Title: Speech at a seminar of the Housing Reform Association
text: Matti Louekoski, Vice Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Bank of Finland Housing Reform Association seminar, Ostrobotnia Ballroom Helsinki 21.3.2001 The importance of housing finance in the national economy Funding is an adaptive factor As a general observation in housing production in today's Finland, it can be said that the biggest problems are by no means on the financing side, but somewhere else entirely. Finance is an adaptive factor in housing (and otherwise) business. That's just a good thing. Developments in recent years have led to the fact that the person who needs a mortgage, within the limits of his ability to pay, receives the type of financing that he wants. Competition between financiers also works reasonably well, which has increased the choice of the person who needs funding. Thus, the price of money is no longer solely determined by the lender. The price is increasingly determined by market conditions. A completely different matter is that the price of the object, the apartment, is usually not up to the borrower to choose. This choice is substantially limited by the orientation of production. In fact, production is far from being geared to the needs. In recent years, housing production has increasingly become a typically business. In regions where demand is strong, society's share of financiers has decreased. Developers and builders are increasingly sensitive to the situation of demand. In this market, prices are determined by my demand. On the other hand, from the point of view of financing, it has to be said that the developer or the construction company receives, within the limits of its collateral and solvency, the type of financing that it needs and wants. The price is determined by competition between the builder and the developer on market terms. In this way, the builder, the developer and the buyer of my apartment are in a way in the same position. The basic focus on the financing side is the market situation. In the provision of finance, the product range is still quite one-sided. The products do not meet all kinds of needs of customers. However, in competing financial markets, new products are now emerging quite quickly if: a) customers are able to define their special needs clearly enough, and b) the demand is large enough so that the production of specialized financial products or the compilation of "packages" is a profitable transaction for the provider at a price that customers are willing to pay. The development of suitable financial products and the compilation of packages is the task of the market, not the state or other authorities. The role of the authorities in the financial markets is to ensure that the playing field in the financial industry is even from the point of view of competition, that the risk management of companies is in order and that the interests of customers are safeguarded in case of abuse. It used to be different It is also instructive for future developments to compare the current situation with the time of the strict regulation of the financial markets. The supply of finance was dominant, since in a period of regulated interest rates and high inflation, demand permanently exceeded supply. In this situation, financiers, mainly banks, had a clear upper hand over their customers in terms of direct power. At that time, the Bank of Finland also had power over the bank. to whom. In this situation, the funding sold by the state, ARAVA, was of great importance. In many cases, absolutely crucial. It sat naturally into a regulated financial environment, where the state, as it were, stepped in as a savior for those homebuyers who would have been regulated out of the market by the banks. At that time, high inflation, interest deductions and tax exemption on deposits ensured that significant support was transferred from depositors to mortgage borrowers. The depositor, as it were, watched from the sidelines as the real value of the savings fell and passed through the subsidization of debts to the debtors. The depositors also accepted the situation, believing that diligent saving would, at the time, give the bank manager a mythical head in financing his own projects. The housing finance system during the period of regulation and high inflation left long marks, which are still visible in urban structures, housing types and, above all, attitudes. The old system had the following effects, among others: "It made it possible to produce high housing in the 1960s and 1970s, which was necessary due to rapid migration. At the same time, however, it supported, for example, the concentration of construction activities and, through regional construction, unnecessarily fragmented the urban structure, which has later been found to be a rather expensive solution. -When combined with rent regulation, the system contributed to the spread of small-sized owner-occupied housing so that it became the basic type of Finnish new production. -Credit regulation required a rapid circulation of credit. This was possible when real interest rates after taxes were severely negative. The level of housing was increased precisely with the support of tax benefits. -Owner-occupied dwellings became a key tool for accumulating wealth. This contributed to the development of capital markets. However, under regulatory conditions, development would not have been very rapid anyway. The upheaval occurred with the liberalization of the financial markets The liberalisation of the financial markets began in the early 1980s and progressed gradually and at an accelerating pace towards the end of the 1980s. My development is accompanied by an intermediate stage in which housing financing shaped the development of the national economy. The result has certainly not been very positive in the late 1980s. Indeed, the disappearance of regulation brought pent-up demand for mortgages to the surface. Demand was further boosted by the fact that many did not notice the development of real interest rates under regulated conditions. They cannot turn negative in the free market. Taught by a long and relatively stable history, it was believed that in apartments the value of money is preserved. However, this illusion was shattered as a result of sudden demand pressure, the ensuing price bubble and the loan policy. Interest rates rose to the limit of solvency, even more than that. At the same time, the widespread recession in society pulled prices down. Many borrowers were trapped, which they still haven't survived. I will return to the opening remarks of my presentation. Looking back at the moment and for a long time now, acquiring a home has not been dependent on the possibility of obtaining a loan. It has just as little to depend on funding to start a new business, if the idea has been a good one. Looking at the present, and especially in the face of the challenges of the future, this vision that I have presented is too narrow. For this reason, we still need to look at a few factors that I believe will have a significant impact on Finnish housing and the financing of housing production. Is there still a need for financial support from society? On some occasions, I have heard it said that buying an apartment is a similar operation to buying boots. Whoever needs, goes to the store and buys. The model is pretty simple, but is it functional? What if the money is only enough to buy one boot. At the moment, the Finnish housing market is deeply divided. In places with strong economic growth, demand far exceeds supply, which has led to a rapid increase in prices. In the emptying countryside and in many medium-sized cities, prices have either been falling or at least stagnant despite the boom. So the law of supply and demand works. From the perspective of the Bank of Finland and the national economy, properly directed and sufficient housing production can be viewed as one of the factors of production. If housing is missing, it can become a crucial niche in production. The same applies, of course, to the unequal price of housing to the ability of those who need it to pay. In such a situation, it is necessary to turn our attention again to both the state and the municipalities. My impression is that the boot example really does not work. My knowledge may be very lacking, but I do not know of a single society in which housing problems could have been satisfactorily solved by market forces alone. A wide range of regulatory and support systems have been needed. In my opinion, they are needed in my Finland. This idea can certainly be turned into a positive one. When I say that regulation is necessary, I mean that the government is active in controlling production. One crucial form of guidance is active land policy. Cities that are primarily responsible for securing the basic services of their residents must be active in the procurement of raw land, town and country planning and other aspects of securing the conditions for production. The period of regional construction in the 1960s and 1970s, which I mentioned earlier, left behind many problems that can and will be avoided now and in the future by keeping control in the hands of urban decision-makers. The best way to do this is to have an active land and land policy. I would like to stress once again the long-term nature of this action. In too many cities, including my hometown of Espoo, the action has been tempo-packed and the results are visible. I may be somewhat old-fashioned, but I too am one of those who still believe in society's need for reception, especially in the field of rental housing. It is not a question of big money, but, above all, of opening up certain bottlenecks. The bottlenecks seem to lie more on the attitude side than on the quantitative needs of funding. There are many examples of this in the Helsinki metropolitan area and elsewhere in the country. A kind of eternal question in housing finance is my, using social support to support production or housing itself. Taking the latter as the main target ensures that the support goes directly to the needy, the low-income resident. The aid thus directed does not distort competition between producers, nor does it encourage concentration, nor does it encourage so-called 'soft law'. category housing. However, I do not have a clear answer as to how the aid should ultimately be directed. The fact at the moment, however, seems to be that far too many people are falling out of the housing market due to the rapid market-based transformation. What kind of help from society? Having led myself above to the idea that public intervention is necessary in our country, as in all other countries, in order to properly finance housing production, it is worth looking at where the focus of society's funding should be. When it comes to organising funding, the public authorities, as well as the state and the municipalities, face more or less the same marginal costs and prices as other market participants. If the state and municipalities become involved as financiers, they will obviously have to deviate from the market-based approach. For example, when selling interest subsidies, it must be borne in mind that this is a subsidy on a special basis, the offsetting of housing costs. As with other public support schemes, it is necessary to assess the effects of aid as incentives for housing policy and as a descriptor of behaviour. This arrangement includes an obligation to compare such aid with any other alternative form of aid on the table. When it comes to public funding or other support, it is natural to keep in mind the mismatch of impacts. Measures to stimulate demand for housing will obviously not work in the right way unless, at the same time, care is taken to ensure a corresponding increase in supply. Otherwise, the aid will pass through the borrower or beneficiary to the seller through rising house prices. In this way, the support is actually directed to the party that does not need the support. For this reason, I will return to the central part of our current housing policy problem, supply. In my view, this cannot be solved by a direct increase in funding, apart from directing funding or other support towards basic production issues such as land acquisition, town and country planning, the construction of municipal infrastructure, etc. These sites are, of course, fundamental to the actual housing policy, but as such they are indirect. Rahoitusta jrjestessn julkinen valta, yht hyvin valtio ja kunnat, kohtaavat jokseenkin samat rajakustannukset ja hinnat kuin muutkin markkinoiden osapuolet. Title: Speech at the European Day reception of the Association of Southwest Finland
text: BANK OF FINLAND Press release FINLANDS BANK Pressmeddelande BANK OF FINLAND Press release 9.5.2001 Vice Chairman of the Executive Board Matti Louekoski Speech at the Reception of the Europe Day of the Regional Council of Southwest Finland 9.5.2001 in Turku A single currency, a single Europe The idea of the euro  a common economy requires a single currency Monetary and exchange rate cooperation between the Member States of the European Union has gradually deepened since the establishment of european economic cooperation. As early as the Treaty of Rome in 1957, member states were obliged to coordinate their economic policies, as strong exchange rate fluctuations were seen to create difficulties for economic cooperation between member states. More concrete soundings of economic and monetary union between the Member States of europe were first made at the turn of the 1960s and 1970s. In 1970, a plan was published, named after Pierre Werner, the then Prime Minister of Luxembourg, who was at the heart of the project, with the aim of moving to economic and monetary union in three stages by 1980. The plan was adopted the following year, but its implementation was interrupted by a very short increase in international inflation, a lack of coordination of economic policies and a system of fixed exchange rates, the so-called 'exchange rate system'. As a result of the disintegration of the Bretton Woods Agreement. Closer monetary and exchange rate cooperation between the Member States of the European Union was returned to in 1978, when leading French and German politicians took the initiative to create an economic area of monetary stability. This initiative became concrete in 1979 with the establishment of the European Monetary System (EMS). The system consisted of an Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM), a notional currency unit and financial engineering arrangements to enable foreign exchange interventions and the financing of external trade deficits. Progress towards economic and monetary union gained new momentum at the end of the 1980s, thanks to favourable economic developments and increased political commitment. It was then that it began to be seen that the more efficient functioning of the internal market required a fixed economic and monetary union and, ultimately, a single currency. In 1989, a committee chaired by Jacques Delors, then President of the European Commission, published a report on the roadmap for monetary union. The preparatory work outlined in the report resulted in a concrete treaty on European Union, which was signed by the Heads of State or Government in Brussels on 7.2.1992 and entered into force on 1.11.1993. According to the Treaty, progress towards Economic and Monetary Union will take place according to a three-stage plan. At this stage, the key issue was to dismantle all internal obstacles to the free movement of capital within the EU. The second stage of EMU began on 1.1.1994. At this stage, the coordination of economic policies between the Member States began to be deepened. During the phase, e.g. The European Monetary Institute (EMI), the forerunner of the European Central Bank, banned the financing of the public sector by central banks and special rights in relation to financial institutions, and issued guidelines to avoid excessive government deficits. From the beginning of the second stage, the convergence criteria agreed in the Maastricht Treaty were used to monitor and compare the member states' economies. Attention was paid to the balance and indebtedness of public finances, inflation, interest rates and exchange rates. The third stage of EMU began on 1.1.1999. The Eurosystem, made up of the European Central Bank and the national central banks of the Member States which adopted the euro, assumed responsibility for the single monetary policy of the euro area. At the same time, the euro was adopted as the official currency. Coordination and multilateral surveillance of economic policies, in particular the fiscal policies of the Member States, were stepped up. As a basis for peer pressure, Member States were obliged to draw up stability and convergence programmes to monitor budgetary developments. In addition, work began on jointly agreed recommendations for the broad economic policy guidelines of the Member States. All this is intended to ensure that the economic development of all euro area countries is as stable and uniform as possible, so that the single monetary policy does not exacerbate economic development in any of the euro countries. The third stage of economic and monetary union will culminate at the beginning of 2002 with the issue of euro banknotes and coins by the European Central Bank and the national central banks of the euro area. Underlying the creation of economic and monetary union is the firm belief that closer economic cooperation and, ultimately, the single currency will stabilise economic development and increase the well-being of europe's citizens. Consumers and businesses alike will be significantly chilled when nearly 300 million European citizens adopt the single currency. Trade in services and goods between euro area countries will be facilitated, which will strengthen the European Union's internal market. Exporters and importers will no longer have to worry about exchange rate fluctuations except when trading with countries outside the euro area. My tourists have an advantage over the euro. When euro notes and coins are introduced at the beginning of next year, travellers from one euro area country to another will no longer have to exchange money or pay commissions. Moreover, as the same currency is used in 12 countries, it is easy to compare prices in different euro area countries. It is hoped that these developments will lead to increased competition between countries and increased prosperity throughout the euro area. The individual Member States of the European Union have had a wide range of political and economic motives to develop closer cooperation with each other. The aim of securing a more stable development of the economy was a key motive when Finland decided to join the EU-euro cooperation. Economic arguments seem to be gaining a great deal of weight in the debate on the enlargement of the European Union and the euro area. However, in many of the applicant countries, accession to the European Union is seen primarily as a political choice. The beginnings of the euro have been a success The euro is intended to be at least as stable as the euro area's previous most stable national currencies, such as the DEM. The primary objective of the Eurosystem, which is made up of the European Central Bank and the national central banks of the euro area, is therefore to maintain price stability in the euro area and thus protect the purchasing power of the euro, in other words, to ensure that a thousand euros can be used to purchase about as many goods and services next year as they do now. By ensuring price stability, the Eurosystem's monetary policy is the best way to support favourable developments and high boredom in the economic environment. Both inflation and deflation can both become very expensive for society, both economically and socially. Provided that the primary objective of price stability is not jeopardised, the Eurosystem will also support the common's general economic policies and respect the principles of an open market economy, as laid down in the Treaty establishing a European Community. In order to make it easier for the general public to assess the success of the single monetary policy, the objective of price stability has been precisely defined. By definition, price stability means an annual increase in consumer prices of less than 2%. There are no other definitions  and no other objectives. As monetary policy does not provide full control over price developments over the short term, the aim is to maintain price stability over the medium term. Seasonal fluctuations or other very short-term effects do not jeopardise compliance with the objective of price stability. If you look at the development over the past two years, you can see that the beginnings of the euro have been a success in many terms. Despite the rise in the price of the euro and the depreciation of the external value of the euro, the euro has retained its purchasing power quite well. Consumer prices in the euro area rose by an average of 1.1% in 1999 and by 2.4% in 2000, i.e. for a thousand euros you can still buy about the same amount of goods and services as in January 1999. In addition, financial market information suggests that the European Central Bank is expected to be able to keep euro area consumer prices stable in the future. In particular, the relatively stable development of long-term market interest rates over the past year suggests that market forces have a strong belief in the European Central Bank's willingness and ability to maintain its price stability objective. In addition, the transition to the single currency and monetary policy has gone smoothly from a technical point of view. In order to achieve their objectives, all developed central banks have at their disposal a number of monetary policy instruments: refinancing operations safeguard the liquidity of the banking system, regulate interest rates and communicate the broad line of monetary policy; the standing facilities are used to regulate liquidity over the banking system; the minimum reserve system is used to smooth out the demand for central bank money and the movement of money market interest rates; with the help of the payment system, large payments are transferred. As the Eurosystem is a consortium of 12 national central banks and the European Central Bank, in which decisions are made centrally, but most operations are carried out on a decentralised basis, it was necessary to create a single set of instruments for the Eurosystem's use on the basis of varying national instruments. The job turned out to be demanding and the schedule tight. Nevertheless, when the market opened on 4.1.1999, it could be said that everything was in order. Over the past two years or so, the toolbox has worked flawlessly, which has certainly contributed to increased confidence in the euro and in the functioning of the Eurosystem. Since its introduction, the external value of the euro has fluctuated quite a bit in relation to the other major currencies in the world. At the moment, the euro in the dollar is more than 20% and the yen exchange rate is about 16% cheaper than in The Month of January 1999. In terms of a basket of currencies formed from weighted average rates, the euro has weakened by about 10%. Although the changes in the external value of the euro have been quite large, they are not a cause for concern for the stable development of the euro area. In view of this, there has been a disproportionate amount of interest in the development of the exchange rate of the euro. The euro floats and its external value in relation to the currencies of other countries is determined by supply and demand on the foreign exchange markets , sometimes quite absurdly. However, as the share of external trade in euro area GDP is relatively small1, the stability of the internal value of the euro, i.e. the price level in the euro area, is essentially a more important objective for citizens than the stability of the external value of the euro. Developments over the past two years make it impossible to assess whether the external fluctuation of the euro has been exceptionally high or what the equilibrium exchange rate of the euro is. At the moment, however, it appears that the evolution of the euro's dollar and yen rates has reflected the imbalances between the US and Japanese economies and the perceptions of currency traders that these imbalances are unravelling rather than the weakness of the euro area economy. In the United States, the overheating of the economy has been followed by a sharp decline in economic activity and a drastic interest rate stimulus by the Federal Reserve There. In Japan, economic growth has been almost at a standstill for several years, despite the Bank of Japan's zero interest rate policy, and structural problems in the economy are still awaiting a sustainable solution. On the other hand, the euro area economy has grown and looks set to grow quite steadily in the coming years, and confidence in the European Central Bank's willingness and ability to keep consumer price inflation in check is strong. In addition, ongoing economic restructuring programmes in many euro area countries will improve the conditions for economic growth in the euro area as a whole. The introduction of euro notes and coins is a consistent end point for the long way to go For citizens, the most concrete phase of the transition to economic and monetary union will begin on 1.1.2002, when the new euro banknotes and coins will enter into circulation. From the beginning of next year, seven euro banknotes and eight euro coins will be legal tender in Belgium, Germany, Greece, Spain, France, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Austria, Portugal and Finland, i.e. in all twelve euro area member states. Markka banknotes and coins will be accepted as means of payment in Finland until 24 p.m. on 28.2.2002, after which the national currencies of member states that have adopted the euro will cease to be legal tender and euro notes and coins will become the only valid currency throughout the euro area. Commercial banks are obliged to exchange markka notes and coins for euro notes and coins at a fixed conversion rate, at least for parallel proceedings. Even after 10 years, the Finnish marks can still be exchanged for euros free of charge at the Bank of Finland. The launch of the new single currency has been a long and demanding process, culminating in the introduction of new notes and coins. In order to ensure a smooth transition to the use of euros, provision has been made for sharing information on a broad front. Finland's official information on the euro is provided by the Minister of Finance, the European Union, the Finnish Consumer Authority and the Bank of Finland. In addition to its own national information campaign, an important part of the Bank of Finland's information campaign on the euro is the Euro2002 information campaign, which is shared by the European Central Bank and the national central banks of the euro area. Both the Bank of Finland's own and the pan-European Euro 2002 campaign will focus on the presentation of the new euro banknotes and coins. In 2000, exports to non-euro area countries accounted for 15.7% of euro area GDP according to trade balance figures and 19.3% according to current account figures. In the United States, exports accounted for 11.0% of gdp in 2000, according to gross domestic product figures. The main themes of the Bank of Finland's information campaigns on the euro are: the design of euro banknotes and coins, such as colours and dimensions, the authentication factors used to distinguish a genuine euro banknote or coin from a false one, monetary values different from those of markka banknotes and coins, and general arrangements for operation. Through its campaigns, the Bank of Finland aims to inform the general public about euro notes and coins, but especially for professional groups that deal with cash or are able to effectively disseminate information about the new currency. The information campaigns are divided into a number of areas to be implemented on a parallel basis, and the campaigns and the campaign materials distributed have tried to take into account the specific needs of specific groups such as schoolchildren, the visually and hearing impaired and the elderly. The main objective of both the Bank of Finland's own and the pan-European Euro 2002 campaign is to familiarise citizens with the appearance of euro coins and, in particular, with the details that ensure their authenticity, as well as with the timetable for issuing them. The smooth transition from mark notes and coins to euro notes and coins requires citizens to be able to rely on their own ability to recognise the correct euro banknote or coin when they first hold one in their hands. It should be possible to create such confidence through euro information campaigns. This will be the most important criterion when assessing the success of campaigns afterwards.

Suomen Pankin eurotiedotuskampanjoiden paiheet ovat  euroseteleiden ja kolikoiden ulkoasu, kuten vrit ja mitat,  aitoustekijt, joiden avulla aidon eurosetelin tai kolikon erottaa vrst,  rahojen arvot, jotka poikkeavat markkaseteleiden ja kolikoiden arvoista ja  kyttnottoon liittyvt yleiset jrjestelyt. Suomen Pankki pyrkii kampanjoillaan tiedottamaan euroseteleist ja kolikoista suurelle yleisle yliptn mutta etenkin ammattiryhmille, jotka ksittelevt kteisrahaa tykseen taipystyvt tehokkaasti levittmn tietoa uudesta rahasta. Tiedotuskampanjat jakautuvat useisiinrinnakkain toimeenpantaviin osa-alueisiin ja kampanjoiden toteutuksessa ja jaettavassa kampanjamateriaalissa on pyritty ottamaan huomioon my erityisryhmien kuten koululaisten, nk- ja kuulovammaisten sek vanhusten erityistarpeet. Sek Suomen Pankin oman ett yleiseurooppalaisen Euro 2002 kampanjan keskeisimpn tavoitteena on tutustuttaa kansalaiset eurorahojen ulkonkn ja erityisesti niiden aitouden varmistaviin yksityiskohtiin sek liikkeellelaskun aikatauluun. Juoheva siirtyminen markkaseteleist ja kolikoista euroseteleihin ja kolikoihin edellytt, ett kansalaiset voivat luottaa omaan kykyyns tunnistaa oikea euroseteli tai kolikko, kun pitvt sellaista ensimmisen kerran kdessn. Tllainen luottamus pitisi pysty eurotiedotuskampanjoiden avulla luomaan. Tm tuleekin olemaan keskeisin kriteeri, kun kampanjoiden onnistumista jlkikteen arvioidaan.

Title: Conference: "Economic and Monetary Union: Challenges and Risks"
text: SUOMEN PANKKI FINLANDS BANK BANK OF FINLAND 11.5.2001 Sinikka Salo Member of the Board Bank of Finland The economic dimension of the single currency: the Finnishperspective Remarks in the conference Economic and Monetary Union: Challenges and Risks, organised by the EuroCollege, University of Tartu and Eesti Bank, Tartu May 11-12, 2001. Talking about the economic impact of the monetary union, with its common monetary policy andthe broad co-ordination of other aspects of economic policy, I must begin by mentioning a couple of caveats. First, I will talk from a particularly Finnish perspective, and from Finnish experience. Ibelieve that the effects of EMU membership can well be different for different countries, dependingon their particular starting points and the problems or strengths they have to begin with. So,experiences of one member cannot be always generalized to others, and the impact of the union onsome new member could be different from its effects on older members. Another caveat is that one cannot really judge the impact of the EMU on its members just bylooking at the statistics, by checking what happened to a country's economic situation after joining the monetary union. For one thing, EMU is still very young. It has been in operation for less than three years, and we do not have experience of its operation over a full economic cycle. On the other hand, many of the effects of EMU started to work their way already before membership. Let us take Finland as an example. When Finland joined the EU in 1995, it was stated that the aimwas to participate also in the monetary union in the first group of countries joining it. From that point on at least, the Maastricht criteria and the foreseeable policy regime of the EMU served as clear orientation points for the Finnish economic policy strategy, and for Finnish firms as well. In fact, because of this advance adjustment, the start of the monetary union on the first day of 1999was by no means a big bang in any practical terms. Rather, it was just a seal on the developments which had occurred over several years already. Despite this, I think that we can learn from each others experience, and the accession countries should try to look at the experience of the "old" EMU countries. This must not be mechanical, however. It must be done with great caution and applying a high degree of judgement in theprocess, considering the experience of other countries against the particular situation andbackground in each new member country. I think that the conference organizers' idea of using Gordon Brown's five tests for the EMU membership as a basic framework for this conference is an excellent one and I shall structure my presentation accordingly. I'll try to explain how I see each of the five tests in the case of the Finnish EMU membership -these five being: effects on the business environment, on financial services, thechallenges caused by cyclical asymmetry, flexibility requirements for member states, and last butnot least, the effect of the monetary union on the general macroeconomic performance of the country. I'll start from the last point in Gordon Brown's list, namely the effect on overall economic performance. Has joining the EMU helped to promote higher growth, stability, and a lasting increase in jobs? As you know, the latter half of the 1990's, i.e. the period after Finland joined the EU, has been a period of unprecedented growth and transformation in the Finnish economy. Even though the unemployment rate still remains far too high, as in most of Europe, it is fair to say that there is now a very broad consensus among Finnish economists and policymakers that the stability of theeconomy is now much better than is used to be, and the policy trade-offs are much more favourable. To fully appreciate the change which seems to have happened, one should understand the frustrating instability of the Finnish economy in the previous decades. The economy used to be veryinflation-prone, its structural current account deficits led to recurrent balance-of-payments crisesand devaluations, and the corporate sector was notorious for its weak capital structure. Growth was relatively fast, it is true, but instability was a major problem. Another problem, for most economists, was the relative inefficiency of investment, in the sense that very high investment rates were required to generate the growth we had. Among the most important changes which have taken place since are the following (see the charts and tables attached): Productivity growth has accelerated significantly, compared to the experience of the previous 20 years or so. This has enabled the economy to grow much faster than used to be thought possible; The growth-vs.-inflation trade-off has improved significantly, judging from the fact that the recent rapid growth in the economy has been realized with less acceleration in inflation than one would have anticipated based on our historical experience; The growth-vs.-current account trade-off has also improved markedly. Despite several years of high growth, the persistent tendency of the current account to be in deficit, which used to be thought as structural, has disappeared. Instead, there is now a very large and apparently still growing surplus in the current account; The capital structure of firms has strengthened dramatically. In a sample of 500 largest companies in Finland, the average debt-equity ratio has decreased from about 1,9 in 1994 to 1.2 in 1999; Now, it is very difficult to say with certainty to what extent these significant changes which have occurred are in fact results from the Finnish membership in the EMU. Some alternative explanations can be found as well: for example, the so-called "new economy" has been credited for the moderation of inflationary pressures and the lower investment requirements for growth (thiscould in turn explain the improvement on the current account). Moreover, broadly similar and parallel improvements in price stability and the balance of payments have been experienced also in Sweden although it has not yet joined the EMU. However, it seems to me that the changes I just listed have a common denominator, so to speak:there is an underlying factor which can (in theory at least) explain them all. Since this factor is also connected with the monetary union, it seems a quite reasonable hypothesis that the improvement ofthe Finnish economic performance has in fact been partly improved by the monetary union. Thiscommon underlying factor is an improvement in the credibility of monetary policy. Let me explain. First, better credibility can explain the improvement in the output-inflation tradeoff,as wage inflation does not take off as easily as before. Second, as monetary policy is not seen as prone as before to bail out export industries in the event of problems, firms now act more prudently and invest with more caution than before. This may explain the decrease in the investment intensityof growth and hence the improvement in the structural current account. A more credible monetarypolicy has also made capital markets work more efficiently, which may explain the improvedsolvency of firms and perhaps the acceleration in productivity growth as well. Of course, the improvement in the credibility of monetary policy, which seems to have occurred in Finland in the course of the 1990s, is not quite the same thing as monetary union. Improvement in credibility just requires the adoption of stability oriented policy and strong, independent institutions to implement it. But it seems that monetary union has helped a great deal in achieving this. Perhaps it was indispensable: there is no way to tell whether the political and economic conditions for a credible monetary policy could have been cemented in Finland without EMU. In the 1960s, 70s and 80s, they were not. Having said this, it is already clear how I assess the first item on Gordon Browns list - namely Has adopting the common currency created better conditions for firms in the long-term perspective? What we know is that after the EU and EMU memberships became a reality, Finnish firms have become much more international than before, in terms of ownership and operations. Also, the economy has become even more export oriented than before. At the same time, the industry structure has changed so that the share of the electronics and IT sectors have grown enormously. In the Finnish case this has meant an increased diversity in the structure of exports, as the electronics exports (such as mobile phones) have emerged as the third major export category alongside themore traditional paper and heavy engineering products. It would be simplistic to attribute the success of this internationalization and diversification of industry mainly to the currency arrangement Finland has chosen. Causes for the Finnish IT miracle - if there is a miracle - must be sought elsewhere. But as I said, there is reason to believe that thestabilization of expectations and the consequent improvement in the functioning of labour andcapital markets has to do with the monetary union, and so part of the positive business environmentwhich we have had recently must be attributed to EMU membership. It is also the case that thebroad economic policy co-ordination in the EFC and Ecofin, has helped policy makers to focus onmedium to long run stretegic programming and hence the policy co-ordination processes have made business environment more stable and predictable than they otherwise might have been. Turning from industry to finance and banking, one can take up the next question, namely How have the country's financial services been affected? As you would know, the Finnish financial sector has been almost completely transformed after the financial crisis of early 1990s. Banks have become more cost efficient and profitable, there is nowa strong if not dominant multinational player in the market, and the stock market has grown andinternationalized beyond all expectations. However, regarding this change in our financial services industry, it is again not easy to distinguishthe effect of the monetary union from other powerful forces of internationalization which have swept the country in general. Certainly, the Finnish financial system has been completely transformed in the run-up to the EMU. But it is not at all clear that joining the EMU has been a decisive force here. We know that actually the Nordic bank mergers have not paid too much attention on the ins/outs question. Geographical location seems to have been a much more significant factor in selecting merger partners than the local currency arrangement, be it EMU,ERM or floating. So, perhaps EMU has been only a minor factor in the banking development so far and other strategic and technological factors have been more influential. In the money and capital markets, the effects of EMU have been more clear. National benchmark instruments and national benchmark rates have virtually disappeared in all of the small EMUcountries, as they have been replaced by the Euribor and Bund markets. This unification of moneyand capital markets may have hurt some traders who lost their business, but on balance the effectfor the member economies is clearly positive. This is essentially because of the elimination ofunnecessary exchange rate risk. For example, Finnish pension funds are now able to diversify theirrapidly growing asset portfolios internationally, something which was previously prevented byexchange rate risk. These diversification possibilities are also utilized on a rather large scale. In the future, as the monetary union develops its financial regulation activity, the Finnish membership in the EMU may well have even more easily identifiable effects on our banks and financial markets. This could result from a more international approach to regulation within the union. For example, if the ECB and the Eurosystem develop their roles in banking supervisionfurther, as I hope they will, then membership in the inner circle of EMU countries may beextremely useful to supervisory authorities and central bankers for understanding what is going onfor developing joint action if necessary. This kind of development is likely to follow soon ifinternational banking mergers become more common in the euro area. The next point has to do with the cost of abandoning national monetary policy. The question is, Are business cycles compatible so that we can live comfortably with common, euro interest rates? Before joining the EMU, the problem of asymmetric business cycles was discussed to some extent in Finland. In particular, it was pointed out that the Finnish business cycle had usually been very different from the "core" European countries. The worry was that common monetary policy, geared to "average" European needs, would be sometimes too lax and sometimes too tight for Finland. The former situation would cause inflation to get out of control; in the latter case, policy would curtail aggregate demand too much and could cause an unnecessary recession. I do not want to sound imprudent, but I think that the limited experience which we have so farsuggests that these fears were probably exaggerated. It is true that during the Finnish EMU membership, until now at last, economic growth has been very fast and inflation has been higher than in the Euro area on average. Some time ago the Bank of Finland, OECD, IMF and some government officials all expressed worries about the possibility of overheating in Finland. However, now it appears that the acceleration of inflation has been small in relation to the scale of the economic upswing, and the situation remained under control. Why have things worked out better than originally expected? It seems that membership in a largemonetary union has removed two destabilizing factors which used to be important to the traditionalFinnish business cycle. First, the balance-of-payments constraint and its monetary consequenceshave almost disappeared in its traditional sense. It used to be the case that whenever the current account was seriously in deficit, the money market reacted to that by tightening and interestdifferentials vis-a-vis the rest of the world would start to rise. (Correspondingly, balance-ofpayments surpluses used to create excess liquidity and absorption problems which were difficult tomanage.) Now, for a small member in a monetary union, international liquidity is not nearly asvulnerable as before. Hence this monetary channel in business cycle transmission is no longer thereand this has probably made the dynamics of the Finnish business cycle much smoother and lessextreme than before. The other factor which has probably changed the Finnish business cycle dynamics for the better isthe increased stability of inflation expectations which I have already mentioned. This is basicallybecause the suspicion that monetary policy would, in the end, accommodate excessive costincreases has now disappeared. With a more stable anchor for price expectations, the labour andreal estate markets in particular will be now calmer than before, meaning that they are less prone tooverheat in economic booms. This means that the likelihood of generating an unsustainableincrease in domestic costs should be less than it used to be when we had a national currency. I am not as frivolous as to claim that the Finnish economy no longer is capable of ending up in an unpleasant disequilibrium. Even if the dynamics of the economy now appear to be more favourable than before, shocks do occur from time to time which require adjustment. Therefore, it is reasonable to raise the last point on the test list, namely: If problems emerge, is there sufficient flexibility to deal with them? (test 4) The flexibility discussion contained by this criterion for membership has been actually very much in the forefront in the Finnish discussion on the effects of the EMU. This discussion has revolved around three main themes: the role of fiscal policy in facilitating business cycle adjustment in the new policy environment; the role of incomes policy in avoiding irreversible erosion of competitiveness of the economy; the need for microeconomic reform of labour markets to make the labour market more flexible. Turning to fiscal policy first, the last decade has been dominated by a consistent effort to improvethe government budget balance. This has also been very successful, and the Finnish budgetary position is now very strong by European standards. This effort to pay back debt fast has been motivated by two different reasons, one of which has to do with stabilization policy. This reason is that a solid fiscal position is desirable to generate leeway for fiscal policy which could be used to"buy time" in the event of an unexpected recession. This does not imply the view that future recessions could be cured by fiscal expansion; I don't think there are many who trust in that kind of strategy these days. But it means understanding that re-balancing the budget after some negative shock can happen in a more gradual and less disruptive way if the government debt level is initially small. This has been an important point in the Finnish policy. The other reason  quite unrelated to EMU  why strengthening of public finances has had a high priority is the fact that the population of Finland is ageing fairly rapidly and the government wants to accumulate pension funds and reduce debt in anticipation of the coming increase in the pensions expenditure. I want to emphasize that even the first of these two reasons for pursuing a very prudent fiscal policy is related to the EMU only indirectly. More specifically, I do not think that the fiscal criteria of the Maastricht treaty or the Growth and Stability Pact have been significant constraints of incentives to Finnish fiscal policy. The genuinely economic motives for prudence have been so much more demanding, that the policy has been satisfying the external, formal criteria voluntarily, and by a clear "safety margin" at that. Regarding the role of incomes policy next, you probably know that Finland is one of the fewcountries where the position of centralized incomes policy has been very strong, and even continued to strengthen. The unions do not only strike centrally co-ordinated wage bargains: the actual scope of incomes policy is larger than that. Much of labour market policy, taxation, and social security policy is in fact negotiated in a tripartite fashion between the labour unions, employer organizations, and the government. Experience shows that this incomes-policy oriented way of formulating economic and social policyhas actually become even more dominant after it became clear that Finland joins the EMU in the first wave of countries and there are no clear signs that this development would be reversed in the near term at least. One may speculate why the EMU membership seems to have increased the bargaining power of labour unions in general economic policy. One plausible explanation is that because of theirtraumatic historical experience, Finnish policy makers are extremely keen to avoid getting into an irreversible cost crisis, which would result from wages rising too much for a prolonged period. In the past, that kind of situations used to lead to forced devaluations of the currency, When Finland joined the EMU, it was immediately obvious to everybody that the kind of situations which used tobe solved by devaluations must never emerge again. The very high priority of cost control for thegovernment has then given the unions quite a lot of leverage on other aspects of policy. Similar developments may have occurred in some other small EMU countries (Ireland, Austria, theNetherlands to some degree), but I think Finland is actually a bit special in this regard. Finally, there is the question of labour market flexibility. How much more should we have? This issue has been politicized quite a bit in Finland, and is connected to the status of incomes policy in the society. I think that one way to look at the Finnish situation is to distinguish between micro andmacro flexibility. Macro flexiblility of labour markets has to do with the ability of the labour markets to weathergeneral, macroeconomic shocks. It is the kind of macro flexibility which may be needed in the event of unpleasant shocks, when national monetary and exchange rate policy are lacking. For that purpose, wage moderation of the kind sometimes achieved by incomes policy may be an instrumental form of flexibility. Many labour market organizations (especially in manufacturingindustries) have also taken a positive attitude towards developing more innovative models of wagedetermination, for example profit sharing systems and the so-called buffer funds where excess unemployment insurance contributions are collected to insurance funds when the economy isgrowing fast, for the purpose of reducing indirect labour costs when economic activity is weak. The effect of the EMU membership in Finland has been that developing and using these forms of flexibility are now actively discussed among the labour market partners and the government, Micro flexiblility, on the other hand, relates more to the ability of labour markets to match jobs withpeople and their skills, and to equilibrate individual wage demands with the individualproductivities of individuals. Here the performance of the Finnish economy is disappointingly weak as the unemployment rate is high, hovering still around 10 per cent (and much more if you include people on measures). It may be that this problem has less to do with the monetary union membership than with taxation and other structural factors. However, it needs to be noted that the existence of high and persistent long-term unemployment has also some bearing on the cyclicaladjustment of the economy: it casts doubt on the ability of the labour market to deal with adverseshocks and structural change. Moreover, high unemployment costs are a burden to the government budget and hence limit the ability of the budget to absorb negative shocks in the short run. At the time when joining the monetary union was first discussed, some people thought that the EMUmembership would in due course force the labour market to change so that it would become more flexible even in the micro sense. So far, there is no evidence of that kind of development. At this point, I would like to emphasize the positive role of the Broad Economic Policy Guidelines and other processes of economic policy co-ordination within the EU. It is clear that these coordination processes produce only recommendations and initiatives. However, their importance inhelping governments to develop their economies should not be overlooked. I am not speaking only about peer pressure for reform; I think that national policy makers do genuinely benefit from thebenchmarking of policies and institutions which take place within these policy co-ordinationprocesses. The processes also force countries to analyze their respective situations in certain wayswhich might otherwise not happen. All this creates focus and incentive for policy development which must not be underestimated. In view of the unemployment problems of Europe, it is clear thatthe tasks are especially large in the field of developing the functioning of labour markets. *** To sum up, I think I have given a rather positive picture of the effects of EMU on the Finnisheconomy, and on balance, I indeed see the effects as overwhelmingly positive. I hope I have alsosucceeded in describing some of the effects of EMU in their relation to the Finnish historical andpolitical background. On the basis of this analysis, it seems to me that a very large part of theeconomic benefits of joining the EMU are in fact due to increased credibility of monetary and fiscalinstitutions -better trust on the value of money and the medium-term balance of the budget. As a result of this better credibility, inflationary expectations have been much lower and more stable than before, and asset and labour markets have been able to work without the macro problems which waves of inflationary fear would otherwise cause. It is clear that, to join the monetary union in a smooth and not disruptive way, countries must adaptwell in advance both in terms of the macroeconomic aggregates and in terms of the microeconomicmaturity of their markets. At the same time, the recent improvements in the performance of the Finnish economy demonstrate that EMU membership, and even the prospect of it, greatly facilitatesovercoming some of the most difficult problems of economic policy, especially if these problemshave to do with less than perfect credibility of policy strategies and institutions.
