Title: Speech at the seminar "Hirvensalmi in Europe"
text: SUOMEN PANKKI FINLANDS BANK BANK OF FINLAND Member of the Executive BoardSinikka Salo Speech at the seminar "Hirvensalmi in Europe" 8.7.2001 EMU, THE EURO, FINLAND AND HIRVENSALMI Dear moose Strait people, I am very pleased to have this opportunity to come and tell you about EMU and the euro. These titles are familiar from the media, but their contents are still unavoidably not very clear to everyone. Since these are issues that concern us all, I chose the title of my speech as 'EMU, the euro, Finland and Hirvensalmi'. We have now been living in the era of EMU for two and a half years. Monetary union is the most important step in the process of European integration in the economic field and when it became operational at the beginning of January 1999, Finland adopted a single European monetary policy. The exchange rates between the currencies of the individual countries of the euro area have been fixed definitively and a single monetary unit has been introduced. At the beginning of next year, the change will eventually affect every Finn in everyday life, as euro-denominated notes and coins will be used. Following the transition to monetary union, the Bank of Finland became part of the Eurosystem, the new system of central banks consisting of the European Central Bank (ECB) in Frankfurt and the twelve national central banks of the euro area. One of them is the Bank of Finland. I have structured my speech as follows: 1)First, I will briefly outline the objective of the single monetary policy. 2) I will then try to shed light on the effects of EMU on the Finnish economy and, in particular, on regional and public finances, including local government finances. 3) Finally, I would like to say a few words about the Bank of Finland's activities in emu conditions and, in particular, about the role of the Bank of Finland in the conversion of banknotes and coins into euros. 1. The ECB's monetary policy objectives The monetary policy of the euro area is also the monetary policy of Finland At the outset, I would like to remind you that neither Finland nor any other Member State of the European Monetary Union has given up its monetary policy, but finland, together with 11 other countries in the euro area, has brought together its monetary policy as a common cause. Although Finland does not have a separate monetary policy, it has its own monetary policy, which is common to the euro area countries: the common monetary policy of the euro area is therefore also Finland's monetary policy. So: there is no longer a separate Finnish monetary policy, but it is clear to me that in the current globally networked conditions, in the 'global economy', a completely independent monetary policy would not be possible for an economy as small and dependent on international trade as Finland.Isolation is not a realistic option, and I do not believe that the Finns would want to return to the conditions of monetary regulation. Finland participates as a full member in the decision-making process on monetary policy in the euro area But Finland still has  or shall I say more so  influence over monetary policy. The structure of the European System of Central Banks - or more precisely the "Eurosystem" - is formed in such a way that no euro area member state is just an object of monetary policy, but a monetary policy subject, that is, a factor. When the Governor of the Bank of Finland attends meetings of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank (ECB) at which monetary policy is decided, he or she has one vote, as do all the other members of the Council, such as the Governor of the German Bundesbank or the Banque de France  the Governing Council is composed of the Governors of the national central banks of the euro area and the members of the Executive Board of the ECB. Such a 'one member, one vote' principle is based on the fundamental convergence of the monetary policy interests of the Member States. The average price stability objective of the ECB's monetary policy in the euro area as a whole means that the policy is not tailored to the needs of any single country or group of countries. That is exactly how it should be. For example, even if we Finns were to be able to decide on the monetary policy of the euro area on our own, it would still not be worthwhile for us to take only the cyclical situation in Finland as the starting point for the interest rate measurement of the entire monetary union. Not even if our own situation is somewhat different from the others, as it was a year or two ago. It is in the interest of each Member State and finland that the euro area economy as a whole remains in balance. Under the single currency, we are all in the same boat, equally dependent on price stability in the euro area and, in particular, on the confidence it enjoys. The institutions and objective of the ECB's monetary policy decided democratically The framework for monetary policy in the euro area is defined in the Maastricht Treaty, which has been signed by governments and ratified by parliaments. In this Treaty, the objective of monetary policy is clearly set out: monetary policy in the euro area is responsible for maintaining price stability in the euro area. This reflects the fact, confirmed by experience, that by maintaining price stability, the central bank can best support long-term stable growth, boredom and the well-being of society. We Finns have had very unpleasant experiences with the depreciation of money, the rapid rise in prices, i.e. inflation over the decades  for example, inflation led to large and arbitrary redistributions of income and wealth from savers to debtors, as a result of inflation, a low, even negative real interest rate led to poorly thought-out investments and thus to capital inefficiency, etc. Price stability is defined by the Governing Council as the annual increase in consumer prices, i.e. inflation, below 2% over the medium term. The primacy of the objective of price stability as an objective of monetary policy also underlines the fact that the central bank has neither the means nor the responsibility to maintain economic growth or dynamism directly - beyond what it takes to maintain price stability. It is the responsibility of the other economic policy sectors to influence these. Price stability is a primary objective of monetary policy, but the Treaty of Tampere also states that, without jeopardising price stability, the common (EU) general economic policy will be supported. It should also be noted that monetary policy in the euro area does not have an exchange rate target, although market commentators and the press often comment on it in relation to exchange rate developments  the dollar value of the euro is of particular interest. This is certainly natural, because exchange rates fluctuate on a daily basis, but sometimes the importance of the exchange rate is exaggerated. The ECB has not set any target level for the exchange rate. The aim is the stability of the purchasing power of the euro within the euro area, not exchange rate stability per se. Of course, the exchange rate plays a role in inflation in that the depreciation of the euro on foreign exchange markets can lead to higher import prices and thus inflationary pressures in the euro area. Of course, the conduct of monetary policy is not mechanical in nature, although the ECB has a well-defined so-called monetary policy. monetary policy strategy. (It is well described, for example, in the ECB's monthly publication.) The conduct of monetary policy is based on the idea that economic measures that predict inflation developments need to be carefully interpreted and weighed in order to distinguish between weak disturbances and long-term changes. This requires not only economists' technology, but also a lot of wisdom, vision and a sense of what is happening in the euro area economies. Monetary policy decision-making and the final interpretation of the situation will therefore take place in the Governing Council meeting in Frankfurt, which, through the various governors of the national central banks, has a broad understanding of economic developments in the euro area as a whole. In this consideration by the Council, the national central banks will make a significant contribution. At the last meeting of the Governing Council of the ECB, the ECB did not change its monetary policy, leaving interest rates unchanged - i.e. the Eurosystem's so-called 'green card'. the lower limit for interest rate offers on the main refinancing operations, the minimum bid rate remained at 4.50%. The Governing Council underlined the medium-term forward-looking approach of its monetary policy strategy. The heads to keep interest rates unchanged reflect the assessment that interest rates are now at a level that ensures price stability over the medium term. Commitment to this goal will have a beneficial effect on the economy as a whole. The single monetary policy has been able to keep inflation expectations low since the start of EMU. As a result, long-term interest rates in the euro area are low, contributing to economic growth and boredom. Consumer prices in the euro area are currently still rising rapidly, mainly reflecting past trends in energy and food prices. The annual increase in the Harmonised Consumer Price Index was 3.4% in May. Inflation is expected to decline over the course of this year and next year (below 2% in 2002). Inflation developments are mainly made uncertain by the potential second-round effects of wage negotiations. Naturally, all factors affecting price stability will continue to be closely monitored. The most important such factors include: in addition to wage developments, monetary developments - monetary and credit growth - and the general development of the economy, the growth of gross domestic product. 2. EMU and local government finances There is already so much experience of monetary union that the picture of its effects  the clots and the adaptation needs it causes  is beginning to become clearer. Interest rates and exchange rates have been determined by the single monetary policy, and monetary policy decisions must have been somewhat different from what we would have done under the conditions of a floating mark. But this should not be overstated. As I said above, strong links bind the economies of all European countries to each other  both the members of the monetary union and the non-monetary UNION EU countries. When considering joining the monetary union, there was quite a lot of discussion in Finland about what monetary union is would mean for Finland's regional economy and public finances. Both themes are central to municipalities, as they account for two-thirds of public finances and when it is the municipalities that face the problems of regional development first. As is well known, Finland is undergoing a remarkably rapid regional structural change, which includes the concentration of economic growth and new jobs in growth centres. It is clear to focus on a limited number of technically and knowledge-intensive sectors, such as the electronics industry. It is possible that Finland's membership of the monetary union has played some part in the success of Hi-Tech Finland. The permanently locked exchange rate in relation to continental Europe has certainly contributed to the availability of capital and encouraged Finnish companies to participate in competitive pricing. However, I do not believe that monetary union is the main driving force behind the structural change under way. The general trend towards globalisation, 'globalisation', is almost certainly a much stronger factor of change than monetary union. From the point of view of regional development, it actually seems that Finland's membership of the monetary union has softened the adaptation of regions dependent on the forestry sector and agriculture to structural change. If the Finnish markka had floated, it is very possible that, under conditions of such rapid economic growth and a record trade surplus as we have experienced recently, the markka would have been under considerable pressure to strengthen. The real incomes of this forestry and agricultural sectors would have been lower than they have enjoyed under the conditions of monetary union. In this sense, EMU membership has maintained the income base of agriculture and forestry rather than the reasons for it. This has been counterbalanced by the concentration of new jobs in knowledge-intensive fields in university towns, triggered by strong globalisation. The most important objective of European economic integration in the 1990s has been to balance and keep public finances in balance. In this context, fiscal policy, i.e. budgetary policy, has agreed on the standards for limiting public debt, which are currently included in the EU's Stability and Growth Pact. Although the EU Member States are independent and alone in their budgetary policy, the purpose of these standards is to ensure that the single currency is not destabilised in any country by unsustainable fiscal policies. Sometimes you hear the Stability and Growth Pact criticised for limiting the room for manoeuvre in public finances too much. After all, the Pact requires that, in the medium term, each country's public finances should show an average deficit of 3% and, even on a cyclical basis, (except in specified situations of exceptionally deep recession, where the deficit could be higher). In my opinion, this kind of criticism is mostly misguided. The treaty hardly excludes any sound economic strategies. The same goes for my so-called .... the broad economic policy guidelines adopted annually by the European Council for eu countries. In fact, the prospects for public finances in European countries are so worrying due to ageing that the obligations of the Stability and Growth Pact can rightly be considered unnecessarily lenient. In Finland, too, the public sector shows a large surplus, especially due to the accumulation of social security funds. Such a surplus should be considered justifiable, especially in the recent high economic climate, where there has been room to correct balance sheets damaged by the recession. The Growth and Stability Pact has not required us to have such a surplus, so it does not, in the current circumstances, in any way create a tightening "straitjacket" for Finland's economic policy. Admittedly, the requirement for scarcity in public spending is entirely due to economic considerations  the population and the risks associated with the tax base, and not EMU. By this I do not in any way wish to play down the seriousness of the issues relating to the finances of municipalities. Municipal the situation as part of the dynamics of the public sector is exceptionally difficult because of such uneven regional development and because the challenges of ageing will put a strain on the budget moments of municipal health and care activities in the future. In addition to these well-known issues, there is still the question of preparing for future cyclical fluctuations. The future development of the tax base will inevitably not always be as favourable in the future as it has been in many municipalities in recent years. The finances of municipalities should therefore be approached even more cautiously than central government finances, even in the case of cyclically-oriented deficits. 3. Tasks of the Bank of Finland Bank of Finland links Finland to European monetary finances In addition to the fact that the Bank of Finland is in the process of deciding on monetary policy in the euro area, one of the most important things a national central bank can do in monetary union conditions for the economic success of its home country is to ensure that the general public, both professionals and laypeople, understand monetary policy as well as possible and, as little as possible, make errors of judgement as to where the policy is going. Communication with the Domestic general is not an ancillary function for the Bank of Finland, but part of its core tasks. That's why this opportunity to come and talk to you here at the Alder Festival is very pleasant and important. The Bank of Finland continues to be a guardian of stability in Finland. Its task is to analyse the risks to price stability in Finland and to remind other domestic policymakers of them. As an independent monetary authority, it is well placed to do this, which is why the Bank of Finland invests heavily in research and economist analysis. An important area of activity is also central banking at both domestic and European level. The Bank of Finland is responsible for the smooth circulation of banknotes in Finland. A major topical challenge is the exchange of marks for euros at the turn of next year, which I will tell you more about in a moment. The Bank of Finland is involved in the implementation of monetary policy, i.e. market operations carried out by the Eurosystem on a decentralised basis by the national central banks under the coordination of the ECB. Finnish banks make their payments and other central bank matters as before with the Bank of Finland. For its part, the Bank of Finland supervises and secures the functioning of the Finnish financial markets. At the European level, the Bank of Finland is represented in all the committees and working groups through which the operation of the Eurosystem is prepared and verified. At the moment, bank officials of the Bank of Finland participate in the activities of 13 different committees and 40 permanent members of the ECB. In addition, the Bank of Finland participates in the European economic and integration debate in various EU for a, and not only on monetary policy. This is very important for a small country that has only been in the EU for 61/2 years. In the new EMU conditions, the Bank of Finland's operations are increasingly focused on expert tasks in monetary policy and financial markets. The Bank of Finland of the future will be somewhat smaller than the current one, but not very much. The Bank remains a vibrant monetary influencer linking Finland to the monetary economy of the rest of Europe. It must be European in Finland and Finnish in Europe. 4. The Bank of Finland's most topical challenge - the exchange of money from euros to marks The euro, its concrete introduction at the beginning of next year, is a more concrete symbol of this link between the Finnish and other European monetary finances. As I said, the bank of Finland's biggest challenge at the moment is to ensure the smooth use of the euro in Finland. The two functions are above all others: 1) The national central banks are each responsible for issuing banknotes in their own country - the Bank of Finland takes care of the issuance of euros in Finland; 2) and the Bank of Finland's task is to familiarise citizens with their new currency. Monetary union has therefore been in force since the beginning of 1999, i.e. we have been living in the euro era for more than two years in monetary policy - we already have experience of the economic policy and financial market effects of monetary union, both in terms of the cold and in the challenges that have required adjustment. At the micro level in the life of the ordinary person, on the other hand, the effects of monetary union will not really be felt until January and February 2002. This is where euro notes and coins will be used. According to the EU recommendation, the vast majority of cash payments would be made in euros as early as two weeks from the beginning of 2002. In monetary terms, the exchange of money no longer means big, it is, as it were, just the final seal on top of the change that has taken place. As a logistical operation, of course, it is very demanding. Some 130 million banknotes (denominated in finnish marks) are withdrawn and almost as many new ones are put into circulation (denominated in EUR 100 million). On the coin side, the number of pieces is roughly tenfold (back 2500 million coins of marks are replaced by 950 million coins in euros). The demanding operation of money exchange is my general, for companies, trade, etc. , all of which will have to convert their invoicing, accounting and other information systems into new monetary units. The costs of the changeover to the euro (transitional period from 1.1.1999 to 31.12.2001, and the exchange period from 1.1.2002 to 28.2.2002) will be considerable and there will be difficulties in using it. It should be remembered, however, that the hymns are also large, although they often only accumulate over a long period of time, in the years to come and in the decades to come. The use of euro banknotes and coins requires extensive communication from the Bank of Finland. The Bank of Finland participates in the Euro 2002 information campaign, which is a joint effort of the euro area central banks and the ECB, and is also implementing a Complementary Finnish campaign. The aim of the central banks is to familiarise citizens, in particular, with the externality and authenticity of euro coins and with the timing of issuance. The target group is not only a large general group, but also those occupational groups that deal with cash or are able to effectively disseminate information about the new currency. The main groups are banks, retail and tourism, as well as the police and education administration. Through this, we hope to reach e.g. schoolchildren. The Bank of Finland has concluded some 65 partnership agreements. with entities. The Bank of Finland assists partners in communicating the euro and, in return, the partners take care of informing their own people and customers. The most visible part of the Bank of Finland's mass media campaign will take place at the end of 2001. Then we will see, for example, an extensive TV advertising campaign. The use of the euro in Finland is reported by the Minister of Finance and the European Union's joint euro information campaign. Different campaigns are coordinated with each other to avoid duplication and information gaps. 5. Finally The euro area is on a par with the United States in terms of population and area. There are 300 million in the euro area. inhabitants, in the United States 270 million. The euro area accounts for 16% of the world's gross domestic product, the United States about 21%. The euro area is a relatively closed economy, which is therefore capable of generating economic growth even internally, i.e. its openness in terms of exportrelation to GDP is only about 17%, i.e. close to that of the United States (10%). (Eg. When viewed alone, finnish openness is around 40 per cent). By being part of such a large internal market and currency area, the opportunities for the Finnish economy in a globalising economy have clearly improved. Finnish entrepreneurs operate in the euro area in the domestic market, where there is no exchange rate risk, among other things. At the beginning of next year, prices on these domestic markets will become more readily comparable, which is likely to promote the functioning of the market for retail consumers. By providing a single monetary policy, Finland will achieve "basic stability" in its economy After all, the aim is stability and minimizing unexpected twists and turns. Money should be a point of reference in the economy and not a distraction. That is why monetary policy in EMU will be all the more successful and Finland's membership of the monetary union all the more robust and predictable the ECB's monetary policy will be. So, the more boring it is, the better monetary policy is. In this respect, the experience with the ECB's monetary policy is successful: we can rely on the ECB's monetary policy and price stability in the euro area. This basic stability, which finland will have to enjoy in a major monetary union, is important. It facilitates the planning of purchases for households and businesses, reduces the risks associated with investment  is likely to promote growth and, consequently, boredom. The political and psychological impact of EMU has been great. We have all been able to see how Finland's weight in European economic policy has increased, and from the 'outer ring' of Europe we have, in a way, moved on to the 'inner ring'. This has, of course, had not only its political and economic consequences. When, in the past, a well-known Spanish banker was asked why he was in favour of his country joining the monetary union, he said that the Spaniards had suffered enough to be regarded as an 'exotic currency'. The same applies to our mark. In the past, exotic, or bad, notoriety was paid for as quite a instability, when trust in the markka varied from unduly good to unduly bad. The result was not only fluctuations in interest rates, but also unnecessary difficulties for the foreign operations of small and medium-sized enterprises. Of course, living in a monetary union also requires flexibility, composure and discipline on the part of us, in the pricing practices of companies, in public finances - so that our inflation rate does not exceed the average inflation rate in the euro area, thereby eroding our price competitiveness. However, such discipline is necessary for more general reasons than simply belonging to a monetary union. The potential of a small economy has always been and is based not only on the ability to innovate but also on greater flexibility and the rapid depletion of the opportunities offered. In my opinion, this applies not only to small countries at the myregional level and to small municipalities. Naturally, changes are needed. The countryside has changed a lot in recent decades. There are fewer people. (Although I noticed from the statistics of your municipality that Hirvensalmi is a migration gain municipality, and the birth rate is also at a good level.) Agriculture has become more technical, more competitive, which certainly seems daunting. On the other hand, technological progress has shortened distances, opened up access to information and thus enabled more diverse entrepreneurship in rural areas. I believe that there are opportunities for original activities that seek to combine traditional know-how using technology. Naturally, my clean and well-maintained surroundings and clean foods will be more and more appreciated in the future  you can understand that especially when you look at things from the tips of crowded Central Europe. I understand very well that the hospitable Hirvensalmi, which I am now visiting for the first time in my life, fascinates German summer guests, among others. There have been many more opportunities and markets for originality, richness of ideas, initiative and entrepreneurship since eu and EMU membership. These opportunities should be used, and I believe that you, as a municipality that invests in good service and the environment, are well equipped to take on the challenges. *** When, in concrete terms, the euro comes in the form of notes and coins at the beginning of next year, we must feel a little sad. After all, we have had our markka since 1860, that is, before Finland was an independent state. But I am sure that we will adopt the euro quite quickly. It must be remembered that we in Finland have spent many kinds of money over the years  including thalers and rubles. (When the Bank of Finland was founded in 1811, it issued kopecks and rubles.) The most important thing about money, however, is the preservation of its value, that is, price stability. In that sense, I dare to predict much better times for us than the average markka's history has been.

Title: Speech at the Euro Enters Everyday Life seminar
text: Matti Louekoski The euro enters everyday life seminar Turku 5.10.2001 THE EURO, EMU AND FINLAND 1. For background The single currency and monetary policy have been part of everyday life in the euro area countries for almost three years. At the beginning of next year, the transition to the single currency will reach its end when euro notes and coins are introduced and the markka becomes part of our monetary history after some 140 years of service. Experience with the euro and the single monetary policy to date supports the assessments expressed in the preparations leading up to Finland's accession to EMU1: the euro and EMU membership in general have been a stabilising factor for the Finnish economy. Despite the strong financial market turmoil that has hit the global economy in recent years  such as the Russian crisis in 1998, the Brazilian crisis in 1999 and recent events in the United States  interest rate and exchange rate developments have remained calm and have supported the maintenance and raising of economic prosperity in Finland. In fact, the stabilisation of interest rate and exchange rate developments in Finland began earlier in the 1990s, when Finland's membership of the EU and later its membership of EMU began to be confirmed. The exchange rate of the mark against the German mark settled around 3 at the end of 1994 and remained close to it until the beginning of the third stage of EMU on 1.1.1999. The long-term interest rate differential between Finland and Germany (10-year government bonds) narrowed below 1/2% by the beginning of 1997. From a broader perspective, the euro has been a stabilising factor. Recent events in the financial markets have shown that, on a global economic scale, the existence of the euro and the Eurosystem has contributed to the de-escalation of the situation and the reduction of uncertainty. One large currency, under these circumstances, has been more than the sum of its shares. It has also been a bulwark against speculative attacks. 1 The concept of 'EMU membership' has been used in this context to refer to membership in stage three of economic and monetary union. 2. On the fundamentals of the ECB's monetary policy The primary objective of the ECB's monetary policy is to maintain price stability in the euro area. This task is entrusted to the ECB (ESCB) by the Treaty establishing the European Community. Within this target in autumn 1998, the Governing Council specified the following: price stability refers to an annual increase in the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices in the euro area of less than two per cent. At the same time, the Council underlined the need to understand this objective as a medium-term objective. Thus, the rate of increase in consumer prices may temporarily  for example, due to external price disturbances, such as fluctuations in the price of ljy  differ from the above. but in the medium term price developments must return to line with the target. The Council also underlined that the objective applies specifically to the euro area as a whole  in the case of individual countries, price developments may be somewhat different, perhaps for longer periods of time. This may be the case, for example, where the price level of a lower-income country gradually approaches the euro area average. In addition to the above-mentioned priority objective, the ECB has also been given the task of supporting the rest of the general economic policy, but in such a way that it must not jeopardise the achievement of the primary objective of price stability. In order to achieve the above-mentioned objective of price stability, the Governing Council has chosen a monetary policy strategy consisting of two components, the so-called "monetary policy strategy". Pillars. The first pillar gives the euro area money volume a prominent role in monetary policy. This role, which reflects the view of inflation as a monetary or monetary indicator, includes a reference value for the annual growth of the broad monetary aggregate M3 (measured as a three-month moving average of a 12-month change). This reference value is 41/2%. In the Governing Council's view, if the rate of monetary growth in the euro area exceeds this reference value, it signals the existence of risks to price stability. However, it should be noted that this is only a reference value, not the objective itself. Deviations from the reference value do not, therefore, automatically lead to changes in monetary policy, but are always carefully and thoroughly assessed with the aim of identifying the factors behind such deviations. The second pillar of monetary policy involves a broad examination of future price developments and risks to price stability. This analysis covers a very wide range of indicators of price and cost developments, including inflation forecasts, asset prices (exchange rates, etc.), exchange rate developments, etc. Under the second pillar, the Eurosystem produces a broad macroeconomic projection twice a year, i.e. a forecast calculation, which is published in the ECB's monthly publication. In its activities, the ECB has strived to pursue an open and transparent approach, which is also reflected in its active communication with the media. In this way, the Council considers that it will contribute to the comprehensibility and acceptability of monetary policy in the euro area. 3. How has the ECB's monetary policy succeeded in achieving its objective? Inflation in the euro area remained at the level of the price stability objective in 1999. On average, inflation at that time was 1.1%, the same as in 1998. Towards the end of the year, however, it became increasingly clear that risks to the volatile sector were on the increase. This was reflected in the signals given by both the 1st and 2nd pillars of the monetary policy strategy. The pace of monetary growth was picking up and credit growth remained brisk. At the same time, economic growth was intensifying, the external value of the euro was depreciating and the price of ljy rose substantially. As a result, as of the second half of 1999, the Governing Council moved the monetary policy stance in a more acrimonious direction in order to maintain favourable price developments and to avoid an increase in inflation expectations. The development continued in the same way until the autumn of 2000. From November 1999 to October 2000, the Governing Council raised its key interest rate to a total of 2.25%, to 4.75%. Despite the tightening of monetary policy, inflation in the euro area increased during the rest of 1999 and 2000, reaching a maximum of almost 3% in November 2000. The average inflation rate for the full year 2000 was 2.3%. In early 2001, inflation fluctuated at a still high level, even rising above 3% in late spring. A key factor in the increase in inflation between 1999 and 2001 was the sharp rise in import prices, above all the price of raw materials. The weakening of the euro contributed to this development, as did the crises in the food market. The latter factor was significant, especially in early 2001. However, the increase in inflation cannot be interpreted as a failure of monetary policy. As the Governing Council stated as long ago as 1998 in its decision on the monetary policy strategy, in the short term there may be deviations in price developments from the objective of price stability that monetary policy cannot or does not even wish to prevent. The volatility of oil prices is a good example of this type of development, which can cause inflationary fluctuations in the euro area. In the medium term, this type of fluctuation should even out. As a result, the ECB's interest rate hikes over the period 1999-2000 were aimed at dampening the knock-on effects of, inter alia, the rise in the price of ljy and at preventing an intensification of inflation expectations that could threaten the maintenance of price stability over the medium term. Based on the development of long-term interest rates and various inflation expectations surveys, for example, this was quite successful. 4. The economic situation in the euro area towards the end of 2001 and the outlook for 2002 During this year, the situation regarding both growth and inflation prospects in the euro area has changed. Growth in the euro area has slowed down substantially, as in the rest of the global economy. In recent months, inflation has also started to decline. At the same time, risks to price stability over the medium term have diminished. Accordingly, the Governing Council eased its monetary policy stance by a total of 1/2% in May and August. Since then, the terrorist attacks on the United States have further darkened the growth prospects of both the global economy and, to a lesser extent, the euro area. In recent weeks, the ECB has contributed to the stability of international financial markets. In September, in the midst of the terrorist attacks in the United States, the Eurosystem facilitated the functioning of euro area money markets by conducting liquidity-providing fine-weather operations and conducted currency swaps to provide European banks with the dollars they needed. The Governing Council lowered its key interest rate by 1/2% to 3.75%. At the same time, several other central banks lowered their key interest rates, although there was no question of any coordinated rate cut. The ECB's recent downward trend has been based on the assessment that the medium-term inflation outlook for the euro area has shifted in a direction favourable to price stability. Inflation in the euro area is expected to continue to decline in the near term, provided that energy prices, especially raw materials, remain stable (or fall, as has happened in recent days) and the inflationary effects of rising food prices diminish as expected. 5. The euro has stabilised the Finnish economy The main justification for Finland's membership of emu and the use of the euro was the promotion of monetary stability. This can be understood as stable interest rate and exchange rate conditions and, ultimately, as the stability of price developments. Price stability, on the other hand, is seen as contributing to economic growth and an increase in general well-being in Finland in the longer term. The sustainable achievement of the stability objective requires various structural changes to take place in our economy.2 These changes have already been made and are still needed in both the food and labour markets. As this is a matter of changing structures, the time that has elapsed is still partly too short to make the final decisions. However, some of the fears and hopes associated with monetary union can already be assessed. First of all, it can be undeniably stated that emu membership and the euro have in recent years protected the Finnish economy from disturbances in the international financial markets and thus stabilised economic development. The Russian crisis of 1998, as well as the very recent events on the world financial markets, clearly demonstrate the importance of EMU membership for Finland. This has been reflected above all in the stability of interest rate developments: interest rate spikes similar to those experienced in the past  which are very easily seen in a small open economy as general uncertainty increases and risk supplements rise  have not been. It is noteworthy that this stabilising effect was already visible before the start of the third stage of EMU in the context of the Russian crisis in 1998. Stable interest rate developments have meant, for example, a safe environment for households to operate in, as major decisions are made  especially in the housing market. Although the external value of the euro has deteriorated considerably since the beginning of 1999, membership of the Economic and Monetary Union and the existence of the euro have nevertheless meant a very stable trading environment for a significant part of Finland's foreign trade. This applies in particular to the part of the trade that takes place between Finland and 2 One of these is increased competition. It will help to reduce the pricing power of local monopolies and promote the adoption of more efficient production methods and thus the growth of welfare. between euro area countries, but more widely to the extent that the euro has been used; in trading, e.g. as a pricing currency. The use of the single currency has facilitated transactions and reduced, among other things, the costs of hedging against currency risks. In relation to Sweden, for example, we have an advantage in this respect. In recent years, the role of the information and communication technology (ICT) sector in the Finnish economy has grown strongly. This has been reflected in many ways, not only in the speed of economic growth, but also in the development of prss courses, for example. Recently, however, the outlook for the sector has changed rapidly and uncertainty about the future has increased. In the past  under the conditions of one's own money  this kind of development would most likely have caused large fluctuations in the external value of the markka. Between 1999 and 2000, the markka would obviously have been under strong pressure to strengthen, as foreign investors would have competed to increase their investments in the shares of companies in the sector. On the other hand, these events in the Finnish ICT sector have had little effect on the exchange rate of the euro. The achievement of the key rationale for EMU membership, namely monetary stability, can ultimately be assessed from the perspective of price stability. Inflation in Finland increased substantially since the end of 1999, peaking at over 4% in the second half of last year, as measured by the Consumer Price Index. Since then, inflation has declined to around 21/2% and is projected to continue declining during the rest of the year and next year. The increase in inflation between 1999 and 2000 was quite universal: the rate of increase in consumer prices accelerated not only in Finland, but also in the rest of the euro area, as well as in many other countries. The acceleration was largely due to an external price shock, i.e. higher prices of raw materials. In Finland, however, inflation has also been fuelled by domestic factors, especially in the services sector, when economic development has been strong. However, there has been no general overheating in the economy  despite the very rapid growth of the economy and the lightness of the monetary economy  but has largely been a matter of regional and sector-specific problems, which have been caused, for example, by the strong growth of the ICT sector. This has been reflected both in some segments of the labour market and, for example, in the housing market and perhaps more generally in the prices of assets. At the moment, these problems seem to be receding or have already receded. The discipline required for membership of economic and monetary union has been implemented reasonably well in terms of the average rate of wage growth. On the other hand, there is concern that wages in low-productivity sectors have risen like in other sectors, thus preventing the emergence of new jobs. Above all, however, this has to do with the form of income solutions, not emu membership itself. On the whole, finland's wage developments in recent years can be seen as supporting the point raised in the debate on EMU membership that economic and monetary union may increase discipline through the tyarchies. The idea is that, under the conditions of the single currency, strong trade unions have no interest in pushing for wages at the peak of the economic cycle, because competitiveness cannot be saved by devaluation when the economic cycle deteriorates. "Although Sweden was excluded from the third stage of EMU, wage discipline has also been achieved there. The differences in wage developments between Finland and Sweden have been relatively small, but the period is still too short to draw strong conclusions. In the context of economic and monetary union, the responsibility for ensuring the balanced development of the economy has often been seen to rest largely on the labour market and public finances. The functioning of the labour market has contributed to achieving stable economic development in Finland in recent years. From the point of view of public finances, both the public sector debt and deficit criteria linked to EMU membership and the stability and growth pact in force have contributed to the rather disciplined and responsible fiscal policy pursued in Finland in recent years, which has contributed to achieving stable economic development. The sharp and rapid deterioration of our country's economic prospects during this year, as well as the spill-over effects of this development on public finances, especially public finances, are a good illustration of the importance of the efforts made in recent years to stabilise public finances. As a result of these efforts, a structural surplus has been created in the state budget, which, in the event of a weakening of the economic cycle, allows the economy to become so-called "greenback". operation of automatic stabilizers. These stabilisers are currently operational and are softening the effects of the economic downturn. Care must be taken to ensure that this room for manoeuvre is maintained in public finances and elsewhere in public finances in the future as well. Therefore, when the revenue base is very sensitive to the economic cycle, expenditure policy must be reticent. What do the very recent events in the global economy mean for Finland? In September, the Bank of Finland published a revised forecast, according to which the economic growth of our country will remain at only 11/2% this year. As recently as the spring, growth was expected to reach nearly 4 per cent. My growth estimate for next year was dropped to about 21/2 percent. Since the forecast was completed, economic development in the world has continued to weaken, mainly due to the terrorist attacks on the United States. From today's perspective, the forecast is probably too optimistic, at least for this year. (Gdp growth of around 1% would seem likely at the moment this year). In addition, there is a great deal of uncertainty about next year. However, there is no room for excessive pessimism, as the fundamentals of our economy are in order: public finances, as well as corporate balance sheets, are in good shape, inflation is falling, interest rates are low and stable, and the current account is firmly in surplus. Thus, a recovery in growth in the near future is likely.
