Tmn pivn nkulmasta arvioituna ennuste lieneekin liian optimistinen, ainakin tmn vuoden osalta. (Noin 1 prosentin bkt-kasvu tuntuisi tll hetkell todennkiselt tn vuonna). Lisksi ensi vuotta koskeva epvarmuus on hyvin suuri. Liialliseen pessimismiin ei kuitenkaan ole aihetta, sill taloutemme perustekijt ovat kunnossa: valtiontalous samoin kuin yritysten taseet ovat hyvll tolalla, inflaatio on hidastumassa, korkotaso on alhainen ja vakaa ja vaihtotase on tukevasti ylijminen. Siten kasvun elpyminen lhitulevaisuudessa on todennkist.

Title: Speech at the Finance 2002 seminar
text: Matti Louekoski Funding 2002 seminar Finlandia Hall, Helsinki 11.10.2001 Monetary policy 2002 1. The ECB's monetary policy kick-off ? The primary objective of the ECB's monetary policy is to maintain price stability in the euro area. This task is entrusted to the ECB (ESCB) by the Treaty establishing the European Community. Within this target in autumn 1998, the Governing Council specified as follows: price stability refers to an annual increase in the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices in the euro area below two per cent over the medium term. Thus, the rate of increase in consumer prices may temporarily d0 for example, due to external price disturbances, such as fluctuations in the price of ljy d0 differ from the above. but in the medium term price developments must return to line with the target. The Council also underlined that the objective applies specifically to the euro area as a whole d0 in the case of individual countries, price developments may be somewhat different, perhaps for longer periods of time. This may be the case, for example, where the price level of a lower-income country gradually approaches the euro area average. The same is true when a temporary 'growth spike' in a country brings with it a 'price spike'. In addition to the above-mentioned priority objective, the ECB has also been given the task of supporting the rest of the general economic policy, while not jeopardising the achievement of the primary objective of price stability. In this respect, the ECB's agenda is, for example, to: Clearly different from the FED. ? In order to achieve its objective of price stability, the Governing Council has chosen a monetary policy strategy consisting of two so-called monetary policy strategies. Pillars. The first pillar gives the euro area money volume a prominent role in monetary policy. This role, which reflects the view of inflation as a monetary or monetary indicator, includes a reference value for the annual growth of the broad monetary aggregate M3 (measured as a three-month moving average of a 12-month change). This reference value is 41/2%. In the Governing Council's view, if the rate of monetary growth in the euro area exceeds this reference value, it signals the existence of risks to price stability. However, it should be noted that this is only a reference value, not an objective in itself. Deviations from the reference value do not, therefore, automatically lead to changes in monetary policy, but the situation is always carefully assessed with the aim of identifying the underlying factors. Most recently, in the context of the decision to reduce the interest rate in August, the Council analysed very carefully (also in its communication) the importance of the monetary aggregate and the internal element of monetary policy. The second pillar of monetary policy involves a broad examination of future price developments and risks to price stability. This analysis covers a very wide range of indicators of price and cost developments, including inflation forecasts, asset prices (exchange rates, etc.), exchange rate developments, etc. Under the second pillar, the Eurosystem produces a broad macroeconomic projection twice a year, i.e. a forecast calculation, which is published in the ECB's monthly publication. ? In its activities, the ECB has strived to pursue an open and transparent approach, which is also reflected in its active communication with the media. In this way, the Council considers that it will contribute to the comprehensibility and acceptability of monetary policy in the euro area. However, there has been a lot of public controversy about transparency. Many consider the previous show of openness to be quite modest. In any case, the practices adopted by the ECB are already new to European central bank policy in terms of its overall approach. 2. On the achievements of monetary policy ? Inflation in the euro area remained at the level of the price stability objective in 1999. On average, inflation at that time was 1.1%, the same as in 1998. Towards the end of the year, however, it became increasingly clear that risks to price stability were increasing, as reflected in the signals given by both the 1st and 2nd pillars. The pace of monetary growth was picking up and credit growth remained brisk. At the same time, economic growth was intensifying, the external value of the euro was depreciating and the price of ljy rose substantially. As a result, since the end of 1999, the Governing Council has changed its monetary policy in a more acrimonious direction. The development continued in the same way until the autumn of 2000. From November 1999 to October 2000, the Governing Council raised its key interest rate to a total of 2.25%, to 4.75%. ? Despite the tightening of monetary policy, inflation in the euro area increased during the rest of 1999 and 2000, reaching a maximum of almost 3% in November 2000. The average inflation rate for the full year 2000 was 2.3%. In early 2001, inflation fluctuated at a still high level, even rising above 3% in late spring. A key factor in the increase in inflation between 1999 and 2001 was the sharp rise in import prices, above all the price of raw materials. The weakening of the euro contributed to this development, as did the crises in the food market. The latter factor was significant, especially in early 2001. However, the increase in inflation cannot be interpreted as a failure of monetary policy. In line with the ECB's monetary policy strategy, deviations in price developments from the objective of price stability may occur in the short term that monetary policy cannot or does not even want to prevent. The volatility of oil prices is a good example of this type of development, which can cause inflationary fluctuations in the euro area. In the medium term, this type of fluctuation should even out. As a result, the ECB's interest rate hikes in 1999-2000 were aimed at dampening the second-round effects of, inter alia, the rise in the price of ljy and at preventing inflation expectations. Based on the development of long-term interest rates and various inflation surveys, for example, this was quite successful. 3. Outlook for the euro area for 2002 ? During this year, the situation in both the euro area growth and inflation outlook has changed substantially. Growth in the euro area has slowed down substantially, as in the rest of the global economy. In recent months, inflation has also started to decline. At the same time, risks to price stability have diminished. Accordingly, the Governing Council eased its monetary policy by a total of 1/2% in May and August. Since then, the terrorist attacks on the United States have further darkened the growth prospects for both the global economy and the euro area. In recent weeks, the ECB has contributed to the stability of international financial markets. In September, in the midst of the terrorist attacks in the United States, the Eurosystem facilitated the functioning of euro area money markets by conducting liquidity-providing fine-weather operations and conducted currency swaps to provide European banks with the dollars they needed. The Governing Council lowered its key interest rate by 1/2% to 3.75%. At the same time, several other central banks lowered their key interest rates, although there was no question of any coordinated rate cut. At the request of the Bank of Japan, the ECB has also intervened in the foreign exchange markets on its behalf. In recent weeks, the Bank of Japan has been working to prevent the yen from strengthening. ? The ECB's recent downward trend has been based on the assessment that the medium-term inflation outlook for the euro area has shifted in a direction favourable to price stability. Inflation in the euro area is expected to continue to decline in the near term, provided that energy prices, especially raw materials, remain stable (or fall, as has happened in recent days) and the inflationary effects of rising food prices diminish as expected. ? The slowdown in economic growth should contribute to reducing inflationary pressures. Recent developments in producer and import prices in the euro area support the view of a decline in inflation. The use of euro cash may have a minor temporary impact on the rate of increase in consumer prices, possibly by pushing the prices of food products upwards. Similarly, however, these efforts are likely to reduce price increases in the future. In addition, many prices are likely to be pushed downwards. ? Recent monetary developments in the euro area do not appear to change the above conclusion on inflation. Although the recent increase in the broad monetary aggregate (M3) above 6%, does not necessarily indicate that future price developments will be subject to upward pressure over the medium term. When the impact of non-euro area items1 is eliminated, the growth rate of M3 was around 51/2% between June and August. It should also be noted that the weak performance of international stock markets, as well as the flatness of the yield curve, have in recent months increased the demand for liquid forms of deposits, which has been reflected in the increase in monetary amounts. Furthermore, the slowdown in the growth rate of credit sold to the private sector suggests that there is no reason to draw too strong conclusions from the recent rise in monetary growth, anticipating an increase in inflation. ? The near-term growth prospects for the euro area had already deteriorated before the terrorist attacks. This reflected partly the downward revision of growth projections in the rest of the global economy and partly the weaker-than-expected development of domestic demand in the euro area during the first half of the year. For example, the growth forecasts for this year and next year in the United States were generally lowered at the turn of August and September, as the outlook for consumer demand, which has maintained growth so far, was fading due to the weakening of tulle and, among other things, the fall in share prices. As a result of the attacks, perceptions of near-term economic developments in the United States and the rest of the global economy have continued to deteriorate. While the shocks are not expected to have a lasting negative impact on growth in the United States d0 the country's production potential has not suffered significantly from what has happened d0 the start of economic growth is likely to be clearly postponed until next year, as households are likely to be even more cautious in their consumption behaviour and businesses in their investment decisions. However, the recovery in growth in the United States is supported by a strong easing of monetary policy (already nine interest rate cuts this year), tax cuts, substantial increases in public spending following terrorist attacks and possibly the progress of the stock adjustment, as evidenced even before the terrorist attacks. It should be noted, however, that the monetary easing has been counterbalanced by a broad decline in the long ranges. It dampens the revitalizing effect of the interest rate endings made. One of the reasons for the development of long-term interest rates is the fear that the balance of general government finances will be clearly weaker than previously estimated. In addition, there is a risk for growth that tax cuts will shift to saving as uncertainty about future developments has increased, asset values have fallen and the outlook for boredom has deteriorated. The increase in public expenditure, and in particular its focus on military and other consumption expenditure, is not conducive to an increase in the long-term growth potential of the economy. ? As a result of recent events, the short-term outlook for growth in the euro area has continued to deteriorate somewhat and uncertainty has increased. Euroalu 1 These include money market and short-term debt securities held by non-euro area residents. Growth is likely to be weaker than previously expected in the near future and the recovery will be delayed. However, there is no reason to overdramatize the situation. In any case, the indirect impact of the attacks on, for example, the climate of confidence is likely to be smaller in the euro area than in the United States. In addition, the conditions for strengthening economic growth in the euro area are good: the tax cuts implemented in many countries are timely for the cyclical situation and will help to address structural problems, including in the labour market, by reducing the tax wedge. Inflation is expected to decline further, supporting the growth of domestic demand, in particular consumer demand. The consolidation of public finances carried out in previous years gives leeway to the operation of automatic stabilisers in those countries where consolidation has progressed sufficiently far. Finally, the monetary situation in the euro area as a whole is currently light and accommodative, with low market interest rates and low external value of the euro. For its part, the ECB's interest rate decisions have created the conditions for a recovery in economic growth in the euro area. ? Recent events in the United States have also been reflected in the external value of the euro, which has strengthened somewhat in recent weeks. This is no surprise d0 the greatest uncertainty has been directed at the US economy and its near-term development. In this situation, the euro as a major currency has been a safe alternative investment. Despite its strengthening, the euro is still a good 10% weaker than in the early months of 1999 in terms of the trade-weight currency index. Although the changes in the external value of the euro have been quite large in recent years, they are not of particular concern for the stable development of the euro area. As the share of external trade in the gross domestic product of the euro area is rather low, the internal value of the euro, i.e. price stability in the euro area, is fundamentally more important for citizens than the stability of the external value of the euro. As a conclusion, the ECB has been very successful in fostering internal stability.
text_original: Matti Louekoski Rahoitus 2002 seminaari Finlandia-talo, Helsinki 11.10.2001 Rahapolitiikka 2002 1. EKP:n rahapolitiikan lhtohtia  EKP:n rahapolitiikan ensisijaisena tavoitteena on hintavakauden yllpitminen euroalueella. Tm tehtv on annettu EKP:lle (EKPJ:lle) Euroopan Yhteisn perustamissopimuksessa. EKP:n neuvosto tsmensi tavoitteen sislt syksyll 1998 seuraavasti: hintavakaudella tarkoitetaan euroalueen yhdenmukaistetun kuluttajahintaindeksin alle kahden prosentin vuosittaista nousua keskipitkll aikavlill. Kuluttajahintojen nousuvauhti voi siis tilapisesti  esimerkiksi ulkoisten hintahiriiden kuten ljyn hinnan heilahtelujen takia  poiketa em. tavoitteesta mutta keskipitkll aikavlill hintakehityksen pit palautua tavoitteen mukaiseksi. Neuvosto my korosti, ett tavoite koskee nimenomaan euroaluetta kokonaisuutena  yksittisten maiden kohdalla hintakehitys voi jossain mrin olla erilainen, kenties pidempikin aikoja. Nin voi olla esimerkiksi tilanteessa, jossa jonkin alemman tulotason maan hintataso vhitellen lhenee euroalueen keskiarvoa. Samoin on asian laita, kun jonkin maan tilapinen kasvupiikki tuo mukanaan my hintapiikin. Edell mainitun ensisijaisen tavoitteen lisksi EKP:lle on annettu my tehtvksi muun yleisen talouspolitiikan tukeminen kuitenkin siten, ett se ei saa vaarantaa ensisijaisen tavoitteen eli hintavakauden saavuttamista. Tss suhteessa EKP:n agenda on esim. FED:ist selkesti poikkeava.  Hintavakaustavoitteen saavuttamiseksi EKP:n neuvosto on valinnut rahapolitiikan strategian, joka koostuu kahdesta ns. pilarista. Ensimminen pilari antaa euroalueen rahan mrlle nkyvn roolin rahapolitiikassa. Tm rooli, joka heijastaa nkemyst inflaatiosta rahataloudellisena eli monetaarisena ilmi, pit sislln viitearvon lavean raha-aggregaatin M3 vuotuiselle kasvulle (mitattuna 12 kuukauden muutoksen kolmen kuukauden liukuvana keskiarvona). Tm viitearvo on 4 prosenttia. EKP:n neuvosto katsoo, ett mikli rahan mrn kasvuvauhti euroalueella ylitt tmn viitearvon, se on merkki hintavakautta uhkaavien riskien olemassaolosta. On kuitenkin huomattava, ett kyseess on vain viitearvo, ei tavoite itsessn. Poikkeamat viitearvosta eivt siten johda automaattisesti muutoksiin rahapolitiikassa vaan tilannetta arvioidaan aina huolellisesti ja pyrkien selvittmn poikkeamien taustalla olevat tekijt. Viimeksi elokuisen koron alentamisptksen yhteydess neuvosto varsin tarkoin analysoi (mys tiedonannossaan) raha-aggregaatin merkityst ja sislt rahapolitiikan elementtin. Rahapolitiikan toinen pilari pit sislln tulevan hintakehityksen sek hintavakauteen kohdistuvien riskien laaja-alaisen tarkastelun. Tm tarkastelu hydynt hyvin laajaa joukkoa erilaisia hinta- ja kustannuskehityst kuvaavia indikaattoreita, mukaan lukien inflaatioennusteet, varallisuusesineiden hinnat (pssikurssit ym.), valuuttakurssikehitys jne. Toiseen pilariin liittyen eurojrjestelm laatii kahdesti vuodessa laajan kokonaistaloudellisen projektion eli ennustelaskelman, joka julkaistaan EKP:n kuukausijulkaisussa.  Toiminnassaan EKP on pyrkinyt noudattamaan avointa ja lpinkyv toimintatapaa, mit heijastaa mys aktiivinen kommunikointi tiedotusvlineiden kanssa. Tll tavalla neuvosto katsoo edistvns rahapolitiikan ymmrrettvyytt ja hyvksyttvyytt euroalueella. Julkisuudessa avoimuudesta on tosin paljon kiistelty. Monet pitvt thnastista nytt avoimuudesta varsin vaatimattomana. Joka tapauksessa EKP:n omaksuma kytnt jo nykyiselln on uutta eurooppalaisessa keskuspankkipolitiikassa sen kokonaisuutta ajatellen. 2. Rahapolitiikan saavutuksista  Euroalueen inflaatio pysytteli vuoden 1999 aikana hintavakaustavoitteen mukaisella tasolla. Keskimrin inflaatio oli tuolloin 1.1 % eli sama kuin vuonna 1998. Vuoden loppua kohden alkoi kuitenkin kyd yh selvemmksi, ett hintavakautta uhkaavat riskit olivat kasvussa, mik nkyi sek 1. ett 2. pilarin antamista merkeist. Rahan mrn kasvuvauhti oli nopeutumassa ja luotonannon kasvu jatkui ripen. Samanaikaisesti talouskasvu oli voimistumassa, euron ulkoinen arvo heikkeni ja ljyn hinta nousi tuntuvasti. Vuoden 1999 loppupuolelta lhtien EKP:n neuvosto muuttikin rahapolitiikkaansa kiristvmpn suuntaan. Kehitys jatkui samantyyppisen aina vuoden 2000 syksyyn asti. Marraskuusta 1999 lokakuuhun 2000 EKP:n neuvosto nosti keskeist ohjauskorkoaan yhteens 2.25 prosenttiyksikk, 4.75 prosenttiin.  Rahapolitiikan kiristmisest huolimatta euroalueen inflaatio kiihtyi loppuvuoden 1999 ja vuoden 2000 aikana ja oli enimmilln liki 3 % marraskuussa 2000. Koko vuoden 2000 keskimriseksi inflaatiovauhdiksi muodostui 2.3 %. Alkuvuodesta 2001 inflaatio vaihteli yh korkealla tasolla, jopa kiihtyen loppukevst yli 3 prosentin. Keskeisen tekijn inflaation kiihtymisess vuosina 1999-2001 oli tuontihintojen  ennen kaikkea raakaljyn hinnan  voimakas nousu. Euron heikentyminen vaikutti osaltaan kehitykseen samoin kuin elintarvikemarkkinoiden kriisit. Jlkimminen tekij oli merkittv erityisesti alkuvuonna 2001. Inflaation kiihtymist ei kuitenkaan voida tulkita rahapolitiikan eponnistumiseksi. EKP:n rahapolitiikan strategian mukaisesti lyhyell aikavlill hintakehityksess voi esiinty sellaisia poikkeamia hintavakauden tavoitteesta, joita rahapolitiikalla eivoida tai ei edes haluta est. ljyn hinnan heilahtelu on hyv esimerkki tmntyyppisest kehityksest, joka voi aiheuttaa inflaatiovaihteluita euroalueella. Keskipitkll aikavlill tmntyyppisten vaihteluiden pitisi tasoittua. EKP pyrkikin vuosien 1999-2000 koronnostoillaan vaimentamaan mm. ljyn hinnan noususta aiheutuvia kerrannaisvaikutuksia ja ehkisemn inflaatio-odotuksia. Pitkien korkojen kehityksen ja mm. erilaisten inflaatio-kyselyjen perusteella tss onnistuttiinkin varsin hyvin. 3. Euroalueen nkymt vuodelle 2002  Tmn vuoden aikana tilanne niin euroalueen kasvu-kuin inflaationkymiss onoleellisesti muuttunut. Euroalueen kasvu on hidastunut tuntuvasti muun maailmantalouden tapaan. Viime kuukausina inflaatiokin on alkanut hidastua. Samanaikaisesti hintavakautta uhkaavat riskit ovat vhentyneet. EKP:n neuvosto kevensikin rahapolitiikkaansa touko- ja elokuussa yhteens  prosenttiyksikll. Sittemmin Yhdysvaltoihin kohdistuneet terrori-iskut ovat synkentneet edelleen niin maailmantalouden kuin mys euroalueen kasvunkymi. EKP on osaltaan tukenut viime viikkoina kansainvlisten rahoitusmarkkinoiden pysymist vakaina. Syyskuussa  vlittmsti Yhdysvaltain terrori-iskujen jlkeen  eurojrjestelm helpotti euroalueen rahamarkkinoiden toimintaa toteuttamalla likviditeetti lisvi hienostoperaatioita sek teki valuuttaswappeja, joilla eurooppalaiset pankit saivat tarvitsemiaan dollareita. EKP:n neuvosto my alensi ohjauskorkoaan  prosenttiyksikl, 3.75 prosenttiin. Useat muutkin keskuspankit alensivat samanaikaisesti ohjauskorkojaan, vaikka mistn koordinoidusta koronlaskusta ei ollutkaan kysymys. EKP on mys Japanin keskuspankin pyynnst intervenoinut valuuttamarkkinoilla sen puolesta. Viime viikkoina Japanin keskuspankki on pyrkinyt ehkisemn jenin vahvistumista.  EKP:n viimeaikaiset koronlaskuptset ovat perustuneet arvioon siit, ett euroalueen keskipitkn aikavlin inflaationkymt ovat muuttuneet hintavakauden kannalta suotuisaan suuntaan. Euroalueen inflaation odotetaan jatkavan lhitulevaisuudessa hidastumistaan, mikli energian  ennen kaikkea raakaljyn  hinta pysyy vakaana (tai laskee, kuten viime pivin on tapahtunut) ja elintarvikkeiden hintojen nousun inflaatiovaikutukset pienenevt oletetulla tavalla.  Talouskasvun hidastuminen vhentnee osaltaan inflaatiopaineita. Euroalueen tuottaja- ja tuontihintojen viimeaikainen kehitys tukee nkemyst inflaation hidastumisesta. Kteisen eurorahan kyttnotolla voi olla vhinen tilapinen vaikutus kuluttajahintojen nousuvauhtiin, kun hydykkeiden hintoja mahdollisesti pyristetn ylspin. Pyristykset kuitenkin vastaavasti vhentnevt hintojen nousua vastaisuudessa. Lisksi monia hintoja todennksesti pyistetn my alaspin.  Rahan mrn viimeaikainen kehitys euroalueella ei nyttisi muuttavan edell esitetty inflaatiota koskevaa johtoptst. Vaikka lavean raha-aggregaatin (M3) kasvuvauhti on viime aikoina kiihtynyt yli 6 prosentin, se ei vlttmtt viittaa siihen, ett tulevaan hintakehitykseen kohdistuisi keskipitkll aikavlill nousupaineita. Kun euroalueen ulkopuolisten tahojen hallussa olevien erien1 vaikutus poistetaan, M3-rahamrn kasvuvauhti oli kes-elokuussa noin 5 %. On mys huomattava, ett kansainvlisten osakemarkkinoiden heikko kehitys samoin kuin tuottokyrn loivuus ovat viime kuukausina lisnneet likvidien talletusmuotojen kysynt, mik on heijastunut rahamrien kasvussa. Mys yksityiselle sektorille mynnettyjen luottojen kasvuvauhdin hidastuminen viittaa siihen, ett rahan mrn kasvun viimeaikaisesta nopeutumisesta ei ole syyt vet liian voimakkaita, inflaation kiihtymist ennakoivia johtoptksi.  Euroalueen lhiajan kasvunkymt olivat heikentyneet jo ennen terrori-iskuja. Ne heijastuivat osin kasvuarvioiden korjausta alaspin muualla maailmantaloudessa, osin odotettua heikompaa kotimaisen kysynnn kehityst euroalueella alkuvuoden aikana. Mm. Yhdysvaltain tmn ja ensi vuoden kasvuarvioita oltiin elo-syyskuun vaihteessa yleisesti alentamassa, kun thn saakka kasvua yllpitneen kulutuskysynnn nkymt olivat hiipumassa tyllisyyden heikentymisen ja mm. osakekurssien laskun myt. Iskujen seurauksena ksitykset lhitulevaisuuden talouskehityksest Yhdysvalloissa ja my muualla maailmantaloudessa ovat edelleen heikentyneet. Vaikka iskuilla ei odotetakaan olevan pysyvi negatiivisia kasvuvaikutuksia Yhdysvalloissa  maan tuotantopotentiaali ei ole mainittavasti krsinyt tapahtuneesta  talouskasvun kynnistyminen siirtynee selvsti ensi vuoden puolelle, kun kotitaloudet todennkisesti ovat entistkin varovaisempia kulutuskyttytymisessn ja yritykset investointiptsissn. Kasvun elpymist Yhdysvalloissa tukevat kuitenkin rahapolitiikan voimakas keventyminen (jo yhdeksn koron alennusptst tn vuonna), veronalennukset, julkisten menojen tuntuvat lisykset terrori-iskujen jlkeen sek mahdollisesti my varastosopeutuksen eteneminen, josta oli merkkej jo ennen terrori-iskuja. On kuitenkin huomattava, ett rahapolitiikan keventmisen vastapainona pitkt ko-rot eivt ole juurikaan alentuneet. Se vaimentaa tehtyjen korkoptten elvyttv vaikutusta. Pitkien korkojen kehityksen taustalla on mm. pelko siit, ett julkisen talouden tasapaino tulee muodostumaan selvsti aiempia arvioita heikommaksi. Lisksi riskin kasvun kannalta on, ett veronkevennykset siirtyvt sstmiseen, kun epvarmuus tulevasta kehityksest on kasvanut, varallisuusarvot laskeneet ja tylisyysnkymt heikentyneet. Julkisten menojen kasvu ja erityisesti sen painottuminen sotilas- ja muihin kulutusmenoihin ei mykn ole omiaan edistmn talouden pitkn aikavlin kasvupotentiaalin nousua.  My euroalueen lyhyen aikavlin kasvunkymt ovat viimeaikaisten tapahtumien seurauksena edelleen heikentyneet jonkin verran ja epvarmuus kasvanut. Euroalu 1 Nm pitvt sislln euroalueen ulkopuolisten hallussa olevat rahamarkkinapaperit ja lyhytaikaiset velkapaperit. een kasvu muodostuneekin lhiaikoina aiemmin odotettua heikommaksi ja elpyminen lykkntyy. Tilannetta ei kuitenkaan ole syyt ylidramatisoida. Iskujen vlilliset vaikutukset mm. luottamusilmapiiriin jnevt joka tapauksessa euroalueella pienemmiksi kuin Yhdysvalloissa. Lisksi talouskasvun voimistumisen edellytykset ovat euroalueella hyvt: Monissa maissa toteutetut veronkevennykset ajoittuvat suhdannetilanteen kannalta oikeaan aikaan ja ne auttavat my rakenteellisten ongelmien korjaantumista mm. tymarkkinoilla, kun verokiilaa kavennetaan. Inflaation odotetaan edelleen hidastuvan, mik tukee kotimaisen kysynnn, ennen kaikkea kulutuskysynnn kasvua. Julkistalouksien aiempina vuosina toteutettu konsolidointi antaa pelivaraa automaattisten vakauttajien toiminnalle niiss maissa, joissa konsolidointi on edennyt riittvn pitklle. Lopuksi, rahatalouden tila kokonaisuudessaan on euroalueella tll hetkell keve ja kasvua tukeva, kun markkinakorot ovat matalat ja euron ulkoinen arvo alhainen. EKP on omalta osaltaan korkoptksilln luonut edellytyksi euroalueen talouden kasvun elpymiselle.  Yhdysvaltain viimeaikaiset tapahtumat ovat heijastuneet mys euron ulkoiseen arvoon, joka on viime viikkoina jonkin verran vahvistunut. Tm ei ole ylltys  on-han suurin epvarmuus kohdistunut juuri Yhdysvaltain talouteen ja sen lhiajan kehitykseen. Euro suurena valuuttana on ollut tss tilanteessa turvalliseksi koettu vaihtoehtoinen sijoituskohde. Vahvistumisestaan huolimatta euro on kauppapainoisella valuuttaindeksill mitattuna edelleen reilut 10 % heikompi kuin vuoden 1999 alkukuukausina. Vaikka euron ulkoisen arvon muutokset ovat olleet viime vuosina varsin suuria, ne eivt kuitenkaan ole erityisen huolestuttavia euroalueen vakaan kehityksen kannalta. Koska ulkomaankaupan osuus euroalueen bruttokansantuotteesta on melko pie-ni, euron sisinen arvo eli euroalueen hintavakaus on kansalaisten kannalta olennaisesti euron ulkoisen arvon vakautta trkempi. Johtoptksen voinee todeta, ett sisisen vakauden vaalimisessa EKP on onnistunut varsin hyvin.

Title: Presentation at the Studia Alumnorum event at the University of Helsinki
text: SUOMEN PANKKI FINLANDS BANK BANK OF FINLAND Sinikka Salo Member of the Board of Directors Globalisation and the role of international organisations Presentation at the Studia Alumnorum event of the University of Helsinki 23.10.2001 In recent years, the debate on economic policy and even on society has largely revolved around two megatrends: the 'new economy' and the 'globalisation'. In fact, these controversial concepts are so closely related that neither can be properly understood separately. Interestingly, still, they are usually viewed very differently. Not so long ago, the new economy d0 a term that I think is quite lame d0 was seen as a positive revolution, promising a rapid increase in prosperity in the world without much inflation or a polluting 'chimney industry', and which could free people up for truly global, mediated interaction and communication on the terms of the recipient. Now, for some reason, public interest in the 'new economy' seems to have waned, even though technology is advancing all the time and the opportunities it creates have not disappeared anywhere. Globalisation, on the other hand, often appears in public debate mainly as a threat, which has also provoked a strong civic movement of activists opposed to it. Criticism of globalisation has received a great deal of publicity for linking it to demonstrations at major international economic meetings such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Trade Organisation (WTO). The criticism is directed, among other things, at the social and environmental underpinnings of globalisation. It is based on the fear that the development trends known as globalisation will simultaneously lead to the escalation of the problems of humpbacks in developing countries, the destruction of jobs in the industrialised countries and the accelerated destruction of the environment. A significant part of the criticism also focuses on how globalization is affecting the relationship between economic and political power in the world. It is feared that the power of the market has gotten out of hand and under the control of governments. It is thought that when the market has become so large that no national government can control it, it will in turn begin to control the governments. This leads to a decrease in national sovereignty. However, the fates of the whole world are believed to be transferred from people to market forces. It is feared that a situation will arise, as if the spacecraft on Earth did not have a captain to control it: "nobody is in charge". On the other hand, it is also suspected that the power of the market with which globalisation is identified is not as anonymous and value-free as the market optimists suggest. It is thought that power is increasingly concentrated in the hands of large multinationals, which today, with the turnaround of power in their favour, would supposedly be able to dictate the internal economic policy and the direction of economic development worldwide. Another equally criticised concentration of power is the international economic organisations, in particular the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the World Trade Organisation (WTO) and the World Bank. Critics know that they are acting in favour of globalisation and already consider it to be the wrong policy by definition, or often think that these systems at least promote the wrong kind of globalisation and act in an un-ecological, undemocratic and unfair manner. I would like to take this opportunity to reflect on what globalisation is all about and what the international organisations are actually doing around it. I will talk a little about the International Monetary Fund and the World Trade Organisation, for example, because they are at the heart of the globalisation policy. My vision is economic, because it is my profession, but at the same time I believe that international economic policy cannot be thought of except in connection with people's values and way of life. "Global Village", globalization On reflection, the globalisation of the economy is not an isolated manifestation with clearly distinguishable "own" effects: it must be seen in a broader context. As early as the 60s, the famous media researcher MarshallMcLuhan coined the term "global village", which then quickly banalized in the hands of business consultants and TV intellectuals to the point where it became difficult to use in a serious conversation. However, I do not believe that a better concept has yet been invented to describe the manifestations that have given rise to the current debate on globalisation. McLuhan saw the world changing everything because of the growing importance of the mass media. However, he couldn't even have a clue about the even more revolutionary possibilities of today's technology offering: what's new in the development of the last ten years is that there has been a shift from one-way mass media to interactivity. Thanks to the Internet, the comparison with the "village" describes the world of electronic communication now better than ever before. Globalisation is often seen mainly as an economic or market-driven development. After all, the recent debate has been very much about the political, social and ecological consequences of the fact that the market and business in general are increasingly crossing national borders. However, the economic outlook is very superficial and can easily lead to deceptively simple conclusions about how to deal with the climate of globalisation. The merit of the McLuhan global village concept lies precisely in the fact that it prioritizes the most important factors influencing globalization: technological change and the resulting cultural change. From the point of view of the concept of 'global village', globalisation is clearly not just an economic manifestation, but is being used by the general expansion of people's spheres of life, which technology has made possible. Life is fundamentally globalized for two reasons. Firstly, thanks to new technologies, cultural influences and market information, in ever-increasing streams, are spreading more and more rapidly everywhere and reaching an increasing proportion of the world's people. It is becoming easier and easier for us to find out from the world things we are interested in, whether this interest is commercial, entertainment or cultural. It is precisely the same technological advances that lead to the talk of a 'new economy' that are globalising the whole circle of people's lives. And since technological progress is, in a way, irreversible once invented, it is not easy to invent it - you can also expect globalisation to be "one-way". Along with technology, another reason for globalization is the political changes that have occurred in recent years. After the fall of communism and many right-wing dictatorships, governments today no longer restrict people's international contacts in nearly as many countries as they once did. This would be increasingly difficult in the modern technological environment. The political changes that have led to an increase in democracy and civil liberties in the world have apparently not been independent of technological progress. It strongly seems that technological progress has not led to a society controlled by the 'big brother' as George Orwell once feared, but quite the opposite: centralised control of behaviour and information has become increasingly difficult. The opening up of people's circles of contact and the similarity of their visions played a part in the collapse of my communism as a social system. The globalisation of the economy in one way or another is an inevitable consequence of the emergence of a global village and the associated spread of a democratic and free model of society. That is precisely why the idea that the globalisation of the economy can somehow be separated from the general cultural change that is taking place is something that makes sense. The market is made up of how modern people live: consume, push, save and move, what entertainment or culture they follow, and so on. The transformation of people into the inhabitants of the global village, and most importantly, hopefully at the same time its citizens, will globalise their economic relations, as well as their other interactions. The functioning of the market then reflects their needs and skills, but also their morality. Criticism of globalization and its criticism Against this background, it is actually a little strange that the cultural and value criticism of Western lifestyles is directed precisely against 'globalisation'. If we are dissatisfied with what we consume and produce as a single person, as a society or as a human race, why should this dissatisfaction be directed against the expansion of international trade and other interactions? One cynical explanation, hopefully untrue, could be that the criticism is fundamentally hypocritical: it would only be the resistance to change that has arisen in rich societies to the new situation caused by the entry of developing countries into the world economy as increasingly serious competitors. There are therefore fears, for example, of the loss of jobs in sectors where production in developing countries is increasing and, in general, of ever greater structural changes. If that were the case, then criticism of globalisation would be nothing more than a new, more hypocritical form of the demand to protect the industries of the industrialised countries from competition, to halt the structural change in the world economy and thus to condemn developing countries in the future to cockiness and dependence on the financial aid of rich countries instead of being able to stand on their own two feet. Another easy explanation that disparages the criticisms that have been made could be that it is based on knowledge of the situation in developing countries: as if we had not realised the fact that globalisation, and only it, offers the people of developing countries a real chance for an economically better future, or as if it had not been realised that in developing countries globalisation mainly threatens the economic and political elites of those countries, and only to the extent that they have hitherto been may have artificially shimmered from protectionism and isolationism. The first option available for globalisation is not a natural idyll, but stagnation, cobbling and a lack of alternatives. However, I do not want to believe that criticism can only be explained by selfishness or ignorance. Yes, there are genuine values behind the debate and the criticism of globalisation. After all, criticism appeals to ideals such as opposition to cobwebs, environmentalism and democracy, with which one cannot disagree. In that sense, it is a positive indication of how strong a force public opinion based on moral principles can be. Unfortunately, however, criticism generally seems to be based on a very superficial view of the causes and consequences of globalisation. It is also often based on a seemingly completely erroneous picture of the motivations of international economic policy organisations such as the Monetary Fund and the World Trade Organisations when they try to develop the economic and political structures required by a globalising world economy. In my opinion, criticism of globalisation has a mythical meaning if and when it leads to ever higher ethical demands in terms of what is bought, what is produced and how it is produced. It should be noted that the controlling influence of global public opinion on the activities of multinationals is precisely the political manifestation characteristic of the 'global village'. It is precisely the existence of multinationals and their desire to maintain their corporate image and the market value of their brands that brings production in developing countries under the influence of Western values and ethics. Criticism also has a mythical meaning when it leads international organisations to operate more transparently and to show how their objectives and strategy relate to generally accepted values. Therefore, while I believe that a critical public debate on my globalisation is valuable, illegalities, hooliganism and other leniency under the guise of criticism are, of course, totally unacceptable. In my opinion, however, criticism of globalisation is completely misguided if it wants to limit the opening up of the world and the lowering of barriers, including economic and commercial barriers. Globalisation is not only irreversible, but in essence a huge positive force. It is precisely those people and the common people who do not share in globalisation and the opportunities it offers that are the greatest problems. It should also be remembered that the alternative to the development based on intergovernmental agreements that the international organisations are building is not harmony led by an ideal, enlightened autocrat, but the economic and political fragmentation of the world into competing trading blocs. The result would be a slowdown in economic development and an even more obvious transformation of trade into an instrument of power politics by the strong players in the world economy. And given the link between economics and politics, commercial fragmentation is very likely to lead to an increase in political tension. The world is getting smaller and smaller, inevitably, and that is why I do not think that globalisation policy can start from the question of whether globalisation is good or bad, but we have to ask what challenges it poses and how to respond to these challenges. The Global Village responds to these challenges by creating a global civil society that will increasingly globalize the values of politics and societies. In this sense, Walt Disney and Amnesty International are part of one and the same globalization of culture and values. Governments, for their part, are responding to the challenges of globalisation by creating international standards andinstitutions for the joint management of the economy, the environment and security. In a shrinking world, the ability of nation states, and even their right to define the conditions under which their citizens live, regardless of global values and systems, is no longer self-evident. Politics and economic policy are losing their national character. Functioning of international financial markets, IMF One of the most prominent challenges of globalisation is the development of international capital markets, and as a central banker, I am particularly interested in it. In the debate on globalisation, a great deal of attention has been paid to the functioning of international financial markets, and in particular to the disturbances that have occurred in it. After all, of the various sectors of the economy, the root finance market is particularly universal, as money is well suited for electronic trading. In fact, it was the financial crisis in South-East Asia, which began in Thailand and Indonesia in 1997, that really aroused the current widespread interest in globalisation. The crisis had very serious social consequences in the region, and its political consequences are also proving far-reaching. A considerable part of the criticism of globalisation has been directed precisely against the social effects of international capital movements. It has to be said at the outset that, like other markets, the transformation of the financial markets into a truly global one is in itself a mythical thing because, if it functions well, the international capital markets will chill both the countries that give up and receive capital, and both employees and investors such as pension funds, etc. For example, developing countries can only prosper in practice if they draw more capital from the developed countries in the form of investments, and this is definitely one of the key conditions for reducing humpbacks in the world. Countries with an ageing population, on the other hand, should save for their future, and this creates assets that are looking for investment opportunities in the world's financial markets. If the international financial system were to function properly, the savings surplus of the industrialised countries would be effectively reduced in order to create better jobs in developing countries. In terms of the economic development of these countries, foreign capital is a practical necessity: attempts to accelerate the financing of investment by the country itself (i.e. by saving more) are incompatible with the objective of reducing the hump. The development aid provided by the industrialised countries or the investments made by the World Bank and other similar development credit institutions are in no way realistically sufficient to solve the problem of capital scarcity in developing countries, even though they have an important role to play, especially in the most populous and economically hopeless regions. In practice, ever greater private equity investment in developing countries would be avoided in order to pull these countries from the margins of the world economy to a position to properly escape the opportunities offered by globalisation. And a particularly important type of international investment is the direct investment of multinational companies, which transfer not only money but also technology and management and marketing know-how to target countries. In practice, direct investments mean, for example, the establishment of an investor-owned industrial facility in the target country. When, due to the relative scarcity of capital, investment return expectations in developing countries can be high, at least when political conditions are stable, there has occasionally been plenty of capital available for them. However, the weight, unfortunately, is on the word from time to time. Indeed, repeated financial crises have demonstrated the vulnerability of international financial markets. The resulting instability is also largely responsible for the criticism levelled at the internationalisation of the financial markets. Instability and vulnerability have their own reasons. The market can only function properly under conditions where the underlying political system is stable and transparent, where reliable information is available to all parties, and where the responsibilities of the various market participants, such as investors and borrowers, are accurately and credibly predetermined. It is precisely the lack of these conditions that can be attributed to market instability. When the causes of financial crises have been investigated, it has been concluded that one of the factors that has hampered the functioning of the markets is that up-to-date information on the economies and economic policies of developing countries has been too scarce and unreliable, which has tended to provoke unnecessarily large fluctuations in waves of confidence and mistrust. In addition to general economic statistics, this problem concerns the weak so-called monetary and fiscal policy stance. transparency in general and thus goes deep into the relationship between administrative practice and the various institutions. In economic policy, transparency goes hand in hand with democracy and with perseverance and predictability d0 the so-called stability orientation. Another cause of the crises is that the own risk management systems of banks and other financial institutions that broker international capital and the banking supervision of public authorities have not been at a sufficiently high level. Again, this is not just a technical problem, because advanced risk assessment involves an assessment of political stability. Prudential and other regulations restricting banks' risk-taking are now widely recognised as too general and formulaic. Thirdly, the role of investors in the event of problems has been a problem. There have been dangerously distorted incentives in the market, with banks selling credit feeling so secure that credit has been sold on short-term basis. The multiplicity of investors has made debt restructuring too difficult in the event of problems, since there have been no pre-established mechanisms to represent investors in these situations. In this sector, the central international forum is the International Monetary Fund (IMF), within which governments and central banks work together to promote the stable functioning of the foreign and financial markets. Traditionally, most of the IMF's work has been 'fire brigade activities': supporting countries caught up in a currency crisis with loans conditional on the pursuit of an economic policy that would rebalance the crisis. The success in this has been mixed, and the Fund has been criticised for its excessive interference in the internal affairs of countries and for not interfering in the activities of corrupt governments. At one point it has been criticised for being too reticent in its policy of aid, which destabilises countries in difficulty, and at other times for being too lax, which only serves to fuel the carelessness of private lenders in the future. At present, the International Monetary Fund and other international organisations are working to improve the prevention of crises, and the so-called 'disaster prevention'. to create a new international financial architecture. This is intended to ensure a more stable functioning of international financial markets and thus to increase the security of the position of countries dependent on capital markets (i.e. those in need of credit or investment). This is a programme of enormous proportions, a long-term demanding programme consisting of many different areas. It addresses precisely those areas that I have mentioned: the development of economic policy transparency and access to economic information;the creation of international quality standards for the supervision and infrastructure of financial markets; and to increase investor responsibility and coordination in the event of a problem. The Fund will play a key role in the development of these reforms and in coordinating and supervising the implementation of these reforms. Of course, the IMF's traditional operational role as a creditor to countries in difficulty is important in itself, but with the aim of the overall architecture project to prevent crises from arising in advance, the IMF's role is hopefully developing to be increasingly consultative and conducive to the creation of international standards. However, its tasks in projects to strengthen the financial architecture are mainly expert and supervisory in nature. Thus, as with the development of the global economic system in general, the strengthening of the international financial architecture does not involve the creation of a world government, but the implementation and management of new international norms and standards is primarily a national responsibility - although in the EU and EMU the role of common European bodies such as the ECB and the Commission is also important. As for the progress of the use of the architecture project, it can be said in passing that, for example, just last spring, an overall assessment of the financial sector was carried out in Finland in the form of a so-called financial architecture. In accordance with the Financial Sector Assessment Program (FSAP), and on the basis of this assessment, a special ROSC (Report on Observance of Standards and Codes) is published on how Finland complies with international standards and codes for the functioning of financial markets. Liberalisation of international trade, WTO However, better functioning of the financial markets alone will not be enough to bring about sufficient globalisation for developing countries, i.e. the transfer of productive resources from the richer to the more mature countries. There is also a need to safeguard and extend the freedom of trade flows. Developing countries need to get better prices for their exports and have a wider market for them. In order for the developing countries to become viable targets for venture capital investment and to be able to genuinely shy away from foreign loans and direct investment, these countries will have to generate more foreign exchange income than before. Without foreign revenues, capital investment by developing countries will only accumulate into an ever-increasing debt burden, which in the end will not be able to be managed. Thus, financing will not solve development problems unless it is accompanied by the liberalisation and growth of trade in goods. Debt problems and a lack of capital are not just financial market issues, they are also trade policy. Therefore, in order for the most cobbled together countries to be able to take better part in the benefits of rapidint integration of the world economy, the richest countries should have the courage to open up their markets to their products. This would cause adjustment difficulties for a small proportion of the population in the richest countries, but both the developing countries and the majority of the people in the industrialised countries would freeze, the former in terms of better earnings, while the latter in terms of low prices and new consumer goods. In addition, the prosperity of developing countries would create new markets for the products in which the rich industrialised countries specialise. Another key issue for developing countries would be the reduction of subsidies for the export production of industrialised countries. These subsidies keep the world market prices of many products, such as agricultural products, artificially low and hinder the development of production in countries that cannot afford to subsidise their own production. Subsidies are, on the whole, unquestionably harmful, with the only mosquitoes being those in the industrialised countries who rely on subsidies in the industries. The WTO has vigorously pushed for a reduction in subsidies, noting, among other things, that the amount of money spent on agricultural subsidies in the EU roughly corresponds to the combined gross domestic product of sub-Saharan Africa as a whole. Against this background, it is strange that, in recent years, the very groups of people who feel that they are on the side of developing countries have been attacked by the WTO. In a couple of weeks' time, the fourth WTO Ministerial Conference will begin in Doha, Qatar. The intention is to launch a new round of liberalisation of world trade. Topics discussed include tariff reductions, the liberalisation of trade in agricultural products, textiles and services, the link between consumer and environmental protection and trade regulation, and so on. The success of this round is important for both developed and developing countries. The industrialised countries need a boost to world trade, whose growth has recently slowed down. The industrialised countries also need a coordinated reduction in the various subsidies, because they are too expensive for the states and threaten to increase. An example of this is the recent support packages for air transport. However, the developing countries have the most to gain. The UN Secretary-General, Kofi Annan, has stated that the theme of this round of negotiations must be improving the position of developing countries. In the run-up to the WTO meeting, the EU has decided on the so-called 'Everything But Arms' initiative, under which the products of the 48 most populous countries will be unilaterally exempted from all customs duties and import restrictions, with the exception of the arms trade. However, in the case of sugar, rice and bananas, there will be a gradual liberalisation. The EU hopes that this will lead, more generally, to the liberalisation of imports from developing countries in all industrialised countries. On the decision-making structures of international organisations It is well known that one of the criticisms of both the Monetary Fund and the World Bank, and also of the WTO, has been the decision-making structure of these organisations and the distribution of power within the systems. In the case of either decision, the majority of member states cannot decide on matters by a majority of their members. In practice, the WTO has to move forward through agreements, by putting together 'packaged solutions' in which all signatory countries feel that they are winning something. In a monetary fund, on the other hand, which is actually a credit institution, voting according to the capital invested, as in the case of a stock company. It decides who pays. There are certainly at least two opinions on the fairness of these procedures, but I personally tend to think about things from the point of view of realpolitik. In practice, the only viable solution in an intergovernmental, ultimately voluntary, international cooperation is to proceed in such a way that all the important parties feel it makes sense for them to participate in this stupidity and to implement the agreements reached. This, of course, sets its own real limits on how decisions can be made on different issues. Better this way, however, than without international agreements. In fact, the fact that, over the past few decades, the international community has come this far in its organisation is cause for optimism. It also shows that trade policy is not a zero-sum game, but that countries have a wide range of issues where their interests coincide and agreements have been reached. It has been possible to achieve significant liberalisation of world trade and, despite all the inequalities, the fruits of economicdevelopment have been reaped in the smaller countries. The Secretary-General of the World Trade Organisation, Mike Moore, recently stated that, thanks to economic development and the spread of technology, infant mortality in developing countries has halved since 1960, and the proportion of malnourished people among the population has fallen by a third. Although the multilateral free trade system is only one part of this progress, however, it is the most avoidable part. Finally Professor Stanley Fischer, the former Deputy Director-General of the IMF and a distinguished professor who has also worked at the World Bank, has said that citizens' concerns about globalisation must be heard and addressed constructively and openly, but he has also emphatically called for globalisation to speak out in favour of globalisation and for the institutions that seek to promote its best. It should not be untrue to tell the truth and the fact is that the last half century has been an unprecedented advance in the history of the world. More people and a larger proportion of the world's population than ever before have become wealthier and more prosperous. At the global level, real gross domestic product per capita has almost tripled in the last 50 years. The developing countries, which have opened up their economies, have also been overwhelmed by the increase in trade and capital flows. Joseph Stiglitz, one of the winners of this year's Nobel Prize in Economics, points out that even in Africa, where economic growth was negative in many countries in the 1970s and 1980s, things are finally starting to get better in economic terms. One of the reasons he cites is the improved and more tailored development strategies of the international financial instruments, the IMF and the World Bank. The world situation, in which attention has focused on the recent terrorist attacks and the responses to them, as well as the fall of the world economy into recession, puts the globalisation debate into a somewhat new perspective. The world seems to have awakened to a new awareness of the universality of certain fundamental values and of how much to lose in the international community if international integration turns to fragmentation and if the economic dependence of peoples is jeopardised. Perhaps this awareness will also help to see globalisation and the importance of the international agreement system on which it is based in the right light, and to take a leap forward in promoting the good effects of globalisation.

Title: Speech at a seminar organised by the University of Helsinki's Research in German-speaking Countries and the Aue Foundation
text: 1 (4) Sinikka Salo Member of the Executive Board 30.10.2001 "Woher d0 wohin?" d0 Training of German-speaking European experts and experts at the University of Helsinki Speech at the seminar organized by the University of Helsinki's Research on German-speaking Countries and the Aue-s8a8at 31.10.2001 First of all, I would like to thank the organisers of this event for the opportunity offered to me to come and tell you why I think it is important d0 even avoiding d0 for Finns to know German. This is particularly pleasing to me, because the biggest surprise for me was - after returning to my native Finland after 51/2 years in Frankfurt at the European Central Bank and its predecessor, the European Monetary Institute, the alienation and prejudice that finns seem to have quite a lot towards Germany, the whole of continental Europe and European integration in general. I even feel it is my personal duty to bring forward my own observations and thus try to influence the development of this issue for the better. My main observation, to make matters a little more acute, is that in Finland we talk about EU matters as if they were not our own business, we talk about the EU saying "they are there", when in fact we have moved from the "outer ring" of Europe to the "inner ring" of Europe, to the unique integration process in which countries peacefully, through negotiations, seek to build common prosperity and promote European values. There is no doubt that Finland belongs to this group. The fact that we experience alienation is perhaps due to the fact that during the Cold War the Finns sort of isolated themselves from EEC Europe and have not yet completely returned to their central European roots. Finns became citizens of the European Union when we joined the EU. But citizenship is not just, and not even predominantly, a legal concept, but includes membership of a common Europe-wide civil society d0 the formation of a European political, social and cultural community and our belonging to it. Of course, not everyone has to write general section articles for the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (or Le Monde) any more than membership in Finnish civil society has required participation in Finnish cultural or other discussion. European citizenship means, however, that we should have the feeling at European level that, in principle, we could participate in them from a non-purely provincial point of view. The fact that modern economic interaction requires cultural knowledge and a deep understanding of the "customer" is, of course, quite self-evident. 2 (4) Sinikka Salo Member of the Executive Board 30.10.2001 It is therefore in Finland's interest to participate fully and constructively in the EU and in the debate on the future of the EU that has now begun d0 from within. In my opinion, this requires much deeper monitoring and knowledge of continental European affairs, above all, of course, of Germany and France, the founding countries of the EU. In this speech, I am going to reflect on my own experiences what kind of fun and pleasure I have had for my knowledge of German. My warm relationship with Germany began as early as the 1960s, more precisely in 1962, when I went on my first trip abroad on my first trip abroad without my family via Kpenhamina to Eckernfrde near Kiel, where the Jugendrotkreuz camp was held. The next time I was in Germany, in the Black Forest in 1966, after I graduated from high school, I visited a family whose daughter had been at my home the previous summer. I had read the so-called. short German, but strangely enough I survived with it d0 thanks to my German teacher who memorized German poems and to my mother and aunt, who were enthusiastic about German and Viennese music d0 I knew many German schlagers and Viennese songs. When I presented these in a suitable place, my German language skills received (perhaps meritless) appreciation. However, I already learned from these experiences how even a little language skills can open doors and build lifelong friendships. But more seriously - for which you need nothing but English. I spent 51/2 years in Frankfurt, the European Central Bank and its predecessor, the European Monetary Institute, where the staff consists of citizens of 15 EU countries. Tyielena is English, and I can say that you can work there without knowing other European languages, if you are limited to "technique". After all, the language of the money market and economics is English, that is, the main market reviews are usually written in English. But even in international, European central banking, there is a chill if you understand and speak German and French. After all, compromises often have to be made. And we humans are such that spiritual relationships always matter, and in these personal relationships it matters if you speak the language of your colleague and know the culture of his country. As soon as you take a slightly broader perspective on how things are handled, even in the economic sphere, it is not enough just to have English. And not only more "broad", but my deeper interaction and familiarization requires knowledge of the partner's language and culture! Nowadays, the emphasis is precisely on the fact that a good turn 3 (4) Sinikka Salo Member of the Executive Board 30.10.2001 the effect starts from the ability to understand the other party's way of thinking. This applies the more we go into political and social issues, joint research projects, not to mention trade in culture. I think we should at least learn German and French if we want to make a difference in the EU. With the help of these languages, it is already better to "swim" into Europeanism and into this joint project of our integration. As is known, language is not only a mechanical understanding of the intentions of the other, but language leads to the understanding of my culture, to understanding between citizens. It is clear to me that getting to know continental European and EU affairs is not just a matter of following English-language sources. Take, for example, the monetary policy of the European Central Bank, which I am, of course, most familiar with. It is quite absurd that, for example, Finnish newspapers mostly quote only the Financial Times, the Economist or the Wall Street Journal when commenting on the euro area economy. Although these magazines are, of course, very important, they are nevertheless outside the euro area, even outside Europe. It is probable that the vision they reflect differs from that of the countries in the region. A concrete example is the writing about the openness and transparency of the ECB's monetary policy. The ecb's monetary policy transparency has been praised by independent academic evaluators. You can't get this idea by reading, for example. The Financial Times or the vast majority of Finnish newspapers that have, in my opinion, rightly criticised the ECB compared to the Fed, for example. It would also be quite unavoidable for the reviews in the German and French economic press, for example, to be read and published. (To avoid any misunderstandings, I would like to say that I am calling for more comprehensive evaluation, and I am by no means calling for a boycott of the Anglo-Saxon press or any kind of censorship d0 after all, this is not a zero-sum game!) The same is even more true when moving in the social sphere and in politics. In my opinion, Finns should really get to know the way of life in modern Germany, also by following the debate in Germany in this area. In Finland, I have developed perceptions and prejudices that have nothing to do with Germany, which is a reality, that is to say, a modern pluralistic and open society that cherishes its democracy. In Germany, with a population of eighty million, there are interesting revelations, spirits, conversations that are in no way transmitted to Finland unless you know German. What has been absolutely amazing to me has been the open-mindedness and openness that this kind of discussion is about. Needless to say, these "pearls" often do not translate into Finnish. For example, do any of you know Marion Dhof or Alice Szhwarzer? The former is v. 4 (4) Sinikka Salo Member of the Executive Board 30.10.2001 1909 Born in East Prussia, perhaps germany's most famous journalist, founder of the prestigious magazine Die Zeit, countess who lived a very interesting life. The latter the most famous feminist in Germany, the founder of the magazine Emma. Suddenly, these women shouldn't have much in common. However, a few years ago, Alice Schwarzer wrote a portrait and biography of Marion Dhof. This unusual connection produced a very interesting book that I wouldn't have been able to get to know if I didn't know German. Germany is also a country with a wide range of debating clubs, such as Die neue Mittwochsgesellschaft, which was also revived by Marion Dnhoff. The original debating club had been founded in 1863, but its activities were cut off in July 1944 when four of its members were hanged for participating in an anti-Hitler attetat. The booklet "Gespr8ache ber Probleme von Bger und Staat", published in 1988, reflects very broadly, in a European way, on morality, the ethics of the market economy, the individual and the responsibility of society. The reflectors include Egon Bahr, Helmut Schmidt, Antje Vollmer and Richard von Weizs8acker. Such little gems are almost never turned over. However, I think they give a grip on today's Germanness and Europeanism. And, of course, German speakers are needed as translators. I was very pleased that, for example, the biography of Germany's best-known literary critic, Marcel Reich-Ranich, originally a Polish Jew, who last year addressed the German general, has been translated into Finnish. I was pleasantly surprised that the book I had been thinking of recommending to be translated by a publisher d0 Bernhard Schlink's Der Vorleser d0 had already been translated into Finnish. Ladies and gentlemen, German has been both amusing and chilling for me. I hope that even with these examples I have convinced you that German is definitely worth studying. We Finns are part of Europe, part of the EU and EMU. I think it is quite clear that we are in our right reference group there. Anyone who has stayed in Germany in the slightest will recognize that our culture has its roots there. Our customs, our traditions, have come from there, either directly or via Sweden. However, we need to reassert this European identity, and this will come naturally by strengthening our knowledge of German. Proficiency in German opens the way for us to an integrated citizens' Europe.

Me suomalaiset olemme osa Eurooppaa, osa EUta ja EMUa. On mielestni aivan selv ett me olemme siell oikeassa viiteryhmssmme. Jokainen joka on vhnkn oleskellut Saksassa tunnistaa ett meidn kulttuurimme juuret ovat siell. Tapamme, traditiomme ovat tulleet sielt, joko suoraan tai Ruotsin kautta. Meidn tytyy kuitenkin uudelleen vahvistaa tt eurooppalaisuuttamme ja se tapahtuu luontevasti vahvistamalla saksan tuntemustamme.
