Title: Speech at the Women's Europe Seminar at the House of the Estates
text: SUOMEN PANKKI FINLANDS BANK BANK OF FINLAND Bank Manager Sinikka Salo The welfare state and the conditions for sustainable growth in Europe d0 A glimpse into the future of Europe Speech at the Women's Seminar on Europe at the House of the Estates 1.12.2001 I have now been in my home Finland for over a year and, in a way, reoriented to mys-Finnish society after almost six years abroad, for example by meeting and talking with citizens from different fields and social groups. Two of the issues that have come up particularly at these meetings have been EMU, European integration in general and the future of the welfare society, both of which are, of course, for me, issues that I have given a great deal of thought to, that are challenging and in whose good future there is reason to believe. So, in my speech, I am going to address these issues and their interlinkages: so I will look first at the welfare state and then at the other conditions for sustainable growth in Europe d0 hence my professional background, above all EMU and the framework of monetary and economic policy pursued within it. Financing welfare services I would like to begin this speech by looking at the future of the Finnish welfare state from the point of view of its financing. This is a key issue not only in Finland, but also more broadly in Europe, where the issue of improving happiness and solutions to the problem of ageing is being considered. It is therefore natural to take a peek at the rest of Europe through this issue. Apart from the fact that the subject is important for society as a whole, it is particularly close to women - after all, women, both as users and producers of these services, play a very important role. As I have said: the welfare state is more important to a woman than diamonds (unlike what Marilyn Monroe has sung)! The key factors in preserving the welfare state are the management of the costs of ageing, economic growth and the intensification of the production of welfare services, and remuneration in these predominantly female-dominated sectors. In my speech, I will focus primarily on increasing the efficiency of the welfare state, which I believe is particularly important not only for the taxpayers who use the services, but also for the development of the salaries of the staff (most of whom are women) who are working there. Population ageing and pension expenditure I am therefore ignoring the management of the costs of ageing, i.e. the issue of pensions, for example, only by saying that, according to the available calculations, in 2015 both pension expenditure and the contributions levied on employees and employers would already account for more than a quarter of the wage income of employees, and the increase in contributions would continue long after that. The solution to this 'pension bomb' is commonly seen as the increasing involvement of older people in the workplace. The government has set itself the goal of raising the average retirement age by 2-3 years from the current average retirement age of 59 years. Of course, the question of pensions is closely linked to the problem of poverty: an improvement in employment would increase the number of 'payers' in the national economy and, secondly, pension expenditure competes, in a way, for the same resources as labour expenditure (i.e. taxes and contributions collected by the public sector). It would be easier to bear the increase in pension contributions if, at the same time, the burden on public finances from unemployment were to be reduced. Economic growth As far as economic growth is concerned, quantitative economic growth alone cannot be relied upon to finance the welfare state. Until now, growth has not eliminated social problems in Finland, and the increase in the production of goods alone will not do so in the future either. Although economic growth basically brings more to share in the national economy, so to speak, it does not, in practice, provide an automatic solution to the question of the financing of the welfare state. The reason for this is the so-called Baumol disease, an unfortunate but universal economic manifestation caused by the fact that the production of public services does not normally lead to a sparing increase in productivity almost as much as in the private sector, and especially in industry. As a result, the provision of public services becomes, in relative terms, more and more expensive the more productivity in the private sector increases. The tax base and tax revenues will increase in line with economic growth, but at the same rate will the cost of producing public services, as wages will in the long run follow the growth of productivity in the private sector. As a result, unless taxation is constantly increased, there will be no improvement in public services. As Baumol's disease progresses, its political symptoms are the growing dissatisfaction that the quantity and quality of public services, without a constant increase in taxation, will not keep pace with the general development of living standards, as well as the pressure to solve this dilemma through administrative cost savings d0 either by tightening the pace of public service provision or by allowing public sector wages to constantly lag behind what is paid by the private sector. These drugs can work momentarily, but it is clear that neither means offers a solution that works in the long term, at least one that is likely to attract and retain skilled workers in the field, which in turn is essential for the provision of high-quality services. Does Baumol's disease threaten the future of the Finnish welfare state? And if there is a threat, can the disease be cured? The situation is worrying in the sense that the trend of increasing taxation in order to finance a welfare society seems exhausted. Improving boredom, which is absolutely essential both for economic reasons and in order to reduce social exclusion, would require a reduction in the overall tax burden, not an increase. On the other hand, when talking about Baumol's disease, it should be noted that in Finland, at least the productivity of the health care sector and possibly some other functions of the welfare state has clearly improved over the past ten years. Based on OECD studies, Finland's development in recent years looks quite exceptional in this respect, both historically and internationally. The general reduction in the cost of health care services has apparently stopped the progression of Baumol's disease for several years and shows that this disease is not a law of nature, but at least sometimes avoidable. Surely a large part of this increase in productivity has been achieved by means that have now been exhausted, it may be that some more than that, but hopefully there will be an impact of product development and technology, i.e. a development that can continue in the future. After all, Baumol's disease can be mitigated, and perhaps cured altogether, if the growth of the national economy can be dragged on a broader basis than just dependent on an increase in industrial productivity. Firstly, economic growth based on an improvement in employment will bring more resources to the national economy and the public sector without baumol's disease being eradicated. This means that the more successful it is in raising the employment rate, hopefully beyond the 70% target set by the government, the better the development of welfare services can be reconciled with an ageing population and a stable (or decreasing) tax rate. Increase efficiency in the production of public services Another viable possibility is to reform the production of public services in such a way as to reduce the difference in productivity development between public services and private goods production. I am by no means offering any tightening of the pace as a solution, but I mean the rise in innovation-based productivity, the constant hype of new technologies and product development in the production of welfare services. How can this be achieved? How can organisations providing services be made more and more actively looking for ways to improve the quality of services and their production methods? And how can we ensure that innovations are implemented quickly? One way is to encourage more extensive use of private outsourced services and also to encourage competition between municipal service organisations. Experience shows that, by doing so, significant improvements can be achieved in quality, managerial practice and cost-effectiveness compared to relying on non-monopolistic civil service organisations as service providers. What, then, are the links between European policy, integration and EMU and the financing of a welfare state and sustainable growth in general? Monetary policy Let me start with monetary policy. As is well known, the institutional framework for monetary policy in the euro area is defined in the Maastricht Treaty, where the objective of monetary policy is clearly set out: the ECB's monetary policy (now also finland's monetary policy) is responsible for maintaining price stability in the euro area. Price stability, on the other hand, has been defined by the Governing Council in order to keep the annual increase in consumer prices below two per cent over the medium term. The ecb's monetary policy objective and the broad independence of political decision-makers given to the central bank reflect the widely shared understanding of that experience. that by maintaining price stability, the central bank can best support long-term stable growth, boredom and prosperity. The primacy of the objective of price stability underlines the fact that the central bank has neither the means nor the responsibility to maintain employment or growth directly - beyond what price stability will bring. It is the responsibility of the other economic policy sectors to influence these. However, since my presentation is not really about monetary policy, I will simply say that the ECB's monetary policy has been successful d0 a policy of low interest rates and small changes in interest rates is credible and provides a solid basis for economic policy-making, including labour market and economic policies. Fiscal policy As far as fiscal policy, public spending and revenue are concerned d0 even in EMU circumstances, this is a nationality. Each member state decides on its own national policy. However, the Treaty establishing the European Union provides for the coordination of the economic policies of the Member States. According to Article 99 of the Treaty, Member States regard their economic policies as a matter of common interest. The budgetary stance, mainly the evolution of the general government gross debt and budget balance, is monitored quantitatively through specific stability and convergence programmes. As a result, known limits have been set on gross debt and budget deficits (60% of GDP, deficit 3%), which are to be prevented from being exceeded in order to ensure the sustainable development of the public sector and to safeguard the single monetary policy. In addition, efforts are being made to coordinate structural policy measures within the EU. As a result of progress in integration and the accumulation of experience and changes in the economic situation, the coordination of the EU's economic policies has changed in recent years, to such an extent that the economic policy framework of the Member States can be considered to have changed. The agenda is defined and solutions to problems are now sought largely through various joint processes. It is worth emphasising that the reason for this change is not the pressure from Brussels, but rather the fact that the problems of economic policy are largely and increasingly common and the Member States have d0 perhaps with a little groping d0 learned a new approach to tackling the problems of economic policy. As a result of changes in circumstances and political decisions, the so-called .... the broad economic policy guidelines have become a key instrument for economic policy coordination. They have grown into a wide-ranging and multifaceted document. At the same time, priorities have changed. In addition to the issues of fiscal stability, the scope of the guidelines has largely expanded to include structural issues. It is quite obvious that sustainable growth in Europe cannot be achieved without the contribution of women and this has been recognised in the broad economic policy guidelines referred to above, which pay particular attention to the ageing of the population in almost all euro area countries and state that preparing for it requires strengthening public finances, including by reducing public debt, improving boredom and, where necessary, reassessing pension systems, health care and, where necessary, the need for care for older people. In the broad guidelines, some topics have been agreed to be raised above the rest d0 such as the need to increase boredom rates by increasing the participation rate of women and older people. Furthermore, it has been mentioned in the guidelines that this requires, among other things, the provision of adequate childcare facilities. All in all, the document defining the broad economic policy guidelines is quite balancedd0 it contains both macroeconomic elements that emphasise stability and a reform-oriented structural policy aimed at absorbing all resources. An efficient Finnish welfare state is an export product - a model for the rest of Europe Ladies and gentlemen, in my opinion, the conditions for sustainable growth and well-being in Finland depend on how the welfare state can be maintained. Above, I have strongly highlighted the need to improve the efficiency of service production in order to guarantee the quality of services, to ensure that skilled, trained workers can be attracted to the production of services. And, as I said, by increasing productivity I mean, among other things, an innovation-based better use of technology and a more efficient organisation of service chains in the public sector, rather than an increase in productivity by means of personnel that are now exhausted and perhaps beyond. Maintaining a good level of welfare services is central to the realization of work participation and better boredom. Here I see a big role for women to take on these issues, to get involved in reflecting on and implementing these issues - also in a European forum. In these matters, the Finnish and Nordic model has proved to be fundamentally sustainable d0 these countries have the highest participation rates of women in Europe d0 at a level that central Europe is only dreaming of. Although these issues have been recognised in principle, for example, in the broad economic policy guidelines, it would be important to take them to a more concrete level in the debate. It must be shown that, in order to increase the level of boredom, we need better opportunities for reunification and family life, caring for children and caring for the elderly. The Europe of the future cannot afford to leave the increasingly educated resources of women untapped. Ladies and gentlemen, because of my professional background, my speech above all deals with the economic arguments relating to the welfare state and participation in employment. Naturally, things can and should be dealt with from my moral point of view - from the point of view of justice and equality. However, I believe that what I have just said does not contradict these key authors either.
text_original: SUOMEN PANKKI FINLANDS BANK BANK OF FINLAND Pankinjohtaja Sinikka Salo Hyvinvointivaltio ja kestvn kasvun edellytykset Euroopassa  Kurkistuksia Euroopan tulevaisuuteen Puheenvuoro Naisten Eurooppa-seminaarissa Stytalolla 1.12.2001 Olen nyt ollut runsaan vuoden ajan koti-Suomessa ja tavallaan uudelleenorientoitunut myssuomalaiseen yhteiskuntaan lhes kuuden ulkomailla vietetyn vuoden jlkeen, mm. tapaamalla jakeskustelemalla eri aloja ja yhteiskuntaryhmi edustavien kansalaisten kanssa. Kaksi aihetta, jotkaniss tapaamisissa ovat erityisesti tulleet esille ovat olleet EMU, Euroopan integraatio yleens jahyvinvointiyhteiskunnan tulevaisuus, jotka molemmat ovat luonnollisesti minulle asioita, joita olen paljon pohtinut, jotka ovat haasteellisia ja joiden hyvn tulevaisuuteen on syyt uskoa. Niinp puheenvuorossani aion ksitell nit kysymyksi ja niiden liittymkohtia: Siis tarkastelen ensin hyvinvointivaltiota ja sen jlkeen muita kestvn kasvun edellytyksi Euroopassa  ammattitaustanivuoksi ennen kaikkea EMUa ja sen puitteissa harjoitetun rahapolitiikan ja talouspolitiikan kehikkoa. Hyvinvointipalvelujen rahoittaminen Haluan aloittaa tmn puheenvuoroni tarkastelemalla suomalaisen hyvinvointivaltion tulevaisuuttasen rahoituksen kannalta. Tm on keskeinen kysymys paitsi Suomessa, mys laajemminEuroopassa, jossa pohditaan tyllisyyden parantamista ja ikntymisongelman ratkaisuja. On siten luontevaa tehd kurkistus muuhun Eurooppaan tmn kysymyksen kautta. Paitsi ett aihe on trke koko yhteiskunnan kannalta se on erityisen lhell naisia - ovathan naiset sek niden palvelujen kyttjin ett tuottajina varsin keskeisess asemassa. Kuten olen sanonut: hyvinvointiyhteiskunta on naiselle trkempi kuin timantit (toisin kuin Marilyn Monroe on laulanut)! Hyvinvointivaltion silyttmisen kannalta keskeisi tekijit ovat vestn ikntymisestaiheutuvien kulujen hallinta, taloudellinen kasvu ja hyvinvointipalvelujen tuotannon tehostaminenja my palkkaus nill pasiassa naisvaltaisilla aloilla. Keskityn tss puheenvuorossani ensisijaisesti hyvinvointivaltion tehokkuuden lismiseen, joka mielestni on erityisen trke paitsi palveluja kyttvien veronmaksajien kannalta mys siell tyskentelevn henkilkunnan (jostaposa naisia) palkkakehityksen kannalta. Vest ikntyminen ja elkemenot Sivuutan siis vestn ikntymisest aiheutuvien kulujen hallinnan eli mm. elkekysymyksen ksittelyn vain toteamalla, ett kytettviss olevien laskelmien mukaan vuonna 2015 sek elkemenot ett tytekijilt ja tyantajilta kannettavat tylkemaksut olisivat jo yli neljnnes tyntekijiden palkkatuloista, ja maksujen nousu jatkuisi viel pitkn sen jlkeenkin. Tmn "elkepommin" ratkaisuna nhdn yleisesti ikntyvien lisntyv osallistuminen tylmn. Valtiovalta onkin ottanut tavoitteekseen keskimrisen elkkeelle jmisin kohottamisen 2-3 vuodella nykyisest 59 vuoden keskimrisest elkkeelle siirtymisist. Luonnollisestielkekysymys nivoutuu kiintesti mys tyttmyysongelmaan: tyllisyyden paraneminen lisisimaksajien joukkoa kansantaloudessa, ja toiseksi, elkemenot kilpailevat tavallaan samoistavaroista tytyysmenojen kanssa (toisin sanoen julkisen sektorin kermist veroista jamaksuista). Elkemaksujen nousu olisi helpompi kantaa, mikli tyttmyydest julkiselle taloudelletuleva rasitus samaan aikaan alenisi. Taloudellinen kasvu Mit tulee taloudelliseen kasvuun, pelkstn mrllisen talouskasvunkaan varaan ei voida hyvinvointivaltion rahoittamisessa tuudittautua. Kasvu ei ole thn asti poistanut Suomestayhteiskunnallisia ongelmia, eik pelkk tavaratuotannon lisntyminen tee sit jatkossakaan. Vaikka taloudellinen kasvu tuokin periaatteessa kansantalouteen niin sanotusti lis jaettavaa, se eikuitenkaan kytnnss tuo automaattista ratkaisua hyvinvointivaltion rahoituskysymykseen. Syyn on niin sanottu Baumolin tauti, harmillinen mutta yleismaailmallinen taloudellinen ilmi joka johtuu siit, ett julkisten palvelujen tuotannossa ei normaalisti tapahdu tyt sstvtuottavuuden kasvua likikn niin paljon kuin yksityisell puolella ja varsinkin teollisuudessa. Tst on seurauksena, ett julkisten palvelujen tuottaminen tulee suhteellisesti aina vain sit kalliimmaksi, mit enemmn tuottavuus yksityisell sektorilla kasvaa. Veropohja ja verotulot kyll kasvavattaloudellisen kasvun myt, mutta samaa tahtia nousevat mys julkisten palvelujentuotantokustannukset, koska palkat pitkn plle seuraavat yksityisen sektorin tuottavuuden kasvua. Seurauksena on, ett ellei verotusta koko ajan kiristet, julkisia palveluja ei pystyt parantamaan. Baumolin taudin edetess sen poliittisina oireina ovat kasvava tyytymttmyys siihen, ett julkisten palvelujen mr ja laatu eivt ilman verotuksen jatkuvaa kiristymist pysy elintason yleisen kehityksen tahdissa mukana, sek paineet ratkaista tm dilemma hallinnollisin kustannussstin  joko kiristmll tyahtia julkisessa palvelutuotannossa tai sitten antamalla julkisten sektorin palkkojen jd jatkuvasti jlkeen siit, mit yksityisell puolella maksetaan. Nm lkkeet voivat tepsi hetkellisesti, mutta on selv, ett kumpikaan keino ei tarjoa pitkn plle toimivaa ratkaisua, ainakaan sellaista, joka olisi omiaan houkuttelemaan ja pitmn alalla osaavaa tyoimaa mik puolestaan on vlttmtt korkealaatuisten palvelujen tuottamiselle. Uhkaako Baumolin tauti suomalaisen hyvinvointivaltion tulevaisuutta? Ja jos uhkaa, voidaanko tauti parantaa? Tilanne on siin mieless huolestuttava, ett trendinomaisesti kiristyvn verotuksen tiehyvinvointiyhteiskunnan rahoittamiseksi tuntuu loppuun kuljetulta. Tylisyyden parantaminen, joka on ehdottoman trke sek taloudellisista syist ett my yhteiskunnallisen syrjytymisenvhentmiseksi, vaatisi nimittin kokonaisverorasituksen keventmist eik kiristmist. Baumolin taudista puhuttaessa on toisaalta pantava merkille, ett Suomessa ainakin terveydenhuoltosektorin ja mahdollisesti eriden muidenkin hyvinvointivaltion toimintojentuottavuus on selvsti parantunut viimeisten kymmenen vuoden aikana. OECD:n selvitysten perusteella Suomen viime vuosien kehitys nytt tss suhteessa aika poikkeukselliselta sekhistoriallisesti ett kansainvlisesti vertaillen. Terveydenhuoltopalvelujen kustannustason yleinenlaskeminen on ilmeisesti meill pysyttnyt Baumolin taudin etenemisen useiksi vuosiksi ja osoittaa, ett kyseinen tauti ei ole luonnonlaki, vaan ainakin joskus vltettviss. Varmaankin suuri osa tst tuottavuuden noususta on saavutettu sellaisin keinoin, jotka on nyt loppuun kytetty, voi olla ett osin ylikin, mutta toivottavasti mukana on my tuotekehittelyn ja teknologian vaikutusta, eli sellaista kehityst joka voi jatkua tulevaisuudessakin. Baumolin tautia voidaan nimittin lievent, ja kukaties kokonaan parantaakin, jos kansantaloudenkasvu voidaan vet laajemmalle perustalle kuin riippumaan vain teollisuuden tuottavuuden noususta. Ensinnkin, sellainen talouskasvu, joka perustuu tyllisyyden paranemiseen, tuo kansantalouden ja my julkisen sektorin kyttn lis voimavaroja ilman, ett Baumolin tauti syne pois. Tm merkitsee sit ett mit paremmin tyllisyysasteen kohottamisessa menestytn, toivottavasti yli hallituksen mrittelemn 70 prosentin tavoitteen, sit paremmin hyvinvointipalvelujen kehittminen on sovitettavissa yhteen ikntyvn vest ja vakaan (tai alenevan) veroasteen kanssa. Lis tehokkuutta julkisten palvelujen tuotantoon Toinen varteenotettava mahdollisuus on uudistaa julkisten palvelujen tuotantoa siten, ett ero julkisten palvelujen ja yksityisen tavaratuotannon tuottavuuskehityksess pienenee. En nyt missn tapauksessa tarjoa ratkaisuksi mitn tytahdin kiristmist, vaan tarkoitan innovaatiopohjaistatuottavuuden nousua, uuden teknologian ja tuotekehittelyn jatkuvaa hyyntmist hyvinvointipalvelujen tuotannossa Miten thn voidaan pst? Miten palveluja tuottavat organisaatiot saadaan yh aktiivisemmin etsimn keinoja palvelujen laadun ja niiden tuotantomenetelmien kehittmiseksi? Ja miten turvataan innovaatioiden nopea hydyntminen? Yksi keino on laajamittaisempi yksityisten ostopalvelujen kytt ja my kunnallisten palveluorganisaatioiden vlisen kilpailun rohkaiseminen. Kokemus osoittaa, ett nin toimien voidaan saavuttaa huomattavia parannuksialaadussa, johtamiskytnniss ja kustannustehokkuudessa verrattuna siihen, ett nojaudutaanpalvelutuottajina monopoliasemassa toimiviin virkamiesorganisaatioihin. Mitk sitten ovat Eurooppalaisen politiikan, integraation ja EMUn yhteydethyvinvointivaltion rahoitukseen ja yliptn kestvn kasvuun? Rahapolitiikka Aloitan rahapolitiikasta. Kuten tunnettua, euroalueen rahapolitiikan institutionaaliset puitteet on mritelty Maastrichtin sopimuksessa, jossa rahapolitiikan tavoite on asetettu selkesti: EKP:nrahapolitiikka (joka on nyt mys Suomen rahapolitiikkaa) on vastuussa hintavakauden yllpitmisest euroalueella. Hintavakaus on puolestaan EKP:n neuvoston toimesta mriteltykuluttajahintojen vuotuisen nousun pysymiseksi alle kahden prosentin keskipitkll aikavlill.EKP:n rahapolitiikalle asetettu tavoite ja keskuspankille annettu laaja riippumattomuus poliittisistapttjist heijastaa sit kokemuksen tuomaa laajalti jaettua ksityst. ett hintavakaudensilyttmll keskuspankki voi parhaiten tukea pitkn aikavlin vakaata kasvua, tylisyytt ja hyvinvointia. Hintavakauden tavoitteen ensisijaisuus korostaa sit, ett keskuspankilla ei olekeinoja eik vastuuta tyllisyyden tai kasvun yllpitmisest suoraan - yli sen mink hintavakaudenvaaliminen tuo. Nihin vaikuttaminen on muiden talouspolitiikan lohkojen vastuulla. Koska esitykseni ei kuitenkaan ole varsinaisesti rahapolitiikasta, totean vain ett EKP:n rahapolitiikka on ollut onnistunutta  alhaisilla koroilla ja pienill korkomuutoksilla operoiva politiikka on uskottavaja tarjoaa vakaan pohjan taloudelliselle ptksenteolle, ml. tymarkkina- ja talouspolitiikalle. Finanssipolitiikka Mit tulee finanssipolitiikkaan, julkisista menoista ja tuloista pttmiseen  se on EMU-oloissakinkansallista. Kukin jsenmaa ptt omasta kansallisesta politiikastaan. Euroopan unioninperustamissopimuksessa on kuitenkin sovittu jsenvaltioiden harjoittaman talouspolitiikanyhteensovittamisesta. Sopimuksen 99 artiklan mukaan jsenvaltiot pitvt talouspolitiikkaansayhteist etuaan koskevana asiana. Finanssipolitiikan linjaa, lhinn julkisyhteisen bruttovelan jabudjettijmn kehityst seurataan snnllisesti erityisten vakaus-ja lhentymisohjelmien avulla. Bruttovelalle ja budjettialijmlle onkin asetettu tunnetut rajat (velalle 60 % BKT:hensuhteutettuna, alijmlle 3%), joiden ylittminen pyritn estmn julkisen sektorin kestvn kehityksen turvaamiseksi ja my yhteisen rahapolitiikan varjelemiseksi. Lisksi rakennepoliittisia toimenpiteit pyritn EU:n piiriss koordinoimaan. Integraation edistymisen ja kokemusten kertymisen ja taloustilanteen muutoksen myt EU:n talouspolitiikan yhteensovittaminen on muuttunut viime vuosien aikana, jopa siin mrin ett jsenmaiden talouspolitiikan puitteiden voidaan katsoa muuttuneen. Asialista mritelln jaratkaisuja ongelmiin etsitn nykyisin paljolti erilaisten yhteisten prosessien kautta. On syyt korostaa, ett syyn thn muutokseen ei ole Brysselin suunnalta tuleva painostus vaan pikemminkin se, ett talouspoliittiset ongelmat ovat paljolti ja enenevsti yhteisi ja jsenvaltiot ovat  ehk hieman hapuillen  oppineet uuden lhestymistavan selvitt talouspolitiikan ongelmia. Olosuhteiden muutosten ja poliittisten ptsten seurauksena ns. talouspolitiikan laajoistasuuntaviivoista on tullut talouspolitiikan yhteensovittamisen keskeinen vline. Title: Globalisation and the challenges of housing construction
text: Bank Director Sinikka Salo, Bank of Finland: Globalisation and the challenges of housing construction Speech at the autumn seminar of the Small House Industry Association in Helsinki 9.11.2004 Ladies and gentlemen! When I came back to Finland in late 2000, I mentioned in a newspaper interview that if I had to mention one thing I would like to change in my home country, it would be living for Finns  especially in the Helsinki metropolitan area. Our housing level has lagged behind other increases in living standards to such an extent that it is beginning to be problematic in view of global competition. I would like to express my sincerest thanks to the organisers of the event for the opportunity to come and talk to you about housing and for allowing me to choose "Globalisation and the challenges of housing construction" as my title. Housing plays a key role in the global competition to attract companies and experts to Finland. Naturally, there are many factors that influence the location of companies and attract talent to the country. However, I would especially like to highlight housing, where we Finns would have good opportunities not only to improve the quality of life of our people, but also to increase the attractiveness and competitiveness of our country in a globalizing world. It is to you, ladies and gentlemen of the single-family house industry, that I would like to address my appeal to improve the quality of housing. In Finland, we need more high-quality, larger-sized detached houses that are implemented either by domestic or other producers. High-quality single-family house production is also your future competitive advantage in an integrated market. *** In my speech, I would therefore like to draw attention to housing as a competitive factor in a globalising world. As a former expatriot, I know that housing is one of the first things to look at in a new environment: what kind of housing level can be obtained either in the rental market or by buying. In this respect, the Helsinki region in particular is not flattering. This becomes apparent when interviewing experts who have moved to Finland and their family members. For example, an interview study conducted by senior researcher Mika Raunio at the University of Tampere has a descriptive quote from a family of experts who have moved to our country from abroad: "It is somehow surprising that people live in such a sparsely populated country so cramped and expensive. We were shocked by the prices because living here is almost as expensive as in Boston, but the apartments are smaller". Finnish housing policy must also be thought of from this new and broader perspective, which must be international. Housing policy must also respond to globalisation. In addition to the China report, attention to the London report In the old industrialised countries, to which Finland also belongs, the fiercest competition is to determine in which country and regions highly skilled work is carried out, where the amount of value added and the level of wages are highest. It is therefore a question of, for example, the location of activities such as research and development, marketing, management and finance. A characteristic feature of these activities is that they focus on the proximity of each other. In the old industrialized countries, such metropolises are growing and thriving, where universities and headquarters of large companies, research institutes and financial markets interact with each other. As physical production recedes, the growth sectors are lagging away from these business and intangible production activities, which are concentrated in the largest growth centers. I think we should also talk about the London report as a counterweight to the China report. After all, London is an example of a European metropolis that has experienced strong growth and has been based on activities that have been more chilled by globalisation than by it. For Finland, this structural change underway in western countries is a particularly major challenge. During the technology boom of the last decade, we have perhaps been too lulled into believing that large investments in technical education and product development will secure Finland's economic success. However, the technological lead is a rapidly consuming competitive factor, and the maturation of technical products from revolutionary novelties to cheap bulk goods is happening under the influence of globalization at an ever faster pace. At the same time, the transformation of the largest Finnish companies into multinationals or the merger into international groups has made Finland less and less an obvious location for the central management of companies. If the headquarters leave Finland, the growth opportunities for Finnish design, marketing, law and finance will wither away. However, it is precisely these activities that must be determinedly developed in high-income countries  including ourselves in Finland  in the future. It is here that I see a clear connection between globalisation and the challenges of Finnish urban planning and housing policy. In Finland, we must ensure that our urban structures and housing markets support Finland's success in this international competition between metropolises. We have traditionally paid a great deal of attention to income policy and tax policy as a means of safeguarding the competitiveness of companies. Much has also been invested in direct and indirect support for research and development. However, it is clear to me that finland should also ensure that Finland, and in particular the Helsinki metropolitan area, offers an attractive and competitive location for the high value added activities I have already mentioned above and an attractive place of residence for the experts who make up these activities. All in all, I consider the London report I referred to above, i.e. competition between metropolises, to be more threatening for Finland than the China report. The decline of Helsinki to the periphery would be a real threat to the development of finland. Low housing level of Finns At the moment, the situation is not good. One problem is that in Finland, and especially in the Helsinki region, apartments are small by international comparison. Finland has the lowest housing among the old EU countries, although Finland's high income level and low population density might suggest otherwise. The average floor area of a dwelling in Finland is 76.5 m2 (in 2000), while in Denmark it is 108.9 m2 and in Holland, for example, 98 m2. Even the average size of a household, which in Finland is quite small, does not explain the small size of the dwellings. Even in Sweden, the per capita housing sector is almost 30% larger than in Finland. The average size of apartments is undeniably slowly increasing in Finland, but we are not catching up with our competitors, because the average size of new apartments in Finland lags well behind what is being built in other countries that are closest to ours. Another problem that weakens the competitiveness of Finnish housing is that the quality of the housing stock does not correspond very well to the wishes of the residents. Finns mostly live in blocks of flats. Only about 40% of Finns live in detached houses, while in densely populated Denmark, for example, 59% and in the Netherlands as much as 71%. Even in Sweden, living in detached houses is more common than in Finland. We only have one-family houses, compared to 51% in Sweden, 60% in Denmark and 74% in the Netherlands. This is despite the fact that, according to studies, the majority of Finns would like to live in detached houses, and although in principle we should have more space for construction than in most other countries. All this means that finland's housing stock should be improved quickly, especially in the Helsinki metropolitan area. Above all, the size of the apartments available must be increased and the quality of the apartments should better meet the wishes of the residents - this means, among other things, a rapid increase in the proportion of high-quality detached houses. The third factor that negatively affects the competitiveness of the Finnish housing market is the thinness and weak functioning of the rental housing market, especially the low supply of high-quality rental housing. The private rental housing market should also be made to function better. This is relevant not only for the stay of a foreigner, perhaps a temporary tyrant, but also for domestic mobility. Moreover, a well-functioning rental housing market helps to reduce the risks to households arising from fluctuations in housing prices. With a view to the development of a well-functioning rental housing market, efforts should be made, inter alia, to revive the interest of institutional investors, such as insurance companies, in the production of rental housing. Recent housing production. After all, in recent years, the assets of hugely inflated tylake funds have increasingly been invested in foreign securities, and domestic investments in, for example, rental housing, have lost their relevance. *** The two fundamental issues of housing policy have traditionally been the land issue and the financial issue. To this could be added the design, that is, the architecture. Are these factors in order? Do they create unnecessary obstacles to the improvement of the quality of housing in Finland and especially in the Helsinki metropolitan area? Does Finland have any strengths that could be hyped up? Access to housing finance is not a problem Housing finance, which for decades was a chronic scarcity factor in Finland, is no longer a problem. The stabilisation of Finland's monetary conditions when joining the European Monetary Union changed the situation, and today the normal, commercial market provides financing at such a low cost that the state housing financing system has had to consider the need and legitimacy of its existence. Low and stable interest rates mean that lack of financing or costs are not a key factor limiting the development of Finnish housing. Naturally, when measuring their borrowing, households must take into account the fact that interest rates could rise from their current low level by 2-3% and one per cent as economic conditions in the euro area pick up. Banks have a role to play in this end. Banks should be reminded of this and carry out "stress tests" on the solvency of their customers. However, thanks to the credibility of the ECB's monetary policy, there is no need to be prepared for interest rate jumps such as those experienced in markka conditions in the early 1990s. One of the factors in which Finland differs from other EU countries is the low fixed interest rate on mortgages. By taking out a fixed-rate mortgage, you can protect yourself from the increase in loan servicing costs caused by the increase in interest rates. When comparing the costs of a fixed-rate and a variable-rate loan  as is usually the case when comparing the cost of a loan, it is worth evaluating things in the long term. From the point of view of the stability of the national economy, a fixed rate would be desirable, as countries with more fixed rates have also found less volatility in the housing market/price volatility. According to the ECB's report, housing market fluctuations are strongest in the United Kingdom, Ireland and Finland, where floating rates prevail. It is to be hoped that the long-term fixed-rate mortgages that we already have available will become increasingly popular, which would be likely to stabilise the housing market. It should be noted that, among other things: In the UK, serious attention has been paid to increasing fixed interest rates in mortgage lending. There, the Finance Minister presented a report on housing finance. The author of the study, Professor David Miles (Imperial College), drew attention to the benefits of fixed rates in managing household risks and the stability of financial markets. He called for new ways for banks to finance fixed-rate loans and make their pricing more transparent. Apartment design could be a strength Another potential strength could perhaps be design, but I believe that in this regard, Finns should return to the roots of their own tradition before this strength can be made more widely used. Finnish architecture is one of the most important building blocks of national identity for us. Its international reputation is based above all on Alvar Aalto's stupidity. Aalto sought to reform the functionalist way of building by bringing humanism and naturalness to it. He did not believe in rationalistic or mechanical solutions, but wanted to give way to the unpredictability and diversity of life. At a time usually dominated by an otherwise blunt romance of efficiency and vulgar social functionalism, Aalto sought inspiration in antiquity and the Italian Renaissance cities. Finnish architecture's unique gift to the world is the humane "third way", which is placed between narrow efficiency thinking and inhuman monumentalism. At least that's how it should be. Despite the fine traditions of Finnish architecture, Finnish housing construction has for decades invested more in quantitative efficiency than in quality. Of course, it can be said that social reasons have forced it. In the midst of the housing shortage, the notion spread that cheap construction with minimum standards represented the highest social morality: ornamentation was a crime, and beauty and quality were also things to compromise on. The number of apartments to be produced has been solved, and cost savings were sought through serial production. Aalto saw early on that such an approach to housing construction should remain a temporary stage of development. As early as 1939, he referred to the "new individualism which, as the production machinery continues to develop and the forms of organisation improve, makes it possible to take a more flexible individual account of the myself, where today the still semi-developed machinery of primitive mass production gives its stamp to dwellings." Perhaps the time that Aalto longed for has finally arrived. If and when globalisation triggers competition between metropolitan areas in terms of the quality of housing and living environments, it can be said that we cannot afford to miss out on the opportunities offered by diverse, humane construction based on the needs of its inhabitants. Construction technology is not a hindrance. I hope not the puritanism of urban architects or municipal politicians either. From the point of view of society, high-quality construction is not even a cost factor, but an avoidance. What is needed for this is more permissive zoning and urban planning, which would give room for solvent demand to influence the quality and orientation of construction. Supply must be made more flexible In Finland, efforts have traditionally been made to develop housing through measures to support demand. In the future, attention must be turned from measures to support demand in general to making housing supply more flexible: the demand for housing must have a greater impact on the orientation and quality of construction activities. Making supply more flexible will also help to moderate house prices (see chart). Now, for example, low interest rates are becoming capitalised in the prices of dwellings in growth centres due to the inflexibility of supply. In order to make supply more flexible, a special and decisive role is played by municipal zoning and plot policies. Through their plot policies, municipalities could also increase competition and supply in the private non-subsidised rental housing market. In a globalizing world, the disadvantages of bureaucracy and restrictive regulation are exacerbated in all areas of life, in my housing, and this requires the development of new approaches to housing policy and zoning. I think it is clear that coping with the challenges of the metropolitan area's plot policy for the next 10 years requires a substantial acceleration of the pace of zoning and a much more liberal approach to land use. In the Helsinki metropolitan area, it seems to be enough news that 18 new single-family house plots will be zoned this year. This can be considered a scandal from the point of view of the development of the Helsinki metropolitan area! Perhaps there is indeed a need for special action by the state to make more room for high-quality housing construction here. However, this is an issue that has a fundamental impact on the economic vitality and future of the country as a whole. Ladies and gentlemen! The age of globalisation requires housing policy and, in connection with it, urban planning, zoning and architecture to be competitive and to be able to see residents as subjects and not as objects of politics. Developing the competitiveness of the housing sector requires looking for the natural strengths of Finland's growth centres and, in particular, the Helsinki metropolitan area in housing. These strengths are related to the space available in Finland, the proximity to nature and, I hope, the designers' ability to draw on the human traditions of Finnish architecture. Competitiveness is not a pocket calculator concept, but it means realizing and accepting the needs of customers  in this case, residents. This means, for example, that the concept of quality in housing must not only, or even primarily, mean building technology, but that people's diverse, even diverse, needs determine the trends in housing. This is also a challenge for you in the single-family house industry.

Features of global development The list could go on longer, but I'm slowing down on bringing up these fetees. I shall interpret the developments and assess what the risks are in the current situation, how serious the imbalances are and what the possibilities are to correct them in a controlled manner. Facts and their interpretation Rates The fact that the euro was weakened in its first years was f many a surprise and f many even a disappointment. For some fetag, it was a happy surprise, which they didn't exactly trumpet. Figure 3. Real handelsvagd exchange rate 1998-2004 The figure shows the effective, i.e. trade-weighted, rate of the euro and the dollar. Here we can see how the euro was weakened and later strengthened. However, the figure shows only one fetish. The effective rates have also fluctuated sharply in the past, the bilateral rates even more strongly. This is clearly visible in the second figure. The first figure is reproduced in the small box. Figure 4. Real handelsvagd exchange rate 1980-2004 From a historical perspective, today's weak dollar or strong euro are not entirely exceptional. They are not far from the long-term averages. Striking, on the other hand, is the dollar's exemplary strength in the first half of the 1980s. So strong was the dollar's effective rate not during the IT boom despite reaching extremely high levels. How is this to be interpreted? A fairly common interpretation is that the events in the United States have affected the effective course of the dollar much more than the events in the Riga world. In the early 1980s, the dollar exchange rate was pushed up by an initially very tight monetary policy, followed by expansionary fiscal policy in the region of the Reagan administration. High interest rates attracted investment in dollars and expansionary fiscal policy drove up domestic demand at the expense of exports. At the turn of the millennium, the IT boom and optimistic return and growth expectations contributed to an influx of foreign equity and direct investment. In this wave of investment, the dollar was strengthened, something that even in the US was not particularly bad about. But, everything has an end. In the mid-1980s, the dollar exchange rate turned steeply downwards and continued to fall for several years. A couple of times it was done to influence the fall in the share price through joint interventions. Similarly, it went f a couple, three years ago. As IT optimism faded, growth expectations became more moderate, share prices sjk and foreign equity and direct investment in the US slowed down. The dollar was booming its long-held outhill climb, which would probably have been even steeper without Asian central bank investments in dollar assets. These investments have also contributed to long-term interest rates not rising as expected. The U.S. eased monetary policy extremely much and the budget deficit was allowed to grow. The problem was that the U.S. ran into double the deficit that many economists had expressed their concerns about. The US double deficit The US current account deficit erupted to grow again in the 1998 IT boom. The budget deficit, on the other hand, had been decreasing since 1993 and was accounted for around the turn of the millennium in a surplus of around two per cent. Figure 5. US deficit The fact that the current account deficit grew during the IT boom is understandable, as resources were fully exploited and domestic demand was growing at a rapid pace. However, the current account deficit has grown even after the IT boom. As its counterpart, household and especially central government indebtedness has continued to a. On the other hand, the indebtedness of the companies sector is not a problem in the US, as the financial position of the companies (cash flow to capital spending) has significantly improved in recent years. The debate has been about whether the double deficits pose a threat to stable development in the United States and thus also to global development. The optimists point to us dynamics and flexible markets as well as having growth potential. In addition, it points to the inflet of investments with high returns and low risk and to the dollar's overriding role as a reserve and investment currency and international means of payment. Even if deficits can't grow forever, the U.S. economy will in due course get rid of these problems, the optimists argue. The pessimists again point out that investors have already been reeling from their dollar investments, and this is skewing the financing of deficits. These developments show that the current budget and current account deficits are already unsustainable. If deficits remain at current levels or years, U.S. foreign and federal debt will respite the limit at which dollar investments are no longer of interest. This leads to a collapse in the dollar and a fall in the price of dollar bonds. The latter means rising long-term interest rates. Monetary policy Historically, monetary policy easing in the United States in 2001-2003 was unusually large, but in the years before, monetary policy had also tightened more than in other countries. Figure 6. Central bank interest rates. The Fed and the ECB In the United States, short-term real interest rates have been slightly negative over the past two years, while in the euro area countries they have also been around zero. Figure 7. Short real interest rate (3 months) Expansionary monetary policy has so far not affected inflation. Inflation expectations have risen slightly since 2003 in both the US and the euro area countries, but the figure is marginal. This does not mean that the ease of monetary policy would not have affected prices as well. The expansionary monetary policy has, for its part, driven up asset prices in the United States as well as in other countries. Share prices rose in 2004. Bond prices have remained in the offing and this is reflected in low long-term interest rates. Investors have lower returns in riskier assets, and the interest rate spread has thus been small (the yield difference between BBB and AAA-rated bonds, the yield difference between developing countries' loans and the corresponding loans for developed countries). The rise in house prices is also likely to be a global blemish. House prices have risen at a fairly rapid pace in almost all OECD countries except Germany and Japan. In international comparison, housing prices in Finland are only at the average level. The upturn in house prices has been clearly stung by the expansionary monetary policy. In this way, monetary policy has also helped to boost domestic demand, especially in the United States, but also in some euro area countries, including Finland. In the recent debate, one has wondered why the low real interest rates have not caused Europeans to change homes or build new homes. Finland is a derogation in this respect, as are Spain and Ireland. The expansionary monetary policy has also indirectly affected commodity prices. This has been done by the fact that the US's easy monetary policy has had an impact in some Asian countries that have changed their exchange rate policies. 1 Interventions have kept the exchange rate stable against the dollar or have counteracted the appreciation of the currency. The liquidity has been used to finance the rapid growth, especially in China. The ha growth in Asia has driven up commodity prices. A direct channel has also existed. Cheap money has stood to ffogande f various speculative positions. 1 The situation is reminiscent of the last years of the Bretton Woods period, when the United States financed the Vietnam War with loans and other countries' central banks were forced to finance the U.S. current account deficit through k of dollar assets to keep their exchange rate at a fixed parity. Liquidity and deflating inflationary pressures were thus transferred to other countries, until Germany had enough and decided to revaluate the Deutschmark. On the comparison with the Bretton Woods period, see Dooley, M. D. Folkerts-Landau and P. Garber, "An Essay on the Revived Bretton Woods System," NBER Working Paper 9971, September 2003. All in all, this means that the prolonged expansionary monetary policy at a time of globalization and h productivity growth has inflationary effects.2 It only takes longer than fut f them to break through in an upturn in the general price level. Perhaps a contributing factor to price stability is the damaged credibility of central banks, which has led to low inflation expectations. The trend for price appreciation is greater when central banks are trusted to keep inflation down. This means, of course, that central banks must continue to pursue a monetary policy that preserves credibility. Low inflation Price stability or low inflation can by now be said to be expected and widely accepted in all OECD countries. An inflation rate of 3-4 percent is currently considered h. Figure 8. Rate of increase in consumer prices The transition to low inflation has been facilitated by high productivity growth in many industries and competition as more and more economies have pushed up their limits in trade and investment. The prices of many industrial products have fallen as production has shifted to low-cost countries and measures have been taken to maintain productivity. However, the low level of inflation is mainly due to the change in monetary policy. Central banks have been made independent, and low inflation has become their main target. There may be differences in inflation dynamics between countries or different regions, although in all the rates of pricing would be equally low. For a year now, the European System of Central Banks has been running an extensive research project aimed at clarifying inflation dynamics. The Bank of Finland has also participated in this work. A comparison of the voluminous material clearly shows that Europe is affected by persistent inflation in a completely different way than the United States. Prices don't change as often as in the U.S. This applies in particular to the services sector. This is one of the reasons why inflation in the euro area has stubbornly remained at just over two per cent.3 Productivity Productivity growth was for a long time faster in Europe than in the United States. This was due to two circumstances. On the one hand, Europe narrowed the productivity gap that had arisen during the Second World War and, on the other hand, the rapidly rising labour costs in Europe in the 1970s and in the early 1980s led to 2 Se Korhonen, T. After the middle of the decade, the keep-up has been the opposite. Productivity gains picked up in the U.S. and slowed in Europe. Productivity growth in the US increased by one percentage point over the period 1995-2001, compared with productivity growth in 1990-1995. Retail and wholesale trade and the financial services sector, including ancillary services, account for 95% of this in productivity growth.4 Figur 9. Largest contributors to productivity acceleration in the USA In Europe, productivity declines during the same period in most countries (excluding Greece, Ireland and Portugal). But Europe also has industries, such as telecommunications, that can report relative productivity growth. However, evidence that productivity has picked up in the services sector and in sectors using ICT technologies is lacking. Figur 10. In China, growth has been very strong for a long time, and nothing indicates that the Chinese economy could not continue to grow yet for a decade or two.5 China's added weight as an economic act is evidenced by the fact that China is now the third most important country in the world in terms of foreign trade. Figure 11. Percentage of world imports China's share of world oil consumption is approaching a tenth: China accounted for about 40% of oil consumption between 1999 and 2003. China is the world's largest steel consumer. Figure 12. Stalkonsumtion and is expected in 2005 to go the U.S. as the world's largest collector of aluminum. Figure 13. Aluminium consumption 4 Figurerna har lanats ur Finlands Banks farska rapport, se Sinkkonen, J., " Labour Productivity Growth and Industry Structure: The Impact of Industry Structure on Productivity Growth, Export Prices and Labour Compensation", Bank of Finland Discussion Papers 2005 (forthcoming). 5 Birch, T., "Will China's rapid growth continue?", Euro & economy 4/2004, pp. 27  32. 6 (13) The rapid growth of China and other emerging market economies bodes well for the world economy. Here are locomotives for growth. The development also means that a large part of the goods and services that were previously produced in developed countries are now manufactured in these low-cost countries. The production structures of developed countries must be adapted to the new division of labour. In some countries or regions, adaptation poses more problems than others. At the same time, new opportunities are emerging as the rapid growth in China and other countries means that their imports are also moving at a rapid pace. This, in turn, means that other countries have the opportunity to quickly increase their exports. China is special in that it mainly finances its own large investments itself, even though it is poor. China's savings rate is very high, and the country's current account is showing a rebound. Strong growth and expectations of returns have led to an infle of capital from abroad. In order to counteract the appreciation of the currency, the Chinese authorities must constantly use foreign currency. The growing foreign exchange reserves contribute to a credit expansion that finances both efficient and inefficient investments. This, too, is part of the global imbalance, if it is considered that development is not sustainable in the longer term. Correction of the US double deficit I have described and interpreted a number of very well-known facts. The interpretation is, of course, caricatured and schematic to say the least. I shall now gather the pieces together and deal with the double US deficit, which I believe is an imbalance for the aforementioned reason: budget and current account deficits cannot continue to grow much longer. Already de-ras current level is unsustainable but may persist for some time yet. Imbalances of this kind, as a rule, are corrected in one way or another, uncontrolled or controlled. Uncontrolled correction An uncontrolled correction could mean a steep, possibly verse, decline in the dollar exchange rate as foreign investors exit their dollar positions. In this situation, interest rates on dollar bonds are rising. The situation could be further aggravated if rising long-term interest rates push down house prices, and this in turn would lead to a sharp rise in the us household savings rate. In such a situation, stock prices would also turn downwards, causing a global surge. The U.S. economy would fall into a severe recession, dragging the rest of the world economy with it. As a counterbalance to the dollar's weakening, the euro would strengthen strongly, especially if Asian central banks continued to peg their currency to the dollar. The stronger euro and the global recession would push the eurozone towards deflation. Although an uncontrolled correction can be prevented, a properly oriented economic policy will not only succeed. Economic structures must also be adapted to the new economic conditions in the world. However, action in just one region or country is not enough, but measures and adaptation are needed in the US as well as in China and Europe. Controlled correction There has been talk of an uncontrolled correction for a couple of years already. But it has not happened. In the market, the risk of such a correction has so far not been priced particularly ht. There, many have been able to keep up the possibility of a controlled correction. What are the elements then? Among other things, it has been mentioned: USA penningpolitiken fortsatter att stramas at successivt budgetunderskottet fas successivt att minska hushallens sparkvot ar China den verhettade ekonomin kyls av bland annat genom revalvering Euro area penningpolitiken fortsatt tillvaxtframjande euroomradet blir starkare och produktiviteten ar framf allt i tjanstesektorn Figure 14 . Imbalances are corrected These elements are readily acceptable at least in terms of monetary policy, the US budget deficit and the saving rate of US households. The perception also sts of various model calculations. A year ago, the Bank of Finland made model calculations with alternative scenarios for the adjustment of the US current account. The starting point was a 2 percentage point decrease in the current account in relation to GDP. Two different paths came to this result. In one option, consumers' permanent income (the discounted present value of expected income) was lowered, thereby reducing the household saving rate. In the second option, the risk premium on dollar investments is re-measured.6 The latter option corresponds to an uncontrolled correction: the dollar is nominally weakened by just over 20 percent, inflation is accelerating in the United States with monetary tightening and rising interest rates as a result. Consumption and investment are decreasing. The current account deficit shrinks as exports fall and imports decline. In the Riga world (euro area), domestic demand is rising, but shrinking net exports are pushing GDP growth down to zero. Prices are falling, and monetary policy is reaching the zero interest rate limit. The first option, us households' savings, is much more positive and represents a controlled correction. There, too, the dollar is weakened real but not nominal. No inflationary pressures arise and monetary policy can be eased in both the US and the riga world (euro area). This option is the fact that the US budget deficit is being reduced, which would also reduce the need to reduce the household saving rate. However, the saving rate is not easy to influence with direct economic policy measures. The OECD Secretariat has made similar calculations. The results were presented in a report in the summer of 2004.7 Even according to these calculations, a controlled adaptation is very difficult if it takes place only through one channel. A two percentage point reduction in the trade balance deficit would require a significant weakening of the dollar (20-25% effective) or a very large change in the budget balance (6% of GDP) or a sharp shift in demand for US-made goods (market share of 2%). The best result is achieved if all factors influence at the same time. All options expect that a reduction in the US current account deficit would dampen growth elsewhere in the world as well. Interesting is the OECD's alternative of a structural change in the world's import demand in the direction of US-produced goods and services. It is easy to accept, but the question is whether it is realistic. It can hardly be influenced by any economic policy measures whatsoever. Still on the list is a reduction in the US budget deficit and a reduction in the saving rate of US households, which is accompanied by a gradual tightening of monetary policy. In the euro area, growth-friendly monetary policy will continue as long as inflation and inflation expectations are kept low. This does not mean that in the coming years interest rates could not slowly rise towards more neutral levels. That leaves two elements: China's exchange rate policy and a stronger Europe. China's vaxelkurspolitik China has received nagging from both the U.S. and Europe to revalue its currency or let it float. The Europeans justify the goal by saying that the brdan should be de-lased: since the reasons for the dollar shift stem from the United States, the eurozone has to bear an unreasonably large part of the adjustment burden where China and some other countries want to fludge the dollar. The Americans would again provide a stronger renminbi to reduce competition from China in the U.S. market. However, the importance of China's exchange rate policy is likely to be exaggerated. A revaluation of the Chinese currency is not a reflection on the problems that a correction of the US double deficit would bring. Revaluing the renminbi by 10% would weaken the US effective (trade-weighted) exchange rate by only 1%. That's not much as the effective rate has already been reduced by 20 percent. No conceivable revaluation of renminbi changes the fact that the cost level in China remains low in relation to the United States or other developed countries. If the renminbi were allowed to float, it would most likely be strengthened, but the question is whether the financial system and money market mechanism in China are mature for a free-floating currency.8 In order to function well, capital flows should be free and the domestic money market should be well developed so that price formation in the market effectively reflects all available information including monetary policy expectations. This is how far the development in China has not yet come. A revaluation of the Chinese currency could, for its part, facilitate adjustment, but it cannot be given much importance. The fact that the Chinese authorities themselves see it as a means of reducing credit expansion or dampening inflationary pressures is best justified. China makes its own decisions at its own pace when the time is right. European challenges Europeans have traditionally reacted more strongly to exchange rate changes than Americans. This is understandable as each European currency area from EMU was small in comparison with the UNITED STATES. In small, low-income economies, exchange rate changes have a large impact, while in large, closed economies, the effects are small. The situation should be different now that the euro area is also a large and comparatively closed currency area. Trade to countries outside the area accounts for 17-18% of GDP. In the US, the corresponding figure is even lower. Precisely because abroad 8 Se Koivu, T., "The challenge of choosing an optimal exchange rate regime for China", BOFIT Online 1/2005. trade in relative terms is so insignificant, a very large exchange rate change is required to enable the external balance to be affected to a greater extent. Europeans have been inclined to blame others for the problems of the strong euro and to expect others to take corrective action. Examples include calls for the US budget deficit to be reduced and the Chinese currency to be revalued. As I already mentioned, there are good grounds for these cases. But it is also appropriate to ask what can be done in Europe to alleviate the problems of the strong euro and to promote a controlled correction of global imbalances. Expansionary monetary and fiscal policy Many commentators have advised eurozone countries to aligned domestic demand with the help of expansionary monetary and fiscal policies. To fling this Council would mean accepting tighter budget deficits than hitherto regardless of the limits of the Stability and Growth Pact and would lead to an even more expansionary monetary policy than a futile one. It has even been suggested that the European Central Bank should counterattack and deliberately weaken the euro through interest rate cuts and currency interventions. It is difficult to see how extensive fiscal stimulus in euro area countries could help reduce the US budget deficit. For the first part, domestic demand may not be due to the measures. The growing deficits may only be the willingness of Europeans to save. But if domestic demand were indeed hitting, it would largely apply to services and to a very small extent to U.S. imports. The risk of rising prices for services would a, and at least this would not facilitate a growth-friendly monetary policy. Monetary policy is currently pro-growth and may continue to be so as long as inflation and inflation expectations are kept low. This does not mean that short-term interest rates in the euro area too would not rise towards more neutral levels in due course. It would be a good idea to explicitly weaken the euro by means of monetary easing or foreign exchange interventions. This would be similar to competing devaluations and lead even further away from a controlled correction of global imbalances. Productivity of the euro area services sector At first glance, productivity developments in the euro area services sector and the controlled correction of global imbalances should have nothing to do with each other. The rule of thumb is that a productivity decline or an ad productivity growth leads to a strengthening of the real exchange rate. With higher productivity and a stronger currency, the country's financial position and competitiveness in relation to other countries have nevertheless improved. Now, however, it is not this simple when you consider that most of the consumption demand concerns goods and services that are not five years old in international trade. In most industries, there is also a home bias in consumption. This means that as the demand for goods that are five years old for international trade grows, a small proportion refers to goods produced in the home country than to goods produced abroad, although they do not differ significantly in quality. This has recently been brought to the attention of US researchers Maurice Obstfeld and Kenneth Rogoff.9 They present calculations according to which non-tradables productivity in the euro area would make the adjustment of the US current account more painless for all parties. How can a productivity shift in the euro area services sector make a positive contribution to the controlled correction of imbalances of US origin? It is not entirely self-evident. The mechanism is largely finicky. All adjustments include a weakening of the real dollar exchange rate. This means that American products are becoming cheaper and that the demand for them is growing in Europe. At the same time, euro area exports are declining or not as fast as before. Productivity in the services sector in the euro area countries indirectly helps to reduce problems in the export sector as well. Firstly, the prices of services are falling, thereby rising consumers' real incomes. The relative price of services (non-tradables) decreases with the result that the demand for services is at the expense of goods (tradables). However, the demand for goods is rising overall, as real income is also reflected in demand for goods. If you add to this the typical home bias of all countries, a greater proportion of demand for goods is attributed to goods produced in their home country (the euro area) than to imported goods, and this in turn compensates for the loss of exports. The fastest way to drive up productivity in the services sector is to arouse competition in the services and goods markets. Here we come back to the same issues that have already been discussed in Europe for a long time, namely structural reforms. The reforms are robust even without global imbalances. At present, they would help to facilitate the correction of imbalances in a controlled manner. The fact that only the productivity of the services sector is highlighted does not mean that productivity did not also have to be seen in the production of goods. Of course, an improvement in industrial productivity would make it easier to withstand the strengthening of the euro. However, it cannot be expected that productivity in euro area industry could have so much that price competitiveness was restored as measured by relative unit labour costs. But the greatest pressure for productivity improvement and structural reforms arises from the fact that the relative share of goods production is shifting to countries outside old Europe and the United States. Summary As an expression of the global imbalance is the double US deficit. Of imbalance, one can speak in the sense that the current situation is clearly unsustainable: the US budget and current account deficits cannot remain at such levels for all eternity. Both deficits must be brought down from time to time. The current account deficit is not fully evened out as demographic developments in the US are so far favourable and the labour force is growing thanks to immigration. Nor is indebtedness the alarming hg of European injustice. Time thus exists f a controlled adaptation. The double deficits are not only america's problem but also a global source of concern. Growth and the export-promoting economic policy strategy in Asian countries have helped to create room for a renewal of the US current account. European supply-side is such that Europe is suffering more from the euro's strengthening than the US suffered from the dollar appreciation a few years ago. Since the double deficits are still mainly america's problem, a controlled adjustment is only possible if domestic demand growth slows down. This requires a gradual tightening of monetary policy and a gradual reduction in the budget deficit. In addition, the household saving rate eventually b a. One challenge for Europe is to strengthen its capacity for adaptation. At the same time, sensitivity f reduces exchange rate fluctuations. An adaptable economy can better respond to changes in the world around us. It also creates incentives to achieve productivity in all industries. Rapid productivity growth in the services sector over the past ten years is what separates the US from Europe. It is now up to Europe to catch up. Stress competition is automatically the pressure for a productivity boost in the services sector. Such a development would, in the current situation, also help to facilitate a controlled correction of global imbalances. Thank you for your attention.
