Title: Speech at My Company 2005
text: VTT Sinikka Salo Member of the Board of Directors The euro, financial markets and entrepreneurship Speech at My Company 2005 event in Helsinki 15.3.2005 First of all, I would like to thank you for this opportunity to speak to you entrepreneurs or those who may intend to become one, because you are key people in finland's future challenges. This is better understood in Finnish society and later in the EU at large  I am just referring, by way of example, to the EU's Lisbon Strategy, which aims to boost the EU's competitiveness and growth, and which was recently given a boost by the EU Commission  and many of the actions to promote entrepreneurship at a purely attitudinal level. The atmosphere in Finland is clearly more favourable for entrepreneurship than, for example, 30 years ago. And it is precisely the desire to encourage small and medium-sized enterprises in the service sector, where great opportunities are seen in terms of boring. After all, Finland has traditionally admired great things  we are rightly proud of our forest companies operating on the world market, not to mention Nokia. In the 1990s, the Finnish business world has been characterised by enormous internationalisation and an increase in the size of companies. This was not possible in a small market area of Finland. Only a larger market will make intensive investments in product development and new technology profitable. Today, more than 60% of the production and personnel of our large companies are abroad. The resources of such a small country are not enough to create and maintain very many large enterprises. In order to bore the Finns, we also need small businesses, for which the domestic market has now expanded to include the euro area and the EU. It must be remembered that even great success stories start small. This is a challenge not only for Finland, which is known to have exceptionally few small and medium-sized enterprises, but for the whole of Europe. In the information society, therefore, the best benefits may be obtained in those economies that succeed in mobilising small businesses. "Think small if you want to create more jobs"  you have to think small if you want more jobs  wrote Professor Graciela Chichilnisky (Columbia University) in a column for the Financial Times in May 2004, commenting on the China denunciation in the United States as well, i.e. the disappearance of traditional jobs in developing countries. Between 1991 and 2000, 60 to 80% of all new jobs in the United States were created in small and medium-sized enterprises. He drew attention to the fact that whereas in the past research and product development were dominated by large companies with large budgets, now, in the creation of new products that serve and promote the information society, small dynamic companies have improved their position. The network economy provides opportunities for small companies to apply strategies that were previously only available to large companies. In this context, he referred, among other things, to the open Linux system developed by our compatriot Linus Torvalds. In addition to business activities and financial services, opportunities are also seen in the production of more traditional services  for example, in it applications for various welfare services and in the production of personal services. In these sectors, the Finnish economy is clearly underdeveloped. Now, however, we are perhaps finally getting out of the "do it yourself" mentality and are learning to make our everyday life easier by buying, for example, renovation, laundry, cleaning, etc. Facilities. The increased outsourcing of public sector services by ordering these services from private service companies will increase the demand for personal services, as well as the general increase in demand for services among the ageing population. There is potential for starting your own business. Of course, I am not an expert in business or entrepreneurship, so my speech will focus, in accordance with my professional background, on the importance of the integration of the euro and the financial markets around business. Through its actions, the Central Bank can support business activity and, for its part, create a favourable framework for business activity. The generally accepted view is that the best way for a central bank to promote business conditions is to pursue a long-term and consistent monetary policy and thereby establish and maintain permanently stable monetary conditions. The central bank's task is also to promote the functioning of the financial system, in particular the smooth flow of payments. In my speech, I will examine the opportunities for business offered by the euro and our single monetary policy and the integrating European financial markets. *** The euro - a key element of the European Single Market Agenda Our single currency, the euro, and the context in which European entrepreneurship operates are very closely linked. The single currency is part of the EU's single market programme, which aims to build a large domestic market in Europe that provides the best possible conditions for entrepreneurship. In an open and extensive common market, it is more profitable to innovate and productise than it would necessarily be in a small national market. The idea of a large common market is at the heart of the eu as a whole and, at the same time, the Union's greatest achievement in terms of business. The single market programme has many facets, such as trade policy, harmonisation and reduction of technical standards, eu-level supervision of competition policy, and so on. The single currency, which has been created in order to make a real common market a reality, is of key importance. It should be remembered that the EU Commission pushed ahead with the monetary union project with the symbol 'one market  one money'. The euro brings stability  the ECB's monetary policy a success The most visible significance of the non-use of the euro was that previously significant exchange rate risks within the euro area were eliminated and thus the euro area markets have become more closely interlinked. The disappearance of exchange rate risks and the absence of exchange costs have chilled the consumer and improved the opportunities for companies to internationalise. The disadvantages that used to be caused by the "exoticism" of one's own currency and own financial conditions in international activities have now disappeared. The starting points of competition in this respect have evened out, not only for large companies, but right up to the grassroots level  including small and medium-sized entrepreneurs. After all, it is understandably more difficult for small businesses to operate in several currencies and to hedge against exchange rate risks than for large companies. It is undeniable that, in its first few years, the European Central Bank's monetary policy has been more successful than hardly anyone could have anticipated or even hoped for beforehand. The conditions have been challenging  I am referring in particular to the strong fluctuations in the international economic cycle and in the prices of jy and other raw materials. However, the European Central Bank has managed to keep inflation low in the euro area. Interestingly, in fact, price stability has been achieved without even having to resort to a heavy-handed monetary policy. The European Central Bank managed to quickly gain the confidence of the public and the markets in its monetary policy or, as economists say, to ensure the credibility of its monetary policy. The credibility of the single monetary policy is clearly and tangible reflected in the current low market interest rates and low inflation in the euro area financial markets. The single monetary policy and the climate of stability built by the European Central Bank have created a financially stable environment for companies and households, which, for example, in Finland, has sustained domestic demand and employment development even during the international recession. Furthermore, as a major currency, the euro is not the same easy target for speculative currency surprises as many of its predecessor currencies and, in this sense, it also provides protection for the inhabitants of the euro area from speculative pressures on the foreign exchange markets, although fluctuations in the exchange rate of the euro towards currencies outside the euro sphere, including the dollar, are, of course, a fact of life under the conditions of monetary union and cannot be overcome by intra-European arrangements. Indeed, experience seems to suggest that a large currency area can offer entrepreneurship a better start in the long run than a small currency area. The second reason for the low level of speculative pressure, which is at least as important in the case of the euro area, is the independence guaranteed to the European Central Bank  the fact that the monetary policy decision-making of the European Central Bank is protected from the pressures of political decision-making and benefit systems. The external value of the euro, despite its strong appreciation, is now only more or less at the 1999 level, as is, for example, Finland's price competitiveness. I would remind you that Finland joined the euro area at an exchange rate that was generally considered to be undervalued rather than overvalued. Despite the appreciation of the euro, the profitability of industry is at a good level, largely thanks to its own previous efforts. Thus, at least from the point of view of Finnish companies, the appreciation of the euro is best understood as a return from the previous exceptionally low level to the normal level, and not as a deviation from the normal level to an exceptionally high level. One might ask what would have happened if Finland still had its own currency and if the markka had strengthened against the US dollar by 50% in four years and the markka's currency index by 30%. It is never possible to get a real answer to this question. However, in the light of past experience, it is not inconceivable that we should now  and probably have had a long time in the past  a lively debate on the correction of the exchange rate of the markka and that, in addition to economists, economic lobbies and various political forces should take full part in this debate. Nor would it be inconceivable that, perhaps for purely expedient reasons, the main focus of the debate should have been on recent developments in the exchange rate since the year 2000. In a small open economy, such an atmosphere of debate easily leads to suspicions of currency devaluation and high interest rates, and often expectations begin to feed themselves. In such a situation, it is difficult for the central bank to maintain a climate of stability for very long. The danger of continuing our long-standing spiral of devaluation and inflation would have been obvious; the currency would once again have been allowed to devalue in a situation where it should have been revalued. The scenario is, of course, completely hypothetical, and there can never be full clarity on the matter. However, I think it is fair to suggest that our previous exchange rate debate and policy contained a significant dose of short-term devaluation. This policy was thought to support the country's growth and investment, and probably in many quarters it was believed to support my entrepreneurship. I think this was a misunderstanding. Instead of entrepreneurship, support was given to traditional sectors in difficulty, mainly the forest industry, and to firms in difficulty, especially large export companies. However, by shackling the functioning of the financial markets and directing scarce financial resources primarily to existing large-scale industry, the emergence and development of small and innovative enterprises was made more difficult  apparently unintentionally. Joining the euro area has significantly clarified the division of responsibilities in economic policy and, more generally, economic responsibilities. The responsibility for national price stability and competitiveness  that is, price stability vis-a-vis the rest of the euro area and competitiveness in global markets  clearly lies with fiscal and budgetary policy, ultimately with the individual decision-makers in various quarters, not least in companies. Mistakes in economic policy or business cannot be corrected afterwards by means of exchange rate policy. In my opinion, most decision-makers in Finland have understood this quite well. Both the public sector and companies were able to use the income from the previous boom and the weak euro wisely, and inflation remained well under control and appears to remain low even in the current upturn. Caution should be exercised in the future. The global economy is now experiencing a boom, but there is no guarantee that it will continue to be as strong as it is today for a long time. Exchange rate developments are even more difficult to predict than real GDP developments, but past experience suggests that large fluctuations in exchange rates are still possible and even probable in the future. The euro area single market was not yet fully absorbed by entrepreneurs Although, in a way, the domestic markets of companies expanded beyond the euro area, they do not seem to have managed to absorb their enlarged domestic markets particularly well in almost any of the euro countries so far. For example, exports from Finland to other countries in the euro area did, however, increase after the emergence of the euro area and peaked at around EUR 17 billion in 2000. Since then, however, annual exports to the euro area have decreased and remained at just under EUR 15 billion last year. At the same time, exports have increased from EUR 33 billion to around EUR 34 billion. These figures do not exclude the possibility that the introduction of the euro has in itself strengthened exports to the euro countries, possibly considerably. The effects may have only been masked by the opposite effects of the international economic cycle. I believe, however, that entrepreneurs  my Finns  could try to make better use of the opportunities offered by the home market, which has, in a way, expanded to sell the euro. I believe that small and medium-sized enterprises in particular would do well to redouble their efforts to conquer the vast and prosperous markets of Central Europe. Europe-wide, truly integrated financial markets play a key role in promoting business ... With the advent of the euro, the opportunities for creating a truly Pan-European financial market have improved. The introduction of the euro considerably calmed down the monetary conditions in Europe. This has already had its own mythical effect on the integration of European financial markets. We are closer to the objective of having access for companies to a Europe-wide financial market that guarantees the widest range of services at the most competitive prices, and that it should not matter from the point of view of invoicing and the management of payment transactions whether there are transactions between different countries in the euro area or within one country. Indeed, after the introduction of the euro, a certain part of the euro area's financial markets were almost fully integrated very quickly; for example, the unsecured interbank short-money market currently operates smoothly and uniformly throughout the euro area. Progress has also been made in other market segments. Despite the political will at the level of the strategy, the creation of common financial markets is progressing slowly and euro area financial markets remain segmented in many respects. Although the introduction of the single currency removed one of the main obstacles to the single market in the euro area, the emergence of a common financial market remains constrained by a number of major frictions. These are partly based on the acceptance of existing conditions and the short-sighted defence of local interests. In particular, there is fierce wrestling going on to defend financial centers. On the other hand, there are also genuine legislative (such as tax and bankruptcy law) and differences in supervisory and administrative authorisation systems, as well as technical differences. Financial market infrastructures, such as securities clearing houses, operate differently in different countries and are not easy to combine into a single entity. The differences are essentially due to the fact that national systems and legislation have been gradually formed from each country's own perspective. Although market integration now seems obvious, in the past it has not been foreseen at all, at least not on the current scale. When I have been asked to speak to entrepreneurs on various occasions, I have wanted to highlight precisely the need for integration of the EU's financial markets. Although there are many frictional factors holding back integration, I am optimistic about the integration process in the EU's financial markets. The benefits of a truly unified pan-European financial market are simply too great for us to ignore. The revival of entrepreneurship and economic dynamism is crucial to Europe's boredom, competitiveness and the future development of countries' budgetary finances. In turn, well-functioning, truly Europe-wide financial markets have a key role to play in reviving economic dynamism. Without well-functioning, EU-wide financial markets, the EU's single market will not function properly and businesses will not be able to fully reap its benefits. The development and regulatory integration of financial markets has been, and will continue to be, at the heart of the EU's economic policy cooperation over the next few years. It is now important to implement the financial market legislation and supervisory framework contained in the Financial Services Action Plan (FSAP), which is coming to an end. In the future, the aim will be a single European payments area instead of the current fragmented payment system structure. Cross-border payment transactions becoming easier The latter objective of a single payment area is a good example of long-term cooperation at EU level. Initially, the European Commission and the European System of Central Banks (ESCB) will both work to promote retail payments in euro in the euro area on the basis of voluntary cooperation between banks. However, no significant progress could be observed. When the euro cash was introduced at the beginning of 2002, the Commission began to prepare a regulation at a rapid pace to develop cross-border retail payments in euro. In July 2002, a regulation on retail payments entered into force, requiring uniform pricing for domestic and crossborder retail payments in euro to customers. Initially, the regulation only applied to card payments and ATM withdrawals, but since July 2003 it has extended to transfers of less than EUR 12,500.- The regulation significantly accelerated the efforts of BANKS in EU countries to improve the efficiency of cross-border payments. In June 2002, the largest banks and EU banking associations set up the European paymets council (EPC). He started to draw up plans for the creation of a single euro payment area (SEPA) in the euro area by 2010. The aim is, among other things, that already in 2008, the basic services for citizens  ordinary credit transfers, instant transfers and direct debits  would operate on a SEPA-wide basis. Finland's representatives in the EPC cooperation have been, in particular, Nordea and the Finnish Banking Association. The EU regulation on the pricing of payment services can in itself be seen as a small but significant step forward in the integration of European financial markets. The regulation will have little effect on the payment transactions of large international companies, but it will make it easier and cheaper for small and medium-sized enterprises  and also ordinary Finns  to make payments abroad. Perhaps the most important aspect of the regulation, however, is that it has stimulated cooperation between European banks. However, there are still concerns about the timetable for implementation. Last week, EU Single Market Commissioner Charlie McCreevy strongly urged banks to step up their efforts to achieve this goal. He specifically said that the Commission would not stand by and watch the slow progress as idle, but "if necessary, the Commission will make some of the jointly agreed standards mandatory and include a timetable for a single charging area in the draft law". The European Central Bank has also expressed its concern about the slowness of the timetable. One of the basic tasks of the ESCB is to promote the smooth operation of payment systems under the Treaty (Article 105.2). The combination of nationally segmented financial markets into a single, well-functioning and safe European financial market provides an excellent example of the very important, but largely unforeseeable, economic policy cooperation within the Framework of the EU, which is of great importance for our future prosperity. It is obvious that seamless legislative cooperation between the Commission, the Member States  not least in the Council of the EU  and the European Parliament is of paramount importance here. Perhaps even more important in practice, however, are the voluntary efforts of the various parties involved in the financial markets to develop the European market. Much to be done to improve risk capital opportunities  for example, the importance of venture capitalists When it comes to risk finance, the US financial markets provide a good example of the financing opportunities that well-developed financial markets offer to companies. Entrepreneurship-based companies and the innovations they carry out, i.e. the commercial clotting of inventions, have had a considerable impact on the strong competitiveness of the country's economy and on its ever-rapid growth. The rise of entrepreneurship in the United States has only been possible to a large extent thanks to active and skilled venture capitalists who, in addition to providing finance to the start-up company, also provide management support and at the same time also control the company. Intensifying competition in an expanding market is creating problems for those companies that are unable to offer quality that stands out from the rest. On the other hand, the opening up of markets will bring great opportunities for those entrepreneurs who will be able to take the initiative into their own hands and will put off the high potential demand there from the euro area and the eu's internal market as a whole.

Title: Presentation at the seminar "Lapland and the challenges of internationalisation"
text: Sinikka Salo Member of the Executive Board Bank of Finland FINLAND, EUROPE AND THE CHALLENGES OF GLOBALISATION Presentation at the seminar "Lapland and the challenges of internationalisation" at the Kemij8arvi Cultural Centre 22.3.2005 Ladies and gentlemen, My sincerest thanks for the invitation to Kemij8arvi. The challenges of globalisation in this region have quickly become concrete. There can be no doubt that you too think that my topic of 'Finland, Europe and the challenges of globalisation' is topical. At the same time, the topic is also quite broad. I cannot possibly hope that I will be able to offer anywhere near an exhaustive presentation of it d0 let alone solutions to the problems of adaptation that the 'China-manifest', i.e. the disappearance of traditional jobs in developing countries, will inevitably cause in the short term. Instead, I hope that I will be able to give some impetus to think about the increased opportunities for Finland and the Finns in the ongoing globalization process. Challenges are always my opportunities! I have broken down my presentation as follows. Let me first look at globalisation in a slightly more general way d0 above all to clarify what is meant by it. After that, I reflect on Finland's position and challenges in the mainstream of globalisation, in which case eu integration and the significance of Finland's membership of the EU must inevitably be examined. As a representative of the Central Bank, I naturally consider the importance of the euro and the single monetary policy for Finland's survival strategy. I consider the euro to be a 'great equaliser', which gives much the same financial and marketing prospects to entrepreneurs, regardless of whether the location is in the heart of Central Europe or northern Finland and Lapland. Globalization is life in the "global village" Markets are becoming more international and open up. In addition to the mobility of various industrial products, as well as capital, technology and work, is increasing worldwide. Indeed, the opening up of different markets is easier to see in globalisation and, at least in the short term, perhaps the most important part for businesses and industry. However, globalisation is significantly more than the opening up of markets. It means a reduction in the importance of geography as a political and cultural factor. We live in a 'global village' d0 I think this characterisation illustrates well that globalisation is clearly not just an economic manifestation, but is being used by the general expansion of people's spheres of life. Life is fundamentally globalized for two somewhat interdependent reasons. Firstly, new technologies have in many respects reduced the importance of the distance between countries and peoples in interaction with each other. New products are typically lighter than old products and are therefore easier to transport even over long distances. Through this, the new technology has actually shrunk the distances in the market. The shrinkage of distances has been particularly evident in the production and transmission of information or information. Telecommunications are the dynamic core of the new technology. Thanks to new technology, the effect teas and information, in ever-flowing streams, spread more and more rapidly everywhere and reach an increasing proportion of the world's people. It is becoming easier and easier for us to find out from the world about things we are interested in, whether this interest is commercial, entertainment or cultural. Thanks to the interactive transmission of information made possible by the Internet, the comparison with the 'global village' is becoming more topical. It can be said that technological advances are globalising the whole circle of people's lives. And since technological progress is irreversible - once invented cannot be easily invented - then globalisation can be expected to be "one-way". Along with technology, another reason for globalization is the political changes that have occurred in recent years. After the fall of communism and many right-wing dictatorships, governments today no longer restrict people's international contacts nearly as much as they used to. The political changes that have led to the increase in democracy and civil liberties have not been independent of technological progress. New technologies and the resulting reduction in barriers to the flow of information have made a significant contribution to the spread of democracy in Central and Eastern Europe as elsewhere. I think it is more correct to think that the transformation of people into global villagers will at the same time globalise their economic relations than that the globalisation of economic relations will globalise all other relations. The market is formed by how modern people live: consume, tinker, save and move, what entertainment or culture they follow, and so on. This is despite the fact that economic relations have been at the forefront of globalisation in some respects. In addition to technological progress and political changes, the importance of geographical location has therefore diminished and continues to decline. At the same time, the hype from the large size of land is also diminishing as more and more countries open up their trade and economies. Against this background, globalisation seems to be promising good times for Finland in the future. Finland is a good example of globalisation from an economy that has been in a state of flux at an early stage. Without the export of wood and paper products and, subsequently, many other industrial products, we would not have been able to build the welfare society in which we now live. In addition to globalisation and economic integration, countries have had to compromise their national self-sufficiency. In a way, this is the price that we have had to pay and will have to pay for a high standard of living. Many industries, which were also important in their time, have shrunk to almost nothing in Finland, thanks to the development of international division of labour. That is as it should be. Otherwise, we would not have been able to concentrate on high-tech products, on which our current standard of living rests entirely. New industries and new jobs can therefore only emerge if the old industries wither away and the old jobs die. This idea, originally conceived by the Austrian, later Americanized economist Joseph Schumpeter, is known as the so-called "black market". as creative destruction. It argues that destruction, i.e. the growing pains of the economy, and the creation of new, more productive jobs are two sides of the same growth process. Finland's challenges are the same as in the EU more generally d0 increasing the degree of participation in work and increasing productivity Secondly, Finland has thus done reasonably well in the process of globalisation. Our economy grew rapidly after the recession of the early 1990s. According to international evaluators, we have many competitive advantages - the quality of public institutions, the high level of technology, the high quality of our basic education, etc. We can be proud of what we are doing, but we must not stop at complacency. We have produced many reports which expressly d0 and rightly d0 warn of this. I will not go into these recommendations in detail. However, I would like to say that the central message of all of them is clear and true: Finland's success has always been based on flexibility and dynamism d0 we cannot afford to stand still. Our main concern relates to the ageing of the population. The economic growth that is avoided in order to maintain and increase well-being comes from the workload d0 the quantity of stubs d0 and productivity d0 from how well and efficiently we produce goods or services. The challenges of both Finland and the EU as a whole to maintain economic growth and well-being are related to both of these components of growth. In greying Finland and throughout Europe, the growth of tyanos is fading. It is estimated that, on average, total EU production is growing at a rate of up to one per cent slower than in the United States, simply because the number of workers on the Old Continent is not increasing, while in the United States there are more workers, e.g. migrants. Even in terms of productivity, we have not yet managed to completely exhaust the opportunities offered by information technology, for example. For this reason, it is essential to try to increase the degree of participation in employment and to increase productivity, above all by using information technology. A key challenge for the future for the Finnish economy and society is to manage the costs of ageing d0 and, in connection with this, to finance the welfare state. According to forecasts, the expected ageing trend in Finland will be dramatic, and a particular milestone will be the retirement of the baby boomers, which is expected to culminate around 2010. Future changes in population will increase social expenditure related to ageing, especially the ratio of pensions paid to the income of employees. There is no opportunity on this occasion to go into this matter in great depth. I would just like to point out that, in addition to increasing the number of taxpayers, that is, increasing the degree of boredom, it is important to reform the production of public services in such a way as to reduce the difference in productivity development between public services and private goods production. The productivity of basic public services must be increased. Otherwise, the financial basis of the welfare state will crumble. Let the example calculation shed some light on the matter: a5 Basic services provided or dependent on public funding - education, health, social services d0 currently employ just over 300,000 people (300,800 in 2003), or 16% of the total number of tulles. As people get older, the need for basic services continues to increase. If the current structure of service production remained unchanged and productivity in the production of services did not increase, about 55,000 new stubs would be needed over the next three decades. When the number of employees decreases, this means that the number of employees providing basic public services would rise to 20% of the workforce! This would be despite the fact that the long-term calculation assumes a slight increase in the employment rate and a reduction in the employment rate to around 6%. a5 If, on the other hand, productivity in public basic service production could be increased by one per cent per year by reorganising practices and freezing information technology, the additional need for work would be more or less eliminated and public finances would be in surplus. There would even be room for tax cuts in public finances, despite the weakening of the public dependency ratio. According to various studies, public service provision has the potential to increase productivity, i.e. to increase the productivity of services without compromising the quality of services. Of course, I am not a connoisseur of the details of streamlining measures in the service sector, but e.g. Sitra's studies show that there will most certainly be genuine rationalisation in the provision of public services, from which both service providers and service users will benefit. It should be noted that cutting services or reducing the quality is not about streamlining, but productivity means rationalizing production methods, doing the right things in the right place and at the right time, i.e. an innovation-based increase in productivity, the continuous use of new technologies and product development, as well as modern logistical solutions in the production of welfare services. This calculation illustrates how big an issue productivity growth is and thus supports the government's goal of increasing productivity. It can be said that the success of Finnish society in the coming decades can be measured to a large extent by how the public sector d0 mainly the municipal sector d0 copes with its efficiency challenge. Both increasing the level of participation in employment and increasing productivity are enshrined in the EU's Lisbon Strategy, agreed by the governments in spring 2000, and which has recently been accelerated in order to improve competitiveness and growth. After all, it was drawn up in order to enable the EU to meet the challenges of global competition and the development of information technology. The European structures, which were good when mechanical engineering production prevailed, are no longer competitive in the production structure that nurtures information technology. On the other hand, the opening up of China, India and many other developing countries to free trade, through which their chances of getting rid of the hump have vastly improved as globalisation has progressed, has increased competition and challenges from outside the EU much more rapidly than was envisaged when the strategy was being formulated in 2000. That is why the rapid implementation of the strategy for European renewal has become all the more important and needs to be accelerated. In order to preserve the European social model, which focuses on social cohesion, we need to improve our competitiveness, to create more entrepreneurship and, consequently, new jobs. Increasing entrepreneurship is absolutely central both in the EU and in Finland The Lisbon Strategy targets a participation rate of 70% by 2010. This is equivalent to creating around 21 million new jobs in the EU. The Finnish Government Programme aims to increase the participation rate to 75 per cent and to create 100,000 new jobs in the next few years. Entrepreneurs and businesses play a key role. This is better understood in Finnish society than before. I refer to a number of measures to promote entrepreneurship at a positive level. The atmosphere in Finland is clearly more favourable for entrepreneurship than, for example, 30 years ago. And it is precisely the desire to encourage small and medium-sized enterprises in the service sector, where great opportunities are seen in terms of boring. And it must be remembered that even great success stories begin small. Indeed, the information society may have the best clot in those economies that succeed in mobilising small business. Whereas in the past research and product development were dominated by large companies with large budgets, now, in the creation of new products that serve and promote the information society, small dynamic companies have improved their position. The network economy provides opportunities for small companies to apply strategies that were previously only available to large companies. In this context, reference is often made, for example, to the open Linux system developed by Linus Torvalds. In addition to business activities and financial services, opportunities are also seen in the production of more traditional services d0 for example, in it applications for various welfare services and in the production of services for people. In these traditional service sectors, the Finnish economy is clearly underdeveloped, but we are perhaps finally getting out of the "do it yourself" mentality and we are learning to make our everyday life easier by buying, for example, renovation, laundry, cleaning, etc. Facilities. The increased outsourcing of public sector services by ordering these services from private service companies will increase the demand for personal services, as well as the general increase in demand for services among the ageing population. There is potential for starting your own business. Entrepreneurship is supported and facilitated by our EU membership and our common currency, the euro. That's next. The EU and the euro as a cover in the mainstream of globalisation The beginning of this year marked the 10th anniversary of Finland's accession to the EU. In general d0 and rightly so d0 it is believed that EU integration has progressed at a dizzying pace, and Finland has also suspended its place in it, both by freezing membership itself, but at the same time by acting constructively to promote the EU's common goals. Although the european Union may well be seen as its origins in the post-war effort to ensure that peace is maintained in Europe, the EU has evolved more and more clearly over time as a response to the challenges of globalisation for European countries. Examples of the EU's role in managing globalisation include its influence in multilateral organisations and its efforts to harmonise global standards. a5 For example, in the World Trade Organisation (WTO) or the International Monetary Fund (IMF), whose activities seek to manage globalisation in order to promote its virtues, the EU's influence may, of course, be much greater than that of any single Member State, especially a small one. Take, for example, the EU's trade policy power at global level. It is more difficult to discriminate against Finnish products when the EU is behind it. a5 Another concrete example relates to the creation of uniform regulations in globalising financial markets. Our large companies that list in the New York PRS have to comply with both us and Finnish/EU regulations in their accounts, which is inconvenient and entails additional costs. If we want to integrate these d0 and thus save costs d0 it is clear that the EU has more opportunities to take things in this direction than, for example, the Finnish authorities alone. Naturally, the same applies to all international, treaty-based activities. The prerequisite, of course, is that the EU countries are able to agree among themselves on their common positions first d0 something that the EU is increasingly working towards. These examples are important, but the most important thing for entrepreneurship d0 especially for companies in the SME sector d0 is the creation of an EU-wide domestic market. This opens up new opportunities, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises. I therefore believe that it would be worthwhile for these companies to redouble their efforts to conquer the large and prosperous markets of the euro area. Improving the functioning of the single market is also at the heart of the Lisbon Strategy. The AIM of the EU's single market programme is to build a large domestic market in Europe that provides the best possible conditions for entrepreneurship. In an open and extensive common market, it is more profitable to innovate and commercialise than it would be in a limited national market. The idea of a large common market is at the heart of the eu as a whole and, at the same time, the Union's greatest achievement in terms of business. The euro is an essential element in the completion of the common market. As a result of the introduction of the single currency, previously significant exchange rate risks were eliminated and exchange charges were eliminated for intraeuro area transactions. This laid the foundations for the functioning of a genuine common market. Let us remember that the European Commission pushed ahead with the monetary union project with the symbol 'one market d0 one money'. In line with my professional background, I will now focus on the importance of the integration of the euro and the financial markets around business. The generally accepted view is that the best way for a central bank to promote business conditions is to pursue a long-term and consistent monetary policy geared towards price stability, thereby establishing and maintaining permanent monetary stability. The central bank's task is also to promote the functioning of the financial system, in particular the smooth flow of payments. In my speech, I will examine the opportunities for business offered by the euro and our single monetary policy, as well as the integrating European financial marketsd0 especially for small and medium-sized enterprises in the service sector, which in Finland and the EU more generally are considered to have exploited opportunities. The euro brings stability d0 the ECB's monetary policy a success The most visible significance of the non-use of the euro was that previously significant exchange rate risks within the euro area were eliminated and thus the euro area markets have become more closely interlinked. The disappearance of exchange rate risks and the absence of exchange costs have benefited the consumer and improved the opportunities for companies to internationalise. Competition in this respect has evened out, not only for large companies, but right down to the grassroots d0 for small and medium-sized entrepreneurs. After all, it is understandably more difficult for small businesses to operate in several currencies and to hedge against exchange rate risks. It is undeniable that, in its first few years, the European Central Bank's monetary policy has been more successful than hardly anyone could have anticipated or even hoped for beforehand. Despite the challenging conditions d0 I am referring in particular here to the strong fluctuations in the international economic cycle and in the prices of ljy and other raw materials d0 the European Central Bank has managed to keep inflation low in the euro area. Interestingly, in fact, price stability has been achieved without even having to resort to a heavy-handed monetary policy. The European Central Bank managed to quickly gain the confidence of the public and the markets in its monetary policy or, as economists say, to ensure the credibility of its monetary policy. The credibility of the single monetary policy is clearly and tangible reflected in the current low market interest rates and low inflation in the euro area financial markets. Furthermore, as a major currency, the euro is not as easy a target for speculative currency jumps as many of its predecessor currencies and, in this sense, it also provides good protection for the inhabitants of the euro area from speculative pressures on the foreign exchange markets, although fluctuations in the exchange rate of the euro against non-euro currencies, such as the dollar, are, of course, a fact of life under the conditions of monetary union and cannot be overcome by intra-European arrangements. The second reason for the low level of speculative pressure, which is at least as important in the case of the euro area, is the independence of the European Central Bank d0 the fact that the monetary policy decision-making of the European Central Bank is better protected from pressure from political decision-making and preferential systems than the central banks of most small currency areas. For example, the external value of the euro, despite its strong appreciation, is now only more or less at the 1999 level, as is, for example, Finland's price competitiveness. It should be remembered that Finland joined the euro area at an exchange rate that was generally considered to be undervalued rather than overvalued. Despite the appreciation of the euro, the profitability of industry is at a good level, largely thanks to its own previous efforts. Thus, at least from the point of view of Finnish companies, the appreciation of the euro is best understood as a return from the previous exceptionally low level to the normal level, and not as a deviation from the normal level to an exceptionally high level. One might ask what would have happened if Finland still had its own currency and if the markka had strengthened against the US dollar by 50% in four years and the markka's currency index by 30%. It is never possible to get a real answer to this question. However, in the light of past experience, it is not inconceivable that we should now d0 and probably have had a long time in the past d0 a lively debate on the correction of the exchange rate of the markka and that, in addition to economists, economic lobbies and various political forces should take full part in this debate. Nor would it be inconceivable that, perhaps for purely expedient reasons, the main focus of the debate should have been on recent developments in the exchange rate since the year 2000. In a small open economy, such an atmosphere of debate easily leads to suspicions of currency devaluation and high interest rates, and often expectations begin to feed themselves. In such a situation, it is difficult for the central bank to maintain a climate of stability for very long. The danger of continuing our long-standing spiral of devaluation and inflation would have been obvious; the currency would once again have been allowed to devalue in a situation where it should have been revalued. The scenario is, of course, completely hypothetical, and there can never be full clarity on the matter. However, I think it is fair to suggest that our previous exchange rate debate and policy contained a significant dose of short-term devaluation. This policy sought to support growth and investment and was probably believed in many quarters to support entrepreneurship. I think this was a misunderstanding. Instead of entrepreneurship, support was given to traditional sectors in difficulty, mainly the forest industry, and to firms in difficulty, especially large export companies. However, by shackling the functioning of the financial markets and directing scarce financial resources primarily to existing large-scale industry, the emergence and development of small and innovative enterprises was made more difficult d0 apparently unintentionally. The single monetary policy and the climate of stability built by the European Central Bank have created a financially stable environment for companies and households, which, for example, in Finland, has sustained domestic demand and employment development even during the international recession. The euro has significantly clarified the division of responsibilities in economic policy and, more generally, economic responsibilities. The economic policy responsibility for national price stability and competitiveness d0 that is, price stability vis-88-vis the rest of the euro area and competitiveness in global markets d0 clearly lies with fiscal and labour market policies, ultimately with individual decision-makers in various quarters, not least companies. Mistakes in economic policy or business can no longer be corrected retrospectively by means of exchange rate policy in the same way as they have often been in the past. In my opinion, most decision-makers in Finland have understood this quite well. Both the public sector and companies knew how to use the income from the previous boom and the weak euro wisely, and inflation remained well under control. Caution should continue to be exercised. The global economy is now experiencing a boom, but there is no guarantee that it will continue to be as strong as it is today for a long time. Exchange rate developments are even more difficult to predict than real GDP developments, but past experience suggests that large fluctuations in exchange rates are still possible and even verifiable in the future. Europe-wide, truly integrated financial markets play a key role in promoting business ... With the advent of the euro, the opportunities for creating a truly Pan-European financial market have improved. The introduction of the euro considerably calmed down the monetary conditions in Europe. This has already had its own mythical effect on the integration of European financial markets. We are closer to the objective of having access for companies to a Europe-wide financial market that guarantees the widest range of services at the most competitive prices, and that it should not matter from the point of view of invoicing and the management of payment transactions whether there are transactions between different countries in the euro area or within one country. Indeed, after the introduction of the euro, a certain part of the euro area's financial markets were almost fully integrated very quickly; for example, the unsecured interbank short-money market currently operates smoothly and uniformly throughout the euro area. Progress has also been made in other market segments, but the creation of truly common financial markets is progressing slowly. Financial markets in the euro area remain segmented in many respects. Although the introduction of the single currency removed one of the main obstacles to the single market in the euro area, the emergence of a common financial market remains constrained by a number of major frictions. These are based in part on the acceptance of existing conditions and the short defence of local interests. In particular, there is fierce wrestling going on to defend financial centers. On the other hand, there are also genuine legislative (such as tax and bankruptcy law) as well as differences in technical control systems and administrative authorisation procedures. Financial market infrastructures, such as securities clearing houses, operate differently in different countries and are not easy to combine into a single entity. The differences are essentially due to the fact that national systems and legislation have been gradually formed from each country's own starting points. When I have been asked to speak to entrepreneurs on various occasions, I have wanted to highlight precisely the need for integration of the EU's financial markets. While the friction that hinders integration there are a lot of them, I am optimistic about the integration process of the EU's financial markets. The benefits of a truly unified pan-European financial market are simply too great for us to ignore. A well-functioning, truly Pan-European financial market has a key role to play in reviving economic dynamism. Without well-functioning, EU-wide financial markets, the EU single market will not function properly and its benefits will not be fully absorbed by businesses. The development and regulatory integration of financial markets has been, and will continue to be, at the heart of the EU's economic policy cooperation over the next few years. It is now important to implement the financial market legislation and supervisory framework contained in the Financial Services Action Plan (FSAP), which is coming to an end. In the future, the aim will be a single European payments area instead of the current fragmented payment system structure. Example: Cross-border payment transactions becoming easier The latter objective of a single payment area is a good example of long-term cooperation at EU level. Initially, the European Commission and the European System of Central Banks (ESCB) will both work to promote retail payments in euro in the euro area on the basis of voluntary cooperation between banks. However, no significant progress could be observed. When the euro cash was introduced at the beginning of 2002, the Commission began to prepare a regulation at a rapid pace to develop cross-border retail payments in euro. In July 2002, a regulation on retail payments entered into force, requiring uniform pricing for domestic and crossborder retail payments in euro to customers.
