EU:n yhteismarkkinaohjelman pyrkimyksen on rakentaa Eurooppaan laajat kotimarkkinat, jotka antavat yrittmiselle parhaat mahdolliset edellytykset. Avoimilla ja laajoilla yhteismarkkinoilla innovaatioiden tekeminen ja tuotteistaminen on kannattavampaa kuin mit se olisi suppeilla kansallisilla markkinoilla. Ajatus laajoista yhteismarkkinoista on koko EU:n ydin ja samalla unionin suurin saavutus yritystoiminnan kannalta. Euro on keskeinen osa yhteismarkkinoiden toteuttamista. Yhteisen rahan kyttnoton seurauksena aikaisemmin merkittvt valuuttakurssiriskit poistuivat ja valuutanvaihtokulut jivt pois euroalueen sisisiss taloustoimissa. Nin luotiin pohja todellisten yhteismarkkinoiden toiminnalle. Muistakaamme, ett EU:n komissio ajoi rahaliittohanketta mrtietoisesti eteenpin tunnuksenaan "yhdet markkinat  yksi raha". Keskityn seuraavaksi ammattitaustani mukaisesti ksittelemn euron ja rahoitusmarkkinoiden integraation merkityst yritystoiminnan ympristlle. Yleisesti hyvksytty nkemys on, ett keskuspankki edist yritystoiminnan edellytyksi parhaiten harjoittamalla pitkjnteist ja johdonmukaista hintavakauteen thtv rahapolitiikkaa ja luomalla ja silyttmll tt kautta pysyvsti vakaat rahaolot. Keskuspankin tehtvn on my edist rahoitusjrjestelmn toimivuutta, etenkin maksuliikenteen sujuvuutta. Nist keskuspankin lhtohdista tarkastelen puheenvuorossani euron ja yhteisen rahapolitiikkamme sek integroituvien eurooppalaisten rahoitusmarkkinoiden tuomia mahdollisuuksia yritystoiminnalle  erityisesti palvelusektorin pienille ja keskisuurille yrityksille, joissa Suomessa ja EU:ssa yleisemminkin katsotaan olevan kyttmtti mahdollisuuksia. Euro tuonut vakautta  EKP:n rahapolitiikka onnistunutta Euron kyttnoton nkyvin merkitys oli sit, ett aikaisemmin merkittvt valuuttakurssiriskit euroalueen sisll poistuivat ja nin euroalueen markkinat ovat entist tiiviimmin kytkeytyneet toisiinsa. Valuuttakurssiriskien hviminen ja valuutanvaihtokulujen jminen pois on hydyttnyt kuluttajaa ja parantanut yritysten kansainvlistymismahdollisuuksia. Kilpailun lhtohdat silt osin ovat tasoittuneet, ei vain suuryrityksille vaan aivan ruohonjuuritasolle asti  pienille ja keskisuurille yrittjille. Pienten yritystenhn on ymmrrettvist syist suuria vaikeampaa toimia useissa valuutoissa ja suojautua valuuttakurssiriskeilt. Kiistatta voitaneen sanoa, ett ensimmisten vuosiensa aikana Euroopan keskuspankin rahapolitiikka on onnistunut paremmin kuin tuskin kukaan osasi etukteen odottaa tai edes toivoa. Vaikka olosuhteet ovat ollet haastavat  viittaan tss erityisesti kansainvlisten suhdanteiden sek ljyn ja muiden raakaaineiden hintojen voimakkaisiin vaihteluihin  Euroopan keskuspankki on onnistunut silyttmn inflaation alhaisena euroalueella. Mielenkiintoista on, ett itse asiassa hintavakaus on onnistuttu varmistamaan tarvitsematta edes turvautua kovaotteiseen rahapolitiikkaan. Euroopan keskuspankki onnistui saamaan rahapolitiikalleen nopeasti kansalaisten ja markkinoiden luottamuksen tai kuten ekonomistit sanovat, varmistamaan rahapolitiikkansa uskottavuuden. Yhteisen rahapolitiikan uskottavuus nkyy euroalueen rahoitusmarkkinoilla selvsti ja kouriintuntuvasti nykyisiss matalissa markkinakoroissa ja alhaisessa inflaatiossa. Lisksi suurena valuuttana euro ei ole samanlainen helppo kohde spekulatiivisille valuuttahykkyksille kuin monet sen edeltjvaluutat, ja tss mieless se my tarjoaa hyvn suojan euroalueen asukkaille valuuttamarkkinoiden keinottelupaineilta, vaikkakin euron kurssivaihtelut euroaleen ulkopuolisiin valuuttoihin, mm. dollariin, nhden ovat tietenkin tosiasia my rahaliiton oloissa, eik niit voida Euroopan sisisin jrjestelyin voittaa. Toinen, euroalueen tapauksessa vhintn yht trke syy keinottelupaineiden vhisyydelle on Euroopan keskuspankin riippumattomuus  se, ett Euroopan keskuspankin rahapoliittinen ptsenteko on paremmin suojassa poliittisen ptsenteon ja etujrjesten tahoilta tulevilta paineilta kuin useimpien pienten valuutta-alueiden keskuspankit. Esimerkiksi euron ulkoinen arvo on voimakkaasta vahvistumisestaan huolimatta nyt vain jokseenkin vuoden 1999 tasolla, kuten on esimerkiksi Suomen hintakilpailukykykin. On muistettava, ett Suomi liittyi euroalueeseen vaihtokurssilla, joka yleisesti katsottiin pikemminkin ali-kuin yliarvostetuksi. Euron vahvistumisesta huolimatta teollisuuden kannattavuus on hyvll tasolla, paljolti teollisuuden omien, aikaisempien toimien ansiosta. Ainakin suomalaisten yritysten nkkulmasta euron vahvistuminen on siis parhaiten ymmrrettviss paluuna aikaisemmalta poikkeuksellisen alhaiselta tasolla normaalitasolle, ei poikkeamana normaalitasolta poikkeuksellisen korkealle tasolle. Voidaan kysy, mit olisi tapahtunut, jos Suomella olisi edelleen oma valuutta ja jos markka olisi neljss vuodessa vahvistunut Yhdysvaltain dollariin nhden 50 prosenttia ja markan valuuttaindeksikin 30 prosenttia. Thn kysymykseen ei ole mahdollista saada koskaan todellista vastausta. Aikaisemman kokemuksen valossa ei kuitenkaan ole mahdotonta, ett meill kytisiin nyt  ja todennkisesti olisi kyty jo pitkn aikaisemmin  vilkasta keskustelua markan valuuttakurssin korjaamisesta ja ett thn keskusteluun ottaisivat ekonomistien ohella osaa tysipainoisesti talouselmn painostusryhmt ja eri poliittiset tahot. Mahdotonta ei olisi sekn, ett phuomio keskustelussa olisi ehk puhtaasti tarkoituksenmukaisuussyist kiinnittynyt nimenomaan valuuttakurssin viimeaikaiseen, vuoden 2000 jlkeiseen kehitykseen. Pieness avoimessa taloudessa tllainen keskusteluilmapiiri helposti johtaa valuutan devalvoitumisepilyksiin ja korkeisiin korkoihin ja usein odotukset ryhtyvt ruokkimaan itsen. Tllaisessa tilanteessa keskuspankin on vaikea pit yll vakauden ilmapiiri kovin pitkn. Vaara pitkn kestneen devalvaatio-inflaatiokierteemme jatkumisesta olisikin ollut ilmeinen; valuutan olisi jlleen kerran annettu devalvoitua sellaisessa tilanteessa, jossa sen olisi pitnyt revalvoitua. Skenaario on tietenkin tysin hypoteettinen, eik asiaan voida saada koskaan tytt selvyytt. Kuitenkin mielestni voidaan perustellusti esitt, ett aikaisempaan valuuttakurssikeskusteluumme ja -politiikkaamme sisltyi tuntuva annos lyhytjnteist devalvaatiopolitiikkaa. Tm politiikka pyrki tukemaan kasvua ja investointeja ja varmaan monilla tahoilla sen uskottiin tukevan mys yrittjyytt. Tm oli mielestni vrinksitys. Yrittjyyden asemasta tuettiin vaikeuksiin joutuneita perinteisi toimialoja, lhinn metsteollisuutta, ja vaikeuksiin joutuneita yrityksi, erityisesti suuria vientiyrityksi. Rahoitusmarkkinoiden toimintaa kahlitsemalla ja ohjaamalla niukat rahoitusresurssit ensisijaisesti olemassa olevalle suurteollisuudelle vaikeutettiin kuitenkin  ilmeisesti tahtomatta  pienten ja innovatiivisten yritysten syntymist ja kehittymist. Yhteinen rahapolitiikka ja Euroopan keskuspankin rakentama vakauden ilmapiiri ovat luoneet yrityksille ja kotitalouksille rahataloudellisesti vakaan toimintaympristn, joka on esimerkiksi meill Suomessa yllpitnyt kotimaista kysynt ja tyllisyyskehityst kansainvlisen taantumankin aikana. Euro on selkeyttnyt talouspolitiikan vastuunjakoa ja yleisemminkin taloudellisia vastuita tuntuvasti. Talouspoliittinen vastuu kansallisesta hintavakaudesta ja kilpailukyvyst  siis hintavakaudesta suhteessa muuhun euroalueeseen ja kilpailukyvyst globaaleilla markkinoilla  kuuluu selkesti finanssi- ja tymarkkinapolitiikalle, viime kdess yksittisille ptksentekijille eri tahoilla, ei vhiten yrityksiss. Talouspolitiikan tai yritystoiminnan virheit ei voi en paikata jlkikteen valuuttakurssipolitiikan keinoin samalla tavalla kuin useasti aikaisemmin. Tmn ovat mielestni useimmat ptksentekijt Suomessa varsin hyvin ymmrtneet. Sek julkinen sektori ett yritykset osasivat kytt edellisen noususuhdanteen ja heikon euron mukanaan tuomat tulot viisaasti, ja inflaatio pysyi hyvin kurissa. Varovaisuuteen on syyt jatkossakin. Maailmantaloudessa on nyt meneilln nousukausi, mutta ei ole mitn takeita siit, ett se jatkuisi pitkn yht voimakkaana kuin nykyisin. Valuuttakurssien kehityst on viel vaikeampi ennustaa kuin kokonaistuotannon kehityst, mutta aikaisemman kokemuksen perusteella kurssien suuret vaihtelut ovat tulevaisuudessakin mahdollisia ja jopa todennksi. Euroopan laajuiset, aidosti integroituneet rahoitusmarkkinat keskeisess asemassa yritystoiminnan edistmisess  Euron my my mahdollisuudet luoda aidosti Euroopan laajuiset rahoitusmarkkinat ovat parantuneet. Euron kyttnotto rauhoitti tuntuvasti Euroopan rahaoloja. Tll on jo ollut oma myteinen vaikutuksensa Euroopan rahoitusmarkkinoiden yhdentymiseen. Olemme lhempn tavoitetta, ett yritysten kytss olisivat Euroopan laajuiset rahoitusmarkkinat, jotka takaavat laajimmat palvelut kilpailukykyisimpiin hintoihin ja ett laskuttamisen ja maksuliikenteen hoidon kannalta ei pitisi olla merkityst, asioidaanko euroalueen eri maiden vlill vai yhden maan sisll. Euron kyttnoton jlkeen tietty osa euroalueen rahoitusmarkkinoista integroituikin erittin nopeasti lhes tysin; esimerkiksi pankkien vliset vakuudettomat lyhyen rahan markkinat toimivat nykyisin kitkatta ja yhtenisesti koko euroalueella. Edistyst on tapahtunut muillakin markkinalohkoilla, mutta aidosti yhteisten rahoitusmarkkinoiden luominen etenee hitaasti. Euroalueen rahoitusmarkkinat ovat edelleen monessa suhteessa lohkoutuneet. Vaikka yhteisen rahan kyttnotto poisti euroalueella yhden merkittvimmist yhteisten markkinoiden esteist, yhteisten rahoitusmarkkinoiden syntymist rajoittavat edelleen monet merkittvt kitkatekijt. Nm perustuvat osaksi olemassa olevien olojen hyvksymiseen ja paikallisten intressien lyhytnkseen puolustamiseen. Erityisesti finanssikeskusten puolustamiseksi kydn ankaraa painia. Toisaalta yhdentymisen tiell on mys aitoja lainsdnnllisi (kuten verotus-ja konkurssilainsdntn liittyvi) sek teknisi valvontajrjestelmien ja hallinnollisten lupamenettelyjen eroja. Rahoitusmarkkinoiden perusrakenteet kuten arvopapereiden selvityskeskukset toimivat eri maissa eri tavoin, eik niit ole helppo yhdist yhdeksi kokonaisuudeksi. Erot johtuvat olennaisesti siit, ett kansalliset jrjestelmt ja lainsdnnt ovat muodostuneet asteittain kunkin maan omista lhtohdista ksin. Kun minua on pyydetty puhumaan erilaisissa tilaisuuksissa yrittjille, olen halunnut tuoda esille nimenomaan EU:n rahoitusmarkkinoiden integraation tarpeellisuuden. Vaikka yhdentymist jarruttavia kitkate kijit on paljon, olen optimistinen EU:n rahoitusmarkkinoiden yhdentymiskehityksen suhteen. Edut aidosti yhtenisist Euroopan laajuisista rahoitusmarkkinoista yksinkertaisesti ovat liian suuret, jotta voisimme jtt ne hydyntmtt. Talouden dynamiikan elvyttmisess hyvin toimivat, aidosti Euroopan laajuiset rahoitusmarkkinat ovat keskeisess asemassa. Ilman hyvin toimivia, EU:n laajuisia rahoitusmarkkinoita EU:n sismarkkinat eivt toimi kunnolla eivtk yritykset voi tysimrisesti hyyttaa niiden etuja. Rahoitusmarkkinoiden kehittmisty ja stelyn yhtenistminen on ollut ja on vastedeskin EU:n talouspoliittisessa yhteistyss keskeisell sijalla lhivuosina. Nyt on trke panna toimeen pttymss olevaan rahoituspalvelujen toimintasuunnitelmaan (Financial Services Action Plan  FSAP) sisltyv rahoitusmarkkinalainsdntja valvontakehikko. Jatkossa tavoitteena on yhteninen eurooppalainen maksualue nykyisen pirstoutuneen maksujrjestelmrakenteen sijaan. Esimerkki: Rajat ylittv maksuliikenne helpottumassa Viimemainittu tavoite yhtenisest maksualueesta on hyv esimerkki pitkjnteisest EU-tason yhteistyst. Aluksi EU:n komissio ja Euroopan keskuspankkijrjestelm (EKPJ) pyrkivt kumpikin edistmn euromrist vhittismaksamista euroalueella pankkien vapaaehtoisen yhteisty pohjalta. Merkittv edistyst ei kuitenkaan voitu havaita. Kun eurokteinen otettiin kyttn 2002 alussa, komissio ryhtyi valmistelemaan nopeassa tahdissa asetusta rajan ylittvn euromrisen vhittismaksamisen kehittmiseksi. Heinkuussa 2002 tuli voimaan vhittismaksamista koskeva asetus, joka edellytti kotimaisten ja rajanylittvien euromristen vhittismaksujen yhtenist hinnoittelua asiakkaille. Aluksi asetus koski vain korttimaksamista ja automaattinostoja, mutta heinkuusta 2003 se on ulottunut my alle 12.500,- euron mrisiin tilisiirtoihin. Asetus nopeutti merkittvsti EU-maiden pankkien toimia rajat ylittvn maksamisen tehostamiseksi. Isoimmat pankit ja EU-pankkiyhdistykset perustivat keskuussa 2002 eurooppalaisen neuvotteluelimen EPC:n (European paymets council). Tm ryhtyi laatimaan suunnitelmia yhden yhtenisen maksualueen (SEPA=Single euro payment area) luomiseksi euroalueelle vuoteen 2010 menness. Tavoitteena on mm., ett jo vuonna 2008 kansalaisten peruspalvelut tavalliset tilisiirrot, pikasiirrot ja suoraveloitukset  toimisivat SEPA-laajuisesti. Suomen edustajina EPC-yhteistys ovat olleet erityisesti Nordea ja Suomen Pankkiyhdistys. Maksupalvelujen hinnoittelua koskevaa EU-asetusta voidaan sinns pit pienen mutta merkittvn edistysaskeleena Euroopan rahoitusmarkkinoiden integraatiossa. Suurten kansainvlisten yritysten maksuliikkeeseen asetus ei juuri vaikuta, mutta pienten ja keskisuurten yritysten  ja my tavallisten suomalaisten  maksut ulkomaille hoituvat sen ansiosta helpommin ja halvemmin.  Yhten esimerkkin Pohjois-Suomen elinkeinoista, jonka voikin odottaa lisntyvsti hyyvn euros-ta on matkailu. Matkailun alueella toimivat yritykset ovat pieni, mutta monilla niist on markkinointikontakteja laajalti Manner-Euroopassa. Sit mukaa kun asiakkaat lisntyvss mrin kyttvt interneti hankkiessan tietoa niden yritysten matkailupalveluksista, markkinointikontaktit muuttuvat sit paitsi yh enemmn ruohonjuuritasolle ja Suomen matkailumarkkinat integroituvat osaksi laajempia, Euroopan sismarkkinoita, euroalueen markkinoita. Hinnan noteeraaminen kotoisessa eurovaluutassa koko laajalla alueella, jossa asuu yli 300 miljoonaa ihmist, on tehostanut toimintaa olennaisesti. Matkailumarkkinat laajenevat ja kynnys tulla Suomeen madaltuu entisestn, kun maksuliike ra-jan yli helpottuu. Asetuksen ehk trkein merkitys on kuitenkin siin, ett se on vauhdittanut eurooppalaisten pankkien keskinist yhteistyt. Huolta on kuitenkin edelleen kannettava toteuttamisen aikataulusta. Viime viikolla EU:n sismarkkina-asiain komissaari Charlie McCreevy kehotti painokkaasti pankkeja tehostamaan toimiaan tavoitteen saavuttamisen suhteen. Hn nimenomaan sanoi, ett komissio ei aio katsoa hidasta edistymist sivusta toimettomana, vaan "tarvittaessa komissio tekee joistakin yhdess sovituista standardeista pakollisia ja sisllytt aikataulun yhtenisest maksualueesta lakiluonnokseen". Mys Euroopan keskuspankki on tuonut esille huolensa aikataulun hitaudesta. Paljon tehtv riskirahoitusmahdollisuuksien parantamiseksi  esimerkkin pomasijoittajien merkitys Mit tulee riskirahoitukseen, Yhdysvaltain rahoitusmarkkinat tarjoavat hyvn esimerkin rahoitusmahdollisuuksista, joita hyvin kehittyneet rahoitusmarkkinat tarjoavat yrityksille. Yrittjyyteen perustuvilla yhtill ja niden toteuttamilla innovaatioilla eli keksintjen kaupallisella hydyntmisell on ollut huomattava vaikutus maan talouden vahvaan kilpailukykyyn ja jatkuvasti nopeaan kasvuun. Yrittjyyden nousu Yhdysvalloissa on ollut paljolti mahdollista vain aktiivisten ja taitavien pomasijoittajien ansiosta, jotka sen lisksi, ett tuovat alkavaan yritykseen rahoitusta, my tarjoavat liikkeenjohdollista tukea ja samalla mys kontrolloivat yrityst. Ekonomistit, yritysjohtajat ja poliittiset ptksentekijt ovatkin nykyisin laajalti yht mielt siit, ett elinvoimainen pomasijoitustoiminta on maan innovatiivisuuden trkeimpi avaintekijt. Samalla tavoin uskotaan laajalti, ett pomasijoitustoiminnan heikkous on Euroopan talousdynamiikan heikkouden trke syy. Riskipoman tarjonta asukasta kohden on ollut Euroopassa karkeasti ottaen vain noin viidennes Yhdysvaltain tasosta. Toimet riskipomien tarjonnan lismiseksi Euroopassa ovat tervetulleita. EU ja jsenvaltiot ovatkin pyrkineet viime aikoina kiinnittmn huomiota pienten ja keskisuurten yritysten riskipoman saatavuuden turvaamiseen. On kuitenkin syyt huomata, ett rahoitusmarkkinat muodostavat tavallaan yhden kokonaisuuden ja ett esimerkiksi pomasijoitustoiminnan kukoistus Yhdysvalloissa perustuu paljolti rahoitusmarkkinoiden muiden lohkojen toimivuuteen. Mainitsen tst vain yhden esimerkin: Mahdollisuudet irtaantua tehdyist sijoituksista kannattavasti vaikuttavat huomattavasti pomasijoittajien halukkuuteen tehd sijoituksia ja kert uutta pomaa uusiin sijoituksiin. Pomasijoitustoiminnan kehitys riippuu siten mys siit, kuinka hyvin rahoitusjrjestelm tuottaa irtaantumismahdollisuuksia. Irtaantuminen tapahtuu esimerkiksi listautumalla prssiin. Pienill kansallisilla rahoitusmarkkinoilla irtaantumismahdollisuudet vistmtt ovat rajalliset. Tm kvi hyvin ilmi Elinkeinoelmn tutkimuslaitoksen selvityksest, jonka mukaan  huolimatta 1990-luvun vahvasta kehityksest  kotimaiset rahoitusmarkkinat eivt vlttmtt vastaa pomasijoittajien irtautumistarpeisiin. Syin thn ovat selvityksen mukaan mm. listautumismahdollisuuksien voimakas syklisyys, osakemarkkinoiden volatiilisuus sek ert muut kotimaisten markkinoiden ominaisuudet. Selv on, ett Euroopan poma- ja rahoitusmarkkinoiden yhdentyminen tarjoaisi merkittvi mahdollisuuksia parantaa pomasijoittajien irtaantumismahdollisia ja kehitt sit kautta koko pomasijoitustoimintaa. Integroitujen  laajojen ja syvien - riskirahoituksen markkinoiden kehittminen on trket innovatiivisille PK -yrityksille ja siten mys uusien typaikkojen synnylle. Erityisen paljon voitettavaa on niill yhtiill, jotka ovat periaatteessa kyllin suuria herttkseen ulkomaisten sijoittajien kiinnostusta, mutta kuitenkin sen verran pieni, ett osakkeiden markkinointi ulkomaille on thn asti ollut niiden toiminnan laajuuteen nhden liian kallista. Arvoisat kuulijat! Globalisaatio ei ole vain taloudellinen ilmi vaan sen juuret ovat yht selkesti kulttuuriset ja poliittiset. Globalisaatioprosessi on ilmin vanha, se on kiihtynyt 1990-luvulta lhtien ennenkaikkea tietoteknologian kehityksen ansiosta niin ett voimme oikeastaan sanoa, ett elmme jo nykyn maailmankylss. Globalisaatiota ei voi peruuttaa. Globalisaatio on pitklle kaikkien eduksi, mutta se aiheuttaa lyhyell aikavlill sopeutumisongelmia ja haasteita taantuvilla toimaloilla. EU:n integraatio on hyv asia. Ilman EU:n jsenyytt Suomi olisi yksininen lastu globalisaation valtavirrassa. Rahaliiton jsenyys ja euro ovat tuoneet yrityksille ja kuluttajille rahataloudellista vakautta ja te hostaneet eurooppalaisten sismarkkinoiden toimintaa nin tarjoten pk-yrityksillemme parempia mahdollisuuksia laajentaa toimintaansa euroalueen varakkailla markkinoilla. My mit tulee rintamaiden ja reuna-alueiden vliseen suhteeseen, pidn euroa suurena tasoittajana, joka antaa pitklti samat rahoitukselliset ja markkinointilhtkohdat riippumatta siit onko sijaintipaikkana Keski-Euroopan ydinalue tai Lappi. Haluan kuitenkin korostaa, ett rahatalous tai talouspolitiikan keinot yleisemminkin voivat vain luoda edellytyksi menestyksellisen yritystoiminnan todellisille perustekijlle  niin ett innovatiivisuus, yrittjyys ja ahkeruus psevt vaikuttamaan. Niss perustekijiss yritykset ja yrittjt itse ovat tietenkin aivan keskeisess asemassa. Reuna-alueilla taloudellinen menestys vaatii kunkin alueen oman erityisluonteen ja edellytysten oivaltamista ja sen nkemist kansainvlisen asiakkaan nkulmasta. Ja lopuksi viel: Suomi on ollut homogeeninen ja verrattain eriytynyt maa nihin aikoihin asti. Uudessa globaalissa verkottuneessa taloudessa eletn ympristss, jossa on kyettv kulttuurien vliseen keskusteluun. Suomalaisten on kehitettv kulttuurisia valmiuksia  opittava elmn ja toimimaan monikulttuurisessa ymprists  opittava my vastaanottamaan siirtolaisia muualta. Pohjolasta ja Euroopasta ksin meidn suomalaisten on paitsi osattava kyd kauppaa my annettava oma panos globaalien ongelmien ratkaisemisessa.

Title: Speech on "Change in the operating environment of banks and prospects for the future" at OP Group's annual meeting
text: President and CEO Erkki Liikanen: CHANGE IN THE BANKING ENVIRONMENT AND FUTURE PROSPECTS OP Group's annual meeting 31.3.2005, Finlandia Hall, Helsinki Mr President, dear people of cooperative banks, my intention today is to deal with the changes in the environment in which banks operate. The OP group that you represent is a good example of how a financial group that relies heavily on a national strategy can successfully adapt to the change in its operating environment, the key features of which are integration and internationalisation. Key features of the change in the operating environment Until the early 1980s, the Finnish financial markets were heavily regulated and poorly developed. After that, the development of the deregulation and financial markets accelerated rapidly. The unprecedented growth in lending associated with the transition period significantly overheated the national economy. When the economic cycle turned, the Finnish economy entered a deep recession and the banking sector was plunged into a serious crisis. During and after the recession and the banking crisis, the development and structural changes in the Finnish financial markets have continued to be strong. The pace of change has been increased by many global and EU-level factors, but there have also been national specificities. The sharp fall in the prices of information and communication technologies and services has enabled the rapid development and non-use of financial innovation. Technical developments have had a major impact on the distribution channels, risk management and market infrastructure of financial institutions as a whole. In particular, the expansion of internment has had a strong impact on the production and provision of banking services. Finland's membership of the EU in 1995, which was preceded by a one-year EEA period, marked a major change. A key objective of the EU has been to liberalise the movement of goods, goods, services and capital between its member states. This was the basis for the creation of the EEC in 1958, but the breakthrough in the creation of the internal market came three decades later, when the internal market was covered by a fixed majority. Since 1993, however, the common internal market has been a reality with a few important exceptions, perhaps the most important of which has been the financial markets. Since then, efforts have been made to accelerate the integration of financial and capital markets through a dedicated financial services action plan. Progress has been made, yet it will take several more years to implement the entire programme in national legislation. The launch of the third stage of economic and monetary union (EMU) at the beginning of 1999 significantly changed the operating environment of Finnish financial institutions and other companies. It removed exchange rate risk from intra-euro area transactions and stabilised interest rates around the euro area. FIGURE 1. 3-month interest rate for euro area countries FIGURE 2. 10-year interest rate for euro area countries The single currency and the single monetary policy also contributed to the acceleration of the integration of financial markets between the euro area countries. Integration has progressed most far in the wholesale financial market and, in particular, in the short-money debt market. In contrast, retail market integration has progressed more slowly. Of course, the introduction of the euro cash has improved the cross-border comparability of prices for products and services. But households and SMEs make relatively little use of financial services from other countries. FIGURE 3. Developments in the importance of interbank lending in the euro area At the same time, demographic factors  especially ageing and prosperity  have had a significant impact on the demand for various savings products. The pool of small investors has expanded as the population has become wealthier. FIGURE 4. Households' financial assets in Finland Many Finns have also started saving and investing to supplement the income provided by the pension after the end of their employment. The share of alternative forms of saving to bank deposits began to grow significantly in Finland at the end of the last decade. Key knock-on effects in the banking sector Over the past two decades, the Finnish financial markets have undergone unprecedented changes. The internationalisation of financial markets has intensified competition. Institutions that have traditionally operated in the market have found themselves in a situation where regulatory protection has weakened, shareholder return requirements and market discipline have increased, while competition has intensified with the arrival of new institutions either in the market or in the face of a significant increase in the threat of entry. In order to succeed in today's environment, a financial services company must operate efficiently. The capacity of banks has been reduced to about half of the period before the banking crisis of the early 1990s. Efforts have been made to increase service channels through the Internet and mergers and cooperation agreements. FIGURE 5. Development of the distribution network of banks OP Group's customers paid only about 6% of their invoices as customer service at branches, and Internet payments accounted for more than 50% of personnel invoices in 2004. Productivity development in the Finnish financial sector has been exceptionally good. This has been influenced by investments in information technology that have already begun under the conditions of interest rate regulation, by increased competition and by the new IT-based services and processes created as a result of these combined, and at the same time by strong cost control. The change in the competitive situation has been reflected in the development of interest margins on bank credit  different interest margins on mortgages sold to households have fallen significantly; From the level of the late 1990s. Interest margins on corporate loans are more sensitive to cyclical fluctuations in the economy than on household loans. FIGURE 6. Development of interest margins on new housing and business loans Another key knock-on effect in the financial sector has been strong structural change. The banking sector has experienced the biggest structural changes, but there have been significant developments in other segments of the financial markets. The benefits of co-production of financial services have been sought through mergers and collaborations. Returns have been sought both in new financial services sectors and across borders. The demarcation barriers between the banking and insurance sectors have largely already fallen. Impact on banks' customers The most visible effects of the actual development have been on households and, in particular, on the housing market. Over the past five years, house prices in Finland have risen by an average of about 3.5% per year in real terms. The growth rate of mortgage lending over the same period has been considerable  in 2004, the stock of mortgage loans grew by just over 15%. Cost-burdening of owner-occupied housing  the so-called "cost burden" that takes into account changes in interest rates and loan periods. the extended debt burden index  has declined clearly in Finland since the start of the third stage of economic and monetary union. FIGURE 7. Burden indices of owner-occupied housing The annual financial expenditure (sum of interest expenses and repayments) arising from the acquisition of one residential unit has substantially decreased relative to the disposable income of the median household. This is due to both a decrease in interest rates and an increase in loan periods. Indeed, the rise in house prices in recent years can largely be explained by the demand factor: the combined effect of rising household incomes, lower interest rates and longer borrowing periods. In the corporate sector, the most visible impact  in addition to the significant stabilisation of foreign exchange and interest rates  has been the increased range of financing options and the growing importance of foreign financing. FIGURE 8. Breakdown of the stock of credit in the non-financial corporations sector by lender The increase in the role of foreign lenders has been mainly reflected in large companies, as the financing of small and medium-sized enterprises is still strongly at the national level. Looking at the domestic lending sectors alone, we see that deposit banks accounted for a record high of around 64% at the end of 2004. Correspondingly, the relative importance of other financial institutions and insurance and employment pension schemes as financiers of enterprises has decreased. Looking at the demand for credit in the corporate sector, it should be noted that the deep recession of the early 1990s, changes in taxation and expectations of the tightening competitive environment through EU membership forced the Finnish corporate sector to strengthen its financial structures. Non-financial corporations increased their equity financing and sharply reduced their indebtedness in the late 1990s. This change in demand forced the financial services sector to adjust supply and invest in new products. Near-term challenges Banks play a strong role in financing households and providing savings instruments. The importance of households as customers of Finnish banks has become more pronounced  in 1990, corporate loans still accounted for about half of banks' lending to the general public, but at the end of last year only good one-third. The first challenge for banks is related to the high level of indebtedness of Finnish households in recent years. The stock of credit in the household sector has grown faster than disposable income since 1998 and the indebtedness ratio has risen to over 15% and 75% in six years. FIGURE 9. Households' indebtedness and interest expenses in Finland The ratio of households' stock of mortgage loans to disposable income exceeds the pre-recession level of the early 1990s. By contrast, there are clearly fewer consumer and student credits and other credits, mainly related to business activities, relative to income than at the end of the 1980s. However, as already mentioned above, thanks to the fall in interest rates and the lengthening of loan periods, the debt servicing burden has fallen markedly in recent years. In addition, the average indebtedness of Finnish households is still reasonable both historically and internationally. The concerns raised by the high level of household indebtedness relate, on the one hand, to the potentially uneven distribution of the debt burden in the household sector and, on the other hand, to interest rate fixing on credit. Unfortunately, very recent statistics on the distribution of households' debt burden are not available. Households heavily indebted in 2002  i.e. those with housing loans that were at least three times their annual income  just over 7% of households. Under two per cent of debtors had large mortgages of over EUR 150,000. They accounted for more than 7% of the total mortgage portfolio. Over the past two years, the share of these heavily indebted households has probably grown. More than 90% of the euro-denominated loan portfolio sold by deposit banks to households is tied to variable interest rates  the vast majority in the 12-month euribor, which is reviewed every year. Thus, indebted households are exposed to significant interest rate risk. Although household risk awareness seems to have increased and an increasing number of households with housing loans have already taken out bank-provided loan protection insurance or other protection against rising interest rates, it is worth monitoring the development of the situation very carefully. Demand for household credit is likely to continue to grow, but at a slower pace. It is in the interests of all parties that, in due course, the inevitable slowdown of the household credit boom to normal levels should take place in an orderly manner. Another challenge in the near future relates to the change in the structure of bank funding. FIGURE 10. Ratio of MFI credits and deposits Even before the start of the third stage of economic and monetary union, banks had more deposits than loans, but the situation has changed dramatically in recent years. As the growth rate of the credit portfolio has long exceeded the growth rate of the deposit stock, banks have increasingly resorted to market-based financing to finance lending. In the current conditions of exceptionally high global liquidity, market-based financing is historically available at a low price  although clearly more expensive than deposit money. We are currently living in an exceptional time and the current situation cannot be permanent. Euro area-wide money and capital markets provide an effective channel for mobilising market-based financing. However, market-based money is sensitive and reacts quickly to changes in credit rating, for example. The changed situation poses greater challenges to banks' liquidity management. The third factor worth noting is the development of the competitive situation. Price competition from banks in the mortgage market is fierce, which has been reflected in a clear narrowing of interest margins. On the other hand, price competition for consumer credit, as well as for most savings products, has so far been rather subdued. As EU integration progresses and deepens, as well as the impact on the retail financial services market, the pressure for tightening of competition in other areas of the banks' business is also likely to increase in the future. Medium- and long-term challenges Banks' medium- and long-term challenges are linked to the future prospects of the Finnish economy  after all, the basis of banks' performance is fundamentally very strongly linked to general economic development. For several years now, economic growth in Finland has been about double the average growth rate in the euro area. Last year, growth picked up above expectations. Growth is expected to remain relatively strong by European standards in the following years. After 2006, however, growth will slow down markedly unless productivity improves significantly and the boredom rate rises. There are many indications that supply constraints are gradually beginning to become an obstacle to economic growth. This is most clearly visible in the increase in imports. As a result, the current account surplus has almost halved since 2000. The problem of matching cannons has worsened. This can be seen in the fact that the number of open jobs has increased rapidly in relation to the number of girls. Residential construction is slowing down due to the shortage of plots. Normally, inflationary pressures intensify as economic growth begins to fall into supply constraints. There is no sign of this in Finland. Inflation is projected to remain low in the coming years. By all accounts, Finland's sensitivity to inflation has decreased. It has been influenced by many factors. The objective of price stability in the Economic and Monetary Union has shifted to expectations, which has affected wage formation and pricing decisions both in Finland and in other euro area countries. Increased competition keeps pricing in check even in times of good demand. While the appreciation of the euro has its own negative effects on exports, it has contributed to containing inflationary pressures in the euro area, thereby maintaining conditions in which interest rates could be kept very low. Global economic growth is projected to remain relatively high. The global economy thus provides opportunities for Finnish exporters. The essential question is how Finland will be able to make use of these opportunities. The growth in Finnish export volumes is expected to lag well behind the growth in export markets, as the growth of export markets is measured by the growth of imports from our most important export countries. This means that, in terms of export volumes, Finland will continue to lose market share in world trade. The decline in market shares may not be a serious acute problem, but from the point of view of a small open economy, it gives cause for concern about longer-term developments. It is to be feared that the problems of Finland's production structure and real export competitiveness will continue. Outside the electronics industry, investment in fixed investments and the development of competitive products has remained limited. Without sufficient investment, there is a risk that Finland's traditional export industry will run into even greater difficulties due to new competitors and that the structure of exports will not diversify quickly enough. If the productive structure of the economy were to solidify and unable to respond to changes in international demand, the prerequisites for productive activity and boring in Finland would weaken. For the financial sector, this would mean not only an increase in credit risks, but also a contraction of new business opportunities domestically and a slow growth in credit. Investment is the single most important use of financing by companies and thus has a significant impact on the demand for financial services. There is still a need for a quantitative increase in both fixed investment and R&D expenditure, although there is no going back to the overinvestment of the 1980s. Ultimately, more important than the volume of investments is their orientation to support the growth of productivity in the national economy as a whole and a more diversified production structure. In the light of the near-term economic outlook, we can therefore expect a favourable development for Finnish banks. However, for the longer-term development of the national economy, it would be important to increase the production potential. It requires investment and investment to improve productivity. This, in turn, would improve the conditions for economic activity in the long term everywhere, including in the banking sector.

Title: Speech at a seminar on cooperation between public administrations and entrepreneurs entitled "The impact of integration on the interaction between the school world and companies"
text: VTT Sinikka Salo Director Bank of Finland European cooperation in a globalising world Speech at the seminar "The impact of integration on the interaction between the school world and companies" at the House of the Estates 8.4.2005 In recent years, the debate on economic policy and even society in Finland has largely revolved around two megatrends: globalisation  which actually entered the Finnish debate only very recently in the so-called "green light". As a China phenomenon, i.e. the relocation of traditional industrial jobs to developing countries  and around the European megatrend of our time, i.e. EU integration. From Finland's point of view, these two parallel integration processes are closely linked to each other and should, in my opinion, be considered together. What I mean is that when discussing Finland's strategy in the global economy, neither Europe nor the EU can be bypassed. The EU is a key instrument for Finland, both economically and politically, when we participate in globa integration. It can be said that the EU is, in many respects, a kind of stepping stone by which Finland will take to the global stage. As a small country, we benefit a great deal from European cooperation, probably even more than the large Member States of the Union, which on the other hand, I believe need the EU more than they often admit. Eu cooperation is, of course, beneficial for Finland in itself, from the point of view of managing Europe's own internal affairs. But the globalisation processes that are now taking place in many respects add value to European cooperation, including for the business world. Let me give you some of the most important examples of this, in my opinion. The most obvious example of how the EU helps Finns on a global level is the EU's trade policy force. When Finnish business is aiming for a truly global market, it is vital that Finnish products are not discriminated against, but that they get on the same starting line as products from competing countries, so to speak. The EU's common commercial policy is working to keep the market open to Finnish living life with all the power that the EU has as a major trading power in the world. There is a kind of paradox that the more Finland's exports are directed outside the EU, the more central the EU's common commercial policy, and thus the activities of the EU Commission, become for us. Of course, there is a danger in the common trade policy that if trade wars or other conflicts arise, we Finns may suffer retaliation, the causes of which lie entirely outside our country's borders. However, these are exceptional situations and, under normal circumstances, the position of Finnish companies is certainly stronger thanks to the EU's trade policy than without it. Another form of European cooperation that is equally important for Finnish business is the internal market, which was established in 1992. After all, it was then that the general principle came into force that a product that is on the market in one country must not be discriminated against in other Member States either. In terms of the growth potential of SMEs in particular, it is an enormous achievement to create a single domestic market with a population of more than 450 million, where a determined effort has been made to put an end to all forms of discrimination and a 'level playing field' has been created. This is of great importance for the global success of companies, as studies show that a sufficiently large domestic market is a key success factor when growing companies seek to make their way through the wider international market. It is true that there is still work to be done to achieve the objective of a fully integrated market, for example in the areas of trade in services, the European patent system and the integration of payment systems, but what has already been achieved so far is nothing short of astonishing when you consider all the political obstacles that opening up to competition always faces. The third form of European integration that supports the activities of Finns at a global level is the common currency, the euro. Before the establishment of monetary union, many European countries, including Finland, suffered from chronic financial instability. Exchange rate uncertainty and, owing to persistent inflation expectations, high interest rates undermined the success and internationalisation of the economies of these countries. The financial policy system established by the Maastricht Treaty, consisting of a single currency and an independent and credible system of central banks administering it, has succeeded in building a historically exceptional monetary stability for the euro area as a whole. In Finland, this can be seen, for example, in the unprecedentedly low and stable interest rates and the easing of access to loan capital. This is a significant competitive factor, even from a global point of view. By the way, the Bank of Finland is now certainly one of the most European organisations. Together with the ECB and the national central banks of the other euro area countries, it forms the Eurosystem, which is responsible for monetary policy in the euro area. The policy is jointly prepared, decided by the Governing Council and implemented by the national central banks under the auspices of the ECB. When monetary union was established at the end of the 1990s, there were many doubts as to whether European cooperation could go this far, whether such a difficult and 'tough' issue as monetary policy could be entrusted to the management of a common institution. Wouldn't national conflicts of interest soon destroy the whole project, it was doubted. Doubts have proved futile. I have been able to participate in European monetary cooperation from the perspective of both Frankfurt and Helsinki, and I can say that cooperation between central banks has worked amazingly well. Nor is it a question of sacrificing the interests of the people in favour of the system. All the central banks that have joined the system understand that balanced development of the euro area as a whole is a necessary condition for the success of their own country. It is also noteworthy that it is precisely in these areas, where the benefits of EU integration have been greatest, that the central role of policy-making is played by the European institutions: the Commission is responsible for the common commercial policy and the internal market, and the ECB, together with the national central banks, for the single monetary policy. The greatest strength of EU integration apparently lies precisely in its supranational institutions, and it is on them that its greatest successes are based. As Jean Monnet said: 'Without people, nothing is possible, without institutions, nothing is permanent'. This means, among other things, that the deepening of in-integration is most obviously and most likely to occur through institutional development. But there are no institutions without the political will to establish them and give them the legitimacy they need. Personally, I believe that strengthening the EU's common institutions is the most effective way forward for economic and non-European economic progress. *** At the moment, however, there seems to be a great deal of uncertainty about the future direction and speed of development of the European Union. On the one hand, European integration has made great, historic progress in recent years. The most important of these have been the single market, the establishment of monetary union and a stable monetary policy, which I have already mentioned, and most recently the entry of the former socialist countries into the Union among the other European democracies. On the other hand, there are worrying signs that the integration momentum, which has worked so well in the past, is now weakening-now. Indeed, many observers have asked whether the EU's favourable development has stalled. There are several concerns. The EU's economic development has been disappointing in recent years and Europe has not been properly involved in the recovery in agricultural growth in recent years. Progress in the EU's competitiveness objectives and in bringing dynamism to the economy, as set out in the Lisbon strategy of 2000, has come close to as hoped. The weakness of economic growth has made it difficult to balance budgets in a number of Member States, and this has now led to a revision of the Stability and Growth Pact, which is intended to ensure budgetary discipline among members. The question has been asked as to whether the coordination of the EU's economic policy has been drastically impaired. At the same time, difficulties have been encountered in building a single internal market, as important elements such as the Services Directive and the Community patent system have proved politically difficult to implement. It is also uncertain whether the draft EU Constitution will be adopted in all the referenda to which it is submitted in the various Member States. These concerns are all real, and it is in Finland's interest  as, I believe, with other Europeans  that these problems can be resolved and that European cooperation can continue to develop in the future in line with the challenges of a changing world. I believe that being European  and being Finnish in it  is an excellent starting point for success in a globalising world as well, as long as we know how to make use of and develop what is best about being European: the cultural richness of our part of the country and the long cultural traditions. The best way for Europe to succeed is through ever-deepening cooperation, which will build a common, broad and open home ground for European decks and businesses, through which they will also be able to play a role in the global interaction that is now expanding at an unprecedented pace. When considering the current situation of the EU and its future development prospects, it would be worth remembering how remarkable the achievements of European integration have been. Even fiscal policy, on which there have been many gloomy opinions in recent weeks and months, has nevertheless seen a significant improvement compared with the pre-Maastricht period, when the public finances of many EU countries were on a much worse trajectory than they are now. And the improvement that took place was largely due to the EU. The Maastricht Treaty, which set clear targets for member states' budget deficits and indebtedness, has certainly played a significant role in ensuring that deficits over the last decade have not been even greater than they have been. In my opinion, this shows that political coordination within the EU, despite all the criticism, has a clear positive value. *** Globalisation is the opening up of markets. But it is also much more than that. On a more general level, it means a reduction in the importance of geography as a political and cultural factor. We live in a "global village", to use a familiar expression. This term  he coined by the famous media scholar Marshall McLuhan back in the 1960s. The term subsequently quickly banalized in the hands of business consultants and TV intellectuals, so much so that its use in serious conversation became difficult. However, I do not believe that a better concept has yet been invented to describe the phenomena that have given rise to the current debate on globalisation. McLuhan saw the world change, above all because of the growth of the importance of the mass media. However, he couldn't even have a clue about the even more revolutionary opportunities offered by today's technology: what's new in the development of the last ten years is that there has been a shift from one-way mass media to interaction. Thanks to the Internet and other new communication technologies, the comparison with the "village" is now much more apt than it was in McLuhan's time. In my opinion, the concept of a global village is a good illustration of the fact that globalisation is clearly not just an economic phenomenon, but is driven by the general expansion of people's spheres of life, which technology has made possible. Economic integration is only one manifestation of globalization. However, the economy is the lifeblood, and that is why the question arises as to what are the keys to economic success in the context of globalisation. In this context, it has become customary to emphasise the intensification of competition and the importance of competitiveness. The other and positive side of the same thing, however, is that the playing field of economic activity, that is, the market, is becoming wider and therefore the commercial opportunities opened up by excellent know-how  or know-how, as they say today  are greater than ever before and are still growing. *** In the Finnish debate on globalisation  most recently in the globalisation report prepared under the leadership of Director-General Brunila on behalf of the Prime Minister  this has been understood and rightly highlighted the importance of competence as part of the Finnish success strategy. He is also associated with the central importance of research and education, which no one in Finland today disputes. However, I would like to raise my concern here about whether the content of competence and competitiveness in Finland is understood too narrowly and technology-oriented. In fact, I think there are good arguments for arguing that this can be dangerous. At the very least, it may lead to efforts to develop national competitiveness ignoring some important issues. Technical and natural science knowledge is becoming more and more transferable and an increasing number of countries in the world are now already at a sufficiently high level of technical knowledge to be able to be technologically competitive and to be able to quickly absorb new technological innovations. The half-life of a technical competitive advantage is short and apparently becoming shorter and shorter. The conclusion to be drawn from this is that sustainable competitiveness is precisely one that is based on excellence in the area of so-called tacit knowledge. After all, tacit knowledge refers to competences that are difficult to write down on paper or formalise, difficult to transfer from one organisation to another  competences based on experience, cultural background and values. Its relative value increases as other things in the world become more and more mobile and accessible. Tacit knowledge is unique. As I said, it is not easily copied or moved. Therefore, an organisation, company or society as a whole, whose competitiveness is based on broad cultural competences, superior interaction skills and networks, shared values that support innovation and collaboration, is competitive in a deeper and more sustainable way than one that can provide a mere high level of technological performance. In my opinion, this means that excellence on the intangible side of industry, creativity, business and marketing skills and cultural competence will be the key prerequisites for the competitiveness of the 'old industrialised countries'  including the developed countries of Europe. This is not just philosophical speculation, it already has its very concrete manifestations. Recently, the Bank of Finland has on a couple of occasions drawn attention in its economic reports to the fact that the prices of Finnish exports have a persistent downward trend. The goods from which our national economy receives its export subsidies have become cheaper every year, and the volume of exports should therefore increase more rapidly if the real income of the national economy is to be kept growing. This phenomenon is due to the focus of our exports on high-tech equipment, the prices of which are trendingly becoming cheaper as the know-how needed to manufacture them is constantly spreading. In this respect, economies  such as great Britain, for example  are in a better position than us  and a significant proportion of their exports consist of financial services, management, marketing services and cultural products. These are examples of areas of business where tacit knowledge is central. Finland is not Britain and I do not believe that Helsinki is becoming a centre of international funding and marketing like London. However, as globalisation places particular emphasis on the market value of tacit knowledge, I believe that in Finland, too, it is worth paying more and more attention to developing competitiveness, precisely in those areas of tacit knowledge where we are naturally well-founded. We also need to pay a lot of attention in education and business management to the accumulation and utilisation of cultural competence based on specific experience. This does not necessarily or primarily mean any particular high culture, but culture in its more mundane form: the full use of the rich European home ground that EU integration has opened up for Finnish companies and citizens. *** In this context, I would like to raise one more area of European cooperation, which I consider to be essential, and which is of far-reaching importance, both human and economic. I am thinking of cooperation in the field of education and, in particular, of international student exchanges. This is also very much linked to the subject of our seminar today. Every year, about 4000 Finnish students participate in international student exchange, of which about two-thirds through exchange programmes organised by the EU. This may not yet be as high as it should be, but it is still very significant in terms of its impact. The international mobility of young people is increasingly making Europe a real "home ground" for Finns, on which they move naturally and from which it is also good to venture into the world of farther afield. We should be proud of the Finnish youth, who today have a completely different class in terms of international capabilities and also international experience than my generation once was. This must be nurtured and supported. Care must be taken to ensure both language skills and the general ability to act in multicultural contexts. The ever-closer European cooperation gives reason to expect that these skills will be needed and that their use will go much further. This also bodes well for Finland's continued economic success. *** Ladies and gentlemen. In this presentation, I have tried to justify my view that making full use of our MEMBERSHIP of the EU and our Europeanness is a key key to economic success, including at global level. The fact that we are in Europe like our home makes us strong in the wider world as well. A large and open, European home market not only helps companies to grow and specialise, but also rewards product development and the commercialisation of ideas much better than small home markets. The extensive domestic market also supports global business. As residents of a small country, it is therefore worthwhile for Finns to work to create as uniform a market area as possible throughout the EU. For us, being European is also cultural capital, a source of tacit knowledge that Finns should increasingly actively evaluate and increase. It also bears in global competition.

Toinen ja suomalaiselle elinkeinoelmlle yht trke eurooppalaisen yhteistyn muoto on sismarkkinat, jotka perustettiin vuonna 1992. Tllinhn tuli voimaan se yleisperiaa-te, ett tuotetta, joka on markkinoilla yhdess maassa, ei saa syrji muissakaan jsen-maissa. Varsinkin PK-yritysten kasvumahdollisuuksien kannalta on aivan valtava saavu-tus, kun nin luotiin nyt yli 450 miljoonan asukkaan yhteninen kotimarkkina-alue, jolla kaikkinainen syrjint on mrtietoisesti koetettu lopettaa ja on luotu "tasainen pelikent-t". Tll on suuri merkitys yritysten globaalin menestyksen kannalta, sill tutkimukset osoittavat, ett riittvn laajat kotimarkkinat ovat keskeinen menestystekij, kun kasvavat yritykset pyrkivt lymn itsens lpi laajemmilla kansainvlisill markkinoilla. On tot-ta, ett tysin yhtenisten markkinoiden tavoitteeseen psemisess on viel tehtv, mm. palvelujen kaupan, eurooppalaisen patenttijrjestelmn ja maksujrjestelmien yhte-nistmisen alueilla, mutta jo thnastisetkin saavutukset ovat suorastaan hmmstytt-vi, kun ajattelee kaikkia niit poliittisia esteit, mit kilpailun avaamisella aina on. Kolmas eurooppalaisen integraation muoto, joka tukee suomalaisten toimintaa globaalilla tasolla, on yhteinen valuutta, euro. Ennen rahaliiton perustamista monet Euroopan maat, mys Suomi, krsivt kroonisesta rahataloudellisesta epvakaudesta. Valuuttakurssiep-varmuus ja sitkeitten inflaatio-odotusten takia korkeat korot heikensivt niden maiden elinkeinoelmn menestyst ja kansainvlistymist. Maastrichtin sopimuksella luotu ra-hapoliittinen jrjestelm, joka koostuu yhteisest rahasta ja sit hallinnoivasta itsenisest ja uskottavasta keskuspankkijrjestelmst, on onnistunut rakentamaan koko euroalueelle historiallisesti poikkeuksellisen rahataloudellisen vakauden. Suomessa tm nkyy muun muassa ennennkemttmn matalana ja vakaana korkotasona ja lainapoman saatavuu-den helpottumisena. Tm on globaalistikin katsoen merkittv kilpailutekij. Suomen Pankki on muuten suomalaisista organisaatioista nyt varmasti yksi eurooppalai-simpia. Se muodostaa yhdess EKP:n ja muiden euromaiden kansallisten keskuspankkien kanssa Eurojrjestelmn, jonka vastuulla euroalueen rahapolitiikka on. Politiikka valmis-tellaan yhdess, siit ptetn EKP:n neuvostossa ja se toteutetaan EKP:n johdolla kan-sallisten keskuspankkien toimesta. Kun rahaliittoa 1990-luvun lopulla perustettiin, esiin-tyi paljon epilyksi voiko eurooppalainen yhteisty menn nin pitklle, voidaanko niin vaikea ja "kova" asia kuin rahapolitiikka uskoa yhteisen instituution hoitoon. Eivtk kansalliset eturistiriidat piankin tuhoa koko hankkeen, epiltiin. Epilykset ovat osoittau-tuneet turhiksi. Olen pssyt osallistumaan eurooppalaiseen rahapoliittiseen yhteistyhn sek Frankfurtin ett Helsingin nkkulmista ja voin sanoa, ett keskuspankkien vlinen yhteisty on toiminut hmmstyttvn hyvin. Kysymys ei myskn ole siit, ett kansal-linen etu olisi uhrattu systeemin hyvksi. Kaikissa jrjestelmn liittyneiss keskuspan-keissa ymmrretn, ett koko euroalueen tasapainoinen kehitys on vlttmtn ehto oman kotimaan menestykselle. Merkillepantavaa muuten on, ett juuri nill alueilla, joissa EU-integraatiosta saatu hy-ty on ollut suurin, keskeinen politiikan muotoilun rooli on unionitason toimielimill: ko-missio vastaa yhteisest kauppapolitiikasta ja sismarkkinoista, ja EKP yhdess kansallis-ten keskuspankkien kanssa yhteisest rahapolitiikasta. EU:n integraation suurin voima onkin ilmeisesti juuri sen ylikansallisissa instituutioissa, ja niihin perustuvat sen suurim-mat menestykset. Kuten Jean Monnet sanoi: Ilman ihmisi mikn ei ole mahdollista, ilman instituutioita, mikn ei ole pysyv. text: Director-General Erkki Liikanen Competition and productivity National Economic Association 13.4.2005 FIGURE 1. Introduction Global imbalances have been a cause for growing concern recently. There is therefore particular cause for concern at this very moment when we look at the problems of the external and internal balance of the United States and the fact that the United States is facing a process of rebalancing its current account anyway. There has been particular concern in Europe, because it has been feared that it would be here that the costs of rebalancing through the exchange rate would be most severely borne. In the following, my intention is to address this problem and to consider how stronger productivity developments, particularly in the services sector in European countries, could reduce the vulnerability of our region to both external and internal shocks. Figure 2: Double deficits in the USA The U.S. economy grew strongly after the mid-1990s. Productivity rose, investment and consumption increased substantially. My real exchange rate appreciated. At the same time, however, the external balance of the economy began to deteriorate sharply: the current account deficit has continued to grow even after the technology boom. The expansion of the current account deficit during the technology boom was understandable, since resources were in full use and domestic demand was growing rapidly: Domestic production was no longer enough to sustain the increased demand, and it was discharged into imports. However, the drivers of the growth in domestic demand were related to a deeper technological upheaval and an acceleration in total factor productivity growth that started in the open sector: This explains the simultaneous appreciation of the real exchange rate and the deepening of the trade deficit in the so-called "real exchange rate". With the help of the Balassa-Samuelson effect. The dollar began its downturn, which would likely have been even steeper than experienced without the dollar-supporting investments by Asian central banks. Us monetary policy was driven exceptionally light and the budget deficit was allowed to increase. This resulted in a double deficit that is of concern to many. However, the observed increase in productivity growth and the above-described impact in BalassaSamuelson1 are not yet sufficient to explain the strength of the appreciation of the real exchange rate in the United States at the end of 1990. The second explanation offered is that at the turn of the millennium, the technology boom and optimistic perceptions of returns on investment and long-term economic growth made U.S. investments the most attractive. As a result of these factors, the dollar appreciated even more in real terms2. Adjusting the US current account deficit  and how it will happen  is not unimportant for Europe, the rest of the world, or even Finland. All the calculations presented to the public conclude that the narrowing of the US current account deficit will slow down economic growth in other parts of the world. Optimists believe in the dynamism of the USA, flexible markets and the undoubted importance of the dollar as a reserve and investment currency. Pessimists, on the other hand, point out that investors' capital flows have already begun to turn away from dollar investments, making it difficult to finance deficits. 1 Balassa-Samuelson arises when productivity grows faster in the open sector than in the domestic sector (e.g. due to external competition). Furthermore, assuming that domestic sector wages follow wage developments in the export sector, domestic firms will only be able to maintain their profitability by raising the prices of their products1. On the other hand, for example, Croke et. AL. Nancy et al. (2005) have studied the dynamics of current account deficits in industrialised countries and concluded that all periods of current account adjustment are accompanied by a rather strong slowdown in GDP growth. The real issue, which is relevant for Europeans, is, on the one hand, how the real economy in the United States will react to the adjustment of the current account deficit and, on the other hand, how large the exchange rate changes in the dollar will be. Europeans have traditionally tended to take a stronger approach to exchange rate changes and disruptions to the world economy than the Americans. This is understandable in that, before Economic and Monetary Union, each European currency area was small compared to the United States. In small and open economies, the real economic impact of exchange rate changes and disruptions to the global economy is large, while in large and closed economies these effects are small. As far as exchange rate changes are concerned, the situation should be different now that the euro area is also a large and relatively closed currency area. Trade outside the region accounts for 17-18% of GDP. In the United States, of course, the corresponding figure is even lower. It is precisely because the share of foreign trade is very small that a major change in the exchange rate is needed in order for it to have a significant impact on the external balance. How, then, can Europe be better prepared for the disruption of economic development caused by external shocks? A number of researchers have put forward various solutions, mainly related to improving the functioning of hyyke and artillery institutions, regulating the jelly market and the openness of European economies. American researchers Maurice Obstfeldt and Kenneth Rogoff3 have also wondered whether an increase in productivity in the non-tradables sector in the euro area could make the us current account adjustment process less painful for all parties involved. The real depreciation of the dollar, which is inevitably associated with the adjustment of the current account, means that American products will become cheaper and demand for them in Europe will increase. Similarly, exports from euro area countries will contract or grow more slowly. However, if productivity were to rise in the services sector in euro area countries, it would counteract the appreciation of the currency. As the prices of services fall, citizens' real income increases, which is reflected not only in the increased demand for services but also in goods. This would chill both US exports and domestic demand in the Euro area. Of course, the above is not the primary reason why europe deserves attention to the development of service productivity. In terms of the economy as a whole, Europe has lagged behind productivity developments in the United States between 1995 and 2002, while in the early 1990s Europe was still stronger than that of the United States. This is illustrated by the following table, which looks at the growth of labour productivity in the economy as a whole and in different industries: Figure 4: Growth in labour productivity in various industries A key explanation for the faster productivity development in the United States lies in services using information and communication technologies, as well as in the ict-producing manufacturing industry. In these sectors, productivity growth in the United States accelerated sharply, while it slowed down in Europe. The EU, on the other hand, has had a competitive advantage in the areas of traditional industrial production. Productivity growth has been faster than in the United States in industries with low use of information technology. Figure 5: Acceleration of productivity growth in the US, divided into key industry contributions. If you look more closely at the sectoral division, you will see that productivity, above all in wholesale and retail trade, has grown rapidly in the USA, which in turn has been very slow in the EU. In the United States, the retail and wholesale trade and the financial services sector, with their ancillary activities, explain 95% of the acceleration in productivity growth by a good percentage between the periods 1990-1995 and 1995-2001. In Europe, productivity growth slowed down over the same period in most countries. Indeed, a major difference to the USA has arisen above all in the productivity development of the service sector. Of course, there is at least one industry in Europe, such as telecommunications, where productivity growth has been clearly faster than in the USA. It has been a highly competitive industry and mobile communications have made a significant contribution to this. Competition and productivity at industry level Lack of competition and regulated services markets have been cited as one of the reasons for the poor productivity development4. Although the internal market is already functioning quite well for goods, mobility and competition in services have not materialised. This has been referred to extensively in the recent debate as a barrier to competition and efficiency in the services sector. My OECD has criticized Europeans in several country surveys  including Finland  for the lack of competition in industries, especially in the non-tradable sector. For example, the OECD country report on Finland (H and Wise, 2004) states that barriers to competition in the jelly market were rapidly dismantled in Finland in the early 1990s, but since then the pace has slowed down. Companies operating in the export sector are exposed to foreign competition, and productivity development there has been better. By contrast, several sectors in the non-tradable sector, in particular the services sector, are poorly competitive. Indeed, there is a lot of industry-specific evidence of the positive effects of increased competition on productivity - both theoretical and empirical. For example, according to the theory of Michael Porter (1990), competition encourages companies to differentiate products and streamline practices in order to maintain a leading market position and increase cost-effectiveness. Many other researchers5 have come to the same conclusion in their empirical studies, the results of which suggest a positive dependence between competition and the innovativeness and productivity of companies. One of the explanations that contributes to competitive productivity growth is related to the fact that, in a competitive situation, the need arises, for example, to make full use of information and communication technologies and to look for new business models and processes to improve productivity. A good example of this is telecommunications services, the liberalisation of which has increased the productivity and competitiveness of the sector in Europe. Another example in the Nordic countries is banking services. Private and public services are problematic sectors. Studies have shown, for example, that the productivity of health services has decreased in Finland6. As such, measuring productivity in the public sector contains many problems. More recent views on the interdependence between competition, business innovation and, consequently, productivity highlight the inverse U-curve relationship between innovation and competition7. In these reviews, the goal of product development is to bring qualitatively better products to the market than the competitor and thus achieve, at least temporarily, a monopoly position. However, the depressing effect of competition on product development arises from the fact that the 4 OMahony-van Ark (2003) 5 Geroski (1995), Blundell, Griffith ja Van Reenen (1999) 6 Aaltonen-Jarvi-Luoma-Raty (2004) 7 Aghion  Harris-Vickers (1997), Aghion  Harris Howitt -Vickers (2001) when very tight, companies can no longer afford to continue product development, or at least product development may slow down. There is some recent evidence of this in the electronics industry, where competition has intensified to the extreme and at least some companies have started to cut R&D expenditure. The effects of intra-industry competition on innovations have been studied to some extent in My Finland with company-level data. The empirical results of Kilponen and Santavirta (2004) show that there seems to be an inverse U-curve relationship between intra-industry competition and innovation. In this sense, the adoption of the Services Directive, which is being discussed in the Council of the EU, is important: it would open up the non-tradable sector to wider competition and ensure faster productivity development in the services sector, as the use of technological innovations would expand more rapidly to the non-tradable sector. As such, despite the public debate, this is a fairly moderate reform that would fill one of the major gaps left in the completion of the internal market. Macroeconomic impact of competition As has already been said, the positive impact of increased competition on business innovation and productivity is quite clear. However, sectoral reviews do not yet reflect the overall economic impact of competition. It is also important to show that the effects of competition on productivity should be reflected in an increase in the well-being and standard of living of households, for example by increasing income and, consequently, consumption opportunities. This point is clarified by the following graph, which looks at the development of GDP per capita over the past twenty years. Graph 6: GDP per capita: cumulative change (log.) since 1980 Using GDP per capita in PPS as a measure of living standards, we see that at the end of 2002 the standard of living in the EU was about a third lower than in the United States. The gap in living standards with the US has widened by about 7% since the early 1980s. As far as Finland is concerned, the situation looks brighter: Finland has been able to close the gap in living standards with the United States significantly in the 1990s. On the other hand, it should be remembered that Finland is on average in terms of living standards among OECD countries. The gap in living standards between the United States and Europe is explained by about a third of lower productivity than in the United States and two-thirds of lower boredom, as can be seen in the following graphs. Figure 7: Gdp components in the EU and the US: cumulative change (log.) since 1980 Sector-specific analyses do not usually indicate how the national economy is adapting to the new competitive environment and what possible negative effects an increase in competition could have. Industry-specific analyses are typically only partial equilibrium analyses, in which case, for example, spillover effects are ignored. It is difficult to assess the overall economic impact of increased competition, but in this context, the so-called 'green light'. dynamic models of general balance have proven to be chilly. Such models, one of which is the Aino model developed by the Bank of Finland, are based on economic theory and the rational and optimal behaviour of housekeepers within the prevailing constraints. Dynamic models of general equilibrium are chilly because they allow complex adjustment mechanisms for the real economy to be examined. On the other hand, of course, it must be remembered that the calculations made with such models are always only indicative. In the following, I will examine the effects of increased competition on the overall economy in the light of the model calculations obtained (GEM, AINO). However, before going into the calculations, it is probably worth recalling a little how different competitive situations can be described and what the adjustment dynamics of the real economy might look like in the light of economic theory. Imperfect competition in the meat market, for example, means that the economy is in a balance where companies produce less, but at a higher price in relation to the competitive equilibrium.
