Title: Presentation at the Economic Summit 2005
text: VTT Sinikka Salo Director Bank of Finland Cyclical outlook for the euro area and the global economy Presentation at the Economy Summit 2005 17.5.2005 1. The world economy The world's total production is growing rapidly. The trend growth in production has been accelerating for a long time, since the 1970s, and is currently estimated to be around four per cent per year. Against the background of the favorable development, there are strong economic forces. A significant factor has been the rapid development and introduction of new technologies. On the other hand, countries that had previously pursued inward-looking economic policies have increasingly opened up and integrated themselves into world trade in goods. The development of financial markets has promoted the mobility of capital and technology worldwide. The structural changes inevitably associated with rapid growth have created tensions almost everywhere. Restructuring at company level, which has often shifted production from mature market economies to emerging economies, has received a great deal of publicity. Global economic tensions are also reflected in the overall economic indicators of the various countries and regions, and the gradually intensifying macroeconomic imbalances could therefore jeopardise the continuation of the positive development of global gdp in the coming years without interruption. Last year, the world's combined total output grew at a rate of more than 5%, the highest growth rate in more than three decades. Global growth continued to spread in Latin America, the Middle East and Africa, while emerging Asian economies further improved their already strong growth rates. China, India and Russia were at the top of the growth. Of the highly developed countries, the growth of the United States has, of course, played a major role in the development of the world economy as a whole. In Europe and the euro area, growth also recovered as a result of the international upturn, although growth rates were not high by international comparison. According to recent forecasts by the International Monetary Fund, the European Commission and the Bank of Finland, global economic growth will continue to be relatively strong this year and next, although the growth rate will slow down slightly to around 4-41/2% per year. Growth remains clearly above average in asia's emerging economies and in Russia. China's growth rate is expected to moderate only slightly, while India's growth is expected to pick up further. Thus, the focus of global economic growth remains on emerging market economies. Growth in the United States has been supported in recent years by highly expansive monetary and financial policies. The policy has led to a large current account and fiscal deficit, and the 41/2% GDP growth rate experienced last year is not sustainable. Although growth is projected to slow down from last year's trend to around 31/2% this year and next, the growth rate of the US economy remains at the top of the list of industrialised countries. The Japanese economy, like the rest of the global economy, recovered during the boom of recent years, partly driven by the success of the Chinese economy. Domestic demand, especially business investment, also showed signs of an end to the long-term stagnation of the economy. Over the past year, however, growth stopped at a new level. In the next few years, the Japanese economy is likely to recover, but only slowly. Continued deflation, major imbalances in the public sector and difficulties in the corporate and financial sectors continue to act as a brake on economic growth. In the euro area, growth was 2% last year. This year, it is estimated to remain at 11/2%, from which it is expected to recover to just over 2% in 2006. I will come back to the outlook for the euro area in more detail later. While the key outlook for the global economy is positive, the possibility of slower-than-forecast growth is also on the horizon. The most obvious risk factor is the increase in the price of oil and other raw materials. Strong growth throughout the global economy has increased the demand for oil and many raw materials and pushed up their prices. Strong demand, especially in China, has contributed significantly to the rise in commodity and oil prices. Although the rise in oil prices was smaller in real terms last year than during the shocks and the industrialised oil-importing countries have reduced their dependence on oil following the oil shocks, the sharp rise in prices (32% on the previous year) dampened the growth of the global economy in the second half of the year. In the first quarter of this year, oil prices continued to rise, to a nominally record high between 55 and 60. In line with the rise in oil prices, the underlying oil price assumptions have been adjusted upwards. At the moment, it appears that oil prices will remain close to recent levels this year and next year. High and highly volatile oil prices have a negative impact on the prospects for growth in the near term and pose a key risk to the forecast outlook. After the bullish phase at the beginning of the year, stock market indices have declined. This is partly related to the results of the first half of the year, in particular for ICT companies, which were estimated to have been cut by increased competition. At the same time, companies' visions of the future have been revised to be a little more cautious. The weakening of the outlook is also illustrated by the fact that in April the size of long-term government bonds in both the United States and Europe fell again back to very low levels at the beginning of the year. Long-term interest rates are historically low in both nominal and real terms. They reflect relatively moderate growth and inflation expectations. At the same time, interest rate differentials between emerging economies and corporate bonds and government bonds have widened slightly and various risk awareness indicators have risen. Overall, financial market indicators signal a somewhat more cautious expectation of near-term global economic developments. Even on the basis of this recent information, a clearer possibility of downward risk can be attached to the above-mentioned forecast picture. The downward risk to the relatively favourable forecast picture is also caused by the gradual accumulation of gender imbalances in the global economy over the past few years, the emergence of which has largely been influenced by the monetary and fiscal policy choices of different countries. Since the beginning of 2001, central banks eased monetary policy strongly, mainly in the United States, but also elsewhere. At their lowest, short-term nominal market interest rates in both the United States and the euro area were clearly lower than at any time since 1960. With the central international role of the dollar and the dollar-linked nature of several currencies, the light monetary policy of the United States spread widely to the world economy, even to countries where the purpose of the light monetary policy was not apparent. On a global scale, light monetary policy has led to strong growth in liquidity over the past few years. The ratio of money and credit to gross domestic product has risen generally in industrialised countries, but fastest in East Asia. Debt reserves in many countries have become so high that they are already raising concerns. The effects of light monetary policy and excessive liquidity have been reflected in a stronger and broader-than-expected recovery in economic growth in the global economy. This is, of course, a positive and desirable thing. But on the other hand, the light situation has also given rise to less desirable phenomena: - Due to strong demand, the world market prices of oil and other raw materials have risen significantly over the past 1-2 years. Not only through economic growth, low interest rates and ample liquidity have supported the demand for raw materials, but also through speculative position-taking. - Globally, inflation is still quite low, but in the United States, consumer price growth has already picked up markedly. - The easing of financial conditions has led to an increase in private sector debt in many countries. " The housing market has become hotter and housing prices have risen high in many countries in recent years. In the current context, real interest rates remain low, in many countries even lower than the growth rate of the economy. This raises concerns about the long-term outlook for world inflation. At the same time, however, when the increase in competition brought about by globalisation is putting downward pressure on prices, it is difficult to assess the correct conduct of monetary policy. In the United States, a light monetary policy stance has been strongly combined with fiscal policy that supports the growth of demand. The policy mix has brought strong demand growth to the country. At the same time, however, the country's austerity and investment imbalances have widened further, combined with a large fiscal deficit. The U.S. current account deficit and indebtedness initially reflected confidence in the strength of the U.S. economy, which prompted foreign investors and firms to invest capital in the United States through both direct and equity investments. Recently, however, foreign investment in the United States has largely been directed towards securities issued by the public sector. The public sector has had to finance its large deficit with foreign funding because of the very low level of household savings. The spiral of indebtedness in the US public sector and the economy as a whole is excessive and it is necessary for it to break or at least slow down considerably at some point. Indeed, one of the risk factors for the international economy has been considered to be the fact that, due to the current account deficit, the dollar will at some point depreciate strongly even further than it is at present. This would help the country's external balance, but could slow down economic growth elsewhere. Europe, and especially the euro area, accounts for a small share of us foreign trade, only in the order of a fifth. About the same is the joint share of China and Japan, so the United States trades most of its trade with smaller countries. The neighbouring countries of Canada and Mexico together are already responsible for about a third of the United States' foreign trade. Thus, the correction of the US current account deficit cannot be based solely on trade between the US and the euro area. There must also be changes in trade flows to other countries. On the other hand, in the structure of us demand, the share of foreign trade is rather low (exports 14%, imports 16%). Therefore, it is quite likely that imbalances cannot be corrected solely through the exchange rate. This is also indicated by the fact that the weakening of the dolla-ri does not seem to have had a major impact on the current account deficit so far. In order to correct the current account, changes are needed in the US national economy so that an even greater proportion of the country's investments can be financed from domestic sources in the future. Us monetary policy has already taken steps in the direction of correcting the balance between investment and saving. The central bank raised its key monetary policy rate in June 2004, while signalling that it was time for interest rate policy to move from a strongly expansionary stance towards a more moderately neutral interest rate level. Since then, the FED has raised its policy rate at regular intervals by a percentage point to the fourth at a time, so that the policy rate is currently 3%. According to market expectations, the FED will continue to raise the policy rate over the current year towards a level of around 4%. With regard to us fiscal policy, the current administration has set itself the objective of halving the general government deficit by the end of its term. However, credible efforts to achieve this goal are lacking for the time being. As a mirror image of the development of the United States, asian countries' financial claims against the United States have increased. Asian countries have traditionally had high saving rates, and in many countries  but not in China  the investment rate declined as a result of the Asian financial crisis. This freed up funds for foreign investment objects. Indeed, the us current account deficit has been countered by current account surpluses and capital exports in key Asian countries. Asian countries have acquired a large number of dollar-denominated targets and in this way contributed significantly to the financing of the US exchange balance sheet and the public sector deficit. By the same token, it is clear that such developments may entail significant risks for international exchange rate and interest rate developments. Indeed, there has been pressure on the markets against the exchange rates of countries linked to the US dollar. The Chinese currency (renminbi) has been at the center of market and also political attention. In Asian countries, inter-ventricular activities have also increased bank liquidity and the supply of credit in the local currency, and may have contributed to undermining the balanced development of economies. The imbalance between savings and investment in the United States and Asian countries has been the subject of debate in many meetings of international organisations and industrialised countries. Imbalances can be corrected through policy measures or through the guidance of market forces. The policy measures to be taken in each country or region are well known, but it is clear that sufficiently effective measures have not yet been taken. The correction of imbalances, primarily under the guidance of market forces, i.e. mainly through strong changes in exchange rates and long-term interest rates, may be rapid, but may be accompanied by significant disruptions to the global economy. Perhaps the best option would be an appropriate combination of more effective policy measures and market adaptation. 2. Cyclical outlook for the euro area Growth in Europe and the euro area also recovered last year, although growth rates were not high by international comparison. Last year, however, supported by strong global trade growth, the growth rate in the euro area rose for the first time in four years to close to the estimated potential growth rate, with euro area output growing by an average of 2% over the whole year. Over the past year, the "engine" of growth in the euro area shifted from external demand in the first half of the year to domestic demand in the second half of the year. In domestic ky-synna, the change in investments turned from negative to positive starting from the second quarter. Overall, however, domestic demand remained subdued. Private consumer demand has still not been a major driver of growth in the euro area. Although economic growth in the euro area is not high internationally, it is close to its potential and is expected to return to its potential growth in the course of this year. According to the EUROPEAN Commission, the euro area will grow at an annual rate of 1.6% this year, from which it is forecast to accelerate to 2.1% next year. In its recently published forecast, the IMF arrived at almost the same figures. Economic policies, the moderation of inflation, favourable financing conditions, an increase in corporate profit margins, progress in structural reforms and a strong global environment support a slight recovery in growth. The vibrant housing market in several countries also boosts wealth and supports consumption. At present, interest rates in the euro area can be considered low when compared with historical interest rates or with estimates of neutral interest rates. The key ECB interest rate is 2% and short-term market rates are at the same level. Long-term 10-year market interest rates are 31/2-4% in nominal terms and just under 2% in real terms. Even in the euro area, monetary growth has been ample in recent years, well above what inflation-free growth would require. At the same time, credit to the private sector has also grown rapidly. Over the past year, however, the growth in the amount of money seems to have moderated. Despite the appreciation of the euro, financing conditions in the euro area can be considered dynamic. Monetary policy has been accommodative. The ECB has assessed that the increase in inflation above the price stability target ceiling, mainly due to higher oil prices, is temporary and that price stability does not appear to be threatened over the medium term. The key interest rates for financial policy have thus been maintained. The economic policy of economic and monetary union consists of a whole of monetary policy, fiscal policy and structural policy. They all contribute to the common objectives of stability, growth and employment, and to boosting Europe's production potential and competitiveness so that Europe can cope with increasing global competition. The most successful of the various policy areas is monetary policy, which can be considered to have achieved its own objective of price stability and, consequently, low interest rates  relatively well. By contrast, fiscal policy has not yet achieved the objectives set for balanced budgetary developments and long-term sustainability. Last year, the general government deficit in the euro area was estimated at 2.7% of GDP and exceeded the 3% mark in France, Germany and Greece. A total of a dozen of the current EU member states are subject to the excessive deficit procedure defined by the Stability and Growth Pact. The application of the Stability and Growth Pact has come up against conflicts between the Commission, the Council of Ministers and the Member States. At the same time, confidence in the fiscal system as a whole has been shaken. Throughout its existence, the Stability and Growth Pact has been the subject of strong criticism. However, the agreement has been better than its reputation. As a result, eu countries have improved their budgetary balances, reduced inflation and lowered interest rates. The European Council has agreed to reform the Stability and Growth Pact. The Council's conclusions did not address the rules-based fiscal framework or the main objective of the Stability and Growth Pact to avoid excessive deficits. The cornerstones of the pact  the 3% deficit reference value and the 60% debt reference value  remained unchanged. However, it was decided to amend the Stability and Growth Pact to give Member States more room for manoeuvre in fiscal policy. This was done, inter alia, by specifying more precisely which relevant factors can be taken into account if the deficit exceeds the 3% reference value. However, the overrun must be temporary in nature and of a minor size before these factors can be taken into account. Despite its changes, the Stability and Growth Pact remains an essential cornerstone of economic and monetary union. It is important that the credibility of the agreement is restored when the reformed pact is implemented. Rule-based fiscal policies, such as the Stability and Growth Pact, will only work if they are respected. The budgetary challenges facing European countries in the context of an ageing population are great. In order to finance the expenditure caused by the ageing of the population in the future, public debt must fall, not increase. The credibility of the rule should not be risked by abandoning its application because of short-sighted political pressures. Of the policy areas, structural policy appears to have been by far the least successful, especially in the large euro area Member States. Although some reforms have been carried out, overall, the success in implementing structural measures remains modest. The ambitious lisbon targets to be achieved by the end of this decade are in danger of being largely a pipe dream. 3. Loppupaatelmia The global economy has experienced a period of strong growth and is projected to continue, albeit with a slight weakening. The strong undertone is driven by more or less permanent fundamentals, such as the introduction of new technologies and the integration of developing countries into the world economy. These fundamentals for global economic growth will enable growth to continue at a rapid pace in the future. On the other hand, growth has also been accompanied by macroeconomic imbalances. Perhaps the most significant risk to the continuation of the favourable development of the global economy is the uncontrolled unwinding of the austerity and investment imbalances accumulated between the United States and Asian countries. The necessary policy measures are fairly well known  to increase savings in the US and to make exchange rates more flexible in the emerging Asian economies  but sufficiently effective measures have clearly not yet been achieved. In the euro area, the balance between saving and investment is reasonably well balanced, but the problem is structurally due to too low growth in real GDP  and even in the output potential. In order to revive the growth dynamics in the euro area and safeguard the conditions for long-term growth, structural measures are primarily needed. The strategy defined in Lisbon five years ago set municipal reform objectives for the EU countries, but they have not been fully implemented in the desired way. Against this background, it is easy for me to agree with the widely accepted view, including at the Spring European Council, that, in order to speed up the implementation of the Lisbon strategy, the strategy should place a clear emphasis on growth and employment. It is essential to make Europe a more attractive place to invest and work. At the same time, investment in knowledge and innovation must be increased and more and better jobs created. The best way for the Member States to achieve these objectives is to define  and implement  their structural reform projects in a very concrete way. As I said at the beginning, globalisation and the rapid growth of the world economy that has taken place as a result are inevitably accompanied by structural changes and adaptation needs almost everywhere. This means that structural changes must also be strongly involved in the examination of the short-term cyclical outlook.
text_original: VTT Sinikka Salo Johtokunnan jsen Suomen Pankki Euroalueen ja maailmantalouden suhdannenkymt Esitelm Talous Summit 2005 tapahtumassa 17.5.2005 1. Maailmantalous Maailman kokonaistuotanto kasvaa nopeasti. Tuotannon trendikasvu on nopeutunut pitkn, jo 1970-luvulta alkaen, ja tll hetkell sen arvellaan olevan noin nelj pro-senttia vuodessa. Suotuisan kehityksen taustalla on vahvoja taloudellisia voimia. Merkittv tekij on ollut uuden teknologian nopea kehitys ja kyttnotto. Toisaalta aikaisemmin sisnpin kntynytt talouspolitiikkaa harjoittaneet maat ovat avautu-neet ja integroituneet enenevsti maailman tavarakauppaan. Rahoitusmarkkinoiden kehitys on edistnyt poman ja teknologian liikkuvuutta maailmanlaajuisesti. Nopeaan kasvuun vistmtt liittyvt rakennemuutokset ovat synnyttneet jnnitteit lhes kaikkialla. Runsaasti julkisuutta ovat saaneet yritystasolla tehdyt saneeraukset, joissa usein on siirretty tuotantoa kypsist markkinatalousmaista nouseviin talouksiin. Maailmantalouden jnnitteet nkyvt mys eri maiden ja alueiden kokonaistaloudel-lisissa tunnusluvuissa ja vhitellen voimistuneet makrotaloudelliset eptasapainotto-muudet saattavatkin vaarantaa lhivuosina maailman kokonaistuotannon mynteisen kehityksen jatkumisen keskeytymttmn. Viime vuonna maailman yhteenlaskettu kokonaistuotanto kasvoi yli 5 prosentin vauhtia, mik oli suurin kasvuluku yli kolmeen vuosikymmeneen. Globaali kasvu jatkoi levimistn Latinalaisessa Amerikassa, Lhi-Idss ja Afrikassa samalla kun Aasian nousevat taloudet paransivat jo entisestn vahvaa kasvuvauhtiaan. Kasvun krjess olivat Kiina, Intia ja Venj. Pitklle kehittyneist maista Yhdysvaltojen kasvun merkitys on luonnollisesti ollut suuri koko maailmantalouden kehityksen kannalta. Mys Euroopassa ja euroalueella kasvu elpyi kansainvlisen noususuhdan-teen myt, vaikka kasvuluvut eivt olleet kansainvlisess vertailussa suuria. Kansainvlisen valuuttarahaston, EU:n komission ja Suomen Pankin tuoreiden ennus-teiden mukaan maailmantalouden kasvu jatkuu verrattain vahvana mys tn ja ensi vuonna, vaikkakin kasvuvauhti hidastuu lievsti noin 4-4 prosenttiin vuodessa. Sel-vsti keskimrist voimakkaampaa kasvu on edelleen Aasian nopeasti kehittyviss talouksissa sek Venjll. Kiinan kasvuvauhdin odotetaan maltillistuvan vain hie-man, kun taas Intian kasvun odotetaan viel nopeutuvan. Maailmantalouden kasvun painopiste pysyy siis edelleen nousevissa markkinatalousmaissa. Yhdysvaltojen kasvua on viime vuosina tukenut erittin ekspansiivinen raha- ja fi-nanssipolitiikka. Politiikka on johtanut suureen vaihtotaseen ja julkisen talouden ali-jmn, eik viime vuonna koettu 4 prosentin bruttokansantuotteen kasvuvauhti ole kestv. Vaikka kasvun ennustetaan vaimenevan viimevuotisesta kohti trendikas-vun tasoa eli noin 3 prosenttiin tn ja ensi vuonna, Yhdysvaltojen talouden kasvu-vauhti silyy yh teollisuusmaiden krkipss. Japanin talous elpyi muun maailmantalouden tavoin viime vuosien nousun aikana, osin Kiinan talouden menestyksen siivittmn. Mys kotimainen kysynt, ennen kaikkea yritysten investointitoiminta, osoitti merkkej talouden pitkaikaisen pysh-tyneisyyden tilan pttymisest. Viime vuoden aikana kasvu kuitenkin pyshtyi uu-delleen. Lhivuosina Japanin talous elpynee, mutta vain hitaanpuoleisesti. Deflaation jatkuminen, julkisen sektorin suuret tasapaino-ongelmat ja yritys- ja rahoitussektorin vaikeudet jarruttavat edelleen talouden kasvua. Euroalueella kasvu oli viime vuonna 2 %. Tn vuonna se j arvioiden mukaan run-saaseen 1 prosenttiin, mist sen odotetaan elpyvn runsaaseen 2 prosenttiin vuonna 2006. Palaan euroalueen nkymiin yksityiskohtaisemmin myhemmin. Vaikka maailmantalouden keskeinen ennustenkym on mynteinen, nkpiiriss on mys ennustettua hitaamman kasvun mahdollisuus. Ilmeisin riskitekij on ljyn ja muiden raaka-aineiden kallistuminen. Voimakas kasvu koko maailmantaloudessa on lisnnyt ljyn ja monien raaka-aineiden kysynt ja nostanut niiden hintoja. Etenkin Kiinan vahva kysynt on vaikuttanut merkittvsti raaka-aineiden ja ljyn hintojen nousuun. Vaikka ljyn hinnannousu oli viime vuonna reaalisesti vhisempi kuin l-jysokkien aikana ja teollistuneet ljyntuojamaat ovat vhentneet ljysokkien jlkeen riippuvuuttaan ljyst, jyrkk hinnannousu (32 % edellisvuotisesta) vaimensi maail-mantalouden kasvua vuoden jlkipuoliskolla. Kuluvan vuoden ensimmisell neljn-neksell ljyn hinta nousi edelleen, nimellisesti enntyskorkeaksi 55 ja 60 dollarin vlille. ljyn hinnannousun mukana ennusteiden taustalla olevia ljynhintaoletuksia on kor-jattu ylspin. Tll hetkell vaikuttaa silt, ett ljyn hinta pysyy tn ja ensi vuonna lhell viimeaikaisia lukemia. Korkea ja voimakkaasti vaihteleva ljyn hinta vaikut-taa negatiivisesti lhitulevaisuuden kasvunkymiin ja muodostaa keskeisen ennus-tenkymiin liittyvn riskin. Alkuvuoden nousuvaiheen jlkeen osakemarkkinoiden indeksit ovat laskeneet. T-mn liittyy osaksi eriden etenkin tieto- ja viestinttekniikan yritysten alkuvuoden tu-loksiin, joita kilpailun kiristymisen arvioitiin leikanneen. Yritysten tulevaisuuden n-kymi on korjattu samalla hieman varovaisemmiksi. Nkymien heikentymist kuvaa mys se, ett pitkaikaisten valtionobligaatioiden ko-rot laskivat huhtikuussa niin Yhdysvalloissa kuin Euroopassakin uudestaan takaisin alkuvuoden erittin alhaiselle tasolle. Pitkt korot ovat historiallisesti alhaiset sek nimellisesti ett reaalisesti. Ne kertovat verraten maltillisista kasvu- ja inflaatio-odotuksista. Samalla kehittyvien talouksien ja yritysten obligaatioiden korkoerot val-tionobligaatioihin nhden ovat kasvaneet hieman ja erilaiset riskitietoisuutta kuvaavat indikaattorit ovat nousseet. Kaiken kaikkiaan rahoitusmarkkinoiden indikaattorit viestivt aiempaa jossain m-rin varovaisemmasta odotuksesta maailmantalouden lhiajan kehityksen suhteen. Tmnkin viimeaikaisen informaation perusteella edell todettuun ennustekuvaan voidaan liitt aiempaa selvempi alasuuntaisen riskin mahdollisuus. Alaspin suuntautuvan riskin suhteellisen suotuisalle ennustekuvalle aiheuttavat mys maailmantalouteen muutaman viime vuoden aikana vhitellen kertyneet tasa-painottomuudet, joiden syntymiseen ovat paljolti vaikuttaneet eri maiden raha- ja fi-nanssipolitiikan valinnat. Vuoden 2001 alusta lhtien keskuspankit kevensivt rahapolitiikkaa voimakkaasti ennen kaikkea Yhdysvalloissa mutta mys muualla. Matalimmillaan lyhyet nimelliset markkinakorot olivat sek Yhdysvalloissa ett euroalueella selvsti alhaisempia kuin kertaakaan vuoden 1960 jlkeen. Dollarin keskeisen kansainvlisen aseman ja usei-den valuuttojen dollarikytkennn myt Yhdysvaltain kevyt rahapolitiikka levisi maailmantalouteen laajalti  sellaisiinkin maihin, joissa kevyen rahapolitiikan tarkoi-tuksenmukaisuus ei ollut ilmeist. Kevyt rahapolitiikka on johtanut globaalisti likviditeetin voimakkaaseen kasvuun viime vuosien aikana. Rahan mrn ja luottojen suhde bruttokansantuotteeseen on noussut yleisesti teollisuusmaissa, mutta nopeimmin It-Aasiassa. Velkavarannot ovat monissa maissa nousseet niin korkeiksi, ett ne herttvt jo huolestumista. Kevyen rahapolitiikan ja liiallisen likviditeetin vaikutukset ovat nkyneet maailman-taloudessa talouskasvun odotettua voimakkaampana ja laaja-alaisempana elpymisen. Tm on tietysti mynteinen ja toivottu asia. Mutta toisaalta kevyt tilanne on mys saanut aikaan vhemmn toivottavia ilmiit: - ljyn ja muiden raaka-aineiden maailmanmarkkinahinnat ovat vahvan kysynnn vuoksi nousseet tuntuvasti viimeisen 1-2 vuoden aikana. Paitsi talouskasvun kautta, alhainen korkotaso ja runsas likviditeetti ovat tuke-neet raaka-aineiden kysynt mys spekulatiivisen positioiden ottamisen kautta. - Globaalisti inflaatio on yh melko alhainen, mutta Yhdysvalloissa kulut-tajahintojen nousu on nopeutunut jo selvsti. - Rahoitusolosuhteiden keventyminen on johtanut yksityisen sektorin vel-kaantumisen lisntymiseen monessa maassa. - Asuntomarkkinat ovat kuumentuneet ja asuntohintojen nousu on ollut suurta monessa maassa viime vuosina. Nykyisess tilanteessa reaalikorot ovat edelleen alhaisia, useissa maissa jopa pienem-pi kuin talouden kasvuvauhti. Tm antaa aiheen huoleen maailman pitkn aikavlin inflaationkymist. Kun globalisaation aiheuttama kilpailun lisntyminen kuitenkin aiheuttaa samanaikaisesti paineita hintojen laskun suuntaan, rahapolitiikan oikean vi-rityksen arvioiminen on vaikeata. Yhdysvalloissa kevyeen rahapolitiikkaan on yhdistynyt voimakkaasti kysynnn kas-vua tukeva finanssipolitiikka. Politiikkayhdistelm on tuonut maalle vahvan kysyn-nn kasvun. Samalla kuitenkin maan sstmisen ja investointien eptasapaino on kasvanut entisestn ja siihen on yhdistynyt julkisen talouden suuri alijm. Yhdysvaltain vaihtotaseen alijm ja velkaantuminen heijasti alkujaan maan talou-den vahvuutta kohtaan tunnettua luottamusta, joka sai ulkomaiset sijoittajat ja yrityk-set sijoittamaan pomia Yhdysvaltoihin sek suorien ett osakesijoitusten kautta. Viime aikoina ulkomailta Yhdysvaltoihin tulleet sijoitukset ovat kuitenkin suuntautu-neet paljolti julkisen sektorin liikkeelle laskemiin arvopapereihin. Julkinen sektori on joutunut rahoittamaan suuren alijmns ulkomaisella rahoituksella, koska kotitalo-uksien sstminen on hyvin alhaisella tasolla. Yhdysvaltain julkisen sektorin ja koko talouden velkaantumiskierre on liiallinen ja sen on vlttmtnt jossakin vaiheessa katketa tai ainakin hidastua tuntuvasti. Yhte-n kansainvlisen talouden riskitekijn onkin pidetty sit, ett vaihtotaseen alij-mn takia dollari heikkenee jossakin vaiheessa voimakkaasti viel nykyisestn. T-m auttaisi maan ulkoista tasapainoa, mutta voisi hidastaa taloudellista kasvua muual-la. Euroopan ja varsinkin euroalueen osuus Yhdysvaltain ulkomaankaupassa on pieni, vain viidenneksen luokkaa. Siten Yhdysvaltain vaihtotaseen vajeen korjautumi-nen ei voi nojata pelkstn Yhdysvaltain ja euroalueen vliseen kauppavaihtoon. Mys kauppavirroissa muihin maihin tulee tapahtua muutoksia. Vaihtotaseen korjaamiseksi tarvitaan muutoksia Yhdysvaltain kansantalou-dessa siten ett entist suurempi osa maan investoinneista voidaan tulevaisuudessa rahoittaa kotimaisista rahoituslhteist. Yhdysvaltain rahapolitiikassa on jo otettu askeleita investointien ja sstmisen tasa-painoa korjaavaan suuntaan. Keskuspankki nosti rahapoliittista ohjauskorkoaan kes-kuussa 2004 ja antoi samalla ymmrt, ett korkopolitiikassa on aika siirty vahvasti elvyttvst virityksest maltillisesti kohti neutraalimpaa korkotasoa. Sen jlkeen FED on nostanut ohjauskorkoaan snnllisin vliajoin prosenttiyksikn neljnnek-sen kerrallaan, niin ett ohjauskorko on tll hetkell 3%. Yhdysvaltain finanssipolitiikassa nykyinen hallinto on asettanut tavoitteekseen julki-sen talouden alijmn puolittamisen kautensa loppuun menness. Uskottavat toimet tmn tavoitteen saavuttamiseksi kuitenkin puuttuvat toistaiseksi. Yhdysvaltojen kehityksen peilikuvana Aasian maiden rahoitussaatavat Yhdysvallois-ta ovat kasvaneet. Aasian maat ovat hankkineet runsaasti dollarimrisi si-joituskohteita ja tll tavalla osallistuneet merkittvss mrin Yhdysvaltain vaihto-taseen ja julkisen sektorin alijmn rahoitukseen. Kotimaisessa ky-synnss investointien muutos kntyi toisesta neljnneksest alkaen negatiivisesta positiiviseksi. Kokonaisuudessaan kotimainen kysynt pysyi kuitenkin edelleen mel-ko vaisuna. Yksityisest kulutuskysynnst ei vielkn ole ollut kasvun merkitt-vksi vauhdittajaksi euroalueella. Vaikka euroalueen talouskasvu ei ole nopeaa kansainvlisesti, sen on lhell potenti-aaliaan ja sen odotetaan palaavan potentiaalista kasvua vastaavaksi viel tmn vuo-den aikana. Talouspolitiikka, inflaation vai-meneminen, suotuisat rahoitusolosuhteet, yritysten voittomarginaalien kasvu, raken-neuudistusten edistyminen ja vahva globaali ymprist tukevat kasvun liev elpy-mist. Mys vilkkaat asuntomarkkinat useassa maassa nostavat varallisuutta ja tuke-vat kulutusta. EKP:n trkein ohjauskorko on 2 % ja lyhyet markkinakorot ovat samalla tasolla. Pitkt 10 vuoden markkinakorot ovat nimellisesti 3- 4 prosenttia ja reaalisesti vajaat 2 %. Rahamrn kasvu on ol-lut euroalueellakin viime vuosina runsasta, selvsti yli sen, mit inflaatiota kiihdyt-tmtn kasvu edellyttisi. Samalla luotot yksityiselle sektorille ovat samalla kasva-neet nopeaa vauhtia. Viimeisen vuoden aikana rahamrn kasvu nytt kuitenkin maltillistuneen. Euron vahvistumisesta huolimatta euroalueen rahoitusolosuhteita voidaan pit ke-vein. Rahapolitiikkaa on ollut kasvua tukevaa. Ra-hapolitiikan ohjauskorot on siten pidetty ennallaan. Talous- ja rahaliiton talouspolitiikka muodostuu rahapolitiikan, finanssipolitiikan ja rakennepolitiikan kokonaisuudesta. Ne kaikki tukevat osaltaan yhteisi tavoitteita  vakautta, kasvua ja tyllisyytt ja Euroopan tuotantomahdollisuuksien ja kilpailuky-vyn kohottamista niin, ett Eurooppa prj kiristyvss globaalissa kilpailussa. Eri politiikkalohkoista parhaiten on menestynyt rahapolitiikka, jonka voidaan katsoa saavuttaneen oman tavoitteensa  hintavakauden ja sen myt alhaisen korkotason  verrattain hyvin. Finanssipolitiikassa ei sit vastoin ole viel saavutettu julkisen talouden tasapainoi-selle kehitykselle ja pitkn ajan kestvyydelle asetettuja tavoitteita. Viime vuonna julkisen talouden alijmn euroalueella oli arviolta 2.7 % bruttokansantuotteesta ja ylitti 3 prosentin rajan Ranskassa, Saksassa ja Kreikassa. Kaikkiaan kymmenkunta nykyisist EU:n jsenmaista on vakaus- ja kasvusopimuksen mrittelemn liiallisen alijmn menettelyn piiriss. Vakaus- ja kasvusopimuksen soveltamisessa on trmtty komission, ministerineuvos-ton ja jsenmaiden vlisiin ristiriitoihin. Samalla luottamus koko finanssipoliittista jrjestelm kohtaan on horjunut. Vakaus- ja kasvusopimus on ollut koko olemassaolonsa ajan voimakkaan kritiikin kohteena. Sopimus on kuitenkin ollut mainettaan parempi. Sen ansiosta EU-maiden julkisen talouden tasapaino on kohentunut, inflaatio on hidastunut ja korkotaso laske-nut. Eurooppa-neuvosto on sopinut vakaus- ja kasvusopimuksen uudistamisesta. Neuvos-ton ptelmiss ei puututtu sntihin perustuvaan finanssipolitiikan jrjestelmn, eik vakaus- ja kasvusopimuksen ptavoitteeseen liiallisten alijmien vlttmisest. Sopimuksen kulmakivet  3 prosentin viitearvo alijmlle ja 60 prosentin viitearvo velalle  silyivt ennallaan. Vakaus- ja kasvusopimuksesta ptettiin kuitenkin muuttaa siten, ett se tarjoaa jsenvaltioille entist enemmn finanssipolitiikan liik-kumavaraa. Tm tehtiin mm. mrittelemll tarkemmin mit relevantteja tekijit voidaan ottaa huomioon, jos alijm ylitt 3 prosentin viitearvon. Ylityksen tulee kuitenkin olla luonteeltaan tilapinen ja kooltaan vhinen, ennen kuin nm tekijt voidaan ottaa huomioon. Muutoksistaan huolimatta vakaus- ja kasvusopimus pysyy talous- ja rahaliiton olen-naisena kulmakiven. On trke, ett sopimuksen uskottavuus onnistutaan palautta-maan, kun uudistettua sopimuksesta pannaan toimeen. Sntn perustuva finanssi-politiikka, kuten vakaus- ja kasvusopimus, toimii vain, jos sit noudatetaan. Euroo-pan maiden julkisen talouden haasteet vestn ikntyess ovat suuria. Jotta vestn ikntymisen aiheuttamat menot voidaan rahoittaa tulevaisuudessa, julkisen talouden velkaantumisen pit alentua, ei lisnty. Snnn uskottavuutta ei tulisi riskeerata sill, ett sen noudattamisesta luovutaan lyhytnkisten poliittisten paineiden takia. Politiikkalohkoista selvsti heikoiten nytt menestyneen rakennepolitiikka, etenkin euroalueen suurissa jsenmaissa. Vaikka joitakin uudistuksia on saatu toteutettua, ko-konaisuutena ottaen menestys rakennepoliittisten toimien tytntnpanossa on j-nyt vaatimattomaksi. Lissabonissa asetetut kunnianhimoiset tavoitteet, jotka on mr saavuttaa kuluvan vuosikymmenen loppuun menness, uhkaavat jd suurelta osin haaveiksi. 3. Loppuptelmi Maailmantaloudessa on eletty vahvaa kasvukautta ja sen ennustetaan edelleen jatku-van, tosin lievsti heikentyen. Vahvan pohjavireen taustalla ovat enemmn tai v-hemmn pysyvt perustekijt kuten uuden teknologian kyttnotto ja kehittyvien maiden integroituminen maailmantalouteen. Nm maailmantalouden kasvun perus-tekijt mahdollistavat kasvun jatkumisen nopeana mys tulevaisuudessa. Toisaalta kasvuun on liittynyt mys makrotaloudellisia eptasapainoilmiit. Ehk merkitt-vimmn riskin maailmantalouden suotuisan kehityksen jatkumiselle muodostaakin Yhdysvaltojen ja Aasian maiden vlille kumuloituneen sstmisen ja investointien eptasapainon purkautuminen hallitsemattomasti. Tarvittavat politiikkatoimet ovat melko hyvin tiedossa  sstmisen lismist Yhdysvalloissa, ja valuuttakurssien joustavoittamista Aasian kehittyviss talouksissa  mutta riittvn tehokkaisiin toi-miin ei selvstikn ole viel psty. Euroalueella sstminen ja investoinnit ovat kohtuullisen hyvin tasapainossa, mutta ongelmana on rakenteellisista syist johtuva kokonaistuotannon  ja tuotantopotenti-aalinkin  liian hidas kasvu. Euroalueen kasvudynamiikan elvyttminen ja pitkn ai-kavlin kasvuedellytysten turvaaminen vaatii ensisijaisesti rakenteellisia toimia. Lissabonissa viisi vuotta sitten mritelty strategia asetti EU -maille kunninhimoiset uudistustavoitteet, mutta niiden toteuttamisessa ei ole onnistuttu tysin toivotulla ta-valla. Tt taustaa vasten minun on helppo yhty siihen laajalti  mm. kevn Eu-rooppa -neuvostossa  hyvksyttyyn nkemykseen, ett Lissabonin strategian toi-meenpanon vauhdittamiseksi strategiassa on syyt selkesti painottaa kasvua ja tyl-lisyytt. Olennaista on tehd Euroopasta entist houkuttelevampi paikka investoida ja tehd tyt. Samalla tulee list investointeja tietoon ja innovaatioihin sek luoda enemmn ja parempia typaikkoja. Niden tavoitteiden saavuttamisessa jsenvaltiot onnistuvat parhaiten mrittelemll rakennepoliittiset uudistushankkeensa hyvin konkreettisesti  ja mys toteuttamalla ne. Kuten alussa totesin, globalisaatioon, ja sen seurauksena tapahtuneeseen maailmanta-louden nopeaan kasvuun liittyy vistmtt rakennemuutoksia ja sopeutumistarpeita lhes kaikkialla. Tm merkitsee, ett lyhyen ajan suhdannenkymienkin tarkastelus-sa on pidettv vahvasti mukana mys rakenteelliset muutokset.

Title: 35th ISC-Symposium at the University of St. Gallen
text: Pentti Hakkarainen, Member of the Board, Bank of Finland 35th ISC-Symposium at the University of St. Gallen, Switzerland, May 19  20, 2005 The main topic of the symposium: "Liberty, Trust and Responsibility" SOURCES OF SUCCESS FOR AN ECONOMY  AND THE ENTERPRISES IN IT  IN THE EURO AREA In my presentation to you today, I would like to put before you some of the impacts, benefits and perhaps some restrictions Finland faced and still faces, due to membership of the EMU, the Economic and Monetary Union. The membership for its part has shaped the environment and formed conditions for all agents of the economy. Despite the fact that Finland is the example, the focus of the presentation is on most relevant general impacts and issues, which may be applicable to any country having discussions of the monetary union. It is important to point out that when Finland joined the euro, the country had just recovered from a very severe economic and financial crisis. This means that the effects of our membership are intrinsically mixed with the effects of the crisis, such as the significant depreciation of the currency, a sudden increase in government debt, a rise in the number of mergers and acquisitions as well as privatisations in both banking and industry. The Finnish experience in the early 1990s stood out from similar experiences of its neighbouring Nordic countries; not least because of the coinciding sudden collapse of the Soviet Union and its export markets which strongly intensified the crisis. During a period of only a few years, our GDP decreased by an unprecedented 10% and the unemployment rate increased from below 4% close to a staggering 18%. While another factor  and one that makes it difficult to isolate the positive effects of the EMU  is the remarkable impact of the so-called new economy. From late 1990s onwards Finland's economic performance has been dominated by the exceptional growth of our high tech industry, led by the success of Nokia. The information and communications sector as a whole contributed to so strong a boom that the effects of the new monetary regime are hard to distinguish from the technology- related changes in the economy. Now we have to ask how Finland and her economy have done during the time of EMU membership. That can be assessed logically through firstly highlighting some of the deliberation that went on behind the decision to enter the EMU. It is really interesting to see what was expected and what was actually accomplished. One should bear in mind that the effects of the EMU started to materialise even before formal entry. Conclusions and future challenges It may still be too early days to say to what extent if any, membership of the EMU has benefited Finland and her economy. Positive development and success regarding the economy itself and enterprises in it are obvious; however one has to point out that the effects of the membership, as such, are intrinsically mixed with the effects of other measures taken to recover from the crises of the 1990s. Having seen the economic development in Finland today, it is even more difficult to argue that Finland would have had to stay outside the EMU. It could be easier to name some threats and potential adverse effects resulting from the decision to stay outside than find plausible explanations that argue for the benefits of not joining the monetary union. A very practical reason for the popularity of the euro, to the man in the street in Finland, is that there is no need to exchange money when travelling around Europe. The typical Finn feels proud that it is Finland's own money that is valid and accepted extensively around the world. In the coming years and not far in the future, the aging of the population, a heavy tax burden and persistently high unemployment levels challenge the sustainability of the economy and force actions that must result in overcoming these foreseeable challenges. These actions must be taken; independent of whether Finland is inside or outside the monetary union and membership provides us with the environment where we can face these more confidently. Through membership we gain the liberty of an open market in which to operate, the trust that comes from a credible monetary policy and allows us to exercise the responsibility of being able to take care of adjusting our own economy. (Please also see the slides of the presentation)

Title: Speech entitled "Ageing and financial markets" at a seminar for the State Pension Fund's 15 years
text: PUBLICATION FREE 25.5.2005 at 15.00 Director General Erkki Liikanen State Pension Fund 15th anniversary seminar 25.5.2005 Helsinki Ageing and financial markets (Figure 1.) It is a pleasure to be part of the seminar of the State Pension Fund. For two reasons. Firstly, the challenges of ageing in the financial markets are a key topic in the debate on the financial markets. Secondly, in 1989 I was involved in the decision to establish the State Pension Fund. It could be seen that state pension expenditure is growing rapidly. At the same time, there was a large surplus in the state economy. The aim of the solution was to influence both. The aim was to prepare for future pension costs and perhaps, in particular, to prevent the surplus from being used for new current government expenditure. Therefore, in the budget, 4.4 billion marks were transferred to the pension fund. At that time, it corresponded to just under one per cent of gross domestic product. Today, however, I would like to focus on the first topic. Far away in the midwestern U.S., in the small mountain village of Jackson Hole in the state of Wyoming, the famous Central Bank Symposium is held every August. The symposium was hosted by one of the U.S. regional central banks, the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City. Last August's symposium focused on "Global Population Structure Change: Economic Impacts and Policy Challenges" with Chairman Alan Greenspan as the first speaker. The symposium identified a long list of the channels of influence of ageing on economic development. Ageing was found to have an impact on factors such as interest rates, natural employment rates, potential growth rates, monetary policy transmission mechanisms, financial claims prices and financial market stability [Bean, Jackson Hole 2004]. Not many economic reports of interest to the central bank were left out of the list. The discussion at the symposium reflects the fact that the ageing of the population has become a permanent part of the international economic policy debate. There has been a lot of talk about whistleblowing in recent years. Still, when studying the forecasts of the population, the pace of aging and the global scale are startling. (Figure 2.) Manifests itself, from a practical point of view, to every country in the world. In its latest forecast, the UN predicts that the median age of the European population will increase by almost 10 years from 2000 to 2050. In Asia (and South America), the rise in median age is even faster: In China, for example, the median age is projected to rise from 30 years to 45 years at the turn of the millennium by mid-century. The increase in median age is smallest in North America, only about six years. At this very moment, the world median age rises by about eight days every month. It is easy to understand that a change of this magnitude in the structure of the population must affect the functioning of the economy in many ways. What exactly these effects will be is a more difficult question. There is very little experiential information on changes in the age structure of the population. To put it mildly, there is one observation of a sharp increase in the birth rate worldwide (baby boomers), one observation of its downturn (from the 50s and 60s onwards), and one observation of a trend-like increase in life expectancy. From such statistical data, a genuine breakdown of the effects of the age structure is somewhat impossible. Therefore, when studying the report, a lot of theoretical analyses and model calculations have to be resorted to. In this presentation, I will go through a few of the channels of influence of ageing in the financial markets and fork out the possible magnitudes of the effects. Let me start by talking about the importance of saving for retirement as a source of funding in the international financial markets. I will then discuss the impact of changes in the age structure and pension reforms on the formation of the international real interest rate. And finally, a few comments on how the Finnish pension system and pension reform respond to the challenges of ageing. Pension savings in the financial markets Preparing for old-age expenses is one of the most significant motives for saving and a key source of funding. Pension funds are the largest players in the financial markets. However, they are only one aspect of the aging manifestation of the financial markets. Even outside pension funds, a large proportion of private equity holdings, fund investments, bank deposits, etc. reflects the contingency of preparedness for old age. How much, is impossible to estimate. There can be many motives for saving, and the share of each of them cannot be unambiguously defined. However, a simple thought play can help you understand the situation. Take, for example, a developed country where the birth rate, retirement age and life expectancy are such that the old-age dependency ratio (ratio of over 65 to the liked population) is 23%, which is the current average for developed countries. It is thought that everyone over the age of 65 is retired and all employees are in tile. Let us continue to imagine that the country has a fully funded pension system with a pension of 60% of the average salary at each point in time. If we add in a few typical assumptions about productivity growth, the real interest rate and production technology, we can estimate the size of pension funds that would accrue in the long term. The answer is about 340% of gdp! This is a wild figure. As a reference point, you can take the value of Finland's national wealth, which, depending on the definition, is perhaps 4-5 times the value of gross domestic product. (Figure 3) Then let's add the aging of the population to the figure. The UN estimates that the old-age dependency ratio in developed countries will rise to 44 per cent by 2050. If the calculation described above is repeated, assuming that the old-age dependency ratio is 44 per cent instead of 23 per cent, the required amount of pension funds will rise dramatically. In the long run, the size of the funds would increase to about 640% of GDP! With different assumptions, slightly different results would be achieved, but the orders of magnitude would be sa-mat. What do such highly typed calculations tell us? Not everything, but maybe two things. Firstly, the fact that it is difficult to organise the expected level of pension provision exclusively through funded pension schemes. Funds that are six times the size of gross domestic product cannot be maintained, either nationally and certainly not globally. Profitable investments simply run out. An economy with a real wealth of more than six times that of gross domestic product would be heavily overcapitalized and a return on capital would be significant. It is therefore clear that a large part of the funds spent on pensions will inevitably be covered by pay-as-you-go systems. Secondly, the message of the calculations is that even if pension liabilities were mainly settled through pay-as-you-go schemes and only a small part were funded, the volumes of pension funds would in any case be very high. The conclusion is that the way in which pension management is organised between funded and pay-as-you-go systems is one of the key factors shaping the future of financial and capital markets. Baby boomers and "financial market meltdown" Some years ago, the term 'financial market meltdown' came into the debate on the prospects for the development of the financial markets the collapse of the financial markets. It refers to the impact that the retirement of the post-war baby boomers will generate, according to some calculations, on the financial markets. When the baby boomers, when they retire, stop saving for retirement and start spending their accumulated wealth, the balance of the financial markets is upset: buyers disappear from the market, while pension funds start to liquidate their wealth. The prices of wealth items are plummeting and, with them, the value of pension savings disappears - that is how the argument goes. For the most part, recent research arrives at a less dramatic view of the future. At the Jackson Hole Symposium I mentioned, the main conclusions were that the change in the age structure will be reflected in fluctuations in the demand for different types of financial instruments in the financial markets rather than in the form of a general price collapse. In particular, the increase in demand for insurance-type instruments was highlighted. (Figure 4.) The financial market impact of baby boomer retirement is softened by at least three factors. Firstly, attention has been drawn to the fact that the actual consumption behaviour of pensioners does not seem to correspond to the assumptions of the models: pensioners do not realise their wealth at nearly the rate that theoretical models would expect. Financial wealth does decrease in retirement, but the decline is slow, and a significant part of the financial wealth remains until the end of life. Taking this observation into account in the calculations will significantly reduce the projected impact of ageing on the financial markets. The effects may be small to such an extent that it may be difficult to distinguish the effects from normal financial market volatility. Another factor preventing sudden price movements is that the retirement of the baby boomers is very predictable. Predictable factors in rational financial markets do not cause collapses, but are gradually reflected in prices. Thus, if the retirement of the baby boomers is seen to change the balance between supply and demand for financial claims, the market will price it out gradually, even years before the baby boomers retire. The third point that will increase the resilience of the financial markets is that, at least in countries where pension provision is largely based on private saving, the link between the retirement of the baby boomers and the price of wealth is a two-way, self-correcting process. If, as described above, the expectation of the baby boomers' retirement begins to pile up sales pressures in the asset market and lowers the prices of stocks, bonds, and housing prices, the value of the wealth of the baby boomers will fall. Many pension savers find themselves in a situation where reduced pension assets no longer allow for the desired level of living in retirement. Some of those planning to retire will have to continue working longer than planned. The amount of pension savings is increasing, the number of pension consumers is decreasing. The balance in the financial markets will improve and there will be no price collapse. A recent study1 by Tuomas Saarenheimo, VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland, on the effects of ageing on the international financial markets, recently completed at the Bank of Finland, brings yet another view that has been overlooked in international debate. The whole debate on the collapse of the financial markets is largely based on a partial examination of one of the elements of ageing  the birth rate and the shrinking age groups. It has been studied what kind of effects it has when shrinking age groups go through a life cycle that remains unchanged. In the models used, cohort after cohort goes through a life in which childhood, like and retirement follow each other predetermined and unchanged in length. Such an approach covers only part of the ageing problem, as ageing is not just about the decline in the birth rate. An equally important element is the change in the life cycle, more precisely, the increase in life expectancy and, in particular, in the time spent in retirement. From 1950 to the present, the life expectancy of a 60-year-old increased by about five years to 22 years. By 2050, it is projected to grow further by about five years. The development is more or less the same everywhere, with the exception of the African countries most affected by AIDS. In particular, from the point of view of the resilience of public pension systems, it would be desirable for part of the lengthening life cycle to be channelled into an extension of the hernia. Until now, however, this has not been the case. It is therefore likely that most of the additional years will continue to extend the period of retirement. In the coming decades, the period spent in retirement can be expected to increase by up to a quarter. It is clear that an increase of this magnitude at the end of the life cycle increases the need to prepare for the financing of pensions. More than twenty years spent in retirement will cost more than fifteen. Some of the increased costs (especially in continental Europe) will be financed through public pay-as-you-go schemes, but the need and desire for private retirement savings is increasing. According to a study conducted by the Bank of Finland, the increase in saving is significant. The study predicts that the saving rate of a typical 62-year-old European approaching the end of his hernia, which, according to the model, is now just over 30% of disposable income, will increase to around 40% by 2050 as a result of the increase in life expectancy. This is despite the fact that public pension schemes cover most of the costs of retirement. If public pension benefits are cut to a more sustainable level, the increase in the saving rate may be even stronger. Global saving is thus shaped by two factors that influence opposite directions. On the one hand, the reduction in the number of age groups will reduce the number of pension savers in relation to the retired and saving age groups. On the other hand, the lengthening of the life cycle increases the propensity of employees to save. The calculations mentioned above suggest that the latter effect would be more pronounced, at least for the next couple of decades. It would not be until around 2030 that the lowering effect of the shrinking age groups on saving would begin to dominate. Even then, the impact would be gradual, and would mainly be reflected in a slowdown in the growth of new investment assets entering the financial markets, not in the form of a collapse. Of course, such calculations should not be treated as forecasts. Predicting economic development on the horizon for decades is not realistic, nor has it been attempted in the calculations made at the Bank of Finland. The aim has been to analyse the impact of certain demographic trends, which are already relatively predictable, on the economy in a mainstream model framework of economics. One more, more speculative motive can be added to the list of factors that increase pension savings. People's attitudes towards retirement seem to be changing. In time, the boredom was left out when the tyky had been reduced so that there were no longer any prerequisites for productive work. Now expectations have changed. More and more people have many more healthy years ahead of them after the accident. Many now see retirement time as an opportunity to enjoy their free time in a way that was not possible in working life. In other words, expectations of the level of consumption during retirement seem to be on the rise. Increasing willingness to consume means increasing needs for saving for retirement. It is difficult to estimate how great the impact of such a change in attitudes in the financial markets will be, but the direction of the impact is likely to be clear. This debate can therefore be summed up by saying that ageing, and in particular the retirement of the baby boomers, will slow down the growth of financial market volumes, but current estimates show that growth will continue and there is no need to fear sudden or strong price shocks. Ageing, real interest rates and public pension systems Although the collapse in asset prices is not visible, ageing still affects many things in the economy and financial markets. The growth of tyoima in the developed world slows down and turns - without strong immigration - into a contraction of the workoma. The decrease in the supply of labour weakens the profitability of investments and reduces investments. Thus, the growth of the capital stock slows down. When the employment rate decreases and the growth of the capital stock slows down, the growth in output of the economy as a whole remains modest. All these factors influence the formation of a equilibrium interest rate in the financial markets  that is, the real level of interest rates that balances investment and saving and is consistent with price stability and balanced growth. The magnitude of such interest rate effects has been estimated in many studies, including the Bank of Finland's calculations mentioned above. More or less without exception, studies show that ageing lowers both the propensity to save and the propensity to invest. The key question for the formation of the real interest rate is which reacts more strongly, saving or investing. In the most comprehensive calculations, the result is usually that the decrease in the propensity to invest is stronger than the propensity to save, resulting in a decrease in the equilibrium interest rate of the economy. For example, in the light of the research literature in the field, the Bank of Finland's calculations reach a fairly typical conclusion that demographic changes would reduce the global real interest rate  ceteris paribus  by about 0.7% over the next quarter of a century. Public pension systems play a central and interesting role in these projections. As I said at the beginning, the extent to which provision is made for the payment of pensions through funding (through the first, second or third pillars) and the extent to which public pay-as-you-go systems are used is absolutely crucial to the provision of funding. At present, the share of public pay-as-you-go systems predominates, especially in Europe. However, the future of pay-as-you-go systems is unclear. It is known with certainty that if pension systems are not radically reformed, pension contributions to pay-as-you-go systems will rise dramatically in the future. According to calculations by the Bank of Finland, pension contributions in Europe would rise from the current 16 per cent of the payroll to around 28 per cent by 2040. Japan, where the temperature is lower, would end up at the same level. Even in the United States, where ageing is clearly slower, the pension contribution rate would rise from 11% to almost 20%. (Figure 5.) If implemented, such an increase in pension contributions would mean the unprecedented large intergenerational tax transfer. At the same time, the increase in care expenditure for the elderly brings pressure to increase other taxes. There is reason to doubt whether pension contributions could actually rise by this much, especially as the constant increase in the international mobility of workers and capital reduces the fiscal room for manoeuvre of the nation state. Many experts have drawn attention to the tightening of tax competition, including Professor Brsch-Supa's assessment of the Finnish pension reform. Putting pension systems on a more sustainable footing has been a key part of the economic policy agenda throughout the developed world. In Finland, considerable progress has already been made in this project, and many other countries have more work to do. From the point of view of the financial markets, the most significant common feature of the pension reforms has been the attempt to reduce the share of the pay-as-you-go system in the provision of income for the elderly. This does not necessarily mean more funding within public pension systems. From a macroeconomic point of view, the same result can also be achieved simply by cutting or restricting access to pay-as-you-go benefits. Such reforms mean a reduction in transfers from future generations to current generations. As a result, the expected income stream of current generations will decrease, the desire of citizens to acquire replacement private pension provision will increase, and the saving rate of the entire national economy will increase. Everyone knows what the political challenges are for such reforms. As noted above, the financial volumes of public pension systems are so huge that reforms to them can have a large macroeconomic impact. The aforementioned study by the Bank of Finland forked out the magnitudes of these effects with a calculation that assumed that pension contributions from public pension systems would be frozen all over the world from 2010 onwards. After this date, the ageing of the population was reflected in the calculation as a clear reduction in the benefits paid by pension schemes. According to the calculation, such a measure would steepen the fall in real interest rates over the next quarter century by more than half a percentage point: Now, until the 2030s, interest rates would fall by 1.3 percentage points instead of 0.7 percent. We can already talk about a massive reduction in real yields. Apart from cutting pension benefits, the sustainability of pension systems can, of course, be improved by selling pensions, i.e. by increasing the number of contributors and reducing the number of beneficiaries. Interestingly, the effects of raising the retirement age on the balance of the financial markets are exactly the opposite of cutting benefits. Postponing retirement would slow down the growth of pension costs, increase labour supply, improve returns on investment and boost economic growth. As a result, the fall in interest rates would be small or non-existent. In the above calculation, an increase of about four years to the end of the hernia (worldwide) would be enough to neutralize the real interest rate-lowering effect of aging. These calculations are thought exercises in nature and are not worth taking literally. What is clear, however, is that the development of pension savings and public pension systems are among the main factors shaping the supply of finance and the future of the financial markets. Transparency and credibility of pension systems Regardless of the extent to which future pensions end up being funded, two vital characteristics of pension systems are required for balanced economic development: transparency and credibility. Transparency means that those in the pension system understand what kind of security the pension system gives them and what its costs are for them. The pension system must be comprehensible  it must not deceive its customers into over- or underestimating the level of their pension provision. This is, of course, clear from the human and social point of view, but it is also important from an overall economic point of view: sooner or later, misunderstandings will become clear, and then there may be sudden changes in people's saving and investment behaviour that will rock the financial markets. Professor Bsch-Supan drew attention to this fact in his assessment of the pension reform in Finland: the reform has many advantages, but as a result, the system is very complex and difficult to understand. Take the life expectancy coefficient as an example. It is an innovative element that is important for the fairness and sustainability of the pension system, but do people understand its importance? Life expectancy is a rather distant and abstract concept for a private person. Will it happen that those who retire in a couple of decades' time will be dismayed by their unexpectedly small pension, while those approaching retirement age will be frightened and will quickly start to increase their savings? Perhaps effective education can avoid surprises  otherwise there may be reasons to simplify the system. Credibility means the ability of a system in all situations to deliver on its promises. If the financing of the pension system is based on a very sharp increase in pension contributions, then the question arises as to whether the payers of the short-term system will actually be sold in the future, or whether, at some point, emergency braking will have to be applied. It is obvious that many European pension systems suffer from such a credibility problem. The rise of ageing and its economic consequences to the headlines and the political legend has been hoped for and necessarily, but the knowledge has added to the pain. Many Europeans have realised that the pension promises on which they have planned their lives are largely unfunded. And unfortunately, it seems that even more people still have this realization ahead of them. It is clear that such a realisation upsets people's sense of security and affects their economic decisions. Often the result is an overreaction: faith in public pension provision collapses and citizens start saving more than would be economically justified. Something like this can be seen in the current situation in Germany. There is another important aspect to the credibility of the pension system, which relates to the nature of public pension contributions and the incentive effects. In a credible, actuarially fair pension system, pension contributions fully accumulate the beneficiary's personal pension assets and, in that sense, constitute savings. Such pension contributions do not have the unfavourable incentive effects associated with taxes. Pension contributions begin to acquire the characteristics of a tax only when there is a deviation from this ideal. The further away one moves away from a credible, actuarially fair pension system, the more pension contributions approach taxation in nature. In this way, faith in the future sustainability of the pension system is linked to the current incentives for stubbornness. If citizens' faith that they will get a fair return on their pension contributions falters, they will begin to perceive pension contributions as taxes. Incentives to work are weakening, the winner is the shadow economy. The guideline of these reflections for the preparation of pension reforms is clear: the aim must be a clear and long-term sustainable pension system. Partial reforms, which postpone the crisis in the system for a few years, only serve to highlight the depth of the problems and frighten the citizens. They cause more problems than they solve. It is obvious that the credibility of the Finnish pension system improved with the reform. Whether credibility is guaranteed permanently is already a more difficult question. Now that genuine information about the operation of the new system is beginning to accumulate, it is important to continue with the impact assessment. Over the next two or three years, it must be possible to form a realistic assessment of the extent to which the reform will actually be able to curb the rise in pension contributions. If it is found that the objectives set are not being met, or if it is possible that the objectives were originally set too modestly, the ability to take new action must be increased. On the one hand, the long-term sustainability of the system must be guaranteed and, on the other hand, citizens must be offered a clear and unvarnished picture of the level of their public pension security as a basis for mental life planning. It is clear that the desire and need for private pension and long-term savings is also growing in Finland due to ageing and the prosperity of citizens. In recent years, the tax treatment of such savings has been considered in various ways. It is important that the nature of the scheme is such that, in terms of tax treatment and the instruments used, it offers flexible conditions for private saving to fill the gaps in pension provision that the public pension system inevitably leaves behind. These questions will certainly be returned to in the future. Johtopaatkset Various conclusions can be drawn from the calculations made on the effects of aging. What is clear, however, is that the world is facing changes, and the impact of these changes on the economy and the financial markets will be enormous. On the one hand, stagnation and a downturn in labour growth in many countries seems to reduce investment demand. On the other hand, the change in the population structure tends to reduce saving flows and the supply of financing. At the same time, the longer life cycle, especially the increase in the number of years after work, increases the need for self-financing of pension provision. At the moment, it seems likely that the combined effect of these forces in different directions on the financial markets will be gradual and perhaps smaller than expected. There is no sign of a collapse in asset prices or other sudden disruptions. The biggest expected change is the gradual reduction in real returns on capital. Three mutually supportive elements are needed to manage the economic and social consequences of ageing. The volumes needed to finance pensions require, first of all, that the system should always be based on a public pay-as-you-go system. On top of that, we need a solid funded element that evens out the disruptions, distributes the burden between generations and thus contributes to the adaptation of the economy to demographic changes. The third pillar requires clear conditions for private pension savings, which will allow for one-sided life planning and fill gaps in the public system. The long-term credibility of the public pillar of the pension system is vital. Pension systems that are questionable in terms of sustainability and share false promises create uncertainty and are a source of disruption to the economy and financial markets. This fact is widely understood and action has already been taken in many countries. Finland is at the forefront on this journey and is an example in many respects. However, it is likely that we have not quite reached our destination here either
text_original: JULKAISUVAPAA 25.5.2005 klo 15.00 Pjohtaja Erkki Liikanen Valtion Elkerahasto 15 vuotta -juhlaseminaari 25.5.2005 Helsinki Ikntyminen ja rahoitusmarkkinat (Kuvio 1.) On ilo olla mukana Valtion Elkerahaston seminaarissa. Kahdestakin syyst. Ensinnkin ikntymisen haasteet rahoitusmarkkinoilla ovat keskeinen aihe rahoitusmarkkinoita koskevassa keskustelussa. Toiseksi olin mukana tekemss vuonna 1989 ptt Valtion elkerahaston perustamisesta. Oli nhtviss, ett valtion elkemenot kasvavat nopeasti. Samaan aikaan valtiontaloudessa oli suuri ylijm. Ratkaisulla haluttiin vaikuttaa molempiin. Haluttiin varautua tuleviin elkekustannuksiin ja ehk aivan erityisesti est, ettei ylijm kytetty uusiin valtion juokseviin menoihin. Siksi budjetissa siirrettiin 4.4 miljardia markkaa elkerahastoon. Tuolloin se vastasi vajaata prosenttia bruttokansantuotteesta. Tnn haluan kuitenkin keskitty ensimmiseen aiheeseen. Kaukana USA:n keskilnnessa, pieness Jackson Holen vuoristokylss Wyomingin osavaltiossa jrjestetn joka elokuu kuuluisa keskuspankkisymposium. Symposiumia isnni yksi USA:n alueellisista keskuspankeista, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City. Viime elokuun symposiumin aiheena oli "Globaali vestrakenteen muutos: taloudelliset vaikutukset ja politiikkahaasteet" ja ensimmisen puhujana puheenjohtaja Alan Greenspan. Symposiumissa identifioitiin pitk lista ikntymisen vaikutuskanavia talouskehitykseen. Ikntymisen todettiin vaikuttavan mm. korkotasoon, luonnolliseen tytmyysasteeseen, potentiaaliseen kasvuvauhtiin, rahapolitiikan vlittymismekanismeihin, rahoitusvaateiden hintoihin ja rahoitusmarkki- noiden vakauteen [Bean, Jackson Hole 2004]. Listan ulkopuolelle ei jnyt montaakaan keskuspankkia kiinnostavaa taloudellista ilmit. Symposiumin keskustelu kuvastaa sit, ett vestn ikntymisest on tullut pysyv osa kansainvlist talouspolitiikkakeskustelua. Ilmit on puhuttu viime vuosina runsaasti. Silti vestennusteita tutkiessa ikntymisen vauhti ja globaali mittaluokka htkhdytt. (Kuvio 2.) Ilmikoskettaa kytnnllisesti katsoen jokaista maailman maata. YK ennakoi tuoreimmassa vestennusteessaan Euroopan vestn mediaani-in nousevan vuodesta 2000 vuoteen 2050 menness lhes 10 vuodella. Aasiassa (ja Etel-Amerikassa) mediaani-in nousu on viel nopeampaa: Esimerkiksi Kiinassa mediaani-in ennakoidaan nousevan vuosituhannen vaihteen 30 vuodesta 45 vuoteen vuosisadan puolivliin menness. Mediaani-in nousu on pienin Pohjois-Amerikassa, vain noin kuusi vuotta. Koko maailman mediaani-ik nousee juuri tll hetkell noin kahdeksalla pivll joka kuukausi. On helppo ymmrt, ett tmn suuruusluokan muutoksen vestrakenteessa tytyy vaikuttaa talouden toimintaan monella tavalla. Minklaisia nm vaikutukset tulevat tarkasti ottaen olemaan, on vaikeampi kysymys. Kokemusperist tietoa vest ikrakenteen muutoksista on hyvin vhn. Vain hieman krjisten voi sanoa, ett maailmanlaajuisesti on olemassa yksi havainto syntyvyyden voimakkaasta lisntymisest (suuret ikluokat), yksi havainto sen kntymisest laskuun (50-60luvuilta eteenpin), ja yksi havainto elinajanodotteen trendinomaisesta noususta. Tllaisesta tilastollisesta aineistosta ikrakenteen vaikutusten aito erittely on jokseenkin mahdotonta. Siksi ilmi tutkittaessa joudutaan turvautumaan paljolti teoreettisiin analyyseihin ja mallilaskelmiin. Tss esityksess kyn lpi muutamia ikntymisen vaikutuskanavia rahoitusmarkkinoilla ja haarukoin vaikutusten mahdollisia suuruusluokkia. Aluksi puhun elkesstmisen merkityksest rahoituksen lhteen kansainvlisill rahoitusmarkkinoilla. Sen jlkeen ksittelen vestn ikrakenteen muutoksen ja elkereformien vaikutusta kansainvlisen reaalikoron muodostumiseen. Ja lopuksi muutama kommentti siit, miten Suomen elkejrjestelm ja elkeuudistus vastaavat ikntymisen haasteisiin.
