Title: Speech at the Influencer Forum
text: Bank manager Sinikka Salo Bank of Finland Integration of banking markets in the EU Speech at the Influencer Forum in Vanajanlinna 25.5.2005 The creation of an EU internal market to improve the EU's competitiveness and thereby increase the well-being of Europeans has been a key objective of EU integration since the Treaty of Rome. The EU's single market programme, which aims to create a large, open and integrated domestic market for European businesses and households as possible, has many facets, such as trade policy, the reduction of technical standards, the monitoring of competition policy at EU level, and so on. From my point of view, the closest issues are, of course, the single currency and the integration of the financial markets, which only allow the common market to become a reality. There is already a single currency in the euro area, and that means much more than 300 million people using the same banknotes. This means, among other things, that previously significant mutual exchange rate risks have disappeared. It means a credible monetary policy to safeguard price stability in the euro area. The single currency will also make it possible for businesses and households to have access to a Pan-European financial market that guarantees the widest range of services at the most competitive prices, and that it should not matter for invoicing and payment management whether there is business between different countries in the euro area or within one country. These objectives have not yet been fully realised. It is all the more important that the central banks, other public authorities and various private bodies, including banks, work resolutely to create a truly integrated financial market and a single payments area in the euro area. Some of the euro area's financial markets are already fairly fully integrated. The best example is the interbank unsecured short money market, which operates almost smoothly throughout the euro area. Significant progress has also been made in other areas, such as sovereign bond markets, but despite the single currency, euro area financial markets in general remain heavily segmented along national lines. The transformation into a truly pan-European market is therefore at most halfway through. The integration of financial markets is high on the EU's economic policy priorities. This can be clearly seen, for example, in the lisbon strategy adopted jointly by the Member States, which is accompanied by a very concrete financial services action plan, the Financial Services Action Plan (FSAP). This action plan, which aims to create a pan-European market for financial services, has required extensive legislative work at EU level; in total, it contains more than 40 measures (recommendations and directives). Much of the action plan has already been implemented on schedule, but significant efforts are still needed to complete its implementation. Hardly anyone is able to accurately assess all the consequences of financial integration. However, according to a number of seemingly reliable estimates, integration has considerable advantages. One example of the link between financial markets and economic efficiency and growth is the United States. It is fairly widely believed that the large, deep and well-functioning US financial markets are a significant  but of course not the only  driver of the country's high productivity and rapid economic growth. If this assessment is correct, then the full integration of the financial markets and the associated intensification would have a similarly positive impact on employment, competitiveness and, consequently, on the budgetary finances of the European countries. That is why it is worth making an effort to achieve a common financial market. In this speech, I will address three key aspects of the interdependence of the EU banking market: the emergence of pan-European (cross-border) banks, the integration trends in banking and insurance, and the efficiency of cross-border payment transactions. The emergence of pan-European banks  "The Nordea case" Although banks have increased their crossborder transactions in Europe, even since the introduction of the euro, this has been the case in quite segmented areas of the business, mainly wholesale bank picking. There are not very many actual pan-European banks that would provide services in full in many countries. There are around 6500 credit institutions in the euro area and around 8800 in the enlarged EU, but only a small number of them  around 40 banks  are of real relevance to cross-border banking. In the Nordic countries, we are avant-garde in this respect, and for that reason alone it is interesting to look at the questions of these banks a little more closely, above all the topical question of the organisation of these banking groups  either in the form of a subsidiary bank or in the form of a side-branch. The choice between a branch form or a subsidiary bank form is not just a pure organizational decision for a bank. When a bank establishes a branch in another EU country, the bank's corporate structure and balance sheet remain one. The bank does not need to release separate capital for the branch, but can rely on the parent bank's capital and financing efficiently and, more importantly, the bank only needs one licence, it must comply with only one regulation and it is sufficient for it to report to one supervisor. If, on the other hand, the bank is or-ganised in the form of a subsidiary bank, these activities are multiplied depending on the number of countries in which the activity takes place. This implies a complex structure and high cost for the pan-gui. So far, the majority of banks operating cross-border within the EU have continued to establish themselves outside their home country in the form of subsidiaries. This is actually quite surprising given the additional costs of regulatory practices and controls. The reason may be, for example, that in mergers, as a result of which a pan-European bank is often born-now, the bank, in the form of a subsidiary bank, can retain its local name and proximity to customers. This has been the case, for example, in the new Member States, whose banks have merged with a foreign banking group. But it is obvious that crossborder banking in the form of branches will increase, especially now that, under the EU Company Regulation, which entered into force in 2004, mergers across borders within the EU became possible under Community law. For example, Nordea's plans to transform into a European company are understandable. A branch bank is not only more cost-effective, but also much simpler in terms of structure and also more transparent. From the point of view of supervision and regulation, the transformation of a bank from a branch to a pan-European one is not entirely straightforward. A single market for financial services is based on two basic principles: the so-called 'single market'. a single passport and the related home country control. These principles should best support fair competition between business procedures and regulatory practices, thereby improving the quality of financial services. This is the core of the integration of the entire EU's financial markets and the driving force behind it. If implemented, the transformation of the Nordea Group from a group of subsidiaries in the various Nordic countries to a European company based in Sweden will mean  according to Nordea's current plans in 2007  that the entire banking supervision of Nordea will be carried out by the Swedish Supervisory Authority (Finansinspektion). The Nordic supervisors are therefore considering what kind of requirements Nordea's new corporate structure places on cooperation between supervisors and, in particular, what expectations the supervisors of the host countries place on the home state supervisor, Finansinspektion. In any case, the Finnish Financial Supervisory Authority and the Norwegian and Danish supervisory authorities are left to monitor the liquidity of the branch network in their own country, as well as the general interest and procedures of the market. Another important issue that needs to be resolved when Nordea becomes a European Company is related to the deposit guarantee scheme and its coverage in the different Nordic countries. The level of deposit protection regulations differs from one Nordic country to another, and in Nordea's case, the deposit guarantee for a European company is agreed upon from the customer's point of view. At present, the main principle of the Deposit Guarantee Scheme Directive is that the deposit guarantee for branches located abroad is in accordance with the state of origin, in this case the Swedish state. It is clear that this is problematic for Nordea's plans. In the summer of 2004, Nordea announced that it had asked the European Commission (the Commissioner for Internal Markets) to make an addition to the deposit guarantee scheme directive that would allow deposits by a subsidiary bank that had become a branch of a European company to remain covered by the deposit guarantee scheme in the country in which it is located. The Commission has therefore launched an investigation into the amendment of the Deposit Guarantee Scheme Directive, but the issues concerning, among other things, the financing of deposit guarantee schemes, coverage, the definition of deposits and the 'topping up' issue - are politically difficult and will probably take a long time to amend the directive. The third important point relates to the stability of the financial markets. Due to its size, Nordea is a key player in all the Nordic and Baltic countries. Nordea's market share of the Finnish financial market, for example, is just under 40%. From the point of view of stability, the functioning of payment systems and the harmoniously functioning links with the euro area are of strategic importance both for Nordea itself and for the Bank of Finland and the European Central Bank. The key  and difficult  issues are agreeing on arrangements and responsibilities in possible crisis situations. These issues ultimately require a legislative solution at EU level. So far, there has been insufficient interest in these matters at European level, as the number of cross-border bank mergers and the number of pan-European branch banks has been low outside the Nordic countries. However, the issue is becoming the subject of wider attention and has also begun to be discussed in all key areas (Commission, relevant EU committees, ESCB). Toimialaliukumat  Bankassurance Another integration trend affecting the financial markets is known as the so-called "black market". as a slippage. This means, above all, the merger and cooperation of banks and insurance companies. The term bancassurance was originally used  and is still used  for the phenomenon, which also indicates the root of the phenomenon. The first banking and insurance joint ventures were formed in France and Belgium as early as the 1970s. In general, cooperation between banks and insurance companies has been much stronger in Europe than, for example, in the United States, where, for example, the Bank Holding Act prevented banks from offering insurance products well into the late 1990s. In Europe, legislation has been more permissive in relation to the universal banking principle. Cooperation between banking and insurance has been aimed not only at reducing costs (unit costs) but also at broadening the revenue base and risk diversification  economies of scale. The benefits of cogeneration have also driven cooperation through one-stop shopping and the use of common distribution channels  mostly bank branch networks  to serve common customers. The low interest rates obtained as a result of monetary policy have meant a reduction in the attractiveness of traditional bank deposits and created a demand for insurance products as long-term savings targets. This demand has also been reinforced, especially in Europe, by the ageing of the population. The forms of bancassurance cooperation are very varied: banks have bought or set up insurance companies, a bank and an insurance company have contracted with each other, or a bank cooperates with one or more insurance companies. Cooperation between banks and insurance companies has, at least on the other hand, been stronger, primarily on the life insurance side. For example, in Finland, the market share of bank-linked life companies is 63 %. In France, the share of banks is at the same level, in Spain it is even higher at around 70%. Cooperation or activity between banks and a non-life insurance company under the same group has so far been less frequent, but some examples can be found, for example, Allianz  Dresdner from Germany and our Sampo Group, in whose turnover the non-life insurance company If accounts for more than 60% (about half of the personnel). The industry drift between banks and insurance seems to be only getting stronger, although there has also recently been a break with cooperation between banks and insurance companies: As an example of this, Citigroup announced in January 2005 that it would sell its Travellers insurance company. The increasing interconnectedness of banks and insurance companies has presented new challenges for financial market supervisors. Monitoring and control must be able to assess cross-ownership and the possible emergence of risk concentration, 'distorted' competition within a group, the potential risks of crisis transmission in financial conglomerates, and also the operational risks arising from cultural conflicts between banks and insurance companies. In many cases, banks have also had to recapitalise fast-growing insurance companies they own. The fact that non-life insurance companies are part of a group further complicates supervision. In several countries, banking and insurance supervision has been reformed over the past 10-15 years, for example by harmonising banking and insurance supervision. For example, among the EU countries, banking and insurance supervision is combined in Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark, Germany, Ireland, Sweden, as well as Estonia, Hungary and Malta. In those countries where there is no combined surveillance, most of them have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU). All euro area central banks have a very close relationship with supervision or part of it. For example, in France and Ireland, as well as in Finland, supervision, or part of it, is attached to the Central Bank. In the Netherlands, the whole of supervision has recently been brought into the central bank. It is obvious that these issues will be a matter of concern to the authorities both at the bancas-surance group's home country and also more broadly at EU level, as the group is increasingly pan-European, i.e. its different parts operate in different countries. Prospects for EU payments Thirdly, as an important and topical issue relating to the integration of the banking market, I would like to mention the creation of a single payments area in the euro area and in the EU. The role of banks in this is absolutely central. Promoting the smooth operation of payment systems is also one of the basic statutory tasks of the European System of Central Banks as defined in the Treaty. In order to be implemented, the single monetary policy requires that liquidity effects, and with them short-term money market interest rates, level off across the euro area, i.e. a payment system at least euro area-wide must be available to help even out liquidity and interest rate differentials between participating countries. At an early stage in the development of the payment systems of the European central banks, preparations were therefore made for this, and national systems were finally linked together at the start of monetary union in the so-called 'single currency'. TARGET, where large interbank payments across the border are made in central bank money in real time. TARGET has fulfilled its role as an EU-wide central bank money intermediation system very well. It has made it possible to implement monetary policy in a decentralised manner through the national central banks. At the same time, it has also played an important role in contributing to the fact, which I mentioned earlier, that the unsecured short-money market between banks is the most integrated segment of the financial markets in Europe. A new centralised system is now under construction, with the aim of streamlining and harmonising the TARGET services of central banks and replacing the existing separate national systems. In its narrow segment, the change represents a step towards universal, integrated and common systems. On the retail payments side, integration has not progressed as quickly. Initially, the European Commission and the European System of Central Banks (ESCB) will both work to promote retail payments in euro in the euro area on the basis of voluntary cooperation between banks. However, no significant progress could be observed. When the euro cash was introduced at the beginning of 2002, the Commission began to prepare a regulation at a rapid pace to develop cross-border differential retail payments. In July 2002, a regulation on retail payments entered into force, requiring uniform pricing for domestic and crossborder retail payments in euro to customers. Initially, the regulation only applied to card payments and ATM withdrawals, but since July 2003 it has also extended to transfers of less than EUR 12,500,- The regulation significantly accelerated the efforts of BANKS in EU countries to improve the efficiency of cross-border payments. In June 2002, the largest banks and EU banking associations established the European Financial Council (EPC). He set out plans for the creation of a single euro payment area (SEPA) in the euro area by 2010. The aim is, among other things, that already in 2008, the basic services for citizens  ordinary credit transfers, instant transfers and direct debits  would operate with uniform practices throughout the SEPA area. Finland's representatives in the EPC cooperation have been, in particular, Nordea and the Suo-men Banking Association. In the preparation of sepa, the ESCB and the EU Commission have both had internal committees and cooperation groups with market participants. Finnish representatives from the banking sector, ministries and Suo-men Bank have been active in these groups, and the aim has been, among other things, to ensure that the modern payment methods used in Finland are taken into account. The EU regulation on the pricing of payment services can in itself be seen as a small but significant step forward in the integration of European financial markets. The regulation does not have much effect on the payment transactions of large international companies, but it will make it easier and cheaper for small and medium-sized enterprises  and also locally Finnish companies  to make payments abroad. In the future, when we hope to achieve uniform practices regarding the format of payment orders, invoicing, reference numbers, etc. the benefits of this relationship are multiplying and are also beginning to grow with larger companies, especially those that deal directly with large groups of consumers. Perhaps the most important aspect of the regulation is that it has stimulated cooperation between European banks. However, there are still concerns about the timetable for implementation. Some time ago, EU Internal Market Commissioner Charlie McCreevy strongly urged banks to step up their efforts to achieve this goal. He specifically said that the Commission would not stand by and watch slow progress as inaction, but 'if necessary, the Commission will make some of the jointly agreed standards mandatory and include a timetable for a single charging area in the draft law'. The European Central Bank has also expressed its concern about the slowness of the timetable. Finally I have given some examples of ongoing topical issues relating to the development of a pan-European banking market. In my opinion, the emergence of pan-European banks, the industry drift between banks and insurance companies and the existence of a single, unified payment platform for retail payment intermediation already illustrate the diversity of regions. Even a cursory inspection of this kind shows that a great deal is going on. And I have not now touched on the many other major projects  Basel II or the harmonisation of accounting practices, the introduction of common international accounting standards and many other FSAP-related measures, the implementation of which will inevitably lead to greater integration of eu financial markets, including banking markets. Nor have I just referred to the supervisory committees  through which the cooperation of supervisors and the whole supervisory framework have been more clearly reformed into a so-called supervisory framework at EU level. As a Lamfalussy structure. This is a step towards the development and simplification of controls. I believe that a good start has now been made at EU level. But, of course, much remains to be done before we reach deep European financial markets. In the final analysis, it is a question of coordinating national procedures and regulations, which will be put to the test, for example, in the national implementation of FSAP legislation. The parties involved in the various countries should therefore look beyond national short-term interests, as the benefits of an undeniably coherent, well-functioning pan-European financial market for europe's life cycle and citizens are significant.

Syyn voi olla esimerkiksi se ett fuusioissa, jonka seurauksena pan-eurooppalainen pankki usein on synty-nyt, pankki voi tytrpankkimuotoisena silytt paikallisen nimens ja l-heisyytens asiakkaisiin. Nin on tapahtunut esimerkiksi uusissa jsenmais-sa, joiden pankki on fuusioitunut ulkomaiseen pankkiryhmittymn. Mutta on ilmeist, ett sivukonttorimuotoinen rajat ylittv pankkitoiminta tulee lisntymn, etenkin nyt kun EU:n vuonna 2004 voimaan tuleen euroop-payhtiasetuksen mukaan fuusiot maiden rajojen yli EU:n sisll tulivat yh-tioikeudellisesti mahdollisiksi. Esimerkiksi Nordean suunnitelmat muut-tua eurooppayhtiksi ovat ymmrrettvi. Sivukonttorimuotoinen pankki on paitsi kustannustehokkaampi mys huomattavasti yksinkertaisempi ra-kenteeltaan ja mys lpinkyvmpi. Valvonnan ja stelyn kannalta pankin muuttuminen sivukonttorimuotoi-seksi pan-eurooppalaiseksi ei ole aivan yksinkertaista. Rahoituspalvelujen yhdet markkinat perustuvat kahteen perusperiaatteseen: ns. yhteen toimilupaan (single passport) ja siihen liittyvn kotipaikkamaan valvontaan (home country control). Niden periaatteiden pitisi parhaim-millaan tukea tervett kilpailua liiketoimintamenettelyjen ja stelykytn-tjen vlill ja siten parantaa rahoituspalvelujen laatua. Tm on koko EU:n rahoitusmarkkinoiden integraation ydin ja sit ajava voima. Nordea-konsernin muuttuminen eri pohjoismaissa toimivien tytrpankkien muodostamasta konsernista Eurooppa-yhtiksi, jonka kotipaikaksi tulee Ruotsi, merkitsee toteutuessaan  Nordean nykysuunnitelmien mukaan vuonna 2007  sit, ett koko Nordean pankkivalvonnasta vastaa Ruotsin valvontaviranomainen (Finansinspektion). Pohjoismaiden valvojien kesken pohditaankin, minklaisia vaatimuksia Nordean uusi yhtirakenne asettaa valvojien yhteistylle, ja erityisesti, mit odotuksia isntvaltioiden valvo-jat asettavat kotivaltion valvojalle, Finansinspektionille. Suomen Rahoitus-tarkastukselle ja Norjan ja Tanskan valvontaviranomaisille j joka tapauk-sessa omassa maassaan olevan konttoriverkoston maksuvalmiuden sek markkinoiden yleisen edun ja menettelytapojen valvonta. Toinen merkittv asia, joka Nordean muuttuessa eurooppayhtiksi on rat-kaistava, liittyy talletussuojaan ja sen kattavuuteen eri Pohjoismaissa. Talle-tussuojasdksien taso on erilainen eri Pohjoismaissa, ja Nordean tapauk-sessa eurooppayhtit koskeva talletussuoja asiakkaan kannalta on sopimat-ta. Talletussuojadirektiivin pperiaate on nykyiselln se, ett ulkomailla sijaitsevien sivukonttoreiden talletussuoja on kotimaan valtion mukainen eli tss tapauksessa Ruotsin valtion mukainen. On selv, ett tm on ongelmallista Nordean suunnitelmien kannalta. Kesll 2004 Nordea ilmoitti pyytneens EU:n komissiolta (sismarkki-noista vastaavalta komissaarilta) sellaisen lisyksen tekemist talletussuojaa koskevaan direktiiviin, joka mahdollistaisi sen, ett eurooppayhtin sivu-konttoriksi muuttuneen tytrpankin talletukset voisivat jd sijaintimaan talletussuojan piiriin muutoksen jlkeenkin. Komissio onkin kynnistnyt talletussuojadirektiivin muuttamisen selvittmisen, mutta kysymykset, jotka koskevat mm. talletussuojan rahoitusta, kattavuutta, talletusten mrittely ja topping up-kysymyst - ovat poliittisesti hankalia ja direktiivin muut-taminen kestnee kauan. Kolmas trke kohta liittyy rahoitusmarkkinoiden vakauteen. Kokonsa vuoksi Nordea on keskeinen toimija kaikissa Pohjoismaissa ja Baltian maissa. Nordean markkinaosuus esimerkiksi Suomen rahoitusmarkkinoista on vajaa 40%. Vakauden kannalta maksujrjestelmien toimivuus ja nor-maalisti toimivat yhteydet euroalueeseen ovat strategisesti trkeit niin Nordealle itselleen kuin Suomen Pankille ja Euroopan keskuspankille. Keskeisi  ja vaikeita  kysymyksi ovat mahdollisiin kriisitilanteisiin liit-tyvist jrjestelyist ja vastuista sopiminen. Nihin kysymyksiin tarvitaan viime kdess EU -tasoinen lainsdnttasoinen ratkaisu. Toistaiseksi nihin asioihin ei ole ollut eurooppalaisella tasolla riittvsti kiinnostusta, koska rajan ylittvien pankkifuusioiden mr ja pan-eurooppalaisten sivukonttorimuotoisten pankkien mr on ollut vhinen muualla kuin Pohjoismaissa. Asia on kuitenkin tulossa laajemman huomion kohteeksi ja siit on alettu keskustella mys kaikilla keskeisill tahoilla (komissio, asiaan liittyvt EU:n komiteat, EKPJ). Toimialaliukumat  Bankassurance Toinen rahoitusmarkkinoilla vaikuttava integraatiotrendi tunnetaan ns. toi-mialaliukumana. Tll tarkoitetaan ennen kaikkea pankkien ja vakuutusyh-tiiden yhdistymist ja yhteistyt. Alun perin ilmist kytettiin  ja edel-leenkin kytetn  termi bancassurance, mik kertoo mys ilmin juuris-ta. Ensimmisi pankki- ett vakuutustoiminnan yhteisyhtiit muodostet-tiin Ranskassa ja Belgiassa jo 1970 -luvulla. Yleenskin yhteisty pankkien ja vakuutuslaitosten vlill on ollut Euroopassa selvsti vankempaa kuin esimerkiksi Yhdysvalloissa, jossa mm. Bank Holding Act esti pankkeja tar-joamasta vakuutustuotteita pitklle 1990-luvun loppupuolelle saakka. Eu-roopassa lainsdnt on yleispankkiperiaatteeseen (universal banking) liit-tyen ollut sallivampi. Pankki- ja vakuutustoiminnan yhteistyll on pyritty sek kulujen (yksikkkustannusten) alentamiseen ett tulopohjan laajenta-miseen ja riskien hajauttamiseen  suurtuotannon etuihin. Mys yhteistuo-tannon edut ovat olleet ajamassa yhteistyhn palveluita keskittmll (one stop shopping) ja hydyntmll yhteisi jakelukanavia  useimmiten pankkien konttoriverkostoa  yhteisten asiakkaiden palvelemiseksi. Uskot-tavan rahapolitiikan myt saadut alhaiset korot ovat merkinneet perinteis-ten pankkitalletusten houkuttelevuuden vhenemist ja luoneet kysynt vakuutustuotteille pitkaikaisina sstkohteina. Tt kysynt on mys vahvistanut etenkin Euroopassa vestn ikntyminen. Bancassurance -yhteistyn muodot ovat hyvin vaihtelevia: pankit ovat os-taneet tai perustaneet vakuutusyhtiit, pankki ja vakuutusyhti ovat fuusi-oituneet keskenn tai pankki tekee yhteistyt yhden tai useamman vakuu-tusyhtin kanssa. Pankkien ja vakuutusyhtiiden yhteisty on ainakin tois-taiseksi ollut vahvempaa ensisijaisesti henkivakuutuspuolella. Esimerkiksi meill Suomessa pankkisidonnaisten henkiyhtiiden markkinaosuus on 63 %. Ranskassa pankkien osuus on samalla tasolla, Espanjassa viel kor-keampi, noin 70 %. Pankkien ja vahinkovakuutusyhtin vlinen yhteisty tai toiminta saman konsernin alla on ollut toistaiseksi vhisemp, mutta joitakin esimerkkej lytyy, mm. Allianz  Dresdner Saksasta ja meidn Sampo-konsernimme, jonka liikevaihdosta vahinkovakuutusyhti If:in osuus on runsas 60 % (henkilststkin noin puolet). Toimialaliukuma pankkien ja vakuutustoiminnan kesken nytt vain vahvistuvan, joskin pankkien ja vakuutusyhtiiden yhteistyss on viime aikoina ollut havaitta-vissa mys irtoamista yhteistyst: Esimerkkin tst Citigroup ilmoitti tammikuussa 2005 myyvns Travellers -vakuutusyhtins. Pankkien ja vakuutusyhtiiden kytkentjen lisntyminen on tuonut rahoi-tusmarkkinoiden valvojille uusia haasteita. Seurannassa ja valvonnassa on pystyttv arvioimaan ristiinomistusta ja riskikeskittymisen mahdollisia syntymisi, konsernin puitteissa tapahtuvaa vristynytt kilpailua, mah-dollisia kriisien tartuntariskej finanssikonglomeraateissa sek mys opera-tiivisia riskej, joita syntyy pankki- ja vakuutusyhtiiden vlisist kulttuu-rieroista. Useissa tapauksissa pankit ovat mys joutuneet pomittamaan omistamiaan, nopeasti kasvavia vakuutusyhtiit. Vahinkovakuutusyhtii-den kuuluminen konserniin monimutkaistaa edelleen valvontaa. Useissa maissa pankki- ja vakuutusvalvontaa onkin viimeisen 10-15 vuo-den aikana uudistettu mm. siten, ett pankki- ja vakuutusvalvonnat on yh-distety. Esimerkiksi EU -maista pankki- ja vakuutusvalvonta on yhdistetty Belgiassa, Hollannissa, Iso-Britanniassa, Irlannissa, Ruotsissa, Saksassa ja Tanskassa sek Virossa, Unkarissa ja Maltalla. Niiss maissa, joissa val-vontaa ei ole yhdistetty, on useimmissa allekirjoitettu yhteistyt koskeva pytkirja (Memorandum of Understanding, MoU). Kaikilla euroalueen keskuspankeilla on varsin lheinen suhde valvontaan tai sen osaan. Esimer-kiksi Ranskassa ja Irlannissa samoin kuin meill Suomessa valvonta tai osa sit on keskuspankin yhteydess. Hollannissa koko valvonta on kokonai-suudessaan vastikn tuotu osaksi keskuspankkia. On ilmeist, ett nm asiat tulevat puhuttamaan viranomaisia sek bancas-surance -konsernin kotimaassa ett mys laajemmin EU-tasolla, kun kon-serni viel yh useammin on pan-eurooppalainen eli sen eri osat toimivat eri maissa. EU:n maksuliikenteen nkymi Kolmantena trken ja ajankohtaisena asiana, joka liittyy pankkimarkki-noiden integraatioon haluan ottaa esille yhtenisen maksualueen luomisen euroalueelle ja EU:hun. Tss pankkien merkitys on aivan keskeinen. Maksujrjestelmien moitteettoman toiminnan edistminen on mys Euroo-pan keskuspankkijrjestelmn perustamissopimuksessa mriteltyj laki-steisi perustehtvi. Yhteinen rahapolitiikka vaatii toteutuakseen, ett likviditeettivaikutukset ja niiden mukana lyhyet rahamarkkinakorot tasaantuvat koko euroalueen laa-juisesti, eli kytettviss tulee siksi olla vhintnkin euroalueen laajuinen maksujrjestelm, joka auttaa tasoittamaan osanottajamaiden likviditeetti- ja korkoerot. Euroopan keskuspankkien maksujrjestelmien kehittmisen varhaisessa vaiheessa tllaiseen valmistauduttiinkin ja kansalliset jrjestel-mt linkitettiin rahaliiton alkaessa lopullisesti yhteen ns. TARGET-jrjestelmksi, jossa yli rajan menevt isot pankkien vliset maksut suorite-taan keskuspankkirahassa reaaliaikaisesti. TARGET on tyttnyt tehtvns EU-laajuisena keskuspankkirahan vlitysjrjestelmn mainiosti. Se on tehnyt mahdolliseksi rahapolitiikan hajautetun toimeenpanon kansallisten keskuspankkien kautta. Samalla se on omalta trkelt osaltaan ollut vai-kuttamassa mys siihen aikaisemmin mainitsemaani seikkaan, ett pankki-en vliset vakuudettomat lyhyen rahan tukkumarkkinat ovat parhaiten in-tegroitunut rahoitusmarkkinoiden lohko Euroopassa. Nyt rakenteilla on uu-si keskitetty jrjestelm, jonka tavoitteena on tehostaa ja harmonisoida kes-kuspankkien TARGET-palvelut ja joka korvaa nykyiset kansalliset erillis-jrjestelmt. Muutos merkitsee kapealla lohkollaan askelta kohti yleiseu-rooppalaisia, integroituja ja yhteisi jrjestelmi. Vhittismaksamisen puolella integraatio ei ole edennyt yht nopeasti. Aluksi EU:n komissio ja Euroopan keskuspankkijrjestelm (EKPJ) pyrki-vt kumpikin edistmn euromrist vhittismaksamista euroalueella pankkien vapaaehtoisen yhteistyn pohjalta. Merkittv edistyst ei kui-tenkaan voitu havaita. Kun eurokteinen otettiin kyttn 2002 alussa, ko-missio ryhtyi valmistelemaan nopeassa tahdissa asetusta rajan ylittvn eromrisen vhittismaksamisen kehittmiseksi. Heinkuussa 2002 tuli voimaan vhittismaksamista koskeva asetus, joka edellytti kotimaisten ja rajanylittvien euromristen vhittismaksujen yhtenist hinnoittelua asiakkaille. Aluksi asetus koski vain korttimaksamista ja automaattinostoja, mutta heinkuusta 2003 se on ulottunut mys alle 12.500,- euron mrisiin tilisiirtoihin. Asetus nopeutti merkittvsti EU-maiden pankkien toimia rajat ylittvn maksamisen tehostamiseksi. Isoimmat pankit ja EU-pankkiyhdistykset pe-rustivat keskuussa 2002 eurooppalaisen neuvotteluelimen EPC:n (Europe-an payments council). Tm ryhtyi laatimaan suunnitelmia yhden yhteni-sen maksualueen (SEPA=Single euro payment area) luomiseksi euroalueel-le vuoteen 2010 menness. Tavoitteena on mm., ett jo vuonna 2008 kansa-laisten peruspalvelut  tavalliset tilisiirrot, pikasiirrot ja suoraveloitukset  toimisivat yhtenisin kytnnin koko SEPA-alueen laajuisesti. Suomen edustajina EPC-yhteistyss ovat olleet erityisesti Nordea ja Suo-men Pankkiyhdistys. SEPA:n valmistelussa EKPJ:ll ja EU-komissiolla on molemmilla ollut sisisi komiteoita ja yhteistyryhmi markkinaosapuol-ten kanssa. Suomalaiset edustajat pankkisektorilta, ministeriist ja Suo-men Pankista ovat toimineet niss ryhmiss aktiivisesti ja tavoitteena on mm. ollut varmistaa, ett Suomessa kytss olevat modernit maksutavat otetaan huomioon. Maksupalvelujen hinnoittelua koskevaa EU-asetusta voidaan sinns pit pienen mutta merkittvn edistysaskeleena Euroopan rahoitusmarkkinoi-den integraatiossa. Suurten kansainvlisten yritysten maksuliikkeeseen ase-tus ei juuri vaikuta, mutta pienten ja keskisuurten yritysten  ja mys taval-listen suomalaisten  maksut ulkomaille hoituvat sen ansiosta helpommin ja halvemmin. Jatkossa, kun toivottavasti pstn yhtenisiin kytntihin maksutoimeksiantojen muodon, laskutuksen, viitenumeroiden jne. suhteen hydyt moninkertaistuvat ja alkavat kasvaa mys suurempien yritysten pu-lella, varsinkin niiden, jotka harjoittavat asiointia suoraan laajojen kulutta-jajoukkojen kanssa. Asetuksen ehk trkein merkitys on siin, ett se on vauhdittanut eurooppa-laisten pankkien keskinist yhteistyt. Huolta on kuitenkin edelleen kan-nettava toteuttamisen aikataulusta. Jokin aika sitten EU:n sismarkkina-asiain komissaari Charlie McCreevy kehotti painokkaasti pankkeja tehos-tamaan toimiaan tavoitteen saavuttamisen suhteen. Hn nimenomaan sanoi, ett komissio ei aio katsoa hidasta edistymist sivusta toimettomana, vaan "tarvittaessa komissio tekee joistakin yhdess sovituista standardeista pa-kollisia ja sisllytt aikataulun yhtenisest maksualueesta lakiluonnok-seen". Mys Euroopan keskuspankki on tuonut esille huolensa aikataulun hitaudesta. Lopuksi Olen edell esittnyt muutamia esimerkkej meneilln olevista ajankohtai-sista kysymyksist, jotka liittyvt Euroopan laajuisten pankkimarkkinoiden kehittymiseen. Pan-eurooppalaisten pankkien synty, toimialaliukuma pank-kien ja vakuutuslaitosten toiminnan vlill ja yhden yhtenisen maksualu-een saaminen vhittismaksujen vlitykseen kuvaavat mielestni jo sit kuinka moninaisilla alueilla toimitaan. Tllainen pintapuolinenkin tarkaste-lu osoittaa, ett paljon on tekeill. Enk ole nyt ksitellyt niit monia muita suuria hankkeita  Basel II tai kirjanpitokytntjen yhdenmukaistumista, yhteisten IAS -standardien kyttnottoa kirjanpidossa ja monia muita FSAP-ohjelmaan liittyv toimenpidett, joiden toimeenpano vistmtt lis EU-alueen rahoitusmarkkinoiden ml. pankkimarkkinoiden yhdenty-mist. Enk ole myskn kuin viitannut valvontakomiteoihin  joiden kautta valvojien yhteisty ja koko valvontakehikko on uudistunut selke-mmin EU-tasoiseksi ns. Lamfalussy-rakenteeksi. Tm on askel valvon-nan kehittmisess ja yksinkertaistamisessa. EU-tasolla on mielestni nyt psty hyvn alkuun. Mutta luonnollisesti paljon on viel tekemtt ennen kuin pstn Euroopan laajuisiin syviin rahoitusmarkkinoihin. Viime k-dess kysymys on kansallisten menettelyjen ja snnsten yhteensovittami-sesta, joka tulee testiin mm. FSAP -ohjelman lainsdnnn kansallisessa toimeenpanossa. Eri maiden osapuolten olisikin katsottava kansallisten ly-hytaikaisten intressien yli, sill kiistatta yhtenisist hyvin toimivista Eu-roopan laajuisista rahoitusmarkkinoista tuleva hyty Euroopan elinkei-noelmlle ja kansalaisille on merkittv.

Title: Speech entitled "Competition increases productivity and investment" at the STTK Economic Policy Seminar
text: Director-General Erkki Liikanen COMPETITION INCREASES PRODUCTIVITY AND INVESTMENT STTK Economic Policy Seminar 16.8.2005 1. Membrane: Competition increases productivity and investment Finland and the whole world are becoming more international. And globalization does not enter the pa-size. From the point of view of companies and employees, the globalizing world is challenging in many ways. Companies need to manage increasingly complex production and logistics processes. At the same time, increasing the share of knowledge in work requires higher and more diverse skills from employees. Companies and workers must also be able to prepare for and adapt to changing international competitive conditions. The innovativeness of companies and employees has also become an essential part of the competitive factor of a successful company. The same applies to a large extent to national economies. However, one key difference between the national economy and the enterprise is that the national economy cannot change its location and its factors of production are given in the medium term. This is particularly true of the labour force, which is  for a variety of reasons  a very immobile factor of production, especially at international level, but also at national level. A company, on the other hand, can change its competitive position by changing its location or by decentralising its activities. This has always been known, but in a globalising world, changes in the activities and location of companies across borders occur faster and more frequently. National economies and regions that are not sufficiently prepared for this find the changed international environment more difficult. 2. Membrane: The challenges of internationalization The reason is that changing the location of companies  or decentralising activities  involves a wide range of costs as the company adjusts its production structure and factors of production. From the point of view of the enterprise, such activities are "profitable" as long as the expected increase in profits from the reorganization of production exceeds the costs incurred by it. At the level of the national economy, the situation is much more problematic. The cost of adaptation is often allocated quite unevenly in terms of area and time, as we have seen throughout history. They can also be targeted at a very disadvantageous situation for employees in situations where it is difficult and takes a very long time to find a job. Costs are also incurred where companies move. Costs arise from the retraining of the workforce, recruitment and, through investment, the rebuilding of productive capital. How, then, can an individual economy or region - such as the EU - prepare for this changed situation? Traditionally, public debate calls for a flexible labour market, together with a suitably set-up economic safety net, to mitigate and offset these costs. This is, of course, true. However, a major challenge arises from the fact that the importance of international competition in companies' investment decisions is inevitably emphasised. The question is whether Finland will be able to maintain a sufficient competitive advantage over other countries in key sectors? In the same way, at European level, the question is whether Europe, as a region, should be able to compete for international investment in relation to the United States and the rapidly developing Asian countries. As far as Finland is concerned, it is quite clear that, as a high-wage country, we are not in a position to attract international productive investment to those basic industries where the production itself is very labour-intensive. There have been plenty of examples of this over the years. Finland faces two challenges at the same time. On the one hand, the growth of the productive capital stock in Finland slows down with the fall in the investment rate and, on the other hand, the supply of labour gradually decreases with the ageing of the population. These require that the use of factors of production can be further developed. In principle, this can be done in two different ways: Labour productivity can be directly affected, for example, by reorganising work and 'smarter', and also by training. Increasing the productivity of capital, on the other hand, requires investments that improve the management of production processes and information. The fragmentation of production chains caused by globalisation also requires the effective use of information technology in the management of production chains and customer relationships. In this context, competition policy and the deregulation of markets have also become increasingly important in the European economic policy debate. This has been achieved by analysing the reasons for the rapid growth in the United States and Asian countries. In particular, perhaps the most important reason for the US economic lead has been considered to be its competitiveness and the openness of markets: the dynamic benefits of a competitive environment are currently being reflected in the innovativeness of companies and, consequently, in the speed of technological development. Let us look at the situation a little in the light of statistical data. The following figure ha persecutes the development of GDP per capita in the United States, Europe and Finland in an internationally comparable way. 3. Pattern. GDP per capita: cumulative change (log.) since 1980 The figure shows at least the following. Since the early 1980s, Europe's standard of living gap with the United States has been steadily widening. At the end of 2002, europe's gdp per capita was about a third lower than that of the United States. For Finland, ti-lanne looks a little brighter. In the 1990s, Finland has been able to close the gap in living standards to the United States significantly. This has largely been due to the exceptionally rapid increase in productivity in the electronics industry. Pohjola and Jalava1 have estimated that between 1995 and 2002, about a third of GDP growth was generated by the production of information and communication technologies. And interestingly, according to their calculations, the combined contribution of information and communication technology to the growth of labour productivity was just over 40%. The high productivity contribution of ICT is explained by the fact that the industry in the sector is producing a large number of general-purpose technologies that, at their best, are rapidly spreading into use, thereby affecting the productivity and living standards of the economy as a whole. In Europe, productivity grew faster than in the United States between 1973 and 1995. But what is worrying is that, since the mid-90s, Europe has lost its lead in terms of productivity development. This fact is further illustrated by the following two patterns. 4. Pattern. Private consumption per capita: cumulative change (log.) since 1981 1 Jalava, Jukka ja Pohjola, Matti (2005) "ICT as a Source of Output and Productivity Growth in Finland". HECER Discussion Papers No. 52 The first figure compares, by international comparison, the development of private consumption in Europe, Finland and the United States since 1981. The figure tells much the same story as the previous one, but it also shows that although Finland has achieved the United States in terms of living standards in terms of gross domestic product, this has not been the case in terms of private consumption. Europe as a whole is also steadily lagging behind the United States in terms of private consumption. In the following figure, GDP growth is broken down into growth in labour productivity and employment. 5. Pattern. Components of GROSS DOMESTIC PRODUCT since 1980 This graph shows that about a third of the living-level gap between the United States and Europe is explained by lower labour productivity in Europe and two-thirds by lower employment. Finally, the following tabular lock examines the growth of labour productivity in Europe and the United States, both between the economy as a whole and between different sectors. 6. Table. Growth in labour productivity in various industries The table shows that the key explanation for the faster productivity trend in the United States can be found in ICT-enabled services and ict-producing manufacturing. In these sectors, productivity growth in the United States picked up sharply, while it slowed down in Europe. The EU has enjoyed a competitive advantage in traditional industrial production. Productivity growth in Europe has been faster than in the United States in industries with low use of information technology. If you look more closely at the sectoral breakdown, you will see that, above all, wholesale and retail productivity has grown rapidly in the US, while growth in the EU has been very slow. 7. Pattern. Contributions to accelerate productivity growth in the US In the United States, the retail, wholesale and financial services sectors and their links explain 95% of the acceleration in productivity growth between 1990-1995 and 1995-2001. In Europe, productivity growth slowed down over the same period in most countries. Indeed, a major difference to the United States has arisen above all in the development of productivity in the service sector. Of course, there is at least one industry in Europe where productivity growth has been clearly faster than in the United States, namely telecommunications. What, then, could explain the weaker productivity performance in the European service sector? One explanation offered is precisely the lack of competition.2 For example, the OECD has criticised Europeans in a number of country studies, including Finland, for the lack of competition, particularly in the non-tradable sector. The OECD country report on Finland3 states that barriers to competition in product markets were rapidly dismantled in Finland in the early 1990s, but that since then the pace has slowed down. Companies operating in the export sector are exposed to foreign competition, and productivity development in this sector has been better. By contrast, several sectors in the non-tradable sector  in particular the services sector  are poorly competitive. It should also be noted that the provision of services is very labour-intensive and often the nature of the services is such that the customers and the producer are close to each other. This means that the risk of the production of services moving away from the domestic market is lower than in many other sectors of the economy. On the other hand, it should also be noted that, although the European internal market functions well in terms of goods and capital, it is not reflected in an increase in competition in the services sector to the same extent as in other sectors of the economy. In this sense, the problems and fears that have arisen in the EU Council and Parliament about the so-called 'black market' have arisen. there are concerns in the handling of the Services Directive. Despite the public debate, this is a rather moderate reform which would have filled one major gap in the completion of the internal market: the directive would make it easier for service providers to compete across borders and thus create a European internal market for services as well. 2 OMahony ja van Ark (2003). 3 High yes Wise (2004). However, further efforts are needed to create a European internal market for the services sector. In the future, it will be one of the key engines of economic growth. It is also a sector whose growth has a high employment impact due to its labour intensity. The opposition to the Services Directive is a good illustration of the conflicts of interest between the various economic units in terms of competition and rationing policies: the benefits and costs of the reform may be unevenly distributed, both regionally and temporally, between the different economic units. The opposition perhaps also illustrates the uncertainty surrounding the effects of economic reforms on the individual, the company, and the national economy as a whole. This uncertainty can be mitigated, at least to some extent, by relying on available economic studies. The Institute for Economic Research, together with the Finnish Competition Authority, organised a seminar on the subject last autumn, at which it was noted that economic research in the field in Finland is still limited and fragmented. That is certainly the case. However, there is already quite a lot of research experience in the international field. In many recent studies, competition has been seen to improve economic performance, in particular through so-called dynamic productivity effects. However, the effects of competition and deregulation are complex, so a detailed analysis of them requires the use of macroeconomic models. Model calculations relating to increased competition have been carried out by the Imf and also by the Bank of Finland using modern macroeconomic models. Taking into account the behavioural and proactive behaviour of housekeepers, the models can be used to assess the evolution of key economic variables such as investment, consumption and employment as the economy adapts to the new competitive environment. On the basis of the calculations, it is also possible to assess the effects on the long-term well-being of consumers, as well as how the costs of the reform are distributed regionally and over time between different units of the economy. In these model calculations, increased competition in commodity markets can be interpreted as a situation where prices are temporarily rising more slowly than in other parts of the world. Similarly, increased competition in the labour market can be interpreted as a situation in which the rate of wage growth is temporarily slowed down. Such a temporary decline in inflation may be due, for example, to the fact that companies are changing their pricing behaviour precisely because of increased competition. There is plenty of evidence of this in Finland, for example, in the grocery trade and in the pricing of telephone calls. 8. Table. Increased competition in Europe: assessing the long-term impact with the GEM model Calculations made using a model developed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF)4 show that if product market competition in the euro area were to increase to the same level as in the United States, the long-term impact on the real economy would be considerable. Calculations suggest that output in the euro area could improve by just under 10%. Consumption and employment could also grow by a marginal 5%. As a result, consumer welfare could increase by as much as a couple of per cent in the long term. It should also be noted that such a reform could also have the effect of significantly increasing investment. All in all, these effects would lead to a narrowing of the gap in living standards between the United States and Europe. On the basis of model calculations, it would appear that differences in competitiveness between product and labour markets would explain about half of the difference in living standards between Europe and the United States. Increased competition in the euro area would also have spill-over effects on the rest of the world. Production andconsumption could increase by around one per cent in relation to a baseline situation in which producers' price margins would remain unchanged. Spill-over effects on the rest of the world would arise mainly from the effects of picking up demand in the euro area. The effects of increased competition have also been assessed from the point of view of the Finnish economy. The Bank of Finland has used the Aino model to make preliminary calculations of the effects of increased competition in commodity markets. These calculations were based on similar results to those of the IMF: in the long term, increased competition in commodity markets would lead to an increase in consumption and investment. 4 See e.g. Bayomi et al. (2004). The model is abbreviated as GEM. In March 2005, the Bank of Finland's 'Euro & talous' magazine examined, as calculated by the IMF, a situation in which competitiveness would increase in both product and labour markets at the same time. The main results of these calculations are shown in the following table. 9. Table. Increasing product and labour market competition in Finland: Simulation results with the Aino model The table shows that once the economy has adapted to the new competitive situation, private production in Finland would increase by about 3%. In the new competitive situation, price and wage margins have been reduced by a total of 2 and 5 percentage points compared to the baseline. The growth of private production is fuelled by a 2.5% increase in private consumption. This is reflected in the long-term growth of just under 2 per cent in employment and an increase of good 3.5 per cent in investment. The real wage would rise by just under 3%, and household welfare would eventually increase by about one per cent. Overall, the calculations also show that the increase in competition in the commodity market explains a larger part of the results, about 2/3 part. The table also shows how it will take time for the economy to adapt to the new competitive situation. However, the short-term effects of the reforms can be painful for economists. 10. Membrane: Intensifying competition  the mecca of adjustment of the real economy Increased competition means, at least temporarily, a reduction in profits for companies, as they have to adapt their activities to the new competitive situation. The entry of new competitors eats into market shares and may require significant adjustments to price margins. In the short term, the tightening of competition is thus also reflected in the deterioration of employment and, through the effects on wealth, in the weakening of household incomes and consumption. If the development of public sector expenditure were kept unchanged, this development would also create pressure for a slight increase in the tax rate. In the longer term, however, the effects are clearly positive, although the direct impact of competition on increasing productivity would not even be taken into account. The productivity effects of increased competition are likely to become apparent only after some time. This is due to the fact that the reorganization of production processes takes time. Similarly, the development and marketing of new products absorb the resources of companies, and this is out of the productive tna. Of course, such model calculations are only indicative, but the basic message of these calculations is also supported by other research results. Already in the medium term, increased competitiveness is reflected in an increase in economic performance and an increase in the standard of living of consumers. In the short term, adaptation can entail costs when, for example, not all companies are able to adapt to the demands of increasing competition.

Reformien lyhyen aikavlin vaikutukset voivat olla taloudenpitjille kuitenkin kipeit. 10. Kalvo: Kilpailun kiristymi-nen  reaalitalouden sopeutumismeka Kilpailun lisntyminen merkitsee yrityksille ainakin vliaikaisesti voittojen supistumista, koska yritykset joutuvat sopeuttamaan toimintojaan uuteen kil-pailutilanteeseen. Uusien kilpailijoiden tulo markkinoille sy markkinaosuuk-sia, ja tm voi edellytt huomattaviakin hintamarginaalien tarkistuksia. Kil-pailun kiristyminen nkyy lyhyell aikavlill nin mys tyllisyyden huono-nemisena ja varallisuusvaikutusten kautta kotitalouksien tulotason ja kulutuk-sen heikentymisen. Jos julkisen sektorin menokehitys pidettisiin ennallaan, syntyisi tst kehityksest mys paineita lievn veroasteen nostoon. Pidemmll aikavlill vaikutukset ovat kuitenkin selkesti positiivisia, vaik-ka kilpailun tuottavuutta lisv suoraa vaikutusta ei edes otettaisi huomi-oon. Kilpailun kiristymisen tuottavuusvaikutukset tulevat esiin todennki-simmin vasta jonkin ajan kuluttua. Tm johtuu siit, ett tuotantoprosessien uudelleenorganisointi vie aikaa. Samoin uusien tuotteiden kehittely ja mark-kinointi imevt yritysten resursseja, ja tm on pois tuotannollisesta tnasta. Tllaiset mallilaskelmat ovat tietenkin vain suuntaa antavia, mutta niden las-kelmien perusviesti tukevat mys muut tutkimustulokset. Jo keskipitkll aikavlill kilpailullisuuden lisntyminen nkyy talouden suorituskyvyn kasvuna ja kuluttajien elintason kohoamisena. Lyhyell aikavlill sopeutu-misesta voi aiheutua kustannuksia, kun esimerkiksi kaikki yritykset eivt vlt-tmtt kykene sopeutumaan lisntyvn kilpailun vaatimuksiin.

Title: Speech entitled "Statistics quality for decision-making" at Statistics Finland's 140th anniversary seminar
text: PUBLICATION FREE 4.10.2005 at 15.30 Director-General Erkki Liikanen Statistics Finland's 140th anniversary seminar 4.10.2005, Finlandia Hall STATISTICS PROVIDE QUALITY FOR DECISION-MAKING During my time in the European Commission, one cabinet official shared his experiences l8aksi8aisiss8a: When I received the appointment to the cabinet, everyone said that I would now move to the political level. I waited with excitement to see what all that would mean. Are we going to start giving political advice to Commissioners all the time? When a political decision is taken, is it different when you no longer have to struggle with details and facts? But it wasn't. 80% of the work was still about finding things out, finding facts, analyzing statistics. The supervisor wanted to be sure that the facts were correct. After that, 10% went to its evaluation what this reality, formed from known material, perhaps obscures. Is there qualitative information or familiarity with changes that are only visible in the statistics afterwards. And only then began to study the options for what political solutions to make. And there, too, had to neutrally find out the pros and cons of the various exchanges and only finally make your own recommendation on the political solution." The speaker was a Dutch expert and civil servant in the information society. A similar situation, but the opposite conclusion, was reported by a high-ranking Finnish decision-maker in the 1970s. He told about a good economist who became a political assistant. This estimates that: in politics, you can get by with much less. No need to do the same basic work, you can jump straight into the line bets. Since politicians know less about everything anyway, there is no need to use the root capacity to find out the facts, but can focus on the "big questions". The dutch official's insight was correct. A policymaker who takes responsibility for solutions long into the future, wants to make sure that you are on as solid a foundation as possible. All possible information must first be used and analyzed. There is never a ready-made solution, the choice is always made in the end on the basis of incomplete information. And then you have to take risks. But if all the existing information has not been used, then you can for the decision-maker to take an unreasonably difficult and rocky road when pushing for reforms. * The compilation of statistics plays an absolutely crucial role in creating the most correct picture possible. Therefore, a high level of statistical activity is the first condition for high-quality decision-making. The statistical function must be independent. The European Commission also went through a long learning process. How to interpret the general government deficit? When the Stability and Growth Pact sets precise limits, the famous 3 % annual deficit, what is the Commission's role in this? The end result today is that the figures are always based on the work of Eurostat and are not interfered with at the political level. Therefore, confidence in Eurostat is extremely important. But of course, there is also discretion at the level of decision-making, if there is accurate information e.g. the government's actions to reduce the deficit in the following year. It can be taken into account before processes are started. My own position is that here, too, equal treatment of Member States must be guaranteed, regardless of size regardless. There are therefore great demands on the consideration; all situations of the same type must be addressed; in absolutely the same way, regardless of the country. However, sometimes situations have arisen in which statistical data comes late or does not measure real changes. This is what happened in the USA in the 1990s. In 1996, Alan Greenspan, who is retiring from the Fed at the end of the year, began talking about the fact that the use of information and communication technologies by companies has apparently led to changes in productivity growth. And that explains why the economy is growing exceptionally strongly, and inflationary pressures are not increasing. This was a new insight. In 1987, Nobel economist Robert Solow had said his famous management decision: I see computers everywhere, except in productivity statistics. Central bank economists argued against Greenspan for years, no evidence is provided by statistical data. But then gave in, as statistics evolved, hedonic indices better described the contribution of information technology, and the analysis deepened anyway. How then Greenspan could have seen this earlier is a big question. He had contacts companies that, with the help of information technology and the Internet, changed their work processes and ways of working. Hierarchies narrowed, the circulation of stocks and capital accelerated; it increased productivity and sooner or later the change had to come to the fore in the statistics as well. And so it happened; Productivity growth in the USA had accelerated since 1995. Investment and universality in ICT, combined with training and business reorganisation, has meant a major change. This well-known case teaches central bankers and others that statistical action and economic models are essential for analysis and decision-making. But that alone is not enough. Must follow the world vigilantly and try to analyze everything they see and experience. * The Bank of Finland and Statistics Finland have a long history of cooperation. The most concrete part of the cooperation has been in the areas of financial and balance of payments statistics. During monetary union, the Bank has substantially increased its own statistical production, on the basis of cooperation agreed within the Eurosystem. The new obligations on the financial markets have been part of the European Central Bank's independent statistical policy. It has required resources. In recent months, we have raised the question of whether all new statistics should be requested Necessary. It is clear that what is needed to conduct monetary policy or to analyse the stability of financial systems must be done. But we have become increasingly critical of the new statistics for collecting solely on the grounds that "it would be nice to know". Such a thing not only takes an inordinate amount of resources from the Bank, but it also puts a strain on the companies that have to respond. The general economic analysis carried out at the Bank of Finland is still mainly based on data produced by Statistics Finland. The Central Bank wants to carefully monitor and forecast Finland's own economic development. This is the Bank of Finland's contribution to the economic analysis of the euro area at the European Central Bank d0 and so are the central banks of the other participating countries. Of course, the Bank of Finland also wants to participate as an expert in the debate on the domestic economy and economic policy. * According to theories, the main statistical needs of monetary policy are quite limited. Monetary policy the starting point most often is a strategy based on a few economic variables. This clarify the presentation of the policy to the market and the general public. The primary objective of monetary policy is usually price stability. The European Central Bank's strategy is aimed at price stability over the medium term. The aim is to keep inflation close but below two per cent. The strategy is based on two pillars which, on the one hand, emphasise the importance of the amount of money on the one hand and various other factors that tend to change prices in the short term, on the other. When monetary policy focuses on price stability, a great deal of attention has to be paid to the price index. The primary indicator of inflation used by the Eurosystem is the harmonised consumer price index. Efforts have been made to make it uniform for all euro area countries. It is essential, among other things, that it contains very high housing costs. There is a lot of debate about the extent to which it is precisely house prices that should be taken into account in monetary policy, and it is often even suggested that share prices should be taken into account. Particularly difficult issues in price indices are the rapid change in the commodity basket in today's world and, on the other hand, the increasingly difficult distinction between services and the quantities and prices of technically more diverse goods. Attempts have been made to solve this by compiling the mentioned hedonic price indices. However, their problem is that the assessment of quality improvement is inevitably quite subjective. The same problem can be seen in the statistics describing productivity. Monitoring productivity is very important for monetary policy. The real interest rate is linked to productivity developments. Similarly, the price competitiveness of a national economy depends on productivity developments vis-88-vis competitors. Careful monitoring of these phenomena d0 with careful statistics as a backdrop d0 are key issues for economic policy. I will come back to the productivity problem later. The problem with communication is that citizens' own perceptions of price developments and the price index differ from each other. It is still often said that the changeover to the euro raised the price level, even though the consumer price indices tell us otherwise. When you then ask the public what prices have risen, the answer is coffee at the market, tabloids or similar small purchases, which are repeated frequently but have a small weight in the indices. Few people follow the price action, knowing the weights of the index, let alone the index theories of the T9arnqvis-tin. Statistics Finland, the Bank of Finland and other authorities still face a communication challenge in this regard. * The Bank of Finland's general economic analysis is mainly based on national accounts, price statistics, production and productivity statistics, employment statistics, public sector financial statistics and the use of forward-looking indicators describing these areas. Statistics focusing on the financial and foreign exchange markets are produced extensively by the Bank of Finland d0 partly also by the ECB d0 but the Statistical Tasks of the Bank of Finland are rather limited compared to Statistics Finland's extensive statistical production. The public sometimes gets the impression that the central bank does nothing but prepare interest rate decisions. In fact, central banks have a very wide range of tasks d0 and correspondingly statistical needs d0 in supervising the stability of the financial system, in implementing interventions in the monetary and foreign exchange markets, the maintenance of the payment system and the banknote system, the development of international financial and foreign exchange markets and other areas. Financial cooperation is extensive in various international organisations. For these activities, statistical data on a wide range of monetary and financial institutions, balance of payments data, securities market statistics, financial data on central government finances, financial items of enterprises and households, as well as international financial statistics, must be managed extensively. For these regions, the Eurosystem's common statistical output is also extensive. * The common pain of both the authors and the users of the statistics is that the world is becoming increasingly difficult to compile statistics. The phenomena to be monitored become more complex. The economy and its institutions are changing, making the continuity of time series is a problem for builders of economic models, for example. For different analytical needs, the boundaries of the statistical phenomenon should often be drawn in different ways. The world economy is becoming integrated. Breakdown of phenomena by country, as well as by function, institution and according to the instrument becomes more difficult. In this respect, good examples include the problems in compiling statistics on Nokia's and Nordea's domestic operations, which can be said to make it genuinely difficult to interpret the economy and the financial markets at times. The consistency of statistics has been developed in international organisations, in particular the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) in the area of financial statistics. Statistical intrusions are well illustrated by statistical manuals that are becoming increasingly thick and difficult to read. Users, the general public, the media and also policymakers are demanding clear basic statistics: what is the right inflation rate, what is the really right unemployment rate, etc. However, for the clarity of the statistics the associated ideals seem to be escaping further and further away. A significant proportion of statistical data are inevitably difficult in terms of conceptualisation and uncertain content. The responsibility not only of the statisticians, but also of the users of the statistics, is increasing. We need to know more precisely what the statistics tell us and what they do not tell us. It is realistic that statistics should always be interpreted with caution. Perhaps the statistics should be accompanied as a footnote by the statistician's critical assessment of the overall reliability of the statistics, the sources of error and problems of interpretation. According to experience, a particularly abnormal observation in the preliminary data is usually a statistical error. The application of statistical theoretic subtleties should be in appropriate proportion to the general accuracy of the statistical material. A critical attitude to statistics does not in any way mean that the compilation and use of statistics are being disregarded. Without a statistical basis, the analysis is pure guesswork. The interpretation of economic and financial developments must be based precisely on statistics. Despite all their problems, the statistics are objectively interpreted in the light of the the best indicators of the phenomenon. Perhaps more emphasis should be placed on the production of reduced indicators in the production of statistics. At the same time, the logic of the aggregation of economic statistics is an important part of the statistical package. Theorical compatibility of statistics also provides an important test for the reliability of separate statistical data. The receivables and liabilities side of the balance sheets are always equal and in all timeframes, and in all markets the purchases and sales correspond precisely to each other. Balance sheets closely link the behaviour of different sectors. * In today's economy and democracy, the central bank and the statistical authority are subject to many similar requirements. Of particular importance is the fact that both are required to be independent in some key aspects of their activities, but also to be very transparent. The independence of the central bank, based on EU regulations, guarantees the central bank the freedom of action necessary for the performance of its basic task. The regulations on independence apply to a wide range of areas. The financial independence of the Central Bank is stronger than that of Statistics Finland. As far as the statistical authority is concerned, the importance of independence is therefore emphasised differently. The statistical authority is: subordinate to the government not only directly in terms of its financial resources, but also in terms of the types of areas and subjects for which statistics are produced. However, within these limits, the content of statistical production must be determined on the basis of separate, autonomous statistical criteria. This guarantees the reliability of the statistics produced by the statistical authority, and does not arise suspicions that the statistics will be influenced by outsiders in a direction that focuses on their interests. No one, not even the state, should interfere in the details of statistics in order to promote their own interests. It is absolutely essential that there is confidence in the independence of statistical production. No such doubts have been expressed with regard to Statistics Finland. Statistics Finland is known not only In Finland, also abroad as an efficient and reliable statistical authority. On the other hand, both the central bank and the statistical authority must be transparent about the reasons for their actions. The central bank is required to have a liability obligation, i.e. it must justify its actions and present its Results. The statistical authority, for its part, is obliged to present in a transparent manner the principles for compiling statistics. This guarantees confidence in the consistency of the production of statistics and is very important in terms of interpretation of statistical data. Although both institutions rightly emphasize their independence, both should also emphasize cooperation and communication in different directions. The Bank of Finland has been working to increase its communication and has recently during the years, they encouraged their superiors and experts to speak out in matters related to their specific areas. Such activities, on the one hand, give feedback from outside the bank, and on the other hand, open up new perspectives. For Statistics Finland, transparency means both active appearances to the outside world and to the listening to statistical wishes and critically considering how to take them into account. Statistics Finland has to: invest more in educating and educating people about statistics. * Finally, I would like to return to my own specific area of interest, namely the development of productivity in the national economy. It was an important theme in my previous work at the EU Commission and is also in my current job in the Central Bank. After all, the concept of productivity, with all its dimensions, is very detailed a variable that is difficult to perceive. All parties involved in public policy should address this issue. Previously, the link between labour productivity and well-being was quite fixed on the level of the national economy. In modern integrated economies, however, growth in output and productivity may differ substantially from the growth of real national income, mainly because of the development of the terms of trade and capital payments abroad. An increase in productivity in one country can go to the benefit of foreign consumers. We have special experience of this in Finland. These factors must be taken into account when assessing the wage-payment reserve d0 as well as the dividend payment reserve and the economy's indebtedness reserve. Goods produced by the public sector do not normally have a market price, so productivity cannot be measured as the ratio of output to input. Productivity estimates have been made by comparing the performance rates of different activities with real inputs. The big problem is that the number of deliverables variable is very heterogeneous, and changes in quality cannot usually be taken into account. Although the estimates made are uncertain, they suggest that the productivity of health centres and the total productivity of municipalities, for example, have even weakened in recent years. Large size of the public sector in view of this, the measurement of the productivity of public services must be regarded as a very central objective of statistics. In practice, public administrations are partly subject to fairly simple and mechanical indicators. Strong efforts should be made to develop these. However, public administration and service must operate according to the same basic logic as in economic activity in general: there must be more return on the funds invested, quantitatively and qualitatively. Of course, the productive activity of the private sector is now also increasingly multidimensional, both in terms of the quantity and quality of inputs. At the beginning of my presentation, in the Greenspan example, I have already stated that measuring the productivity growth generated by information technology and education is by no means self-evident. Measuring, among other things, the quality of labour input is a challenging task for Statistics Finland; for example, how much the increase in the average age of the workforce affects productivity. The efficient use of funds for education and training will be one of the major challenges of the coming years. How much does the last engineering student admitted to college increase productivity? On the other hand, statistics finland's challenges relate to improving the quality of existing indicators, on the other hand, the development of new indicators due to globalisation, among other things. High speed of production technology development requires new metrics. So there is a lot of work to be done, for each of them. Best wishes to Statistics Finland on its anniversary!
