Title: Speech on "The four challenges of the economy" at the ECONOMIC 2006 event
text: Director-General Erkki Liikanen ECONOMY 2006 Finlandia Hall 27.10.2005 THE FOUR CHALLENGES FACING THE ECONOMY Challenge 1: PRODUCTIVITY GROWTH Economic growth in Finland, as elsewhere, is based on growth in productivity and labour input. Our standard of living is now more than 12 times higher than it was a hundred years ago, even though the number of hours worked per capita is lower. The explanation is that the productivity of ty has increased 14-fold. In the long term, therefore, our standard of living may eventually rise mainly through increased productivity. This is what it has done throughout our economic history. Although the long-term growth of the economy cannot be based on the growth of the tyanos, I do not want to underestimate the importance of tulle. An increase in the level of participation in the form of an increase in the contribution rate is of considerable importance for the sustainability of the pension system and public finances. A high level of participation not only reduces the need for transfers, but also facilitates the accumulation of pension reserves. Therefore, any attempt to increase the degree of happiness is important. And it is to be hoped that the pension reform will increase the number of jobs. But productivity growth is a source of rising living standards. Productivity can increase through two channels: the first factor is capital gain and the second is the increase in total factor productivity, which describes technical progress, the use of technology in the organization of companies and processes, the recipe for smarter management of labour and capital inputs. First, let's look at capital empowerment.. Investments in machinery and equipment, Figure 2. The decline in investments in machinery and equipment in Finland is particularly worrying. Capital domination occurs when the growth of the capital stock is stronger than that of tyanos. The productivity of a stub worker increases when more or better machines, equipment and technology are given to help or facilitate the stubborn worker." A significant feature of capital is that very often a new production technology is tied to new capital. This raises concerns that slow capital growth may hold back productivity growth in the longer term. Components of GDP and labour productivity growth in Finland between 1995 and 2002, Figure 3. Capital domination has traditionally been an important source of growth. The structural change of the last decade is strongly reflected in the capital domination: due to the collapse of boredom, the growth of capital domination accelerated sharply in the early 1990s, after which it turned to a decline that lasted almost a decade. In the current decade, the growth of the capital stock has been slow. Jalava and Pohjola (2005, ICT as a source of productivity and economic growth) examine the significance of capital domination for productivity growth between 1995 and 2002. Of the 2.5 per cent growth rate in productivity, only half a per cent fell on the shoulders of capitalisation. This growth contribution relied exclusively on capital domination in the form of information and communication technologies (ICT capital), as the contribution of other capital was negative. However, the contribution of ICT capital to productivity growth has been even greater in the United States and the United Kingdom. However, the main source of productivity growth is total factor productivity. Total factor productivity refers to that part of the growth in output that cannot be explained by the growth of inputs, capital and labour. According to Jalava and Pohjola, the growth in total factor productivity explained 4/5 of the productivity growth between 1995 and 2002, i.e. the contribution of the increase in total factor productivity to productivity growth was 2 per cent. There are many poorly measurable aspects of the increase in total factor productivity. These include innovation capacity, organisational structures, financial systems, education, etc. I would like to highlight here a challenge in terms of education. In recent years, we have been able to bask at the forefront of PISA research. The teacher's rooms in primary schools are flooded with foreign guests. This strengthens Finland's reputation and increases interest. It is especially great to see that learning achievements are also good for those students who, for one reason or another, have worse starting positions than others. In other words, the competence of schoolchildren does not depend only on the top individuals. In other words, secondary and tertiary education institutions receive good pupil material from comprehensive school, and the basis for further education is solid. The amount of tertiary education is high, Figure 4. What is the level of education of our people after basic education? In a broad sense, the share of people with tertiary level education among the working-age population in Finland is among the best in the world. We are second in terms of this metric, just behind Canada. Do we have enough top-level education? Figure 5. When we confine ourselves to more than three years of higher education, the picture is no longer the same. We remain in the middle caste of the industrialised countries. Why could this slow down productivity growth? A recent study provides an explanation model for the connection of education to our growth history. It is based on the observation that the general level of education explains to a considerable extent the differences in growth when looking at all countries. However, the explanatory power of the general level of education is weakened when the examination is limited to industrialised countries only. It has since been observed that differences in productivity growth in industrialised countries are particularly affected by the number of employees with the highest level of education. This finding, according to the researchers, may be due to the following: A strong investment in secondary education helps countries and companies behind the forefront of technological development to catch up with the forefront by imitating them. However, when a company or country is at the forefront of technological development d0 as Finland is in many industries d0 imitation is no longer enough. It is necessary to invent completely new products and production methods. Success requires the ability to invent new recipes. In order to produce innovations, therefore, stub workers with the highest level of education are needed. It would seem that the difference between Europe and the United States is reflected precisely in the amount of tertiary education. And the number of studies alone is not enough, but equally important is the quality and orientation of the studies. I understand the concerns of the business community about this view. Economic research is comforting in the fact that more education does not seem to lead to the polarization of society, but the innovation output of the highly educated increases the demand for less educated people. Investment in education at the highest level may be one of the explanations for the fact that productivity growth in the USA has been faster than in Europe since 1995. Another factor has been the difference in it investment and its exploitation d0 which is hardly a matter entirely independent of educational attainment. In the USA, there has been a strong development, especially in the productivity of services. To a small extent, it is explained by the higher level of IT investments, but the biggest difference has arisen in the process changes they enable. The strong competitive situation on the market has forced companies to innovate in their organisation and processes. In European countries, including Finland, the lack of competition has not brought the same incentives. I will come back to this subject. Challenge 2: EXCHANGE RATIO The weak development of export prices in recent years is becoming a structural problem for Finland. From the point of view of households, the decline in the terms of trade is a real problem when it is no longer compensated by the fall in the prices of durable goods, as in recent years. Households' indebtedness reserves and the tax base of general government finances may thus grow clearly more slowly in Finland than the general economic picture would suggest. Export prices, large euro area countries Finland, Figure 6. Export prices, small countries, Figure 7. Exports seem to be increasingly focused on product groups where competition is fierce and demand growth is slow. Strong competition, especially in the electronics industry, has encouraged productivity-enhancing measures. The electronics industry has managed to keep the growth in production volume strong. But the competitive situation has forced the transfer of productivity growth to prices. Indeed, prices in the electronics industry usually fall by 10, sometimes 15%, per year. The average productivity figures of our national economy will be high, but at the same time they will deteriorate due to the terms of trade, and the majority of the benefit will go to consumers on the world market, and the income will not be distributed to the home country as much as could be inferred from the production volumes alone. At the same time, our other important export industry, the forest industry, has been struggling with falling export prices. Traditionally, the demand for paper and the increase in prices followed the general development of the economy. This is no longer the case. Even during the period of growth in world trade, price developments have been subdued. There must have been reasons on both the demand and supply sides. The Internet and the changed reading habits of young people may have reduced demand and new producer countries have increased competing supply. Cumulative change in real GDP and in purchasing power real GDP, % Graph 8. The decrease in the terms of trade resulting from falling export prices can only be improved by a structural change in exports. This can happen both through improved productivity growth in traditional export sectors and through the development of new export products with a high degree of processing. Our traditional export industry clusters still have productivity growth potential. This arises from the business services that they take advantage of in production. Think of product development, standards and brand management, marketing, business planning or legal services. Business services are a significant intermediate input for them, as for other companies. This ties productivity growth in the services sector to growth in the competitiveness of the export sector. A report submitted to the Economic Council last week shows that the productivity development of services supporting business operations has been subdued in Finland. As exports of manufactured goods and services become increasingly interlinked, both export potential and opportunities for better export price development are lost. A major challenge for mature export industries is that the price elasticity of their demand is not very high. Before long, the increase in productivity in these sectors will be reflected in a decrease in the industry's inputs d0 such as labour. It is therefore to be hoped that new export industries will emerge d0 most certainly in the form of services d0 in sectors where the price elasticity of demand and therefore the potential for growth is high. So far, only the software and hardware manufacturing of communication technology has been able to do this. Increasing competition in the services sector is not only a domestic challenge, but also a European one. The so-called 'green card' proposed by the previous Commission. the Services Directive should therefore be adopted. Unfortunately, the reform that is being avoided here has been halted by political struggles within some countries. The Commission should just press on and the British Presidency will show its mettle. Innovation can take place in both new and old companies. However, there is no incentive for old companies to innovate if it is not subject to competition from new companies d0 or the threat of their emergence. The emergence of new companies has been found to have a positive effect on growth. The growth impact has been great when we are at the forefront of technological development. Entrepreneurship should therefore be viewed from this perspective of innovation and competition. The sophistication of financial markets plays an important role in screening viable ideas. The financial markets are chewing on this information. And they assess the eligibility of recipes when deciding on funding. . 3. Challenge: INSTITUTIONS AND POLITICAL DECISION-MAKING Recent research has found that the main factor explaining differences in productivity growth rates is social infrastructures. Social infrastructure refers to those institutions and government policies that affect the economic incentives of individuals and companies. These incentives, in turn, encourage increased productivity through the accumulation of training, the development of new products and production technologies. In turn, incorrectly set incentives can encourage evasion of regulations, corruption and theft. Poor social infrastructures can become obstacles to general prosperity. The basic structures of society create a breeding ground for the development of productivity. Three weeks ago, the World Economic Forum's competitiveness survey was again published. Finland was once again number one in the overall assessment and also at the top in many areas. This measure of competitiveness includes many factors that are part of the basic social fabric. I'll list a few of them here Mittareiden mukaan korruption taso on Suomessa hyvin alhainen. Corruption is harmful because, the time and resources spent on it are out of production. Furthermore, corruption affects the market to the advantage of the old players, creates barriers to entry and thus prevents healthy competition. Poliittinen p8a8atsentekoj8arjestelm8amme on pystynyt aika ajoin venym8a8an t8arkeill8a hetkill8a nopeaan ja m8a8ar8atietoiseen p8a8atsentekoon ja on toiminnaltaan hyvin l8apin8akyv8a8a. I will come back to this important theme even later. Omistusoikeudet ja v8ahemmistomistajien oikeudet on meill8a hyvin m8a8aritelty. These are the avoidances for the emergence of a functioning market. Lakeja noudatetaan laajasti, eik8a tyanosta hukkaannu vankiloissa. The resources of society and the individual are not lavishly wasted on supervision. The basic structure of society is among the best in the world, Figure 9. What, then, is the link between this and productivity growth? Looking at the link between economic growth and indicators of the quality of social infrastructures through a wide range of countries, a clear positive link between economic growth and the quality of institutions is easily observed. The situation will change if the review is limited to the industrialised countries. The differences in this are very small and there is no clear statistical connection anymore ldy. When economic infrastructures are in good enough shape d0 as in key industrialised countries d0 small differences in infrastructure no longer affect investment decisions and productivity growth. The political decision-making system is part of the basic social fabric. The challenge of making decisions is often that the problems of many reforms only come to light much later than the disadvantages associated with it. This is the case with the reforms relating to increased competition. Legislators and authorities create the framework within which competition takes place. Structural reforms are often followed by uncertainty and the dynamic growth effect of the economy is only visible with a delay. It puts the reform advocate in a challenging position. Calculations made by the Bank of Finland on the large-scale removal of barriers to competition confirm this view. As price margins contract, with increased competition, profits fall, at least temporarily, and as a result, the wealth of owners, ultimately households, falls. Increased competition through lower prices will increase consumers' real earnings. Demand begins to strengthen, after that employment and investment increase . And importantly, the growth potential of the economy increases. The pain after the final act turns into an increase in well-being. The problem for the political decision-maker is that the disadvantages are front-loaded and the hymns are back-loaded. Of course, it must be acknowledged that the Finnish decision-making system has stretched a couple of times in recent years in a way that is exceptional. One example is the implementation of pension reform. It is home to both the tripartite and the legislator. In many countries, a similar reform is still in the planning stages. Another good example of the ability of the Finnish political decision-making system to function is the debate, the government's proposal and the parliament's decision on a new nuclear power plant. Such stretching is still needed many more times. Service restructuring is one such area. Challenge 4: MONETARY POLICY Long-term interest rates, Figure 10. In real terms, long-term interest rates are at historically low levels in the same countries. There are at least three reasons for the low level of long-term interest rates Firstly, the supply of finance has had a major impact: surplus countries such as producer countries and Asian countries have been looking for high-quality investment targets worldwide. This has tended to push up the prices of these investments d0 in this case, long-term interest rates. Secondly, low inflation expectations affect interest rates. Market participants are counting on central banks to ensure that price stability is maintained in the future. Thirdly, demographic developments have been seen as one of the reasons for the low level of long-term interest rates. Due to ageing, growing pension funds and voluntary pension investments are part of this trend in the increased demand for investment targets. Ageing slows down economic growth and leads to a slowdown in investment growth. Thus, the supply of weather stars remains high in relation to demand, i.e. investment, which pushes interest rates down. Ample liquidity has sought new assets, which has pushed up the prices of homes and many other assets and reduced yields. The risk premiums related to corporate loans and the yields on credits in developing countries are small compared to previous years. House prices are rising rapidly and household indebtedness continues at an alarming rate in many countries. Monetary policy has been accommodative in recent years, and the weak development of investment in the euro area is not due to monetary policy at least. The level of short-term interest rates in the euro area has been close to zero in real terms since 2003. Despite repeated interest rate hikes by the Central Bank, the real short-term interest rate in the United States is still very low. Short-term (3-month) interest rates, Figure 11. Monetary growth increases the inflation potential of the world economy, and for this reason alone monetary policy has to pay attention to it. On the other hand, if monetary easing continues for a long time, it will increase the vulnerability of national economies as indebtedness ratios rise. An increase in interest rates, a deterioration in the financial situation or a fall in asset prices can easily provoke a sharp change in behavior. The global economy is threatened with recession if the saving rate starts to rise simultaneously in several countries and risk premiums start to rise again. In conclusion, due in particular to the rise in the price of jy and petrol, the estimate of short-term price developments has had to be revised broadly. Inflationary pressures over the medium term in the euro area remain contained, but significant risks to their increase need to be taken into account. In addition, the monetary analysis has identified risks relating specifically to the continued rapid growth of money and credit. The ECB's monetary policy strategy pays attention to both the real economy and the monetary factor. The main points are based on a comparison of the data according to both angles of vision. At the moment, a cross-check of the strategy's two pillars confirms that greater vigilance is needed from monetary policy in order to keep inflation expectations in line with price stability. By keeping medium-term inflation expectations firmly anchored in line with price stability, monetary policy can continue to make a significant contribution to the recovery of economic growth.

text: Director-General Erkki Liikanen Akava Autumn Union Meeting Akava House 21.11.2005 EDUCATION AND TECHNOLOGY AS COMPETITIVE FACTORS IN FINLAND Many international evaluations have placed Finland in the top positions in recent years and months. They have increased the reputation of our country, and that is important capital. Finland has also experienced faster economic growth in recent years than in most other euro area countries. While we are enjoying this success, it is worth looking at where the risks in our economy are increasing or whether there have already been negative developments. Over the past couple of years, the Bank of Finland's publication has paid a lot of attention to the development of our exports. Finland has lost market share in exports and export prices have fallen. Our position as a high-tech exporter is no longer as strong as it was a few years ago. Another factor undermining the conditions for growth in our economy is the contraction of the supply of labour. Since the baby boomers in Finland were born earlier than in other European countries, the ageing of the population will also begin to affect our economic growth earlier. It already limits our ability to grow typanos. In the short term, it will help to increase the employment rate by postponing retirement, but in the long term, Finland's economic growth is increasingly dependent on the growth of the quality of employment and labour productivity. Would there be a common recipe for these problems limiting our economic growth? Our current account has been in surplus for several years. Now the surplus is gradually melting away. [Slide 2: Finland's current account] The deterioration of the current account is due to the fact that domestic demand is growing rapidly and the share of net exports is decreasing due to rising imports. The increase in imports and the weakening of the current account balance reflect the increasing supply constraints of the economy, including the decline in labour availability. However, a key reason for the decline in the current account surplus has been the unfavourable development of the terms of trade, i.e. export and import prices. [Slide 3: Finnish export and import prices and terms of trade] Finland's terms of trade have been deteriorating continuously since 2002, and the deterioration is projected to continue. When export prices fall and import prices rise, we have to export more products to pay for the same amount of imports. The weakening of the terms of trade means that part of the growth in national product flows abroad at lower prices, thus limiting the growth of the real purchasing power of citizens. [ Slide 4: GDP growth and purchasing power developments] The unfavourable development of foreign trade prices has slowed down the rise in the standard of living in Finland over the past 10 years by a total of about 5 per cent. The impact has been particularly strong between 2000 and 2004, when the deterioration of the terms of trade has cut real GDP purchasing power growth by around 3% individually. The impact could have been greater if the fall in import prices for durable durables had not had the effect in the other direction. The assessment of the economic situation often focuses too much on the cyclical picture based on GDP growth. If the effect of the terms of trade on actual purchasing power is not taken into account, this may result in miscalculations about, for example, the development of tax revenues. There is also a risk that households will base their indebtedness decisions on unrealistic income expectations. [Slide 5: International comparison of Finland's export price development] The development of Finnish export prices has been exceptional in Europe. Although economic growth in Germany, for example, has been slow in recent years, Germany's export success and the development of export prices have been clearly better than in Finland. This indicates a different structure of exports. German exports include a lot of capital goods, the price development of which has been more favorable than that of many other products. On the other hand, it is precisely in the export sectors that are important to us, the electronics industry and the paper industry, that export prices have been falling for several years. The forest industry has been struggling with falling export prices for a long time. Traditionally, the demand for paper and the development of prices have been very cyclical, but have followed, on average, the growth of the national product. Cyclical fluctuations continue to sway demand, but long-term trends indicate a structural change in paper demand. New technology has affected the paper industry in two different ways. The development of information and communication technologies has begun to affect the demand for paper. Ict, for example, has contributed to reducing the demand for both newspaper use and office paper. In some cases, such as the United States, we have seen a decrease in volumes, while in Western Europe demand has also been slower than the growth of national product. On the other hand, the new technology has also increased the productivity of the paper industry, which, together with increasing competition, has contributed to lower prices. The demand for paper is still growing as economic prosperity continues to grow in many developing countries, such as China and Russia. On the other hand, new paper producers have entered the market, with low production costs and guaranteed availability of raw materials. The electronics industry is characterized by rapid technological progress. It allows for a sharp increase in productivity. However, the competitive situation on the world market has forced the transfer of the benefit of productivity growth to consumers. Indeed, prices in the electronics industry are falling by about 1015% per year. Our problem with the terms of trade indicates that the structure of our exports needs to be developed and diversified. It requires research and development, innovation and investment in machinery and equipment. [Slide 6: Investments in Machinery and Equipment] The development of machine and equipment investments in Finland has been very modest. Capital domination has traditionally been an important source of productivity growth. In the current decade, the growth of the capital stock has been slow, accounting for only about a fifth of productivity growth since the mid-1990s , also almost exclusively thanks to information and communication technologies. Increasing the degree of added value in exports would require more results from R&D and innovation. Both the OECD and the IMF have been reproaching us recently for the fact that, although we are adept at producing new technology, we do not know how to apply and productise it ourselves very well. This may have been driven by a way of thinking in which the great importance of services is not fully understood. As innovators and marketers of service products, we are still newbies compared to many other countries. The fact is, however, that the kind of future blockbuster products in which Finland can be competitive in the longer term are most likely to be replaced by high-tech, freezing smart services. One could imagine that product development in this direction would be needed, for example, in the field of welfare services and business services. Here the importance of human capital will be very great. Over the past 20 years, there has been a marked qualitative change in the way the euro area operates, with a sharp rise in the level of education in the workplace. Indeed, research shows that human capital growth has played a greater role in productivity growth in the euro area than expected in recent decades. The most important factors affecting the quality of tyano are the age structure and level of education of the tyano. Productivity is considered to be at its highest at around the age of 35-55. This age group is called in the literature by the so-called .... a prime age group, which I guess can be translated as being in the "best of tats". Those younger than that still lack work, and on the other hand, in groups older than that, productivity has been found to gradually decrease as a result of aging. (Although we 55-year-olds don't believe it.) In the euro area, demographic developments have been favourable over the past 20 years. In most European countries, baby boomers were born in the 1950s and 1960s, so they have come to the best place in the last twenty years. In this way, the quality of the workload has, by definition, improved. The share of education in development was particularly high in the late 1980s and early 1990s, as the share of university-educated employment among employed persons increased in the euro area. Investment in education at the highest level may be one of the explanations for the fact that productivity growth in the USA has been faster than in Europe since 1995. Another factor has been the difference in it investment and its exploitation. In the USA, there has been a strong development, especially in the productivity of services. To a small extent, it is explained by the higher level of IT investments, but the biggest difference has arisen in the process changes they enable. The strong competitive situation on the market has forced companies to innovate in their organisation and processes. Over the past couple of decades, improvements in the quality of tyanos have, on average, been due to just under a third of productivity growth in the euro area. In the early 1980s, this proportion was still only about 15%, but it has risen to 35% in the early 2000s. The slowdown in the qualitative development of labour input appears to have contributed to the slowdown in productivity growth in the euro area during the 1990s. In Finland, the ageing of the population has already begun to have an impact on the growth of stub productivity. Thus, the importance of education in increasing the quality of work input is more important to us than in other countries. [Slide 7: Share of higher education in different countries] It is worth considering separately the so-called. the level of general education and the so-called. the importance of the highest level of education in productivity development. In Finland, the general level of education has risen over the past couple of decades. It has received flattering recognitions, for example, through the famous PISA study, where the Finnish school system has been raised as a model example for other OECD countries. That is a good thing. The share of people with tertiary level education among the liked population in Finland is also among the best in the world. We are second on this metric, just behind Canada. That, too, is important. But if you look at higher education that has lasted more than three years, Finland falls short of the average caste of industrialized countries in comparison. [Slide 8: Do we have enough top-level education?] According to studies, the general level of education and the number of people with the highest level of education have different significance for productivity development and economic growth. The general level of education explains growth differences when all countries are examined. It is likely that a strong investment in secondary education will help countries and companies behind the forefront of technological development to catch up by imitating them. By contrast, differences in productivity growth between industrialised countries are particularly affected by the proportion of employees with the highest level of education. However, when a company or country is already at the forefront of technological development  as Finland is in many industries  imitation is no longer enough. It is necessary to invent completely new products and production methods. In order to produce innovations, stub workers with the highest level of education are needed. In October, the latest competitiveness survey of the World Economic Forum was published. In it, Finland was once again number one in the overall assessment and also at the top in many areas. This measure of competitiveness includes many factors that are part of the basic social fabric. According to the indicators, the level of corruption in Finland is very low. Our political decision-making system is efficient and very transparent in its operation. We also have well-defined property rights that are important for a functioning market. An important competitive factor is also social peace, as laws are widely observed in Finland. The importance of these factors as contributors to economic growth is emphasised when comparing very different countries, such as a developing country and an industrialised country. On the other hand, the differences in the basic structures of society between industrialised countries are relatively small, and there is no longer a clear statistical link between these differences and differences in economic growth. [Slide 9: The basic structure of Finnish society is among the best in the world] On the other hand, even smaller structural differences can play a role in creating long-term differences in development between industrialised countries. These factors include, for example, the competitive nature of the market. The Bank of Finland has carried out calculations on the effects of removing barriers to competition. At first, the effects can be negative for many groups, but over time the positive effects are accentuated. Competition lowers prices, raises real wages and thus increases demand. This, again, after a certain delay, increases jobs and investment, and ultimately the well-being of the nation. Unfortunately, the disadvantages are front-loaded, and the advantages are rear-weighted. The EU is still working on a proposal to liberalise services to international competition. Despite all the controversy, it is clear that more competition in the internal market would increase tulle and growth in Europe. And it would have a mythical effect on productivity growth, which is a prerequisite for increasing real earnings. In public administration and services, the concept of productivity has often been understood very one-sidedly. Productivity is identified only with grinding. The standard of living does not rise if the same soup is cooked at a faster pace from one decade to the next, or if the orchestra plays faster. Productivity comes from inventing better recipes, organizing more intelligently. At all levels. I refuse to believe that an annual improvement of two or three per cent is not possible in the public sector. We have a better trained spirit. Its creative power must be unleashed and leadership developed. And use resources better. The major challenge in the coming years will be how to make the tymarket system work in such a way that centralised agreements keep inflation down while at the same time taking into account: enterprise and individual productivity growth. The system should also encourage the accumulation of human capital, particularly through training. Here we still face major challenges. Docent Rita Asplund has studied these questions extensively. Productivity developments are an important factor in containing inflation. It lowers production costs, which, in a functioning competitive market, will eventually pass into price reductions to the benefit of consumers. For this reason, central banks also have particular reason to be interested in productivity developments. The role of the European Central Bank is to ensure price stability in the region. The aim is to keep inflation rates in the euro area below, but close to, 2% over the medium term. Healthy competitiveness and high productivity contribute to achieving this goal. [Slide 10: Inflation developments in the euro area] The euro's journey so far has been a success story, as inflation rates in the euro area countries have fallen markedly compared to what they were in the middle of the last decade. The general price development can also be influenced by national means. Of these, the key factors are increased competitiveness, productivity growth, public taxes and charges, and wage developments. [Slide 11: Short-term interest rates (3 months) in the euro area and the US] In the euro area, interest rates have recently been at historically low levels. The level of short-term interest rates in the euro area has been close to zero in real terms since 2003. These developments have increased households' real disposable income and purchasing power, thereby supporting economic activity. Interest rates have not been a barrier to investment. [Slide 12: Long-term interest rates in the euro area and the US] In addition, long-term interest rates have been at historically low levels, which indicates, firstly, that market participants have confidence in the ability of central banks to ensure that price stability is maintained in the future. Secondly, the surplus countries' investments in long-term debt securities have pushed interest rates down. And thirdly, demographic trends have been seen as one of the reasons for the low level of long-term interest rates. Ageing leads to a gradual decline in investment. Ageing also increases pension funds and increases voluntary pension savings. Thus, the supply of savings assets remains high in relation to demand, i.e. investment, which pushes interest rates down. In conclusion, I would like to stress that the two key problems of the Finnish economy  the weakening of the terms of trade and the reduction in the labour force  can in principle be cured with the same prescription. The main objectives are to diversify the structure of exports and increase the degree of added value, as well as to increase the productivity of ty. Increasing productivity can take place through increased training, physical capital and technological progress. The key factor in Finnish competitiveness is competence: education and high technology. The key question is how we can make the most of the new technology. Education plays an important role in how well new technologies can be absorbed and how, for example, the use of information and communication technologies can be used to increase productivity in more and more new sectors. On the other hand  by increasing productivity  new technology frees up highly educated work for development and innovation. We can also ask if we can take full advantage of the good education and skills of our work. Even if the pension reform and the intensification of the education system could increase the number of jobs done, the ageing of the population will, in the long term, reduce the number of domestic jobs. In order to increase productivity, the qualitative development of labour input, especially through training, is key. It is important that the structures and incentive systems of society support the accumulation of competence both at the level of monosyllabics and at the level of my companies. Education should be rewarded already at a young age group. At the institutional and systemic level, the key word is intelligent organisation, which combines both efficiency and long-term development objectives. It is high time to look at how the provision of public services has been organised, how new technologies have been developed and the competence of both employees and the organisation as a whole has been taken care of.

Title: Speech on "The next stage of European financial integration as an objective and challenge" at the negotiating day of the media management and the Board of the Banking Association
text: President Erkki Liikanen Meeting day of the Media Management and the Board of the Banking Association 24.11.2005 THE NEXT PHASE OF EUROPEAN FINANCIAL INTEGRATION AS AN OBJECTIVE AND CHALLENGE Ladies and gentlemen, I would like to start by thanking the Finnish Banking Association for the opportunity to appear at your negotiating days. It is both pleasant and chilling to meet such a representative group of key media and banking influencers at once and discuss what the current challenges in the banking sector look like from the central bank's perspective. The banking sector as part of the financial markets has been subject to strong forces of change for years and the change continues. The amendment has three separate articles: firstly, there will be cross-border integration and, secondly, cross-sectoral integration. And thirdly, the use of information and communication technologies continues to cause major changes both in the distribution network and in the internal processes of banks. A common feature of these is the effort to improve productivity and, consequently, competitiveness and profitability. In addition to these three elements of change, I intend to deal with my four topics, regulation, regulation. Striving for continuous structural change and productivity improvement Banking European in the banking sector is welcome and necessarily. European economic policy rakennemuu the main challenge is to revive the economic dynamism of the continent. Economy must continue other and social problems, such as employment and the financing of public finances, are largely due to a lack of growth dynamics and investment. In their revitalization, the financial sector plays a significant role. The development of financial markets plays a key role in the economic growth and stability of the EU region as a whole The European economy cannot reform unless the financial markets are reformed and made more efficient. This is not only due to the financial weight of the financial sector itself, but even more so to the central importance of financial services and markets for the functioning of the economy in general. This role is twofold. First of all, banks, capital markets and the financial sector in general play a key role in evaluating, pruning and growing innovations and new business ideas. In this way, the financial sector not only takes care of the pursuit of the market, but also contributes to the continuous development of the economy. Secondly, the payment system that the banks manage is the basic structure that can unite the market into a single whole. Without a well-functioning payment system, the market would be fragmented locally, regionally or nationally. Only an efficient and uniform payment system will allow for a large and competitive market. * * * The current orientation of European financial market policy underlines the objective of market integration. Here are both challenges and opportunities for banks that banks should look at carefully. The reason for the integration of the financial markets is that it has been assessed as essential for the revival of economic growth in Europe. Financial integration drives growth for three reasons: ensinnakin investointien tuottovaatimus alenee, koska paaomaa can be obtained from the market at a lower price. As a result, investments grow and the tulle improves. toiseksi kuluttajat saavat valitta hytya, kun lainojen marginaalit ja whereas service charges are reduced in response to competition, and kolmanneksi rahoituspalvelujen tarjonta ja tuotevalikoima laajenee ja diversifies, which also lowers the cost of financing. Furthermore, the integration of financial markets will make the euro area economy more stable, as single financial markets also act as risk equalisers between countries. The effects of country-specific economic fluctuations will be dampened and evened out as the ownership and trade of financial claims and investments between countries expands and deepens. In the USA, a large part of those characteristic of the regions, so Public authorities and legislators have built the conditions for the unification of EU financial markets... ... but the main responsibility for the development of the financial system lies with the markets, my banks to say, asymmetric income fluctuations are smoothed out through financial markets. Monetary policy still has a particular interest in ensuring that the financial markets in the euro area are as cohesive as possible. This is an advantage in order to prevent the effects of monetary policy from targeting the various member states of the monetary union too asymmetrically. Today we have a common monetary policy, but not an internal market for financial services. * * * A key instrument for creating an integrated financial services market has been the Financial Services Action Plan (FSAP), adopted in 1999. In support of this, a special committee structure was created to harmonise supervision, bearing the lamfalussy name. The action plan contained a large number of measures, as many as 42, almost all of which have already been implemented at EU level. For many projects, national implementation is still ongoing, the most important of which is the reform of the capital requirements of credit institutions in line with Basel II. Last year, the Commission started preparing a follow-up to the action plan. However, there is no new comprehensive legislative package to come. Commissioner McCreevy has so often assured me, during his visit to Finland in early autumn. The Commission has underlined the 'better regulation' objective. In accordance with the principles adopted just over three years ago, any new proposal must first go through an extensive consultation process, always using the Internet as well. In addition, a careful impact assessment of all proposals must be carried out, particularly in terms of costs and costs, before any decision is taken on the need for a new legislative initiative. So the authorities have been active. Is the reform of the European financial markets therefore a 'revolution from above'? Of course not. Focus on the payment system, securities trading and financial supervision The harmonisation of the euro area payment system is a policy priority and bank cooperation in this area is favoured Ultimately, progress in the integration of the European financial system will not be achieved by public authorities or by means of regulation. Banks and other financial service providers are responsible for generating added value for customers. Therefore, integration becomes a reality only when market participants, such as banks, develop their business. It is the task of the authorities to remove obstacles and to ensure that supervision is developed. The three main areas in which financial integration should now be taken forward are all part of the market infrastructure. The first is the construction of a single European market in retail banking, particularly in payments. The second is the streamlining and harmonisation of clearing and settlement systems for securities transactions. The third is the harmonisation and coordination of financial supervision. I'm going to touch on these in the following. * * * The development of a uniform and technically efficient payment system requires cooperation and coordination, both between banks and more widely. On the other hand, economic efficiency requires that this cooperation must not turn into a restriction of competition contrary to the interests of customers. We must therefore favour cooperation within the industry, but at the same time be careful that this interaction does not abuse market power. The requirement for transparency in the systems offers one solution, but at the same time raises the question of incentives for product development. Open standards and compatibility are needed, and there must also be incentives in the market to develop new payment methods and business models. This tension between coordination and competition and the associated problem of the balance between the unity and innovation of systems is the central issue of charging system policy. Both the Eurosystem central banks and the EU Commission consider the promotion of integration to be a priority in payment system policy. One of the problems identified is the fragmentation of the European retail payment system, especially in the euro area. The Single European Payments Area (SEPA) is an important project... ... whose technological up-to-dateness must be ensured One example of this measure was the European Commission's regulation, which two years ago banned the levying of different prices for domestic and intra-euro area cross-border payments. Banks viewed it negatively for various reasons. However, this regulation was an unavoidable step that removed one of the striking obstacles to the functioning of the single market in the euro area. The European Commission is continuing its efforts in the same area. It is now preparing a proposal to reduce the delay in the value of cross-border credit transfers to a maximum of three days. The creation of a single European payments area (SEPA) has become an important internal market objective. The European Payments Council, set up by the banks, is welcomed as a sign of the commitment of financial institutions to this objective. The objective of the single payments area is that the instruments available to the final customer  the payer and the payee  should be compatible throughout the euro area and that the level of service would in no way depend on whether or not the payment exceeds borders between Member States. This would be of great importance in promoting economic integration. The single European payments area is of great importance to the banking sector because it does not only mean the creation of common European payment gateways and instruments, but also involves the dismantling of certain nationally differentiated payment systems. Credit transfer, direct debit and card payment would receive uniform specifications. Banking competition would intensify, for example, due to the elimination of the need for companies to keep several payment accounts in different euro area countries. Each company could make its payments at a single point across the euro area. The aim is to have a single European payments area by 2010. The schedule is municipally ambitious and requires a strong commitment. From the point of view of Finnish banks and my customers, a unified payment area allows for great benefits, but the project is not without its problems. Finland is a pioneering country in telegrams and online payment systems. It would be a good idea to expand the cooperation between Finnish parties in the development of payment systems The worst option would be for the Single European Payments Area to rely on models in which network solutions and Internet banking are not sufficiently involved. However, the ECB has rightly stressed as its own requirement that the future system must enable the automation of transactions throughout the process in order for the payment system to be cost-effective, not only in banks but also in customer companies. This requires uniform standards at the interface between banks and customers. The Finns should not be arrogant about the establishment of a single payments area, even though our own systems today are technologically well advanced. Everything possible must be done to ensure that common payment systems are based on future solutions. Then the current level of service will be maintained and improved in the transition to a single payment area. A unified and efficient internal market in this field will ultimately bring great benefits to everyone, including us Finns. In order to achieve the objective of developing payment systems, it is necessary to ensure a closer partnership between the central bank, banks, businesses, system suppliers and consumer organisations. If necessary, competition and telecommunications authorities should also be invited. The Bank of Finland has its own channel of influence as part of the Eurosystem. Banks have their own avenues. In order for influencing to be effective and coordinated, a common Finnish payment platform may be necessary. It would help to develop and expand existing forms of cooperation between public authorities and the private sector. The forum can be light, free of any bureaucracy, but available when needed. The forum could promote both the impact of Finns in European contexts and the dissemination of information on future changes in the payment system here in Finland. The Bank of Finland is ready to convene one. The European securities markets are still too heterogeneous Integration also places demands on the development of Finnish securities trading systems This type of role as a facilitator of cooperation between domestic parties is currently played by the authorities, not only permitted, but also derived from the bank's statutory duties. When it comes to market restructuring, the most technologically advanced, fastest adjusters usually turn out to be winners. That is why I believe that Finnish banking know-how will put off new markets as efforts to improve the efficiency of payment transactions in the euro area continue. * * * Next, there is another problem with the infrastructure of European financial markets, the structure of the securities markets. The problem is the lack and heterogeneity of the depth and liquidity of the market. The main problem has been localised to the fragmentation of clearing and settlement systems, which is partly responsible for the high cost of securities trading in Europe. This is particularly the case for cross-border stock trading, the high costs of which are precisely what perpetuates market fragmentation. This creates problems both for issuers in the form of lower prices and for my investors and financial service providers in the form of higher transaction costs. Thus, the market infrastructure has too much influence on the choice of trading platform and investment decisions. In this situation, everywhere, including in Finland, the national specificities of the clearing and settlement system must be examined from the perspective of their future in a converging infrastructure. At the present stage of development of the Nordic securities market, this is no longer just a national issue, but also a Nordic one, and increasingly a European issue. From Finland's point of view, two special features are highlighted in this review: on the one hand, the structure of the book-entry system, which we have based on the direct ownership of individual investors, and, on the other hand, the absence of a central counterparty in securities trading in the Nordic countries. Financial supervision structures need to keep up with the times In Finland, financial supervision should be harmonised It is important for Finnish business life that the financial sector provides it with competitive and developing services also in the future, and that there are good operating conditions for the production of financial services in Finland. The greater the changes that the upcoming integration entails, the earlier it is worth starting to prepare for them. * * * Financial supervision is the third element of market infrastructure affected by cross-border integration and cross-sectoral integration of financial markets. Financial supervision is not an end in itself, but aims to safeguard the stability of the financial system and support the efficient functioning of markets. Therefore, supervisory arrangements cannot, in the long term, be independent of market restructuring. Today, the remit of financial supervision is increasingly international. As the financial sector in the euro area becomes more integrated, internationality will continue to be emphasised. The field of supervision is also increasingly sector-wide, as banking, securities markets and insurance activities are closely interlinked. In Finland, due to the convergence of the financial and insurance industries, there is a need to examine the national structures of financial supervision without prejudice. This is both a safety and cost issue. The current financial supervision has worked well since the banking crisis. In recent years, however, cross-border mergers between countries and sectors have changed the sector significantly. The largest bank is also large in the life insurance market and the next two are now major players in both the life and non-life insurance markets. In addition, Finland has its own historical peculiarity, statutory employment insurance. However, it is precisely because of this special status that it can be excluded from the review today. In modern administration, the starting point is that the client has one counterparty in the control field. On the other hand, for public oversight, when risks are concentrated, it would be important for them to be assessed by a single supervisory authority. International structures for financial supervision must be strengthened It is also important to avoid the risk of fragmentation of resources and multiplication of management. For the sake of this simple but irresistible logic, the same authority should have the main responsibility for the supervision of financial conglomerates, regardless of the importance of banking and insurance activities in their business. In any case, banks and life insurance supervision should be carried out by the same supervisory authority. Non-life insurance has its own special features, but it is also such an essential part of the activities of large financial conglomerates that it would be more effective to carry out supervision by a single authority. Of course, this issue will be put forward by the government of the country. And laws are decided by parliament. And I don't want to go to their field. But what is undeniable is that the banking and insurance field has changed fundamentally. At the same time, the administration should change in order to be able to carry out its tasks in the best possible and effective way. As far as the financial system is concerned, efficiency is important. But beyond that, it must be remembered that financial systems have always been vulnerable to disruption in a way that is different from other sectors. In them lies the so-called. the risk of systemic risk, which, if realised, can spread rapidly from one company to another and now from one country to another, which is one of the problematic aspects of integration. Promoting financial stability is therefore one of the key objectives of the EU and the Eurosystem, in addition to efficiency. The line taken by the EU authorities at the moment is that there is now no desire to interfere in the institutional system of surveillance and safety nets. The development of the market is passing by this. The role of the host country is, for example, a key issue for Finland, but also for many eu countries, especially the new ones, that voluntary agreements are hardly enough to secure it. We will have to look for a stronger legal basis. * * * Banks operating in Finland have good starting positions Banks need to remember to be adequately prepared for lending risks In my opinion, the banks are in a position to succeed in the conditions of the structural changes I have outlined here are good, if not excellent, as long as the challenges are properly identified and responded to in time. The results and solvency of the banking sector have been good by international comparison. After the dip at the beginning of the decade, profitability has improved again and is among the best in Europe. My productivity is at the top of the international rankings. Banks had invested heavily in information technology before the major crisis. After that, competition and the need to restore profitability forced a sharp increase in productivity. At that time, the investment made in information technology was taken full throttle. The processes were automated and online services were widely used. What has been important in Finland is that online services were not created alongside traditional distribution channels, but in their place. Thus, productivity increased sharply. And what are the challenges ahead? The restructuring of the sector must proceed with a view to further improving productivity and cost-effectiveness. For financial groups, synergy challenges are still a separate issue. Profitability and solvency must be kept in good condition. Basel II has a major impact here. New prudential requirements should lead to the development of risk management and a more efficient use of capital in banks. However, it is not a question of easing capital requirements that would allow banking to become more risky. On the contrary, the aim is to increase stability. When moving to a new prudential regime, excessive credit growth must be avoided and the wisest thing to do is to proceed prudently and risk-acknowledging. In addition to the minimum capital required by the new regulations, banks also need larger solvency buffers, for example because, under the new solvency rules, capital requirements will be more variable than before. Banks' R&D activities have a broad societal significance We are now in good times, and we are used to the fact that credit risks are low. However, the good times do not go on forever, and when they end, the dynamics of Basel II begin to take effect. The capital required of banks will start to grow if the cyclical situation deteriorates and the risk content of the loan portfolio also increases due to the increase in credit risk. * * * And finally. Banks play a key role in European productivity efforts. Their activities and the development they carry out, alongside their business value, play a key role in society. These roles do not compete with each other. The social function of the banking system is realised precisely through good, long-term business and competition in the market economy.

Painopistein maksujrjestelm, arvopaperikauppa ja rahoitusvalvonta Euroalueen maksujrjestelmn yhtenistminen on politiikassa etusijalla ja pankkien yhteisty tll alalla suositaan Viime kdess Euroopan rahoitusjrjestelmn integraation eteneminen ei toteudu viranomaisten toimesta eik sntelyn keinoin. Pankit suhtautuivat siihen kielteisesti eri syist. Tm regulaatio oli kuitenkin vlttmtn edistysaskel, joka poisti yhden silmiinpistvn euroalueen yhtenismarkkinoiden toimintaa haittaavista esteist. Yhtenisen eurooppalaisen maksualueen merkitys pankkisektorin kannalta on suuri sen takia, ett se ei tarkoita pelkstn yhteisten eurooppalaisten maksuvylien ja -instrumenttien perustamista, vaan se sislt mys tiettyjen kansallisesti eriytettyjen maksujrjestelmien alasajon. Markkinoiden rakennemuutoksissa teknologisesti edistyneimmt, nopeimmat sopeutujat yleens osoittautuvat voittajiksi. Siksi uskon, ett suomalainen pankkiosaaminen lyt uusia markkinoita kun maksuliikkeen tehostamispyrkimykset euroalueella jatkuvat. * * * Seuraavaksi toisesta eurooppalaisen rahoitusmarkkinoiden infrastruktuurin ongelmakohdasta, arvopaperimarkkinoiden rakenteesta. Ongelmana on markkinoiden syvyyden ja likvidisyyden puute ja epyhtenisyys. Keskeisimmksi ongelmaksi on paikallistettu selvitys- ja toimitusjrjestelmien pirstoutuneisuus, joka on osaltaan syyn siihen, ett arvopaperikaupan kustannukset Euroopassa ovat korkeat. Tm koskee erityisesti rajat ylittv osakekauppaa, mink suuret kustannukset juuri yllpitvt markkinoiden pirstoutuneisuutta. Tst seuraa ongelmia sek liikkeeseenlaskijoille matalampien hintojen muodossa, ett my sijoittajille ja rahoituspalvelujen tuottajille korkeampien liiketoimikustannusten muodossa. Markkinoiden infrastruktuuri vaikuttaa siis liikaa kaupankyntipaikan valintaan ja sijoitusptksiin. Tss tilanteessa on kaikkialla, Suomessakin, tarkasteltava selvitys- ja toimitusjrjestelmn kansallisia erityispiirteit siit nkulmasta, mik niiden tulevaisuus on yhtenevss infrastruktuurissa. Pohjoismaisten arvopaperimarkkinoiden nykyisess kehitysvaiheessa tm ei ole en vain kansallinen, vaan my pohjoismainen kysymys, ja yh enenevss mrin my eurooppalainen kysymys. Suomen kannalta korostuu tss tarkastelussa kaksi erikoispiirrett, yhtlt arvo-osuusjrjestelmn rakenne, joka meill perustuu yksittisten sijoittajien suoraan omistukseen, ja toisaalta arvopaperikaupan keskusvastapuolen puuttuminen Pohjoismaista. Rahoitusvalvonnan rakenteiden on seurattava aikaansa Suomessa rahoitusvalvonta olisi yhtenistettv Suomalaisen elinkeinoelmn kannalta on trke, ett rahoitusala tarjoaa sille kilpailukykyiset ja kehittyvt palvelut mys tulevaisuudessa, ja ett rahoituspalvelujen tuotannolle Suomessa on hyvt toimintaedellytykset. Mit suurempia muutoksia edess oleva integraatio aiheuttaa, sit aikaisemmin niihin valmistautuminen on syyt aloittaa. * * * Rahoitusvalvonta on kolmas markkinoiden infrastruktuurin osa, johon maiden rajat ja rahoitusmarkkinoiden sektorirajat ylittv integraatio vaikuttaa. Rahoitusvalvonta ei ole itsetarkoitus, vaan sill pyritn varjelemaan rahoitusjrjestelmn vakautta ja tukemaan markkinoiden tehokasta toimintaa. Valvonnan jrjestelyt eivt siten voi pitkn plle olla riippumattomia markkinoiden rakennemuutoksesta. Nykyisin rahoitusvalvonnan tehtvkentt on entist kansainvlisempi. Kun rahoitussektori euroalueella yhtenistyy, kansainvlisyys edelleen korostuu. Suomessa on rahoitus- ja vakuutustoimialan lhentymisen vuoksi tarvetta tarkastella ennakkoluulottomasti rahoitusvalvonnan kansallisia rakenteita. Tm on sek turvallisuus- ett kustannuskysymys. Nykyinen rahoitusvalvonta on toiminut hyvin pankkikriisin jlkeisen ajan. Viime vuosina maiden ja sektorien rajat ylittvt fuusiot ovat kuitenkin muuttaneet alaa merkittvsti. Suurin pankki on my suuri henkivakuutusmarkkinoilla ja kaksi seuraavaa ovat nyt merkittvi toimijoita sek henki- ett vahinkovakuutusmarkkinoilla. Sen lisksi Suomella on oma historiallinen erikoisuutensa, lakisteinen tylkevakuutus. Juuri tmn erityisasemansa vuoksi se voidaan jtt kuitenkin tnn tarkastelun ulkopuolelle. Modernissa hallinnossa lhdetn siit, ett asiakkaalla on yksi vastapuoli valvontakentll. Toisaalta julkisen valvonnan kannalta, kun riskit keskittyvt, olisi trke, ett ne arvioidaan yhden valvontaviranomaisen toimesta. Rahoitusvalvonnan kansainvlisi rakenteita pit vahvistaa On my trke vltt voimavarojen hajottamisen ja hallinnoinnin moninkertaistamisen vaara. Tm yksinkertaisen, mutta vastaansanomattoman logiikan vuoksi saman viranomaisen tulisi olla pvastuussa finanssiryhmittymien valvonnasta riippumatta pankki-ja vakuutustoiminnan merkityksest niiden liiketoiminnassa. Muutenkin tulisi pankkien ja henkivakuutusvalvonnan tapahtua saman valvontaviranomaisen toimesta. Vahinkovakuutuksessa on omat erityispiirteens, mutta sekin on niin oleellinen osa suurten finanssikonglomeraattien toimintaa, ett valvonta olisi tehokkaampaa suorittaa yhden viranomaisen toimesta. Tst asiasta tekee tietysti esityksen maan hallitus. Ja laeista ptt eduskunta. Enk halua menn heidn kentlleen. Mutta kiistatonta on, ett pankkija vakuutuskentt on muuttunut oleellisesti. Hallinnon pitisi muuttua samalla kyetkseen parhaalla mahdollisella tavalla ja tehokkaasti hoitamaan tehtvns. Rahoitusjrjestelmn osalta trke on tehokkuus. Mutta sen lisksi on muistettava, ett rahoitusjrjestelmt ovat aina olleet hirialttiita muista sektoreista poikkeavalla tavalla. Niiss piilee ns. systeemiriskin vaara, jonka toteutuessa hirit voivat levit nopeasti yrityksest toiseen ja nykyisin maasta toiseen, mik onkin integraation ongelmallisia puolia. Rahoitusjrjestelmn vakauden edistminen onkin tehokkuuden ohella EU:n ja Eurojrjestelmn keskeisi tavoitteita. EU:n viranomaisten linja tll hetkell on, ett valvonnan ja turvaverkkojen institutionaaliseen jrjestelmn ei nyt haluta puuttua. Markkinoiden kehitys on kulkemassa tmn ohitse. Isntvaltion rooli on esimerkiksi Suomen, mutta mys monien varsinkin uusien EU-maiden tapauksessa niin keskeinen kysymys, ett sen turvaamiseksi vapaaehtoisuuteen pohjautuvat sopimukset tuskin riittvt. Joudutaan etsimn vahvempaa juridista pohjaa. * * * Suomessa toimivien pankkien lhtohdat ovat hyvt Pankkien on muistettava riittv varautuminen antolainauksen riskeihin Pankkien lhtkohdat menesty tss hahmottelemieni rakennemuutosten oloissa ovat mielestni hyvt, elleivt erinomaiset, kunhan haasteet oikein tunnistetaan ja niihin ajoissa reagoidaan. Pankkisektorin tulokset ja vakavaraisuus ovat olleet kansainvlisesti vertaillen hyvt. Vuosikymmenen alun notkahduksen jlkeen kannattavuus on uudelleen parantunut ja on Euroopan krkitasoa. My tuottavuus on kansainvlist krke. Pankit olivat investoineet runsaasti tietotekniikkaan ennen suurta kriisi. Sen jlkeen kilpailu ja kannattavuuden palauttamisen tarve pakottivat nostamaan tuottavuutta voimakkaasti. Tehdyist tietotekniikkainvestoinneista otettiin silloin tysi hyy. Prosessit automatisoitiin ja verkkopalvelut otettiin laajasti kyttn. Trke Suomessa on ollut nimenomaan se, ettei verkkopalveluja luotu perinteisten jakelukanavien rinnalle vaan tilalle. Nin tuottavuus kasvoi voimakkaasti. Ent mitk haasteet ovat nyt edess? Alan rakennemuutoksessa on edettv pyrkien samalla edelleen parantamaan tuottavuutta ja kustannustehokkuutta. Finanssiryhmille synergiahaasteet ovat viel oma kysymyksens. Kannattavuus ja vakavaraisuus on pidettv hyvss kunnossa. Basel II:n vaikutus on tss suuri. Uusien vakavaraisuusvaatimusten pitisi johtaa riskienhallinnan kehittymiseen ja poman tehokkaampaan kyttn pankeissa. Tarkoituksena ei kuitenkaan ole sellainen pomavaatimusten keventminen, joka sallisi pankkitoiminnan muuttumisen aikaisempaa riskipitoisemmaksi. Pinvastoin, tavoitteena on vakauden lisntyminen. Uuteen vakavaraisuusjrjestelmn siirryttess on vltettv liiallinen luotonannon kasvu ja viisainta on edet harkiten ja riskit tunnistaen. Pankit tarvitsevat uusien mrysten edellyttmn vhimmispoman lisksi mys entist suurempia vakavaraisuuspuskureita mm. siksi, ett uusien vakavaraisuusmrysten vallitessa pomavaatimukset ovat aikaisempaa vaihtelevammat. Pankkien tuotekehitystoiminnalla on laaja yhteiskunnallinen merkitys Nyt edetn hyvi aikoja, ja on totuttu siihen, ett luottoriskit ovat pieni. Hyvt ajat eivt kuitenkaan jatku ikuisesti, ja kun ne loppuvat, Basel II:n dynamiikka alkaa vaikuttaa. Pankeilta vaadittu poma kntyy kasvuun, jos suhdannetilanne heikkenee ja lainasalkun riskipitoisuus luottotappioriskien kasvun myt kasvaa. * * * Ja lopuksi. Pankeilla on keskeinen rooli eurooppalaisissa tuottavuusponnistuksissa. Niiden toiminnalla ja my niiden harjoittamalla kehitystyll on liiketaloudellisen arvonsa rinnalla keskeinen yhteiskunnallinen merkitys. Nm roolit eivt kilpaile keskenn.
