Title: Bank Manager Sinikka Salo's speech at the Institutional Investors' Decision-Making Days "Aatos and Ehtoo"
text: VTT Sinikka Salo Director Bank of Finland Institutional investment challenges in today's markets Presentation at the Institutional Investors' Decision-making Days "Aatos ja Ehtoo" in Espoo 24.11.2005 I have been asked to speak at this event on the challenges of institutional investment in today's markets. This broad topic can be approached from several different angles. In this speech, I will examine the challenges of institutional investment from the perspective of economic development, the integration of financial markets and newer investment targets, mainly private equity. Economic development Global economic growth has continued to be relatively vigorous and the outlook for growth remains favourable, although global economic growth is projected to decelerate from a rate of 5% to around 4% in the coming years (2005-2007, Euro & Economy 3, 2005). The growth of the agricultural economy has been going on for several years without disturbances. A number of threats d0 related to the overheating of the Chinese economy or the imbalances in the US economy d0 have not materialised. The impact of the rise in oil prices on the growth of the world economy has also been less than estimated, at least for the time being. The stable development of the international economy has also supported the stability of the financial system. The financial markets have survived the recent shocks that have hit them (Enron, Parmalat, the difficulties of the automotive industry in the United States, etc.) without any more serious problems. As a result of favourable economic developments, financial actors d0 such as banks, insurance companies, pension providers d0 have been able to improve their performance and strengthen their balance sheets. At the same time, the resilience of the financial system to shocks has improved, and this is also the case in our home country. The performance of non-financial corporations in advanced economies has also been good on average and corporate indebtedness moderate. As a result of good profit performance and subdued investment, companies have been able to strengthen their balance sheets. However, the global economic outlook is not without risks. Us indebtedness problems continue to worsen, household and public sector indebtedness continues to rise, both in the United States and in several European countries. The evolution of wealth prices, especially house prices, is also one of the concerns almost everywhere. The ample liquidity in the financial markets has been reflected not only in the United States, but also in the housing markets of several European countries in the form of rapid price increases and has increased the risk of rising inflation. Ample liquidity has also contributed to the exceptionally low interest rates on long-term bonds, and the risk premiums on lower-quality bonds remain low despite their slight rise. In view of the robust development of the global economy, there is a risk that the effects of high liquidity would unwind in the financial markets uncontrollably. This kind of stability disorder in the financial markets could be accompanied by an increase in longterm interest rates, a sharp fall in stock prices and strong volatility in the foreign exchange markets, which could significantly disrupt both global and domestic developments. The level of long-term interest rates has long been exceptionally low. The low interest rate level is due to factors such as: - The global investment gap or 'overspending', i.e. saving, has exceeded the demand for credit for investment for years. - Asian countries, especially China, have been able to finance their growing investments with their own high savings. The rapidly growing foreign exchange reserves of Asian countries have been substantially invested in the United States' fixed income markets, i.e. demand for fixed income securities has remained strong and long-term interest rates have remained low, as have risk premia. - The ageing of the population has also already contributed to lowering the level of long-term real interest rates. For example, according to a study conducted at the Bank of Finland (Tuomas Saarenheimo: Ageing, market interest rates and financial flows, Bank of Finland Discussion Initiatives 2/2005), ageing would have a negative impact on the international real interest rate level over the next two decades. The prices of long-term bonds therefore appear to be on the rise in the coming decades. The ageing of the population and the increase in the expected retirement period increase the need to save in advance for retirement, while as the population ages, the growth rate of the labour force slows down, which lowers the demand for investment. - The prolonged decline in long-term interest rates, including capital gains, has maintained low interest rate expectations and continued to support bond investments for several years. However, for new bond investments, the low level of interest rates has posed a challenge, at least for the functioning of the insurance sector. In this respect, the yield requirements of old guaranteed income commitments exceed the current long-term interest rates and, in this respect, additional returns must be sought not only from the sovereign loan market, but also from riskier fixed income markets or other securities markets such as the stock market or new investment targets - for example, hedge funds or venture capital (which I will come back to later). The portfolios of most institutional investors are fixed income or bond-oriented, and a rapid rise in long-term interest rates would pose challenges for fixed income portfolio managers. Finland's economy The growth prospects for the Finnish economy have remained relatively good. This year's growth will remain at 1.6% due to contractual disputes in the paper industry (SP forecast), but will accelerate to a growth path of just over 3.5% in 2006. Growth is based on strong domestic demand and exports are supported by favourable developments in the global economy. In addition, Finland's growth is supported by the strong development of the Russian economy. Although the outlook for Finland's near-term economy is quite favourable also from the point of view of investment activities, the future development of our economy nevertheless entails some risks arising from the structures of our economy. The good income development has maintained the purchasing power and optimism of households. Household borrowing has grown rapidly, for example, the growth rate of bank mortgage lending is already well over 16%. A reversal in house prices, coupled with a significant rise in interest rates, could rapidly weaken household consumer demand and weaken the growth of our economy rapidly. The decline in Finland's terms of trade has continued continuously for several years. This is mainly due to the weak development of export prices. Due to the weakening of the terms of trade, the real income of the national economy grows more slowly than GDP at constant prices, which is usually always examined. In this situation, it is therefore legitimate to consider, for example, that the rapid growth in household indebtedness has been based on overly optimistic income expectations. The weakening of the terms of trade may also be reflected in the weakening of the financial balance of the non-financial corporations sector in the future. This, too, would have significant macroeconomic implications (lower employment, public sector tax revenues, etc.). The outlook is challenging from the perspective of both fixed income and equity investors. Will companies' risk ratings take a downward turn, and how will stock prices behave in the next few years? Internationalisation and integration of financial markets The creation of the EU's internal market and the introduction of the single currency radically changed the operating environment of Finnish investors. The main significance of the introduction of the euro was the elimination of past exchange rate risks between euro area countries and, at the same time, the establishment of closer links between euro area financial markets. The elimination of exchange rate risks has particularly benefited kor-suitors and, for example, investment opportunities for earnings-related pension assets expanded from Finland to the entire euro area. With the single monetary policy, the stability of interest rate markets has increased. Financial integration plays a key role in the EU's economic policy. Integration of the financial markets is expected to make a significant contribution to economic growth in the EU. According to studies commissioned by the European Commission, the growth effect of financial market integration is estimated to mean an increase of up to 0.5d00.8% in the annual gdp growth. Such estimates are, of course, subject to a high degree of uncertainty, and such high figures are to be treated with caution. However, it is evident that the integration of financial markets is a significant positive factor for the EU's growth potential. Promoting the integration of the EU's financial markets in such a way as to maximise this growth potential is therefore a key challenge for integration policy. As the previous Commissioner for the Internal Market, Mr Bolkestein, has said, improving the competitiveness of the EU and also of the financial markets has often boiled down to the protection of short-sighted national interests through the activities of public authorities or market standards. Overcoming such barriers will also be one of the key challenges in the future of promoting financial integration. The important role of financial market integration was also reflected in the Lisbon strategy adopted by the Member States in 2000, which is closely linked to the Financial Services Action Plan (FSAP) and the Risk Capital Action Plan (RCAP). The main objective of the action plans was to create a pan-European, single market for financial services. The final report of the Venture Capital Action Plan (RCAP) was published in 2003 and the measures set out in the report have been taken into account in the preparation of some EU directives. The Financial Services Action Plan, the FSAP, has required a considerable amount of legislative work at EU level: it contains more than 40 measures, either recommendations or directives. The projects under the action plan are either completed or are in the process of being completed, but considerable efforts are still needed to complete implementation, including at national legislative level. For example, it is excellent to use the so-called . implementation of the Directive regulating financial market instruments (MiFID, i.e. Markets in Financial Instruments Directi-ve). This is a comprehensive reform of the structure of the securities market, the procedures to be followed in the provision of investment services, the requirements for service providers and investor protection, which requires a number of amendments to the existing financial markets legislation, such as amendments to the Act on the Market in Accounting Securities and the Act on Investment Firms. The Commission has just recently published an FSAP evaluation analysing the financial impact of FSAP. In this context, the Commission is seeking the views of various parties on issues such as the preparation of financial market directives, i.e. both the FSAP process and the Lamfalussy process used in the preparatory work, which, in simple terms, will serve to improve the preparation of legislation at EU level and to work towards regulatory harmonisation. In addition to the authorities, market participants also have the opportunity to present their views on the eu-level law drafting process if they so wish. Nordic integration Financial operators operating in Finland have invested in Nordic cooperation and a marketplace, perhaps even at the expense of euro area integration in the last couple of years. This has contributed to a broad and lively debate both from the point of view of financial market supervision and also from the point of view of Helsinki's position as a marketplace. The most concrete example of the issues raised by the integrating financial markets is Nordea's plan to merge the group's banks and turn them into branches of the Swedish European company. However, due to problems with the EU Deposit Guarantee Scheme Directive, the project is progressing more slowly than originally planned. The transformation of a multinational bank into a European company is a challenge from the point of view of supervising the financial markets, but also from the point of view of maintaining the stability of the financial markets, since in principle it is a Swedish bank supervised by the Swedish supervisory authorities. It may also be increasingly challenging for investors to analyse the activities of multinational financial groups. Another example of the progress of integration that is slightly broader than in the Nordic countries is the mainly Swedish-owned stock exchange OMX AB, which, in addition to the Tukhol, Helsinki and Copenhagen stock exchanges, also includes the Baltic stock exchanges. The Icelandic Stock Exchange is also considering joining the OMX Group. The size of the group has grown and the conditions for the Nordic stock market have basically been created. The next question remains whether the size of the group is sufficient in terms of competition between European stock exchanges. In July, the Helsinki Stock Exchange adopted the international standard industrial classification already used on the other stock exchanges of the NOREX Consortium. After the new industry classifications, the Nordic stock exchange listings will be more comparable than before, and it has been hoped that this will benefit both domestic and international investors. Concerns have been expressed about the decline in visibility among smaller listed companies. Based on brief experience, it can be said that there has been no - at least no significant - reduction in the visibility of small and medium-sized enterprises. The Nordic control group with its uniform industry classifications enables, at least in principle, the creation of a wider market for smaller listed companies as well. Stock exchange integration has progressed rapidly, but post-trade integration has been slower and the field of activity remains fragmented. The Central Securities Depositories of Finland (APK) and Sweden (VPC) have merged, but otherwise the Nordic and Baltic countries still operate separately. In this respect, I believe that the structural arrangements will continue at some stage. Changes in investment activities Changes in real estate investment In our country, real estate investments have traditionally focused on direct real estate investments or real estate companies. Finland has lacked both fund-based and bond-based real estate investments. The legislation on real estate funds has been in force for several years, but the closest thing to that is related to the taxation of funds has meant that none of them have been able to do so. no real estate fund under the law has been created in our country. The Ministry of Finance is about to publish its proposal for amendments to the Real Estate Funds Act. The Ministry of Finance's interim report showed that tax issues related to real estate funds are quite difficult to solve in such a way as to create operating conditions for the funds. From several points of view, it would be desirable for the legislation to be amended so that real estate fund operations could also be launched in Finland. With real estate funds, the liquidity of real estate investments would improve and real estate investments would also be possible with fewer inputs than before. Making adequate legislative changes is therefore primarily a challenge for both legislators and decision-makers. As far as investors are concerned, I would see the start of the real estate fund market as a very positive development. The market for mortgage-backed bonds, on the other hand, seems to be getting off to a better start than real estate funds. Mortgage banks have already issued bonds both domestically and on the international market. The expansion of this market would also be desirable from the point of view of the Central Bank for a number of reasons. The risks of real estate financing would be more widely diversified from the perspective of both financiers and investors. Mortgage-backed bonds would bring more new, low-credit risk investments to the market that have not been available in our market. From the central bank's point of view, mortgage-backed bonds would also be subject to a widening of the material base eligible as collateral for banks' central bank financing. P8a8aomasijoittaminen Over the past few years, capital investments made in Finland have become quite reasonable in terms of volume. Relative to the size of the economy, the investments made in Finland over the past five years clearly exceed the EU average, ahead of the United Kingdom, Sweden and the Netherlands. Although the amount of investments made has remained fairly stable, EUR 350-400 million per year throughout the 2000s, the amount of new capital raised has started to decline. This is likely to be reflected in weakening investment opportunities in new growth companies in the future. Indeed, our venture capital markets are currently in a kind of period of generosity. New capital accumulates slowly and, on the other hand, uninvested capital is quite abundant. Reversing this trend is one of the key challenges facing our private equity markets from a future perspective (Appendix table: Venture capital markets). The sources of funds directed to capital investments are quite diverse in our country and, for example, the share of the banking sector in investments made is clearly lower than in continental Europe. Compared to the Anglo-Saxon countries, the amount of risk capital received by both universities and research institutes in the research and seed phase is low. In recent years, a significant proportion of new venture capital investments made by institutional investors have come from pension institutions or insurance companies. According to the last yearbook of the Finnish Venture Capital Association, about a quarter of the investments made in the past five years have come from the insurance sector and almost the same amount of venture capital has come from employment pension schemes. As far as venture capital is concerned, the problem is probably not so much the lack of funding available, but how the funding is allocated. It is obvious that we have a ti-latte similar to that in the whole of Europe, there is a need for more seed or start-up capital injections. Here is a clear difference between Europe and the United States. Furthermore, in Europe, initial capital investments seem to be directed towards numerous, small investments, which then cannot be managed into productive activities. There is a need for more seed and early-stage venture capitalists. With the increase in wealth, one would hope, for example, that the number of business angels in our country will increase. The number of other players investing in the early stages of risk capital activities should also increase. There are discontinuities in the Finnish venture capital market that weaken the opportunities for new growth companies to develop innovative business and product ideas into a productive and employable business. The chain from innovation to a productive company does not work well enough in Finland. The Ministry of Trade and Industry has done a great deal of creditable work to address the shortcomings. The challenge for decision-makers is to build a better framework for venture capital investment than before in order to increase the supply of capital, especially for early-stage growth companies. In an international comparison of the financing opportunities of growth companies, Finland is not capable of competing. According to the Benchmarking Euro-pean Tax and Legal Environments (May 2004) study conducted by the European Venture Capital Association (EVCA), Finland's ranking among 21 countries was only 17. According to the report, both legislation and taxation have curbed the channelling of private capital into seed and early-stage companies. From Finland's point of view, a weak picture is also given by the fact that although Finland is considered a strong technology country, the targeting of risk capital investments at technology companies is low. However, the results of the survey should be viewed with mild reservations, for example, Sweden, which has one of the busiest venture capital activities in Europe, is only a few notches above Finland. Despite legal and tax obstacles, there is a wide range of activities in Sweden by the standards of our part of the country. In Finland, biotechnology accounted for 1.4%, electronics for 4.6% and Internet technology for 1.6% of last year's private equity investments (Source: Finnish Capital Investment Association, yearbook 2004). A major challenge, especially from the perspective of the future, can be considered how to find early-stage venture capitalists in our country who would also invest in growth companies in the technology sector. The investment of earnings-related pension funds is the subject of lively debate. What, then, could be the role of employment pension schemes in private equity? At the end of September, employment pension schemes' capital investments amounted to close on EUR 1.3 billion. The share of domestic private equity investments in investments was good one-fifth. Thus, the weight of private equity investments seems to be strongly in foreign investments. One of the challenges can be seen as to whether these placements could be directed more widely to the home country. With regard to domestic investments, consideration should also be given to whether the capital investments of employment pension schemes can be directed towards initial or seed-stage capital investments and, if so, in what scale and in what form. After all, it is not clear that the core competence of employment pension schemes supports participation in the evaluation of the operations of growth companies and in the supervision of owners. If this is the case, an attempt should be made to encourage pension providers to use fund-type intermediaries specialised in growth companies in their venture capital activities. Another possibility is that pension companies will ally themselves in their financial projects with other, specialised venture capitalists. The allocation of pension funds to the different stages of the development of venture capital investments is one challenge, another is the question of which sectors should be invested in in order to best increase the activity and dynamism of the economy. In order to achieve good results in the allocation of funds, the flow of information between funders, research institutes and existing growth companies in various ways should be further enhanced. Tyelkevarojen sijoittamisesta kydn vilkasta keskustelua. Mik tyelkelaitosten rooli voisi pomasijoittamisessa sitten olla? Syyskuun lopussa tyelkelaitosten p-omasijoitukset ylsivt vajaaseen 1,3 miljardiin euroon. Kotimaisten pomasijoitusten osuus sijoituksista olivat runsas viidennes. Title: Speech at the announcement of the J.V. Snellman commemorative coin
text: Director-General Erkki Liikanen Announcement of the J.V. Snellman commemorative coin in Kuopio 8.1.2006 Ladies and gentlemen, one can hardly imagine a more apt way to celebrate J.V. Snellman's jubilee than the issuance of a commemorative coin dedicated to him, as Snellman is, after all, in the minds of most Finns, the father of Finland's own currency. In fact, the image of Snellman as a monetary politician is so strong, perhaps thanks to the statue in front of the Bank of Finland, that it may be worth reminding ourselves of other aspects of Snellman's activities. The commemorative coin that has now been announced, designed by sculptor Tapio Kettunen, is, in my opinion, very successful in this respect as well. The commemorative coin does not depict the most familiar Snellman figure, a senator of mature age and a head of finance, but a young Snellman, which takes the thoughts to the beginning of his literary and political activities. Kuopio is the best place to announce a commemorative coin depicting the young Snellman, because he made his most significant contribution as a national revivalist during his term in Kuopio, as the editor of his magazines "Saima" and "Litteraturbladet". In this city, Snellman founded the Finnish political press. Snellman's magazines were not the first newspapers in Finland, but they were ambitious and aware of their own mission in a new way than the previous ones. Journalist Snellman was not content with entertainment and small news, but started a public social debate in Finland. Thanks to him, Kuopio can be considered not only as the birthplace of Finnish journalism, but also as the beginning of what is now called civil society. The Finnish development strategy created by Snellman based on the national education programme, which he propagandised in his magazines, is the most enduring part of his thinking. Snellman was a nationalist, and after the terrible history of Europe in the 1900s, nationalism is rightly in disarray. But Snellman's nationalism is another country. It is not aggressive, but it is based on the premise that it is up to nations, and through them individual people, to make their own unique contribution to the development of all mankind. The national nature of the programme does not mean national selfishness, but the idea that only on a truly own basis can something unique be achieved, not copied, but something new to contribute to the development of humanity. There is much in Snellman's opinions that we reject today as outdated and downright reactionary. His insistence on the homogeneity of national culture fits poorly with the multicultural reality of modern open society. We cannot accept Snellman's views on, for example, the emancipation of women or her scepticism about democracy and parliamentarianism. But the idea that a nation's strength and success stems from its civilisation and ability to offer something new for the use of all mankind is, as a vision, staggering and far more modern than other economic policy or state programs of his time. It also shows how patriotism and internationalism can be reconciled. Snellman's vision was extremely idealistic, but at the same time it was full of realpolitik. The development of Finland over the past 150 years has also proven to hold that vision in practice. Today's Finland's reputation as a producer of cutting-edge technology or a leading country in PISA studies is based on the fruits of Snellman's educational programme. It is precisely by adhering to this strategy that Finland has risen from a cobbled european backwater to a level where it is capable of equal commercial, cultural and political interaction with any other country. It is also Snellmanism that the nation's political goal is set in just that way. But let's return to Snellman and the Finnish markka. It may seem paradoxical to celebrate Snellman, mark's father, at a time when the mark has just recently been abandoned. It is not so straightforward, however, and on closer inspection you will see that the monetary reform of 1865, for which Mr Snellman is praised, was in fact a measure along the same lines as Finland's entry into the euro area in 1999. This idea of the parallelism between the use of the markka and the abandonment of it is probably so surprising that it is worth explaining it a little more closely here. The chain of events that led to the creation of the silver mark and the de facto detachment of Finland from the Russian monetary system did not start from any separatist motives, but were motivated by economic reasons. It was a question of stabilizing the value of money and strengthening Finland's commercial links with Europe. Before the Crimean (or Ooland) War, roubles were used as money in Finland, and the country was on a silver standard together with Russia. In Finland, the coins consisted of silver banknotes issued by the Bank of Finland and Russian silver coins. In addition, Russian banknote rubles were also legal tender, so the Bank of Finland had to redeem them with silver on demand. The outbreak of war in 1854 triggered a monetary crisis in Russia and My Finland, as a result of which the exchangeability of the ruble for silver had to be abolished. The detachment of the ruble from silver caused a whole range of difficulties. When the value of money was no longer tied to silver, it quickly began to decline. There was a shortage of change because the silver coin disappeared from the general circulation into the coffers of speculators. Perhaps the worst thing was that exchange rates in relation to traditional trading partners in Sweden and northern Germany began to fluctuate. This made it difficult to trade and use foreign credit. In response to the finns' catches to resolve the monetary question, in 1860 the emperor sold Finland his own monetary unit, the markka, which, however, was defined in relation to the banknote ruble, as its quarter. When the ruble of banknotes still remained legal tender, this reform did not yet bring a solution to the main problem, namely the question of how to return to the silver standard. When Snellman became head of finance in 1863, the markka already existed, but Snellman saw the restoration of the silver stock as his most important task. For this, a sufficient silver reserve was needed for the Bank of Finland and, in addition, Russia's consent to the fact that the status of the ruble as legal tender in Finland would cease. Snellman traveled to St. Petersburg to negotiate with the Russian side on the matter. The result of the trip was the emperor's consent that the mark could be redefined, not as a quarter of the ruble in general, but specifically of the silver ruble. This is Snellman's main achievement in the history of the Finnish markka. The Imperial Manifesto, which stipulated that domestic and Russian silver coins would henceforth become the only legal means of payment in Finland, was published on November 12, 1865. It is said that Snellman had to tip the barnkeeper to prevent the declaration from leaking to the public before the deadline, but despite this, the Board of Directors of the Union Bank was alerted to the matter and informed the bank's branches in advance by telegram. After the manifesto, the obstacles to returning to the silver standard were removed and the Bank of Finland began to redeem its banknotes with new silver marks at the beginning of March 1866. At the same time, the value of the markka stabilised in relation to other silver-bearing countries, such as Sweden and Germany, which were therefore our most important western trading partners already at that time. It is interesting in what way the exchange rate stabilized in relation to the French franc: since the silver value of the franc, 4 1/2 grams of silver, coincidentally was exactly the same as that of the mark, the exchange rate of the franc relative to the mark became exactly 1:1, which, except for minimal fluctuations, remained in force for decades, until 1914. In connection with Snellman's monetary policy activities, it is worth mentioning another landmark event concerning the Bank of Finland. Snellman was the person who handed over from the bank of Finland's board of directors "to the administration of the Riksdag and to answer", as it was then called. As head of finance, Snellman had been the head of the board of directors of the Bank of Finland, even though the estates had already wanted to take over the bank in 1862 and had elected four bank delegates to supervise the bank. Snellman was sceptical about handing over the bank because he feared that their actions could jeopardise the return to the silver standard. Snellman managed to postpone the matter until the next Diet, where the matter was finally decided. According to the first account of the banking delegates, on January 7, 1868, "Senator Snellman, on behalf of the Imperial Senate, left to the Estates the original and mortgage funds under the name Bank of Finland and with the purpose of the previously enacted Gracious Decree". By the way, after the economic crises of the mid-1860s, the bank was not at all in good shape at the time. More than half of its assets, about 12 million marks, were caught in bankruptcies or under foreclosure. From those years, however, Finland's economic boom began, as a result of which GDP by the First World War quadrupled. The development was possible because Finland at the same time opened up to international trade and economic power, and the international unity of the monetary system strongly supported this development. Markka's origin story shows that getting finland its own money was a way to be involved in the world, not separatism. Later, in the light of the events of 1917, it has begun to be seen as the first step in Finland's detachment from Russia, even though it was at one time more of a means of connecting to the West. Of course, the development of its own national institutions, such as money, was part of Finland's maturation into state independence, but it is worth remembering that even in the 1800s, when the world was living first under the conditions of a silver standard and then a gold standard, an independent national monetary policy, separate from other countries, was by no means one of the hallmarks of an independent state. On the contrary, the ideal was participation in a global monetary system based on a common measure of value, gold or silver. The history of money and the history of my Bank of Finland are extremely fascinating topics, which, by the way, are currently being studied in a special history project of the Bank of Finland. The task of this project is to write a comprehensive overview of the bank's history for publication on the bank's 200th anniversary in 2011. Surely Snellman's monetary policy, which has been praised in previous literature for being remote and criticized as unnecessarily harsh, will also shed new light on this project. It is customary to say that every generation must rewrite history. Today's Finns will probably be particularly interested in looking at Finland's monetary history in its international context. Now Finland is a member of the European Monetary Union and it is often said that Finland no longer has its own monetary policy. Should Finns even be interested in monetary policy anymore, or is it worth studying it in Finland? The answer to these arguments and doubts is that Finland has its own monetary policy, which is the single monetary policy of the euro area. The Bank of Finland participates in its formulation as one of the full members of the Eurosystem, and it can be said that the Finns now have more influence on the monetary economy of our continent than ever before through monetary union. But this influence is "Snellman's" in nature: it exists only to the extent that we are able to contribute new elements to the making of the single monetary policy, not copied from others, but genuine original from the inside. This is a challenge for the Bank of Finland, but it is also a challenge for Finnish economic research and financial journalism, because Finns have just as good a reason to engage in monetary debate and research as, for example, Germans or French. Meeting this challenge is a prerequisite for us to be in the position of the citizen, not the object of power, in European monetary policy. Snellman's analysis of national strategy is unmissable on this issue as well. This year marks the 200th anniversary of the birth of J.V. Snellman, dozens, even hundreds of Snellman-themed events will be held in Finland. It is to be hoped that the jubilee year will not be used only to commemorate or glorify a great man placed on top of the nation's closet. Snellman's jubilee year also provides a good opportunity to discuss such topical issues as the role of the nation state in an integrating world, the importance of social cohesion in a Finland that is becoming multicultural, the future of the Finnish language as a tool for the highest level of teaching and research, and also economic policy, which Snellman also dabbled a lot in. Hopefully, the issuance of this commemorative coin will serve as a stimulus for such a debate and thus contribute to the success of the jubilee year.
text_original: Pjohtaja Erkki Liikanen J.V. Snellman -juhlarahan julkistamistilaisuus Kuopiossa 8.1.2006 Hyvt kuulijat, voi tuskin kuvitella osuvampaa tapaa juhlistaa J.V. Snellmanin juhlavuotta kuin hnelle omistetun juhlarahan liikkeeseen lasku, sill onhan Snellman useimpien suomalaisten mieless juuri Suomen oman rahan is. Kuva Snellmanista rahapoliitikkona on itse asiassa niin vahva, ehk Suomen Pankin edess olevan patsaan ansiosta, ett voi olla syyt erityisesti muistuttaa Snellmanin toiminnan muistakin puolista. Nyt julkistettu juhlaraha, jonka on suunnitellut kuvanveistj Tapio Kettunen, on tsskin mieless mielestni hyvin onnistunut. Juhlarahaan ei nimittin ole kuvattu kaikkein tutuinta Snellman-hahmoa, kypsn ikn ehtinytt senaattoria ja valtiovarainpllikk, vaan nuori Snellman, mik vie ajatukset hnen kirjallisen ja poliittisen toimintansa alkupuolelle. Kuopio on paras paikka julkistaa nuorta Snellmania kuvaava juhlaraha, koska merkittvimmn panoksensa kansallisena herttjn hn teki juuri Kuopion kaudellaan, lehtiens "Saiman" ja "Litteraturbladetin" toimittajana. Tss kaupungissa Snellman perusti suomalaisen poliittisen lehdist. Snellmanin lehdet eivt olleet Suomen ensimmisi sanomalehti, mutta ne olivat uudella tavalla kunnianhimoisia ja omasta tehtvstn tietoisia kuin aiemmat. Lehtimies Snellman ei tyytynyt ajanvietteeseen ja pikku-uutisiin, vaan aloitti julkisen yhteiskunnallisen keskustelun Suomessa. Hnen ansiostaan Kuopiota voidaan pit paitsi suomalaisen journalismin syntypaikkana, my sellaisen yhteiskunnallisen osallistumisen alkukotina, mit nykyn sanotaan kansalaisyhteiskunnaksi. Snellmanin luoma kansalliseen sivistysohjelmaan perustuva suomalainen kehitysstrategia, jota hn lehdissn propagoi, on hnen ajattelunsa kestvint sislt. Snellman oli nationalisti, ja nationalismi on Euroopan 1900-luvun kauhean historian jljilt syystkin huonossa huudossa. Mutta Snellmanin nationalismi onkin toista maata. Se ei ole aggressiivista, vaan se lhtee siit, ett kansakuntien ja niiden kautta yksittisten ihmisten tehtvn on antaa oma ainoalaatuinen kehityspanoksensa koko ihmiskunnan kehityksen hyvksi. Ohjelman kansallinen luonne ei tarkoita kansallista itsekkyytt, vaan ajatusta, ett vain aidosti omalta pohjalta voidaan saada aikaan jotakin ainoalaatuista, ei kopioitua, vaan jotakin uutta annettavaa ihmiskunnan kehitykseen. Snellmanin mielipiteiss on paljon sellaista, mink tnn hylkmme aikansa elneen ja suorastaan taantumuksellisenakin. Hnen vaatimuksensa kansallisen kulttuurin homogeenisuudesta sopii huonosti nykyajan avoimen yhteiskunnan monikulttuuriseen todellisuuteen. Emme voi myskn hyvksy Snellmanin ksityksi esimerkiksi naisten emansipaatiosta tai hnen epilev suhtautumistaan demokratiaan ja parlamentarismiin. Mutta ajatus, ett kansakunnan voima ja menestys johtuvat sen sivistyksest ja kyvyst tarjota jotakin uutta koko ihmiskunnan kyttn on visiona huikea ja paljon modernimpi kuin hnen aikansa muut talouspoliittiset tai valtiolliset ohjelmat. Se mys nytt, miten isnmaallisuus ja kansainvlistyminen ovat yhteen sovitettavissa. Snellmanin visio oli rimmisen idealistinen, mutta se oli samalla tytt reaalipolitiikkaa. Suomen kehitys viimeisten 150 vuoden aikana on my osoittanut tuon vision kytnnss pitvksi. Nykyisen Suomen maine huipputeknologian tuottajana tai PISA -tutkimusten krkimaana perustuu snellmanilaisen sivistysohjelman hedelmille. Juuri sit strategiaa noudattamalla Suomi on noussut kyhst Euroopan takapajulasta tasolle, jolla se pystyy tasavertaiseen kaupalliseen, kulttuuriseen ja poliittiseen vuorovaikutukseen mink tahansa muun maan kanssa. Snellmanilaisuutta on sekin, ett kansakunnan poliittinen tavoite asetetaan juuri tuolla tavoin. Mutta palataan Snellmaniin ja Suomen markkaan. Voi tuntua paradoksaaliselta juhlia Snellmania, markan is, aikana, jolloin markasta on juuri vain vhn aikaa sitten luovuttu. Asia ei ole kuitenkaan nin yksioikoinen, ja asiaa lhemmin tarkastellen huomaa, ett vuoden 1865 rahauudistus, josta Snellmania kiitetn, oli itse asiassa tavoitteiltaan samansuuntainen toimenpide kuin Suomen liittyminen euroalueeseen vuonna 1999. Tm ajatus markan kyttnoton ja siit luopumisen samansuuntaisuudesta on varmaan sen verran yllttv, ett sit kannattaa tss selostaa vhn tarkemmin. Tapahtumaketju, joka johti hopeamarkan syntyyn ja Suomen tosiasialliseen irtoamiseen Venjn rahajrjestelmst, ei lhtenyt liikkeelle mistn separatistisista vaikuttimista, vaan taustalla olivat kytnnn taloudelliset syyt. Kysymys oli rahan arvon vakauttamisesta ja Suomen kaupallisten yhteyksien vahvistamisesta Eurooppaan. Ennen Krimin (tai Oolannin) sotaa Suomessa olivat rahana ruplat ja maa oli hopeakannassa yhdess Venjn kanssa. Suomessa rahana olivat Suomen Pankin liikkeeseen laskemat hopeaan vaihdettavat setelit ja venlinen hopearaha. Lisksi mys venliset seteliruplat olivat laillisia maksuvlineit, joten Suomen Pankin piti lunastaa niitkin hopealla vaadittaessa. Sodan syttyminen vuonna 1854 kynnisti Venjll ja my Suomessa rahakriisin, jonka tuloksena ruplan vaihdettavuus hopeaan jouduttiin lakkauttamaan. Ruplan irtoaminen hopeasta aiheutti monenlaisia vaikeuksia. Kun rahan arvo ei en ollut sidottu hopeaan, se alkoi nopeasti heiket. Vaihtorahasta tuli puutetta, koska hopearaha hvisi yleisest liikkeest keinottelijoiden kirstuihin. Ehk pahinta oli, ett valuuttakurssit suhteessa perinteisiin kauppakumppaneihin Ruotsissa ja Pohjois-Saksassa alkoivat vaihdella. Tm vaikeutti kauppaa ja ulkomaisen luoton kytt. Vastauksena suomalaisten tekemiin pyyntihin rahakysymyksen ratkaisemiseksi keisari mysi vuonna 1860 Suomelle oman rahayksik, markan, joka kuitenkin oli mritelty suhteessa seteliruplaan, sen neljsosaksi. Kun setelirupla viel ji lailliseksi maksuvlineeksi, ei tm uudistus viel tuonut ratkaisua pongelmaan, eli kysymykseen, miten voitaisiin palata hopeakantaan. Kun Snellman tuli valtiovarainplliksi vuonna 1863, markka oli jo olemassa, mutta Snellman nki hopeakannan palauttamisen trkeimmksi tehtvkseen. Tt varten tarvittiin Suomen Pankille riittv hopeavaranto ja lisksi Venjn suostumus siihen, ett ruplan asema laillisena maksuvlineen Suomessa lakkaisi. Snellman matkusti Pietariin neuvottelemaan venlisen osapuolen kanssa asiasta. Matkan tuloksena oli keisarin suostumus sille, ett markka voitiin mritell uudelleen, ei yleisesti ruplan, vaan nimenomaan hopearuplan neljsosaksi. Tm on Snellmanin pasiallinen saavutus Suomen markan historiassa. Keisarillinen manifesti, jossa mrttiin, ett kotimainen ja venlinen hopearaha tulisivat tst lhtien ainoiksi laillisiksi maksuvlineiksi Suomessa, julkaistiin marraskuun 12. pivn 1865. Kerrotaan, ett Snellman joutui antamaan latojalle juomarahaa, jotta julistus ei vuotaisi julkisuuteen ennen mraikaa, mutta siit huolimatta Yhdyspankin johtokunta sai asiasta vihi ja tiedotti siit shkeell pankin sivukonttoreille etukteen. Manifestin my esteet hopeakantaan palaamiselta poistuivat ja Suomen Pankki alkoi lunastaa seteleitn uusilla hopeamarkoilla maaliskuun alussa 1866. Samalla markan arvo vakiintui suhteessa muihin hopeakantamaihin, kuten Ruotsiin ja Saksaan, jotka siis olivat trkeimpi lntisi kauppakumppaneitamme jo tuolloin. Mielenkiintoista on, mill tavalla kurssi vakiintui suhteessa Ranskan frangiin: koska frangin hopea-arvo, 4  grammaa hopeaa, oli sattumalta aivan sama kuin markankin, frangin valuuttakurssiksi suhteessa markkaan tuli tasan 1:1, mik pysyi minimaalisia vaihteluita lukuun ottamatta voimassa vuosikymmeni, aina vuoteen 1914 saakka. Snellmanin rahapoliittisen toiminnan yhteydess kannattaa mainita toinenkin Suomen Pankkia koskeva merkkitapahtuma. Snellman oli nimittin se henkil joka luovutti Suomen Pankin hallituksen alaisuudesta "valtiopivin hallintoon ja vastattavaksi" niin kuin silloin sanottiin. Snellman oli valtiovarainpllikkn ollut my Suomen Pankin johtokunnan esimies, vaikka sdyt olivat jo vuonna 1862 halunneet ottaa pankin haltuunsa ja valinneet nelj pankkivaltuusmiest pankkia valvomaan. Snellman suhtautui epluuloisesti pankin luovuttamiseen, koska pelksi pankkivaltuusmiesten voivan toiminnallaan vaarantaa hopeakannalle paluun. Snellman onnistuikin lykkmn asian seuraaville valtiopiville, jossa asiasta vihdoin ptettiin. Pankkivaltuusmiesten ensimmisen kertomuksen mukaan, tammikuun 7. pivn 1868 "Senaattori Snellman, Keisarillisen Senaatin puolesta, jtti Styjen haltuun alkuperisen ja hypoteekki-rahastot nimell Suomen Pankki ja sill tarkoituksella kuin ennen mainittu Armollinen Asetus sti". Pankki ei muuten tuohon aikaan ollut 1860-luvun puolivlin talouskriisien jljilt ollenkaan hyvss kunnossa. Yli puolet sen varoista, noin 12 miljoonasta markasta, oli kiinni konkursseissa tai ulosoton alaisena. Noista vuosista kuitenkin alkoi Suomen taloudellinen nousu, jonka tuloksena BKT ensimmiseen maailmansotaan menness perti nelinkertaistui. Kehitys oli mahdollista, koska Suomi samalla avautui kansainvliselle kaupalle ja taloudelliselle tyjaolle, ja rahajrjestelmn kansainvlinen yhtenisyys oli tt kehityst osaltaan vahvasti tukemassa. Markan syntytarina osoittaa, ett oman rahan hankkiminen Suomelle oli keino olla mukana maailmassa, ei separatismia. Myemmin se on alettu nhd vuoden 1917 tapahtumien valossa ensi askeleena Suomen irtoamisessa Venjst, vaikka se aikanaan oli enemmn keino kytkeyty lnteen. Totta kai omien kansallisten instituutioiden, kuten rahan, kehittyminen oli osa Suomen kypsymist valtiolliseen itsenisyyteen, mutta kannattaa kuitenkin muistaa, ett viel 1800-luvulla, kun maailmassa elettiin ensin hopeakannan ja sitten kultakannan oloissa, ei itseninen, muista maista erillinen kansallinen rahapolitiikka missn tapauksessa kuulunut itsenisen valtion tunnusmerkkeihin. Pinvastoin, ihanteena oli osallisuus globaalissa rahajrjestelmss, joka perustui yhteiseen arvonmittaan, kultaan tai hopeaan. Rahahistoria ja my Suomen Pankin historia ovat rimmisen kiehtovia aiheita, joita muuten parhaillaan tutkitaan erityisess Suomen Pankin historiaprojektissa. Tmn projektin tehtvn on kirjoittaa kattava yleisesitys pankin historiasta julkaistavaksi pankin 200vuotispivn vuonna 2011. Varmasti Snellmanin rahapolitiikka, jota aikaisemmassa kirjallisuudessa on sek kiitelty kaukonkisyydest ett kritisoitu tarpeettoman ankaraksi, saa mys uutta valaistusta tmn projektin myt. Tapana on sanoa, ett jokaisen sukupolven on kirjoitettava historia uudelleen. Tmn pivn suomalaisia kiinnostaa varmaan erityisesti tarkastella Suomen rahahistoriaa sen kansainvlisiss yhteyksiss. Nyt Suomi on Euroopan rahaliiton jsen ja kuulee usein sanottavan, ettei Suomella ole en omaa rahapolitiikkaa. Kannattaneeko suomalaisten en olla edes kiinnostuneita rahapolitiikasta, tai kannattaako sit Suomessa tutkia? Nihin vitteisiin ja epilyihin voi vastata, ett Suomella on oma rahapolitiikka, joka on euroalueen yhteinen rahapolitiikka. Suomen Pankki osallistuu sen muotoiluun yhten eurojrjestelmn tysivaltaisena jsenen, ja voi sanoa, ett suomalaisilla on rahaliiton kautta nykyn enemmn vaikutusvaltaa maanosamme rahatalouteen kuin koskaan aikaisemmin. Mutta tm vaikutusvalta on "snellmanilaista" luonteeltaan: sit on vain siin mrin, kun pystymme kontribuoimaan yhteisen rahapolitiikan tekoon uusia aineksia, ei muilta kopioitua, vaan aitoa omaperist sislt. Tm on haaste Suomen Pankille, mutta se on my haaste suomalaiselle taloustutkimukselle ja talousjournalismille, koska suomalaisilla on aivan yht hyv syy harjoittaa rahapoliittista keskustelua ja tutkimusta kuin vaikkapa saksalaisilla tai ranskalaisillakin. Thn haasteeseen vastaaminen on ehtona sille, ett olemme Euroopan rahapolitiikassa kansalaisen, emme vallankytn kohteen asemassa. Snellmanin analyysi kansallisesta strategiasta on ohittamaton tsskin kysymyksess. Kun tn vuonna tulee kuluneeksi 200 vuotta J.V. Snellmanin syntymst, Suomessa jrjestetn kymmeni, jopa satoja Snellman-aiheisia tapahtumia. On syyt toivoa, ett juhlavuotta ei kytet vain kansakunnan kaapin plle asetetun suurmiehen muisteluun tai ylistmiseen. Snellmanin juhlavuosi antaa my hyvn mahdollisuuden kyd keskustelua sellaisista ajankohtaisista kysymyksist kuin kansallisvaltion roolista integroituvassa maailmassa, sosiaalisen yhteenkuuluvuuden merkityksest monikulttuuriseksi muuttuvassa Suomessa, Suomen kielen tulevaisuudesta korkeimman opetuksen ja tutkimuksen vlineen, ja talouspolitiikastakin, jota Snellman mys paljon harrasti. Toivottavasti tmn juhlarahan liikkeeseen lasku omalta osaltaan toimisi virikkeen tllaiseen keskusteluun ja nin myvaikuttaisi juhlavuoden onnistumiseen.

Title: Finland - and Her Economy - in the Euro Area
text: Pentti Hakkarainen, Member of the Board, Bank of Finland Finnish-American Business Council of the Greater Washington Area Speech at the Coctail Buffet at the Embassy of Finland, Washington D.C. on Tuesday, 10 January 2006 Finland  and Her Economy  in the Euro Area It is a great pleasure to give this presentation to you today. The topic is very current since there are discussions in Europe on how different members of the Eurosystem have carried out their economic policies. I would like to put before you some of the impacts, benefits and perhaps some restrictions Finland faced and still faces, due to membership of the EMU, the Economic and Monetary Union. The membership for its part has shaped the environment and formed conditions for all agents of the economy. It is important to point out that when Finland joined the euro, the country had just recovered from a very severe economic and financial crisis. This means that the effects of our membership are intrinsically mixed with the effects of the crisis, such as the significant depreciation of the currency, a sudden increase in government debt, a rise in the number of mergers and acquisitions as well as privatisations in both banking and industry. The Finnish experience in the early 1990s stood out from similar experiences of its neighbouring Nordic countries; not least because of the coinciding sudden collapse of the Soviet Union and its export markets which strongly intensified the crisis. During a period of only a few years, our GDP decreased by an unprecedented 10% and the unemployment rate increased from below 4% close to a staggering 18%. While another factor  and one that makes it difficult to isolate the positive effects of the EMU  is the remarkable impact of the so-called new economy. From late 1990s onwards Finland's economic performance has been dominated by the exceptional growth of our high tech industry, led by the success of Nokia. The information and communications sector as a whole contributed to so strong a boom that the effects of the new monetary regime are hard to distinguish from the technology- related changes in the economy. Now we have to ask how Finland and her economy have done during the time of EMU membership. That can be assessed logically through firstly highlighting some of the deliberation that went on behind the decision to enter the EMU. One should bear in mind that the effects of the EMU started to materialise even before formal entry. It is crucial to extend our observations to also cover several years before the point of time of official membership acceptance. Then we can look at some relevant macroeconomic indicators. Private individuals form a very important group of agents in all economies and it is worth studying how households and private individuals have perceived the common currency. Finally we can draw conclusions. Deliberations around the EU/EMU Political motives played an important role when the decision to join the monetary union was made. It was seen as means of being part of the inner circle of the European Union and enhancing the country's influence in future European development. In all respects, economic considerations were also crucial. Finnish monetary policy had traditionally suffered from a lack of credibility where devaluation was repeatedly used as a means of restoring competitiveness and was directly reflected in interest rates. Critics blamed this for many of the country's structural problems, such as large investment rates relative to growth and chronic weakness of the current account. It was anticipated that monetary policy would be strengthened, that interest rates would be lower and more stable if the country were to join the monetary union. This should in turn enhance investment and economic growth. Biggest benefits were expected in the form of better credibility of monetary policy which would in turn result in lower interest rates and thus enhancing economic growth. It was also seen that an external lever was needed to create the right mindset, in order to have moderate wage increases, a reduction of costs and an improvement in the country's competitiveness in a bigger global market. However, there were also some concerns expressed regarding losing our current independent monetary policy and the possibility of devaluating our currency in case of unforeseen economic adverse shocks. Generally speaking when there are shocks affecting different countries differently, i.e. so called asymmetric shocks, each country can use its monetary policy or exchange rate movements to adjust accordingly. It should be pointed out that most of the studies made before the EMU showed that Finland's economic structure deviated clearly from the rest of the EU. Therefore the expected difficulty of adjusting to asymmetric economic shocks without national money was considered to be one of the main objections to Finland's membership. In addition to the potential threat in the form of asymmetric shock, inflexibility of labour markets and whether the country's public finances were strong enough and possessed sufficient buffers to adjust to a difficult economic cycles were also mentioned. Balancing positive expectations with some negative expectations was highlighted in quite heated and not in all cases very rational debates. Also issues such as the loss of our symbol of independence, our own currency, were taken up. There was undeniably a lot of tension in the discussions of that time. Finland and Sweden have about the same structures in their economies, especially when you compare a breakdown of their exports by countries and products. It is interesting to analyse reasons for the opposite conclusions of the monetary union. Different decisions concerning membership were due to a major difference in approach. In Sweden it was thought that first one should improve the economic position and then contemplate entry into the EMU, only when everything is strong enough. In Finland, economists shared the same worries as in Sweden; however there was the assumption of a more flexible labour market and potentially more responsive fiscal policy in Finland than in Sweden. Also it was seen that membership, as such, forces changes in public policy and private sector behaviour and thus would take care of critical success factors inside the monetary union. Economic environment Looking at GDP growth since the mid 1990s, one can see that the growth expectations have already materialised, to quite a large extent. Finnish economic development has clearly exceeded the average of the other Eurosystem members. This is partly due to a powerful but favourable asymmetric shock in the form of an IT boom. The boom was much stronger in Finland than in other euro area countries, on average. In Sweden there was a similar shock and its overall economic development has been equally strong. What is noteworthy is the fact that even with strong growth the Finnish currency could not appreciate - because of its commitment under the ERM  whereas a clear strengthening of the Finnish markka would have been likely, if Finland still had the free hands of its own monetary policy. The expectation of better credibility of the monetary policy has materialised. Both long-term and short-term interest rates have not only been at a lower level than previously but also been more stable. There have not been fluctuations despite the write-downs in the ICT sector and difficulties of the neighbouring Russian economy, and shocks such as corporate scandals in the international financial markets. Not only interest rate levels have lowered but also risk spreads have narrowed. Finland used to pay risk premium in the form of higher interest rates on its debts compared with government debts of more credit worthy countries. As public finances in Finland have been balanced, we have seen a narrowing of spread e.g. over the ten year German bond rate. Observations on competitiveness A country's competitiveness can be measured by the real effective currency value. That is not the only measurement which is valid. There are different assessments of a country's competitiveness, striving towards a comprehensive observation, and including several other criteria than just economic ones. When comparing the competitiveness of various countries, the best known institutions are the Swiss business management institute IMD and the World Economic Forum (WEF). According to the IMD's competitiveness comparisons Finland ranks in 6th place. And the first place is given to the United States of America. And WEF ranks Finland as the first, with the USA being the second. Both institutes measure, in principle, the same thing i.e. the country's real and structural competitiveness and the state of its economy. Because of different criteria the results are also not entirely comparable. One could note that if in the comparisons all so-called soft criteria were to be left out and the assessment is only economic, the position of Finland would drop substantially. According to the IMD report, the main weaknesses Finland has, in the comparison, are among other things the high wage costs of industrial production, a heavy overall tax burden and slow growth of the work force. Also the welfare system as a whole does not currently provide adequate incentives to search for employment. Unemployment Unemployment is perhaps the worst problem in the Finnish economy. During severe economic crises in the early 1990s unemployment rocketed to unprecedented levels. Despite quite rapid economic growth in the recent years, it seems that unemployment remains stuck at quite a high level, indicating a mismatch between those who are seeking for a job and the number of vacancies. Productivity In the Finnish economy we have seen very rapid productivity increases in several sectors. The highest increase has been seen in banking services and telecom sector. As an illustration one could note that the outcome of the recovery of the banking crises in the early 1990s led to a radical reduction of the number of bank branches and a rapid increase in the use of state-of-the-art technology. Over a period of five years the work force in the banking sector decreased by more than half. Today roughly 90% of all banking transactions are made electronically. In corporate banking services this development has been even stronger, showing that 99.9% of corporate banking transactions are made in electronic form. Openness of businesses Without doubt one essential development has been the increasing level of openness in the economy. This has taken place at several levels as the share of exports in the country's GDP has increased. But the change has also been substantial in the financial markets through use of euro which is recognised globally. Exports have increased steadily since 1990. The breakdown by countries which are the main trading partners of Finnish exports have remained close to the proportion they were 15 years ago. This breakdown illustrates well how dispersed the Finnish export business is and how, for its part, it is contributing to better economic growth than on average in the EU. Finland and her economy benefited from fast growing economies outside the European Union. During the period we have also seen the emergence of Finnish multinational companies on an unprecedented scale. This development was led by Nokia, the mobile phone manufacturer, but there has been also strong internationalisation of more traditional companies. Much of the internationalisation and expanded activities abroad has been done in the form of acquisitions and takeovers. More international financial markets Since 1990 capital markets have internationalised as well. This development can not be directly related to EMU membership. However disappearing currency risks have facilitated both investments to Finland and Finnish investments abroad. Pension funds and companies in particular have been active in diversifying their portfolios and investing abroad. The internationalisation of the capital market has also been seen in the foreign ownership of the Finnish shares. In the Helsinki Stock Exchange the foreign ownership peaked at over 70% of the market capitalisation of the stock exchange at the beginning of 2000. Foreign ownership is still today over 50% and Helsinki Stock Exchange is one of the most international stock exchanges in the world. This, for its part, has been contributing to the possibilities for raising equity capital. It is very difficult to distinguish unambiguous and concrete impacts of EMU membership in the stock market. Nonetheless it is obvious that the common currency has facilitated equity offerings for Finnish companies. All in all a huge change has taken place in capital markets, in the debt market in particular. In international markets the euro has overtaken the US dollar as the most used currency of bond issues. Partly that may be due to the fact that the European actors have been more active in launching bonds than US issuers in the last three years. Among all European issuers, perhaps naturally, the euro has been clearly favoured and by far more than other currencies. Trends in the international market have also been reflected in Nordic issuance. The euro has been by far the most important currency in bond issues by Nordic issuers as well. This is noteworthy since only Finland is a member of the euro area and Swedish issuers rely on the common currency euro in the bond markets. Financial management There are also some effects at the company level that can be studied by looking at the concrete implications of the common currency in financial management through specific company example. Otherwise it is very difficult to see what benefits or disadvantages the euro has brought with it for running businesses. As an example, and a case study, we can take a Finnish industrial company which has activities in more than 30 countries around the world. Roughly 90% of its EUR 7 billion turnover is generated outside Finland. This means that it has substantial flows of currencies in and out. Perhaps a word of caution is necessary however. The case study shows only a specific impact on the company, and may not be applicable to all enterprises and may therefore be wise not to generalise too much. In the long term financing an increasing number of companies in Finland have been gaining from broader bond and loan markets. Not only bond issuance but also other borrowings in the form of syndicated loans as well as normal bank loans are done in international financial markets. Number of lenders has increased due to the common currency. This means that companies such as this case study company have had more financing sources at their disposal. As an important fact facilitating debt raising is of course the fact that now Finnish companies can use their own currency. The euro has a very liquid market and is widely used in global international financing. In Europe we have seen an increase and improvement of the medium-term note market which is in use for Finnish companies as well. All companies having a decent rating have been able to tap the MTN market which is deep and liquid to cover medium term financial needs. Companies also seem to have benefited in the area of cash management. Now it is possible to integrate electronic banking services with accounting and main client ledger systems together using a single currency. In the case study, one person can take care of European wide cash management systems. All banking transactions are made in electronic form, which generates automatically entries into the company's accounting system. Management of financial risks In the area of risk management the common currency makes market conditions more stable. In particular interest rate risk management is easier today than before, since more predictable and more stable interest rates help to hold bigger open interest rate risk exposures. One could even argue in these more stable times, that interest rate risk exposure as a concept has diminished. The case study company can have most of its loans on a floating rate basis and needs not to match all maturities of its assets and liabilities, as in the era of more fluctuating interest rate. Another area of financial risk management where companies can reach substantial savings, is foreign exchange management. This is due to the fact that when both in and outflows are more often in euros, i.e. the accounting base currency, the natural currency risk exposure, and the need to hedge this, is clearly smaller than in the case of having bigger revenues and costs in several currencies. In the case study the need to make foreign exchange deals has decreased almost by 40% based on the common currency. Additional savings in foreign exchange management can be reached through narrower spreads i.e. more competitive prices between different currencies, when the other one of the currency pairing is the very liquid euro instead of the Finnish markka, as was the case earlier. Through both the diminished currency exposure and very narrow spreads, annual costs on FX dealing have gone down from EUR 4.4 million, to EUR 1 million. Private individuals Let me then turn to private individuals and the household sector. Again it is difficult to distinguish the impacts of the euro as such on the behaviour of households. However based on more stable interest rates, which have dropped to very low levels, it is obvious that households are willing to raise loans for both housing and other purposes. A remarkable increase has been seen in household indebtedness since the late 1990s, when the amount of household debt in Finland increased from the EUR 30 billion level up to about EUR 70 billion. Despite the rise in absolute terms, household borrowing is still relatively low in relation to GDP, compared with most European countries. After the very gloomy period of low private consumption at the beginning of the 1990s, consumer demand has risen to quite a stable level and has now maintained a growth rate of 2% annually. Bearing in mind our continuing high levels of unemployment this remarkable development may be seen as unconventional. In Finland consumer confidence has also been clearly stronger than in most EU countries. Confidence was not eroded by either Asian crises, difficulties in the Russian economy, or the bursting of the IT bubble. The man in the street in Finland sees the euro as being beneficial to the country. According to the latest Euro barometers assessing how people in different countries perceive the euro and its advantages, Finland ranked as one of the most satisfied euro countries. More than two thirds of all individuals perceive the euro as a good thing. Conclusions and future challenges It may still be too early days to say to what extent if any, membership of the EMU has benefited Finland and her economy. Positive development and success regarding the economy itself and enterprises in it are obvious; however one has to point out that the effects of the membership, as such, are intrinsically mixed with the effects of other measures taken to recover from the crises of the 1990s. Having seen the economic development in Finland today, it is even more difficult to argue that Finland would have had to stay outside the EMU. It could be easier to name some threats and potential adverse effects resulting from the decision to stay outside than find plausible explanations that argue for the benefits of not joining the monetary union. A very practical reason for the popularity of the euro, to the man in the street in Finland, is that there is no need to exchange money when travelling around Europe. The typical Finn feels proud that it is Finland's own money that is valid and accepted extensively around the world. In the coming years and not far in the future, the aging of the population, a heavy tax burden and persistently high unemployment levels challenge the sustainability of the economy and force actions that must result in overcoming these foreseeable challenges. These actions must be taken; independent of whether Finland is inside or outside the monetary union and membership provides us with the environment where we can face these more confidently. Title: Productivity of services  a bottleneck for growth? on Store Days
text: Trade Day Marina Congress Center 23.1.2006 Director-General Erkki Liikanen Service productivity  a bottleneck for growth? When analyzing the national economy and its key figures, great attention is paid to industrial production and its various sectors. A lot of information and statistics are available. Industry is therefore important. The construction of Finnish industry was a major driver of the post-war boom. And the growth of finland's national economy itself began with the industrial revolution in the 1870s. Until then, neither the national economy nor the standard of living increased at all. This was due to the fact that there was no increase in productivity. An increase in living standards depends precisely on an increase in productivity. Productivity increases when investment is made, as the level of education improves and as better and smarter ways of organising work are developed It requires new technologies and innovations in the organisation of work. Often it means better logistics. Slide 2: Value added in the economy, Euro area 2004 So industry is important. But let's take a closer look at the development of the economy. The importance of services has grown strongly. Today, services account for almost 70 per cent of value added in euro area countries, while manufacturing accounts for 23 per cent. And the share of services is increasing and the share of industry is decreasing. However, it should be remembered that industry and services are well integrated today. Without competitive services, industry cannot operate competitively. And many such activities that were carried out in the industry before have passed to service entrepreneurs. How, then, is the service sector divided? Trade accounts for a quarter of that. Slide 3: Value added in private services, Euro area 2004 Retail and wholesale trade account for 11 1/2 per cent of the value added of the economy of the euro area countries as a whole, which is thus one-half of the value added in manufacturing. Trade therefore plays an extremely important role in the development of the economy and employment. 4. Membrane: Increasing competition  adjustment mechanisms for the real economy Increased competition means, at least temporarily, a reduction in profits for companies, as they are forced to adapt their activities to the new competitive situation. Likewise, the development and marketing of new products absorb the resources of companies, and this is out of the productive sphere.
