Title: Opening speech by Bank Director Sinikka Salo at the Account and Tax Days of the Finnish Financial Administration Association
text: 1 (7) Bank Manager 23.1.2006 Sinikka Salo THE EURO, THE EUROSYSTEM AND FINANCIAL INTEGRATION Opening speech at the Account and Tax Days of the Association of Finnish Accounting Firms 23.1.2006 Ladies and gentlemen! First of all, I would like to express my sincerest thanks to the organisers for this opportunity to open this year's account and tax days. I have chosen the title 'The euro, the Eurosystem and the integration of financial markets'. 11 years of EU membership, including 7 years in monetary union, has been a success for Finland overall. And although the eu's integration process at the moment seems to be faltering  because of the headwinds faced by the ratification of the Constitutional Treaty  I believe that progress is being made. The benefits of integration are so great that we cannot afford to leave them unaddressed in the long term. My intention in this presentation is to highlight the challenges we face in the development of the EU's common market, particularly in the financial markets. The emergence of the euro gave an important new impetus to the process of integration of the financial markets and has perhaps for the first time opened up the possibility of creating deep and almost pan-European financial markets. In this area, there are significant benefits to be gained in promoting the functioning of the common market and, consequently, growth and prosperity. Promoting the integration of financial markets is also one of the objectives of the Bank of Finland and the Eurosystem as a whole, i.e. the European Central Bank and the national central banks of the euro area. The integration of the financial markets is important in many ways. In an integrated, deep and broad financial market, firms and households have access to a wide range of services at competitive prices, and when making different financial transactions, it does not matter whether transactions are carried out within the euro area as a whole or within a single country alone. Integration will promote competition and technological development in financial markets and broaden and deepen financial intermediation. As a result, it leads to an intensification of capital flows and a strengthening of the growth potential of real GDP. The magnitude of the pitfalls still to be gained from the integration of the euro area and the EU's financial markets will depend on how far the financial markets are already integrated. The unabashed hymns are large if the integration of the market is only just beginning and, correspondingly, smaller if the integration is already somewhat complete. One might therefore ask how far the financial markets in the euro area are already integrated, in which areas integration is already at an advanced stage and which, in turn, are the areas where there is still a great deal of potential to erode the benefits of integration. I shall begin my presentation by examining the current integration situation of the euro area financial markets in the light of the differences in interest rates between the euro countries. According to this analysis, pricing in euro area securities markets is already fairly uniform. Indirect financing, i.e. financing intermediated by banks and other financial institutions, on the other hand, still has large differences in interest rates per country. A different view of the degree of integration of financial markets is obtained when we look at market structures rather than prices. Both the activities of financial institutions and the cross-border provision of financial services, especially in retail markets, remain rather modest, and financial market infrastructures such as supply and settlement systems or payment systems have remained fragmented. Thus, at this stage of the process of financial integration in the euro area, a situation has emerged in which pricing is already functioning fairly uniformly, but the structure of the market, in particular as regards retail markets and infrastructure, remains cumbersome and inefficient. The clots of integration have not yet been exhausted. In my opinion, the opposite is true, i.e. we are at most only halfway to the creation of a European market, and the most important benefits of integration have therefore yet to materialise. However, the success of the clots of integration requires determined efforts to develop the structures of the financial markets. In this presentation, I will examine two projects aimed at rationalising the infrastructures of the financial markets, namely the euro payments area for private banks and the new eurosystem payment system. To conclude, I would like to make a few more assessments of the importance of the integration of the financial markets, particularly for the financial management of a prss-listed company. Will the one-price law be implemented in the euro area financial markets? According to the simplest definition, the financial markets are fully integrated when the so-called "green belt" is realized in it. the law of one price. The identical prices of claims generating cash flows are the same regardless of the country in which the claim was originally issued or in which country the claim was originally settled. In the financial markets, the price is often expressed in terms of interest, and thus the integration of the financial markets can be viewed by comparing the interest rates on similar claims in different countries. In the euro area short-term debt securities market, pricing has already become very much more integrated in some respects. Money market interest rates  i.e. interbank short-term interest rates up to the 12-month maturity  have been almost fully integrated since the euro was used. To the extent that interest rate differentials between countries are no longer quoted on the money market at all, these are usually very small, not exceeding one hundredth of a percent. Before monetary union, the differences could be several percentage points. Interest rates on short-term debt securities issued by the public sector are, in practice, almost the same in all euro area countries. The market for short-term corporate debt securities, on the other hand, has remained segmented, but important steps have also been taken to create a common market. In this context, I can mention the STEP (Short-Term European Paper) initiative, which aims to harmonise standards and market practices for short-term corporate debt securities. STEP is an initiative of market participants, but at least in the early stages of its operation, the Eurosystem will provide support for it. The first STEPpapers are expected to hit the market soon this year. In the market for long-term debt securities, price formation is more complex and, correspondingly, it is more difficult to examine interest rate differentials than in the money market. Bonds differ significantly in areas such as repayment structure, liquidity, credit rating and market practices, and it is even more difficult to compare corporate shares than long-term debt securities. In the markets for long-term debt securities and equities, the existence of potential price differences between countries has to be assessed using model-based analyses. It should be mentioned that the European Central Bank has started to monitor the integration of capital markets through model reviews. The intention is to assess the state of market integration on an annual basis, and the first report was published last October. According to this report, interest rate formation on government bonds and, to some extent, on other long-term bonds is fairly uniform throughout the euro area. The stock market, on the other hand, still seems to have national barriers, and the euro area cannot yet be regarded as a single prss area as, for example, the United States. One permanent obstacle to cross-border trade in euro area equities and other securities is the fragmented clearing and settlement system for securities. However, the preference for domestic equities (i.e. the so-called home-bias) has declined markedly since the euro was not used, especially for institutional investors. This has also been noticed in the debate in Finland. In my opinion, however, it would be backwards if attempts were to be made to favour domestic stocks in some way artificially, as might be inferred from the complaints that have been made about the diversification of investments. Assessing the pricing trend of financing mediated by banks and other financial institutions is even more difficult than that of long-term securities or stocks. Estimates have to be based on statistics with rough classifications and may include, for example, products that differ from each other in terms of interest rate fixing or loan guarantees and collateral. The eurosystem's new harmonised statistics on interest rates provide some opportunity to assess the pricing of bank loans in the euro area. In light of these statistics, pricing looks different in different segments of banking. Wholesale banking, which relies heavily on the money market, can be considered to be highly integrated in terms of interest rate formation. Interest rates on retail bank loans, on the other hand, vary quite clearly from country to country. If we compare retail loan agreements with similar interest rates, the lowest interest rate differentials between countries are attributed to large corporate bonds. In recent years, the range of average interest rates on new loans between euro area countries has been no more than about half a per cent. Large corporate loans are usually highly competitive everywhere, and so it is not surprising that their interest rate differentials remain quite small. The average interest rates on smaller loans to non-financial corporations of up to one million euros differ more than those on large loans, and the range of interest rates between countries has been more than one per cent in recent years. These loans are mainly taken out by small and medium-sized enterprises, and variations in interest rates may reflect differences in their bargaining position and competition in banking in different countries. The variation in interest rates on new mortgages has been of the same magnitude as on smaller corporate loans. The dispersion of interest rates on consumer loans by country has been substantially greater than that of other loans. Partly for statistical reasons, but partly for interest rate differentials are undoubtedly real. To sum up the interest rate formation in euro area financial markets and financial intermediation, pricing differs from one part of the financial system to another. Of course, the key monetary policy rates are exactly the same in all the euro countries, and the law of one price is also closely implemented in markets close to the single monetary policy, above all in the interbank money market. In the case of bonds, and now perhaps even stocks, we can also talk about a fairly uniform market in terms of pricing. In retail banking, the one-price law would seem to hold true worse than in the money and capital markets. Whether financial structures in the euro area have become more harmonised A second view of the integration process is obtained if, instead of pricing, we look at the corporate structure of the market or the basic structures of the market, such as payment systems or securities settlement and settlement systems. From this perspective, the financial markets can be considered fully integrated when national borders have no effect on the structure of the financial markets. Increased competition since the emergence of the euro and in general has forced the financial institutions of the euro area to increase their efficiency. This is demonstrated, among other things, by the fact that the number of credit institutions operating in the euro area fell from around 8700 in 1997 to around 6400 in 2004. The structure has become more compact, mainly through the formation of larger national units. Although foreign acquisitions and mergers have also started to increase in recent years, the degree of domesticity of financial institutions is still considerable. For example, foreign banks  i.e. branches and subsidiaries  account for less than 15% of banking in most euro area countries. However, in some countries, such as Finland, the share of foreign banks is clearly higher than this. In addition, the cross-border retail supply of financial services is limited. In principle, there are no longer major obstacles to the provision of cross-border funding, for example legislative ones. However, cross-border use of retail services has remained limited, and, for example, depositing or lending via the Internet across borders has not become much more common even after the euro has been used. In addition to habits and habits, the cross-border procurement of financial services is hampered by a number of frictions, such as national differences in the use of collateral in loans and deposit guarantees in deposits. Thus, since the introduction of the euro, the euro area financial markets have certainly become more compact and efficient, but both the corporate structure and the various infrastructures of the market have remained largely unchanged and the markets have been segmented at national level. Due to the segmentation of the market, large-scale benefits have only been partially eroded and cost structures have remained heavy. Euro area financial markets are not yet able to provide a wide range of services to all market participants at competitive prices. There is no doubt that large, globally operating companies will be able to implement their financial decisions at a very competitive price today, regardless of the country in which they are headquartered. For small and medium-sized enterprises, as well as for households, access to financial instruments is more limited, especially in a small country, and these market participants may also encounter large margins of interest rates in their financial transactions. Financial system infrastructures on the EU agenda The integration of financial system infrastructures , such as payment systems and securities clearing and settlement systems, therefore has significant potential economies of scale as a result of cost-effectiveness and market liquidity of larger size. Structural reform is therefore high on the agenda of both the various EU institutions and market participants. Among the reform projects, I would like to highlight the desire to create a single payments area in Europe, which is understandably very important for the functioning of the internal market as a whole: the free movement of goods and services requires that the associated payments be made quickly and efficiently. There will therefore be a strong effort to steer the development of european payment systems in the coming years with a view to creating a single payments area. With regard to small payments, the EU intervened in the pricing of payment services by means of a regulation which, since 1.7.2003, has restricted the right of banks to charge higher fees for cross-border credit transfers in euro than for domestic payments. From the beginning of this year, the regulation will apply to payments of up to EUR 50 000. Of course, the regulation as such does not affect the payment systems themselves, the modification of which requires action by payment service providers, i.e. mainly banks. Euro area banks have responded to the challenges of payment systems by setting up a joint body called the European Payments Council, which has set itself the objective of implementing a single euro payments platform (Single Euro Payments Area, SEPA) by 2010. In 2008, it is planned to achieve the so-called "green belt". sepa, i.e. all euro area citizens would then have access to mutually compatible payment methods that are independent of national borders. National debit cards, credit transfers and direct debits would be phased out in 2010, thus achieving a perfectly unified payment area across the euro area. The Eurosystem, i.e. the ECB and the national central banks of the euro area, is not involved in the SEPA project as a party, but rather as an active catalyst. This role includes not only close monitoring of the progress of the project, but also negotiations and discussions with banks and other parties. The Eurosystem can support the progress of the project, in particular in the event of conflicting interests between decision-makers. On the other hand, the Eurosystem, together with the competition authorities, must ensure that interbank cooperation does not become a price cartel and an abuse of market position. In December, the European Commission published a proposal for a directive on payment services, which, if implemented, will create a legal framework for the SEPA project. The proposal for a directive aims to remove all remaining legal barriers to cross-border retail payment services and to make payments to another EU country as easy, affordable and secure as at home. The new directive will apply to all EU Member States and will apply to all EU currencies, while the 2001 regulation only applied to payments in euro. One major obligation for banks is that, from 2010 onwards, payments for one currency must be made in a maximum of one day. The directive also introduces direct debits from one country to another. In this context, I would also like to mention the attempt to develop a system for the wholesale money market, that is to say, for the transmission of large payments. A key development in this area is the Eurosystem's new target 2 payment system, which is to be phased in from November 2007. TARGET 2 replaces the current TARGET system, which was typically built on national payment systems during the current phase of eurofinancial integration. Under the new system, a private bank enters into an account relationship with the national central bank, but the production of services is centralised and banks in all euro area countries offer the same services. It goes without saying that under the new system, pricing will be the same for cross-border payments as for domestic payments. The system also allows a banking group operating in several countries to combine its accounts with different central banks of the euro area into a single virtual account, which can be managed and used as if it were a single account during the day. Building new systems covering the whole of the euro area or even the whole of the EU requires considerable costs and is not easy anyway. In many cases, painful national and institutional conflicts of interest are addressed, for which there may not be easy, mutually satisfactory solutions. This is the case, for example, in cases where economies of scale are significant and the 'natural' solution would be to limit the number of operators to one. Despite the potential conflicts of interest, companies operating in the financial markets and national authorities should be reassured that the one-eyed defence of national systems and markets prevents us from getting a complete glimpse of the process of european financial integration. The focus on short-term costs and mosquitoes easily masks the achievable longer-term clots, which over time are of a different order of magnitude than the costs. According to seemingly realistic estimates, the gross domestic product of the euro area could be increased by as much as several percentage points  that is, by as much as tenths of a per cent per annum  over a ten-year horizon if the remaining obstacles to financial integration could be completely removed. I believe that these estimates give a reasonably good picture of the economic importance of a well-functioning and deep financial market. On the unification of financial management Accurate and up-to-date reporting by companies is essential for the functioning of financial markets. For this reason, the issuer of a publicly traded share or other security is obliged to disclose, without undue delay, the main facts and other facts that materially affect the value of the security. The aim is to ensure equal, equal and simultaneous access to information for all investors. In recent years, the driving force behind the process of regulatory convergence in the EU's financial markets has been the Financial Services Action Plan (FSAP), jointly adopted by the Commission and the Member States, which started in 1999 and for the most part the legislation on which was completed as planned last year. The plan included more than 40 different measures. A significant measure was the adoption of common accounting standards by companies. IFRSs entered into force in all EU countries at the beginning of 2005 and apply to the consolidated financial statements of all listed companies. The aim of the reform was to improve the international comparability of financial statements and to make financial information more up-to-date. With common financial statements, companies' financial reporting and, at the same time, control will become more uniform and international. A new common dimension has emerged in the financial reporting of companies, which forces the company's financial administration, auditors and the tax authorities to pay attention to the application of common standards not only in their own country, but also in the rest of the EU. It is important for the functioning of financial markets that common accounting standards are applied as similarly as possible throughout the EU. On the other hand, however, due to differences in tax and joint regulations, for example, it is unlikely that it will be possible to apply standards in a completely uniform manner. In drawing up economic reports, difficult choices have to be made between the uniformity of standards and national applicability. One of the consequences of the deep integration of the financial markets, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises in a small country, is the expansion of the range of financial instruments available. Some of the new instruments are complex and difficult to understand, which makes their management and handling in the company's financial reporting challenging. It may be difficult to assess the appropriateness of using new instruments. Suunnitelma piti sislln yli 40 erilaista toimenpidett. Merkittv toimenpide oli yritysten yhteisten tilinptsstandardien omaksuminen. IFRS-tilinptstandardit tulivat voimaan kaikissa EU-maissa vuoden 2005 alusta ja ne koskevat kaikkien listattujen yritysten konsernitilinptksi. Uudistuksen tavoitteena oli tilinptsten kansainvlisen vertailtavuuden parantaminen ja tilinptinformaation ajantasaisuuden lisminen. Yritysten talousraportointiin onkin muodostunut uusi yhteisllinen dimensio, joka pakottaa yrityksen taloushallinnon, tilintarkastajat ja verottajan kiinnittmn huomiota yhteisten standardien soveltamiseen paitsi omassa maassaan my muualla EU:ssa. Rahoitusmarkkinoiden toiminnan kannalta on trke, ett yhteisi tilinptstandardeja sovelletaan mahdollisimman samalla tavalla koko EU:n alueella. Toisaalta mm. vero- ja yhtilainsdnnn erojen takia standardien tysin yhteninen soveltaminen tuskin kuitenkaan on mahdollista. Talousraportteja laadittaessa joudutaankin tekemn vaikeita valintoja standardien yhtenisyyden ja kansallisen soveltuvuuden vlill. Ers rahoitusmarkkinoiden syvllisen integraation seurauksista erityisesti pienen maan pienten ja keskisuurten yritysten kannalta on kytettviss olevien rahoitusinstrumenttien joukon laajentuminen. Osa uusista instrumenteista on monimutkaisia ja vaikeasti ymmrrettvi, mik tekee niiden hallinnan ja mys ksittelyn yrityksen talousraportoinnissa haastavaksi. Uusien instrumenttien kytn tarkoituksenmukaisuutta saattaa olla vaikea arvioida. Esimerkit erityisesti Yhdysvalloista mutta my muualta osoittavat, ett pitklle kehittyneiden markkinoiden instrumentteja voidaan kytt eptarkoituksenmukaisesti tai jopa suorastaan vrin. Ptksentekijt ja asiantuntijat joutunevatkin tulevaisuudessa pohtimaan entist enemmn sit, miten rahoitusmarkkinoilla avautuvia uusia mahdollisuuksia voidaan parhaiten kytt yrityksen ja yhteiskunnan edun mukaisesti. Tm edellytt rahoitusinstrumenttien ja -markkinoiden syvllist tuntemusta. Rahoitusvaihtoehtojen lisntyess kasvavat mys yrityksen mahdollisuudet verotuksellisesti edullisten vaihtoehtojen valintaan. Valtiot voivat reagoida verotuksessaan rahoitusmarkkinoiden yhdentymiseen eri tavoin. Yhtlt ne voivat pyrki kyttm verojrjestelm kilpailukeinona tai jopa kaupan teknisen esteen yritysten sijoittumisesta kilpailtaessa. Toisaalta integraation etenemisen my kasvavat paineet verotuksen erojen poistamiseksi ja ajanoloon ehk my verotuksen harmonisoimiseksi. Yrityksen tilintarkastajien ohella yritysten tilinptsi ja muuta taloudellista raportointia valvovat EU-maissa eri viranomaiset, Suomessa Suomen Pankin yhteydess toimiva Rahoitustarkastus. Rahoitustarkastus mys osallistuu Suomen edustajana standardien yhdenmukaista soveltamista koskevaan eurooppalaiseen yhteistyhn. Rahoitustarkastuksen noteerattuja yrityksi koskeva valvonta perustuu paljolti yhtiiden julkistamiin raportteihin. Sen mahdollisuudet onnistua valvonnassaan riippuvat siten ratkaisevasti siit, ett yritysten taloushallinnosta ja tilintarkastuksesta vastaavat tahot hoitavat ensin oman tyns moitteettomasti. Hyvt kuulijat! Hyvin toimivat, aidosti Euroopan laajuiset rahoitusmarkkinat ovat keskeisess asemassa, kun EU pyrkii rakentamaan taloudellisesti yhtenisemp ja dynaamisempaa Eurooppaa. Tmn pmrn saavuttamiseksi kannattaa ponnistella. Kitkatekijst huolimatta olen EU:n rahoitusmarkkinoiden tulevan yhdentymiskehityksen suhteen optimistinen. Edut aidosti yhtenisist Euroopan laajuisista rahoitusmarkkinoista ovat kustannuksiin verrattuna yksinkertaisesti liian suuret, jotta voisimme jtt ne hydyntmtt. Askeleita oikeaan suuntaan otetaankin jatkuvasti sek viranomaisten ett yksityisen rahoitussektorin toimesta. Eurojrjestelm ja sen mukana Suomen Pankki osallistuu thn prosessiin aktiivisesti paitsi rahaviranomaisena my markkinaosapuolena ja maksupalvelujen tarjoajana. Lopuksi haluaisin todeta, ett hyvinkn toimivat rahoitusmarkkinat eivt yksin riit ratkaisemaan Euroopan talouden kaikkia ongelmia, joiden juuret ovat enimmkseen muualla kuin rahoitustaloudessa. Rahoitustalous voi vain luoda edellytykset sille, ett kilpailukyvyn menestyksen todelliset perustekijt  kuten hyv koulutustaso, innovatiivisuus ja ahkeruus  psevt vaikuttamaan. Hyvin toimivat rahoitusmarkkinat edistvt yritysten menestyst, mutta viime kdess yritysten ja koko kansantalouden menestys riippuu kuitenkin muista kuin rahataloudellisista tekijist, ennen kaikkea yrityksiss tehtvst mrtietoisesta tyst. Title: Information, opportunity, threat, security? at the Internal Security Influencer Seminar
text: Internal Security Influencer Seminar 2006 7.2.2006 Marina Congress Center Director-General Erkki Liikanen Knowledge and communication have become a key factor in the development of the economy and society. In order to better understand information networks and the security associated with them, it is worth looking at how this has come about. The development of information networks and, above all, the spread of the Internet and the World Wide Web have been a revolutionary step forward in the exploitation of information systems. For a long time, automatic data processing was handled by large mainframes or mini-computers. Security was handled by physical security mechanisms, as central units, terminals and other peripherals formed uniform, but single wholes. The breakthrough of open communication networks changed everything. Separate and even built computers from different manufacturers could be connected to others. A captivating new vision was born; everything could be connected to each other, freely and without restrictions. The first area of computer networks was universities and research institutes, as well as some large enterprises. In the 1980s, personal computers, PCs and the local area networks formed by offices exploded. And then, in the early 1990s, the widespread use of web technology brought the internet network to the public consciousness. Data sharing between systems laid the foundation for a whole new level of productivity gain. Databases could be shared, information costs dropped drastically. Businesses and communities moved into the online world. Increasingly critical functions became network-dependent. First came the great vision of the freedom and ease of everything. But then we woke up; security risks increased sharply. Online security became a major issue. The ideology of free connectivity did not make it possible to equip business-critical objects of use with networked systems. Computer viruses were the first examples of system vulnerability. Figure 1: Network and information security  the first part of network security The security of information and communication systems has become a key challenge for decision-makers. However, finding policy responses has become increasingly challenging. Communications services are no longer provided by state-owned monopolies, but by a number of private operators and service providers in competition with each other, not only domestically, but increasingly at European or global level. Networks are converging: they are able to support the same services, they are increasingly interconnected and they partly use the same infrastructure. Figure 1: Network and information security  part two cybercrime, third part hacking Cybercrime was born. Hacking rose to the top of the concerns. However, the various manifestations of cybercrime have been evolving at the same pace as the size of the economic or public interests handled in information networks has increased. For a long time, cybercrime was largely the play of clever nerds, "teasing" or financial goals. The situation has changed and financial crime through networks has increased. We have read expert reports on cooperation between organised crime and IT experts. And we have read about how home computers have been hijacked as spam distribution centers. Figure 1: Network and information security  the fourth part of the privacy policy The high productivity contribution of networks is related to the fact that data, including personal data, can be stored and processed in the online environment. It is easy and economical. But at the same time, there are increased risks in terms of privacy. It is essential to protect citizens and their personal data. Extensive databases and efficient information retrieval tools enable very accurate profiling of individuals. If users' data and privacy cannot be protected, people will be frightened and the great economic and social potential of the information society will not be realised. Figure 1: Network and information security  the fifth part of identity theft Identity theft is a serious threat related to the services provided on information networks. Identity theft refers to the acquisition and misuse of personal data to make commitments, such as opening accounts or making purchases in an online store. Millions of crimes of this type are recorded in the United States and the United Kingdom every year, and the phenomenon threatens trust in the use of online services. In order to ensure a minimum level of security, a large number of legal provisions have been adopted at both national and EU level within the framework of the telecommunications regulatory framework and data protection legislation. These provisions must be applied effectively in a rapidly changing environment. The challenge with regulations is that technologies and also their misuse are advancing rapidly. That is why the legislator and the authorities face challenges. At the same time, it is important that companies are constantly developing solutions to overcome security problems. Both should go hand in hand, with regulation and technological innovation. Security has become a commodity to be bought and sold on the market and an element of agreements between the parties. Economists say that the price mechanism balances the cost of producing security with specific security needs. However, many safety risks remain unresolved or the market uptake of solutions is slow  players who have achieved a significant market position have put the brakes on the overall use of competing solutions. Specific policy measures addressing these shortcomings can strengthen the market process while improving the functioning of the regulatory framework. Such actions must be part of a European approach to ensure the internal market, to benefit from common solutions and to be able to act effectively at global level. Figure 2  The development of the European information society The European information society has progressed in the eEurope2002 and eEurope2005 programmes. In the area of information security, the first major line was set out in a Commission communication in July 2001. It did not receive much attention at the time. But September 2001 changed everything. Online security was at the top of the list of concerns. The Commission then proposed the creation of a European Network and Information Security Agency (ENISA). As Finns, we can be proud of the fact that we have received significant tasks related to the Agency, as its Board of Directors is chaired by Kristiina Pietikainen from Finland. I am very pleased that my successor, Viviane Reding, has presented a graduate programme, i2010, in which safety continues to play a key role. The programme highlights interoperability, security and reliability, identity management, rights management and ease of use as significant challenges. The information security debate is shifting from technical security to achieving public trust in the digital world. The challenges of the European information society after 2005 highlight trust and reliability: information networks must be both secure and reliable. Consumers expect the protection of privacy and the fight against illegal trading practices and illegal content. And the infrastructures of modern life are largely built on information and communication technologies and are interdependent, so malfunctions can have serious consequences. European developments have also brought with them security factors, the impact of which causes conflict. The debate on the obligation to store electronic communications identification data is certainly familiar to this public as well. The background to this obligation is the fight against terrorism. In practice, this means that telecom operators must store data related to telephone calls and e-mail communications for a fixed period of time (6-24 months). This has been perceived as a threat to privacy while at the same time entailing significant costs for operators. In connection with this topic, a study on cost sharing has also been launched in Finland. Finland has played an active role in information security matters. In 2003, the State Council approved the National Information Security Strategy, which has received attention. At the best of times, work is underway to draw up a similar European strategy, in which Finland has been a pioneer. During the upcoming Presidency of the Council of the EU, special attention will be paid to information security issues. Figure 3:"What is the most common way you pay your bills?" The banking system is among the most active users of online services. This is how the opportunities and threats of the online world are present in the banking world every day. Finns, on the other hand, are among the world leaders in the areas of electronic banking services and card payments. The survey-based comparison shown in the figure shows that 64% of respondents have reported the Internet as the most common way to pay bills. I mentioned identity theft above as a serious challenge to NIS reform. Banks are at the heart of this problem. Phising is related to identity theft. Last December, we witnessed an attempt to collect identification information from customers of one bank using a fake email. In the area of card payments, reliable identification is advancing with the emv system based on chip card technology standardised by the key credit card companies (Eurocard, Mastercard, Visa EMV). The introduction of EMV will affect cards, payment terminals, ATMs and back-end systems. The aim of the EMC is to prevent card fraud, reduce abuses, speed up payment transactions and ensure international sharing. Figure 4: Bank payment intermediation and machine-readiness rate The financial sector is a good example of an area where ICT has made it possible and continues to enable the emergence of new types of services, distribution channels, operating models and even banks. The figure shows the development of payment intermediation from the mid-1990s onwards, and we can see that the degree of machine-language proficiency is almost 100%. The financial sector is highly dependent on functioning information systems and networks. Crisis exercises in the sector have shown that the provision of services through manuaa supplements is very limited. Up-to-date account information and well-functioning payment intermediation are prerequisites for providing banking services. Disruptions to information systems and the availability of electricity are highlighted as threats. Recent natural disasters have made ensuring critical infrastructure in society a key security issue. Part of this work is also to ensure the functioning of the financial markets. Solutions are on the horizon in which systems are consolidated into more efficient entities. In many cases, new services are subject to doubts about their reliability and safety. When developing new solutions, safety is a key enabler. Figure 6: National Information Security Day Today, 7.2.2006, is the third National Information Security Day. The digital world and information networks have become a significant part of both work and leisure time. It has made life easier. However, we have read the warnings of apocalyptic forecasters - there are in the depths of technology as elsewhere - that the internet is coming to an end and the digital world is on the verge of collapse. This is not the case. But favorable development requires awareness of information security also at the individual level. Mobile workstations, communicators and other handhelds have detached us from the constant guidance of IT professionals. When it comes to home machines, we often feel that we are "on our own". Therefore, it must be remembered that the user also has his own responsibility. It is important to know the alphabet of information security. With your own behavior, you can significantly reduce the risks. In the world of risks, one should not panic, but remain vigilant.

Title: Presentation by Bank Director Sinikka Salo at the Economic and Financial Forum in the Local Government Sector
text: Presentation by Bank Manager Sinikka Salo at the Municipal Economic and Financial Forum 15.2.2006 THE EU AND WORLD ECONOMY IN A NEW SITUATION, HOW EUROPE AND FINLAND ARE DOING For a long time, total world production has developed favorably. Apart from temporary cyclical fluctuations, output growth has been steadily increasing since the 1970s and is currently estimated at around four per cent per annum in global gdp. Against the background of this favorable development, there are strong economic forces. A significant factor has been the rapid development and use of new technologies. On the other hand, many countries that had previously pursued inward-looking economic policies have opened up and increasingly integrated into world trade in goods and services. Globalisation has also made rapid progress in the financial markets, which has encouraged the mobility of capital and technology worldwide. The prolonged period of rapid growth in the global economy has not been possible without major changes in production and demand structures and the associated growing pains. Great attention has been paid to the relocation of industrial workers to low-cost countries, i.e. the so-called low-cost countries. China--as a result of which redundancies in low-productivity sectors in industrialized countries have increased. The disappearance of low productivity jobs is a natural and permanent part of the process of economic growth, but the pace of change has accelerated with globalisation and, as a first-hand experience, it can undoubtedly be difficult and difficult to get caught up in structural change in the global economy. As global GDP growth has accompanied an increase in demand for scarce natural resources, and it is not surprising that commodity prices have risen as a result of rapid economic growth. In recent years, especially jy and jy products have become considerably more expensive. Thanks to the development and integration of financial markets, countries with deficits have been able to finance their current account deficits easily, while countries with surpluses have been able to easily invest their surpluses on international financial markets. Current account surpluses and deficits have thus become larger than they were used to in the past. This can be considered a natural consequence of the general internationalization trend. On the other hand, the fact that financial flows have been directed towards a prosperous and highly developed United States, financed by countries in the Middle East and East Asia, which are well below their level of development and wealth, cannot be regarded as a natural consequence of internationalisation. I will begin this presentation with the current state of the world, EU and Finnish economies and the forecast outlook for the near term. The key scenario is a mythical one. Real GDP growth is expected to remain relatively high throughout the global economy, and in the EU and Finland it is even expected to pick up slightly. On the other hand, the development of the global economy is overshadowed by various uncertainties, which also foresee the possibility of slower-than-forecast growth. Among the uncertainties in the global economy, I will take a closer look at the high prices and, in particular, the current account imbalances. Although Europe's own current account balance is, on the whole, more or less well balanced, the uncontrolled unwinding of global current account imbalances could cause a major shock to our economic development. I will conclude with a few thoughts on how Europe and Finland will cope with their future challenges, especially if global economic risks materialise and real GDP growth temporarily weakens. The development of world total production from myths Last year, global gdp is estimated to have grown at a moderate pace of its trend growth of just over 4%, and growth is expected to continue at almost the same rate this year. This growth can be considered good, although it is lower than in the peak year of 2004, when the global economy recorded an annual growth of just over 5%. Growth in 2004 was the fastest in more than three decades. The rapid growth in real GDP is largely due to Asian countries. According to new statistical figures, china's economy has been growing at an annual rate of about 10% for more than ten years. In China's wake, India and other emerging asian economies have been increasing their output at a rapid pace, although asia's small emerging economies have not now gotten off to the same pace as before their economic crisis at the end of the last decade. In Japan, the deflationary period seems to be finally coming to an end and production is recovering. Among the industrialized countries, the engine of growth has long been the United States. Last year, the country's total production increased by 3-4%, and this year growth is expected to remain more or less unchanged. Economic growth in the United States has been sustained in recent years by strong domestic demand, above all consumption. Consumption has been supported by an increase in household disposable income as a result of improved labour market conditions and, in particular, tax relief in the past. In addition, U.S. households have consistently saved less and less of their income, and last year they spent  for the first time since the Depression of the 1930s  more than they earned. The significant increase in the value of apartments has been one of the factors that has pushed consumption and indebtedness. The bush administration's fiscal policy has been relatively slow, leading to a deterioration in public finances and, in part, in the external budgetary position. In relation to total output, general government finances currently show a deficit of around 3%, compared with a surplus of just over one per cent in 2000. Last year and the year before last, however, the deficit did not increase much. The formation of the public deficit has been influenced by previous tax cuts and the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. For a long time, monetary policy in the United States was also light. However, in June 2004, the Central Bank raised the key monetary policy rate from one per cent to 1.25%, while signalling that it was time for monetary policy to move from a strongly accommodative stance towards a more moderately neutral level of interest rates. Since then, the central bank has gradually raised the key interest rate, which is currently 4.50%. Recent strong economic figures have increased market expectations that the central bank will raise its key interest rate somewhat more. However, the market expects that the current period of policy rate increases is already beginning to draw to a close. In contrast to the key monetary policy rates and short-term money market rates, us long-term interest rates have remained broadly unchanged, although they rose slightly towards the end of last year. The U.S. ten-year rate has recently been around 4 1/2 percent. Long-term interest rates are also low outside the United States and in real terms  i.e. inflation - they have remained well below the growth rate of the economy almost globally. Various explanations have been offered for the low level of long-term interest rates. As a result of the previous very light monetary policy  in countries other than the United States  the market for asset hype has been flooded with liquidity, which has driven the prices of long-term bonds, i.e. long-term interest rates, among other assets, have fallen. On the other hand, much has been said about the global oversupply of saving, that is, the abundance of saving compared to investment. I will come back to this explanation later in this presentation. Low long-term interest rates undoubtedly reflect moderate inflation expectations in the global economy over the medium to longer term, driven, inter alia, by confidence in monetary policy. The explanation has also been offered that pension funds and other institutional investors have directed a larger part of their investment portfolio towards fixed-rate investments. Whatever the reasons for the low long-term interest rates, the financing conditions in the global economy can still be considered relatively light. The light financial market situation has contributed to strong and broad-based economic growth. This is, of course, a mythical and desirable thing. On the other hand, it has contributed to the emergence of some less desirable revelations: -Due to strong demand, the world market prices of jy and other raw materials are have risen substantially in the last couple of years. Ample liquidity and low interest rates are supported the demand for raw materials, not only the consumption of raw materials, but also the accumulation of stocks and perhaps through taking my speculative positions. -Easing financing conditions have led to increased private sector indebtedness, and at the same time, the housing market has heated up and housing prices have risen rapidly. -The rise in consumer prices has accelerated clearly due to higher prices of ljy and ljy products. Rising prices can spread from the jy products market and the housing market to other hyy market and on to wages and costs, which gives cause for concern over a long period of time kavalin inflaationakymista. Growth in the euro area is slow but accelerating In 2004, for the first time in four years, euro area output growth reached its potential growth rate of just over 2%. Even this modest growth spurt was short-lived, and in early 2005 growth stopped almost completely. Towards the end of the year, however, euro area economic indicators started to improve and, in particular, the business outlook picked up to some extent. Supported by exports, total output in the euro area grew by an estimated 1.5% last year. Signs of a recovery in euro area domestic demand, in particular private consumption, have been few and far between. Household confidence has remained relatively weak and other indicators do not indicate a rapid pick-up in private consumption either. The improvement in the labour market situation in the euro area has also been slow. The subdued level of consumer demand is explained in particular by the weak development in Germany. The key ecb monetary policy rate, the two-week auction rate, was 2% for a long time, but last December the Governing Council decided to raise it to 2.25%. An increase does not necessarily mean further increases in the future, but the market expects a couple more similar interest rate hikes from the ECB during the current year. Long-term market interest rates have also remained low in the euro area. The 10-year market rate is currently around 31/2% in nominal terms and 1-2% in real terms. Overall, financing conditions in the euro area can continue to be broadly accommodative. This year, real GDP growth in the euro area is expected to rise to around two per cent. Favourable financing conditions, a slowdown in inflation, an increase in corporate profit margins, progress in structural reforms and a strong global economy support a slight recovery in growth. My vibrant housing market boosts wealth and supports consumption in several euro area countries. In Finland, economic growth remained low in the first half of 2005 due to weak industrial production. At the beginning of last year, the strong growth in the metal and electronics industry came to a temporary halt, and in the second quarter, the labour market dispute in the forest industry dropped industrial output considerably. The annual growth in real GDP, around two per cent, was almost entirely based on domestic demand. On the other hand, last year's low reference level raises this year's growth figures, and GDP growth in 2006 is projected to be 3-4%. The production of private services is growing faster than total output, while the growth in the production of public services remains sluggish. Risks to the global economy Despite prolonged high growth, there are risks to the global economic outlook and growth is no longer as solid in all respects as it used to be. The impact of high oil prices on economic growth has, at least for the time being, been less than feared. This is partly explained by the fact that the root cause of the price increase has been strong economic growth, which has increased the demand for ljy, especially in the emerging asian economies and the United States. Moreover, in the industrialised countries, energy use has become much more efficient since the sharp crises of the 1970s and 1980s. The relatively minor effects of higher oil prices on growth are also partly explained by the fact that the indirect effects of the rise in the prices of other products and wages of other products have remained small. This has been helped by the high credibility of monetary policy, which has kept the inflation expectations of economists moderate despite the rise in the price of the pound products. In turn, the moderation of inflation expectations has supported the maintenance of low long-term interest rates and the maintenance of high economic growth. As a result of the integration of world financial markets, the opportunities to issue and take on debt, regardless of national borders, have improved. This has allowed countries to accumulate larger current account deficits and surpluses. This possibility has been exploited to a considerable extent in recent years. The US current account has been negative  i.e. the country has been financed from abroad on a net basis  since the early 1990s. Initially, foreign companies and investors financed the country's productive investments in the form of both direct and portfolio investments, but with the bursting of the internet bubble, foreign investment in the U.S. corporate sector declined. Since then, foreign funding has increasingly been used to finance households' and public sector expenditure. At the moment, the current account deficit of the United States is already more than six percent of gross domestic product. The duration and magnitude of the deficit is unprecedented for the industrialised country. Another thing that makes the situation exceptional is that the world's largest economy is experiencing a large deficit. The current account deficit in the United States has been financed mainly by east Asian countries, in recent years also by producer countries. Export earnings of oil-producing countries increased rapidly as the price of ljy rose, and they have not been able to adjust their consumption and investment to match their increased incomes. Much of the accumulated funds have been recycled to finance the US current account deficit. East Asian countries have traditionally both saved and invested heavily. Following the Asian financial crisis, investment in relation to GDP declined in the countries affected by the crisis, while saving remained at a reasonably high level. The accumulated funds have been used to map foreign exchange reserves, which are largely invested in short-term or long-term bonds issued by the US government. The increase in foreign exchange reserves has dampened the pressure on the appreciation of the currencies of east Asian countries. At the same time, it has increased the liquidity of banks and the supply of credit in the local currency. The foreign exchange reserves of Asian countries have become large. The best example is China, whose foreign exchange reserves at the end of last year amounted to just over USD 800 billion, or about USD 200 billion more than a year earlier. The country's current account is facing a growing surplus thanks to abundant domestic saving, and foreign exchange reserves have been boosted by imports of capital from abroad. If foreign exchange reserves continue to grow at their current level, China is likely to overtake Japan as the world's largest holder of foreign exchange reserves by the end of this year. Compared to the size of the economy, China's foreign exchange reserves are already enormous, between 35% and 40% of gross domestic product. Thus, the US current account deficit is mainly financed by the central banks of the exporting and East Asian countries, and their investments in us financial markets are mainly in liquid assets. This makes the situation in the United States fragile, and it is obvious that there may be considerable risks in the future to finance the country's current account deficit. Until now, the United States has had no difficulty in financing its deficit, but the situation can change quickly. Even if the United States were to be able to finance its current account deficit without difficulty, the pace of its indebtedness would be forced to slow down sooner or later. The current account deficit at the current level is simply sustainable in the long run. The tightening of monetary policy in the United States has supported the correction in current account balances by restraining aggregate demand growth. On the other hand, it has supported the dollar in the international foreign exchange market. However, the temporary appreciation of the dollar appears to have stalled at the end of last year and market expectations of a weakening dollar are now picking up again. An orderly weakening of the dollar would help to reduce the current account deficit. A tightening of the US fiscal stance, which is in any case necessary to safeguard the sustainability of the country's public finances, would be counterproductive in order to correct the current account imbalances. President Bush's administration has set itself the objective of reducing the public sector deficit to two per cent by the 2009 budget year. This objective may be considered modest, but in the absence of decisive action, it may also prove difficult to achieve. Countries with current account surpluses have not done much to reduce their surpluses. The current account surplus is not seen as much of a problem in economic policy as the current account deficit. Furthermore, a surplus current account and the accumulation of foreign exchange reserves may have been a sensible policy, especially for those Asian countries that bitterly experienced the disadvantages of too few foreign exchange reserves in the context of the Asian financial crisis. There are also structural reasons behind the current account surpluses of Asian countries. The recovery in domestic demand is hindered, on the one hand, by poorly functioning financial markets, which force companies to finance their investments with income financing, and, on the other hand, by a lack of social protection, which forces households to save heavily in order to prepare for a rainy day. In the international debate on current account imbalances, a great deal of attention has been paid to the exchange rate policies of the East Asian countries. There have been calls on countries to abandon their fixed exchange rate policies or at least to allow their currencies to appreciate. In some countries  in particular Korea  indeed, the currency has appreciated markedly since 2004. China has come under the greatest pressure to change exchange rate policy. Indeed, the country announced last July that it would change its exchange rate policy in a more flexible direction by abandoning the dollar switch of its currency and switched to guided floating based on a basket of currencies. At the same time, the renminbi was revalued by about two percent. In practice, changes in China's exchange rate policy have, at least until now, remained very minor. Large imbalances in current account balances cannot last indefinitely, and sooner or later capital flows will have to level off and perhaps even turn in the other direction. This can happen in several different ways. It would be detrimental to the development of the world economy if the new equilibrium were to be applied at a lower level of aggregate demand and a higher level of interest rates than at present. The growth of global gdp could slow down considerably. In a more positive scenario, a slowdown in U.S. demand growth would be offset by an increase in demand elsewhere. Real GDP growth could continue at a rapid pace, while current account imbalances would gradually be corrected. The current account of the euro area is broadly balanced. Despite this, the region will not be safe if the major imbalances in the global economy unravel uncontrollably. It would be particularly detrimental to the euro area if global growth were to slow down and the US dollar weakened, above all, against the euro. The adjustment in the euro area would be facilitated by the fact that the currencies of the surplus countries would strengthen not only against the dollar against the my euro, but would increase their imports not only from the United States but also from Europe. Europe's economic policy challenges The economic policy of the euro area is made up of a whole of monetary policy, fiscal policy and structural policy. They all contribute to supporting the common objectives of the Member States' economic policies  stability, growth and a high level of tulle. The most successful policy area is monetary policy. In the short period of its existence, the European Central Bank has managed to acquire considerable monetary credibility capital and, when deciding on a monetary policy stance, it does not need to fear speculative attacks on the euro or a sudden rise in inflation expectations. A credible monetary policy is especially valuable when the euro area is facing external demand disruptions, such as the slowdown in international economic growth. In the face of weakening economic growth and the threat of deflation, the ECB can reduce its key interest rates credibly. This will allow it to maintain price stability in the euro area while supporting aggregate demand growth. As regards fiscal policy, on the other hand, the room for manoeuvre of euro area countries is very limited. Despite favourable developments in the global economy, few euro area countries have achieved the objectives set for the balanced development of public finances and long-term sustainability. If economic growth slows down from its current level, deficits would seek to increase from their current level without any savings. In many countries, fiscal policy decisions would find themselves in a difficult gap, with the choice between austerity measures that deepen the cyclical downturn or increasing deficits and jeopardising the long-term sustainability of public finances. Finland's general government finances are in better shape than in several other EU countries. Mainly thanks to social security funds, general government finances are in surplus, last year around 2 per cent relative to GDP. Despite this, the room for manoeuvre in fiscal policy is not particularly large for us either. The difficulties are rearing their heads in different parts of the public sector, not least in local government finances, where expenditure is increasing, especially in terms of health care expenditure. Despite the rise in tax burdens, local government finances have already run into a financial deficit, and as the population ages, the pressure to increase the deficit may increase further. In principle, the deficit of municipalities could be compensated for by current transfers from the state, but it is difficult to see such savings in central government finances that they would create significant additional space for increases in municipal expenditure. Substantial tax increases would be detrimental to economic growth and, furthermore, tougher international tax competition will limit their use even more in the future. Among the economic policy areas, structural policy, which has been the least successful in Europe, is structural policy, which, like fiscal policy, is mainly national. The success of the EU countries in implementing structural policies has so far remained rather modest. Reforms are needed both in the tyarchies and product markets, as well as in the financial markets. Decisive action to improve the functioning of markets would significantly improve not only the growth potential of economies, but also their flexibility and ability to face external shocks. Ladies and gentlemen, The global economy has experienced a period of strong growth and this is expected to continue. The strong undertone of the global economy is driven by more or less permanent fundamentals, such as the use of new technologies and the integration of developing countries into the world economy. These fundamentals will allow growth to continue at a rapid pace in the future. On the other hand, global economic growth has been accompanied by macroeconomic imbalances, in particular large current account deficits and surpluses, the unwinding of which could lead to a cyclical weakening of growth. Despite a balanced current account and a credible monetary policy, Europe may be in a vulnerable position if the global economic downturn materialises. In most EU countries, the room for manoeuvre in fiscal policy is limited, if not non-existent. The main problem, however, is the cumbersome and rigid structures of the economies, which have left the trend of gdp growth in European countries and their ability to adapt to external shocks modest. In order to revive Europe's growth dynamics, Europe should be made a more attractive destination for investment and work. At the same time, investment in knowledge and innovation should be stepped up. The EU Member States have identified these priorities, but the practical efforts to achieve the targets have so far remained rather limited. In order to achieve results, it would probably be worthwhile for the Member States to define their structural plans in a very concrete way and to pay more attention to their implementation. The new national Lisbon programmes provide a good starting point for accelerating economic renewal, as long as the projects they contain are implemented with determination. In many respects, Finland is in a better position than most other EU countries to cope with the future challenges of the global economy. However, this does not entitle us to rest on our laurels. The globalizing economy will change the international division of labour drastically in the future as well, and My Finland will have to look again and again for new ways to survive in a rapidly changing world. Success requires adapting to constantly changing circumstances, which is why it is worth constantly making changes  as we have done before. Good adjustment capacity is particularly needed in the event that global economic risks are triggered and global growth slows down, at least for some time. I see no reason why we cannot do well in this case as well. But, of course, tougher efforts and better adaptability are required in difficult circumstances than in easy conditions.
