Title: Challenges of productivity and the development of working life in Finland at the TYKES 10th anniversary seminar in Helsinki
text: TYKES 10th anniversary seminar 16.5.2006 Helsinki Director-General Erkki Liikanen Challenges in the development of productivity and working life in Finland Tykes' development programme defines as its vision a qualitatively sustainable productivity growth in a way that supports the improvement of the quality of working life and thus the retention of employees in working life. The aim is therefore both rapid productivity growth and a high employment rate. Both are important: together with productive capital, they are fundamental pillars of our economic well-being and therefore of our standard of living. The population is getting older. This means that unless something changes, our economic well-being can no longer be increased by increasing the number of stubs. The average retirement age in Finland is still low. The aim of the pension reform is to increase it. The financial incentive to continue working is now greater than before. But what is very important when making mental decisions is how the competence and experience of the mature worker is valued in the field and how well the employee is able to take into account the differences due to the age-related factors of the worker. ********************* Today, however, I will focus on the challenge of productivity growth. Why productivity growth is becoming more central and why changes and organisation of the world of work play a major role in this? The increase in total factor productivity means that more intelligent work is done and the available capital is managed more efficiently than before. The growth in total factor productivity is mainly due to technological development. Many economists compare technology to a recipe  it includes information on how to make food ingredients into an even better meal. Technology is the knowledge of how inputs can be used to turn into products and services. In the early 1990s, it was still generally thought in Europe that productivity growth was in order here. Indeed, since the sharp crisis in the United States in the early 1970s, productivity growth had been clearly lower than in Europe. Unlike in Europe, in the United States, the main source of growth at that time was the increase in employment. The situation changed in the mid-1990s, although it was only discovered later. In the United States, economic growth accelerated sharply. A key reason for this was the acceleration of productivity growth. In Europe, on the other hand, the pace of economic growth slowed down. One of the reasons was the decrease in the number of jobs entering the market. An even more important factor, however, was the slowdown in productivity growth. As a rule, the turning point is only detected afterwards. Delays are therefore one of the greatest challenges for policy-makers: when the Lisbon Summit was held in March 2000, nothing was said yet about the problems of slow productivity growth. Not too much about the challenge posed by Asia. Today, neither topic is ignored. In the European Commission, since 2000, we have invested a great deal of research into finding out why the difference between Europe and the United States in terms of productivity growth is due. The study showed that the difference is related to the development of computers and information and communication technologies. Their development is as significant a thing as the telegram, which began about 100 years ago. The development of ICT technologies explains the difference in productivity growth between Europe and the United States for two reasons: on the one hand, because in the United States the ICT manufacturing industry is an important industry. On the other hand, productivity growth in the United States has been accelerated by the large-scale adoption of ict in various sectors of the economy, especially in services. Robert Solow, a Nobel economist, had said in 1987, "I see computers everywhere except in productivity statistics." This may have been the case at first, but not anymore. The weight of the ICT industry in the USA is much greater than in Europe. Therefore, its favourable productivity performance is reflected significantly more in the indicators of the economy as a whole than in Europe. One of the reasons for Finland's high productivity figures by European standards has been the high share of the ICT industry in our economy. Another important explainer has been the development of services. Computers alone were not enough for this, but the sales effect of various information and communication networks and the Internet was needed. When, for example, databases could be shared cheaply from anywhere, information costs plummeted. Retail and wholesale trade were the biggest gainers in the US, but financial services have also increased their productivity sharply. The same thing has not happened in Europe. What to do? In the case of private services, only competition encourages companies to innovate and also to increase productivity. As the pressure of competition increases in the market, it forces companies to take advantage of the opportunities created by ICTs to improve productivity. In this way, competition forces innovation and increased productivity. Competition my lowers prices. This, in turn, increases real earnings. When real earnings increase, demand rises. This, in turn, creates jobs and investment. And this will increase growth and well-being. The Bank of Finland has made a whole series of calculations on the matter using its own Aino model. ********************* Economic growth is quite young in history. It began with the Industrial Revolution. Finland fell into disrepair at the beginning, but caught up with the strong development of the 1900s. In the 1900s, Finland was one of the fastest growing national economies in Europe. Finland learned to hyphenate telegrams quickly. Telegram was used to refine forests and ores, and thanks to it, productivity grew rapidly: When Finland closed down to other industrialized nations after the war, productivity increased by at best 5 percent per year. It was then that the standard of living of citizens doubled in 14 years. It should be remembered that in the last century the working week was reduced from 60 hours to less than 40 hours. Still, the standard of living per capita increased 12-fold. This, if anything, tells us how productivity growth is at the heart of economic growth and increased well-being: In one hour of work, we can produce more than ten times more different products and services than we did 100 years ago. By the 1970s, Finland had exhausted the great potential of telegram as a driver of productivity. The ICT revolution has come since then. The capacity of microprocessors has doubled in a year and a half and the nominal price has remained unchanged. This has meant a sharp fall in real prices. At the same time, the prices of various telecommunications services have fallen the steepest among the services. What ICT technology and teletechnology have in common is that they are of general use: Telegram spread to almost all sectors of the economy, and industrialisation based on its use produced machines and equipment for people capable of processing raw materials into products more efficiently than by mere muscular power. The new information technology revolution, on the other hand, gives us the tools to use information more efficiently, it increases the "capacity of our brains". Falling prices have created countless new opportunities for the use of information technology. What, then, was the reason for Solow's dilemma: for a long time, computers appeared everywhere except in productivity statistics? ********************* Changes in organizations and work processes In advanced economies, productivity growth depends not only on technological innovation itself, but also on the organisational changes that technological innovation makes possible. The widespread use of information and communication technologies and computers makes it possible to develop new, better production and jobs in almost all sectors of the economy. Ict has enabled, for example, major changes in working processes and in the organisation of companies and institutions. Significant new innovations have become also possible in the value and supply chains or in the organization of customer relationships. In order for new technologies and production methods to be successfully introduced, further efforts are needed in the organization of work, organizational renewal and the processes of enterprise and management. They also require significant investments in skills. When studying the impact of computerisation on the output of enterprises, it has been found that initially the increases in output roughly correspond to the cost of the investment. But in the longer term (3-7 years), the output can exceed the cost many times over.1 The increase in longer-term output can be 2-5 times the short-term output. These figures help to understand why private companies operating in a competitive market may have a strong incentive not only to adopt new technologies, but also to try to reorganise and change the way they operate in the past. Depending on the situation, the increased productivity achieved as a combined effect of these changes may be a source of survival, competitive advantage, or both for the company. There can be many types of organizational changes. One study has compared two different reforms, increasing the grouping and lowering the hierarchy2. Lowering the hierarchy affects the flow of information in the company, while increasing the grouping affects the flow of information in a project or task. The study found that the benefits of IT investments are clearly greater if combined with organisational changes in the workplace. The differences in productivity gains caused by thinning the hierarchy and increasing grouping were quite small. It was considered to mean that the key productivity benefits in both are the same: improved information flow and increased motivation among employees. The relationship between ICT use and organisational change has generally been guided by two conclusions: The successful implementation of change requires innovative leaders and a person with a positive attitude towards change. 1 Brynjolfsson Erik ja Hitt, Lorin M: Computing produvtivity: firm level evidence, MIT 2003 2 Bertchek,Irene ja Kaiser, Urlich: Productivity Effects of Organizational Changes, Microeconomic Evidence, Mannheim 2003. ********************* On the importance of education and skills Often, the productivity impact of information technology is considered to require not only a change in the organization and work of the company, but also an increase in the level of education of the employees. To return to an earlier recipe parable: You can't get a tasty meal from a dish even with a good recipe unless the chef has the basic skills needed for cooking. On a general level, as the development of information and communication technologies has accelerated, it has been observed that the demand for unskilled workers has declined and employment has increased. The better the education of the worker, the less stupidity there is. This is partly explained by the fact that the successful introduction of new technologies has required the recruitment of well-trained workers. When we take a closer look, the connection between education and information technology is more complex. When we talk about companies with a high level of investment in research and development, the importance of high education is very great. This is particularly the case in the ICT industry and innovation. On the other hand, when you look at the use and application of ICT, it is not that straightforward. Studies have examined how, for example, the steel smelting process uses INFORMATION AND COMMUNICATION TECHNOLOGIES and how it has changed the training requirements and jobs of workers.3 I believe that the same conclusions apply to many sectors of the process industry. Until twenty years ago, the worker was often a very concrete part of the ty and production process: he was physically part of it and performed mechanical tasks. Today, gunners monitor and monitor the process from computers. The process itself may not have changed much and therefore it must be mastered by the worker. The advantage of new computer applications lies in the fact that software helps to control and control the production process as a whole: They collect information about the entire process and transfer it for the user to see. At the same time, he now sees much more. The big difference in the most advanced companies is that the focus of stub and training has shifted from mechanical tasks to problem solving and better information sharing. The working ones are changed more often. In the past, the situation may have been different: When a problem arose, the stubborn conveyed information about it to his superior. Now he seeks to solve it himself, before small problems become big ones. If the problems are major, he will urgently convene a group of people who know the different sides of the issue. 3 Shaw, Kathryn: By What Means Does IT Affect Employment and Wages seka Chennels, Lucy ja van Reenen, John: Technical Change and Structure of Employment and Wages; teoksessa Productivity, Inequality and the Digital Economy , ed. Greenan, Nathalie etc., MIT 2002, I said above that it is in the field of services that productivity has risen the most since the use of information technology. Does this always mean that basic training for workers should at the same time rise rapidly? If this were the case, the changes would be slow. It is essential for productivity growth that all the workers involved in the process are able to use the information technology required for it. Often the best solution is for a significant number of employees to be involved in the project when new information or control systems are developed and applied in practice. They are familiar with the products and services and their flow. For control systems, the whole process becomes more transparent and easy to perceive. The same work is done, but more meaningfully and efficiently. This insight is pivotal. Therefore, training can be effective if it is done alongside work. When a company operates in a competitive situation, the pressure of competition is an important incentive for the company's management. If a company is unable to increase its productivity, competitors of the new one threaten to push it out of the market. Those competitors can come from home or from outside. But on the other hand, raising productivity requires investment, the renewal of companies and their processes, and the training and broad commitment of personnel. How to succeed in this task? It is important that the entire personnel knows and knows the company's situation in the market and the challenges it brings, and that it shares the company's vision and values. It is the foundation of commitment. Secondly, it is important to understand that increasing productivity does not simply mean increasing "grinding". Increasing productivity in the IT environment requires the introduction of new processes and production methods, as well as the development of new products and services. Getting everyone's creative power and also independent judgment and decision-making ability to develop a company is key. Thirdly, the great challenge is that external changes can be unpredictably rapid. They are always a challenge for corporate management. But on the other hand, unless the staff trusts that increasing productivity will improve the company's future prospects and thus the retention of jobs in the future, the confidence required for commitment may be too low. Therefore, in a situation of change, it is important to safeguard trust. ********************* What about the public sector? Above, I said how more competition forces companies to innovate and increase their productivity. This has happened and will continue to happen, particularly in the private service sector. But what to do on the public side, which is often protected from competition? For the public sector, ageing creates its own additional challenges. There will be fewer stubs in the workplace than there will be in retirement. Even more so than before, the development of well-being depends on an increase in productivity. It is precisely for these reasons  that is, the lack of competition and the ageing of the population  that improving the productivity of public services is a major challenge for our national economy. At the same time, however, it is a my chance, because many public services are very knowledge-intensive. This means that their digitization will allow for a high increase in productivity and better services for people. In Finland, a lot of effort has been put into measuring the productivity of public services. It is not without its problems. How to take into account the quality of services? How to measure safety? Productivity figures do not always measure the actual performance of public services. It may also happen that if some unnecessary bureaucratic task is abandoned, it means in mechanical calculations that productivity will fall. But even then, the same productivity logic must work in public services. We need to do more with tax money: we need to be able to produce either more services or better quality, or preferably both. Of course, progress has been made in some areas in Finland. For example, the tax reporting procedure has been modernized. Declarations are processed digitally and the citizen receives a tax proposal, which in most cases is accepted. Many steps forward have been taken in this agreement. But in large areas of public services, such as health care, the potential is extraordinarily great in relation to achievements. We need compatible systems, we need secure solutions and we need determined and committed management. Often, the organizational and process changes required for productivity growth fail due to internal opposition or mutual hand-wringing within the administration. A breakthrough will come only if the management has a strong vision and a lot of perseverance. Productivity is not increased by IT specialists, although their input is required. Productivity rises only when work and its processes are reorganized. And that's something that management can't delegate to anyone. Municipal decision-makers and senior officials of government agencies and institutions are a lot of guards. Finland has a wide and well-educated population. It is important to unleash the creative power of everyone to seek better solutions for the organization of jobs and services. It requires good leadership and the right incentives. ********************* In conclusion, I would like to emphasize that future prosperity will be based on increased productivity. Information and communication technologies make this possible, but the prerequisite is the renewal of work organisations and processes combined with the training of personnel. This requires innovative leadership and the commitment of the personnel. Everyone has their own responsibility.

Title: Remarks by Ms Sinikka Salo in the conference "Changing Foresight Practices in Regional Development - Global Pressures and Regional Possibilities"
text: FINANCIAL INTEGRATION FROM A REGIONAL PERSPECTIVE Remarks by Ms Sinikka Salo in the conference "Changing Foresight Practices in Regional Development  Global Pressures and Regional Possibilities" in Turku 9th June 2006 1. Introduction Financial markets are often seen as forerunners in globalisation. This is understandable, since the immaterial and weightless nature of money seems to make geography less relevant in the world of finance than in most other industries. It is easy to present examples which lend support to the view of finance-led globalisation. Money can move from one part of the world to another in seconds, and contracts worth hundreds of millions of euro are made daily in the financial markets, over the telephone, between parties based on different continents. In Helsinki, for example, we may check the prices of shares traded on the New York Stock Exchange at least as quickly and with greater precision than the prices of vegetables in the open-air market of our home town. The picture of financial markets as extremely globalised is only partly true, however. It is true that, for some parts of the financial markets, geography has lost its importance already a long time ago, but there are others where international and regional integration is still incomplete and on-going. In the last ten years, highly significant progress has taken place in this area. Let me start my brief survey of what financial integration means from a regional perspective by considering some of the recent developments in Europe and in the world as a whole. After that, I will discuss the regional implications of the ongoing integration process and finally close with some policy-related remarks. 2. Trends in financial integration in Europe Let me review European financial markets first. Europe has, of course, a long history of international capital movements, both in the form of short-term hot money flows and as foreign direct investment in industries across national borders. Trueintegration of European financial markets is much more recent, however. The most visible sign so far of financial integration in Europe is the euro, the creation of which indeed started a new era of financial integration in the area. After the adoption of the common currency in 1999, money markets in the euro area were rapidly integrated and interest rates were unified as the result. So, financial conditions in the macroeconomic sense are now pretty much the same throughout the whole euro area. However, in Europe, and more specifically in the euro area, large and very important parts of the financial market are not yet completely integrated. Retail banking markets, for example, today remain mainly national in nature, so that a cross-border supply of housing loans or deposit accounts is a rare exception rather than the norm. Securities markets are similarly still organised on a national, country-by-country basis so that the trading of stocks issued in another country usually requires rather expensive custody arrangements. The clearing and settlement stage of international share transactions in particular is much more expensive than similar transactions in the domestic market. Other areas where Europe is still financially fragmented include the payment system and the venture capital market. In practice all this fragmentation means that, at least for entities other than banks and large multinational companies, national borders still matter a great deal in European finance. The European situation is not stagnant, however. EU authorities, and the Commission and also the European Central Bank in particular, are pushing hard towards a more complete financial integration of the EU. Last December, the Commission published an important White Paper defining its financial services strategy for the following five years. The goals listed in this paper include a stronger integration of retail markets in banking, insurance, securities, and asset management. Another goal is international supervisory convergence, which is obviously important in the context of financial integration. Finally, the Commission wants Europe to be active also on the global stage, going for active liberalisation of financial services in the context of the WTO negotiations, and intensifying regulatory dialogue with the US and other trading partners of the EU in the international financial markets. Parallel to the work of the Commission and the ECB, the private sector  markets themselves  is also preparing for much closer integration. Very important in this regard are the attempts of the stock exchanges to create larger European and even global market places for the trading of securities. Stock exchange business in its modern form requires large fixed investments in information infrastructure and has therefore very large economies of scale. Trading costs can be greatly reduced if the processing of trades is concentrated into bigger centres. At first, mergers and acquisitions within the stock exchange industry seek to exploit these economies of scale through sharing technology and possibly also processing capacity, and by doing so, cutting costs of trading to a fraction of present levels. In the medium term, the integration of stock exchanges can also be expected to result in the pooling of listings to form larger, European-level trading lists and the creation of truly unified market places. Turning to financial institutions, the international consolidation of banking and insurance industries has been long overdue, with the exception of the Nordic area and the Benelux Countries, but it is very likely to gain pace at some not too distant point in the future. The reasons are not too different from those which are now transforming the stock exchange industry. The increasing complexity of both technology and regulation is increasing the economies of scale in banking, too, and is therefore building up pressure for reorganisations in the form of mergers and acquisitions. Meanwhile, the largest euro area commercial banks have formed a new organisation, the European Payments Council, to coordinate the creation of a Single Euro Payments Area as required by the ECB and the Commission. 3. Globalisation and finance Globally, the degree of financial integration achieved so far is obviously less than in the euro area or even in the EU as a whole. However, the changes which have taken place at the global level, and are still on-going, have such huge proportions that calling them epic would be no exaggeration. The most important part of these developments is the entry of developing Asia into the global financial markets, both as a target and a source of international investment. In particular, the emergence of China as a major player in international financial markets has brought 1, 300 million people in contact with worlds capital resources for the first time. The financial liberalisation of India, with its 1, 000 million inhabitants, has as large potential as China to transform the world economy. It seems certain that not more than a small part of the eventual impact on the world financial markets arising from the opening up of these giant Asian economies has been felt up till now, and much more is yet to come. As we all know, this prospect has attracted an enormous amount of public attention in the last years. Much of the current globalisation debate has been in terms of an alleged flight of capital to Asia but the facts do not support this idea. In fact, developing Asia has been a large scale capital exporter, rather than importer, ever since the Asian crisis of 1997. What this means is that any investment from the developed west to developing Asia has been more than matched by investment to the opposite direction, from these relatively poor countries to world financial markets  ultimately much of it in U.S. government securities. In view of this, a fair characterization of the Asian participation in globalisation so far could be that it has mainly happened in markets for industrial exports and raw materials imports rather than in capital markets. It has been mainly based on rapid acquisition of technological and commercial know-how, and the deregulation which has allowed the Chinese and Indian factories to put this know-how into use. True, much of the technological transfer has been made possible by foreign direct investment in China and India, but so far the net capital flow has scarcely reflected the meeting of China's and India's capital needs and the capital resources of the developed world. The reasons why the full potential of developing Asia has not yet been felt in the international financial markets can be found in the painful experience of the Asian crisis of 1997. The crisis was caused by extensive over-borrowing by a number of countries in the form of short-term bank loans. The lesson from the crisis was that it exposed the weakness of institutions which are needed to channel capital from developed to the developing world. Serious problems existed in the risk management of the lending banks, but especially in the management practices, economic transparency, and the legal systems of the Asian countries. Since the crisis, Asian governments have been reluctant to allow large-scale dependence on foreign capital, and are effectively using all funds flowing into their countries to accumulate foreign exchange reserves rather than importing more capital goods. Thus they have chosen an export-led growth strategy which uses domestic saving as the ultimate source of financing their rapid growth. This cautious strategy has caused a lot of frustration in the West, as developing Asia exports much more to the developed world than imports from it. However, after the Asian crisis, the international community has started a large scale effort to increase the stability of the global financial markets and so to create better, more secure environment for investing in the developing countries. The International Monetary Fund, in particular, started to work consistently for ensuring sound economic governance in all countries of the world. Traditionally, the role of the IMF was to provide emergency support for countries getting into balance-of-payments difficulties such as currency crises. The new role of the IMF is more preventive. It has started two very important programmes for benchmarking economic policy and economic institutions across the world. Under the so-called ROSC programme, the IMF reviews the observance of international standards and codes in the areas of (1) economic and fiscal transparency and availability of data; (2) financial sector standards such as the state of financial supervision, reliability of the payments system, and combating the financing of terrorism; (3) market integrity, including standards for corporate governance, accounting and auditing, and (4) insolvency procedures and creditor rights in each country. In another important programme, the so called Financial Sector Assessment Program, the IMF looks at and reports on the soundness and stability of the financial sector in each country. Participation in these IMF programs is voluntary, and the Asian giants have not yet joined in, but peer pressure and the prospect of concrete benefits in the form of better creditworthiness encourages more and more countries to join these efforts to improve the performance and stability of international financial markets. All in all, this brief review of current developments in international financial integration suggests that even though financial markets are global, they are far from being fully integrated yet, and the full effects of financial integration are still to be felt. 4. Regions in financial integration The world economy as a whole should benefit greatly from more integration. Financial integration is expected to accelerate economic growth and productivity, as the growing supply of finance and new productive investment opportunities projects are matched more efficiently with each other than before. The distributive and regional effects of integration are much more complicated, however. An analysis of the effects on economic regions of the kind of financial integration we are currently experiencing is particularly challenging. This is due to two main reasons. First of all, the current financial integration cannot be analysed simply as a case of economic regions moving from financial isolation to sharing a common financial market. That would be the standard approach of international economics, but it does not apply very well. In fact, regions  meaning areas smaller than a country  have been for a long time already financially integrated at the national level. In Finland, for example, the national financial markets have been quite well unified for a long time  certainly for decades  so that speaking of some specific financial markets of the Turku region, where we now are, is not very meaningful. Money, credit and financial investments flow quite smoothly within Finland from one region to another and financial conditions are not too different in different parts of the country. The same can be said of all developed countries nowadays. This being the case, the impact of financial integration on economic regions cannot be analysed satisfactorily by using the simplest tools of international economics or economic geography. Instead, we must ask, how financial integration between nations affects economic regionswithin countries. This is a much more complicated question, because we cannot assume that international financial integration will have a similar impact on all regions within a given country, and secondly, because regions have different policy concerns than nations: national economic policy has to do with "hard" things like taxation and financial regulation. Regional policy makers, however, are more concerned on things which can be regionally differentiated, like infrastructure and education, as well as promoting cooperation between firms in regional industrial clusters, etc. Hence, the emphasis on soft and proactive kinds of policy is greater at the regional than national level. The second reason which complicates the analysis of the impact of financial integration is that we are not mainly interested in the impact of integration on the financial services industry itself, but rather on the impact of financial integration on the regional economy as a whole. This contrasts with the standard approach which would analyze the effect of integration of an industry on the structure and performance of that same industry. Here, however, we are mostly interested in the effects outside the financial services industry. Focusing on these "second-round" or indirect effects of financial integration is essential because in most regions, the financial services industry is relatively small part of the economy. In Finland, for example, financial services account for about 1.6 per cent of all jobs, and in Germany, 3 per cent. While the direct employment effects of financial services are not negligible, it is clear that the indirect effects of the financial industry are much greater. This is because finance is a necessary input to virtually any sector of the modern economy, and the performance of financial markets is therefore a precondition of good performance of the economy as a whole. How does finance influence the rest of the economy? The financial markets are, firstly, a market for channelling savings to investment; secondly, a market for risk; thirdly, a market for corporate control; and, finally, they provide an infrastructure for making payments. These functions of financial markets are in fact studied by quite different branches of economic theory, and a unified theory of the role of financial markets in the economy is therefore not really available. The market for savings is analysed by macroeconomics; the market for risk is analysed using the theory of finance; and the market for corporate control is analysed using the theory of industrial organisation. Finally, the intermediation of payments is usually analysed in the context of monetary theory (or recently, network economics). In many financial relationships, these different functions of financial markets appear intertwined, but nevertheless they are conceptually separate and their purposes and impacts on financial integration are also different. 5. The functions of finance in the economy 5.1. Market for savings The ongoing financial integration process concerns each of the four functions of financial markets. Therefore, we must take all of them into account when trying to get a full picture of what future financial integration will mean to regions. Let us look at the macroeconomic aspect first. Viewed from this perspective, what the financial markets do is transfer resources in time and in space. From the point of view of a saver, financial markets are useful, because they help them to transfer their resources forward in time  just as from the point of view of a borrower, the markets enable a transfer of resources backwards, from the future to the present. From the geographic point of view, however, the very same transfer of resources happens in space: the resources flow from the location of the saver to the location of investment. From that perspective the perspective of financial intermediation in space the resources are not moved in time at all, but only from one place to another. There is reason to believe that the importance of intercontinental capital flows could even grow in the future. This is because some economic fundamentals suggest that regional differences in the propensity to save and invest should grow in the future. One of the fundamentals is population ageing in the highly developed parts of the world. This ageing, especially in Europe and Japan will increase saving in these parts of the world and keep investment demand there relatively subdued. This could mean that Europe would join Japan as one of the significant capital exporters of the world  unless Europes government deficits remain too large and use resources which otherwise could be invested productively in the emerging economies of the world. The effect of financial integration of the market for savings is that the market rates of return on capital will generally converge as a result of it. At the same time, both saving and investment will increase, because on average, savers will get a higher rate of return for saving, and similarly on average, investors capital costs will decline. Who actually collects the benefits from this process depends on the initial situation of savers and investors in different parts of the world. The classical view of this process emphasises the equalising force of financial integration. According to this view, the rate of return for capital is generally highest in countries or regions where capital is relatively scarce and other resources relatively ample; by the same token, the rate of return is lowest where capital is relatively ample. The effect of financial integration is, consequently, to equalise the capital intensities of regions and hence equalise productivity and real income differentials as well. The classical view may, however, be too simplistic. As the result of the emergence of the so-called "new economic geography" (a school of thought associated especially with Paul Krugman and his co-authors), the classical view is no longer seen as the whole story. New economic geography emphasises the importance of economies of scale in many industries. In those industries, the rate of return on capital is not necessarily a declining function of previous investment, but may well be anincreasing function of the amount of capital which has previously been invested ("sunk") in a particular industry in a particular region. For these kinds of industries, the integration of markets can lead to agglomeration and concentration to centres where the economies of large-scale operation can be best achieved. A perfect example of the economics of agglomeration is the financial services industry itself. Especially in securities markets, the benefits of large scale operation are so important that the financial services industry concentrates in great cities such as London or Frankfurt even though the cost of labour and land is higher in these financial centres than in other cities. Fortunately, the benefits of concentration emphasised by new economic geography can also be achieved in smaller cities, at least in the case of narrowly focused niche industries. Even Finland has several examples of firms which are world class players in their markets even though they may not be very big companies as such and even if they are not located in some large metropolis. 5.2. Market for risks Let us now turn to the second function of financial markets, to transfer risk. Financial markets allow investors to diversify their assets so that the overall riskiness of their portfolios is reduced. Also, the markets allow entrepreneurs to sell some of their business risks to outside investors so that firms can grow faster and take more investment risk. The markets also price risks and this affects capital costs for firms and the return expectations of savers. Generally, riskier projects must have higher rates of return than less risky ones in order to be realized. Financial integration will mean that some of the risks which were not possible to get rid of before, will become diversifiable risks after integration. So, the process of financial integration reduces the prices of those risks which it helps to diversify. Because of this, capital costs of firms are reduced and, at the same time, the obtainable risk/return mix is improved for savers. Because certain risks will become cheaper, they depress financial asset prices less than before integration and therefore required rates of return decline and asset prices generally appreciate as a result of increased diversification possibilities. The biggest gainers from this are the companies which, before integration, represented dominant risks in their home country but which thanks to integration can spread their ownership and their business risks internationally. Nokia is a perfect example of this. It would be very risky and virtually impossible to have an industrial giant like Nokia in Finland without the broad international ownership made possible by financial integration. What then is the regional dimension of the increasing possibilities to diversify investment risks in world markets? An important effect is that integration makes it possible for companies, operating in their home regions, to finance larger investments and specialise in a more courageous way than they otherwise could. Thus, financial integration favours, or even enables, greater regional specialisation and concentration of business, especially for those companies which are large enough to benefit from the possibility of an internationally diversified ownership. Another side of the same coin is that, as a result of increased diversification of asset holdings, savers are able to isolate themselves better from economic fluctuations happening in their home region. 5.3. Market for control The third function of financial markets is to transfer control. Buying a large number of shares in a company will give the investor some control in its management. Actually, corporate control is at least as important object of trading in the stock market than funds themselves. This has very important economic functions, because if the market works well, control will end up with those owners who can put resources to most efficient use. Also, selling some corporate control to outside investors will enable innovators get much more capital than would be possible otherwise. This is actually the main principle of the venture capital industry. In financial integration, the market for corporate control will work so as to spread the most efficient management methods from region or country to another. Companies which could be better managed will change owners and be reorganised. The effect of this is that the market value of "best practice" management and "best practice" technologies will increase at the expense of substandard management and production practices. The market for corporate control is thus crucial for innovation and productivity improvements. Over the last ten years, financial integration has had the greatest effect just through the market for corporate control. This is apparent from the example of China, which has been a major exporter of capital since 1997, for about 10 years now. As I already mentioned, in net terms, China has been investing abroad more than other countries have invested in China. But for Chinese development, the important thing has not been the net capital flow  which was outward in any case  but foreign direct investment. The effect of this is that instead of capital as such, China has been importing foreign control, management and technology in a very large scale and this has actually revolutionized the Chinese economy and also the world economy in the process. In the public debate in the press about international financial integration, the corporate control aspect of integration is carried out under the rubric "foreign ownership". In the media, the question is posed by contrasting international, distant ownership with local or national ownership. The popular worry is that distant ownership is by its nature destructive, whereas local ownership is often seen as more sensitive to requirements of fairness. Regionally, the international integration of the market for corporate control means that global instead of national best practice increasingly becomes the norm for the efficiency of corporate management. Another beneficial effect is that new start-up companies could have a wider choice of potential investors to contact, and consequently a higher probability of finding one with enough expertise to understand the particular business idea in question, whatever than may be in each case. The importance of control and trust for financial relationships is very important. At the fundamental level this is so because of problems of asymmetric information which are inherent to financial contracts. Economists classify these problems to cases of "hidden action", where monitoring and shared responsibility is needed to ensure that both parties fulfil their share of the contract, and to cases of "hidden information" where screening and risk sharing is important to make sure that projects or securities are as good as they are claimed to be when financial contracts are made. The importance of monitoring, screening and control emphasise the value of proximity. This is why information concerns put certain limits to how far financial integration can go. As I have already pointed out, financial integration in itself is a force which favours the concentration of financial activities to larger units and to large financial centres. However, this force will mainly be felt in those financial services which are possible to render "at arm's length". These services include securities, deposits, payments, and nowadays even routine insurance and consumer credit. It can be argued, however, that there also exist categories of financial services which cannot be commoditised to be rendered at arm's length. These are services where tacit information on companies, individuals or investment projects is necessary for successful business. The best example of this is the venture capital finance of start-up companies. Private equity investment to small and medium-sized companies is by definition not commoditised, because if it was, the stock could be traded in open markets. But the nature of information problems implies that the stocks in small firms are more valuable to the venture capitalist that knows the firm and its management and has some control in the way it is developed. Private equity investment does not necessarily need to be locally or regionally based. Indeed, financial integration can well increase such investment in the long range, because specialised expertise can be at least as important for successful investment as geographical proximity. However, other things being equal, distance does matter in private investment. Thus, we can predict that information concerns will remain a counterforce to pressures for geographic concentration, in those categories of financial services in which private information is essential. 5.4. Provision of a payment system Last but not least in the list of the functions where financial integration will matter is the payment system. The current fragmentation of the payment system is most serious in the segment of retail payments, meaning the payments to and from households and small firms. This is, first and foremost, a hindrance to effective competition in the financial services industry. If fast, reliable, and unified international systems of account transfers and direct debit were established, the market for such financial services as mortgages, time deposits, asset management, and life insurance would become much more competitive. The currently high fees charged on international credit card transactions could also be reduced by more intense competition in that sector. In the medium term, further progress in the international integration of the payments industry can mainly be expected in the euro area where the creation of the Single Euro Payments Area is already under way. The completion of that project will not only facilitate payments in the area but also make financial services more competitive. In this way, the benefits to businesses from operating in the euro are would be strengthened. 6. Conclusions from a regional perspective To conclude, financial integration holds great promise in terms of growth efficiency and economic opportunities, but also requires significant adjustments in public policy and private business performance. Financial integration is a great equaliser in the sense that the more it progresses, the less geography matters for the provision and availability of financial services. However, this does not necessarily mean that regions will become more equal as a result. When financial barriers go down, the importance of other regional factors than finance is emphasised. This means that the quality of less mobile factors such as the skills of the labour force, communications and other local infrastructure, and the level of informal business networks in the region, will become much more important for economic success than before. Where these prerequisites for success are not competitive, the region will suffer economically from financial integration despite the increasingly equal access to financial services. In fact, it is the increasingly equal access to finance which is precisely the reason why other dimensions of competitiveness will grow in importance. It is interesting to note that those dimensions of competitiveness which are emphasised by financial integration are usually the responsibility of policy makers at the local or regional level. This means that financial integration increases the responsibility of local governments for the economic success of the regions where they work and also emphasises the importance of regional coordination of policies regarding things such as infrastructure, education, and business promotion. However, there are limits to how far financial integration can proceed. As I mentioned, these limits are determined by the fact that many financial relationships require trust and information that is hard to establish from a distance. As the structure of financial services is likely to consolidate in the future to bigger units and continue to concentrate in large cities, these information concerns constitute a counterforce to these tendencies, especially in the financing of small, growing, and medium sized firms. But even the venture capital industry and the financing of SME's cannot escape the fact that sufficient scale is necessary for financial services. Also in the future, small and diverse concentrations of firms will find financing more difficult than larger and more specialised ones. Therefore, in order to combine the benefits of specialised information, geographic proximity and efficient size, the creation of strong, specialised business clusters will be even more essential in the future to ensure the success of region in the environment of international financial integration, financial consolidation, and tougher competition. It is the challenge of local policy makers and business communities to act as catalysts for the formation of such structures.

Title: The EU and post-industrial Finland
text: Dr. Sinikka Salo, Member of the Governing Board bank of Finland The EU and post-industrial Finland Lecture in Vienna on 20.6.2006 Dear Sir or Madam! This year Finland celebrates the 200th birthday of the philosopher and statesman Johan Vilhelm Snellman, after whom this seminar is named. In the field of finance, Snellman's most important achievement is not Finnmark, as is often assumed. Rather, as chairman of the Senate Finance Committee d0 according to today's terminology as Minister of Finance d0 he played a decisive role in pegging the Finnish mark to the price of silver and removing the peg to the Russian ruble. Actually, the mark only became a real currency. The Tsar approved the monetary reform in November 1865 and it came into force in early March 1866. A good 130 years later, at the beginning of January 1999, Finland became one of the first EU countries to join the European Monetary Union, and responsibility for Finnish monetary policy went to the European Central Bank. Although this reform appeared to be the complete opposite of the currency reform of 1865, the same motive was behind it: the desire to stabilize Finnish monetary relations through the close link to the monetary stock of Western European countries. The next phase of our monetary integration began in 2002, when the Finnmark was also replaced by the euro in cash transactions. Before joining monetary union, there were lively discussions in Finland about the advantages and disadvantages of this step. The focus was on the specific characteristics of the Finnish economy: the one-sided industrial structure, the large share of trade with non-euro area countries and the economy's traditional susceptibility to inflation. There was a risk that so-called asymmetric congestion would have a stronger economic impact in Finland than in other euro area countries. According to the critics, the asymmetric structures were a serious, if not the decisive argument against joining the monetary union. I do not share this view myself, but I can understand it to a certain extent in the light of our history. Snellman and most of his contemporaries were unfamiliar with the idea of compensating for economic fluctuations through monetary policy measures. Critical voices arose at the time, however, because Finnish monetary policy was very strict under the extraordinarily difficult conditions after the currency reform of 1865 in order to ensure the convertibility of Finnmark. We have now been a member of the monetary union for a good seven years. What is interesting is that many of the asymmetric strands that opponents of monetary union have warned about seem to have already occurred in this relatively short period of time. At the turn of the millennium, the information technology and telecommunications sector, which is very important for the Finnish economy, first experienced an Internet boom and then a recession. The exchange rate of the euro fell by almost 30 percent against the US dollar in the first two years and then recovered by 50 percent. The price of oil has risen many times over during the time of monetary union. Contrary to what critics expected, however, the external pressures of the turn of the millennium did not plunge the Finnish economy into an inflationary spiral. The recession in the information technology and telecommunications sectors and the strengthening of the euro have also risen to the country without any major damages. In retrospect, it can be said that the common monetary policy of the Finnish economy is very well developed despite the asymmetric structures. The clearest evidence is that inflation in Finland is in line with the European Central Bank's definition of price stability. In recent years, Finland has been one of the EU countries with the lowest inflation rate, while employment and output have grown quite well compared to most euro area countries. The profitability level of the industry is also good, largely thanks to the industry's own measures. The Finnish experience seems to suggest that a large currency area and the stability provided by a strong institution such as the central bank offer better economic opportunities for citizens and companies in the long run. The separate monetary policy of a single small economy always has a harder time creating in the conflict of roles between the market and politics and can therefore fluctuate slightly. As a large and strong currency, the euro is a good protection for euro area countries against the pressure of the foreign exchange markets because it does not lend itself to speculative attacks in the same way as many of its predecessor currencies. At least as important for the security of the euro is the fact that monetary policy decisions in the euro area are largely independent of policy and pressure from different stakeholders. Economically highly developed countries are often referred to as industrial nations. This is in a way a paradox, because the production share of industry in these countries has steadily declined in recent decades. Services have become more important and now account for the largest share of production and employment in most industrialised countries. Instead of industrialized countries, one should speak more correctly of post-industrial countries. As can be seen from the title of my presentation, I count Finland among the post-industrial countries. Although the Finnish service sector has traditionally had a rather modest volume, it has grown in importance over the last twenty or thirty years. In 2003, the production share of the service sector in Finland was around 66 percent. By way of comparison, the share of services in total production in France in the same year was 73d074 percent and in Germany it was 70 percent. The service sector is less vulnerable to external activity than industry. Therefore, the high share of services in production explains why the common monetary policy is suitable for Finland and the other countries of the monetary union. A special feature of the Finnish service sector d0 and this also applies to the other Nordic countries d0 is the great importance of public welfare services such as health care, day care for children and care for the elderly. Public welfare services have given women the opportunity to combine their role as mothers with participation in the labour market, while at the same time providing them with jobs in the public sector. About 80 percent of the workers in this sector are women. Women's employment in Finland is already well above the 60 percent target set by the EU for 2010. Due to the high level of employment of women, the overall employment rate in Finland is relatively high at 68 percent, higher than in most EU countries. Almost a quarter of Finland's workforce works in the public sector. The EU aims to increase the share of research and product development to three percent of gross national product by 2010. In Finland, this goal has already been achieved. Expenditure on research and development amounted to 3.5 percent of gross national product in 2004. Expenditure on research and product development accounts for only around one per cent of gross national product; the largest part of the expenditure in this area is financed by private companies. Half of the expenditure on research and development goes to information and communication technology. This reflects, on the one hand, the importance of this sector in Finland and, on the other hand, the importance of research in this sector. It is estimated that the mobile phone and telephone network manufacturer Nokia accounts for thirty percent of total research and product development expenditure in Finland and almost ffzig percent of private financing. The specialization in information and communication technology since the beginning of the nineties has been a great success for Finnish industry and has accelerated the growth of production and exports. However, Finland seems to have already left the peak growth in this area behind. International competition has intensified. In order to work close to the customer and reduce costs, the companies have distributed their production and procurement to different parts of the world. What is interesting about this development is that it was relatively easy to relocate the production of these products d0 including high-tech products d0 to emerging markets, while the service-rich parts of the production chain such as headquarters, research and product development tend to remain in the country. Finland seems to be moving closer to Sweden, where the share of high-tech production and exports is only in line with the international average, even though research intensity is at world level. This has nothing to do with the fact that the competitiveness of the companies has decreased or the market shares have shrunk, but with the fact that production has been relocated abroad. In the coming decade, Finnish production growth will hardly affect the technology industry in the same way as it did last year. An expansion of the private sector is also unlikely; on the contrary, this sector faces the challenge of introducing new technologies and increasing labour productivity. The increase in production and exports in Finland will increasingly depend on private services. Above all, information-intensive industries such as services for companies have a key role to play. Service companies that use technology and innovation have expanded faster than other companies in recent years. This rapid growth is expected to continue. The driving force behind the expansion of service companies is not only the aforementioned global division of labour with a focus on a high degree of further processing, but also the fact that industrial companies concentrate on their core competencies and outsource other activities to service companies. In addition, various intangible factors such as delivery times and delivery methods, trademarks and product image as well as maintenance and servicing are becoming increasingly important in competition, which further frustrates the demand for services for companies. Services play a crucial role not only in Finland, but also in the other post-industrial countries of the EU. The expansion of activity abroad is more or less imperative, especially for service companies in small countries, if they want growth and efficient production. The EU's internal market offers service companies in the member states good conditions for internationalisation. Internal market legislation has removed technical, legal, brocratic, cultural and protectionist barriers to trade between Member States. The introduction of the euro has removed an important obstacle to the proper functioning of the internal market, namely the uncertainty associated with the exchange rates of the Member States. In the field of services, the internal market has become a mixed reality. Certain segments of the financial markets are already well integrated and the internal market is already functioning very well for financial services. In 1999, the Commission proposed an action plan to fully liberalise the financial services market by 2005. Most of the plan's 42 initiatives have been implemented, but the financial services market has not yet unified to the end. The creation of a Single European Payments Area will be an important step forward for the financial services industry. This simplifies payment transactions in the euro area or the entire EU and can be processed just as securely and quickly as they are today within a country. This project of the private banks is to be fully implemented by 2010. For services other than financial services, the formation of the internal market is often still in its infancy. In order to improve the situation, in 2004 the European Commission drew up a proposal for a directive on services in the internal market. Last April, the Commission presented a new proposal which largely takes into account the compromise negotiated in the European Parliament. Although the new proposal dilutes the freren in some respects, it continues to cover a significant part of the services and thus nevertheless holds out the prospect of a significant improvement in the current situation. In Finland, a good forty percent of the workforce and turnover of all companies is expected to fall within the scope of the new proposal. I think it is important that the Commission's proposal be adopted without further weakening. Of course, the directive as such cannot remove all the obstacles to the proper functioning of the internal market in services, but it is in any case a step in the right direction. Dear Sir or Madam! Finland's experience with monetary union suggests that national differences and special interests are often overemphasized when weighing the pros and cons of common policies, while commonalities and common interests are easily overshadowed. Despite all doubts, the common monetary policy was also good for Finland, where the euro area seemed to deviate most from the "optimal currency area" in the run-up. This shows that post-industrial Finland is not as different from other EU countries as often thought. Finland is part of the post-industrial EU. Services account for the largest share of production and employment in the post-industrial EU. With regard to commercial growth, information-intensive service sectors such as business services play a particularly important role. Without an efficient pan-European internal market, there will be no expansion in this area. The internal market is particularly important for dynamic service enterprises in small countries whose growth opportunities are limited by the volume of the domestic market. There are still many obstacles to the well-functioning internal market in services. Eliminating them requires work and mhe from many sides, but I think that this work and mhe will be worthwhile. At best, the internal market in services will one day prove to be as successful as the euro and the common monetary policy.
text_original: Dr. Sinikka Salo, Mitglied des Direktoriums Bank von Finnland Die EU und das postindustrielle Finnland Vortrag in Wien am 20.6.2006 Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren! In diesem Jahr feiert Finnland den 200. Geburtstag des Philosophen und Staatsmanns Johan Vilhelm Snellman, nach dem dieses Seminar benannt ist. Auf dem Gebiet der Finanzwirtschaft ist Snellmans wichtigste Leistung nicht die Finnmark, wie oft angenommen wird. Vielmehr hat er als Vorsitzender des Finanzausschusses des Senats  nach der heutigen Terminologie als Finanzminister  entscheidend daran mitgewirkt, dass die finnische Mark an den Silberpreis gekoppelt und die Bindung an den russischen Rubel aufgehoben wurde. Eigentlich wurde die Mark erst damit zur echten Whrung. Der Zar billigte die Geldreform im November 1865 und Anfang Mrz 1866 trat sie in Kraft. Gut 130 Jahre spter, Anfang Januar 1999, trat Finnland als eines der ersten EU-Lnder der Europischen Whrungsunion bei, und die Verantwortung fr die finnische Geldpolitik ging an die Europische Zentralbank er. Obwohl diese Reform dem Augenschein nach das vollkommene Gegenteil der Whrungsreform von 1865 darstellte, stand dasselbe Motiv dahinter: das Bestreben, die finnischen Whrungsverhltnisse durch die enge Bindung an den Geldbestand der westeuropischen Lnder zu stabilisieren. Die nchste Phase unserer monetren Integration begann 2002, als die Finnmark auch im Bargeldverkehr durch den Euro ersetzt wurde. Vor dem Beitritt zur Whrungsunion gab es in Finnland lebhafte Diskussionen er die Vor- und Nachteile dieses Schritts. Dabei standen die besonderen Kennzeichen der finnischen Wirtschaft im Mittelpunkt: die einseitige industrielle Struktur, der groe Anteil des Handels mit Lndern, die nicht zum Eurogebiet gehren, und die traditionelle Inflationsanflligkeit der Wirtschaft. Es bestand die Befrchtung, dass so genannte asymmetrische Stungen in Finnland strkere wirtschaftliche Auswirkungen haben wrden als in anderen Lndern des Eurogebiets. Nach Meinung der Kritiker waren die asymmetrischen Strungen ein schwerwiegendes, wenn nicht gar das entscheidende Argument gegen den Beitritt zur Whrungsunion. Selbst teile ich diese Ansicht nicht, doch kann ich sie im Lichte unserer Geschichte bis zu einem gewissen Grad verstehen. Snellman und den meisten seiner Zeitgenossen war der Gedanke, Konjunkturschwankungen durch geldpolitische Manahmen auszugleichen, fremd. Kritische Stimmen erhoben sich seinerzeit jedoch, weil die finnische Geldpolitik unter den auerordentlich schwierigen Verhltnissen nach der Whrungsreform des Jahres 1865 sehr streng war, um die Konvertierbarkeit der Finnmark zu sichern. Jetzt sind wir gut sieben Jahre Mitglied der Whrungsunion. Interessant ist, dass viele der asymmetrischen Strungen, vor denen die Gegner der Whrungsunion gewarnt haben, bereits in dieser relativ kurzen Zeitspanne eingetreten zu sein scheinen. Die fr die finnische Wirtschaft sehr wichtige Informationstechnik- und Telekommunikationsbranche erlebte zur Jahrtausendwende erst einen Internet-Boom und danach eine Rezession. Der Wechselkurs des Euro sank im Verhltnis zum US-Dollar in den ersten zwei Jahren um fast 30 Prozent und erholte sich dann um 50 Prozent. Der lpreis ist in der Zeit der Whrungsunion um ein Vielfaches gestiegen. Anders als von den Kritikern erwartet, haben die externen Strungen der Jahrtausendwende die finnische Volkswirtschaft jedoch nicht in eine Inflationsspirale gestzt. Auch die Rezession in der Informationstechnik-und Telekommunikationsbranche und die Erstarkung des Euro hat das Land ohne grere Schden erstanden. Im Nachhinein kann man sagen, dass die gemeinsame Geldpolitik der finnischen Wirtschaft trotz der asymmetrischen Strungen sehr gut bekommen ist. Der deutlichste Beweis dafr ist die Tatsache, dass die Inflation in Finnland mit der Preisstabilittsdefinition der Europischen Zentralbank im Einklang steht. In den letzten Jahren gehrte Finnland zu den EU-Lndern mit der niedrigsten Inflationsrate, whrend die Beschftigung und die Produktion im Vergleich zu den meisten Euro-Lndern recht gut zugenommen haben. Auch das Rentabilittsniveau der Industrie ist gut, weitgehend dank eigener Manahmen der Industrie. Die finnischen Erfahrungen scheinen darauf hinzudeuten, dass ein groes Whrungsgebiet und die durch eine starke Institution wie die Zentralbank gegebene Stabilitt den Brgern und Unternehmen auf lange Sicht bessere wirtschaftliche Mglichkeiten bieten. Die separate Geldpolitik einer einzelnen kleinen Volkswirtschaft hat es im Rollenkonflikt von Markt und Politik stets schwerer zu erzeugen und kann deshalb leicht schwanken. Als groe und starke Whrung ist der Euro fr die Bger des Eurogebiets ein guter Schutz gegen den Druck der Devisenmrkte, weil er sich fr Spekulationsangriffe nicht so anbietet wie viele seiner Vorgngerwhrungen. Mindestens ebenso wichtig fr die Sicherheit des Euro ist der Umstand, dass geldpolitische Entscheidungen im Eurogebiet weitgehend unabhngig von der Politik und dem Druck unterschiedlicher Interessengruppen getroffen werden. *** Wirtschaftlich weit entwickelte Lnder werden gern als Industrienationen bezeichnet. Dies ist in gewisser Weise ein Paradox, weil der Produktionsanteil der Industrie in diesen Lndern in den letzten Jahrzehnten kontinuierlich zurckgegangen ist. Dienstleistungen sind wichtiger geworden und haben in den meisten Industrielndern heute den grten Anteil an der Produktion und der Beschftigung. Statt von Industrielndern sollte man richtiger von postindustriellen Lndern sprechen. Wie bereits aus dem Titel meines Vortrags hervorgeht, zhle ich Finnland zu den postindustriellen Lndern. Obwohl der finnische Dienstleistungssektor traditionell eher ein bescheidenes Volumen hatte, hat er in den letzten zwanzig, dreiig Jahren sprbar an Bedeutung gewonnen. 2003 lag der Produktionsanteil des Dienstleistungsgewerbes in Finnland bei rund 66 Prozent. Zum Vergleich sei gesagt, dass sich der Dienstleistungsanteil an der Gesamtproduktion in Frankreich im selben Jahr auf 7374 Prozent belief und in Deutschland auf 70 Prozent. Der Dienstleistungssektor ist weniger anfllig fr Stungen von auen als die Industrie. Deshalb ist der hohe Anteil der Dienstleistungen an der Produktion eine Erklrung dafr, warum die gemeinsame Geldpolitik fr Finnland und die anderen Lnder der Whrungsunion geeignet ist. Ein besonderes Kennzeichen des finnischen Dienstleistungssektors  und das gilt ebenso fr die anderen nordischen Lnder  ist die groe Bedeutung der ffentlichen Wohlfahrtsdienstleistungen wie Gesundheitsversorgung, Tagesbetreuung fr Kinder und Altenpflege. Die ffentlichen Wohlfahrtsdienstleistungen haben den Frauen die Mglichkeit gegeben ihre Rolle als Mutter mit Teilnahme am Arbeitsmarkt zu verbinden, und auch gleichzeitig ihnen Arbeitspltze im ffentlichen Sektor geboten. Etwa 80 Prozent der Arbeitnehmer in diesem Sektor sind Frauen. Die Beschftigung der Frauen liegt in Finnland schon jetzt deutlich ber dem Niveau von 60 Prozent, das sich die EU fr das Jahr 2010 zum Ziel gesetzt hat. Durch den hohen Beschftigungsgrad der Frauen ist der Beschftigungsgrad in Finnland mit 68 Prozent insgesamt relativ hoch, hher als in den meisten EU-Lndern. Fast ein Viertel der finnischen Erwerbsttigen arbeitet im ffentlichen Sektor. Die EU strebt an, den Anteil von Forschung und Produktentwicklung bis zum Jahr 2010 auf drei Prozent des Bruttosozialprodukts zu erhhen. In Finnland ist dieses Ziel bereits erreicht. Die Ausgaben fr Forschung und Entwicklung beliefen sich 2004 auf 3,5 Prozent des Bruttosozialprodukts. Die fentlichen Aufwendungen fr Forschung und Produktentwicklung tragen nur rund ein Prozent zum Bruttosozialprodukt bei; der grte Teil der Ausgaben in diesem Bereich wird von privaten Unternehmen finanziert. Die Hlfte der Ausgaben fr Forschung und Entwicklung fliet in die Informations- und Kommunikationstechnik. Darin spiegeln sich einerseits die Bedeutung dieses Wirtschaftszweigs in Finnland, andererseits der Stellenwert der Forschung in dieser Branche wider. Schtzungen nach hat der Mobiltelefon- und Telefonnetzhersteller Nokia an den gesamten Aufwendungen fr Forschung und Produktentwicklung in Finnland einen Anteil von dreiig Prozent und an der privaten Finanzierung einen Anteil von fast ffzig Prozent. Die Spezialisierung auf Informations- und Kommunikationstechnik seit Anfang der neunziger Jahre war fr die finnische Industrie ein groer Erfolg und hat das Wachstum von Produktion und Export beschleunigt. Die Wachstumsspitze scheint Finnland in diesem Bereich jedoch schon hinter sich gelassen zu haben. Der internationale Wettbewerb hat sich verschrft. Um kundennah zu arbeiten und Kosten zu senken, haben die Unternehmen ihre Produktion und die Beschaffung auf verschiedene Teile der Welt verteilt. Interessant ist bei dieser Entwicklung, dass es verhltnismig einfach war, die Fertigung dieser Produkte  auch Hightech-Produkte  in aufstrebende Mrkte zu verlegen, whrend die dienstleistungstrchtigen Teile der Produktionskette wie Hauptgeschftsstelle, Forschung und Produktentwicklung eher im Land bleiben. Finnland scheint sich an Schweden anzunhern, wo der Anteil der Hightech-Produktion und des Hightech-Exports nur dem internationalen Durchschnitt entspricht, obwohl die Forschungsintensitt Weltspitzenniveau erreicht. Das hat nichts damit zu tun, dass die Wettbewerbsfhigkeit der Unternehmen abgenommen htte oder die Marktanteile geschrumpft wren, sondern damit, dass die Produktion ins Ausland verlegt worden ist. Im kommenden Jahrzehnt wird sich das finnische Produktionswachstum kaum in gleicher Weise auf die Technologieindustrie stzen knen wie im vorigen. Auch eine Expansion des fentlichen Sektors ist unwahrscheinlich; dieser Sektor steht vielmehr vor der Herausforderung, neue Technologien einzufhren und die Arbeitsproduktivitt zu erhhen. Der Produktions-und Exportanstieg wird in Finnland zunehmend von den privaten Dienstleistungen abhngen. Vor allem informationsintensiven Branchen wie Dienstleistungen fr Unternehmen kommt dabei eine Schlselrolle zu. Dienstleistungsunternehmen, die Technologie und Innovationen nutzen, haben in den letzten Jahren schneller expandiert als andere Unternehmen. Es wird erwartet, dass dieses schnelle Wachstum anhlt. Triebmotor fr die Expansion der Dienstleistungsunternehmen ist nicht nur die bereits erwhnte globale Arbeitsteilung mit dem Schwerpunkt auf einem hohen Weiterverarbeitungsgrad, sondern auch der Umstand, dass sich die Industrieunternehmen auf ihre Kernkompetenzen konzentrieren und andere Ttigkeiten an Dienstleistungsunternehmen auslagern. Darber hinaus werden verschiedene immaterielle Faktoren wie Lieferzeiten und Lieferarten, Warenzeichen und Produktimage sowie Wartung und Instandhaltung im Wettbewerb immer wichtiger, was die Nachfrage nach Dienstleistungen fr Unternehmen weiter frdert. Dienstleistungen spielen nicht nur in Finnland, sondern auch in den anderen postindustriellen Lndern der EU eine entscheidende Rolle. Die Ausdehnung der Ttigkeit ins Ausland ist vor allem fr Dienstleistungsunternehmen in kleinen Lndern mehr oder weniger zwingend, wenn sie Wachstum und eine effiziente Produktion anstreben. Der Binnenmarkt der EU bietet den Dienstleistungsunternehmen in den Mitgliedslndern gute Voraussetzungen, um sich zu internationalisieren. Die Binnenmarktgesetzgebung hat technische, rechtliche, brokratische, kulturelle und protektionistische Handelshemmnisse zwischen den Mitgliedslndern beseitigt. Die Einfhrung des Euro hat ein bedeutendes Hindernis fr das reibungslose Funktionieren des Binnenmarktes aus dem Weg gerumt, nmlich die Unsicherheit, die mit den Devisenkursen der Mitgliedslnder verbunden war. Im Bereich der Dienstleistungen ist der Binnenmarkt uneinheitlich Wirklichkeit geworden. Bestimmte Segmente der Finanzmrkte sind schon weit integriert, und bei Finanzdienstleistungen funktioniert der Binnenmarkt bereits sehr gut. Die Kommission hat 1999 einen Aktionsplan vorgeschlagen, nach dem der Markt fr Finanzdienstleistungen bis 2005 ganz liberalisiert werden sollte. Die meisten der 42 Initiativen des Plans sind umgesetzt worden, doch bis ins letzte hat sich der Finanzdienstleistungsmarkt noch nicht vereinheitlicht. Die Bildung eines einheitlichen europischen Zahlungsverkehrsraums wird ein wichtiger Fortschritt fr die Finanzdienstleistungsbranche sein. Damit vereinfacht sich der Zahlungsverkehr im Eurogebiet oder der gesamten EU und lsst sich ebenso sicher und schnell abwickeln wie heute innerhalb eines Landes. Dieses Projekt der Privatbanken soll bis 2010 vollstndig umgesetzt sein. Bei anderen als den Finanzdienstleistungen steckt die Bildung des Binnenmarktes vielfach noch in den Anfngen. Um die Situation zu verbessern hat die Europische Kommission 2004 einen Vorschlag fr eine Richtlinie er die Dienstleistungen im Binnenmarkt ausgearbeitet. Im vergangenen April hat die Kommission einen neuen Vorschlag vorgelegt, der den im Europischen Parlament ausgehandelten Kompromiss in weiten Teilen bercksichtigt. Obwohl der neue Vorschlag den freren in mancher Beziehung verwssert, deckt er weiterhin einen bedeutenden Teil der Dienstleistungen ab und stellt damit trotzdem eine erhebliche Verbesserung der gegenwrtigen Situation in Aussicht. In Finnland werden voraussichtlich gut vierzig Prozent der Mitarbeiter und des Umsatzes aller Unternehmen in den Geltungsbereich des neuen Vorschlags fallen. Ich halte es fr wichtig, dass der Vorschlag der Kommission ohne weitere Schwchung angenommen wird.
