Die Richtlinie als solche kann natrlich lngst nicht alle Hindernisse beseitigen, die dem reibungslosen Funktionieren des Dienstleistungsbinnenmarktes im Weg stehen, ist aber in jedem Fall ein Schritt in die richtige Richtung. *** Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren! Die finnischen Erfahrungen mit der Whrungsunion deuten darauf hin, dass die nationalen Unterschiede und Sonderinteressen bei der Abwgung der Vor- und Nachteile der gemeinsamen Politik oft zu stark betont werden, whrend die Gemeinsamkeiten und gemeinsamen Interessen leicht in den Schatten treten. Trotz aller Zweifel war die gemeinsame Geldpolitik auch fr Finnland gut, wo das Eurogebiet im Vorfeld am strksten vom optimalen Whrungsraum abzuweichen schien. Das zeigt, dass sich das postindustrielle Finnland doch nicht so sehr von den brigen EU-Lndern unterscheidet wie hufig gedacht. Finnland ist ein Teil der postindustriellen EU. Dienstleistungen haben in der postindustriellen EU den grten Anteil an der Produktion und der Beschftigung. Im Hinblick auf das kftige Wachstum kommt vor allem den informationsintensiven Dienstleistungszweigen wie Dienstleistungen fr Unternehmen eine wichtige Rolle zu. Ohne einen effizienten europaweiten Binnenmarkt gibt es in diesem Bereich keine Expansion. Besonders wichtig ist der Binnenmarkt f die dynamischen Dienstleistungsunternehmen in den kleinen Lndern, deren Wachstumsmglichkeiten durch das Marktvolumen im eigenen Land beschrnkt sind. Auf dem Weg zum reibungslos funktionierenden Dienstleistungsbinnenmarkt gibt es noch viele Hindernisse. Sie zu beseitigen bedarf es Arbeit und Mhe von vielen Seiten, aber ich denke, dass sich diese Arbeit und Mhe lohnen werden. Im besten Fall wird sich der Dienstleistungsbinnenmarkt eines Tages als ebenso groer Erfolg erweisen wie der Euro und die gemeinsame Geldpolitik.

Title: The basics and implementation of monetary policy at the economic seminar of the Parliamentary Finance Committee
text: Director-General Erkki Liikanen Economic seminar of the Parliamentary Finance Committee on 6 September 2006 Basics and implementation of monetary policy Over the past couple of years, the global economy has been going through a strong upswing. During this period, the prices of crude oil and many other raw materials have sharply increased and capacity utilisation rates have increased. Indeed, inflationary pressures have increased in many countries. Central banks have set out to unwind the monetary easing that has contributed to accelerating global economic growth in recent years. The monetary policy stance has changed everywhere. This year alone, more than 20 central banks have raised their key interest rates. At the beginning of August, the European Central Bank (ECB) raised its key key interest rate for the fourth time since early Last December, to 3%. In the Us, the policy rate rose to 5.25% at the end of June d0 overall, the central bank has raised interest rates 17 times in a row over two years. FIGURES 1, 2, 3, 4 THE BANK OF FINLAND'S CORE ACTIVITIES CHART 5 KEY MONETARY POLICY RATES Perhaps the best indication of a change in the global monetary policy stance, however, comes from Japan. There, the country's central bank announced last March that it would begin to exit the so-called "black market". from its monetary policy based on quantitative easing and moving towards market guidance based on interest rate policy. In July, the central bank raised its key interest rate for the first time in several years. With interest rate expectations still bullish for many countries, markets are interested in any information that would help anticipate future interest rate movements. This also applies to the euro area. Thus, the Governing Council seeks to communicate in such a way as to give the most accurate picture possible of how it sees the current situation and on what basis future decisions are taken. However, it should be remembered that interest rate policy intentions are always conditional on new information and analysis of the economic situation. Therefore, at least as important as the formulation of the interest rate outlook is how the opinions characterise the economic outlook and the monetary situation. What is the aim of monetary policy? The actual objectives of monetary policy in the world are more consistent than the formal definitions of the objective in the various central banks would suggest. Price stability is now recognised as a key objective of monetary policy in practically all developed countries. This means that monetary policy counteracts fluctuations in the general price level, such as inflation and deflation. FIGURE 6 MONETARY POLICY OBJECTIVES In the case of monetary policy in the euro area, the objectives are clearly defined. Price stability was set as an objective of the European System of Central Banks by the Maastricht Treaty. According to the Treaty, price stability is the primary objective of monetary policy and the ECB must support the other objectives of the Community's economic policy insofar as price stability is not jeopardised. The Governing Council has since formulated that the concept of price stability refers to the annual rate of increase in consumer prices, which is close to, but below, two per cent over the medium term. The monetary policy objectives of the euro area have often been compared with those of the United States. Parallel objectives, such as price stability and maximum employment, have been defined by law for the central bank system of the United States. Interestingly, despite such legal differences, both the ECB and the Us Federal Reserve, as well as the other key central banks, see their role in much the same way: the key objective is to keep inflation low and stable in the medium term, because this is also essential for sustainable growth and employment. The objective of price stability is directed at the general level of prices for goods and services. Thus, the objective of monetary policy is not to stabilise the prices of individual commodities, but to examine the price level at the level of the economy as a whole, in the euro area and specifically at the level of the euro area as a whole. In the euro area, price developments are measured by the so-called "price action curve". the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices, the principles of which have been harmonised in all EU countries. Some central banks use different core inflation indicators that exclude some items from the CPI, such as energy or unprocessed food prices or changes caused by taxes. However, this has not been the case in the euro area, because the consumer price index itself is the one that ultimately affects the lives of citizens and to which the ECB's objective of price stability must therefore also be considered to apply. This is precisely about the prices of goods and services, so monetary policy does not, in principle, aim at the stability of assets, such as share prices or house prices, although fluctuations in these often cause concern to central banks. Indeed, fluctuations in stock prices may have an impact on monetary policy in that they reflect market expectations for growth, inflation and interest rates. Even then, stock prices are only one factor to consider when assessing the economic situation, not a goal. Monetary policy decisions affect inflation with a delay of one year or a year and a half. As a result, monetary policy cannot aim to guide general price developments in the short term, but must have a longer-term perspective, in the 'medium' term. Monetary policy decision-making is therefore strongly forward-looking. Why price stability? Thus, the achievement of a price stability period, which is understood to imply a low and stable inflation rate, has generally become the primary objective of monetary policy. Price stability is a goal for a number of reasons. FIGURE 7 DISADVANTAGES OF INFLATION Price stability helps consumers to distinguish changes in relative prices from changes in the general price level, thereby making the price mechanism work more efficiently in the economy. It reduces the risk premium of inflation in the return on investment requirements and thus lowers the 'natural' interest rate. It also reduces the need for economic managers to spend resources on hedging inflation and prevents unfair and arbitrary redistributive effects of inflation. In the past, it was thought that controlling inflation and pursuing economic growth and high employment were contradictory objectives. However, both practical experience and theoretical research have shown that this is not the case. The current view is that maintaining price stability is a key condition for sustainable economic growth in the long term. In situations where there are threats to price stability stemming from fluctuations in aggregate demand, monetary policy gearing price stability also directly smooths out cyclical fluctuations. If economic growth picks up at the same time as inflation risks increase, as has happened this year in the euro area, a tightening of monetary policy is warranted, both from a cyclical point of view and from a cyclical point of view, in order to safeguard price stability over the medium term. In the early years of the millennium, the situation was reversed: at that time, growth in the euro area slowed down substantially as a result of supply and demand shocks, but monetary policy was able to provide significant support for growth while inflationary pressures remained under control. Historical experience shows that a consistent monetary policy geared towards price stability has produced good results. Inflation and its costs have been brought down significantly throughout the world. While in 1980-84 the average rate of increase in consumer prices without land was about 14%, in 2000-05 it fell to just under 4%. The difference with the instability of the 1970s is startling. GRAPH 9 RATES OF INCREASE IN CONSUMER PRICES FIGURE 8 FACTORS INFLUENCING REAL GDP GROWTH IN THE EURO AREA The orientation of monetary policy towards maintaining price stability has contributed to a sharp fall in inflation. Globalisation has also played a role in the same direction. It has brought new, low-cost countries into international trade and, at the same time, substantially increased the supply of cheaper industrial products. In the industrialised countries, increased competition has also changed the pricing behaviour of companies and the nominal wage targets on the workers' side in a more moderate direction. The result has been a slowdown in the price-wage cycle in many of the old industrialised countries. Inflation expectations depend on the credibility of monetary policy The current problems of monetary policy are closely linked to the question of managing inflation expectations. The Governing Council's communication has repeatedly underlined the role of monetary policy to "anchor" inflation expectations in line with the price stability objective. Anchoring inflation expectations is an essential condition for monetary policy, while controlling inflation, to be able to support growth and employment. GRAPH 10 MONETARY POLICY AND INFLATION EXPECTATIONS The arguments for the importance of inflation expectations in monetary policy can be found in economic research. The picture of the functioning of the economy in modern monetary research is strongly "forward-looking". This means that both inflation and aggregate demand are largely determined by expectations for the future. For example, the rate of inflation is determined by what citizens, businesses and trade unions expect from the upcoming inflation. Demand for goods and services, on the other hand, depends on expectations of future revenues and real interest rates. Inflation expectations, in turn, depend on the credibility of monetary policy. This means that there is confidence in the central bank's willingness and ability to achieve its monetary policy objectives. If credibility is good, the central bank will be able to achieve the price stability it seeks, even with a very moderate monetary policy. If credibility is low, the defence of the value of money requires a heavy-handed monetary policy that disrupts economic growth and employment and may not even succeed in controlling inflation. In practice, attempts have been made to build the credibility of the Central Bank mainly by three complementary means. GRAPH 11 INCREASING THE CREDIBILITY OF MONETARY POLICY The first of these is to ensure the independence of the Central Bank. Since the late 1980s, institutional reforms of monetary policy have emphasised the independence of central banks. The European Central Bank has also been made fully operationally and economically independent of the EU's political institutions. The independence of a central bank does not mean that it should be able to choose the objectives of its activities. On the contrary, today the emphasis is on the independence of central banks so that they can reliably play the very role they have been given in the democratic order d0 that is, to maintain price stability with their monetary policy. Another key means of increasing the credibility of monetary policy is to build a reputation for reliability. It can be acquired over time by means of a coherent, effective and well-founded policy. The third way is to coordinate the rest of economic policy with price stability. This applies in particular to fiscal policy. A disciplined fiscal policy that avoids excessive deficits and indebtedness is not only a hallmark of good economic policy, but also a prerequisite for a successful monetary policy. Without it, the central bank will not be able to achieve price stability in the long term. In order to coordinate economic policies, Europe's Economic and Monetary Union has established a comprehensive economic policy coordination mechanism, with the Stability and Growth Pact at its core. The idea of the pact is precisely to prevent the increase in public budget deficits and public sector indebtedness, thereby ensuring the credibility of monetary policy, that is, to prevent an unnecessarily tight monetary policy from being trapped. As is well known, the surveillance mechanisms and sanctions relating to the Stability and Growth Pact have been put to the test. In the last few months, however, the commitment to the Stability and Growth Pact has been reaffirmed. Successful management of inflation expectations Despite its young age, the European System of Central Banks has been able to build confidence, which is reflected in the fact that inflation expectations in the euro area have been broadly in line with the objective of price stability. In this respect, the ECB has benefited from the trust and credibility that the Bundesbank had gained over the decades. CHART 12 INFLATION EXPECTATIONS In central banks, inflation expectations of the public and the markets are closely monitored, for example through surveys and quotations of index-linked bonds. In the euro area, there have been no signs of inflation expectations falling significantly above two per cent. This can be considered a good achievement. Communication is an integral part of monetary policy The credibility that has been achieved cannot be taken for granted, but must be carefully preserved. For this reason, the ECB attaches great importance to both policy coherence and predictability in monetary policy. Monetary policy communication plays a key role in guiding expectations and supporting the predictability of policies. The increased credibility of monetary policy has also meant an increase in the importance of communication in the activities of central banks. FIGURE 13 MONETARY POLICY AND COMMUNICATION In the past, central banks often sought to make their interest rate decisions unexpectedly, and even considered it a matter of honour. However, in recent years, the transparency of central bank policies has been decisively increased. This has been done in order to contribute to the stable functioning of the financial markets. The forms and content of communication on current monetary policy are currently being treated with great seriousness in central banks, in the markets and in the media. What is told about interest rates is almost as important as what is done with interest rates. This is because expectations also play a decisive role in the functioning of financial markets. This is because market interest rates are not determined solely on the basis of the prevailing guide rate at any given time, but are forward-looking: market rates depend to a large extent on the type of interest rate movements expected by the central bank in the coming months. In Finland, for example, most mortgages are linked to the 12-month Euribor rate, which fluctuates from day to day, even if the key ECB interest rate remains unchanged. CHART 14 THE INSTRUMENTS OF MONETARY POLICY IN DIFFERENT AREAS OF THE YIELD CURVE The graph below shows the yield curve in the euro area d0 i.e. the level of short- and long-term interest rates d0 and the change in interest rates since the summer of last year. Three areas are also marked in the figure, which illustrate how different factors affect different parts of the yield curve. The very shortest interest rates closely follow the development of the central bank's key interest rate. By contrast, as we move into the middle of the yield curve, central bank communication is becoming increasingly important. The figure shows how the change in the level of interest rates since July 2005 has been greatest in the middle of the yield curve, which is most affected by expectations of the central bank's future interest rate decisions. The changes at the beginning of the yield curve correspond to changes in the level of the policy rate. Finally, at the long end of the yield curve, long-term growth and inflation expectations are reflected. By anchoring inflation expectations to low levels, the central bank is also influencing these. The European Central Bank's monetary policy is framed by the strategy published by the Bank. It outlines both the deliberations on monetary policy in the Bank's Governing Council and the report given after the meetings. The strategy consists of two pillars, the first of which covers an economic analysis of inflationary pressure, including projections of developments by ECB and national central bank staff, and the second a monetary analysis, which provides information on inflationary pressures in money supply and credit developments. The final monetary policy consideration is based on a comparison of the information contained in these different pillars. Finally On Thursday last week, the Governing Council held its last monetary policy meeting. All 18 members of the Council were present: 12 governors of euro area central banks and 6 members of the ECB Executive Board. Following careful review of the economic formulation and thorough deliberations, the Council decided to keep the key ECB interest rate unchanged at 3%. At the ensuing press conference, the President of the ECB presented the conclusion of the meeting in an opinion justifying the decision taken in a wide-ranging manner while at the same time shedding light on the Council's views on near-term economic developments. In the markets, the Council's message was interpreted as the ECB continuing its interest rate hikes during the rest of the year. Since the meeting, market inflation expectations have remained stable, around two per cent. CHART 15 MARKET INTEREST RATE EXPECTATIONS Summary: The main contribution of the Central Bank to economic growth and employment comes from the stabilisation of inflation expectations. The stability of inflation expectations is reflected in the financial markets as a low level in relation to the history of long-term interest rates. This will contribute to supporting the continuation of investment activity in the euro area countries and thus to further economic growth and employment.

Nin ollen rahapolitiikan tavoitteena ei ole yksittisten hydykkeiden hintojen vakauttaminen, vaan hintatasoa tarkastellaan koko talouden tasolla, euroalueel-la nimenomaan koko euroalueen tasolla. INFLAATION HAITAT Hintavakaus auttaa kuluttajia erottamaan suhteellisten hintojen muutokset ylei-sen hintatason muutoksista ja tehostaa niin hintamekanismin toimintaa talou-dessa. Samaan suuntaan on vaikuttanut mys globalisaatio. Se on tuonut uusia, alhaisen kustannustason maita mukaan kansainvliseen kauppavaihtoon ja samalla lisnnyt tuntuvasti entist halvem-pien teollisuustuotteiden tarjontaa. Kilpailun kiristyminen on mys muuttanut teollisuusmaissa yritysten hinnoitte-lukyttytymist ja tyntekijpuolen nimellispalkkatavoitteita aiempaa maltil-lisempaan suuntaan. Seurauksena on ollut hinta-palkkakierteen vaimeneminen monissa vanhoissa teollisuusmaissa. Inflaatio-odotukset riippuvat rahapolitiikan uskottavuudesta Rahapolitiikan tmnhetkinen problematiikka liittyy lheisesti kysymykseen inflaatio-odotusten hallinnasta. EKP:n neuvoston viestinnss on toistuvasti korostettu rahapolitiikan tehtvn olevan inflaatio-odotusten ankkurointi hintavakaustavoitteen mukaisiksi. Inflaatio-odotusten ankkurointi on vlttm-tn edellytys sille, ett rahapolitiikka, samalla kun se kontrolloi inflaatiota, pystyy tukemaan kasvua ja tyllisyytt. KUVIO 10. RAHAPOLITIIKKA JA INFLAATIO-ODOTUKSET Perusteet inflaatio-odotusten merkityksen korostumiseen rahapolitiikassa ly-tyvt taloustutkimuksesta. Nykyaikaisen rahataloudellisen tutkimuksen kuva talouden toiminnasta on voimakkaasti "eteenpin katsova". Tll tarkoitetaan, ett sek inflaatio ett kokonaiskysynt mrytyvt suurelta osin tulevaisuutta koskevien odotusten perusteella. Esimerkiksi inflaatiovauhti mrytyy sen mukaan, mit kansalaiset, yritykset ja ammattiliitot odottavat tulevasta inflaa-tiosta. Tavaroiden ja palvelujen kysynt taas riippuu tulevia tuloja ja reaalikor-koja koskevista odotuksista. Inflaatio-odotukset riippuvat vuorostaan rahapolitiikan uskottavuudesta. Tm tarkoittaa, ett keskuspankin haluun ja kykyyn saavuttaa rahapolitiikkansa ta-voitteet luotetaan. Jos uskottavuus on hyv, keskuspankki pystyy saavuttamaan tavoittelemansa hintavakauden hyvin maltillisellakin rahapolitiikalla. Jos uskottavuus on huo-no, rahan arvon puolustus vaatii kovaotteista rahapolitiikkaa, joka aiheuttaa hiriit talouskasvuun ja tyllisyyteen eik silti vlttmtt edes onnistu in-flaation kontrolloimisessa. Kytnnss keskuspankin uskottavuutta on pyritty rakentamaan lhinn kol-mella toisiaan tydentvll keinolla. KUVIO 11. RAHAPOLITIIKAN USKOTTAVUUDEN LISMINEN Ensimminen nist on keskuspankin itsenisyyden varmistaminen. 1980-luvun lopulta alkaen rahapolitiikan institutionaalisissa uudistuksissa on koros-tettu keskuspankkien itsenisyytt. Mys Euroopan keskuspankki on toimin-nallisesti ja taloudellisesti tehty tysin itseniseksi suhteessa EU:n poliittisiin toimielimiin. Keskuspankin itsenisyys ei tarkoita, ett sen pitisi itse voida valita toimin-tansa tavoitteet. Pinvastoin, tnn korostetaan keskuspankkien itsenisyytt siksi, ett ne voisivat luotettavasti toimia juuri siin tehtvss, joka niille on demokraattisessa jrjestyksess annettu  siis yllpit hintavakautta rahapoli-tiikallaan. Toinen keskeinen keino rahapolitiikan uskottavuuden lismiseksi on luotetta-van maineen rakentaminen. Sen voi hankkia aikaa myten johdonmukaisella, tuloksekkaalla ja perustellulla politiikalla. Kolmas keino on muun talouspolitiikan yhteensovittaminen hintavakauden kanssa. Tm koskee varsinkin finanssipolitiikkaa. Kurinalainen finanssipoli-tiikka, joka vltt liiallisia alijmi ja velkaantumista, on paitsi hyvn talo-uspolitiikan tunnusmerkki, mys onnistuneen rahapolitiikan edellytys. Ilman sit keskuspankki ei voi pitkll aikavlill onnistua hintavakauden saavutta-misessa. Euroopan talous- ja rahaliitossa on talouspolitiikan yhteensovittamiseksi ra-kennettu kattava talouspolitiikan koordinaatiomekanismi, jossa keskeist on vakaus- ja kasvusopimus. Sopimuksen ideana on juuri est julkisten budjetti-vajeiden ja julkisen sektorin velkaantumisen kasvu ja nin varmistaa rahapoli-tiikan uskottavuus, eli ehkist tarpeettoman kiren rahapolitiikan loukkuun joutuminen. Kuten tunnettua, vakaus- ja kasvusopimukseen liittyvt valvonta-mekanismit ja sanktiot ovat olleet koetuksella. Aivan viime kuukausina kui-tenkin sitoutuminen vakaus- ja kasvusopimukseen on taas vahvistunut. Inflaatio-odotusten hallinnassa onnistuttu Euroopan keskuspankkijrjestelm on nuoresta istn huolimatta pystynyt saavuttamaan luottamuksen, mik nkyy siin, ett euroalueella vallitsevat in-flaatio-odotukset ovat olleet varsin hyvin hintavakauden tavoitteen mukaiset. EKP on tss hytynyt siit luottamuksesta ja uskottavuudesta, jonka Saksan keskuspankki Bundesbank oli vuosikymmenten mittaan saavuttanut. KUVIO 12. INFLAATIO-ODOTUKSET Keskuspankeissa yleisn ja markkinoiden inflaatio-odotuksia seurataan tiiviisti esimerkiksi kyselytutkimusten ja indeksisidonnaisten obligaatioiden noteeraus-ten avulla. Euroalueella ei ole ollut merkkej inflaatio-odotusten rystytymi-sest merkittvsti kahden prosentin ylpuolelle. Tt voidaan pit hyvn saavutuksena. Viestint on olennainen osa rahapolitiikkaa Saavutettua uskottavuutta ei voida pit itsestnselvyyten, vaan sit on huo-lella varjeltava. Tst syyst EKP kiinnitt rahapolitiikassa suurta huomiota sek politiikan johdonmukaisuuteen ett ennustettavuuteen. Rahapoliittisella viestinnll on keskeinen odotuksia ohjaava ja politiikan ennustettavuutta tu-keva merkitys. Uskottavuuden korostuminen rahapolitiikassa on merkinnyt mys viestinnn merkityksen korostumista keskuspankkien toiminnassa. KUVIO 13. RAHAPOLITIIKKA JA VIESTINT Takavuosina keskuspankit usein pyrkivt tekemn korkoptksens ylltt-en, ja pitivt sit jopa kunnia-asianaan. Keskuspankkien politiikan lpinky-vyytt on kuitenkin viime vuosina mrtietoisesti listty. Nin on pyritty mytvaikuttamaan rahamarkkinoiden vakaaseen toimintaan. Ajankohtaista rahapolitiikkaa koskevan viestinnn muotoihin ja sisltn suh-taudutaan sek keskuspankeissa, markkinoilla ett tiedotusvlineiss nykyisin suurella vakavuudella. Mit koroista kerrotaan, on melkein yht trke kuin mit koroille tehdn. Tm johtuu siit, ett odotuksilla on ratkaiseva merki-tys mys rahoitusmarkkinoiden toiminnassa. Nin siksi, ett markkinakorot eivt mrydy vain kulloinkin vallitsevan oh-jauskoron perusteella, vaan ne ovat eteenpin katsovia: markkinakorot riippu-vat suureksi osaksi siit, millaisia korkoliikkeit keskuspankin odotetaan teke-vn tulevina kuukausina. Esimerkiksi Suomessa useimmat asuntolainat on kyt-ketty 12 kuukauden Euribor-korkoon, joka vaihtelee pivittin, vaikka EKP:n ohjauskorko pysyisi ennallaan. KUVIO 14. RAHAPOLITIIKAN VAIKUTUSKEINOT TUOTTOKYRN ERI OSA-ALUEILLA Oheisessa kuviossa on esitetty euroalueen tuottokyr  siis lyhyiden ja pitkien korkojen taso  sek korkojen muutos viime vuoden kesst. Kuvioon on li-sksi merkitty kolme aluetta, jotka kuvaavat sit, miten eri tekijt vaikuttavat tuottokyrn eri osiin. Aivan lyhyimmt korot seuraavat lheisesti keskuspankin ohjauskoron kehitys-t. Tuottokyrn keskivaiheille siirryttess keskuspankin viestinnll on sen sijaan yh suurempi merkitys. Kuviosta nhdn, miten muutos korkojen tasossa vuoden 2005 heinkuun jl-keen on ollut suurin tuottokyrn keskivaiheilla, johon odotukset keskuspankin tulevista korkoptksist vaikuttavat eniten. Tuottokyrn alkupn muutok-set vastaavat ohjauskoron tasoon tehtyj muutoksia. Lopuksi, tuottokyrn pit-kss pss heijastuvat pitkn aikavlin kasvu- ja inflaatio-odotukset. Ankku-roimalla inflaatio-odotukset matalalle tasolle, keskuspankki vaikuttaa mys nihin. Euroopan keskuspankin rahapolitiikan kehikkona toimii pankin julkaisema strategia. Se jsent sek rahapolitiikan ksittely pankin neuvostossa ett mys kokousten jlkeen annettua selostusta. Strategia koostuu kahdesta pilarista, joista ensimminen kattaa inflaatiopainei-ta arvioivan taloudellisen analyysin, mukaan lukien EKP:n ja kansallisten kes-kuspankkien asiantuntijoiden laatimat kehitysarviot, ja toinen rahataloudellisen analyysin, jossa esiin tulee rahan tarjonnassa ja luotonannon kehityksess n-kyv inflaatiopaineita koskeva informaatio. Lopullinen rahapoliittinen harkinta tapahtuu niden eri pilarien sisltmn informaation vertailuun perustuen. Lopuksi EKP:n neuvosto piti viime viikon torstaina viimeisimmn rahapoliittisen ko-kouksensa. Paikalla olivat kaikki neuvoston 18 jsent: 12 euromaan keskus-pankkien pjohtajaa ja 6 EKP:n johtokunnan jsent. Huolellisen talousin-formaation lpikynnin ja perusteellisen harkinnan seurauksena neuvosto pt-ti pit EKP:n ohjauskoron ennallaan 3 prosentissa. Kokousta seuranneessa tiedotustilaisuudessa EKP:n pjohtaja esitteli kokouk-sen johtoptksen lausunnossaan, jossa perusteltiin laaja-alaisesti tehty p-tst ja valotettiin samalla neuvoston ksityksi lhiajan talouskehityksest. Markkinoilla neuvoston viesti tulkittiin siten, ett EKP jatkaa koronnostojaan loppuvuoden aikana. Kokouksen jlkeen markkinoiden inflaatio-odotukset ovat pysyneet vakaina, kahden prosentin tuntumassa. KUVIO 15. MARKKINOIDEN KORKO-ODOTUKSET Yhteenvetona: Keskuspankin pasiallisin anti talouskasvulle ja tyllisyydelle tulee inflaatio-odotusten vakauttamisen kautta. Inflaatio-odotusten vakaus nkyy rahoitus-markkinoilla pitkien korkojen historiaan nhden alhaisena tasona. Tm on osaltaan tukemassa investointitoiminnan jatkumista euroalueen maissa ja siten talouskasvua ja tyllisyytt mys jatkossa.

Title: Difficult choices for Finnish well-being at Aamulehti's 125th anniversary seminar
text: Director-General Erkki Liikanen Aamulehti's 125th anniversary seminar Tampere University Ballroom 29.9.2006 "Difficult choices for Finnish well-being" Jacques Delors, the long-time President of the European Commission, used to say that we need competition because it creates economic incentives and solidarity, because it holds society together. The EU summit in Gothenburg in the summer of 2002 again underlined that: that 'sustainable development offers the European Union a positive long-term vision of a society that is more prosperous and fair, in which both our generation and our children and grandchildren can enjoy a high quality of life'. The idea comes from the famous Brundtland Committee: Growth and increased prosperity must be achieved without jeopardising the well-being of future generations and the potential for economic growth. The summit continued: "It requires the implementation of sustainable economic growth while supporting social progress and protecting the environment. In addition, social policy must support economic productivity and environmental policy must be implemented effectively." This underlines the interlinkage between economic, social and environmental sustainable development. Without economic development, society cannot guarantee social justice. The decline in economic activity and the high level of unemployment are undermining the community to work for the benefit of the environment. Economic growth without solidarity in sustainable development leads to a socially fractured society; the cohesive cohesion is broken. Sustainable development requires a competitive economy. A strong economy alone is not enough, but it alone creates the conditions and resources for a policy that maintains safety nets and social integrity. Therefore, today I want to begin by highlighting the basic premise: The choices made by the Finnish welfare state are the more difficult the growth of our economy and the less able we are to secure our competitiveness. In the worst case, there are no alternatives. Of course, there is also the argument that if the economy grows, the choices will become more politically and psychologically difficult, because there are resources to share. Decisions come about only when things are going very badly, the economy is not growing at all or the national product is even contracting, in other words, during a deep crisis. However, I do not believe that anyone is proposing that the objective of economic policy should therefore be low growth or a crisis. That is why I want to focus today on how to increase the growth potential of our economy in Finland and Europe. And at the same time, I would argue that increased competition and deregulation, particularly in commodity markets, are the most important tools for raising our standard of living and influencing the conditions for long-term growth of the national economy. Increasing competition in the market affects our standard of living and the speed of its rise through at least two different channels: The first channel is that competition in commodity markets reduces price-margins. It lowers the price level from what it would otherwise be and leads to an increase in real earnings and purchasing power in the medium term. In this way, consumption increases, increased demand leads to investment and creates new jobs. These effects of increased competition have been assessed both in international studies and in the Bank of Finland's Aino macroeconomic model.1 The Aino model is tailored to describe the most important sectors and actors in our national economy and can also be used to assess the effects of increased competition. The preliminary results obtained at the Bank of Finland clearly show that households' real income and well-being will increase as the economy has adapted to the new competitive situation. The problem for the decision-maker is that the costs are realized in the short term and the increasing benefits of the dynamics of the economy in the medium and long term. 1 J. Kilponen ja A. The second channel is that increased competition in the intermediate and final product markets will accelerate productivity growth in the economy and thus further long-term economic growth. I will return to the link between competitiveness and economic growth in more detail in a moment. It is worth emphasizing that the calculations I have mentioned with the Aino model take into account only the first of the two channels described above, that is, how a decrease in price margins increases purchasing power, consumption, etc. They therefore do not take into account the latter channel, i.e. the direct impact of competition on the rate of productivity growth. Nevertheless, the effects of the competition were found to be positive. Today, I will focus above all on the latter, namely how and why increased competition in the market is important for long-term productivity growth. Adam Smith has already said that sustainable economic growth is based on an increase in productivity. The rate of productivity growth is therefore crucial for the future development of our standard of living. The effect of increased competition on productivity growth is not self-evident. If that were the case, we would not hear companies complaining that excessive competition has reduced their ability to innovate. These examples can also be found in Finland. This point of view, which some industries and companies have come up from time to time, is based on the understandable idea that competition in the sector itself may reduce the expected returns and revenues from innovation. It reduces the incentives for companies to sacrifice resources to make/invent them. Several models of economics developed by the mid-1990s provided support for this view. According to them, companies' willingness to do product development, for example, weakens as competition intensifies and eventually stops altogether. The positive effects of increased competition are not self-evident either because we have a patent system that restricts competition at the same time, as well as competition legislation aimed at increasing competition and the Finnish Competition Authority, which oversees it. If we deliberately exacerbate this confrontation, we end up wondering why inventions and innovations are granted patents designed to protect the inventor/innovator from the effects of competition  and why, at the same time, it is felt necessary to promote, among other things, free entry into the sector and price competition by another authority. Does the left hand know what the right one is doing? It is worth seeking clarity on the seemingly contradictory views expressed above. So it is necessary in order to understand how and why competition, as a rule, accelerates productivity growth. In recent years, a great many new studies and studies on the link between competition and economic growth have been published.2 These studies have sought to examine in particular the relationship between competitive activity in sectors and innovation. The studies mentioned have searched for and also found new answers to the following questions, among others:  Question 1: What are the conditions under which increased competition is most likely to accelerate productivity growth?  Question 2: What policy measures can contribute to the competitiveness of the sector by increasing innovation activity?  Question 3: Why might some market participants have a natural incentive from their point of view to oppose or at least put the brakes on increased competition? I think these are good and interesting questions. It is right to consider the answers to them and the answers found in a little more detail. Question 1: What are the conditions under which increased competition is most likely to accelerate productivity growth? When considering the link between competition and innovation, it is important to emphasise the dynamic nature of competition. This is because, traditionally, competition has been treated as a rather static phenomenon: for example, competition has been assessed on the basis of companies' current market shares. Consumers, on the other hand, have been thought to benefit, above all because, as a result of intense competition, they can obtain from existing manufacturers and producers the products already on the market at low prices. The dynamic effects of competition mean that competition and its acceleration are a source of structural change that accelerates productivity growth. This structural change is evidenced, for example, by new products and operating methods entering the market, as well as the entry of new companies into the sector and the exit of old ones from the sector. According to this way of thinking, changes in the market shares of companies, and therefore not so much their current level, can be considered as an indicator of competition (at least indirect). The impact of the competitive nature of the industry on the innovation performance of individual enterprises should be examined at two different points in time: How intense the competition is before the company has made a potential innovation (pre-innovation) and how intense it is after the innovation is made (post-innovation). An important finding is that while increased competition in commodity markets may in fact reduce the expected returns from successful innovation, it may still increase the incentives for companies to carry out R&D activities. This is the case if increased competition comparatively erodes more profits that a company earns before it has taken an enthusiastic call than it undermines the profits it earns after a potential innovation. To many, that may sound like some sort of theory-mongering by economists. But it is not. It's a kind of stick-and-carrot effect: Tightening up the competition today is a stick with a tighter stroke that encourages you to be better than others tomorrow. The carrot is the competitive advantage of innovation vis-a-vis other companies in the industry and the additional profits that this advantage brings. If the (current) competitive situation in the industry becomes tougher, the company should have good incentives to pursue innovation. These innovations can be new and better products or services, related to the intensification of production methods, or mean reforms of the organization or business models that will help it to stand out from other companies in the industry in the future. How profitable it is for a company to sacrifice resources and effort to make demands for innovation depends on how effectively successful innovation helps the company to "escape" the competition (escape competition effect). The aim is to gain a competitive advantage over other companies in the industry. What has been said above can also be described differently. As competition in the market (co-mpetition in markets) intensifies, incentives to escape the current state of low profitability or the threat thereof intensify. Thus, competition for markets ends up being competed for by diversifying (differentiating) existing products and services, developing entirely new goods or creating completely new technologies and markets. These two different dimensions of competition may therefore be complementary and not substitutable, as has sometimes been thought. Question 2: What kind of policy measures can influence the competitiveness of the industry by increasing innovation activity? I said above that competition enhances the incentives for companies to innovate if it reduces the profitability of today's business more than it reduces the company's future, post-innovation profitability. This finding helps to understand why there is no contradiction between a patent system that contributes to competition and competition law aimed at increasing competition:  The actions of competition authorities are a way of raising the cost of not innovating.  The patent system, on the other hand, rewards successful innovation. The increase in patent protection is therefore equivalent to a more juicy or mouth-ribbed carrot in the example I mentioned, in the example of carrots and sticks I mentioned. This brings us back to the earlier question: does the right hand of those who design policy measures not know what the left is doing? Maybe you know after all. Competition in commodity markets can intensify in many different ways. One of the main reasons for the natural intensification of competition is the entry of new companies into the sector. The removal of barriers to entry into the sector and European integration have made it easier for new companies, on the one hand, and foreign operators, on the other, to enter the sector in Finland, and for Finnish companies to enter other markets. This development is to be welcomed and supported in the future. I do not think I am very wrong when I say that, for example, the increase in labour productivity experienced in Finland in recent years in the retail sector is in many, if not all, partly the result of the fact that the old players who were already in the sector have responded to the influx of foreign companies, or at least to the threat thereof. There is a risk that this entry into the industry will increase unless something changes in the industry. It is therefore a question of the effects of increased competition and the defence of market positions by increasing productivity (escape entry effect). More generally, the increase in international trade and the entry of foreign companies into the market have been found in Finland to accelerate the change in establishment structures and the exit of old inefficient companies from the sector.3 This structural change has been an important source of productivity growth. International studies also suggest that deregulation and increased competition in product markets have accelerated overall productivity growth in recent decades4. Question 3: Why might some market participants have a natural incentive from their own point of view to resist or at least put the brakes on competition? Increasing competition also has opponents. This is understandable from many perspectives.5 Firstly, even if the overall impact of increasing competition is positive for the national economy, tightening up or deregulating competition may strengthen the position of some players but correspondingly weaken others. It is obvious that increased competition is undermining the profitability of inefficient companies in particular. The profitability of efficient and innovative companies suffers less. With successful innovation and the detachment it enables, it can even improve. This should mean that inefficient companies, in particular, have an incentive, from their own point of view, to try to put the brakes on increasing competition. One type of way of opposing deregulation and influencing decision-makers. Uncertainty about the distribution of positive impacts between different actors may also be greater than uncertainty about the allocation of costs. In this case, there is resistance to reform because there is no certainty as to what will happen to oneself.6 Secondly, the different timing of costs and benefits may have an impact on support for reforms that increase competition. Often the costs come in advance, but the benefits only come later. This can make it more difficult to push through reforms. For example, facilitating the entry of new companies into the market may, in the early stages, destroy more establishments than new ones and establishments will be created. In addition, the structural change brought about by increased competition and the acceleration of productivity growth will only increase investment and growth later on. Thirdly, the positive effects of competition on product markets are of a macroeconomic nature, the most important of which is the general increase in living standards brought about by the acceleration of productivity growth. The detection of positive effects of this kind and its association with increased competition has not been obvious even to economists, let alone to the people on the street. On the other hand, the negative effects of increased competition can be quite tangible. For example, as I said earlier, increased competition can force inefficient companies to either renew themselves or leave the market. In an extreme case, increased competition is reflected in the closure of establishments and in the bankruptcy of companies that are least successful in the competitive situation. These consequences are tangible and we often learn about them from the media. Even when work is believed to be moving away from one's home country, difficult discussions arise. Bankruptcies and closures of companies also destroy jobs. This is happening at the same time as new jobs are being created in new enterprises and in growth companies that have succeeded in innovation. The 'creative destruction' of this business sector and productivity growth go hand in hand. It is quite clear that an increase in the productivity of a national economy or an improvement in the efficiency of an industry as a result of structural change is a meagre consolation for the part of the people who lose their jobs. Losing a job for a long time or even a lifetime is a painful experience, the importance of which for individual people or families can hardly be overestimated. A significant number of people are re-employed fairly quickly, but those who are less fortunate need a public safety net to get back into work. Public safety nets and retraining are particularly needed when and if competition and its tightening are a source of structural change that accelerates productivity growth7. Similarly, a safety net and retraining are also needed when, as a result of the change in the global division of labor, activities are transferred to countries with lower production costs and similar jobs are no longer available. Changes in the competitive nature of product markets may also have an impact on changes in the functioning of other markets. OECD:n tutkimusten mukaan usein edel-tnyt kilpailua lisvt muutokset hydykemarkkinoilla muutamia vuosia aikaisemmin.8 Nyttisi siis silt, ett kilpailun lisntyminen hydykemarkkinoilla johtaa mys tymarkkinoiden uudistumiseen. Hydykemarkkinakilpailu luo edellytyksi muillekin uudistuksille.9 Toi-mivat tymarkkinat vhentvt riski, ett kiristyneen hydykemarkkina-kilpailun vuoksi alalta poistuvien yrityksien tyntekijt jisivt tyttmksi. Taloustutkijoiden keskuudessa on varsin suuri yksimielisyys siit, milt toimivat ja kilpailulliset hydykemarkkinat ainakin periaatteessa nyttvt. Tymarkkinoiden osalta mielipiteet ovat huomattavasti moninaisempia. Ei ole yht selv, millaiset tymarkkinainstituutiot toimivat parhaiten eri ym-pristiss ja tilanteissa.10 Tymarkkinoiden suurin haaste on, miten sa-maan aikaan edistetn kilpailun ja tuottavuuden kannalta trke yritys-kentn uusiutumista ja toisaalta turvataan ihmisten toimeentulo ja mahdolli-suudet uuteen alkuun mys vaikeissa muutostilanteissa. Ja lopuksi: Me teemme tnn ptksi sek oman sukupolvemme tulevasta elintasos-ta ett mys tulevien suomalaisten sukupolvien hyvinvoinnista. Suomalai-sen hyvinvointivaltion tulevien valintojen vaikeusaste on sit alhaisempi, mit vauraampana ja kilpailukykyisempn pysymme. Vestn ikntymi-sen mukanaan tuomat haasteet on kohdattava jo lhitulevaisuudessa. Julkis-ten palveluiden ja tulonsiirtojen yllpitminen ja kehittminen edellytt vankkaa talouskasvua mys jatkossa. Olen keskittynyt erityisesti hydykemarkkinakilpailun ja talouskasvun yh-teyteen. Meill on yh enenevss mrin tietoa ja ymmrryst kilpailun ja tuottavuuden kasvun vlisest positiivisesta yhteydest. Uskon, ett kilpai-lun lisminen markkinoilla on yksi trkeimmist kytssmme olevista in-strumenteista, jolla voimme vaikuttaa kansantalouden pitkn aikavlin kas-vuedellytyksiin ja siten valintamahdollisuuksiimme. Kilpailu ja sen mukanaan tuoma tuottavuuden kasvu eivt kuitenkaan yksin riit. Kilpailun lisksi tarvitsemme yhteisvastuuta, solidaarisuutta, joka pi-t yhteiskuntaa koossa ja varmistaa, ettei kukaan j osattomaksi kilpailun ja tuottavuuden tuomista hedelmist. Julkisia turvaverkkoja on yllpidett-v ja kehitettv, jotta mys kilpailun kiristymisest krsineill on mahdol-lisuus pysy tyelmss ja aktiivisina. Nin varmistetaan osaltaan kilpai-lulle ja hyvinvoinnin kasvattamiselle suotuisan ilmapiirin jatkuminen yhteiskunnassamme.

Title: 100th anniversary celebration for the full political rights of Finnish women
text: 1 (3) Bank Manager Sinikka Salo Bank of Finland Keynote speech "At the 100th anniversary of the full political rights of women" in Vaasa 8.10.2006 Ladies and gentlemen, celebratory women! The first unicameral parliament elected 100 years ago had many interesting women. One of them was Liisi Kivioja from the southern constituency of Vaasa, one of the six female MPs of the Finnish Party. She had graduated as an elementary school teacher and lived with her family for years in the United States. In Parliament, Liisi Kivioja, along with other women representatives, supported the right of women to all government posts, the hiring of a hand in municipalities, the fullness of their own and their property for married couples aged 21 and over, the improvement of the insurance legislation for mothers and the improvement of the status of illegitimate children, but also, among other things, general compulsory education and assistance to national libraries. Liisi Kivioja was widowed in 1909, and in the second Diet of the same year she participated in national politics for the last time. He was ready to start a new stage of life. In order to get a permanent position already at the age of 50 and to secure the livelihood of his own and the family's foster son, he went to Kuopio to become the director of a school for the blind. When she had to leave her position due to the school's financial difficulties in 1918, she was elected to a position that was rare for a woman, as the head of the local branch of the National Equity Bank in Kalajoki. He held this position until his death in 1925. Handsome and interesting career! Presenters like Liisi Kivioja have contributed to the fact that all doors are now open for a Finnish woman, at least in principle. According to Kaari Utrio, the last woman to open the post of road master was in 2000. Women have been involved in building Finnish well-being and have played a significant role in finland's rise from being one of the richest countries in the world. So it's a pleasure to be a Finnish woman! But still, we face challenges. Gender equality has not been fully realised. This is reflected in many ways in society. The fact that women are important builders of economic well-being is not reflected, for example, in the same proportion in economic decision-making and its preparation. And yet it is precisely in solving perhaps the most important economic challenge of Finnish society that women play a key role and have special expertise. What is this challenge? Aging. The population of Finland  like the rest of Europe  is getting older. In 2030, the number of people aged over 65 in Finland will be almost double that of those aged over. This so-called. the dependency ratio will then be the highest in the eu as a whole. Economic growth, which consists of both the number of employees and productivity, i.e. how efficiently services and goods are produced, is in danger of fading as the number of people who like it decreases. On the other hand, pension expenditure is increasing. We need both women's productivity and productivity in order to survive. 2 (3) In Finland, the participation rate of women in employment has traditionally been high, and the challenge is, first of all, to keep women in the lurch and to improve their high level of education in order to increase productivity. In addition, care must be taken to ensure that the development of the population remains favourable for the future, i.e. that the birth rate does not collapse, but that it is possible to reconcile employment and family life. This, in turn, requires support for the reconciliation of parenthood and merit: good childcare facilities and care services for the elderly. The construction and maintenance of such an infrastructure to such an extent that it keeps the participation of women at a sufficiently high level of merit has not been successful with private money alone. The Nordic welfare state model, in which tax revenue is used to participate in the production of care services, provides the basis on which economic growth can be built. The Finnish welfare model as one of the manifestations of the Nordic model has worked well so far. But it needs modernization. Although the Finnish economy is on a more stable footing than in most other EU countries, the financing of the welfare state poses a challenge to our economic policy as our population ages. Taxation is already at such a level that it is no longer possible to raise it. We too have a government debt-to-GDP ratio of over 40%. It should be remembered that the higher the debt, the higher the debt servicing costs, which are absent, for example, from the financing of welfare services. For example, despite the low interest rates, a significant part of the expenditure on the public sectors of the EU's heavily indebted countries goes to debt servicing. A huge amount of common resources, at least 5-6% of GDP, are therefore spent in those countries not on welfare services but on interest on debts. In the coming decades, the success of Finnish society will be measured to a large extent by how the best principles of the highly popular Nordic welfare state and reasonable taxation can be maintained as the population ages. Economic growth is needed, but quantitative economic growth alone cannot be lulled into financing the welfare state. A viable, if not the only, way to secure the financing of our welfare system is to increase the efficiency of the welfare state. This is particularly important not only for the taxpayers who use the services, but also for the development of the salaries of the staff who work there (the majority of whom are women). In order to defend the welfare state, the productivity of the public sector must be stepped up  and I do not mean that women in the public sector should be torn even more from their backs. That is probably no longer possible. It may even be the case that this has gone too far. Instead, we need to think about how to integrate the Nordic welfare state into the information society so that efficiency increases and organisations are streamlined. That is, doing the right things in the right place at the right time. Sitra's studies, for example, show that there will most certainly be genuine rationalisation in the provision of public services, from which both service providers and service users will benefit. When the system works efficiently, it also makes sense to the people involved. With a system that provides efficient quality services, we can afford and want to pay the taxes that keep it afloat. If the welfare state deteriorates and services are not available or of poor quality, the desire to pay stops. 3 (3) That is why it is also in the interests of women to improve the efficiency of the public sector. I believe that women in particular can bring great added value to this rationalisation! Even a cursory acquaintance with Liisi Kivioja and her female colleagues in the first Parliament gives the impression that there was a group of incredibly energetic and, in many areas of life, women who took the initiative at the same time. Brave and personal women! They would probably be quite happy with the development of the status of a modern woman in 100 years. Instead, they might feel disappointed in at least a couple of things: First of all, Liisi Kivioja, as a bank manager, would probably be disappointed that there are so few women in the top management of banks and in the management of companies in general. I am not in favour of lashing out at the boards of private companies  they are contrary to the market economy and private property rights  but instead I have on several occasions encouraged women to use market-based means to promote a more female-faced economy. For example, women could only invest in shares in companies that also have women on their management boards. That is the 'means of exerting pressure' that money offers. I recently read a statement by a Swedish investment fund manager  a male person  about the investment policy of his fund: they do not invest in companies that do not have any women on their boards. Although our neighbouring country is probably more mythical than we are about equality, I believe that this is happening not only for the sake of equality, but because women are a significant and well-informed group of investor customers in Sweden as well. Secondly, the women of the first Parliament would probably be quite surprised that representative democracy has not progressed further in terms of the gender criterion. Although the 37% share of women MPs in our current Parliament is at a good international average, our pioneering tradition as the world's first women to achieve both the right to vote and to stand for election obliges us to achieve a better result! Here's my challenge for women in next year's election! Quoting Economic Counsellor Hedvig Gebhard  a member of parliament in the first parliament he too  "Where a capable female candidate is, every conscious woman votes for her."
