Title: Nation State and European Integration at the annual meeting of the Paasikivi Society
text: Director-General Erkki Liikanen Paasikivi Society's annual meeting 27.11.2006: The nation state and European integration The Finnish Cultural Foundation announced an important decision at its annual celebration in February. It had bought Louis Carre's house in Bazoches-sur-Guyonne, a village of just under 500 inhabitants located 40 kilometers outside Paris. This was an important cultural act, as Maison Carre is one of the most significant private houses designed by Alvar Aalto. It is often mentioned even alongside Villa Mairea. Louis Carre was a Parisian art dealer whose gallery sold works by great artists such as Matisse, Leger and Picasso. Maison Carre was rich in paintings by Leger. Acquired by Maire Gullicshen, the Villa Mairea collection reflects the same taste in art. In addition to Louis Carre, the presentation of the municipality mentions that another prominent figure lived in the same area. He was Jean Monnet, the 'founding father' of the European Union, as the French used to say. Monnet, originally the son of a cognac merchant from Cognac, made a remarkable career in international positions and banking, and after the war settled in this small village. Louis Carre and Jean Monnet were neighbors. Maison Carre was part of the unofficial part of President Urho Kekkonen's visit to France in October 1962. Louis Carre had also invited Maire Gullicshen. According to a small news item in one of the columns in Helsingin Sanomat, Urho Kekkonen met Jean Monnet at Carre's house and talked with him at length in English. By that time, Monnet had already resigned from the leadership of the European Coal and Steel Community and was committed to promoting European unity through the popular movement. We do not know the content of kekkonen's and Monnet's discussion. But it is well known that Monnet and President de Gaulle, the host of Kekkonen's visit, represented opposing views on the principles of European integration at the time of the visit. According to De Gaulle, national sovereignty was inviolable, he did not accept strong European institutions and he was opposed to qualified majority voting. A few years later, with his "empty chair policy", he froze the EEC. Monnet took the opposite view: he considered that the objectives of the EEC and its effective decision-making could only be safeguarded by qualified majority rules and common institutions. He advocated a gradual but determined deepening of integration. When, a year later than Kekkonen's visit, Eisenhower met de Gaulle in Paris, he asked about Monnet, the president replied: "He makes good cognac. Unfortunately, that's not enough for him". De Gaulle is even said to have made sure that Monnet was not even invited to Robert Schuman's funeral. Juhani Suomi tells about Kekkonen's visit to France in his book The President. Finland considered that in de Gaulle "it was justifiable to see a guarantor that the development of the organisation (i.e. the EEC) would not endanger Finland's interests". There is no account of monnet's meeting or his views in the book. Which path is in Finland's interests four decades later, now as a member of the European Union? The world and Europe have changed. But the big issue of debate is still the relationship between the Member State and the European Union  or, if you like to put it more generally, the relationship of the national to the European community and internationalism in political, economic and wider terms. It was here that there was a great disagreement between de Gaulle and Monnet. The winter marked the 50th anniversary of the election of Urho Kekkonen as President of the Republic. In the autumn of the same year, first Risto Ryti left our midst and later in December J.K. Paasikivi. Throughout this year, we have been paying attention to J.V. Snellman, whose birth marked the 200th anniversary of his birth in May. Examining the thinking of Snellman, Paasikivi and Ryti and their heritage from this perspective, which is the relationship of the national to the European community or internationality, is very interesting and topical. Paasikivi is considered the real politician par excellence: well-known is his Carlyle quote, according to which the beginning of wisdom is the recognition of facts. Paasikivi's guiding star in international relations was prudence, a policy of negotiations and mediation. He adopted this line already as a young man, when during the period of oppression he joined the Old Finns Party. It examined the relationship between Finland and Russia as a political and historical question rather than as a matter of state law. Paasikivi started from the premise that in relations between states, "real interests take precedence over ideological and other irrational influences." Although he was a political realist, Paasikivi did not admire the politics of power. Nor was he a cynic who would have regarded the ideal of justice in international relations as naive fantasies. Conversely. In his memoirs, Paasikivi strongly condemned Bismarck's thesis, according to which great things are solved "with blood and iron". He noted how powerful and mighty Germany, by applying that doctrine, had twice fallen into ruin. When you read his diaries, or Hannu Immonen's fine summary of Paasikivi's philosophy of history, you will see that Paasikivi was very interested in major questions of principle, and especially in justice and justice also in international relations. The interest was based on Paasikivi's concern about the fate of a small nation under the pressure of power politics. Already in the 1930s, Paasikivi had considered the relationship between nationalism and internationalism. In his diary, on 26.6.1931, he wrote the following words: "Both the idea of nationality and the idea of large entities is right. Both ideas are right. Task: they must be reconciled. Not impossible. Pan-Europe? Is that the solution?" The war understandably brought darker tones to his annotations. During the last weeks of the Continuation War in July 1944, he wrote in his diary: "We have relied on the power of justice and justice. History does not seem to give a basis for this. Reading history, one becomes a pessimist.  The states acted on Staatsrason's soil. It's awful  blutrotig. It is outside of good and evil. (...) Staatsrason's limitation, its relationship to morality, is a question on the resolution of which the future of small states in particular depends in the first place, but also, in the end, the success of the large and the entire human community." The excerpt simultaneously sums up Paasikivi's pessimistic realism and, on the other hand, it also shows the principled side of Paasikivi's thinking. He believed that justice should prevail in international relations instead of brutal power politics. He considered the restriction of the sovereignty of states to ultimately be in the interest of all, including large states. Although he is more pessimistic about the possibilities of international law, he considers it even more necessary. Reflecting on the importance of power and justice in international politics, Paasikivi had to return to Snellman's ideas and take a stand on them again and again. Snellman was an important ideological starting point for him as an Old Finn. As Hannu Immonen has shown, Paasikivi became increasingly critical of many of the features of Snellman's thinking as he grew older. Paasikivi's criticism concerned, among other things, Snellman's position on the language issue and, in particular, his kind of Darwinist image of international politics. Paasikivi's attitude to the language issue was more open-minded than Snellman's, but of course the time was different. He accepted Snellman's national education program and considered it important, but rejected Snellman's simple theory, which identified the language community with nationality. For Snellman, nationality meant the common consciousness of the nation, and he considered this consciousness to be strongly language-bound, based on language and literature in one's own language. Paasikivi does not politicise the language issue in the same way. Paasikivi also could not agree with Snellman's views on relations between nations. Snellman had not put much hope into international law. In fact, he did not believe in its existence. He considered world politics to be a field of merciless competition between peoples, in which they, organized as states, fought for leadership in the world. In Snellma-n's view, morality had no place in international affairs and the people "had to rely only on their it". In his "Memoirs of the Years of Oppression", published in the 1950s, Paasikivi took Snellman's ideas under critical scrutiny. He says that he has read over and over again the last chapters of Snellman's Political Science, which deal with international problems. Paasikivi defined Snellman as a staunch real politician because he gave justice no place in international relations: "The right of nations is power" and "There are no laws for foreign policy in the first place", Snellman had said. On the other hand, Snellman had emphasized non-material factors. "The power of the nation lies not in the number of men fit for war, but in the patriotism and civilization of the people". He also held that "if a people really wants to achieve and maintain its independence, it will always have the ability to defend it." Paasikivi considered Snellman's belief in the power of national spirit and civilisation to be insufficient in itself to secure the existence of small nations. Although he criticized Snellman for his "realpolitik", Paasikivi considered Snellman too optimistic in this regard. In Paasikivi's opinion, the sheer power of civilisation did not provide sufficient security against violence. Sometime in the 1930s, Mannerheim came to talk to Paasikivi about the basichanhands of the Finnish Defence Forces. When Paasikivi had said that there had been opposition to the procurement programme, Manner-heim had asked what the opponents of the programme were then trusting. "Cultural defence," Paasikivi replied. Mannerheim had said to this: "Oh! So they trust the Academic Bookstore". Paasikivi considered Mannerheim's remark to be hurtful. Paasikivi himself explained his disagreement with Snellman by the fact that Snellman had lived in the "idyllic" conditions of the 1800s, when Finland was not subject to the threat of direct violence. Paasikivi's conceptions of the state, on the other hand, had developed first during the oppressive period at the turn of the century and then during the totalitarian dictatorships of the first half of the 1900s and the great wars they started. At that time, the conditions were so harsh that submission to the forces of history seemed, at least from the point of view of a small nation, too disgusting  downright unacceptable. On the other hand, paasikivi felt that simply "relying on one's own strength" was too demanding of a small nation and proved to be disastrous in the lives of even large nations. Paasikivi wanted to find an answer to this dilemma in international relations. It is difficult to say how realistic he considered these things to be, but at least he considered them necessary and wanted to work on them. * * * Paasikivi's criticism of Snellman was directed at Snellman's views on the international legal order (or its impossibility). On the basis of this criticism, however, one cannot form a true picture of Snellman's thinking, and certainly not of the significance of his actions. Of course, Snellman's political agenda was not to submit to violence. Rather, Snellman held that violence had no chance of success in the long run, but that the triumph of freedom was a historical necessity, but that freedom had to be earned by one's own strength, specifically by one's own strength. This was related to his Hegelian conception of history. Snellman's significance, however, lies neither in his rugged visions of world history, in which nations fight for the leadership of mankind, nor in his Hegelian conception of Morasalism, which always accepts the so-called right of the victor. What is most original and valuable about Snellman's philosophy of nationality is his educational programme. In reality, Snellman's nationalism is not at all aggressive, but he assumes that it is the task of nations, and through them individual people, to make their own unique contribution to the development of all mankind. Snellman's special feature is precisely the emphasis on the power of civilisation. Snellman's education programme was national. However, this does not mean national egotism, but the idea that only on a truly own basis can something uniquely be made new contribution to the development of humanity. There is much in Snellman's opinions that we reject today as outdated and downright reactionary. His demand for the homogeneity of national culture, based on the philosophy of language, fits poorly with the multicultural reality of modern open society. Nor can we accept Mr Snellman's views on the position of women, for example, or her scepticism about democracy. But Snellman's idea that a nation's strength and success are due to its civilisation and ability to make something new available to all mankind is, as a vision, staggering and much more moderate than other economic policy or state programs of his time. It also shows how patriotism and internationalism can be reconciled. Snellman's vision was idealistic, but at the same time it was realpolitik. Finland's development over the past 150 years has also shown that this vision to hold true in practice. The prosperity of finland today and its reputation as a producer of cutting-edge technology or as a spearhead of PISA studies are based on the fruits of the Snellman education programme. It is precisely by following this strategy that Finland has risen from a poor backward country in Europe to a level capable of equal commercial, cultural and political interaction in Europe and globally. * * * Economic integration is one of the key dimensions of internationalisation. A visible expression of this is our membership of the European Economic and Monetary Union. Finland joined the euro area in pursuit of greater monetary stability and inclusiveness of the single market. It was a historic step, but still not unique in our history. It may seem paradoxical to celebrate Snellman, mark's father, at a time when the mark has been abandoned. However, it is not that simple. On closer inspection, you can see that the monetary reform of 1865, for which Snellman is praised, was in fact a measure along the same lines as Finland's entry into the euro area in 1999. Why is that? The chain of events that led to the creation of the silver mark in 1865, and with it the de facto detachment of the Finnish monetary system from Russia, did not start with separatist influences, but were motivated by practical economic reasons. The reform was about stabilising the value of the money and strengthening Finland's commercial links with Europe. In the past, in Crimean (or Oolannin) Finland, the currency was silver-exchanged banknotes issued by the Bank of Finland and Russian silver coins. In addition, Russian banknote rubles were also legal tender, so the Bank of Finland had to redeem them with silver as required. All in all, the situation was quite confusing. The outbreak of war in 1854 then triggered a monetary crisis in Russia and also in Finland, as a result of which the convertibility of the ruble for silver had to be abolished. It brought many difficulties. When the value of money was no longer tied to silver, it quickly began to decline. There was a shortage of exchange money because the silver coin disappeared into the coffers of speculators. The worst thing for Finland was that exchange rates in relation to their traditional trading partners in Sweden and Northern Germany began to fluctuate. Trade and access to foreign credit became more difficult. The Finns wanted a solution to the question of money. The emperor responded by awarding Finland its own currency, the mark, in 1860. However, it was defined in relation to the banknote-ruble, its quarter. When the banknote ruble still remained legal tender, this reform did not yet bring a solution to the main problem of how to return to the silver standard. Thus, the markka already existed when Snellman became head of finance in 1863. He took as his main task the restoration of the silver stock. For this, a sufficient silver reserve was needed for the Bank of Finland and, in addition, Russia's consent to the fact that the status of the ruble as legal tender in Finland would cease. Snellman traveled to St. Petersburg to negotiate. As a result of the trip, the emperor's consent was obtained that the mark could be redefined, not as a quarter of the ruble in general, but specifically as a quarter of the silver ruble. This is Snellman's most important achievement in the history of the Finnish markka. The Imperial Manifesto, which stipulated that domestic and Russian silver coins would henceforth become the only legal means of payment in Finland, were published in November 1865. As a result, the obstacles to returning to the silver standard were removed and the Bank of Finland began to redeem its banknotes with new silver marks in March of the following year. At the same time, the value of the markka stabilised in relation to other silver-bearing countries, such as our important trading partners Sweden and Germany. An interesting detail is that the silver value of the French franc, 4 1/2 grams of silver, coincidentally was exactly the same as that of the mark. Thus, the exchange rate of the franc in relation to the mark became exactly 1:1, which remained in force for decades, until the First World War. Markka's origin story shows that acquiring its own money for Finland was a way to be involved in the international economy. Later, in light of the events of 1917, the acquisition of one's own money has begun to be seen as the first step in Finland's detachment from Russia, although in time it was more of a means of seeking stability and a way of connecting to the European market. Of course, the development of its own national institutions, including its own currency, was part of Finland's maturation into state independence. However, it is worth remembering that in the 1800s the world lived first in the conditions of the silver standard and then the gold standard. An independent national monetary policy, separate from other countries, was not one of the hallmarks of an independent state at that time. On the contrary, the ideal of the time was participation in a universal monetary system based on a common measure of value, gold or silver. * * * The stability achieved by Snellman's monetary reform was lost in the whirlwinds of the First World War. After Finland became independent, a new basis had to be sought for the country's monetary system. Now the most important influencer was Risto Ryti, first as a young minister of finance and then as the governor of the Bank of Finland since 1924. Ryti set himself the goal of integrating the Finnish markka into the international monetary system, which was then being rebuilt. In his presentation on the subject, Ryti stated: "it is not enough to have a good monetary system, it is also required that our monetary system be such that it is trusted abroad". Ryti's purpose was to strengthen Finland's international creditworthiness in order to attract foreign investment to the country. He wanted to normalize Finland's high interest rates and help Finnish industry gain foreign capital. He thought that, as a capital-poor country, Finland could benefit from foreign loans and investments for a long time to come, and stabilising the value of the markka was a way for him to increase confidence. Ryti soon established himself as governor of the Bank of Finland after becoming president of the Finnish markka in relation to the U.S. gold dollar, and with the monetary law that entered into force in 1926, Finland formally returned to the gold standard. During the 1920s, most other countries adopted a gold-standard monetary system. However, the common paint-wide monetary system thus created did not last long and soon succumbed to the Great Depression of the 1930s. What is interesting for the present is that at that time, as in Snellman's time, a separate monetary policy was not considered to be one of the necessary characteristics of an independent state. Instead, Ryti's economic policy aimed to integrate Finland as well as possible into the international economy and to make international interest rates effective also in Finland. Ryti was also the first Finn to be active in multinational economic political cooperation. He represented Finland both in the Economic Committee of the League of Nations and in the meetings of the International Settlement Bank (BIS). It was from these connections that Ryti enjoyed even after the end of the war in English banking circles. In the 1930s, Ryti had to see firsthand the difficulty of international economic policy cooperation. Nevertheless, he did not renounce his view that it was vital for the country of Finland in particular to align its economic policy, and especially its monetary policy, with the international economic system. In 1937, Ryti wrote an article for the publication celebrating the 20th anniversary of Finland's independence, in which he discussed the international connections of Finnish monetary policy. He considered the future development of the international monetary system to be difficult to predict, but nevertheless considered it in Finland's national interest to be involved in future monetary cooperation. He wrote: "... whatever direction the development takes, and whatever the outcome, our small country has little choice but to go along with developments in the great world and to prepare in every way, at the right moment, for accession to the monetary system which best meets our interests and needs." * * * When you look at Paasikivi' s, Snellman's and Ryti's attitudes towards nationality and internationality, you will see that despite the differences, there is an important common feature in their thinking: they saw that Finnishness could best be realized only in international interaction. Their patriotism was thus neither isolationist nor aggressive in nature, but meant an effort to make Finland an equal and constructive part of the international community. However, they highlighted different aspects of international interaction. The aging Paasikivi examined the problems of international interaction from the perspective of national security. He hoped that international relations could be based on law, so that the "Staatsrason" and the politics of power would not be dominant in them. He hoped that the sovereignty of states could be limited to their common good, and clearly considered an international order based on law to be compatible with the idea of nationality. Snellman examined the relationship between the national and internationalism, especially from a cultural point of view. He used the concept of civilization in its broadest sense, to refer to all human construction work. For Snellman, therefore, the cultural perspective was not a partial perspective that would have excluded something relevant to human life. For him, it included everything that carried the development of mankind forward. In the stark picture painted by Snellman of the nation's development mission, its "quantity is to make its way from national one-sidedness to general humanity" and "... at the same time, the national independence of a nation must not be national, but the general power of mankind, of the spirit of the world." In practice, Snellman's nationality programme meant an effort to elevate Finland as a nation to a level where it could truly contribute to the cultural construction of humanity  including culture, economy, politics  in its own, meaningful and irreplaceable way. Ryti, on the other hand, was a banker and for him internationality meant above all participation in international economic interaction and division of labour. He saw that every country needed international interaction in order to be able to fully exploit its own resources and opportunities. He often stressed in particular that Finland was more dependent on international trade than almost all other countries. Ryti advocated free trade and a unified, free international monetary system, to which Finland was also supposed to be a part. This would ensure finland's financial stability and access to international capital markets. * * * As a central banker, I would like to mention here one of the most successful results of European integration, the single currency. When Finland is a member of the European Monetary Union, it is often said that Finland no longer has its own monetary policy. Is monetary generosity gone? Should Finns even be interested in monetary policy anymore? The answer to these arguments and doubts is that Finland has its own monetary policy, which is the single monetary policy of the euro area. It is a question of the mutual unification of sovereignty on terms that are well defined by the agreement of the Member States. The Bank of Finland participates in the formulation and implementation of practical monetary policy as one of the full members of the Eurosystem. It is fair to say that the Finns now have more influence on the financial economy of our continent than ever before through monetary union. In this area, we are at the heart of decision-making. But this influence is of a 'Snellmanian' nature: there is only influence to the extent that we are able to bring new elements to the making of the single monetary policy, not original content from others, but genuine original content. This is a challenge for the Bank of Finland. That is why the Bank invests in high-quality research and economic analysis. But it is also a challenge for Finnish economic research and financial journalism in general, because Finns have just as good a reason to engage in monetary-political research and debate as, say, Germans or French. Meeting this challenge is a prerequisite for us to be a citizen in European monetary policy, not as an object of power. Snellman's analysis of national strategy is unmissable on this issue as well. * * * The political future of Europe depends fundamentally on how the European Union develops in the future. The future development of the Union does not seem to be without its problems right now. Many have seen a weakening of european commitment, not only at the level of citizens, but also in the policies of governments. There has been discussion about the strong commitment of the governments of the various EU countries to the European project. The fate of the draft Constitution has remained open. As confusion sets in, it is worth returning to the eu's founding principles. At different stages of history, attempts have been made to unite Europe by subjecting our continent to a single hegemony. Those efforts have caused a great deal of destruction and suffering. The European Union differs from all previous attempts in that it is non-hegemonic, no one can gain supremacy. At the same time, however, efforts have been made to ensure the effectiveness of decision-making by means of qualified majority regulations. Indeed, non-hegemony and decision-making efficiency are two key characteristics that must be nurtured. The draft Constitution strengthens and clarifies these characteristics of the Union. However, it does not transfer to the Union new competences of a Member State. For this reason, the Government has acted correctly in proposing that the draft Constitution be ratified in Parliament. It is also good international practice that what a government with the confidence of a parliament signs, it also submits it for ratification by parliament. Nist yhteyksist oli perisin se arvostus, jota Ryti viel sodan ptyttykin nautti englantilaisissa pankkipiireiss. Ryti joutui omakohtaisesti 1930-luvulla toteamaan kansainvlisen talouspoliittisen yhteis-tyn vaikeuden. Siit huolimatta hn ei luopunut ksityksestn, ett varsinkin Suomen kal-taiselle maalle oli elintrke sovittaa talouspolitiikkansa ja varsinkin rahapolitiikkansa kan-sainvlisen talousjrjestelmn osaksi. Vuonna 1937 Ryti kirjoitti Suomen itsenisyyden 20-vuotisjuhlajulkaisuun artikkelin, jossa hn ksitteli Suomen rahapolitiikan kansainvlisi kytkentj. Hn piti kansainvlisen raha-jrjestelmn tulevaa kehityst vaikeasti ennustettavana, mutta katsoi kuitenkin Suomen kansallisen edun mukaista olevan olla mukana tulevaisuuden valuuttayhteistyss. Hn kir-joitti: "mit suuntaa kehitys kulkeekaan, ja millainen lopputulos sitten onkaan, on meidn pie-nell maallamme tuskin muuta mahdollisuutta kuin kulkea suuressa maailmassa tapahtuvan kehityksen mukana ja valmistella kaikin tavoin liittymist oikean hetken tullen rahajrjes-telmn, joka parhaiten vastaa meidn intressejmme ja tarpeitamme." * * * Kun tarkastelee Paasikiven, Snellmanin ja Rytin suhtautumista kansallisuuteen ja kansain-vlisyyteen, huomaa, ett eroista huolimatta heidn ajattelussaan on trke yhteinen piirre: he nkivt suomalaisuuden voivan parhaiten toteutua vain kansainvlisess vuorovaikutuk-sessa. Heidn patriotisminsa ei siten ollut luonteeltaan eristytyv eik aggressiivista, vaan se tarkoitti pyrkimyst saada Suomi tasavertaiseksi ja konstruktiiviseksi osaksi kansainvlis-t yhteis. He korostivat kuitenkin kansainvlisen vuorovaikutuksen eri puolia. Vanheneva Paasikivi tarkasteli kansainvlisen vuorovaikutuksen ongelmia kansallisen turvallisuuden nkkulmasta. Hn toivoi, ett kansainvliset suhteet voitaisiin perustaa laille, niin ett Staatsrson ja voimapolitiikka eivt olisi niiss mrvin. Hn toivoi, ett valtioiden suvereenisuutta voitaisiin rajoittaa niiden yhteiseksi eduksi, ja selvsti piti oikeuteen perustuvaa kansainvlist jrjestyst yhteensopivana kansallisuusaatteen kanssa. Snellman tarkasteli kansallisen suhdetta kansainvlisyyteen erityisesti sivistykselliselt kannalta. Hn kytti sivistyksen ksitett sen laajimmassa merkityksess, viittaamaan kaikkeen inhimilliseen rakennustyhn. Snellmanille sivistyksellinen nkkulma ei siten ollut mikn osittaisnkkulma, joka olisi rajannut pois jotakin inhimillisen elmn kannalta merkityksellist. Hnelle se sislsi kaiken, mik vei ihmiskunnan kehityst eteenpin. Snellmanin maalaamassa jylhss kuvassa kansakunnan kehitystehtvst sen mrn on raivata tiens kansallisesta yksipuolisuudesta yleiseen ihmisyyteen ja "kansakunnan kansallisen itsenisyyden ei samalla pidkn olla kansallista, vaan ihmiskunnan, maail-manhengen yleist mahtia". Kytnnss Snellmanin kansallisuusohjelma merkitsi pyrki-myst kohottaa Suomi kansakuntana tasolle, jolla se pystyisi todella tuomaan panoksensa ihmiskunnan sivistykselliseen rakennustyhn  sislten kulttuurin, talouden, politiikan  omalla, merkityksellisell ja korvaamattomalla tavallaan. Ryti puolestaan oli pankkimies ja hnelle kansainvlisyys merkitsi ennen kaikkea osallisuutta kansainvliseen taloudelliseen kanssakymiseen ja tynjakoon. Hn nki, ett jokainen maa tarvitsi kansainvlist vuorovaikutusta voidakseen tyteen mittaan hydynt omia voimavarojaan ja mahdollisuuksiaan. Hn korosti usein erityisesti, ett Suomi oli miltei kaikkia muita maita riippuvaisempi kansainvlisest kaupasta. Ryti kannatti vapaata kauppaa ja yhtenist, vapaata kansainvlist rahajrjestelm, johon mys Suomen piti kuulua. Tm turvaisi Suomelle rahaolojen vakauden ja psyn kansainvlisille poma-markkinoille. * * * Keskuspankki-ihmisen haluaisin tss ottaa esille Euroopan integraation ern menestyk-sellisimmist tuloksista, yhteisen rahan. Kun Suomi on Euroopan rahaliiton jsen, kuulee usein sanottavan, ettei Suomella ole en omaa rahapolitiikkaa. Onko rahapoliittinen suve-reenisuus mennytt? Kannattaneeko suomalaisten en olla edes kiinnostuneita raha-politiikasta? Nihin vitteisiin ja epilyihin voi vastata, ett Suomella on oma rahapolitiikka, joka on euroalueen yhteinen rahapolitiikka. Kysymys on suvereenisuuden vastavuoroisesta yhdis-tmisest ehdoin, jotka on jsenmaiden sopimuksella hyvin mritelty. Kytnnn rahapoli-tiikan muotoiluun ja toteutukseen Suomen Pankki osallistuu yhten eurojrjestelmn tysi-valtaisena jsenen. Voi perustellusti sanoa, ett suomalaisilla on rahaliiton kautta nykyn enemmn vaikutusvaltaa maanosamme rahatalouteen kuin koskaan aikaisemmin. Tll alu-eella me olemme ptksenteon ytimess. Mutta tm vaikutusvalta on "snellmanilaista" luonteeltaan: vaikutusvaltaa on vain siin mrin, kun pystymme tuomaan yhteisen rahapolitiikan tekoon uusia aineksia, ei muilta ko-pioitua, vaan aitoa omaperist sislt. Tm on haaste Suomen Pankille. Sen vuoksi Pankki panostaa korkeatasoiseen tutkimuk-seen ja talouden analyysiin. Mutta se on mys haaste yleens suomalaiselle taloustutkimuk-selle ja talousjournalismille, koska suomalaisilla on aivan yht hyv syy harjoittaa raha-poliittista tutkimusta ja keskustelua kuin vaikkapa saksalaisilla tai ranskalaisilla. Haasteeseen vastaaminen on ehtona sille, ett olemme Euroopan rahapolitiikassa kansalai-sen, emme vallankytn kohteen asemassa. Snellmanin analyysi kansallisesta strategiasta on ohittamaton tsskin kysymyksess. * * * Euroopan poliittinen tulevaisuus riippuu keskeisesti siit, miten Euroopan Unioni jatkossa kehittyy. Unionin tuleva kehitys ei juuri nyt nyt ongelmattomalta. Monet ovat nhneet Eu-rooppa-sitoutumisen heikkenemist paitsi kansalaisten tasolla, mys hallitusten politiikassa. Keskustelua on kyty siit, kuinka vahvasti eri EU-maiden hallitukset ovat sitoutuneet eu-rooppalaiseen projektiin. Perustuslakiesityksen kohtalo on jnyt avoimeksi. Kun hmmennys valtaa alaa, on syyt palata EU:n perusperiaatteisiin. Historian eri vaiheis-sa Eurooppaa on yritetty yhdist alistamalla maanosamme yhden hegemonian alaiseksi. Ne pyrkimykset ovat aiheuttaneet paljon tuhoa ja krsimyst. Euroopan unioni poikkeaa kaikista aikaisemmista yrityksist sen vuoksi, ett se on ei-hegemoninen, kukaan ei voi saada ylivaltaa. Mutta samalla ptksenteon tehokkuus on pyritty turvaamaan mrenemmistsdksin. Ei-hegemonisuus ja ptksenteon tehok-kuus ovatkin kaksi keskeist ominaisuutta, joita on vaalittava. Perustuslakiesitys vahvistaa ja tsment nit Unionin ominaisuuksia. Se ei kuitenkaan siirr Unionin toimivaltaan uusia jsenvaltion toimivaltuuksia. Tmn vuoksi hallitus on toiminut oikein esittessn perustuslakiesityksen ratifioimista eduskunnassa. On mys hy-v kansainvlist kytnt se, ett mink parlamentin luottamusta nauttiva hallitus allekir-joittaa, sen se esitt mys parlamentin ratifioitavaksi. Kirkkaissa periaatteissa pysyminen tekee ptksentekotilanteen selkeksi. Aika sitten nytt, kuinka perustuslain ksittely EU:n tasolla etenee. Ensi kevt on seuraava tarkastelukohta. * * * Kirjoittaessaan "Staatsrsonin" rajoittamisesta Paasikivi ei voinut arvioida, kuinka realistisia tai eprealistisia hnen toiveensa olisivat. Euroopan integraation saavuttamat konkreettiset edistysaskeleet  rahaliitto ei ole niist vhisin  ja sen tuottamat tulokset rauhana, liikku-misvapautena ja vaurautena kuitenkin osoittavat, ett kysymys ei ollut vain haaveilusta. On kiistatonta, ett Suomen kansainvlinen asema on nyt paljon vahvempi kuin Paasikiven kirjoittaessa mietteitn kansainvlisest politiikasta. Tai kun Kekkonen vuonna 1962 kvi keskusteluja De Gaullen kanssa Pariisissa ja tapasi Jean Monnetn Maison Carrssa. Vas-taavasti suomalaisten, niin kansalaisten kuin yritystenkin, asema nyt, eurooppalaisina, on aivan toinen kuin tuolloin. Tm hyv kehitys on suureksi osaksi tapahtunut juuri sen seurauksena, ett olemme voi-neet tysivaltaisesti osallistua syvenevn eurooppalaiseen integraatioon, eik tst integraa-tiosta huolimatta. Euroopan unioni, jonka ptksenteon tehokkuudesta pidetn huoli ja jonka toiminnan jatkuvuuden takaavat yhteiset instituutiot, on siksi meidn etumme. .

Title: Innovation, business growth and financial markets, at the 100th anniversary seminar of Parliament in Kauhajoki
text: Innovation, business growth and financial markets Presentation at the 100th anniversary seminar of parliament in Kauhajoki 2.12.2006 Dear Jubilee General, First of all, I would like to thank you very much for the invitation to Kauhajoki. This is a very special joy, as Kauhajoki is my birthplace, where I lived my first five years. Thus, at the entrepreneur seminar, it should be mentioned that my parents were here when they were young  just over 20 years old  preparing to become entrepreneurs, to continue my grandfather's trade activities a little further north in Southern Ostrobothnia, in Kortesjarvi. My father was here as a store manager for a co-operative shop in the village, and my mother owned half of Kauhajoki's Kotikutomo! Ladies and gentlemen! Over the past hundred years, Finland's total production has developed as favourable as before. This has made it possible to make progress in the field of my health, social care and other welfare services. The general improvement in living conditions is perhaps better illustrated than any other single indicator by the increase in life expectancy. The expected life span of a newborn is now about 32 years longer than a hundred years ago. Total output per capita has increased, on the one hand, as a result of the capitalisation of production and, on the other hand, the increase in productivity of the producers of production  ty and capital. Of the two, productivity growth is estimated to have been clearly more significant over the past hundred years. Its importance has become even more pronounced since the 1980s, when the growth of the capital stock has slowed down. In an economy that operates efficiently and consumes advanced technology, productivity growth requires investment in new technologies. The commercial and economic exploitation of scientific and technical inventions  i.e. innovation  means new and better products and services or new, more efficient ways of producing former products and services. Expenditure on research and product development is an essential contribution to innovation, although the results of the activity - successful innovations - do not, of course, depend solely on them. Financial markets channel economic resources from low-productivity industries and firms to high-productivity industries and firms. In other words, they finance the restructuring of the economy. In connection with industrialization, the work was transferred from agriculture to industry. A new structural change is now underway, in which the factors of production are shifting from the manufacture of industrial products to high-productivity services. This structural change is part of the globalisation of the economy, an essential element of which is the strong internationalisation of the financial markets. Financial markets also provide financing for investments aimed at accelerating the growth of business productivity. The use of new technologies in a company is often accompanied by investments in machinery and equipment, but increasingly productivity is increased through innovation and other intangible investments. Enterprises that have already established themselves can finance their usual innovation activities largely with income financing. By contrast, starting a new technology company or implementing a major innovation project almost invariably requires external funding. In a well-functioning financial market, a company's risks can be diversified effectively. This allows innovation companies to focus on what they do best and grow very quickly when conditions allow. International risk diversification also enables companies operating in small countries to become world leaders in their field. The theme of this presentation, in a nutshell, is the blessing of the internal market and, in particular, of an integrated European financial market for growth companies. Let me first look at what qualities are required of a good venture capital market  after all, financing innovations is almost always risk finance. Here, of course, the developed and deep us financial markets provide a good basis for comparison and illustrate why there is a need for an integrated financial market in Europe as well. After that, a few words about finland's innovation financing system and why our growth companies could also jump out of the integrated venture capital markets. Finally, I will briefly assess the stage at which we are in the process of European integration of the financial markets and what measures are needed to remove the remaining obstacles to a single financial market. Characteristics and importance of good venture capital markets for innovation and growth Financing innovation is almost always risk finance. This is primarily due to the fact that the distribution of revenue from innovation projects is skewed. In other words, there are a lot of failures, and few real successes - but the returns from successful projects can be very high, up to a thousand times the initial contribution. Identifying profitable innovation projects is a challenging and professional task not only for innovative companies but also for financiers of innovation projects. The biggest opportunities, but at the same time the biggest risks, lie in new, fast-growing sectors and in financing new companies that are just starting out. The challenge of financing decisions for these companies is increased by the fact that the cost of developing innovations can be high, and in some sectors it may take a very long time to become profitable. During the implementation of a project, there is often no capital accumulate that could be used as collateral for financing, and financiers may have an unclear picture of the real potential of the project at all times. Well-functioning venture capital markets allocate funding to projects with a good expected return. On the other hand, they are cutting back on projects with poor prospects in relation to their risks. Risk investments are not in themselves a new invention, but have been made in various forms for centuries, if not millennia. However, in developed financial markets, risk finance markets have differentiated into a separate market segment. The current kind of professional private equity investment activity based on special funds has its origins in the United States, where the first venture capital firms aimed to commercialize technologies developed during the Second World War. *** One feature of recent economic developments that has received a lot of attention is that, since the 1990s, real GDP and productivity growth has been faster in the United States than in Europe. Productivity growth in the United States has accelerated faster than in Europe, especially in services that use a wealth of information and communication, such as retail, wholesale and financial services. While productivity growth in Europe has been slower than in the United States, European companies have invested less in development and research than U.S. firms. In relation to total output, US expenditure on research and development is one and a half times higher than in the EU. In addition, the share of enterprises in total R&D expenditure in the United States is clearly higher than the European average. The stronger investment of enterprises in innovation activity is estimated to be one of the factors explaining the favourable productivity development in the United States. Differences in the performance of financial markets may explain part of the different innovation activity in Europe and the United States. The corporate finance market in the United States is generally more developed than in Europe. There is no doubt that large, globally operating European companies will be able to implement their financial decisions at a very competitive price today, regardless of the country in which they are headquartered. In the case of small and medium-sized enterprises, on the other hand, access to financial instruments is more limited, especially in small countries, and they may also encounter relatively large interest rate margins in their financial transactions. In particular, those parts of the financial system that focus on financing the upstream and growth phases of high-skilled companies are still quite mature in Europe. This applies to both private equity and IPO activities. Investments in the private equity market are estimated to be many times higher in the United States than in Europe. In the United States, there are also a large number of venture capital investments made by private individuals (i.e. so-called business angels), the total amount of which is estimated to exceed the total amount of investments made by private equity funds in start-up and growth-stage companies. One explanation for the underdevelopment of European venture capital is probably that their markets in Europe are still largely national. This may redirect funding to small projects and make it more difficult to delay funding for projects that directly target the european market as a whole. In Finland, for example, the financing of the latter-mentioned companies is central  after all, it is based on Finland's innovation activity concentrated, innovation funding fragmented Finland is considered a model country for competence. In 2005, Finland's R&D expenditure relative to GDP was about 3.5%, of which enterprises accounted for about 70%. Finland's figures stand up well to comparison with the United States and by European standards: After Sweden, Finland is the most research-intensive country in Europe. Research and development has also been quite effective. One indication of this is that more patents are sold per capita to Finns than to citizens of any other EU country, with the exception of Germans. The productivity of my production workers has increased well compared to other EU countries or even the United States. In some areas, such as telecommunications technology, it has already reached the top of the world rankings. However, R&D in Finland is highly concentrated. Most of the activities are carried out in the ict sector. One enterprise, Nokia, is estimated to account for around one-third of the R&D expenditure of the entire national economy and close on one-half of the R&D expenditure of the non-financial corporations sector. The concentration of research and development is, of course, largely indicative of the strength and success of the ICT cluster. On the other hand, it suggests that the research effort of other companies is relatively modest. When surveying the innovation activity of enterprises in the EU, it has been found that the number of enterprises with innovation activity in Finland is only the same as in the EU countries on average. *** Finland's corporate finance environment has changed and developed strongly over the past 10-15 years. Our financial system has diversified and its bank-centricity has decreased. I am hardly too optimistic if I think that access to finance is generally no longer a major problem, even for small and medium-sized enterprises. However, risk finance is needed to commercialise and finance innovations. It is important for the growth dynamics of the economy that we have a risk investment industry that channels equity financing efficiently  and selectively where necessary. A notable feature of our corporate finance system is that it is home to a wide range of organisations providing public corporate finance and support. Public business funding is provided and the R&D and development activities of enterprises are supported by e.g. Finnish Funding Agency for Technology and Innovation Tekes, Finnish Industry Investment, Sitra, Finnvera, and Industry Investment and Employment and Economic Development Centres, i.e. the so-called Finnish Industry Investment Agency. TE Centres. The public provision of finance cannot be considered to be negligible on the whole. According to a survey by the Bank of Finland and the Minister of Trade and Industry, 40% of large industrial companies had used public corporate financing during the past year. It is also estimated that approximately one in three Finnish SMEs would have ever received some form of public funding or support. Despite developments in financial markets, the provision of public finance may still be necessary in some cases. I do not want to dispute that. However, I think it is good to remember the various problems associated with the abundant provision of public funding. We must have the courage to ask under what circumstances an individual organisation channelling public corporate finance, or, more generally, the entire public corporate finance system, will be able to solve problems that private financial market participants have failed to solve on market terms. At the same time, we will have to consider the effectiveness of our current system of public corporate finance, which seems rather fragmented, at least to outsiders. In addition to the effectiveness of the public corporate finance system, attention must be paid to the fact that private risk finance is abundant and that financiers are able to take on even high risks if necessary. This is the kind of activity that should be pursued in my Finland. The Finnish venture capital market can certainly be improved through national measures. However, I believe that the most important thing for My Finland is the development of the entire EU venture capital market. When making investment decisions, the importance of national factors decreases and the importance of sector-specific factors increases. For a remote country like Finland, this is an advantage. The creation of deep and well-functioning financial markets in the EU is key to providing European companies  including Finnish growth companies  with a large and open domestic market. It is clear that without a single, borderless financial market, a common market for services and goods cannot function optimally and companies will not be able to pursue their innovations on a Europe-wide basis and productise them in the best possible way. As I have emphasised, this is particularly important for Finnish innovation companies. In other words, the whole idea of the internal market will remain halfway through unless we get deep and liquid financial markets in Europe. Integration will promote competition and technological development in financial markets and broaden and deepen financial intermediation. In this way, it enhances the use of capital and strengthens the growth potential of real GDP. Although the volume of cross-border investments and investments has increased, the integration of venture capital markets in Europe is still at an early stage. Last year, more than 60% of the investments made by European venture capital funds went to the fund's home country and only 35% to other European countries.1 The national segmentation of European venture capital markets is often explained by legislative, fiscal and administrative barriers that hamper both cross-border risk investing and cross-border investments. In addition, regulation varies from country to country, which also contributes to making it more difficult for risk investors to operate effectively on a Europe-wide basis. A more integrated environment would provide European venture capitalists with a wider and better functioning market, supporting innovation and growth by companies. The example of the United States shows that large and deep capital finance markets offer opportunities to finance even significant projects by dynamic companies. An integrated market would also make it possible to finance, on a larger scale, projects aimed directly at the european market as a whole. The Europeanisation of venture capital would also bring benefits to venture capitalists, who, by pooling their resources, could diversify the 1 In addition to venture capital funds, these figures also include so-called venture capital funds investing in mergers and acquisitions and more mature companies. buy-out funds. risks and to make more efficient use of scarce expert resources in the field. In addition, in a large and well-functioning financial market, it would be easier to exit investments, either through an IPO or an acquisition, which is important for the long-term development of the private equity industry. In order to achieve truly integrated financial markets in Europe, both legislative work and efforts by the various parties involved in the financial markets are needed to integrate the infrastructure of the financial markets. A great deal of this largely unseen has been done in Europe in recent years and, as a result, a number of major joint projects aimed at restructuring and improving the efficiency of financial markets are being implemented and planned in the EU. In the next few years, it will be topical to deepen the integration of retail banking and clearing and payment systems in particular. *** Ladies and gentlemen! Well-functioning, pan-European financial markets are key to the EU's efforts to build an economically cohesive and dynamic Europe. Significant progress has been made in the process of integrating the financial markets without the use of the euro. However, many other sectors of the financial markets, such as venture capital, are still segmented nationally. With regard to the future integration of the EU's financial markets, I believe that there is reason to be optimistic. The advantages of creating a truly unified financial market are simply too great in comparison with the costs to leave them unabashed. But optimism does not mean that the development will take place without a strong commitment to it. The importance of financial integration must therefore be kept on the political agenda both here in Finland and at EU level. Although I have talked above mainly about the development and provision of finance in the business finance environment, Finland's problem is probably not only the availability of financing or even risk finance. It's all about entrepreneurship and willingness to take risks. Here in Ostrobothnia, entrepreneurship has traditionally been valued and entrepreneurs relatively more than elsewhere in Finland. However, surveys show that, on average, Finns prefer to be employees rather than entrepreneurs (less than 30% prefer to be entrepreneurs) and that the difference to the United States, for example, is large in this respect (just over 30% individual). Compared to the rest of Europe, the willingness to engage in entrepreneurship is low in Finland. However, in view of the conditions for the growth of our economy, it would be important for there to be a sufficient number of entrepreneurs in our country and for those who have the ability and, above all, the desire to bear the risk, to identify significant commercial applications and to lead the economic activity required for this commercialisation should be selected as entrepreneurs. Throughout its activities, the Parliament has strived to create a good and competitive operating environment for Finnish business. This has contributed to the favourable development of real GDP and productivity over the past hundred years. In the future, we must ensure that the preconditions for business operations remain good in Finland. Finns can only succeed in the globalizing global economy if our society is capable of renewal, we offer companies a competitive and flexible operating environment, and if we produce and nurture the latest know-how and knowledge better and faster than others. This means that the importance of parliament as a guarantor of the renewal and competitiveness of society will be emphasised even more in the future.

Nin yrittjseminaarissa mainittakoon, ett vanhempani olivat tll nuorina  vain hieman yli 20-vuotiaina  valmentautumassa yrittjiksi, jatkamaan isoisni kauppatoimintaa vhn pohjoisempana Etel-Pohjanmaata, Kortesjrvell. Isni oli tll kirkonkyln osuuskaupan myymlnhoitajana ja itini omisti puolet Kauhajoen Kotikutomosta! Hyvt kuulijat! Suomen kokonaistuotanto on kehittynyt sadan viime vuoden aikana ennennkemttmn suotuisasti. Tm on tehnyt mahdolliseksi edistyksen my terveyden, sosiaalihuollon ja muiden hyvinvointipalveluiden alalla. Tutkimus- ja tuotekehittelymenot ovat innovaatiotoiminnan oleellisia panoksia, vaikkakaan toiminnan tulokset - onnistuneet innovaatiot - eivt tietenkn riipu pelkstn niist. Rahoitusmarkkinat kanavoivat talouden voimavaroja alhaisen tuottavuuden toimialoilta ja yrityksilt korkean tuottavuuden toimialoille ja yrityksille. Nyt meneilln on uusi rakennemuutos, jossa tuotannontekijt siirtyvt teollisuustuotteiden valmistuksesta korkean tuottavuuden palveluihin. Tm rakennemuutos on osa talouden globalisaatiota, jonka olennainen osa on rahoitusmarkkinoiden voimakas kansainvlistyminen.
