Box 160, 00101 HELSINKI Phone (09) 1831Fax (09) 611 694, 658 424 Telegram mail info@bof.fi PB 160, 00101 HELSINGFORS Telefon (09) 1831Fax (09) 611 694, 658 424E-post info@bof.fi P.O. Box 160, FIN-00101 HELSINKI, FINLAND Phone International 358 9 1831 Fax 358 9 611 694, 358 9 658 424Email info@bof.fi In 1865, the monetary reform carried out under the leadership of J. V. Snellman finally realized the goal of the Finns: the markka was detached from the ruble and connected to silver. At the same time, exchange rates against other silver currencies locked in. This was important because silver was the predominant monetary metal in all of Northern Europe and Scandinavia at that time. From today's point of view, it is interesting to note that the emergence of the Finnish markka was therefore by no means due to an attempt to provide the country with a special national monetary room for manoeuvre, but on the contrary, the aim was to stabilise the value of money and, at the same time, to integrate the monetary system into important trading partners in northern Germany and Sweden. After all, in a metal-based monetary system, there could not really be an independent monetary policy. The next monetary reform, the abandonment of silver and the linkage of the markka with the gold standard in 1878, were also due to the same reasons. During the 1870s, the gold-bearing monetary system had spread from England into a pan-European monetary system in practice, and the value of silver had become unstable at the same time. Finland thus threatened to be left alone with its silver currency. The spread of the gold standard was, in fact, an integral part of the great wave of globalisation of the 1870s, which included the growing importance of railways, humblers and the telegraph, as well as the rapid increase in foreign trade. The Finnish markka was linked to the gold standard in such a way that the gold value of the Finnish markka was set exactly equivalent to the French franc. In this respect, Finland was not alone. Around France, the so-called "guerrillas" had already arisen in the past. Latin monetary union, whose monetary units of the member states were identical to the French franc, although the names varied. In practice, however, the French, Belgian and Swiss francs, the Spanish pesetas and the Italian lira were all of equal value. Finland joined this group in 1878, albeit with a one-sided decision. Indeed, the exchange rate of the Finnish markka against all the currencies of the Latin Monetary Union was simply 1:1 for the entire period in which the gold standard system was in force, that is, until the First World War: 37 years. In a way, we were already in monetary union at that time  at the time when Ville Wallgren and Albert Edelfelt were creating cultural links for us in Paris. After Finland gained independence, the monetary system had to be rebuilt again, now in order to stabilise the value of the markka in the wake of the inflation caused by the world war and the confused monetary affairs of the early years of the young republic. The aim was to reconnect with the international gold standard system, which was successful from the beginning of 1926. However, the gold standard system between the world wars could not withstand the depression and financial crises of the 1930s, either here or elsewhere. After the collapse of the international gold standard in the autumn of 1931, the markka floated for about a year and a half, after which the Bank of Finland linked it to the pound sterling, part of the so-called pound sterling. pound club. After all, England was Finland's most important trading partner at the time. Since the Second World War, the world's monetary system has been the subject of multilateral international cooperation. The agreement is based on the Treaty establishing the International Monetary Fund, which Finland signed in 1948. From this point on, the Finnish monetary system was part of the international so-called monetary system. The Bretton Woods system, the idea of which was that currencies were linked to the dollar and, through it, indirectly to gold. The greatest achievement of the system was the interchangeability of the currencies of the western industrialised countries, which was crucial for the growth and economic development of world trade, including in Finland. However, the system collapsed when the US dollar entered a crisis of confidence in 1971. The dollar-linked exchange rate system was soon abandoned worldwide, and the main currencies began to float against each other. The Fund began to focus on the prevention and aftermath of monetary crises. After the fall of the Bretton Woods system, finland, as in the other Nordic countries, was looking for ways to restore stability to the monetary system. For us, the solution was to link the markka to the currency index, a kind of basket of currencies that included the currencies of all the main trading partners. The markka was officially pegged to such a basket of currencies in 1977, and the system remained in force until 1991, when the Economic Crisis in Finland and political changes in Europe consigned it to history. The economic crisis in Finland undermined the monetary policy pursued up to that point. There was no possibility of fixing the exchange rate, so the guidelines for monetary policy had to be sought elsewhere. The markka had to be devalued in the autumn of 1991 and allowed to float in the autumn of 1992. At this critical juncture, the inflation target was made the primary objective of monetary policy: at the beginning of 1993, the Bank of Finland announced that monetary policy would aim to keep inflation below two per cent. It was not yet known that this would be very precisely the same thing that the European Central Bank would later adopt as the main objective of monetary policy for the whole of EMU. In a way, therefore, it can now be said that Finland's convergence towards the monetary system of EMU began already at that time, although it could not be guessed at the time. Finland joined the EU at the beginning of 1995, and immediately began building the capacity to join the monetary union that the old EU countries had already decided on in Maastricht three years earlier. "However, the final decision on accession was not made in Finland until the spring of 1998. The birth and institutions of monetary union The idea of a European monetary union is not new. It was already being developed in the early 1970s within what was then the European Economic Community (EEC). Known as the Werner Plan, the project lived on for a few years but did not come to fruition before collapsing into the upheavals of the international economy, such as the great thunder crisis of 1973. The EEC countries were forced to lower their ambitions for monetary integration for a long time. When, in the 1970s, after the collapse of the Bretton Woods system, the world's major currencies began to float in relation to each other, European countries decided to link their currencies together, forming the so-called "currencies". the currency snake, which in the early 1980s developed into the European Exchange Rate System (ERM). The purpose of the arrangement was to reduce exchange rate fluctuations between THEEC countries and thus stabilise the conditions of competition in the single market area. The aim was, so to speak, a level playing field in which exchange rate changes would not solve the competitiveness of companies or national economies. In practice, the ERM was a system in which other countries more or less closely linked their currencies to the German mark, which became known as the anchor currency. German monetary policy thus rose to a leading position in Europe. The dominant role of German monetary policy was only accentuated during the 1980s, when capital movements in the EEC countries were liberalised and efforts were made to increase the mutual stability of exchange rates in the ERM system. The ERM system had certain operational and political problems that led to the idea of a European monetary union being revived in the late 1980s. From a political point of view, the dominance of the Deutsche Bundesbank was difficult, although the monetary policy pursued by the Bundesbank was generally considered to be successful and enjoyed a high degree of confidence. However, the Bundesbank was "only" the Deutsche Bundesbank, its monetary mandate was only German and not European, and its main bodies were elected by the Germans and consisted only of Germans. This did not satisfy the other Member States of the economic community, in particular the French and the Italians. From a functional point of view, there were my problems with the ERM system. Firstly, several of the currencies in the system were not able to achieve full market confidence, although the countries made quite close efforts to follow German monetary policy. The lack of confidence was reflected in the fact that inflation expectations and interest rates in these countries rose at times well above those in germany, the anchor country of the system. It was clearly discernible, for example: In Italy and Spain, and occasionally in my France. The lack of credibility of monetary policy posed a major economic policy problem in many European countries, especially in combination with the very slow growth in Western Europe in the early 1980s. There was talk of 'Eurosclerosis'. Another operational problem with the ERM system was that the existence of separate national currency units significantly increased the cost of exchanging currencies within the European economic community, especially as economies were highly integrated so that trade and travel among member states was very extensive. Comparing prices between different countries was not as easy as the idea of a single European market would have required, which reduced competition and thus the overall dynamism of the economies. Solving these political and economic problems was only possible by forming a monetary union that would give all Member States an equal position in monetary policy, put an end to the pressure on exchange rates between European countries due to a lack of confidence and create the conditions for the creation of a truly unified European market area. That is why the idea of a monetary union between the EEC countries was dug out of naphthaline in the mid-1980s and a committee of experts was set up to consider the possibility of establishing a monetary union. The Committee was chaired by Jacques Delors, a very influential President of the European Commission. The Delors Committee report was submitted in 1989 and the Maastricht Treaty, written on the basis of it, was signed in February 1992. Monetary union entered into force in practice at the beginning of 1999. Talln Finland was already a member of the EU and joined the monetary union in the first group together with ten other countries. The Maastricht Treaty, which defined the organisational structure of economic and monetary union and the timetable for its transition to it, was very much in line with the delors committee's recommendations. In fact, the structure of the agreement is very similar to the original Werner plan from the early 70s. The institutional structure of monetary union has been formulated very carefully. Its architecture places particular emphasis on the issues required to conduct a credible and stable monetary policy, as well as on the legitimacy of the system for the Member States. The task was not entirely simple, because in order to ensure credibility and stability, the central bank that governs the single currency had to be made independent and isolated from politics. The real unification of monetary systems required a fairly centralised decision-making system and uniform technical systems throughout the monetary union. On the other hand, however, the legitimacy of the system in the eyes of member states and citizens, as well as a proper understanding of local conditions, require that the central bank to be established should have solid roots in all Member States and their national financial centres. Thus, no distant 'ivory tower' could be built from the Common Central Bank. The main principles of the system were a system of central banks made up of national central banks and a single European Central Bank, in which decision-making is centralised, but in practice, including banking transactions, the implementation of monetary policy is mainly carried out by the national central banks. The national central banks of the euro area and the European Central Bank, which together are responsible for monetary policy in the region, are called the Eurosystem. The closest reference point to this structure is the US Federal Reserve system, which in a similar way consists of twelve regional central banks and the Federal Reserve Board in Washington. The National Central Banks own the European Central Bank and play a decisive role in its decision-making process. The highest decision-making body of the ECB is the Governing Council, which comprises the governors of all the central banks participating in monetary union. From Finland, the Council thus includes Matti Vanhala, President of the Bank of Finland. In addition to the governors of the national central banks, the governing council is also composed of six members of the Executive Board of the ECB. The Executive Board of the ECB is the operational steering body, which is permanently based in Frankfurt and prepares the meetings of the Governing Council and is responsible for implementing the decisions taken therein. The Executive Board of the ECB is supported by a total of thirteen committees composed of representatives from all ncbs and the ECB. These committees each specialise in their respective areas of central banking. So we have the Monetary Policy Committee, the Market Operations Committee, the Payment Systems Committee, and so on. The importance of the committee institution lies in the fact that cooperation within the Eurosystem is not limited to formal decision-making and its implementation according to common guidelines. Thanks to the committees, the implementation of monetary policy and the preparation of various development projects are now carried out in close cooperation on a system-wide basis. There are still a large number of different groups and task forces operating under the auspices of the committees. Civil service central banks  such as the Bank of Finland  are now very international in nature due to committee work, for example. In order to safeguard the political independence of monetary policy in the Maastricht Treaty provided that both the NCBs and the ECB must be financially independent and, in their decision-making, independent. The persons elected to the executive boards of central banks are inseparable from practice during their term of office and may not take orders from any outside body, not even national governments or parliaments, in monetary matters. The fact that Europe is a federation of nation states and not a federation like the United States is reflected in the structure and functioning of central banking systems. In Europe, it is the national central banks, and through them the nation states, that own the system and ultimately decide how it works. The NCBs also have a majority in the Governing Council of the ECB, which makes important monetary policy decisions. In the United States, on the other hand, the Federal Reserve Board is a federal agency, and in the so-called "federal reserve" that decides monetary policy. in the Open Market Committee, a majority of votes are cast by directors appointed by the President. The governors of the regional banks have fewer votes. In the decision-making process of the Governing Council, all members shall have one vote. When President Vanhala attends meetings of the Governing Council, where monetary policy is decided, he therefore has the same number of votes as all the other members of the Council  for example, Ernst Welteke of the German Bundesbank or Jean-Claude Trichet of France. Only when deciding on the ECB's own finances, such as its distribution of profits, are the number of votes proportional to the size of each member state. Such a 'one member, one vote' principle is based on the fundamental convergence of the monetary policy interests of the Member States. If this were not the case, the whole system would naturally be impossible and would not have been built in this way in the first place. It is worth emphasizing this point. The ECB's monetary policy objective is to pursue price stability throughout the euro area. 'The euro area as a whole' means that the policy is not tailored to the needs of any single country or group of countries. There was no contradiction in this from the point of view of an individual Member State: even if we Finns were to be able to decide on the monetary policy of the euro area on our own, it would still not be worthwhile for us to take only finland's cyclical situation as the starting point for the monetary policy of the entire monetary union, even if our own situation was different from the others. It is in the interest of each Member State, and thus of Finland, that the euro area economy as a whole remains in balance. In the context of the single currency, we are all in the same boat, equally dependent on the stability of the price level of the euro area, that is, the value of the euro, and, in particular, on the confidence it enjoys. As a result, the monetary policy interests of the countries that have joined the euro area largely coincide, and this is the starting point for a decision in the Governing Council. The ECB's monetary policy But what are the objectives and operating principles of monetary policy in practice? The Governing Council has defined a monetary policy strategy consisting of the following elements: an operational definition of price stability and two "pillars" that structure the decision-making process. The ECB Charter, which entrusts the bank with the task of maintaining price stability in the euro area, does not define what price stability means. The Governing Council has therefore had to define this concept itself. The definition is that, in a context of price stability, the rate of increase in consumer prices should remain below two per cent over the medium term. Consumer prices are measured by means of the so-called Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices, which is calculated in the same way in all EU Member States. - In recent months, inflation in the euro area has exceeded the two per cent mark and has gone as high as three per cent. However, according to forecasts, inflation is now on the decline, so the definition of price stability, which refers to the 'medium term', is unlikely to be breached. In addition to defining the objective, the strategy includes two pillars that describe how monetary policy in practice aims to achieve its objective. The first pillar is monetary. A reference value for the pace of monetary growth has been set for the monitoring of monetary developments. According to the reference value, annual monetary growth of around 41/2% can be expected to be consistent with price stability. The amount of money is measured by a special M3 figure, which includes not only cash but also bank deposits and securities issued by banks to a very large extent. -The interpretation of monetary growth has recently been clearly hampered by investment movements between the euro area and other countries, as well as by the fact that, during falling stock prices, the popularity of bank deposits in Europe has increased greatly. The second pillar of the monetary policy strategy is a "broad assessment of future price developments and related risks", which refers to the real economy, forward-looking analysis. Attention is paid here, for example, to the relationship between supply and demand in the jelly and cannon calendars of the euro area, as well as to inflationary pressures from commodity prices, such as the prices of grain. In the context of analyses under the second pillar, macroeconomic projections, or rather estimates, which the Eurosystem produces as a basis for the Council's work, play an important role. These estimates have now begun to be published in a regulatory  semi-annual  manner, which it is hoped will clarify the rationale for monetary policy in terms of the money market and the wider general. The strategy of the two pillars of monetary policy is not of a mechanical nature. It is based on the idea that both monetary growth and the general inflation outlook must be carefully interpreted and weighed in order to distinguish transient interference from long-term changes, and to correctly weight the signal values of various indicators. This requires not only the technology of economists, but also a lot of wisdom, vision and a sense of what is really happening in the economies of the euro area. That is why monetary policy decision-making and the final interpretation of the situation will take place in the Governing Council, which, through the governors of the various national central banks, has a broad understanding of economic developments in the euro area as a whole. In this consideration by the Council, the contribution of the national central banks is significant. The shape of the ECB's monetary policy and the functioning of its strategy in practice can be followed by any interested person. Once a month, the Governing Council meeting is followed by a press release on monetary policy and a press conference is held at which Ecb President Wim Duisenberg answers questions from the press. Both the press release and a summary of the press conference will be posted on the ECB's website as soon as the press conference ends. When you read the press release, you will immediately see that it is organised by means of strategic pillars: firstly, you comment on the growth of money and bank credit under pillar one, and then you move on to the second pillar, such as cost pressures and the demand situation. The same structure is observed in the monetary policy reviews that the ECB regularly publishes in its monthly bulletin. This publication is also available in Finnish  conveniently on the Internet, and you can pick it up from the Bank of Finland. In the economic press, monetary policy in the euro area is often commented on in relation to exchange rate developments  the dollar value of the euro is of particular interest. This is natural, because exchange rates fluctuate on a daily basis, but sometimes the importance of the exchange rate is exaggerated. The ECB has not set any target level for the exchange rate, and the monetary policy objectives have been defined solely in terms of price stability. The aim is therefore to stabilise the purchasing power of the euro within the euro area and not to maintain exchange rates as such, and monetary policy is in no way dictated by exchange rate developments. Of course, the exchange rate plays a role in inflation, in that the weakening of the euro in the foreign exchange markets may cause higher import prices and thus inflationary pressures in the euro area. It is only in this way that the exchange rate is linked to the monetary policy strategy, i.e. as part of the broad assessment of inflationary pressures in the 'second pillar' to which I have just referred. In the early days of monetary union, the exchange rate of the euro attracted a great deal of attention because the value of the euro against the dollar fell almost continuously from the beginning of 1999 to the autumn of 2000. Since then, the euro has fluctuated somewhat, but has no longer been depreciating in a trend-like manner. At the same time, the debate on the exchange rate has been diluted. Effects of monetary union on Finland There is already so much experience of monetary union that the picture of its effects  its causes and the adaptation needs it causes  is beginning to become clearer in Finland as well. One of the intermediate effects of joining the monetary union was, of course, the elimination of exchange rate fluctuations vis-a-vis the other euro countries. Since 1999, there have not really been exchange rates between the Finnish markka and the monetary units of the other euro countries, but fixed conversion rates, which will also remain in use at the turn of next year when the euro definitively replaces the national monetary units. The stabilisation of exchange rates and the single currency unit will link the Finnish economy more and more closely to the euro area markets as a whole and increase the foreign competition that companies face. At the same time, they benefit the consumer and improve the opportunities for internationalisation, especially for small businesses. Approximately one third of Finland's exports go to the euro area, so for us these effects of the elimination of internal exchange rates are not quite as decisive as in many continental European countries, whose exports are even more clearly directed within the euro area. Another intermediate effect of monetary union is the convergence of interest rates. The interest rates applied in Finland are currently determined by a euro area-wide money market with a uniform level of interest rates. This has not led to the full harmonisation of bank lending rates or deposit rates in the euro area, but interest rates have converged quite a bit and I believe that developments in the banking market will increase competition and harmonise bank interest rates even further than they are at present. Interest rates have been lower in recent years than they have been for a long time, in fact we have to go back to the years of the gold standard in history before we meet interest rates as low as those we have enjoyed in recent years. The difference from recent decades is particularly clear: in the past, Finland suffered from a persistent problem of inflation and, therefore, from higher interest rates than other European countries. Monetary union has now eased these problems. When considering joining the monetary union, there was a lot of discussion in Finland about what monetary union means for national cyclical policy. The question was, will the incomparable instrument of national economic policy be lost when one's own interest rate policy can no longer respond to Finland's specific cyclical problems? And what are the risks when the opportunity to compensate for the loss of competitiveness caused by excessive wage increases, for example, by means of devaluation, is omitted? And can or should we try to compensate for the end of national monetary policy by other means? These questions can hardly be answered with certainty, even in retrospect. However, it is clear that the need for a national cyclical policy depends at least on whether Finland's economic cycle differs from that of the rest of Europe: the more the economic cycles of the Finnish economy fluctuate at the same rate as in the other euro countries, the better the common monetary policy can be expected to fit finland's needs. If you look at recent developments, you will see that the cyclical fluctuations we have actually had significantly synchronised with the rest of the euro area, although the fluctuations we have had have been relatively steeper than the average development of monetary union. This can be seen, for example, in the growth of industrial production. As for the risks of competitiveness and the need for devaluation, it must be remembered that the possibility of devaluation was always a double-edged sword. While exchange rate flexibility made it possible to restore lost competitiveness by a simple means of economic policy, the very existence of this instrument maintained inflation expectations and the temptation to avoid difficult economic policy problems by resorting to inflationary solutions. The fact that exchange rate policy is not definitively excluded from the toolbox of Finnish economic policy is therefore not only a challenge, but also an opportunity. If the previous inflation sensitivity of our economy was due to the low credibility of monetary policy, now this problem should no longer exist. Membership of the monetary union has put an end to devaluation speculations and forces all policy-makers to come up with solutions compatible with stable monetary stability. Wage and price developments in recent years are encouraging in this respect. Fortunately, although finland's national economy has grown rapidly, it has fortunately been possible to avoid an increase in inflation well above the general level of the euro area. Hopefully, this will be a sign of the stabilising effect of monetary union membership on inflation expectations and wage formation. However, the greatest effects of monetary union have  as expected  been political and psychological. We have all been able to see how Finland's weight in European economic policy has increased, and from the 'outer ring' of Europe we have, in a way, moved on to the 'inner ring'. This has, of course, had not only political but also economic consequences. This is where psychology and confidence come into play. When, in the past, a well-known Spanish banker was asked why he was in favour of his country joining the monetary union, he replied that the Spaniards had suffered enough from the fact that their money was considered an 'exotic currency'. Surely this mark of ours, like the peseta, has suffered from its exoticism from time to time. Exoticism, or bad notoriety, was paid for in the past as quite a instability, as trust in the mark ranged from meritlessly good to unduly bad. The result was not only fluctuations in interest rates, but also unnecessary difficulties for the foreign operations of small and medium-sized enterprises. In the second half of the 1990s, Finland experienced a record long period of rapid economic growth. Over a period of seven years, total production grew at an annual rate of about five per cent, that is, almost one and a half times during that period. This period of rapid growth is now over, and economic growth in Finland has stopped last spring and summer and even turned negative. This is mainly due to the contraction in output in the INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY sector, which started in the United States last year and has since spread to other parts of the world and other industries. Uncertainty about future developments has increased. In recent weeks, economic uncertainty has been exacerbated by the terrorist attacks in the United States and their military repercussions. I believe that it is precisely in such very uncertain circumstances that Finland is in a quandary about membership of the monetary union. The fact that we are part of a European currency area means that Finland's exceptionally high dependence on the telecommunications sector, which has now suffered setbacks, has not been passed on through exchange rate fluctuations or interest rate reactions as instability to the rest of the economy. EMU has therefore been a stabilising factor in the current situation. It is clear that monetary union as such cannot solve economic problems that have non-monetary roots. On the other hand, in the stable environment created by monetary union, economic fundamentals such as productivity, competitiveness, corporate solvency and innovation  have the best influence. As these basics of the economy are in better shape in Finland today than they have been for decades, the conditions for a recovery in economic growth are good for us despite the setbacks of recent months. The role of the Bank of Finland Finally, I would like to say a few words about the impact of joining the monetary union on the position of the Bank of Finland. The Bank of Finland is certainly the Finnish institution that has been most affected by monetary union. The biggest changes lie in the bank's institutional position, rather than in its practice. The central bank, which managed its own money and acted under the guidance of the Parliamentary Banking Council, has become an independent part of the Eurosystem, which plays an active role in the preparation of European monetary policy and represents Finland in the Eurosystem. Another, equally important role of the bank is to represent the Eurosystem in Finland. This is partly operational: the Bank of Finland must participate in the operational implementation of monetary policy, which within the Eurosystem is decentralised to the various national central banks. Payment transactions between commercial banks, the deposit of their reserves, money market operations that control interest rates, the issue of banknotes and coins, the investment of national foreign exchange reserves  almost all central bank transactions are carried out by the national central banks, and in Finland this is done by the Bank of Finland. But representing the Eurosystem in Finland also means an obligation to communicate and market, on the one hand to gather views from the Finnish economic debate and, on the other hand, to present assessments of the demands that European monetary policy places on finland's economy and economic policy. Due to its position, the Bank of Finland has an obligation to analyse these issues and a unique opportunity to see both the economic development of Finland from the perspective of European monetary policy and the effects of European monetary policy from the perspective of the Finnish economy.

Rahaliiton suurimmat vaikutukset ovat  odotetusti  kuitenkin olleet poliittiset ja psykologiset. Title: Presentation at the Talousforum 2005 seminar
text: Vice President Matti Louekoski PRESENTATION AT TALOUSFORUM 2005 SEMINAR 25.1.2005 FINLAND'S NEAR-TERM ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT 1. THE GLOBAL ECONOMY  Global economic growth intensified at the end of 2003, driven by the United States, Japan, China and even Russia. U.S. growth exceeded 4% last year, but Japan's economic development weakened during the spring and fall (Figure 1).  The prolonged growth of the global economy, and in particular china, pushed the price of crude oil up sharply since the end of 2003 (Graph 2). The rise in oil prices was halted by last year's lo-bun. Rather than too little supply, the increase in oil prices was influenced by factors related to supply uncertainty, for example. Risks associated with oil production in Iraq and Russia.  According to the latest forecasts by international organisations, global economic growth is expected to continue at a moderate but slower pace this year than last year.  The appreciation of the euro, together with global growth, has dampened the growth of euro area exports over the past summer and autumn. Euro area domestic demand has not been able to compensate for the weakness in exports and growth in the euro area is expected to remain modest in the near term.  On the basis of the medium-term inflation outlook, the European Central Bank has maintained its key interest rate at 2% since June 2003. During the autumn of 2004, the market's expectations of an increase in interest rates have been dampened by the weakening of the economic outlook and the appreciation of the euro. (Figure 3). 2. FINLAND'S ECONOMIC OUTLOOK  Economic growth in Finland has strengthened during 2004 (Figure 4). Real GDP growth has been around three per cent over the past year. In the light of indicator data, the development at the end of last year may be slightly weaker than in the third quarter. This year and next year, real GDP growth is projected to remain broadly at the current rate.  Growth is supported by production in the electronics industry (Nokia), private consumption and housing investment. Investments in machinery and equipment are also recovering. The growth in output in the forest industry has been at a standstill in recent months.  The growth in the volume of exports has remained small in relation to the growth in export markets, even though exports are currently at historically high levels. The increase in the revenue stream generated by exports has also remained small compared to the increase in volume, as the fall in export prices has continued.  Export prices have been falling in the electronics industry for a long time. Paper export prices have stagnated. However, the rise in metal prices has sustained the export prices of other basic industries (Figure 5).  However, production in the electronics industry has continued to be highly profitable thanks to strong productivity growth.  Export growth has been hampered by the appreciation of the euro against the dollar and the yen, which has weakened the price competitiveness of Finnish companies in regions outside the euro area and also in euro area countries with imports from outside the euro area.  The slow growth in the euro area, and in particular in Germany, has recently had a negative impact on economic growth in Finland. On the other hand, the rapid growth in Finland's neighbouring regions has improved growth prospects. In particular, Finland's trade with Russia has grown strongly.  The number of employed persons has grown rapidly since last summer and the employment rate rose to nearly 68 per cent in November. In particular, the number of persons working part-time has grown, but in November the number of persons in continuous full-time work was also clearly higher than one year earlier. In turn, the unemployment rate was better than before in November, i.e. 8.7 per cent (Figure 6).  Consumer price growth in Finland has recently been the slowest in the euro area. The development has been affected by the decrease in alcohol tax and car tax, as well as increased competition in Finland. The effect of the decrease in the alcohol tax was most noticeable. Competition has increased, particularly in the telecommunications and retail sectors (Figure 7). The 12-month growth rate of consumer prices was only 0.3 per cent in November last year. Inflation is expected to pick up in the coming months as the effects of tax and fee changes fall short of the 12-month comparison of inflation rates. 3 YRITTaJaILMAPIIRI  Finland needs to increase the employment rate and productivity in order to secure the sustainable development of public finances, i.e. the financing of the welfare state. The balance of public finances in the coming years will be jeopardised by the retirement of the baby boomers, persistently high unemployment and globalisation.  Globalisation has meant that new establishments for large companies have moved closer to the market to countries with lower labour costs in order to secure their operations in the face of increasing international competition. This development has been visible as a weakening of the employment of large enterprises in Finland (Figure 8).  The importance of small and medium-sized enterprises in safeguarding employment in Finland has been emphasised. Last year, they employed 61.2 per cent of all persons working in private sector enterprises, that is, 800880 persons (Figure 9).  Given the increased importance of entrepreneurship, recent governments have had an important objective to support entrepreneurship through entrepreneurship programmes. In 2003, the European Commission published the so-called "Green Paper". a Green Paper on improving the conditions for entrepreneurship in EU countries. The prerequisites for entrepreneurship in Finland as such are not much different from other EU countries.  The governments of Lipponen and Vanhanen have made significant reforms to support entrepreneurship in Finland. These include the reduction in the taxation of wage earners' earned income through several measures (reducing labour costs and increasing the supply of work) by both the Lipponen and Vanhanen governments, the reform of the taxation of corporate and capital income that will enter into force at the beginning of this year, the generational change relief in the Inheritance and Gift Tax Act, the abolition of the tax on the transfer of property, the reduction in the taxation of private companies, the graduation of value added tax for small businesses and the staggering of labour for salaried employees in the ma-tala reductions in social security contributions and an increase in entrepreneurship training in all educational establishments.  None of these measures in itself will decisively improve the conditions for entrepreneurship in Finland, but they are significant steps to improve the entrepreneurial climate. The entrepreneurial climate in Finland has been found to be weak in international comparisons, in the sense that the willingness of Finnish young people to become entrepreneurs is even the weakest by international comparison.  The current government's renewed entrepreneurship programme emphasises the importance of growth companies for employment. International studies have shown that between 3% and 5% of new businesses can create up to 75% of the jobs created by new businesses. However, it is difficult to identify growth companies among the new companies that are emerging, so it is to be hoped that the strong growth of new companies will also increase the likelihood of the emergence of growth companies. Thus, a general improvement in the entrepreneurial climate would also increase the number of growth companies. 4 SOME STRUCTURAL CHALLENGES FOR FINLAND'S DEVELOPMENT  AGEING fastest in Europe brings with it a reduction in public revenues while the demand for services increases, and the unit price of services will rise  THE FALL IN EXPORT PRICES appears to have been going on for several years; whether high-tech products have become "sleds" (Figure 5)  The structure of TAXATION does not favour Finland in the expanding situation of tax competition 5 FUNDAMENTALS OF ECONOMIC GROWTH  Only sufficient growth secures well-being  One of the most important factors in Finland's growth is the continuous increase in productivity

Indikaattoritietojen valossa viime vuoden lopun kehitys voi jd hieman heikommaksi kuin kolmannella neljnneksell. Viennin mrn kasvu on jnyt vhiseksi suhteessa vientimarkkinoiden kasvuun, vaikka vienti onkin tll hetkell historiallisesti korkealla tasolla. Mys viennin aikaansaama tulovirran kasvu on jnyt mrn kasvuun verrattuna vhiseksi, kun vientihintojen lasku on jatkunut.  Vientihinnat ovat laskeneet elektroniikkateollisuudessa jo pitkn. Paperin vientihinnat ovat polke-neet paikallaan. Metallien hintojen nousu on kuitenkin pitnyt yll muun perusteollisuuden vienti-hintoja (Kuvio 5).  Elektroniikkateollisuuden tuotanto on ollut kuitenkin edelleen erittin kannattavaa tuottavuuden voimakkaan kasvun ansiosta.  Viennin kasvua on haitannut euron vahvistuminen dollariin ja jeniin nhden, mik on heikentnyt suomalaisten yritysten hintakilpailukyky euromaiden ulkopuolisilla alueilla ja mys euromaissa alueen ulkopuolisen tuonnin kanssa.  Euroalueen ja erityisesti Saksan hidas kasvu on viime aikoina vaikuttanut negatiivisesti Suomen talouskasvuun. Toisaalta Suomen lhialueiden nopea kasvu on parantanut kasvunkymi. Varsin-kin Suomen Venjn kauppa on kasvanut voimakkaasti.  Tyllisten mr on kasvanut viime kesst lhtien ripesti ja tyllisyysaste nousi marraskuussa lhes 68 prosenttiin. Erityisesti osa-aikatyt tekevien mr on kasvanut mutta marraskuussa mys jatkuvaa kokoaikatyt tekevien mr oli selvsti suurempi kuin vuotta aiemmin. Kilpailu on lisntynyt etenkin televiestinnss ja vhittiskaupassa (Kuvio 7). Kuluttajahintojen 12 kuukauden nousuvauhti oli viime vuoden marraskuussa vain 0,3 prosenttia. Inflaation odotetaan nopeutuvan lhikuukausina, kun vero- ja maksumuutosten vaiku-tukset jvt pois inflaatiovauhdin 12 kuukauden vertailusta. 3 YRITTJILMAPIIRI  Suomi tarvitsee tyllisyysasteen ja tuottavuuden nostoa julkisen talouden kestvn kehityksen eli hyvinvointivaltion rahoituksen turvaamiseksi. Julkisen talouden tasapainoa tulevina vuosina vaa-rantavat suurten ikluokkien elkkeelle siirtyminen, korkeana jatkuva tyttmyys ja globalisoitu-minen.  Globalisoituminen on merkinnyt suurten yritysten uusien toimipaikkojen siirtymist lhemmksi markkinoita alempien tyvoimakustannusten maihin, jotta yrityksen toiminta on pystytty turvaa-maan kovenevassa kansainvlisess kilpailussa. Tm kehitys on nkynyt suurten yritysten tyllis-tvyyden heikkenemisen Suomessa (Kuvio 8).  Pienten ja keskisuurten yritysten merkitys tyllisyyden turvaajana Suomessa on korostunut. Yrittjyyden korostuneen merkityksen vuoksi viime hallituksilla on ollut merkittvn tavoitteena yrittjyyden tukeminen yrittjyysohjelmien avulla. Euroopan komissio julkaisi vuonna 2003 ns. vihren kirjan, jossa pohditaan yrittmisen edellytysten parantamista EU-maissa. Yrittmisen edel-lytykset sinns Suomessa eivt juuri poikkea muista EU-maista. Title: Speech at the Decision-Making Day event
text: Vice-Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Bank of Finland Matti Louekoski Decision-maker's day event Helsinki 10.3.2005 OVERVIEW OF THE GLOBAL AND FINNISH ECONOMY THROUGH INSTITUTIONAL FROM AN INVESTOR'S PERSPECTIVE World economy - Global economic growth has slowed down from 5% to around 4%. The growth phase has actually been one of the strongest in recent decades. The development of the global economy has also been positive in that the rise has been quite broad-based, generally covering also emerging economies. - Growth is still strong in the United States and especially in Asia, especially in China and Inti-a. It is important for Finland that russia's growth also seems to continue strong. Global economic growth is likely to remain consistently strong also in the coming years. It is also expected to even out in that the growth differentials between countries and major regions will narrow. - China is apparently slowly taking Japan's place as asia's most significant economy. In nominal terms, it is still only half of the Japanese economy, but in terms of purchasing power, it is already two times higher. It has already overtaken Japan as the world's third-largest exporter after the U.S. and Germany. - Growth remains weak in Japan and, for example, in some of the large euro area countries. - There are opposing pressures on the world's inflationary trend. Oil and commodity prices have broadly risen, as have house prices in many Western countries, but on the other hand, competition from developing and transition economies is pushing down the prices of many industrial products. __________________ - The easing of monetary and fiscal policy in the United States is the driving force behind the country's recent rapid growth, but also its many imbalances. In the United States, both public finances and the private sector are getting into debt, which is reflected in the country's large current account deficit. - The availability and price of energy are uncertainties, as is the current account deficit in the United States, which has already risen to almost 6% of GDP. It is higher than the deficits of the other deficit countries in the world put together. - There are significant surpluses in many Asian and European countries, as well as in oil producers. The international financial markets are very large in gross terms, and the immediate financing of the US deficit does not necessarily come from the countries with a financial surplus. In China, for example, the financing provided by the current account surplus is only a small part of the assets that the People's Bank invests in the United States as foreign reserve assets. Most of the funds come from foreign investment in China. - Us deficits increase the risks of exchange rate and interest rate developments. The dollar's exchange rate has wide-ranging effects on the world economy, and developments in the United States are also having a major impact on interest rates in other parts of the world, even on Finnish interest rates. The euro area economy - Of the large euro area countries, Germany and Italy have been experiencing economic difficulties, while most of the smaller countries have maintained moderate growth rates. The situation in Germany is particularly problematic. It is burdened by the problems of the former East Germany, a markedly weakened population structure and the costly burdens that have contributed to the relocation of production to the foreign countries. - Uncertainty has led to precautionary savings in Germany. As investment has fallen, Germany's current account surplus has returned to the highs of the past decades. - Low-growth countries are also characterised by difficulties in complying with the Stability and Growth Pact. The economic policy of the euro area is characterised by slow movement. The internal pressures are partly left-handed, which means that no quick solutions can be found. - The euro area has a small current account surplus, there is no significant external debt and price stability is close to being in line with the objectives. The financial market situation is light. Interest rates are low and liquidity is abundant, even suspiciously abundant. __________________ Finland's economy - In terms of economic growth in Finland, last year has turned out to be more positive than expected, growth rose to almost 4 per cent. Exports recovered slowly, supported by household consumption and investment in housing. At the very end of the year, there was a brisk export spurt, but it may remain momentary. - In the Finnish economy, price stability and the current foreign balance are in fairly good shape, but employment development is not. The rate of household indebtedness requires intensified monitoring, but housing debt is still quite reasonable in international comparison. The increase in debt is also due to the lengthening of mortgage loan periods. - The long-term problem is the lack of investment by companies. Investment activity recovered slightly last year and looks set to strengthen this year as well. However, the investment rate of the Finnish economy is still low, although it slightly exceeds that of Sweden, Germany and the United Kingdom. - The low level of productive investment is a widely common problem for western countries. Investments depend on profit prospects. In the United States, investments are still being made on the back of strong domestic demand; elsewhere, investors are cautious. _______________________ - In Finland, and perhaps even more so in Sweden, the behaviour of companies has been characterised by an unusually high distribution of dividends. Of course, if there are no own investment opportunities for the company's assets, it is justified to distribute the accumulated liquidity in the company to the owners so that they can invest it in more profitable objects. When the distribution of generous and even extra dividends is very wide in the corporate field, one is left wondering where the owners can then find better investment targets for their loose assets. - A large part of the distributed dividends have gone directly to foreign owners. In other respects, the va-rat has largely come to other companies and only to a small extent directly to households. The ability to channel funds back to Finnish companies has been limited, and e.g. share issues have been limited in recent years. Companies have not needed new equity financing to finance their business operations, and credit financing is also cheap. The obvious answer to the use of distributed dividend assets is the strong growth in foreign investment in investment funds in recent years and more recently. Already about 2/3 of their investments are abroad. __________________ - The limited importance of access to finance for investment is evident when discussing the use of occupational pension funds invested abroad to stimulate domestic investment. Under the conditions of financial regulation, such management of capital flows could be done, but hardly anymore in today's world. "The investments of Finnish companies do not depend on where the pension assets are invested. It is essential to invest pension funds in efficient real investments and in secure and productive foreign financial liabilities. The extensive investment of these assets in foreign countries and various claims is also justified from the point of view of risk diversification. - It is, of course, understandable that the question of additional investments in the home country arises when almost 2/3 of these funds are already in foreign investments, mainly in the allocations of euro area countries. The amount abroad is already very large in relation to the Finnish economy, about 40% of GDP. It would perhaps be good if more of these were used domestically, but that depends on the effective investment of companies and their financing arrangements. - Significantly, premiums written cannot be replaced by returns on foreign investment. ________________ The riddle of low market interest rates - Almost everywhere in developed countries, interest rates have been low in recent years. This applies to both monetary policy rates and long-term market rates. A particularly bold policy of low interest rates has been implemented by the Federal Reserve. - Since the dollar is the world's most important reserve currency, the light monetary policy of the United States has spread widely throughout the world economy. Many countries have pursued low interest rates, even from their own targets. - Central banks do not set long-term market interest rates and are not able to influence them very much directly. Market interest rates move as a result of a great many factors, and only a component among these is - at least in the short term - the monetary policy of the Central Bank. __________________ - Bond and stock prices depend on expectations of yields. Also in the preparation of monetary policy, it is necessary to carefully study the views of the market on the factors affecting the development of interest rates, stock prices and exchange rates. - Particular attention was drawn when Alan Greenspan wondered about long-term interest rates remaining low, even falling at a time when the Fed has been making interest rate hike decisions. Greenspan considered this an enigma, conundrum. In general, the long-term interest rate has jumped upwards when tightening US monetary policy. - The long-term nominal interest rate broadly reflects (1) leakages in the economy (productivity), (2) inflation expectations, and (3) different debtor-dependent risk, liquidity, etc. Factors. In the formation of the nominal interest rate, the importance of inflation is obvious. The setting of the real interest rate at the level of real growth, on the other hand, basically comes from the fact that, at equilibrium, the interest rate must correspond to the return on an alternative real investment. _____________________ - Looking at current risk-free interest rates, it can be seen that the long-term growth and inflation forecasts together are clearly higher than the long-term interest rate. The expectations of real growth in the economies appear to be far too low. - Based on the 10-year French government index bond, the euro area's long-term inflation expectation has been just over 2% in recent months, but the real return expectation is just under 11/2%. For the United States, the expectation of a similar real return is about the same, which is even more bizarre, as in general the US is expected to grow faster than Europe. Thus, when monetary policy in the euro area aims to keep inflation at just below 2%, and growth potential is generally considered to exceed 2%, the long-term interest rate should therefore remain above 4% rather than 3.5%. So there really is something special about heels. - Low inflationary pressures in recent years have contributed to the pressure on nominal interest rates. Low inflation has been affected by the tightening of price competition. - The moderate inflationary trend in western countries has not required a tight monetary policy. Loose monetary policy has countered general deflationary fears. The general expansionary economic policy is the background to upward pressure on energy and other commodity prices. This has also been reflected in the housing market. _________________ - The exceptionally low market rate may be affected by (1) global overspending and concomitant low demand for credit for investment, (2) abundant investment by Asian central banks in U.S. government papers, and (3) the U.S. Central Bank's ability to inform far in advance of its low-interest rate policies. " Strong international savings are reflected, for example, in current account surpluses. Asian countries, in particular, finance their large investments with their savings. In Europe, too, the level of saving has remained satisfactory. In Europe, the Stability and Growth Pact also limits the issuance of government debt. An element is increased preparedness for the pension problem. It is well known that saving in the United States has historically become exceptionally low. - Europe is characterised by prudence in real investment. There is no desire to find good investment targets for long-term investment capital, which weighs on the interest rate level. The low level of investment is likely to be linked, among other things, to the ageing of the population and uncertainty about the change in the structure of the world economy. __________________ - The primary criterion for the foreign exchange reserves investment policy of central banks is not the return on investment. Many Asia central banks tend to maintain a relatively stable dollar exchange rate. Foreign reserve assets are typically invested in government debt securities, although mainly in short-term ones. Asian central banks have occasionally financed most of the U.S. shortfalls, pushing down dollar market interest rates at the same time. - The risk of the dollar has been the shift of central banks and other investors from the dollar to other currencies. The shifts in reserve investments of central banks are not large in relation to the total volume of the market, but they seem to be of great psychological importance. ___________________ - The consistent interest rate policies of central banks may also be part of the reason for the behaviour of long-term interest rates. The increase in price stability and inflation targets and the increase in credibility may have led to too strong a belief in the maintenance of low interest rates. If the central bank announces its interest rate policy for a long period of time, the long-term interest rate is quite likely to react to this. Alan Greenspan's consistent policy of low interest rates has contributed to pushing U.S. interest rates. - Central banks do not seek to directly influence the long-term interest rate, nor can they influence it except indirectly. In principle, short-term interest rate control also affects the long-term interest rate  after all, the long-term rate is the average of the expected short-term (forward) rates. However, this simple math usually does not apply. The interest rate curve is moving, driven by expectations, with a credible tightening of interest rates raising the yield curve for the near term but lowering it in a few years' time. This is the case when policies are expected to keep inflation within the medium-term objective. ___________________ - Interest rates react strongly to political crises, etc. common problems, although the effects are usually short-lived. Bond prices and interest rates are also often swayed by shocks in other markets, especially the stock market. Strong tendencies away from equities drive down their prices, often pushing up bond prices and vice versa. - Also regulatory changes, investor protection strategies, etc. similar factors periodically create the need to increase or decrease long-term fixed income investments. For example, in some European countries, the need to invest more and more in long-term claims, which has arisen from the new regulations on pension insurance, has recently been on the agenda. - The internationalisation of real interest rates makes it more difficult to assess the development of interest rates in an individual country. In the world of free capital movements and free-floating exchange rates, the risk-free expected real interest rates in different countries cannot differ very much from each other. Harmonisation creates problems for countries with low returns on real investment. The main ones flee to more productive destinations abroad.
