Title: Presentation in The Round Table Hosted by De Nederlandsche Bank
text: PRESENTATION IN THE ROUND TABLE HOSTED BY DE NEDERLANDSCHE BANK ON 14 OCTOBER 2005 CENTRAL BANK RESERVE MANAGEMENT: A EUROPEAN VIEW ON RETURN VERSUS LIQUIDITY Pentti Hakkarainen, Member of the Board Suomen Pankki  Bank of Finland Let me first say how delighted I am to have an opportunity to share my views on this important topic with such a prominent group of people. What could be a European view on central bank reserve management and especially on return versus liquidity? This was probably the question I pondered the most when outlining this short presentation. Management of central bank reserves is such a global topic and subject to such a spectrum of principles, that applying any geographical viewpoint when addressing the issue seems somewhat artificial. Having said that, however, one can also see specific developments which have taken place in Europe and in the euro area during the last 5 to 10 years  developments which may have led us to have a slightly different angle when approaching this interesting topic. Just by observing what central banks in Europe have done to their balance sheets and investment policies allows one to draw some general conclusions. Before going further, I would like to mention the well known fact that the level as well as the composition of central bank reserves is always a result of various factors. Some of these factors are more under the control of the current central bank decision makers and some are less so. There are many valid reasons why central banks cannot make large, rapid and regular changes to their reserves and investment policies, even though the underlying willingness to do so may exist. 1. Reserve management framework in the Bank of Finland Let me start by briefly characterising the reserve management framework in the Bank of Finland, which has remained largely unchanged since Finland joined the euro. It may not be the best example of a trend in Europe, however it does illustrate one approach. After the EMU entry the Bank has invested in corporate bonds, increased duration of investments and started "active investment management". In accordance with our strategic policies, the Bank of Finland takes the long-term perspective in managing its foreign reserves and handles them in a professional and active manner, on the basis of strict risk management principles. The Bank of Finland holds foreign reserves in order to meet any additional transfer needs of foreign reserves to the ECB and the financing requirements of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), as well as to prepare for contingencies, such as serious disruptions in the financial markets. When measured in euro terms, the size of the Bank's foreign reserves has remained stable. The key objectives of the Bank's investment policy  security, liquidity and return  have remained unchanged. The security objective refers to the requirement that the market value of foreign reserves must not fluctuate excessively as a result of the various risks involved. In addition, part of the reserves must be sufficiently liquid; it must be possible to convert it into cash sufficiently quickly and at low cost, whenever needed. Within these constraints, the aim is to obtain the best possible return. The cornerstone of our investment policy is effective portfolio diversification. This especially concerns currency diversification, since the Bank of Finland holds only foreign (non-euro) assets. The fact that the Bank of Finland does not have a euro portfolio distinguishes it from most other euro area central banks. The Bank of Finland attempts to limit exchange rate risk by spreading its holdings of foreign reserve assets among six different currencies (USD, GBP, DKK, SEK, CHF and JPY). The benchmark currency distribution is reviewed at 23 year intervals. Between the reviews, the actual currency distribution is kept as close as possible to the benchmark currency distribution. Since November 2002, the benchmark currency distribution has remained unchanged. The interest rate risk associated with the reserves has been mainly measured and managed in terms of duration. The target duration of 2.5 years is applied to all the currencies included in the foreign reserves. Also the value-at-risk (VaR) method has been adopted for risk management purposes. Most of the reserves are invested in the government (sovereign) paper, but approximately a quarter of the foreign reserves are invested in debt instruments issued by entities with a high credit rating, such as corporates. The credit risk inherent in the credit portfolio is also measured using the VaR method. Effective portfolio diversification is crucial in the management of credit risk. Diversification is achieved by setting maximum limits and minimum credit rating criteria for issuers and counterparty banks and maximum limits for the VaR figures derived for the credit risk on the credit portfolio. The portfolio that is assessed as being best suited to the Banks long-term investment objectives is expressed in terms of currency distribution and currency-specific benchmark portfolios. The currency distribution and the structure of benchmark portfolios largely determine the return on invested reserves. The aim of active investment is to obtain a return on invested reserves that is higher than the return on the benchmark portfolios. This, briefly, describes the reserve management framework in the Bank of Finland. Let me now take a wider and somewhat more general perspective. 2. Determinants and policy requirements for central bank reserve management frameworks In a simplified framework, the objectives for holding central bank reserves can be seen as stemming from two types of risk; macroeconomic risks and microeconomic risks. 2.1. Macroeconomic and microeconomic risks Macro risks will always remain the primary risks for a country (or a central bank) to hold reserves against, as they concern not only the risks to monetary, foreign exchange and financial stability, but also risks to the safe functioning of the national economy or the currency area. The fact that it is the central bank as holder of the country's reserves against macroeconomic risks originally results from an innate division of labour within the country. Due to the nature of a central bank's objectives and other functions, it is the natural institution for the task of holding reserves on behalf of the society it serves. Although micro risks are also very important, but only secondary when compared to macro risks, as they "only" concern the financial result of the central bank. In this respect, micro risks have implications not only for the financial result of the central bank itself but also its stakeholders, e.g. the Government, to which at least a part of the financial result of the central bank is transferred normally. In order to fully see the relative importance of macro and micro risks, it is worth emphasising the causality between them. Macro risks are the reason for holding reserves, whereas micro risks are a consequence of holding reserves. There is a trade off between macro and micro risks. This is partly due to the very different nature of these risks. A central bank may try to eliminate micro risks which can lead to exposing the country more to macro risks. Similarly, by trying to minimise the country's exposure to macro risks, the central bank may tend to face more micro risks. 2.2. Changing weights of macro and micro risks in Europe Managing macro and micro risks, and the trade-off between them, is difficult since these risks are not perceived as being fixed over time. The weights given to these risks by society and decision makers vary over time. As macro risks materialise during financial turbulence or otherwise hard times, the weight given to them tend to decrease when good times prevail. When thinking about the framework for defining the level of reserves, liquidity and the composition, a crucial decision concerns the weights placed on macro and micro risks. Although there are many sophisticated tools, techniques and frameworks to approach this problem, one cannot hide from the fact that these weights are often only defined implicitly and they characterise how the world is perceived. Assessment of the risks is, to a significant degree, a highly subjective matter. The reason that this task is primarily given to central bankers probably results from the expectation that central bankers have a longer horizon than other national decision makers and therefore have a comparative advantage in avoiding myopia and getting carried away when times are good. Looking at the global and European experience in this respect, I would like to make three observations. First, when reserves are increased  deliberately or otherwise  the central bank becomes stronger in facing macro risks. However this means that micro risks, ie the risks concerning financial results of the bank, may increase. This has been evident not only in Asia during the last few years, but also in some countries in Europe. For instance, a strong inflow of foreign capital has resulted in a significant accumulation of foreign reserves in the new EU member states. Second, it also appears that in the euro area macro risks are now deemed smaller than they were before the introduction of the common currency and the monetary union. There are probably many good reasons for this attitude. The change, in this respect, differs from one country to another. A common factor, however, seems to be that the institutional framework supports this trend. It appears that the creation of the Eurosystem has freed a part of the reserve management constraints which was held against macro risks and which is now available for more active management, ie creating potential micro risks. Personally, I do not believe that macro risks as such have significantly decreased since the introduction of the euro. However, I believe that with the Eurosystem we are provided with more tools to manage macro risks. We have new institutions which share the management of some macro risks with the national central banks. The best example of this is the ECB which, with its foreign reserves, now takes primary responsibility for possible FX interventions. In addition, for many euro area countries the euro is a more usable currency to hold against macro risks than previous national currencies. For instance, the Finnish markka was not, in our case, a reserve currency to hold against macro risks, whereas the euro has many favourable characteristics in this respect. My third observation concerns the increased freedom that the euro area central banks have today in arranging their financial assets. The euro area central banks have an indisputably independent position from which to carry out their tasks, in comparison to other European or governmental bodies. Independence has not only offered freedom, but also an obligation to have a more efficient, skilful and careful approach to managing micro risks. Euro area central banks are more accountable than ever for showing, through their actions, that they fully deserve their independent role. 3. Liquidity and return characteristics of central bank reserve management Although the specific words may differ from one central bank to another, safety, liquidity and return are the objectives of reserve management which are most often set by central banks. The Bank of Finland is no exception to this rule. 3.1. Liquidity reserves In order to simplify the task of defining investment policy for total reserves on the basis of these three objectives, there is a tendency to divide total reserves in two parts, at least metaphorically. I shall refer to these two parts as liquidity reserves, which are held primarily against macro risks, and investment reserves which can be managed concentrating more on maximising return at the chosen level of financial risks. In the current financial markets this division may not lead to different returns, since these reserves can be managed based on almost similar risk-return -ratios. Liquidity reserves should be managed in a way which keeps the probability of losses very low over the short-term. Against this background, it is not difficult to see why liquidity and safety take priority over the search for return, when the investment policy is formulated. The reason for emphasising liquidity and capital preservation naturally is that at a time when macro risks materialise, it would be excessively costly for a country without access to reserves and especially foreign assets. The inability to deliver foreign assets in stress situations and turbulent market conditions can have drastic effects on the real economy and lead to a significant reduction of national income and wealth. Therefore, having determined the level of liquidity reserves, the very nature of the reserves obliges the implementation of a conservative investment policy. The obligation to be conservative is normally not a great challenge for a central banker. Liquidity reserves are thus invested in a manner which guarantees, as far as possible, that the assets are usable practically immediately when the central bank or the country needs them the most. For this reason liquidity reserves are normally allocated to a small number of major international currencies and invested in the most liquid and creditworthy assets in those currencies. For instance, at the Bank of Finland we concretize the liquidity requirement as expecting that 25% of invested reserves should be highly liquid. In terms of high liquidity, only government securities, up to one month repurchase agreements and up to one month deposits in the six reserve currencies can be defined as such. 3.2. Investment reserves and how to manage them As regards investment reserves, the investment horizon and maintenance period are longer than for liquidity reserves and restrictions regarding safety and liquidity are looser. The investment policy can put more emphasis on maximising return. The investment policy which is optimal for liquidity reserves is not applicable to investment reserves. When setting an investment policy for investment reserves, central bankers should probably listen more carefully to what asset management professionals, investment bankers and why not even other long term investors have to say. Although the optimisation of a central bank's investment portfolio still comprises restrictions which are not common to the private sector long term investors, the goal of reaching for an efficient frontier is in fact not that different. So, what advice can asset management professionals give us central bankers, today? Most recently, at least, the following recommendations have reached my ears most often. First, investment bankers tell us that we should differentiate the currency allocation from the country allocation. Placements can be made separately from managing foreign exchange exposure with currency overlay and thus making use of the best characteristics of both markets. As the currency and bond returns have a relatively low correlation, this would give a significant opportunity to reduce risk without having a negative effect on the return of the total portfolio. What makes this advice especially interesting in my view is the fact that following it would not necessarily increase the cost of liquidating the portfolio, even in distressed conditions. Second, investment bankers tell us to relax individual duration constraints within each country sector and focus more on total portfolio risk. Being more efficient in taking advantages of the various shapes of yield curves and different covariance amongst the maturity sectors delivers opportunities to both increase return and reduce risk. In essence, for most central banks this also means higher durations. Third, investment bankers tell us to relax the credit constraints on our portfolios and to widen the array of instruments. Allowing the portfolio to extend into investment-grade credits or even beyond and into instruments like ABS and MBS would again allow improvement in efficiency of the total portfolio, as measured by the Sharpe Ratio type criteria. As we are nowadays continuously reminded, moving away from government risk to credit risk actually allows us to reduce the total risk of the portfolio while increasing returns. This is supported by the Bank of Finland's experience with corporate debt. The advice given by investment bankers is, of course, correct when judged on the basis of the models and assumptions used. However, the advice may often be derived from too narrow a framework. By this I mean that the advice is often asset management oriented rather than having a more comprehensive asset and liability management framework behind it. Intuition tells us that central banks which are separate legal entities, more and more like private companies, with their own balance sheets and income statements cannot overlook their liabilities when formulating asset management and investment policies. Even though central banks have unique tasks and objectives which differ from the private sector, it should not mean that central banks can be complacent about their funding structures, about their obligations and about what is done in the world of investment management in general. In this respect, I would like to put a number of open questions to you. How do central banks generally see their balance sheet liabilities, such as banknotes and equity? What are their costs and interest rate characteristics? Should the way in which the central bank assets are financed affect the way they are invested? For instance, should we see banknotes as having a redemption obligation and if so, should this have an effect on the duration guidelines when setting investment policies? Should part of the assets be earmarked as financed through equity? An opponent to this approach could of course say that what suits pension funds, for example, is not really applicable to central banks. Central banks are entities which can actually set the cost structure of their balance sheets by, for example, deciding on policy interest rates. Central banks can create funds through issuing banknotes. Yet, on-balance sheet liabilities may not fully characterise the total liabilities of the central bank, for instance, in a serious financial stress. However, central banks have more and more similarities with private sector long term investors, such as pension funds. Both have long-term liabilities or objectives. Confidence is the core element in both businesses. Both have to demonstrate reliably that future obligations can be met. Since obligations materialize in the distant future, both institutions require decent return on assets invested to maintain or increase the real value of the assets. Both have increased demand to carry out their activities, also when it concerns the area of investment, in a transparent manner. In general, central banks are not yet required to report on their financial performance more than annually. It may only be a question of time when evaluation of performance is carried out more often. Despite some similarities, it is perhaps needless to say that they are not identical or comparable peers as such. In any case, I think it is fair to say that more attention should be paid to comprehensive asset and liability management in central banks too. The liability side of the balance sheet always contains crucial information on dependencies between different balance sheet items and understanding them fully is a prerequisite for setting an investment policy that maintains a strong central bank balance sheet. The characteristics of liabilities naturally have an impact on the entire interest rate risk of the balance sheet and certainly on defining the duration of the invested assets. Perhaps one weakness in the recommendations offered to central bankers is the fact that they are often derived by simple mean-variance optimisation frameworks. The models use estimated parameters, such as correlation coefficients, which are often treated as stable. This may be a serious weakness, since central banks' investment policies have traditionally been defined especially for those periods when these parameters tend to break down. Central banks may not be prepared to accept losses, and thus understanding the asymmetry of dispersion and the potential negative outcomes is necessary. It is important to emphasise that central bank specific restrictions significantly limit setting investment policies for investment reserves. Again, these restrictions probably vary among central banks in their nature and number. Also the size of the central bank and its role in the global scene has an effect on how restricted it feels. Developments during recent years seem to confirm this observation. In general, it can be said that European central banks have probably fewer restrictions and they can move faster and more flexibly than 10 years ago. Even though the trend in reserve management has provided more freedom, there is one abstract and important restriction; the so-called reputation risk. There are many ways to define reputation risk. None of the definitions are exhaustive and can sometimes be deemed contradictory. For instance, reputation can be damaged when a central bank incurs loss due to the default of a debt security, even though the effect on the total portfolio return can be marginal. There may be some practical hindrances to implementation of a modern investment policy for investment reserves like, for example, IT systems, experience and skills. In some cases, it may not be possible to include a new financial instrument in the investment universe, due to the IT system available or a lack of skills, even though it would be optimal from the portfolio performance point of view. Of course, this would give the incentive to an investment banker to offer advice using external asset management (i.e. outsourcing) to circumvent these restrictions. The justification for a central bank to manage liquidity reserves is clear and often written in national legislation. The justification for managing investment reserves or assets in the excess needed for macro risks is not as clear. In fact, if the central bank does not manage investments and risks efficiently following the highest professional standards, one should not be surprised to hear occasional comments questioning the birthright of the central bank to manage them. Especially, when investment reserves are mostly held in domestic currency, their link to central bank policy tasks may not be that clear to outside observers. On top of which, one can expect more regular comparisons with the performance of similar investors managing wealth, such as pension funds. As a result of increased transparency and accountability requirements, central banks cannot avoid this kind of exposure. 4. Conclusions I would like to end now by drawing the following conclusions. It is clear to me that the liquidity requirement today, as seen in its strictest form, is applicable to a smaller proportion of central bank reserves in the euro area than it was before the introduction of the euro. The common currency and its track record so far support the notion that the macro risk burden of a national central bank is partly carried by the European institutional framework and therefore, national foreign reserves have been reduced. However, this may not have diminished the need for reserves. The euro may have partly just substituted foreign currencies in central banks' financial assets since it may be deemed useable in crisis situations, as any foreign currency. At the same time, as we are due to hear in the next session in greater detail, one can see that the balance sheets of the euro area central banks are not becoming smaller. On the contrary, the continuous growth of the Eurosystem liabilities due to the strong demand for euro banknotes has meant that also the asset side of the Eurosystem balance sheet has continued to grow. Following these two effects, both of which interestingly result from the success of the common currency, many euro area central banks are facing a situation where their investment reserves are on a progressive path. This has meant, and will continue to mean, that the portfolio-theoretic thinking and the return objective will take a larger role when setting investment policies in the euro area central banks. From both the European and the euro area point of view the return and liquidity determinants for setting investment policies have indeed changed. In terms of asset allocation, there is more leeway between foreign currency and domestic euro assets. In this environment concentrating only on asset management techniques is probably too narrow an approach and more attention should be paid to the liability side of the central bank balance sheet. In any case, euro area central banks have become increasingly accountable for managing national wealth through the exercise of prudent stewardship.

Title: Speech at the Finance 2005 seminar
text: Speech by Director-General Erkki Liikanen at the Finance 2005 seminar . Speech . Thursday14 October 2004, 12:00 AM MONETARY POLICY CHALLENGES IN AN UNBALANCED INTERNATIONAL CONTEXT World economy Over the past year, global economic growth has been faster than expected. Both the United States and Asian countries d0 Japan, China and India d0 had stronger-than-expected economic figures in the early part of the year. Also noteworthy is the rapid development of the Russian economy. The growth spread both regionally and by industry. In Europe and the euro area, too, optimism finally began to pick up. Of course, the growth figures were not high, but still slightly higher than expected. Today, it seems that in the global economy, the fastest phase of the cyclical upturn has probably already passed. Data from summer and early autumn show that the growth rate has moderated. The most obvious reason has been the rise in oil prices. But there are also major imbalances in the global economy and a reduction in the impact of expansionary economic policies. However, according to forecasts, global economic growth will continue at a rate of about 4% in the near future. It is stronger than average in asia's industrialising economies as well as in transition economies. In the EU-15, growth is projected to remain at just over 2% in the near future. The assumption in these scenarios is that oil prices will gradually fall from current levels (ca. 50 a barrel) to 30-35 a barrel, and that global imbalances will not lead to shocks that could upset economic developments. The outlook is therefore overshadowed by oil prices and major imbalances. The light monetary policy stance in industrialised countries in recent years has supported the recovery in the global economy, but at the same time led to strong liquidity growth. The global abundance of liquidity has raised concerns. These concerns concern the threat of rising inflation and the accumulation of financial imbalances, as well as their spill-over effects from major industrialised countries to other countries. In the United States, current account and fiscal deficits have remained high or even increased during the current economic upturn. As a mirror image of this development, asian countries' financial receivables have increased, and in connection with this, exchange rate pressures have increased. The very strong growth in China has had a significant impact on commodity and oil price developments. The financial and structural problems of the public sector in the Japanese economy remain unresolved, although some progress has been made in recent years. Correcting these imbalances is a very demanding challenge for economic policy. Problems can to be corrected as a result of economic policy measures or in a market-driven manner. The former option can be slow and somehow predictable, the latter fast and surprising. Perhaps the best option would be an appropriate amount of each. It will depend on how the global economy will eventually develop in the next few years. This presentation of these issues focuses on the challenges posed by abundant global liquidity. This issue is close to and a concern for the monetary policy industry. The liquidity problem of the global economy Light monetary policy and exchange rate policy of Asian countries The last few years have been a very exceptional time for the world's monetary economy: inflation has been low; monetary policy has been light; interest rates have been at record lows and liquidity has accumulated ample in the global economy. Today, that amount of liquidity is a key challenge for future monetary policy. How did this situation come about? From the beginning of 2001, monetary policy was heavily eased by central banks, mainly in the United States, but also in Europe and Japan. Last summer, short-term nominal market interest rates were around 1% in the Us, 2% in Europe and around zero in Japan. Long-term 10-year market rates were around 4% in the US and Europe and just under 2% in Japan. Interest rates were clearly lower than at any time since 1960. Perhaps most clearly, the general easing of the monetary policy stance is illustrated by the fact that the central bank's policy rate, weighted together by these three economies (USA, JAP, EUR), is now about 3 percentage points lower than the so-called "central bank interest rate", which is consistent with the long-term balanced development of the economy. natural rate. The natural or neutral interest rate is usually defined as the sum of the long-term average real growth rate of the economy and the inflation target and varies from country to country. In the United States it is estimated at around 4-5%, and in the euro area it is slightly less. The substantial easing of monetary policy has led to strong credit expansion. Liquidity metrics d1 such as monetary and credit growth d1 have risen sharply. The ratio of money and credit to GDP has risen generally in industrialised countries, but fastest in East Asia. Debt reserves in many countries and sectors are already so high that they give cause for concern. The strong easing of monetary policy in the United States was prompted by a sharp turnaround in the economic cycle and an attempt to prevent the problems it might cause. With the central international position of the dollar and the general dollar interweaving of different currencies, very light monetary policy spread widely throughout the world economy. This is especially true for countries that have followed the dollar in their exchange rate policy. However, a light monetary policy has been deliberately pursued not only in the United States, but also in other countries. A looser-than-average monetary policy compared to the rest of the world, coupled with a sharp loosening of fiscal policy, has brought the United States a large current account and a fiscal deficit. In other parts of the world, despite expansive economic policies, current account balances have generally improved or been in clear surplus. In key Asian countries, in addition to a light monetary policy, an important factor in the money supply has been the current account surplus and capital imports. In Asia, the development of the balance of payments has been accompanied by intervention by the monetary authorities, which has increased the liquidity of banks in the local currency. In Japan, the financing of public deficits has also led to a sharp increase in the money supply. The U.S. deficit and indebtedness also initially reflected the strength of the country's economy, which prompted foreign investors and companies to invest heavily in the United States. In recent years, investments from abroad have: were largely targeted at public sector securities. A growing share of investment has come from central banks in Asian countries. Despite the many advantages of its currency, the spiral of US indebtedness is currently excessive and is bound to break or at least slow down considerably at some point. Indeed, one of the risk factors for the international economy has been considered to be the fact that the dollar will weaken sharply at some point due to the deficit. It would help to rebalance foreign trade, but could slow down economic growth elsewhere, especially in Europe. As a continuation of this scenario, it is necessary to build scenarios against which currencies the dollar weakens, since different countries have different exchange rate policies. China and Japan have so far tried to prevent the dollar from weakening against their own currency. The pressure on the fixed US dollar exchange rate policy pursued by Asian countries is increasing. In Europe, there have been fears that the floating euro will have to carry the whole load. Such an image is easily created if you look only at the large countries. However, the importance of a single bilateral exchange rate should not be overstated. Europe, and especially the euro area, accounts for a small share of us foreign trade, only in the order of a fifth. About the same is the joint share of China and Japan, so the United States trades most of its trade with smaller countries. Neighboring Canada and Mexico alone together already account for about a third of U.S. foreign trade. In the structure of demand in the United States, the share of foreign trade is quite small (exports 14%, imports 16%). It is quite likely that imbalances cannot be corrected solely through the exchange rate. Domestic demand will also have to adjust, which means that household savings will eventually have to rise. AMOUNT OF MONEY AND INFLATION The monetary ratio of the global economy has risen in relation to GDP over the last ten years, and particularly sharply in recent years. For example, China's real growth has been in the order of 8% annually, but the growth of monetary and credit aggregates is still much more drastic. In China, both limited and large amounts of money in relation to GDP have almost doubled since the mid-1990s. Banks' outstanding amounts to almost 150% of GDP. The effects of loose monetary policy and excessive liquidity have been reflected in a stronger and broader-than-expected recovery in economic growth in the global economy. This is, of course, a positive and desirable thing. But the light situation has also given rise to phenomena that raise concerns in the long run: -the prices of raw materials and oil on the world market have risen significantly over the past 1-2 years due to strong demand. The prices of these have been pushed up by strong demand from the United States and Asian countries, as well as by the risk premium for oil prices caused by various crises in Iraq and other producing countries. Traditionally, the rise in commodity prices has signalled a strengthening of global demand and rising inflationary pressures. -globally, inflation is still quite low, but in the United States and Europe, consumer price growth has picked up somewhat since the beginning of the year. Recent inflation forecasts have been accompanied by an upside risk. -the housing market has become hotter and housing prices have risen high in many countries (UK, Spain, France, Sweden, and Finland) in recent years. -the easing of financial conditions has led to an increase in private sector indebtedness in many countries. Private sector indebtedness has given rise to great concern from a monetary policy point of view. -it can be said that while inflation is still low, the abundance of funding may rise to the point that it threatens to upset the sustainability of the ongoing economic upturn. MONETARY POLICY CONCERNS Future monetary policy therefore faces many concerns and challenges. The traditional concern for monetary policy is that ample liquidity will increase inflationary pressures over time. In the current context, where real interest rates are well below the long-term natural interest rate, one may rightly be concerned about the long-term outlook for inflation. If the real interest rate remains very low for a long period of time, the result will be overheating of the economy and an increase in inflation expectations, as in the past in similar situations. Exchange rates are quite inflexible in many countries. Many Asian countries have intervened in the markets to keep the nominal exchange rate of their currencies stable, especially against the dollar. The policy has prevented normal fluctuations and changes in exchange rates. Currency interventions can amplify the risk of inflation if they prevent the currency from strengthening and lead to a more expansionary policy that would otherwise be desired. Ample liquidity undermines monetary stability, especially in countries that pursue such policies. The liquidity created in the United States, Japan and Europe has led to an influx of private capital, especially into emerging economies, which offer the highest nominal returns. Capital flows to emerging economies have increased sharply since 2002. This has led to a dramatic easing of financial conditions in developing countries, which threatens the stability of financial markets. At the moment, the main concern in many central banks is probably how to get rid of the recent long period of loose monetary policy. Recent, increasingly contradictory signals about the economic situation and high oil prices are making it difficult to find a solution. A tightening of monetary policy could help to stem the formation of new liquidity. However, due to oil prices and indebtedness, prudence in politics may be in place in the short term. U.S. households and businesses are heavily indebted in many respects, both domestically and abroad (albeit fortunately in dollars) and the debt is still growing rapidly. However, there are still no significant debt problems, as interest rates have remained low. In large Asian countries, large debts are domestic, which is why the problem is, in principle, easier. On the other hand, both Japan and China already have a very widespread and difficult problem of unmanaged credit. In Europe, too, debt reserves have risen markedly in most countries, but the overall financial situation is more balanced. Especially in small countries, external imbalances have often ended up in a currency crisis over a long period of time. In the case of the United States, such a risk is less, since the country is large and its currency occupies a key position in the world monetary system. China is not suffering from a current account deficit, but is at risk of excessive credit expansion and the threat of a banking crisis. However, China's financial system is still heavily regulated and supported by the public authorities. Japan has a large net foreign asset, so it does not depend on the behavior of foreign investors. The debt problem lies purely between domestic economic entities. Among the concerns is the rapid increase in government debt and the high level of bank non-performing loans. In any case, the continuation of financial growth trends increases the vulnerability of economies and even the likelihood of crises. In any case, the rapid growth of money and credit will sometimes have to be reversed, which could significantly limit global economic growth. MONETARY POLICY IN THE EURO AREA A turnaround in monetary policy in the United States Financial markets began to react to the acceleration of global economic growth and symptoms of inflation last spring, with the release of data on better-than-expected early-year growth figures and employment gains in the United States. The market's interest rate expectations changed rapidly. In line with expectations, the Federal Reserve raised the monetary policy rate in June, while signalling that it was time for interest rate policy to move from a strongly expansionary stance towards a more moderately neutral level of interest rates. Since then, the FED has raised its policy rate twice during the summer and early fall, by a percentage point a quarter at a time, to 1.75%. On the basis of the FED's statements, the shift in interest rate policy towards a more neutral level of interest rates can be expected to continue unless there is a downward turn in economic developments. According to market expectations, the fed's key policy rate will be 2% at the end of this year. For next year, market expectations are divided. According to the market consensus outlook, the FED will continue moderate rate hikes next year. Due to the slightly weaker economic figures expected in recent weeks, some economists expect the FED to take a "pause for reflection" early next year. The approaching presidential elections have curbed the current debate on economic policy and possibly also decision-making. In any case, the winner of the elections will probably have to curb the indebtedness of public finances. ECB MONETARY POLICY STANCE Over the past year, the European Central Bank and its Governing Council have been closely monitoring economic developments and threats to price stability. The ECB has assessed that the increase in inflation above the price stability target ceiling, mainly due to higher oil prices, is temporary and that price stability does not appear to be threatened over the medium term. According to the ECB's latest forecast, the euro area economy will grow by about 2% this year, from 1.8% to 2.8% in 2005. Inflation will exceed the price stability cap for another six months or so, after which it is expected to fall below 2% in the first half of next year and remain below 2% on average in 2005. This forecast is based on the assumption that the price of oil will fall to an average of about 37 in 2005. An upside risk has been identified in the inflation forecast. Indeed, in its bulletin following its last meeting of the Governing Council (7.10), the Council stated that: "A number of upside risks to price stability remain. Oil price developments remain a cause for concern, in particular as regards the realisation of second-round effects stemming from wage and price-setting." *** "Overall, annual inflation rates are expected to fall below 2% in 2005, but a number of threats to price stability over the medium term need to be carefully monitored. -... the materialisation of risks to price stability needs to be monitored with particular vigilance." At present, interest rates in the euro area are relatively low when compared to historical interest rates in euro area countries or to estimates of neutral interest rates in the euro area. The key ECB interest rate is 2%. Short-term market interest rates are around 2% in nominal terms and slightly negative in real terms. Long-term 10-year market interest rates are just over 4% in nominal terms and around 2% in real terms. Monetary growth has been abundant in recent years, well above what non-inflationary growth would require. However, over the past year, the pace has moderated. Credit to the private sector has grown rapidly. Overall, financing conditions have been accommodative and monetary policy has continued to be accommodative. The financial market information shows the market's expectations regarding inflation and interest rate developments. According to the latest data, inflation expectations in consumers and financial markets have not risen, although oil prices have risen and remained high during the autumn. The market's expectations of a rate hike have also moderated slightly in late summer and autumn from what they were in early summer. Now the market expects the ECB to raise interest rates for the first time in the second quarter of next year, by 0.25 percentage points. However, in line with the nature of financial markets, these interest rate expectations may change sensitively with the information on the economic outlook. The expectations of the market are only their view of the future development of interest rates. The ECB's interest rate decisions are fully based on its own assessment of the outlook and risks to price stability, and the Governing Council is following developments very closely. SUOMEN TALOUDEN HAASTEET <d0> TUOTTAVUUDEN LIS<80><80>MINEN Ennusteiden mukaan ty<9a>ik<8a>inen v<8a>est<9a> alkaa Suomessa muutaman vuoden p<8a><8a>st<8a> supistua, el<8a>kel<8a>isten m<8a><8a>r<8a> nopeasti lis<8a><8a>nty<8a> ja ik<8a><8a>ntymiseen liittyv<8a>t menot kasvaa. Ty<9a>n tuottavuuden kasvua koskevissa kansainv<8a>lisiss<8a> vertailuissa Suomi on yleens<8a> k<8a>rkisijoilla. Suomessa palvelujen hinnat ovat yleisesti korkeat, mink<8a> vuoksi yksityisten palvelujen k<8a>ytt<9a> on v<8a>h<8a>ist<8a>. Julkisiin sosiaali-ja terveydenhoitopalveluihin tulee kohdistumaan kasvava menopaine. Kustannusten nousun rajoittamiseksi palvelujen tehokkuutta on pystytt<8a>v<8a> lis<8a><8a>m<8a><8a>n. T<8a>rke<8a><8a> olisi l<9a>yt<8a><8a> kannustimet ja keinot julkisten palvelujen tuottavuuden kohottamiseksi. Tuottavuuden kohottamisessa my<9a>s ulkomaankaupan avoimuudella ja kilpailun lis<8a><8a>ntymisell<8a> on t<8a>rke<8a> rooli. Kannustimet tuottavuuden kohentamiseen puuttuvat, jos kilpailu on v<8a>h<8a>ist<8a>. EU:n laajentuminen on merkinnyt vastaavanlaisen kilpailuasetelman syntymist<8a> vanhojen ja uusien EU:n j<8a>senmaiden v<8a>lille. Laajentuminen on johtanut vanhojen EU-maiden teollisuuden tuotannon ja tuotantoketjujen levi<8a>miseen uusiin j<8a>senmaihin, joissa voidaan hy<9a>dynt<8a><8a> paitsi halvempaa ty<9a>panosta usein my<9a>s uudempaa tekniikkaa ja hyv<8a><8a> tuottavuutta. Nyt tilanne on muuttunut monella tavalla; kulutamme v<8a>hemm<8a>n kuin tuotamme ja teolliset ty<9a>paikat v<8a>henev<8a>t. Uusia ty<9a>paikkoja voidaan synnytt<8a><8a> palvelutarjontaa lis<8a><8a>m<8a>ll<8a> ja monipuolistamalla. Ty<9a>llisyysasteen nostaminen on tarpeen, jotta voidaan varautua v<8a>est<9a>n ik<8a><8a>ntymisen aiheuttamiin ongelmiin. Yht<8a> t<8a>rke<8a><8a> on luoda ymp<8a>rist<9a>, joka kannustaa tuottavuuden jatkuvaan kohottamiseen. Tavoitteet eiv<8a>t ole vastakkaisia. Title: Speech on "the challenges of the Finnish economy" at Nordea's Employee Seminar in Pori
text: President and CEO Erkki Liikanen's speech on "Challenges for the Finnish economy" at Nordea's Employee Seminar in Pori . Speech . Tuesday 18 October 2005,12:00 AM Challenges for the Finnish economy First about growing: Measuring well-being is a challenging task. However, the generally accepted measure of living standards is considered to be: real national income per capita. National income per capita is not enough, safety, health, a good living environment, equality of starting points, etc. are also important. Unfortunately, however, low national incomes also mean great difficulties in achieving these other objectives. Economic growth, on the other hand, is characterised by the change in real income per capita. Growth is important again, because then jobs can be better preserved and new ones created, funds will be created for the development of common services and companies and society will be able to invest in a better environment. As such, growth is not a very old phenomenon. Until the Industrial Revolution, there was no growth at all. The growth that began in the 1870s continued strong until World War 1. The interwar period was overshadowed by the Great Depression. Again, from the Second World War to the oil crises, growth was very strong throughout the industrialized states. After that, it slowed down, but historically it was still significant. Where does growth come from? Growth is generated by growth in labour input and productivity. In Finland, labour input grew strongly as the baby boomers and women entered the labour market extensively. Now we are approaching a situation where baby boomers are starting to retire. If that day can be postponed with the pension reform, it will contribute to sustaining growth and, in particular, helping to finance pension and health costs. In any case, when labour growth slows down, growth can only be achieved by increasing labour productivity. And that means that the per capita output of labor increases. Many say that productivity always means grinding. That's not quite the case. Productivity can also be increased by investing in new machinery and equipment and training. And ultimately, what is important is the overall productivity, which tells about the "recipe" of how to use labor and capital. The standard of living does not rise from boiling more of the same soup, but from inventing better "recipes". In the same way, total productivity arises from finding smarter, why not wiser, ways of organising work, often by using new technologies. In the long term, well-being has primarily increased precisely through increased productivity. Wage and salary earners are well aware that real earnings can grow on average by no more than the growth in productivity. If so, how can productivity growth be increased? 1. Investments are needed, first of all, in machinery, equipment, new technologies. Through investments, the per capita output of work may increase. That is why it is extremely important that investments in machinery and equipment in Finland grow. Construction investments have developed satisfactorily. There is a lot of international investment in research and product development in Finland, but little in new machines and equipment. 2. Investment in education is needed. The more competent the workforce, the higher the productivity, if the work is properly organized. In Finland, comprehensive school has gained a lot of fame around the world. That is a good thing. Great system. But we face a lot of challenges at all levels of education after this. 3. We need an environment open to competition. We need to increase the overall productivity, the "recipe". New information and communication technologies make it possible to process information cheaply through great savings. But experience shows that companies make such changes only in a competitive situation. The pressure to organise work more intelligently increases if there is a risk of being overtaken by competitors. Competition is an important incentive. Investment in information and communication technologies and staff training is necessary, but it is only competition that has forced a reorganisation of work. The Bank of Finland has carried out a lot of research on the matter. As a result, the following chain of events is seen: As competition intensifies, first the profits of companies fall. But at the same time, the prices of products are falling, people's purchasing power is improving, they can buy more, it strengthens demand, creates new jobs, leads to investment and, ultimately, to growth. Secondly, on the terms of trade: Two important export sectors in Finland are the forest and electronics industries. There, companies are world famous. Productivity, especially in the electronics industry, has grown strongly. This is also reflected in the figures of the national economy. At the same time, competition for market share has been fierce. As a result, prices have fallen, often by 10-15% per annum. And when companies export the vast majority of their production, the advantage is also mainly transferred to the foreign consumer. The export prices of forest products have also fallen. At the same time, import prices have risen on average. What does it mean? We need more exports to finance the same imports. This is the weakening of the terms of trade. In this way, part of the growth of the Finnish economy and also of productivity is drained abroad. Our national product is growing more than the purchasing power of our citizens. The answer is not to leave export prices uncalculated. Then the export market goes to others and exports stop. Prices are determined by fierce competition on the world market. More new products need to be developed that can be valued. It requires research and development, but it also requires investment in machinery and equipment. If our service sector, through competition, improves its productivity, it can also add value to exports and reduce the problem of the terms of trade. Thirdly, on finland's economic outlook: Finland's economic development has been good in recent years compared to many European countries. Consumers' confidence in their own economy has been strong and it has kept consumption high. This has been based on an increase in real purchasing power and improved employment trends. This has also been compounded by exceptionally low interest rates and longer loan periods. In the long term, however, we face threats. In order to combat them, it is necessary to be able to increase productivity throughout the economy. The challenge concerns not only the private sector, but also the public sector. We have a more skilled workforce. Investments, the use of new technologies and new ways of organising work can also increase productivity in public administration and services. At the same time, we need to add value to our products and services. We need new companies that are looking for growth. What is needed is research and development and a more imaginative exploitation of research results. Innovation is needed. And, of course, competent and motivated staff is the basis of any success. To conclude on price outlook: In Finland, the rise in prices has been well under control in recent years. Of course, it has also been affected by changes in the taxation of alcohol and cars. But nevertheless. In recent months, the prices of oil products have been at a higher level than before. In the 1970s, tax and wage settlements began to compensate for the rise in oil prices in many countries. The benefits of compensation trickled down to oil producers. Inflation accelerated further and governments faced large deficits. As a result, economic development slowed down sharply and unemployment increased. Now it is important to avoid those mistakes. The role of the European Central Bank is to ensure price stability. That is why we now have to be more vigilant in monitoring price developments.

Title: Speech at the Independence Day celebration in Korso, Vantaa
text: Speech by Director-General Erkki Liikanen at the Independence Day celebration in Korso, Vantaa . Speech . Tuesday 6 December 2005,12:00AM Finland has been independent today for 88 years. During these years, the world has changed enormously and Finland even more so. The growth of the economy and, at the same time, prosperity is only a short stage in the history of mankind. It began only 200 years ago after the Industrial Revolution, which means that it reached Finland during the period of autonomy. Until then, the population and production had grown at the same rate. In other words, the average standard of living had remained unchanged. Since then, production has grown more than the population on a global scale, so that the standard of living has risen yhdeks8ankertaiseksi. In Finland, economic and standard of living growth began later, but it has been faster than others. We have caught up with others. Today, Finland is among the 15 most developed countries in terms of standard of living. The volume of Finland's national product has grown more than 20-fold. Of this, 1/3 has been due to an increase in the number of employed persons. The remaining 2/3 has been due to productivity gains. In other words, what has been absolutely crucial in this long period of time has been the increase in output per capita. If we look at the development per employee, it must be remembered that working time has been reduced by more than a third. The working week has been reduced from 60 hours to less than 40 hours. But still, the standard of living per capita has increased 12-fold. This has been possible precisely because of the increase in productivity. Indeed, productivity growth is the key to economic development and an increase in living standards, as much negative as the word is associated with it. Productivity has increased as a result of investment in machinery and equipment, the country has become more capitalised. Many physically strenuous work phases are carried out mechanically. But beyond that, the training of the workforce has risen drastically. First, general compulsory education was created, and then, in the 1970s, a comprehensive school. Vocational and higher education has expanded. All this has improved the quality of the workforce and this, too, has increased productivity. During the trip, new and better ways of combining labor and capital have also been invented, better recipes have been invented. The standard of living does not rise from boiling more of the same soup. If finland were now cooking ten times as much of the same potato soup or making the same amount of potatoes and sauces compared to the post-war years, it would not have raised our standard of living or quality. It has risen due to new and better recipes. And it has not meant refinement, but better training and better ways of organizing work, companies and services. Less work has resulted in more quantity and better quality. The standard of living arises from the work done, but its increase from the increase in productivity. When considering the development of our country in the long run, throughout the period of independence, the importance of productivity was overwhelming. For the first time in its history, Finland is facing the challenge of ageing. After the war, the birth rate was exceptionally high. An average of four children were born to women, which meant 100,000 or more children per year between 1945 and 1950. Since then, the birth rate has fallen to a completely different level. Today, 1.76 children are born to us per woman. It is not a low figure in a European comparison. However, already the year before last, Finland moved to a situation where the age group leaving working age was smaller than the one entering working age. Our challenge from now on is how to continue to rise living standards and well-being when fewer new workers enter the labour market than retire from working life. This is a challenge for the financing of welfare services and pensions. The aim of the pension reform is to ensure that people continue their working lives longer. The last few years raise the pension more than the earlier ones. If, in addition, work communities learn to value the experience of those who have grown up more and the work is organized taking into account their needs, it is possible that the retirement age will increase from the current 60 years. That would be a welcome change and would make it easier to face the challenge of ageing. Yet, in the long term, the rise in our standard of living cannot be built on an increase in the labour force, because the age groups have become smaller. Even more so than before, the increase in well-being depends on how productivity increases. And by this I certainly do not mean laborious grinding, but better and smarter ways of organizing work, both in the private and public spheres. Information technology and its application is the most important tool in this. We have an increasingly extensive and better educated population and workforce. The creative power of all must be unleashed to seek better solutions for the organisation of work and services. It requires good leadership and the right incentives. When good training and the use of information technology are combined in such a way that processes within the company's administration are simplified and stairs are reduced, contacts with customers and citizens are handled by avoiding bureaucracy, and procurement is made more efficiently, the output of each work rises. Let's do the right things and do them better. Throughout history, it has an extraordinary meaning. In the post-war years, when Finland caught up with other Western countries, finland's productivity grew by 5 percent per year. It was then that the standard of living of a citizen doubled in 14 years. Now that productivity is growing by 2.5% per annum, living standards are doubling in 28 years. If productivity does not increase at all, raising the standard of living of one person or group means that the real income of others will correspondingly fall. That is the kind of world we lived in until the early 1800s. *** In 1917, Finland was a very poor country. Only one in fifty apartments was such that there were amenities, electricity or a toilet inside. Today these are in all permanent residences. The development has been enormous. No stage in history knows anything like it. This is always good to remember. Still, it doesn't diminish our need to work for better housing or other living conditions. The last few years have seen one big jump on this side. Mortgages had been regulated until the last decade. Loan periods were short and, especially during the recession, interest rates jumped to unbearable heights. In 1999, Finland joined the European Economic and Monetary Union. The euro replaced the marks less than five years ago. Financial conditions have changed completely. Loan periods have lengthened. And interest rates are historically low. And are still like that after last week's interest rate decision. The development of financial markets has created a lot of new opportunities. When interest rates ate up 10% of Finns' income in 1990, now they account for 3 %. Low interest rates and current loan periods create opportunities to build a life far into the future. Still, everything has its risks. On average, Finns are not very indebted, but the averages mask below an important fact. Only one in three Finns is in debt. And for some young people, the debts are high, the risks of servicing which increase significantly when faced with unemployment or family crises. It is also important to make sure that all this does not literally spill over when the price of land rises. Construction costs have remained reasonably under control, but the price of land has risen threateningly in some places. *** What has happened to public health? When Finland became independent, infant mortality was high, twelve out of a hundred children died in childbirth. With many major reforms, especially the maternity and child health clinic system, infant mortality has virtually disappeared. Our health situation has also improved. Tuberculosis and many other diseases have almost been defeated. This has dramatically increased people's lifespans. The life expectancy of a person at the time of our country's independence was less than 50 years. Today it is more than 75 years for a man and more than 80 years for a woman. And grows so that in 2030 the figure for men will exceed 80 years, and for women - 85 years. When our country became independent, young people inherited their parents when entering the world of work. In the future, it is common, and even today it is not uncommon, for a child to inherit his parents upon retirement. What a change! The increase in life expectancy is a positive thing. At the same time, it will change the country and the world so that there will be interesting challenges for politics. *** The last couple of decades have also been a time of breathtaking change. When I moved to Brussels 15 years ago, the Soviet Union was still a superpower and Finland was a small and unknown country behind the Nordic countries, a neighbor of the Soviet Union. The Berlin Wall had already fallen and then the Soviet Union fell apart. At the right time, Finland applied for membership of the European Union. The goal was to be around the table where decisions are made. Already during the war, J.K. Paasikivi dreamed of a Europe in which relations between countries would be determined by law and not by force. This is precisely the essence of the European Union. A treaty is a law that determines relations between countries. No one can have hegemony. But even so, decisions can be taken when they can be taken by qualified majority. The EU Constitution would increase qualified majority voting almost everywhere and would therefore strengthen the Union and Finland. Let us hope that a solution can be found to push this reform through. Membership of the European Union made Finland familiar. Finland came to be known as a country, is a country that has had a rich, albeit heavy, history. It is a Nordic country, but different in many ways. History and experience made it easier to adapt to a community based on the law and the rule of law. But at the same time, many of Finland's achievements are known to everyone. The once much-debated primary school is of international interest due to learning outcomes. In various research, innovation and competitiveness comparisons, Finland ranks first. The Finnish administration is at the top or second in the list of the least corrupt countries. These achievements are something to be proud of. And remember that they are the result of years of work. And we must take the credit we deserve in the world. But at the same time you have to see behind them. Efforts must be made to further develop primary school and improve pupils' motivation. Vocational training must be developed so that vacancies and jobseekers meet. And unemployment would be reduced. Innovation and entrepreneurship must be encouraged so that new businesses are created and existing ones develop and create more work. And it is necessary to develop with an open mind common services. We know that resources are always limited. Defending the welfare state is its development. Often it also means painful solutions in the short term in order to achieve the benefits in the long term.

Jos katsotaan kehityst<8a> ty<9a>ntekij<8a><8a> kohden, on muistettava, ett<8a> ty<9a>aika on supistunut yli kolmanneksen. Ty<9a>viikko on lyhentynyt 60 tunnista alle 40 tunnin. Mutta silti elintaso henke<8a> kohden on kasvanut 12-kertaiseksi. Se on ollut mahdollista juuri tuottavuuden kasvun vuoksi. Tuottavuuden kasvu onkin talouden kehityksen ja elintason nousun avain, niin paljon kielteist<8a> kuin sanaan liitet<8a><8a>nkin. Tuottavuus on kasvanut, kun on investoitu koneisiin ja laitteisiin, maa on p<8a><8a>omaistunut. Monet fyysisesti raskaat ty<9a>vaiheet tehd<8a><8a>n koneellisesti. Mutta sen lis<8a>ksi ty<9a>voiman koulutus on noussut rajusti. Ensin luotiin yleinen oppivelvollisuus ja sitten 1970.luvulla peruskoulu. Ammatillinen ja korkeakoulutus on laajentunut. T<8a>m<8a> kaikki on parantanut ty<9a>voiman laatua ja t<8a>m<8a>kin on lis<8a>nnyt tuottavuutta. Matkan aikana on my<9a>s keksitty uusia ja parempia tapoja yhdist<8a><8a> ty<9a> ja p<8a><8a>oma, on keksitty parempia reseptej<8a>. Ei elintaso siit<8a> nouse, ett<8a> keitet<8a><8a>n enemm<8a>n samaa soppaa. Jos Suomessa keitett<8a>isiin nyt sodanj<8a>lkeisiin vuosiin verrattuna kymmenkertainen m<8a><8a>r<8a> samaa perunakeittoa tai teht<8a>isiin saman verran lis<8a><8a> perunaa ja kastiketta, ei se meid<8a>n elintasoa tai laatua olisi nostanut. Se on noussut uusien ja parempien reseptien vuoksi. Eik<8a> se ole tarkoittanut hiostamista, vaan parempaa koulutusta ja parempia keinoja organisoida ty<9a>, yritykset ja palvelut. V<8a>hemm<8a>ll<8a> ty<9a>ll<8a> on saatu aikaan enemm<8a>n m<8a><8a>r<8a><8a> ja parempaa laatua. Elintaso syntyy tehdyst<8a> ty<9a>st<8a>, mutta sen kasvu tuottavuuden lis<8a>yksest<8a>. Kun tarkastellaan maamme kehityst<8a> pitk<8a>ll<8a> aikav<8a>lill<8a>, koko itsen<8a>isyyden ajalta, tuottavuuden merkitys oli ylivoimaisen suuri. Suomi on historiansa aikana ensimm<8a>ist<8a> kertaa ik<8a><8a>ntymisen haasteen edess<8a>. Sodan j<8a>lkeen syntyvyys oli poikkeuksellisen suuri. Naisille syntyi keskim<8a><8a>rin nelj<8a> lasta, mik<8a> merkitsi vuosittain 100 000 lasta tai ylikin vuosina 1945<d0>1950. Sen j<8a>lkeen syntyvyys on laskenut kokonaan toiselle tasolle. T<8a>n<8a><8a>n meille syntyy 1.76 lasta naista kohden. Se ei ole alhainen luku eurooppalaisessa vertailussa. Silti jo toissa vuonna Suomi siirtyi tilanteeseen, jossa ty<9a>i<8a>st<8a> poistuva ik<8a>luokka oli pienempi kuin ty<9a>ik<8a><8a>n tuleva. Haasteemme t<8a>st<8a> eteenp<8a>in onkin, kuinka jatkaa elintason ja hyvinvoinnin nousua, kun ty<9a>markkinoille tulee v<8a>hemm<8a>n uusia ty<9a>ntekij<9a>it<8a> kuin ty<9a>el<8a>m<8a>st<8a> siirtyy el<8a>kkeelle. T<8a>m<8a> on haaste hyvinvointipalvelujen ja el<8a>kkeiden rahoitukselle. El<8a>keuudistuksella pyrit<8a><8a>n siihen, ett<8a> ihmiset jatkaisivat ty<9a>uraansa pitemm<8a>lle. Viimeiset vuodet nostavat el<8a>kett<8a> varhaisempia enemm<8a>n. Jos lis<8a>ksi ty<9a>yhteis<9a>iss<8a> opitaan arvostamaan enemm<8a>n varttuneempien kokemusta ja ty<9a>t j<8a>rjestet<8a><8a>n heid<8a>n tarpeensa huomioon ottaen, on mahdollista, ett<8a> el<8a>kkeelle siirtymisik<8a> nousee nykyisest<8a> 60 vuodesta. Se olisi tervetullut muutos ja helpottaisi kohtaamaan ik<8a><8a>ntymisen haasteen. Silti pitk<8a>ll<8a> aikav<8a>lill<8a> elintasomme nousu ei voi rakentua ty<9a>voiman kasvuun, koska ik<8a>luokat ovat pienentyneet. Viel<8a> enemm<8a>n kuin ennen, hyvinvoinnin kasvu riippuu siit<8a>, miten tuottavuus kasvaa. Ja t<8a>ll<8a> en todellakaan tarkoita puurtavaa hiostamista, vaan yh<8a> parempia ja <8a>lykk<8a><8a>mpi<8a> tapoja j<8a>rjest<8a><8a> ty<9a>, niin yksityisell<8a> kuin julkisellakin puolella. Tietotekniikka ja sen soveltaminen on siin<8a> t<8a>rkein v<8a>line. Meill<8a> on yh<8a> laajemmin ja paremmin koulutettu v<8a>est<9a> ja ty<9a>voima. On vapautettava kaikkien luova voima hakemaan parempia ratkaisuja ty<9a>n ja palvelujen j<8a>rjest<8a>miseen. Siihen tarvitaan hyv<8a><8a> johtamista ja oikeita kannustimia. Kun hyv<8a> koulutus ja tietotekniikan k<8a>ytt<9a> yhdistet<8a><8a>n niin, ett<8a> yrityksen hallinnon sis<8a>ll<8a> prosesseja yksinkertaistetaan ja portaita v<8a>hennet<8a><8a>n, yhteydet asiakkaisiin ja kansalaisiin hoidetaan byrokratiaa v<8a>ltt<8a>m<8a>ll<8a> ja hankinnat tehd<8a><8a>n tehokkaammin, nousee jokaisen ty<9a>n tuotos. Tehd<8a><8a>n oikeita asioita ja tehd<8a><8a>n ne paremmin. Historian saatossa sill<8a> on tavaton merkitys. Sodanj<8a>lkeisin<8a> vuosina, kun Suomi otti kiinni muita l<8a>nsimaita, maamme Suomen tuottavuus kasvoi 5 prosenttia vuodessa. Silloin kansalaisen elintaso kaksinkertaistui 14 vuodessa. Nyt kun tuottavuus kasvaa 2,5 prosenttia vuodessa, kaksinkertaistuu elintaso 28 vuodessa. Jos tuottavuus ei kasva lainkaan, merkitsee yhden henkil<9a>n tai ryhm<8a>n elintason nostaminen sit<8a>, ett<8a> muiden reaalitulot vastaavasti laskevat. Sellaisessa maailmassa me elimme 1800-luvun alkuun saakka. *** Suomi oli vuonna 1917 todella k<9a>yh<8a> maa. Vain joka viideskymmenes asunto oli sellainen, ett<8a> siell<8a> oli mukavuuksia, s<8a>hk<9a> tai WC sis<8a>ll<8a>. T<8a>n<8a><8a>n n<8a>m<8a> ovat kaikissa vakituisissa asunnoissa. Kehitys on ollut valtaisaa. Mik<8a><8a>n historian vaihe ei tunne vastaavaa. T<8a>m<8a> on aina hyv<8a> muistaa. Silti se ei v<8a>henn<8a> tarvettamme ty<9a>skennell<8a> parempien asumis-tai muiden elinolojen puolesta. Viimeiset vuodet ovat n<8a>hneet t<8a>ll<8a> puolella yhden suuren hypp<8a>yksen. Asuntolainat oli s<8a><8a>nnelty viime vuosikymmenelle saakka. Laina-ajat olivat lyhyit<8a> ja varsinkin laman aikana korot hypp<8a>siv<8a>t siet<8a>m<8a>tt<9a>miin korkeuksiin. Vuonna 1999 Suomi liittyi Euroopan talous-ja rahaliittoon. Eurot korvasivat markat vajaat viisi vuotta sitten. Rahoitusolot ovat muuttuneet t<8a>ysin. Laina-ajat ovat pidentyneet. Ja korot ovat historiallisen alhaisia. Ja ovat sellaisia edelleen viime viikon korkop<8a><8a>t<9a>ksen j<8a>lkeen. Rahoitusmarkkinoiden kehitys on luonut paljon uusia mahdollisuuksia. Kun korot s<9a>iv<8a>t suomalaisten tuloista 10 % vuonna 1990, nyt niiden osuus on 3 %. Alhaiset korot ja nykyiset laina-ajat luovat mahdollisuuksia rakentaa el<8a>m<8a><8a> pitk<8a>lle tulevaisuuteen. Silti kaikella on riskins<8a>. Keskim<8a><8a>rin suomalaiset eiv<8a>t ole kovin velkaantuneita, mutta keskiarvot peitt<8a>v<8a>t alle t<8a>rke<8a>n tosiasian. Suomalaisista velkaa on vain joka kolmannella. Ja osasta nuoria velat ovat suuria, joiden hoitamisen riskit nousevat merkitt<8a>v<8a>sti ty<9a>tt<9a>myyden tai perhekriisien kohdatessa. On my<9a>s t<8a>rke<8a><8a> pit<8a><8a> huoli, ettei t<8a>m<8a> kaikki kirjaimellisesti valu maahan maan hinnan noustessa. Rakennus.kustannukset ovat pysyneet kohtuullisesti hallinnassa, mutta maan hinta on noussut er<8a>in paikoin uhkaavasti. *** Miten on k<8a>ynyt kansanterveyden? Kun Suomi itsen<8a>istyi, imev<8a>iskuolleisuus oli suurta, kaksitoista sadasta lapsesta kuoli synnytykseen. Monien suurten uudistusten, varsinkin neuvolaj<8a>rjestelm<8a>n my<9a>t<8a>, imev<8a>iskuolleisuus on k<8a>yt<8a>nn<9a>ss<8a> poistunut kokonaan. Terveystilanteemme on my<9a>s parantunut. Tuberkuloosi ja monet muut taudit on miltei voitettu. T<8a>m<8a> on pident<8a>nyt ihmisten elinik<8a><8a> dramaattisesti. Ihmisen odotettavissa oleva elinik<8a> oli maamme itsen<8a>istyess<8a> alle 50 vuoden. T<8a>n<8a><8a>n se on miehell<8a> yli 75 vuotta ja naisella yli 80 vuoden. Ja kasvaa niin, ett<8a> vuonna 2030 miesten luku ylitt<8a><8a> 80 vuoden ja naisten 85 vuoden. Kun maamme itsen<8a>istyi, nuoret periv<8a>t vanhempansa ty<9a>el<8a>m<8a><8a>n siirtyess<8a><8a>n. Tulevaisuudessa on tavallista, eik<8a> t<8a>n<8a><8a>nk<8a><8a>n harvinaista, ett<8a> lapsi perii vanhempansa el<8a>kkeelle siirtyess<8a><8a>n. Mik<8a> muutos! Elini<8a>n kasvu on my<9a>nteinen asia. Se muuttaa samalla maata ja maailmaa niin, ett<8a> politiikalle tulee mielenkiintoisia haasteita. *** Viimeiset pari vuosikymment<8a> ovat olleet my<9a>s heng<8a>stytt<8a>vien muutosten aikaa. Kun siirryin Brysseliin 15 vuotta sitten, Neuvostoliitto oli edelleen suurvalta ja Suomi pieni ja tuntematon maa Pohjoismaiden takana, Neuvostoliiton naapurina. Berliinin muuri oli jo murtunut ja sitten hajosi Neuvostoliitto. Suomi haki oikealla hetkell<8a> j<8a>senyytt<8a> Euroopan Unionissa. Tavoite oli olla sen p<9a>yd<8a>n ymp<8a>rill<8a>, jossa p<8a><8a>t<9a>kset tehd<8a><8a>n. Jo J.K. Paasikivi unelmoi sodan aikana Euroopasta, jossa maiden v<8a>lisist<8a> suhteista m<8a><8a>r<8a>isi laki eik<8a> voima. T<8a>m<8a> on juuri Euroopan unionin ydin. Perussopimus on laki, joka m<8a><8a>ritt<8a><8a> maiden v<8a>liset suhteet. Kukaan ei voi saada hegemoniaa. Mutta silti p<8a><8a>t<9a>ksiin pystyt<8a><8a>n, kun ne voidaan tehd<8a> m<8a><8a>r<8a>enemmist<9a>ll<8a>. EU:n perustuslaki lis<8a>isi m<8a><8a>r<8a>enemmist<9a>p<8a><8a>t<9a>sten teon l<8a>hes kaikkialle ja siksi se vahvistaisi Unionia ja Suomea. Toivokaamme, ett<8a> ratkaisu l<9a>ytyy t<8a>m<8a>n uudistuksen ajamiseksi l<8a>pi. Euroopan Unionin j<8a>senyys teki Suomen tutuksi. Suomi opittiin tuntemaan maana, on maa, jolla on ollut rikas, vaikka raskas historia. Se on Pohjoismaa, mutta monessa erilainen. Historia ja kokemus helpottivat sopeutumista yhteis<9a><9a>n, joka nojautui lakiin ja oikeusvaltion periaatteisiin. Mutta samalla monet Suomen saavutukset ovat kaikkien tiedossa. Aikanaan paljon kiistelty peruskoulu on kansainv<8a>lisen kiinnostuksen kohteena oppimistulosten vuoksi. Erilaisissa tutkimus-, innovaatio-ja kilpailukykyvertailuissa Suomi on k<8a>rkisijoilla. Suomalainen hallinto on k<8a>rjess<8a> tai toisena v<8a>hiten lahjottujen maiden listalla. N<8a>ist<8a> saavutuksista pit<8a><8a> olla ylpe<8a>. Ja muistaa, ett<8a> ne ovat vuosien ty<9a>n tulosta. Ja on otettava maailmalla se kunnia, mik<8a> meille kuuluu. Mutta samalla on n<8a>ht<8a>v<8a> niiden taakse. Pit<8a><8a> ponnistella, jotta peruskoulua kehitet<8a><8a>n edelleen ja oppilaiden motivaatio paranee. On kehitett<8a>v<8a> ammattikoulutusta, ett<8a> avoimet ty<9a>paikat ja ty<9a>nhakijat kohtaisivat. Ja ty<9a>tt<9a>myys saataisiin alenemaan. On kannustettava innovaatiota ja yritt<8a>jyytt<8a>, jotta uusia yrityksi<8a> syntyisi ja entiset kehittyisiv<8a>t ja loisivat lis<8a><8a> ty<9a>t<8a>. Ja on kehitett<8a>v<8a> avoimella mielell<8a> yhteisi<8a> palveluja. Tied<8a>mme, ett<8a> voimavarat ovat aina rajoitettuja. Hyvinvointiyhteiskunnan puolustaminen on sen kehitt<8a>mist<8a>. Usein se merkitsee lyhyell<8a> aikav<8a>lill<8a> my<9a>s kipeit<8a> ratkaisuja, jotta edut voitaisiin saavuttaa pitk<8a>ll<8a> aikav<8a>lill<8a>.

Title: At the unveiling of Matti Vanhala's portrait
text: Speech by Director-General Erkki Liikanen at the unveiling of Matti Vanhala's portrait . Speech . Friday 31March 2006, 12:00 AM Today it is two years since my esteemed predecessor Matti Vanhala was subjected to a serious illness to leave office as Governor of the Bank of Finland. After a long career in the Ministry of Finance, the International Monetary Fund and, above all, in various positions at the Bank of Finland, Matti Vanhala was appointed Chairman of the Bank's Board of Directors on 5 June 1998. At that time, we were going through an extremely important phase for the Kingdom and the Bank of Finland. One month earlier, legislative amendments guaranteeing the independence of the Bank of Finland had entered into force. They were a prerequisite for Finland to be able to join the Euro system. The European Central Bank had become operational on 1.6.1998. Exchange rates were fixed and the new currency euro entered into force on 1.1.1999. The third stage of economic and monetary union was launched. It marked a new era in European economic integration. The final milestone then was the introduction of the euro cash on 1.1.2002. During and after those times, many things changed at the Bank of Finland and in Finnish society. There In the process of change, Matti Vanhala's contribution to the bank was decisive. This work is greatly appreciated by the Bank of Finland. The portrait that is now being unveiled partly reflects this appreciation. A painted portrait is capable of conveying even things that a photograph cannot. The portrait goes deeper  at its best, it captures a lot of humanity, personality and nuances from the model. The portrait that is now being unveiled is a good example of this. It describes Matti Vanhala as he is remembered and we want to remember him. He didn't bring himself up, but he impressed. He always had a watchful gaze. A smile was on his lips. He was youthful and approachable. You, painter Markku Kolehmainen, have had an interesting but challenging artistic interpretation task. It has been particularly demanding because you have had to paint a portrait of someone you did not have the opportunity to meet. The end result shows that you have reached a lot and essential things about Matti Vanhala. This work is a high-quality addition to the series of portraits of former Governors of the Bank of Finland. On behalf of the bank, I would like to thank the artist for this successful outcome. In addition, I would like to present to Liisa Vanhala my sincerest thanks for his valuable contribution to the success of this portrait project. I ask that the portrait be revealed.
