Title: Challenges for the financial sector at a seminar of Aktia Sstpankki Oyj
text: PUBLICATION FREE 28.4.2006 at 15:15 Director-General Erkki Liikanen AKTIA SAVINGS BANK PLC SEMINAR IN VAASA 28.4.2006 CHALLENGES FOR THE FINANCIAL SECTOR 1. Changes in the Finnish financial industry The recent history of Finnish banking is characterised by one thing: change. The magnitude of the change is revealed when you think back to what the banking sector in Finland was like just over 10 years ago. Let's think about the following:  Bank performance and structural changes. Only 10 years ago, the combined credit losses of Finnish banks were higher than their operating profit. It was not until 1995 that the banking market became profitable after the banking crisis. Since then, profitability and profitability have been in good shape in the banking sector. At times, the results are even excellent Figure: Operating profit (loss) of Finnish banking, credit losses and valuation discounts 19802005 The banking crisis of 19911994 forced drastic efficiency improvements and permanently restructured the Finnish banking structure. The structures of the Finnish and Nordic financial sector are completely different and more international today than they were 10 years ago. New banking groups and groups have emerged rapidly. In recent years, new banks have been established in Finland and more foreign parties have entered the market. This can be seen as a sign that the banking and financial sector is looking to the future. The financial industry is currently a very profitable industry. The productivity of the financial sector has grown strongly in recent years, which has had a major positive impact on the national economy. Businesses and households have benefited from an environment in which Economic and Monetary Union has created low and stable interest rates and where good productivity developments in the banking sector have allowed for fierce competition.  Network of services of banks and the Internet. Just over 10 years ago, bank branches played a significant role in ordinary banking and payment transactions. Since then, the nature of the branches has changed to a very different one. Today, they are more like service and counselling centres than places for day-to-day financial management. Telephone and especially online services have taken their place. 1(6) 10 years ago, internet banking was just beginning. Today, no bank can do without functional and high-quality online banking services. The change has been profound and irreversible. The exploitation of new technologies and the Internet has given banks huge opportunities to become more efficient and better. It can be said that the banking sector was able to take advantage of the opportunities brought about by technological progress. This can be seen, for example, in the change in the nature of bank payment intermediation, where the machine-readability rate is currently 95%. Graph: Domestic bank payment intermediation 1986-2005  Customers. In Finland, customers have embraced the use of new banking technology well. The nature of banking transactions today is quite different from that of 10 years ago, for example in terms of payment methods. In addition, ordinary bank customers are more affluent. A wide range of services related to prosperity and prosperity are now an essential part of Finnish banking. As recently as 10 years ago, for example, regular fund investing was very small-scale and concerned only a small part of the customer. In the long term, the financial assets of Finnish households have changed considerably structurally Graph: Households' financial assets in Finland 19902005 2. Rahoitustoimialan muutostekijat On a more general level, the financial industry everywhere is shaped by a few drivers of change, perhaps the most important of which is technological progress and the transformation of information technology. It changes the nature of the activity permanently. New business opportunities are opening up and things can be done more efficiently than before. The pace of technological progress is not slowing down, but accelerating. So the change is accelerating. Title: At Bank of Spain -conference
text: Governor Erkki Liikanen at Bank of Spain -conference . Speech . Thursday8 June 2006,12:00 AM INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCE "CENTRAL BANKS IN THE 21ST CENTURY" HOSTED BY THE BANCO DE ESPANA IN MADRID COMMENTS ON oFINANCIAL STABILITY AND GLOBALISATION: GETTING IT RIGHTo BY F. MISHKIN (PAPER FOR A BANK OF SPAIN CONFERENCE, 8-9 JUNE 2006) On the paper Professor Frederic Mishkin provides a very insightful and comprehensive paper on potential pitfalls in financial liberalization and globalization, and discusses policy responses to well-manage such a transition both macro (monetary, fiscal and trade policies) and microeconomic (legal system, corporate governance, information disclosure, financial supervision). On these policies, there is both a balanced account of the literature and some recommendations in the paper. The paper mostly deals with developing countries. While liberalization and globalization are needed for supporting financial deepening, an almost immediate consequence in several countries was a period of severe financial instability or a full-blown financial crisis. The high cost of these crises makes their prevention and effective resolution a policy priority. oAnatomyo of crises since early 1980s There is striking amount similarity in the past crises, even though details of the crises may differ. Most of the financial crises experienced since the early 1980s followed a fairly standard pattern of deregulation, lending boom, asset price booms, business cycle and asset price shocks, and large-scale bank failures, and eventually a financial crisis . Crisis was usually triggered by an external shock (e.g. unforeseen recession or ex-change rate collapse). Crisis resolution was often similar as well. Insolvent banks were either temporarily nationalized or forcibly merged, after separating obad loanso in a state agency. In some cases, a blanket government guarantee was also given that all financial institutions would meet their obligations. Examples of similar crises include the crises in Latin America (Argentina, Mexico in early 1980s), the US Savings and loans institutionso crisis (early 1980s), and the three Scandinavian banking crises (Norway, Finland, Sweden in early 1990s). The crises in merging market economies in late 1990s (Korea, Philippines etc.) also reflected the same pattern, by and large. The Finnish crisis fits well with the major source of instability highlighted in the paper: the danger of accumulating indebtedness in foreign currencies and the resulting currency mismatches in the closed sectors of the economy. Once the Finnish currency depreciated heavily after its flotation, many firms could no longer repay their debt and bankso ac-crued vast amount of credit losses. Four viewpoints for discussion The points below are suggested as complements to the paper not necessarily as points of disagreement (even though these elements are missing or hidden in the paper): Financial globalization raises difficult issues related to supervision and crisis management of cross-border and cross-sector financial institutions Focus also on the quality of supervision by developing risk-based approaches (not only on the institutional framework); Avoid rigid policy solutions (one-size-fits-all) for countries with different circumstances; The next crisis could result from different risks and require different preventive or resolution measures. We should be prepared to prevent and handle future crises not the past ones. 1. Financial globalization raises difficult issues related to supervision and crisis management of cross-border and cross-sector financialinstitutions The paper argues, rightly, that opening up the domestic markets to foreign financial institutions may promote higher-quality domestic regulation and supervision by, inter alia, putting pressure on the domestic government to make reforms that will make the financial system work more efficiently. However, as is well-known, big market shares of foreign-owned banks in many small countries create potential problems for both prudential financial supervision and the maintenance of financial stability in those countries. One of the key issues in the international regulatory debate is how to divide the tasks, powers, and responsibility between different countries in supervising cross-border financial institutions and dealing with these institutions in financial distress. In the EU, the di-vision of tasks, powers, and responsibilities is currently based on home-country control. The home country is responsible for supervising financial institutions that are headquartered in that country and its foreign branches. Foreign subsidiaries, on the other hand, are supervised by the host country supervisor. The home country supervisor, in addition, is responsible for the consolidated supervision of the financial group. Today, financial institutions cross-border and cross-sector activities are increasing at fast speed. Currently, for example, there are at least over 40 banks and banking groups that are active in more than three EU countries. In addition, financial institutions increasingly work along global business lines and less along national borders. For financial groups which are expanding cross-border a part of synergies is derived from centralizing functions along business lines, not necessarily along country borders. Concerning the legal form of banks foreign operations, the relative importance of banks foreign branches (as opposed to that of foreign subsidiaries) is likely to increase substantially as banks start to take advantage of the European Company Statute and operate as a single entity. As illustrated by these changes, the current and future European banking market is very different from that in which role of banks cross-border and cross-sector operations and banks foreign branches was negligible. The problem of the current set-up is the gap, on the other hand, between the legal powers and mandates and, on the other hand, the abilities and responsibilities of the home and host supervisors. This gap becomes a problem once there is a financial institution that is systemically relevant in a host country. The problems are starkest in the event of a crisis in the banking group, as all national authorities have a clear mandate to protect only their depositors and systems. In particular, if the institutions presence in the host country is a branch, it is the home country supervisor who is responsible for managing a crisis. Although the branch can systemically important in the host country, all its authorities can, to put it bluntly, do is to hope that the home country authorities take the interests of host country into account when dealing with the crisis. It is clear that because of integration, the EUs current regulatory set-up will be under increasing pressure in the future. Therefore, it is not a surprise that various alternative models to the current home-host set-up have been presented. The alternatives range from considerably strengthening the role of the home supervisor (lead supervisor model) to creating a European Financial Supervisor with full supervisory powers over branches and subsidiaries of cross-border banks. However, despite the pressures, the EU is likely for the time being to stick to the current European supervisory principles and structures and try to improve the functioning of the current regime by, inter alia, increasing supervisory cooperation and convergence of supervisory methods. A thorough discussion of the European supervisory arrangements would require a sepa-rate presentation. In this context, it might be sufficient to say that the financial globalization raises very challenging issues related to the supervision of cross-border and cross-sector financial institutions. These issues, in addition to those presented in Mishkins paper, should be addressed in any regulatory reform agendas. 2. Focus also on the quality of supervision bydeveloping risk-based approaches An appropriate institutional framework (deposit insurance, disclosure regime, property rights, independence and accountability of supervisors etc.) is clearly a prerequisite for well-managing liberalization and preventing crises. However, one of the biggest lessons from the crises (also from the Finnish one) is that bankso risk management and supervisory practices were not yet developed enough to address the risks in the new environment. This resulted in uncontrolled risk taking by banks as such risk taking was made possible by the liberalization. Mishkin discusses as a central issue the need to put in place proper institutional setting (foremost supervision) before liberalization, but does not spend space on the issue of the quality of supervision. Before the crises, supervision was (and can still sometimes be) mostly legalistic checking of compliance with current regulations, rather than focused on risks. But risk-based supervision is at the core of having preventive (i.e. forward.looking) supervision rather than responding to problems when it is already too late. This is an issue of both supervisory culture and resources (a large enough number of qualified risk analysts working as supervisors). What is needed is a systematic plan to develop risk-based supervision, which one should acknowledge takes many years to institute in a supervisory authority. Even developed countries have further efforts to make in this area. A key element of such a plan is to put emphasis on institutionso own risk management, as risks are getting so complex and fast moving that they cannot be observed real-time by supervisors, or prevented through simple supervisory limits. Independent supervisory as-sessment is needed to prevent moral hazard and to avoid problem institutions from shifting risk to the government. Basel II reform supports this development by instituting a regular supervisory risk review (which is the second Pillar of the Basel package). 3. Avoid rigid solutions (one-size-fits-all) for all countries Policy measures need to be adjusted to individual countrieso circumstances (economic structures and development stage, financial system structure, political systems etc). While lessons on policy mistakes from the crises can be (reasonably) clear, this does not mean that a simple recipe can prevent future crises, or represent otherwise suitable policy options in all circumstances. The paper does not advocate uniform solutions very strongly; in general it is quite balanced. It only has this flavor at instances. Some examples are below. (International institutions (IMF, World Bank) can have a stronger tendency for one-size-fits-all recommen-dations). Floating exchange rates (recommended with caveats in the paper) can be more stabilizing than fixed and allow using monetary policy to cool down fast credit growth. However, a currency board could be a good option for oimportingo monetary policy and bringing down inflation. Deposit insurance is often recommended (by World Bank, IMF and in the paper) to be avoided, at least by less institutionally developed countries because of moral hazard and increased risk taking by banks. However, deposit insurance can be a commitment device for governments to rescue only depositors and not other creditors of banks, and thus to support market discipline. Without deposit insurance the true policy adopted in a crisis can be a blanket guarantee for all bank creditors. Market discipline is only possible when some creditors have their money at stake (with some positive ex ante probability) in a crisis. Disclosure of information is needed, but it does not generate market discipline unless the previous condition is met. Hence, explicit and limited deposit insurance explicitly protecting depositors only and leaving out other creditors could be a step forward especially in a country (like Scandi-navian countries in late 1980s / early 90s) with a history of blanked guarantees and weak market discipline. Explicit deposit insurance also needs to be coupled with ef-fective supervision to cub any moral hazard effects. Stringent (and simple?) regulatory capital requirements are recommended (in the paper) for banks in less developed countries. However, a large and simple require-ment (such as a leverage ratio) would not support the development of bankso own risk management and ability to function in a liberalized environment as it is not risk-based. On the other hand, advanced aspects of the highly risk-based Basel II may not be feasible due to lack of expertise and data in banks, but nothing prevents from gradually moving towards a more flexible and risk-based approach in less developed countries (where Basel II is not obligatory and its timing is not pre-specified like in Europe). One could implement e.g. the standard Basel II model for sovereign and bank counterparties based on external ratings and thus avoid the present low risk weight on government bonds under Basel I. Advanced methods for calculating capital charges for firms and households could and should be adopted only over time with more experience in banks and the supervisory authority. Limiting currency mismatches (recommended in the paper) in closed sectors of the economy would only be feasible by limiting foreign currency-denominated borrow-ing. This would be canceling liberalization, actually, so other indirect measures should probably be considered. What those measures could be will depend on the local tax system (possibility to use taxes to curb lending growth), monetary policy etc. This is an actual issue for many New Members States of the EU with high credit growth, often in foreign currencies. 4. The next crisis could result from different risks and require different preventive or resolution measures The past crises were mainly due to credit risk and were national in scope. While credit risk often still is the most important risk for banks, the structure of the financial system has been changing in a profound way and the next crisis could come from a different source. First, a rapid increase in bankso and other financial institutionso (e.g. insurance companies and pension funds) financial market-related activities has increased their exposure to financial markets (and counterparty risks to other market players) and earnings sensitivity, suggesting that financial instability may increasingly result from market instability. This refers to equity, bond and derivative markets as distinguished from more traditional exposures of banks to real estate price and exchange rate movements. Second, the past separation between financial institutions and markets has been replaced by an increasing integration of markets and banks, as well as between banks and other financial institutions. Hence, systemic risks could result from non-bank financial institutions (such as hedge funds, private equity funds etc.), at least to the extent that major financial institutions are exposed to them. Third, liquidity conditions and contagion risks play an increasingly important role due to the rapid increase in financial marketso activities and bankso increased reliance on market sources of funds. Fourth, internationalization of the financial system has spread rapidly. Capital controls and restrictions on cross. border bank operations have largely been eliminated. National markets can no longer be viewed as isolated entities, but tend to be embedded in a complex system of interlinks. This holds true especially for EU countries due to the Single Market and spreading of cross-border banking, but also globally and for many developing countries as well, because in their financial systems international banking groups can play an important role. In New EU Members States the ownership of foreign banks in the local banking system is 70-100%. Policies and measures taken to foster financial stability must take into account these developments in case of both developed and developing economies . Failure to upgrade policies to mach financial system developments can be very costly as the previous lessons show.

Title: Reform of the European payment system  SEPA
text: Director-General Erkki Liikanen: Reform of the European payment system  SEPA . Speech . Tuesday 28 November 2006, 12:00 AM REFORM OF THE EUROPEAN PAYMENT SYSTEM  SEPA Director-General Erkki Liikanen Presentation by the Finnish Commerce Federation 28.11.2006 Speech associated kalvosarja (/globalassets/NR/rdonlyres/6988501F-F610-4E70-9929. AAF0D70ACAF1/0/061128ELKaupanL.ppt) (Slide 1) I have been to the events of the predecessors of the Finnish Trade Association often. Once, as an ambassador, I introduced eu membership. For the second time, as Commissioner, I spoke about Economic and Monetary Union and the introduction of the euro. Today it is a pleasure to talk again about a major European project, which is linked to my current role at the Bank of Finland and is again very important for trade. The Single European Payments Area (SEPA) is a project to increase the benefits of integration in payment transactions. Background to integration(slide 2) A key objective of the EU is an effectively functioning single market that promotes growth, employment and consumer welfare. Goods are already moving smoothly within the Union and people are already moving around, despite the occasional difficulties. There are still many obstacles to the movement of services and payments. Economic and monetary union and the euro, the common means of payment, have been important steps towards integration. Common legislation has also been used to promote the integration of financial markets. Progress has certainly been made, but securities trading and clearing, retail banking and retail payments are still handled in a fragmented manner and often at high costs. Tasks of the Bank of Finland today (slide 3) One of the bank's core tasks is to contribute to the decision-making of the single monetary policy of the euro area. Influencing it requires high-quality research and research. On the other hand, the Bank is responsible for the stability and reliability of financial markets and promotes the efficiency of financial markets. Thirdly, the Bank of Finland acts as a bank for banks with the task of safeguarding the liquidity of the banking system, brokering large payments between banks and investing financial assets (including foreign exchange reserves). And the fourth task is money supply, responsibility for the issuance of banknotes and coins in Finland. The Bank of Finland's task is to safeguard the condition and authenticity of the cash. The Bank of Finland manages the money supply in cooperation with banks and companies specialising in money supply. Role of financial market supervision (Slide 4) Promoting the stability and efficiency of financial markets is one of the key tasks of the Central Bank. The Bank of Finland is responsible for the oversight of the financial and payment system as a whole. The Financial Supervisory Authority, which is independent but operates in conjunction with the Bank of Finland, in turn supervises companies operating in the financial markets, such as banks. Financial market surveillance aims to prevent crises from occurring. But it also has a responsibility for crisis management capabilities in the event of serious disturbances in the financial markets. The stability of financial markets is promoted through the highest possible level of analysis and evaluation. Oversight of financial markets is carried out in cooperation with the Eurosystem and other EU countries. This cooperation will become more important as integration progresses. The integration of financial markets increases the efficiency of the internal market and supports economic growth. That is why the Bank of Finland supports the creation of a common and efficient financial market. At the same time, we want to work towards the wider use of digitalised services that we have found to be effective in the euro area and the EU. What is SEPA(Slide 5) Effective payment transactions are oil in the wheels of the economy, as the European Commission says. One of the company's financial managers has said that it takes as much time to process a few foreign payments as it does to handle a multiplically larger domestic payment transaction. Why, then, is it so much more difficult to pay across borders than, say, sending a mobile phone call or text message? After all, both data flows digitally. The reasons can be found in the different laws and trade barriers of countries. In addition, the standardisation work is ongoing and the systems are not compatible. Intra-European trade can be made more efficient and simplified by creating harmonised payment systems. Payments must be handled in the same way, with standardised systems throughout Europe. In this way, payment services can also be put out to tender. Creating a SEPA is a process(Slide 6) Creating a unified payment area is a long process. The 2001 Euro Payments Regulation stipulated that payments denominated in euro, within Europe, up to a maximum of EUR 50,000 may be charged at the same price as similar domestic payments. The decision was made through a legislative route. The European Commission no longer relied on voluntary progress. The banks then decided to speed up the integration process on their own initiative. The intention, apparently, was that in the future more progress could be made on the so-called 'green card'. the path of softer regulation. The banking sector joined forces to form the European Payments Council (EPC). And the Payments Council then announced a project to create a single euro payments area, or SEPA. Sepa as an area comprises the European Union as well as Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein and Switzerland. It concerns payments denominated in euros, which is why the emphasis is on the euro area. But the rules of the directives apply to all EU countries, regardless of currency. The EEA countries and Switzerland have announced their accession to SEPA. This requires them to amend their national legislation accordingly. The Commission's proposal for a directive on payment services supports the creation of SEPA by harmonising the conditions for payment intermediation. It would eliminate surprises related to delivery times or fees or complaints for cross-border payments. During its Presidency of the Council of the EU, Finland has strongly promoted the proposal for a directive. The directive would create the necessary legislative framework for the implementation of SEPA. The Commission's objective is to create a single payment area that makes effective use of information technology and supports Europe's economic development. This year, the Commission has submitted a consultation document for the opinions. It stresses that voluntary progression is a priority. But if there is no progress, the Commission will, if necessary, exercise its right of initiative by means of legislation. Common European payment methods (Slide 7) In the common payment area of SEPA, payments will be made by means of uniform credit transfers, direct debits and payment cards. These are services that we are familiar with in themselves. Transparent standards will be created for payment methods and the payment intermediation infrastructure will be obliged to use these standards. The benefits of uniform standards that are open to Finns are clear, but in the rest of Europe the reform is very significant. There is no limit on the amount of the fee. After all, there has been a limit of EUR 50,000 in the Euro Payments Regulation. SEPA schedule (slide 8) According to the schedule, in 2008, the basic services, i.e. credit transfer and direct debit, will be in use. The aim is that the majority of European payments, whether within the borders of one country or from one country to another, should use these common payment methods by 2010. As for card payments, the standards will not be ready until the beginning of 2008. A uniform way of paying with a card in the terminal, and the possibility of transmitting card payment transactions through competitive tendering to the selected refunder of transactions, is unlikely to become a reality until closer to 2010. These schedules must be taken into account in the investment and upgrade plans for the systems in the coming years. Trade plays a key role (Slide 9) Trade is the industry with the highest inputs in the development of SEPA. It is a large user of payment services in all respects; in the case of credit transfers, recurring payments and card payments. This can be seen in the figures on the film, which are based on the statistics of the Banking Association and the enlightened estimates of the Finnish Commerce Federation and the Bank of Finland. That is why it is valuable that it is the Finnish Trade Association that has organised this presentation event in the maksujarjestelmauudistuksesta. Trade plays an important role in the development of both the economy and employment. Retail and wholesale trade account for 11.5% of the value added of the euro area economy as a whole. It is very important how trade reap the benefits of the Single Euro Payments Area. What's changing  there are plenty of challenges(Slide 10) Payment practices vary across Europe and are not easy to reconcile. We Finns consider ourselves  and rightly so  to be progressive and modern payers when we utilise cards, internet services and automate the operations of companies. SEPA represents a major step forward for the vast majority of Europe. We're probably well into the 2010s before everyone has given up their checks, or even started using payment services. Similarly, it takes time for all the services in the common payment area to meet the requirements of modern, automated financial management. The work will not end even in 2010, but streamlining and integrating payment transactions into financial management processes is constantly looking for innovations and new, more efficient solutions. The Bank of Finland strives to ensure that a common payment area does not mean a deterioration in existing services anywhere. The ECB and the European Commission have taken our position on this: they also believe that SEPA must not mean a lower level of service or an increase in prices for anyone. What will change with SEPA? (Slide 11) So what will change? The goal is for one bank account in Europe to suffice  cash management and liquidity management should consider how they can benefit from this. When payments are made in the same way and the terms of payment intermediation are uniform, any customer can put payment service providers out to tender on the same line. Increasing competition challenges service providers to make their production more efficient, which is reflected in lower prices for customers  a logic that is familiar to trade. That is what has always been demanded of the trade. Now commerce should benefit from the same increase in competition in its payment transactions. There will be uniform standards for payments. They make it possible to automate financial management for all European payments A common standard for card payments is being prepared. This means that the functions of the payment terminal will be harmonised. Stores are at the best time switching to EMV chip cards. reading terminals. Sepa's card standard is based on EMV, and the upcoming SEPA change will certainly be much easier to implement as a device upgrade. The payment terminal forms a record of each payment transaction, which is sent to the party crediting the transactions, usually the merchant's bank or Credit Union in Finland for further processing. This content of the transaction record, i.e. the terminal message, is also standardized. This means that commerce is free to compete for the refund of card transactions at European level. According to many studies, Finnish card payment fees are among the lowest in Europe, so this will perhaps bring a greater competitive advantage to Finnish creditors of card transactions than to trade. Heikki Kapanen will probably talk more about this in his speech. The retailer has been concerned about the internationalisation of cards used in Finland, as Finnish banks have announced that they will abandon bank cards. The first cards belonging to international card brands, which are attached directly to a bank account, are already in the hands of customers. The bank card has been very affordable for both retailers and consumers. If the cost of card payments is to increase, card issuers and creditors must be prepared to justify clearly and transparently the basis on which this can happen. The clear political message from both the European Commission and the European Central Bank is that the switch to SEPA payments must not reduce the level of service, nor must it increase the prices of existing or equivalent SEPA services. At the same time, efforts have been made to promote the cost-reflectiveness of prices. There are still challenges(Slide 12) Standardisation has got off to a good start. But things familiar to Finns in all parts are not yet included. E.g. the reference in its current form is essential for automatic payment recording. It can continue to be used, but checking the correctness of the reference may remain a domestic additional service. The future of recurring payments used in the payment of wages is still open. Finnish banks are expected to announce in the near future how this will be implemented. In addition, electronic invoices have not yet been included in SEPA's standards. On the positive side, however, EPC has set up a working group to prepare e-and-m payments. This has also always been the will of the Commission and the ECB. Implementation of SEPA(Slide 13) There is a clear division of labour in the implementation of SEPA: Policymakers have set a target at European level and are following developments closely. The Bank of Finland, in cooperation with the European Central Bank, is actively involved in this monitoring. The european payments council, the cooperation organisation of the banks, has the responsibility for implementation at European level. Nationally, every bank is committed to complying with the SEPA plan. The role of system vendors is also important. They are responsible for implementing the new SEPA payment methods into the systems in such a way that daily payment transactions run smoothly. In addition to banks, system suppliers are important partners for trade in the implementation of SEPA. Sepa's stakeholders will ultimately be all European retail payment parties, businesses, the public sector and individuals. Trade plays a key role in this as a whole. That is why it is so important for trade to be active in the introduction and exploitation of a single payment area.

Title: Finland, EMU och euron, Stockholm
text: Chefdirekt9ar Erkki Liikanen: "Finland, EMU och euro", Stockholm . Speech . Tuesday 23January 2007, 12:00 AM Chefdirekt9ar Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland The Network Meeting Point Swedish-speaking Finland Stockholm 23.1.2007 FINLAND, EMU AND THE EURO Before Finland joined EMU in 1999, there was a lively and intense discussion about the pros and cons of joining as well as sweden. The benefits of economic efficiency were recognised, such as reduced exchange rate uncertainty, lower foreign exchange costs, more comparable prices, increased competition and a more efficient money and other financial markets. But opinions differed sharply on the impact on economic stability. Some were convinced that EMU and the single monetary policy would contribute to a more credible monetary policy. If a lack of credibility for monetary policy was the cause of the traditional Finnish problems of inflationary pressures and declining competitiveness, price stability and competitiveness could be improved in EMU. It also envisaged more stable and average lower interest rates in monetary union than under conditions of an independent monetary policy. But a lot of interest was devoted to the so-called asymmetry of the Finnish economy. While macroeconomic developments were broadly uniform in the EU's core countries of Germany, France and benelux, in Finland it went in a different direction. Economic cycles shifted at a different pace and fluctuations were deeper in Finland than in other countries. Similar features also characterized Sweden, albeit to a lesser extent. As common policies would be adapted to the economic cycles of the euro area as a whole, it was feared that the direction might be inappropriate or even very inappropriate for the Finnish economy. The following reasons were given for the asymmetry towards the other euro area countries: Production and exports in Finland were concentrated in a small group of industries. The paper and pulp industry still accounted for the lion's share. These industries are sensitive to the economic cycle in terms of both prices and volumes. During the 1990s, the ICT industry grew rapidly, largely driven by the success of a single company, Nokia. The Finnish economy thus became vulnerable to developments in the telecom sector, but at the time of the asymmetry debate, one could not realize the extent of it. One-third of exports went to the euro area, which made Finland vulnerable to disruptions from other countries as well. In particular, the concerns related to exchange rate movements: it was feared that the movements of the US dollar and other currencies against the euro would have a strong impact on the competitiveness of Finnish production. The traditional method of countering competition problems, i.e. devaluation, would no longer be possible in monetary union. For the opponents of EMU, this was the heaviest argument, especially if our important trading partners Sweden and the United Kingdom chose to stay outside the currency union and possibly also outside the exchange rate mechanism ERM2, which later turned out to be the case. Fears of asymmetric shocks were reinforced by the still fresh memory of the unusually deep economic and financial crisis of the early 1990s. The crisis, which was deeper in Finland than in Sweden, was preceded by a boom in the late 1980s partly driven by financial deregulation. The collapse of trade with the Soviet Union, rising interest rates in Europe and the problems of a fixed exchange rate regime paved the way for a depression and banking crisis. Behind the final choice to join the ERM and participate in EMU lay economic and political reasons. It was believed that the benefits of monetary union in terms of economic efficiency and a credible monetary policy would outweigh the costs and loss of an independent monetary policy. But the political motives were at least as important as the economic ones. Finland wanted to sit at all the tables where decisions are made and participate in the "inner circle", if such a club emerged within the EU. In Finland, too, the decision was not easy. For a long time, there was uncertainty about what kind of eu countries would switch to the euro, and in some circles there were doubts about whether EMU would be achieved at all. Our Nordic neighbors chose to remain outside. And at first, public opinion in Finland was clearly opposed to participation. In the autumn of 1996, the majority, 62 percent, were against and only 29 percent in favor. During the discussion and after the government declared its position and parliament sanctioned participation, support for the euro began to increase. In 2001, it was up to 72 percent. Finland's experience of EMU We now have over eight years' experience of monetary union. Interestingly, many of the asymmetric shocks feared by opponents of the euro have already materialised in this relatively short period of time. Our ICT industry experienced strong economic fluctuations (boomd0bust cycle) at the turn of the century as well as in the Swedish one. The ICT-dominated index of the Helsinki Stock Exchange fluctuated more than the corresponding index elsewhere. In Finland, the economic downturn was reflected in growth expectations and asset prices rather than output volumes. The euro's exchange rate against the dollar first fell by close to 30 percent and then rose by 50 percent. Furthermore, the price of oil has multiplied during the existence of the euro. Contrary to the fears of opponents of EMU, neither the positive external shock at the turn of the century nor the initial euro weakening have plunged the Finnish economy into any inflation spiral. The economy has weathered the ICT recession and the large fluctuations of the euro quite painlessly. The Finnish inflation rate, which stabilised in the pre-EMU period through an inflation targeting policy, has been broadly equivalent to the EMU average since 1999. Since 2000, inflation has remained mostly at a level that falls within the ECB's definition of price stability. In recent years, inflation in Finland, as well as in Sweden, has actually been among the lowest in the entire EU. Finland's GDP growth has fluctuated more or less in line with that of the euro area, but average growth has been around one percentage point higher in Finland than in the euro area. Factors behind Finland's macroeconomic development Finland's economic development reflects both cyclical and structural factors. Growth has normalised after the 1990s crisis and the recovery effects were still visible in output growth in the first years of EMU. Unfortunately, unemployment remains relatively high, although it is now far from the record figures of the early 1990s. In recent years, demand has grown rapidly outside the euro area, and the open economy has benefited the export industry and the entire Finnish economy. At the same time, global competition and output growth have dampened increases in the prices of exported industrial goods and imported goods, thereby also dampening inflationary pressures from strong demand. Inflation targets and successful fiscal consolidation combined with Finland's accession to the EU in 1995 contributed to low inflation becoming something obvious and acceptable even before the start of EMU. Factors such as a clear nominal anchor for inflation expectations and increased competition in product markets have contributed to profound changes in price and wage formation and enabled relatively rapid growth without inflation. But I can perhaps mention three contributing factors that explain an important part of the positive growth trend over the last ten years. First, since the 1980s, policymakers have consistently pledged to promote an innovation-driven economy. Research and development expenditure in Finland accounts for 3.5 per cent of GDP, which is highest in Europe besides Sweden and on a par with the United States. An important part of the research has focused on ICT. Finland and Finnish companies have always participated actively in EU research programmes. Secondly, free trade and liberalised markets are a prerequisite for growth in a small country. Without free trade, no companies of any great stature are created and only a competitive domestic market enables innovation. The crisis of the 1990s contributed to the realization that reforms were needed. Various coalition governments have sought to maintain a business-friendly climate. The liberalisation of the capital market and rapidly increasing risk finance stimulated growth, the diversification and internationalisation of the ICT sector, and the whole economy. The third factor that has contributed to the development in Finland is the emergence of the ICT industry. Deregulation and open standards supported rapid development in the telecoms industry and services. This accelerated productivity growth in Finland. The same applies to Sweden. I would also like to draw attention to the changes in the banking sector. After the crisis of the 1990s, the banking sector was capital restructured. The number of employees and offices was halved. The productivity of the banking sector also increased thanks to increased competition and the use of new information technologies and Internet services. This contributed to Finland's economic growth. A few words about the education Innovation-driven development has required the interaction of several fundamental factors, such as an effective education system, a consistent and predictable policy environment and sound basic infrastructure. Most of these conditions were met even before the 1990s. Our school system has been reflected in the OECD PISA survey of 15-year-olds' knowledge and skills (Programme for International Student Assessments). Finland's top rankings in the surveys have often been used as examples of results that can be achieved with both equal and high-quality teaching. The supply of graduates in science and technology has fostered innovation but at the same time helped to keep the salaries of researchers and engineers in ICT clusters moderate despite high demand. Strong exchange balance and international portfolio diversification ICT growth is reflected in the current account, which has been in surplus since 1994. Large surpluses are a marked difference from the past. Current account surpluses are not only the result of a competitive open sector and strong export growth, but also reflect rather weak growth in domestic demand after the 1990s crisis. The corporate sector adopted a more prudent investment strategy by reducing its debt exposure and increasing its Buffer Stock. The general government sector has been in surplus for several years. As a result of the international diversification of investors' portfolios, the holdings of foreigners on the Helsinki Stock Exchange increased to just over 70 per cent of the total market capitalisation in 2000. The exposures of the Finnish economy in the ICT price bubble at the turn of the century decreased, as the ownership risk was mostly borne by foreign investors. Fiscal policy under control After the crisis of the 1990s, there was a clear need for an economic policy compatible with the free movement of capital across national borders. Broad support has been developed for stability-oriented fiscal policies as a basis for longer-term stable economic development. Fiscal policy has been effectively based on explicit guidelines such as spending limits over the entire parliamentary term and, in line with this, public finances have been consolidated. As a result of fiscal policy, the general government sector is running a surplus. The surplus is 2-3% and is expected to remain at that level. Risks and challenges Of course, everything does not look bright. Lurking on the horizon are major risks and economic policy challenges. I will mention two here. One concern is the terms of trade, which has deteriorated in recent years and, according to forecasts, continues to deteriorate. The prices of ICT products are falling globally as a result of technological developments and increased competition. Price development in the forest industry has also been rather weak. The challenge is to keep productivity growth high and increase value added in exports. Another concern is fiscal policy as the population ages faster in Finland than in other industrialized countries including Sweden. The reason is the large cohorts from 1945d050. Expenditure on public services and pensions is increasing, while the scope for financing additional expenditure is becoming more limited. We are thus faced with the great challenge of improving the productivity of public services. Conclusion All in all, Finland's EMU membership in the early years seems to have fulfilled most of the promises and avoided most of the risks. The benefits were, as expected, an efficient economy and a credible monetary policy, and there is no indication that macroeconomic stability would have deteriorated, quite the contrary. Finally, a few words on the effects of EMU on central bank work: For the Bank of Finland, the new institutional the surroundings were almost transformative. As part of the Eurosystem, the Bank of Finland is now part of the world's second largest central banking system, which policies vis-88-vis the world's second-largest currency. Alongside this, the Bank continues to function as finland's national central bank. For the Governor, this means full membership of the Governing Council and participation in the ECB's key decision-making together with d0 since the turn of the year d0 twelve other national managers and the ECB's full-time Executive Board. This provides insight into and responsibility for European as well as for global issues in a completely different way than we have become accustomed to in Finland. Those of us who sit in the Council all have a voice in deciding on monetary policy and other policy issues. For me personally, EMU means in practice biweekly Council meetings in Frankfurt and, for a large group of Bank of Finland officials, regular trips to committee meetings in Frankfurt in the same way that their colleagues from the Ministry of Finance and other ministries in Finland d0 as well as in Sweden d0 travel to Brussels. But it's still more a matter of substance than travel. Therefore, we, a small central bank, have chosen to invest in research, analysis and assessment. Only in this way can we create as good a basis as possible in the preparation of decision-making in the Council as well as for our other activities in the Eurosystem.

Tuesday 23January 2007, 12:00 AM Chefdirekt<9a>r Erkki Liikanen Finlands Bank N<8a>tverket Tr<8a>ffpunkt Svenskfinland Stockholm 23.1.2007 FINLAND, EMU OCH EURON Innan Finland gick med i EMU <8c>r 1999 f<9a>rdes en livlig och intensiv diskussion om f<9a>r-och nackdelarna med ett intr<8a>de liksom ocks<8c> i Sverige. Men <8c>sikterna gick kraftigt is<8a>r om effekterna p<8c> den ekonomiska stabiliteten. En del var <9a>vertygade om att EMU och den gemensamma penningpolitiken skulle bidra till en trov<8a>rdigare penningpolitik. Om bristande trov<8a>rdighet f<9a>r penningpolitiken var orsaken till de traditionella finska problemen med inflationstryck och avtagande konkurrenskraft, kunde prisstabiliteten och konkurrenskraften f<9a>rb<8a>ttras i EMU. Man r<8a>knade ocks<8c> med stabilare och genomsnittligt l<8a>gre r<8a>ntor i valutaunionen <8a>n under f<9a>rh<8c>llanden med en sj<8a>lvst<8a>ndig penningpolitik. Men mycket intresse <8a>gnades den s<8c> kallade asymmetrin i den finska ekonomin. Medan den makroekonomiska utvecklingen var i stort sett likriktad i EU:s k<8a>rnl<8a>nder Tyskland, Frankrike och Benelux, gick den i Finland i en annan riktning. Konjunkturerna v<8a>xlade i en annan takt och sv<8a>ngningarna var djupare i Finland <8a>n i andra l<8a>nder. Liknande drag k<8a>nnetecknade ocks<8c> Sverige om <8a>n i mindre omfattning. Eftersom den gemensamma politiken skulle anpassas efter konjunkturerna i hela euroomr<8c>det, befarade man att inriktningen kunde bli ol<8a>mplig eller rent av mycket ol<8a>mplig f<9a>r den finska ekonomin. F<9a>ljande sk<8a>l angavs f<9a>r asymmetrin mot de andra eurol<8a>nderna: Produktionen och exporten i Finland var koncentrerade till en liten grupp industrier. Pappers-och massaindustrin stod fortfarande f<9a>r lejonparten. Dessa industrier <8a>r konjunkturk<8a>nsliga i fr<8c>ga om b<8c>de priser och volymer. Under 1990-talet v<8a>xte IKT-industrin snabbt, till stor del p<8c>driven av framg<8c>ngarna i ett enda f<9a>retag, Nokia. Den finska ekonomin blev d<8a>rigenom s<8c>rbar f<9a>r utvecklingen i telekomsektorn, men vid tiden f<9a>r asymmetridebatten kunde man inte inse vidden av det. En tredjedel av exporten gick till euroomr<8c>det, vilket gjorde Finland s<8c>rbart <8a>ven f<9a>r st<9a>rningar fr<8c>n andra l<8a>nder. S<8a>rskilt g<8a>llde oron v<8a>xelkursr<9a>relserna: man befarade att US-dollarns och andra valutors r<9a>relser mot euron skulle ha en kraftig inverkan p<8c> den finska produktionens konkurrenskraft. Den traditionella metoden att motverka konkurrensproblem, det vill s<8a>ga devalvering, skulle inte l<8a>ngre g<8c> att tillgripa i valutaunionen. F<9a>r EMU-motst<8c>ndarna var det h<8a>r det tyngsta argumentet, framf<9a>r allt om v<8c>ra viktiga handelspartner Sverige och Storbritannien valde att stanna utanf<9a>r valutaunionen och m<9a>jligen ocks<8c> utanf<9a>r v<8a>xelkursmekanismen ERM2, vilket senare visade sig vara fallet. Bakom det slutliga valet att intr<8a>da i ERM och delta i EMU l<8c>g dels ekonomiska och dels politiska sk<8a>l. Man trodde att f<9a>rdelarna med valutaunionen i form av ekonomisk effektivitet och en trov<8a>rdig penningpolitik skulle motv<8a>ga kostnaderna och f<9a>rlusten av en sj<8a>lvst<8a>ndig penningpolitik. Men de politiska motiven var minst lika viktiga som de ekonomiska. Finland ville sitta vid alla bord d<8a>r beslut fattas och delta i den <d3>inre kretsen<d3>, om en s<8c>dan klubb uppstod inom EU. Inte heller i Finland var beslutet l<8a>tt. Det r<8c>dde l<8a>nge os<8a>kerhet om en hurudan samling av EU-l<8a>nder som skulle <9a>verg<8c> till euron och i vissa kretsar nyste man tvivel om huruvida EMU <9a>verhuvudtaget f<9a>rverkligas. V<8c>ra nordiska grannar valde att st<8c> utanf<9a>r. Och till en b<9a>rjan var den allm<8a>nna opinionen i Finland klart mot ett deltagande. H<9a>sten 1996 var majoriteten, 62 procent, mot och endast 29 procent f<9a>r. Finlands erfarenheter av EMU Vi har nu <9a>ver <8c>tta <8c>rs erfarenhet av valutaunionen. Intressant <8a>r att m<8c>nga av de asymmetriska chocker som befarades av motst<8c>ndarna till euron redan har realiserats under denna relativt korta tid. V<8c>r IKT-industri upplevde starka konjunktursv<8a>ngningar (boom<d0>bust-cykel) vid sekelskiftet liksom ocks<8c> i den svenska. I Finland speglades konjunkturnedg<8c>ngen snarare i tillv<8a>xtf<9a>rv<8a>ntningar och tillg<8c>ngspriser <8a>n i produktionsvolymer. Eurons kurs mot dollarn sj<9a>nk f<9a>rst med n<8a>ra 30 procent f<9a>r att sedan stiga med 50 procent. Vidare har oljepriset m<8c>ngdubblats under den tid euron har funnits. Tv<8a>rtemot EMU-motst<8c>ndarnas farh<8c>gor har varken den positiva externa chocken vid sekelskiftet eller den initiala eurof<9a>rsvagningen st<9a>rtat den finska ekonomin i n<8c>gon inflationsspiral. Ekonomin har r<8a>tt sm<8a>rtfritt klarat sig igenom IKT-recessionen och eurons stora fluktuationer. Den finska inflationstakten, som under tiden f<9a>re EMU stabiliserades genom en politik med inflationsm<8c>l, har sedan 1999 i stort motsvarat EMU-genomsnittet. Efter 2000 har inflationen mestadels legat p<8c> en niv<8c> som ryms inom ECB:s definition av prisstabilitet. Under de senaste <8c>ren har inflationen i Finland liksom ocks<8c> i Sverige faktiskt h<9a>rt till de l<8a>gsta i hela EU. Finlands BNP-tillv<8a>xt har fluktuerat mer eller mindre i takt med euroomr<8c>dets men genomsnittstillv<8a>xten har varit omkring en procentenhet h<9a>gre i Finland <8a>n i euroomr<8c>det. Faktorer bakom Finlands makroekonomiska utveckling Den ekonomiska utvecklingen i Finland speglar b<8c>de cykliska och strukturella faktorer. Tillv<8a>xten har normaliserats efter 1990-talskrisen och <8c>terh<8a>mtningseffekterna syntes <8a>nnu i produktionstillv<8a>xten under de f<9a>rsta EMU-<8c>ren. Tyv<8a>rr <8a>r arbetsl<9a>sheten fortfarande relativt h<9a>g <8a>ven om den nu ligger l<8c>ngt fr<8c>n rekordsiffrorna under tidiga 1990-talet. Under senare <8c>r har efterfr<8c>gan <9a>kat snabbt utanf<9a>r euroomr<8c>det, och den <9a>ppna ekonomin har gynnat exportindustrin och hela ekonomin i Finland. Samtidigt har den globala konkurrensen och produktionstillv<8a>xten d<8a>mpat pris<9a>kningarna p<8c> exporterade industrivaror och importvaror och d<8a>rigenom ocks<8c> d<8a>mpat inflationstrycket fr<8c>n den starka efterfr<8c>gan. Forsknings-och utvecklingsutgifterna i Finland utg<9a>r 3,5 procent av BNP, vilket <8a>r h<9a>gst i Europa vid sidan av Sverige och i niv<8c> med USA. En viktig del av forskningen har fokuserat p<8c> IKT. Finland och finska bolag har alltid deltagit aktivt i EU:s forskningsprogram. F<9a>r det andra <8a>r frihandel och avreglerade marknader en f<9a>ruts<8a>ttning f<9a>r tillv<8a>xt i ett litet land. Utan frihandel skapas inga bolag av n<8c>gon st<9a>rre dignitet och endast en konkurrensutsatt inhemsk marknad m<9a>jligg<9a>r nyskapande. 1990-talskrisen bidrog till insikten om att reformer beh<9a>vdes. Olika koalitionsregeringar har f<9a>rs<9a>kt uppr<8a>tth<8c>lla ett f<9a>retagsv<8a>nligt klimat. Avregleringen av kapitalmarknaden och snabbt <9a>kande riskfinansiering stimulerade tillv<8a>xten, IKT-sektorns diversifiering och internationalisering samt hela ekonomin. Den tredje faktorn som har bidragit till utvecklingen i Finland <8a>r uppkomsten av IKT-industrin. Avreglering och <9a>ppna standarder st<9a>dde en snabb utveckling i telekomindustrin och telekomtj<8a>nsterna. Det h<8a>r satte fart p<8c> produktivitets<9a>kningen i Finland. Det samma g<8a>ller f<9a>r Sverige. Jag vill ocks<8c> f<8a>sta uppm<8a>rksamhet vid f<9a>r<8a>ndringarna i banksektorn. Efter 1990-talskrisen omstrukturerades banksektorn kapitalt. Antalet anst<8a>llda och kontor halverades. Banksektorns produktivitet <9a>kade ocks<8c> tack vare <9a>kad konkurrens och utnyttjande av ny informationsteknik och Internettj<8a>nster. Det h<8a>r bidrog till den ekonomiska tillv<8a>xten i Finland. N<8c>gra ord om utbildningen Den innovationsdrivna utvecklingen har f<9a>rutsatt en samverkan mellan flera fundamentala faktorer, s<8c>som ett effektivt utbildningssystem, ett konsekvent och f<9a>rutsebart politiskt klimat och en sund grundl<8a>ggande infrastruktur. De flesta av dessa villkor var uppfyllda redan f<9a>re 1990-talet. V<8c>rt skolsystem har <8c>terspeglats i OECD:s PISA-unders<9a>kning av 15-<8c>ringars kunskaper och f<8a>rdigheter (Programme for International Student Assessments). Finlands topplaceringar i unders<9a>kningarna har ofta anv<8a>nts som exempel p<8c> resultat som kan n<8c>s med b<8c>de j<8a>mlik och h<9a>gklassig undervisning. Starkbytesbalans och internationellportf<9a>ljdiversifiering IKT-tillv<8a>xten speglas i bytesbalansen, som har visat <9a>verskott sedan 1994. Stora <9a>verskott <8a>r en markant skillnad mot f<9a>rr. Bytesbalans<9a>verskotten <8a>r inte bara f<9a>ljden av en konkurrenskraftig <9a>ppen sektor och stark exporttillv<8a>xt utan speglar ocks<8c> en r<8a>tt svag tillv<8a>xt i den inhemska efterfr<8c>gan efter 1990-talskrisen. F<9a>retagssektorn antog en f<9a>rsiktigare investeringsstrategi genom att minska sin skuldexponering och <9a>ka sina buffertlager. Den offentliga sektorn har g<8c>tt med <9a>verskott i flera <8c>r. Som en f<9a>ljd av den internationella diversifieringen av investerarnas portf<9a>ljer <9a>kade utl<8a>nningarnas innehav p<8c> Helsingforsb<9a>rsen till drygt 70 procent av det totala b<9a>rsv<8a>rdet 2000. Den finska ekonomins exponeringar i IKT.prisbubblan vid sekelskiftet minskade, d<8c> <8a>garrisken till st<9a>rsta delen bars av utl<8a>ndska investerare. Finanspolitiken under kontroll Efter 1990-talskrisen fanns ett klart behov av en ekonomisk politik som var f<9a>renlig med den fria r<9a>rligheten f<9a>r kapital <9a>ver nationella gr<8a>nser. Ett brett st<9a>d har utvecklats f<9a>r en stabilitetsinriktad finanspolitik som grund f<9a>r en l<8c>ngsiktigare stabil ekonomisk utveckling. Finanspolitiken har effektivt baserats p<8c> uttryckliga r<8a>ttesn<9a>ren s<8c>som utgiftsgr<8a>nser <9a>ver hela valperioden och i linje med detta har de offentliga finanserna konsoliderats. Som resultat av finanspolitiken g<8c>r den offentliga sektorn med <9a>verskott. <85>verskottet ligger p<8c> 2<d0>3 procent och ber<8a>knas ligga kvar p<8c> den niv<8c>n. Risker och utmaningar Sj<8a>lvfallet ser allt inte ljust ut. Vid horisonten lurar stora risker och ekonomisk-politiska utmaningar. Jag ska h<8a>r n<8a>mna tv<8c>. Ett bekymmer <8a>r bytesf<9a>rh<8c>llandet, som under de senaste <8c>ren f<9a>rs<8a>mrats och enligt prognoserna forts<8a>tter att f<9a>rs<8a>mras. Priserna p<8c> IKT-produkter sjunker globalt till f<9a>ljd av den tekniska utvecklingen och <9a>kad konkurrens. Ocks<8c> prisutvecklingen i skogsindustrin har varit ganska svag. Utmaningen ligger i att h<8c>lla produktivitets<9a>kningen h<9a>g och <9a>ka f<9a>r<8a>dlingsv<8a>rdet i exporten. Ett annat bekymmer <8a>r finanspolitiskt d<8c> befolkningen <8c>ldras snabbare i Finland <8a>n in andra industril<8a>nder inklusive Sverige. Sk<8a>let <8a>r de stora <8c>rskullarna fr<8c>n 1945<d0>50. Utgifterna f<9a>r offentlig service och pensioner <9a>kar medan utrymmet f<9a>r finansiering av extra utgifter blir mer begr<8a>nsat. Vi st<8c>r allts<8c> inf<9a>r den stora utmaningen att f<9a>rb<8a>ttra produktiviteten av de offentliga tj<8a>nsterna. Slutsats Sammantaget verkar Finlands EMU-medlemskap under de f<9a>rsta <8c>ren ha infriat de flesta l<9a>ftena och undvikit de flesta riskerna. F<9a>rdelarna blev som ber<8a>knat en effektiv ekonomi och en trov<8a>rdig penningpolitik, och inget tyder p<8c> att den makroekonomiska stabiliteten skulle ha f<9a>rs<8a>mrats, snarare tv<8a>rtom. Till slut n<8c>gra ord om effekterna av EMU p<8c> centralbanksarbetet: F<9a>r Finlands Bank har den nya institutionella omgivningen varit n<8a>rap<8c> omv<8a>lvande. Som en del av Eurosystemet <8a>r Finlands Bank nu med i v<8a>rldens n<8a>stst<9a>rsta centralbankssystem som bedriver politik visavi v<8a>rldens n<8a>stst<9a>rsta valuta. Vid sidan av det h<8a>r forts<8a>tter banken att fungera som Finlands nationella centralbank. F<9a>r centralbanksschefen betyder det h<8a>r fullv<8a>rdigt medlemskap i ECB-r<8c>det och deltagande i ECB:s centrala beslutsfattande tillsammans med <d0> sedan <8c>rsskiftet <d0> tolv andra nationella chefer och ECB:s heltidsanst<8a>llda direktion. Det h<8a>r ger insyn i och ansvar f<9a>r europeiska s<8c>v<8a>l som f<9a>r globala fr<8c>gor p<8c> ett helt annat s<8a>tt <8a>n vi vant oss vid i Finland. Vi som sitter i r<8c>det har alla var och en en r<9a>st vid besluten om penningpolitiken och andra politikfr<8c>gor. F<9a>r mig personligen betyder EMU i praktiken r<8c>dsm<9a>ten i Frankfurt varannan vecka och f<9a>r en stor grupp tj<8a>nstem<8a>n vid Finlands Bank regelbundna resor till kommitt<8e>m<9a>ten i Frankfurt p<8c> samma s<8a>tt som deras kolleger fr<8c>n finansministeriet och andra ministerier i Finland <d0> liksom i Sverige <d0> reser till Bryssel. Men det <8a>r <8a>nd<8c> mera fr<8c>ga om substans <8a>n resor. D<8a>rf<9a>r har vi, en liten centralbank, valt att satsa p<8c> forskning, analys och bed<9a>mning. Bara p<8c> det s<8a>ttet kan vi skapa en s<8c> god grund som m<9a>jligt i f<9a>rberedelserna f<9a>r beslutsfattandet i r<8c>det liksom ocks<8c> f<9a>r v<8c>r <9a>vriga verksamhet i Eurosystemet.

Title: Kekkonen and Monnet at Carr's House at the FAQ Heritage Association
text: President and CEO Erkki Liikanen's speech "Kekkonen and Monnet at carre's house" at the UKK Heritage Association . Speech . Thursday25 January 2007, 12:00 AM Director-General Erkki Liikanen UKK Perinneyhdistys 25.1.2007 Kekkonen and Monnet at Carre's house President Urho Kekkonen began his second term in March 1962 with a major election victory. Behind them were the note crisis and discussions in Novosibirsk with Prime Minister Hrutshev. John F. Kennedy was halfway through his short presidency. The domestic political situation was still tense, especially between the Center Party and the Social Democrats. 39-year-old Ahti Karjalainen became Prime Minister for the first time.
