Ja se oli <d0> "Kiina, maailman rikkain valtakunta, on siit<8a> kiist<8a>m<8a>t<9a>n esimerkki. Siell<8a> ei kaupungeilla ole mit<8a><8a>n etuoikeuksia, eik<8a> mit<8a><8a>n eroja tehd<8a> kaupunki-ja maalaiselinkeinojen v<8a>lill<8a>; sen t<8a>hden koko maa on kuin kaupunki ja kaikki kaupungit ihaninta maaseutua<c9>k<8a>sity<9a>t ovat siell<8a> vapaat, siksi ty<9a>mies on ahkeruudessaan v<8a>sym<8a>t<9a>n, ja monitoimisuus menee itsest<8a><8a>n maanpakoon lakien tarvitsematta sinne sit<8a> karkoittaa" Hollanti ja Englanti olivat ihannetta l<8a>hinn<8a>, mutta sittenkin niin kaukana: kukaan ei ollut antanut luonnonlakien vallita niin vapaasti kuin kiinalainen, muut ovat sokeita, paitsi hollantilaiset ja englantilaiset, jotka ovat toissilm<8a>isi<8a>. Vastoin n<8a>it<8a> esimerkkej<8a> Ruotsi oli uskonut yksinoikeuksien, rajoitusten ja monenlaisten kieltojen heit<8a> rikastuttavan. N<8a>ill<8a> vahvoilla argumenteilla aloitti Chydenius itse asiassa puheenvuoronsa Pohjanmaan kaupunkien kauppaoikeuksien laajentamisen puolesta. Keskustelua ei pid<8a> irrottaa omasta aikakaudestaan. Mutta Kiina oli tuolloin maailman suuri talousmahti, ja my<9a>s t<8a>n<8a><8a>n se kasvaa voimakkaasti, vaikka onkin viel<8a> kaukana johtavan mahdin asemasta. Kuinka s<8a><8a>dell<8a> v<8a>ltt<8a>m<8a>t<9a>n ja v<8a>ltt<8a><8a> ylis<8a><8a>ntely, on suuri keskusteluaihe edelleen, esimerkiksi Euroopan unionin piiriss<8a>. *** Lopuksi muutama sana Chydeniuksen ja Tokoin toiminnan olennaisista piirteist<8a> nykyajan n<8a>k<9a>kulmasta katsoen: Chydenius ajoi ulkomaankaupan vapautta ja elinkeinovapautta ja vastusti hattupuolueen subventioihin ja kieltoihin perustuvaa elinkeinopolitiikkaa. H<8a>n ajoi rahan arvon vakauttamista sen vallitsevan arvon pohjalle; h<8a>n ajoi sananvapautta, hallinnon avoimuutta ja vastusti sensuuria; ja h<8a>n halusi lis<8a>t<8a> palkollisten oikeuksia ja laajentaa uskonnonvapautta. On selv<8a><8a>, ett<8a> liberaali Chydenius n<8a>ki maailman monessa asiassa hyvin eri tavoin kuin sosialidemokraatti Tokoi. Varsinkin heid<8a>n ratkaisunsa sosiaalisiin ongelmiin olivat erilaiset ja heid<8a>n suhtautumisensa markkinatalouden mekanismeihin oli erilainen ja joskus jopa vastakkainenkin. Mutta sek<8a> Chydeniuksella ett<8a> Tokoilla poliittisen ohjelman perusteluna oli sosiaalisen oikeudenmukaisuuden v<8a>hent<8a>minen ja erilaisten valta-asemaan perustuvien etuoikeuksien kumoaminen. Chydenius vaati "Kansallisessa voitossa", ett<8a> "kaikki keinot el<8a><8a> ilman ty<9a>t<8a> katkaistaan, eik<8a> kukaan muu kuin ahkera voi tulla varakkaaksi". T<8a>m<8a> vaatimus olisi sopinut my<9a>s Tokoin suuhun. My<9a>s Chydeniuksen huoli palkollisten suojattomasta asemasta ja ajatus, ett<8a> ep<8a>demokraattisessa valtiossa lait sortavat k<9a>yhimpi<8a>, yhdist<8a><8a> h<8a>nt<8a> Tokoihin. Molemmat olivat vakaumuksellisia demokraatteja ja suhtautuivat kielteisesti s<8a><8a>ty-yhteiskuntaan. Sek<8a> liberalismin ett<8a> poliittisen ty<9a>v<8a>enliikkeen juuret ovat valistuksessa, ja Chydenius on hyv<8a> esimerkki valistusajan poliittisista uudistuspyrkimyksist<8a>. *** Molempien el<8a>m<8a>ntarinassa on t<8a>m<8a>n p<8a>iv<8a>n valossa sensaatiomaisiakin piirteit<8a>. Sek<8a> aatteen ett<8a> toiminnan miehin<8a> molemmat panivat itsens<8a> likoon ja saivat my<9a>s kokea sen seuraukset. Chydeniuksen ajatusten kaukon<8a>k<9a>isyys ja kielen ter<8a>vyys on vaikuttavaa. Niin monet asiat ja ongelmanasettelut ovat s<8a>ilytt<8a>neet ajankohtaisuutensa t<8a>h<8a>n p<8a>iv<8a><8a>n asti. H<8a>nen toimintansa vaikutti Pohjanmaan talouteen ja tuntuu viel<8a> t<8a>n<8a><8a>nkin sek<8a> Ruotsin ett<8a> Suomen poliittisessa el<8a>m<8a>ss<8a> esimerkiksi avoimuuden ja sananvapauden korkeana arvostuksena. Tokoin el<8a>m<8a>ntarina on v<8a>rikk<8a><8a>mpi, suorastaan ainutlaatuinen. H<8a>n eli Yhdysvalloissa yli nelj<8a>kymment<8a> vuotta, n<8a>ki yht<8a><8a>lt<8a> kaksi lamaa ja toisaalta Yhdysvaltain nousun. H<8a>n oli ensimm<8a>isen eduskunnan j<8a>sen, ensimm<8a>inen p<8a><8a>ministeri, toinen SAJ:n puheenjohtaja, kansanvaltuuskunnan j<8a>sen, vahva demokratian puolustaja ja ennen kaikkea selviytyj<8a>. Anders Chydeniuksesta on tehty merkitt<8a>v<8a> el<8a>m<8a>nkerta. Sellainen tarvitaan my<9a>s Oskari Tokoista.

Title: Climate change, economy and investment Nordea Private Banking AutumnSSatoa seminar
text: President and CEO Erkki Liikanen: "Climate change, the economy and investment", Nordea Private Banking AutumnSatoa seminar, Finlandia Hall . Speech . Wednesday12 September 2007,12:00AM Director-General Erkki Liikanen Nordea Private Banking AutumnSatoa seminar, 12.9.2007 Finlandia Hall Speech associated kalvosarja (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and. . interviews/documents/nordea_diat12092007.pdf) INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIC SITUATION The international economic situation can be examined by dividing the issue into two. Firstly, what it looked like in early August and secondly, what it will look like after that. At the beginning of August, we noted that global economic growth has remained strong in the first half of the year. It is generally predicted that despite the cooling of the US economy, global economic growth will reach around 4.5% this year, meaning that the growth rate will slow down only slightly from last year. This means that the boom that began in 2003 will be one of the longest in the post-war period. Figure 2: Global economic growth, 1998-2008 (IMF; 25.7.2007) What has been exceptional about this boom has been the geographical breadth. The developing countries of Asia, especially China and India, have experienced strong economic growth. Growth has also been strong in Russia and the new EU Member States. The economies of South America, and also of Africa, have now had their share of global economic growth and lively world trade. At the same time, the welfare gap between low-income countries and the old industrialised countries has narrowed, albeit slowly. Since the second week of August, the attention of those who follow the economy has been focused on the tightening of the monetary and financial markets. The problems in the US mortgage market have been well known, but now their effects have become widespread with the new instruments in the financial markets. What has happened has had a negative impact on the confidence of investors, especially in the money and financial markets. Today, it is still difficult to estimate the extent to which the perceived shocks will have on the real economy. The sign is likely to be negative. Most assume that the global impact will be quite small, although the US economy will slow down markedly towards the end of the year. This is due to the fact that the global economy faced the August shocks in a period of strong growth and thus has resilience against financial turmoil. However, we must carefully monitor all new economic information. Despite strong global economic growth, inflationary pressures remained surprisingly low in key economic areas for a long time. The euro area has remained close to the 2% level. Although the inflation rate of the fast-growing emerging economies is clearly higher than this, they have not so far seen the strong acceleration in consumer price growth typical of previous booms. The credibility of monetary policy has kept inflation expectations anchored. Furthermore, globalisation, i.e. the opening up of global product and labour markets to competition, has helped to keep price pressures under control. Figure 3: Inflation expectations 2003-2007 (Bloomberg) Globalisation has also meant a major upheaval in the international labour market. The available labour force in the global economy has quadrupled in twenty years as China, India and the former socialist countries of Eastern Europe have integrated into the global exchange economy. Global competition in the labour market has significantly curbed the rise in labour costs in the old industrialised countries, thus helping to keep inflation under control. ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENTS IN THE EURO AREA AND ECONOMIC POLICY CHALLENGES Graph 4: Structure of growth in the euro area (PATU 19482) The euro area economy entered the growth cycle of the international economy later than others. Over the past two years, economic growth in the euro area countries has also strengthened markedly. Growth has been boosted by increased investment activity, as investments in machinery and equipment have increased, supported by strong demand, good corporate profitability and favourable financing conditions. At the same time, the strong pull in the housing market has kept residential construction buoyant in many euro area countries. Graph 5: Unemployment rate and spare capacity in the euro area (RPR graph 27) Gradually, the growth dynamics within the euro area economy have also intensified, as employment growth has started to be reflected in household incomes and confidence. In the first half of this year, the unemployment rate in the euro area has fallen to around 7%, the lowest figure for the euro area in more than twenty years. As a result of the rapid growth in employment, the euro area labour market has clearly tightened, despite the fact that labour supply has also increased as a result of immigration. In some countries, the tightening of the labour market has also started to be reflected in wage developments. While this is partly a shift to more productivity-oriented sector- and company-specific wage agreements, there is a risk of wage inflation spreading and exiting productivity developments. Graph 6: Oil prices (RPR Figure 5) Inflation risks in the euro area remain upside, especially over the medium term. Economic growth in the euro area is projected to remain close to, or even slightly above, potential output growth rates. As a result, production bottlenecks are forming in some regions, which may lead to upward pressure on the industry's input and output prices. In such a situation, there is also a growing risk that sharply increased energy and raw material costs will begin to be passed on more strongly to the prices of intermediate and final products. Figure 7: Monetary aggregates (RPR Figure 30) Inflation risks over the medium term are also indicated by the ongoing strong monetary expansion, namely: the rapid growth of monetary and credit volumes. According to the latest statistics, the broad monetary amount in the euro area, M3 and the public lending of euro area MFIs, continue to grow at an annual rate of around 10%. Thus, while the euro area economic fundamental picture remains positive, recent financial market shocks have somewhat altered the risk balance. ENVIRONMENTAL PROBLEMS AND FINANCIAL MARKETS Economic impacts of climate change Climate change has quickly become the great challenge of our era, starting to threaten our living environment, economic development and human well-being. Climate change in itself is not a new phenomenon: in the long run of history, the earth's climate has experienced cold and hot, as well as rainy and dry periods. What is new now is that the ongoing climate change is largely caused by humans themselves. Figure 8. Global carbon dioxide emissions In addition, global warming appears to be happening faster than previously estimated. The negative consequences of warming in the form of droughts, floods and storms, for example, are no longer a distant future, but problems for us and for our immediate generations. Long-term environmental risks are now seen as so significant that they are also beginning to be reflected in the financial markets. At the same time, consideration has begun to be given to how financial markets could contribute to the fight against climate change and to the adaptation of societies to change. Climate change affects economic development in at least three different ways. The much-publicised report by the British economist Nicholas Stern focuses in particular on the wealth effects of climate change, i.e. the destruction of physical wealth and productive capital as a result of droughts, floods and storms. The report is impressive. It estimates that the economic effects of climate change could be more severe than those of the world wars or the depression of the 1930s. However, according to Stern's assessment, such a disaster scenario can be avoided if strong measures are taken to reduce carbon dioxide emissions. The most decisive of these measures, the report considers, the definition of a global price for carbon dioxide, either through taxation or emissions trading. Next comes the technological approach, i.e. investing in low-carbon and energy-efficient products. Climate change also weakens the ability of the economy to function by making it more difficult to access resources. An example of this is the availability of water, which has become a major problem in many countries as drought and desertification have become more common. Global agricultural production can also suffer significantly if desertification and rising seawater levels reduce the cultivatable surface area and rising water and energy prices limit production potential. Climate change can have a significant negative impact on economic development through increased uncertainty and the consequent increase in risk premia. The increase in uncertainty stems not only from the direct unexpected effects of climate change (storms, increased weather variations, etc.), but also from uncertainty about how consumer behaviour and economic policies will react to climate change (changes in consumption patterns, taxation, emissions restrictions, etc.). It is very possible that in the increased prices of oil and other energy sources, we are already seeing a risk premium related to climate change, which reflects uncertainty about how climate change will affect the availability of different energy sources and what kind of measures will be targeted at the supply and prices of different energy sources as a result of climate change. ENVIRONMENTAL PROBLEMS AND ECONOMIC POLICY The Kyoto Protocol to the UnFCCC was adopted in 1997 and entered into force in 2005. The Kyoto Protocol is an important step forward in preventing global warming by including binding quantitative targets to limit and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Figure 9: EU climate targets Greenhouse gas emission allowances and their trading play a key role in achieving both the European Union's own climate policy objectives and the commitments under the Kyoto Protocol. Emission allowances aim to internalise, i.e. create a cost for the negative externalities of greenhouse gases. Emissions trading is a cost-effective climate policy, as the functioning of the market is guided by the reduction of emissions where it is most affordable. Figure 10: The market for carbon dioxide emission allowances in 2006 The role of financial markets in implementing measures to mitigate climate change has increased significantly with the development of emissions trading. Over the past three years, carbon emissions trading has become one of the fastest growing market segments of the financial markets, which is being competed for by large investment banks and a number of smaller institutions. The World Bank estimates that emissions trading rose to around 30 billion last year, three times the previous year's support. By far the largest emissions trading mechanism in terms of both participants and trading volumes is the European Union's greenhouse gas emission allowance trading, the volume of which reached around 22.5 billion last year. How large the trading volumes of emission allowances in the next few years will be depends. political decisions; the pace at which new countries will join emissions trading and how strict the country-specific emission limits and emission targets will be set. According to the most daring estimates, emissions trading could reach up to 1000 billion in a decade, making it the world's largest raw materials market. CLIMATE CHANGE AND INVESTMENT Climate change affects the financial markets in many other ways as well. Long-term environmental risks are also becoming increasingly visible in financial markets, as environmental and living conditions factors affect the creditworthiness of housekeepers and financial market prices. After all, the prices of financial assets and financial contracts should reflect expected economic developments and the associated risk. For example, in the pricing of insurance contracts, shares and long-term debt, the review period is so long that even long-term environmental risks become very significant. The ultimate task of the financial markets is to direct financing from savers to investors. The price and allocation of assets in the financial markets depend on the expected returns and risks of investments. As climate change accelerates, the need to increasingly direct energy investments towards the production of renewable energy, such as solar, bio- and wind power, has become more pronounced. However, from the investor's point of view, there are risks associated with the production of renewable energy in the early stages. Renewable energy production facilities are often small compared to those powered by conventional energy sources. Similarly, technology is often new, and although it is developing rapidly, there is still no long-term experience of it. Another significant risk for the investor is that the profitability of renewable energy production is highly dependent on the price level of traditional energy sources, such as oil. For these reasons, it is understandable that the public sector plays a significant role in financing the production of renewable energy and, in particular, product development. However, the situation is rapidly changing. In recent years, investments in renewable energy have grown rapidly, and now such a critical mass has been reached that private investors have also "discovered" this sector. Figure 11: Share of different forms of energy in energy production in OECD countries, 2004 (IEA, World Energy Outlook 2006) Despite the development of technology, the world's need for energy is growing rapidly all the time. For example, the IEA (International Energy Agency) has estimated that by 2030, global investment in the energy sector will cumulatively reach 10-15 trillion euros. A growing share of this is directed towards renewable forms of energy, which still account for a relatively low share of energy production at the moment. For example, in OECD countries, wind power, bioenergy, geothermal heat and other new forms of energy currently account for less than 5% of total energy production, and even if hydropower is included, it remains below 10%. Figure 12: Global investment in renewable energy, 2004-2006, USD billion (UNEP) The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) has estimated that last year global investment in renewable energy reached more than 70 billion. This year is expected to rise to around 85 billion. At the same time, the forms of financing used have also become significantly more diverse. Alongside government subsidies, a wide range of private financing has developed. The fastest growing of these in recent years has been private equity investments and equity investments directly or through stock exchanges in companies producing renewable energy. Figure 13: Global investment in renewable energy by form of financing in 2006 (UNEP) Also on the asset management side, environmental factors are becoming an increasingly important factor. This is due both to increased environmental awareness among investors and to the product development of banks and funds, which offers greater opportunities to take social and environmental factors into account when making investment decisions. In the United States, one-tenth of the assets under active asset management are already so-called asset managers. socially responsible investments. They seek to invest in companies that are committed to sustainable development and corporate social responsibility. Investments in this sector are also growing rapidly in Europe and Finland. Graph 14: DJIA index and DJ sustainability index The investor base is aware of the importance of environmental issues and the opportunities that this rapidly developing sector offers. This interest and profit potential is also reflected in the stock exchange rates of companies investing in sustainable development, which on average have risen faster than the general price development. The values of sustainable development have also become part of the investment philosophy of institutional investors. In Europe, especially in the most funded pension systems, such as the UK and the Netherlands, socially responsible investing is rapidly becoming part of the mainstream of investment. In other countries, too, socially responsible investing is becoming part of the investment market. In recent years, several EU countries have introduced an obligation for investors in pension assets to disclose whether and how social responsibility is taken into account in their investment activities. Finnish legislation does not contain any specific provisions on the social responsibility of the investment of earnings-related pension funds. However, earnings-related pension insurers have voluntarily adopted the general principles of socially responsible investment, which they independently apply in their own investment activities. This increase in investor social awareness has a significant guiding effect.

Title: Speech in Mikkeli
text: Speech by President and CEO Erkki Liikanen in Kuopio, Savon Sanomat 100 years . Speech . Friday 12 October 2007, 12:00 AM President and CEO Erkki Liikanen Savon Sanomat 100 years Kuopio 12.10.2007 Dear festive audience! Ladies and gentlemen! Dear friends! There are hardly any countries where the press plays such an important role as in Finland. Newspapers are read by us much. In addition to that, many of them in international comparison would be counted in quality magazines. The number one newspapers in the provinces have a particularly strong position. They have played an important role in raising the identity of the provinces and in developing the provinces. There is no strong provincial center without a strong provincial newspaper. The more open the newspapers have been to different opinions, the more valuable their contribution has been to the compilers of the provinces. I would like to congratulate Savon Sanomat, which is celebrating its 100th anniversary, and it has been and is one of the best in the Finnish press. It has also been the driving force behind many projects in the province, assembling troops and conveying the message But these years have not been a downhill climb. In order to stay strong, the magazine has had to keep the economy in order, the magazine itself to be of high quality, and at the same time be able to invest in the last technology in order to keep it at the forefront of development. It is the newspaper production process that has undergone a major upheaval. When Savon Sanomat celebrated its 60th anniversary, i.e. only 40 years ago, the production of the magazine was from another world. The clashes between Kuopion Palloseura and the Mikkeli teams were hot news at the time. When the young assistant in Mikkeli had finished the story, he called it by phone to Kuopio, where Jarmo Karjalainen or even Reino Myohanen rewrote it about dictation. After that, he took the text to the barnkeeper, who did it for the third time. Today, in the world of ICT, an assistant writes a story on his computer; it will be in the magazine in no time. The original text can be edited, but not rewritten, it goes to the electronic folding table, and from it directly to the printing presses. Technology has made it possible for one to do what used to take three. This is an increase in productivity. Indeed, the basis for the growth of well-being is precisely in the growth of productivity. At the time of the founding of this magazine, Finland and Savo were the most underdeveloped regions in Europe. First, machines and equipment that use electricity began to replace wood and in metal processing to replace muscle and steam power. Later, the processes and methods of production began to be changed by exploiting information and communication technologies. This has meant a sharp increase in productivity for 100 years and, as a result, the standard of living per capita today is 14 times higher, even though the working day has become shorter. But the challenges do not subside: Finland faces ageing quickly and more drastically than others. The labor force begins to contract already after three years. After that, all growth will be based on productivity. We need investment in new technologies, new ways of producing and organising and training. Just as has been done in the newspapers. But we need to be able to increase productivity everywhere, in industry and services, in the public and private sectors. If productivity development does not improve in public services, it will not be possible to maintain the current service provision. Productivity needs to be improved by developing smarter and more creative ways of working. Not grinding brings a solution. The standard of living does not rise from cooking more of the same soup, but from doing the right things and with better recipes. The ICT industry and the widespread exploitation of ICT have been a key driver of domestic growth over the past decade. The relocation of jobs to lower-cost countries, for example, in composition, cannot be prevented, but by focusing on tasks with high value added, we can maintain and raise our standard of living in the future. In the process of change, society's safety nets are necessary, but they must not lock in people or change, but they must encourage them to seek new challenges. In international competition, we must claim our place every day in order to keep up with developments and maintain our current standard of living. Last year we celebrated J.V. Snellman's jubilee year all over Finland, but especially here in Kuopio. I was here to issue a commemorative coin dedicated to him. This was a good way to honour Snellman, as Snellman is, after all, in the minds of most Finns, the father of Finland's own money. Kuopio was the best place to announce a commemorative coin depicting the young Snellman, because he made his most significant contribution as a national revivalist during his term in Kuopio, as the editor of his magazines "Saima" and "Litteraturbladet". In this city, Snellman founded the Finnish political press. Snellman's magazines were not the first newspapers in Finland, but they were ambitious and aware of their own mission in a new way than the previous ones. Journalist Snellman was not content with entertainment and small news, but started a public social debate in Finland. Thanks to him, Kuopio can be considered not only the birthplace of Finnish journalism, but also the beginning of what is now called civil society. As in Snellman's time, democracy grows largely with the support of a press that is aware of its task. The press also plays a key role in promoting and transforming the cultural aspirations of its region. It is a pleasure to say that Savon Sanomat has maintained Snellman's legacy well. I have had the opportunity to work first as an assistant, but later in various social tasks in cooperation with three editors-in-chief of Savon Sanomat. First we had a long collaboration with Mauri Auvinen, then with Reino Myohanen and most recently with Tapani Lepola. It has to be acknowledged that the subscribers and readers of Savon Sanomat have had good luck. The editors-in-chief have been tolerant and open-minded people who have not been trapped in their complacency or in their backbenchers, as is sometimes the case. They have known that the doors must be kept open everywhere if the forces of the province are to be rallyed. They have been curious and interested in the changes in Finland, Europe and the world and have conveyed this important attitude to their editors and readers. Information and communication technology revolutionised the production of the magazine already during the reign of Mauri Auvinen and Reino Myohanen. Under Tapani Lepola, the Internet revolution began. It also began to change the distribution channels of magazines. Editor-in-Chief Jari Touruse's big challenge is how to secure the position of Savon Sanomat now that the Internet is challenging the printed newspaper. At a time of globalization and fragmentation of knowledge, I believe that the value of provinciality, locality and communality will increase. People want to belong to something, to be from somewhere. In Finland, too, citizens' identity is largely based on people's local participation in the economy and social activities of their own region. This is wealth. It gives a great opportunity to the provincial newspaper. On the other hand, when information is fragmented, there is always a need for quality suppliers who put the pieces together and give background and connections to things. It may not be the job of a journalist to say what a person should think, but he can provide tools for understanding the world and the earth and thus for forming his own perception. It is not always easy. Let's take one example from the current field of activity, for example. How is it possible that mortgages with low creditworthiness in the American market - subprime loans, as they are called - are rocking the money and financial markets around the world? How long can the current crisis of confidence continue? If it drags on, what will be the impact on our national economy, households and entrepreneurs? There are many experts at the Bank of Finland and elsewhere who have invested in analysing the problem and also in finding solutions to safeguard the functioning of the money and financial markets. But in order to analyse this information and convey the message, we need professional journalists and media that citizens trust. Monetary policy itself is both decisions and communication. A good story and good content will always live on. But every generation of business leaders and editors has to struggle to create business models that making a magazine is a profitable business. There will be enough challenges and we do not know all the answers today. Finally, I would like to thank Savon Sanomat for the much it has given over the years. It has always provided a forum if there has been anything to say. But it has also conveyed the feelings of women and men in the province to decision-makers. It has brought a lot of friends from the circle of numerous journalists. But it has also been an important common bond for many of us Savonians who have, in one way or another, lived within it. There are a lot of names buzzing in the mind. There was Matti Korhonen. There are Jouko Loikkanen and Juhani Koskinen. There are Paavo Lipponen and Seppo Kaariainen. There are Lasse Lehtinen and Markku Hyvarinen. And dozens, maybe hundreds more. Without Savon Sanomat, many chains would have been broken.
text_original: P<8a><8a>johtaja Erkki Liikasen puhe Kuopiossa, Savon Sanomat 100 vuotta . Speech . Friday 12 October 2007, 12:00 AM P<8a><8a>johtaja Erkki Liikanen Savon Sanomat 100 vuotta Kuopio 12.10.2007 Arvoisa juhlayleis<9a>! Hyv<8a>t naiset ja miehet! Hyv<8a>t yst<8a>v<8a>t! Ei ole juuri maita, joissa sanomalehdist<9a>ll<8a> on niin t<8a>rke<8a> asema kuin Suomessa. Sanomalehti<8a> luetaan meill<8a> paljon. Sen lis<8a>ksi monet niist<8a> kansainv<8a>lisess<8a> vertailussa luettaisiin laatulehtiin. Erityisen vahva asema on maakuntien ykk<9a>slehdill<8a>. Ne ovat olleet t<8a>rke<8a>ss<8a> asemassa maakuntien identiteetin nostajina ja maakuntien kehitt<8a>jin<8a>. Vahvaa maakuntakeskusta ei ole ilman vahvaa maakuntalehte<8a>. Mit<8a> avoimimpia lehdet ovat taas olleet erilaisille mielipiteille, sit<8a> arvokkaampi niiden panos on ollut maakuntien kokoajina. Haluankin onnitella 100 vuotta t<8a>ytt<8a>v<8a><8a> Savon Sanomia, se on ollut ja on suomalaisen sanomalehdist<9a>n parhaimmistoa. Sen on ollut my<9a>s monien maakunnan hankkeiden taustavoima, joukkojen kokoaja ja viestin v<8a>litt<8a>j<8a> Mutta eiv<8a>t n<8a>m<8a> vuodet ole olleet silkkaa my<9a>t<8a>m<8a>ke<8a>. Pysy<8a>kseen vahvana, on lehden t<8a>ytynyt pit<8a><8a> talous kunnossa, itse lehti laadukkaana ja kyet<8a> samalla investoimaan viimeiseen teknologiaan, jotta se pysyisi kehityksen k<8a>rjess<8a>. Juuri sanomalehtien tuotantoprosessi on k<8a>ynyt l<8a>pi suuren mullistuksen. Kun Savon Sanomat t<8a>ytti 60 vuotta, siis vain 40 vuotta sitten, lehden valmistus oli toisesta maailmasta. Kuopion Palloseuran ja mikkelil<8a>isjoukkueiden yhteenotot olivat tuolloin kuumia uutisia. Kun nuori avustaja Mikkeliss<8a> oli saanut jutun valmiiksi, soitti h<8a>n sen puhelimella Kuopioon, jossa Jarmo Karjalainen tai jopa Reino My<9a>h<8a>nen kirjoitti sen sanelusta uudelleen. Sen j<8a>lkeen h<8a>n vei tekstin latojalle, joka teki sen kolmanteen kertaan. T<8a>n<8a><8a>n tieto-ja viestint<8a>tekniikan maailmassa avustaja kirjoittaa jutun tietokoneellaan; se on lehdess<8a> hetkess<8a>. Alkuper<8a>ist<8a> teksti<8a> voidaan muokata, mutta ei kirjoiteta uudelleen, se siirtyy s<8a>hk<9a>iseen taittop<9a>yt<8a><8a>n ja siit<8a> suoraan painokoneisiin. Teknologia on mahdollistanut sen, ett<8a> yksi tekee sen, mihin ennen tarvittiin kolme. T<8a>m<8a> on tuottavuuden kasvua. Hyvinvoinnin kasvun perusta onkin juuri tuottavuuden kasvussa. Suomi ja Savo olivat t<8a>m<8a>n lehden perustamisen aikaan Euroopan alikehittyneint<8a> seutua. Ensin s<8a>hk<9a><8a> k<8a>ytt<8a>vill<8a> koneilla ja laitteilla alettiin puun ja metallinjalostuksessa korvata lihas-ja h<9a>yryvoimaakin. My<9a>hemmin tuotantoprosesseja ja -tapoja ryhdyttiin muuttamaan tieto-ja viestint<8a>tekniikkaa hyv<8a>ksik<8a>ytt<8a>m<8a>ll<8a>. T<8a>m<8a> on merkinnyt tuottavuuden voimakasta kasvua 100 vuoden ajan ja sen vuoksi elintaso henke<8a> kohden on t<8a>n<8a><8a>n 14-kertainen, vaikka ty<9a>p<8a>iv<8a> on lyhentynyt. Mutta haasteet eiv<8a>t hellit<8a>: Suomi kohtaa ik<8a><8a>ntymisen nopeasti ja muita jyrkemmin. Ty<9a>voima alkaa supistua jo kolmen vuoden kuluttua. Sen j<8a>lkeen kaikki kasvu perustuu tuottavuuteen. Me tarvitsemme investointeja uuteen tekniikkaan, uusiin tuotanto-ja organisaatiotapoihin ja koulutukseen. Juuri niin kuin on tehty sanomalehdiss<8a>. Mutta tuottavuuden kasvuun pit<8a><8a> pysty<8a> kaikkialla, teollisuudessa ja palveluissa, julkisessa ja yksityisess<8a>. Ellei tuottavuuskehitys parane julkisissa palveluissa, ei nykyist<8a> palvelutarjontaa kyet<8a> pit<8a>m<8a><8a>n yll<8a>. Tuottavuutta on parannettava <8a>lykk<8a><8a>mpi<8a> ja luovempia ty<9a>tapoja kehitt<8a>m<8a>ll<8a>. Ei hiostaminen tuo ratkaisua. Ei elintaso siit<8a> nouse, ett<8a> keitet<8a><8a>n lis<8a><8a> samaa soppaa, vaan siit<8a>, ett<8a> tehd<8a><8a>n oikeita asioita ja paremmilla resepteill<8a>. Tieto-ja viestint<8a>tekninen teollisuus ja tieto-ja viestint<8a>tekniikan laaja hyv<8a>ksik<8a>ytt<9a> ovat olleet kotimaisen kasvun keskeinen voima viimeisen vuosikymmenen ajan. Ty<9a>paikkojen siirtymist<8a> alemman kustannustason maihin esimerkiksi kokoonpanossa ei voi est<8a><8a>, mutta keskittym<8a>ll<8a> korkean arvonlis<8a>yksen teht<8a>viin, voimme yll<8a>pit<8a><8a> ja nostaa elintasoamme tulevaisuudessa. Muutosprosessissa ovat yhteiskunnan turvaverkot tarpeellisia, mutta ne eiv<8a>t saa lukita ihmisi<8a> eiv<8a>tk<8a> muutosta, vaan niiden pit<8a><8a> kannustaa hakeutumaan uusiin haasteisiin. Kansainv<8a>lisess<8a> kilpailussa meid<8a>n on lunastettava paikkamme jokaisena p<8a>iv<8a>n<8a> pysy<8a>ksemme kehityksess<8a> mukana ja s<8a>ilytt<8a><8a>ksemme nykyisen elintasomme. Viime vuonna vietimme kaikkialla Suomessa, mutta varsinkin t<8a><8a>ll<8a> Kuopiossa J.V. Snellmanin juhlavuotta. Olin t<8a><8a>ll<8a> laskemassa liikkeelle h<8a>nelle omistettua juhlarahaa. Se olikin hyv<8a> tapa kunnioittaa Snellmania, sill<8a> onhan Snellman useimpien suomalaisten mieless<8a> juuri Suomen oman rahan is<8a>. Kuopio oli paras paikka julkistaa nuorta Snellmania kuvaava juhlaraha, koska merkitt<8a>-vimm<8a>n panoksensa kansallisena her<8a>tt<8a>j<8a>n<8a> h<8a>n teki juuri Kuopion kaudellaan, lehtiens<8a> "Saiman" ja "Litteraturbladetin" toimittajana. T<8a>ss<8a> kaupungissa Snellman perusti suomalaisen poliittisen lehdist<9a>n. Snellmanin lehdet eiv<8a>t olleet Suomen ensimm<8a>isi<8a> sanomalehti<8a>, mutta ne olivat uudella tavalla kunnianhimoisia ja omasta teht<8a>v<8a>st<8a><8a>n tietoisia kuin aiemmat. Lehtimies Snellman ei tyytynyt ajanvietteeseen ja pikku-uutisiin, vaan aloitti julkisen yhteiskunnallisen keskustelun Suomessa. H<8a>nen ansiostaan Kuopiota voidaan pit<8a><8a> paitsi suomalaisen journalismin syntypaikkana, my<9a>s sellaisen yhteiskunnallisen osallistumisen alkukotina, mit<8a> nyky<8a><8a>n sanotaan kansalaisyhteiskunnaksi. Niin kuin Snellmanin aikana my<9a>s nyky<8a><8a>n demokratia kasvaa pitk<8a>lti teht<8a>v<8a>st<8a><8a>n tietoisen lehdist<9a>n tukemana. Lehdist<9a>ll<8a> on my<9a>s keskeinen rooli alueensa kulttuuripyrint<9a>jen edist<8a>j<8a>n<8a> ja muutosvoimana. On ilo todeta, ett<8a> Savon Sanomat on pit<8a>nyt Snellmanin perint<9a><8a> hienosti yll<8a>. Olen saanut ty<9a>skennell<8a> ensin avustajana, mutta sittemmin erilaisissa yhteiskunnallisissa teht<8a>viss<8a> yhteisty<9a>ss<8a> kolmen Savon Sanomien p<8a><8a>toimittajan kanssa. Ensin meill<8a> oli pitk<8a> yhteisty<9a> Mauri Auvisen, sitten Reino My<9a>h<8a>sen ja viimeksi Tapani Lepolan kanssa. On pakko tunnustaa, ett<8a> Savon Sanomien tilaajilla ja lukijoilla on ollut hyv<8a> herraonni. P<8a><8a>toimittajat ovat olleet suvaitsevaisia ja avarakatseisia ihmisi<8a>, jotka eiv<8a>t ole j<8a><8a>neet omahyv<8a>isyytens<8a> tai taustajoukkojensa vangeiksi, kuten joskus k<8a>y. He ovat tienneet, ett<8a> ovet on pidett<8a>v<8a> auki kaikkialle, jos halutaan koota maakunnan voimat. He ovat olleet uteliaita ja kiinnostuneita Suomen, Euroopan ja maailman muutoksista ja v<8a>litt<8a>neet t<8a>m<8a>n t<8a>rke<8a>n asenteen toimittajilleen ja lukijoille. Tieto-ja viestint<8a>tekniikka mullistivat lehden valmistuksen jo Mauri Auvisen ja Reino My<9a>h<8a>sen kaudella. Tapani Lepolan aikana alkoi Internetin vallankumous. Se alkoi muuttaa my<9a>s lehtien jakelukanavia. P<8a><8a>toimittaja Jari Tourusen suuri haaste onkin, kuinka turvata Savon Sanomien asema nyt kun Internet haastaa painetun sanomalehden. Globalisoitumisen ja tiedon sirpaloitumisen aikana uskon maakunnallisuuden, paikallisuuden ja yhteis<9a>llisyyden arvon kasvavan. Ihmiset haluavat kuulua johonkin, olla jostain kotoisin. Suomessakin kansalaisten identiteetti perustuu suurelta osin ihmisten paikalliseen osallistumiseen oman alueensa talouteen ja yhteiskunnalliseen toimintaan. T<8a>m<8a> on rikkaus. Se antaa suuren mahdollisuuden maakuntalehdelle. Toisaalta kun tieto sirpaloituu, tarvitaan aina laatutoimittajia, jotka asettavat palaset kokonaisuudeksi ja antavat asioille taustaa ja yhteyksi<8a>. Journalistin teht<8a>v<8a> ei ehk<8a> ole sanoa, mit<8a> ihmisen pit<8a><8a> ajatella, mutta h<8a>n voi antaa v<8a>lineit<8a> maailman ja maan ymm<8a>rt<8a>miseen ja siten oman k<8a>sityksen muodostamiseen. Se ei ole aina helppoa. Otetaanpa yksi esimerkki vaikka nykyiselt<8a> toimikent<8a>lt<8a>. Miten on mahdollista, ett<8a> amerikkalaisilla markkinoilla heikon luottokelpoisuuden omanneet asuntolainat -subprime-lainat, niin kuin niit<8a> kutsutaan -heiluttelevat raha-ja rahoitusmarkkinoita ymp<8a>ri maailman? Kuinka kauan nykyinen luottamuskriisi voi jatkua? Jos se pitkittyy, mitk<8a> ovat vaikutukset meid<8a>n kansatalouteemme, kotitalouksiin ja yritt<8a>jiin? Suomen Pankissa ja muualla on paljon asiantuntijoita, jotka ovat panostaneet ongelman analysoimiseksi ja my<9a>s sellaisten ratkaisujen aikaan saamiseksi, mill<8a> raha-ja rahoitusmarkkinoiden toiminta turvataan. Mutta t<8a>m<8a>n tiedon analysointiin ja viestin v<8a>litt<8a>miseen me tarvitsemme ammattitaitoisia toimittajia ja tiedotusv<8a>lineit<8a>, joihin kansalaiset luottavat. Rahapolitiikka itsess<8a><8a>n on sek<8a> p<8a><8a>t<9a>ksi<8a> ett<8a> viestint<8a><8a>. Hyv<8a> tarina ja hyv<8a> sis<8a>lt<9a> el<8a><8a> aina. Mutta jokaisen yritysjohtaja-ja toimittajapolven on kamppailtava sellaisten liiketoimintamallien luomiseksi, ett<8a> lehden tekeminen on kannattavaa liiketoimintaa. Siin<8a> tulee haasteita riitt<8a>m<8a><8a>n emmek<8a> tied<8a> kaikkia vastauksia t<8a>n<8a><8a>n. Haluan lopuksi viel<8a> kiitt<8a><8a> Savon Sanomia paljosta, mit<8a> se on vuosien mittaan antanut. Se on aina tarjonnut foorumin, jos on ollut sanottavaa. Mutta se on my<9a>s v<8a>litt<8a>nyt maakunnan naisten ja miesten tuntoja p<8a><8a>tt<8a>jille. Se on tuonut paljon yst<8a>vi<8a> lukuisten toimittajien piirist<8a>. Mutta se on ollut my<9a>s yksi t<8a>rke<8a> yhteinen side meille monille savolaisille, jotka ovat tavalla tai toisella el<8a>neet sen piiriss<8a>.. Nimi<8a> vilisee paljon mieless<8a>. Oli Matti Korhonen. On Jouko Loikkanen ja Juhani Koskinen. On Paavo Lipponen ja Seppo K<8a><8a>ri<8a>inen. On Lasse Lehtinen ja Markku Hyv<8a>rinen. Ja kymmeni<8a>, ehk<8a> satoja muita. Ilman Savon Sanomia moni ketju olisi katkennut.

Title: Speech in Kuopio
text: Speech by Director-General Erkki Liikanen in Mikkeli, Mikkeli Employment and Economic Development Centre 10 years . Speech . Friday 12 October 2007, 12:00 AM Director-General Erkki Liikanen Mikkeli Employment and Economic Development Centre 10 years 12.10.2007 Mikkeli When assessing the state of the economy, it has become customary to share the image of the world with perception before and after the middle of last August. Until the beginning of August, global economic growth was exceptionally strong, still at an annual rate of 4.5%. The growth had continued for as much as the fifth year, which is the longest growing season in more than 30 years. Although U.S. growth was already fading, Asia was a strong driver of the world economy. Europe, too, had finally embarked on a path of sustainable growth, and Latin America and Africa were closing the gap in living standards. In other words, the fundamentals of the world economy seemed to be in order. Then, on 9 August, we woke up to the liquidity crisis in the money and financial markets. The overnight interest rate on loans granted by banks to each other rose sharply. Normally, the overnight rate should have stayed around the key ECB rate of 4%, between 4.06% and 4.08%, but now it jumped more than half a percentage point at once. In addition, commercial papers based on housing, real estate and similar collateral suddenly did not sell at all. In particular, if the debt securities contain even the slightest bit of American subprime credits as collateral, the buyers will not touch them. As market liquidity dried up, companies were forced to turn to banks where they have their credit lines. Banks, on the other hand, borrowed from central banks. The interest rate differential between secured and unsecured loans rose sharply as confidence in market participants had disappeared. For example, euribor rates are just such rates on unsecured, interbank loans. In particular, the 3-month Euribor rates have risen sharply and the corresponding risk premium has also risen by about 0.6 percentage points in the 12-month Euribor rates. Finnish (secured) mortgages are mostly tied to an unsecured 12-month euribor, so households have to pay an extra risk premium. In a conventional mortgage of 100000 euros, the increase in costs is already 200-300 euros per year compared to the level of last July, and the difference is even greater if the reference point is the secured market rate. Admittedly, mortgage interest rates are still reasonable compared to the growth rate of income. The cost of financing for companies has also risen and the availability of financing has decreased. On the other hand, in the corporate bond market, the return of risk premiums to normal levels has, of course, been healthy, as it reduces unnecessary speculation. The only problem today is that the turbulence in the money and financial markets also has an impact on the real economy. How big it is, it cannot be said with certainty, but its sign is negative. The effect can come through many channels. Firstly, the correction of risk pricing will increase the financing costs of companies. Similarly, if banks are forced to take on their balance sheets debt papers that were outside them, which are now unfit for the market, it may impair their ability to lend. Secondly, the volatility of the money and financial markets may have a negative impact on stock market prices and, consequently, on the future expectations of businesses and also of citizens. The third channel of influence may be a slowdown in the growth of consumption, something that is feared right now in the United States. The US Federal Reserve has already cut its key interest rate. The European Central Bank refrained from making the increase already expected by the markets in September. Economic operators are therefore following all new information with great vigilance in order to form the most accurate picture possible of the direction of development. As I said above, the fruits of a long period of growth in the world economy are spread over an exceptionally wide geographical area. Similarly, the long-term growth of the Finnish economy has begun to be felt in an even wider area. It has also been visible in Southern Savonia. Matti Kellokumpu wrote in the annual report that the economic development in South Savo has been reflected especially in the positive development of the metal industry and services. That's the good news. The big question is how Finland and South Savo will fare in the future as economic expectations become more uncertain again. Where do growth factors come from? Finland and also South Savo are facing the retirement of the baby boomers. We take on the challenge of ageing first in Europe and more drastically. When the net labour force begins to decline, the potential for growth is entirely dependent on productivity. What to do? The first step should be to find out whether working lives could be extended. In many professions requiring important manual skills, qualified professionals and women are retiring and young people are just entering education. There are actually three risks; firstly, labour shortages threaten to undermine growth, secondly, the retirement of older people will result in a lot of important tacit knowledge from companies and, thirdly, the financial pressures in the public sector will become more acute. The pension reform will provide better financial incentives for prolonging working lives. But does the atmosphere in the workplace encourage it? Is the contribution of a mature employee sufficiently valued? Should flexibility in working hours also be considered from their point of view? Secondly, even if some continue in working life longer than planned, increasing productivity is key. On average, the wage level in Finland is high, the level of developed countries. Only high productivity will make it possible for work to be maintained in the country and province and for new jobs to be created. In increasing productivity, on the other hand, investments and total productivity, i.e. better recipes, play a key role. The profit development of enterprises has been good on average. Despite the uncertainty in the financial markets, interest rates are below the historical average. If companies' labour needs can be met and the market is good, there should be a basis for investment. The South Savo TE Centre is also delivering regional policy investment subsidies in this field. Traditionally, the productivity of the province has risen as machines that use electricity have replaced muscle power in work processes. Now investment in information technology and better recipes is at least as important. The organization of the company has historically been very hierarchical; the employee has had a foreman, he has his own master and control. ICT-based systems have made it possible to thin out business organisations. Tasks become more independent, everyone's creative ability and imagination can be put to use in solving problems. And that's where the key to productivity growth lies. Three things are needed for this. First on the list are investments in information and communication technologies, which create the conditions. In addition, the use of information technology must be used to continuously develop processes within and between companies, and here, again, the right incentives are important. Finally, we must invest in education and training so that everyone has equal access to the new tools and to be part of the new processes. Thirdly, investments in research and development and innovation are necessary in order to obtain more value added to products and services and, consequently, more room for companies to pay salaries. High productivity and the added value generated by R&D and innovation are both prerequisites for success in an openly competitive market. The public authorities, and here especially the South Savo TE Centre, can play an important role in providing important support to companies. Fourthly, public administration and services face the same challenges in order to increase productivity and also to develop services and processes. Initiative and innovation are equally important here. From a management point of view, the problem is made more difficult by the fact that the feedback or metrics provided by the private sector market test are not always available. Nevertheless, I am sure that indicators can also be applied to the development of public administration and services, which will be drawn up together with the staff. It is important to evaluate not only the inputs, but also the results of the work qualitatively and quantitatively. Well-built metrics are an important tool for change management.

Friday 12 October 2007, 12:00 AM P<8a><8a>johtaja Erkki Liikanen Mikkelin ty<9a>voima-ja elinkeinokeskus 10 vuotta 12.10.2007 Mikkeli Talouden tilaa arvioitaessa on tullut tavaksi jakaa maailman kuva k<8a>sitykseen ennen ja j<8a>lkeen viime elokuun puoliv<8a>lin. Elokuun alkuun saakka maailmantalouden kasvu oli poikkeuksellisen voimakasta, edelleen 4.5 prosentin vuosivauhtia. Kasvu oli jatkunut per<8a>ti viidett<8a> vuotta, mik<8a> on pisin kasvukausi yli 30 vuoteen. Vaikka Yhdysvaltain kasvu oli jo hiipumassa, niin Aasia toimi maailman talouden vahvana veturina. Eurooppakin oli vihdoin p<8a><8a>ssyt kest<8a>v<8a>n kasvun uralle ja Latinalainen Amerikka sek<8a> Afrikka olivat kuromassa elintasokuilua suppeammaksi. Toisin sanoen, maailman talouden perus-tekij<8a>t n<8a>yttiv<8a>t olevan kunnossa. Sitten, elokuun 9. p<8a>iv<8a>n<8a> havahduttiin raha-ja rahoitusmarkkinoiden likviditeettikriisiin. Pankkien toisilleen my<9a>nt<8a>mien lainojen y<9a>n yli -korko nousi rajusti. Normaalisti y<9a>n yli koron olisi pit<8a>nyt pysy<8a> EKP:n ohjauskoron eli 4 % tuntumassa, 4.06 -4.08 %:n v<8a>lill<8a>, mutta nyt se hypp<8a>si kerralla yli puoli prosenttiyksikk<9a><8a>. Lis<8a>ksi, asunto-, kiinteist<9a>-ja vastaaviin vakuuksiin nojanneet yritystodistukset eiv<8a>t yht<8a>kki<8a> menneet kaupaksi juuri ollenkaan. Erityisesti, jos velkapaperissa on v<8a>h<8a>nkin amerikkalaisia subprime-luottoja vakuutena, eiv<8a>t ostajat koske niihin. Markkinoiden likviditeetin kuivuessa yritykset joutuivat k<8a><8a>ntym<8a><8a>n pankkien puoleen, joissa heill<8a> on luottolimiittins<8a>. Pankit taas lainasivat keskuspankeilta. Vakuudellisten ja vakuudettomien lainojen korkoero nousi rajusti, kun luottamus markkinaosapuoliin oli kadonnut. Suomen (vakuudelliset) asuntolainat on useimmiten sidottu vakuudettomaan 12 kuukauden euriboriin, joten kotitaloudet joutuvat maksamaan ylim<8a><8a>r<8a>ist<8a> riskilis<8a><8a>. Tavanomaisessa 100000 euron asunto-lainassa kustannusten kasvu on jo 200 -300 euroa vuodessa verrattuna viime hein<8a>kuun tasoon ja ero on viel<8a> suurempi, jos vertailukohtana on vakuudellinen markkinakorko. Tosin asuntolainojen korkotaso on edelleen kohtuullinen verrattuna tulojen kasvuvauhtiin. My<9a>s yritysten rahoituksen kustannukset ovat nousseet ja rahoituksen saatavuus heikentynyt. Toisaalta yrityslainamarkkinoilla riskilisien paluu normaalille tasolle on toki ollut tervett<8a>, sill<8a> v<8a>hent<8a><8a>h<8a>n se tarpeetonta spekulaatiota. Ongelmana t<8a>n<8a><8a>n on vain se, ett<8a> raha-ja rahoitusmarkkinoiden turbulenssilla on vaikutuksensa my<9a>s reaalitalouteen. Kuinka suuri se on, sit<8a> ei varmuudella voi sanoa, mutta sen etumerkki on negatiivinen. Vaikutus voi tulla montaa kanavaa pitkin. Ensinn<8a>kin riskihinnoittelun korjautuminen nostaa yritysten rahoituskustannuksia. Samoin jos pankit joutuvat ottamaan taseeseensa niiden ulkopuolella olleita, nyt markkinoille kelpaamattomia, velka-papereita, se saattaa heikent<8a><8a> niiden luotonantokyky<8a>. Toiseksi, raha-ja rahoitusmarkkinoiden ep<8a>vakaus saattaa vaikuttaa p<9a>rssikursseihin alentavasti ja sit<8a> kautta yritysten ja my<9a>s kansalaisten tulevaisuuden odotuksiin. Kolmas vaikutuskanava voi olla kulutuksen kasvun hidastuminen, mit<8a> juuri nyt Yhdysvalloissa pel<8a>t<8a><8a>n. USA:n keskuspankki on jo laskenut ohjauskorkoaan. Euroopan Keskuspankki pid<8a>tt<8a>ytyi tekem<8a>st<8a> jo markkinoiden odottamaa korotusta syyskuussa. Talouden toimijat seuraavatkin suurella tarkkaa-vaisuudella kaikkea uutta informaatiota voidakseen muodostaa mahdollisimman tarkan k<8a>sityksen kehityksen suunnasta. Kuten edell<8a> totesin, maailmantalous pitk<8a>n kasvukauden hedelm<8a>t ovat jakautuneet maantieteellisesti poikkeuksellisen laajalle alueelle. Samoin Suomen talouden pitk<8a><8a>n jatkunut kasvu on alkanut tuntua entist<8a> laajemmalla alueella. Se on n<8a>kynyt my<9a>s Etel<8a>-Savossa. Matti Kellokumpu kirjoitti vuosi-kertomuksessa, ett<8a> Etel<8a>-Savon suhdannekehitys on n<8a>kynyt erityisesti metallialojen ja palvelujen my<9a>nteisen<8a> kehityksen<8a>. Se on hyv<8a> uutinen. Suuri kysymys on se, kuinka Suomi ja Etel<8a>-Savo p<8a>rj<8a><8a>v<8a>t tulevaisuudessa talouden odotusten muuttuessa j<8a>lleen ep<8a>varmemmiksi. Mist<8a> kasvun tekij<8a>t? Suomen ja my<9a>s Etel<8a>-Savon edess<8a> on suurten ik<8a>luokkien siirtyminen el<8a>kkeelle. Otamme vastaan ik<8a><8a>ntymisen haasteen ensimm<8a>isen Euroopassa ja muita jyrkemp<8a>n<8a>. Kun ty<9a>voima alkaa netto-m<8a><8a>r<8a>isesti v<8a>henty<8a>, niin kasvun mahdollisuudet j<8a><8a>v<8a>t kokonaan tuottavuuden varaan. Mit<8a> tehd<8a>? Ensimm<8a>iseksi olisi selvitett<8a>v<8a>, voitaisiinko ty<9a>uria pident<8a><8a>. Monissa t<8a>rkeit<8a> k<8a>den taitoja vaativissa ammateissa p<8a>tev<8a>t ammattimiehet ja -naiset ovat siirtym<8a>ss<8a> el<8a>kkeelle ja nuoret ovat vasta hakeutumassa koulutukseen. Riskej<8a> on itse asiassa kolme; ensinn<8a>kin ty<9a>voimapula uhkaa vied<8a> kasvulta pohjan, toiseksi ik<8a><8a>ntyvien el<8a>kkeellesiirtymisen my<9a>t<8a> l<8a>htee yrityksist<8a> paljon t<8a>rke<8a><8a> hiljaista tietoa ja kolmanneksi julkisen sektorin rahoituspaineet k<8a>rjistyv<8a>t. El<8a>keuudistus tuo entist<8a> paremmat taloudelliset kannustimet ty<9a>uran pident<8a>miselle. Mutta kannustaako siihen ilmapiiri ty<9a>paikoilla? Arvostetaanko varttuneen ty<9a>tekij<8a>n panosta riitt<8a>v<8a>sti? Olisiko ty<9a>ajan joustoa mietitt<8a>v<8a> my<9a>s heid<8a>n n<8a>k<9a>kulmastaan? Toiseksi, vaikka osa jatkaisikin ty<9a>el<8a>m<8a>ss<8a> suunniteltua pitemp<8a><8a>n, tuottavuuden kasvattaminen on avainasemassa. Suomen palkkataso on keskim<8a><8a>rin korkeaa, kehittyneiden maiden tasoa. Vain korkea tuottavuus mahdollistaa sen, ett<8a> ty<9a> s<8a>ilyy maassa ja maakunnassa ja ett<8a> uusia ty<9a>paikkoja syntyy. Tuottavuuden nostamisessa taas avainasemassa ovat investoinnit ja kokonaistuottavuus eli paremmat reseptit. Yritysten tuloskehitys on ollut keskim<8a><8a>rin hyv<8a>. Rahoitusmarkkinoiden ep<8a>varmuudesta huolimatta korkotaso on alle historiallisen keskiarvon. Jos yritysten ty<9a>voimatarve voidaan tyydytt<8a><8a> ja markkinat ovat hyv<8a>t, tulisi investoinneille olla pohjaa. Etel<8a>-Savon TE-keskus on v<8a>litt<8a>m<8a>ss<8a> my<9a>s t<8a>ll<8a> kent<8a>ll<8a> aluepoliittisia investointitukia. Perinteisesti maakunnan tuottavuus on noussut, kun s<8a>hk<9a><8a> k<8a>ytt<8a>v<8a>t koneet ovat korvanneet lihasvoimaa ty<9a>prosesseissa. Nyt investoinnit tietotekniikkaan ja parempiin resepteihin ovat v<8a>hint<8a><8a>n yht<8a> t<8a>rke<8a>ss<8a> asemassa. Yrityksen organisaatio on historiallisesti ollut hyvin hierarkkinen; ty<9a>ntekij<8a>ll<8a> on ollut ty<9a>njohtaja, h<8a>nell<8a> oma p<8a><8a>llikk<9a>ns<8a> ja kontrollinsa. Tieto-ja viestint<8a>tekniikkaan perustuvat j<8a>rjestelm<8a>t ovat mahdollistaneet yritysorganisaatioiden ohentamisen. Teht<8a>vist<8a> tulee itsen<8a>isempi<8a>, jokaisen luova kyky ja mielikuvitus voidaan ottaa k<8a>ytt<9a><9a>n ongelmien ratkaisussa. Ja siin<8a> on avain tuottavuuden kasvuun. T<8a>h<8a>n tarvitaan kolme asiaa. Ensimm<8a>isen<8a> listalla ovat investoinnit tieto-ja viestint<8a>tekniikkaan, jotka luovat edellytyksi<8a>. Lis<8a>ksi tietotekniikkaa hyv<8a>ksik<8a>ytt<8a>en on pyritt<8a>v<8a> jatkuvasti kehitt<8a>m<8a><8a>n yrityksen sis<8a>isi<8a> ja yritysten v<8a>lisi<8a> prosesseja ja t<8a>ss<8a> taas oikeat kannustimet ovat t<8a>rkeit<8a>. Lopuksi on panostettava koulutukseen niin, niin ett<8a> kaikilla on yht<8a>l<8a>iset mahdollisuudet k<8a>ytt<8a><8a> uusia v<8a>lineit<8a> ja olla osana uusissa prosesseissa. Kolmanneksi panostukset tutkimus-ja tuotekehitystoimintaan ja innovaatioihin ovat v<8a>ltt<8a>m<8a>tt<9a>mi<8a>, jotta tuotteisiin ja palveluihin saadaan enemm<8a>n arvonlis<8a><8a> ja siten my<9a>s yrityksille palkanmaksuvaraa. Korkea tuottavuus ja T&K-toiminnan ja innovaatioiden tuoma arvonlis<8a> ovat molemmat menestymisen edellytyksi<8a> avoimesti kilpailluilla markkinoilla. Julkinen valta ja t<8a><8a>ll<8a> erityisesti Etel<8a>-Savon TE-keskus voivat olla antamassa t<8a>rke<8a><8a> tukea yrityksille. Nelj<8a>nneksi julkista hallintoa ja palveluja koskevat samat haasteet tuottavuuden nostamiseksi ja my<9a>s palvelujen ja prosessien kehitt<8a>miseksi. Aloitteellisuus ja innovatiivisuus ovat t<8a><8a>ll<8a> yht<8a> t<8a>rkeit<8a>. Johtamisen kannalta ongelman tekee vaikeammaksi se, ett<8a> yksityisen sektorin markkinatestin antamaa palautetta tai mittareita ei ole aina k<8a>ytett<8a>viss<8a>. Silti olen varma, ett<8a> my<9a>s julkisen hallinnon ja palvelujen kehitt<8a>miseen voidaan soveltaa mittareita, jotka laaditaan yhdess<8a> henkil<9a>kunnan kanssa. On t<8a>rke<8a><8a> arvioida ei vain panoksia, vaan my<9a>s ty<9a>n tuloksia laadullisesti ja m<8a><8a>r<8a>llisesti. Hyvin rakennetut mittarit ovat t<8a>rke<8a> muutosjohtamisen v<8a>line.

Title: Similarities and differences between the Nordic EU economies
text: Erkki Liikanen, Director General: Similarities and differences between the Nordic EU economies. Finnish-Swedish Chamber of Commerce, Stockholm . Speech . Monday15 October 2007,12:00 AM Chefdirektor Erkki Liikanen Finnish-Swedish Chamber of Commerce, Stockholm 15.10.2007 at 12.00 Represent (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and. . interviews/documents/finsk_svenska_handelskammaren.ppt) (ppt) SIMILARITIES AND DIFFERENCES BETWEEN THE NORDIC EU ECONOMIES Figure 1. Similarities and differences between the Nordic EU economies Figure 2. Monetary policy Finland, Sweden and Denmark all have different monetary policies. Finland, together with the other countries in the euro area, has embarked on a single monetary policy and has the euro as its currency. Sweden has its krona and its own monetary policy based on inflation targets. Denmark also has its krona left, but unlike Sweden, has chosen to peg the krona's rate to the euro. Figure 3. The people appreciate the euro in Finland Thus, we have three textbook examples of different monetary regimes in the Nordic EU countries; we have a country (Finland) that has chosen to join a monetary union; a country (Denmark) that has chosen to hold its own currency but to link it to the euro via the ERM II cooperation; and a country (Sweden) that has chosen to hold its national currency and to conduct an independent monetary policy with direct inflation targets and floating exchange rates. Norway's monetary policy regime is close to the Swedish one. The same can be said of Iceland, but Iceland differs in that it has had a greater degree of sensitivity to what is happening to the currencies of the so-called growing economies. In future, I will simplify the analysis and concentrate on Finland, Sweden and Denmark, the Nordic EU economies, well aware that Norway and Iceland are also, of course, Nordic economies. Similarities between the Nordic countries 1. GDP growth Economic development in Finland, Sweden and Denmark has been strong in recent years. The development has also been very similar, surprisingly similar, in these three countries, and one wonders how this is possible? Figure 4. The growth rate in GDP Compared with the growth of other Western European countries, GDP growth in the Nordic countries has been very strong in recent years. In the early 2000s, all three EU countries experienced an economic downturn, but since then the trend has been strong. In 2006, both the Finnish and Danish economies grew by over 5% per year and the Swedish economy grew by almost 5%. The picture shows that finnish and swedish development in particular are closely linked, while the development of the Danish economy sometimes differs from the rest, for example in 2005. 2. Productivity The higher GDP growth in Sweden and Finland in recent years than in the euro area countries on average stems mainly from the faster growth in labour productivity. So what is behind this development? Why has labour productivity developed so favourably with us? Figure 5. Sectoral contribution to labour productivity In general, growth stemming from what is known as deepening ICT capital has been greater in the Nordic countries than in the euro area in general. The Nordic countries have both increased their use of ICT and used ICT for reorganization and streamlining. Nordic companies have used ICT to increase productivity both in service industries and in more traditional industries. Recently, empirical research has shown that investments in information and communication technologies, ICT, have noticeably affected productivity growth in the United States. This supports the theory that Scandinavian productivity growth could stem from higher investment in ICT. Major investments in education and research are also likely to have played a decisive role in the development of labour productivity. The productivity development of Sweden and Finland has differed from that of Denmark. As you can see from the picture, the development of Finland and Sweden during the years 1995-2004 has been very smooth and at a very high international level. However, Sweden's labour productivity has grown more in trade and transport, while Finland's labour productivity growth has concentrated more on manufacturing. Denmark's productivity growth has been lower than in Finland and Sweden, but still higher than the European average. (During the first half of 2007, productivity growth has been weaker than expected in Sweden, but it is better to be cautious before drawing conclusions based on two quarters.) A potential explanation for why the Nordic countries' productivity increases have been higher than the European average may also be found in the pro-competitive liberalisation of the product market. The Nordic countries have relatively little regulation of the product market and economic policy has focused on promoting and highlighting the competitiveness of companies. The liberalisation of product markets usually leads to the efficiency of organisations and thus to the use of various technological tools. Empirical research shows that there is a positive relationship between product market deregulation and productivity growth. 3. Inflation Figure 6. Inflation Inflation developments have been similar in the Nordic EU economies in recent years. This development is to some extent surprising, since it is precisely in monetary policy that the three countries have chosen their three different regimes. However, the goal of monetary policy coincides; price stability is sought in all these countries, only the approaches are different. 4. Large public sector and high taxes Let us turn for a moment to another common Nordic factor; the large public sector. All the Nordic countries have a large public sector. Sweden has the largest public expenditure per GDP: about 56%. Finland and Denmark also have a government expenditure share exceeding 50% of GDP and are thus among Europe's "top throws" vis-a-vis the size of the public sector. Figure 7. Share of civil servants in total employment This has led to a large amount of public employment, which to various extents has also helped to keep employment high, especially in Sweden and Denmark. There, public employment accounts for over 30% of total employment. Finland's figure is around 25%, while the corresponding figure in the US is 15%, in Ireland 13% and in the Netherlands 11%. In order to finance the large public sector, extensive social security and employment policy, the Nordic countries have high taxes. Both the average tax wedge and the marginal tax rate for highly paid individuals are very high, especially in Sweden. Figure 8. General government surplus/deficit Figure 9. General government debt Hand in hand with the high taxes goes the fiscal discipline of the Nordic economies. The Nordic countries have long been characterised by a healthy public sector with funding surpluses and relatively small public debt. The picture shows that all three countries have surpluses in public finances. The following picture again shows that public debt is falling. The level is internationally low. However, it should be borne in mind that public finances must be strong at the moment, as we are still enjoying a relatively favourable age structure. 5. Even distribution of income The fifth and final similarity, which I choose to mention today, is the even distribution of income in the Nordic countries. Sweden has the most even income distribution, followed by Finland and Denmark. Although income inequality is small, there are still signs of increased income inequality in the Nordic economies. Inequality in gross income has increased steadily over the past decade in all the Nordic countries. However, this development has been slower than in the Anglo-Saxon countries. The development of the Nordic countries has thus been astonishingly similar in recent years. One would think that three different monetary policy regimes would lead to different economic developments. Many also believed when Finland joined the euro area that it would lead to the similar economic development of the Nordic economies starting to differ more and more. However, this has not happened. In addition to the Nordic countries, Ireland is an example of a small, remote country with fiscal discipline that has managed to use its position between North America and Europe to build its economy. Ireland's economic growth rate has exceeded the performance of the Nordic countries for some time. How do the Nordic countries differ from each other? Figure 10. How do the Nordic countries differ from each other? 1. Attitude towards the EC/EU Despite the fact that the Nordic economies have developed surprisingly similarly in recent years, there are also differences to point to. Perhaps the clearest difference between Finland, Sweden and Denmark is the attitude towards the EU and the former EC. For Finland, entry into the EU meant safety and security in a different way than for Denmark and Sweden and a noticeable change from the somewhat isolated situation in which the country had found itself. A similar situation arose with the entry into the euro area, when the euro was introduced. For Finland, it was very important to take part in the decisions at the core of Europe. In Sweden and Denmark, they thought along partly different lines and were more concerned about their own "independence". They chose to keep their own currencies and their own monetary policy. However, the differences between the Nordic economies extend beyond the purely political decisions that have been chosen to be taken. 2. Labour market The structure and functioning of labour markets is one of the great things that separates the Nordic countries. Compared to the other countries in the euro area, Finland appears to be very much like a model country with high female employment, low long-term unemployment and a high employment rate in general. When looking at Finnish development from a Nordic perspective, the picture is not as positive. Finland is currently lagging behind in terms of both employment and unemployment. One explanation for why this is the case can be found in the employment of the elderly. Here, Finland has failed compared to Sweden and Denmark. Finland's development is also weak in terms of employment among young people compared to Denmark, but in that comparison Finland is doing better than Sweden. Figure 11. Youth unemployment Perhaps the biggest difference between Finland and the other two countries concerns the employment rate. Our employment rate is about 70% while Sweden's is about 73% and Denmark's is about 77%. Figure 12. Employment rate Figure 13. Share of part-time employment Another noticeable difference between Finland and the other two countries is the share of part-time employment in employed persons. The strong growth of part-time jobs has become a trend across Europe in recent years. This trend has not been reflected in Finland to the same extent as elsewhere, mainly due to the high level of full-time employment of women. However, this has an impact on the employment statistics, which for Finland look worse. The picture shows that the share of part-time employment in all employment is almost 10 percentage points higher in Sweden and Denmark than in Finland. The great differences between the labour markets of Denmark and Finland in particular also stem from the labour market policies pursued. Denmark's labour market is seen as one of Europe's most flexible and the model is also sometimes referred to as the "flexicurity" model. Wage negotiations in Denmark are conducted at company level. The low level of redundancy cover is compensated by very generous unemployment protection. Active labour market policies are used very extensively and the low marginal tax wedge in Denmark provides incentives for mobility and productivity increases. In addition, young people under the age of 25 are subject to some coercive measures aimed at activating them in the labour market. Sweden, and especially Finland, certainly has a great interest in studying the Danish model, even though no model can be directly copied from one country to another. Figure 14. Arbetskraftsbrist Despite national deviations, the Nordic labour markets also have a common growing problem and that is the lack of skilled labor. All three countries that I have examined here have a high labour shortage in the construction industry. Especially in Denmark, the shortage has spread to other sectors quickly. Denmark's low unemployment rate means that the labour shortage risks becoming even more acute than in Finland and Sweden, but the problem is characteristic of all these countries. The picture shows the shortage of labour in industrial enterprises. The problems are thus growing in all three countries, but Sweden's situation looks significantly brighter than That of Finland and Denmark. 3. Structure of the enterprise sector and the structure of production A final important feature that separates the Nordic economies is the countries' different corporate structure and production structure. Our economy is still based on industry to a greater extent than the other countries. Finland's industrial orientation stems from strong traditional large industry: the forest industry, the metal industry and later the high-tech industry. Figure 15. Branschvis bruttovardeokning, 2006 The growth of service industries has not been as strong in Finland as in the rest of Europe. The picture shows that both the share of financial services in gross value added and that of other services is noticeably lower in Finland than in Sweden and Denmark. Nevertheless, the role of services in Finnish society is also growing all the time. The company structure itself also differs between countries. Denmark is characterized by an ownership structure that is often based on institutional ownership in listed companies. Finland and Sweden have been quicker to integrate business into the world economy through acquisitions, while in Denmark there have been significantly fewer foreign acquisitions. The differences in business structure between Finland and Sweden on the one hand and Denmark on the other are quite large. In Sweden and especially Finland, large companies (with more than 250 employees) account for the absolute majority of value added, 62% and 65% respectively. In Denmark, on the other hand, large companies generate only about 53% of value added. The difference in the structure of enterprises comes from the fact that small enterprises (with 10-49 employees) and medium-sized enterprises (with 50-249 employees) in Denmark create a larger share of the increase in value than in Finland and Sweden. Conclusion The Nordic countries that I have examined here are characterized by many similarities, but also by some differences in addition to the different monetary policy regimes. Economic development in recent years has been convincing and many eyes are on the Nordic region as an example region. As is well known, people sometimes talk about the "Nordic model" when examining the institutional solutions typical of Nordic welfare policy, but also when you think about the positive developments in the region. Whether it is correct to talk about a model or just about similar policies may be unsaid. But what are the reasons why the Nordic economies have done so well despite the large public sector? Finland, Sweden and Denmark are small open economies. Foreign trade is very important for the prosperity of all three countries and all three countries have favoured free trade. At the same time, they are all pro-competitive and have repeatedly demonstrated an understanding of the importance of market forces for economic growth. Finland, Sweden and Denmark have also had a tight fiscal policy and thus a healthy public sector despite the large public sector. The Nordic countries are also constitutional states, with a highly developed judiciary and low corruption. Of course, we must take into account that the large EU countries have "even greater" problems with demography and public finances, and this helps to ensure that the Nordic countries come out well in comparative statistics. (But the fact that the challenges are relatively less severe than in the rest of the EU does not make them "absolutely" lessened!) What is a fact is that many similar economic policy decisions have been taken in Sweden, Finland and Denmark. In particular, decisions relating to economic liberalisation, the promotion of competition and efforts to increase productivity and thus economic growth have been important for our, Swedish and Danish successes in recent years. Common to the three economies is also the idea of an inclusive society that tries to avoid individuals being excluded. This requires a flexible and economical organization of social systems, in which productivity grows. Such a system is a challenge but at the same time also an asset. The Nordic countries also have common future challenges: One challenge is the productivity of the public sector. This challenge is becoming more and more pressing as the demand for social and health care services grows. Another challenge is to ensure that we have enough labour in the future. We need to discuss what measures we should take to solve these problems. We cannot avoid the issue of labour supply and labour taxation. The Nordic countries still have a lot to learn and they have many new challenges ahead of them. Economic success requires continuous reforms. Keeping a country competitive, growing strongly and with high employment while maintaining a comprehensive welfare society is no easy feat.
