Title: Does the turmoil in the financial and financial markets threaten growth prospects?
text: President Erkki Liikanen: Is the turmoil in the financial and financial markets threatening growth prospects? Parliamentary Finance Committee . Speech . Wednesday17 October 2007,12:00AM Director General Erkki Liikanen Parliamentary Finance Committee 17.10.2007 Speech associated kalvosarja (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and. . interviews/documents/071017eltalousvaliokunta.pdf) Figure 2: The three main questions of the introduction The unrest in the money markets, which began in August, has been partly unprecedented. In the next introduction, the intention is to try to answer three questions. Firstly, what has happened in the money markets, secondly, why the unrest started and, thirdly, what are the consequences for the growth of the national economy and the development of the financial markets. WHAT WAS THE UNREST IN THE MONEY MARKETS? Figure 3: Northern Rock stock price Turmoil surfaced in the money market on Thursday, August 9, when the demand for liquidity, short-term liquidity, rose sharply. In the euro area money markets, this led to a sharp overnight rise in interest rates. Why is overnight rate so important? It is very important because the overnight interest rate is the first step in the mechanism through which monetary policy decisions are transmitted to the economy. Graph 4: Overnight interest rate in the euro area When we decide on interest rate policy in the Governing Council of the European Central Bank, we decide on the level of the policy rate. This policy rate has been 4% since the June meeting. In order to ensure that the money markets operate on the basis of the monetary policy set by the Council, the ECB aims to keep the overnight interest rate as close as possible to the key interest rate through its market operations. In general, the overnight rate has been stable, hovering between 0.06 and 0.08 percentage points over the policy rate. But on August 9, this overnight rate jumped to 4.6%, or more than half a percentage point above the policy rate. The situation was completely exceptional and at odds with the monetary policy decided. It should also be remembered that the overnight rate is the starting point of the yield curve and the anchor of the time structure of interest rates. It is the interest rate on the shortest deposit and credit and normally the interest rates on longer-term investments gradually increase from it. A stable overnight interest rate is an important factor for the functioning of the market, as the market has tied other financial instruments (e.g. swaps) to it. Graph 5: Overnight rates of the euro, dollar and pound Similar turmoil also occurred in the United States, however, due to the time difference a little later (In fact, the demand for Euro liquidity took off from the demand for dollar liquidity). Overnight in Britain, too, interest rates rose in the same way. The events were not limited to just overnight interest rates. In the interbank market, the interest rate differential between secured and unsecured money was wide-ranging. For example, the interest rate differential between a secured and an unsecured three-month loan has for years been in the order of less than a tenth of a percent. This low interest rate differential was based on trust between banks. Banks that had extra money in the coffers lent it with a low margin to those in need of liquidity without collateral. The reference rate for these loans is called euribor. Figure 6: Interest rate on an unsecured and secured 3-month loan But then confidence declined and people began to suspect that the opposing parties had risks that were not exactly known. The interest rate on unsecured money rose sharply, in three-month investments by as much as half a percentage point. When, in particular, the three-month Euribor rate and the 12-month Euribor rate  although slightly less  rose as a result of the unrest, so did the linked credit rates. Chart 7: The price of hedging against credit risk in the euro area The rapid growth in mistrust and risk awareness was also reflected in the corporate finance markets. Today, corporate finance has evolved in such a way that a bank may grant a large loan to its corporate client, even if it does not take the entire loan risk, because it would be too large for one part of the company. For a fee, the bank may transfer e.g. half of the risk of the loan to investors who are compensated for bearing the risk a little like interest. The increase in the price of risk hedging means an increase in the cost of corporate financing for the company. Risk awareness grew rapidly everywhere. When it is not known exactly where the risks are, everyone is suspected. In such a situation, investors want to put the money in a place where there is no risk of bankruptcy and from which they can get their money out very quickly if necessary. Such an investment object is a government bond. A Western state does not go bankrupt, and if you want to sell a bond, it is easy to do so. When suddenly many people want to buy government bonds, high demand raises the price of these debt securities and, accordingly, lowers the interest income from them. Let's see what happened in the sovereign bond market in the US and Europe last August. Chart 8: Interest yield on US 2-year and 10-year benchmark government bonds In August, investors fled the risky market and transferred their money to a safe haven. Due to the huge demand for loan papers, interest rates fell sharply, even by more than half a percentage point in a matter of days and by a total of just over one percentage point. Graph 9: Yields on euro benchmark 2- and 10-year government bonds The same development was also visible in Europe. Concern about the risks grew sharply and the money was wanted for security. Interest rates on two-year loans fell by more than half a percentage point in mid-August. If the government issued a bond at that time, it received money cheaply. At the same time, the cost of financing in the private sector rose. Risk premiums, i.e. interest rate differentials between the state and risks of varying degrees the loans between private companies had been reduced to unduly small amounts over the past few years. The situation changed rapidly in August. Graph 10: Risk premium on banks' 10-year loans compared to government loans The figure shows the evolution of the difference in interest rates on bank loans and government loans in recent years. Indeed, in August, the risk premiums on bank loans rose sharply after a long period of exceptionally low levels. Still, when you compare the increased risk premiums with the beginning of the decade, their level is by no means exceptionally high. What did the central banks do in this situation? Did they really just pump billions of money into the market, as some media reported? One of the basic tasks of the Central Bank is to ensure that the money market has sufficient liquidity in all circumstances. Banks need liquidity, liquidity, for example, to clear interbank payments, to meet depositors' cash needs and to acquire banknotes to be passed on to the public. The instruments of monetary policy, while at the same time ensuring liquidity, are market operations, the standing facilities made available to credit institutions and the minimum reserves required of credit institutions. It is through these instruments that the shortest money market interest rates are kept close to the policy rate, i.e. the policy rate. What did the European Central Bank do on August 9, when it was seen that overnight interest rates had jumped to 4.6%? Due to the time differences, it was the ECB that faced the unrest as the first Western central bank. Immediately after the turbulence began, on Thursday 9 August, the ECB launched an additional market operation called a fine-tuning operation. With its help, the Central Bank offered banks the opportunity to lend excess liquidity overnight. Banks had to provide normal security for the credit and in this first operation the borrowing rate was 4%, the key ECB interest rate. The decision was preceded by an exchange of information and discussion between eurosystem central banks. The Bank of Finland was involved in this. Even before the operation was carried out, the markets were informed that the Central Bank was aware of the problems in the money market and would act accordingly if necessary. Graph 11: The ECB's fine-tuning and longer-term refinancing operations Overnight, the rise in the interest rate was halted, but uncertainty and mistrust led to a sharp rise in unsecured money market rates, especially the three-month Euribor rates, as reported above. However, monetary policy is not a tool to eliminate uncertainty or mistrust between private banks. The market tension was not only limited to overnight interest rates, but also extended over a longer period. In order to respond to strong demand, the Governing Council decided to provide additional liquidity against collateral for a period of 3 months (in maturity). These longer-term operations, which were part of the monetary policy toolkit, were intended to give market participants time to repriced their portfolios and also to write off potential losses, which is necessary to reduce mistrust in the markets. Measures to stabilise financial markets continue. WHAT TRIGGERED THE UNREST IN THE MONEY AND CAPITAL MARKETS? As is well known, the unrest in the financial markets originated in the United States. The trigger was the rapidly increasing payment difficulties in the so-called "payment". in the subprime market in the United States, when low-credit households that took out mortgages ran into difficulties due to rising interest rates and stagnation in house prices. A subprime loan applicant is a person who cannot get a mortgage on the market under normal conditions because his credit history does not meet the basic requirements. As a result, they end up paying a higher interest rate on their loans. Figure 12: What is behind market unrest? In early 2007, the picture of a worrying development quickly strengthened. Why? Approximately 14% of the mortgage portfolio consists of these subprime loans, of which 9 percentage points are variable-rate and 5 percentage points fixed-rate. The loan was often issued on the principle of 2 28, that is, first two payment-free years, often also at a very low interest rate and without self-financing. After these two years, the borrowing rate rises sharply and repayments begin. Even those with low solvency survived the situation during rising housing prices, because after two years they could sell the apartment, pay off the debts and start the project from scratch, or negotiate a subprime loan into a better loan as the credit history improved. But when the rise in house prices stopped or house prices even fell at the same time as interest rates jumped first, for example. To 9%, and then to 12%, households quickly ran into great difficulties. Customers were unable to pay interest on loans and loan amortization. Payment defaults spread quickly. But how, then, do the defaults of low-income American mortgage lenders lead to turmoil in financial markets around the world? It is linked, on the one hand, to the low interest rates of recent years and, on the other, to the intensive development of new financial instruments. Graph 13: Innovation in financial instruments has a shared credit risk The securitisation of mortgages started already in the 1970s. The aim was to immediately bring long-term mortgage receivables into a marketable and liquid form. When a lender securitizes a large bundle of mortgages, it sells the rights to interest and amortization to investors and gets the money instantly. This has also provided opportunities for the rapid growth of banks. Graph 14: Traditional mortgage securitisation The development and use of new financial instruments gained new momentum in the early 2000s from exceptionally low interest rates, especially in the United States. The US policy rate was only 1%, and both short-term and long-term market rates were lower than investors were used to. For this reason, more and more people wanted investments with a clearly higher return than this. However, high returns were not obtained from traditional investments, so it was necessary to look for increasingly innovative and, at the same time, higher-risk investment products. Financial institutions responded to this by developing increasingly complex debt securities. It is precisely these new, complex financial products that have been at the centre of the unrest in recent weeks. There are many species, but I will go through one in the following. Graph 15: Subprime credit and secured debt securities The first actor in the chain is a salesman who goes to meet a loan customer. He can have products from up to five banks in his portfolio. Once he has agreed on a loan with the client, he takes the loan papers to the bank and receives a commission on the sale. His contribution ends here. The bank then bundles the loan with other similar mortgages into a package, which it sells to a separate company out of its own balance sheet. Thus, from the very beginning of the bank, a thin connection with the client is broken. Together with the credit rating agencies, the new company will refine these loans into bonds with different risks, with different privileges on the cash flow generated by the loans, i.e. interest and amortization. The highest credit rating is given to those slices of the package that are the last to suffer from the insolvency of debtors. Slices are sold to international investors. In recent years, investors increasingly included special investment companies set up by banks, which financed the purchase of bonds by issuing very short-term commercial papers themselves, secured by purchased bonds. Since short-term interest rates are lower than the interest rate on long-term debt securities investments, the special investment company makes a good profit by taking advantage of this difference in interest rates. The risk is also considered manageable, as credit rating agencies have given a high rating. However, in case there are temporary problems with the liquidity of the special investment company, the company agrees with one or more banks on a separate credit line. Where, then, did the problem arise and spread? As information about the increasing defaults on subprime loans spread more widely, international credit rating agencies  in the opinion of many, too late  started to downgrade the credit ratings of securities structures containing subprime loans in June and July. In August, investors no longer wanted to buy these papers or take them as collateral for commercial papers. The perception of risks spread, but when it was not known exactly where and how great the risks were, everyone was suspected. Graph 16: Consequences for money markets Investors withdrew from the market for these securities, almost completely halting the issuance of new (mortgage) secured debt securities and secondary market trading. SSAs could no longer finance the (mortgage) secured debt securities they bought from the bank with short-term commercial papers, and instead had to resort to a credit line agreed with the bank. The need for liquidity shifted to banks, and many banks were squeezed with their own financing. As a result of the collapse in the financing of special investment companies, banks are forced to write off a large amount of the debt securities they sell back to their balance sheets and to make provision for write-downs. The losses incurred by the banks as a result of these are considerable. Major international investment banks have already published information on the size of write-downs, and some banks are seeing a loss in their third-quarter results. In Germany, two banks have been rescued from the subprime crisis by means of structural arrangements. The lack of confidence and liquidity problems in the interbank money market are a major problem and, if they persist for a long time, a serious threat. In this regard, an increase in information about the real losses of banks improves the situation. The increased risk premiums are reflected in the loans granted by banks. The situation that has arisen speaks of mistrust between financial market participants and increased uncertainty about one's own and counterparties' financial situation. Interest rates on unsecured loans have risen. Commercial paper sales have continued to be sluggish. It has become more difficult to put together financial packages related to large acquisitions. WHAT ARE THE CONSEQUENCES FOR THE FINANCIAL MARKETS? WHAT ABOUT THE NATIONAL ECONOMY? To begin with, the money and capital markets. If we look at the development of stock prices in the United States and Europe, we can see that the general trend has been steady, but the rates of banks and other credit institutions have fallen. Graph 17: Us stock price developments Graph 18: Stock price developments in Europe What has been interesting about the financial sector has been that while banks have announced losses related to the unrest and subprime credit of recent months, their share prices have since risen. Investors' doubts about the extent of the risks are high, but when banks do a repricing of their products and write off their losses, it restores confidence. It should be remembered that banks have had strong results for a long time and, as a result, balance sheets are also strong. Overall, the direct participation of European banks in the US subprime loan market has been limited and therefore direct losses from there will be limited. But many European banks have been active and major players in the market for various subprime-linked debt securities and are therefore forced to record losses. The Nordic banks are expected to make relatively small losses out of the market turmoil. According to the Financial Supervisory Authority, the subprime risks of Finnish banks are very low. Whether everything will return to normal after the turbulence is an important question. In the money and capital markets, many believe in at least three changes as a result of the unrest in late summer and autumn: Figure 19: What changes does turbulence bring to financial markets? 1. The pressure increases in the direction of greater transparency. Investors need more information about new products and their real risks, or they do not buy them. 2. Banks are unlikely to reclaim all loans on their balance sheets and securitisation will continue. However, the importance of liquidity and liquidity will be emphasised in all risk management solutions. 3. The role of international credit rating agencies in creating and classifying new financial instruments will remain the subject of critical debate for a long time to come. What, then, are the effects on the Finnish and European economies? The sign of the effects is negative. The extent of the effects depends on how long and how deep the agitation continues. The role of financial markets in the global economy is perhaps more significant than at any time in economic history. As has been seen, market-based pricing and close international links between different segments of the financial markets and instruments spread shocks quickly and widely. Graph 20: Impact on the national economy The turbulence of recent months primarily means a deterioration in financial conditions and friction in the transmission of finance. The supply of financing is limited by increased risk awareness and tightening of credit conditions. The demand for financing, on the other hand, is curbed by increased risk premiums, which have raised the price of financing. More realistic pricing of risks is healthy, but some investment plans with higher financing costs are no longer as attractive as they used to be. Worsening financial conditions may also weigh on consumption, as reference rates for housing and consumer credit, for example, have risen. If, as a result of turbulence, stock prices and other asset values fall, it increases the negative impact on consumption. However, perhaps the most significant role in terms of risks to economic development is played by the effects of disturbances on the climate of confidence in business and households. The latest statistics on confidence indicators point to a decline in confidence in key industrialised countries. It is still too early to say how large and long-lasting these effects will be. However, it is worth remembering that the world, European and Finnish economies have faced financial market unrest in a period of strong growth. Growth has been rapid for an exceptionally long time, and the balance sheets of companies and financial institutions are strong due to good profit development. In addition, the engine of international growth is in the emerging economies of Asia, that is, relatively far from the center of turbulence in the financial markets. This strengthens the ability of the economy to absorb negative shocks. Therefore, the effects of short turbulence are manageable, but protracting would raise more question marks. Stock indices in key economic areas are well above levels at the beginning of the year, suggesting that financial markets expect the negative effects of the turmoil to be largely confined to the financial sector. The development has also been influenced by changed interest rate expectations.

Title: Current state of the economy and financial markets
text: Erkki Liikanen, Governor: The current state of the economy and financial markets, Bank of 81land Business Day, Mariehamn . Speech . Thursday24 January 2008, 12:00 AM Chefdirekt9ar Erkki Liikanen Bank of 81land Business Day, Mariehamn 24.1.2008 Diaserie (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and-interviews/documents/080124_el_alandsbanken.pdf) [S1] The banking sector in Finland has been in constant change for more than 20 years. Of the bank names we were used to seeing in the 1980s, most have disappeared. There have been turbulent periods in the past as well, but they are far back in time. In the midst of this change, the Bank of 81land is one of the oldest commercial banks in Finland. The bank emerged unscathed even from the depressions of the 1930s and 1990s, when many competitors were forced to cease operations. The mere desire to remain independent would not have made the bank so long-lived. Making the right choices and avoiding fatal mistakes have been prerequisites for continued operations. So what does the outlook for the economy and banking look like today in a broader perspective? The future holds far more uncertain than just a few months ago. [S2] Increasing uncertainty is something new that we really only started to notice this summer. The world economy has been growing strongly for a long time, and the Finnish economy even longer. This has led, for example, to unemployment falling almost continuously since the mid-1990s. This is how 81land, for example, has been able to report even enviable unemployment figures: in December 2007, according to 8cland's statistics and research agency, unemployment in the region was as low as 2.1%. In Finland, output growth has been limited by a lack of capacity rather than weak demand. Households' confidence in their income development has remained strong and this has kept up domestic demand. In contrast to the situation in many other countries, this has not led to current account deficits in our countries, as export demand has also always been strong. Ever since the end of the summer, in the midst of a period of strong growth, we have encountered a new problem: turbulence in the financial markets. The outlook for continued good economic development seems increasingly uncertain, although hardly anyone predicts a direct recession. Economic history has been marked by countless crises, panic reactions and disruptions of various nature and strength in the financial markets. History has not repeated itself, but each phenomenon has had its own characteristics. And once again, we've been surprised by a brand new market disruption. At the center this time is so-called structured financing. In its current scope and complexity, structured finance is something completely new. And it is therefore also the first time that we are dealing with the problems that it has given rise to. Structured finance shows an impressive diversity of species. One must therefore use the expression 'usually' or 'in general' when talking about funding, as there are almost always exceptions. Extremely complex and variegated instruments have seen the light of day. In any case, the financing includes securitization, securities issues in tranches, investment companies issuing structured finance instruments (of the structured investment vehicle type, SIV, and conduit) as well as monoline insurance companies. [S3] Traditional securitisation forms the basis for many different arrangements. The bank sells receivables to a special company set up for the purpose. Such a company normally has neither staff nor premises. It finances itself by issuing bonds and uses the assets to buy receivables that are securitized. As a rule, these receivables have been relatively homogeneous, for example only housing loans. Typically, in securitization, the issued bonds are divided into different tranches according to credit risk or sometimes according to some other characteristic. [S4] In traditional securitization, no new credits have been taken into the company after the transaction has been completed. On the other hand, in a collateralized debt obligation (CDO) you can collect many different receivables and buy from them when old credits are amortized. The securitizing bank carries on the credit risk. Structured financing has increased the distance between the final risk taker and the debtor. The risk assessment has been transferred to the rating agencies, i.e. credit rating agencies, which assess the credit risk in each individual tranche. Any credit losses are distributed according to the seniority of the tranches, first the junior part is affected and last the senior part. For each tranche, credit ratings are sought from rating agencies. Banks often point out that securitisation helps to free up capital for other purposes as it reduces lending on the balance sheet. Economic theorists have come up with more sophisticated explanations. They relate to asymmetric information or to divergent optimal financial structures in different projects. Securitization began to be practiced in the United States as early as the 1970s and still has its largest spread there today. In Finland, securitisation has not gained much popularity, while it has been more common, for example, in the United Kingdom, Spain and the Netherlands. [S5] Thus, for structured financing there are special investment companies, often started by banks. They issue certificates in their own name. They also have credit lines in banks that guarantee financing, for example, if they cannot refinance themselves in the certificate market. They may have a broad asset mass that includes, among other things, securitized receivables. A large part of the financing through the market is short-term, while investments are long-term. Investment companies are not credit institutions in the legal sense and are thus not subject to banking legislation. The so-called monoline insurance companies play a central role in many securitization transactions. They carrying out only one form of activity: they grant guarantees for securities issues. The demand for such a company's services is in all parts dependent on the company having a very high credit rating. Structured finance is a typical global economic phenomenon. Securitisation gives rise to bonds that are sold in large quantities across borders from one country to another. Banks have never before conducted such extensive borrowing and lending in countries where they are not physically established. Structured financing has been on the agenda in recent months mainly because of the problems it has caused. In today's globalized economy, we are affected by both positive and negative events even in countries far away. The market turbulence we are now experiencing has propagated from across the Atlantic. [S6] The word "subprime" has constantly reappeared in recent financial news. A few years ago, households that did not meet the conditions for traditional housing loans, i.e. households that were not so-called prime customers, also began to be granted in the UNITED STATES. Subprime loans were mainly given to people with poorer than normal credit ratings. The subprime lending conditions are d0 or perhaps more accurately were d0 at the beginning, i.e. usually in the first two years, very favourable. After that, the interest rate rose significantly and became variable. The margin against the reference rate is often even five percentage points. Until 2007, it was believed that the credit risk in the loans was insignificant. The fact that the loans had housing as collateral was considered to be a guarantee of the lenders' claims. Subprime loans have been securitised to a very large extent and large quantities of securities with subprime loans as underlying assets have been issued. [S7] The chain of events in the subprime mortgage market begins with the seller agreeing on a home loan with the client. The seller can have up to five different banks' products in their portfolio. The seller receives a fee from the bank and thus he has played his role. After that, the bank puts the loan together with other corresponding home loans into a package that it sells to an investment company. At the same time, the already weak connection between the bank and the client is broken. Together with a rating agency, the investment company refines the loans into certificates with different credit risk and different order of priority in terms of cash flow, i.e. interest and amortization. The various tranches are sold to international investors. [S8] The credit risk in subprime loans has now turned out to be greater than previously assessed. For a year, house prices in the United States have been falling. If the original lender banks had kept the credits on their balance sheets, many of them would now be grappling with major problems. The fact that structured financing is international means that we are in a new situation. Through complicated arrangements, credit risk has ended up in different parts of the world among the most surprising investor groups. Of course, the arrangements do not eliminate credit losses. They only direct the losses in a new way, and also to foreign banks. Without structured financing, it would be almost impossible to imagine that, for example, a European bank could have credit risks in the miami or boston housing market. We do not yet know how extensive the losses from subprime credits will be. Large new losses will still occur in 2008. According to some observers, the combined losses can reach up to 200-400 billion. Most of the commercial banks that have reported large subprime losses will, by all accounts, still not show loss for 2007. Their owners will have to be content with weaker than expected wages and lower dividends. The situation of monoline companies is weakening as the guarantee commitments are fulfilled. The monoline companies' operations are based entirely on high creditworthiness. If creditworthiness fails, the classification of all bonds guaranteed by the company in question must be reviewed. Extra capital has already been needed to keep credit ratings unchanged. Monoline companies have often also guaranteed other securities whose credit rating and market price are questioned if the companies' creditworthiness is lowered. Not all investment companies have subprime risks. However, investors cannot be completely sure of this. Since you do not know for sure where exactly the risks are, everyone is suspicious. Many investment companies have therefore become the object of suspicion and their certificates are no longer sought-after investment objects. The lack of transparency is the most serious problem at the height of uncertainty. [S9] Banks' operations are based on the fact that they raise short-term financing more cheaply and invest it in longer-term investments with higher returns. Last autumn, many investment companies ran into difficulties when they could not finance themselves with short-term certificates. The investment companies had to seek help from the banks with which they had agreed on a credit limit. Although the bank's guarantee commitment is not of a formal nature, the bank may be forced to assist its investment company with emergency financing, obviously at its own risk, in order to protect its name and reputation. In the next step, the link with the investment companies led to liquidity problems in the banks. Liquidity became the key word in the turbulence. Even the deposits in bank accounts, which have been considered safe, have proven to be unsafe if trust is lost. Proof of this is the bank attack by the British bank Northern Rock. Banks' awareness of the vulnerability of their liquidity has contributed to further weakening market liquidity. The banks have, just in case, hoarded liquidity instead of granting credit on the financial market. Investors have shown less interest than in the past even in banks' certificates. [S10] In the money market, a situation has arisen where the interest rate differential between secured and unsecured loans, euribor, is exceptionally large compared to the past. Until 9 August last year, hardly anyone considered whether money market rates should be measured on the basis of secured or unsecured credit. The difference was almost non-existent. It was hardly suggested to anyone that euribor rates reflect the interest rates on unsecured credit in the interbank market, i.e. the market where banks borrow from and to each other. That day, the situation changed abruptly. The large interest rate difference between secured and unsecured loans describes the suspicion that spread through the banking system. The rise in euribor interest rates after the summer is not due to monetary policy expectations, for example. [S11] The central banks have looked at the situation very seriously. They have maintained liquidity with available funds. For example, the Eurosystem has strengthened banks' liquidity through a large number of short-term fine-tuning operations and longer-term credit, although the key ECB rates have not changed. Central banks have also provided long-term credit. Without these measures, the situation at the turn of the year could have been even more worrying. Through these operations, central banks provide banks with loans against collateral. Central banks have also shown that they can cooperate on a broad front. In December 2007, together with the US Federal Reserve, the ECB provided us dollar counterparties with Eurosystem counterparties. It has very rarely happened that central banks have been involved in providing financing in foreign currencies. [S12] So far, the effects of the turbulence have been limited mainly to the financial market. It is still unclear how strong the impact of the turbulence will be on the real economy. Every day we receive new information and it is important to evaluate when it is a question of temporary castes and when there are permanent changes. It is clear, however, that the effect has a negative character. The channels of influence are many. The extent of the effects depends on the duration of uncertainty in financial markets. Recently, a number of international institutions have written down their growth forecasts for the world economy. [S13] In recent years, the strong demand in the US has been central to growth throughout the world economy. It has been common for U.S. households to mortgage their houses and use the money for consumption. When house prices fall, this possibility is curtailed with the result that consumption demand decreases. In addition to housing construction, this is one reason why growth expectations in the US have weakened. The price of financing has risen and, according to recent reports, the availability of financing has also decreased. This has an impact on business investment and on the growth prospects. At least one consequence of the turbulence is positive. The indirect effects of the upheavals reduce the current account deficit in the United States. The deficit has been one of the central problems in the imbalances in the world economy. [S14] It has been said that even in the worst case, subprime losses do not correspond to more than the loss in value on a single bad day in the US stock market. However, a temporary decline in share prices is far from having the same effect on the national economy as credit losses in banks. Equity investments are often long-term. Price slumps are part of everyday life for equity investors. But we must remember that the effects on the national economy of large credit losses in the banks come via the balance sheet. If credit losses eat into the bank's capital, the bank may be forced to cut lending even tenfold. Subprime losses can thus have major knock-on effects on national economies. [S15] According to the Financial Supervisory Authority's survey, Finnish banks have hardly any direct risks in the market for subprime-related securities. From this, however, we cannot conclude that the subprime problems could not affect banking operations in Finland. Subprime risks can be found in completely unexpected groups, including the foreign counterparties of Finnish banks in different markets. This increases the risks of our banks. In recent years, bank lending has grown significantly more strongly than deposits. In order to finance the difference, banks have had to rely on market financing, which has now become more expensive. More expensive financing weakens net interest income. However, the situation is facilitated by the structure of lending by the banking sector. A large part of the credits are tied to euribor. The market turbulence thus contributes to a gradual increase in the average interest rate on loans as the credit stock is repriced under the terms of the agreement. But there are also risks for banks. An increased interest burden strains borrowers' ability to pay and increases credit loss risk. Experiences are always instructive, and most of them are generally learned from the mistakes. It is perhaps still too early to draw any definitive conclusions from what has happened, but I think some circumstances can be addressed now. [S16] Banks' tasks traditionally include checking the ability of borrowers to pay. This is, of course, an impossible task for the depositors and they have therefore renounced it. The banks have a very strong motive for this control as any credit losses eat into their equity. Securities investors on another continent cannot control the borrower's ability to pay. Outsourcing the credit risk assessment to rating agencies does not correspond to the bank's own careful assessment. Investors have learned that it is not worth blindly trusting the credit ratings of rating agencies. Even the best classification is only an appraiser's opinion, albeit an important one. In addition, the classifications assess credit risk only in a narrow sense and do not take into account, among other things, liquidity risk. The risk in an investment is always borne by the investor. [S17] Rating agencies, and their shareholders, have already felt the turbulence. Share prices in the industry have been clearly falling. The position of rating agencies in the market is in many respects special. They receive their fee from the issuers while the classifications are made for the investors. On the other hand, the demand for classifications is entirely dependent on the good reputation of institutions. Embellished judgments quickly lose their credibility, and for such no one is willing to pay. Many market participants have complained that rating agencies' methods and criteria are not sufficiently transparent. The lack of transparency is also an obvious problem in the structured finance market. Accurate information is available to too little extent, and to a much lesser extent than, for example, on traditional banking. Ultimately, it is the financial firms themselves that suffer most from the lack of transparency. The conditions for these special investment companies to finance themselves in the market are disturbed during bad times. Lack of transparency coupled with weak capitalization means that they are the first to suffer from liquidity problems. Structured finance has increased the link between banks and insurance companies. When banks first grant credit and then securitise them, a large part of their lending ends up on the balance sheets of insurance companies. After all, insurance companies are among the most important investors in the bond market. For this reason, too, it is rational to concentrate the supervision of the financial and insurance industry in one and the same authority, as has been decided to do in Finland. The subprime crisis has once again shown how strongly the risks in the financial markets are associated with the rest of the economy. This time, the problems arose in the housing market in the United States. Next time, they may arise elsewhere in the world. Supervisors must have detailed knowledge of the conditions in the countries where supervised companies have risks. The legal homeland of the bank is of minor importance. The EU has in its time issued rules according to which the supervisory authority of one bank's home country is also responsible for supervising the bank's branch in another EEA country. At that time, banks had quite few and comparatively small foreign branches. Today, the situation is quite different, and the share of branches will most likely continue to grow. In the worst-case scenario, you could end up in a situation where the banking sector in any EU country is made up of a few large players, each supervised by its supervisor. No supervisory authority then has an overall picture of the situation anymore. Foreign supervisory authorities may lack sufficient resources, language skills or other expertise. This is by no means intended to promote effective supervision. It is high time to recast the financial supervision directives by strengthening the supervisory role of the host country. In any case, however, it is important to learn from the turbulence. The most important lessons for banks this time are perhaps the following: [S18] The risk analysis should not be outsourced, at least not entirely. Credit ratings by an ECA alone are not sufficient to provide banks or other investors with sufficient information. Rating agencies measure credit risk, but there are also other risks. Liquidity risk is still significant. The lack of transparency increases the problems. Previously, liquidity was regulated by various regulations that were gradually abolished. It was considered that a solid bank can always finance itself in the market. The regulation has therefore in recent years come to apply primarily to capital adequacy, but liquidity problems are still not a thing of the past. On the contrary. [S19]

Om de ursprungliga l<8c>ngivarbankerna hade h<8c>llit krediterna i sina balansr<8a>kningar skulle m<8c>nga av dem nu brottas med stora problem. Att den strukturerade finansieringen <8a>r internationell g<9a>r att vi befinner oss i en ny situation. Via komplicerade arrangemang har kreditrisken kommit att hamna p<8c> olika h<8c>ll i v<8a>rlden hos de mest <9a>verraskande investerargrupper. Uppl<8a>ggen eliminerar sj<8a>lvfallet inte kreditf<9a>rluster. De bara styr f<9a>rlusterna p<8c> ett nytt s<8a>tt, och ocks<8c> till utl<8a>ndska banker. Utan strukturerad finansiering skulle det vara n<8a>rmast om<9a>jligt att t<8a>nka sig att till exempel en europeisk bank kan ha kreditrisker p<8c> bostadsmarknaden i Miami eller Boston. <80>nnu vet vi inte hur omfattande f<9a>rlusterna fr<8c>n subprimekrediterna blir. Stora nya f<9a>rluster uppst<8c>r <8c>tminstone <8a>nnu 2008. Enligt vissa bed<9a>mare kan de sammanlagda f<9a>rlusterna n<8c> upp till 200-400 miljarder dollar. De flesta av de aff<8a>rsbanker som har rapporterat stora subprimef<9a>rluster kommer av allt att d<9a>ma <8a>nd<8c> inte att visa f<9a>rlust f<9a>r 2007. Deras <8a>gare f<8c>r l<8c>ta sig n<9a>jas med svagare l<9a>n-samhet <8a>n v<8a>ntat och l<8a>gre dividender. Monolinebolagens situation h<8c>ller p<8c> att f<9a>rsvagas efter hand som garanti<8c>tagandena infrias. Monolinebolagens verksamhet bygger helt och h<8c>llet p<8c> h<9a>g kreditv<8a>rdighet. Sviktar kreditv<8a>rdigheten m<8c>ste klassificeringen av alla obligationer som bolaget i fr<8c>ga garanterat ompr<9a>vas. Extra kapital har redan beh<9a>vts f<9a>r att h<8c>lla kreditklassificeringarna of<9a>r<8a>ndrade. Monolinebolagen har ofta garanterat <8a>ven andra v<8a>rdepapper vars kreditbetyg och marknadspris ifr<8c>gas<8a>tts om bolagens kreditv<8a>rdighet s<8a>nks. Alla investeringsbolag har inte subprimerisker. Helt s<8a>kra p<8c> detta kan investerarna dock inte vara. D<8c> man inte med s<8a>kerhet vet var exakt riskerna finns <8a>r alla misst<8a>nkta. M<8c>nga investeringsbolag har d<8a>rf<9a>r blivit f<9a>rem<8c>l f<9a>r misstankar och deras certifikat <8a>r inte l<8a>ngre eftertraktade investeringsobjekt. Bristen p<8c> transparens <8a>r det allvarligaste problemet n<8a>r os<8a>kerheten <8a>r som st<9a>rst. [S9] Bankernas verksamhet bygger p<8c> att de skaffar kortfristig finansiering billigare och placerar den i l<8c>ngfristigare investeringar med h<9a>gre avkastning. I h<9a>stas r<8c>kade m<8c>nga investeringsbolag i sv<8c>righeter d<8c> de inte kunde finansiera sig med kortfristiga certifikat. Investeringsbolagen var tvungna att s<9a>ka hj<8a>lp hos de banker som de avtalat om kreditlimit med. <80>ven om bankens garanti<8c>tagande inte <8a>r av formell natur kan banken tvingas bist<8c> sitt investeringsbolag med n<9a>dfinansiering, sj<8a>lvfallet med egen risk, f<9a>r att skydda sitt namn och rykte. Anknytningen till investeringsbolagen ledde i n<8a>sta steg till likviditetsproblem i bankerna. Likviditet blev nyckelordet i turbulensen. Till och med inl<8c>ningen p<8c> bankkonton, som har betraktats som s<8a>ker, har visat sig vara os<8a>ker om f<9a>rtroendet f<9a>rloras. Ett bevis p<8c> detta <8a>r den uttagsanstormning som den brittiska banken Northern Rock r<8c>kade ut f<9a>r. Bankernas medvetenhet om hur s<8c>rbar deras likviditet <8a>r har bidragit till att ytterligare f<9a>rsvaga marknadslikviditeten. Bankerna har f<9a>r s<8a>kerhets skull hamstrat likviditet i st<8a>llet f<9a>r att bevilja krediter p<8c> finansmarknaden. Investerarna har visat mindre intresse <8a>n tidigare <8a>ven f<9a>r bankernas certifikat. [S10] P<8c> penningmarknaden har uppst<8c>tt en situation d<8a>r r<8a>nteskillnaden mellan krediter med s<8a>kerhet och krediter utan s<8a>kerhet, euribor, <8a>r exceptionellt stor j<8a>mf<9a>rt med tidigare. Fram till den 9 augusti i fjol var det knappast n<8c>gon som funderade <9a>ver om penningmarknadsr<8a>ntorna borde m<8a>tas utifr<8c>n krediter med s<8a>kerhet eller krediter utan s<8a>kerhet. Skillnaden var n<8a>stan obefintlig. Det f<9a>resv<8a>vade knappast n<8c>gon att euriborr<8a>ntorna <8c>terspeglar r<8a>ntorna p<8c> krediter utan s<8a>kerhet p<8c> interbankmarknaden, dvs. marknaden d<8a>r bankerna l<8c>nar av och till varandra. Den dagen f<9a>r<8a>ndrades situationen abrupt. Den stora r<8a>nteskillnaden mellan l<8c>n med s<8a>kerhet och l<8c>n utan s<8a>kerhet beskriver den misst<8a>nksamhet som spred sig genom banksystemet. Uppg<8c>ngen i euriborr<8a>ntorna efter sommaren beror inte p<8c> exempelvis penningpo-litiska f<9a>rv<8a>ntningar. [S11] Centralbankerna har sett p<8c> situationen med stort allvar. De har uppr<8a>tth<8c>llit likviditeten med tillbudsst<8c>ende medel. S<8c> har till exempel Eurosystemet st<8a>rkt bankernas likviditet genom ett stort antal kortfristiga finjusterande transaktioner och l<8c>ngfristigare krediter fast<8a>n styrr<8a>ntorna inte har <8a>ndrats. Centralbankerna har tillhandah<8c>llit <8a>ven l<8c>ngfristiga krediter. Utan dessa <8c>tg<8a>rder hade l<8a>get vid <8c>rsskiftet kunnat vara <8a>nnu oroligare. Genom de h<8a>r transaktionerna ger centralbankerna bankerna l<8c>n mot betryggande s<8a>kerheter. Centralbankerna har ocks<8c> visat prov p<8c> att de kan samarbeta p<8c> bred front. Tillsammans med den amerikanska centralbanken tillhandah<9a>ll ECB i december 2007 motparterna i Eurosystemet finansiering i US-dollar. Det har ytterst s<8a>llan h<8a>nt att centralbanker varit med om att tillhandah<8c>lla finansiering i fr<8a>mmande valuta. [S12] Hittills har effekterna av turbulensen begr<8a>nsats fr<8a>mst till finansmarknaden. Det <8a>r fortfarande oklart hur stark inverkan turbulensen har p<8c> realekonomin. Vi f<8c>r varje dag ny information och det g<8a>ller att utv<8a>rdera n<8a>r det <8a>r fr<8c>ga om tillf<8a>lliga kast och n<8a>r det <8a>r fr<8c>ga om best<8c>ende f<9a>r<8a>ndringar. Klart <8a>r dock att effekten har negativt f<9a>rtecken. P<8c>verkanskanalerna <8a>r m<8c>nga. Effekternas omfattning beror p<8c> hur l<8a>nge os<8a>kerheten p<8c> de finansiella marknaderna h<8c>ller i sig. Den senaste tiden har en rad internationella institutioner skrivit ned sina tillv<8a>xtprognoser f<9a>r v<8a>rldsekonomin. [S13] De senaste <8c>ren har den starka efterfr<8c>gan i USA varit av central betydelse f<9a>r tillv<8a>xten i hela v<8a>rldsekonomin. Det har varit vanligt att amerikanska hush<8c>ll bel<8c>nat sina hus och anv<8a>nt pengarna f<9a>r konsumtion. N<8a>r bostadspriserna faller kringsk<8a>rs denna m<9a>jlighet med f<9a>ljden att konsumtionsefterfr<8c>gan minskar. Ut<9a>ver bostadsbyggandet <8a>r det h<8a>r en orsak till att tillv<8a>xtf<9a>rv<8a>ntningarna i USA har f<9a>rsvagats. Priset p<8c> finansiering har stigit och enligt f<8a>rska rapporter har ocks<8c> tillg<8c>ngen p<8c> finansiering minskat. Det h<8a>r <8c>terverkar p<8c> f<9a>retagens investeringar och den v<8a>gen p<8c> tillv<8a>xtutsikterna. <81>tminstone en konsekvens av turbulensen <8a>r positiv. De indirekta effekterna av omv<8a>lvningarna minskar bytesbalansunderskottet i USA. Underskottet har varit ett av de centrala problemen i obalanserna i v<8a>rldsekonomin. [S14] Det har sagts att subprimef<9a>rlusterna <8a>ven i v<8a>rsta fall inte motsvarar mer <8a>n v<8a>rdef<9a>rlusten under en enda d<8c>lig dag p<8c> den amerikanska aktiemarknaden. En tillf<8a>llig nedg<8c>ng i aktiekurserna har dock l<8c>ngtifr<8c>n samma effekt p<8c> samh<8a>llsekonomin som kreditf<9a>rluster i bankerna. Aktieinvesteringarna <8a>r ofta l<8c>ngsiktiga. Kurssvackor h<9a>r till vardagen f<9a>r aktieinvesterare. Men vi m<8c>st minnas att effekterna p<8c> samh<8a>llsekonomin av stora kreditf<9a>rluster i bankerna kommer via balansr<8a>kningen. Om kreditf<9a>rlusterna t<8a>r p<8c> bankens kapital kan banken tvingas sk<8a>ra ned utl<8c>ningen till och med tiofalt. Subprimef<9a>rlusterna kan s<8c>ledes ha stora f<9a>ljdeffekter p<8c> samh<8a>llsekonomierna. [S15] Enligt Finansinspektionens enk<8a>tunders<9a>kning har de finl<8a>ndska bankerna knappast alls n<8c>gra direkta risker p<8c> marknaden f<9a>r subprimerelaterade v<8a>rdepapper. Av detta kan vi <8a>nd<8c> inte dra den slutsatsen att subprimeproblemen inte skulle kunna p<8c>verka bankverksamheten i Finland. Subprimerisker kan finnas hos helt ov<8a>ntade grupper, ocks<8c> hos finl<8a>ndska bankers utl<8a>ndska motparter p<8c> olika marknader. Detta <9a>kar v<8c>ra bankers risker. Under de senaste <8c>ren har bankernas utl<8c>ning <9a>kat betydligt kraftigare <8a>n inl<8c>ningen. F<9a>r att finansiera skillnaden har bankerna tvingats ty sig till marknadsfinansiering som nu har blivit dyrare. En dyrare finansiering f<9a>rsvagar r<8a>ntenettot. Situationen underl<8a>ttas dock av strukturen p<8c> banksektorns utl<8c>ning. En stor del av krediterna <8a>r bundna till euribor. Marknadsturbulensen bidrar s<8c>ledes till att successivt h<9a>ja medelr<8a>ntan p<8c> utl<8c>ningen efter hand som kreditstocken enligt avtalsvillkoren priss<8a>tts p<8c> nytt. Men h<8a>r finns ocks<8c> risker f<9a>r bankerna. En <9a>kad r<8a>nteb<9a>rda anstr<8a>nger l<8c>ntagarnas betalningsf<9a>rm<8c>ga och <9a>kar kreditf<9a>rlustrisken. Erfarenheter <8a>r alltid l<8a>rorika, och mest l<8a>r man sig i allm<8a>nhet av misstagen. Det <8a>r kanske <8a>nnu f<9a>r tidigt att dra n<8c>gra definitiva slutsatser av det som skett, men jag tror att n<8c>gra omst<8a>ndigheter kan tas upp redan nu. [S16] Till bankernas uppgifter h<9a>r traditionellt att kontrollera l<8c>ntagarnas betalningsf<9a>rm<8c>ga. Detta <8a>r sj<8a>lvfallet en om<9a>jlig uppgift f<9a>r ins<8a>ttarna och de har d<8a>rf<9a>r avst<8c>tt fr<8c>n den. Bankerna har ett mycket starkt motiv f<9a>r denna kontroll d<8c> eventuella kreditf<9a>rluster t<8a>r p<8c> deras eget kapital. V<8a>rdepappersinvesterare p<8c> en annan kontinent kan inte kontrollera l<8c>ntagarens betalningsf<9a>rm<8c>ga. Utl<8a>ggning av kreditriskbed<9a>mningen till ratinginstitut motsvarar inte bankens egen omsorgsfulla bed<9a>mning. Investerarna har f<8c>tt erfara att det inte l<9a>nar sig att blint lita p<8c> ratinginstitutens kreditbetyg. <80>ven den b<8a>sta klassificering <8a>r bara en bed<9a>mares uppfattning, om <8a>n en viktig s<8c>dan. Klassificeringarna bed<9a>mer dessutom kreditrisken bara i sn<8a>v bem<8a>rkelse och tar bland annat inte h<8a>nsyn till likviditetsrisken. Risken i en investering b<8a>rs alltid av investeraren. [S17] Ratinginstituten, och deras aktie<8a>gare, har redan f<8c>tt k<8a>nna av turbulensen. Aktiekurserna i branschen har varit klart fallande. Ratinginstitutens st<8a>llning p<8c> marknaden <8a>r i m<8c>nga avseenden speciell. De f<8c>r sitt arvode av emittenterna medan klassificeringarna g<9a>rs f<9a>r investerarna. <81> andra sidan <8a>r efterfr<8c>gan p<8c> klassificeringar helt och h<8c>llet beroende av institutens goda rykte. F<9a>rsk<9a>nade bed<9a>mningar mister snabbt sin trov<8a>rdighet, och f<9a>r s<8c>dana <8a>r ingen villig att betala. M<8c>nga marknadsakt<9a>rer har klagat <9a>ver att ratinginstitutens metoder och kriterier inte <8a>r tillr<8a>ckligt transparenta. Bristen p<8c> transparens <8a>ven i <9a>vrigt <8a>r ett uppenbart problem p<8c> marknaden f<9a>r strukturerad finansiering. Exakt information finns i alltf<9a>r liten omfattning, och i betydligt mindre utstr<8a>ckning <8a>n exempelvis om traditionell bankverksamhet. Det <8a>r sist och slutligen de finansiella f<9a>retagen sj<8a>lva som mest lider av bristen p<8c> transparens. F<9a>ruts<8a>ttningarna f<9a>r dessa speciella investeringsbolag att finansiera sig p<8c> marknaden rubbas under d<8c>liga tider. Bristande transparens i f<9a>rening med svag kapitalisering g<9a>r att de <8a>r de f<9a>rsta som drabbas av likviditetsproblem. Den strukturerade finansieringen har <9a>kat kopplingen mellan banker och f<9a>rs<8a>kringsbolag. N<8a>r bankerna f<9a>rst beviljar krediter och sedan v<8a>rdepapperiserar dem hamnar en stor del av deras utl<8c>ning slutligen i f<9a>rs<8a>kringsbolagens balansr<8a>kningar. F<9a>rs<8a>kringsbolagen h<9a>r ju till de viktigaste investerarna p<8c> obligationsmarknaden. <80>ven av den orsaken <8a>r det rationellt att koncentrera tillsynen av finans-och f<9a>rs<8a>kringsbranschen till en och samma myndighet, s<8c>som man beslutat g<9a>ra i Finland. Subprimekrisen har <8a>n en g<8c>ng visat hur starkt riskerna p<8c> de finansiella marknaderna <8a>r f<9a>rbundna med den <9a>vriga ekonomin. Den h<8a>r g<8c>ngen uppstod problemen p<8c> bostadsmarknaden i USA. N<8a>sta g<8c>ng uppst<8c>r de kanske p<8c> n<8c>got annat h<8c>ll i v<8a>rlden. Tillsynsmyndigheterna m<8c>ste ha ing<8c>ende k<8a>nnedom om f<9a>rh<8c>llandena i de l<8a>nder d<8a>r f<9a>retagen under tillsyn har risker. Bankens juridiska hemland <8a>r av mindre betydelse. EU har p<8c> sin tid utf<8a>rdat regler enligt vilka tillsynsmyndigheten i en banks hemland svarar f<9a>r tillsynen <8a>ven av bankens filial i ett annat EES-land. P<8c> den tiden hade bankerna r<8a>tt f<8c> och j<8a>mf<9a>relsevis sm<8c> utl<8a>ndska filialer. I dag <8a>r situationen en helt annan, och filialernas andel kommer med st<9a>rsta sannolikhet att v<8a>xa <8a>ven i forts<8a>ttningen. I v<8a>rsta fall kan man hamna i en situation d<8a>r banksektorn i n<8c>got EU-land utg<9a>rs av n<8c>gra f<8c> stora akt<9a>rer, var och en <9a>vervakad av sin tillsynsmyndighet. Ingen tillsynsmyndighet har d<8c> l<8a>ngre en helhetsbild av l<8a>get. Utl<8a>ndska tillsynsmyndigheter kanske saknar tillr<8a>ckliga resurser, spr<8c>kkunskaper eller annan sakkunskap. Detta <8a>r ingalunda <8a>gnat att fr<8a>mja en effektiv tillsyn. Det <8a>r h<9a>g tid att omarbeta direktiven om finanstillsyn genom att st<8a>rka v<8a>rdlandets tillsynsroll. I alla fall g<8a>ller det dock att ta l<8a>rdom av turbulensen. De viktigaste l<8a>rdomarna f<9a>r bankerna den h<8a>r g<8c>ngen <8a>r kanske f<9a>ljande: [S18] Riskanalysen b<9a>r inte l<8a>ggas ut p<8c> entreprenad, <8c>tminstone inte helt och h<8c>llet. Enbart kreditbetyg av ett ratinginstitut r<8a>cker inte f<9a>r att banker eller andra investerare ska f<8c> tillr<8a>cklig information. Ratinginstituten m<8a>ter kreditrisken, men det finns ocks<8c> andra risker. Likviditetsrisken har fortfarande betydelse. Bristen p<8c> transparens <9a>kar problemen. Tidigare reglerades likviditeten genom olika best<8a>mmelser som successivt slopades. Det ans<8c>gs att en solid bank alltid kan finansiera sig p<8c> marknaden. Regleringen har d<8a>rf<9a>r de senaste <8c>ren kommit att g<8a>lla framf<9a>rallt kapitalt<8a>ckningen, men likviditetsproblemen h<9a>r <8a>nd<8c> inte till det f<9a>rg<8c>ngna. Tv<8a>rtom. [S19]

Title: SEPA, a single euro payments area, will be launched
text: President Erkki Liikanen: Sepa launches single euro payments area. Commission representation in Finland . Speech . Monday28 January 2008, 12:00 AM President Erkki Liikanen: "Sepa launches single euro payments area" Information and discussion on the premises of the European Commission Representation in Finland 28.1.2008 ECONOMIC GROWTH NEEDS EFFICIENT PAYMENT INTERMEDIATION Payments in the same way, under the same conditions, throughout Europe Ladies and gentlemen, Payment intermediation is the oil in the wheels of the internal market, says the European Commission on its website. On the whole the market economy always requires functioning payment systems. The revolution in information and communication technologies and the liberalisation of regulation have meant that information and services move online in the blink of an eye. With a mobile phone, you can easily send e-mails, pictures and videos to another mobile phone regardless of the borders of the countries. It's hard to fathom that it can still take several days to make a payment from one account to another across borders  and in some European countries, even within a country' s borders  and can be subject to high fees. However, it is about the same transport of bits and information content. The European Commission has taken a number of initiatives to improve the efficiency of the European internal market, including in the area of payment intermediation. The banks have responded to the challenges presented and set out to build uniform business rules and standards for euro payments. The Eurosystem has supported these efforts. We are here to witness the first concrete evidence of this work. A common European credit transfer for euro payments is being introduced throughout Europe today. The Single Euro Payments Area, or SEPA, is becoming a reality. The reform is not spectacular and concrete in the same way as the introduction of euro notes and coins seven years ago. However, the Single Euro Payments Area is changing the way payments intermediation works in a very fundamental way. Payment service providers have undertaken to mediate payments in euro in a harmonised manner. Common payment methods with the Payment Services Directive, which will enter into force next year, will ensure that anyone can pay anyone in euros across borders in Europe in the same way as they do within a country. This is how the vision of sepa, the single euro payments area, is becoming a reality. Payment is an integral part of all economic activity, and by simplifying and facilitating payment, we facilitate the functioning of the economy as a whole. When all european euro payments are transmitted in a uniform format, the differences in the efficiency of service providers and infrastructures will become visible. Both customers when choosing payment services and banks when choosing their infrastructure suppliers can compare the level and price of service. This inevitably leads to the fact that the best benefit and the weaker have to improve their performance in order to survive. In this way, increasing competition will make operations more efficient and, above all, benefit customers. The European financial markets cannot be modernised and diversified without the development of intermediation mechanisms, that is to say payment and settlement systems. Although payment intermediation in national markets is often already efficient and there is competition in services, cross-border payments have been slow and expensive. Retail payments infrastructure has not developed as efficient as domestic payment intermediation systems for cross-border payments. The Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA) will enable businesses operating in Europe to simplify and streamline their own cash management. One of the obstacles for companies in the domestic market to expand their markets to the rest of Europe will be removed. In this way, sequential payments area will also bring efficiency gains to the business sector as a whole, which goes beyond payment intermediation. Users of payment services must realise the opportunities now available and switch to a single euro payments area transfer as soon as possible. At the same time, the implementation of the efficiency gains it provides becomes possible. Maintaining overlapping payment gateways is costly. Therefore, the shortest possible transition period for banks is also advantageous. The benefits of SEPA for final customers are obvious. Today, the Commission is publishing an external study which calculates that the net benefit to the European economy in the next six years could be as much as more than EUR 120 billion. The banking sector has pointed out that SEPA primarily raises banks' costs by requiring investment and reducing the potential for returns. That is certainly the case in the short term, but there is also a flip side to the coin. The investments required by SEPA can be made with new technologies with lower production costs. SEPA enables, and certainly does, the centralisation of payment volumes, which increases efficiency. Intensifying competition is forcing banks to look at their processes even more critically and thus seek more efficiency. There is no doubt that there are banks in Europe that are unable to meet the challenges of a changing environment. In my opinion, however, Finnish banks are well aware of the factors that must be used to respond to the change and to benefit from a single euro payments area. Could payment intermediation services be a competitive advantage for Finnish banks in an integrated European market? We have long experience in electronic, machine-readable payment intermediation, which we can utilize in an even wider market. We also have the impression that the sepa-format credit transfer that is now being introduced is only the first, but important, step towards more efficient payment intermediation in Europe. Finnish banks have supported SEPA's further work and expansion into e.g. internet and mobile payments and electronic invoicing. That is the direction in which SEPA must be taken. It is also possible for banks to offer these services to customers in areas where companies are not yet very advanced in automating their financial management. By developing a Single Euro Payments Area to support end customers' demand for integrated services, the indirect impact of SEPA on society could be many times greater than what has been proposed so far. Estimates have been made that the growth stimulus of the whole process for the European economy could be in the order of one percentage point on an annual basis. Europe should not miss such an opportunity. Thank you.
