Title: The Nordic Model
text: Erkki Liikanen, Director General: The Nordic Model, ESV Day, Swedish Financial Control Agency, Stockholm, 16 October 2008 . Speech . Thursday16 October 2008, 12:00 AM Slide show (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and. interviews/documents/161008_el_stockholm.pdf) [Fig. 1] What is the Nordic model? [Figure 2: The Nordic Model] The Nordic countries have many common features. The Nordic model can be described as a welfare system in which the market economy functions freely within the framework conditions set by society. The Nordic model is based on free trade, strong consensus-oriented institutions, human capital and know-how, collective risk allocation and a responsible economic policy. The core of the Nordic model has been built up over many decades. The practical solutions have certainly changed over the years and are different in the different countries. However, the solutions have the common core as a basis. How has the Nordic model worked? The Nordic model has received a lot of attention in recent years. Analyses of different countries' conditions for success in the world have shown that the Nordic countries have been able to create wealth for citizens at a rate that stands up in an international comparison but does not increase income inequality. This has been considered surprising because countries with a large public sector, a generous social security, a tight taxation and a narrow income range are not normally considered dynamic, high-growth economies. The Nordic countries  for practical reasons I will limit my presentation to the EU countries Finland, Sweden and Denmark  have undoubtedly done well in a European perspective measured by all the more important indicators. The countries have a high employment rate, high productivity growth and good competitiveness. Welfare growth is very evenly distributed and social mobility is high. [Figure 3: The Nordic countries have done well] Countries' fiscal policies are responsible and predictable, public finances are in surplus and public finances are in surplus debt is decreasing relative to GDP. Despite the countries' different institutional solutions  Finland is in EMU, Denmark has pegged its krona to the euro through ERM2 while Sweden has a floating exchange rate regime with an inflation target  their monetary policy is credible and focused on steadily increasing purchasing power. [Figure 4: The Nordic countries have done well] Productivity growth is an important source of increased national prosperity. Other sources are increased labour input and increased capital input. As population growth slows and with it the growth of labour input, national prosperity can only increase through increased capital use per employee in production, so-called capital deepening, and increased productivity (TFP, total factor productivity). Since the mid-1990s and especially in the 2000s, productivity growth has slowed down most clearly on average in most old EU countries. In Sweden and Finland, on the other hand, productivity growth has accelerated. In the US, too, productivity has been growing at a rapid pace. [Figure 5: Produktivitetstillvaxt] Various reports show that the rapid productivity growth in the Nordic countries, and especially in Sweden and Finland, is due to many factors. Among the most important are the wider and more integrated use of information and communication technologies and new, more sophisticated production methods. Thanks to ICT training  i.e. training in information and communication technology  the workforce has been able to take advantage of the opportunities offered by the new technologies. Large investments in research and product development have ensured that companies have kept pace with technological developments. For their part, the relatively liberalised product markets and increased competition have contributed to productivity growth. All this can be seen as a consistent expression of the principles that have been the basis of the Nordic model over the years, if you like. Why has the Nordic model worked? When considering future success opportunities, it is worth asking why the Nordic countries in particular seem to have found a working recipe. What do the Nordic countries have that other countries do not have or what do the Nordic countries do that other countries do not? Which of the typical features of the Nordic model that I mentioned earlier have particularly contributed to the favourable development? Professor Andre Sapir has studied the labour market, income distribution and social security systems in the old EU countries, what we usually call the EU-15. He has divided the countries into four groups according to their ability to utilize their available labor-force resources and fairly distribute the increase in wealth among the citizens. Sapir measures production efficiency using the employment rate and the degree of fair income distribution using the at-risk-of-poverty rate. [Figure 6: European social models ala AndreSapir] In this comparison, only the Nordic welfare model, which according to Sapir is represented by the Netherlands in addition to Sweden, Finland and Denmark, has been able to combine production efficiency and a fair distribution of income. Sapir concludes that countries with less than average capacity to use their labour resources should learn from countries with more efficient use of labour resources. According to Sapir, the nordic model's most important success factor is the combination of high unemployment protection and relatively low employment protection. For example, flexible Danish employment protection flexicurity  flexibility and security. The idea of the flexicurity model is that employees can accept relatively low employment protection as a high unemployment protection ensures financial compensation in the event of unemployment. Low employment protection makes it easier for them to get a new job. At the same time, the state is investing large sums in an active labor market policy to make it easier to look for and get a new job. The true belief in the flexicurity model is evidenced by the fact that its key principles are now being launched in other EU countries as well as part of the efforts to achieve growth and the employment objectives of the Lisbon Strategy. Just under a year ago, a Nordic expert group of six top economists published a report on the most important features of the Nordic welfare model and its challenges. The expert group came to the same conclusions in part as Professor Sapir. The economist group noted that there is an important and positive interaction between the open economy in the Nordic countries and the equalisation of the risks posed by transparency. According to the group, the collective risk equalisation in the Nordic model has contributed to a successful combination of flexibility, which is a prerequisite for productivity growth and economic growth, and security, which citizens strive for. Northerners are prepared to accept the risks of an open economy in the knowledge that the welfare state's safety net will catch those affected. What challenges do the Nordic countries face? [Figure 7: Globalisation and ageing population create challenges] Will the Nordic model continue to work in the future? Globalisation and the ageing of the population are megatrends with challenges that the Nordic countries also face. The starting point is good, but can you get by with old recipes? The Nordic model and globalisation First, let us look at globalisation. Globalisation means increasing global labour supply, reducing barriers to trade and exploiting the new information and communication technologies. ICT developments have profoundly changed the organization of production processes and made it possible to fragment the production chain. At the same time, the increased integration of emerging economies  notably China and India  into the international economy has increased global labour supply. All this has made it possible to integrate the international division of labour  to move jobs and jobs from one country to another. [Fig. 8: Varldshandelstillvaxt] Globalization has been rapid in recent years. World trade has grown at an extremely high pace and on a broad front. The increase in trade has increased prosperity in the developed countries of the West but above all in the emerging countries. Even the traditional developing countries have benefited from globalisation. Differences in living standards between developed and emerging countries have shrunk and the number of people living in extreme poverty has decreased. All this is extremely positive. At the same time, however, the downsides and risks of globalisation have also become apparent. Although globalization has led overall to higher living standards everywhere in the world, individual regions, industries, companies and citizens have seen their competitiveness disappear due to the increasingly integrated international division of labour. The increasing uncertainty and adaptation problems have increased criticism of globalisation and, at the same time, more and more people are calling for protectionism. Nevertheless, I do not believe that globalisation will come to a halt even in the long term. Although differences in competitiveness, production costs and living standards have narrowed, they still exist. Therefore, globalisation continues to create unlimited opportunities for those who can adapt to changes in the world around them, such as an increasingly integrated international division of labour and increased competition. Winners are those who can create favorable conditions to take advantage of the opportunities. It has been argued that the Nordic model, with its focus on openness and free trade, its collective distribution of the risks of production changes and its investments in education, research and product development, creates the conditions for exploiting these opportunities also in the coming years. The starting point for the Nordic countries is good. Through education, research and product development, knowledge capital is created that is a prerequisite for sustainable competitiveness. In order for knowledge capital to be utilized, it is again necessary that resources can be flexibly directed to the most competitive industries and companies. The welfare state's many-handed safety nets alleviate the problems of flexible adaptation. It is essential that the Nordic countries, thanks to their safety nets, do not have to waste resources on supporting non-viable industries and companies. Safety nets are not there to exclude citizens from a productive working life, but to help them adapt to changing circumstances and to seek new opportunities. With the help of safety nets, individual citizens can also see globalisation as an opportunity rather than a threat. [Figure 9: Globalisation and ageing population create challenges] Even if the starting position is good, we must not rest on our laurels. More efficient product and labour markets and a more stimulating tax and social security system are needed in the face of intensifying international competition. Globalisation has made labour demand even more sensitive than before to changes in labour costs. At the same time, globalisation has amplified the negative effects of rigidities in labour market flows. The need to streamline the labour market and review wage formation mechanisms has increased. There is a need for both coordination with a focus on the whole and flexibility at company level. Denmark and Sweden are already well advanced in their efforts towards macroeconomic coordination and micro-flexibility in the labour market. In Finland, too, the debate on the need to review wage formation mechanisms has begun. By increasing microflexibility without forgetting macro coordination, one can better match the demand and supply of labor. At the same time, the ability of enterprises and the entire national economy to adapt to changes in the operating environment will increase. The changes are increasing as the world globalizes and becomes increasingly difficult to predict. It is important that social security systems are primarily there to insure individual citizens in the event of a downturn and to secure the livelihoods of individual citizens who are unable to cope financially. The social security system must not passiveise citizens so that they become dependent on benefits and live on benefits and benefits. The social security system should enable citizens to seek new opportunities. These offer, for example, education, new careers or entrepreneurship. The importance of market economy mechanisms as a guiding factor behind the choices made by companies and individual citizens should not be underestimated. This has been highlighted by several researchers who have analysed the success criteria of the Nordic model. The measures to reduce regulation in product and labour markets, promote competition and provide tax incentives and social security systems have been an important factor in the favourable development of the the Nordic countries. The Nordic model and population ageing The Nordic countries are well placed to survive in globalisation. But the ageing of the population poses threats to which the Nordic model is vulnerable. The basic problem is that it is expensive to maintain a comprehensive public safety net and an extensive range of public services and that the tax rate is therefore high. The Nordic countries' well-developed safety nets, extensive provision of public services and high tax levies mean that the ageing of the population is creating increasing pressure on public finances. It is somewhat paradoxical that the Nordic model has elements that contribute to the adaptation of globalisation but at the same time threaten to erode the financing of the welfare model. [Figure 10: The social agreement  net taxes andtransfers] The Nordic welfare model is designed in such a way that those who have jobs pay for the population's education, pensions and social and health care. The large transfers from people in the workplace to those outside the world of work are widely accepted because it is known that at different stages of life you receive quid pro quos for taxes and contributions paid  education in youth, retirement in old age, health care throughout life and basic financial security in worse times. The financing of the model rests on a secure basis when the public sector  except in the event of cyclical deviations  spends the same amount of money on benefits, allowances and services that can be levied in the form of taxes and fees. As the population ages  as the working population begins to decline and the number of pensioners increases  broad support for the Nordic model threatens to plummet. Those who work may no longer be willing to fund the system when they realize that during their lifetime they will not receive the benefits and services for which they consider themselves to have already paid taxes and fees. Without broad acceptance among citizens, the Nordic welfare model will inevitably crumble. It is no longer possible to turn a blind eye to the problems caused by the ageing of the population and the measures required. In all the Nordic countries, pensioners will very soon start to increase the dependency ratio  the number of people outside working life in relation to the number of employed persons  and reduce labour input. In this respect, the development in Finland is somewhat faster than in the other Nordic countries and other EU countries. [Figure 11-21: Aging baby boomers] The population structure is changing surprisingly fast in Finland. The projected changes in the number of people reaching retirement age and the number of people of working age are staggering. Finland's declining population structure is due to the fact that men were at the front for five years, from 1939 to 1944. The birth rate was understandably very low, but instead very many children were born in the years after the war. On this great dance [SLIDE 11] you can see that during the late 1940s significantly more children were born in Finland than in Sweden and Denmark. Over the years, the major grades have gotten older [SLIDE 12, etc.]  and older. [Figure 22: Age structure of the population] The number of pensioners in Finland is already growing at a rapid pace and will increase even faster in the years to come when the large age groups born in 19451949 reach statutory retirement age. In 2007, the number of people who reached retirement age for the first time the number of people entering the labor market. In 2010, the number of people reaching retirement age is already almost 80,000 more than those entering the labour market. At the same time, the growth in the number of working-age Finns, i.e. aged 15 to 64, will be halted. According to the population projection, the working-age population will start to decline in 2010  first by 10,000 people and after 2010 by around 20,000 people per year. In 2020, Finns of working age are approximately 170,000 fewer than in 2007. In line with ageing, pension expenditure and demand for public sector welfare services threaten to increase and the funding base for the public sector will stop growing so that general government revenue no longer covers expenditure. [Figure 23: Age-related expenditure 2004-2050] The European Commission has calculated how much the growth in age-related expenditure will be borne by the public finances of eu countries. The most recent estimates are from 2006. They show that the load in the Nordic countries is highest in Finland and almost as great in Denmark, while in Sweden it is clearly less than in Denmark and Finland. In both the euro area and EU member states on average, the load will still grow significantly after 2030, but will still be smaller on average than in Denmark and Finland. An ageing population and a generous welfare state are a difficult combination. According to the Commission, the risks that threaten long-term sustainable financing of the public sector are small in all Nordic countries. In Finland, however, the Ministry of Finance has calculated that the financing of the Finnish public sector is not based on a sustainable basis in the long term. There are several ways to reduce the sustainability deficit. The deficit can be covered by increased revenues, reduced expenses or borrowing. Finland has chosen a combination of measures aimed at increasing the growth of the public sector's financing base, reducing growth in public expenditure and reducing public debt. [Figure 24: Globalisation and ageing population create challenges] Integrated tax and social security systems with increased incentives are necessary to ensure an increased funding base for the public sector. It is important to increase the labor input in the economy in every way. The so-called diligence traps in the systems must be reduced. Similarly, the risk of falling into a benefit trap must be reduced, a risk typical of a comprehensive social security system. The financing problems of the public sector will not be solved by increased taxation. Taxation and especially taxation of labour is already very high in the Nordic countries. As a result, the tax wedge  the difference between the gross income that the employer has to earn and the net salary that the employee receives in hand  is already large. A large tax wedge has serious anti-employment effects. In addition, globalisation has limited the ability of individual states to tax companies and capital in particular. Globalisation has also increased the distortive effects of taxation. Jobs are disappearing to other countries even though the workforce remains. In order to curb the growth in public spending, productivity in the production of public services must be increased  that is a mantra that we often hear. But what does increased productivity in the public sector really mean? Basically, it's about doing the right things, and doing them well. In English, one speaks of effectiveness and efficiency. "To do the right thing  and to do it well". Let me give you an example: in Finland, a few decades ago, we invested a great deal of money in long-term care and in building old people's homes. But experience showed that when the old people had ended up in a sickbed, they never got up again. The system became both inhumane and expensive. Instead, major investments are now being made so that our senior citizens can live at home for as long as possible. It's about effectiveness  investing in what's right. If you do not do what is right, there is no point in increasing productivity. There is nothing more frustrating for a worker than to do something that everyone knows is of no real use, and to be forced to do so in a more stressful way. The next step is efficiency and for public services that are often very information-intensive, this means that three things should be done at the same time:  firstly, investments in IT; that is, communication networks, computers, mobile technology, and so on. Such efforts are a necessary, but not a sufficient, condition for increased productivity;  secondly, employers, together with their staff, must develop more intelligent work processes. People who are employed in, for example, county councils and municipalities should be encouraged to take the initiative themselves for better organization of work and work routines. Employees need to feel involved so that they can really influence how the work is done.  and thirdly, training is required. Everyone needs a certain basic education so that they can effectively use the new technologies in their work. Increasing productivity in the public sector costs money, and it is important to distribute resources correctly. If you invest SEK 20 million in IT and computers, you should allocate SEK 80 million on improved work processes and on training of staff. 20/80 is a good rule, I think. Finally, I am convinced that it is possible to increase productivity in the public sector. And it can look in a way that is beneficial and beneficial both to those who work in the public sector and to those who are covered by the services that are produced. Faster productivity growth would, in turn, significantly improve the sustainability of public finances. And that is exactly what is needed if we are to be able to secure welfare in a situation where the population is getting older. But an increase in productivity alone is not enough. Title: Financial market turmoil and Finland
text: President and CEO Erkki Liikanen: Financial turmoil and Finland, Autumn meeting of the National Defence Course Association, Helsinki, 30.10.2008 . Speech . Thursday30 October 2008, 12:00 AM Autumn meeting of the National Defence Course Association, Finlandia Hall, Helsinki 30.10.2008 FINANCIAL TURMOIL AND FINLAND Speech Membranes (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and. interviews/documents/081030_maanpuolustuskurssiyhdistys.ppt) Ladies and gentlemen, The stability of financial markets is one of the key issues of national and international security. In good times, the stability of the financial system is taken for granted. Society's dependence on the ability of the financial system to function is forgotten. However, the international financial crisis, which has escalated in recent weeks, has made the link between financial market stability and economic security even more prominent. Political decision-makers and authorities have taken this issue seriously. The exceptionally swift and decisive action of both the EU countries and the United States in the event of a crisis is a good indication of this. In particular, the ability of European political leaders to cooperate in crisis management has often been questioned. This autumn's activities show that there is a willingness to cooperate and the ability to make joint decisions. SLIDE 2: Financial Markets and Security The underlying concern is well-founded. Malfunctions in the financial markets can severely paralyse the functioning of the entire national economy. When the most difficult international financial market crisis to date took place in the 1930s, it had a bad impact on both the well-being of citizens and international security. In modern society, the dependence of core activities on the financial and payment system has grown even greater. For Finns, the financial crisis reminds us of the banking crisis and recession in the early 1990s. It was a tough experience, but it still gives only a partial picture of what a serious international financial crisis could cause at its worst. The Finnish banking crisis cost taxpayers a lot, and thousands of loan customers suffered as a result of the disruption of banks' lending capacity. This seriously undermined the operating conditions of companies and employment. Nevertheless, in the Finnish crisis, the financial system was able to remain operational in its essential parts: the funds deposited in banks remained available to depositors, the payment system functioned without disruption, and foreign payment relationships also continued without severe interruptions due to lack of trust or regulation. One can only imagine what the situation would have been like if these basics had also been disrupted. The stability and ability of the financial markets to function is not just a national interest. Stability is inevitably an international issue, because both the market and the parties involved, above all the banks, are international and therefore the risks do not look at national borders. The monetary infrastructure that is vital for the economy - payment systems, account registers and securities settlement systems - is also largely international. The widespread dependence of production and consumption on foreign trade, the country's foreign liquidity and the smooth flow of international payment transactions has long been a fact. In a highly connected global economy, no country can isolate itself from international monetary shocks, especially a small, developed and economically specialized country like Finland. If a serious crisis on the financial markets were to uncontrollably destroy the basic structures of the monetary system, unilateral action by one country, even extreme ones, would not be able to prevent significant economic and social damage. The international institutions of the financial markets are part of the peace project of the international community. The crisis of the 1930s contributed to the tightening of international relations and the rise to power of dictatorships in many European countries. At that time, international cooperation did not work. In 1933, an international economic conference was held in London to try to resolve the then crisis. However, the conference failed because Hitler's Germany had turned away from the democratic path and President Roosevelt refused international treaties binding on the United States. It was only at the end of the Second World War that the Bretton Woods Conference in the United States congratulated on the establishment of a multilateral international financial architecture, thanks to which we have the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank and the World Trade Organisation( WTO). The current financial crisis has once again given rise to the idea of strengthening and rebuilding the international financial architecture. G20 leaders have been invited to a summit in Washington in mid-November. Finland will be represented through the EU and the Bank of Finland will be represented as part of the European Central Bank and the Eurosystem. SLIDE 3: Features of the Current Crisis The current crisis in the financial markets began in August 2007. At the time, there was still talk of financial turmoil. It escalated into seriousness no later than 15 September last, when the US investment bank Lehman Brothers collapsed. This marked the beginning of the current phase, which is characterised by banks' mistrust of each other and their overgrown desire to improve their own liquidity. Over the past decades, the world's financial system has relied on banks to base their liquidity on their ability to borrow money from each other in the interbank deposit market if necessary. Now this strategy is no longer working, as banks' confidence in each other's creditworthiness and liquidity has deteriorated. They are no longer willing to give each other unsecured credit as usual. As access to borrowed money has become more difficult, banks are now trying to secure their own solvency by acquiring more liquid investments for themselves  the best treasury bills and central bank deposits. This rush to liquid assets has spirallingly exacerbated the state of the interbank money market. Banks' desire to increase the liquidity of their investments has also made them more cautious in their lending. The decline in interbank confidence is driven by a sharp increase in the volume of securitised real estate loans over the course of this decade. These were loans that banks turned into securities for resale in large bundles. The idea was to free up the capital committed to the loans and diversify the credit risks involved in them in the market. SLIDE 4: Mortgage Create and Diversify Model The so-called "mortgage securitization" however, the create-and-diversify model included, at several levels, poor incentives, which led to a deterioration in the quality of the loan portfolio and an increase in uncertainty about it. The system rewarded volume growth and not risk control. When the long rise in real estate market prices last year stalled, first in the United States, it turned out that the market for mortgage-backed securities was built on a deceptive foundation. The value of securities fell and their sellability  liquidity  plummeted. The banks and insurance companies that had invested in them, or guaranteed them in the market, ran into a new situation. Capital dwindled and liquidity deteriorated rapidly. Where did this flood of mortgage-backed securities come from? One of the reasons for the unhealthy phenomena in real estate financing was, in retrospect, the overly light monetary policy of the early 2000s, which sustained the rise in real estate prices. Another reason was the prolonged imbalances in the global economy, as part of which the huge balance of payments surpluses of Asian countries brought large amounts of capital seeking new investments to the market. A third factor behind the crisis was also the recklessness of banks as they became heavily indebted to short-term money markets. The fourth factor was the shortcomings of financial supervision. The most significant example of this is that in the United States, investment banking was practically outside normal banking supervision. The fifth factor that accelerated the growth of the market was the incentive scheme just mentioned. Now, mortgage-backed securities have turned into "problem waste" that no one wants to buy. Wall Street's illustrious flagships, investment banks, have in a short time gone down in history. All parties to the market are feverishly trying to reduce their dependence on short-term debt and change their wealth to the most liquid form possible. This threatens to lead to a self-perpetuating negative spiral, which at worst is a credit crunch. The Finnish financial system had not been significantly directly exposed to the events that triggered the current crisis, American real estate loans or the bankruptcies of large banks. Liabilities in Icelandic banks were also small. Indeed, the effects of the financial market crisis have come to us indirectly, as the general state of the global financial markets has changed. The solvency and liquidity of Finnish banks are good today. However, Finland is by no means isolated from the ever-changing situation on the international market. The increase in the cost of market financing and the sharp fall in stock prices have an impact on the financing costs of financial sector companies and the value of investments. How the Finnish economy as a whole copes with the current turmoil will depend crucially on the development of the global economic cycle. What is clear is that economic growth is slowing down markedly here too. The slowdown in global economic growth and the general decline in confidence have an impact on the development of exports and, in particular, on investment and, consequently, on employment. The rise in financing costs and the tightening of financing conditions have already begun to affect business investment. Customers' financing difficulties have reduced export orders. SLIDE 5: Crisis management interventions and the role of central banks How have we tried to manage this crisis? Ronald Reagan once said the well-known phrase: 'Government is not the solution, government is the problem'. Now market optimism has failed. The functioning of the market requires that supply and demand meet and that the parties have confidence in each other's ability to pay and liquidity. In the financial crisis of recent weeks, these conditions ceased to apply. Strong intervention by states, governments and central banks became necessary. The state became a solution because it has the right to collect taxes, and from the Central Bank, because it can create money. The principles of the division of labor between authorities are clear. Central banks take care of the liquidity of banks and the monetary system as a whole. The way out is for the Central Bank to provide banks with credit in exchange for adequate collateral. However, the tasks of central banks do not include covering the losses of banks. If there are so many losses that the solvency of the banks is jeopardised, it is up to the governments and finance ministries to decide on capital support. The means are either government equity investments in banks  the so-called "equity investments". recapitalisation  or the purchase of banks' risky assets  illiquid loans or securities  into the hands of the state and thereby the easing of banks' balance sheets. Although these principles are clear, in practice the responsibilities of central banks and the state in crisis management are intertwined, because liquidity and solvency are twins: when granting credit and deciding on the collateral for credit, the Central Bank has to take a stand on the solvency of banks, and, on the other hand, when ministries of finance provide guarantees to banks or buy their assets from banks, they make liquidity policies. Close coordination between central banks and ministries is therefore essential. The third important element in crisis management is financial supervision. It supervises individual banks and their solvency. Therefore, it is the owner of important information. It is also capable of directly intervening in the activities of banks. In the early stages, from August 2007, the focus of crisis management was on securing the liquidity of banks and the money market as a whole. As the interbank money market began to dry up, banks' need for liquidity increased, and central banks lent banks large amounts of central bank money to banks. Bank reserves, ie. the amount of central bank money circulating in the banking system increased in an unprecedented way. The press likes to talk about "pumping" money into the market, but it is a question of short-term loans to banks by central banks against various collateral, usually securities collateral. This activity has been very widespread since August last year and has been growing, both in the United States and in Europe, as banks have still not wanted to lend to each other, and money between them now flows largely through central banks. The role of governments in this crisis has only been highlighted this autumn after the bankruptcy of the Lehman Brothers investment bank. Since the crisis has escalated in Europe and the United States, extensive programmes have been adopted to safeguard the recapitalisation of banks where necessary. The summit of euro area heads of state held in Paris on 12 October endorsed the principles, which were later confirmed by all EU countries in the Council of the EU. The decisions provided strong support for central banks' efforts to ensure banks' liquidity. At the same time, governments committed themselves to safeguarding the functioning of the financial system through three different means: 1. a fixed-term State guarantee for new bank borrowings, 2. the provision of additional capital to viable banks in the form of state investments, and 3. preventing the failure of important financial institutions in difficulty, if necessary by capital investment. SLIDE 6: Balance sheet effect of losses Crisis management is, of course, aimed at minimising disruptions to the functioning of financial markets. At the same time, however, both central banks and governments must be careful that crisis management measures do not in themselves cause harm. For their part, central banks must ensure that the objective of monetary stability over the medium term is not jeopardised. This presupposes that measures to increase central bank money are measured flexibly and correctly in relation to the demand for central bank money that exists in the banking system. This task is made very challenging by the fact that the effects of monetary policy and the financial market crisis on inflation will only materialise after a fairly long delay. Even in conditions of high uncertainty, monetary policy should be able to navigate correctly between controlling inflation and combating the risk of deflation. There are examples in history where, if inadequately managed, the financial market crisis has, in a couple of years' time, led to a deflationary spiral that is difficult to manage. Governments and finance ministries, on the other hand, when supporting the solvency of the banking system, must ensure that the risks and potential costs to taxpayers do not become excessive. An equally important aspect is that the safety net that is tuned under the financial system does not lead to the so-called "black market". moral hazard, i.e. the fact that banks will continue to take too much risk precisely by relying on the existence of a safety net. For this reason, state interventions, while increasing the operational capacity and solvency of the targeted bank, must also ensure that the bank's management and owners bear their share of the realised risks, losses. State intervention is also always accompanied by the risk that aid given in one country will distort the competitive situation between banks and countries. Crisis management in one country could exacerbate the situation in a neighbouring country. It is therefore essential that measures to be taken in Europe are agreed at EU level. This was the case with the state guarantees and recapitalisation of banks' new credits and, albeit belatedly, with regard to the deposit guarantee scheme. SLIDE 7: What about after the crisis? Today, we do not know when the financial markets will finally calm down and the global economy will be put on a more stable footing. What is clear, however, is that the crisis has been so deep and painful that there is no going back to the time before it. There will be changes both in the structures of the financial markets and in their regulation and supervision. One structural change already taking place is the increased role of the public authorities as the owner of the financial markets. Both the United States and some European countries have invested large amounts of capital in banks and insurance companies. It is difficult to predict how long this increased ownership will continue and what strategic importance it will take on the activities of financial institutions after the financial crisis. However, I think it is likely that, for various reasons, governments will be reticent about exercising direct influence in the banking sector once the former management and shareholders have assumed their responsibilities. They will probably want to sell their investments reasonably soon, once the market situation has returned to normal. In order to ensure that new, wider state ownership does not distort the competitive conditions in the financial markets, competition authorities must be vigilant when safety nets for the financial sector, which have been set up during the crisis, and also when the time comes to dismantle them after the crisis. It is clear that the financial system cannot remain permanently covered by a comprehensive guarantee from the state. Competition between international banking groups in the global economy and with a guarantee from the public sector is an impossible combination that would eventually lead to major trade policy problems and dangerous distortions in the functioning of the financial markets. The world shortage of the 1930s led to a general trade war, which essentially deepened the then crisis, especially in small countries. When the general guarantees offered by the public sector need to be fixed-term, after the crisis the financial sector must return to normal. The actual responsibility for the stability of the financial system must lie with the banks and insurance companies themselves. It is there that strategic and operational decisions are made on loans and other investments, on the structures of information systems, and on the ratio of equity and risk. But at the same time, it is clear that the one-way competition between financial centers for who regulates the least will come to an end. The focus of regulatory development shifts to who regulates best and where the financial markets are most transparent. On the other hand, we need to improve proactive crisis management preparedness, especially at international level. SLIDE 8: For better financial supervision How will regulation change? I am convinced that all the major players in the financial markets will be subject to public scrutiny. In this respect, the reform of Finland's financial supervision, which is being discussed in Parliament, goes in the right direction by bringing together the supervision of banks, insurance companies, pension funds and the securities markets. In addition, the following changes are necessary: 1. In prudential supervision, significantly more attention needs to be paid to measuring risks. 2. Credit rating agencies lost ground. Neither banks nor supervisors will be able to outsource their risk assessment to credit rating agencies to the same extent as before. 3. The authorities responsible for financial supervision will have to change their approaches. In addition to solvency, more attention should be paid to the regulation and supervision of liquidity. It is essential that banks are not overexposed to uncertain sources of short-term financing. 4. International supervisory cooperation must be intensified. in the EU. This means that the home country principle currently in force will be supplemented. According to the home country principle, the supervisor of the head office country is responsible for supervising the bank. In future, in the case of a multinational bank, supervisors from all countries in which the bank has significant activities will have to participate in supervision and have access to supervisory information about the bank. A new EU-level financial supervisory organisation is needed to supervise the largest multinational institutions. Such an EU supervisor may consist of national supervisors and their common central organisation, which would have binding decision-making powers in relation to certain matters concerning multinational financial institutions and other supervised entities. Even if the regulation and supervision of financial markets are improved, the possibility of further crises can never be completely ruled out. International cooperation in crisis management must also be strengthened. Cooperation requires a legal framework, a well-functioning organisation and different skills that develop as a result of joint crisis exercises and experiences. Going through different threat scenarios and scenarios helps to prevent or at least impound many problems. SLIDE 9: Two Types of Threats and Crises The development of crisis preparedness everywhere, including in the financial sector, is based on the definition of threat scenarios. Serious disturbances in the financial markets - or threat scenarios - can be divided into two parts. The first type of threat is the serious realisation of risks in financial operations. It is in this region that the current crisis has occurred. Iceland, in particular, is an example of a country where risks in the financial sector have, when realised, been reflected in society as a whole. Elsewhere, although in a milder form, we have gained experience of the consequences of serious disruption to the normal functioning of the financial system. A crisis in the financial system can be the instigator of a crisis in the economy as a whole. The second threat relates to the serious disruptions to the infrastructure of the financial system. We are talking about critical telecommunications or system failures, interruptions in energy supply or a major accident. A particularly serious threat scenario is a possible terrorist attack aimed at the infrastructure of the financial system. Both types of threats can, at worst, lead to so-called risk factors. the materialisation of systemic risk. Systemic risk refers to a situation in which, as a result of the materialisation of risks, the entire financial system is in danger of collapsing: institutions go bust like bowls because banks and other institutions are broadly intertwined. They have considerable mutual liabilities and claims against each other and to other participants in the financial markets. Many classifications of threat models have been made in Finland and they have also been applied to the financial sector. SLIDE 10: Strategy for safeguarding the vital functions of society Securing the vital functions of society, i.e. the so-called "security". The YETT strategy was completed in Finland in 2006. It provides a good basis for society's preparatory work in preparing for threats and crises. Many of the threat models outlined in it have direct and indirect effects on the financial markets. SLIDE 11: Government decision on safeguarding the security of supply With regard to safeguarding the security of supply, the Government decided in August this year to define the objectives for Finland's security of supply. Safeguarding financial systems is central to this. The Government's decision to safeguard the security of supply emphasises that the availability and preservation of up-to-date information must also be ensured in situations where systems and their maintenance move across national borders. It is therefore required that there must be adequate contingency arrangements for the management of interbank payments even after the transition to the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA). The Government's decision precisely lists the objectives related to the functionality of payment transactions and the preservation of data. As stated above, the key is that companies and institutions operating in the financial sector have well-functioning risk management systems, that they are solvent and that their internal control is in order. Preparedness must be seen as a continuous activity and it must be focused on already when the situation in the industry is good and the operating environment is favourable. In addition to the financial companies' own efforts, maintaining preparedness naturally requires cooperation with the authorities and their own measures. As the last few weeks have visibly shown, the financial sector is an international activity in which the effects of various events spill from one country and institution to another in an instant. This poses particular challenges for preparedness in Finland precisely in the financial sector, which is highly international in nature. In the following, I will briefly discuss the tasks of the Bank of Finland and the work that is being done in Finland with regard to the preparedness of the financial markets. SLIDE 12: The Four Core Activities of the Bank of Finland The Bank of Finland has four core functions. When it comes to monetary policy, we are a fully-fledged decision-maker in the Eurosystem. With regard to money supply, the Bank of Finland is responsible for issuing new euro banknotes and coins and for ensuring that the means of payment in circulation are authentic and correct. During this crisis, two core functions have been highlighted. In the banking area, the ECB's monetary policy implementation and liquidity operations are carried out on a decentralised basis by the national central banks . Accordingly, the Bank of Finland provides central bank credit against approved collateral to counterparties operating in Finland. Because of the responsibility associated with the liquidity of the banks, we are therefore here in the market every business day. With regard to financial supervision, the tasks are divided between the Financial Supervisory Authority and the Bank of Finland. The task of the Financial Supervisory Authority is to monitor the solvency of individual banks. The Bank of Finland's task is to safeguard the stability and efficiency of the entire financial system. This task is emphasised in times of crisis, because the Bank of Finland is, if the situation so requires, the Bank of Finland is a so-called bankrupt. lender of last resort, an emergency funding provider in addition to normal central bank financing. During the current global crisis, the Bank of Finland has not granted emergency funding to any operator in Finland. In many countries, the current crisis has also highlighted the importance of general supervision by central banks, because from one bank the crisis can spread rapidly to the entire sector due to the effects of contagion. In order to carry out this task, the Bank of Finland conducts a financial market stability analysis, in which financial stress tests are an integral part. The National Emergency Supply Agency is a key authority in Finnish crisis management. Financial supply is one of its priorities. There is a lot of cooperation between the National Emergency Supply Agency, companies in the sector and the authorities. The Bank of Finland has its own key responsibility as part of the financial services pool formed by the sector. The pool is a good example of how in a small country all key players can be effectively involved in cooperation. The result of the work of the funding pool is, among other things, the financial market's contingency guidelines, which contribute to implementing the statutory obligation of companies and organisations in the sector to prepare for serious disturbances and exceptional circumstances by means of plans and advance arrangements. The functionality of the contingency guidelines has been tested with separate banking procedures, i.e. so-called banking procedures. With PATO exercises. SLIDE 13: Participation of the Bank of Finland in crisis exercises Given the internationalisation of financial markets, joint international crisis exercises are very important. The Bank of Finland has participated in many such international crisis exercises. We have done this between the Nordic central banks, because many of the banks that operate in finland play a significant role in more than one Nordic country. We have also participated in joint ECB-Eurosystem crisis exercises. In addition, together with the Ministry of Finance, we have also been involved in a financial crisis exercise at EU level. What lessons have been learned from these crisis exercises? Crisis scenarios have been made as real as possible. We have had to test the cooperation between different actors. We have had to analyse how quickly the crisis spreads from one country to another. We have had to make assessments in real time of whether a crisis that started with liquidity problems will turn into a solvency crisis. Cooperation with the Central Bank, the Ministry of Finance and the Financial Supervisory Authority must then be seamless. In the exercises it has proved difficult to create the so-called .... private sector solutions in which the actors in the sector would resolve a serious crisis among themselves, without the help of public authorities or public authorities. Such solutions always take precedence among the options, because they save taxpayers' money. In general, however, there is a need for a coordinating or at least supportive role for the authorities. The solution that emerged in Finland for the branch of the Icelandic bank, Kaupthing, was based on the activities of the private sector, which, however, also required state support in the form of guarantees. Furthermore, could the global crisis that began in August 2007 have been avoided with better crisis training by the authorities and market participants? The answer is no; negative market phenomena and imprudent behaviour cannot be changed by exercises alone. However, the crisis exercises have been of significant benefit. They have shown the participants in advance what kind of situations and in what kind of avalanche they may be solved. They have confirmed the view that, in a Financial Market integrated in Europe, the solutions to crises must also be properly coordinated and multinational. However, they are also based on the initiative and cooperation of the national authorities. SLIDE 14: Future Prospects Ladies and Gentlemen, The international financial crisis that we are currently experiencing is serious and will continue. The consequences of the crisis for the real economy, its effects on production, employment, public finances and people's well-being are certainly, for the most part, still to come. We know that these effects will be negative, but any estimate of how great they will be is still very uncertain. What is positive about the experience of recent weeks is the ability shown by the authorities and political leaders to cooperate across national borders. This cooperation has played an important role in not seeing a more serious collapse of the financial system. The capabilities for first-stage crisis management have proved satisfactory, to say the least. The crisis has shown that, in the future, it will be necessary to move from international cooperation in the supervision of the financial markets to building more permanent rules of the game and multilateral institutions. The reform of the international financial system is a major project that has not even properly begun yet, but its importance from an economic and world political point of view cannot be overestimated. For the European Union, the crisis represents a challenge to develop its own institutions and capacity to act. Community-level powers in the field of financial supervision must be increased. The Union also needs to step up its presence on the international stage at a time when the writing of the rules of the game, also known as world financial architecture, has been put on the agenda. This is particularly in the interests of the smaller Member States, as it is through the EU and the ECB that their say in the design of future financial market structures can be most strongly realised. In the past, EU integration has often deepened precisely in response to economic challenges. The whole organization began as a response to the problems of the coal and steel industries in the 1950s, and it was not until the currency crises of the early 1990s that several Member States convinced of the need for a single currency. Of course, German reunification also created a political opportunity for this. It is to be hoped that the current crisis will give the EU the impetus to strengthen common policies, including on financial market issues. History shows that economic interests have been the motive for the EU's political integration, but this does not contradict the idea that the EU is, in essence, a project of peace and a mitigator of conflicts between states. From Finland's point of view, our membership of the EU and the euro area has been an advantage during the crisis. Membership of the monetary union means unprecedented security for Finland and other Member States against balance of payments crises. A collapse in international economic relations, which has hit some developing countries in the past, and which most recently threatened Iceland, would be almost impossible in the case of a member state of the euro area. In addition to the financial protective effect of the euro on the financial markets, our membership has enabled Finland to be an active, constructive and full member in all the forums where solutions to the problems of the financial markets have been sought. Finland's experience, expertise and contribution to european financial crisis management have also been appreciated. Eu membership and participation in economic and monetary union will continue to be a key means for us - not forgetting our membership of the International Monetary Fund  to be involved in influencing the regulation of financial markets and to the development of the structure at European and global level. It is in Finland's interest that the EU presents itself as a united, proactive and constructive party in this process, which is only just beginning.

Title: Finland, Europe and slowing global economic growth. A challenge to competitiveness
text: President Erkki Liikanen: Finland, Europe and slowing global economic growth. A challenge to competitiveness. Seminar of the autumn meeting of the Confederation of Finnish Industries 27.11.2008, Helsinki . Speech . Thursday27 November 2008, 12:00 AM Director General Erkki Liikanen Seminar of the autumn meeting of the Confederation of Finnish Industries 27.11.2008, Helsinki FINLAND, EUROPE AND SLOWING GLOBAL ECONOMIC GROWTH. A CHALLENGE TO COMPETITIVENESS Speech Related Membranes (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and. . interviews/documents/081127_el_elinkeinoelama_final.ppt) (PPT) Puheeseen Related Membranes (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and. . interviews/documents/081127_el_elinkeinoelama_kalvot.pdf) (PDF) Link to the speech summary (/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and-interviews/2008/paajohtaja-erkki-liikanen.. would-the-labour-market-be-synthesis-time-summary-of-speech-of-the-business-life-union-autumn-meeting. seminar-27.11.2008-helsinki/) Just over six years ago, Matti Vanhala, President of the Bank of Finland, gave a speech in Helsinki titled "Market-driven wage formation boosts employment". The central message of the speech was: time had overtaken the traditional incomes policy of agreeing on uniform wage increases covering the entire labour market. We were on our way to a world where there could be a shortage of labour in one industry or region, while in another, the redundant labour force became unemployed. Vanhala called for the need to give the labour market room to function, to allow wages to adjust in all relevant dimensions  by industry, region, occupational group and skills  so that the available labour force could be channelled into the most productive and thus the best paid use. It was not easy for everyone to accept the message of the speech. It was most difficult for those who had put a lot of effort into making the income policy decisions of the time. This was particularly the case in the trade union movement. It is widely accepted today that wage-setting is not only about distributing the common good in a fair way, but that the labour market is also a key part of the market economy. But views differ widely on what should replace traditional income policy solutions. How important is macro-level coordination, what is its relationship with industry-level or local wage formation? While it has been difficult for the trade union movement to give up the hut, this seems to be difficult for employers. I will come back to that later. *** What are the current challenges for the European and Finnish economies? The global economy is in the throes of unprecedented turmoil. The infrastructure of the global financial sector is faltering, access to finance is tightening and the value of international trade is likely to fall next year. No one is in any doubt that the challenges to our economy are extraordinarily great. The seeds of the crisis were sown a long time ago. Symptoms appeared in the summer of 2007. The US subprime market is the trigger for the crisis. A phase began that we called the financial market turmoil. The rapidly increasing use of leverage by international banks since the beginning of the decade was the real cause of the problems. (Figure 2. Over-indebtedness of the international financial system) An increasing share of lending and investments was financed by market financing. The share of deposits in bank financing contracted. Investments were made in securities that at the time had a high credit rating and therefore tied up less equity. As investments were revalued after the turbulence resumed, their value declined while access to market financing became significantly more difficult. Lightened risk buffers, lower relative equity proved insufficient. (Figure 3 chronology of events) The disturbance of just over a year smouldered, flared up at times, but subsided again for a while. The situation escalated into a crisis just over two months ago. First, in mid-September, Lehman Brothers, one of the major US investment banks, went bankrupt. Lehman soon pulled after one of the world's largest insurance companies, AIG, which had to be rescued with federal funds. In the previous week, the giant US housing financiers Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac had fallen into the arms of the federation. There is no entity on the international financial markets that has not been touched in any way by the bankruptcy or brink of bankruptcy of these four major financial players. In a modern financial market, all players are financially linked to each other  either directly or indirectly through common counterparties. It was known that the dominoes were starting to fall, but no one could have foreseen which way  which brick would fall next. When it was not known exactly where the risk was, everyone was suspected. (Figure 4. Risk premiums in interbank markets in the euro area) Panic immediately spread around the world. Trade in the interbank market stalled and prices rose. The cost of long-term fundraising for banks increased sharply. So did the price that holders of bonds issued by banks had to pay for insuring the credit risk inherent in their investment. (Figure 5. Banking CDS) At the same time, in some banks around the world, signs of deposits trickling out began to appear. Cash flows dwindled and liquidity tightened. It was clear that if nothing was done, the financial markets were heading towards a massive systemic collapse. Governments and central banks took action at a pace that is unparalleled. Central banks wanted to ensure access to liquidity for the banking sector. For the Eurosystem, this meant abandoning the quantitative restriction on central bank money to be distributed to banks and giving them all the liquidity they were willing to take at the key ECB interest rate. (Figure 6: The ECB's liquidity operations) When the weakening of the foreign exchange market led to a shortage of dollars among European banks, the ECB, through an agreement with the Federal Reserve, the Fed, also began to provide banks with dollar liquidity without quantitative restrictions. States also implemented a wide range of confidence-building support measures. A summit was held in Paris on 12 October, which summarised a common European policy. (Figure 7. Decisions of the Paris Meeting) Two measures supported bank borrowing. Firstly, the deposit guarantee for bank deposits was improved. Secondly, it was agreed to provide state guarantees for bank fundraising. At the same time, agreement was reached on measures by which governments invest funds in order to improve the solvency of banks and thus safeguard their lending. (Figure 8. Example of the balance sheet effect of losses, why capital support is needed) (Figure 9. Example of the impact of losses and risk aversion on the target size of a bank's balance sheet) The support measures were successful in that the international financial markets did not collapse. The fall of the dominoes stopped. Confidence in banks' solvency began to improve, which was reflected, among other things, in the lower price of banks' credit risk insurance. However, the situation is far from normal. The exchange has not recovered in the interbank financial markets, but the flow of money between banks is largely channelled through central banks. Despite the ECB's interest rate cuts, euribor rates have remained high due to risk premiums  a fact that the majority of finnish mortgage borrowers perceive in the breakdown of their loans and its companies see in their financing costs. From the point of view of Finland and the global economy, an even greater concern than the price of money is its availability. Information from various sources suggests that while the threat of collapse has receded, the financial taps have remained tight. (Figure 10. Net share of banks that have tightened credit policy in the US and the euro area) Access to credit has become more difficult for the small customer at the bank counter, it has become more difficult for large companies to raise syndicated borrowing, and it has become more difficult for governments to obtain financing. The global financial markets' attitude to risk has fluctuated from one extreme to the other: after another year and a half of seeing risks almost nowhere, risk-averseness is now beginning to take on an over-the-top character. The collapse of funding is strangling the global economy in many ways. Investment plans are being cancelled, which will hit the Finnish engineering industry hard, whose production has focused on capital goods. Financial arrangements relating to international trade are becoming more difficult, which slows down the development of world trade in general. Especially in countries with current account deficits, the lack of funding forces a reduction in domestic demand. The key threat to the future of the world economy no longer concerns the stability of the financial sector, now we are talking about the stability of the real economy. The current crisis involves many phenomena that have to be described as unprecedented. One of them is the pace at which the international forecasting agencies have revised their economic forecasts for 2009 downwards. As recently as mid-September, both the euro area and the US economies were expected to grow by just over one percentage point next year. Now, a couple of months later, growth forecasts have been updated by a couple of percentage points downwards, meaning that both economies are now expected to contract markedly. (Figure 11: Growth forecasts for 2009) If all goes well, growth in the euro area could start to recover sometime in the next year. If things go badly, it will take much longer to get back to normal. In anticipation of the turnaround, the good employment trend of recent years will be interrupted and unemployment will start to rise. Traditionally, recessions in Europe have been long in coming. While the US economy has generally adapted and emerged from the pit quickly, europe's more rigid structures have slowed down the recovery and left unemployment high for a long time after periods of decline. Over the next few years, it will be tested whether the increase in employment experienced in Europe reflects a genuine improvement in economic structures or whether it has been onnenkantamoinen. *** Finland is approaching a downturn in the global economy in a balanced position. General government finances are strong, corporate indebtedness is low, and the Finnish economy is not burdened by the same kind of debt-driven housing market bubble as some other countries. The position of the banking sector is also stable in international comparisons. Still, the turmoil has hit Finland hard. The structure of Finnish exports is sensitive to the slump in investment and world trade. The confidence indicators are at rock bottom and the monthly indicator of total output has already made a downturn. The economic figures for the next few quarters will make for sad reading. The ECB's monetary policy and liquidity management measures are softening the real economic impact of the financial crisis in Finland as well. The strong position of public finances also allows the state to build a bridge over the economic downturn. A wide range of measures are also being prepared to secure companies' access to finance. The international recession is an opportunity to schedule public construction projects in a way that is beneficial to the national economy and the taxpayer. The projects must be justified and the readiness to get off the ground must be good. Even in a recession, the use of public funds must be prudent. *** The challenges for the Finnish economy in the coming years will therefore be considerable. Many companies will have to adjust the number of their staff to the changed situation and, despite public action, unemployment will rise. However, companies should also try to look beyond the economic downturn as well. The most important challenge facing the Finnish economy and labour market in the next few years and decades has not changed. Finland is ageing and the working-age population will soon begin to decline rapidly. In the short term, there may be an oversupply of labour, but as growth recovers, labour shortages are looming again. (Figure 12. The number of people of working age is shrinking) The ageing of the population will be costly for public finances, and preparing for the costs requires a brisk increase in the employment rate. In recent years, there has been a promising move in the right direction. If the impending recession now begins to push people into retirement and leads to a decline in participation rates, then during the economic upturn, labour shortages will be even worse and the challenges of ageing will be even greater. Effective wage formation is an important part of meeting these challenges. The financial crisis places a wide range of demands on wage formation in Finland. From Finland's point of view, the sharp slowdown in global economic growth is a strong macroeconomic shock  a macroeconomic one in the sense that it affects the economy as a whole. The economic outlook for the next couple of years is also exceptionally uncertain, and the risk of further macroeconomic shocks is high. Economic research shows that when the economy is hit by major macroeconomic shocks, effective macro-coordination in contract negotiations is important. A shock affecting the competitiveness of the national economy as a whole may require a broad-based adjustment of wages. Indeed, regardless of the contractual system, the labour market forces wages to adjust sooner or later, but macro-level coordination will speed up the adjustment and thus minimise the damage to the economy and employment. The possibility of macro-coordination is an important part of the contract system, but it alone is not an adequate response to the challenges of economic uncertainty. Although the financial crisis itself is global, its effects differ between companies. Similarly, the conditions for companies to withstand prolonged difficulties in financing or a drop in demand vary. Companies with a strong liquidity position are in a better position to maintain their capacity to function and the conditions for growth. On the other hand, companies whose activities have relied more heavily on external funding will run into problems more quickly. In such circumstances, different ways of building a bridge over the economic downturn are needed for businesses with healthy businesses. It is absolutely essential to ensure that the financial system is able to function. Although finland's challenges in this respect are smaller than in countries where banks have had to resort to crisis support, here, too, there is a need to ensure the liquidity of the financial sector and capital buffers. The government's efforts to secure funding are therefore justified. Local agreements can also be a way of providing flexibility at company level, so that companies with basic needs are not forced to close down due to temporary difficulties caused by the crisis. *** Finland therefore needs a model of agreement that has the ability to adapt to the needs of the situation. On the one hand, it must stabilise the economy and the labour market in the face of macroeconomic turmoil and, at the same time, provide flexible conditions for agreement at company level, too, when the situation of the company so requires. Such a model of agreement would help Finland in the difficult times ahead, but it would provide a flexible basis for agreeing also as the economic cycle improves. It would be important to create the conditions for agreeing at the level that best suits the situation. Agreement at the company and workplace level must always play an important role. This is the level at which decisions on recruitment and redundancies are made. It also provides the best information on what kind of skills are needed at any given time and how much they have to pay for it in the prevailing labour market. Local agreement is the instrument that enables the national economy to adapt flexibly to the structural changes that are constantly taking place in the economy. There is plenty of work to be done in developing systems to support company-level and workplace-level agreements. Some industries are already further along in this respect, but there is certainly room for improvement in all sectors. The increase in local agreement does not mean that the time for centralised coordination is over. Local agreement needs to be supported by a tool capable of responding to phenomena that have an impact at the macroeconomic level. The need for coordination is likely to vary from year to year, but it is important that the capacity to do so is created and maintained. What, then, should be the role of the industry level in agreeing on wages and working conditions? Its importance should not be underestimated. A wide range of economic shocks and technological advances can affect different industries in different ways. That is why the sectoral level is one of the dimensions within which the agreement system must allow for sufficient flexibility. (Figure 13. Finnish unit labour costs, compensation of employees) It has to be said, however, that the limited experience gained in recent years from industry-level contract rounds is not a positive one. An example of this is the round from a year ago. Certainly, in many industries, the situation was exploited and a genuine attempt was made to solve the kind of sectoral problems that had accumulated during the long tupoperiod. (Figure 14. Rate of increase in compensation of employees in relation to the development of labour productivity and the terms of trade) Nevertheless, it seems clear that the sectoral situation was not always the determining factor. There was cross-industry glancing and peeking, and as the round of agreements progressed, the level of increases moved upwards all the time. The general level of wage increases became high, and it is unclear whether even the wage structure of the national economy moved in a direction that supports employment. The process and outcome of last year's round of agreements were very closely reminiscent of what two well-known economists, Calmfors and Driffill, predicted twenty years ago in their classic article on contract systems: the mutual squabbling between the unions led to a level of wage increases that ultimately did not benefit anyone. (Figure 15. Labour costs per hour, total national economy) Wages must also be able to be flexible between sectors, but this must not be the only or even the main dimension of wage flexibility. When industry-specific rounds are made, it is equally necessary that, even then, there is a mutual agreement on an anchor to stay at. This would prevent a race between sectors. In general, a commitment to a sustainable wage line requires that the parties have a common understanding of the line before the first agreements are concluded. We can also learn from the experience of other countries. *** Six years ago, Matti Vanhala stressed the importance of pay flexibility in relation to coordination. At the time, he was instigating a debate that is continuing. Today it is recognized that, as important as the average wage development in the national economy, is the adjustment of the wage structure according to the needs of the economy so that the supply and demand of labor meet. But there is still a lot of work to be done in considering how to build these elements into the contract system. This issue should be discussed openly and without prejudice. The need for coordination has by no means gone away. Although Vanhala called for flexibility, he did not deny the importance of coordination. If implemented correctly, coordination can be an element that increases flexibility and enables it. If the "tupo" was thesis, and the "eitupo" antithesis, would we Snellman's heirs have the ability to develop a synthesis? In synthesis, strong wage coordination would create an anchor for nominal increases that correctly takes into account the growth of productivity in the national economy and the development of the terms of trade. Sector-specific and, in particular, company-specific arrangements would again seek solutions to company-specific differences in productivity and competitiveness. Now, after the last round of agreements, Finland is facing a sharply deteriorating global economy with an even heavier cost load and declining competitiveness. If employment is the only adjuster, the costs are unnecessarily heavy. Ladies and gentlemen! Europe and Finland face many common challenges. Financial market problems require action at national, European and global level. We have been on the move quickly, but there are still major problems ahead. Fiscal policy has its potential when public finances are in order. The Finnish Government has room for manoeuvre here, and it is right that it should be used. The more joint efforts in different countries go in the same direction, the greater their effectiveness. Structural policy reforms will improve the resilience and resilience of the economy. Studies carried out at the Bank of Finland have shown that by increasing competition in product and labour markets, the growth of the national product and economic dynamism are strengthened. In Europe and Finland, investing in knowledge, technological change and innovation must remain a high priority. Investments in research and product development play a key role.
