Title: Cooperation between the USA and the EU in resolving the financial crisis
text: Director-General Erkki Liikanen: US-EU cooperation in resolving the nuclear crisis. Foreign Policy Institute. Helsinki, 11.12.2008 . Speech . Thursday11 December 2008,12:00AM Director-General Erkki Liikanen Obama's choices d0 perspectives on the policies and impacts of the new US administration Foreign Policy Institute Helsinki, 11.12.2008 US-EU COOPERATION IN RESOLVING THE FINANCIAL CRISIS International financial crisis The crisis, which originated in the US subprime mortgage market, quickly spread to various areas of the financial markets, including euro-denominated money markets. Already in early autumn 2007, the Eurosystem and the Federal Reserve faced a significant challenge, when liquidity in the money markets suddenly declined and the interbank liquidity equalisation ended in a lack of confidence. The globalisation of the financial markets has shown its downside. No country seems to escape the harmful side of the crisis. The crisis is also spreading to the real economy and could lead to a serious recession in both Europe and the United States. When the market is functioning normally, banks balance liquidity in the interbank market. Those banks that have a surplus sell the surplus at the end of the day to those banks that, for one reason or another, need short-term money to cover their own payment flows. In other words, banks' liquidity is based on the ability to borrow from other banks if necessary, and the central bank is only used as a last resort. The operation is based on trust between banks. The counterparty risk is perceived as small. The Eurosystem's role has been to ensure that the market has provided sufficient liquidity to meet the needs of banks. Now the situation is different. As the crisis has progressed, bank confidence has eroded and the desire to give other banks unsecured credit has dried up. Coordinated operations The crisis has also posed new challenges for the European Central Bank and its Council, as well as for the Fed. In the midst of the chaos in the financial markets, central banks have done everything they can to secure the operating conditions of the financial markets. The Eurosystem and the FED have shown considerable ingenuity and flexibility in their efforts to safeguard the liquidity of financial markets in the face of difficult conditions. Traditional monetary policy frameworks are not predetermined. In the changed circumstances, both the Central Banks of Europe and the United States have open-mindedly changed the practices of trying to maintain the functioning of the market in the best possible way. As market tensions have risen, the FED in particular has expanded its activities to areas that are not common to the central bank. It rescued the investment bank Bear and Stearns, which was not a deposit bank. On the other hand, the FED did not bail out investment bank Lehman Brothers, which was later assessed as a mistake. The FED also lent to the insurance company AIG (American International Group). As the financial crisis has escalated, the Eurosystem and the Federal Reserve have stepped up their cooperation. This cooperation has led, above all, to new joint monetary policy operations, including foreign exchange and interest rate operations. The first joint operation with currencies took place as early as the end of 2007 in December, when steps were taken to secure the availability of dollars in Europe. Euro area banks had expressed concerns about the adequacy of dollars, and as a result of which the Governing Council of the European Central Bank announced that it would supply dollars to euro area banks in cooperation with the US Federal Reserve. The dollars were delivered to banks through the NCBs in exchange for normal Eurosystem collateral. Joint foreign exchange operations have also been conducted in 2008, for example through currency swaps. In the operation, the ECB has delivered euros to the FED for a fixed period of time and, accordingly, received dollars from the FED to replace the euros. These operations have ensured sufficient availability of dollars in the euro area. Historically, the most significant joint operation was the decision to simultaneously reduce interest rates on both sides of the Atlantic on October 8. On that day, the Governing Council of the European Central Bank, the Federal Reserve and four other central banks (the Central Banks of Canada, England, Sweden and Switzerland) decided to cut interest rates. This extraordinary codecision aimed to maximise the impact of the interest rate cut on the markets and to signal that central banks were determined to counter the deepening recession. In connection with the interest rate reduction, the Governing Council of the European Central Bank also announced that it would provide the market with euro liquidity in the main refinancing operations in an unlimited manner and at a fixed interest rate. It was a unique decision. It is worth noting that the Bank of Finland is the only central bank in the euro area that has used a similar method already in 1996. Also interesting is the fact that shortly thereafter, the Federal Reserve announced (13.10) that it would switch to a similar system. Other forms of cooperation in international for a In addition to the many joint operations, the European and US central banks are in close contact in a number of for a. The governors of both banks meet regularly at meetings of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the G7. There is also cooperation within the Financial Stability Forum (FSF) and the so-called Financial Stability Forum. Basel Committee. The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) has developed into a forum for cooperation between the world's key central banks. At present, the BIS is both a bank and an international organisation. The BIS is a kind of central bank of central banks and provides central banks with services related to the investment of foreign exchange reserves and gold, among other things. On the other hand, it is home to important cooperation committees between central banks and financial market supervisors. An integral part of the BIS's activities are its bimonthly meetings of central bank governors. The Governor of the Bank of Finland will also take part in these meetings. The meetings provide an excellent opportunity to discuss informally issues related to the development of the global economy. The BIS has a wide range of committees and working groups, both permanent and ad-hoc, which provide a good tool for cooperation between the Eurosystem and the FED. Perhaps the most well-known of these is the so-called .... The Basel Committee, which has prepared conditions for, among other things, the solvency of banks. The Basel Committee has formulated extensive standards and guidelines for control. Although the Basel Committee has no legislative powers, many of its recommendations have been transposed into national law. BIS also provides secretarial services to a number of independent expert organisations, the most important of which is the Financial Stability Forum (FSF). The Forum was established in 1999 and its mission is to contribute to the stability of international financial markets. There are also working groups attached to the Forum. The Central Banks of Europe and the United States regularly participate in the work of the Forum. In the spring of 2008, the FSF published an extensive multi-area list of measures aimed at more stable market conditions. Paulsonin roskapankkiehdotus In the autumn of this year, US Treasury Secretary Hank Paulson drew up a plan to set up a junk bank to support banks in trouble (The Troubled Asset Relief Programme , TARP). The intention was that 'toxic' and illiquid claims would be transferred from banks' balance sheets to the junk bank, thereby reorganising the banks. The arrangement is somewhat reminiscent of the Finnish solution in 1993, when Savings Bank Finland was split up and healthy parts of the bank were sold to competitors, but non-performing loans were transferred to a separate junk bank called Arsenal. According to Paulson, it took USD 700 billion to set up a junk bank. However, the project immediately faced headwinds in the US Congress. More left-wing critics thought the project would only protect Wall Street. Right-wing critics feared that the initiative violated the principles of a free market economy. Many criticised the fact that the Ministry of Finance is given a free hand to manage such a large sum. A number of questions remained unresolved, including how accountability would be organised. Although the motion did not touch bank ownership, the most conservative representatives in Congress saw the project as a threat to American capitalism. Many economists considered the direct recapitalization of banks to be a more transparent and efficient solution. For example, owning preferred shares would be a better solution for taxpayers than spending money on acquiring risky and hard-to-price securities. There was no obvious pricing method by which bad loans could be bought. A capital increase of one dollar would also allow banks to increase lending by about ten dollars. This was considered an effective remedy to combat credit crunch. In addition, the banks' shares still had some price on the market, which cannot be said to have been available with "toxic" ones. Although the issue was politically sensitive, Paulson stuck to the original plan. Partial socialization of the banks would have seemed an even worse option. Interestingly, however, when major investor Warren Buffet invested a substantial amount of money in Goldman Sachs' preferred stocks, he was highly praised in the market. Paulson's original motion was three pages long, but as other elements began to be incorporated into the junk bank bill in Congress, it swelled in a matter of weeks into a bill of more than 450 pages. The initiative was finally adopted on 3 October by a clear majority. In the vote, the bill was supported by 263 deputies and opposed by 205 deputies. After the decision, Paulson announced with determination that he would use the new powers. The US deposit guarantee scheme was increased from 100,000 to 250,000. Gordon Brown's alternative In the same week in Europe, the Irish Government baffled the leaders of other EU countries by unexpectedly announcing that the government would guarantee bank deposits in Irish banks for two years. The decision was a panic reaction and the result of reports that Irish banks had been subjected to a flight of deposits. The increase in the deposit guarantee scheme was not coordinated by any EU body and was considered by other EU countries to be a measure distorting competition. The Irish decision set in motion a process that resulted in the minimum amount of deposit guarantee in the EU countries being raised to EUR 50000. But, for example, the German government announced that it would guarantee all German private deposits in full. The decision was prompted by the accumulated problems of the German bank Hypo Real Estate and the fear of flight from deposits. In Finland, the notification of the Government's proposal to Parliament to increase finland's deposit guarantee scheme from EUR 25000 to EUR 50000 was issued on 8.10.2008. Perhaps the most important decision in principle to help distressed banks was taken in England on 8 October. Less than a week after the US Congress's decision on junk banking, British Prime Minister Gordon Brown announced a massive bank support operation. However, it was not a question of setting up a junk bank in the American way, but of recapitalising English banks and, consequently, of partially socialising the banks. The government was prepared to increase the capital of English banks in exchange for preferred shares (a350 billion). On the same occasion, the government announced that it would grant state guarantees for bank funding and the Bank of England announced a special liquidity programme through which the central bank undertook to exchange liquid government papers for banks' less liquid securities. Gordon Brown's performance was a completely different option from Paulson's and was widely praised in the European media. Immediately after Brown's decision, the idea of recapitalizing banks began to warm up in the USA as well. The debate highlighted the positive aspects of recapitalisation and ideological differences were allowed to recede. Paulson's idea of a junk bank suffered a shipwreck and a debate began in the United States about how much of the 700 billion set aside. can be used to recapitalize banks. Paris Declaration In Europe, the events of the eventful weeks culminated when the heads of the euro countries (and Gordon Brown) met in Paris on 12 October. The aim of the meeting was to agree on common principles and operating methods for the management of the financial crisis and, in particular, for problem banks. In particular, there was a desire to commit to common rules of the game. The Paris Declaration, published after the meeting, agreed on common principles and actions. First of all, it was decided that the states would start providing guarantees for unsecured fundraising by banks. Banks could apply for guarantees on a voluntary basis and they would be remunerated. In Finland, the maximum amount of guarantees is planned to be db50 billion. Eur. Secondly, principles were agreed on the possible recapitalisation of banks. Recapitalisation could take place either out of a desire to improve the lending capacity of viable banks or out of a desire to save the bank. In Finland, a maximum of db4 billion is planned for this purpose. Eur. Thirdly, it was agreed to increase the deposit guarantee to EUR 50,000. In the United States, the wind is turning Just a few days after the Paris declaration, the US government announced the historic decision to buy preferred shares in banks. A total of USD 250 billion was earmarked for the operation, of which USD 125 billion was earmarked for the operation. it was immediately decided to use the capitalization of nine large American banks. In this way, the US Government finally adopted the path chosen by Europe to deal with the financial crisis. At the moment, more than USD 160 billion has been spent on the purchase of preferred shares in the US. The idea of a junk bank was buried on November 12, when Paulson officially announced that the project had failed. Instead, Money from The Troubled Asset Relief Programme would be used to support car, credit card and student loans, among other things. In many American reflections, the decision-making capacity of economic policy in the euro area has been considered weak. However, the events of October show that Europe, which used to be seen as slow and fragmented, was capable of taking rapid decisions and, because of its activity and speed, of influencing us decision-making in managing the crisis. Does the internationalfinancial architecture need to be reformed? As the financial crisis deepens, the question has been raised of the ability of the international financial architecture to function and its reform. The G201 met to reflect on these issues at a summit in Washington on 15/11. The meeting had been convened by President Bush. As the meeting approached, it was suspected that, given President Bush's impending term of office and the short period of preparation, the outcome of the summit would not be very tangible. The outcome of the meeting would not be unambiguous and tangible. However, the decision-makers of the world's economic powers said that the mistakes of the market economy must be tackled decisively. The meeting mapped out ways to improve the financial architecture and, in fact, the result was more than many expected. Unanimously, the decision-makers of the G-20 countries agreed on general principles and measures for 2009. At the end of the meeting, the so-called "green paper" was published. Washington's Declaration. It contains general principles to which the leaders of the G20 countries commit themselves. The resolution contains a 45-point action plan. Some of the measures should be implemented by the end of March next year. Given the length of the list of measures and the number of countries involved, it is fair to say that the targets are ambitious. It is evident that the ongoing financial crisis has increased the search for consensus among the participating countries. Although the role of the various G conglomerates in the international financial architecture was not discussed, it is clear that the role of the G20 countries was strengthened as a result of the meeting. It is important to note that the Washington meeting was the first meeting of G20 leaders. The leaders announced that the G20 countries would meet again by April 30, 2009. G-20 policymakers agreed that regulation should extend to all market segments, products and operators. However, over-regulation should be avoided. The aim is to increase the transparency, regulation and supervision of the market The aim is to make operators in the sector accountable and market products transparent and understandable. The Washington meeting identified the need for, among other things, improved risk management by banks, international cooperation between supervisors, high standards for credit rating agencies and improved accounting standards. The participants in Washington agreed that we now need to start preparing concrete reforms. The problem, however, is how EU cooperation is organised in practice. Only the eu's large member states, England, Italy, France and Germany, are involved in the G20 cooperation. England will also hold the presidency of the G20 in 2009. There is a risk that the big EU countries will agree on reforms, regardless of the smaller ones. When the practical preparations for next year's April meeting get under way at full speed, the eu's true unity will be weighed up. 1 G20 countries include Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, China, Germany, India, Indonesia, Italy, Japan, Mexico, South Korea, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, the United States and South Korea. In addition, the G20 meetings are attended by the EU (presidency), as well as the IMF and the World Bank.

AB6633EB323F/0/090129_Taloustieteellinenyhdistys_en.ppt) For starters, I would like to congratulate the Finnish Economic Association, which from the start of the year combines under one roof the activities of the Finnish Economic Association and the Finnish Society for Economic Research. Since then, much has happened. At the time, that is, in my presentation in spring 2007 I said: oMonetary policy needs to pay attention to credit and money variables not only in the assessment of the potential inflationary impact of aggregate demand, but also because changes in indebtedness affect the stability of the financial markets and the whole economy. For one thing, the stability of the banking sector is a necessary prerequisite for the pursuance of successful monetary policy. For another, corporate and house-hold indebtedness affects the susceptibility to disturbances of the whole economy. The higher the indebtedness of the economy, the faster aggregate demand reacts to different negative distur-bances, such as fluctuations in economic outlook.o I doubt that anyone could have foreseen that this threat would began to materialise already in the summer of 2008. Back in August 2007, there was an abrupt turn in one segment of the US housing loan system, the market for subprime loans, which triggered liquidity problems across the fi-nancial sector. Soon huge credit and currency losses and consequent capital adequacy problems surfaced along with the liquidity problems. We are now witnessing a odeleveraging processo, whose impacts on the real economy can be seen everywhere. Growth of aggregate demand in the world economy has come to a halt as economic agents en masse try to repair their balance sheets at the same time. Throughout last year and even in January of this year, growth forecasts for 2009 have been revised downwards. According to recent forecasts, the GDPs of developed countries will contract substantially this year. World trade will also shrink, and this will notably slow the growth of emerging economies that rely on export-driven growth strategies. The idea that emerging Asian economies could offset the decline in US demand in the world economy is not being realised. This was the rationale for the so-called soft landing and decoupling scenarios of recent years. Confidence indicators are at historical lows. Not only have growth forecasts been revised substantially downwards; the associated uncertainty still exceeds the usual levels. Due to the abrupt slowing of growth, inflation has receded quickly. In particular, following the sharp rise of recent years, the prices of raw materials have dropped just as sharply. In some countries the halt in price increases has brought fears of deflation. The financial crisis has highlighted the extent to which national financial systems are intertwined and how interdependent are the different economies. How is it that the worldos financial markets are so highly sensitive to a change in the economic outlook? The underlying cause is a protracted and oversized accumulation of debt and an underestimation of risks. The structure finally broke where it was most vulnerable, in the US housing finance system. Many US financial market innovations in the last few years have been in the area of housing finance. One of these, the originate-and-distribute model of securitisation, which was also employed in the financing of subprime housing, functioned smoothly as long as housing prices kept on rising. However, when the price rise stopped in 2006, the problems began to surface. And when housing prices went into decline in 2007, the system collapsed. Subprime loans had a structural defect. After two amortisation-free and low-interest years, the interest rate would be set at levels as high as Libor6 percentage points. Because prices began to decline at the same time, many borrowers whose ability to repay had always been doubtful had to walk out of their homes. Fire sales worsened the downward spiral in the housing markets. On the other hand, US indebtedness was enabled and fuelled by expanding investment flows from the Asian surplus economies. These countries amassed huge stocks of investment assets and exported relatively cheap capital to the United States, which only acerbated the imbalances in the world economy. The expansion of the financial crisis to the global scale illustrates how dependent on US investment vehicles the international financial system has been in recent years. Central bankso monetary policy and the financial crisis The core functions of a central bank can be summarised as four areas: 1. monetary policy: preparation and implementation 2. banking operations: monetary policy operations, settlement of large payments and portfolio management 3. financial oversight: stability analysis, potential emergency funding) 4. currency supply: availability of banknotes and coins and control of their quality and authenticity. The crisis has brought changes to all of these areas. I will concentrate on the first three, although the crisis has also been felt in connection with currency supply. Changes are taking place in how we think about monetary policy and how its implementation is organised. Some of the changes are exceptional solutions for crisis situations, but the present crisis will also have a permanent impact on the operation of central banks. Under normal circumstances, the central bankos primary focus is on monetary policy aimed at price stability. Now I believe the financial crisis is also impacting our thinking about monetary policy strategy, both in the central banks and in academia. The one and half decades or so preceding the crisis were a time of growing support for direct inflation targeting. The often-prevailing notion was that monetary policy was simply interest rate policy and that a sufficient aim of interest rate policy was to hit inflation forecasts that were consistent with the price stability objective. In this context, quantitative magnitudes such as money and credit stocks played a secondary -if any -role. The European Central Bank has not strictly adhered to a strategy of direct inflation targeting; instead, it has always conducted its monetary policy on the basis of a otwo pillaro system. In this framework, inflation forecasts are in oeconomic analysiso pillar and growth of the money stock is in the omonetary analysiso pillar. In past years, this two.pillar framework at times aroused heated criticism and was considered old-fashioned and theoretically opaque. One cannot exclude the possibility that at some point the present problems will be ascribed to overly lax monetary policy in the pre-crisis years. Neither is it far-fetched to conclude that it would have been better if central banks around the world had paid more attention to controlling the growth of money and credit stocks. Now that it has become clear how crucial credit expansion and liquidity are for the emergence of the present problems and for the conduct of monetary policy in the crisis, I suspect that monetary policy will be viewed from a broader perspective than before. Policy interest rates have now sunk to historic lows, as current business conditions would demand. In the United States, monetary policy has even faced the zero-interest-rate constraint. The Fedos target level for the interbank overnight rate (Federal Funds Rate) has been cut to the range of zero to 0.25%. It is impossible to go much lower since the zero rate on cash holdings constitutes a type of floor for policy rates. Previous experiences with bottom-level interest rate policy are mainly those of Japan in the 1990s and in the United States in the 1930s. These two episodes show that lowering policy rates to zero may not be enough to get you out of a credit crunch and deflation. How can monetary policy be eased further when the traditional interest rate measures are exhausted? Japan already has a long experience with oquantitative easingo. The Federal Reserve has now resorted to roughly similar measures. The balance sheet total of the Federal Reserve system has tripled, from USD 800 bn to USD 2400 bn, as the Fed has extended its lending to new participants and introduced entirely new means of lending -finance facilities -which enable it to provide loans to the private sector. Discussion about zero interest rates and quantitative easing has also emerged elsewhere. However, the situation in Europe, at least for the time being, is different. There is less chance of deflation here. This should be taken into account in discussing how low ECB policy rates can go. At the same time, it should be borne in mind that the ECB's price stability objective means keeping inflation close to, but below, two percent in the medium term. Zero inflation -not to mention falling prices is not within the scope of this objective. Even expectations of deflation would be detrimental for total demand and for the real-estate markets. Stability issues Besides price stability, central banks also strive to ensure the stability of the financial system, a task that is highlighted in times of crisis. At times, emergency funding may also be needed. In normal times, an important way to ensure financial stability is to succeed in controlling the value of money. Sufficiently calm monetary conditions both contain inflation and prevent credit bubbles that could jeopardize stability. The other side of the coin is that pursuance of sound monetary policy is much easier if financial markets function in a reliable and stable manner. Under normal circumstances, financial market stability is a concern of regulation and supervision, with central banks mainly monitoring conditions and maintaining crisis management capabilities. However, a stabile situation may be disrupted and, as witnessed recently, the central banks may end up on the front lines, confronting issues such as whether and under what conditions emergency funding can be provided to problem-ridden banks. However, if regulation, competition and market transparency (the information base) are not up to par, even a good monetary policy environment cannot guarantee financial stability. It has even been claimed that an era of stability leads to a reduction in risk-awareness and the underestimating of risks, which only worsen and lead up to the next crisis. This odisaster myopia hypothesiso was enunciated by Hyman Minsky already in the 1960s and has recently attracted renewed interest. If the hypothesis is true, then no regulatory-supervisory system can withstand good times and the resultant liberalisation pressures, and so crises will inevitably recur from time to time. The central bank in acting as emergency financier faces some well known risks. Excessive reliance on liquidity support from the central bank may, at worst, induce banks and other market participants to pay insufficient attention to liquidity or even solvency. On the other hand, denial of emergency funding may have consequences such as we witnessed last autumn in the liquidation of Lehman Brothers. The dilemma is a tough one; but there is no way around it. Many central banks have recently faced it -fortunately not the Bank of Finland. The upshot is that proper performance of the central bankos task of ensuring stability requires a good system of regulation and supervision that prevents the omoral hazardo problem of excessive risk-taking due to the existence of a safety net. The crisis has laid a firmer foundation for international consensus on supervision issues. One step in that direction was the euro countrieso summit in Paris in October, where the countries made a commitment to secure the continuity of systemically important financial institutions and correspondingly promised to strengthen the structures of financial supervision. I will return to the pros-pects for supervision in more detail at the end of my presentation. Changes in implementation mechanisms of central bankpolicy The third key task of a central bank -as bankerso bank -has also been highlighted in the current crisis. As liquidity in the financial system dried up, banks set out to secure their own payment capacity, which led to a freezing-up of the interbank market. This gave the central banks an even more important role, beyond securing overall liquidity of the banking system: mediating liquidity between banks. Before the financial crisis, central banks' banking operations were considered to be basic technical services provided in the shadow of monetary policy. Now the situation has changed completely, as the crisis has forced us to pay close attention for example to the auction procedures of monetary policy operations and the central bankos collateral policy and collateral management. Suddenly these functions assume a very central and changing role on the stage of monetary policy. Within the Eurosystem, acting as bankerso bank is a task of the national central banks. Although ECB market operations are decided on a centralised basis, they are implemented on a decentral-ised basis by the national central banks, including the Bank of Finland. The reception and management of collateral for lending is also a job for the national central banks. Hence the financial crisis has spotlighted the role of national central banks within the Eurosystem. In contrast, in the US, the Fed decides on operations on a centralised basis, but the New York Federal Reserve Bank operates alone in the markets. This division of tasks remains unchanged. In other respects, however, the Federal Reserve has, since August 2007, made more changes in its operations than in its entire previous history. The number of counterparties has increased significantly, collateral procedures have been substantially revamped, etc. In the past, the Fed's market operations were restricted to short-term government paper, and private sector paper was approved as collateral only at the discount window, which provided funding solely for extraordinary and temporary payment difficulties. The ECBos operational framework, on the other hand and for historical reasons, from the onset included a large number of counterparties, and the pool of securities and bank loans approved as collateral for refinancing operations was extensive already before the financial crisis. Therefore it has been possible to respond even to pronounced changes in the operating environment of the euro area, primarily by adjusting existing operating procedures and resetting framework parameters. However, a lot has also happened in the euro area. After all, the financial crisis has been the historically most significant test of the operational framework of monetary policy. The financial crisis has proceeded in a gradual manner. Initial symptoms of problems in the financial markets surfaced in some sectors already in early 2007, but operation of the money market -the actual home base of the central bank -was not badly disrupted until August 2007. This first stage, labelled a disruption or turbulence, was characterised by a persistent lack of money market liquidity. Two changes were made already in the early stage. First, together with the US Federal Reserve, the ECB decided to offer collateralised dollar-denominated refinancing to euro area banks acting as its counterparties. The reason for such joint operations was the decoupling of the euro interest rates on the dollar from the interest rates in the later-operating US money markets. The widening of the interest rate spread was largely due to a dearth of trust between banks on opposite sides of the Atlantic Ocean, and the central bank cooperation was aimed at securing a frictionless flow of dollar liquidity across the Atlantic. Secondly, the demand for longer-maturity central bank money beyond the normal one-week period -increased sharply at the outset of the financial turbulence. Therefore the Eurosystem substantially extended the average maturity of central bank refinancing. Prior to the turbulence, the regular one-week basic refinancing operations accounted for about two-thirds of total refinancing, and the longer-term operations covered a third. [Slide 1.] After the financial disruption in late summer of 2007, the Eurosystem began to increase the size and variety of longer-term refinancing operations. Soon the proportions were reversed: only a third was for one-week maturity and the remaining two-thirds were for the longer maturities of 1d6 months. In September 2008, the financial disturbance turned into a full-fledged crisis in the wake of the Lehman Brothers bankruptcy. Concern about a significant expansion of credit risk paralysed money markets around the world. It was especially at this stage that the problems of the US money markets swiftly spread around the world. Activity in the interbank money markets virtually came to halt, and conditions in the financial markets worsened materially. Risk premia in the interbank money markets, which were already at high levels, jumped to new highs -in the euro area and elsewhere in the world. Uncertainty about the future state of the financial markets and the economy increased sharply. [Slide 2.] Uncertainty as to how much money would be auctioned off induced banks to notably raise their bid rates in a race to obtain liquidity from the central bank. The situation became unsustainable from the central bankos perspective when the average accepted bids exceeded the policy rate set by the Governing Council by nearly 75 basis points at worst. In other words, at that point the price of central bank money was almost three normal rate hikes above the target level. At the same time, Euribors in the interbank markets began to have a life of their own, decoupled from the ECB policy rate. The danger was that the ECB would lose its grip on actual conditions in the money markets: the transmission mechanism of monetary policy had been seriously weakened. At that stage, two major changes were made in the ECBos basic refinancing system, the first relating to the liquidity auction mechanism and the second to collateral policy. Previously, the ECB announced the minimum price of auctioned liquidity and at the same time controlled the amount of liquidity distributed. An individual bank would not obtain the liquidity it wanted if its bids were below the marginal auction rate. If it bid at the marginal rate, it obtained only a part of the requested amount. The marginal rate itself was determined by the bids and the ECBos target level of liquidity. At the start of October, the Governing Council revised the system by introducing fixed-price auctions. Here, the bankso quantity-bids are accepted in full if they have enough eligible collateral to cover them. In these ovolume tenderso, the central bank announces the price of liquidity, at which the supply is perfectly elastic. The banks inform the central bank of the amounts of liquidity they are willing to borrow at the given price. The move to volume tenders immediately eliminated the gap that had developed between the effective rate and the policy rate and, in a technical sense, the operability of the first link of the monetary policy transmission mechanism was restored. It took much longer before the Euribors -even the shortest ones -converged again to the policy rates. In recent weeks, the situation in this regard has become more normal, and one could probably say that the ECB and Eurosystem have regained their usual grip on the level of money market prices. This has also contributed to a rapid decline in market rates. [Slide 3.] However, the uncertainty facing the banks and the heterogeneity of the banking sector continue to impact the markets. Whereas banks previously trusted in being able to borrow short-term finance from the markets whenever necessary, they are now holding large excess reserves liquidity buff-ers -in their central bank accounts. The massive amounts of excess reserves were instrumental in the Governing Councilos decision to narrow the interest rate corridor from two to one percentage point in connection with the introduction of volume tenders. If a bank made an overnight deposit in the central bank of money bor-rowed from the central bank, it incurred a cost of half a percentage point -half of the previous cost. Last week, the two-percentage-point corridor was restored, so that now if a bank deposits such borrowed money in the central bank, it earns interest at one percentage point less than the policy rate. Correspondingly, banks pay one percentage point over the policy rate for overnight loans from the marginal lending facility. The purpose of restoring the original interest rate corridor is to give banks the incentive to once again even out liquidity among themselves on market terms. Collateral policy was another area of significant change in the policy implementation mechanism. In October 2008, the Governing Council revised the collateral policy of the Eurosystem so as to ensure that bankso liquidity supply would not dry up because of a shortage of assets for use as collateral. The importance of this action in the context of a financial crisis should be obvious. The collateral pool was expanded by adding certain dollar, pound sterling and yen-denominated marketable debt securities and by lowering the rating threshold of eligible instruments from A-to BBB-. I noted earlier the differences between collateral policies of the Eurosystem versus other major central banks. Because the treaty establishing the Eurosystem prohibits the favouring of government debt, private debt instruments -including not only securities but also certain bank loans meeting specific criteria -comprised an important segment of collateral accepted by the ECB already in the years before the crisis. This is an important factor in the modesty of the changes that have been made in ECB collateral policy even in the midst of financial crisis. In contrast, many central banks have been forced to make fundamental revisions in the principles of collateral policy as the crisis has deepened. In formulating collateral policy, central banks must always weigh the safeguarding of financial stability against the ballooning risks of their credit operations. The choice is neither easy nor straightforward. In light of experience gained so far, the operational framework of Eurosystem monetary policy has proven flexible and functional. It has enabled the effective maintenance of market liquidity. With the changes made last autumn, it has also improved the transmission of the Governing Councilos monetary policy actions into market interest rates. The central bankos policy measures taken during the worst phase of the financial crisis have solidi-fied the critical role of the Eurosystem in the context of financial market disruptions. Strong, financially sound banks are able to readily utilise the Eurosystem as a source of liquidity even when the interbank money markets are frozen. The model of centralised decision-making and decentralised implementation has worked well in the euro area. The role of national central banks in putting together the systemos liquidity management toolbox has been underlined by their close relationships with counterparty banks. The model of centralised decision-making and decentralised implementation can also be credited at least partly for the ECBos ability to react rapidly in the early stage of the crisis in August 2007 as well as for the Eurosystem's ability to revise its liquidity management practices throughout the crisis. In this respect, the Bank of Finland has not stayed on the sidelines. Thanks to our own analytical work and previous experiences, we have been actively involved in adjusting the interest rate steering system. Cooperation between central banks during the crisis Due to the global nature of the crisis, its management has required joint efforts by major central banks, such as the ECB and those of the UK, Japan, Switzerland and the US, to secure liquidity in the international money markets and to alleviate the impacts of the financial crisis on the real economy. The dialogue between economists in different central banks and decision-makers, which is active even under normal circumstances, has intensified in the course of the crisis, and the exchange of ideas has been supplemented by unprecedented joint interventions in the money markets. It was pointed out above that the Eurosystem and many foreign central banks have offered dollar liquidity in their open market operations in cooperation with the Federal Reserve. In addition to the dollar refinancing operations, the Eurosystem has provided its counterparties with Swiss francs. All of these operations are proof of central bankso desire and ability to act in money markets in the common interest when the situation requires it. As the most visible evidence of exceptionally close cooperation between central banks, one could mention the coordinated 50 basis-point rate cut of last October. Central bank policy rates in the developed countries have been rapidly eased to historical lows. In addition to multilateral operations between major central banks, the large central banks (particularly the ECB) have supported smaller currency areas by granting swap limits to their central banks, allowing the smaller central banks to calm their money markets. Willfinancial supervision change because of the crisis? While the financial crisis has resulted in crisis management operations on an unprecedented scale, it has also spurred discussion about reform of the supervision-regulation systems. The institutional structure of financial supervision has previously been reformed following experiences of financial crisis. Crises help to get over the institutional frictions often related to supervisory reform. Changes are also partly driven by development trends in the markets. Supervisory reforms are now on everybodyos agenda. Supervision is surely being reinforced and its scope extended in many ways due to the crisis. A commitment to that effect was made also at the political level in the G20 summit in Washington last November. One common area of development, particularly in Europe, is the internationalisation of supervision. Financial supervision in the EU is currently based on three basic pillars: responsibility of the national supervisory authority, the principle of home state control, and cooperation and coordination arrangements between supervisory authorities. The number of financial institutions operating in several countries has increased in recent years in the EU area. For example, by the end of 2007, there were 45 European banking groups with significant activities outside the home state. These banking groups operating in many countries account for two-thirds of the EU's banking markets. Banking groups try to centralise their key businesses, such as funding, wholesale market and trading operations, as well as the management of market risk and partly also credit risk. As a result, not just branches but also subsidiaries are often managed in a highly integrated manner. These changes in the financial sector have added to the pressure to reform the EUos financial supervision structures. When a bank is systemically relevant in more than one country, the solution has been to improve cooperation between the supervisor in the head office country (home supervisor) and the supervisor in the country of location of the branch or subsidiary (host supervisor) by establishing ocolleges of supervisorso. Progress has been made in this respect, which is important to Finland, and a corresponding legal basis is being established at the EU level. The ongoing financial crisis has also revealed problems in the institutional structure of the EUos current supervisory system. There is a chance that in a crisis, efforts will be made to protect the interests of national interest groups even when crisis management concerning financial institutions operating in many countries would require a systemic perspective and seamless cooperation between authorities. An important question going forward is how to organise supervision at the level of the EU or euro area of large international banks operating in several countries. When the number of countries involved is large and the bank is systemically relevant also to the entire EU area, a college of supervisors is no longer a satisfactory way to arrange supervision. A group chaired by Jacques de Larosiere, former managing director of the IMF, is preparing a proposal on the issue. In many areas of the EUos internal market policy, supervision solutions have been designed so that the national supervisor independently deals with nationally relevant issues and then the supervisors together form a supervisory structure that is responsible on a centralised basis for issues or companies with broader influence in the internal market. Examples can be found for instance in the areas of pharmaceuticals or competition -and why not also in chemicals. Another model is the European System of Central Banks. Financial supervision is a highly diverse and multifaceted issue. Nonetheless, one should be openminded about finding a solution for supervision at the level of the EU or euro area also in this field. Experiences with the present financial crisis now offer an opportunity to implement reforms. One alternative at hand is that the supervision of large banks operating in many euro area countries be established in connection with the ECB. With respect to supervision of the banking sector, this reform could be effected without revising the Treaty. Therefore it would be a pragmatic way to move on. However, this would require that the division of tasks between supervisors at the European and national levels be clearly defined. In addition, a solution has to be found for how monetary policy and financial supervision can be conducted in the new structures separately and independently enough, while also ensuring proper exchange of information and interaction. To be sure, there are other issues that have to be explored, all with an open mind. In addition to the internationalisation of supervision, another key reform area is increasing the coverage and uniformity of supervision across sectors. In a G20 statement, commitment was made to regulate or supervise all financial market products and agents. Previously, US investment banks for example operated outside the scope of banking supervision. The fading of sector borders and interlinking of risks has added to the pressure to reorganise and combine the networks of sector-specific supervision and regulation authorities. In this respect, Finland is on top of market developments. The new financial and insurance supervision authority, the Financial Supervisory Authority (FIN-FSA), commenced operations on 1 January 2009. The FIN-FSA, generally speaking, took over the tasks of the previous Financial Supervision Authority and Insurance Supervision Authority. The Financial Supervisory Authority is independent in its decision-making but operates in connection with the Bank of Finland. The solution has aroused much interest elsewhere. The advantage of the Finnish model, besides uniformity of supervision, is that it supports coordination and information flows precisely at the interface where it is most needed, between the supervisory authority and the central bank, which may have to consider the need for emergency funding. Finally In this presentation, I have focused on a review of the impacts of the financial crisis and the challenges posed by it from the perspective of the central bank. Monetary and fiscal policies have their division of responsibilities and central banks have their independence, which they are deter-mined to hold on to. Nonetheless, it is clear that economic policy can effectively alleviate the negative impacts of a financial crisis only by means of joint efforts among the various policy segments. Central banks consider measures taken by governments to ensure and reinforce bankso capital adequacy to be crucial. It is good that proposals to that effect have also been made in Finland. Reinforcement of bankso capital also promotes the objectives of monetary policy and supports the efforts of central banks to ensure the continuous functionality of the financial sector.

Title: International economic crisis and Finland
text: Director-General Erkki Liikanen: The international economic crisis and Finland. Venture capital date. Helsinki, 3.2.2009 . Speech . Tuesday 3February 2009,12:00 AM President and CEO Erkki Liikanen Venture Capital Day Porssisali, Helsinki 3.2.2009 INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIC CRISIS AND FINLAND Speech Membranes (PPT) (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and. . interviews/documents/090203_el_porssi.ppt) Puheen Membranes (PDF) (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and. . interviews/documents/090203_el_porssi.pdf) Ladies and gentlemen, First of all, for the sake of clarity, I would like to inform you that a member of the Governing Council will not make any comments on monetary policy during the week preceding the interest rate meeting. The Council's interest rate meeting is this coming Thursday, so this opportunity falls into that period. Fortunately, we have plenty of other issues to deal with today. First, let's look at a few more patterns as a background. Figures 2-5 The international financial crisis came to a head on 15 September last year when the US investment bank Lehman Brothers sought protection from its creditors. As a result, the already weakened trust between banks collapsed, threatening to paralyse the interbank lending market and destabilise the entire international financial system. However, thanks to the exceptional measures taken by the public authorities, the most critical phase of the financial crisis so far was clarified. Since then, the functioning of the interbank loan market has gradually improved. I will come back to that at the very end. Figure 6. Risk premiums in the interbank money market This pattern shows the first phase of turbulence in August 2007 and then the crisis in September 2008. Since then, the financial crisis has not only escalated into a global economic crisis, but also progressed to the next stage, a key feature of which is the reduction of excessive debts of over-indebted banks and other economic entities. In English, this deleveraging is referred to as deleveraging. Banks are forced to reduce their indebtedness because credit losses and write-downs of investment assets have depleted banks' own capital. In order to meet the minimum capital requirements required by law, banks are forced either to sell their assets, reduce their lending or raise additional capital. Figure 7. Losses and problems with market financing began to limit bank lending Due to the loss of selling portfolio investments in thin and falling markets and the reluctance of investors to provide banks with new capital or other financing, banks are under great pressure to contain or reduce their new lending. Restricting lending weakens the operating conditions for companies and other bank customers. The worst threat has been a credit crunch, in which a large number of fundamentally healthy companies are forced to close down or drastically reduce their activities due to lack of funding. Figure 8. Banking in a pinch: deleveraging The low liquidity of the securities markets and the extreme risk aversion of investors have made it even more difficult for companies to finance. The lack of confidence among investors has increased the financing costs of both financial and non-financial corporations and lowered their share prices. In turn, the increased risk aversion has reduced the international movement of capital, as banks and investors often provide financing primarily to domestic customers and companies. The fall in asset prices has, on the other hand, reduced the collateral values of companies' assets and thus weakened the creditworthiness of companies. In addition, banks have generally tightened their credit conditions. Figure 9. Credit conditions in the euro area: mortgages and loans to large enterprises Figure 10. Credit terms in the UNITED STATES: large and medium-sized companies, as well as mortgages For these reasons, companies' access to finance has become more difficult globally and the cost of financing has risen. An even more serious problem for Finnish companies and the Finnish national economy than financing is the rapid contraction in exports caused by the slowdown in global economic growth and trade. In this presentation, however, I will confine myself to examining the transmission of the financial crisis to Finland through the domestic and international financial system. In particular, I will examine the effects of the crisis on the availability of financing for Finnish companies, the sources and composition of their debt financing, and the measures taken and planned to secure the financing of Finnish companies. The financial situation of Finnish companies has deteriorated The Finnish financial system had hardly been exposed to the events that triggered the current crisis. The effects of the economic crisis have mainly come to Finland from outside our country's borders. Despite the severity of the financial crisis, the liquidity and solvency of Finnish banks and other financial institutions have remained good in international comparison. Unlike banks in many other countries, Finnish banks do not have the need to deleverage as described above. The Finnish securities market has suffered more than banks from the crisis. The availability of financing for Finnish companies on both domestic and foreign markets has become more difficult and the price of financing has risen. As a result, large companies that relied on financing from the market have returned to the counters of domestic banks. The lending capacity of Finnish banks may, without special measures, be too small to cover the rapidly growing demand for bank credit from companies. Yritystodistusmarkkinat Large, mostly highly creditworthy, companies obtain debt financing on the financial markets, including by issuing short-term, mainly unsecured commercial papers, and longer-term bonds. As a result of the financial crisis, the relative importance of these sources of financing has decreased and the relative importance of bank financing has increased. Figure 11. Sources of debt financing for Finnish companies before the financial crisis and at the moment Finnish companies have issued commercial papers mainly in Finland. Commercial paper issued domestically has typically accounted for about 90% of all commercial papers. The largest investors in commercial paper include earnings-related pension companies and other insurance companies, as well as short-term interest funds. Companies with a liquidity surplus also invest in commercial paper instead of deposits. Since the onset of the financial crisis, investors quickly began to cash out of short-term funds, as a result of which the investor base for commercial paper has rapidly shrunk. The value of Finnish short-term interest funds decreased by over EUR 7.5 billion between August 2007 and the end of 2008. Figure 12. Size of short-term interest funds registered in Finland Over the same period, the stock of commercial paper in circulation in Finland has declined by around EUR 3 billion and that of commercial papers in circulation abroad by around half a billion euros. Figure 13. Commercial papers in circulation in Finland Figure 14. Cumulative changes in commercial paper stocks since Q2 2007, broken down by ownership sector Since large companies typically use the funds they raise with commercial paper to finance their short-term financing needs, such as working capital, companies have needed replacement financing quickly. This is what they have acquired from domestic and foreign banks by withdrawing loans within the credit lines they have previously agreed. The return of large companies as loan customers of domestic banks threatens to displace smaller companies from the credit counters of banks. The situation is exacerbated by the fact that corporate bond financing has also become more difficult. Joukkovelkakirjalainat Unlike commercial paper, Finnish companies have issued bonds mainly to international financial markets. Bonds issued abroad account for almost 80% of all corporate bonds. Mainly the largest Finnish companies raise financing from the international bond market. At the moment, it is difficult for companies to obtain new bond financing. Investors' risk appetite is low and their approach to credit risk is cautious, which makes new bond financing costly for companies. The drive of over-indebted banks and other investors to reduce their balance sheets by selling their securities is also weighing on the prices of securities. The number of new bond issues issued by Finnish companies is currently very small. Figure 15. Annual change in the stock of corporate bonds issued in Finland. However, the stock of Finnish non-financial corporations' outstanding bonds has declined more slowly than that of commercial paper in circulation. Title: Financial crisis and the Nordic region
text: Erkki Liikanen, Director General: The financial crisis and the Nordic countries. Nordic Co-operation Committee of the Labour Movement SAMAK, Helsinki 10.2.2009 . Speech . Tuesday 10 February 2009, 12:00 AM Chief Executive Erkki Liikanen Nordic Co-operation Committee of the Labour Movement Helsinki 10.2.2009 THE FINANCIAL CRISIS AND THE NORDIC COUNTRIES The global economic crisis surprised everyone The crisis that began in the U.S. subprime mortgage market in 2007 spread rapidly within the financial system and into the real economy. The rapid and simultaneous economic slowdown worldwide in October and November last autumn still surprised everyone. Even a year ago, there was talk of 'decoupling'. The idea was that the emerging economies of Asia will take on the role of locomotives as the United States lags behind. The scenario didn't kick in. Economic growth is slowing at the same rate everywhere. In emerging market economies, the pace will be higher but the impact just as profound. Since January last year, each new forecast has been worse than the previous one. Two weeks ago, the Imf estimated that the world economy will grow by only 0.5% this year and that world trade will even decline. If that happens, we will see the end of a period of several years of growth as a result of favourable world trade developments. We must remember that, in the years 2004-2008, not only the emerging economies of Asia, but also sub-Saharan Africa and the economies of Latin America grew much faster than the industrialised countries and the gap in living standards narrowed. Gdp is now declining clearly in the three major economic areas of the UNITED STATES, Europe and Japan. No European country is outside the crisis either, even though the negative growth shocks have come from elsewhere. All open economies are affected by the global economic slowdown, not least the most export-dependent countries. The financial sector is also shrinking, most in areas where the sector's share of GDP has been highest. Where housing construction has been expansionary through increased debt, the slowdown has been very rapid. How have the Nordic countries fared in the turbulence? Has it mattered that they have different monetary policy systems? Finland is a euro area country. Denmark has its krona but it is pegged to the euro. The euro is floating against other currencies and the Eurosystem's primary objective is to maintain price stability. Sweden and Norway have their crown currencies and a monetary policy with inflation targets. Iceland has had to resort to exceptional measures due to major economic difficulties. The financial sector was exceptionally large relative to the rest of the economy. Despite the differences in the monetary policy systems, four of the Nordic countries have done well in recent years. Now they have all been hit by the crisis equally hard but at different rates. Gross domestic product will contract markedly in 2009 and the employment situation will also deteriorate. How could the subprime problems in the U.S. trigger such a major global crisis? In international banks in particular, balance sheets have swelled at an increasing rate during this decade. Subprime loans that were packaged together with other loans, were securitized and lifted out banks' balance sheets, contributing to the banking sector's over-indebtedness in the United States. Housing loans were granted to households with weak repayment capacity and the decoy was two non-repayable years with low fixed interest rates. Then the interest rate was raised to Libor plus 6 percent. As long as house prices rose, the system worked. After two years, the loan could be renegotiated or the home sold. Once the loan had been lifted off the bank's balance sheet, the bank was able to grant a new loan with the capital. But prices began to fall, the loan amount was soon higher than the value of the home, and the system collapsed. In the complex loan packages, subprime loans with increasing payment defaults were increasingly found. When they were not known where they were and at what amounts, no one bought these loan products anymore, nor did anyone give loans against them. Liquidity in the banking system dried up. Market interest rates rose. At first, liquidity dried up, but then credit losses began to materialize. The losses were eating away at equity. As equity decreases, the bank's lending capacity decreases tenfold. Banks were forced to cut back on their lending. The major international banks withdrew to their homeland. They left behind a large gap in corporate finance in the Nordic region as well. Access to loans decreased and the price rose. Centralbanksoperationer Central banks were among the first to react to the market turmoil. They have significantly increased their lending to banks against adequate collateral. When markets function normally, banks even out the liquidity of the interbank market. In other words, the liquidity of banks rests on the possibility of borrowing, if necessary, from other banks and from the Central Bank as a last resort. The interbank market is based on trust between the banks and counterparty risk is perceived as low. When banks' confidence is destroyed, the willingness to give other banks unsecured loans decreases. Central banks have had the task of providing markets with sufficient liquidity for the banks' needs. The Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and the Nordic central banks have, through joint operations, allocated dollar liquidity to the nordic central banks' customer banks. The historically unique coordinated rate cut in October also testifies to central bank cooperation. The ECB, the Fed and, among others, the Riksbank decided to cut key interest rates by half a percentage point at the same time. Monetary policyis not enough: junk banking or capitalization? As the crisis continued and deepened following the bankruptcy of the Lehman Brothers investment bank, the banks' financial position weakened further, and their capital adequacy and the stability of the entire banking system were threatened. Risk premia rose sharply and, in line with them, market interest rates and lending tightened further. In October, the US and some European countries ran into acute problems when banks needed capital appreciation and have the illiquid loans (junk bonds) lifted off their balance sheets. Ronald Reagan sade n8ar han tilltr8adde: d3Government is not the solution, government is the problem.d3 Now they say: The crisis is so deep that there are no other solutions than government, state and central bank. Why? Because only the government has an unshakable right to tax revenue. Only the central bank can issue money and provide liquidity in the banking system. In many countries, the Nordic banking crises and solutions from the 1990s were intensively studied. First, Britain embarked on the path of capitalization followed by the EU and, after some hesitation, the United States as well. Capital injections were the fastest and most open way to strengthen the banking system. The banks' long-term borrowing had also become more difficult and expensive. The states decided to provide guarantees for banks' borrowing so that lending could continue. The financial system is the bloodstream of the economy; if the blood stops circulating, the entire economy is threatened. Policymakers have had no easy task: they must ensure that bank lending, which is so vital to the economy, continues, but at the same time ensure that taxpayers' money is not wasted. Everyone has faced the same dilemma; For its part, the ECB has tried to contribute to a solution by establishing a common understanding of best practice. About capitalization and guarantees, it has succeeded. The issue of so-called junk banks is still open in most countries. If the state has already taken over a bank, then the solution is simple: then, after all, it will be a question of an internal transfer. But problems arise with private banks: How should the illiquid loans be priced? If valued at market prices, the write-downs lead to losses that erode the bank's capital and lending capacity. If the loans are priced at book value higher than the market price, it becomes a state aid that gives the bank a competitive advantage. Many countries are still looking for a solution to the problem. What went wrong in the financial system? The banks had thus built up a business that was too dependent on market financing and they had allowed their capital buffers to be thinned out. Many other reasons were also behind the problems: 1) The credit rating agencies had failed in their risk assessments of the complex loan products. 2) Banks and investors relied too much on credit rating agencies' credit assessments and did not make their own. 3) With the modern risk diversification methods, it was imagined that it was possible to postpone the risk and believe that it would never be realized. 4) The lending criteria lost their effect when the lender in the long securitisation chain lost contact with the borrower. 5) The bonus systems in the banks tempted to expansive lending and risk-taking. The bonuses were linked to loan volumes, not repayments. 6) It was trusted that liquidity would never run out. It was not realised that mistrust is spreading when the first banks start accounting for losses and that the payment system is then paralysed. How should banking supervision and the international financial architecture be reformed? Many have rightly asked themselves why the crisis could not be better predicted and prevented. It has been the hottest theme in many meetings lately. 1) 1) Perhaps the most important was the G20 summit in Washington last November. Expectations for the summit were high. However, no tangible results were expected. But there they were mistaken. The heads of government of the major economies announced that work on improving the international financial architecture must begin quickly and decisively. The meeting resulted in a Washington declaration. It contains a comprehensive action plan that is both ambitious and demanding due to tight timetables. The declaration summarises proposals from many international organisations such as the IMF, BIS, the EU and the Financial Stability Forum. The Nordic countries are represented in the first three. The current international financial architecture was created after the war. It should be remembered that the Bretton Woods institutions were formed as part of the great peace project. Attempts to create a financial architecture were made as early as 1933 after the Depression, but Hitler had already chosen his own path and President Roosevelt had enough of the domestic problems and did not want to commit to any international commitments. Crises have also led to changes in the financial architecture in the past. Due to the Vietnam War and the US balance of payments problems, the Bretton Woods system with its fixed exchange rates was abolished in 1971 and market forces were given more leeway with exchange rates. When the Berlin Wall was torn down in 1989 and the Soviet Union split in 1991, the IMF and the World Bank gained many new members and became genuinely global institutions. The next G20 meeting will be held in London in April. The crisis has contributed to the fact that consensus, consensus, has been reached on many fundamental issues. Firstly, transparency and accountability in financial markets must be strengthened. The market must know the products and the economic position of financial firms. Incentives must be changed so that they do not tempt excessive risk-taking. Secondly, financial supervision must be strengthened so that all financial markets, products and operators are subject to some degree of regulation. Credit rating agencies must also be monitored. Thirdly, the integrity of the financial markets must be strengthened. Consumer protection shall be improved, illegal market manipulation shall be prevented and conflicts of interest shall be avoided. Fourthly, international cooperation between supervisory authorities and other authorities is to be strengthened. We have been working for this for a long time here in the Nordic region. And fifthly, the international financial institutions are to be reformed. In recent years, the Nordic countries have worked intensively to reform the Bretton Woods institutions. The main challenge will be to ensure the position of emerging market economies and the resources of institutions. Nordic co-operation in the IMF is based on a long tradition. Iceland and Norway joined the fund as early as December 1945 and Sweden as the last Nordic country in August 1951. The joint constituency for the Nordic and Baltic countries was formed in 1992 when the Baltic states became independent. The Nordic-Baltic constituency has proven to be a successful move over the years. The countries share much the same values and the management of the constituency is much more democratic than in most other constituencies, where a large country often dictates the positions. In the Nordic-Baltic constituency, there is consultation on all issues and there is a great deal of solidarity. The constituency's work in the Foundation has been marked by our independence from international power politics. It has allowed us to speak out in situations where attempts have been made to use the fund for political purposes for the benefit of some country group. Independence has also given us the opportunity to support management when the fund's integrity has been in the balance. From a Nordic point of view, it is important that Europe achieves a common understanding on the development of the financial architecture and that the consensus is then effectively championed in the preparation of the G20 summits. The EU has started work to achieve a common understanding in all focus areas and mobilised key EU actors for it. It remains to be seen whether the international community can agree on how to reform the structure. 1) The G20 includes Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, India, Indonesia, Italy, Japan, Mexico, Russia, Saudi Arabia, The United Kingdom, South Africa, South Korea, Turkey and the United States. The G20 meetings are also attended by the EU (presidency), the IMF and the World Bank.

Tillg<8c>ngen till l<8c>n minskade och priset steg. Centralbanksoperationer Centralbankerna h<9a>rde till de f<9a>rsta som reagerade p<8c> marknadsoron. De har markant <9a>kat sin utl<8c>ning till bankerna mot fullgod s<8a>kerhet. N<8a>r marknaderna fungerar normalt j<8a>mnar bankerna ut likviditeten p<8c> interbankmarknaden. Med andra ord vilar bankernas likviditet p<8c> m<9a>jligheten att vid behov l<8c>na av andra banker och av centralbanken som en sista utv<8a>g. Federal Reserve, Europeiska centralbanken och de nordiska centralbankerna har genom gemensamma transaktioner tilldelat de nordiska centralbankernas kundbanker dollarlikviditet. Om centralbankssamarbetet vittnar ocks<8c> den historiskt unika samordnade r<8a>ntes<8a>nkningen i oktober. ECB, Fed och bland annat Riksbanken beslutade att samtidigt s<8a>nka styrr<8a>ntorna med en halv procentenhet. Penningpolitik<8a>r inte nog: skr<8a>pbank eller kapitalisering? N<8a>r krisen fortsatte och f<9a>rdjupades efter investmentbanken Lehman Brothers konkurs f<9a>rsvagades bankernas finansiella st<8a>llning ytterligare, och deras kapitalt<8a>ckning och hela banksystemets stabilitet hotades.
