I oktober fick USA och n<8c>gra europeiska l<8a>nder akuta problem n<8a>r bankerna beh<9a>vde kapitalf<9a>rst<8a>rkning och f<8c> de illikvida l<8c>nen (skr<8a>pobligationerna) lyfta ur sina balansr<8a>kningar. Ronald Reagan sade n<8a>r han tilltr<8a>dde: <d3>Government is not the solution, government is the problem.<d3> Nu s<8a>ger man: Krisen <8a>r s<8c> djup att det inte finns n<8c>gra andra l<9a>sningar <8a>n regering, stat och centralbank. Varf<9a>r? D<8a>rf<9a>r att endast regeringen har orubblig r<8a>tt till skatteinkomster. Endast centralbanken kan ge ut pengar och s<9a>rja f<9a>r likviditeten i banksystemet. I m<8c>nga l<8a>nder studerade man intensivt de nordiska bankkriserna och l<9a>sningarna fr<8c>n 1990-talet. F<9a>rst slog Storbritannien in p<8c> kapitaliseringsv<8a>gen f<9a>ljd av EU och efter en viss tvekan ocks<8c> USA. Kapitalinjektioner var det snabbaste och <9a>ppnaste s<8a>ttet att st<8a>rka banksystemet. Bankernas l<8c>ngfristiga uppl<8c>ning hade ocks<8c> f<9a>rsv<8c>rats och blivit mycket dyr. Staterna beslutade st<8a>lla garantier f<9a>r bankernas uppl<8c>ning s<8c> att utl<8c>ningen kunde forts<8a>tta. Det finansiella systemet <8a>r blodomloppet f<9a>r ekonomin; om blodet slutar cirkulera hotas hela ekonomin. De politiska beslutsfattarna har inte haft n<8c>gon l<8a>tt uppgift: De ska garantera att den f<9a>r ekonomin s<8c> livsviktiga bankutl<8c>ningen forts<8a>tter men samtidigt se till att skattebetalarnas pengar inte sl<9a>sas. Alla har st<8c>tt inf<9a>r samma dilemma; ECB har f<9a>r egen del f<9a>rs<9a>kt bidra till en l<9a>sning genom att f<8c> till st<8c>nd en samsyn om de b<8a>sta metoderna. Om kapitalisering och garantier har det lyckats. Fr<8c>gan om s<8c> kallade skr<8a>pbanker <8a>r <8a>nnu <9a>ppen i de flesta l<8a>nder. Om staten redan har tagit <9a>ver en bank, <8a>r l<9a>sningen enkel: d<8c> blir det ju fr<8c>ga om en intern <9a>verf<9a>ring. Men problem uppst<8c>r med privata banker: Hur ska de illikvida l<8c>nen priss<8a>ttas? Om de v<8a>rderas till marknadspris, leder nedskrivningarna till f<9a>rluster som urholkar bankens kapital och utl<8c>ningskapacitet. Om l<8c>nen priss<8a>tts till bokf<9a>rt v<8a>rde som <8a>r h<9a>gre <8a>n marknadspriset, blir det ett statligt st<9a>d som ger banken en konkurrensf<9a>rdel. I m<8c>nga l<8a>nder s<9a>ker man fortfarande en l<9a>sning p<8c> problemet. Vad var det som gick snett i det finansiella systemet? Bankerna hade allts<8c> byggt upp en verksamhet som i alltf<9a>r h<9a>g grad var beroende av marknadsfinansiering och de hade l<8c>tit sina kapitalbuffertar tunnas ut. Ocks<8c> m<8c>nga andra orsaker l<8c>g bakom problemen: 1) Kreditv<8a>rderingsf<9a>retagen hade misslyckats i sina riskbed<9a>mningar av de komplexa l<8c>neprodukterna. 2) Bankerna och investerarna litade alltf<9a>r mycket p<8c> kreditv<8a>rderingsf<9a>retagens kreditbed<9a>mningar och gjorde inga egna. 3) Med de moderna riskdiversifieringsmetoderna inbillade man sig att det gick att skjuta p<8c> risken och tro att den aldrig skulle realiseras. 4) L<8c>ngivningskriterierna f<9a>rlorade sin verkan n<8a>r l<8c>ngivaren i den l<8c>nga v<8a>rdepapperiseringskedjan tappade kontakten med l<8c>ntagaren. 5) Bonussystemen i bankerna frestade till expansiv utl<8c>ning och risktagande. Bonusarna var kopplade till l<8c>nevolymer, inte <8c>terbetalningar. 6) Man litade p<8c> att likviditeten aldrig skulle sina. Man ins<8c>g inte att misstroendet sprider sig n<8a>r de f<9a>rsta bankerna b<9a>rjar redovisa f<9a>rluster och att betalningssystemet d<8c> f<9a>rlamas. Hur b<9a>r banktillsynen ochden internationella finansarkitekturen reformeras? M<8c>nga har med r<8a>tta fr<8c>gat sig varf<9a>r krisen inte b<8a>ttre kunde f<9a>rutses och f<9a>rhindras. Det har varit det hetaste temat p<8c> m<8c>nga m<9a>ten den senaste tiden. 1) 1) Det viktigaste var kanske G20-l<8a>ndernas toppm<9a>te i Washington i november i fjol. F<9a>rv<8a>ntningarna p<8c> toppm<9a>tet var h<9a>ga. Man v<8a>ntade sig <8a>nd<8c> inte n<8c>gra handgripliga resultat. Men d<8a>r tog man fel. De stora ekonomiernas regeringschefer meddelade att arbetet med att f<9a>rb<8a>ttra den internationella finansarkitekturen m<8c>ste inledas snabbt och beslutsamt. M<9a>tet resulterade i en Washingtondeklaration. Den inneh<8c>ller en omfattande handlingsplan som <8a>r b<8c>de ambiti<9a>s och kr<8a>vande p<8c> grund av sn<8a>va tidtabeller. I deklarationen sammanfattas f<9a>rslag fr<8c>n m<8c>nga internationella organisationer s<8c>som IMF, BIS, EU och Financial Stability Forum. De nordiska l<8a>nderna <8a>r representerade i de tre f<9a>rsta. Den nuvarande internationella finansarkitekturen skapades efter kriget. Man b<9a>r minnas att Bretton Woods.institutionerna bildades som ett led i det stora fredsprojektet. F<9a>rs<9a>k att skapa en finansarkitektur gjordes redan 1933 efter depressionen, men Hitler hade redan valt sin egen v<8a>g och president Roosevelt hade nog med de inhemska problemen och ville inte binda sig vid n<8c>gra internationella <8c>taganden. Kriser har ocks<8c> tidigare lett till f<9a>r<8a>ndringar i finansarkitekturen. P<8c> grund av Vietnamkriget och USA:s betalningsbalansproblem slopades Bretton Woods-systemet med sina fasta valutakurser 1971 och marknadskrafterna fick st<9a>rre spelrum med valutakurserna. N<8a>r Berlinmuren revs 1989 och Sovjetunionen splittrades 1991 fick IMF och V<8a>rldsbanken m<8c>nga nya medlemmar och blev genuint globala institutioner. N<8a>sta G20-m<9a>te kommer att h<8c>llas i London i april. Krisen har bidragit till att samf<9a>rst<8c>nd, konsensus, har uppn<8c>tts i m<8c>nga grundl<8a>ggande fr<8c>gor. F<9a>r det f<9a>rsta m<8c>ste <9a>ppenheten och redovisningsskyldigheten (transparency and accountability) p<8c> finansmarknaderna st<8a>rkas. Marknaden m<8c>ste kunna produkterna och de finansiella f<9a>retagens ekonomiska st<8a>llning. Incitamenten m<8c>ste <8a>ndras s<8c> att de inte frestar till alltf<9a>r h<9a>gt risktagande. F<9a>r det andra m<8c>ste finanstillsynen st<8a>rkas s<8c> att alla finansmarknader, produkter och akt<9a>rer omfattas av n<8c>gon grad av reglering. Ocks<8c> kreditv<8a>rderingsf<9a>retagen m<8c>ste <9a>vervakas. F<9a>r det tredje m<8c>ste finansmarknadernas integritet st<8a>rkas. Konsumentskyddet ska f<9a>rb<8a>ttras, olaglig marknadsmanipulation ska f<9a>rhindras och intressekonflikter ska undvikas. F<9a>r det fj<8a>rde ska det internationella samarbetet mellan tillsynsmyndigheter och andra myndigheter st<8a>rkas. Det har vi h<8a>r i Norden arbetat f<9a>r redan en l<8a>ngre tid. Och f<9a>r det femte ska de internationella finansinstitutionerna reformeras. De nordiska l<8a>nderna har under de senaste <8c>ren arbetat intensivt f<9a>r att reformera Bretton Woods-institutionerna. Den st<9a>rsta utmaningen blir att s<8a>kerst<8a>lla tillv<8a>xtekonomiernas st<8a>llning och institutionernas resurser. Det nordiska samarbetet i IMF bygger p<8c> en l<8c>ng tradition. Island och Norge gick med i fonden redan i december 1945 och Sverige som sista nordiska land i augusti 1951. Den gemensamma valkretsen f<9a>r de nordiska och de baltiska l<8a>nderna bildades 1992 n<8a>r baltstaterna blivit sj<8a>lvst<8a>ndiga. Den nordisk-baltiska valkretsen har under tidernas lopp visat sig vara ett lyckat drag. L<8a>nderna delar i m<8c>ngt och mycket samma v<8a>rderingar och f<9a>rvaltningen av valkretsen <8a>r betydligt mer demokratisk <8a>n i de flesta andra valkretsar, d<8a>r ett stort land ofta dikterar st<8a>llningstagandena. I den nordisk-baltiska valkretsen samr<8c>der man i alla fr<8c>gor och samh<9a>righeten <8a>r stor. Valkretsens arbete i fonden har pr<8a>glats av v<8c>rt oberoende av den internationella maktpolitiken. Det har gjort det m<9a>jligt f<9a>r oss att tala ut i situationer d<8a>r man har f<9a>rs<9a>kt anv<8a>nda fonden f<9a>r politiska syften till f<9a>rm<8c>n f<9a>r n<8c>gon landgrupp. Oberoendet har ocks<8c> gett oss m<9a>jlighet att st<9a>dja ledningen n<8a>r fondens integritet har legat i v<8c>gsk<8c>len. Ur nordisk synvinkel <8a>r det viktigt att Europa uppn<8c>r en samsyn om utvecklingen av finansarkitekturen och att samsynen sedan effektivt f<9a>rf<8a>ktas vid f<9a>rberedelserna av G20-l<8a>ndernas toppm<9a>ten. Arbetet med att uppn<8c> en samsyn har EU inlett inom alla fokusomr<8c>den och mobiliserat centrala EU-akt<9a>rer f<9a>r det. Det <8c>terst<8c>r att se om det internationella samfundet kan enas om hur strukturen ska reformeras. 1) Till G20 h<9a>r Argentina, Australien, Brasilien, Indien, Indonesien, Italien, Japan, Kanada, Kina, Mexiko, Ryssland, Saudiarabien, Storbritannien, Sydafrika, Sydkorea, Turkiet, Tyskland och USA. I G20-m<9a>tena deltar ocks<8c> EU (ordf<9a>randelandet), IMF och V<8a>rldsbanken.

Title: Taxation and the economy in recession  what about after that?
text: President Erkki Liikanen: Taxation and the economy in recession d0 what about after that? Tax 2009, Helsinki 11.3.2009 . Speech . Wednesday11 March2009, 12:00 AM Director General Erkki Liikanen Taxpayers' Tax 2009 event Marina Congress Center, Helsinki 11.3.2009 TAXATION AND THE ECONOMY IN RECESSION d0 WHAT ABOUT AFTER THAT? Speech Membranes (PPT) (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and. . interviews/documents/090311_el_vero2009.ppt) Puheen Membranes (PDF) (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and. . interviews/documents/090311_el_vero2009.pdf) Slide 1 The global economy has experienced the effects of the financial crisis everywhere. In August 2007, financial markets reacted very strongly to news from the US housing market as the long-standing rise in the real estate market stalled. In one part of the US mortgage lending system, the subprime lending market, there was a turnaround that triggered a chain reaction leading to liquidity problems in the financial sector. Slide 2: The Create and Decentralize Model and Its Incentive System The subprime 'originate and distribute' model of securitisation, which was also used in mortgage lending, worked without problems as long as house prices continued to rise. Yield expectations for property-backed securities had been based on rising property prices. In addition, yield expectations were particularly sensitive to changes in the price of the underlying collateral. This was due to the structure of sub-prime loan agreements. After property prices finally started to fall in 2007, the system collapsed. It turned out that the pricing models of the securities had not sufficiently taken into account, if at all, the possibility that real estate prices could fall. The notion was based on the fact that real estate prices in the United States as a whole had last fallen in the 1930s. The risks of mortgage-backed securities were severely underpriced. There were already warnings about underpricing risks at the beginning of 2007. There had also been concern about the rapid growth of mortgage credit for a long time. However, the real surprise was related to securitisation and these the rapid spread of market disturbances throughout the money market. The crisis that started in the financial markets spread to the real economy with a delay of about a year. Although it may have been expected, the ferocity of the shock has surprised everyone. In the early part of 2008, economic growth continued to be brisk in the global economy, and world commodity prices reached new highs. However, signs of a slowdown in economic growth began to appear in the summer of 2008. Slide 3: Views change During the autumn, views changed fundamentally. Towards the end of the year, output growth in key economic areas began to slow down and GDP even contracted in the fourth quarter. Emerging economies also played their part then and their growth slowed down by the same slope. Slide 4: U.S. & EU export orders According to many forecasts, the national product of developed countries will contract significantly this year. Global trade is shrinking, and as a result, growth in emerging economies that rely on an export-led growth strategy is also slowing down sharply. Slide 5: Indicators of Japanese and industrial exports Slide 6: NIE value of exports of countries The idea that the emerging economies of Asia could, in the global economy, compensate for the contraction in DEMAND in the United States is not coming true. The so-called "backstop" of the past years. After all, the "soft landing" scenarios were based on that train of thought. A large number of emerging economies are struggling with major economic problems. Even if China and a few other key emerging economies avoid a contraction of their economies, their domestic demand will not be enough to reverse global economic developments. Slide 7: Finland and the euro area Real GDP in the euro area also contracted already in the third quarter of 2008 and, according to preliminary data, the last quarter of the year will be even worse. Exports, in particular, have fallen exceptionally sharply. Finland is falling along with the others. According to the latest ECB forecast, real GDP in the euro area will contract at a rate of between 2.2% and 3.2% in 2009, while growth of between -0.7% and 0.7% is expected for 2010. Inflationary pressures have also declined significantly and the ECB expects inflation rates to decline to between 0.1% and 0.7% in 2009. With the collapse of growth in large economic areas, the international economy now lacks a strong engine. Efforts are being made everywhere to stimulate the economy through both monetary and fiscal policies. The strong easing of monetary policy, as well as the measures taken by governments in support of financial systems, have so far reassured financial markets. Central banks have acted with an open mind in order to get financial intermediation under way. The ECB has cut the key interest rate to a historical low of 1.5%, and in the United States the key interest rate has been lowered to 0.25%. Nevertheless, uncertainty about the economic outlook remains exceptionally high. Under normal circumstances, when interest rates are low, firms and households would be expected to stimulate aggregate demand by investing and spending. However, the financial crisis has led to a reduction in the risk appetite and often the ability of companies and households, as well as banks. Due to the reduced risk appetite or ability, both the supply and demand for credit have decreased and households' savings are not channelled through financial intermediaries to those in need of financing. Slide 8: Through the balance sheet, losses limit bank lending New investment projects cannot be started and are postponed. The growth in aggregate demand has stalled as economists everywhere are simultaneously trying to improve their balance sheets and emerge from the financial crisis unscathed. Slide 9: Corporate risk premiums by credit grade Currently, private sector savings are allocated to low-yield and low-risk assets such as treasury bills and savings accounts. This is reflected in the balance sheets of banks and their reserves. It is also reflected in the yield gap between certificates of deposit issued by companies and treasury bills. This phenomenon is commonly referred to as flight to quality. Financial intermediation has been disrupted and there is a gap between the supply and demand for risky credit. Credit growth has slowed down and the price of risky credit has risen sharply. At the same time, a slowdown in aggregate demand will lower inflation. These phenomena are partly explained by the lower risk appetite of households, companies and banks. The concomitant decline in aggregate demand and the decline in inflation suggest that the economy is experiencing a strong demand shock. This, combined with the problems of financial intermediation, makes the situation very challenging. Furthermore, the effectiveness of interest rate policy is in any case limited in a situation where nominal interest rates are already inherently low and households' risk appetite is low. Slide10: Fiscal stimulus Many are of the opinion that the only way to "start the economy" is through fiscal stimulus. Governments have therefore taken massive fiscal stimulus measures. According to the Commission, by mid-January of this year, EU countries had announced a number of discretionary expansionary fiscal measures for 2009 equivalent to a total of around 1% of the value of the EU's GROSS DOMESTIC PRODUCT. The stimulus measures agreed in the euro area also amounted to around 1% of GDP. The stimulus measures announced for 2010 have, at least for the time being, been smaller, at just over half a per cent. In addition, europe must take into account the automatic stabilisers resulting from progressive income taxation and safety nets, among other things. In the United States, too, a very large-scale stimulus package is being put in place for 2009-2010, mainly in addition to the support measures granted to the housing and financial markets. If implemented in full, the size of the stimulus package could reach more than 5% of GDP. The sums involved are historically high. Public estimates of rising government indebtedness have already raised doubts about the ability of the public authorities to adequately guarantee risks in the private sector. This is reflected in the fact that the risk premia of some government debt instruments and the interest rates on their loans have been rising sharply. There is wide disagreement among economists on the effectiveness of fiscal policy, as to whether an increase in public expenditure financed by public debt can regulate aggregate demand in the economy. The argument for the inefficiency of fiscal policy is based on the fact that economists are looking ahead and therefore see behind a public budget constraint. The increase in government debt, according to this, includes a commitment to raise taxation in the future and to keep the general government surplus until the debt has been restored to a sustainable level. However, in the current economic crisis, there are elements that can make a fiscal stimulus financed by government debt more effective than it would be under "normal circumstances". As households' risk appetite has decreased, private sector savings are now channelled into investments with low risk. From the point of view of households, government debt represents just such an investment object. Government bonds are favoured over other private sector-offered investments with a high risk-return profile. In this case, the marginalization effect of public debt may be less than it would be under normal circumstances. Many economists are sceptical about the fiscal stimulus, citing precisely the ability of households to see behind the public budget constraint, i.e. that the debt taken out today is a commitment to raise taxes in the future. Perhaps, however, a little more economists will agree that high taxation can cause distortions in the economy in the first place and thus lower the productive potential of the economy. This is perhaps also reflected in the fact that, even in Europe, more than half of the fiscal stimulus announced by EU countries appears to be linked to tax cuts. The Commission estimates that 0.6% of GDP of the stimulus measures will reduce public revenue and 0.5% of expenditure. The majority of member states are seeking to revive their economies through direct support to households, in particular through reductions in taxes and social security contributions. Indeed, the stimulus aimed at increasing the purchasing power of households corresponds to almost half of the measures announced. Roughly half of the EU countries also allocate reductions in taxes and social security contributions to enterprises. In Finland, too, a massive fiscal stimulus is needed, and as a result, central government debt will rise considerably in the coming years. Considering that finland's overall tax rate and tax wedge are high from an international point of view, and that ageing will put additional pressure on public finances in the near future, expectations of substantial tax increases in the future would slow down the upside potential of the economy in an already very challenging situation. Slide 11: The role of the tax structure in economic dynamics Let me now turn to the role of the tax structure in economic dynamics. This is an important issue, especially from the point of view of longer-term sustainability. I examine the economic impact of the change in the tax structure in the light of the Bank of Finland's model calculations. These calculations were made at the beginning of 2007, when there was still no information about the crisis and these calculations have been presented in Euro & economy issue 1/2007. The purpose of the calculations was to find out how shifting the focus of taxation from labour to consumption would affect the development of the national economy in the short and long term. The analysis made use of the dynamic general balance model (Aino) developed at the Bank of Finland. The model takes into account the behavioural effects of taxation on labour supply and demand. In addition, households are thought to understand the budgetary constraint of general government finances, i.e. the impact of a potential deficit on the future conditions of general government finances. The main long-term results of these calculations are presented in the table below. It has estimated the effects of a one percentage point increase in consumption tax on the quantities that are key to the balance of the economy in the Aino model in the long term. Slide 12: Shifting the Focus of Taxation; Model calculations of long-term effects As this is a tax revenue-neutral examination, the calculation looked at three different cases. 1) In the first case, the increase in tax revenues resulting from an increase in consumption tax will be used to reduce the taxation of earned income so that public debt/GDP remains unchanged. 2) In the second case, the increased tax revenues are used to reduce the non-wage labour costs of companies. 3) The calculation was supplemented with an examination where the increase in consumption tax is credited to households as income transfers as a lump sum. The latter analysis best illustrates the extent to which the effects on the balance of the economy of the relative price distortions caused solely by consumption taxation are. In the first two cases, the relative prices are distorted by the combined effect of the assumed measures. Let us start from the case where the increase in consumption tax is compensated to households by increasing income transfers (column III). As a result of raising the consumption tax by one percentage point, both consumption and output will decrease by around half a per cent. The decrease in consumption is due to the contraction of the real wage after tax by close on 0.2 percentage points as the price level rises and the rise in the price of consumption relative to leisure time. The increase in the attractiveness of leisure time is reflected in the supply of work, and employment decreases by about 0.25 percentage points. When, in the model, earnings-related pension contributions are allowed to be determined by the budgetary constraint of employment pension schemes, employment 1) follows. of the deterioration, the fact that pension contributions will have to be increased by just under one tenth of a percent This affects the tax wedge, which increases by more than one percentage point. If, on the other hand, the increase in consumption tax is compensated for by a reduction in taxes on labour, the effects on the economy would be positive. This can be seen in columns 1 through 2 of the table. If the increase in consumption tax is compensated by lowering the taxation of earned income, the economy will end up in a balance where consumption and production are good half a per cent higher than the starting point. Compared to the previous option, the effects of raising the consumption tax are almost the opposite. The reason is that the positive impact on supply of a reduction in taxes on labour is clearly stronger than the negative impact on consumption resulting from an increase in consumption tax. This is best illustrated by the fact that, as a combined effect of tax changes, the tax wedge would be reduced by just under one percentage point, thereby reducing the distortive effects of taxation on the relative prices of the economy. However, the positive impact on economic development would be strongest if the increase in consumption tax were compensated by a reduction in non-wage labour costs. Raising the consumption tax by one percentage point would mean that the indirect costs of labour could be reduced by as much as a good three percentage points. Finland would then be considerably closer to the European average when the level of taxation is measured by the total tax wedge. The positive effects of the narrowing of the tax wedge on production and employment reflect the weaknesses of the current tax structure. Such an examination requires certain assumptions and, of course, caution is always in order when considering the exact magnitude of the effects. However, the key element of the calculations is that they highlight the impact of the tax structure on the performance of the economy as a whole in the long term. The above is an analysis of the long-term effects of a tax reform that shifts the focus of taxation in the direction of consumption taxation. However, the adjustment of the economy to the change in the tax structure is taking place slowly. Slide 13: Shifting the Focus of Taxation; Model calculations of short-term effects The table below further describes the adjustment of the key variables of the economy to the one percentage point increase in the consumption tax during the first five years, when the increase in consumption tax is compensated by a gradual reduction in the taxation of earned income. Firstly, the dynamic effects show that the effects of the change in the tax structure are only gradually materialising on the real variables of the economy. Consumption, in particular, reacted moderately at the beginning, as did the real wage after taxes. Both reactions reflect the rigidity of nominal wages, as well as the assumption that taxation on earned income will be slowly reduced. However, the positive reaction of consumption at the beginning reflects households' anticipation of a reduction in income taxation. Companies are also anticipating an increase in future demand by adjusting their investments. Thanks to these forward-looking effects, both production and employment react positively from the outset, even if the tax wedge widens slightly at the beginning. However, it is essential that the effects of taxation may not be immediately visible in the real economy. For this reason, the cyclical timing of fiscal policy, and in particular fiscal policy, is a difficult subject. Slide 14: Conclusion The economic crisis that has started in the financial markets has challenged many of the economic policy perceptions of recent years. The unwavering belief in the efficiency of the financial markets and their ability to correct the mistakes themselves has been severely damaged. According to the theory, for example, the US economy should not have a financial crisis or even serious problems of over-indebtedness, whatever the financial developments, including indebtedness. Financial developments vary in the way that rational economic units see fit, sometimes indebtedness and sometimes debts are paid. Institutional development allows for ever greater financial intermediation and risk diversification, and with it rising debts. Everything is taken care of d0 even large current account deficits d0 when the market is allowed to operate freely in its own optimal way. A lot is changing as a result of this crisis. There is no longer a competition about who regulates the least, but about who regulates the best. Too much regulation kills innovation, but too loose control creates systemic risks. Properly targeted incentives can stimulate economic growth, but unbridled risk-taking for those that are misdirected. And a lot of things change. What is important is that a common line is reached at the G-20 meeting in London in April and that its content can be influenced by all sides. There is a broad consensus today on the need for fiscal stimulus and measures to facilitate financial intermediation. Finland, too, needs a massive fiscal stimulus. This will mean a significant increase in government debt in the following years. At the same time, the financial crisis has shown in a tangible way how important trust is. The short-term fiscal d0 and also monetary d0 solutions that are now being adopted must therefore also be sustainable in the long term. Debt-driven stimulus cannot continue indefinitely and ways must be sought to limit the upward pressure on public debt in the future. One important area is to take measures, also in the field of taxation, to strengthen the growth dynamics of the economy. In an ageing Finland, this is even more important. That is why the broad lines must also look beyond the problem of the economic cycle. 1) In this calculation, the pressure to increase earnings-related pension contributions arises solely from a reduction in the tax base. The calculation does not take into account the effects of aging. The calculation also assumes that only earnings-related pension contributions are flexible.

text: Director-General Erkki Liikanen: European elections 2009: Ball in the game .campaign opening ceremony. Helsinki 20.4.2009 . Speech . Monday20 April 2009, 12:00 AM Director-General Erkki Liikanen European elections 2009: Opening ceremony of the Ball in the Game campaign Helsinki 20.4.2009 HOW DID THE FINANCIAL CRISIS HIT? The years 20042007 were a period of strong growth in the global economy. Economic development of many developing countries . accelerated. Sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America grew strongly; as much as 6% per annum. They are even bridging the gap with the industrialised countries. However, the countries with the fastest growth were emerging economies. Growth was accelerated by the internationalisation of the financial markets. Interest rates and risk premiums were low and credit growth was strong. In August 2007, the financial markets began to cough. The US subprime market triggered the crisis. . Modern financial products turned out to be very risky. When housing prices began to fall, products containing subprime.loan papers became poisoned. Mistrust quickly spread, financial taps began to dry out. International banks began to make large losses. Losses, on the other hand, ate away at their ability to lend. Balance sheets had to be . reduce: Either lending had to be reduced or investments sold In practice, both were done. But after the rates had dropped, there were additional losses from the sale of investments. Lending began to be tightened. First, as far away as possible from the domestic market; developing countries and emerging economies saw international credit taps go off. Mistrust spread to the world economy. The final blow was the bankruptcy of a large investment bank in October . in the USA; after that, investment slowed down and world trade came to a standstill. This year, the world economy will contract somewhat and world trade will even contract considerably. Before the turnaround in the global economy, rising oil and food prices had weakened those developing countries that: . were not exporters of these products. Their position is now being weakened by the contraction of funding and the stagnation of external investment and the rapidly decreasing remittances of those working abroad. WHAT HAS BEEN THE POLICY RESPONSE TO THE FINANCIAL CRISIS? The G-20 meeting in London was an important milestone. Clearly better than several G-7 meetings, but of course . Within the UN and the Bretton Woods institutions, all countries must be able to give their own opinion and contribution to resolving the crisis. Important achievement: Market and control; the division of labour between the market and the state has been redefined. . Firstly, all financial institutions will be subject to supervision. Now many non-bank . financial institutions  such as hedge funds  are unregulated. Any financial institution of systemic importance whose operation or failure may cause great economic damage in society, come under proper regulation. Secondly, credit rating agencies will also be regulated, whose failure has accelerated . over-indebtedness of the financial system. Thirdly, the reward systems that encouraged unbridled lending expansion will also be shifted. History. Bonuses cannot be distributed just because the loan has been signed, it must also be paid. Fourthly, the capital requirements of financial institutions will also be changed so that they do not increase . suhdannevaihteluita. Fifthly, tax havens are being tackled through joint international action. Everyone must agree to the UN. model tax convention. The OECD has published the names of countries that have not met this requirement. WHAT ABOUT NEW RESOURCES? The resources of the International Monetary Fund will be strengthened. 500 billion ( 370 billion euros) will be added . IMF resources. A further 250 billion will strengthen the IMF's SDR capability. At least 100 billion will be allocated to finance multilateral development banks; to their . the ability to lend even to the lowest-income developing countries will be strengthened. WILL THE INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND AND OTHER BRETTON WOODS INSTITUTIONS REFORM? Gordon Brown said in London: ' The time for the Old Washington Consensus is over'. . Of course, a lot is changing: The new balance between the market and regulation that has just been mentioned is one of them. Big. confidence that the market will solve all problems and correct its own mistakes is over. Yet opposing protectionism and promoting world trade and foreign investment are equally . important as before. The IMF has also made major changes to its lending instruments and terms. Member states will be able to get a more . larger loans and with fewer terms. The objective of lending remains to safeguard the balance of the national economy, but value choices remain . as an internal matter for countries. The role of the IMF is therefore crucial, as many foreign donors in crisis countries require the IMF to: . Presence. WHAT WILL BECOME OF THE MILLENNIUM DEVELOPMENT GOALS? The growth rate in developing countries is slowing down and the problems are deepening. IMF estimate; Africa's growth in 2008 5%, halved . in 2009; 2,5 %. Member states must continue their support efforts, not weaken them because of the financial crisis. . The EU is a major donor of development aid. Increased cooperation between member states and the Commission is needed to ensure that support is . as efficient as possible. in 2005, EU countries committed to increasing development cooperation funds to 0.56% of GDP by 2010; big . summons. IMPORTANT RIGHT NOW: It is important to support efforts to resolve the financial crisis now; but equally important is the emphasis on sustainable development, . the realisation of human rights and democratic principles. The involvement of civil society in decision-making everywhere gives depth and more to decision-making. legitimacy, although it does not take away the responsibility of elected decision-makers themselves. The petition talks about the objectives of development policy in relation to trade, agriculture and external relations . Objectives. These do not necessarily conflict. For example, I am convinced that opposing protectionism is also in the interests of development policy. But, of course, the objectives of development policy must not be abandoned in favour of other objectives. . As president of the Red Cross, one clarification: It is important to talk about both development cooperation and humanitarian . assistance at the same time. Both are important, parallel goals. During the years of the Commission, a lot of experience came out of it.

Title: Financial crisis, Europe and Finland
text: President Erkki Liikanen: The financial crisis, Europe and Finland. University of Jyvaskyla 10.6.2009 . Speech . Wednesday10 June 2009, 12:00 AM I. CAUSES OF THE CRISIS [Slide 2] The financial crisis and the subsequent global economic crisis are unique in their scale and also in the mechanisms of their emergence. There are usually three explanations for the crisis. They have sometimes been in competition with others, but rather they are complementary. The first is the macroeconomic explanation related to global current account imbalances. The second explanation is monetary policy, which, in turn, attributes the crisis to the excessively prolonged low interest rates in the United States. [Slide 3] The third explanation relates to the structural problems of the financial system and financial innovation. In this explanation, the regulation and supervision of the authorities failed, but also the risk management and internal control of financial sector companies themselves: among other things, credit rating agencies failed to classify the risks of structured credit products and frontloaded incentive schemes encouraged uncontrolled risk-taking by financial institutions. All these factors contributed to a significant underestimation of risks in the financial sector. The crisis has also raised the question of the procyclicality of the financial system, that is, the property of the financial system to strengthen cyclical fluctuations. This has given rise to a debate on the need to reform the prudential provisions. Below I will discuss in more detail the above-mentioned causes of the crisis. I will then briefly examine what measures are needed for a sustainable recovery of the financial system - and therefore of the global economy. Finally, I will review the proposals made to reform the financial system and the challenges of implementing them. A. VAIHTOTASEIDEN EPaTASAPAINOT [Slide 4: US current account deficit and interest rates] The development of international funding gaps and surpluses is linked to the reshaping of the world order, which has been accelerated in particular by the emergence (or return) of China to the ranks of the major market economy countries and, more generally, by the strong economic growth of Asian countries. With these, a large amount of new production capacity entered the world economy. Over time, these developments created wealth in these transition economies, for which there was a need to look for investment targets. On the other hand, the experience of the Asian financial crisis in the late 1990s created a strong incentive for many transition economies to buffer their economies against potential crises. They therefore accumulated significant current account surpluses. Large surpluses also accumulated in oil-producing countries. A development followed in which investable wealth flowed, especially into the US market. This pressure on the supply of external capital to the United States is well illustrated by the fact that, despite the growing current account deficit of the US economy, long-term interest rates fell. Why did the new wealth look for investment targets, especially in the US market? MIT professor Ricardo Caballero has expressed the view that there is a shortage of reliable investments in the world. The paradox was that investments flowed to the United States, because it was precisely the strength, governance and control of its financial system that was trusted. However, they failed. The oversupply of investable assets contributed to the underpricing of risks and the emergence of financial innovations and practices that, in retrospect, have proven to be unsustainable. B. MONETARY POLICY [Slide 5: Federal Reserve Bank policy rate: actual vs. Taylor rule] Another macroeconomic background explanation given for the emergence of the crisis has been the excessively long period of low interest rates, particularly in the United States. Professor John Taylor has presented an analysis of this, relying on the Taylor Rule of Monetary Policy named after him. The figure below, presented by Taylor, shows how, between 2002 and 2005, the Taylor rule was deviated from by up to three percentage points at most. It was not until 2004 that the policy rate was raised, whereas under the Taylor rule, the increase should have started in 2002. The Federal Reserve justified its choices at the time with care about deflation. Japan's experiences of the 1990s were often referred to. In retrospect, however, it can be argued that interest rates remained too low for too long at a time when the US housing market was overheating. C. STRUCTURAL AND REGULATORY AND SUPERVISORY WEAKNESSES IN THE FINANCIAL SYSTEM 1. The create-and-diversify model and the functioning of credit rating agencies [Slide 6: Create and Decentralize a Template] One of the major changes in banking over the past decade was the strong expansion of the use of the 'originate and distribute' business model and the incorporation of increasingly risky assets. This led to a significant increase in banks' off-balance-sheet items and also to a rapid increase in the dependence of banks' own borrowing on very short-term market money. Banks started to package the loans on their balance sheets and sell them on to investors through special purpose vehicles and other similar arrangements. This was justified by more effective risk diversification, as the risks inherent in credit were basically transferred to a large number of investors away from banks' balance sheets. Similarly, new investment targets could be offered to the wealth that flowed into the United States. This process is called securitization. Securitisation can increase banking financing opportunities, e.g. in banking. with the use of covered bonds. However, there may be problems of principle. In hindsight, it is clear that the securitisation went too far and took on unhealthy characteristics. As early as the end of the 1990s, Professor Raghu Rajan, who at the beginning of the decade also served as chief economist at the IMF, wrote that he was puzzled as to what the true economic rationality of securitisation is and how such a large market could have emerged in the first place. In his reflections, Rajan pointed out that the loans on banks' balance sheets have been understood in banking theory to be marketable due to the asymmetry of the information they contain. The bank knows its customers and the real value of the loans it issues better than an outside investor. It is for this reason that the loans have been issued by the bank, and the borrower has not received them directly from the promissory note market. The problem of asymmetric information was mainly solved in two ways. First, public credit rating agencies such as Standard&Poor's and Moody's took to classifying securitised assets. They awarded the investment products an external evaluator's label. Bengt Holmstrom has compared this to the practices of the diamond trade. There was a symmetry of information among investors, because no one was allowed to look at the 'contents of the diamond bag', in this case the vat of securitised loans. But the level of quality of the frogs and the uniformity between them was ensured by an external quality controller, in this case a credit rating agency. Secondly, the securitisation items were broken down into sections, each with a different risk. The issuing bank often kept the highest proportion of risk on its balance sheet. The purpose of this was also to provide an incentive for the bank itself to cherish diligence and prudence in the underwriting process. However, perhaps the biggest losses for international banks have come from lower-risk mortgage-backed securities (so-called senior/ super senior tranches), which the banks themselves had huge amounts of leveraged and whose low-rated risk the banks did not care to hedge. These securities were initially priced at a very high level due to the low estimated risk. Therefore, since the onset of the crisis, banks have suffered large valuation losses from these investments through the requirement to use fair value. Since the onset of the crisis, it has been shown that the process of classifying and pricing securitised assets did not work properly and that the products had become far too complex. Risks were systematically underestimated, especially for macro risks, and increased systemic risks through complex interbank links were not understood. The possibility of a simultaneous and widespread fall in the price of secured housing across the United States was not taken into account in the models. There has also been much debate as to whether the rating agencies' own financial incentives led to failure and jeopardising their independence. An interesting detail, the centrality of which in the course of events should perhaps not be underestimated, is the so-called encyclopedia. The role of Li's formula in the pricing and classification of securitised receivables. Wall Street financial engineers had long pondered the problem that was the last 'missing piece' in valuing securitised credit pools. How should the probability of a simultaneous default on individual loans in the vat be modelled? Dr. Li published his research in which he took advantage of actuarial mathematics on the life expectancy of spouses, conditional on the passing of one of the spouses. The result was an elegant and easy-to-apply formula that allowed the last missing parameter to be practically calibrated from the market prices of the securitised items. In hindsight, it seems that the growth in the volume of securitised items accelerated considerably as information about Li's formula spread. Eventually, Standard & Poor's and Moody's also adopted it one after the other in the classification of securitised items. This can be considered questionable, since the classifier should rather be able to question the methods used by the market, rather than adopting them as such. Li's formula had a key constraint of which its author was aware. The formula assumed a stable correlation between payment defaults. However, the problem is that correlation structures in financial markets can be very unstable. With regard to the current crisis, there was a fatal change in correlations at the latest when the prices of apartments secured by securitised subprime loans began to decline in the United States. While the role of Li's formula should not be overemphasized, it is one practical example of how the risks of securitised receivables ended up being underestimated. The models were over-relied on when it came to pricing complex products, and there was not enough questioning of the models' assumptions and the sensitivity of pricing to changes in assumptions. Despite the shortcomings of ratings and, apparently, of the pricing mechanism for securitised claims, the financial crisis could have been much milder if risks had genuinely shifted away from banks' balance sheets. Financial researchers at New York University who have recently compiled the book "Restoring financial stability: how to repair a failed system? They ask the question of why, in the end, a significant part of the risks remained on the balance sheets of banks. The answer they offered is that, along with risk diversification, the real motive for securitisation in many cases was to relax banks' prudential requirements. The phenomenon in question is called capital arbitrage. In addition to the shortcomings in risk underpricing and risk management, these prudential regulatory problems are likely to have had a significant impact on the emergence of the crisis. One weakness of the Basel I prudential framework is that it does not contain sufficiently sophisticated instruments for defining the solvency requirements for off-balance-sheet items. Researchers at New York University further suggest that many of the financial innovations related to securitisations in recent years have aimed to convert the risks on a bank's balance sheet into a form that effectively mitigates the solvency requirement on them. In this way, many banks have been able to increase the return on capital employed. This was achieved, for example, by converting some mortgages into AAA-rated securities with a very low solvency requirement through securitisation. As many as half of the AAA-rated securitisation items remained on the balance sheets of the banking sector. Even in cases where securitised products were transferred to special purpose vehicles, the bank usually provided them with a line of credit to secure liquidity. When, in August 2007, the crisis broke out and the commercial paper market dried up, banks were forced to take over the financing of special purpose vehicles and return the company to the bank's balance sheet. [Slide 7: Total claims vs. risk-weighted claims of US banks] The figure below illustrates the evolution caused by capital arbitrage: the total exposures of the largest US banks have grown much faster than the amount of risk-weighted assets on the basis of which the solvency requirement is determined. When considering what could have been done to avoid or mitigate the crisis, it has been suggested that basel II should have been implemented years earlier. It is already in force in Europe, but the United States is only just moving towards its use. The central idea of Basel II is to set solvency requirements according to the actual risk of balance sheet items. In addition, it contains more precise rules for off-balance-sheet items, as well as for what constitutes a real off-balance-sheet transfer of risk and what is not. In this way, a tighter bridle would have been obtained for capital arbitrage. The crisis has shown that there are also problems with the Basel II framework that need to be rectified. For example, the capital requirements for special purpose vehicle credit limits and trading portfolio credit risks are too low in the original Basel II framework. These capital requirements are likely to be substantially increased. [Slide 8: Change in banks' financial structure] Closely related to the create-and-diversify model was the fact that the structure of banks' own fundraising changed radically in the pre-crisis period. The share of deposits declined and the share of short-term market financing increased sharply as banks financed the rapid growth of their asset masses. This exposed banks to liquidity risk, in a way a modern version of bank flight, which materialized when the problems of subprime credit began to come to light. The create-and-diversify model also contributed to how the crisis spread. Risk diversification through securitisations turned into a global contagion channel when the crisis erupted. 2. Governance, risk management and management incentives of financial institutions [Slide 9] For a long time, the prevailing view was that the modern governance of the financial system and the system's own risk management and self-regulation, which is an essential part of it, work and correct errors themselves. The financial crisis has dealt a heavy blow to this belief. In August 2005, professor Raghu Rajan, already mentioned, gave a presentation at the annual symposium of central bank governors in Jackson Hole while he was chief economist at the IMF. The theme of the symposium was " The Greenspan Era". His topic was: Have the evolution of the financial system increased risks in the world? ( Has Financial Development made the World Riskier?) The speech was met with exceptionally harsh criticism and from well-known names. Rajan predicted at the time that risks had increased significantly in the global financial markets. He saw as a key reason the incentive schemes of financial institutions, which rewarded short-term returns, but did not sufficiently take into account the long-term risks associated with whether or not the loan would eventually be paid off. The risks were obscured because the prevailing investment strategies produced steady positive results but left a low probability of a disastrous outcome. Risk re-pricing began in the market in the summer of 2007, when the first wave of the crisis began. It had been two years since Rajan's prophetic introduction. Researchers have since explained the problems of corporate governance by the fact that fierce competition for the most qualified people in the financial sector may lead to a situation where standards of good governance are eroded. Poor governance more easily leads to the structure of reward systems favouring too short-term remuneration. The key people who perform the best are easy to change jobs, In this competition, the ability of financial institutions to develop reward systems that take into account longer-term risks has proven to be very weak. The boards of directors of financial institutions ended up opting for a solution for remuneration systems that is ultimately disadvantageous for everyone and for the system as a whole. This is a major market coordination problem. As a result of the externalities associated with good governance, attempts can be made to improve standards of good governance through regulation or supervision, however demanding that may be. In addition to rewarding healthy risk management, the independent position of risk management, adequate and competent resources should be secured, and active challenge to the results of models should be ensured. Supervisors should sharpen their own criteria, but this does not take away from the fact that responsibility for good risk management and internal control must remain with the companies themselves. 3. Luottojohdannaiset [Slide 10] One financial instrument that has received a lot of attention in the context of the crisis is credit default derivatives, i.e. the so-called credit defaults. CDSs (credit default swap). The problems of the American insurance company AIG were associated precisely with these instruments. A credit default derivative is a credit insurance that provides its buyer with protection against a default on, for example, a promissory note issued by a bank. The market for credit derivatives has functioned as an over-the-counter (OTC) market and therefore trading has not been centralised, for example, on the stock exchange. Counterparty risk for buyers of credit derivatives has been high because the exposures of different parties have not been netted in a central counterparty system. Supervisors have found it difficult to obtain an up-to-date overview of market volumes, pricing and risk developments. The establishment of a centralised clearing and settlement system for credit derivatives is one of the concrete proposals that have been made to improve the stability of these markets and facilitate supervision. II. CONDITIONS FOR RECOVERY - STABILISATION OF THE BANKING SYSTEM [Slide 11] The containment of the financial crisis and the restoration of the functioning of the financial system have required and will require the cooperation of all economic policy areas. Measures in support of the financial sector can be divided into three parts: securing liquidity, providing sufficient capital and cleaning up toxic assets from banks' balance sheets. Already in August 2007, the central banks  the ECB being the first of these  took major steps to safeguard the liquidity of the banking system. A particularly significant change was that, since autumn 2008, the ECB has been issuing the amount of credit at the key interest rate to counterparty banks in its operations. The range of accepted guarantees has also been broadened. In the second phase of the crisis, in October-November 2008, measures were taken to safeguard banks' capital. Within the EU, rules of the game have been agreed whereby the state can, on the one hand, bail out crisis banks and, on the other, invest capital in viable banks in various forms. Viable banks have primarily sought to raise capital directly from the market. They have generally been reticent about government capital investments. Under common EU state aid rules, governments have also been given the opportunity to provide guarantees for long-term financing of banks. These opportunities have also not been used by nearly all banks. For example, banks operating in Finland have failed to use the possibilities of capital support and guarantees because there has been no compelling need to increase the support. The clean-up of banks' balance sheets from problem assets is still ongoing. In the United States, in order to clean the banking system from problem items on balance sheets, Treasury Secretary Tim Geithner introduced the PPIP (Public-Private Investment Program) model. In support of this, banks underwent stress tests to scan their balance sheets. The use of this has not been widespread either. In Europe, too, it has been decided to carry out stress tests of banks with common standards, but carried out by national financial supervisors. Many national financial supervisors  such as Finland  have already accounted for their own separate stress tests, which are carried out as part of their ongoing supervisory work. Support measures for the financial sector alone will not be sufficient to solve the problems of the global economy, but a return of the financial sector to as normal a state as possible is a prerequisite for the sustainable recovery of the economy. The recovery of credit by financial institutions is one of the conditions for the economic recovery of the economy as a whole. Another important question for the normalisation of credit is the extent to which the create-and-diversify model based on securitisation will recover. This market can continue to play a key role in the financing of traditional lending, provided that the necessary solutions are taken to address the major shortcomings identified in the operating models. III. LESSONS FROM THE CRISIS TO IMPROVE REGULATION AND SUPERVISION AND ECONOMIC ANALYSIS [Slide 12] The crisis has, of course, given rise to a lively debate on how to develop the regulation and supervision of the financial system in the future in order to prevent similar crises from arising, or at least from worsening them. There have been many summits around this issue, the most important of which were the Summit of Heads of Eurozone and British Governments last October in Paris and the G-20 summits last November in Washington and April in London. The message of the meetings was clear; A new balance is now being sought between the actions of the public authorities and the market. Confidence in the market's ability to adequately regulate its own operations has gone. There is a need for a common supervisory practice at global level, there is a need to strengthen the so-called 'supervisory framework'. the identification and supervision of systemic risks, the need to bring all major financial institutions, including outside banks, under appropriate supervision, must be prevented from creating incentive schemes that could plunge the entire financial system into crisis, and credit rating agencies must also register and be subject to appropriate supervision. If in the past there was too much reliance on self-regulation by the market, now the big challenge in the midst of a crisis is to avoid excessively onerous regulatory measures. A. CONCRETE REGULATORY DEVELOPMENT MEASURES For its part, the EU has moved forward on the basis of and independently of the decisions of the summits. First, in relation to the create-and-diversify model, the new regulation sets a minimum limit on how much the issuing financial institution must hold on its own balance sheet for the risks of the securitised item. This is to ensure that the issuer has sufficient incentives to take care of the quality of the securitised credits. Information about who ultimately bears the risk will also improve. Secondly, various measures will be taken to regulate the activities of credit rating agencies. Their purpose is to ensure the standards of classifications. The measures will increase the transparency of rating methods and strengthen the good governance of rating agencies. Thirdly, the Commission's recommendation seeks to guide the remuneration policies of financial institutions. The recommendation states that the payment of bonuses should be staggered in such a way that they can be proportional to the possible realisation of the risks of operations at a later date. These basic principles of remuneration are also becoming part of the EU's common financial legislation. Some Member States have already attached conditions to remuneration schemes as a condition for the recapitalisation of banks and state guarantees. B. DEVELOPING MACRO-SURVEILLANCE During the crisis, the European Commission set up a committee chaired by former IMF Managing Director De Larosiere to make proposals for improving financial supervision at European level. The Committee's report has been a key basis for reform projects in the EU. One of the Committee's key proposals, which the European Commission has included in its recent proposal, is the creation of a new Risk Council responsible for macro-supervision of the financial system in the EU. Macro-supervision differs from traditional financial supervision in that its role is to focus on the supervision of systemic risk posed by financial institutions and markets as a whole, not only on the supervision of individual institutions. The crisis has shown that supervision of individual institutions alone may not be sufficient to take into account the risks arising from interinstitutional links, such as counterparty relationships. These risks can cause, as has been seen, unexpected infections from one institution to another and the liquidity of entire markets drying up overnight. Supervision of individual companies may also disregard risk concentrations formed at the level of the financial sector as a whole, for example. with strong overall credit growth. Recently, Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke has published a list of things he thinks macro-surveillance should cover. There are at least four of them: 1) Large and rapidly growing exposures should be monitored at the level of the institutions and the market as a whole, and not only at the level of the balance sheets of individual institutions. As an example of the systemic significance of such liabilities, one can cite the knock-on effects that have arisen from subprime credits. (2) The systemic risks that may arise from changes in risk management practices, a general increase in indebtedness or changes in financial markets or their products shall be assessed. (3) The potential chains of influence generated by counterparty risks shall be analysed. 4) The supervision of individual institutions should be proportional to the risk their failure would pose to the financial system as a whole. Some researchers have also suggested that prudential requirements should also be proportional to the amount of systemic risk in an institution. The crisis has further taught us that systemic risk depends not only on the size of the institution, but also on the structure of its responsibilities. It is important that, in the future, cooperation between supervisors and central banks is further intensified in this supervision of macroprudential financial markets. PROSYKLISYYS [Slide 13] The crisis has also brought into the discussion the development of prudential regulations. The G20 meeting in London, which has already been mentioned, also outlined this. Prudential provisions and other similar provisions should be further developed so that they do not strengthen credit cycles and thus the cyclical fluctuations of the economy. In the event of economic downturns, banks' credit losses and write-downs increase, so their capital buffers in relation to the minimum capital requirements set by the authority are reduced. Given the difficulty or cost of raising external capital in recessions, banks may need to reduce their lending to ensure that their capital requirements are met in all circumstances. A decline in credit, at worst a credit crunch, could further deepen the recession. The procyclic mechanic is characteristic of any prudential regulation, but it is clear that the new Basel II regulation strengthens the mechanism compared to the previous Basel I acquis. In the past, for example, the minimum capital requirement for banks arising from corporate loans was standard, but under the new Basel-II regulations, the requirement is determined by the bankruptcy risk of a corporate customer. As the risks of corporate bankruptcy have been found to increase in a downturn, basel II capital requirements also increase in recessions. Rising capital requirements will further reduce the supply of credit and thus could deepen the recession. Capital requirements, on the other hand, fall during boom periods and the resulting credit supply reinforces the boom. It should be remembered, however, that the United States has always had Basel I in place, so basel II can hardly be blamed for causing the crisis. As we said earlier, there have even been estimates that the earlier implementation of Basel II-type regulation could have mitigated the developments that led to the crisis. At all times - both booms and downs - there are credit customers with different risks. It is therefore important to uphold the principle of differentiating prudential requirements on the basis of customer and receivable risk. However, in order to further develop the Basel II framework, means must be created to reduce procyclicality. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision is expected to present its views on such means by the end of this year. One possibility is to raise the average level of the Basel II minimum capital requirements in boom periods and lower it in recessions. This, of course, requires the selection of suitable indicators for the timing and intensity of the cyclical phases. This can be quite challenging. Another possibility is to require banks to use methods for assessing customer risks that assess risk across the business cycle. A considerable number of research results, mainly based on simulations, have been presented in favour of adjusting the average capital requirements in some way over the economic cycle. The Bank of Finland has also carried out research in this regard. C. FAIR VALUE ACCOUNTING AND DYNAMIC PROVISIONS Another aspect of regulatory development that is indirectly linked to the issue of credit supply in the event of crises is fair value accounting. The issue has also gained attention because, in the United States, the accounting rules of banks were recently amended in a way that is a step away from the fair value principle. This was to mitigate the exposure of banks' balance sheets to market valuations that contain exceptional uncertainty in the context of the crisis or are simply absent. Opinions are divided on the research side. On the one hand, some academic researchers have put forward theoretical arguments as to why the valuation of banks' balance sheet items at market values can further increase volatility, market values may be artificial and exceptionally uncertain in crisis situations. Lending and counterparty business may be disrupted for this reason as well. On the other hand, the defenders of fair value valuation argue that the information value of accounting should be preserved. According to them, it is wrong to 'shoot the messenger', which is what accounting should be seen as in the first place. Defenders also cite the opposite evidence that the uncertainty and mistrust of counterparties towards each other will only increase if balance sheet items are not recorded at fair value. Short-term threats to stability and long-term incentive effects seem to be at odds. In this context, attention has been drawn to the so-called 'green card'. Spanish model. At the initiative of the authorities, Spanish banks made dynamic reserves in the early years of this decade. Provisions were accumulated against potential credit losses, which were estimated on the basis of historical data. If any credit losses are realised, the provisions can be cancelled accordingly. Dynamic provisions allow banks to keep earnings more even, but risks are, in principle, prepared for in a transparent manner. The method also attracted criticism. It was not considered to comply with current international accounting standards and therefore Spain had to modify its system in 2004. As a rule, current standards accept only realized credit losses or similar write-downs. In the near future, we will see in Europe, too, a lively dialogue between accounting experts, financial supervisors, central banks and the private financial sector on how to combine the principle of transparency in accounting and the prudential principle of supervision in a single framework. The issue is also important for reducing the procyclicality of the financial sector. [Slide 14] D. DEVELOPMENT OF SCENARIO ANALYSIS Macro-supervision of the financial system also needs to be supported by analysis based on micro- and macroeconomic models. Surveillance cannot be based only on the forecasted, that is, the most likely course of economic development. Monitoring must also take into account unlikely, even extreme, scenarios. Before the current crisis, the 'lingua franca' of risk management had become the Value-at-Risk analysis, which is based on certain fairly simple probability distributions and the assessment of the probabilities of losses based on them. More attention has now been paid to scenario analysis, which examines the bad options for the future in more detail, but on the other hand, the definition of the probabilities of their realisation is perhaps approached more humbly after the crisis. Scenario analysis has become a topic of increased attention following the recent debate on stress tests. After all, stress tests are based precisely on the elaboration of scenarios for banks' operating environments and the analysis of their impact. International supervisory cooperation has highlighted the need to harmonise the methodology for stress tests. This would be necessary to ensure comparability of results, even if stress testing were carried out in a decentralised manner in different countries and hopefully also in cooperation between supervisors and supervisors. The practices and models of stress tests will be one of the priorities for the development of macro-supervision of the financial system in the near future. Scenarios and stress tests will interestingly form a bridge between macroeconomics and financial supervision Macroeconomic analysis and financial supervision will hopefully converge. On the other hand, it is known that taking into account financial factors or dealing with breakpoints such as the economic crisis are not the most strongly developed areas of current macroeconomics. Cooperation between the various sectors of economic policy should also be discussed. The task of ensuring monetary stability is a matter for the Central Bank and remains their primary task, but the concept of macro-supervision shows that central banks inevitably also play a key role in stability policy. Furthermore, the idea of the independence of monetary stability and the stability of the financial markets as policy objectives has proved to be misleading in the wake of the crisis. The state of financial markets has a decisive impact on the economy as a whole, including on the transmission of monetary policy and aggregate demand, and thus on the achievement of monetary policy objectives. The debate on the integration of asset values as part of the monetary policy strategy has also rekindled with the crisis. I am just referring to the criticism that has been levelled at the monetary policy of some central banks in particular during the real estate boom of the last decade. So far, no central bank has given asset values a formal status as part of its monetary framework. I am open to this issue and I hope that it can be the subject of a thorough and analytical debate at international level and also within the euro area. IV. HOW HAS THE CRISIS AFFECTED FINLAND? A. THE CURRENT CRISIS AND THE RECESSION OF THE EARLY 90S The economic crisis has hit all economies hard. In the spiral of mistrust triggered by the bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers, world trade last autumn fell synchronously and it quickly hit export-dependent economies such as Finland. The financial crisis has contributed to a freeze on investment. The national product of Europe and Finland will contract significantly this year, and there is no prospect of a rapid economic recovery. The question is often asked: how can the current situation be compared to the recession in Finland in the 1990s? There are also major differences. At the beginning of the 1990s, our corporate sector was highly indebted and everywhere, including in the non-tradable sector, there were also a lot of foreign currency liabilities. The devaluation of the Finnish markka caused a devastating impact on the business sector. At the time of the current crisis, corporate liabilities were far from comparable currency risk and their balance sheets are also stronger in terms of equity. Households are now about as indebted as they were then. However, the difference is that while at that time 8-9% of household disposable income went to interest payments, now the corresponding share is about 3.5% and loan periods have lengthened significantly. In a joint stress test conducted by the Bank of Finland and the Financial Supervisory Authority, banks have also been found to survive in conditions of worse economic development, even if this would mean an increase in their losses and a deterioration in their performance. Although the situation is now easier, as described in this way, the current recession still leaves a long mark on our economy. It will take time for the national economy to reach the level of 2008. The weakening of the labour market is felt both in the daily lives of young jobseekers and in the premature withdrawal of experienced workers from the labour market. This also has a major impact on the sustainability of public sector funding. B. THE DEVELOPMENT OF REGULATION AND SUPERVISION IN FINLAND - THE NEW FINANCIAL SUPERVISORY AUTHORITY AND ITS CHALLENGES At the beginning of the year, a new Financial Supervisory Authority, fiva, has started its operations in Finland, which operates in connection with the Bank of Finland and was created as a result of the merger of the Financial Supervisory Authority and the Insurance Supervisory Authority. Finland's solution represents the current mainstream thinking. Risk sharing between the banking and insurance sectors is difficult or even artificial in a systemic analysis. The position of the Financial Supervisory Authority as independent, but in the context of the Bank of Finland, ensures a natural connection and division of labour between micro-supervision and macro-supervision, which is part of the central bank's task. It would also be important to make rapid progress on solutions at European level on both fronts. It is also important for Finland to establish the rules of the game for cooperation between supervisors in the home and host countries of supranational banks. In Finland, there are banks in a significant systemic position that are headquartered in another Nordic country. The subsidiaries are supervised by Fiva in Finland, which is very important. If they ever become branches, the rights of the host state's supervisor must also be safeguarded. V. CONCLUSION We have been living through the most significant international financial crisis since the Great Depression for almost two years. The crisis has been a major challenge for policymakers and monetary policymakers. who, in constant change, have had to make far-reaching decisions and move the frameworks of their policies. Solutions have been sought in an open spirit and extensive international cooperation. Let us hope that the same attitude will endure when the decisions taken at summits have to be implemented. A major challenge lies ahead even when the massive stimulus mobilised as the economy strengthens has to be pulled back in order to prevent the spiral of inflation and excessive public debt. Timing is going to be a difficult question that will also arouse passions. The balance between the public sector and the market is changing. The financial crisis has a major and long-term impact on national economies. That is why better controls are needed to prevent them in the future. At the same time, there is a great risk of over-regulation and excesses when, in the midst of a crisis, long-term ground rules are changed. The crisis will leave its mark on economic and monetary policy, financial control and, in general, the relationship between regulation and the market. But neither economics nor economic research will remain an outsider. On the one hand, economics has cause for introspection: Has research been in relevant areas? Where has research not stood the test of a major crisis? What is the future of rationality assumption and behaviorism in economic analysis? Also at the application level, research has faced many challenges in support of regulatory reform of the financial system. How, on the one hand, to safeguard the possibility of innovation in the financial system and, on the other hand, to prevent the risks that innovations bring with them, which destabilise the entire financial system, from materialising?
