Stressitestith<8a>n perustuvat juuri pankkien toimintaymp<8a>rist<9a>j<8a> koskevien skenaarioiden laadintaan ja niiden vaikutusten selvittelyyn. Kansainv<8a>linen valvontayhteisty<9a> on nostanut esiin tarpeen stressitestej<8a> koskevan metodiikan yhten<8a>ist<8a>miseksi. T<8a>m<8a> olisi tarpeen tulosten vertailukelpoisuuden varmistamiseksi, vaikka stressitestausta teht<8a>isiinkin hajautetusti eri maissa ja toivottavasti my<9a>s valvottavien ja valvojien yhteisty<9a>n<8a>. Stressitestien k<8a>yt<8a>nn<9a>t ja mallit tulevat olemaan yksi rahoitusj<8a>rjestelm<8a>n makrovalvonnan kehitt<8a>misen painopisteit<8a> l<8a>hiaikoina. Skenaariot ja stressitestit muodostavat kiinnostavalla tavalla sillan makrotaloustieteen ja rahoitusvalvonnan v<8a>lille Makrotaloudellinen analyysi ja rahoitusvalvonta l<8a>hestyv<8a>t toivottavasti toisiaan. Toisaalta tiedet<8a><8a>n, ett<8a> rahoitustekij<9a>iden huomioon ottaminen tai talouskriisin tyyppisten murtokohtien k<8a>sittely eiv<8a>t ole nykyisen makrotaloustieteen vahvimmin kehittyneit<8a> alueita. My<9a>s talouspolitiikan eri lohkojen yhteisty<9a> on syyt<8a> keskustella l<8a>pi. Rahan arvon vakaudesta huolehtiminen kuuluu keskuspankille, ja pysyy niiden ensisijaisena teht<8a>v<8a>n<8a>, mutta makrovalvonnan k<8a>site osoittaa, ett<8a> keskuspankeilla on v<8a>ist<8a>m<8a>tt<8a> keskeinen rooli my<9a>s vakauspolitiikassa. Ajatus rahan arvon vakauden ja rahoitusmarkkinoiden vakauden riippumattomuudesta politiikan tavoitteina on sit<8a> paitsi kriisin my<9a>t<8a> osoittautunut harhaanjohtavaksi. Rahoitusmarkkinoiden tila vaikuttaa ratkaisevalla tavalla koko kansantalouteen, my<9a>s rahapolitiikan v<8a>littymiseen ja kokonaiskysynt<8a><8a>n ja sit<8a> kautta rahapolitiikan tavoitteiden saavuttamiseen. My<9a>s keskustelu varallisuusarvojen huomioon ottamisesta osana rahapolitiikan strategiaa on virinnyt uudestaan kriisin my<9a>t<8a>. Viittaan vain siihen kritiikkiin, jota on kohdistettu varsinkin er<8a>iden keskuspankkien rahapolitiikkaan viime vuosikymmenen kiinteist<9a>boomin aikana. Toistaiseksi mik<8a><8a>n keskuspankki ei ole antanut varallisuusarvoille formaalia asemaa osana rahapoliittisessa kehikossaan. Suhtaudun kysymykseen avoimesti ja toivon, ett<8a> siit<8a> voitaisiin k<8a>yd<8a> perusteellinen ja analyyttinen keskustelu kansainv<8a>lisesti ja my<9a>s euroalueella. IV. MITEN KRIISI ON VAIKUTTANUT SUOMEEN? A. NYKYKRIISI JA 90-LUVUN ALUN LAMA Talouskriisi on iskenyt voimakkaasti kaikkiin talouksiin. Rahoituskriisi on osaltaan j<8a><8a>dytt<8a>nyt investointeja. Usein kysyt<8a><8a>n, miten nykyist<8a> tilannetta voi verrata Suomen lamaan 1990-luvulla? Suuria erojakin on. 1990-luvun alussa yrityssektorimme oli hyvin velkaantunut ja kaikkialla, my<9a>s suljetulla sektorilla oli runsaasti my<9a>s valuuttam<8a><8a>r<8a>isi<8a> velkoja. Suomen markan devalvoituminen aiheutti tuhoisaa j<8a>lke<8a> yrityskent<8a>ll<8a>. Nykyiseen kriisiin tultaessa yritysten veloissa ei ollut l<8a>hesk<8a><8a>n vastaavaa valuuttariski<8a> ja niiden taseet ovat vahvemmat my<9a>s oman p<8a><8a>oman osalta. Kotitaloudet ovat nyt suunnilleen yht<8a> velkaantuneita kuin silloin. Ero on kuitenkin siin<8a>, ett<8a> kun tuolloin kotitalouksien k<8a>ytett<8a>vist<8a> tuloista meni korkomenoihin 8-9 %, nyt vastaava osuus on noin 3.5 prosenttia ja laina.ajat ovat pidentyneet merkitt<8a>v<8a>sti. Suomen Pankin ja Finanssivalvonnan yhteisess<8a> stressitestiss<8a> pankkien on todettu selvi<8a>v<8a>n my<9a>s nykyist<8a> huonomman talouden kehityksen oloissa, vaikkakin se merkitsisi niiden tappioiden kasvua ja tuloksen huonontumista. Vaikka tilanne on n<8a>in kuvatulla tavalla nyt helpompi, nykyinen taantuma j<8a>tt<8a><8a> silti pitk<8a>n j<8a>ljen talouteemme. Vie aikaa, ennen kuin kansantalous saavuttaa vuoden 2008 tason. Ty<9a>markkinoiden heikentyminen tuntuu sek<8a> nuorten ty<9a>nhakijoiden arjessa ett<8a> kokeneiden ty<9a>ntekij<9a>iden liian varhaisena vet<8a>ytymisen<8a> ty<9a>markkinoilta. T<8a>ll<8a> on my<9a>s suuri vaikutus julkisen sektorin rahoituksen kest<8a>vyyteen. B. S<80><80>NTELYN JA VALVONNAN KEHITYS SUOMESSA -UUSI FINANSSIVALVONTA JA SEN HAASTEET Suomessa on vuoden alusta aloittanut toimintansa uusi Finanssivalvonta, Fiva, joka toimii Suomen Pankin yhteydess<8a> ja joka syntyi Rahoitustarkastuksen ja Vakuutusvalvontaviraston yhdistymisen tuloksena. Suomen ratkaisu edustaa nykyist<8a> mainstream-ajattelua. Riskien jakaminen pankki-ja vakuutussektorin v<8a>lill<8a> on systeemitarkastelussa vaikeaa tai jopa keinotekoista. Finanssivalvonnan asema itsen<8a>isen<8a>, mutta Suomen Pankin yhteydess<8a> turvaa luontevan yhteyden ja ty<9a>njaon yksitt<8a>isiin yrityksiin suuntautuvat mikrovalvonnan ja keskuspankin teht<8a>v<8a>v<8a><8a>n kuuluvan makrovalvonnan v<8a>lill<8a>. Olisi t<8a>rke<8a><8a> edet<8a> pikaisesti my<9a>s Euroopan tason ratkaisuissa molemmilla kentill<8a>. Suomen kannalta on my<9a>s t<8a>rke<8a><8a> vakiinnuttaa ylikansallisten pankkien koti-ja is<8a>nt<8a>maan valvojien yhteisty<9a>n pelis<8a><8a>nn<9a>t. Suomessa on merkitt<8a>v<8a>ss<8a> systeemisess<8a> asemassa pankkeja, joiden p<8a><8a>konttori on toisessa pohjoismaassa. Tyt<8a>ryhti<9a>it<8a> valvoo Fiva Suomessa, mik<8a> on hyvin t<8a>rke<8a><8a>. Mik<8a>li ne joskus muuttuvat haarakonttoreiksi, is<8a>nt<8a>valtion valvojan oikeudet on my<9a>s silloin turvattava. V. LOPUKSI Olemme el<8a>neet kohta kaksi vuotta merkitt<8a>vint<8a> kansainv<8a>list<8a> finanssikriisi<8a> sitten suuren laman. Kriisi on ollut suuri haaste talouspolitiikan ja rahapolitiikan p<8a><8a>tt<8a>jille. jotka jatkuvassa muutoksessa ovat joutuneet tekem<8a><8a>n kauaskantoisia ratkaisuja ja liikuttamaan politiikkansa kehyksi<8a>. Ratkaisuja on haettu avoimessa hengess<8a> ja laajassa kansainv<8a>lisess<8a> yhteisty<9a>ss<8a>. Toivokaamme, ett<8a> sama asenne kest<8a><8a>, kun huippukokouksissa tehdyt p<8a><8a>t<9a>kset pit<8a><8a> saattaa toimeen. Suuri haaste on edess<8a> silloinkin, kun liikkeelle pantu mittava elvytyspanos talouden vahvistuessa joudutaan vet<8a>m<8a><8a>n takaisin inflaatiokierteen ja julkisen talouden liiallisen velkaantumisen est<8a>miseksi. Ajoitus tulee olemaan vaikea kysymys, joka her<8a>tt<8a><8a> my<9a>s intohimoja. Julkisen sektorin ja markkinoiden tasapaino muuttuu. Finanssikriisill<8a> on suuri ja pitk<8a>aikainen vaikutus kansantalouksiin. Siksi sellaisten est<8a>miseen vastaisuudessa tarvitaan parempaa valvontaa. Samalla ylis<8a><8a>telyn ja ylily<9a>nnin vaara on suuri, kun keskell<8a> kriisi<8a> muutetaan pitk<8a>n aikav<8a>lin peris<8a><8a>nt<9a>j<8a>. Kriisi tulee j<8a>tt<8a>m<8a><8a>n j<8a>lkens<8a> talous-ja rahapolitiikkaan, rahoituksen valvontaan ja yleens<8a> s<8a><8a>ntelyn ja markkinoiden suhteeseen. Mutta taloustiede eik<8a> taloustutkimuskaan tule j<8a><8a>m<8a><8a>n ulkopuoliseksi. Yht<8a><8a>lt<8a> taloustieteell<8a> on aihetta itsetutkiskeluun: Onko tutkimus ollut relevanteilla alueilla? Miss<8a> tutkimus ei ole kest<8a>nyt suuren kriisin testi<8a>? Mik<8a> on rationaalisuusoletuksen ja behaviorismin tulevaisuus talousanalyysiss<8a>? My<9a>s sovellusten tasolla tutkimukselle on tullut paljon haasteita rahoitusj<8a>rjestelm<8a>n s<8a><8a>ntelyn uudistamisen tukena. Miten yht<8a><8a>lt<8a> turvata innovaatioiden mahdollisuus rahoitusj<8a>rjestelm<8a>ss<8a>, ja toisaalta est<8a><8a> samalla innovaatioiden mukanaan tuomien, koko rahoitusj<8a>rjestelm<8a><8a> horjuttavien riskien toteutuminen? Title: Pijt-Hme EntrepreneurShip Festival
text: President and CEO Erkki Liikanen: P8aij8at-H8ame Entrepreneur Festival 2009, Lahti 24.10.2009 . Speech . Saturday 24 October 2009, 12:00 AM President and CEO Erkki Liikanen P8aij8at-H8ame Entrepreneur Festival 2009 Lahti 24.10.2009 It is always a great experience to be here at the Sibelius House in Lahti. Six weeks ago, we were here on a Friday evening to listen to a concert by the Lahti Fine Symphony Orchestra at the Sibelius Festival. In this hall, all the sounds, even the quietest pianissimos, are played sensibly sensitively. The great conductor Jukka-Pekka Saraste conducted the concert. After the concert, my wife and I continued in the dark evening by car to Mikkeli and from there by boat to the island. On the way, we listened to an album we bought here, in which the same orchestra, now led by another great conductor Osmo V8ansk8a, played Sibelius's original Karelian series. What an evening! Today we are meeting at the P8aij8at-H8ame Entrepreneur Festival. We are celebrating it in an exceptional economic situation. The global economy has experienced the most extensive and deepest recession since the war. Imbalances in the global economy and the collapse of financial innovation first triggered the financial market turmoil in late summer 2007. A year ago, they spread to the real economy as if synchronised, at the same time everywhere. Trade finance froze, mistrust spread everywhere, and world trade as a whole began to contract for the first time in decades. The first phase of the financial shocks did not yet affect the development of the Finnish economy, but growth continued to be strong until the autumn of last year. Then, after the bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers, confidence in the economic outlook plummeted everywhere and the financing of exports quickly became more difficult. World trade came to a standstill, and through the collapse of exports, the crisis also spread to Finland. After that, the impact on Finland was stronger than in many other countries, as industrial investment goods and intermediate products represent up to 80% of our exports. Investments were postponed and even cancelled, and industrial and commercial stocks were emptied. While in 2008 exports accounted for almost half of our national product, they have now fallen to just over a third. The growth of globalisation strongly supported Finland's rise between 2004 and 2008. Now its backward steps have hit especially export-oriented countries such as Finland. Today, the free fall of the world economy is over. Growth, especially in emerging economies, has picked up speed. The developed industrial states have also reached the bottom of the recession. The International Monetary Fund has revised its forecasts upwards. However, growth will be slower than before. While the use of leverage accelerated growth in recent years, it is now being held back by reduced indebtedness. Companies, financial institutions and households pay off debt. It slows down the growth of demand. Governments and central banks around the world took extensive stimulus measures last year. The European Central Bank cut its key interest rate rapidly from 4.25% to 1%. In addition, the key interest rate has given banks the amount of liquidity they want, which has pushed short-term market rates even lower than the key interest rate. In Finland, loans to non-financial corporations and households are tied to short-term market interest rates more generally than in other euro area countries. For this reason, the fall in steering and market interest rates in Finland has been passed on faster than others to the interest paid by companies and households. Although banks have raised their margins to some extent, interest rates on loans have fallen to historically low levels. Governments have also stimulated the economy with significant budget deficits. It has been increased by the substantial expenditure increases and tax reductions that have been decided. In addition to them, the so-called. automatic stabilizers have increased the deficit. As unemployment rises and companies' results weaken, central and local government revenues decline, their expenditure automatically increases with the increase in unemployment security expenditure. It was right and important to support the economy through state intervention at a time when the structures of the world economy were destabilised and private investment and consumption were shrinking. The stimulus measures taken by governments and central banks were both indispensable parts of building the bridge over the financial market crisis and the global demand pit that followed. The opposite shore is already looming, but we are not there yet, and therefore it is not yet time to abolish the public stimulus. But when the opposite shore is reached, the construction of the bridge must be stopped, even if the opposite shore does not turn out to be as attractive as had been imagined. As I have just said, in the light of the current economic forecasts, the opposite side is hectic: growth will be modest in the coming years and public finances will not rebalance by themselves. As important as approving the deficit now is to prepare measures to achieve a balanced budget within a reasonable period of time and to break the debt spiral. If citizens do not trust that the balance of public finances will be achieved in the future, it may increase prudential savings and thus reduce consumption for a longer period of time. On the other hand, a growing spiral of public debt would easily lead to higher interest rates in sensitive financial markets. In this way, states and municipalities would for a long time have to make surplus budgets simply to pay interest on debts. A strong continuation of the growth of public debt would also limit the room for manoeuvre of monetary policy. An orderly and timely exit from government emergency measures would facilitate the safeguarding of price stability and give monetary policy time and space to support the functioning of the economy without jeopardising the objective of price stability. Unemployment has risen over the past year. Unemployment has increased particularly strongly among people aged 20 to 29. The Bank of Finland has studied the effects of the recession of the early 1990s on the labour market. The study showed that a significant proportion of young women and men who had been unemployed for a long time were permanently excluded from working life. It is very important to avoid a repetition of that situation. With the help of the state's active labour market policy and other means, care must be taken to ensure that young people entering working age remain attached to or close to working life. In the process of change, society's safety nets are necessary. The livelihoods of both entrepreneurs and employees and the opportunity for a new start must be secured in difficult situations of change. However, safety nets must not lock in people or change, but must encourage people to seek new challenges. At the same time, we must be concerned about the productivity of the economy. Total output per capita is determined by the amount of labour input on the one hand and the productivity of labour input on the other. There are therefore two ways to raise living standards: by increasing labour input or by increasing labour productivity. The standard of living is created by the work done. That is why it is important to extend working careers. After that, however, the age structure of the population and population growth set limits on the amount of work. In the long run, economic growth per capita is mainly based on growth in labour productivity. In principle, labour productivity can increase indefinitely. Its growth is influenced by both the use of capital input and the so-called capitalization. an increase in total factor productivity(s), which increases the productivity of inputs. The increase in total factor productivity is an important source of growth. It encompasses both technological progress and new, better ways of combining work and capital, and of organising production processes and organising working methods, i.e. new 'recipes'. The standard of living does not rise by cooking more of the same soup, but by inventing and using better recipes. Indeed, the mystery of economic growth lies precisely in understanding the factors affecting total factor productivity. Entrepreneurs play a key role in the economy. It is impossible to talk about a functioning market economy without entrepreneurs. The majority of the value added of all developed economies is generated by the private sector. Production in the private sector takes place in individual enterprises and, of course, it is difficult to imagine business activity without entrepreneurs. In Finland, entrepreneur-driven small and medium-sized enterprises account for more than half of the turnover of the entire business sector as well as employment. Entrepreneurs take responsibility for employing themselves, and often also family members and outsiders. Becoming an entrepreneur in itself is a sign of initiative and deserves to be appreciated. There can be no oversupply of such active participation in any society. There seems to be less willingness to take this kind of initiative in Finland than in other countries. According to international surveys, just under 30 per cent of people in Finland would rather work as an entrepreneur than as an employee if they were free to choose. On average, almost half of those in Europe (EU-15) prefer entrepreneurship and two-thirds in the United States, even more so in some southern European countries. You don't have to be born an entrepreneur, even though entrepreneurs often have entrepreneurial parents behind them. Becoming an entrepreneur is a career choice, and there are certainly as many reasons as there are entrepreneurs. As the economy grows, the reasons for choosing a career are different than in a recession. New companies are emerging and old companies are leaving the market at a brisk pace. You are certainly familiar with this, but little attention has been paid to the phenomenon in public debate. International comparisons show that in some European countries up to one in ten of the company stock is renewed every year. In Finland, the corresponding comparable figures are lower than the European average, but even here every year about 7d08% of companies are born and a slightly smaller number leave the market. In terms of numbers, this is not a small group of companies, as around 16,000d020,000 companies are born and exited every year. Especially in the early years, the loss is severe, with only about half of the new companies operating in Finland after five years. This change in the business sector is causing adaptation needs at the individual level for both entrepreneurs and wage and salary earners. On the other hand, it signals great potential for innovation and the fact that many new ideas make it to the market test. For the economy as a whole, it is important that ideas do not remain in drawers. Indeed, new companies and entrepreneurs are often considered important for innovation, but innovations and new ideas can also arise in companies that are already operating. From this we can move on to a theme that you entrepreneurs are very familiar with, namely competition. Competition is an essential part of a functioning market economy. Although competition can be seen as problematic from the point of view of an already established individual entrepreneur or company, it is of paramount importance for the functioning of the economy as a whole. A well-functioning and competitive market with easy access also offers new opportunities for existing entrepreneurs and companies in terms of both the size and direction of the business. Indeed, the renewal or 'creative destruction' described above, as it has also been called in economics, goes hand in hand with an increase in productivity. Increased competition and deregulation are the most important tools for raising our standard of living and affect the long-term growth conditions of the national economy. Increased competition affects our standard of living and the rate at which it rises along at least two different channels. The first channel is that competition reduces price margins and lowers the price level, leading to an increase in real earnings and purchasing power in the medium term. In this way, demand will intensify and lead to investment and create new jobs. At the Bank of Finland, we have made calculations on this with the Aino model for the overall economy. The second channel is that increased competition in the intermediate and final product markets will encourage companies to innovate and accelerate productivity growth in the economy and thus further long-term economic growth. Such innovations can be either new or better products, or equally new services or organizational reforms that make production processes more efficient. There is a wealth of new research data on this channel. Finally, on the role of economic policy in promoting business and collective well-being. It is essential for economic development that economic policy provides the right incentives for individual actors, i.e. entrepreneurs, companies and workers, to pursue economic success. One of the key tasks of economic policy is to ensure a competitive, stable and predictable operating environment for business. This allows entrepreneurs and companies to plan their operations on a long-term basis, invest in production capacity and employ people. The success of export-oriented companies around the world has always been seen as important for the development of Finnish well-being. But the development of the domestic market is also of paramount importance for both the growth of living standards and employment. The creation of a pan-European internal market has broadened the concept of the domestic market in terms of trade in goods, thus opening up new business opportunities for Finnish companies as well. The share of the service sector in value added and jobs has grown in recent decades both in Finland and elsewhere. That is why it is particularly important to increase productivity in services in particular. In Europe, however, the development of labour productivity has slowed down in services over the past ten years, while in the United States, for example, productivity growth has accelerated. For many years, the productivity of services in Finland grew rapidly compared to other European countries. However, due to the low baseline, the level of productivity is still only mediocre. Services have not been part of the internal market and attempts to liberalise trade in services in the European Union have made regrettably slow progress. Opening up a pan-European services market would also bring new opportunities for Finnish companies and much-needed dynamism for the entire European service sector. Maintaining price stability is a priority for the European System of Central Banks. Price stability has been specified to mean inflation rates of just under two per cent. The positive effects of monetary policy based on price stability on business are evident. Already Lenin is reported to have said that the best way to destroy the capitalist economic system is to degenerate (debauch) its money. In a market economy, the functioning of the price mechanism is therefore central to the efficient allocation of resources. Unexpected fluctuations in the price level weaken the information conveyed by prices, increase uncertainty and thus make it difficult for the economy to function. Strong fluctuations in exchange rates and uncontrolled movements are also a factor, which increases uncertainty in the economy. Uncertainty at exchange rates is undesirable as it does not contribute to favourable economic developments or financial stability. From this point of view, the commitment of us economic policy to a strong dollar is justified. From the point of view of the individual entrepreneur, constant fluctuations in costs and purchase prices make it difficult to "correctly" price their own products and may lead to inefficient production and investment decisions. In conditions of high and fluctuating inflation, firms and households are forced to use their resources to hedge inflation rather than productive activities. Inflationary uncertainty is also reflected in the size of risk premia, as investors demand compensation for uncertainty. Fluctuating inflation also leads to a random redistribution of income and wealth. Price stability is an important way to support business and the growth of well-being. In conditions of low and stable inflation, entrepreneurs and companies can plan their future in the long term and focus on productive business and its development. Economic growth, employment and Finnish well-being are created only through the success of companies. The financial crisis has also highlighted the role of central banks in safeguarding the stability of financial markets. The task of the financial supervisor is to monitor the solvency of individual banks. In addition, the crisis has taught us in a tangible way that we must ensure the stability of the entire financial system. This is because interbank links can create shocks throughout the financial system that deepen the volatility of national economies and, at worst, drive the national economy into a deep crisis. Europe has tackled this problem. To manage these systemic risks, we are creating a European Risk Committee with central bank governors as members and financial supervisors involved. It is important to find solutions here this year. In Europe and Finland, banks play a key role in securing the financing of companies. Therefore, it is good to note that Finnish banks are solvent. According to the stress tests, they can withstand a very challenging economic test. Ladies and gentlemen, We have lived and continue to live in a very challenging time financially. The global economy has started to recover cautiously. It is important that Finland can benefit from the strengthening of the global economy as soon as possible. It is not self-evident. The prerequisite is that our economy adapts to change. We must be able to seek new opportunities in the changing market situation. It requires innovation, initiative and entrepreneurship. In addition, the economy must also be competitive in terms of prices. This can only be achieved by increasing productivity; more needs to be done from the same stakes. Finnish entrepreneurs are an important cornerstone in this. When Jari Litmanen from Lahti played his top season for Ajax, he was interviewed in the run-up to the Juventus-Ajax final in a spectacular way for a French sports magazine. He was asked how you can be so patient and unyielding in any situation. Jari Litmanen replied: "Already as a little schoolboy, I always went to school by bike. Once there was a severe frost, more than 20 minus degrees. Mom helped with the dressing. We covered everything, even our faces, only there were small openings in the eyes. When I arrived at school, my eyes were frozen. It taught patience and perseverance." We also need this perseverance in the economy. At the same time, we must tirelessly seek new solutions, new markets and smarter ways of organizing work.

Title: Independence Day celebration of the City of Porvoo
text: Director General Erkki Liikanen: Independence Day celebration of the City of Porvoo, 6.12.2009 . Speech . Sunday 6 December 2009, 12:00 AM Erkki Liikanen Governor of the Bank of Finland / Finlands Banks chefdirekt9ar City of Porvoo Independence Day celebration / Borg8c stads sj8alvst8andighetsfest Linnankoski Upper Secondary School 6.12.2009 DEAR FESTIVE AUDIENCE! LADIES AND GENTLEMEN! MINA DAMER OCH HERRAR! Exactly 200 years ago, the diocesan and high school city of Porvoo was the scene of revolutionary events for four months. As is well known, the Estates of Finland gathered in Porvoo in March 1809. It was an interesting milestone in the history of great power relations and, above all, between Russia and France. But for Finland, it marked an important step in the development of the nation. In a speech in Porvoo, Emperor Alexander had raised Finland as a "nation among nations". The background to the events dates back less than two years. In July 1807, Napoleon and Alexander I had gathered in Tilsit to negotiate a peace treaty. At that time, Russia joined the French-led embargo against England. Sweden remained the only ally of England and at the same time became a potential enemy of Russia. A French historian gave a colourful account of the negotiations in a recent biography of Emperor Alexander. He writes that the negotiations took place in French, which one of the negotiators spoke without dialectal accent, an accent. It was the Russian Tsar who had again received the traditional strong French training of the court. Napoleon was again a Corsican, whose strong, original dialect is well known. The first alliance between Russia and France, agreed in Tilsit, lasted only until 1812, when Napoleon invaded Russia. One of the few, if not the only tangible consequence of this short alliance, was that Russia captured Finland from Sweden. As the war effort continued in March 1809, Emperor Alexander convened the Landtag here in Porvoo Porvoo's Land days have been celebrated here deservedly and with dignity during the year. The festive side of the Landtag has recently received a lot of new attention when Henrika Tandefelt's book Porvoo 1809. Ceremonies and dances were chosen as the winners of the Tieto-Finlandia competition. Porvoo's ceremonies received attention before, for example, in professor Matti Klinge's various books. The language of the well-known speech given by Emperor Alexander in the French language at the Porvoo Landtag stemmed from the Enlightenment. This was reflected in his oft-repeated words: the Finnish people were "exalted among the nations to the crowd". Through home teachers, the Enlightenment had influenced the upbringing of Alexander I and was reflected in his efforts to reform Russia. His chief adviser and supporter in this work was his Secretary of State Mikhail Speranski. Speransky's goal in the reform plan was to divide into self-governing provinces and create a system of government based on a constitutional monarchy. In his capacity, Speranski had now had to familiarise himself with the Swedish constitutions and the administrative system, and he saw a certain exemplary character in them. The conditions in Finland provided a testing ground for future reforms throughout the empire. However, after Speransky's resignation and Napoleon's invasion, the plans remained on paper. In this way, Finland remained a region different from the rest of the Empire. After Speranski's resignation, the presentation of Finnish affairs passed to Gustaf Maurtiz Armflelt, who was appointed as his successor. Over the decades, historians and others have pondered the message of Emperor Alexander and the significance of 1809 in Finnish history. According to Professor Timo Soikkanen, depending on the researcher, the estates met either in the Diet or in the Landtag. On these days, depending on the researcher and interpretation, either a treaty of state or a treaty of domination was concluded. There has also been controversy about whether Finland became an autonomous state at that time or just a Russian province. We do not need to take a stand on all these disputes; unquestionably, the Diet of 1809 was a significant stage in Finland's history. In his new book, Professor Henrik Meinander juxtaposes the years 1809 and 1944 in an interesting way. At the end of the war in 1944, the Finns reflected on their future in a state of great uncertainty. Historical benchmarks were sought as a basis for thinking. Pessimists feared that when, in 1944, Finland had again been pushed closer to Russia's sphere of interest, it could mean the end for Finland as an independent state, as happened for a long time for the Baltic states. Pessimists saw a connection with the years of oppression during the Tsarist period, when autonomy had been tightened and Russia's military grip strengthened. Optimists, on the other hand, believed that, as in 1809, events could result in a new national heyday. History shows that the optimists were also right in 1944. In both cases, many later factors contributed to a happy outcome for Finland. The Diet of Porvoo has also played an important role in the history of the Bank of Finland. Not even scientists are arguing about that. Here in Porvoo, a process began that led to the establishment of the Central Bank two years later. Addressed to the estates, the emperor's question about "money and the MFI" was formulated very general. It stated that the Finnish monetary institution was closely linked to the country's political position, which referred directly to the need to reform the country's monetary conditions in line with Finland's new political position. The Finance Committee of the Estates considered the matter and it was stated that the first thing to do was to put the confused monetary conditions in order. While the war was still going on, both Swedish and Russian money were circulating in the country. In both Russia and Sweden, the official base coin was the silver coin, in Russia the ruble, and in Sweden the peafowl. In practice, the circulation consisted mainly of banknotes of variable value. According to the committee's report, only money tied to silver would ensure that the value of money remains stable in Finland. As for the choice of monetary unit, the only option left was the Russian silver coin and its hundredth, or kopeck. First of all, it was a question of political reality, when Finland had become part of Russia. On the other hand, the division of the ruble into one hundred parts was a convenient scheme. The Swede's system was more complicated. The peafowl was divided into 48 guildinks and the killinki further into 12 plentiful cannons. However, there was a consensus in Porvoo in 1809 that only with the help of its own central bank could the stability of stable monetary conditions be ensured in the future. Estates' wishes to set up the Bank of Finland on the Swedish model under the estates were not quite unrealistic. At that time, the representatives of the estates gathered in Porvoo had no idea that the constitutional flow that still prevailed in Russia in 1809 would remain a short intermediate stage, and they could not have known that the Diet of Finland would not be convened after Porvoo for more than half a century. The emperor's confirmation of the establishment of the bank was received on 12.12.1811, and the first statute was published as Imperial Majesty's Gracious Reglementi Waihetus (W8axeli-) Loan and Depositioni-Contror in the Great Prince of Finland. Later, the institution was renamed the Bank of Finland. Many people had taken part in the preparatory work. In the very final stages of the founding, gustaf Mauritz Armfelt, the newly appointed chairman of the Finnish Affairs Committee, stepped into the picture d0 in a way in the role of a midwife. Regarding translations between different languages, the name Tandefelt is not at all new here in Porvoo. When Emperor Alexander I gave his regent's assurance in 1809, his speech was translated from French into Swedish by Chancellor of Justice Adolf Tandefelt. During the 1800s, Finnish developed into an administrative language in the Grand Duchy of Finland alongside Swedish. Even after Finland gained independence in 1917, Finland has continued to be a bilingual country, with Finnish and Swedish as national languages. I consider bilingualism to be a great wealth for our country. The government and municipalities must continue to offer adequate services in both national languages, Swedish and Finnish. Of course, this also applies to public law communities such as the Bank of Finland. Swedish is not only a national matter, but language is an important means of communication when we meet our Nordic friends. This also applies to central banks. Despite the fact that Finland is a member of the European Union and as the only country has switched to the euro, we have not forgotten about Nordic co-operation at all. During the financial crisis, this cooperation has become more intense than in the past. Especially within the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the Bank of Finland cooperates closely with central banks from the other Nordic countries and also from the Baltic states. 2011 marks the 200th anniversary of the establishment of the Bank of Finland and this year the 10th anniversary of the launch of Europe's Economic and Monetary Union. Finland has been a full member of the Economic and Monetary Union and the euro since its inception. How does the single currency fit into the long line of Finnish history? Let us go back to history for a moment. We can move on from the founding of the Bank of Finland to the monetary reform of 1865. Its father was J.V. Snellman. In terms of its objectives, the reform was a step in the same direction as Finland's accession to the euro area. It also represented the quest for stable monetary conditions. The outbreak of the Crimean War in 1854 had triggered a monetary crisis, as a result of which the exchangeability of the ruble for silver had to be abolished. It brought many difficulties. The worst thing for Finland was that exchange rates in relation to traditional trading partners in Sweden and northern Germany began to fluctuate. Trade and access to foreign credit became more difficult. The Finns wanted a solution to the question of money. Emperor Alexander II responded to the petitions by awarding Finland its own currency, the Mark, in 1860. However, it was defined in relation to the banknote ruble, its quarter. When the banknote ruble remained legal tender, this reform did not yet bring a solution to the main problem of how to return to the silver standard. When Snellman became chief of finance in 1863, he took it upon himself to tie the mark to the silver standard. Snellman obtained the emperor's consent that the mark could be redefined, not as a quarter of the ruble in general, but specifically of the silver ruble. After the imperial manifesto was issued on the matter, the Bank of Finland began to redeem its banknotes with new silver marks in March of the following year. At the same time, the value of the markka stabilised in relation to other silver carrier countries, such as our important trading partners Sweden and Germany. All three major phases, the porvoo Riksdag's declaration of the quest for the most stable monetary conditions, Snellman's monetary reform and joining the euro, have, at their core, sought to do the same; there is a desire to promote the stability of stable monetary conditions. The importance of monetary and economic stability is once again underlined today. Just over two years ago, the world's financial markets experienced their first shocks, which in September a year ago deepened into a deep crisis. After that, the crisis spread to the real economy. The financing of foreign trade ran into difficulties and world trade began to contract for the first time in decades. Confidence in the future deteriorated sharply and investment came to a standstill. The global economy entered a recession. Central banks around the world took unprecedented steps to save the functioning of the financial system. Interest rates were cut sharply and counterparty banks were given the amount of liquidity they needed. Governments also made important commitments. The big banks will no longer be let down. Governments are prepared to recapitalise banks to secure lending, etc. These extensive measures were able to prevent the financial market crisis from deepening. Concrete steps have also been taken to reform the financial market rules. Credit rating agencies will be subject to regulations. Measures have also been put in place to limit incentive schemes to favour excessive risk-taking. Prudential provisions will also be amended to provide adequate buffers for financial institutions in the face of economic fluctuations. As a new measure, a risk committee of central banks and financial supervisors will be present in Europe, with the task of analysing systemic risks and making proposals if necessary. It is not enough to look at individual trees, it is necessary to take care of the entire forest. Stimulus measures by central banks and governments have halted the downward spiral in the global economy. Policy rates have been cut drastically and, supported by various measures, market interest rates have fallen even more than them. This has been particularly visible in the interest costs of households and non-financial corporations in Finland, where interest rates on loans are more tied to short-term market interest rates. The fiscal stimulus has also been significant. Separate stimulus measures have been taken and in many European countries the negative effects of the collapse of world trade on domestic demand and employment have already been softened by automatic fiscal stabilisers. Stabilisers mean that tax revenues from wage earners and businesses as unemployment has risen have fallen and public spending has increased due to safety nets. This has also led to an increase in the general government deficit. Fortunately, finland's general government balance was strong at the beginning of the recession, at least compared to the situation in many other countries. However, the pace of indebtedness is very steep and we must be prepared for the fact that this does not create a spiral of indebtedness. Over the past many years, Finland grew strongly due to the growth of world trade. Our exports increased especially for capital goods. Now that world trade is in shambles and investment is frozen, Finland has faced the recession more strongly than many other countries. Everything possible must be done to ensure that our economy is able to strike strongly as the world economy recovers. It requires innovation, adaptation to changing market situations and competitiveness. It is important to take care of those young people, young people who have no previous work experience. Long-term unemployment among young people increased in the 1990s and too many were completely excluded from working life. It would be important to ensure that similar developments do not materialise in this recession. Ladies and gentlemen I have already talked about Professor Henrik Meinander's new book "1944". Meinander outlines the background to the personal promise that President Risto Ryti made to the German war leadership not to conclude a separate peace with the Soviet Union. In exchange, Finland received weapons support and other military aid, which the hard-fighting Finnish soldiers so badly needed in order to achieve what we usually call a repulsion victory. Basically, according to Meinander, the Second World War in Northern Europe was about two main factors: firstly, the struggle for the Swedish ore fields in Lapland and, secondly, soviet concern for Leningrad's security. Denmark and Norway were occupied by Germany while Finland was forced to take on the Soviet Union. Sweden, with luck and skill, managed to stay out of the pure acts of war. In addition to the heroic efforts of the Finnish soldiers in the summer of 1944, the race to Berlin contributed to Stalin not attempting an outright invasion of Finland. The Soviet troops were needed elsewhere. Finland's independence and democratic society survived by a hair's breadth. With Risto Ryti leaving the presidency, Finland no longer considered itself bound by the promise to Germany not to conclude a separate peace. Under Marshal Mannerheim's leadership as both commander-in-chief and president, Finland was able to conclude an armistice agreement with the Soviet Union. At the Bank of Finland, we have a special respect for Risto Ryti. Ryti was appointed Governor of the Bank of Finland at the age of only 33 in 1923, and he actually returned to that post after serving as prime minister and president. However, his tenure as central bank governor after the war was short (1944d01945), as he was sentenced to ten years of chastisement as a "war officer". Risto Ryti did an important life's work both as Governor of the Bank of Finland and as a politician who helped save Finland's independence during the difficult war years. At the same time as Risto Ryti, as president of the Republic, faced extremely difficult decisions, Juho Kusti Paasikivi was outside the government, but still a kind of outsider of the inner circle. In the summer of 1944, Paasikivi pondered bleakly about the fate of the state. He had become a pessimist while reading history. "The states acted in the interest of the Staatsr8ason state. It's awful, blutrotig blood red." And Paasikivi continued: "So far, no system has been found that would limit the Staatsr8ason, the policy of interests of states, and protect other states against it. He emphasized: "The limitation of the Staatsr8ason, the policy of interests of states, its relationship with morality, is a question on the resolution of which the future of small countries in particular depends in the first place, but also, in the end, the future of the large and of humanity as a whole". Jean Monnet, the French 'founding father' of the European Union, pondered the same questions in 1944 in a completely different way. He stressed that there can be no peace in Europe if states are rebuilt on the basis of national sovereignty leading to a policy of prestige and economic protection. If the countries of Europe are to protect themselves against each other again, then the creation of large armies will be necessary again. And before long, war will ensue. Where Monnet spoke of nationalism and national sovereignty, paasikivi wrote about the staatsr8ason. At its core, both were talking about the same thing. Paasikivi said the key question was how to limit the staatsr8ason, the state's interest policy. Monnet, on the other hand, considered it a fundamental problem how to limit national sovereignty. History had made Paasikivi a pessimist on the one hand and cautious on the other. When Monnet was accused of being overly optimistic in a number of initiatives, he always replied: 'I am not an optimist, I am determined'. Another founding father of the European Union, former French Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Robert Schuman, contributes to: summed up his own thinking in his unpublished memoirs: "The hard school of history has taught me, as a frontier person, that I am skeptical of hasty improvisation or overly ambitious projects. But when mature consideration based on facts or the highest interests of the people leads to new initiatives that are even revolutionary, then we must hold on to them with determination and perseverance". Schuman took the 'revolutionary' initiative, prepared by Monnet, to establish the European Coal and Steel Community in May 1950. Schuman wanted to transfer the raw materials of the war, coal and steel, to the community. This community was supposed to be the first step towards the creation of the European Federation, which was necessary to maintain peace. And Schuman summed up his message: "The solidarity of production thus bound will show that the war between France and Germany will not only be beyond the conceivable, but also materially impossible." The Treaty establishing the European Coal and Steel Community was finally signed in April 1951. Six years later, the European Economic Community , the EEC, was built on much the same foundation. The EEC, on the other hand, deepened and later expanded into the European Union. Finland joined the European Union after the end of the Cold War and the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1995. Schuman, the founding father of European integration, left the post of French Foreign Minister in January 1953. In late winter, the attention of the world and Finland was directed to the Soviet Union. Stalin had died in March. The selection of the new management was followed with great interest. At Stalin's funeral, Prime Minister Urho Kekkonen represented Finland. When he returned, he told President Paasikivi that his minds in Moscow had calmed down. The new leader Malenkov is a man of Stalin's spirit and will pursue the same policy. The new government was organized according to a precise plan and Malenkov and Beria agreed. Around the same time, the Finnish Foreign Trade Association was looking for a well-known French speaker for its event in Helsinki. Heikki Brotherus, press counsellor at the Embassy in Paris, had gotten to know Schuman at Quaker events and therefore knew him. Now that Schuman had withdrawn from the government, Brotherus considered him a good candidate. The leadership of the Foreign Trade Association was in awe. But it was in the picture of time that then the difficulties began. Brotherus received a letter from Tarjanne, permanent secretary of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs, who accused him of high-handedness. According to Brotherus, the Ministry for Foreign Affairs even went so far as to ask the French ambassador in Helsinki to cancel schuman's planned visit to Finland. However, the visit took place in April. At the weekly meeting, Minister Ralf T9arngren told President Paasikivi that the leadership of the Foreign Trade Union wants to make the visit a big deal, but the government does not. He stated, according to Paasikivi's diaries, that "the government does not hold dinner, nor any other attention." That is why Prime Minister Urho Kekkonen did not meet WithChuman. However, President J.K. Paasikivi was listening to Robert Schuman's speech on 9.4.1953 and also received him the next day. It was part of the picture of the time that Pravda wrote about the visit a week later. According to Pravda, it could not be denied that Schuman's visit was not connected with the debate against the revitalization of trade between Finland and the Soviet Union. The article was written by Stefan Smirnov, who later served in the Finland unit of the international department of the NKP until the 1980s. Finland's long road Finland was very far removed from the creation of the Coal and Steel Community and the EEC. The Soviet Union considered the EEC to be the union of the West. Finland's room for manoeuvre was limited, and every move was considered and monitored. Little d0 if any d0 was known about the process of European integration. There was a long way to go until 1992 before our country applied for membership of the European Union. The basic problem of adapting Finland's foreign policy to EU membership took a turn in August-September 1991. This changed the context in which we operate in foreign policy. The coup d'8etat in Moscow failed. The Baltic states gained independence. A new treaty basis was negotiated for the neighbourly relations between Russia and Finland. For Russia, the EU had turned from a threat into a partner. What is most essential in the European Union? The most important thing is that it is the law, not the force, that determines in the Union. The rule of law is the most important principle governing relations between member states. The Commission's role is to monitor respect for the EU Treaties. An independent European Court of Justice shall rule on disputes arising from the legality of the action. The principle of legality and common institutions are an important protection for all Member States, regardless of their size and population. This is particularly the case for the smaller Member States. These principles are now enshrined in the Treaty of Lisbon. Was Finland's membership of the EU one of the solutions to Paasikivi's fundamental problem of staatsr8ason, the state's policy of interests and the fate of small countries? At the beginning of the week, it was the 70th anniversary of the start of the Winter War. The long and heavy war lasted until the autumn of 1944. It was 50 years since the end of the war that Finland became a member of the European Union. Today we are an independent people and, at the same time, we have been a full member of a European Union based on the Treaty and common institutions for 15 years. Neither the sacrifices nor the efforts were in vain. I would like to offer a respectful greeting to the veterans of our wars and to the lot. Hyv8a8a itsen8aisyysp8aiv8a8a! I wish you all a happy Independence Day!

Ja Paasikivi jatkoi: "Toistaiseksi ei ole l<9a>ydetty mit<8a><8a>n j<8a>rjestelm<8a><8a>, joka rajoittaisi Staatsr<8a>sonia, valtioiden etupolitiikkaa, ja suojelisi toisia valtioita sit<8a> vastaan. H<8a>n korosti: "Staatsr<8a>sonin, valtioiden etupolitiikan, rajoitus, sen suhde moraaliin, on kysymys, mink<8a> ratkaisemisesta erityisesti riippuu ensi k<8a>dess<8a> pienten maiden tulevaisuus, mutta loppujen lopuksi my<9a>s suurten ja koko ihmiskunnan tulevaisuus". Jean Monnet, Euroopan Unionin ranskalainen "perustaja-is<8a>" pohdiskeli samoja kysymyksi<8a> vuonna 1944 aivan toisaalla. H<8a>n korosti, ettei Euroopassa voi olla rauhaa, jos valtiot rakentuvat uudelleen sellaisen kansallisen suvereniteetin pohjalle, joka johtaa arvovaltapolitiikkaan ja taloudelliseen suojautumiseen. Jos Euroopan valtiot suojautuvat uudelleen toisiaan vastaan, suurten armeijoiden luominen on uudelleen v<8a>ltt<8a>m<8a>t<9a>nt<8a>. Ja seurauksena on ennen pitk<8a><8a> sota. Siell<8a> miss<8a> Monnet puhui nationalismista ja kansallisesta suvereniteetista, siell<8a> Paasikivi kirjoitti staatsr<8a>sonista. Ytimelt<8a><8a>n molemmat puhuivat samasta asiasta. Paasikivi sanoi avainkysymyksen olevan, kuinka rajoittaa staatsr<8a>sonia, valtioiden etupolitiikkaa. Monnet taas piti perusongelmana, kuinka rajoittaa kansallista suvereniteettia. Historia oli tehnyt Paasikivest<8a> yht<8a><8a>lt<8a> pessimistin, toisaalta varovaisen. Kun Monnet'ta syytettiin lukuisten aloitteiden yhteydess<8a> liiallisesta optimismista, h<8a>n vastasi aina: "En ole optimisti, olen p<8a><8a>tt<8a>v<8a>inen". Toinen Euroopan Unionin perustaja-is<8a>, Ranskan entinen p<8a><8a>ministeri ja ulkoministeri Robert Schuman osaltaan tiivisti oman ajattelunsa julkaisemattomissa muistelmissaan: "Historian kova koulu on opettanut minulle rajaseudun ihmisen<8a>, ett<8a> olen ep<8a>ilev<8a>inen h<8a>t<8a>isen improvisoinnin tai liian kunnianhimoisten hankkeiden suhteen. Mutta kun tosiasioihin tai ihmisten korkeimpiin etuihin perustuva kyps<8a> harkinta johtaa uusiin aloitteisiin, jotka ovat jopa vallankumouksellisia, silloin meid<8a>n tulee pit<8a><8a> niist<8a> kiinni p<8a><8a>tt<8a>v<8a>isesti ja per<8a><8a>nantamattomasti". Schuman teki Monnet<ab>n valmisteleman "vallankumouksellisen" aloitteen Euroopan hiili-ja ter<8a>syhteis<9a>n perustamisesta toukokuussa 1950. Schuman halusi siirt<8a><8a> sodan raaka-aineet, hiilen ja ter<8a>ksen yhteis<9a>n alaisuuteen. T<8a>m<8a>n yhteis<9a>n piti olla ensimm<8a>inen askel Euroopan federaation luomiseksi, mik<8a> oli v<8a>ltt<8a>m<8a>t<9a>n rauhan s<8a>ilytt<8a>miseksi. Ja Schuman tiivisti sanomansa: "N<8a>in sidottu tuotannon solidaarisuus tulee osoittamaan, ett<8a> sota Ranskan ja Saksan v<8a>lill<8a> ei tule olemaan vain ajateltavissa olevan ulkopuolella, vaan my<9a>s materiaalisesti mahdoton." Perustamissopimus Euroopan hiili-ja ter<8a>syhteis<9a>st<8a> allekirjoitettiin lopullisesti huhtikuussa vuonna 1951. Kuusi vuotta my<9a>hemmin paljolti samalle perustalle rakennettiin Euroopan talousyhteis<9a>, EEC. EEC taas syveni ja laajeni my<9a>hemmin Euroopan Unioniksi. Suomi liittyi Euroopan Unioniin kylm<8a>n sodan p<8a><8a>ttymisen ja Neuvostoliiton hajoamisen j<8a>lkeen vuonna 1995. Euroopan integraation perustajais<8a> Schuman j<8a>tti Ranskan ulkoministerin teht<8a>v<8a>t tammikuussa 1953. Lopputalvesta maailman ja Suomen huomio suuntautui Neuvostoliittoon. Stalin oli kuollut maaliskuussa. Suurella mielenkiinnolla seurattiin uuden johdon valintaa. Stalinin hautajaisissa p<8a><8a>ministeri Urho Kekkonen edusti Suomea. Palattuaan h<8a>n kertoi presidentti Paasikivelle, ett<8a> mielet Moskovassa olivat rauhoittuneet. Uusi johtaja Malenkov on Stalinin hengen mies ja tulee ajamaan samaa politiikkaa. Uusi hallitus oli tarkan suunnitelman mukaan j<8a>rjestetty ja Malenkov ja Berija olivat yht<8a> mielt<8a>. Samoihin aikoihin Suomen ulkomaankauppaliitto haki tunnettua ranskalaista puhujaa tilaisuuteensa Helsinkiin. Pariisin l<8a>hetyst<9a>n lehdist<9a>neuvos Heikki Brotherus oli tutustunut Schumaniin kveekarien tilaisuuksissa ja tunsi siksi h<8a>net. Nyt kun Schuman oli vet<8a>ytynyt hallituksesta, piti Brotherus h<8a>nt<8a> hyv<8a>n<8a> ehdokkaana. Ulkomaankauppaliiton johto oli ihastuksissaan. Mutta ajan kuvaan kuului, ett<8a> sitten alkoivat vaikeudet. Brotherus sai kirjeen ulkoministeri<9a>n kansliap<8a><8a>llik<9a>lt<8a> Tarjanteelta, joka syytti h<8a>nt<8a> omavaltaisesta toiminnasta. Brotheruksen mukaan ulkoministeri<9a> meni jopa niin pitk<8a>lle, ett<8a> pyysi Ranskan Helsingin l<8a>hettil<8a>st<8a> peruuttamaan suunnitellun Schumanin Suomen vierailun. Vierailu kuitenkin toteutui huhtikuussa. Ministeri Ralf T<9a>rngren kertoi viikoittaisessa tapaamisessa presidentti Paasikivelle, ett<8a> ulkomaankauppaliiton johto haluaa tehd<8a> vierailusta suuren jutun, mutta hallitus ei. H<8a>n totesi Paasikiven p<8a>iv<8a>kirjojen mukaan, ett<8a> <d3>hallitus ei pid<8a> p<8a>iv<8a>llist<8a>, eik<8a> muuta huomiota<d3>. P<8a><8a>ministeri Urho Kekkonen ei siksi Schumania tavannut. Presidentti J.K. Paasikivi oli kuitenkin kuuntelemassa Robert Schumanin puhetta 9.4.1953 ja otti h<8a>net my<9a>s vastaan seuraavana p<8a>iv<8a>n<8a>. Ajan kuvaan kuului, ett<8a> Pravda kirjoitti vierailusta viikkoa my<9a>hemmin. Pravdan mukaan ei voitu kiist<8a><8a>, ettei Schumanin vierailulla ollut yhteytt<8a> Suomen ja Neuvostoliiton kauppavaihdon el<8a>v<9a>itt<8a>mist<8a> vastaan suunnattuun keskusteluun.. Kirjoituksen oli laatinut Stefan Smirnov, joka my<9a>hemmin palveli NKP:n kansainv<8a>lisen osaston Suomi-yksik<9a>ss<8a> aina 1980-luvulle saakka. Suomen pitk<8a> tie Suomi oli Hiili-ja ter<8a>syhteis<9a>n ja EEC:n luomisestaa kovin et<8a><8a>ll<8a>. Neuvostoliitto piti EEC:t<8a> l<8a>nnen liittona. Suomen liikkumavara oli rajoittunut ja jokaista liikahdusta mietittiin ja seurattiin. Euroopan integraatioprosessia tunnettiin v<8a>h<8a>n <d0> jos ollenkaan. Oli kuljettava pitk<8a> tie aina vuoteen 1992 asti ennen kuin maamme haki Euroopan unionin j<8a>senyytt<8a>. Perusongelmassa eli Suomen ulkopolitiikan sovittamisessa EU:n j<8a>senyyteen tapahtui k<8a><8a>nne elo-syyskuussa vuonna 1991. T<8a>ll<9a>in muuttui ulkopoliittinen toimintaymp<8a>rist<9a>mme. Vallankaappaus Moskovassa ep<8a>onnistui. Baltian maat itsen<8a>istyiv<8a>t. Ven<8a>j<8a>n ja Suomen naapuruussuhteille neuvoteltiin uusi sopimuspohja. Ven<8a>j<8a>lle EU oli muuttunut uhkasta kumppaniksi. Mik<8a> on oleellisinta Euroopan unionissa? Oleellisinta on se, ett<8a> Unionissa m<8a><8a>r<8a><8a> laki, ei voima. Laillisuuden ja oikeusvaltion periaate (rule of law) on j<8a>senmaiden v<8a>lisi<8a> suhteita s<8a><8a>telev<8a> keskeisin periaate. Komission teht<8a>v<8a>n<8a> on valvoa EU:n perustamissopimusten kunnioittamista. Riippumaton Euroopan tuomioistuin ratkaisee toiminnan laillisuudesta syntyneet kiistakysymykset. Laillisuuden periaate ja yhteiset instituutiot ovat t<8a>rke<8a> suoja kaikille j<8a>senmaille niiden kokoon ja v<8a>kilukuun katsomatta. Erityisesti n<8a>in on pienten j<8a>senmaiden kohdalla. N<8a>m<8a> periaatteet on nyt vahvistettu Lissabonin sopimuksessa. Oliko Suomen EU-j<8a>senyys yksi ratkaisu Paasikiven perimm<8a>iseen ongelmaan staatsr<8a>sonista, valtion etupolitiikasta ja pienten maiden kohtalosta? Talvisodan alkamisesta tuli kuluneeksi alkuviikosta 70 vuotta. Pitk<8a> ja raskas sota kesti aina syksyyn 1944. Sodan p<8a><8a>ttymisest<8a> kului 50 vuotta Suomen j<8a>senyyteen Euroopan unionissa. Olemme t<8a>n<8a><8a>n itsen<8a>inen kansa ja samalla olleet jo 15 vuotta t<8a>ysivaltainen j<8a>sen perussopimukseen ja yhteisiin instituutioihin nojaavassa Euroopan unionissa. Uhrit eiv<8a>tk<8a> ponnistukset olleet turhia. Haluan esitt<8a><8a> kunnioittavan tervehdyksen<8a> sotiemme veteraaneille ja lotille. Hyv<8a><8a> itsen<8a>isyysp<8a>iv<8a><8a>! Jag <9a>nskar er alla en trevlig sj<8a>lvst<8a>ndighetsdag!

Title: Future of cash. Mint's 150th anniversary
text: Director-General Erkki Liikanen: The future of cash. Mint's 150th anniversary 6.4.2010 . Speech . Tuesday 6 April2010,12:00AM Director-General Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland greetings at the Mint's 150th anniversary 6.4.2010 Speech Related Membranes (ppt) (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and. interviews/documents/100406_el_rahapaja_150.ppt) Speech Related Membranes (pdf) (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and. interviews/documents/100406_el_rahapaja_150.pdf) The future of cash My pleasant task is to bring the Bank of Finland's greetings to this seminar organised by the Mint of Finland on the "The Future of Cash". This is pleasing because we have worked fruitfully together throughout the 150 years of mint's existence. The Bank of Finland has been a key customer of the Mint. When assessing the future of cash, it is a good idea to first go through history. There you can find many interesting stages and events. First of all, it should be noted that the relationship between the Bank of Finland and the Mint has not always been as straightforward as it is now. On many occasions, the mint has been planned in various government instances, like the banknote printing, as part of the Bank of Finland. Only twenty years have passed since the last debate. However, it is probably better for the mint's own development that there was no reunification. The decisions by which the mint has been developed seem to have successfully taken the company forward in other areas of business than just minting money. In the case of central bank-owned mints, expanding business beyond core activities is rare today. Rather, there has also been a trend towards decoupling in some central banks. Finland is a special country in the sense that we had our own currency and central bank even before independence. Next year marks the 200th anniversary of the establishment of the Bank of Finland. The issuance of its own currency to the Grand Duchy of Finland in the 1860s was also accompanied by a decision to build a mint. However, there had already been a mint in Turku during swedish rule in the 1400s and 1500s, and some kind of minting had already been practised in Finland in the 1000s. [2nd image] The history of cash goes back much further. The first coins were minted already 600 years before the beginning of our era in Lydia. At that time, metal goods money, which served as a means of exchange, was gradually replaced by a more functional means of payment. Among other things, it had a punch stamp to express the characteristics of money. The appearance of the coin gave it more credibility. Although some kind of money made from paper was used to pay in China even before the 1000s, the first banknotes in their current form were issued in the 1660s by the Swedish Stockholm's Banko. It also had a branch office in Turku. Thus, in principle, finns have been involved in the introduction of another form of cash, i.e. banknote money, almost from the very beginning. [3rd image] Finland has a long history of using money, which may partly explain the fact that we have also been leading countries in new payment technology. In Finland, the share of cash in GDP was the lowest among the countries in the current euro area during the Markka period, and it has not changed much since then. This setting provides an interesting starting point for reflecting on the future of cash, the theme of this celebratory seminar. [4th image] The figure below shows the evolution of the value of the euro banknotes in circulation. The blue curve shows the evolution of the value of the euro banknote with a scale on the left vertical axis and the bar graphs showing the annual growth rate with a scale on the right vertical axis. Three clear conclusions can be drawn from the figure: 1. The issuance of the euro began apace and the euro cash quickly gained public acceptance and trust. 2. The issuance has been constantly growing. A significant part of the growth has gone outside the euro area, which means that the euro has risen alongside the dollar as another globally important currency. It is estimated that around one fifth of the euro is in circulation outside the euro area. The euro has gained broad international confidence and credibility. 3. The international financial crisis triggered by Lehman's bankruptcy is clearly visible in the figure as a spike in demand for cash. Euro cash was widely perceived as a safe haven in the turmoil of the financial markets. It is also noteworthy that the accelerated growth continued for a year and that after that the "over-demand" did not return to the central banks, but the trend growth has continued as before. [5th image] The blue curve in this figure shows the development per unit of all small 5, 10 and 20 banknotes in circulation. The red curve, on the other hand, represents the number of units of banknotes of 50 and above. We now see that the growth of euro banknotes in circulation has been due above all to the demand for high-value euro banknotes. This has been the result of the adjustment of the public's cash registers to the low inflation expectations and low interest rates that have prevailed in Europe since the introduction of the euro, i.e. banknotes have become a more important form of preservation of value. Similar confidence in the preservation of the value of banknotes is demonstrated by the developments described above during the financial turmoil. The steady demand for small whalers, which, as a rule, are used for payment, reinforces the notion that the use of cash means of payment no longer significantly increases the amount of cash. [6th image] Let us now look at the evolution of all euro coins in circulation. It has differed from the euro banknotes in that the increase in the number of coins has always outweighed the increase in their value, i.e. demand has been particularly focused on the denomination coins of 1, 2 and 5 cents, as shown in the figure below. The top lilac-colored curve represents the number of coins in circulation of 1, 2 and 5 cents. When banknotes with the largest denominations are used as a form of storage for wealth, and are therefore out of active circulation, then, accordingly, the coins with the lowest value disappear into savings boxes and jars, thereby actively decommissioning. The lowest value euro coins have to be minted continuously in large numbers in those euro countries that, like Finland, do not have a rounding rule. This pattern supports the parliament's decision at the time to introduce a rounding rule. As a result, there was no need to mint and 1 and 2 cent coins in Finland for the use of means of payment. Naturally, from the point of view of the turnover of the organizer of this seminar, the Mint of Finland, the decision was not necessarily positive. The Ministry of Finance may take a different view on the point of hitting them for cost reasons. In contrast, the demand for other euro coins, the green and blue curves in the picture, has developed at a similar annual rate to the number of low-value banknotes, indicating their constant need for small payments and change. [7th image] After looking at cash, I will now deal with payment behaviour in Finland. The information comes from a regular survey conducted by the Federation of Finnish Financial Services on different payment methods. In the picture, we can see that in Finland, the share of cash in the purchase of daily consumer goods has been constantly decreasing and it has been lower than the use of card money for a few years now. In euros, the use of cash in Finland is estimated to have remained more or less unchanged. However, why is cash issuance in Finland constantly growing? The answer is that growth drains abroad. Some research has been carried out and at least the following reasons have been found for the export of cash: the import of used cars, tourism and the wages of foreign labor. According to the method of payment method surveys, the use of cash is still more common elsewhere in Europe than in Finland. Although the trend in the use of different means of payment is similar to that in Finland, the change has taken place more slowly than in Finland. The conclusion from the above review is a kind of paradox. At the same time as the relative share of cash as a means of payment has decreased as new electronic payment methods have become more common, its use as a form of storing wealth has increased. Due to the combined effect of both development trends, the amount of cash in circulation has continued to increase. Cash, therefore, does not seem to be disappearing. Its purpose of use is gradually changing. [8. Image] Based on the above review, what can be said about the future of cash? I believe that two conclusions can be drawn from this. First of all, even in the future there will be demand for such cash that the public trusts. In the situation a year and a half ago, the public relied on euro banknotes as a store of value, which shows that the public considered that the European System of Central Banks had succeeded in maintaining price stability as its primary objective. The success of the Eurosystem in its stability objective will continue to determine confidence in euro cash and the euro's status as a global cash and reserve currency. Secondly, only those means of payment have a future that are easy and cost-effective to use when paying. We can see that electronic means of payment and various forms of mobile payment are developing rapidly. In order to maintain the competitiveness of cash as a means of payment, it requires a more determined intensification of the circulation of banknotes and coins, together with all key market participants and money supply players. Studies show that cash is still an effective means of payment for smaller payments. Finally, it should be noted that there are challenges for the Mint of Finland, on the one hand, in developing the characteristics of coins together with other euro area players and, on the other hand, as part of the Eurosystem for the Bank of Finland as the national monetary authority. By meeting those challenges, we can be confident about the future of cash.

Title: What will change with the financial crisis? How to strengthen the basis for growth in Finland?
text: Director-General Erkki Liikanen: What will change with the nanny crisis? How to strengthen the basis for growth in Finland? Delegation from the Finnish Central Chamber of Commerce Helsinki 26.5.2010 . Speech . Wednesday26 May2010,12:00 AM Director-General Erkki Liikanen Delegation from the Finnish Central Chamber of Commerce Finlandia Hall, Helsinki, 26.5.2010 Speech-related slides (ppt) . (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and. interviews/documents/100526_keskuskauppakamari_el.ppt) WHAT WILL CHANGE WITH THE FINANCIAL CRISIS? HOW TO STRENGTHEN THE FOUNDATION FOR GROWTH IN FINLAND? RAHOITUSMARKKINOISTA It will soon be three years since the start of the global economic and financial crisis. The credit loss outlook for banks has already improved slightly since last spring. For example, a month ago, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) lowered its estimate of total credit losses to financial institutions caused by the financial crisis to USD 2 300 billion, compared with a high of USD 500 billion. The amount is still very high, but the recovery of the financial system had in any case begun. What have we learned from the financial crisis? Firstly,the solvency of the banks had to be safeguarded. Solvency was strengthened in many countries through large injections of public capital. Banks' recently improved profitability has contributed to supporting their solvency. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision is currently preparing proposals to strengthen the prudential regulation of banks worldwide. Banks must have more and more high-quality own funds, which are the primary line of defence against possible losses incurred by banks. Secondly,the liquidity of the banks had to be safeguarded. During the liquidity crisis in autumn 2008, central banks took exceptional measures to safeguard banks' liquidity. Since then, banks have strengthened their liquidity buffers and their resilience to a crisis such as that of autumn 2008 has improved. The Basel Committee is also preparing proposals to strengthen banks' liquidity regulation worldwide. In the future, banks' balance sheets will have to contain significantly more liquid assets  cash and cash at low cost  than they had before the crisis began. Thirdly,the availability of long-term financing by banks had to be guaranteed. In late autumn 2008 and early spring 2009, it was difficult for banks to obtain anything other than very short-term financing from the market. Access to long-term financing is still worse than before the crisis. However, especially profitable and solvent banks have recently been able to obtain long-term financing at a more affordable price. Here, too, the support measures taken by the central banks and governments of the various countries to support the securities markets have played a part. Fourthly, we need to reform the incentive schemes which contributed to unbridled risk-taking. Incentives should not be tied to short-term virtual profits, but to the long-term success of the company. Reducing the vulnerability of the financial system to crises also requires structural, medium-term changes. Above all, imbalances in the global economy and trade need to be corrected. Imbalances fuel indebtedness and bubbles in the financial system, the bursting of which will lead to crises such as those we have today. It is worrying that while deficits and surpluses in some regions have narrowed, major global imbalances have not changed. Repairing the financial system requires an understanding of the lessons of financial crises, both ongoing and past. Let me now turn to three important lessons from the current crisis. The first lesson is that the biggest financial crises may continue to be global. The financial crisis of autumn 2008 revealed how quickly the crisis can progress in interconnected financial markets across borders. It is clear that the remedies for the financial system must also be global. The broad package of reforms being prepared by the Basel Committee will play a key role in this. The tightening of financial regulation also affects those countries whose financial institutions have acted responsibly and whose national financial system did not enter a crisis. Despite this fact, correcting regulation primarily on the basis of national needs would be an inadequate solution. This would lead to a patchwork regulatory environment and encourage cross-border regulatory arbitrage. The problem with global uniform regulations is that they may not be optimal for any single country. However, both public authorities and financial institutions must be prepared to compromise in order to create a safer international financial system and better prevent financial crises. Nevertheless, it is very important that the Basel Committee, and also the European Commission, following the impact assessments carried out, calibrate and phase the implementation of the proposals in such a way that the economic recovery is not jeopardised. The second lesson is that the overall economic cost of global financial crises can be enormous. Often, when assessing the costs of financial crises, only the direct costs to the state economy of rescuing financial institutions are considered. However, many times the real social costs of financial crises are due to lost production and the damage it causes. According to one estimate, total global output in 2009 was around 6.5% lower than it would have been in the absence of the financial crisis. Worst of all, production losses typically don't stay for one year. Some of the production losses can be permanent or at least very long-term. Given the enormous cost of the crises, it is abundantly clear that cosmetic regulatory reforms alone will not be enough. Financial regulation must be radically reformed, as is being done. The third important lesson is obvious in the light of recent events: there are always great dangers associated with excessive indebtedness. This applies to households, financial institutions and other enterprises as well as to public finances. The seeds of the current crisis were sown when U.S. households took out  and were tempted to take out  excessive mortgages relative to their income and debt sustainability. The housing price bubble was then inflated by pretending that these bad loans could be used to create low-risk and high-yielding securities through financial alchemy. The threat of uncontrolled house price development should not be underestimated in Finland either. According to Statistics Finland's preliminary data, prices of old dwellings in blocks of flats rose by over 11 per cent in January to March and by as much as over 15 per cent in Greater Helsinki compared to the first quarter of 2009. In turn, intensified competition from banks for mortgages has reduced the already narrow margins of new mortgages. The rise in house prices appears to be largely due to the temporary shortage of housing supply and exceptionally low interest rates after the recession. In this situation, both those planning to buy a home and banks should exercise great discretion when making a loan decision. In this context, the risks associated with excessive government indebtedness do not need to be further highlighted. If public debt grows out of control, interest rates on government loans will rise. It will increase banks' financing costs even more than this. In addition, there is a risk that public borrowing will crowd out private borrowing in the market, thereby undermining the potential for growth. It is therefore very important that the increase in public debt is brought under control through measures that are transparent and credible. MONETARY POLICY The ECB announced the launch of its bond market programme on 10 May. The aim of the programme is to enable an effective transmission of monetary policy by addressing the dysfunction of the euro area bond market. The bond market programme does not relax the monetary policy stance. The prevailing monetary policy stance is appropriate and the liquidity effects of the bond market programme will be fully eliminated. The ECB's primary objective is price stability, and the ECB will not bow to this objective under any circumstances. The ECB is also an independent actor and takes all its decisions independently. However, when entering into the Bond Market Programme, the ECB took note of the commitment of euro area governments to take the necessary measures to achieve their fiscal objectives and to accelerate the consolidation of fiscal sustainability.
