Title: Opening remarks at the Bank of Finland and Banca d'Italia Conference on Challenges of the Global Crisis to Macroeconomic Theory and International Finance
text: Opening remarks by the Governor Erkki Liikanen, at the Bank of Finland and Banca d'Italia Conference on Challenges of the Global Crisis to Macroeconomic Theory and International Finance, Helsinki 11 June 2010 . Speech . Friday 11 June 2010, 12:00 AM Governor Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland Bank of Finland and Banca doItalia Conference on Challenges of the Global Crisis to Macroeconomic Theory and International Finance Helsinki 10-11 June 2010 Dear friends, After an ECB Governing Council meeting a year ago Mario Draghi told about Jorge Braga de Macedo's initiative. He wanted a memorial conference to be organized as a tribute to the academic work of Pentti Kouri. We both agreed. Rather soon we came to the conclusion that the Bank of Finland and Banca doItalia should co-organise the conference. It should also be held in Finland. We asked Ignazio Visco and Seppo Honkapohja to prepare a programme in close contact with Jorge. Here we are today. We want to thank Ignazio, Seppo, Jorge and all others who have helped to organize this event. About 14 years ago Pentti Kouri published his memoirs in Finnish. His career in the field of economics covers about 30 pages, no more than 10% of the book. As you know, his lifetime activities extended to many other areas, from art to business. Still today our focus is on Pentti Kourios work as an academic. As early as in spring in 1970 Kouri was asked by the Bank of Finland to come for an interview for the IMF's young professionals programme. Already in August of the same year he moved to Washington to start to work at the IMF. We are happy to have with us another young professional of the time, Patrick Honohan, today the Governor of the Irish Central Bank. Already his early papers in IMF created a lot of attention among academic economists. In spring 1972 he was invited to the Wing spread -conference at Chicago University, where he met many of the great names of economic science. Professor Edmund Phelps, the 2006 Nobel Laureate was among them. We are happy to welcome Professor Phelps as the first speaker to our conference. Among others participating in the Chicago conference on 1972 were Rudi Dornbusch, Jacob Frenkel and Stanley Fischer, the present Governor of the Bank of Israel. In autumn 1973, Pentti Kouri was accepted to the PhD programme at the MIT. Stanley Fischer was his thesis supervisor. He tells that Pentti was among his first students. Stan continues: oHe came almost every day after 4 ooclock to talk. Pentti had an incredibly wide scope of interest. So it was very interesting. But finally in April, I told to him that it is nice to talk but not much has happened with your thesis. Only two months later he came back with a very good thesiso. Pentti Kouri writes in his memoirs that he had great time in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and that Mario Draghi became one of his closest friends and remained so. Pentti Kouri got his PhD from MIT and moved briefly back to the IMF. We have two other PhDos from MIT from that period with us today, Professor Francesco Giavazzi and the Chief Economist of IMF Olivier Blanchard. Governor Josz de Gregorio from the Bank of Chile got his PhD from MIT in the 1980os. We are very happy to have you as speakers in our conference. In summer 1975, Pentti Kouri got an offer from Stanford which he accepted. In the same summer he organized, with Franco Modigliani, a seminar for academic and central bank economists in Haikko, 50 kilometres east of Helsinki. The seminar was hosted by Mauno Koivisto, the then-Governor of the Bank of Finland, later president of the Republic of Finland. Pentti Kouri taught at Stanford for two years. It was at Stanford that the former governor of the Bank of Mexico and former president of the BIS, Guillermo Ortiz became his friend. Bengt Holmstrsm was also finishing his dissertation at Stanford at that time. We welcome both Guillermo and Bengt to this conference. During his Stanford years Kouri often visited the Institute for International Economic Studies in Stockholm, which was directed by Assar Lindbeck. Pentti Kouri made a lot of friends in Sweden. We are happy to have Assar Lindbeck on our panel today. Pentti wrote in his memoirs that he was asked then to write an assessment on Franco Modigliani for the Nobel committee. He continued (in 1997), that all other economists he assessed got a Nobel Prize with the exception of Robert Mundell, who deserved it. As we now know, the Nobel Committee agreed with him and Robert Mundell became the 1999 Nobel Laureate. Two years later James Tobin invited Pentti Kouri to Yale. He got an associate professorship in Yale in autumn 1977. In January 1978 in democratic Finland his academic career was interrupted by military conscription. He spent the whole year in the grey uniform of the Finnish army. Pentti Kouri returned to Yale in the beginning of 1979. Professor Jorge Braga de Macedo was then his student and friend. Also James Galbraith was a PhD student at Yale at that time. Jorge will chair the last panel of this conference today. From Yale Pentti Kouri moved to New York University where he got his tenure in autumn 1979. At the same time he was also awarded a professorship at the University of Helsinki. He held two parallel professorships for four years. Pentti Kouri was a leading young researcher in the field of international economics and finance of his time. This is illustrated by the fact that Penttios work was cited in seven out of the eleven major survey articles in the well-known Handbook of International Economics (Volume 2) in 1985. I want to welcome you all to Helsinki. And I want to invite Governor Mario Draghi, who is also the president of the Financial Stability Board, to chair the first session. seminar (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagseminar) crises (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagcrises) macroeconomics (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagmacroeconomics) nance (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagnance)

Title: Global economy is recovering at different speeds
text: Director-General Erkki Liikanen: The global economy is recovering at different speeds. Open hearing in the Parliament's Finance Committee. Helsinki 9.9.2010 . Speech . Thursday9September 2010, 12:00 AM Director-General Erkki Liikanen Open hearing in the Parliament's Finance Committee 9.9.2010 Speech Related Membranes (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and. . interviews/documents/100909_talousvaliokunta.ppt) (ppt) Puheeseen Related Membranes (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and. . interviews/documents/100909_talousvaliokunta.pdf) (pdf) President Liikanen:The global economy is recovering at different speeds The global economy continues to recover from the deep recession it entered after the financial market crisis in late 2008. However, the pace of recovery has been mixed. China's economic growth  which slowed down just slightly during the crisis  was among the first to pick up speed, backed by massive stimulus measures. This was widely reflected in the surrounding Asia and the rest of the world economy. In the United States and Japan, the recovery started a little later in 2009. By contrast, in the euro area, a turnaround could be expected until the spring of this year, when growth strengthened, driven in particular by Germany. Over the summer, there have been signs from China, the United States and Japan that the pace of recovery is leveling off. According to the ECB's forecast, this is also expected to be the case in the euro area. The replenishment of stocks and the expansionary fiscal stance supported growth in many countries until the first half of this year. Now this support is diminishing as the stock adjustment is coming to an end and stimulus measures are moving towards fiscal consolidation. While economic growth is still generally expected to continue, these developments are not without risks. The crisis in some public finances last spring and the accompanying sharp increase in uncertainty in the financial markets were a stark reminder of this. Central banks and governments around the world have continued their efforts to support the economy. Key interest rates have been kept low and the liquidity of financial institutions has been safeguarded by continuing to use non-standard monetary policy instruments. In addition, european countries facing financial difficulties have been supported by bilateral loan programmes and the establishment of specific mechanisms to secure access to finance. However, it is important that the countries facing the problems strictly adhere to the programmes established for the consolidation of public finances and carry out structural reforms that ensure sustainable economic growth. Finland's total output contracted by as much as 8% last year. Above all, this reflected a sharp decline in our exports as a result of the international recession. During the spring and summer, economic growth has also intensified in Finland. Exports of forest industry products and processed metals have grown in particular. On the other hand, the mechanical engineering and metal products industries, as well as the electronics industry, have not yet experienced a similar recovery. During the recession, the state of public finances in our country has sharply deteriorated. Especially this applies to state finances. Fiscal consolidation and sustainable consolidation is of paramount importance. The general conditions for the growth of the national economy must also be taken care of. We need structural reforms that will increase productivity and increase the amount of labour input in the economy. In addition, wage formation should support stable economic development while providing flexible structures for agreeing wages at local level, taking into account productivity developments. The recovery of the financial system requires a restoration of trust between market participants. The bank stress tests carried out in Europe provided transparent information on the condition of European banks' balance sheets and risk tolerance, thereby contributing to the restoration of confidence. The new European Systemic Risk Board will play an important role in identifying risks to the stability of the European financial system. It is to be welcomed that agreement was reached in the EU last week on the details of setting up the committee. The ESRB enables central banks and financial supervisors to work together across the EU. The most important project to reduce the vulnerability of the international financial system to crises is the preparation by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision. The overall Basel III reform, which is entering the final straight. The reform will mean strengthening banks' prudential and liquidity provisions and limiting banks' excessive indebtedness. The reform is important for increasing the stability of the financial system. Recent years have shown the considerable cost of financial crises to national economies. An ambitious reform, with a sufficient transitional period to be implemented, will make it possible to achieve a more sustainable financial system without limiting the lending capacity of banks too much

Title: Opening ceremony of The Cooperative Bank Week
text: President Liikanen's speech at the opening ceremony of osuuspankkiviikko, Hameenlinna 4.10.2010 . Speech . Monday4 October 2010, 12:00 AM The speech does not contain any reference to the ecb's monetary policy stance, on which the Governing Council will take a position on the following once in public on 7.10.2010. Speech Related Membranes (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and. . interviews/documents/101004_osuuspankkiviikko_4_10_2010lyh.finaali.ppt) (PPT) Puheeseen Related Membranes (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and. . interviews/documents/101004_osuuspankkiviikko_4_10_2010lyh.finaali.pdf) (PDF) A cyclical upturn alone will not solve economic problems The global economy is recovering from the deep recession into which it entered after the financial market crisis. In China, economic growth began to pick up among the first, which was widely reflected in the surrounding Asia. In the United States and Japan, the recovery started a little later, but in the euro area and Finland, a turnaround could be expected until the spring of this year. While economic growth is still generally expected to continue, these developments are not without risks. The pace of recovery is leveling off. Top-up stocks and expansionary fiscal policies are no longer as supportive of economic growth as they were in the past. However, central banks around the world have continued their efforts to support the economy. Key interest rates have been kept low and the liquidity of financial institutions has been safeguarded by unconventional monetary policy instruments. In Finland, global economic growth has increased exports of forest industry products and processed metals in particular. Domestic demand has also picked up in low interest rate conditions, driven by private consumption and housing investment. However, the recovery as a whole is not becoming very strong in Finland. According to the Bank of Finland's new forecast, Finland's GDP growth will settle at a rate of just over 2 per cent between 2010 and 2012. However, the production pit caused by the recession will only expire with difficulty by 2012. There can be no return to the pre-recession growth path without structural measures to increase labour supply and improve productivity. During the recession, the state of Finland's public finances has deteriorated considerably. In a short period of time, a surplus of more than 4% of GDP will turn into a deficit of just over 3% of GDP, and the general government debt will grow rapidly. The mismatch between revenue and expenditure will begin to correct as economic growth recovers. However, the importance of cyclical factors should not be considered overestimate. A significant part of fiscal consolidation will be left to other means. The low level of interest rates has significantly supported the Finnish economy in particular during the recession. At the same time, it has maintained the indebtedness of Finnish households. The increase in indebtedness may be accompanied by significant adverse effects on the national economy. Housing prices can rise to a level that is not economically justified. In addition, the high debt burden weakens the ability of households and, at the same time, the economy as a whole, to adapt to various shocks. The recovery of the financial system is still ongoing and requires a restoration of trust between market participants. The bank stress tests carried out in Europe and the ongoing reform of bank regulation have contributed to restoring confidence. The most important project to reduce the vulnerability of the international financial system to crises is the preparation by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision. The basel III comprehensive reform, which has entered the final stretch. The aim of the regulatory reform is to improve banks' risk-bearing capacity and reduce the likelihood of further financial crises, both in Europe and globally. The agreed reforms represent an important step forward towards a more stable financial system. Banks play a key role in the functioning of the economy, and their activities have had to be secured with tax revenue. The crisis has quite rightly raised the question of what all such an industry, under the special protection of public authorities, can be allowed to do.

Title: How to strengthen the basis for growth?
text: President and CEO Erkki Liikanen: How to strengthen the basis for growth? Presentation at Tieto's Tieto Days 12.10.2010 . Speech . Tuesday 12 October 2010, 12:00 AM President and CEO Erkki Liikanen Tieto Days 12.10.2010 Esitelm8a8an Related Membranes (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and. . interviews/documents/101012_el_tieto.ppt) (PPT) Esitelm8a8an Related Membranes (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and. . interviews/documents/101012_el_tieto.pdf) (PDF) HOW TO STRENGTHEN THE BASE OF GROWTH? [FIGURE 1: How to strengthen the bottom of growth?] State of the economy and cyclical outlook I have returned today from a meeting of the International Monetary Fund in Washington. To begin with, a few words about how the meeting saw the state of the world economy. In conclusion, we can say that the global economy will continue to grow, but the recovery will nevertheless be fragile and uneven. It is fragile precisely because it is uneven. [FIGURE 2: GDP growth in key economic areas] At the imf meeting, a forecast for the global economy was presented, which paints a picture of a reasonably favourable but very two-fold development. Many emerging economies, not just China, are growing rapidly. At the same time, the growth prospects of advanced economies are clearly lower. The growth forecast for the US was lowered, while the forecast for the euro area was revised slightly upwards. Within the euro area, too, the outlook for growth is very mixed. The growth engine of the euro area is now an export-driven Germany. Northern Europe is growing more widely. The lowest growth rates are in countries that have undergone major adjustment measures. There are internal and external imbalances in the global economy, which should be reduced. Within countries, stimulus measures have strengthened public demand while private sector is weak. However, sustainable growth will only be sustainable when it is driven by private consumption and investment. In order to reduce external imbalances, deficit countries need to contribute to saving more, while surplus countries need to increase their consumption. The risk of a double recession was considered very low at the meeting. The Finnish economy is also gradually recovering d0 later than others d0 from the deep recession into which it was plunged by the global financial market crisis. Last year, the volume of Finland's GROSS DOMESTIC PRODUCT contracted by as much as 8%. The drop was the largest since 1918. The manufacturing industry was hit particularly hard by the recession. Its value added decreased by one-fifth as exports collapsed. [FIGURE 3: A turnaround in growth occurred in Finland, growth broad-based, but not strong] Finland's GDP started to grow in the second half of 2009. The economic recovery has intensified during 2010 as exports have recovered. Growth has been strongest in traditional export industries in the manufacture of wood and paper products, the processing of basic metals and the chemical industry. Homebuilding and trade in the domestic market have also recovered. [FIGURE 4: Recovery intensified in Finland] The Bank of Finland published its macroeconomic forecast two weeks ago. Its image of the global economy is very much in line with that of the Monetary Fund. According to the forecast, total output will grow more slowly in the next few years than before the economic crisis, but at an annual rate of just under 3%. At this rate, the pre-recession level of output will be reached at the end of the forecast period in 2012. The fact that production returns to pre-collapse levels only slowly is a consequence of both the structure of export production and the change in the productive structure of the economy as a whole. [FIGURE 5: Finnish exports recover more slowly than export markets] Finland's export industry has a high emphasis on capital goods, the demand for which will only recover more strongly when global economic growth stabilizes. Growth in Finland is also curbed by the fact that the share of manufacturing, which is fast-growing in productivity, in the economy's total output and employed, has been slowly decreasing since the turn of the millennium. At the same time, the share of service industries with slower productivity development has grown. [FIGURE 6: Unemployment is slowly falling] In the wake of the turnaround, there has recently been more positive news from the labour market than expected. At the end of 2009, as output gradually recovered, the number of hours worked began to increase, and over the course of 2010 the number of jobs has started to increase. The latest data on employment among both young and older people suggest that the impact of the recession on labour supply is not becoming as long-term and large as feared. The unemployment rate for both young and old people has fallen and the employment rate has risen. Thanks to the lay-off system, the rise in the unemployment rate remained subdued during the recession compared to the contraction in output. Correspondingly, in the first phase, the recovery in the demand for work will mainly be reflected in a decrease in lay-offs, while the decrease in unemployment will be slower. According to the forecast, the unemployment rate will fall to just under 8 per cent in 2012. Improved employment will maintain strong consumer confidence in the future. Together, these factors will support the growth of private consumption in Finland in the next few years. Stimulus and low interest rates have increased residential construction for households. Productive investment will recover as free production capacity decreases. [FIGURE 7: Consumer prices in Finland have risen faster than in the euro area] In such an economic environment, upward pressure on prices remains low in Finland. According to the Bank of Finland's forecast, consumer price inflation will pick up but remain around 2% in the next few years. [FIGURE 8: General government balance and debt] As a result of the recession and the stimulus measures, the general government balance showed a clear deficit in 2009. The deficit threatens to increase further this year. As economic growth strengthens and the fiscal stance changes from expansionary to tightening, the deficit will begin to decline. As a result of deficits, the general government debt is growing rapidly and is projected to reach 55% of GDP in 2012. In this way, the room for manoeuvre created by the decline in the general government debt ratio over the course of a decade will be lost in a few years. At the same time, the need to adjust public finances in order to secure its financing in the long term has increased significantly. From the cyclical pit to the medium-term growth path Although the Finnish economy will emerge from the recession back on a growth path, the prospects for economic growth seem modest compared to the need for sustainable financing of the welfare state. At the same time, the Finnish economy is affected by many structural factors that threaten to limit growth and income generation long after the recession has passed. Demographic change caused by ageing is cutting the labour and productive potential of the economy drastically. [FIGURE 9: Labour force potential contractes for a long time] The age groups entering retirement age are considerably larger than those entering working age. The number of people aged 60 to 64 will clearly exceed the number of 20 to 24-year-olds entering the labour market age over the next two decades. This year, the difference between the age groups is at its highest as 74,000 persons. The imprint of the baby boomers is long in finland's demographic structure. [FIGURE 10d030: The long aftermath of baby boomers: same thing from another perspective] In addition, subdued economic growth may accelerate the exit of older people from the labour market. Experience has shown that those who have left the labour market are less likely to return to work. The large numbers of older people leaving the labour force threaten to significantly reduce the growth potential of the economy in the coming years. At the same time, the Finnish economy continues to undergo a change in the structure of production, which has been accelerated by the global economic crisis. [FIGURE 31: Share of industries in the economy's value added at current prices] Since the turn of the millennium, the share of services in the total output of the economy and in the employed has slowly grown and that of industry has declined. Between 2008 and 2009, this structural change accelerated substantially as output and employment in manufacturing contracted sharply. [FIGURE 32: Change in production structure creates threats] It is likely that some of the change will be reversed as exports and investment recover. But it is possible that some of the change will remain permanent. Breaking down industrial production chains into small parts and relocating them to different countries has been one of the key features of globalisation. It will continue to shape the structure of production in countries. As a result, industrial production is moving from developed countries to developing countries. In addition, there is a risk that at least part of the production that was discontinued in Finland during the recession will be permanently removed from Finland. A decrease in the output share of manufacturing would slow down economic growth, as productivity improvement in the production of services is slower than in manufacturing. [FIGURE 33: Where to find the tools for growth?] So the situation as a whole is challenging. Economic growth and income development in line with the basic picture are not enough to finance the welfare state in the long term. Where are the keys to growth that will maintain the standard of living and welfare society in Finland in the coming years? Towards a renewing Finland Answers to this question have been sought in many state working groups that have recently published their reports. Various pension working groups have proposed ways to extend working lives by improving the quality of working life. A working group chaired by Director Anita Lehikoinen at the Ministry of Education has made proposals to reform the higher education system to better meet the competence needs of society. Minister AnttiTanskanen's growth working group has been looking for ways to accelerate productivity growth in the economy. The report prepared at the Ministry of Finance under the leadership of Director General Jukka Pekkarinen has assessed the content and scale of the measures required to stabilise general government finances and ensure the sustainability of their finances. Undersecretary of State Martti Hetem8aki's working group is currently finalising its proposals for reforming the tax system. [FIGURE 34: Where to find the tools for growth? d0 Goals] What is common in all the recommendations presented is that the structures of the economy should be reformed without prejudice in order to strengthen the basis for growth, maintain the price competitiveness of Finnish production and ensure the financial sustainability of public finances. Sustainable growth through productivity Many of the proposed reforms focus on the functioning of labour and product markets, taxation, the organisation and orientation of education and research, and the basic infrastructure of society. [FIGURE 35: Where do you get the tools for growth? d0 A reforming Finland] It is easy to agree with many of the proposals. Adequate competition should be guaranteed in the various markets. The entry of young people into the labour market should be brought forward and the exit of older people should be delayed. The premature interruption of careers should be tackled decisively. The effectiveness and productivity of basic services provided by the public sector should be increased. In taxation, preference should be given to measures that promote employment growth and employment. A common wage anchor/framework could stabilise the overall development of the national economy, while opportunities to agree on working conditions at the sector and company level would support flexible adaptation and the competitiveness of Finnish production. [FIGURE 36: Strengthening the foundations for growth] Strengthening the conditions for economic growth and maintaining growth are key to meeting the major challenges we face. The growth of the economy and living standards is the result of an increase in labour input and an increase in labour productivity. The ageing of the population threatens to drastically reduce labour input over the next two decades. Therefore, during this period, the growth of the economy and living standards must be sought from the growth of labor productivity. According to the theory of growth, the growth of labor productivity is determined by the number of on the basis of investments, as well as technological developments. Technology refers to "knowledge of how 1) inputs become commodities with which people satisfy their needs' . It means not only the manufacturing technology, but the entire value chain, from raw materials to finished products. What is important are the ideas and recipes for reorganizing work and organizing processes so that more can be done with invested capital and labor. Ultimately, it is technological development that is the most decisive source of productivity and economic growth. Investment in human and material capital is needed when new technologies are introduced. Or, conversely, without technological advances, there is no need to learn new production methods or acquire new types of machinery and equipment. The emergence of information and communication technologies made it possible for globalisation to become the main driver of economic development in the world in this millennium. The development of information and communication technologies (ICT) has revolutionised the management of production processes and made it possible to break down the production chain into small parts that can be carried out in different countries. At the same time, new countries d0 in particular China, India and the former socialist countries of Eastern Europe d0 have been linked to the world economy with great force. Thanks to its strong ICT expertise and the Nokia-driven ICT cluster built on it, Finland was quickly able to participate in benefiting from the opportunities created by globalisation. [FIGURE 37: Level of total factor productivity in different countries d0 corporate sector] The years after the recession of the early 1990s until the crisis in the financial markets and the subsequent global economic downturn were a time of rapid growth in productivity and living standards in Finland. By 2005, Finland had progressed to the top of the list of developed countries with the total productivity of the corporate sector 2)measured. [FIGURE 38: Level of total factor productivity in different countries d0 industry excl. ICT and private services] In addition to the ICT cluster, productivity also grew rapidly in many other industrial sectors and in some service sectors, such as trade and telecommunications. After the recession, changes in establishment structures in particular, where new jobs were created in high-productivity establishments, accelerated productivity growth. I believe that the use of information and communication technologies and the advancement of globalisation are key drivers of the global economy, even after the current recession. [FIGURE 39: The three channels of technological advances to productivity] The development and introduction of information and communication technologies, like any other new technology, will improve labour productivity in three ways. 1) It increases productivity in the manufacture of products with new technologies. 2) It increases productivity in industries that use capital with new technologies. 3) It will increase productivity across the economy as new technologies make businesses, the public sector and households change their ways of working in a more efficient direction. 3) Professor Matti Pohjola has extensively studied the factors behind productivity and economic growth. According to him, in Finland, the positive impact of new technology has been transmitted to the economy due to productivity growth in the production of ICT products. In the United States, on the other hand, the impact has been transmitted mainly through the use of capital containing new technologies. According to studies, there is so far less information about the positive growth effect conveyed through a wide-ranging change in operating methods. However, growth researchers agree that typically major technological disruptions, such as the introduction of steam and electric power, have improved the productivity of the economy and the living standards of citizens in the long term through a profound and wide-ranging change in the way new technologies are introduced into society. The new ways of working made possible by information and communication technologies will be the key to increasing productivity and living standards in the future. The possibilities for technological development are endless. On the other hand, the amount of inputs d0 raw materials and labour d0 is limited. For this reason, the constant increase in the standard of living can only be based on the development of technology and its widespread exploitation in society. Professor Erik Brynjolfsson heads the MIT Center for Digital Business at MIT, whose researchers have investigated the use of information and communication technologies and the spread of new ways of working 4) conditions in enterprises. Brynjolfsson talks about those who have undergone a successful change in operating methods 5) of companies as "digital organizations". [FIGURE 40: Investment in organisation and education outweighs ICT investments] He stresses that, in addition to the actual investment in computers, software and communication equipment, significant complementary investments in new ways of working are needed to enable companies to take full advantage of the opportunities created by INFORMATION AND COMMUNICATION TECHNOLOGIES. The measures that drive the change process forward should focus on ways of managing and managing information, decision-making mechanisms, staff recruitment, rewarding and training, and corporate culture. Brynjolfsson's message is important. It is clear that the objectives set for an increase in productivity and living standards will not be achieved in society if companies are unable to change their business models and to produce higher or even higher or better quality returns with the same or even fewer inputs. We still have a lot to achieve in this area d0 including in industry, where many companies in many sectors are already at the forefront of technological development, but especially in private service provision and, in particular, in public service production, where productivity has improved slowly, if at all, during the emergence of information and communication technologies. Sustainability gap in public finances and productivity in the production of welfare services In Finland, there is a broad acceptance and commitment to maintain a welfare society. This means that health, education and social services want to maintain a high level of service and wide access to services. Even before the recession, it was seen that this welfare model could also withstand the ageing of the population without drastic changes in income criteria. Thus, the central government and municipalities, as well as employment pension schemes, were believed to be able to respond to the growing need for services and increasing income transfers without indebtedness turning to unsustainable growth. The picture of the sustainability of general government finances has become significantly gloomier during 2009d02010. In practice, the recession ate away at the indebtedness with which Finland had prepared for growing expenditure and a shrinking tax base. When ageing is already here in practice, putting public finances on a sustainable footing will be a particularly big challenge. The scale of this challenge and the overall economic impact of various adaptation measures have been assessed in several recent reports by the Bank of Finland. [FIGURE 41: The EU's three-pronged ageing strategy] Within the EU, emphasis has been placed on measures to consolidate the budgetary position and reduce debt, as well as to restructure the economy in a growth- and employment-friendly direction. With the recession, it has become important to move forward on all fronts at the same time. The Bank of Finland's calculations also show that, in practice, the sustainability gap cannot be filled simply by raising taxes. In view of the unfavourable effects of tax increases on the labour market and on economic growth, it is absolutely impossible for any adjustment to be made by changing the tax bases. Although it is obvious that, without a full increase in taxation, government indebtedness is unlikely to be brought under control, sustainability policy cannot be built on that alone. Other means are therefore needed, of which the extension of working lives is essential. A very important element of the sustainability strategy is also the objective of improving the productivity of public service provision. When the share of welfare and health services in the production of the entire economy, and thus in labour resources, is already large, and will rise significantly in the coming decades, productivity growth will have a key impact on the sustainability gap. Productivity growth in public service production has a direct impact on the cost burden of service production. In addition, productivity growth affects the extent to which labor resources are available for market production. If the productivity of basic public services were to increase and public services could be provided more cheaply, the picture of the sustainability gap would become clearly more favourable. [FIGURE 42: Scenario: overall tax rate in an ageing Finland] This is illustrated by the figure below. In it, the basic calculation describes a situation in which the problem of the sustainability of public finances would be fully solved by increasing taxes and charges on labour. Taking into account the dynamics of the economy, the need to increase taxation would rise to around 10 percentage points. In this case, it is assumed that the productivity of basic public services will not increase at all. If, on the other hand, the productivity of public health, social welfare and education grew by one per cent every year during the reference period, the need to increase taxation would decrease to just under a third. According to the calculation, an annual increase in productivity of one per cent would substantially reduce the need for fiscal adjustment. The target seems large when compared to the actual change in productivity. On average, fiscal productivity has not increased at all, or even decreased, over the past 20 years or so. However, it is clear that there is a great deal that can be done to increase the productivity of basic public services when the objectives are clear and the incentives are properly targeted. [FIGURE 43: Improving public sector productivity] Projects aimed at improving productivity in the public sector have been extensively underway in both central and local government. The use of information and communication technologies (ICT) in the provision of services is a key issue. However, ICT can also be seen as a strategic resource that would enable completely new operating models in public administration. These have been discussed in the recently published publication of the Ministry of Finance entitled 'Administration as a balancer of wellbeing and the economy'. According to a report by the Ministry of Finance, the use of ICT could both improve the quality of services and increase the efficiency of the service system. However, achieving the benefits made possible by information technology requires both common operating models and common basic IT solutions between different actors. The report points out that permanent improvements in efficiency and productivity require dismantling silos in public administration, increasing centralised guidance and strengthening knowledge management. The potential for improving fiscal productivity is significant. There are always two important objectives in the organisation of public services: effectiveness and efficiency. You have to do the right things that generate genuine added value and you have to do them efficiently in order to achieve as much as possible. [FIGURE 44: Productivity-enhancing solutions can create a more sustainable basis for Finland's welfare services] It is therefore important that the functions of public finances should be reformed on a long-term basis and that planning should not be limited to existing institutional structures. Constantly considering how to direct services to where the impact is greatest and to organise them in a way that uses tax revenues as efficiently as possible creates the basis for a fiscal strategy that reduces cost burdens. The fiscal crisis, exacerbated by the recession, will help us to better see the sustainability problems of public finances. What is important, however, is that the various proposals form a common line of action, the pieces into a whole. Only so there will be a plot for the story. Change, on the other hand, requires strong commitment both centrally by the state and decentralizedly in municipalities. 1) Pohjola M (2008), "Information and communication technology as a source of productivity growth", Technology Industries of Finland, 2008. 2) Od5Mahony M ja Timmer M P (2009), d3Output, Input and Productivity Measures at the Industry Level: The EU KLEMS Databased3, Economic Journal, Volume 119, Issue 538, pages F374-F403, June 2009. 3) Pohjola M (2010), "What will happen to productivity growth", in "After the crisis", ed. Yhteenvetona voi sanoa, ett<8a> maailmantalouden kasvu jatkuu, mutta elpyminen on kuitenkin haurasta ja ep<8a>tasaista. Se on haurasta nimenomaan sen takia, ett<8a> se on ep<8a>tasaista. [KUVA 2: BKT:n kasvu keskeisill<8a> talousalueilla] Valuuttarahaston kokouksessa esitettiin maailmantalouden ennuste, joka maalaa kuvan kohtuullisen suotuisasta, mutta hyvin kaksijakoisesta kehityksest<8a>. Monet kehittyv<8a>t taloudet, ei vain Kiina, kasvavat nopeasti. Samaan aikaan kehittyneiden talouksien kasvun<8a>kym<8a>t ovat selv<8a>sti alhaisemmat. USA:n kasvuennustetta alennettiin, euroalueen ennustetta taas korjattiin hieman yl<9a>sp<8a>in. My<9a>s euroalueen sis<8a>ll<8a> kasvun<8a>kym<8a>t ovat hyvin kaksijakoiset. Euroalueen kasvuveturi on nyt vientivetoinen Saksa. Pohjoinen Eurooppa kasvaa laajemminkin. Alhaisimmat kasvuluvut ovat maissa, joissa on jouduttu suuriin sopeutustoimiin. Title: Productivity Forum 2010
text: Governor of the Bank of Finland, Erkki Liikanen at the Productivity Forum 2010, 19 October 2010 . Speech . Tuesday 19October 2010,12:00 AM Slides (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and.. interviews/documents/101019_el_macroeconomic_realities_productivityforum.ppt) (PPT) Slides (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and.. interviews/documents/101019_el_macroeconomic_realities_productivityforum.pdf) (PDF) Summary of speech MACROECONOMIC REALITIES The world economy is now recovering from the deep recession that followed the crisis that befell the financial markets at the end of 2008. Economic development has, however, been uneven. Economic growth in China which slowed only slightly during the crisis was one of the first to speed up, supported by considerable expansionary measures. This was broadly reflected in other developing economies in Asia and elsewhere in the world. The upswing in the United States and Japan started a little later, in 2009, while the euro area had to wait until spring 2010 to experience a turnaround. Subsequently, China, the United States as well as Japan have been showing signs of an evening up in their pace of recovery. Growth is expected to continue unevenly. In emerging economies, rapid growth is fostered not only by population structure, but particularly also by their position as technological catch-up countries: It is faster to adopt existing high-level technology than develop it themselves. Additionally, the financial crisis is seen slowing growth more in developed than in emerging economies in the coming years. The reason for which being that the financial crisis had a significantly more pronounced effect on developed than emerging economies. Households have already increased their savings in many countries where leveraging was increasing rapidly before the crisis. Returning indebtedness back to more sustainable levels over the long run is expected to be a protracted process, in many of these countries. This probably will slow down economic growth in these countries for several years. One of the more serious consequences of the crisis has been how rapidly governments have become indebted. Expansionary measures have increased public deficits in, for example, some euro area countries extremely rapidly. These debts only serve to exacerbate future funding pressures. It is possible to survive these debt burdens only under conditions of adequate growth, but structural reforms will also be imperative. Several euro area countries are in a situation where the share of working-age population is starting to shrink. Consequently, population growth no longer supports economic growth; rather it poses a threat in the form of a reduction in hours worked. This leads to a situation where, from the debt servicing point of view, productivity improvements will remain the sole means of achieving the necessary economic growth. In order to sustain high-level of wellbeing, the speeding up of productivity growth is a great challenge and will require both public support as well considerable efforts from the private sector.

Title: Monetary policy measures of the Eurosystem during the financial crisis
text: Erkki Liikanen, President of the European Union: The Eurosystem's monetary policy response during the crisis of the economy. Bank of Finland statement by Parliament's Economic Affairs Committee 23.11.2010 . Speech . Tuesday 23November 2010,4:00 PM Pss Director Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland statement by Parliament's Economic Affairs Committee 23.11.2010 Eurosystem monetary policy measures during the financial crisis Synopsis The primary objective of the European Central Bank's monetary policy is to maintain price stability in the euro area. The price stability objective is a long-term increase in consumer prices but below two per cent over a medium period of time. Achieving the price stability objective safeguards the purchasing power of citizens in the euro area. As the financial crisis that began in 2007 spread, upstream inflationary risks to the real economy disappeared. In the past, the crisis hit international trade hard. At the same time, monetary policy shifts threatened serious shocks on euro area money and credit markets. The euro area economy was at risk of falling into a credit crunch, which would have quickly deepened the crisis in the real economy. As a result of the deteriorating economic situation, the ECB cut interest rates rapidly in the past. The reduction in policy rates started at 4.25% in October 2008 and fell to 1.0% in May 2009. Market interest rates fell further to a markedly lower level as a result of the ECB's liquidity policy. In the euro area, banks play a key role (around 70%) in the financial intermediation. As a result, the Euro Mechanism has taken its non-standard monetary policy measures through the banking sector in advance to secure financial provision. In some respects, this approach has differed from that of the United States, where the role of banks in financial intermediation is clearly more limited (around 30%). The ECB's interest rate and liquidity policies have improved banks' ability to provide financing to firms and households at low interest rates. Liquidity operations have played a key role in restoring confidence. At the same time, in line with its price stability mandate, the ECB has ensured that the measures taken counteract deflation and do not threaten price stability through excessive increases in inflation. The measures are structured in such a way that they can be phased out quickly when the economic situation allows. The development of the financial market crisis and monetary policy measures The credit crisis that started in the United States spread to the euro area money markets in autumn 2007. Banks' uncertainty about the creditworthiness and liquidity of other banks led to rapid difficulties in accessing market finance. In order to counteract the upward pressure on market interest rates, the ECB made the timing of its liquidity policy more flexible and extended the maturity of loans granted to banks against collateral. Nsms operations fell within the normal scope of monetary policy implementation. They alleviated banks' perceived uncertainty about the availability of liquidity. After the collapse of the US investment bank Lehman Brothers in September 2008, the financial market crisis came to an end. The normal liquidity equalisation between banks, which is at the heart of money market functioning, became impossible. In the euro system's auctions, uncertainty took the form of rising interest rates as banks competed fiercely for the central bank liquidity available. The Czech Republic made it difficult to control short-term money market interest rates. Households and non-financial corporations felt that market interest rates were rising even though policy rates were unchanged. In October 2008, governments across Europe, led by the European Commission, took concerted and informed action to safeguard the solvency of failing banks, through guarantees and, where appropriate, recapitalisation. The measures mentioned above, which were also taken by other major economic areas, succeeded in averting the imminent collapse of the global banking system. In addition to the rapid reduction in interest rates, in order to defuse the situation that has arisen on the money markets, the ECB adopted a transition to a policy of interest rates (the so-called distribution and fixed interest rate policy) in order to defuse the situation that has arisen on the money markets. As a result, the transmission of liquidity between banks was replaced by a central bank. As a result of this measure, short-term money market rates fell first to and below the key interest rate. Subsequently, the ECB adopted a policy of distribution at the key interest rate, including for longer-term (3d12-month) credit operations. The reason was to reduce the rise in interest rates on longer-term money market rates (EURIBOR) due to high liquidity demand, while short periods were already at very low levels. In support of the liquidity policy for distribution, the range of approved collateral was extended. Chms took place in all credit operations. At the same time, risk management was made more efficient. This took place, among other things, with undervaluation of collateral and other restrictions on collateral. During the financial crisis, counterparties, i.e. banks, attempted to bring assets that were unrelated to the central bank as collateral. He stressed the need for the ECB to tighten its collateral risk management policy. The guarantee mechanism is part of the ECB's monetary policy policy, which is also taken into account take into account the objectives of the central bank and the functioning of financial markets. In addition, the market for covered bonds, which is critical for bank financing, was supported by a 60 billion purchase programme from July 2009 to the end of June 2010. The programme succeeded in reducing risk premia and capitalising issuances in these markets. combating the negative effects of the financial market crisis and restoring confidence in the financial markets 1) The ECB's liquidity operations have played a key role. The partitioning policy removed liquidity uncertainty and prevented forced sales of liquid assets by providing central bank liquidity against a wider range of collateral. Ns supported banks' ability to provide finance to the public and ensured that low interest rates were passed on to the real economy. As a result of these measures, problems in the supply of credit will be alleviated and the banking system will be able to finance its claims flexibly. The transformation of the financial market crisis into a sovereign debt crisis At the height of the European debt crisis in May 2010, liquidity demand increased again and even exceeded the post-Lehman crisis level (peaking liquidity demand at over EUR 300 billion). This is due to the fact that some banks in troubled countries, in many cases guaranteed by the State concerned, have become dependent on the euro system for their financing, as the loss of credibility of the State guarantee has led to a lack of confidence in the banks also guaranteed. In May 2010, a new asset purchase programme (Securities Markets Programme) was launched, under which securities are purchased on the private, and public bond markets, which are essential for the transmission of monetary policy, as appropriate. Hsirisits was particularly evident in the sovereign bond market, where pricing began to be driven not by fundamental factors but by waves of general nervousness. The functioning of these markets is important because their market may also include other market segments that are important in terms of financial intermediation. Government bonds also serve as a basis for pricing other financial market instruments. Since the beginning of the programme, purchases have been intermittent and well below the initial stage. The liquidity effect of the purchase programme will be sterilised in the amount of purchases corresponding to the volume of purchases. The balance sheet of the euro system will shrink as money markets normalise In order to help normalise money market conditions, including through stress tests, the ECB has gradually begun a gradual return to normal monetary policy implementation. Normalisation has been reflected in a reduction in risk premia in money market trading and improved lending opportunities for banks that have been found to be solvent. Measures affecting the banking sector as a whole have been abandoned and authorities in different countries have been able to concentrate on managing individual failing banks. As a result, lengthy operations of 6 and 12 months have already been abandoned. The timing and gradual progress of the exit from non-standard measures is important. An early exit could have destabilised financial markets and discouraged budding economic growth, tightened lending opportunities and raised risk premia. Gradual progress is intended to ensure the most timely response to changes in the operating environment and to facilitate the halting or even reversal of actions if necessary. Non-standard measures have increased the size of the euro system's balance sheet, but have not restricted the ECB's ability to control interest rates. The ECB will be able to adjust its monetary policy stance to the desired level, even if liquidity support to the banking system continues. The growth of the Eurosystem's balance sheet has been moderate compared with many other central banks. The reason for this is that the ECB's credit operations with banks have been sufficient and there has been no need for large-scale purchase programmes (covered bonds and SMP programme totalling 125 billion). The balance sheet swelled, i.e. as a result of increased credit operations, and rose by 500 billion during the crisis. EUR 2 000 billion the euro (about 20% of euro area GDP). However, the balance sheet has started to shrink as progress towards money market normalisation has reduced demand for senior liquidity in credit operations. 1) Ks. Title: Viable cooperation between Nordic central banks
text: Governor Erkki Liikanen: Viable co-operation between Nordic central banks. Svart8c 27.1.2011 . Speech . Thursday27 January 2011,5:00 PM Erkki Liikanen, Governor of the Bank of Finland Magma Academy seminar Svart8c 27.1.2011 VIABLE CO-OPERATION BETWEEN NORDIC CENTRAL BANKS Ladies and gentlemen, thank you very much for the kind invitation to attend the Magna Academy seminar here at Svart8c Castle. My intention is to highlight the co-operation between the Nordic central banks; a cooperation that has long traditions and is still extremely viable. I will examine the Nordic countries' various integration policy solutions, especially when it comes to the attitude to economic and monetary union EMU, and try to explain why our cooperation is intensive despite the fact that the currency regimes differ between the different countries. Our common interest in the Baltics plays an important role here. Finally, I will talk about where developments are now heading, after the financial crisis, when many forms of international cooperation are being reassessed. Among other things, a new body, the European Systemic Risk Board, has seen the light of day. I note that, in accordance with its strategy, the Magma think tank will "pave the way for new thinking about swedish future in Finland". On this point, I am afraid of disappointing you. I belong to a generation for whom bilingualism is something completely natural. We have two national languages in Finland, Finnish and Swedish. For me, it feels like a matter of course that all schoolchildren in Finland should be taught at least the basics of the second national language. Of course, everyone, both Finnish-speaking and Swedish-speaking, must receive services in their mother tongue from the authorities. And I hope that Swedish d0 or Scandinavian d0 is a cornerstone of Nordic co-operation will be clear in my speech today. Co-operation between the Nordic central banks has long traditions. Between 1873 and 1924, Sweden, Norway and Denmark were part of the so-called Scandinavian Coin Union. In practice, it was about a connection to gold, so that the Swedish, Norwegian and Danish crowns were all worth the same. There were even proposals to establish a single monetary policy authority based in Gothenburg, but that proposal never materialised. Sveriges Riksbank, Norges Bank and Danmarks Nationalbank have held joint meetings at least since 1916, but probably even longer. Eventually, a tradition of annual meetings was introduced. The Bank of Finland joined the cooperation in 1933 and Landsbanki Island in 1937. As cooperation continued after a few years' hiatus after The Second World War, a recurring question was how exchange rates would be determined. Politically, Finland was hard-pressed by the Soviet Union, but this did not prevent the tradition of Nordic central bank meetings from continuing. And Finland joined the IMF and the World Bank at an early stage. The history of the Bank of Finland, which will be published later this year, will shed a lot of new light on this important stage in Finland's history. For a long time, Nordic central bank co-operation was perhaps the most important concrete channel for co-operation beyond national borders. The forum was also used at times to invite representatives of central banks outside its own circle, for example from the Bank of England. In line with international developments and European integration, co-operation between the Nordic central banks and the governors of the central banks has changed, but it has still been quite intense. Cooperation has been characterised by an informal spirit and perhaps also spontaneity and perhaps less bureaucracy. The same applies to Nordic central bank co-operation at departmental level. This has also continued despite the fact that international contacts have increased significantly, especially for the Nordic countries belonging to the EU. A development trend in recent years has been that the heads of the Nordic supervisory authorities such as the Swedish Financial Supervisory Authority have also participated in the meetings. In addition to the more formal meetings, which are usually held in the summer according to a rotation order, the governors of the central banks have already gathered for dinner for a long time about four times a year, usually in one of the Nordic capitals. Most recently, we met over dinner in Helsinki in December, when we thanked our Norwegian colleague who retired. Let me underline that cooperation between the Nordic central banks and the supervisory authorities is still of great substantial importance. In a situation where integration into the financial market in the Nordic region is deepening with several large cross-border banks and insurance companies, it is important that the authorities also cooperate. An example of this is a cooperation agreement on financial stability that was signed last summer between the central banks, supervisory authorities and finance ministries of the Nordic and Baltic countries. The Nordic countries have chosen different solutions when it comes to European integration and the euro. Finland is a member of both the EU and EMU. Sweden is in the EU but still has its krona floating freely, and the Riksbank has an inflation target. The EU country Denmark has chosen a different solution: it retains its national currency, but it is strictly tied to the euro. Commodity-rich Norway is a special case; the country is outside the EU and the central bank in Oslo is pursuing its monetary policy on the basis of an inflation target. Iceland, for its part, has been so shaken by the financial crisis that it has applied for membership of the EU. The point is that as long as fiscal policy and, for example, competition policy have been handled responsibly, the Nordic countries have been able to choose their exchange rate regime quite freely, without it having made cooperation more difficult. In the meetings between the Nordic central bank governors, we traditionally always speak Swedish or Scandinavian. But I must admit that at one stage we made an exception. In the autumn of 2008, when the financial crisis was at its worst, we switched in the discussions to English when it came to the figures in the concrete support for Iceland. Norway, Denmark and Sweden entered into a so-called swap agreement with the Icelanders, to support Iceland's economy. Finland and the Bank of Finland were also cornered by the fact that the Eurosystem d0 i.e. the Eurosystem d0 was in a corner. The European Central Bank and the national EMU central banks d0 were also involved in the process. A third aspect of Nordic co-operation is that we have had common interests when it comes to the Baltics. On the one hand, we have co-operation within the framework of the Nordic-Baltic group of countries in the IMF and, on the other hand, Swedish and Danish banks in particular have made large investments in the Baltic countries. An interesting stage began in the New Year 2011 when the European Systemic Risk Board (ESRB) saw the light of day. The Systemic Risk Board is chaired by ecb president Jean-Claude Trichet and sits the heads of the national central banks and financial supervisory authorities. The ESRB is a new construct that has been created in the aftermath of the financial crisis, and as its name says, it is responsible for monitoring systemic risks in the European financial market. Riksbank Governor Stefan Ingves was elected Chairman of the ESRB's Advisory Technical Committee. From a Nordic perspective, it is positive that Sweden and Denmark are also members of the systemic risk board, despite the fact that they are not members of EMU. Since Finland became a member of the European Union in 1995, the relative weight of Nordic co-operation has decreased, it must be admitted. For Finland and the Bank of Finland, membership of EMU since 1999 has of course been very important. When it comes to co-operation between the Nordic EU countries in particular, there has sometimes been a bit of squeaking in relations. It is, of course, a fact that integration policy solutions differ from country to country. Nevertheless, regional co-operation in the Nordic countries is very much alive. It is natural that countries that are each other's geographical neighbours are significant trading partners and that there is a lively trade and tourism across borders. The fact that we can handle contacts with our Nordic neighbours in one of our two national languages seems to me to be a great advantage and strength for us in Finland. English tends to become the corporate language in large Nordic companies, and english is also becoming more and more in the contact between the authorities, especially when the Baltic countries join. But especially in view of the informal contacts with Sweden, Norway and Denmark, it is important that Finnish officials continue to master Swedish. Can a Finn understand Sweden if he or she does not understand Swedish at all? The Bank of Finland is one of very few institutions that still arranges monolingual Swedish meetings with various stakeholders such as the Swedish Parliamentary Group and the Swedish Yle. But it is also a problem with us that the younger civil servants do not speak Swedish in the same way as older generations. Bilingualism in the public sector must be alive so that the country's Swedish-speaking population receives services in their mother tongue. This is something that the Bank of Finland adheres to both as a national monetary authority and as a member of the Eurosystem. This will apply to everything from internet pages to annual reports and brochures and personal contacts with the authorities. And the contacts to 81land and the 81landers are of course handled in Swedish. Thanks for the attention!

Title: Role and risks of the Bank of Finland in the operations of the Eurosystem
text: President Erkki Liikanen: The Bank of Finland's role and risks in the Eurosystem's operations. Parliament's Finance Committee 1.2.2011 . Speech . Tuesday 1 February 2011, 11:00 AM Director-General Erkki Liikanen Parliament's Finance Committee 1.2.2011 THE BANK OF FINLAND'S ROLE AND RISKS IN THE EUROSYSTEM'S OPERATIONS As part of the Eurosystem, the Bank of Finland participates in the implementation of all ecb monetary policy operations. This also applies to purchases of securities under the Bond Market Programme. In accordance with the rules of the single monetary policy, the Bank of Finland receives a proportional share of the proceeds of monetary policy (including banknotes) corresponding to its relative size. Similarly, contributes its contribution to the risk-bearing nature of the single monetary policy. The Bank of Finland's share of the ECB's capital, the so-called "bank share". the capital key, is 1.8%. The risk buffers on the Bank of Finland's balance sheet are designed to cover the risks of monetary policy operations and own investment activities. In addition, the Bank of Finland has been able to make a significant distribution of profits to the state on an annual basis. From 2007 to 2009, approximately EUR 250 million in profits have been distributed annually. For 2010, the Parliamentary Banking Board will decide on the distribution of profits after the financial statements have been completed. In accordance with the EU Treaty approved by Parliament, monetary policy decisions in the euro area are taken by the Governing Council of the European Central Bank. The Governor of the Bank of Finland is a member of the Council. In addition, the Bank of Finland, like the central banks of other euro area countries, plays a key role in the implementation of monetary policy decisions. The tasks, powers and responsibilities of the Bank of Finland within the Eurosystem are defined in the Statute of the ESCB and in the Act on the Bank of Finland. The Bank of Finland is the bank of the Parliament and is supervised by the Parliament. The Governing Council's judicial review of monetary policy decisions is carried out through the Court of Justice of the European Union. Given the autonomy of the Governing Council, the ECB's monetary policy activities are not subject to political surveillance under the Treaty. The Bank of Finland keeps parliament informed of the ECB's monetary policy measures and the reasons for them. The Bank of Finland has regularly reported on the ECB's activities and the related financial risks to the Board of Governors and to auditors appointed by Parliament. In addition, the Bank of Finland is at the disposal of the Finance Committee when the committee so wishes. In December 2010, the Economic Committee held a detailed briefing on the implementation of monetary policy, collateral policies and risks
