Title: Transformation of the global economy and the challenges of the European economy
text: President Erkki Liikanen: On the transformation of the global economy and the challenges facing the European economy. OP-Pohjola Group Research Foundation's theme day. Helsinki 14.2.2011 . Speech . Monday14 February 2011,11:00AM Director General Erkki Liikanen OP-Pohjola Group Research Foundation Theme Day Helsinki 14.2.2011 ON THE TRANSFORMATION OF THE WORLD ECONOMY AND THE CHALLENGES FACING THE EUROPEAN ECONOMY Speech Membranes (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches/documents/el_op_pohjola110214.ppt) (PPT) . Speech Membranes (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches/documents/el_op_pohjola110214.pdf) (PDF) . The recovery of the global economy from the recession has been fragile and uneven. It has been fragile precisely because it has been uneven. Emerging economies have grown strongly everywhere. The recovery in the industrialised countries has been more subdued. Why did many emerging economies get away with so little of the global economic crisis? On the other hand, why are the industrialised countries suffering so much more? Why did the industrialised countries become so heavily indebted? How can we ensure that Europe and Finland can cope with major changes in the global economy? [Slide 2] The pace of the global economic recovery slowed down somewhat in the second half of last year. However, based on the latest data, growth still seems to have continued to be positive around the turn of the year  also in most industrialised countries. The recovery after the recession was initially driven by both exceptionally strong stimulus policy measures and a reversal of the inventory cycle; companies had to replenish their stocks emptied during the recession. However, the effects of these factors cannot last very long. When they subside, the recovery will continue where the conditions are in place for a more permanent strengthening of private demand. In many industrialised countries, the near-term prospects for private demand are not very good. Businesses and households are indebted, and the pressure to reduce leverage (deleveraging) is great. The availability of borrowed money has also decreased compared to the situation before the recession. Households cannot be expected to increase their demand strongly when their income development is subdued and employment conditions are poor. Business investment, on the other hand, is weighed down by the uncertainty of the economic outlook and the abundant unused production capacity. [Slide 3] In emerging economies, private consumption and investment have increased substantially since the recession and will continue to grow. The recession in emerging economies was both short-lived and subdued compared to industrialised countries. . Of course, there are big differences between emerging economies. The recession was particularly low in Asia and partly also in Latin America. However, in many of Europe's emerging economies, the recession was deep. Why did emerging economies, on the whole, survive the global economic downturn with relatively little? A key background factor is related to international financial flows. Before the recession, the current account balances of emerging economies showed surpluses, especially in Asia, the Middle East and Russia  and still are. At the same time, emerging economies have reduced their dependence on foreign funding. Their foreign claims have increased, as have their foreign exchange reserves. Emerging economies have thus been less vulnerable to shocks in the international financial system. There are also other factors behind the more stable development of emerging economies. The structure of the countries' exports has diversified, as has the structure of their production in general. At the same time, trade between emerging economies, especially in Asia, has increased. It has reduced their dependence on imported demand from industrialised countries. The rise in the average income level of citizens and the strengthening of the middle class have contributed in the same direction. It has increased the relative importance of domestic demand and the ability to cushion the effects of fluctuations in export demand on total output in countries. [Slide 4] In addition, in many developing countries, the institutions of economic policy have strengthened and policies have become more coherent. This can be seen, among other things, in the fact that since the turn of the millennium, inflation has, as a rule, been brought under control in emerging economies  on average, it has remained at single-digit figures. [Slide 5] The rapid growth of emerging economies after the recession means that the trend of the 2000s will continue. Between 2000 and 2009, output in emerging economies increased by an average of around 6% per year. Growth thus accelerated substantially from the 3rd per cent rate of the previous decades. It was significantly faster than the average growth rate in the industrialised countries, which was only 2% between 2000 and 2009. Emerging economies have thus significantly closed the gap in living standards with the industrialised countries. The term 'great convergence' has been used to refer to ongoing developments. The older term 'great divergence' was used to refer to the developments brought about by industrialisation. It was then that the prosperity of the West made a break with the rest of the world. [Slide 6] China is expected to soon become the world's largest economy. This is the result of a catch-up process that has progressed at an astonishing rate since the turn of the millennium. As recently as 2000, China's economy was only slightly more than half the size of the U.S. economy. On the other hand, this is not a historically new issue. China lost its position as the largest economy in the world only in the late 1800s. In 1870, China's economy was still the largest in the world, and in second place was India. At the time, the U.S. and British economies were roughly equal to each other  each just over half the size of China. Let us return to this day. While the outlook for emerging economies for the next few years is now favourable, they too have their challenges. They have to adapt to the fact that indebted industrialised countries, both households and companies tend to reduce their debts. So are the increasingly indebted countries. This weakens the prospects for exports to industrialised countries. Therefore, in emerging economies, domestic demand must increase in relation to exports. Only in this way can rapid economic growth continue. This requires changes in economic policies and, in particular, the strengthening of currencies in some countries. The monetary policy stance therefore has room for tightening, which would at the same time reduce overheating risks in some emerging economies. Rising inflation is already a major concern for many emerging economies. At the same time, the sustainability of economic policy institutions is being tested. Although the ability to pursue coherent policies has improved in emerging economies, the institutions are not as stable as in the industrialised countries. [Slide 7] It is possible that the rapid growth of emerging economies will slow down at some point. However, there is no reason to expect that the slowdown will be long-term or that the success of emerging economies will turn out to have been built on a large-scale economic bubble. The "Great Convergence" may take temporary step backwards, but there are no signs of its end. The most likely scenario is for growth to continue at a brisk pace. Changes in the structure of the global economy will be major and irreversible. There is no going back to the old division of labor. In many respects, development is a good thing. A large number of residents of emerging economies are experiencing a rapid improvement in their material well-being. The major changes under way for industrialised countries also offer opportunities. Consumers will benefit from cheap imported goods, and many companies will receive an increasing share of their profits from emerging economies' markets. At the same time, the challenges are enormous. Many sectors and occupational groups are under great pressure to adapt as competition from emerging economies continues to increase. The successes will be those economies with flexible structures, where public finances are in order and where the competitiveness of domestic production is not eroded. [Slide 8] In the next few years, the industrialised countries will have to contend with many problems. Growth prospects are quite modest. This is partly due to the indebtedness of different sectors of the economy. The decline in debt burdens (deleveraging), which had grown rapidly before the recession, is just beginning and will hold back demand growth for years to come. In many industrialised countries, the conditions for long-term growth are weakened by the fact that the age structure of the population is ageing considerably. The ability of these economies to grow out of debt has clearly declined compared to previous decades of rapid growth  and also compared to many emerging economies. In addition to debt-guzzling, growth is constrained by frictional factors related to inevitable structural changes: in many countries, resources must be transferred from construction to other industries, among other things. The training and skills of workers released from construction are often not directly suited to these sectors. Before the recession, the share of construction in total output increased due to, for example, very light financial conditions. We are now in the process of rapidly adapting economies to the smaller construction sector. Tighter financing conditions will also limit the pace of the recovery. There is no reason to expect a return to the very light pre-crisis financing conditions. Should we even hope for that? Due to the subdued outlook in many industrialised countries, the global economy as a whole cannot be expected to grow very rapidly in the next few years. The outlook is uncertain. One key source of uncertainty at the moment is that financial markets are sceptical about the sustainability of public finances in some euro area countries. [Slide 9] The recession severely weakened the fiscal outlook in most industrialised countries, as the deterioration in real economic developments rapidly reduced the tax base. There are also automatic stabilizers and active stimulus measures increased public deficits. Not all countries had created room for expansionary fiscal policies in the years leading up to the recession. Given that economic development in industrialised countries deteriorated significantly more in the recession than in emerging economies, it is not surprising that it is in the industrialised countries that public deficits have increased. Another factor is that the size of public finances in the industrialised countries is much larger than in the developing countries. In industrialised countries, the ratio of gross government debt to GDP increased from around 70% before the recession to 95% last year. At the same time, in emerging economies, public debt has remained around 35% of GDP. Public deficits in industrialised countries appear to be only slowly declining in the coming years, and public debt will continue to rise. The problem is exacerbated by the fact that the outlook for economic growth is weak in many countries with high public debt. In most EU countries, fiscal problems have now become so great that reversing the stimulus measures put in place during the recession alone will not be enough to ensure the sustainability of public finances. Much more ambitious decisions are needed. [Slide 10] In countries whose fiscal sustainability is questionable in the eyes of the markets, economic growth can no longer be supported by increasing public spending. The question of whether fiscal tightening will undermine economic growth is ultimately theoretical for problem countries. They do not have a realistic alternative. Increasing spending would only undermine confidence in households, businesses and markets and raise the cost of servicing the country's debt. The result would be a knock-on effect in which an increase in interest payments exacerbates the government deficit and feeds ever deeper mistrust in the markets. We must be able to break this cycle of mistrust. Thus, in the countries most affected by debt problems, there is no alternative to rapid fiscal consolidation. In most other EU countries, it is necessary to take rebalancing measures. However, those countries that have maintained a good capacity to raise money on the market have more leeway in terms of the timing of their actions. They have the opportunity to choose a fiscal strategy that will safeguard market confidence on a permanent basis without jeopardising short-term economic growth. In these countries, an immediate and rapid emergency brake on public spending is not the best option. It is essential to build a credible fiscal programme that will be able to stem the growth of public expenditure in the long term below that of the national economy. The credibility of the chosen strategy is key. If the plans to balance public finances are credible, the threat of increasing taxation will be less pronounced in the future. This instantly supports consumption and investment. Institution-building in fiscal policy-making can improve the ability of public authorities to implement a decided programme of measures in an effective and credible manner. The central government spending limits budgeting used in Finland belongs to such institutions. Fiscal consolidation can also be facilitated by accelerating structural reforms that improve the conditions for economic growth. Recent years have shown that economic stability can be shaken very quickly and unexpectedly. There will also be economic crises in the future. Overcoming them without much distress requires the creation of a margin for manoeuvre in public finances. We must therefore be able to reduce debts not only under duress. The room for manoeuvre also facilitates adaptation to changes in the global division of labour. The state of public finances in Finland is better than in many other countries of the European Union. In the years before the recession, there was a clear surplus in general government finances and a decrease in public debt. Efforts have been made in Finland to prepare for the problem of the ageing of the population, because it starts earlier than in other countries and is also bigger than many others. For the time being at least, Finland has avoided the weakening of market confidence and the rise in financing costs that a large number of euro area countries are now having to face. [Slide 11] However, the sustainability of public finances has not been ensured. Without policy changes, Finland's public debt will rise rapidly in the 2020s, as the growth of age-related expenditure accelerates. The so-called fiscal sustainability gap is 5% of GDP, according to a report published by the Ministry of Finance in late 2010. This improvement in the budgetary position should be achieved by 2015 in order to ensure that public finances are sustainable in the long term. The Bank of Finland's september 2010 estimate of the sustainability gap is slightly higher, at around 6% of GDP. One important element in our country's preparation for the aging challenge is the improvement of labor productivity in the production of basic public services. Health and welfare services already account for a significant share of production and employment in the economy as a whole, and it will increase considerably more as the population ages. Calculations show that productivity growth, which appears to be relatively small, would significantly strengthen the sustainability of public finances. Only. an improvement of one per cent per year would already significantly ease the situation. Another key element in preparing for aging is the much-talked-about effort to extend careers, from the beginning, the middle and the end. However, finland's fiscal sustainability strategy cannot be relied solely on longer working lives and improved productivity in basic public services. The sustainability gap in public finances has already grown to such an extent that other structural reforms are also needed  and inevitably a reassessment of expenditure and revenue. Sometimes there is a temptation in the debate to present the need for fiscal adjustment as an "external compulsion". In the long term, however, balancing public finances is about preventing the erosion of education, health services and infrastructure and securing their development in a sustainable way. [Slide 12] The need for structural reforms to improve the conditions for economic growth is at least as topical throughout the EU as it is in Finland. Economic growth in the EU has been rather slow by international comparison in recent decades. The outlook for the next 10 years will certainly not be better unless structural reforms are accelerated. The major financial crisis and the associated recession are estimated to have had a significant negative impact on the productive potential of the EU economy. Experience with financial crises shows that post-crisis economic policy is of great importance in terms of how deep a mark the crisis leaves on economic development. The crises in Japan, Sweden and Finland in the 1990s are often used as an example. Following their crises, the Nordic countries implemented significant growth-friendly structural reforms, and economic growth recovered even faster than before the crises. In Japan, on the other hand, no major reforms were made  with notorious consequences. Structural reforms that promote competition, employment and productivity can improve the conditions for economic growth in EU countries. At the same time, they can significantly facilitate budgetary consolidation efforts and reduce macroeconomic imbalances. Structural reforms are needed to enable economies to make effective use of the various innovations that increase production potential. Economies must also be able to adapt to changes in the external environment. The rise of emerging economies ensures that such changes will continue to exist in the future. [Slide 13] The labour market is in need of major structural reforms in many EU countries. In industrialised countries, cyclical fluctuations are often accompanied by the problem of the persistence of unemployment. Unemployment rises substantially in a recession, but only slowly decreases in a boom. In Western European countries, this problem generally seems to be more difficult than in many other industrialized countries. An encouraging example of the effectiveness of structural reforms in the labour market is Germany. At the beginning of the last decade, unpopular but significant reforms were carried out to increase the supply of labour and the functioning of the labour market was improved. Indeed, unemployment in Germany has fallen substantially since the middle of the decade. The large drop in output in 2009 only led to a slight and temporary increase in the unemployment rate in Germany. Labour market reforms played an important role in the change. Removing barriers to competition is a key way of increasing the productive potential of an economy. Increased competition will increase employment. In addition, it forces more efficient production, increases the volume of innovation and improves the conditions for productivity growth. [Slide 14] In Finland, too, various structural reforms are in a good position to significantly improve the conditions for economic growth. The potential to improve labour productivity in many industries seems to be significant. After all, productivity growth in Finland has been known to have been rapid thanks to the large role played by ICT production. Labour productivity is also high in many industrial sectors in Finland. When the share of manufacturing in value added decreases and the importance of service production rises, it will have a significant impact on future growth prospects. This is due to the fact that the productivity development of services is lower than that of industry. In addition, in many sectors of service production in Finland, labour productivity is significantly lower than in many other industrialised countries. It is important to dismantle restrictions on competition and learn from international best practices to increase productivity. Competition also opens up markets for new innovations. The Finnish economy must also be able to adapt as painlessly as possible to the changing world. The structures of the economy will be constantly in motion. At the same time, the international competitiveness of Finnish production must be ensured. In achieving these goals, wage formation plays an important role. A practice would be needed in the labour market where a common wage framework or anchor would stabilise the overall development of the national economy and, at the same time, provide flexible opportunities for agreement at local level. The starting point should be a common understanding of what level of wage increases would be possible for the sustainable development of the economy. Flexibility would be sought through sector-specific and company-specific agreements. The functioning of such a model would require the construction of an appropriate institutional framework. [Slide 15] The functioning of the financial system is important for the restructuring of the economy. The international financial system is now slowly recovering from the crisis that began a few years ago. The actions of governments and central banks played an important role in mitigating the crisis in the financial system and limiting its impact. Already from August 2007, the central banks  the European Central Bank being the first of them  took major steps to safeguard the liquidity of the banking system. As the crisis progressed, support was also given to the recapitalisation of banks. In addition, public guarantees were given for bank funding. The government also sought to help clear banks' balance sheets of problem assets. In many European countries, the amounts of money attached to these support measures exceeded 5% of GDP. The majority of the sum consists of guarantees, a large part of which is likely to be returned to the exercise of public authority. In some countries, such as Great Britain and, above all, Ireland, public subsidies have been very high. There are also countries, such as Finland, where state money has not been needed to support banks at all. The reduction of bank support measures has already begun. A rapid withdrawal from the support measures  if the stability situation allows  will eliminate the distortions of competition that may result from them and thus make the financial markets healthier. However, the financial sector will not return to normal. The crisis revealed shortcomings in the regulation and supervision of financial institutions. Large-scale regulatory and supervisory reform projects have been carried out or are in the process of being implemented due to the enormous social costs of the financial crisis. It is important to correctly select the sizing and timing of measures. For example, a significant increase in banks' capital requirements is a key and necessary part of regulatory reform. This must be done with skill so that the ability of banks to finance new economic growth in a sustainable and healthy way is not jeopardised. Overall, the government support measures put in place in Europe during the recession were unique in size and scope. They prevented the crisis in the financial system from deepening into a real economic recession. However, it seems that the most difficult and onerous solutions are still ahead of us: those that ensure the sustainability of public finances and the conditions for longer-term economic growth, as well as increasing the stability of the financial system, without prejudice to effective financial intermediation. All EU countries will benefit from a common agreement on sustainable fiscal and banking regulatory standards. Ultimately, however, economic recovery will ultimately come from micro-decisions that improve productivity and adapt to the changing division of labour in the global economy. These most important decisions are taken at national and local level, at company level, at municipal level and in labour market organisations. If these decisions are successful, our chances of successfully coping with the ongoing transformation of the global economy will improve. [Slide 16]

Title: Speech at a seminar of Kunta-asunnot Oy
text: President and CEO Erkki Liikanen's speech at Kunta-asunnot Oy's seminar 10.3.2011 . Speech . Thursday10 March2011,5:00 PM President and CEO Erkki Liikanen's speech at Kunta-asunnot Oy's seminar 10.3.2011 HOUSING AND FINANCIAL MARKETS Speech Related Patterns (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches/documents/elpuhe_10032011.pdf) (pdf) Ladies and gentlemen, The global economy is recovering from the deep recession into which it plunged after the crisis in the financial markets in autumn 2008. The recovery has been uneven and fragile, and much the same is predicted to continue. In Finland, too, total output has started to grow after a sharp drop, and unemployment has started to fall slightly. However, there is no return to the pre-crisis growth path in Finland without measures to improve productivity and increase the supply of work. Different assessments have been made of the causes of the financial crisis. A key factor has often been cited as the large savings surplus of China and other emerging economies, which channelled to developed countries such as the United States and pushed global real interest rates exceptionally low. At the same time, increased competition brought about by globalisation kept inflationary pressures in check. It allowed for low policy rates in key industrialized countries. Low interest rates, in turn, led to the search for returns on riskier investments. As a result, financial firms introduced increasingly complex investment products to the market, which were traded to investors around the world. Often they were various types of securitised assets that banks and other financial institutions in this way transferred off their balance sheets. Large-scale credit securitisation and the associated use of derivatives allowed risks to be passed on in a way that undermined the incentives for banks to ensure the quality of their lending. At the same time, the picture of the risks associated with the functioning of the entire financial system was blurred. This is how a structure was woven, which began to unravel in the second half of 2007, first as a financial turmoil and then, from the autumn of 2008, as an outright financial crisis. The close global links between the financial sector ensured that the effects were felt strongly throughout the global economy. The crisis in the financial markets was followed by a deep recession in the real economy, which led to major difficulties in the public finances of many countries. The public sector debt crisis is still ongoing. Solving it is the key challenge facing economic policy in the near future. The financial crisis of recent years has features that are common to many previous banking and financial crises. These include, above all, the sharp increase in indebtedness in the years leading up to the crisis and the central role of the real estate market - the housing and commercial real estate markets - in the emergence of the crisis. These two things are interlinked. FIGURE 2. Construction investment brisk before the crisis In the early 2000s, construction was generally lively. This was the case, among other things. Ireland and Spain. In particular, investments in housing increased rapidly. Low interest rates and an abundance of available financing - fuelled by the global factors described above - on the one hand increased the demand for housing and, on the other hand, contributed to a substantial increase in new production. Especially in the United States, owner-occupied housing was made available to new population groups through innovations in the financial system. FIGURE 3. Housing prices rose rapidly Despite the increase in housing construction, supply was unable to meet demand, which was reflected in the rapid rise in prices. In Spain, Ireland and the United Kingdom, house prices more than doubled in the 2000s before the onset of the financial crisis. In the United States, too, prices rose substantially, by more than 75%. The rise in prices clearly exceeded the general price level as well as the rate of increase in household income. The prices of many assets other than houses also rose in the years leading up to the financial crisis. This reflected the impact of low interest rates and the abundance of funding. However, in many countries, the development of the real estate market was the factor that, on the one hand, exacerbated the pre-crisis boom and, on the other hand, deepened the recession that followed. The construction of housing and other real estate is a labor-intensive activity, the growth of which often creates a large number of new jobs. The sector also uses a significant amount of intermediate products, which are often manufactured domestically. Thus, the spillover effects of construction on the surrounding national economy are great. This is also reflected in the tax revenues of general government finances. The strong boom in the real estate market is thus fuelling the growth of aggregate demand and increasing tax revenues in many different ways. Similarly, the downturn in the real estate market is negatively reflected in different parts of the economy. This negative linkage is exacerbated by the increase in indebtedness, "leveraging", which is usually inherent in booms in the real estate market. When the boom ends and the prices of housing and other real estate assets begin to fall, indebtedness is usually no longer at a sustainable level. We are then faced with a substantial reduction in indebtedness, the 'deleveraging', which will reduce aggregate demand and thus intensify the economic downturn. FIGURE 4. Households' indebtedness has grown The development of the 2000s has followed the development of indebtedness described above. In the years leading up to the financial crisis, households became heavily indebted in many countries as they invested in housing and increased their consumption. The rise in the value of dwellings and other assets contributed to the fuelling of borrowing: it was possible to take on additional debt against it. Debt was also granted to households whose creditworthiness was, by definition, questionable. This was particularly the case in the United States, where the so-called 'black market' was born. the market for subprime mortgages. As is well known, these loans later became the trigger for the financial crisis. The growth in indebtedness was not limited to households. In many countries, the construction sector also became heavily indebted as new construction projects were started and real estate development projects were launched. This is what happened, for example. Spain, where the volume of credit in the construction sector grew at an annual rate of 20-35% before the crisis. Similarly, the real estate investment industry often operated with high leverage. FIGURE 5. Banks' balance sheets grew strongly The growth in the indebtedness of households and non-financial corporations was also reflected in the strong growth in the balance sheets of financial institutions. Banks and other financial institutions financed their increased lending not only with deposits, but also increasingly with market financing, which could be very short-term. This exposed them to changes in market conditions, as the fate of the British bank Northern Rock visibly demonstrated. The bank in question had built its long-term mortgage lending on short-term market financing. When the market began to malfunction and access to finance stagnated, the bank ran into great difficulties and eventually had to be nationalised in February 2008. Financial institutions also obtain financing by securitising housing and other loans they grant. In the 2000s, this activity was very lively in the United States: before the crisis, the number of new securitisations varied in the range of around EUR 2000-3000 billion per year. In particular, subprime mortgages were securitised in abundance and sold to investors in different parts of the world. This later became a key transmission channel of the financial crisis from the US housing market to the rest of the world economy. FIGURE 6. Securitisation also increased in real estate financing in Europe At the same time, securitisation of loans for housing and commercial real estate in Europe also increased substantially, although it was significantly lower than in the United States. For example, in 2007 - on the eve of the financial crisis - around EUR 300 billion in residential and commercial real estate loans were securitised in Europe, compared with five times as high in the United States. With the financial crisis, the real estate market in many countries declined rapidly. Construction contracted significantly when no new sites were started and projects that were already underway were suspended. The situation in the housing and commercial real estate markets deteriorated particularly sharply in countries such as Spain, Ireland and the United States, where pre-crisis growth had relied heavily on the pull of the real estate market. At the same time, bankruptcies increased and the credit losses of financial institutions in the real estate sector increased. Many households, businesses and financial institutions were forced to deleverage. The result was an increase in the household saving rate and a tightening, or even a contraction, in bank lending. Deleveraging intensified the negative effects of the crisis on gdp and employment in many countries. Lessons have been learned from previous financial crises that deleveraging takes time. This is also the case this time. This slows down the recovery of many developed countries and contributes to the risk that rising unemployment will lead to an increase in structural unemployment. This would weaken the conditions for longer-term growth in real GDP. The construction sector also heated up in Finland before the crisis The financial crisis plunged the Finnish economy into recession, which was one of the deepest among developed countries in terms of loss of production. Gross domestic product contracted by more than 8% in 2009, and the unemployment rate rose by about 3 percentage points. Access to finance became more difficult and its conditions tightened, which affected the activities of many companies. However, the operational capacity of banks in Finland remained at least satisfactory throughout the crisis. Despite the difficulty in accessing finance, the most significant impact of the crisis on the Finnish economy came through a sharp contraction in international trade. Finland's exports decreased by one-fifth in 2009. The contraction in exports was reinforced by the fact that capital goods play a major role in our exports. As a result of the crisis, investment activity generally slowed down in the global economy. Similarly, the strong stock adjustment initiated in different parts of the world reduced the export deliveries of many Finnish companies. FIGURE 7. Construction brisk in Finland before the crisis Part of the reason for the depth of Finland's recession was the strong upturn in the years before the financial crisis. Between 2004 and 2007, Finland's GDP grew by an average of 4% per year. Asset prices also rose: house prices rose by an average of 6% and share prices by more than 17% on average each year. The Finnish economy began to show signs of overheating. This was reflected not only in the labor market, but also in the construction sector. Before the financial crisis, the share of construction investments in GDP rose to its highest level since the beginning of the 1990s, and even in a European comparison, construction was very lively in Finland. Especially business premises construction increased rapidly as new office and retail space was built. Instead, residential construction began to slow down even before the crisis hit, as rising mortgage rates and high house prices cut demand. Shortage of skilled labour and building materials silenced many smaller residential construction sites. In retrospect, it can be said that the calming of the housing market at the height of the economic upturn and the related decline in residential construction was a good thing for Finland's national economy and prevented the damage to our economy that was greater than what we have now seen. The strong construction of business premises in Finland in the years preceding the financial crisis can be seen as a reflection of the developments that prevailed at the same time in different parts of the global economy and global financial markets. Financing was readily available for construction projects, and often its price was cheap in relation to the expected returns. FIGURE 8. Real estate sales picked up speed in 200607 In addition to banks and international financial markets, financing was also found, for example, in domestic pension companies. In addition, the interest of foreign real estate investors in the Finnish market increased. They either bought ready-made properties or set out to finance new projects with large investments, often with considerable leverage. Indeed, the share of foreign buyers in domestic real estate transactions rose to over 50 per cent in 200607. At the same time, the net return requirements for commercial properties decreased. In practice, this meant a significant increase in real estate prices. As a result of the financial crisis, business premises construction has decreased considerably in Finland. In particular, there is plenty of free office space available. It curbs new construction. On the other hand, there are signs of picking up on the retail space side. Of course, the amount of construction is far from the level of the years before the crisis. Real estate transactions have also decreased considerably from their peak figures. Last year, only about a third of the 2007 number of transactions were made. At the same time, the share of foreign investors in transactions has shrunk. As in many other countries, it takes time for the real estate market to recover from the excesses of the years before the crisis. Fortunately, these excesses remained relatively limited in Finland. In addition, the risks were more diversified than before. In addition to domestic sources, foreign investors and their financiers have also suffered. Worrying developments in household indebtedness FIGURE 9. Fall in housing prices was short-lived As a result of the crisis, the Finnish housing market also experienced a correction, during which prices fell, trade slowed down and non-subsidised newbuilding decreased very strongly. However, the movement remained short-lived and mild. The fall in house prices was quite small, on average in the order of just over 6 per cent, and lasted only a few quarters. Prices soon started to rise again, while interest rates fell to an exceptionally low level. Newbuilding has also increased strongly, especially in terms of subsidised construction, and recently non-subsidised production has also clearly recovered. The Construction Business Cycle Group (RAKSU) estimates that the construction of more than 31,000 new dwellings will begin this year, with the main focus on non-subsidised owner-occupied housing production. FIGURE 10. Interest rates on new mortgages in Finland low The relatively mild correction in the housing market was partly due to the fact that the pre-crisis boom avoided the kind of excesses that some countries succumbed to. This was facilitated by the increase in EURIBOR rates, which in Finland was transmitted to household mortgage rates more strongly than the euro area average. In the majority of Finnish households' mortgages, the reference rate is a euribor rate or a bank prime rate that more or less follows the development of euribor rates. Thus, changes in money market interest rates in Finland are quickly transmitted to credit rates. In many other countries, on the other hand, mortgage rates tend to be pegged to longer-term market rates, which means that credit rates change less frequently. In addition, the development of long-term interest rates is influenced by many factors other than monetary policy measures. All in all, it can be said that the tightening of the ECB's monetary policy since 2005 contributed to the stability of the Finnish housing market. Similarly, the substantial easing of the ECB's monetary policy from the end of 2008 onwards was quickly and strongly transmitted to mortgage rates for Finnish households. This contributed to supporting the demand for housing and thus dampened the effects of the crisis on the housing market. Compared to countries where house prices fell sharply as a result of the crisis, the deterioration of the balance sheets of the household sector in Finland was minor and short-lived. This contributed to maintaining household consumer demand during the recession. FIGURE 11. Households' indebtedness has continued to grow While the low level of interest rates has recently supported the economy, it has contributed to the continuation of household indebtedness. In particular, the number of mortgages has increased as the housing market has picked up. Households' indebtedness ratio is estimated to have risen to nearly 110 per cent relative to disposable income during 2010. If the estimated share of households in the debts of housing companies were also included, the debt ratio would become even higher. Thus, on average, households have debts above their annual disposable income. Measured by the indebtedness ratio, Finland belongs to the middle caste in international comparison. Although the combined debt of Finnish households has become high, the average burden of debt servicing on households is currently exceptionally low. This is due to the low level of interest rates. However, debt management problems have not been completely avoided. Although problems are likely to exist in many population groups, typically they have been most prevalent in low-income, young and single-parent households. Despite these problems, the level of non-performing household loans and the resulting credit losses to banks has remained low. According to the Financial Supervisory Authority, non-performing loans accounted for approximately 0.5% of the outstanding credit in the household sector in the fourth quarter of 2010. The situation is very different from the recession of the early 1990s, when the share of non-performing loans in household credit increased more than tenfold compared to the current level. The difference is mainly explained by the level of interest rates, which are now considerably lower than in the early 1990s. It is likely that the number of debt service problems will increase from its current low level as interest rates rise. As the financial crisis of recent years has visibly demonstrated, high household indebtedness is not without risks. This is particularly the case when indebtedness is accompanied by a rapid rise in housing prices and a substantial increase in housing construction. The increase in indebtedness weakens the ability of households and, at the same time, the national economy as a whole to adapt to various shocks. At the same time, it increases banks' credit loss risks. Economic policy should therefore avoid creating incentive structures that increase household indebtedness. This applies, among other things, to the tax system. The right to deduct interest on mortgages, which is included in finland's current tax system, reduces the cost of servicing the loan to households and thus contributes to the growth of indebtedness. This, in turn, is reflected in the demand for housing and can raise the price level of apartments, as the supply of housing is usually rigid even in the longer term. There are therefore good arguments for restricting the right to deduct interest. This has recently been proposed. In its final report published in December, the tax working group chaired by Undersecretary of State Martti Hetemaki proposed a gradual reduction in the right to deduct mortgage interest. The group's presentation should be considered moderate and should be seriously considered. Financial crisis changing the regulation of financial institutions The financial crisis of recent years is leading to a significant reform of the regulation of financial markets at the global level. The new prudential provisions for banks (Basel III) were adopted at the G20 meeting in November 2010 and will gradually enter into force over a long transition period. Under the new regulations, banks will, among other things, be required to have higher quality own funds and, in addition, the minimum own funds requirement will be increased in proportion to risk-weighted receivables. In addition, banks' indebtedness is capped: a new requirement for a leverage ratio defines a minimum level of banks' own funds in relation to risk-weighted exposures. In addition to solvency, new provisions are also aimed at improving the liquidity of banks. For example, the so-called permanent fundraising requirement links the length of banks' fundraising to the length of lending. The more long-term lending a bank has, the longer its borrowing must be. This is to curb banks' over-reliance on short-term liabilities. The regulatory reforms described above will also have an impact on housing and other real estate financing and thus on the development of the real estate market in Finland. In particular, the requirement for permanent fundraising can have significant implications in this regard. Since mortgage lending - and partly other forms of real estate lending - is often long-term, banks need to raise more long-term financing to counterbalance it. This is likely to increase the average cost of bank fundraising and could push up the price of housing and other long-term loans. Ultimately, the magnitude of the impact depends, among other things, on the competitive situation between banks. Another new provision that may affect the development of the real estate market in particular concerns the leverage ratio. As mortgage-focused banks often have large but low-risk balance sheets in terms of risk-weighted capital requirements, the leverage ratio requirement is likely to require more of their own funds. This can affect the price and availability of credit issued by banks. The significance of this provision for Finland will increase considerably if it is extended to include the lending of Kuntarahoitus Oyj. The authorities are currently working on the implementation of the regulation in the EU and Finland. In recent years, municipal financing has played a key role in financing subsidized housing production, and it has carried out this task with a small amount of equity. With the leverage ratio requirement, Municipal Finance should either significantly increase its own funds or reduce its lending. Both the requirement for permanent funding and the leverage ratio requirement are likely to be refined in many details during the transition period. Their introduction will take place only in 2018. However, it is expected that banks will start preparing for the entry into force of the regulations in good time. Thus, the effects on domestic housing and other real estate lending are gradually beginning to be visible. Overall, regulatory reforms can be expected to stabilise the development of the real estate market both in Finland and elsewhere. Although the tightening of the conditions and availability of financing will, under normal circumstances, slow down economic growth, according to calculations made at the Bank of Finland, the overall impact of the reforms will be positive for the Finnish economy in the long run if the reforms succeed in reducing domestic and foreign financial crises and the resulting production losses as expected. Title: State of the economy from a central bank perspective
text: Governor Erkki Liikanen: The state of the economy from a central bank perspective. aland 13.6.2011 . Speech . Tuesday14 June 2011, 1:00 PM Dear listeners, ladies and gentlemen, Storm is something that is familiar to you alanders. The wind often whizzes around the knots out here in the archipelago. In recent years, it has also stormed the world economy. Small gusts have grown into worldwide hurricanes, and we know that the wind has not yet died down, although you can see some blue skies behind the clouds. The situation in the world economy looks quite bright, even though we are currently going through a turbulent period. Despite the rather bright outlook, there are major imbalances in the world economy and there is great uncertainty about the future. Growth in total output has recovered well in many countries from the financial and economic crisis. The developing countries, led by China, have done particularly well. The impact of the economic crisis on China's economy in particular remained limited. China's strong demand has also helped many industrialized countries get back on their feet after the deep downturn. A good example of this is Germany, whose economy is highly dependent on the export of investment goods. Germany has been able to take better advantage of the developing countries' need for increased capital in the form of machines and technology in the post-financial crisis period. This is also the case for several Nordic economies. After the unusually deep fall in gross domestic product during the crisis, Finland and Sweden have seen a strong recovery in the economy. This is partly due to countries' strong dependence on cyclical foreign trade in investment goods. All three of these countries  Germany, Finland and Sweden  have also seen a good development in domestic demand after the crisis. Economic growth is thus on a fairly broad basis, and does not depend solely on the support of developing countries. However, many industrialised countries have fared significantly worse than after the outbreak of the crisis and we are seeing increasingly clear segregation between industrialised countries that have weathered the storm and those that are still in the heart of the storm. Greece, Portugal and Ireland are still in the midst of the storm and must implement major restructuring programmes to enable better growth in the future. Confidence in the future has also remained fairly good in recent quarters. The industry's purchasing managers' index describes how purchasing managers at various companies are experiencing the economy, and as you can see, confidence among these has also improved drastically since 2009. In 2011, however, we have seen a slowdown and downward turn in the indices, especially in Japan. This, of course, reflects the tsunami and the nuclear disaster in Japan, the economic effects of which are now beginning to be discerned. Despite the recent decline, the level of the indices still indicates growth both in the euro area and in the United States. However, the prospects for the world economy are overshadowed by the public debt crisis that several European countries are going through. The ambiguities about how the crisis will develop are reflected throughout the world economy. However, it is not only some European countries that have a heavily indebted public sector. The US and Japan also have major long-term problems to contend with. The problems that need to be solved are therefore not only in Europe, but are a more general problem in the industrialised countries of the world. Although the primary purpose of the Bank of Finland and the Eurosystem is to pursue a monetary policy that promotes price stability, there are also other aspects that are important from a central bank perspective. Of particular importance is what is called macrostability. Macro-stability refers to the sum of stable financial markets and a balanced real economy. The Bank of Finland's tasks also include monitoring financial stability in Finland. So on to Finland's economy and its challenges. The global financial crisis was handled heavily with Finland. Gross domestic product fell by over 8% as world trade fell sharply and financing conditions deteriorated. The fall in total output was a stark reminder of how dependent Finland, as a small open economy, is on the economic development of other countries. Finland's economy has now grown at a good pace for just over a year, while the world economy has recovered. In addition to exports, domestic demand has also gained momentum. Both private consumption and housing investment have increased. According to the Bank of Finland's latest forecast from March (we will issue a new forecast later this week), GDP growth will continue strong after growth of 3.1% last year. GDP will not reach the level of 2008 until 2012. The deep recession will still be reflected in Finland's economy for a long time to come. The strong growth figures we are seeing now reflect the economy's recovery from the bottom of the pit. The growth potential is significantly lower in the longer term. Finland's industrial production has developed in two parts. The machinery and metal industry has developed well after the crisis, although somewhat worse at the beginning of this year. The forest industry seems to have remained at a significantly lower level of production than it was before the outbreak of the crisis. The chemical industry has developed favourably after the crisis, but growth varies greatly from quarter to quarter. Foreign trade has been important for the recovery from the global financial crisis in Finland. The fall in exports was sharp, but so was the upturn. At the beginning of this year, the growth of exports has come to a halt, but despite this, companies' confidence in the future has remained positive. The order books are almost as full as they are on average and stocks have normalized. However, the differences between the companies are large; a quarter of companies still have spare capacity in relation to demand. Households' confidence has also developed positively over the past year. At the same time, the relatively good wage growth has supported the retail sector. However, there are many aspects of household prospects that do not look so bright. One of the concerns of the Finnish economy right now is the rising indebtedness of households. We have not seen any 'deleveraging' in the household sector after the economic crisis. On the contrary, debt is still increasing. Compared with the situation in the mid-90s, the ratio of household debt to disposable income has increased drastically. Loans are getting longer and larger both in relation to income and in relation to collateral. The high and increasing debt-to-equity ratio is a phenomenon that can be seen throughout the Nordic region. More and more households in Finland are heavily indebted and are thus particularly vulnerable to changes in the economic situation. Around 17% of indebted households have a debt-to-income ratio of over 300% of their disposable income, and this share has risen sharply in recent years. Nearly 50% of households' total debt is held by these heavily indebted households. In no case can one speak of this as a marginal phenomenon. It is of the utmost importance that households and banks exercise caution in these matters. Households should take out loans according to their ability to pay and also keep in mind that interest expenses may rise. For their part, banks should not grant excessive loans to households in relation to collateral and ability to pay. Both parties, both the lender and the borrower, should exercise some caution in these matters to avoid disasters in the future. The danger of heavy debt often stems from increased risks. A household with high indebtedness is not as flexible and cannot accommodate as much damage as a household with lower indebtedness. Heavily indebted households are often particularly exposed to risks. In Finland, almost all housing loans are tied to short-term market interest rates, 1-month, 3-month and 12-month euribor, as well as banks' own prime rates. In part, this means that monetary policy is being conveyed quickly and efficiently in Finland, which is a positive thing. But the other side of the coin is that rising interest rates are affecting Finnish loan customers faster than loan customers in most other euro area countries, where home loans are mainly tied to significantly longer interest rates. As market interest rates fall, Finnish households will benefit correspondingly, but fewer risks stem from this phenomenon. One of the biggest risks for a household is always the risk of unemployment. When you become unemployed, your income decreases and thus also the ability to manage your borrowing costs. The larger the loan, the greater the threat posed by unemployment. Unemployment can measure the human cost of a crisis. The consequences of a recession are often protracted and painful for households through this channel. Especially from a central bank perspective, the risk of unspent borrowing costs is an important aspect of unemployment, as this is a channel through which the problems of unemployment can spread further in society via the financial sector. Unemployment rose relatively little during the last economic crisis, but at present it looks as if the decline would be rather slow. Unemployment has now been hovering on the spot between 8 and 9% for some time. In practice, this means that in April of this year we had 207,000 unemployed. In April 2008, there were 55000 fewer unemployed. In a small country like Finland, this is a lot. In the context of a recession, long-term unemployment usually rises with a certain delay because you have to have been unemployed for a year to be counted as long-term unemployed. Consequently, Finland's long-term unemployment started to rise later than unemployment and no decline has yet been discernible. The interesting question at the moment is also how long-term unemployment will develop and what kind of structural problems arise from this. Closely related to rising indebtedness is the development of the housing market, which is also relevant for households, as households are active players in the housing market and a large part of household wealth is linked to the housing market. Finland, like many other countries, has seen a very strong increase in real house prices in the 2000s. Over the period 2000-2008, real house prices rose by around 50%. In an international comparison, this does not seem like much. For example, the development in Sweden during this time period has been stronger than in Finland. Compared to Germany, which otherwise (but not in the housing market) has a fairly similar economic structure as Finland, however, the development is breathtaking. What, then, has enabled such a rise in house prices? The explanations are the same in most countries that have seen a sharp upturn in the housing market; The possibility of getting larger and longer loans, as well as low interest rates and margins, as well as the fact that supply has not really kept up with demand, have all contributed to the development. A general over-optimism about their own economic situation and its future prospects has probably also led some households to make what they perceive in retrospect as non-optimal economic decisions. Risks have been undervalued and one's own future income flow overvalued. However, the development of house prices can largely be explained by the rise in the income level of wage and salary earners. As can be seen from the picture, house prices in relation to incomes are not so much above the historical average at the moment. Compared to the rent trend, you can see that house prices have soared significantly more. Part of the rise in prices can be explained by too narrow supply. Especially in the Helsinki Metropolitan Area, the lack of land is a problem, which has also contributed to the rise in the price of housing. As you can see in this graph, land prices have risen significantly faster than home prices across the country. This is a long-term structural problem in the housing market that is particularly visible in the capital region, a problem that is also found in, for example, Stockholm, and which should be addressed. In Finland, we managed to avoid the worst excesses in the housing market in connection with the economic crisis. Strong growth in construction activity slowed well before the outbreak of the crisis due to, among other things, tightening monetary policy and labour shortages and high construction costs. Thus, we avoided the worst overheating in the housing market. In retrospect, we can state that this was successful. However, the fall in house prices was short. Construction activity slowed rapidly, leading to a widening gap between supply and demand. At the same time, expansionary monetary policy supported the economic situation of households. House prices quickly turned steeply upwards, growing by almost 9% last year. As it takes time to build houses, we are only now approaching a situation where the supply of housing is starting to normalize, which should help to calm down housing price growth going forward. Nevertheless, the risks in the housing market are real. Household indebtedness is only increasing and house prices have risen sharply in the last two years. The problems have not been resolved. Under-Secretary of State Martti Hetemaki's working group has proposed as a measure that the right to deduct borrowing costs in taxation should be abolished. We support the proposal but, at the same time, believe that this will hardly lead to a significant reduction in the level of high indebtedness. Inflation is particularly important from a central bank perspective. The primary mandate of the European System of Central Banks is to keep inflation close to but slightly below 2% over the medium term. In April, inflation in the euro area was 2.8%, i.e. well above the medium-term objective, and there is upward pressure on inflation overall. Inflation has gained momentum mainly due to the fact that commodity prices have skyrocketed as well as food prices. But the price of service and industrial products has also increased in recent months. However, it is expected that inflation will fall back below 2% in 2012 as a result of a fall in commodity market prices. Market inflation expectations also indicate confidence that inflation will fall. Inflation in Finland has always been above 3% this year. Inflation in Finland is thus higher than in the euro area on average. In Finland, food and service prices have risen faster than in the euro area on average. The tax changes implemented in Finland in 2010 also partly explain the differences in inflation. The Governing Council has raised interest rates once in the spring, unlike the other major central banks, which have not raised their interest rates. Many central banks have been wary of tightening monetary policy, others have again been more active, especially smaller central banks. For example, Sveriges Riksbank has raised its key interest rate in several replays to stabilise inflation. As a result of the economic downturn, Finland's public finances weakened sharply. Although the growth we can now see increases tax revenues and reduces cyclical public spending, the government deficit will remain large unless new fiscal measures are taken. At the same time, the entire public sector deficit will continue to exist. When the effects and challenges of ageing are added to this equation in the future, public sector consolidation is already beginning to be urgently needed, and consolidation needs are becoming apparent. According to the Ministry of Finance's assessment, Finland's sustainability gap is approximately 5% of GDP. The Bank of Finland's assessment is similar. The success of public sector consolidation depends a lot on how it is implemented. Priority should be given to those approaches that impair economic growth and employment as little as possible. This should be taken into account especially in solutions related to taxation. In addition to this, the credibility of the chosen stategin is important. If the plans are credible, the threat of future tax austerity is reduced at the same time. This supports consumption and investment at this time. Although Finland's economic outlook looks quite good, there are many challenges in the near future. The public sector sustainability gap has grown so large that structural changes and a reassessment of general government expenditure and revenue are now needed. Ageing will play a central role in Finland's near future. The ageing of the population will reduce the growth prospects of the economy and the working-age population will decrease, while more and more personnel are needed for health care and other health care services. An important aspect is the sustainability of public finances as the population ages. How can we prepare for aging? Labour productivity must be increased in basic public services. This means better and more efficient use of information and communication technologies and the development of new ways of working. The second central element of this equation is the prolongation of professional careers  both at the beginning, at the end and in the middle. In addition to these challenges, the rise of developing countries  although it presents great opportunities  also means increased competition in several markets both in service and more traditional goods markets. At the same time, the core of demand is shifting further and further away from Finland. This entails major adaptation needs for many sectors and occupational groups  and thus for the entire Finnish economy. Especially for industrial production, which fell sharply during the recession, the challenges are great. Even in such circumstances, structural changes can support economic growth. Economy microstructure should be constantly in upheaval so that companies can continuously adapt to the new environment. These are also important for wage formation. As industry's share of the value increase decreases, the importance of the service industry increases. According to existing research, productivity in several service industries is significantly lower in Finland than in many other industrialised countries. This can be seen as a possibility. In these sectors, it should be relatively easy to raise productivity levels by learning from internationally best practice and by removing barriers to competition. Examples of obstacles to competition are regulations regarding planning and regulations that limit business activities. We live in a time of economic break. New solutions and structures are being devised. At the same time, the work is far from finished. The public sector, households and many companies have major challenges ahead of them. One of the challenges is the high level of debt and what should and can be done about it. None of the challenges have clear and easy solution options. At international level, the public debt crisis is still extremely worrying and the challenges of the financial sector have not disappeared anywhere. In addition to these problems, the prevention of systemic risks is a major, but important, challenge for the authorities going forward. It is a question of finding tools that will succeed in preventing the crisis we have been living through from repeating itself without strangling economic growth. At the same time, it is important to create the conditions for new innovations and the development of potential business ideas, which can increase competitiveness in the long term. Thanks!
