Title: Mannerheim and reconciliation
text: Director-General Erkki Liikanen: Mannerheim and reconciliation. Headquarters Symposium, Mikkeli 6.7.2012. . Speech . Friday 6 July 2012, 10:00 AM Erkki Liikanen: Mannerheim and reconciliation Headquarters Symposium, Mikkeli 6.7.2012 at 10 a.m. On February 26, 1919, Regent Mannerheim visited the Mikkeli Lyceum. He had accepted the position two months earlier. Mannerheim spoke to all the Lyceum students: "Let the white snows we see around us today be, and the blue sky curving over them as a metaphor for the moods of the youth; snow, in which no traces of the passer-by are yet visible, and a high trace of the sky, which is not obscured by clouds. May the minds of our youth be as pure and their thoughts just as high. That is the future of our fatherland, the future that we who have lived through the events of the present, wish our beloved Finland bright and happy". Kari Selen states in his book Mannerheim's Speeches that the event certainly pleased schoolchildren, because the regent promised after his speech that the following Monday would be a day off. Mannerheim was still speaking at dinner in the evening at the Seurahuone in Mikkeli with arrangements: "I've already enjoyed the hospitality of this city before. It was then, when there was still a struggle for the future of this country." At the same time, he thanked him for the peace of mind he received in Mikkeli. So that's how it was in February 1919. Between 1964 and 1966, almost half a century later, the Mikkeli City Board and Council discussed the location of the Mannerheim statue on several occasions. In October 1966, it was decided to place it on the Greater Savo Square. At that time, I was a first-year high school student at the same Mikkeli Lyceum where Mannerheim had spoken in 1919. Our history teacher Heikki Palmen commented in class on the council's deliberations on the matter. In 2003, the issue was raised again in the city bodies. Now the council decided to place it in The Government Square. My intention today is to seek answers to four questions: 1) How was national unification after the Civil War and before the Winter War possible? 2) What was Mannerheim's contribution to national defragmentation? 3) Why were the wounds of the civil war still open for so long again after the war? 4) Why was the location of mannerheim's statue such a difficult question in Mikkeli? HeikkiYlikangas wrote in 1993 that the Civil War is neutral compared to the concepts of war of independence, civil war or class war. That is why I am talking about the Civil War today. The overall picture of the Civil War began to take shape in historical research when Jaakko Paavolainen's works Political Violence in Finland appeared. The first part, The Red Terror, was published in 1966 and the second part, The White Terror, in 1967. The books gave the number of victims. I still remember when heikki Palmen, who has read the aforementioned extensively, told me that they were new studies of history for him. He had thought that at least as many, if not more, whites had died. I borrowed the books from the city library and plunged into the stages of the national tragedy. Even later, Paavolainen published the studies Prison Camps in Finland and The National Tragedy. When Jaakko Paavolainen died a few years ago, Professor Timo Soikkanen wrote that Paavolainen's works were revolutionary both in the study of history about 1918 and in the deconstruction of the associated trauma. He put the numbers of casualties killed in and after the war approximately in place. Vaino Linna's trilogy Here Under the North Star had been published earlier, from 1959 to 1962. It was not a study of history, but it was a great literary trilogy of the stages of the nation. The castle also had a significant influence on the discussion of the events of 1918. Immediately after the end of the Civil War, Kyosti Kalliopuhui, the central leader of the Peasants' Union, in the Nivala Church. The line of the rock was reconciliation, not revenge. "We must create a Finland in which there are neither red nor white, but only Finns who love their motherland, citizens of the Republic of Finland, who feel that they are members of society and who enjoy themselves here," said Kallio on May 5, 1918. In the 1917 elections, 92 social democrats or socialists had been elected to parliament. After the civil war, some of them were imprisoned, some had fled to Russia and some did not feel able to participate in parliamentary activities under those circumstances. Only two attended parliamentary sessions. The Parliament was dissolved and the last session of the Stub Parliament was held two days after Mannerheim's visit to Mikkeli. The new Parliament met in April 1919. There, the Social Democratic Party had 80. The Agrarian League had 42 representatives, the Coalition Party 28, the Progressive Party 26 and the Swedish People's Party 22. In July, Regent Mannerheim confirmed the new form of government, and a week later K.J. Stahlberg defeated Mannerheim by a vote of 143 to 50 in parliament. Mannerheim was supported by the National Coalition Party and the Swedish People's Party. The Progressive Party, the Agrarian League and the Social Democratic Party voted for Stahlberg, who became the first President of the Republic of Finland. The attitude towards Mannerheim was deeply divided. He had strong supporters and unyielding opponents. Political conditions were unstable. At first, governments sat for a hundred to two hundred days. Conflicts between the bourgeois parties were related to the aftermath of the civil war and the language issue. The controversy over whether Finland should be a republic or a kingdom had also deeply divided. Under Stahlberg's leadership, the republicans and those who emphasized the importance of reconciliation were neck and neck in the years after the Civil War. It was not easy for everyone to adapt to it. During Stahlberg's term, Mannerheim visited the Presidential Palace only once for dinner and even then left immediately after the meal had ended. Mannerheim took a very different position on many key issues than the president and the government. Mannerheim's speeches at the end of 1919 and in 1920 were sharp. He did not approve of the large-scale amnesty for red prisoners, nor the attempt to start peace negotiations with Soviet Russia. "Mannerheim seemed to be more on the right than the right," it was said. Many also felt that Mannerheim was ready to lead a military force from Finland in support of the troops of Russian white generals soviet. Mannerheim sharply criticized the government's amnesty policy in November 1920: "You will understand that when everything that has been bought by heavy victims within two short years is traded away as a change among the state parties, that when we are ready to open the borders of the country to thousands of those from whose bullets our best sons fell". The severely scarred wound was associated not only with the civil war itself, but especially with executions and prison camps. According to Paavolainen, the victims of the Red Terror rose to 1800 white. Whites, on the other hand, died as victims of terror a total of 8400 Reds, including 364 underage girls. The darkest chapter in the tragedy were the prison camps. As many as 13500 Finns died of disease and malnutrition in the prison camps. Military and civilian authorities blamed each other for what happened after the war. The Finnish Civil War lasted a hundred days and the total number of victims rose to 1% of the population. The Spanish Civil War lasted a thousand days and, according to new studies, the total number of victims rose to between 1.5% and 2% of the population. Both civil wars were total conflicts and they can be compared to each other," says Jukka Kekkonen, Professor of Legal History. A red prison monument was unveiled in Fellman's Park in Lahti 60 years after the Civil War in the summer of 1978. President of the Republic Urho Kekkonen also honoured the occasion with his presence. The unveiling ceremony of the monument was attended by 30,000 citizens. Among them were many who were in the same place as prisoners in the spring of 1918. We went there from Mikkeli by bus. Journalist and municipal politician Maire Haapasalo was on the trip. In Lahti, the impression was left that his family had some connection to the events of Hennala and Fellman. Maire Haapasalo's appreciation is shown by the fact that in 1986 the City of Mikkeli awarded her the prestigious Pro Mikkeli medal. His spouse was long-time Member of Parliament and Minister of the 2nd Government of Ahti Karjalainen K.F. Haapasalo. What was Mannerheim's contribution to the treatment of red prisoners? Matti Klinge says that Mannerheim was absent from Finland since 1.6.1918. That summer, prison camp deaths were at their worst. According to Klinge, Mannerheim had tried to prevent "white terror" during the war and opposed the mass imprisonment of the Reds. In March 1918, he issued an order according to which those who surrendered in the conquest of Tampere must be treated as prisoners of war. There were many foreigners in Tampere who were there to see the events. Mannerheim understood the danger they brought to the country's reputation. In the final stages of the war, Mannerheim had banned summary executions. Each prisoner's case had to be heard in court. However, the executions continued in a confused situation. In his memoirs, Mannerheim wrote that he had proposed to the Senate that ordinary Red Guards, even those who had been imprisoned with a gun in hand, be released from the camps without further ado. Only for serious crimes had to be brought to justice, The Minister of Justice of the time, OnniTalas, vehemently denied Mannerheim's claim. According to him, Mannerheim did not propose the release of prisoners in the spring of 1918. According to Talas, his will would have been fulfilled. Two episodes were related to Mannerheim and the red prisoners after the capture of Tampere. Mannerheim had visited a military hospital with white and red wounded. He reportedly accidentally handed out badge ribbons to the Reds as well. It became clear at the end of the round. He got really angry. Mannerheim had commanded the Reds apart, even into the street. In the end, the order was watered down. The history of the Finnish Red Cross, written by Gunnar Rosen, also tells about another case. A couple of weeks after the previous event, a new order for the day was issued in Mannerheim's name. The impact of food shortages had begun to be seen. The order of the day stipulated that the daily ration of bread and flour for the wounded was 250 grams for the whites and 75 grams for the reds. A.J. Palmen, the chief medical officer who had twice been imprisoned by the Red Guards, protested sharply and wrote that the order was indefensible from the point of view of medical care. He continued: "As I cannot accept the procedure described above, and in no case, as a doctor, do I consider myself capable of taking part in the torture of defeated enemies, I may hereby declare that I will cease to function in the hospital entrusted to me if the procedure laid down in the order is followed". Many doctors, even because of their social backgrounds, were sympathizers of whites, but they adhered to medical ethics in their work and dealt with victims in the same way. In his book Mannerheim, Veijo Merit sums up the discussion about the treatment of red prisoners: When there was constant controversy about who bore the responsibility, no one did. At the same time, hunger and disease killed a startling number of Finnish women and men in prison camps. The prime ministers who led the governments of the early years of independent Finland came from the Agrarian League, the Progress Party or the National Coalition Party. In 1925, LauriKristian Relander of the Agrarian League was unexpectedly elected president of the second Republic. At the end of 1926, kallio's 2nd government was overthrown. The bourgeois parties could not agree on a new government. The formation of a government that would have included left and right is out of the question at the time. In the end, President Relander gave the task of forming a government to the leader of the largest parliamentary group, Vaino Tanner. As expected, Tanner received a negative response from other parties. Relander urged to continue and was even ready to accept a one-party government. Relander told Tanner that the trend so far was unhealthy, the nation was divided, and the events of 1918 still played some part in dealing with politics. It had to be taken away. This is how the Tanner government was formed. Professor Vaino Voionmaa became Minister for Foreign Affairs. For the first time, a woman, Miina Sillanpaa, joined the board. The government's proposal for an amnesty law was one of the most pressing issues. In the end, by a vote of 96 to 94, a motion was passed that pardoned the rest who had been convicted solely of participation in or in connection with the Civil War. Those who suffered the punishment were restored to civic trust. When President Relander fell ill in May 1927, he was in office. President Tanner received a parade of the Defense Establishment, which was also attended by units of the Guards Corps. The issue was the subject of heated debate. Tanner said he had done his duty and therefore the matter did not cause him any conscientious objections. After losing the presidential election in 1919, General Mannerheim was excluded from state duties. Kari Selen stated that Mannerheim was, however, in a way an "outsider" in Finland. He had returned to Finland after 30 years in Russia. The only group to which he firmly belonged were the white generals. In 1918, Sophie Mannerheim, the general's sister, had started to assist, among other things, orphaned children of the Red Guards. He founded a nursing home for them, which was named Children's Castle. He got his brother involved in the idea of creating a nationwide child welfare organization, which happened in 1920. When the organization held its first meeting, Mannerheim said in his opening speech that he was hesitant to take the initiative because he was unfamiliar with the field. Sophie Mannerheim, on the other hand, knew the history of child welfare work. It originated from the call-ups during the Boer War, which revealed in a horrific way a different picture of the health of the people that had been thought. Sophie Mannerheim was similarly awakened by the misery of remote areas. Mannerheim also started a long term later as chairman of the Finnish Red Cross. How did the general come to prevail in this position? The initiator was Richard Faltin, Finland's first military doctor. He was started his career in Krasnoye Selo, Ingria. When the Russian-Japanese War broke out in 1904, Faltin had travelled to Manchuria as chief physician. There was one ambulance and three military hospitals from the Finns. In the great battle of Mukden, the losses amounted to 90,000 men. One day after the fighting, an exhausted, young cavalry lieutenant colonel with a high fever appeared in the Red Cross ambulance. His name Carl Gustaf Mannerheim. Faltin took care of Mannerheim's health. When the same Faltin, who was still Mannerheim's friends, asked him in 1922 to be the chairman of the Red Cross, Mannerheim did not feel able to refuse. Mannerheim also travelled abroad in Red Cross duties. Among other things, he participated in the meetings of the International Red Cross in Geneva. The union was operated by two commissions, one focused on peace, and the other on wartime. Mannerheim led both. He also created the field hospital system that was ready when the Winter War broke out. At that time, the Red Cross was not yet the current NGO. District and basic organizations were created only in the 1950s. In 1928, Mannerheim took two initiatives. First of all, he proposed the establishment of a Red Cross hospital and donated a considerable sum as a nest egg. The hospital was completed with donated funds in 1932. Mannerheim spoke at the inauguration and President Per-Erik Svinhufvud was also present. Mannerheim stated that in the hospital 'to train the most competent forces for the tasks which, according to the lofty principles of the Geneva Convention, are the responsibilities of the Red Cross societies in the event of epidemics, war and persecution'. The hospital is known as Toolo Hospital and is part of the Hospital District of Helsinki and Uusimaa. The initiative of the second concerned the holding of a series of radio presentations. Its purpose would be to "awaken from one's own, small hobbies, strife and strife, and to spread among them civil peace and a sense of community." Mannerheim continued as chairman of the Finnish Red Cross, even though he had to sit full-time in the General Staff from 1931 onwards. In December 1934, Italy invaded Abyssinia (Ethiopia). It was not until October 1935 that the League of Nations found Italy guilty. Abyssinia needed help. The Finnish Red Cross sent a unit there, headed by the aforementioned military surgeon Robert Faltin. The Board of the Finnish Red Cross arranged a farewell party, where Mannerheim spoke to Faltin:  .. we admire the decision you made and want to spend the evening with you before you leave...... I certainly don't want to give you any advice for your trip...... but if, on behalf of the Red Cross, I may express the wish that, having transcended the boundaries of the European cultural circle, you will try, as far as possible for you, to leave behind your dressing personal modesty, which, as part, is associated with your charm, and that in its place you will adopt the sense of race and self-consciousness which fall under the burden of the white man in his dealings with other races ........... we must also try to inspire respect alongside the richer countries and organisations that have been more favoured by the circumstances." Of Mannerheim's surviving public speeches of the time, he gave several of them at events organised by the Finnish Red Cross. Mannerheim had moved to St. Petersburg at the age of 20 in 1887 and returned from there in 1917, when he was 50 years old. For three decades, his contacts with Finland had been limited to a small group of Finland-Swedes. Through the Finnish Red Cross and the Finnish League for Child Welfare, Mannerheim gained a more diverse picture of Finland and the Finns. It may have had a bearing on his perceptions and attitudes. The Red Cross came to the fore even after the war, when the General Staff of the Finnish Defence Forces had donated its assets to the Finnish Red Cross before the abolition. It included property acquired with state money. The Red Cross stuck to the letter of the will. When the negotiations between the Finnish Defence Forces and the Finnish Red Cross reached an impasse, Mannerheim was still looking for help in finding a compromise. In addition to his organizational duties, he represented the Finnish state at a few international events. In November 1932, he attended the commemoration of Gustav Adolf's 300th birthday in Lutzen. There Mannerheim gave Finland's greeting. On the way, he also stayed in Berlin, where The Finnish Envoy was Vaino Vuolijoki. After talking with the general, Vuolijoki wrote to Vaino Tanner that Mannerheim is much better than his reputation and recommended that the Social Democrats should not reproach him too much. The middle-group governments, which were aiming for the middle ground of politics, and also the minority government of the Social Democrats, suffered a setback in the atmosphere of the Great Depression in 1929. The focus of politics shifted to the right. At its core was the anti-communist movement. Svinhufvud returned first as prime minister in 1930 and then as president. According to Timo Soikkanen, Lapuan Liike tore apart the budding defragmentation. The tense mood is illustrated by the fact that, in the run-up to the 1933 elections, the right wing demanded a ban on the Social Democratic Party for treasonous activities. The Social Democrats, on the other hand, demanded that the IKL's relationship with the banned Lapua movement be clarified and that attention be paid to the relations between the IKL and the Coalition Party. Because of this, there was little time left for defragmentation, only the years 19341939 before the wars. In 1967, Kalle Lehmus, who headed the Information Department of the General Staff, published The Unknown Mannerheim, which brought many more nuances. According to him, in the 1930s Mannerheim sought contacts with the social democratic governments of the Nordic countries. One of the objectives was to de-escalate tensions in Finland. In January 1935, Mannerheim held a press conference in which he emphasized the necessity of a Nordic orientation. According to Linden, there were two reasons for this. First of all, Mannerheim believed that anchoring Finland in the direction of neutral Sweden and Norway would convince the Soviet Union that Finland has no intention of supporting the possible belligerent efforts of some superpower, mainly Germany, against the Soviet Union. Another reason for domestic politics; it would make it easier to achieve language peace and, at the same time, cooperation with countries dominated by the labour movement could de-escalate conflicts in Finland as well. In December 1935, parliament adopted a position paper on the Nordic trend. For the right wing, it meant, above all, defence policy, and for the Swedish People's Party and the Social Democrats, it also meant foreign, economic and cultural policy. In 1937, Kyosti Kallio was elected President of the Republic. Svinhufvud returned to Luumaki. Kallio paved the way for red mullet cooperation. The government of Prime Minister A.K.Cajander was the first in which the left and bourgeois parties were together. The government included the Agrarian League, the Social Democrats and part of the Progressive Party. The first red mullet government was a significant step towards the unification of the nation. The right-wing opposition spoke of "the return of the blood flows of 1918." Another factor that laid the foundation for the unification of the nation was strong economic development. It enabled the red mullet government to pursue a reform policy. Finland's national product grew at the top rate in Europe towards the end of the decade. On May 30, 1937, Mannerheim organized a dinner at his home. Among the dinner guests were also two ministers, Vaino Tanner and Vaino Voionmaa. Mannerheim had stated that they were the first social democrats in his home. This was 19 years after the end of the Civil War. According to Tanner' s account, Mannerheim tried to get into a conversation with them for two, but because of the other guests, it did not work out. However, there was one thing Tanner had noted down. When he had asked Mannerheim about the danger of war, he had replied: "War is in some ways a bit like what was once in St. Petersburg with Yevropeiskaja Gastinitsa (a well-known place of restaurants and entertainment). We didn't usually decide to go there specifically, but we always had to go there in some way." On June 4, 1937, Mannerheim turned 70 years old. It was one kind of measure of national unity. The celebration was mainly a non-socialist holiday, but there were hardly any gravelly voices from the left either. Minister Hannes Ryoma was part of the government's congratulatory delegation, and The Speaker of parliament Vaino Hakkila read the parliament's petition at the citizens' party. The changed tone of Mannerheim's speeches was also noticed on the left. Vaino Tanner spoke in Naantali in July 1938 on behalf of the workers: "In its (labour) opinion, bitterness towards the victor of the war, the white General Mannerheim, has evaporated. On the contrary, it has acknowledged his many manly statements in recent years." It is known that Mannerheim and Tanner's views on the possibility of war diverged. In August 1939, Germany and the USSR, the old enemies, concluded a non-aggression pact. It seemed like a bombshell to the opinions of the parties. The extreme right and the communists had justified their policies on the opposing side, but in this way the mother countries betrayed their supporters. Vaino Hakkila wrote polemically that the Berlin-Moscow agreement caused such a "short circuit in the heads of the "supporters of dictatorial doctrines" that indeed all the lights went out. The result was a truly miserable confusion and the collapse of the ideology." The morale of the communists was also deeply influenced by the persecutions carried out by Stalin in Karelia, in which a considerable number of Finnish noble brothers were executed. The far right, on the other hand, collapsed its bottom when Germany invaded stub-Czechoslovakia. It was considered to be directed against all small states and their rights. Lehmus said that Mannerheim had made two decisions with his own authority, by which he was expressly trying to promote reconciliation. First of all, he decided to end the celebration of victory in the War of Independence, which took place on May 16. The Winter War had shown the unity of the nation, and there was no longer any desire to celebrate in public the events that aroused bitter memories in a large part of the population. Instead, a day of remembrance for the fallen began on May 19. Secondly, he also laid a wreath on the graves of the Reds. It was also a recognition to those who fought for the Reds or otherwise acted that they, too, had acted for their convictions with the aim of an independent Finland. Thus, the stigma of treason was removed. Perhaps the biggest and most visible amicable settlement, however, was the January engagement of 23.1.1940. At that time, in the midst of the Winter War, employers issued a declaration in which they recognized trade unions as counterparties. The Parties agree that they will henceforth endeavour to reach an agreement through negotiations. The midwife of the January engagement was K.A. Fagerholm. Lehmus, among others, also claims that Mannerheim and Rudolf Walden, minister of defence and director of the United Paper Mills, were key background influencers. Just over two years later, Mannerheim turned 75. A small-scale birthday party was held in a train carriage in Immola. The birthday is also remembered for the fact that Hitler unexpectedly went to congratulate Mannerheim. That conversation was recorded and the tape has been used a lot because Hitler spoke in a "normal" voice. Before that, however, the President and the government had offered their congratulations and told Mannerheim about the title of field marshal granted to Mannerheim. After that, it was the parliament's turn to congratulate. At that time, the Bureau announced that parliament had decided to give Mannerheim his own home in Helsinki. This is how the Kaivopuisto apartment became Mannerheim's property. Next in line for congratulations were representatives of the Central Organisation of Finnish Trade Unions SAK, the Metalworkers' Union and the Woodworkers' Union. Under the leadership of Eero A. Wuori, President of the Central Organisation of Finnish Trade Unions (SAK), they said the following: "The working people have attached particular importance to your determined efforts, which have been aimed, in particular, at erasing the traces of the 1918 cases from among our people. The working people see that, by doing so, you have been the influential builder of the united front that has been a fundamental prerequisite for the success of the struggles of our people in recent years." Mannerheim attached special importance to the congratulations. He said: "Nothing pleases me more than seeing here with me representatives of the Finnish working people, who make up a huge part of the constructive power of our people. Your beautiful greeting gives me a very special joy and at the same time the satisfaction of seeing in it a testimony of the fulfillment of my dreams and aspirations from decades ago. The contribution of the Finnish working population to the fierce struggle of recent years, both at the front and in the factories and jobs in their home region, deserves great recognition." After the trade union movement, it was the turn of the Finnish Defence Forces, the Union of Brothers in Arms, the Knights of the Mannerheim Cross and the Uusimaa Dragoon Regiment. The greeting from the trade union movement was immediately after the state, which probably shows its great importance to Mannerheim. Why, then, in the 1960s, even in Mikkeli, did the placement of Mannerheim's statue open the wounds of a difficult civil war? This is a question I have often wondered about. One explanation may be given by Timo Soikkanen, to which I referred above. Research data on the civil war was just coming. The traumas were unraveled. A prerequisite for this was correct knowledge. The knowledge base came only later. But something even more had to do with the events in Mikkeli. Eino Liikanen was born in 1925, so he made it to the front during the Continuation War. I remember asking him twice who he had voted for. First in 1958 parliamentary elections. He said that he had voted for A.F.Oar, a silent general, who was a candidate in the Mikkeli constituency. In the 1962 presidential election, he voted for Urho Kekkonen. In 1964, by a couple of close friends, he was asked to stand as the candidate of the Social Democrats in the municipal elections. He was elected to the Mikkeli City Council the same autumn. During the first term, the location of mannerheim's statue was discussed by the council. This became a major point of contention. I asked dad who this was so important to in the council group. He mentioned Maire Haapasalo's name. He appreciated Maire Haapasalo for her general education and willingness to speak. What was Mairen Haapasalo's connection to the events of the Civil War? This has long been a matter of concern. Three weeks ago, I got in touch with his son, Chief Physician Hannu Haapasalo, who lives and works in Tampere. The conversation I had with him and the subsequent contact with the National Archives has brought a response. Hannu Haapasalo said that his mother, Maire Haapasalo, os. Virta was originally from Aitolahti, Tampere. Maire's father, Kaarlo Virta, was the secretary of the Aitolahti Workers' Association, who did not participate in armed activities in the Civil War. However, around the time of the takeover of Tampere, he and his wife Hilja and five children had to flee Tampere. They were arrested on the way and the whole family was transferred to a prison camp in Fellman's field in Lahti. Maire was the youngest of the children, at that time only 2 years old. After a couple of days, the mother and children were released, but the father was taken to Ekenas. Red Guards and participants in the Social Democrats' party activities were transferred to the Ekenas prison camp. On 21 August 1918, Kaarlo Virta was convicted of aiding and abetting treason in the Lappeenranta branch of the State Criminal Court. The sentence was 8 years in a disciplinary chamber. After that, he was still sentenced to forfeit civil trust for 12 years. The decision can be found in the minutes of the State Criminal Court in the National Archives. In the summer of 1918, there were almost 9000 prisoners in the Ekenas red prison camp. Of them, almost 3000  one in three  died of starvation or disease. Kaarlo Virta survived that wave of death. He was pardoned in January 1920. The family moved to Tammela in Tampere, where Virta continued to work as a carpenter. A sixth child was born to the family, Maire's young sister, who passed away shortly after her birth. Neither the father's sentence nor the prison camp time was talked about in front of the children. There was silence about the painful experiences. Finally, my answer to the four questions that were asked at the beginning. How was defragmentation possible? The process of reconciliation of the nation began gradually after the civil war. It was active in the Agrarian League, led by SanteriAlkio and Kyosti Kallio, and the Progressive Party, whose candidate K.J.Stahlberg also served as the first president. The share of the Social Democrats was natural. Lapua's movement halted development. In the second half of the 1930s, national unification gained momentum again. The first government was formed in which the bourgeois parties and the social democrats cooperated. Its work was facilitated by strong economic development. In the end, events in world politics collapsed the bottom of the extremists. And what wasmannerheim's contribution?In the 1920s he was first and foremost a general of the whites. He divided the people. The situation gradually changed in the 1930s. In 1931, Mannerheim became chairman of the Defense Council, who would serve as commander-in-chief during a possible war. In the mid-1930s, he spoke in favor of the Nordic trend. This, in turn, required contacts with the social democratic governments that led the other Nordic countries. After that, he cautiously but consistently took measures in favor of defragmentation. There were also bold solutions for which no one else's authority would have been sufficient. The main ones came during the war. Why did the wounds of the civil war remain open for so long even after the war? I agree with Timo Soikkanen that the series of investigations that only started with the work of Jaakko Paavolainen has brought a knowledge base to replace the rumours and horror stories characteristic of civil wars. That work began very late, only 50 years after the Civil War. Why was it so difficult in Mikkeli in the late 1960s, even though this was the focus of the fighting? People who lost those closest to them or had to suffer greatly as victims of the Civil War are a different matter. Many of them felt that they had experienced unreasonable injustice. In the light of research, undeniably so often. That experience can only be alleviated in time, if that too. And an outsider is not capable of being a judge. Thank you!

Title: Speech on the separation of banking activities
text: Governor Erkki Liikanen, speech on the separation of banking activities, Paris 15.11.2012 . Speech . Thursday15 November 2012,1:00PM AMF Annual Conference, Paris, November 15, 2012 11:00 a.m.-12:30 p.m.; Separation of banking activities Governor Erkki Liikanen: The Expert Group on Structural Reform of the EU Banking Sector, which I chaired, submitted its report to Commissioner Michel Barnier a month ago. The Task of the Expert Group was to examine the need for structural reforms of the EU banking sector, with the aim of establishing a system that is safe, stable and efficient. After taking into account the other ongoing reforms of the banking system and taking into account the lessons learned from the last crisis, we have arrived at a positive response: these structural reforms are indeed necessary. The report we have submitted contains a series of recommendations and our main proposals relate to how banks should be structured in the future. We propose to split the banks into separate legal entities. If a bank wishes to engage in significant trading activities, in the form of trading activities on its own account or market making activities, these activities will have to be separated from its deposit banking activities, grouping them into a separate subsidiary dedicated to these trading activities, known as a trading entity. The latter should be financed and capitalised separately from the deposit bank. Our proposals have generally received constructive reactions. Of course, we had to deal with many questions and some criticisms as well. The separation we advocate has an obvious purpose: By isolating it, it is a question of protecting the deposit bank, whose financing benefits explicitly or perhaps implicitly from a government guarantee system, from the consequences of significant risk-taking carried out in its name. This separation acts directly as a shield protecting both the deposit bank and the taxpayer. It should also improve the incentive systems associated with trading activities of any kind. When the financing of the positions taken must be carried out under conditions that are more those imposed by the market, (with the consequences related to the withdrawal of government safety nets), the propensity to take large risks should be reduced and this should also prevent abnormal and excessive growth in trading activities. Some critics (often from the banks themselves) have said that customers suffer from this separation. According to those critics, the banks' ability to offer their corporate customers a 'one-stop shop' for all their needs is compromised by that separation, which would have the effect of increasing the costs and inconvenience caused to those same customers. That is not the position of our group. We have recognized the value of universal banks as providers of a full range of banking services. This is why we have not insisted on a radical separation of deposit banking activities and trading activities that go so far as to place them under the control of different shareholders. Instead, we proposed that it be allowed for them to be grouped together in a holding company. A banking group could thus continue to market all of its services from the various constituent entities. We also wanted deposit banks to be allowed to carry out, at the request of their clients, trading operations and underwriting of securities and loans issued by companies. However, our panel has noted that positions held in these client-driven transactions should be subject to risk-side limits. These risks should also be adequately covered. So, all things considered, we feel that our proposal has taken into account the benefits of the single window in banking services. Another criticism that has been made of our proposal is that the legal separation of trading activities and deposit banking activities by assigning them to separately capitalised entities would be costly in terms of own funds since the same basic capital could not be distributed between these different entities. If a capital increase fails, the separation of these activities would reduce the size of at least one of the subsidiaries. In response to this argument, we must point out that the sharing of capital between trading activities and deposit banking activities would also mean the sharing of the associated risks, which is precisely what our expert group wishes to avoid, given the resulting incentive effects in terms of risk-taking. In reality, the higher capital requirements are not an undesirable consequence of the separation of these activities. Other regulatory reforms that have had the explicit aim of increasing the capital requirements on banks. It should also be noted that the cost impact of the need for greater capital should not be overestimated. Due to a lower level of debt, the risks borne by shareholders will be lower and they will therefore have moderate demands in terms of return. The reasons why we propose to separate market making activities from deposit banking activities are related to the fact that it is very difficult to distinguish them from proprietary trading activities. Also in times of market turmoil, market making activities may give rise to undesirable risky positions that should not be allowed in order not to jeopardize the solvency of the deposit bank. The difficulty of separating market making activities from proprietary trading activities has been described as the greatest from a practical point of view under the Volcker Rule. To the extent that our proposal would involve separating market-making activities from deposit-taking activities, the criticism we have been made is that the liquidity of bond markets would suffer from new restrictions on market-making activities. It is argued that these restrictions would mean an increase in spreads, greater market volatility and inefficient price formation. How can we react to such criticism? This is based on the idea that the dysfunction of bond markets is such that market making activities should be supported. through their financing by means of guaranteed deposits. Why should trading activities be activities whose specificity justifies their receiving specific support? Implicit support for these activities can even have unfortunate consequences. An artificially high level of liquidity can encourage excessive risk-taking as investors are assured that they can get rid of their securities very quickly in the event of an uncertain climate. As Paul Volcker said, more trading doesn't always mean more efficiency. Not all of the criticisms that were levelled at us said that our proposals were too harsh. On the contrary, some have argued that they are not sufficiently so. When I was asked about this by the parliamentary committee in the United Kingdom, some of its members said that they would have preferred a complete separation. We wanted to avoid asking for a complete separation as had been done in the United States under the Glass-Steagall Act. Such a request would have been too far removed from the European banking tradition and would have broken the universal banking model. The dismantling of all trading and market-making activities within banking groups existing throughout Europe would have had a very disruptive effect by forcing the sale of the entities concerned or the liquidation of their portfolios. Taking into account the advantages of being able to offer a wide range of services has led us to propose a legal separation that does not call into question the structure of these groups. In the event that a credible rescue and resolution plan so requires, we propose that supervisors will have the right to require a broader separation of risky activities from deposit banking activities. Therefore, the rescue and resolution plan is the ultimate instrument serving as a criterion for deciding on the extent of separation. Our proposal for legal separation must be seen in a context where other reforms are underway or have been proposed to support the structural reform process. I would like to mention three in particular. The first relates to the Basel Committee's revision of the rules governing the trading portfolio, which could improve those relating to capital requirements for trading activities. The second relates to the review of how capital requirements for mortgages are determined. Finally, the third concerns the design of bail-in mechanisms and dedicated bail-in instruments that would reduce risk-taking incentives and increase shock-absorbing capacity. As the list of the various measures mentioned above shows, our group did not consider its proposal for the structural separation of banking activities to be a kind of 'miracle cure' in terms of stability and security. This proposal is a necessary component of a balanced package of banking reforms. The ultimate goal of these reforms in their entirety is the same as that defined in the framework of the mandate entrusted to us, namely "the establishment of an efficient banking system, meeting the needs of citizens, the economy of the European Union and the internal market". **

Thursday15 November 2012,1:00PM Conf<8e>rence annuelle de l<d5>AMF, <88> Paris, le 15 novembre 2012 11H00-12H30 ; S<8e>paration des activit<8e>s bancaires Gouverneur Erkki Liikanen : Le Groupe d<d5>experts sur la r<8e>forme structurelle du secteur bancaire de l<d5>UE, que j<d5>ai pr<8e>sid<8e>, a remis son rapport au Commissaire Michel Barnier il y a un mois. Ce Groupe d<d5>experts avait pour mission de s<d5>interroger sur la n<8e>cessit<8e> de mettre en place des r<8e>formes structurelles du secteur bancaire de l<d5>UE, dans le but dtablir un syst<8f>me <88> la fois s<9e>r, stable et efficace. Apr<8f>s avoir pris en consid<8e>ration les autres r<8e>formes en cours du syst<8f>me bancaire et compte tenu des le<8d>ons tir<8e>es de la derni<8f>re crise, nous sommes parvenus <88> une r<8e>ponse positive : ces r<8e>formes structurelles sont effectivement n<8e>cessaires. Le rapport que nous avons remis comporte une s<8e>rie de recommandations et nos principales propositions portent sur la fa<8d>on dont les banques devront <90>tre structur<8e>es <88> l<d5>avenir. Nous proposons de scinder les banques en entit<8e>s juridiques distinctes. Si une banque d<8e>sire s<d5>engager dans des activit<8e>s de trading significatives, sous la forme d<d5>activit<8e>s de trading pour son compte propre ou d<d5>activit<8e>s de tenue de march<8e>, ces activit<8e>s devront <90>tre s<8e>par<8e>es de ses activit<8e>s de banque d<8e>p<99>t, en les regroupant au sein d<d5>une filiale distincte d<8e>di<8e>e <88> ces activit<8e>s de trading, dite entit<8e> de trading. Cette derni<8f>re devrait <90>tre financ<8e>e et capitalis<8e>e s<8e>par<8e>ment de la banque de d<8e>p<99>t. Nos propositions ont re<8d>u d<d5>une mani<8f>re g<8e>n<8e>rale de r<8e>actions constructives. Bien s<9e>r, nous avons d<9e> faire face <88> de nombreuses questions et <88> quelques critiques <8e>galement. La s<8e>paration que nous pr<8e>conisons a une finalit<8e> <8e>vidente : Il s<d5>agit, en l<d5>isolant, de prot<8e>ger la banque de d<8e>p<99>t, dont le financement b<8e>n<8e>ficie explicitement ou peut-<90>tre implicitement d<d5>un syst<8f>me de garantie gouvernementale, des cons<8e>quences d<d5>une prise de risque significative effectu<8e>e en son nom. Cette s<8e>paration agit directement comme un bouclier prot<8e>geant <88> la fois la banque de d<8e>p<99>t et le contribuable. Elle devrait <8e>galement am<8e>liorer les syst<8f>mes d'incitation associ<8e>es aux activit<8e>s de trading, quelle qu<d5>en soit la nature. Lorsque le financement des positions prises doit <90>tre effectu<8e> dans des conditions qui sont davantage celles impos<8e>es par le march<8e>,( avec les cons<8e>quences li<8e>es au retrait des filets de s<8e>curit<8e>s gouvernementaux), la propension <88> prendre de gros risques devrait s<d5>en trouver r<8e>duite et cela devrait aussi pr<8e>venir une croissance anormale et excessive des activit<8e>s de trading. Certaines critiques (<8e>mises souvent par les banques elles-m<90>mes) ont dit que les clients souffrent de cette s<8e>paration. Selon ces critiques, la capacit<8e> des banques <88> offrir <88> leur client<8f>le d<d5>entreprises un <c7> guichet unique <c8> pour l<d5>ensemble de leurs besoins serait compromise du fait de cette s<8e>paration, laquelle aurait pour effet d<d5>augmenter les co<9e>ts et la g<90>ne occasionn<8e>s pour ces m<90>mes clients. Ce n<d5>est pas la position de notre groupe. Nous avons reconnu toute la valeur des banques <88> vocation universelle en tant que fournisseurs d<d5>une gamme compl<8f>te de services bancaires. C<d5>est la raison pour laquelle nous n<d5>avons pas insist<8e> pour une s<8e>paration radicale des activit<8e>s de banque de d<8e>p<99>t et des activit<8e>s de trading allant jusqu les placer sous le contr<99>le d<d5>actionnaires diff<8e>rents. Au lieu de cela nous avons propos<8e> qu<d5>il soit permis qu<d5>elles soient regroup<8e>es au sein d<d5>une holding. Un groupe bancaire pourrait ainsi continuer <88> commercialiser l<d5>ensemble de ses services <88> partir des diff<8e>rentes entit<8e>s le constituant. Nous souhaitions <8e>galement qu<d5>il soit permis aux banques de d<8e>p<99>t d<d5>effectuer, <88> la demande de leurs clients, des op<8e>rations de trading et de la prise ferme de valeurs mobili<8f>res et d<d5>emprunts <8e>mis par des entreprises. Toutefois, notre groupe d<d5>experts a fait remarquer que les positions d<8e>tenues dans le cadre de ces op<8e>rations effectu<8e>es <88> la demande des clients devraient faire l<d5>objet de limites encadrant <8e>troitement les risques encourus. Ces risques devraient aussi faire l<d5>objet d<d5>une couverture ad<8e>quate. Donc, tout bien consid<8e>r<8e>, nous avons le sentiment que notre proposition a tenu compte des avantages associ<8e>s au guichet unique en mati<8f>re de services bancaires. Une autre critique qui a <8e>t<8e> faite <88> l<d5>encontre de notre proposition est que la s<8e>paration juridique des activit<8e>s de trading et des activit<8e>s de banque de d<8e>p<99>t en les affectant <88> des entit<8e>s capitalis<8e>es de fa<8d>on distincte, serait co<9e>teuse en termes de fonds propres dans la mesure o<9d> le m<90>me capital de base ne pourrait <90>tre r<8e>parti entre ces diff<8e>rentes entit<8e>s. En cas dchec d<d5>une augmentation de capital, la s<8e>paration de ces activit<8e>s r<8e>duirait la taille d<d5>au moins l<d5>une des filiales. En r<8e>action <88> cet argument, nous devons faire remarquer que le partage du capital entre les activit<8e>s de trading et les activit<8e>s de banque de d<8e>p<99>t signifierait <8e>galement le partage des risques associ<8e>s, ce qui est pr<8e>cis<8e>ment ce que notre groupe d<d5>experts souhaite <8e>viter, compte tenu des effets incitatifs qui en d<8e>coulent en termes de prise de risques. En r<8e>alit<8e>, les besoins plus <8e>lev<8e>s en termes de fonds propres ne sont pas une cons<8e>quence ind<8e>sirable de la s<8e>paration de ces activit<8e>s. D<d5>autres r<8e>formes r<8e>glementaires qui ont eu pour finalit<8e> explicite d<d5>augmenter les exigences pesant sur les banques en termes de fonds propres. Il faudrait aussi faire remarquer qu<d5>il ne faut pas surestimer l<d5>impact en termes de co<9e>ts r<8e>sultant de la n<8e>cessit<8e> de disposer de fonds propres plus importants. Du fait d<d5>un niveau d<d5>endettement moins important, les risques support<8e>s par les actionnaires seront moindres et ils auront donc des exigences mod<8e>r<8e>es en termes de rendement. Les raisons pour lesquelles nous proposons de s<8e>parer les activit<8e>s de tenue de march<8e> des activit<8e>s de banque de d<8e>p<99>t sont li<8e>es au fait qu<d5>il est tr<8f>s difficile de les distinguer des activit<8e>s de trading pour compte propre. Aussi en p<8e>riode d<d5>agitation des march<8e>s, les activit<8e>s de tenue de march<8e> peuvent donner lieu <88> des prises de positions risqu<8e>es non d<8e>sirables qui ne devraient pas <90>tre autoris<8e>es afin de ne pas mettre en p<8e>ril la solvabilit<8e> de la banque de d<8e>p<99>t. La difficult<8e> qu<d5>il y a <88> s<8e>parer les activit<8e>s de tenue de march<8e> des activit<8e>s de trading pour compte propre a <8e>t<8e> d<8e>crite comme <8e>tant la plus grande d<d5>un point de vue pratique dans le cadre de la r<8f>gle Volcker. Dans la mesure o<9d> la proposition que nous avons faite impliquerait de s<8e>parer les activit<8e>s de tenue de march<8e> des activit<8e>s de banque de d<8e>p<99>t, la critique qui nous a <8e>t<8e> faite est que la liquidit<8e> des march<8e>s obligataires p<89>tirait de nouvelles restrictions impos<8e>es aux activit<8e>s de tenue de march<8e>. Il est avanc<8e> que ces restrictions signifieraient une augmentation des <8e>carts de taux, une plus grande volatilit<8e> du march<8e> et une formation inefficace des prix. Comment pouvons-nous r<8e>agir face <88> une telle critique ? Celle-ci repose sur l<d5>id<8e>e selon laquelle le dysfonctionnement des march<8e>s obligataires est tel que les activit<8e>s de tenue de march<8e> devraient <90>tre soutenues via leur financement au moyen de d<8e>p<99>ts garantis. Pourquoi les activit<8e>s de trading seraient-elles des activit<8e>s dont la sp<8e>cificit<8e> justifierait qu<d5>elles re<8d>oivent un soutien sp<8e>cifique ? Le soutien implicite de ces activit<8e>s peut m<90>me avoir de f<89>cheuses cons<8e>quences. Un niveau de liquidit<8e>s artificiellement haut peut encourager des prises de risques excessives d<8f>s lors que les investisseurs sont assur<8e>s de pouvoir se d<8e>barrasser de leurs titres tr<8f>s rapidement en cas d<d5>apparition d<d5>un climat incertain. Comme l<d5>a dit Paul Volcker, davantage de trading ne rime pas toujours avec davantage d<d5>efficacit<8e>. Les critiques qui nous ont <8e>t<8e> adress<8e>es ne disaient pas toutes que nos propositions <8e>taient trop s<8e>v<8f>res. Au contraire, certaines ont avanc<8e> qu<d5>elles ne ltaient pas assez. Lorsque j<d5>ai <8e>t<8e> interrog<8e> sur la question par le comit<8e> parlementaire, au Royaume-Uni, certains de ses membres ont d<8e>clar<8e> qu<d5>ils auraient pr<8e>f<8e>r<8e> une s<8e>paration compl<8f>te. Nous voulions <8e>viter de demander une s<8e>paration compl<8f>te comme cela avait <8e>t<8e> fait aux <83>tats-Unis dans le cadre du Glass-Steagall Act. Une telle demande aurait <8e>t<8e> trop <8e>loign<8e>e de la tradition bancaire europ<8e>enne et aurait bris<8e> le mod<8f>le de la banque universelle. Le d<8e>mant<8f>lement de l<d5>ensemble des activit<8e>s de trading et de tenue de march<8e> au sein des groupes bancaires existant dans toute l<d5>Europe aurait eu un effet tr<8f>s perturbateur en obligeant <88> la vente des entit<8e>s concern<8e>es ou <88> la liquidation de leurs portefeuilles. La prise en compte des avantages li<8e>s au fait que les groupes bancaires puissent proposer une gamme <8e>tendue de services nous a amen<8e>s <88> proposer une s<8e>paration juridique qui ne remette pas en cause la structure de ces groupes. Dans le cas o<9d> un plan de sauvetage et de r<8e>solution des d<8e>faillances cr<8e>dible la demanderait nous proposons que les autorit<8e>s de surveillance auront le droit d<d5>exiger une s<8e>paration plus large des activit<8e>s <88> risques par rapport aux activit<8e>s de banque de d<8e>p<99>t. Par cons<8e>quent, le plan sauvetage et de r<8e>solution des d<8e>faillances constitue l<d5>instrument ultime servant comme crit<8f>re de d<8e>cision quant <88> ltendue de la s<8e>paration. Notre proposition de s<8e>paration juridique doit <90>tre consid<8e>r<8e>e dans un contexte o<9d> d<d5>autres r<8e>formes sont en cours ou ont <8e>t<8e> propos<8e>es pour soutenir le processus de r<8e>forme structurelle. Je voudrais en citer trois en particulier. La premi<8f>re est li<8e>e <88> la r<8e>vision par le Comit<8e> de B<89>le des r<8f>gles r<8e>gissant le portefeuille de trading et qui pourrait am<8e>liorer celles relatives aux exigences de fonds propres aff<8e>rentes aux activit<8e>s de trading. La deuxi<8f>me est li<8e>e au r<8e>examen de la fa<8d>on dont sont d<8e>termin<8e>es les exigences de fonds propres aff<8e>rentes aux pr<90>ts immobiliers. Enfin la troisi<8f>me concerne la conception de m<8e>canismes de renflouement interne (bail-in) et d<d5>instruments d<8e>di<8e>s au renflouement interne qui r<8e>duiraient les incitations <88> la prise de risques et augmenteraient la capacit<8e> d<d5>absorption des chocs. Comme le montre la liste des diff<8e>rentes mesures pr<8e>cit<8e>es, notre groupe n<d5>a pas consid<8e>r<8e> que sa proposition de s<8e>paration structurelle des activit<8e>s bancaires constituait une sorte de <c7> rem<8f>de miracle <c8> en mati<8f>re de stabilit<8e> et de s<8e>curit<8e>. Cette proposition est une composante n<8e>cessaire au sein d<d5>un ensemble <8e>quilibr<8e> de r<8e>formes bancaires. Le but ultime de ces r<8e>formes dans leur globalit<8e> est le m<90>me que celui d<8e>fini dans le cadre du mandat qui nous a <8e>t<8e> confi<8e>, <88> savoir <c7> la mise en place d<d5>un syst<8f>me bancaire performant, r<8e>pondant aux besoins des citoyens, de lconomie de l<d5>Union Europ<8e>enne et du march<8e> interne <c8>. **

text: Director-General Erkki Liikanen: Great enthusiasm. 10th anniversary of The Frame Association, Helsinki 26.11.2012 . Speech . Monday26 November 2012,3:00 PM Erkki Liikanen, Governor of the Bank of Finland Speech at the 10th anniversary celebration of The Frame Association Helsinki 26.11.2012 Suuriinnostus In 1968, a working group led by Kaj Warras, Secretary General of the Finnish Red Cross, proposed that the state support development cooperation between NGOs. Jaakko Iloniemi from the Ministry for Foreign Affairs replied that although the postponement is unfortunate, it would be beneficial for the matter. Within a larger whole, in due course, such a relatively modest thing can be put in order. It did, but not until six years later, in 1974. In 1969, on the initiative of student organizations, many organizations filed a petition in favor of a "development tax". The petition set out the basic idea of the percentage movement: everyone would issue a power of attorney entitled to withhold 1 % of the income for the chosen development cooperation target. Interestingly, the Association of Finnish Student Unions rejected the proposal. Chairman Kimmo Eskola and Secretary General MattiLouekoski wrote that there has already been too much experimentation with volunteering. "The government likes to look at... citizens' own-initiative development cooperation and voluntary action will completely eliminate the need for government intervention in the same sector". The letter reflects the debate of that time: the actions of society and "charity" were opposite for many Solutions. In 1970, Finland's development cooperation funds amounted to only 0.06% of GDP. TaksvarkkiMosambikiin In January 2007, on the outskirts of Maputo, the capital of Mozambique, in a small printing house, an old but well-kept German Heidelberg printing press pushed out a staff magazine at Maputo airport. When you look at the machine up close, you can see that the work instructions attached to its side with metal tiles are all in Finnish. Where did the Finnish instructions come from? The traces lead to the largest citizens' development project of 1969. On October 10, 1969, tens of thousands of Schoolchildren from Finland participated in a taxi race for the benefit of the Mozambique Institute. The target had been chosen at the Teens' Union Congress in Helsinki after a close vote. The Mozambique Institute operated in the context of Frelimo, the Liberation Movement of Mozambique, but focused on education and humanitarian work. The institute was headed by JanetMondlane, the widow of Eduardo Mondlane, president of Frelimo, who was killed in a bomb attack at the beginning of the same year. The destination divided the Finnish school world. Many rose up against the taxidermy directed at Mozambique. The reasons varied. Some felt that there was still enough shortage in their own country and that there was no need for support abroad. Still others were convinced that all the money, however, goes to weapons or misconduct, and nothing goes to the intended targets. After much controversy, the return was disappointing, 450,000 marks, which in 2012 money, however, is 600,000 euros. Frelimo and the Mozambique Institute were headquartered in Tanzania. The critical debate raised concerns about whether the collection money would get through correctly. In order to secure this, it was decided in January 1970 to send a member of the taxicab committee, 19-year-old Erkki Liikanen, to Dar es Salaam to negotiate the final form, implementation and supervision of the project. Various roads had received a wealth of cautionary information about the problems of implementing projects in Africa. Fortunately for the Finns, there were Finnish development cooperation troops operating in Tanzania at the time, in which the printing expert Kid Ahlfors served. He was hired to be in charge of on-site project execution and staff training. Under Ahlfors' leadership, the project plan was redone. Only machines were procured for which maintenance and spare parts were available in Tanzania. To be on the safe side, the procurements were eventually handled through importers operating in Finland. The bills were paid to them directly from Helsinki. In this way, spending remained under close control. Since finnish importers had ordered the machines, they had been fitted with instructions for use in Finnish. The year 1970 was a time of enormous development optimism. I will forever remember the 10 days I spent in Tanzania in January 1970. The economy grew and the plans were great. We lived through Julius Nyererenparas. Dar es Salaam was a pleasant city on the shores of the Indian Ocean. Everything worked. In the evenings, we met on the terrace of the New Africa Hotel with development workers. I also got to know many representatives of the liberation movements. Under the leadership of Kid Ahlfors, the printing press was launched in 1971. Textbooks were printed there for schools operating in areas decolonized from Portuguese rule. The textbooks wanted to tell about Mozambique from the point of view of the African population. The earlier ones were produced by Portuguese colonial rule. The Carnation Revolution in Portugal changed the country's colonial policy in 1974. In the same year, a transfer of power between the Portuguese Government and Frelimo was agreed. Power was transferred to Frelimo without elections, and Mozambique gained independence in 1975. With independence in 1975, the printing house was moved to Maputo. Tanzanian-Indian Anton PaulSilveira and Mozambican Alfredo Abilio Simang, who ran the printing house, cleared the transfer, put the machines back in place and resumed the printing business. For fifteen years, the main product was still textbooks. It was a pleasure to meet in January 2007 Silveira and Simango, who were about to launch a weight in Tanzania , when I visited it in May 1971. They had handled the machines and the weight strikingly well, the metal was shining, and the places were neatly arranged. The first two years of Mozambique's independence were hard. Mozambique also became part of the struggle between the great powers. The civil war tore the ground apart and caused a huge number of deaths. It was not until 1992 that a peace treaty was reached in Rome, which ended the war. Where did Finland's development cooperation go in the early 1970s? It was mentioned above that Finland's development cooperation funds in 1970 amounted to only 0.06% of gdp. By 1981, they gradually rose to 0.26%. The Development Cooperation Department was established in the Ministry for Foreign Affairs in 1972. Timo Soikkanen writes colorfully in the history of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs about the early stages of the department. When the first head of department, ake Vihtol, was appointed, he said: "The 76 idealists, democrats and some others of the Development Cooperation Office were handed over to me, saying that there are some good ones there." Martti Ahtisaari had hoped for the position of deputy head of department. However, department head MattiTuovinen speculated that a possible appointment would cause "complications". However, Ahtisaari was later appointed to the position. The main recipient countries were finalised in the budget for the first time for 1973. Chile, Nigeria, Zambia and Tanzania were elected. Development cooperation policy was a field of heated political debate, in which the representatives of the baby boomers who came to parliament were active. The guidelines for development policy were prepared by a committee set up in 1976, headed by Jan-Magnus Jansson and ErkkiTuomioja, among others, served as a member. Minister for Foreign Affairs Keijo Korhonen also appointed himself as a member, but during his term of office, the deputy was Jorma Ollila from VTK. Overall, the 1970s were a time of strong development for sub-Saharan Africa. The economy grew by 4% a year. Many countries stepped up their development efforts at the same time. Optimism and faith in the future were great. The Finnish Red Cross was an important player from the very beginning. The Finnish Red Cross Disaster Relief Fund had been established in 1961, and the first development cooperation programmes began in 1964. The first basic course in the international personnel reserve was held in 1970. Huge disappointment 15 years later In 1986, the Parliamentary Committee on Foreign Affairs made a trip to Africa to get acquainted with development cooperation sites and the situation in southern Africa. We had three destination countries, Tanzania, Zimbabwe and Botswana. The delegation included Jutta Zilliacus, Marjatta Vaananen and Inger Hirvela, among others. As chairman of the committee, I was the head of the delegation. We were the first to arrive in Tanzania. Dar es Salaam was a completely different city. There were no more streetlights. From the New Africa Hotel, the windows had been removed; the new ones had been leaning against the wall of a building that had looked abandoned for years. Based on my recommendation, we stayed at the famous Kilimanjaro Hotel. That, too, had collapsed. The rooms lacked either running water or a working electric lamp. We toured through many development cooperation projects under the leadership of a qualified ambassador, Ilkka Ristimaki. There were many great disappointments. The pharmaceutical factory, built with considerable development funds, stood and was rusting when it was unable to import the basic chemicals needed for production. A similar message came from different sides. Of course, there were also positive experiences, but they came from small projects where a lot was done with the input of one person. When there was a need for infrastructure or a functioning administration, the results were bleak. What had happened? The long war with Uganda, the drought, but also irresponsible economic management, weak institutions and corruption had driven the country to a complete impasse. After Tanzania, we traveled to Zimbabwe. It had recently been liberated. Robert Mugabeoli the new leader of the country. Again, everything worked. Nyerere had uttered the famous words to Mugabe: ' You have got the diamond of Africa. Take good care of it". Today we know what has happened. From there we continued on to Botswana. In the capital, the Association of South African Cooperation Sadec held its headquarters. Botswana has been lucky with diamonds. But there have been functioning institutions and administration. Botswana's development continues to be positive. Structural adjustment By the early 1980s, the external funding of many African countries had dried up. Measures had to be taken. The solution was structural adjustment programmes with the International Monetary Fund. The hardest part was with President Nyere. Nyere opposed all conditionality, only his finance minister supported them. Nyere drove the IMF negotiators out of the country and fired his finance minister. The first programs were torso, but the IMF accepted them, despite their shortcomings. Nyere, on the other hand, said that the IMF is a conspiracy by the West aimed at crushing Tanzania's socialist traditions. Since 1986, with the structural programmes, tanzania's economy was gradually liberalised. Exchange rates and prices were allowed to be determined by the market. Companies were privatized. Economic growth was still subdued for a long time. Overall, economic growth in southern African countries fell to two per cent, which was lower than population growth. Countries became poorer per capita. Africa was a lost continent for many, and Africans had almost two lost decades. Finland reached the 0.7% target A year after the Foreign Affairs Committee's trip to Africa, in 1987 I became Minister of Finance. During the Holkeri government, two important things happened in the field of development policy: Firstly, development cooperation funds were increased to 0.7% of the national product. Secondly, the tax deduction for development aid donations was abolished. I admit that I influenced both decisions. In the 20-year history of KEPA by KirsiSalonen and Juha Rekola, the former was not mentioned, the latter yes. It was important that Finland achieved its development cooperation objectives. It was a remarkable step. The country later entered a deep depression, causing these funds to be drastically reduced. Why was the tax deduction for development aid abolished? When a donation is tax-deductible, it causes the state to lose tax revenue, i.e. tax expenses. We looked at whether this would be considered development spending. The answer was no. Did the right to tax deduction increase donations to development cooperation? Did not add. In addition, due to the progression of taxation, the deduction had the effect that the tax benefit from the same amount was greater the higher the income. My choice was clear: Donations are a valued civic activity. But tax deductibility did not increase donations and distorted the distribution of income. Therefore, there was no reason for the state to continue it. Instead, the state's investment was directed towards direct development cooperation funds. With direct assistance, the state could support the development cooperation activities of NGOs. EU and development cooperation Finland joined the European Union in 1995. Development issues were not a problem in the negotiations, and negotiations always focused on problems. However, membership brought us to a new world, where, in addition to our own direct development cooperation, eu development cooperation came into play, which, to my great delight, was joined by the Framework Association. load. The EU's development policy has its own history and its own peculiar financial background. Part is financed directly from the budget. Last week's summit was unable to give a clear indication of the development of this section. The second part is financed by the Development Fund, which is based on the Yaoude and Lome agreements. This dichotomy is not without its problems. It would be better to keep them together under normal circumstances. Now that the Member States are pushing the overall framework to the brink, one might also say that, fortunately, it does not apply to everything. I was involved in the corresponding budget negotiations in Berlin in March 1999. Fortunately, they ended successfully, and the so-called "green light". Agenda 2000 was adopted. We then travelled on holiday to Egypt. The phone rang there on Good Friday. At the end of the phone was Emma Bonino, commissioner for humanitarian aid. "Can you come to my room right away?" "Unfortunately, I'm in Cairo, not Brussels," I replied. But I promised to be there on Easter Monday. Then, when I was there, Emma's room was filled to the brim with papers. Title: Publication of the Collected Writings of Anders Chydenius
text: Director General Erkki Liikanen: Publication of Anders Chydenius' collected writings, Stockholm 15.1.2013 . Speech . Tuesday 15January 2013,12:00 PM Chefdirektor Erkki Liikanen, Finlands Bank The publication of anders Chydenius collected writings Stockholm, January 15, 2013 It gives me great pleasure to be present today at the publication of the collected writings of Anders Chydenius. The Bank of Finland is one of the financiers of the issuance project. The Bank's main contribution has been to have the most important writings translated into English in order to give them wider circulation among international researchers. The resulting collection "Anticipating the Wealth of Nations, the Selected Works of Anders Chydenius" was published last year. The idea behind our participation is that we consider Chydenius to be deserving of a more prominent role in international research circles. I believe that this extraordinary collection, including a miniature biography written by Professor Lars Magnusson, will very much meet expectations. The complete compilation edition, whose publications have now begun to be published in both Finnish and Swedish, is of course at least as important as the English book. It is to be hoped that the broad publication of Chydenius' writings both in the original language and in Finnish will increase interest in this exceptional man's life's work. Even in Finland, which sees Chydenius as one of his national philosophers, we have an unnecessarily narrow view of his activities. It is to be hoped that this will make the picture more diverse and that research on Chydenius will increase. It is particularly gratifying to speak about Chydenius here in Stockholm, where he sat in the Riksdag and authored most of his famous writings. Chydenius is not the only economist with Finnish roots who has been active in economic policy in Sweden. In both economics and economic policy, close contacts have continued even after Finland's withdrawal from Svea Rike. Reputable Finnish-born economists who have been active in Sweden include Karl Langenskiold, who was governor of the Riksbank in the early 1900s, and of course my colleague, the current Governor of the Riksbank, Stefan Ingves. Intellect, of course, has also flowed the other way. Among the Swedes who have had a major impact on economic policy in Finland are Eli Hecksher, who was an advisor at the Bank of Finland when the Finnish markka was pegged to the gold standard in the mid-1920s, and Erik Dahmen, who researched economic development and was one of the foremost architects of structural change in Finland in the 1960s as an advisor to the Bank of Finland's Governor Klaus Waris. *** Chydenius' contributions to contemporary politics spanned a wide range. Best known as an early defender of free trade and the freedom to conduct a business, he is often referred to as Adam Smith's predecessor. The writing "The national profit" dealing with these issues is also Chydenius' most famous writing. Chydenius was successful in his work in lifting the mercantile restrictions in foreign trade. This is surely the main reason why he is still remembered with great gratitude in the Ostrobothnian coastal cities, which in the 1760s were given the right to independently conduct foreign trade instead of selling their products to Stockholm as before. This contributed significantly to the future development of the area. But also other parts of Chydenius' activities, which are perhaps less well known, are worth a mention. His other great success, which  I believe  was even more significant than the freedom of sailing for the Ostrobothnian cities, was his action in introducing freedom of the press in Svea Rike. In 1766, Sweden became the first country in the world to pass a law abolishing political pre-censorship. Chydenius played an essential role in the making of this law, to which he devoted most of his time and energy. Chydenius later wrote in his memoirs that during his first term in the Reichstag he had not worked as diligently on any other issue as on freedom of the press. He was secretary of the parliamentary committee that dealt with the matter and also wrote a voluminous memorandum on freedom of the press entitled "Memorial on freedom of the press and freedom of the press", on which the proposals of the committee and the law that was passed largely came to be based. Although Chydenius' memorandum on freedom of the press is almost 250 years old, it is of great interest even from today's perspective. Chydenius did not see freedom of the press as a danger to the social order. He believed, on the contrary, that the freedom of writing and the press should support the free social order, the free regiment, as he put it. Chydenius wrote: "a cheap freedom of scribbles and freedom of the press is one of the firmest pillars that a free regiment can possess stock up to". With free regiment, Chydenius was referring to the regime during the time of freedom after the king's autocracy had been abolished and the Reichstag ruled the country. Chydenius was a convinced democrat. Such writings as supported autocracy or malicious aristocracy he found so dangerous that their publication could be punished with fines, but only afterwards. Chydenius pointed out that without freedom of the press "the Estates could never possess the requisite knowledge to make good laws, the law-makers no control to follow them in their offices, and obey little knowledge of the claims of the law." According to Chydenius, freedom of speech and public debate were also needed to limit political power. He writes thus: "The freedom of a nation does not consist deruti that almighty estates may act at arbitrariness, but deruti that the light of nations binds the hands of them that they may not be soul-fed". Chydenius already realized the importance of the public sphere, or the third power, as you say here in Sweden. It is worth noting that Chydenius shares the view of the importance of public life as a condition of political freedom with another Finnish political thinker, J.V. Snellman, who is the second of Finland's national philosophers. After all, Mr Snellman took the view that national public life and public debate are the most important component of political freedom; ultimately more important and stronger than formal government bodies. Various surveys show that Sweden and Finland are among the leading countries in the field of press freedom. The road to get there has certainly not been completely straight, but I believe that even today we can be grateful to Anders Chydenius and his pioneering work to build up the free society. Without freedom of the press, a development of Nordic democracy to the current level would not have been possible. *** Interestingly from the perspective of the Central Bank, Chydenius was also active in monetary policy. In Sweden in the 1700s, there was a lively monetary policy debate that Chydenius also participated in, despite the fact that it required a large portion of civil courage from him and ultimately cost him his seat in the Riksdag. Relevant from a Finnish perspective is that Chydenius' publication "The help of the kingdom through a natural financial system" is the first monetary policy study written by a Finn. The main theme of the publication, defending price stability, is just as relevant now as it was then. As an Enlightenment writer, Chydenius did not draw a sharp dividing line between economics, politics and ethics. With the same certainty and courageand only conscience and reason as the guiding principlehe acted in all these areas, which he considered to be tightly interwoven. In the broadened perspective of thought, this is perhaps the reason why Chydenius feels so fresh and current even to the modern reader. Because of the economic crisis that the entire Western world has suffered, we are currently living in a time where economists also have to think in political terms and politicians, in turn, in economic terms. At the same time, the ethical requirements of both people's activities are highlighted. Just like Anders Chydenius in his time, today's decision-makers and citizens are faced with problems relating to economic freedom and justice, competition and regulation, democracy and freedom of the press. The optimism and idealism that Chydenius' writings breathe can also be the inspiration of modern man. As an example, his courage to fight for the values in which he believed also serves. Once again, I would like to thank all those who contributed to the implementation of this great publishing project. Bank of Finland (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagBank of Finland)
