Title: Success factors, threats, and opportunities of our national economy
text: Speech by Director-General Erkki Liikanen: Success factors, threats and opportunities for our national economy. January engagement seminar, Jyvaskyla, 17.1.2013. . Speech . Thursday17 January2013,5:00 PM Erkki Liikanen, President, Bank of Finland Speech at the January Engagement seminar in Jyvaskyla 17.1.2013 Full speech (PDF, 183 KB) . (/globalassets/en/media-and.. publications/speeches/documents/el_puhe_kansantaloutemme_menestystekijat_uhat_ja_mahdollisuudet.pdf) Speech-related presentation (PPT, 0.5 MB) . (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches/documents/el_tammikuun_kihlaus_seminaari_jk_17_01_2013.pptx) SUCCESS FACTORS,THREATS AND OPPORTUNITIES FOR OUR ECONOMY Summary The outlook for the Finnish economy has deteriorated significantly in recent months. Economic activity is becoming even more modest than expected in spring 2012, and this has also worsened the fiscal outlook. At the same time, the outlook for the balance between exports and foreign trade has remained weak, and the direction of our competitiveness is deteriorating. The weakening of the external balance and competitiveness of Finland's national economy, as well as public finances, are important alarm signs of the erosion of Finland's strengths. It is essential to pursue structural reforms that improve the growth potential of the economy and the sustainability of public finances. Reforms relating to the labour market play an essential role in this respect. In addition, the international competitiveness of Finnish production must be revived. Here the importance of wage formation is great. Wage formation plays a key role in reviving the international competitiveness of Finnish production. Improving the balance of employment and foreign trade in the open sector requires that the deterioration of the situation be taken into account in future wage settlements. Wage developments in the non-tradable sector also have a direct impact on the prices of domestic intermediate inputs used by the open sector and, consequently, on competitiveness. Thus, the importance of wage solutions is also emphasized in the non-tradable sector. It is essential that the export sector determines the level at which contractual solutions are also made in other sectors. The problem of the sustainability of public finances could be decisively alleviated by structural reforms that increase labour supply. If policies that increase the employment rate in a sustainable way are not implemented, it will be difficult or impossible for the Finnish economy to cope with the ageing of the population without serious problems. Measures to prolong working lives are key. They can be achieved by implementing structural reforms that prolong working lives upstream, increase the incentive for the supply of work for people of working age or prolong working lives at the end of it. In other words, the economy needs to increase labour input at every stage of one's working life. It would also even out the distribution of the costs of securing the welfare state between different age groups. A change of direction will require significant efforts over a number of years. The decisions taken last spring were important, but on the basis of new economic information, they are proving to be insufficient. Waiting doesn't make the necessary corrections any easier. Title: Democracy and economic crisis: Review of vin Tanner's and Mauno Koivisto's activities
text: Director General Erkki Liikanen: Democracy and the economic crisis: Reviewing the activities of Vaino Tanner and Mauno Koivisto, Lahti 8.2.2013 . Speech . Friday 8February 2013, 3:00PM President and CEO Erkki Liikanen, Bank of Finland Opening speech at the Finnish History Days in Lahti 8.2.2013 at 15.00 DEMOCRACY AND THE ECONOMIC CRISIS: REVIEWING THE ACTIVITIES OF VaINo TANNER AND MAUNO KOIVISTO The Danielson-Kalmari seminar, held at the beginning of this year's Finnish History Days, focused on the far right in Europe in the 1930s. At that time, the economic crisis fuelled various anti-democratic extremists and democracy was put on the defensive in Europe. Finland was a happy exception to the trend that prevailed between the world wars in that our democracy actually became established and strengthened, despite the fact that in Finland, too, nationalist and far-right currents were sometimes very strong. One of the main trends in the history of independent Finland has been the consolidation and development of parliamentarism. The road that led from the royal adventure of autumn 1918 through the presidential republic to the constitution now in force has been long and multi-stage. If you start looking for characters who have had a great impact on this development, K.J. Stahlberg and Kyosti Kallio, for example, will come to the fore. Today, I have chosen as my subject two people who have been important both as promoters of parliamentarianism and as economic politicians in times of crisis. The first is VainoTanner. Tanner was on the sidelines of the Civil War and then fought for decades against the dictatorial tendencies of both the far left and the right, and for parliamentarianism. Tanner's contribution was central to the fact that Finnish democracy was consolidated after the Civil War in the 1920s and 1930s. The second is Mauno Koivisto. His merits in the parliamentaryisation of our political system in the 1980s are undeniable. When you think about the careers of these men, you can find many common features in them. Both were economists who had risen to the top of politics and whose careers took off from the business circle of the labour movement, in Tanner's case from the position of ceo of Elanto, in Koivisto's case from the position of ceo of the Helsinki Workers' Savings Bank. Both served as prime minister (Tanner once, Koivisto twice) and finance minister (Tanner in three, Koivisto in two governments). In their day, they also held key positions in the administration of the Bank of Finland. Both came from humble circumstances. The Bank of Finland is the first public institution in Finland under the control of parliament. The bank was given to the "guarantee and care" of the Diet as early as 1868. For half a century, the bank was the only part of the state apparatus in Finland that operated under the Riksdag and not the emperor. The Bank and Finnish parliamentarianism have long common roots. Vaino Tanner's career in the administration of the Bank of Finland was exceptionally long. Tanner rose to the first unicameral parliament at the age of 26 in 1907. The following year, he was appointed auditor of the Bank of Finland. He was elected bank delegate in 1919. He continued in this position until the spring of 1962. There was only one six-year hiatus due to a war guilty verdict. Thus, the joint history of the Bank of Finland and Tanner spanned as many as seven decades. There is no such thing in the history of the Bank of Finland. It's unlikely to be found. Mauno Koivisto's career at the Bank of Finland was much shorter, but it is a central part of the image of both Koivisto and the Bank of Finland in the memory of the people. Koivisto was appointed director general at the beginning of 1968 after Klaus Waris had resigned after the previous year's great devaluation. Koivisto was on leave of absence twice due to his duties as prime minister and once as minister of finance in Paasio's second government, but otherwise led the bank until his election as president in 1982. As a result, his active time at the head of the Bank of Finland lasted eight years and eight months. At the time of both Tanner and Koivisto, the administration of the Bank of Finland included a severe economic crisis. As a banking delegate, Tanner was a key influencer in monetary policy when Finland's national economy fell into the grip of the global depression at the end of the 1920s. The crisis lasted a long time until the 1930s. The most dramatic phases of Koivisto's presidency also coincide with the international economic crisis. The situation came to a head in Finland between 1975 and 1977, when, in the aftermath of the oil crisis, Finland was plunged into a balance of payments crisis and under the guidance of the International Monetary Fund. The years will be remembered especially for Miettunen's emergency government, which President Kekkonen "ransacked". *** Vaino Tanner's attitude to his social duties is illustrated by the following quote: "I've looked at it from a completely different perspective. I have said to myself, 'If you accept a post, you will take it.' You don't get to choose your dishes very much, but you have to eat both the good and the bad." This is how Tanner responded when he was criticized at the SDP's 1930 party congress for having received, on 16.5.1927, as prime minister and deputy to the president, a parade of patrons on the day of the military flag celebration. It was celebrated in honor of the victory of the White Army. He felt that agreeing to the formation of a minority government of the Social Democrats was an opportunity to influence matters, but then we had to act according to the rules of democracy and also deal with the difficult issues for our own group. Vaino Tanner matriculated from the Real Lyceum in Helsinki, Ressu. When the father worked as a brakeman on the railways and the mother had moved to the capital as the daughter of a crofter, sending the boy to secondary school was not a foregone conclusion. My father was downright opposed to going to high school. Interestingly, the social background of Ressu's classmates did not differ from Vaino Tanner, with a few exceptions. Later studies, i.e. a diploma from the Finnish Businessmen's School of Business and a law degree completed alongside work, provided support for a later career. The Finnish Businessmen's Business School was not a trivial institution. While Tanner was studying, one of the teachers there was a young lawyer named J.K. Paasikivi. Another prominent figure among the teachers was later Yrjo Jahnsson, who became professor of economics and encouraged Tanner to become familiar with cooperatives. I will come back to Mr Jahnsson later. Vaino Tanner served as head of finance of Oskari Tokoi's Senate from March to September 1917. During these turbulent months, Senator Tanner was also at times responsible for the country's food supply. Tanner saw how the working population, both in rural and urban areas, suffered the most from food shortages and the associated sharp rise in the cost of living. The bitterness generated under these circumstances contributed significantly to the tightening of the social climate and the rise to power of radical non-parliamentary currents in the labor movement. Tanner saw how it was impossible for low-income earners to hedge against galloping inflation. Perhaps it was for this reason that the fight against inflation remained the red thread of his monetary policy throughout the decades. Tanner was confronted with monetary issues after becoming a banking commissioner in 1919. In the early stages, the chairman was Wille Lavonius (Progressive Party), who had acquired his spurs as insurance director, followed since 1924 by Professor Ernst Nevanlinna (Conservative Party). At the same time, Tanner became vice-president of the delegates. Later, after Nevanlinna's death, Tanner rose to the position of chairman of the banking council. The position of the banking commissioner was important. When Risto Ryti became president of the bank at the age of 35, in 1924, the president's influence grew, but he, too, was dependent on the support of the banking council in his activities. In practice, the cooperation of Nevanlinna, Tanner and Ryti in monetary policy was generally seamless and marked by mutual respect. Although Tanner and Ryti had differing views on domestic policy issues, such as their attitude to the Reds' amnesties, on monetary issues their views were similar. For Tanner and Ryti, the independence of the central bank was clear, and both saw the role of bank delegates in the same way. Although the banking delegates were elected by parliament, as bank delegates they acted more as independent experts than as messengers for their own parliamentary groups. Tanner's work on the banking council was characterised by pragmatism taken to the extreme. As the director of the elanto cooperative movement, Tanner was also aware of the needs of the business community in terms of monetary policy. Tanner's pragmatism is aptly illustrated by his statement in the banking council: 'No theories are decided here, but concrete issues are dealt with'. When Tanner joined in, the Board of Directors of the Bank of Finland and the banking delegates found a common vision of how to get out of the economic chaos of the time. The first step was to stabilise public finances and move away from banknote financing, which in 1918 was the main source of inflation. After that, it would be the turn of rebalancing Finland's foreign balance of payments and, with it, the stabilisation of exchange rates. After that, it would then be possible to go back to the gold standard. In the 1920s, the reconstruction of the gold standard was the main goal of international monetary cooperation. Tanner received his baptism of fire into international monetary issues in the spring of 1922, when an international economic meeting was held in Genoa, Italy, at which, among other things, recommendations for returning to the gold standard were decided. The Finnish delegation was led by Prime Minister Juho Vennola and the Bank of Finland was represented by bank delegates Nevanlinna and Tanner. Italy, the host country of the meeting, was in an economic crisis and politically unstable. Half a year after the Genoa Conference ended, Mussolini's blackshirts marched to Rome. In Finland, Minister of Finance Risto Ryti and the Bank of Finland, then headed by Otto Stenroth, worked together smoothly. The state finances had been rebalanced astonishingly quickly, and the currency situation was also beginning to improve. In 1924, after Ryti became president of the Bank of Finland, preparations began to be made for taking the final step, the gold coupling of the markka. The Banking Board was unanimous on the main lines of the gold standard policy, and the only thing that gave rise to discussions was selection of a mortgage course. In the end, the value of the markka was fixed in accordance with the position of Director-General Ryti. Public opinion was also in favour of returning to the gold standard. The markka was formally incorporated into the gold standard at the beginning of 1926. Of course, there were also gravelly voices, and the loudest was Tanner's former teacher from the time of the Business School, now Yrjo Jahnsson, who has become a professor of economics at the Helsinki University of Technology. In Jahnsson's opinion, the gold standard was going too strong and monetary policy had been kept too tight. When, during the depression of the 1930s, monetary policy was tightened strongly to ensure that the gold standard remained, Jahnsson became the most implacable critic of Finnish monetary policy and one of the leading figures of the shortage movement. At the same time, the old friendship of Tanner and Jahnsson turned into bitter hostility. In Jahnsson's view, the amount of money needed to be increased and prices allowed to rise. For him, the position of agriculture had to be eased by increasing import duties on cereals. The demand was an abomination for Tanner, because raising the price level of food would directly reduce the real earnings of wage earners. Jahnsson considered people with a party background at the head of the Bank of Finland to be "holy cats", whose raison d'etre was to protect the bank's monetary policy from criticism. Jahnsson attacked Kyosti Kallio of the Agrarian Union, who was a member of the Board of Directors of the Bank of Finland, but the holy cats were also the Social Democrats Vaino Tanner and bank manager Lauri afHeurlin. In Parliament, the pressure on the central bank's activities came mainly from the Agrarian Union, as the representatives of the shortage movement had a strong position in the Agrarian Union. The banking delegates of the Agrarian Union called, among other things, for a strong easing of monetary policy in order to break the deflationary trend and to change the regulations so that the Bank of Finland could start lending to agriculture. This led to a conflict with the majority of the banking council, to which Tanner also belonged. It considered the requirements impossible, even dangerous. 1931 was the most difficult year. A quote from J. K. Paasikivi's diary of 29.6.1931 describes the pressures that prevailed within the banking council and Tanner's position. "I met Nevanlinna when I went to the bank. Walitti, how poorly the Board of Governors of the Bank of Finland has now been assembled. Of the rural allies: Lahdensuo, Westerinen and Leppala (no one understands anything). Of the Social Democrats: W. Tanner (good), Ailio (does not understand, follows Tanner) and Helo(unreliable, does not know where he is at any given time). Of the Swedes: E. Frenckell(who agitated himself instead of Professor af Forselles). At the meeting, a banking delegate from a rural ally had said: 'I have been informed that the Bank of Finland was set up to help farming' !! This terrified Nevanlinna. And yes, it is awful that the management of the State Bank can be influenced by such ignorant people." Both Risto Ryti and the majority of the Board of Governors considered that Finland needed to balance its balance of payments by increasing savings. This strategy led to the establishment of the State Expenditure Reduction Board in the spring of 1931. J. K. Paasikivi (KOP and Kok) was invited as its chairman and Risto Ryti (Bank of Finland and The Progressive Party), Alexander Frey (PYP and Swedish People's Party), Tyko Reinikka (KOP and Agrarian League), Vaino Tanner (Elanto and SDP) as members. So there were four leading bankers, as well as Tanner. As the single largest savings target, the board proposed a general reduction in civil servants' salaries. The reason for this was the deflation of previous years, during which the real salaries of civil servants had risen. For the Social Democratic Party, Tanner's presence on this board, which was occupied by bankers, was a hard pill to swallow, and it was the subject of heated debate even at the party congress. The year 1931 culminated in the European currency crisis, in which Britain and the Nordic countries, Finland with them, had to break away from the gold standard. However, the depression in Finland lasted for a good couple of years after this, and it was not until 1934 that there had been a clear transition to new growth. Finland's political instability escalated precisely when the recession was at its worst in the spring of 1932 with the Mantsala rebellion. The recession years did not change Tanner's basic views on economic policy. His starting point was disciplined state finances, in which public spending would be adjusted according to income. Care had to be taken in raising taxes so that swelling public finances did not hinder capital formation. As a cautionary example, Tanner considered the development of the 1920s, when both the government and especially the parliament had, according to Tanner, increased spending in an overly "sad" way. Thus, government indebtedness had to continue to be guarded, and in good times, savings should be accumulated in cyclical funds, which, if dismantled, would overcome the bad times. This was his central message when, as Minister of Finance in the red-soil government of Cajander in the autumn of 1938, he presented his budget for 1939. Tanner's thrift was also directed at defense spending, which has since been notoriously criticized. The Cajander government, formed in the spring of 1937, was the first coalition government in which the Social Democrats were involved. Tanner admitted that the parties that formed it, the Progressive Party, the Swedish People's Party, the Agrarian League and the Social Democrats, pulled "a different rope in many respects", but he saw this government as a coalition of democratic forces. He said that "with its formation, the final end point had been set for the events of the Lapua period." During the war, there was close cooperation between the Bank of Finland and the Ministry of Finance. Close cooperation was ensured by Tanner's dual role, he served as both minister of finance and chairman of banking delegates. This meant a departure from the principle of the independent status of the Central Bank, but in exceptional circumstances Tanner considered it a workable solution. The question of conflicts of interest was allowed to recede, and there was no legal problem of incompatibility. The war guilty verdict severed Tanner's political activities. He returned to parliament in 1951 and immediately returned to the banking council. In the new political situation, he was no longer elected president of the council, but had to settle for the position of vice-president. Tanner's monetary policy stances had not been greatly altered by the past few years. According to him, the main task of the Central Bank was to ensure the stability of the value of money. According to Tanner, the state relied too easily on the Bank of Finland's banknote machine to meet the state's monetary needs. In many countries, the central bank was not allowed to lend to the state, and this should also be pursued in Finland. This is where Tanner's doctrine of sound government finances surfaced. In 1952, he said: "Governments should get to the point where, when drawing up their budgets and planning government spending, they take into account the extent to which tax revenues and other government revenues can meet these needs. In general, the stresses that go beyond it should not be taken into account". Tanner considered the race between prices and wages, as well as the constantly inflated public finances, to be major problems. Only by strengthening public confidence in the political system could a situation be achieved in which citizens would be prepared to make the sacrifices that would allow the value of the markka to be stabilised. This would strengthen positive expectations of the preservation of monetary value, and the central bank would succeed in its role as a custodian of monetary stability. *** Mauno Koivisto's career in economic policy began around the same time that Tanner's activities were coming to an end. Koivisto, who had become the director of the Helsinki Workers' Savings Bank in 1958, became active as an economic policy debater in the early 1960s. Tanner, on the other hand, stepped aside from politics in the early 1960s, leaving the banking council in 1962. The similarities in the life stages of men begin already in their youth. Koivisto studied alongside work, as tanner did in his time. Both sons of a working-class family therefore completed their academic degrees relatively late, at the age of 30, Tanner in law and Koivisto in sociology. Koivisto began his career as a financial man as the director of the Helsinki Workers' Savings Bank, tanner served as the CEO of the cooperative company Elanto for 30 years. Koivisto had already been elected to head Elanto, but he did not have time to accept the position before Klaus Waris' resignation relieved him of the position of Governor of the Bank of Finland. Koivisto began to specialise in economic policy issues when he was the director of the Labour Savings Bank. At that time, at the end of the 1950s, he also established relations with emerging economic policy stars. Koivisto's economic policy interlocutors were found in the so-called O Group. This was a discussion circle of young economists, which had arisen mainly within the circle of young talents of the Institute of Economic Research of the Bank of Finland. The group consisted of such characters as Olavi Niitamo, Jussi Linnamo, Timo Helela and Jaakko Lassila. Academically, jouko Paunio became the most famous. Mauno Koivisto became known to the general public as minister of finance in rafaelPaasio's People's Front government. At that time, the SKDL returned to the government. The government was formed in May 1966. Vaino Tanner had died a month earlier. I once asked Koivisto if he had time to talk to Tanner earlier about the possibility of skdl joining the board. After all, the issue had been in the public debate for some time. Mauno Koivisto said that he had discussed the matter. In his memoir "Two Seasons", Koivisto says that his attitude towards Vaino Tanner was difficult. Koivisto writes: "In my opinion, he (Tanner) had done great services to the fatherland and had been wrongly and wrongly convicted as a war criminal". Koivisto considered that the Social Democratic Party should establish better relations with the Soviet Union. "Tanner had nothing negative to say about this, he just stressed that dignity must be preserved and outsiders must not be allowed to interfere in internal affairs". Koivisto rose to the position of Governor of the Bank of Finland with the support of Tanner's opponent, Urho Kekkonen. Kekkonen was interested in the income policy that was being introduced to Finland at the time, the President felt that the Governor of the Bank of Finland would need the support of the trade union movement in his work to defend the value of money. Kekkonen wrote in Suomen Kuvalehti, under the cover of his pseudonym "Liimatainen", that Koivisto, as a "man of the left", would have the best chance of gaining the support of the trade union movement for monetary policy. In this way, he ignored the other candidates who came forward in favour of Koivisto, namely his own confidant AhtiKarjalainen and Reino Rossi, who represented the civil service line. Incomes policy was at the top of the economic policy agenda in the early years of Koivisto's presidency. The so-called Liinamaa agreements achieved good results in controlling inflation and helped the economy to grow so fast that Koivisto was already wondering if no other policy was needed. He ironized that the country apparently imagined that income policies would allow "fiscal and monetary policymakers, relieved of their responsibilities, to move quite a bit to the sidelines." The golden age of income policy was eventually cut short as inflation failed to be kept under control. Economic policy pursued growth too ambitiously, and the economy overheated. On top of this came the first oil crisis, which brought inflation figures in the industrialised countries to double digits and collapsed the model of economic growth that had been going on in the West for a couple of decades and was based on cheap energy. In 1974, Finland's national economy was badly out of balance. The background to this was the overheating of the Finnish economy at the same time as western export markets were paralysed. The situation in Finland was different from that in other Western countries, in that our oil imports took place within the framework of bilateral trade from the Ussr. The Soviet Union had to use the oil revenues it received from Finland to buy goods from Finland. The sudden quadrupling of oil prices increased Finland's exports to the East in an unprecedented way. Finland's national economy overheated while western markets went into recession. Inflation in Finland accelerated to an annual rate of 18 per cent and the shortfall in foreign trade deepened to record levels. The Bank of Finland assessed the situation as unsustainable. In the spring of 1975, when the monetary situation continued to deteriorate, Finland, on the initiative of Mauno Koivisto, turned to the International Monetary Fund, asking it for support credits. On behalf of the government, Koivisto presented the Monetary Fund with the stabilisation programme demanded by the organisation, which promised to tighten both fiscal and monetary policy clearly. The programme was based on a set of fiscal measures adopted by the Government and the Bank of Finland's plan to tighten monetary policy. In the spring of 1976, a second, stricter programme had to be presented to the Imf when the adjustment measures had not progressed and a new aid credit had to be applied for. Like the tight monetary policy of the Bank of Finland at the beginning of the crisis of the 1930s, Koivisto's policy also attracted a lot of criticism during the crisis of the 1970s. Professor Jouko Paunio, an old friend of Koivisto from the time of the O Group, was perhaps one of the most prominent and authoritative critics. He severely criticized Koivisto's policy at the time, for example. In a presentation at the Science Days in early 1977. In Paunio's opinion, the economic policies pursued had limited demand too much and he called for devaluation instead. The issue was the subject of much-noticed public debate. Koivisto wanted to hold on to reducing inflation of the success achieved and replied to Paunio by asking, "How much better has economic development been in those countries that have fallen into or otherwise gone into an inflation-devaluation spiral than in those that have kept their inflation in check?" Paunio replied: "Koivisto apparently believes that in the past, frivolous extravagance has instilled in Finnish society, the consequences of which we are now suffering. Since this evil must be eradicated, the Finnish national economy has been made to carry out severe penance exercises, the number and duration of which only Koivisto knows." Koivisto and Paunio were thus caught up in the economic policy debate in a way that strikingly resembles the conflict between Vaino Tanner and his old teacher Yrjo Jahnsson 45 years earlier. When Koivisto talked about countries caught in a spiral of inflation, he was apparently referring at least to Britain, which was plunged into a balance of payments crisis at about the same time as Finland, but allowed its currency to depreciate and allowed inflation to accelerate at a much higher rate than in Finland. At the time of the koivisto-Paunio debate, the British pound had weakened by about 26% against the dollar against the pre-oil crisis exchange rate, while the Finnish markka dollar exchange rate was still almost unchanged. The eventual rise to power of MargaretThatcher in the spring of 1979 and the continuation of the economic regimen under her leadership. Koivisto also gave a speech at the Korpilampi meeting, in which he said that a prerequisite for a new, lighter economic policy was that inflation expectations could be met, and that a lot depended on what positions the interest groups would take. In both cases, the economic policy line consisted of tightening budgetary policy and balancing the balance of payments with a hard monetary policy. Foreign indebtedness had to be stopped and the country's foreign liquidity secured. The alternative of accepting inflation was not tested. *** If we compare Mauno Koivisto's economic policies in the 1970s with how Vaino Tanner acted in the 1930s, there are both common features and differences. Both Tanner's and Koivisto's economic statements emphasised the need for stability in the value of money and balanced central government finances. Both were involved in implementing economic policies in line with these objectives in difficult economic conditions. Of course, the circumstances were different. What was common was a dangerous balance of payments crisis, a recession in the economy and a rise in unemployment. Otherwise, the situation was different. The economic downturn of the 1970s, on the other hand, arose in conditions of rising inflation and sharply rising international interest rates. International economic policy cooperation was able to prevent the growth of protectionism, and Finland also set out to implement its free trade agreement with the EEC. Contrary to what is sometimes claimed, he stuck to economic policy issues in the background and saw it as his task to support the government that enjoyed the confidence of the parliament in question. At one time, during the economic crisis of the 1970s, Urho Kekkonen had warned that if the government and the Bank of Finland were to be "buttoned up against each other", the government would draw a longer straw. The Bank of Finland's historical work, published last year, does not see Koivisto as a key monetary player during his presidency. This picture also corresponds to my own perception. *** At the moment, both Finland and Europe are living in the worst economic crisis of our generation. Public sector indebtedness, the weakening of growth prospects and, consequently, the scarcity of future economic opportunities represent a serious challenge. It is a test of the ability of national political institutions in many countries, and in particular the supranational institutions of the EU. Times and circumstances are also changing, but the position of decision-makers is difficult even now. The issues are complex and decision-makers have to act simultaneously at national and international level, under pressure from citizens and the market. There are more media and the pressure for easy replies is great. However, a sustainable starting point is that the facts are brought to light and solutions are sought on a sustainable basis. Responsible economic management and democratic decision-making must be reconciled. That road takes strength and challenges decision-makers, but all the other options are much worse.

Title: Opening words at the Bank of Finland Payment Forum
text: President and CEO Erkki Liikanen: Opening words at the Bank of Finland's Payments Forum in Helsinki 7.5.2013 . Speech . Tuesday 7 May 2013,10:00 AM Director-General Erkki Liikanen Opening words at the Bank of Finland's Payment Forum in Helsinki 7.5.2013 THE PAYMENT CHAIN WILL CONTINUE TO REQUIRE THE COOPERATION OF ALL PARTIES I would like to warmly welcome you all to this already seventh Payment Forum. The payment forum has become a visible and useful part of the cooperation through which the Finnish payment system has been developed in recent years and its visions for the future have been outlined. As the monetary authority of Finland, the Bank of Finland's duties include, according to the law, "to take care of the payment and other the reliability and efficiency of the financial system and contribute to its development." This task can be carried out by the Bank only in cooperation with the various parties to the payment system and also with others with public authorities. When supervising the development of the payment system, the Bank of Finland does not only consider banks to be its partners, although they are, of course, already a very important reference group even as SP's account customers. The retail payment system is ultimately for businesses and consumers and caters to all aspects of the economy. Players. It is natural that in the development of the payment system, the perspective of payers and payees must be centrally displayed. Opening in this direction was already the goal when the first Payment Forum was organized six years ago. The customer perspective will be equally central in the future. One might perhaps ask what the importance of cooperation such as the Payments Forum can be when, in a market economy, the development of services should normally take place on the basis of competition and the demand expressed in practice by customers. Communication between the parties to the payment system must not be aimed at reducing competition. Competition remains the best engine of efficiency. The aim of the payment forum is also to promote competition and efficiency in such a way that it is best associated with others. the expectations that society has of the payment system. What are these expectations? For my part, I would like to highlight five criteria that must be taken into account when developing the charging system. *** The first of the criteria, which Finland has invested in for decades with good results, is technical efficiency. This has to do with how advances in payment technology are making payment cheaper, faster and safer. There are constant innovations on the technological side, and the challenge is how to implement new, better solutions. This is where efficiency and coordination meet. The payment service is a network-like activity, and in such an industry we are faced with the well-known "egg-and-chicken" problem: it is not worthwhile for any party to switch to new systems on its own, without the knowledge that others are going to decide for themselves the same. In the case of a charging system, cooperation between the various parties may therefore aim to ensure that there is a sufficient awareness of technical advances, the plans and priorities of the various parties so that everyone can plan their activities rationally. On the other hand, communication must be transparent in such a way that coordination does not become discriminatory in relation to the solutions on offer. We can be pleased with how efficient the Finnish payment system has been tuned to be. It is among the most effective by international comparisons. For example, according to a study on the cost of payment carried out by the ECB published last autumn , (which the Bank of Finland also participated in - Finland, together with Sweden and Denmark, belonged to the group of countries with the lowest total social costs of retail payments. The cost-effectiveness achieved in this group of countries was based on advanced payment electronicisation, which was reflected in the prevalence of payment terminals and the high volume of card payments in relation to the number of cash payments. Comparisons of the cost of payment involve a lot of measurement and conceptual problems. However, the results are likely to be very indicative. The overall economic importance of payment systems is underlined by the fact that, despite everything, the economic cost of payment, even in this most advanced group of countries, to which Finland belongs, was estimated at almost one per cent of gdp value (0.8%). *** Another important criterion that has recently been on the table is the accessibility of payment systems for different segments of the population. We can talk about non-discrimination. Non-discrimination means that groups of people whose needs differ from the situation of the vast majority of the population can also use means of payment and payment services without undue effort or cost. When the payment system has sought to be cost-effective and to standardise payment methods, the needs of some groups of people may be overlooked. Last November, the Bank of Finland drew attention to these issues. We announced that we will monitor how the citizens' right to basic banking services is realised. The importance of the non-discrimination criterion as a concern for payment system policy has increased recently as there has been an increasing shift to electronic and network-based services. Although, on average, the availability of banking services is good, not all bank customers, such as the elderly or special groups, are able to take full advantage of electronic services. It must be assumed that, even because of the needs of special groups, the availability of cash and banking services is still part of a well-functioning financial system. Part of the functioning provision of cash services is that banks should provide their customers with the possibility to withdraw their deposits also in cash. The Bank of Finland considers it important that banks ensure sufficient access to cash and banking services. We want to encourage banks to develop new solutions that would combine the requirement for increased efficiency with wide access to services. *** The third criterion relates to pricing. In order for the benefits of an advanced charging system to be effectively exploited in the national economy, the pricing of payments must also be efficient and cost-based. In a market economy, the main rule is that competition prevents the abuse of market power. The issue of pricing is particularly thorny precisely in payment systems, where functions are concentrated and where pricing has traditionally been largely indirect. The cooperation between operators required by payment systems and the economies of scale at different levels of the value chain mean that effective competition in the provision of payment services is not a foregone conclusion. The current situation, in which low interest rates reduce banks' ability to earn on current account interest margins, should accelerate the transition from indirect pricing of payment services to more targeted pricing. Until now, the costs of banks' payment transactions have only been partly covered by the commission income associated with the payment. The fundamental importance of the issue of pricing is further underlined by the nature of payment as a necessity service. Where market power exists and where suitable alternative payment methods are not available, the disincentives to pricing will remain weak. Competition policy is therefore also needed. At EU level, particular attention has recently been paid to the pricing of card payments. Contacts such as the Payment Forum are no substitute for a well-functioning competition policy. However, it can offer service users one way to bring their point of view to the fore if there are obvious flaws in pricing. *** The fourth criterion is related to the continuity of operations and security of supply. The payment system is a neural network of economic life, the uninterrupted and efficient operation of which is essential for the functioning of the market and the smooth running of citizens' everyday lives. It must therefore be sufficiently immune to technical failures. In addition, the payment system must aim for sufficient security of supply in case of exceptional circumstances. This issue has become even more complex in recent years as dependence on electronic payment methods has increased and the possibilities of using cash payments as a comprehensive back-up system have diminished. In addition, the processing of interbank payments has mainly moved beyond Finland's borders. The challenges posed by these developments will be addressed when the financial markets' preparedness guideline for exceptional circumstances is renewed later this year. In the future, this work may also place new demands on the structure of the systems. In addition, the Bank of Finland will continue to monitor the operational reliability of the systems under normal conditions in accordance with its duties. *** The fifth criterion relates to international compatibility. This has been at the heart of our agenda in recent years in the form of the SEPA project. Finland has progressed on schedule and meets the targets well in the implementation of European standards. The integrity of the European payment system is important for the internal market and, in particular, for the European business sector operating internationally. At the end of this project next winter, development resources or brainpower may be freed up for other current payment system projects. However, international compatibility must continue to be borne in mind when considering the introduction of new solutions. Finns seem to have a lot to offer, for example, when it comes to implementing the European standards for e-invoicing. *** It is probably the case that payment is best arranged if you do not notice it separately, but it goes effortlessly and safely. In this regard, it is like human health: only when something goes wrong does greater attention begin to be paid to it. Reliable and efficient payment systems are often taken for granted. However, behind them there is a large number of different parties who need to be able to work smoothly together. In order to ensure the security and efficiency of payment systems also in the future, the cooperation of all parties in the payment chain is needed. In many countries, there is cooperation similar to the Payment Forum and established forms have also been sought for it. The focus has been not only on technical issues, but also on the social dimension of the development of the payment system. We in Finland would also benefit from establishing this type of activity, and at the same time we could create a new medium-term agenda for cooperation on payment systems. *** Let me now turn to our programme today. The morning is reserved for the Payment Forum. As in previous years, this afternoon will be the turn of the SEPA Forum, which is organised by the Federation of Finnish Financial Services and the SEPA core group. The morning Payment Forum has two main themes/sections: 1. European retail payments in transition 2. Paying in a digitalizing world. Both themes aptly illustrate the multifaceted role of today's payment. On the one hand, it has cross-border connections under an EU-level regulatory framework. On the other hand, it is closely linked to other, often digitised, functions of the economy. At the beginning of the morning, we will hear a progress report on the current state of play of regulatory projects. The European Commission is in the process of reforming the legislation on retail payments, including the completion of an update to the Payment Services Directive. At the same time, the Commission is finalising measures on card, online and mobile payments in line with the so-called 'green card' published last year. on the basis of the Green Paper. These regulatory projects will contribute to shaping the playing field for retail payments in Europe. The practical implementation of the transformation of European retail payments is, of course, the responsibility of payment service providers. It is therefore important to hear their views on future developments. How do different representatives of the payment industry see the challenges and opportunities of changing the playing field? This is explained by representatives of card, mobile and online payments. As I have already emphasised, when developing payment methods, attention should also be paid to ensuring that suitable services are available for all categories of users. In the commentary, we hear about the challenges older people face when it comes to paying. *** In the second part of the morning, we will look at payment and its role in a digitalizing world. Economic real-timeization is advancing on many fronts: the digitalization of financial administration and payments opens up plenty of new opportunities for efficiency that need to be seized. In connection with these, we will hear about ongoing projects and their confluences within the framework of Aalto University's Real-Time Economy programme in the recent ICT-2015 working group report on the possibilities of utilising the digital economy. If successfully completed, the ongoing projects enable, among other things, that the information needed to fulfill administrative obligations can be collected from companies' financial management systems as automatic by-products of payroll payments, e-invoicing, payment transactions and bank statements. When considering the domestic and European development of payments, it is important to strive for the widest possible perspective: innovations in retail payments are often born in the global market and can spread rapidly today. In connection with this, we hear about the experiences of an internationally operating company in the operating environments of very different payment methods globally. *** In connection with this year's Payments Forum, the fifth and final SEPA Forum will be held in the afternoon to discuss the final challenges of Finland's SEPA transition. It is valuable that the NGO perspective is also on display in the forum. However, at the end of the SEPA Platform's activities, cooperation on the development of retail payments should continue. The Bank of Finland proposes that a Payment Council be established in Finland as a new cooperation body to continue the activities of the Payment and SEPA Forum. It aims to provide a framework for cooperation between service providers, users and public authorities to ensure secure and efficient payment services in the future, using new technologies and innovations. Pentti Hakkarainen, Vice Chairman of the Board of Directors, will tell more about the next steps in the establishment of the Payment Council at the end of the morning. Kuten edell<8a> jo korostin, maksamistapoja kehitett<8a>ess<8a> tulee kiinnitt<8a><8a> huomiota my<9a>s siihen, ett<8a> sopivia palveluja on tarjolla kaikille k<8a>ytt<8a>j<8a>ryhmille. Kommenttipuheenvuorossa kuulemme ik<8a><8a>ntyneiden ihmisten kohtaamista haasteista maksamiseen liittyen. *** Aamup<8a>iv<8a>n toisessa osiossa tarkastelemme maksamista ja sen roolia digitalisoituvassa maailmassa. N<8a>ihin liittyen kuulemme Aalto-yliopiston Real-Time Economy -ohjelman puitteissa meneill<8a><8a>n olevista hankkeista ja niiden yhtym<8a>pinnoista tuoreeseen digitaalisen talouden hy<9a>dynt<8a>mismahdollisuuksia k<8a>sitelleeseen ICT-2015 ty<9a>ryhm<8a>n raporttiin. Title: Letter from Director General Liikanen
text: Letter from Director-General Liikanen, 04/01/2014 . Speech . Saturday 4 January 2014, 12:00 PM Published in Ilta-Sanomat on 4.1.2014 Dear readers, The start of the new year is encouraging for the international economy. However, the outlook for the Finnish economy is slowly improving. In addition to the recession that followed the financial crisis, Finland has faced a major restructuring of industry. The past year has been a turning point in the Finnish economic debate. For a long time, the debate was dominated by a delusion: Finland's basic problems stem from others, such as Greece or economic and monetary union. The focus was on judging and teaching others. As always happens, arrogance became an injury. Our own problems were not seen in the right light. The drastic contraction of the electronics sector and the adjustment of the forest industry hit Finland at the same time as the international financial crisis. However, these are two separate changes. We must seek a solution to our own crisis in Finland, to the financial crisis in Europe. Many believed that this was just a cyclical pit. A bridge can be built over it with debt. Later it was seen that the second beach was not visible. The bridge becomes a pier and then no money is enough. In the summer, it was understood that we had to tackle our own problems. The cost level in Finland has risen too much, much more than elsewhere. Retrospective adjustment is difficult. But the gap is bound to be bridged, and it won't happen anytime soon. The social partners took their own responsibility for this. Sustainable economic and employment growth can only be achieved through reforms. The need for an economy structural reforms that increase production potential and employment, as well as a successful innovation policy. Important decisions have been taken to respond to the challenges of the economy. When expenditure seems to permanently exceed tax revenue, an unsustainable situation arises that needs to be resolved. The structural reforms proposed by the government seek to find a way to adapt the welfare state to the size that Finland's resources can withstand. Is that enough? The Bank of Finland conducted an economist analysis of the structural package. The summary is that if the scale of the structural package is adhered to, the package will be implemented in its entirety and front-loaded, it will be enough. But if parts are removed from it, you will have to apply for a new one. If it or parts of it are postponed, much more will soon have to be done. The important thing is to get more done with tax money. That is what an increase in the productivity of public services means. Grinding does not help, it is necessary to look for wiser ways to organize the work. Let's do the right things and do better. People have a better education. Information technology will help. Better incentives and leadership are needed. People also live healthier and longer than previous generations. It is not unreasonable for a small part of the additional years to be spent in working life. I do not believe that politics comes only for tactical or power reasons, but because of value choices and a desire to change the world for the better. If the economic facts change, it must be taken into account. It is logical to create a positive program, define things, prioritize them and try to promote them with others. It may be easier to stand in the way of all change, but it does not create solutions. How should Finland act in Europe and other international fields? Here, too, we are most successful when we define our own goals and seek support for them from others. It will only succeed if we are also prepared to give support to others when their demands are justified. When the general line is constructive, you can gain a better understanding when you have exceptional things to defend and are even difficult. Nevertheless, it should be remembered that we have a lot of common interests with others that need to be promoted, and not just focus on rejecting the initiatives of others The banking union is a good example of European cooperation. It is important to end the path where profits are private  but losses are taxpayers'. People's criticism has been entirely justified. A year and a half ago, an important decision was taken in Europe: lessons must be learned from this economic crisis. Everything possible must be done to ensure that it does not happen again. Two important steps have been taken this year: Firstly, there will be a single banking supervision in Europe. Once authorised, banks will be able to operate throughout the EU's single market. It is essential that they are also supervised by a European authority together with national supervisors. Secondly, when a bank gets into trouble or threatens to fail, it is the responsibility of the shareholders and investors. The European crisis management system is an important step in this respect. To support the scheme, a crisis management fund will be set up, to which banks will pay collateral contributions to cover common risks. That is right. Relying on state aid must be avoided at all costs. When profits are private, losses must also be private. Important solutions have been made at European level through a shared awareness of the burning nature of the problem. When the banking system operates across national borders, supervision and crisis management measures must also be at the same level. In the case of large banks, the right level is European, together with national supervisors. Finland's structural problems, on the other hand, must be solved in Finland. We must ensure that the financial basis of the economy and employment, as well as of the welfare state, lasts. Knowledge of history is essential. We must remember finland's great story. I have had the opportunity to attend two memorable events this year. In March, Linda Jakobson recounted one event from 1997 at her father's memorial service. He was walking with his father and they discussed the collapse of the USSR and Finland's accession to the European Union. Suddenly, Max Jakobson had stopped and said: "Listen, it is only in recent years that I have realised that, for the first time in its entire history, Finland is now truly independent". In November, president Koivisto announced on his 90th birthday that he belonged to a generation that first fought for independence and then sought to integrate. They were prepared to give up part of the sovereignty when it was counterbalanced by more influence. "This is what happened. The pessimists were wrong," Koivisto said. What unites them? Both are patriots, including front men. But at the same time, they are committed to being European and international. My concern is that instead of the fine patriotism of Koivisto and Jakobson, passionate nationalism and intolerance will surface. It does not size, but divides. At the same time, they are working against the tradition of tolerance, Europeanism and internationalism that they represent, among other things. Knowledge of history helps to appreciate those who, in difficult times, bear responsibility for national, European and international solutions. It also teaches that cynicism only destroys, but criticality is necessary  it is an important prerequisite for renewal. Erkki Liikanen Governor of the Bank of Finland
