Title: Vin Tanner and Risto Ryti in Finland's monetary policy
text: President and CEO Erkki Liikanen: Vaino Tanner and Risto Ryti on Finnish monetary policy. University of Helsinki, 12.3.2014. . Speech . Wednesday12 March 2014,4:00 PM Director General Erkki Liikanen Presentation at the Vaino Tanner Foundation seminar at the University of Helsinki 12.3.2014 VaINo TANNER AND RISTO RYTI IN FINNISH MONETARY POLICY INTRODUCTION In the history of the Ministry of Finance, which appeared in 2009, there is a graph on which the economic policy influencers of the interwar period are placed. The strongest influencers are in the middle of the chart and the less significant ones are on its outskirts. At the very centre of the inner circle are Risto Ryti, Governor of the Bank of Finland, and J.K. Paasikivi, President of the National Bank of Finland. In addition, the ceo of Osuusliike Elanto, Vaino Tanner, and two export men, RudolfWalden, managing director of the United Paper Mills, and Frans MikaelPitkaniemi, the long-term ceo of the Voin vienti-osuusliike Valio, will be included in the same series. Of these heavyweight influencers, only Ryti and Tanner held public positions, the others represented the business world. Ryti and Tanner had an influence as members of parliament, ministers and monetary policy, especially at the head of the Bank of Finland. Ryti is the bank's longest-serving president and Tanner's longest-serving board member. In the 1930s, Vaino Tanner was chairman of the banking board. Ryti and Tanner formed a pairing, and their cooperation took hold of Finnish monetary policy already in the 1920s and dominated it in the 1930s. Economic policy in the interwar period has always been the subject of lively, sometimes harsh, debate in Finland as well. Recent years have once again increased this interest, as the current financial crisis has been compared to the experiences and lessons of the 1930s. The study of the depression of the 1930s has also had a great deal of influence on economic policy. For example, the active activities of the Federal Reserve in recent years can well be explained by the fact that its recently resigned governor, Ben Bernanke, has devoted a large part of his career to the study of the depression of the 1930s. In Finland, the interwar decades were, on the whole, a period of rapid growth. From 1920 to 1938, the economy grew by an average of 4.5% per year, while modernizing in many respects. However, even in Finland, the economic crisis of 1929-1932, which hit the section of the population that earns their living from agriculture and forestry work the hardest. The forced auctions and unemployment of the time have remained part of the nation's collective memory, even though, from an economic point of view, the recession of the 1930s was clearly milder and shorter in Finland than in most other countries. BACKGROUNDS OF RYTI AND TANNER The comparison between ryti and Tanner's actions is interesting because their backgrounds are diametrically opposed in many respects and yet there was also much the same in them. During the most important years of their political careers, they worked in constant cooperation, which, at least on economic issues, was usually absolutely seamless. It was also evident that they valued each other a lot, even though the starting points were so different. Martti Turtola, who wrote a biography of Ryti, even talks about "the sympathy of souls". Ryti was a liberal who represented the right-wing wing of the Progressive Party and a talent who had risen to leading positions in economic life at a young age, a cosmopolitan who, according to the authors of his biographies, especially when he was younger, was quite a dandy, a yuppie figure of his time. No one has described Ryti as folksy. Tanner was eight years older than Ryti from a working-class family in Helsinki, who, after completing business school, had adopted a social democratic worldview during an internship in Germany and entered politics. By the time he graduated as a lawyer in 1911, Tanner was already a 30-year-old member of parliament. He was a temperance man and an ascetic in lifestyle, with the possible exception of his cigar-smoking hobby. There were also common features. Both were lawyers, and both had become familiar with financial matters through experience gained in business life  Ryti as a lawyer for Alfred Kordelin, the richest man in Finland, while Tanner had started his career as a manager of the Vahavasten Osuusliike in Turku and ended up in the management of the large cooperative company Elanto for 30 years. Tanner's speeches are dominated by sarcastic, sometimes harsh humour. He was concrete in his speeches and excerpts. Ryti, on the other hand, was inclined to theorize and even pedantry. Both were emphatically businesslike as human beings and avoided emotion. The men were united by a commitment to the values of Western democracy. They were also exceptionally international at the time and travelled extensively abroad. Both have served on the committees of the League of Nations since the 1920s. Tanner also worked for the International Cooperative Association, while Ryti worked for the Basel Bank for International Settlements (BIS). Tanner's foreign policy of the 1920s and 1930s emphasized the Nordic trend in particular. Ryti, on the other hand, is considered an Anglophile, and his relationships, especially with the Bank of England, became close, also on a personal level. Montagu Norman, the legendary governor of the Bank of England, described Ryti as unique and wrote in 1935 that hopefully Ryti would never become president, lest he would simply be tarnished in politics. Vaino Tanner's political activities began long before Ryti. Tanner became a member of parliament for Finland's first unicameral parliament elected by universal suffrage in 1907. He had just turned 26 at the time. Before Finland became independent, Tanner was already a senator, head of finance of OskariTokoi's short-lived Senate in the spring and summer of 1917. CO-OPERATION STARTS In the first parliamentary elections of independent Finland in 1919, both Tanner and Ryti were elected to parliament. Both were immediately involved in the administration of the Parliament's bank, the Bank of Finland: Tanner became a member of the banking board and Ryti became the auditor of the Bank of Finland. After a couple of years, Ryti rose to leadership positions in economic policy when, in the spring of 1921, he became Minister of Finance J.H. Vennola's minority government, which consisted half of ministers from the Progressive Party and half from the Agrarian Union. Ryti was 32 years old at the time and is still Finland's youngest ever finance minister. Vennola's government remained standing for more than a year, mainly with the support of the Social Democrats, until the foreign minister was overthrown According to the so-called "encyclopedia" driven by Rudolf Holst. due to peripheral state politics. The biggest issue in the early years of the cooperation between Vaino Tanner and Risto Ryti was the stabilisation of Finland's state finances and the value of the markka after the economic chaos caused by the First World War and the Civil War. By the beginning of the 1920s, the amount of money in circulation had increased tenfold from what it had been when the First World War broke out. The central government had had to cover its expenses by borrowing from the Bank of Finland, and its creditworthiness abroad was non-existent. The value of the markka against the US dollar had weakened to one-sixth of the previous level, and the trend was still deteriorating. Ryti and Tanner quickly found common ground on these issues. Among Vaino Tanner's papers are his notes about a meeting with Ryti in the spring of 1921 after he became Minister of Finance. According to the notes, already at that time the men agreed on the need to balance the state economy and stabilize the exchange rate of the markka. Both felt that the Finnish markka had weakened too much, so it had to be allowed to strengthen at its then level, but not too much. Among them, the stabilisation of the exchange rate had to take place on the basis of the reduced purchasing power of the markka. So neither of them wanted to go after the value of money that had prevailed before the war, as was the case in Sweden, for example. There, the restoration of the value of money caused a severe economic crisis. The inflation experienced in Finland had been so high that it would have been quite unrealistic in practice to start reversing it. Tanner's line on economic stabilisation was already evident at the party congress in December 1919, where he was re-elected chairman of the Social Democratic Party. In economic policy, the hot issue was the currency law, which would have centralized currency trading for the Bank of Finland. At the party congress, Tanner addressed the issue as follows: "I would like to touch (Oskari) Elm's statement if he was talking about currency law. It shows such a foolish notion of the basis on which our economic life rests that one would not think that even an ordinary worker, let alone a man involved in parliamentary life, could pronounce such a thing. He said that there is no point in trying to organise the rise in the value of money and the state economy, best to let it degenerate and go into a hustle and bustle, then we will see what comes. He had no program other than: then we would see what came of it! If such a thing were to be presented at a Labour Congress somewhere else, such a man would be laughed out. Because everywhere else the Social Democrats have, according to their strength, worked to prevent the bankruptcy of the state. In Germany and Austria, where it is under enormous threat, the Social Democrats have worked extremely hard to combat it. I do not think that we, too, have the working class in favour of Elm, but insists that we must put the state's finances in order, otherwise it will become intolerable to live in this country. This is what it means to enact a currency law. It was intended to give the government the power to prevent the extraordinarily dizzying depreciation of the Finnish markka. But if there is no way to prevent it, then there is the Elm let go program. Since June, the value of the Finnish markka has just gone halfway. It is by no means a small question for the working people. The consequence has been that the costs have increased twice as much; but have wages risen? You will not be able to raise wages at the rate at which the mark is falling, and if the parliamentary group does not then consider it its duty to give the government all the weapons that can be given, then it will poorly fulfill its obligations." The Currency Act was enacted, and it remained in force until the fall of 1921. On the side of private banks, the law aroused a lot of bitterness. For Tanner, the emphasis on inflation and the stability of state finances was also due to the experiences of his tenure as head of finance of the Tokoi Senate in 1917. At that time, Finland's food shortage worsened and the state's economy plunged into a deep crisis. As Minister of Finance, Ryti's policy also aimed at improving the health of central government finances and stable monetary value. The goal of his first budget, 1922, was to eliminate the deficit. As the economy recovered faster than expected that year, central government finances turned into surplus and the central government paid off its short-term bill of exchange debt to the Bank of Finland altogether. The state thus got rid of "banknote financing". Inflation stopped and Finland's trade balance turned positive for the first time in all the time it had been recorded. After the fall of Vennola's government, Ryti returned to the position of Finance Minister for the second time after a short break. He joined the government led by KyostiKallio, which served from the beginning to the end of 1923. During his time on Kallio's board of directors, Ryti was appointed governor of the Bank of Finland, but he only accepted the post after the fall of the board. During Ryti's second term as Minister of Finance, a significant surplus was achieved in central government finances. As a result, Ryti proposed substantial tax cuts to Parliament. The state also completely paid off all its short-term debts. At the same time, however, the state took out a long-term dollar loan from abroad, not for the needs of the state, but in order to increase the foreign exchange reserves of the Bank of Finland. The purpose of this was to prepare for the transition to the gold standard. KULTAKANTAPOLITIIKKAA Ryti took over as Governor of the Bank of Finland in February 1924. The early years of his term as governor were dominated by the question of returning to the gold standard. It was a universal quest for stable monetary conditions prior to the First World War. Sweden returned to the gold standard in 1924 and England in 1925. These solutions also created preconditions for Finland's decision. According to both Ryti and Tanner, Finland's entry into the gold standard was an obvious goal. They were both members of the Gold Standard Committee, which in the spring of 1925 was preparing Finland's return to the gold standard. The committee was chaired by the then chairman of the banking council, Ernst Nevanlinna of the Conservative Party, who had once been Tanner's history teacher at the Finnish Real Lyceum in Helsinki  now Ressu Upper Secondary School. The Gold Standard Committee was unanimous in recommending that the mark be tied to the gold standard and thus that its exchange rate be permanently fixed on other gold currencies. The recommended level of the committee in relation to the gold dollar corresponded to what Risto Ryti had paid attention to at the beginning of his term as president. The chosen exchange rate level was somewhat undervalued relative to purchasing power parity. Tanner had previously advocated a slightly stronger mortgage rate, but during 1924 he had come out in support of the Ryti line. In Tanner's opinion, the gold standard was needed to permanently stabilize the value of money. Stable monetary value was considered by Tanner to be an important goal for the working party. His thinking was based on the fact that changes in the exchange rate would cause damaging fluctuations in the standard of living of workers. Ryti presented his thinking on the gold standard extensively in a presentation he gave at the National Economic Association as soon as the work of the Gold Standard Committee was completed. According to Ryti, a key argument in favour of joining the gold standard was to improve Finland's foreign creditworthiness. In his opinion, Finland was a capital-poor country in terms of its natural resources and population growth, and he predicted that Finland would therefore remain a "capital-importing country" for a long time to come. But the creditworthiness of Finland depended on the monetary system. In his presentation, Ryti summed up: "It is not enough to have a good monetary system, it is also required that our monetary system be such that it is trusted abroad." This was a key argument when joining the gold standard. Finland officially entered the gold standard at the beginning of 1926. Practical monetary policy was no longer much affected by this, since the exchange rate against the leading gold currency, the US dollar, had been fixed for two years already. In 1925, presidential electorate elections were held. The first vote of the electors included six presidential candidates, among them both Tanner and Ryti. Tanner received the most votes, 79, and Ryti 33 votes. It was clear that the Social Democrats could not get their own candidate through. In the second round, they, led by Tanner, supported Risto Ryti as President of the Republic. He was considered the most "democratic" of the bourgeois candidates. Even the combined strength of the Social Democrats and the Progressive Party was not enough, and in the end L.K. Relander of the March Union became president with the support of the Conservative Party and the Swedish People's Party. TANNER BOARD OF DIRECTORS At the end of 1926, Tanner became Prime Minister of Finland. His social democratic minority government sat for a year. It was eventually overturned by a dispute over the 1928 budget. The Tanner government would have liked to dismantle agricultural import protection and drastically reduce import tariffs on food. The reductions in customs duties were to be covered by an increase in taxes on income and property. Lowering food prices and increasing the progressive tax on income and property had long been on the social democrats' agenda, and now attempts are being made to push this goal through. However, the budget was not suitable for a majority in parliament, and the government was forced to leave its seat. Indeed, it was not until the 1990s that real progress was made in reducing the import protection of agricultural products when Finland joined the EU. The minority government of the Social Democrats has often been seen as a sign that after the civil war, political conditions began to return to normal. It was one step. However, Vaino Tanner had played a significant role in the administration of the Bank of Finland and in the Tartu peace negotiations before that. From a modern point of view, it may be considered strange that Tanner continued on the banking council, even as its vice-president throughout his term as prime minister. This was the way of the time. Kyosti Kallio served simultaneously as Speaker of the Parliament and as a member of the Board of Directors of the Bank of Finland throughout the 1930s, until he was elected President of the Republic. In the 1950s, ministers sat on the banking council as late as the 1950s, and the members of the Board of Directors of the Bank of Finland often held ministerial duties alongside their own duties. Only the chairman of the executive board, Sakari Tuomioja, had to ask for a leave of absence when he was prime minister. The question of conflicts of interest and disqualification was understood in a very different way than it is today. THE GOLD STANDARD DOES NOT LAST It was hoped that the gold standard would alleviate the capital shortage in Finland and lower interest rates. The Bank of Finland worked to lower interest rates, and the idea was to get closer to the interest rates of stable gold standard countries. In Finland, both the general bank interest rates and the key interest rate of the Bank of Finland were many percentage points higher than the corresponding Swedish and English rates. A lot of foreign credit was received in the country, but the high demand for credit still kept interest rates higher than the Bank of Finland had sought. The corona reduction policy advocated by Ryti and Tanner has later been criticized, as in 1927 and 1928 finland's national economy clearly overheated due to the acceleration of construction activity. When the sawn timber market took a turn for the worse, the situation finally led in the autumn of 1928 to a sudden money market crisis, rising interest rates and an economic downturn. The economic crisis began in Finland about a year before the Wall Street stock market crash started the Great Depression abroad. The depression, or shortage, as it was said at the time, ushered in the most controversial phase of the Bank of Finland's monetary policy. Finland's export market was paralysed and the prices of export products fell sharply. In order to defend the gold coupling of the markka, the Bank of Finland pursued a tight monetary policy. The combination of deflation and tight monetary policy caused debt problems and bankruptcies, especially in agriculture and the sawmill industry. The situation came to a head in the summer of 1931, when the European banking crisis broke out. It began in Austria and spread to Germany. In September, the Bank of England was also subjected to a currency attack and was eventually forced to abandon the gold standard. The other Nordic countries followed England almost immediately, Finland two weeks later. However, monetary policy continued to be tight for more than a year, as the Bank of Finland sought to put the brakes on the currency's flight from the country. After the markka had left the gold standard, it was initially feared that inflation would be rampant. This had happened the last time that the value of money had been cut off after the outbreak of the First World War. Since then, the return to the gold standard and monetary policy in general had been geared towards combating inflation, which was seen as the greatest threat to the monetary system. It took some time before it was realized that in the conditions of the global depression, the risk of deflation was a greater threat than inflation. In practice, the balance of payments largely determined the room for manoeuvre in monetary policy even a couple of years after the exit from the gold standard. There was pressure on the exchange rate, and although interest rates were considered higher than in many other countries, the exchange rate depreciated markedly. The Bank of Finland only began to ease its monetary policy after the pressure on the exchange rate had eased. CONTROVERSY OVER MONETARY POLICY After the exit from the gold standard, there was a rather heated debate in Parliament about whether the Bank of Finland had defended the gold value of the markka for too long or not. In addition, the Bank of Finland was criticised for providing emergency funding and also for investing share capital in Finland's third largest commercial bank, the Provincial Bank. It had entered a crisis at the same time as Finland was struggling to stay in the gold standard. In parliament, accusations were made especially from the Agrarian Union, which in the early 1930s called for a easing of monetary policy. In Parliament, Vaino Tanner strongly defended the Bank of Finland against both accusations. For Tanner, fear of rising inflation largely defined the framework of his monetary policy thinking. In the parliamentary debate on the Bank of Finland's policy in connection with the exit from the gold standard, he said: "I regard as great an accident both inflation, the deterioration of the value of money, as deflation, the deliberate improvement of the value of money. In fact, however, deflation has taken place over the last two or three years and, as far as I can see, the country's economy has largely already adapted to it. If we now begin to deliberately degrade the value of money again, it is, as has often been said, the same as driving the devils out with Belsebub." The dispute over the principles of monetary policy had already begun in the 1920s, when farmers demanded a reduction in interest rates. In the early years of the 1930s, a shortage movement arose, which demanded, in addition to lowering interest rates, other measures to facilitate access to credit for agriculture. It was believed that a light monetary policy would lead to a situation in which deflationary developments could be halted and prices could rise. The shortage movement was partly foreign parliamentary, but it also had a strong influence on the economic policy positions of the Agrarian Union. The monetary disputes of the early 1930s were largely between the Agrarian Union and the management of the Bank of Finland. Differing views culminated in a state commission that considered the organization of public works and price and interest rates issues in 1932. The committee consisted of both Risto Ryti and Vaino Tanner, and its secretary was A. E. Tudeer, Ryti's confidant from the Bank of Finland. The committee's report reflected their view that there was no reason to change the bank's monetary policy principles. However, not all members of the committee were on the same lines. Its chairman, EmilHynninen (director of the Pellervo Society) and Frans Mikael Pitkaniemi (CEO of Valio), attached a dissenting opinion to the report, in which they called for a reduction in interest rates, an increase in the banknote in circulation and active measures by the Central Bank to increase credit to agriculture. In their opinion, the Bank of Finland's regulations on setelinkate should be amended to allow for extended lending for agricultural purposes. The decisive dispute over the direction of monetary policy was fought by the Banking Council in December 1932. On the table was the opinion prepared by the Executive Board on the report of the aforementioned expert committee. In its statement, the Executive Board rejected the demands made in the dissenting opinion of the report and stressed the importance of the continuity of monetary policy. In an uncertain situation, there was no reason to experiment with inflation. The Board of Governors voted through the opinion of the Executive Board. The three rural allied members of the board of governors, led by jalo Lahdensuo, the then chairman of the banking council, maintained the dissenting position in the report but remained in the minority. During 1933, disputes over monetary policy eased. Tanner then rose to the position of chairman of the banking council, and the economic upturn eased the demands of the "shortage men" on the Bank of Finland. When confidence returned, the Bank of Finland was able to lower interest rates without putting further pressure on the exchange rate. The markka was attached to the pound sterling, and the pound exchange rate remained unchanged until the outbreak of world war. SAVINGS IN CENTRAL GOVERNMENT FINANCES The recession put pressure on central government finances. The government program of J.E. Sunila from March 1931 says this: "The current shortage situation has also weakened the position of central government finances, which therefore requires special care to be put in balance. In order to overcome the difficulties, a significant reduction in government spending is necessary. The government is aware that decisive measures are required in this regard, as one may seem in many respects. A reduction in public expenditure is also necessary to facilitate the adaptation of productive life to changed economic conditions." Sunila's government set up a special government spending reduction board, which operated through the spring of 1931. The members of the board were invited to be the heavyweights of economics and politics. The chairman was J.K. Paasikivi, President of the National Equity Bank, and the members were Alexander Frey, President of the Nordic Union Bank, Risto Ryti, Governor of the Bank of Finland, Tyko Reinikka, one of the influential members of the Agrarian Union, and Vaino Tanner of the then opposition party, the Social Democratic Party. The conclusion of the board's report was that the state's finances were becoming a burden on the national economy. "The consequence of this has been that, as has been pointed out earlier, the state has been forced to demand too much of the nation's income to satisfy its needs. There is a risk that the state economy is becoming a burden on the regular development of the national economy. A reduction in taxation would therefore have been necessary for our capital in our poor country in the past. Regardless of the recession, it would therefore have become necessary to undertake a review of the basics of central government finances in order to eliminate unhealthy growths in the state budget and reduce government expenditure." According to the committee's report, the most fundamental phenomenon of the depression was the huge fall in prices, which was reflected in the prices of agricultural products in particular, but also in the prices of raw materials for industry. In turn, the fall in prices, together with the contraction of forestry work, had led to particularly great difficulties for the agricultural community and brought numerous farmers to the brink of bankruptcy. In central government finances, the recession has been visible as a downturn in income since 1929, while central government expenditure has been boosted especially by support measures for agriculture and general work due to unemployment. The majority of central government expenditure was statutory. In the Board's assessment, it limited the means of reduction. It considers a reduction in central government wage expenditure to be the single most effective way. As a result of the fall in the cost of living, the real wages of government officials and other employees had risen, so the consequences of a general salary reduction would not be unreasonable. The concrete proposal was to reduce civil servants' salaries by between 5% and 10%. They had already become acquainted with tokoi's board of directors, and had also worked together in the administration of the Bank of Finland. The Social Democrats were satisfied by commitments to develop social insurance and health care and to change taxation to reduce the tax burden on low-income earners. The Agrarian Union was promised to continue its agricultural support measures and to increase settlement activity. For example, the financing of the army's basic procurement programme should only be done by raising taxes and not by increasing the national debt. In October 1938, Tanner and Ryti publicly discussed Tanner's budget proposal. The discussion went quite amicably. From the outset, Tanner acknowledged that the budget for the following year was relatively optimistic in nature, partly due to the good economic performance of previous years. However, spending had not gotten out of hand and Tanner characterized the budget as balanced. In his speech, Risto Ryti focused on warnings. According to him, the budget did not sufficiently take into account the threats that had arisen in the international economy. Ryti considered it very possible to international the impact of economic difficulties on Finland as well, as a result of which the criteria for the budget could be shaken: "Although now both our national and national finances are much better equipped for a worse time than in the past, I would venture to believe that the cyclical fund, even at the current size, is not in the hands of the government as strong a weapon as perhaps in many quarters imagine." Finally, Ryti returned to his own experiences as Minister of Finance in the early 1920s: "A well-known Finn instructed me that the Minister of Finance should speak like an optimist, but act like a pessimist. Its bottom failed, as is well known, due to far more fateful events than the debaters expected the previous autumn. The outbreak of war linked the fates of Ryti and Tanner together again in a new, and if possible even more serious way. The purpose of Tanner's visit was to persuade Ryti to become Prime Minister of Finland. President of the Republic Kallio also arrived. Tanner and Kallio eventually persuaded Ryti to agree, and his board was appointed in the evening of the same day. Vaino Tanner became its foreign minister. The idea of appointing Tanner as Foreign Minister was Paasikivi's. The fact that Tanner at such a moment just trusted Ryt says a lot about the relationship between the men. On the other hand, it says just as much about this relationship that Ryti wanted Tanner as her foreign minister. The framework of monetary policy has changed many times since the 1930s. Economics and the knowledge base and toolbox available for economic policy have evolved a great deal. Yet the same issues become topical time and time again. The main guiding stars of both Ryti's and Tanner's economic policy efforts were to protect and improve Finland's foreign creditworthiness and to secure a stable monetary value. A necessary condition for achieving these objectives was, in their view, a sustainable balance in central government finances. Not everything has changed. Securing stable monetary stability and the sustainability of public finances are key objectives of economic policy even now. The independence of the Central Bank must be guaranteed if it is to be able to play its role of price stability effectively. Once again, it has become the task of governments and, above all, of finance ministers, to act to ensure the sustainability of public finances. There weren't too many friends in that position in the past decades. And it is not today. But the sustainability of public finances is also now the lifeblood of sustainable growth and employment.

Valtion velka k<8a><8a>ntyi laskuun jo vuonna 1934, jolloin alkanutta ylij<8a><8a>m<8a><8a> ryhdyttiin my<9a>s rahastoimaan erityiseen suhdannerahastoon. PUNAMULTAHALLITUS Vuoden 1933 eduskuntavaaleista l<8a>htien V<8a>in<9a> Tanner alkoi tavoitella sosiaalidemokraattien p<8a><8a>sy<8a> mukaan hallituksiin. Aikaisemmin SDP:ss<8a> oli suhtauduttu kielteisesti hallitusyhteisty<9a>h<9a>n porvarillisten puolueiden kanssa. Tannerin hallituspyrkimysten esteen<8a> oli kuitenkin presidentti Svinhufvud, jolle sosialidemokraattien ottaminen hallitukseen ei sopinut. Vuoden 1936 eduskuntavaaleissa sosiaalidemokraattisen puolueen asema entisest<8a><8a>n vahvistui, ja kun Ky<9a>sti Kallio valittiin seuraavana vuonna tasavallan presidentiksi, tie SDP:n ottamiseen mukaan hallitukseen avautui. Presidentti edellytti maalaisliiton ja sosiaalidemokraattien puolueen hallitusyhteisty<9a>t<8a>. Kallio ja Tanner luottivat toisiinsa. He olivat tutustuneet jo Tokoin hallituksessa, ja olivat toimineet yhdess<8a> my<9a>s Suomen Pankin hallinnossa. Hallitusneuvottelut k<8a>ytiin pitk<8a>lti Tannerin ja maalaisliittoa edustaneen Juho Niukkasenkesken. Yksimielisyyteen siit<8a>, kumman puolueen johdolla hallitus koottaisiin, ei p<8a><8a>sty, jolloin ratkaisuksi tuli edistyspuolueen ottaminen mukaan hallitukseen ja p<8a><8a>ministerin teht<8a>v<8a>n antaminen edistyspuolueelle. Vahvimpina p<8a><8a>ministeriehdokkaina nostettiin esiin Risto Ryti, entinen presidentti K. J. St<8c>hlberg ja kaksi kertaa aikaisemminkin p<8a><8a>ministerin<8a> toiminut mets<8a>hallituksen p<8a><8a>johtaja Aimo Cajander.Tannerille Ryti olisi ollut mieluisin p<8a><8a>ministeri, mutta Ryti kielt<8a>ytyi teht<8a>v<8a>st<8a> ja p<8a><8a>ministeriksi tuli Cajander. Ensimm<8a>isen punamultahallituksen valtiovarainministeriksi nousi itseoikeutetusti V<8a>in<9a> Tanner. Cajanderin hallituksen aloittaessa ty<9a>ns<8a> kev<8a>ttalvella 1937 valtion taloudellinen asema oli hyv<8a>, sill<8a> takana oli jo useampi nopean taloudellisen kasvun vuosi. Jo hallitusneuvottelujen aikana Tanner oli joutunut tinkim<8a><8a>n kahdesta itselleen t<8a>rke<8a>st<8a> tavoitteesta, nimitt<8a>in tuontitullien alentamisesta ja puolustusm<8a><8a>r<8a>rahojen supistamisesta. Oikeistopuolueet puolestaan vaativat maanpuolustuksen m<8a><8a>r<8a>rahojen merkitt<8a>v<8a><8a> korottamista. Tanner ja h<8a>nen puolueensa olivat perinteisesti vastustaneet sotilasmenoja ja korostaneet Kansainliiton roolia rauhan s<8a>ilytt<8a>j<8a>n<8a> maailmassa. Valtiovarainministeriksi tultuaan Tanner joutui kuitenkin tunnustamaan tilanteen muuttuneen. <d3>Kun ei Suomenkaan asema ole maantieteellisesti turvattu, vaan meill<8a>kin, niin pieni ja k<9a>yh<8a> kansa kuin olemmekin, on mahdollisuus joutua valloitushaluisten naapurien hy<9a>kk<8a>yksen alaiseksi, on kysymys varusteluista t<8a><8a>ll<8a>kin tullut p<8a>iv<8a>npolttavaksi. My<9a>s sosiaalidemokraattinen puolue, ajatellessaan niit<8a> vaaroja, joita diktatuurij<8a>rjestelm<8a> on mukaan tuonut ja havaitessaan aatetoveriensa kaikissa maissa luopuneen aikaisemmalta vastustavalta kannaltaan, on katsonut voivansa olla kohtuullisessa m<8a><8a>r<8a>ss<8a> mukana lis<8a>varojen my<9a>nt<8a>misess<8a>. T<8a>ll<9a>in kyll<8a> kirvelee mielt<8a> heitt<8a><8a> hyv<8a><8a> rahaa ja n<8a>in suuressa m<8a><8a>r<8a>ss<8a> niin tuottamattomaan, hy<9a>dytt<9a>m<8a><8a>n ja suorastaan vahingolliseen tarkoitukseen kuin varustelujen lis<8a><8a>minen on.<d3> N<8a>in Tanner ja h<8a>nen puolueensa olivat viimeist<8a><8a>n vuoden 1938 alussa siirtyneet tukemaan esill<8a> olleen laajan perushankintaohjelman toteuttamista. Valtiovarainministerin<8a> Tanner korosti s<8a><8a>st<8a>v<8a>isyyden ensisijaisuutta. Valtion tulot ja menot oli pidett<8a>v<8a> tasapainossa ja valtio saisi ottaa lainoja ainoastaan tuottavien investointien rahoittamiseen. Esimerkiksi armeijan perushankintaohjelman rahoittaminen saisi tapahtua ainoastaan veroja korottamalla eik<8a> valtion velkaa lis<8a><8a>m<8a>ll<8a>. Erityisen t<8a>rke<8a>n<8a> finanssipoliittisena v<8a>lineen<8a> Tanner piti suhdannerahastoa, jota vuodesta 1934 l<8a>htien oli ryhdytty kartuttamaan ja jonka turvin valtiolla olisi pelivaraa mahdollisten taantumien aikana ilman ett<8a> tarvitsisi turvautua lainanottoon. Lokakuussa 1938 Tanner ja Ryti keskustelivat julkisesti Tannerin budjettiesityksest<8a>. Kyseess<8a> oli Kansantaloudellisen yhdistyksen kokous, jossa valtiovarainministeri ensimm<8a>isen kerran esitteli hallituksen talousarvion seuraavalle vuodelle ja johon kommenttipuheenvuoron pit<8a>j<8a>ksi oli pyydetty Suomen Pankin p<8a><8a>johtaja Risto Ryti. Keskustelu sujui melko sopuisasti. Tanner my<9a>nsi alusta l<8a>htien seuraavan vuoden tulo-ja menoarvion olevan perusluonteeltaan suhteellisen optimistinen, mik<8a> osittain johtui edelt<8a>neiden vuosien hyv<8a>st<8a> taloudellisesta kehityksest<8a>. Menot eiv<8a>t kuitenkaan olleet karanneet k<8a>sist<8a> ja Tanner luonnehti budjettia tasapainoiseksi. Risto Ryti keskittyi omassa puheenvuorossaan varoituksiin. H<8a>nen mukaansa tulo-ja menoarviossa ei ollut riitt<8a>v<8a>sti huomioitu kansainv<8a>lisess<8a> taloudessa esiin nousseita uhkia. Ryti piti hyvin mahdollisena kansainv<8a>lisen talouden vaikeuksien heijastumista my<9a>s Suomeen, mink<8a> seurauksena tulo-ja menoarvion perusteet saattaisivat j<8a>rkky<8a>: <d3>Vaikka nyt sek<8a> kansantaloutemme ett<8a> valtiotaloutemme on paljon paremmin varustautunut huonommankin ajan varalle kuin aikaisemmin, rohkenen kumminkin olla sit<8a> mielt<8a>, ettei suhdannerahasto viel<8a> nykyisenk<8a><8a>n suuruisena ole hallituksen k<8a>siss<8a> vaikean pulan sattuessa niin vahva ase kuin ehk<8a> monella taholla kuvitellaan.<d3> P<8a><8a>tteeksi Ryti palasi omiin kokemuksiinsa valtiovaranministerin<8a> 1920-luvun alkuvuosina: <d3>Er<8a>s tunnettu suomalainen antoi minulle sen ohjeen, ett<8a> finanssiministerin pit<8a><8a> puhua kuin optimisti, mutta toimia kuin pessimisti. Paradoksaalisuudestaan huolimatta t<8a>m<8a> ohje n<8a>ytt<8a><8a> viel<8a>kin k<8a>ytt<9a>kelpoiselta.<d3> Budjetti, josta keskusteltiin, koski vuotta 1939. Sen pohja petti, niin kuin tiedet<8a><8a>n, paljon kohtalokkaampien tapahtumien vuoksi kuin mit<8a> keskustelijat edellisen<8a> syksyn<8a> osasivat odottaa. Sodan syttyminen liitti Rytin ja Tannerin kohtalot yhteen j<8a>lleen uudella, ja jos mahdollista entist<8a>kin vakavammalla tavalla. LOPUKSI Joulukuun ensimm<8a>isen<8a> p<8a>iv<8a>n<8a> 1939 V<8a>in<9a> Tanner tuli Suomen Pankkiin heti aamulla pankin ovien auettua tapaamaan Risto Ryti<8a>. Talvisota oli alkanut edellisen<8a> p<8a>iv<8a>n<8a>. Tannerin k<8a>ynnin tarkoituksena oli taivutella Ryti ryhtym<8a><8a>n Suomen p<8a><8a>ministeriksi. Paikalle saapui my<9a>s tasavallan presidentti Kallio. Tanner ja Kallio saivat lopulta Rytin suostumaan, ja h<8a>nen hallituksensa nimitettiin viel<8a> saman p<8a>iv<8a>n iltana. V<8a>in<9a> Tannerista tuli sen ulkoministeri. Ajatus Tannerin nimitt<8a>misest<8a> ulkoministeriksi oli Paasikiven. Se, ett<8a> Tanner t<8a>llaisella hetkell<8a> luotti juuri Rytiin, kertoo paljon miesten v<8a>lisest<8a> suhteesta. T<8a>st<8a> suhteesta kertoo toiselta puolen yht<8a> paljon sekin, ett<8a> Ryti halusi ulkoministerikseen juuri Tannerin. Raha-talouspolitiikan puitteet ovat muuttuneet moneen kertaan 1930-luvun j<8a>lkeen. Taloustiede ja talouspolitiikan k<8a>ytett<8a>viss<8a> oleva tietopohja ja keinovalikoima ovat kehittyneet paljon. Silti samat asiat tulevat ajankohtaisiksi kerran toisensa j<8a>lkeen. Sek<8a> Rytin ett<8a> Tannerin talouspoliittisten pyrkimysten t<8a>rkeimpin<8a> johtot<8a>htin<8a> olivat Suomen ulkomaisen luottokelpoisuuden varjeleminen ja parantaminen sek<8a> vakaan rahanarvon turvaaminen. V<8a>ltt<8a>m<8a>tt<9a>m<8a>n<8a> ehtona n<8a>iden tavoitteiden saavuttamiseksi oli molempien mielest<8a> valtiontalouden kest<8a>v<8a> tasapaino. Kaikki ei ole muuttunut. Vakaan rahanarvon turvaaminen ja julkisten talouden kest<8a>vyys ovat talouspolitiikan keskeisi<8a> p<8a><8a>m<8a><8a>ri<8a> nytkin. Keskuspankin itsen<8a>isyys on taattava, jotta se voisi hoitaa hintavakausteht<8a>v<8a><8a>ns<8a> tehokkaasti. Hallitusten ja niiss<8a> ennen kaikkea valtiovarainministerien teht<8a>v<8a>ksi on j<8a>lleen tullut toimia julkisen talouden kest<8a>vyyden turvaamiseksi. Siit<8a> teht<8a>v<8a>ss<8a> ei ollut liikaa yst<8a>vi<8a> menneill<8a> vuosikymmenill<8a>. Eik<8a> ole t<8a>n<8a><8a>n. Mutta julkisen talouden kest<8a>vyys on my<9a>s nyt kest<8a>v<8a>n kasvun ja ty<9a>llisyyden elinehto.

Title: Experience of global monetary policy cooperation during the financial crisis
text: President Erkki Liikanen: Experiences of global monetary policy cooperation during the nuclear crisis. Finnish Atlantic Society, Helsinki, 13.5.2014 . Speech . Tuesday 13 May2014,11:00AM Bank of Finland Governor Erkki Liikanen Experiences of global monetary policy cooperation during the financial crisis Finnish Atlantic Society, Monetary Museum, 13.5.2014 We warmly welcome you to the Bank of Finland's Monetary Museum. The Finnish Atlantic Society has an important task: to build mutual open debate and to strengthen trust in euro-Atlantic foreign and security policy. The value of trust and cooperation comes to the fore, especially during crises. When the acute phase of a crisis is on, trust is intangible capital that enables swift decision-making, even when decision-makers are forced to act under pressures of time in a state of less or greater uncertainty, or even relying on past experience or their intuition. Mutual trust proved to be valuable capital for central banks in the main economic areas during the financial crisis. Central banks are typically perceived as national institutions whose mandates limit their objectives and tasks mainly to the domestic economy. Central banks maintain price stability and act as banks' banks by providing central bank services to their counterparties. The financial crisis highlighted the tight commitment of national financial markets and the interdependencies between economies. As capital markets are international, cooperation between the world's central banks was also necessary to contain the global economic crisis. Cooperation between central banks did not begin only during the economic crisis, but there has always been a lively dialogue, both among decision-makers and at the level of economists, both bilaterally and in international for a such as the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) and the IMF. With the single currency, the central banks of the Eurosystem will, of course, be in close contact with each other. Today, however, I would like to focus on the cooperation of the major central banks, in particular the Fed and the European Central Bank, and also some other central banks during the financial crisis. Above all, it stabilised the global financial system and prevented the recession from developing into an economic disaster similar to the Great Depression of the 1930s. The financial crisis has also increased cooperation between central banks and governments in reforming financial supervision and regulatory systems, but I will leave supervisory cooperation out of my discussion today. We can, of course, come back to that in the debate. The first symptom of the global economic crisis, the sharp weakening of the mortgage market in 2007, was considered primarily a problem for the United States. Falling house prices and unmanaged mortgages first brought down banks specializing in mortgage lending. Soon, the trouble hit the big investment banks on Wall Street, which had securitised these loans they had acquired from mortgage banks into various structured investment instruments, the so-called "structured investment instruments". property and property-backed securities. In turn, US investment banks sold these safe investment instruments to their clients, including US-based European banks and their special purpose vehicles. The size and number of internationally operating banking groups had increased strongly in Europe, accounting for around two thirds of the EU banking market before the recession. European banks increased their trading in securities offering higher returns from American investment banks. At the beginning of 2008, European banks had more than ten thousand billion dollars' worth of investments in the United States on their balance sheets, and a large part of these investments were in investment banks such as Lehman Brothers instead of traditional banks. The fall in house prices in Florida, through the international affiliations of the financial sector, was soon also a problem for European banks. On August 7, 2007, the Fed's Open Market Committee (FOMC), which makes the Fed's interest rate decision, concluded that the difficulties in the subprime market were the beginning of a salutary adjustment. However, the U-turn came the very next day, when French bank BNP Paribas as the first global commercial bank announced that it would freeze its three funds investing in the US subprime market. Timothy Geithner, the then President of the New York Fed, describes in his memoirs how, above all, the strong reaction of the ECB opened his eyes to the seriousness of the situation. According to Geithner, ECB President Jean-Claude Trichet was known as a conservative central banker, but now he implemented a very nonconservative monetary policy by generously increasing the liquidity of European banks. European banks needed support: investors withdrew their investments from them because they feared that banks would be vulnerable due to large US subprime investments. During the crisis, the Fed was heavily criticized for not working hard enough before the crisis to limit the growth of indebtedness and the emergence of a housing bubble. However, the institutions that grew their fastest lending were not traditional deposit banks, but lending grew almost entirely outside the traditional banking sector, the so-called "bank banks". in the shadow banking sector, which was outside the control of the central bank. Before the financial crisis, the shadow banking sector held more than half of the country's credit, but only a small amount of equity. At the end of 2007, Wall Street's largest investment banks, Bearn Stearns, Lehman Brothers and Merrill Lynch, had equity of only 3% of their obligations. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, the world's largest mortgage banks, had barely one percent equity. The development of derivative instruments used for hedging loan portfolios and falling prices encouraged the shadow banking sector to sluggish lending. The possibility of protecting part of the credit in the event of a client's insolvency not only reduced the risk of an individual loan, but also the overall risk of the financial system. The affordability of hedging against credit risk encouraged banks to grant credit to increasingly risky customers. In the early stages of the crisis in 2007, central banks each focused on managing their own lot: First, the ECB reacted and increased liquidity in the euro area banking system in August 2007. The Fed took action the following week. The Fed lowered the central bank's policy rate on the so-called "greenback". fed funds interest promptly. The Bank of England decided at this point to do nothing and saw the increase in financial costs as a somewhat desirable market correction. Mervyn King, governor of the Bank of England, later stated that in the autumn of 2007 the crisis was generally expected to be over 'by Christmas', as it was in the autumn of the First World War in 1914. The economic crisis revealed the interconnectedness of global financial markets. The US financial turmoil was not only a US problem, but also a problem for the euro area and the UK, Sweden and all EU countries. Before the financial crisis, European banks' balance sheets were in balance in terms of US investment, as banks had roughly the same amount of investments and loans on their balance sheets. When the return on investments in the United States weakened sharply, loans could no longer be serviced with dollars from investments. At the same time, us own financial institutions began to hoard liquidity. Due to the time difference, the dollar and euro markets were open at different times of the day, when in the hours when the European market was trading but the US market was closed, the availability of dollars in the European interbank market was very poor. The European Central Bank was able to support the liquidity of its banks by providing them with euros but not dollars. If the financial markets had functioned normally, banks would have been able to exchange the euros they received from their central banks for dollars on the international foreign exchange markets. However, the persistent financial turmoil had eroded the confidence of the foreign exchange markets and rendered them inoperative. Following discussions in Basel, on 12 December 2007, the Fed, the ECB and the Central Banks of Canada and Switzerland announced that they had concluded mutual currency swaps, i.e. the opening of the so-called swap lines. The Bank of England joined the arrangement later. Under a currency swap agreement, the Fed, for example, can give 10 billion to the ECB. dollars and the ECB for the Fed the equivalent amount of euros. After the exchange, the ECB will have the opportunity to lend the dollars it receives against collateral to its counterparties who are suffering from a shortage of dollars. At the time specified in the agreement, for example after 3 months, the central banks exchanged the currencies they borrowed, with the dollars being returned to the Fed and the euros to the ECB. Thus, in cooperation with the Fed, the ECB was able to provide its counterparties with dollar-denominated financing. The scheme supported the liquidity of European banks to enable them to settle smoothly with faltering US investment banks and the fragile banking system. Similarly, the Eurosystem opened swap lines with the central banks of Switzerland and some non-euro area EU countries, which were suffering from euro shortages. Three years after the swap lines opened, the U.S. Congress lambasted the Fed for supporting European banks. In its response, the Fed stressed how dangerous discriminating banks on the basis of geographical location would have been at the time. By a joint decision, the central banks prevented a vicious circle in which European banks, for lack of dollars, would not have been able to service their dollar-denominated loans to US financial institutions. At the turn of 2007 and 2008, problems with the repayment of loans would have further weakened the US financial system. The Fed's support for European banks was therefore not due to kind-heartedness, but to the fact that European banks played a key role in the US financial system. In January this year, the Bank of Finland's Board of Governors visited the United States. At the Fed, the Banking Board discussed with Governor Bernanke, among other things, the main findings and lessons of the current economic crisis. According to Bernanke, three lessons were learned from the economic crisis: First, when a liquidity crisis threatens the banking system, the central bank must provide good banks with almost unlimited liquidity. Secondly, the central bank had to cut its key interest rates aggressively. Thirdly, Bernanke said that before the financial crisis, however, it was not fully understood how large and complex modern financial institutions are and, on the other hand, how hugely important they are for the economy. However, it was fortunate for the global economic order that the facts mentioned by Ben Bernanke were known, as they had also been the lessons of the Great Depression of the 1930s  the Great Depression  from the 1930s. The Fed's response and decision-making in the financial crisis was accelerated by the fact that Governor Ben Bernanken wanted to avoid the mistakes the Fed had made during the Great Depression. There is still a rapidly dwindling number of people who have personally experienced the Great Depression, but the legacy of the Depression still lives on in the minds of Americans. That legacy has strongly shaped the Fed's monetary policy, in the same way that the hyperinflation of the 1920s continues to influence Germans' collective thinking and, to some extent, the monetary policy line pursued by the Bundesbank. Prior to his career as a central banker, Bernanke had been a professor at mit, a well-known U.S. university. He had studied the causes of the depression of the 1930s and drew on the findings published a little earlier by Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz, in a classic work in the history of economics called A Monetary History of the United States. Prior to the publication of Friedman's and Schwartz's analysis, the cause of the Great Depression was considered to be mainly low demand in relation to the volume of American production. Friedman and Schwartz, however, testified that during the Great Depression, the fed's tight monetary policy, i.e., a sharp contraction in the money supply and interest rate hikes, deepened the crisis strongly. About half of U.S. banks went bankrupt between 1930 and 1933. Due to limited liquidity, financial institutions that had become temporarily insolvent were also bankrupt. During the Great Depression, the Fed did not follow the principle of walter Bagehot, a well-known economist at the time, that during a crisis, the central bank must provide emergency financing for compensation to good and solvent banks to support their liquidity. The result was a fall in the money supply, deflation and economic paralysis. The current lesson that the Fed heeded during this financial crisis was that emergency funding for viable banks had to be provided almost without limits. In addition to the Fed, other central banks also increased the liquidity of the banking system in a variety of maturities. The Fed's second mistake during the Great Depression was interest rate policy. In 1930, Great Britain had been forced to break away from the gold standard because, during the banking panics, the Bank of England's gold reserves dwindled as people exchanged their banknotes for gold. After the collapse of the pound, speculators attacked the dollar. The Fed supported the gold standard system and raised interest rates sharply. Higher interest rates reduced the willingness of currency speculators to exchange dollars stored in accounts with good returns for gold. The Fed succeeded in its gold standard defense operation, but raising interest rates accelerated the fall in the price level and further reduced the money supply. Another lesson of the Great Depression during the financial crisis was precisely that as liquidity tightened, central banks cut interest rates rapidly. The third instructive experience of the Great Depression was that when large financial institutions fail, the economy collapses with them. Lending came to a standstill in the early 1930s and waves of bankruptcy swept through the corporate sector and households. The banking crisis deepened the plight and the 1929 Wall Steet stock market crash spread into a comprehensive economic crisis. In his academic research, Bernanke criticized the Fed for unwillingness to provide banks with emergency funding during the Great Depression. However, the dilemma faced by the Fed in particular in 2008 was that the investment banks struggling with their difficulties were not actual banks. They were outside the stricter regulation of deposit banks and it was precisely because of their lower capital requirement that they were able to pay higher returns to their customers than deposit banks. The Securities and Exchange Commission SEC, which oversees investment banks, was mainly focused on overseeing the interests of clients investing in these banks, and overall financial market risks were not really the responsibility of any institution. Although investment banks were very bank-like in the market and many of them were wall steet's old traditional institutions such as Bearn Stearns, Lehman Brothers, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, they were not counterparts to the Fed's monetary policy and the Fed did not act as a bank for them as a bank for banks like deposit banks. During the financial market crisis, numerous structural arrangements were carried out under the fed's leadership, including acquisitions, mergers and banking system support packages. Similar arrangements were also made in Europe to support the financial system The fall of Lehman Brothers plunged global financial markets into chaos. At this point at the latest, it dawned on market participants that large and influential financial institutions could also fail. Market participants asked themselves why lend money to another financial institution if there were no longer any guarantees of repayment. The cost between bank secured and unsecured lending ruptured. Banks wanted to ensure the security of their own liquidity, thereby drying up the liquidity of the banking system. Many banks perfectly hit the wall: they did not receive financing at all, at any interest rate. Once again, the ECB supported bank liquidity, but banks were short of dollars. Swedish banks were also in great distress, needing both euros and dollars to service their loans. In the most difficult situation of the crisis, the Riksbank even used its gold reserves as collateral to be able to obtain on the market the dollars that its banks desperately need. Four days after the collapse of Lehman Brothers, central banks once again opened currency exchange lines. In addition to the previous participants, this time the central banks of Sweden, Norway, Denmark and Australia also joined in. The shock that started in the financial markets was boosted by the bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers and soon spread to the real economy. The climate of confidence deteriorated unprecedentedly, world trade collapsed and economic growth slowed down in both developed and emerging economies. As demand waned, raw material prices fell rapidly. For example, the price of a barrel of crude oil fell by almost USD 100 in six months by the end of 2008. Inflation declined all over the world and even aroused deflationary fears in some countries. The decline in inflation allowed central banks to ease monetary policy further. Cooperation between central banks during the crisis culminated in a single money market intervention. The economic crisis that began in 2007 highlighted the vulnerability of the global financial system. The role of central banks in economic policy was emphasised and central banks played a leading role in resolving the crisis. After the economic crisis, closer cooperation between central banks continues, as the crisis has not stopped the integration of the financial world. Title: Efficient payment systems for society
text: Director-General Erkki Liikanen: Efficient payment systems for society. Helsinki, 19.5.2014. . Speech . Monday19 May 2014,2:00PM Director-General Erkki Liikanen Maksufoorumi 19.5.2014 SOCIALLY EFFICIENT PAYMENT SYSTEMS The importance of payment systems for the financial system and the functioning of society as a whole is obvious. Whether trading raw materials, securities or paper machines, the final confirmation of the transaction occurs when the margin on the payment is transferred through the payment system. We receive our paychecks by wire transfer to our bank account, pay many of our recurring payments in online banking and in the store with a debit card. Efficient payment services support the productivity and growth of the economy. Finns are dependent on electronic payments. Only a few percent of payments are delivered to the bank branch in a payment service envelope. Approximately 95% of bank transfers are made as machine-readable payments by companies or through online banking, often on the basis of an electronic invoice. According to the statistics of the Federation of Finnish Financial Services, already three out of four purchases are paid at the store's checkout with a card. Payment-related issues are more topical than ever during the eight-year history of the Payments Forum. For example, paying with a mobile phone has been on the agenda for several years before, the first time already in 2008. Over the past year, the first mobile payment apps have finally entered the market. Mobile applications have also appeared on the market that we did not foresee. Online banking applications have been introduced to smartphones, and the possibility to accept payments with a mobile phone, for example, is rapidly becoming more common. Although e-commerce has started slower in Finland than in the rest of the world, it is also starting to take off here. Increasingly, society's services are also being taken online in the name of efficiency. Many digital economy projects have also been discussed in this Payment Forum. The risks of online transactions are different from the risks of physical transactions. Service providers deal with criminals a race to see how online transactions and payments can be carried out safely. Payment security is a big theme that operators may not be able to solve on their own. A joint working group of central banks and banking supervisors has prepared recommendations for online and mobile transactions. The European Banking Authority will continue this work at least with guidance on the use of the payment account. The Bank of Finland has a long tradition of participating in the development of efficient and secure payment systems. Forms of cooperation will be discussed at European level in the future. The transition to a single euro payments area triggered a dialogue between central banks and payment service providers and users. There is a desire to continue to do so. The ECB chairs the Euro Payments Area Retail Payments Council, which is looking for direction for future development projects. Its domestic counterpart is the Bank of Finland's Payments Council, which is a forum for open discussion. The aim of the Payments Council is to identify bottlenecks in the development of payments and to enable them to be resolved in a way that takes into account the views of all stakeholders. In many places, both at EU and national level, it has been considered that the obstacles to development are such that they can only be overcome by regulation. In the European Union, too, a number of regulatory projects are being implemented in the area of payment. The regulation concerns the availability of payment accounts and payment services, as well as the general right to basic banking services, the conditions for the provision of payment services and competitiveness. Recently, the European Parliament adopted the Payment Accounts Directive, which aims to guarantee all Europeans both a payment account and the most common payment methods, such as a payment card directly linked to the account, sending and receiving credit transfers, online banking and depositing and withdrawing cash. In Finland, the right to basic banking services has been written into the Credit Institutions Act, but not as comprehensively as in the new directive. The authorities must find out, preferably in cooperation with representatives of different customer groups, whether Finnish regulations also need to be updated. The dominant role of the two major international payment card systems has been under the scrutiny of the authorities for a long time. They have been suspected of using their dominant position in the market to collect excessive rewards. For this reason, the interchange fee for card payment intermediation is being restricted. A dominant market position is not only a pricing issue, but also an obstacle to the development of new payment methods. Card payments are not designed for the network, and always providing card information separately to each network service used puts confidential information at risk. When the market position is strong enough, normal competition is no longer possible. Partly for this reason, new payment methods that are better suited to the environment have not become more common in online payments. Last year's payments forum provided an overview of the criteria by which we can assess the social effectiveness of payment systems. These criteria concerned technical efficiency, non-discrimination in services, guiding pricing, preparedness for various risks and international compatibility. It is worth looking at how, now that we have moved to the Single Euro Payments Area, these criteria will be implemented. The first criterion was technical efficiency, which is used to seek economies of scale, speed and affordability. Finland is considered to be a pioneer in this respect, and the precise transition to the Single Euro Payments Area proves that we have realized the power of both international standards and networking. Finnish payment service providers, as well as end customers, make full use of European standards and payment systems. The exploitation of the Single Euro Payments Area is linked to another feature of an efficient payment system, namely international compatibility. The EU regulatory framework and international standards enable the exploitation of competitive markets beyond the domestic market. Now that the rest of Europe is practically in common European standards, we can look forward to the consolidation of the systems behind payments and the greater realisation of economies of scale. In Finland, e-invoicing has progressed rapidly, and the transmission of standardised information along with the payment has enabled automation benefits, especially for the financial administration of companies. In Europe, development seems to be progressing more slowly. The impact of e-invoicing on efficiency is intuitively clear, but as far as I know, no actual research has been done on the automation benefits of payment. Here could be a good theme for academic research or the work of the payment council in the future. We do not only need a payment method suitable for Finnish conditions, but an operating model built to be internationally compatible. If we can't find one in today's market, why not be pioneers and use our high level of expertise and even experience in the gaming industry to build a simple, technologically advanced and cost-effective payment method for users? The main thing is that behind innovations is the understanding that development is always made for the whole world. We are excellent in terms of technical efficiency and international compatibility in many respects. More development is required for payment services, which are used as people and businesses move to information networks on a large scale. The third criterion for payment systems that are efficient for society is access to services and non-discrimination. Our current Act on Credit Institutions guarantees basic banking services for everyone, and the implementation of this right is supervised by the Financial Supervisory Authority. In the 2013 survey, it was concerned about the deteriorating situation in some areas and customer groups, even though services are readily available overall. The results of the spring 2014 study are still being prepared, but a preliminary increase in alternative service channels has been identified to possibly replace the lost branch services. In particular, the availability of cash is enhanced by the possibility of withdrawing it at the store's checkout when making purchases, if the store's cash situation allows it. There are positive experiences of this practice in Norway, so why not fit the model for us as well. As online transactions become more common, users are starting to place even tougher demands on user interfaces as well. The one-click shopping experience is unsurpassed. At its best, such a way of working, or an intuitive user interface that is otherwise inherent in the human way of working, for example in a mobile phone, can also enable people to do business online for whom it is not possible with computers and applications like the ones we have today. Despite all the technical progress, there are always situations where the best and perhaps the only possible interface of the service is another person. Personal service can be implemented with the support of information systems efficiently, and thus be provided to those who need it. For some customer groups, a traditional payment service envelope is still the best way to pay. Perhaps we could also be more open-minded about various proxy services: municipal home care could assist older people in delivering payment service envelopes. Withdrawing cash from a store's cashier can be the first step to bringing some limited payment services close to customers to the store. Pricing that guides efficient payment methods is the fourth criterion that can be set for payment systems. When choosing payment methods, people are sensitive to price signals. If and when you pay for the product or service you want, you no longer want to pay separately. We have long talked about cost-based pricing, how the prices charged for services should reflect the cost of their production. When we talk about a necessity such as payment, the matter is not quite simple. An example of this is Ireland. Representatives of the Central Bank of Ireland visited Helsinki in early spring.
