Title: Speech on Europe, Ambassadors' Meeting
text: Director-General Erkki Liikanen: Speech on Europe, Ambassadors' Meeting 26.8.2014, Helsinki . Speech . Tuesday 26August 2014,2:00PM "On the first of August, shortly before seven o'clock in the evening, Germany declared war on Russia. In the evening of the second of August, German troops invaded the Principality of Luxembourg and Belgium after Brussels had received an ultimatum to let the German columns into the country according to Schlieffen's plan. On the third of August at 18:15, Germany declared war on France. Britain said it would secure Belgium if its borders were breached. And by the fourth of August it was clear that Germany had invaded Belgium." 1 The First World War had begun. The quote is from the book La Grande Guerre by the Frenchman Francois Cochet. The background was a complex network of alliances and security guarantees that, after the escalation of the Austro-Serbian conflict, operated in a way that was no longer under anyone's control. It has been said about the First World War that it was a war that arose by accident, and that no one wanted. The showdown, intended as a brief clash, turned into a four-year slaughter. The outcome of the war was also one that no one had sought or foreseen. Empires fell. In Russia, power passed to the Bolsheviks. The Habsburg dynasty collapsed, and a number of new independent states emerged on the territory of the former Austro-Hungary. Britain and France gained control of the Middle East, which was part of the Ottoman Empire, as mandated areas. New land borders were drawn there. Many geopolitical crises are concentrated in that region and in those countries today. What will happen to them is an open question. The First World War largely defined The Whole of Europe in the 1900s. When the empires collapsed, many small nations achieved independence  Finland as one of them. The peace terms aroused resentment in the losing parties and caused great tensions in the international economy. The Second World War can therefore be seen as an extension of 1914. It was even more destructive than its predecessor. After the war, former enemies stated: "Never again." In the early 1990s, Max Jakobson said in Brussels that finns are unfamiliar with the essence of European integration because we were not involved in world war 1. Robert Schuman, the founding father of the EU, knew the 1st World War very personally. His homeland was Alsace-Lorraine, which was part of Germany until World War 1. He served in the German army as a scribe during World War 1. In May 1951, while Robert Schuman was foreign minister of France, dropped a bomb. At the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' weekly press conference at the Quai d'Orsay, he proposed that six European states hand over their sovereignty over coal and steel to common, supranational hands. The show received huge attention across Europe; less in Finland, however. The Finnish Embassy in Paris reportedly first reported on the matter in September, when the negotiations were at a very advanced stage. Robert Schuman visited Finland in the spring of 1953. He had then remained outside the government, and the active press counsellor at the Embassy conveyed to him an invitation from the Finnish Foreign Trade Association to come and speak in Finland. The invitation was made behind the envoy's back. When it came to the attention of the ministry, the permanent secretary tried to withdraw the invitation. However, Schuman arrived in Finland and President Paasikivi was listening to the speech of a high guest and also received him. The government kept a low profile. It decided separately not to hold a dinner in Honour of Schuman and not to pay attention anyway. In 1958, the European Coal and Steel Community was enlarged to become the European Economic Community. The development of the single market took a leap forward in the 1960s when the EC countries abandoned mutual tariffs. Prime Minister Urho Kekkonen did not meet Robert Schuman in Helsinki in 1953, but instead, during a state visit to France in 1962, President Kekkonen met another founding father of the EU, Jean Monnet, at the Louis Carre house designed by Alvar Aalto. At the time, Matti Hakkanen was serving as an assistant in Paris. According to him, the meeting was Carre's idea alone; Monnet was simply Carre's neighbor. There is no report on the discussions. However, in relations with Finland, the EEC had a long period of silence. In 1947, Finland had concluded a trade agreement with the Soviet Union, which was in force until 1992. The trade agreement included an extensive preferential clause, which gave Moscow a tool to monitor Finland's integration solutions. However, Finland sought to develop trade both east and west, even though both sides of the Cold War restricted trade in countries belonging to their own spheres of interest over the Iron Curtain. Jaakko Kalela has stated that the measure of the real success of Finland's neutrality policy during the Cold War was that Finland was able to manage its trade relations in both directions despite these restrictions. The main concern was that Finland's worst competitors, such as Sweden, would not gain an unfair competitive advantage. This was helped by the fact that the Swedes were also prepared to support this, because if Finland had been closed to the Western market, the Iron Curtain could have descended on the Gulf of Bothnia. From 1948 until the end of the Cold War, Finland managed to achieve the same integration arrangements as Sweden in one way or another: GATT, EFTA, the EEC Free Trade Agreement and the EEA. After the war, not only trade relations, but also access to foreign credit, were of great concern. After World War II, the world monetary system was built on principles formulated at a meeting of Bretton Woods in July 1944. This meeting was attended by representatives of 44 allied countries, including from the USSR. Of the Nordic countries, only Iceland and Norway were involved, and Denmark as observers. At the same time as delegations from the Allied countries arrived in Bretton Woods, Finland was engaged in its fiercest battles during the entire Second World War. The soviet union's major offensive, which began in June, had culminated in the battle against Tali-Ihantala, and the United States had severed its diplomatic relations with Finland. The neutral countries, including Argentina, Spain, Portugal, Switzerland and Sweden, were also not invited because they were viewed with suspicion because of their links with Germany. The main features of the new international monetary system were formed on the basis of the plans of the US and British governments, and the key figures in the negotiations were US Deputy Secretary of the Treasury Harry Dexter White and the famous British economist John Maynard Keynes. Finland's relations with the victorious states immediately after the war were governed by the Armistice Agreement signed on 19.9.1944. Among other things, it also had an impact on Finland's creditworthiness, which was overshadowed by doubts about whether Finland would survive the war reparations demanded by the Soviet Union and whether finland's internal political situation would stabilize at all. The history of the Bank of Finland, written by Antti Kuustera and Juha Tarkan, tells extensively about Finland's accession to the international monetary system. Finland ratified the peace treaty already in March 1947, but the Soviet Union only in September due to the delay in the Italian settlement. Ratification and the removal of the Control Commission strengthened Finland's position and reduced obstacles to international cooperation. Finland applied for UN membership already four days after ratification on 19.9.1947, but it foundered due to superpower conflicts. The process leading to Finland's accession to the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank had already begun a year earlier. In September 1946, Paasikivi had invited the US Ambassador Maxwell Hamilton to speak after the Americans refused to negotiate credit with Finland. The ambassador had raised the issue of the World Bank, whose activities had begun in the summer of 1946 and had said that Finland should apply for its credit there. In Paasikivi's view, Finland should first have signed a peace treaty and become a member of the UN, and only then could it become a member of the Bretton Woods institutions. It would also require time and capital, and Finland had neither. Paasikivi's chronology expired in a couple of days. The first annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank began just two days after Hamilton's visit. Italy was accepted as a member of the organizations, although it had not signed a peace treaty. After that, Finland advanced. In November 1946, Matti Virkkunen, Head of the Trade Policy Department of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs, requested a statement from the Bank of Finland on IMF membership. The bank responded two weeks later. After weighing up the different aspects of the issues, the Bank of Finland came to the conclusion that the benefits outweighed the obligations and Finland should aspire to become a member of the International Monetary Fund. Finland officially applied for membership of the International Monetary Fund and the IMF at the beginning of April 1947. Finland was accepted as a member at the second annual meeting of the organizations in September 1947. Although the proposal to join was made by Mauno Pekkala's government, it received criticism in Parliament from the SKDL. Sakari Tuomioja, governor of the Bank of Finland, and the Ministry for Foreign Affairs tried to facilitate the adoption of the agreements by pointing out that Poland and Czechoslovakia were already members and that the accession of the Soviet Union would still be possible. The parliament approved the proposal in December and Finland officially joined in January 1948. In the Imf, Finland initially joined the Eastern European constituency, which also included Poland, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia. The Nordic countries were scattered across constituencies. Sweden had not even joined the Monetary Fund yet. The constituency was not easy, because soon after, relations between Poland and Czechoslovakia with the Monetary Fund became difficult and eventually reached an impasse. The constituency fell apart when first Poland left the organisation and then also T.ekkoslovakia. Finland was left alone. For a long time, Sweden was hesitant about joining the Bretton Woods organisations because it feared that it would conflict with the policy of neutrality. It was only the desire to participate in the GATT's round of tariff reductions that decided the position and Sweden applied for IMF membership in June 1951. Let's go back to the EEC. In the 1970s, the EEC expanded and the EEC deepened. Finland safeguarded its interests through various arrangements, to which I have already referred. Important was the EEC Free Trade Agreement in 1973. The European Economic Area, on which negotiations began in the spring of 1990, was also considered important. At the end of last year and at the beginning of this year, we have reviewed the events that led to changes in Finland's attitude towards EU membership on the occasion of two anniversary days. March marked the 20th anniversary of the conclusion of the membership negotiations, and President Mauno Koivisto turned 90 last November. For a long time, Koivisto considered the EEA Agreement to be an ideal solution for Finland. It would safeguard Finland's economic interests without political burdens. The EEA negotiations started positively, but then ran into difficulties. It soon became clear that, in practice, the EEA does not have to adapt to the EC's supranational decision-making without genuine influence. In addition, first Austria and then, in 1990, Sweden also applied for EC membership. Jacques Delors' idea of an ETA that would postpone enlargement did not work. President Koivisto and Prime Minister Harri Holkeri tried to keep the debate on EC membership in check, but it was no longer successful. The world was changing. The changes of power in the countries of Eastern Europe, the reunification of Germany, the independence of the Baltic states and, finally, the abolition of the Soviet Union changed Europe, both on the map and politically. Finland's position began to change in August 1991 after the moscow coup failed. Certain political parties had already become active in favour of membership. At the end of August, Minister for Foreign Trade Pertti Salolainen proposed that Finland should improve its readiness to make a decision on membership. Koivisto was irritated by the individual soloing, but immediately told Prime Minister Aho that Salolainen was right and that the government had to start preparations immediately. Koivisto also became public at the end of September 1991. The rest is history. At the Maastricht Summit in December 1991, the presidency already discussed the opening of negotiations with Austria and Sweden. The proposal was not adopted, but the message to Finland was clear. Now we had to move if Finland wanted to negotiate alongside Austria and Sweden. Finland acted quickly and decisively. On 18 March 1992, parliament approved the application for EC membership. On the same day, the application for membership, signed by the President and the Prime Minister, was submitted to Brussels. Accession negotiations began in February 1993 and were concluded in just over a year. While the negotiations were under way, the European Community was transformed into the European Union , the Union as we know it, to which Finland, together with Sweden and Austria, joined at the beginning of 1995. It will soon be 16 years since the start of Europe's Economic and Monetary Union. At the beginning of 1999, eleven EU Member States switched to a single currency and monetary policy, with Finland as one of them. With the exception of monetary policy, the rest of economic policy remained largely the responsibility of the Member States themselves. The rules of the game in public finances were defined in accordance with the Stability and Growth Pact and the so-called fiscal framework. with the no bail-out rule. The supervision of banks also remained a national responsibility. The first ten years of monetary union were in many respects an opportune time. The economy grew, unemployment fell and inflation remained low and stable. Interest rates were low compared to previous decades. The euro area current account showed a surplus. The favourable overall development also concealed unfavourable trends. Priority was given to economic developments in the euro area as a whole, leaving the imbalances developing in individual countries unresolved. In some countries, such as Spain and Ireland, economic development had fallen into an unsustainable path as a result of household indebtedness, rising housing prices and overheating of the construction sector. In other countries, such as Italy and Portugal, economic growth had stagnated as a result of weak productivity developments. In Greece, on the other hand, growth had been sustained by increasing the public sector. Easy access to finance allowed problems to develop for a long time. In the first years of the euro, the inflation of indebtedness was mediated by banks, which channelled private sector savings from surplus countries to households and businesses in countries that have since been in crisis. The low-cost money led to poor investments, the realised return of which was lower than expected. In the end, the risks were greater than imagined. The financial crisis that began in the United States hit Europe in August 2007. In the autumn of the following year, the financial crisis escalated into a full-scale banking crisis. The bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers halted credit flows, collapsed world trade and cut off investment. The real economy entered a crisis. At the time, the fear was that the world economy would fall into the same kind of deflation and mass unemployment that had been imposed in the early 1930s. At that time, economic chaos had been followed by political instability, protectionism, the closure of borders and, finally, hatred. The fear of a repeat of the experiences of the 1930s was one of the reasons why the global banking crisis was quickly resolved at the end of 2008. For once, international coordination worked effectively. Coordinated measures succeeded in safeguarding banks' liquidity and restoring the functioning of financial markets. These measures also included a massive easing of monetary policy in several countries at the same time. The structures of Europe's Economic and Monetary Union were put to the test particularly hard during the crisis. EMU under the Maastricht Treaty had proved to be too fragile. Fragility had been caused not only by the tendency of the financial markets to excesses, but also by a lack of compliance with the rules and shortcomings in the rules themselves. The spirit of the Stability and Growth Pact had not been respected. Despite good years, the government debt ratio of several euro area countries did not fall towards the 60% reference value. There were countries where it did not fall at all. These shortcomings have now been addressed by new legislation. The Stability and Growth Pact has been clarified. A new element has been the creation of the macroeconomic imbalances procedure, within the framework of which attention is focused on the balanced development of the national economy as a whole. The new framework of rules has been criticised for penetrating too far into matters within national competence. However, it is still up to the individual member state to decide whether its public sector role is large or small. This value choice is made by the elected parliament of the member state and its government, which enjoys its trust. The financial constraints contained in the common rules are concerned: the financial basis of public finances must be in order. Ultimately, no country inside or outside the EU can live up to this principle. In the medium term, revenue and expenditure must be in harmony. There have also been shortcomings in banking supervision. Monetary union promoted the integration of financial markets and expanded cross-border banking. At the same time, the supervision and resolution of banks remained within the competence of national authorities. When the financial crisis in Europe turned into a sovereign debt crisis, it was discovered that national supervision and supranational banking form a fragile whole. One important characteristic of the euro area debt crisis has been the strong bond between governments and banks. Ireland, Spain and Cyprus have had to resort to support programmes when the banking crisis has exceeded or threatened to exceed the carrying capacity of public finances. In Greece, Portugal and Italy, banks have run into difficulties when the creditworthiness of their home country has been called into question. Banks are not believed if their home country is not believed. The state is not believed if its ability to solve the problems of its banking sector is not believed. It has proved very difficult to break this cycle. Recent years have shown that when there is a common awareness of the burning nature of the problem, big decisions can be made at European level. Two years ago, the European Union took one such big decision: lessons must be learned from this crisis. Everything possible must be done to ensure that it does not happen again. When the banking system operates across national borders, supervision and crisis management must also be at the same level. In the case of large banks, the right level is European, together with national supervisors. Last year, two important steps were taken in this regard. Firstly, there will be a single banking supervision in Europe. The SSM is structured around the ECB. The largest banking groups in the countries joining the banking union will move to joint direct supervision. They total around 130 and hold 85% of the assets of euro area banks on their balance sheets. In addition to these, the supervision of smaller banks can also be brought under the direct authority of the ECB if necessary. A comprehensive and comprehensive assessment of the banks to be transferred to joint supervision is currently being carried out. This will ensure that only banks that are in good condition will be subject to joint supervision. Another important step forward in the banking union is the single resolution framework. Bank resolution is needed for the effective winding down and restructuring of crisis banks. When a bank gets into trouble or threatens to fail, it must be possible to intervene in good time. Only in this way will it be possible to ensure that liability for losses can be limited to the bank's shareholders and creditors. The normal bankruptcy procedure for banks is too slow, which can lead to a crisis in the entire financial system. A slow procedure also destroys the value of the bank being reorganized. In previous banking crises, this has usually become the biggest cost to taxpayers. Now the powers of the authorities are being strengthened and a mechanism is being created that is also suitable for restructuring or shutting down banks operating in many countries. Ultimately, the aim of resolution reforms is to break the unhealthy situation where banks' profits are private but losses are public. This tightening of market discipline relies on investor responsibility, or so-called investor responsibility. bail-in principle. In the future, not only shareholders, but also holders of bank bonds may be held more liable for the costs of winding down a bank. The most significant item exempted from liability are bank deposits subject to the deposit guarantee scheme. The decisions on the banking union were taken quickly and their implementation has also progressed rapidly. The SSM will take over the supervision in November this year. The Single Resolution Mechanism will be built in the course of next year and will be operational at the beginning of 2016. The broad outline of Finland's EU policy during the first 15 years of membership emphasized influencing at common tables. For the first time in its history, Finland was involved in making decisions that affected our European environment either directly or indirectly. Jan Store, who has been permanent representative to the EU for a long time, is coming up with a book that is eagerly awaited. In his final report, he recalled how The Economist defined Finland's way of working in the Union in 1999: "Despite its location on the farthest edge of Europe, since the beginning of their membership in 1995, Finns have mastered the EU's practices in an almost unbelievable way. Many see them as a model example of how a small member state should function in the EU institutions; not preaching like the Swedes, not indulging like the Danes, not too ambitiously as the Austrians, but modestly and purposefully, holding on to both principles and a sense of proportion." With the economic crisis, problems got in the way of Finland's European policy. As a result of the crisis in general, more divisions have been formed throughout the EU. They were formed between countries using the euro and those not participating in the euro. They were also drawn between the countries helping and helping within the euro area. An economic crisis always leads to difficult situations. When total output falls, unemployment rises and public finances fall into deficit, the government is forced to make difficult and unpopular decisions. This time, in addition to these decisions, we were faced with new kinds of decisions. These decisions concerned crisis policy and participation in the euro area. For a long time, the debate was dominated by the illusion that the basic problems of the Finnish economy are due to others, such as Greece or economic and monetary union. The focus was on judging and teaching others. As always happens, arrogance became an injury. The problems were not seen in the right light. The drastic contraction of the electronics sector and the adjustment of the forest industry hit Finland at the same time as the international financial crisis. However, these are two separate changes. In the shadow of the financial crisis, Finland has developed into an independent but serious and long-term structural problem. Solutions to one's own crisis must be sought in Finland, and to the financial crisis in Europe. If the facts change, it must be taken into account. It is logical to create a positive programme, to define things, to prioritise them and to try to promote them together with other countries. It may be easier to stand in the way of all change, but it does not create solutions. How should Finland act in Europe and other international fields? Here, too, we are most successful when we define our own goals and seek support for them from others. It will only succeed if we are also prepared to give support to others when their demands are justified. When the general line is constructive, one can gain a better understanding when there are exceptional issues of one's own defensible and is even tricky. Nevertheless, we must remember that we have many common interests with others that need to be promoted, and not focus on rejecting the initiatives of others. Finland is voluntarily part of a large community with which we share the same values and build common institutions. On the occasion of his 90th birthday, President Koivisto said the mind-blowing words: "We are a generation that first fought for independence and then sought to integrate. We were ready to give up part of independence as we gained more influence. This is what happened. The pessimists were wrong. A toast for peace and work." 1 Nain alkaa Francois Cochet'n kirja The Great War. End of a world, beginning of a century (Ministry of Defense, Paris 2014).

Title: 100 years after the appearance of Eino Leino's "Bank Lords"
text: President Erkki Liikanen: 100 years since the appearance of Eino Leino's "Bank Lords". 9.9.2014, Helsinki. . Speech . Tuesday 9 September 2014,5:00 PM President Erkki Liikanen 100 years since the appearance of Eino Leino's "Bank Lords" Speech with Eino Leino 9.9.2014 "Whoever does not know history is doomed to repeat it," wrote George Santayana in his time. This idea has often come to mind in recent years, when, inspired by the financial crisis, previous crises and their lessons have been discussed. Financial history is being talked about and written about now more than perhaps ever before. Around the world, you can see how researchers and economic policymakers are increasingly interested in economic history and how previous economic crises arose and how they have been overcome. Interest in the business and banking world is also lively these days. That is a good thing. One of the books on the history of financial crises that has attracted the most attention in recent years is the book "This time is different" by americans Carmen Reinhart and Ken Rogoff. The very title tells the main thesis of the authors: Behind the crises, there is an illusion that this time everything will be different. The world has changed and nothing can be learned from the mistakes of the past. Under the power of this fantasy, generation after generation makes the same mistakes. Are we really not learning anything? This is how one reads Eino Leino's "Bank Lords", which appeared 100 years ago. It amazes the modern reader because, as a depiction of the business world, it feels almost timeless. Only mobile phones and tablet computers are missing. * Anyone who argues that human nature, and with it economic life, over the decades is fundamental changed, it would be good to familiarize yourself with the picture left by contemporaries of how it used to be thought. Here is The secret of interest in the "bank lords". Fiction at its best offers research deeper and a more convincing picture of the life and mindset of previous generations. The book is the story of the destruction of the life of a businessman. In a matter of months, conservative bank manager and family man Antti Puuhaara becomes a toss-up, a familyless lifer who eventually ends up murder and suicide. The money world, which he has faithfully served, will eventually abandon him. The background to the story is vividly depicted helsinki of the beginning of the century, especially the restaurants and business palaces in its center. From night to night, the city's upper class amuses "like the last day" in glamorous restaurants, opera and theater. Breakfast classes are spent in Kamp and evenings are celebrated with champagne flowing. Leino describes Helsinki's amusement and nightlife in a way that makes the city seem like a metropolis much larger than its size at the time. Changing the names of the restaurants, the story could just as well be set in Berlin, Paris or St. Petersburg. The picture of Helsinki in 1914, drawn by the "bank gentlemen", is simplistic and deliberately completely upper-class. The main characters of the book belong to a small elite who could afford champagne and trips to Europe. Antti Puuhaara himself, whose background was peasant, had in a few years developed into an "aristocrat" and adopted the worldview of his new environment, which, in Leino's words, was "alienating the people, fearing God, and loving himself". Through the eyes of Bank Manager Puuhaara, Leino marvels at the general loosening of customs and morals and how the celebrating upper class lived by indebtedness beyond its means. The corrupting effect of easy money is an important theme of the book. Eino Leino was not a businessman, but with the artist's instinct, he has managed to draw a plausible picture of the mindset of the businessmen of the time. In a few strokes, he also sketches an economic model with which he explains the celebration of consumption that appears around him. He attributed "incompleteness and bankruptcies, cheating and suicides" to the fact that "the so-called "black market". the solvent upper class did not have the moral courage to look the truth in the eye and to compromise a tiny bit on their former life standards. On the contrary, the general desire for pleasure had taken hold of it too, and it lived day after day, from hand to mouth, ever at an ever-increasing pace, ever more blind with its eyes closed to the impending ruin." "It couldn't take long. After all, the whole nation here already at the mercy of foreign loans. As long as they were available, there were good times in the country. When they ran out and the foreign financial markets tightened, the same misery and misery began again. And no wonder, because the whole nation lived beyond its means. Imports increased enormously, and exports did not show the same signs at all to rise." This sounds all too familiar and could aptly describe the financial crisis of many countries in different decades, whether it be Latin America in the early 1980s, Finland in the early 1990s or southern Europe in the 2000s. Business (or the market economy, or capitalism) appears in the book as a hard and ruthless, value-free mechanism in which human emotions and loyalty are subordinate to economic calculations and thus ultimately irrelevant. The characters who represent capital in the book, one old bank manager who is Puuhaara's supervisor, and the other greedy investor, Cameroon Lichen, do not appear in the book as evils, but instead carry out their role as instruments of simple economic logic. * The description of the business world is not the only subject of "Bank lords". The second topic of the book is related to the status of women. These two themes are interlinked. Leino's criticism is directed at how, in the Helsinki he describes, when traditional life models broke down, gender relations also became money-dependent and commercialised. The situation was exacerbated by the large income inequality of the time, which fuelled the exploitation of people. There are many better experts on this second theme. It should be noted, however, that the central female characters of the story, both Elna, Puuhaara's wife, and his mistress Mrs. Lathe, appear in the book as more humane than the other main characters. Mrs. Puuhaara, who leaves her husband at the beginning of the book, eventually wants to go back to him, but Antti, who has a taste of an enjoyable life, sends her away. Mrs. Sorvi, on the other hand, is destroyed: she embezzles money at her workplace to help Antti get out of debts, but is caught doing it. The third type of woman is the bank manager's young and spoiled daughter Betty, whom Leino calls the heiress. She is presented as a frivolous seductress, whom Antti becomes interested in because of the money. After the moments spent with Betty, Antti dreams of the already imagined millions that marriage with her would bring. Leino's hundred-year-old image of a woman is very traditional and stereotypical from a modern perspective. Well, on the other hand, the heavily caricatured and simplistic characters are also the men in the book. As a whole, the book is a critique of materialism, both in describing business and in dealing with gender relations, and as such it reflects leino's entire work's desire for a life dominated by ideology. The book also flashes the germ of an actual noble novel, when two types of men with their own worldviews, "idealist" and "socialist", join the group of men celebrating Antti's divorce. However, Leino does not develop this sprout any further, but abandons these characters after a few replicas. In its form, "Bank Lords" is a classic tragedy and morality. The main characters, one after another, are destroyed, unable to change their fate. Even the final solution of the book leaves no hope for the better, but is written as a warning example of where materialism and the desire for pleasure, when unleashed, will take you. * The time when "Bank Lords" was written was a time of the astonishing heyday of financial capitalism and, at the same time, financial crises and scandals both in the world and on a smaller scale also in Finland. Leino witnessed this stage of development, and "Bank Lords" shows that he understood that a major upheaval was going on. The years leading up to the First World War have been called the first wave of globalisation. The growth of international trade and capital movements reached unprecedented proportions. It was at that time that Finland, a formerly remote and undeveloped country, became involved in the world economy, and this for the first time triggered the irreversible growth and modernization of the national economy. Economic history speaks of a 'take-off'. Finland's development at the turn of the 1800s and 1900s can be seen as similar to the start of growth that has recently been seen in emerging economies when they have entered the global economy. Helsinki lived through a phase of rapid growth. By the time the "bank lords" appeared, the city's intermediate figure had doubled since the turn of the century, in just over a decade. Lifestyles had also changed. As vividly described in the book, years of unprecedented economic boom had put people's heads on the wheel. Social differences had escalated, and the outbreak of civil war was four years away. Financially, Finland was in the gold standard. In 1878, the Finnish markka was defined as equivalent to the French gold franc. The exchange rate of the markka against other gold currencies had been fixed for more than three decades at the time of the appearance of the "Bank Lords". Joining the gold standard had made it possible to take out large, long-term loans from abroad, which were used, for example, for railways and the construction of urban infrastructure. Abundant capital inflows increased the money supply in the country. Eino Leino refers to this import of foreign capital in the "Bank Lords", and he thinks that this was the driving force behind the sweet life that spread in Helsinki. Experience had also been gained from monetary crises. Abroad, the most significant had been the great money market crisis of 1907, the so-called "money market crisis". The Knickerbocker crisis, which shocked major financial centers, especially in the United States, but also in Europe, such as Amsterdam and Hamburg. That crisis caused, among other things, the creation of a central bank in the United States, the Federal Reserve. The crisis showed the Americans that the banking system was too unstable unless it had the security of a strong central bank capable of emergency lending. In the Finnish money market, the crisis of 1907 did not feel very strong, although it caused quite a setback for export trade for a few years. However, the crisis led to one of the biggest credit losses in the Bank of Finland's history, when haller & Sohle & Co., a respected banking company operating in Hamburg. went bankrupt. The Bank of Finland had kept part of its foreign exchange reserves deposited in Haller & Sohle, and its collapse caused the Bank of Finland to lose approximately FIM 2.3 million. All in all, the money market situation in the early 1910s was more or less as Eino Leino painted it in his book. After the international downturn in 1907, Finland's trade balance had turned into a clear deficit. The deficit was financed by a large influx of capital, the consequences of which Leino also talks about. At the turn of 1912, the influx of capital to Finland stopped and the money market tightened clearly. Leino also refers to this tightening. The tension lasted until the end of 1913. In Finland, however, there was no general experience in these years, the so-called "black market". a systemic financial crisis, one that would have hit our entire banking system as it did in the 1930s or early 1990s. Leino's material in "Bank Lords" is not a comprehensive financial crisis, but some banking scandals related to embezzlement and spectacularly unsuccessful transactions. The biggest bankruptcy in Finland's banking history up to that point had been experienced in 1901, when Suomen Maan maatalouss-ja Teollisuuspankki Oy, had fallen into a state of execution due to large credit losses. The bank's president, Otto Hjelt, was removed from his post and fled to the United States to avoid worse consequences. The estate of the Agricultural and Industrial Bank was surveyed until 1917. The end result of its bankruptcy was that the bank's shareholders lost their investments completely and depositors lost more than 30% of their receivables. Perhaps the most legendary embezzlement in Finnish history had taken place in 1912. At that time, it turned out that Nils Idman, the director of the Tampere branch of the Us Bank of Finland, had misappropriated about 9 million marks through fraud and forgery. Idman received 10 years of discipline for his work. According to the National Biography, Albert Snellman, the manager of the Tampere branch of the Nordic Equity Bank, who was involved in Idman's skein, committed suicide after the case was revealed. Idman had also been granted large loans by the Bank of Finland's Tampere branch, even at the very last minute before he was discovered, and adolf lindeblad, the branch manager of the Bank of Finland, the "commissioner", was forced to resign. At the time of writing "Bank Lords", the most recent Finnish banking scandal was the collapse of Nykarleby Aktiebank at the end of 1913. The bank was small, but the story attracted a great deal of attention. According to sources, Nykarleby Aktiebank had been engaged in "frivolous lending" and its accounts had been falsified. In November 1913, the bank's president, Georg Lonnestrom, committed suicide, after which an audit revealed that the bank was ripe for bankruptcy. The bank's losses turned out to be so great that depositors lost almost 36% of their investments in bankruptcy. The shareholders lost their investments altogether. These cases certainly served as ingredients and a wake-up call when Eino Leino wrote "Bank Lords". However, in terms of describing easy money and speculation, Leino was perhaps moving a little too early. After the outbreak of the First World War, a real banking boom was launched in Finland, which continued until the early 1920s. Its driving force was that the money rush and inflation caused by the war's banknote financing fuelled speculation and unhealthy growth in the banking sector. In a few years, a total of 16 new commercial banks were established in Finland, but only a few of them proved viable once conditions had stabilised. In most cases, the problems that arose were dealt with by merging weak banks with stronger ones, so large bankruptcies were avoided. * Financial market crises and speculation have, of course, been the subject of many other novels. I will single out just two here, which I find interesting to compare with the "Bank lords". Leino's "Bank Lords" has been compared to Tom Wolfe's well-known bestseller "The Bonfire of the Vanities", among others, in which successful investment banker Sherman McCoy is destroyed in 1980s New York. What the books have in common is that the focus is more on the critical description of customs than on the actual speculation, which nevertheless forms the necessary background to the events. The difference between the books is interesting. While Leino's book focuses on the morality of the individual and thus of the entire business class, Wolfe describes extensively the social conflicts caused by the liberalization of the capital markets and the widening wealth gap in New York in the 1980s. What is common is the depiction and critique of a wasteful and frivolous way of life, but instead of Leino's psychological point of view, wolfe's book has a sociological perspective. In Leino's "Bank Lords", the crucial tension is within the main characters, but in Wolfe's "The Stake of Vanities", the tension is between the social classes, Park Avenue and the Bronx, and also between the races. The widening of wealth inequality, which began in the 1980s and has also been accompanied by an increase in the importance of the securities markets, has recently been at the centre of international debate. This is especially the case after the Frenchman Thomas Piketty published his much-noticed book "Capital in the 21st Century". Piketty fears that, due to the concentration of wealth, western countries are returning to the type of societies they were before The First World War  the time described by "Bankers". Leino's book shows the downsides of such a vision of the future. Wolfe warns against it especially effectively, although in the 1980s the development had only just begun. Leino's "Bank lords" also have benchmarks among their contemporaries. One notable one is the small key novel "The Moneychangers", written in 1908 by the American Upton Sinclair, which was also published in Finnish at the time, under the title "Money Changers". By the way, it was translated into Finnish by Yrjo Sirola, the editor of the newspaper Tyomies and later a man who became famous as a communist leader. He had stayed for several years in America, and must have studied Sinclair's book there. Sinclair's "Money Changers" describes the great stock market crash of 1907 that Wall Street has already mentioned, and its background. In terms of its themes, the book closely resembles Leino's "Bank Lords". Sinclair describes the wasteful life of the upper class and the deceitfulness that prevails in the business world. Both books end up with the death of some of the main characters. But while Leino's emphases are moral, sinclair's emphases are clearly political. In "Money Changers", Sinclair focuses on cartels and trusts as the causes of the financial crisis, as well as the corruption of the government and the press in the face of business pressures and temptations. While Leino describes the destruction of people from a psychological point of view, Sinclair describes it from a social and structural point of view. At Sinclair, politics appears, on the one hand, as a corrupt instrument of economic interests, but on the other hand as an opportunity to change things. Thus, at the end of the book, its protagonist, Allan Montague, a business lawyer, announces that he is entering politics to change the world. Leino's book  nor Wolfe's "The Stake of Vanities" offers any such hope. * One of the topical questions in the economic debate right now is whether policy  i.e. legislation and public oversight  can prevent financial crises from occurring in the future. Banking crises have been a recurring phenomenon in a market economy. Since the crises, major changes have often been made in banking regulation, economic policy and the international monetary system. The aim has been to avoid a resurgence of crises. Yet crises arise. The question arises as to why. Do people really not learn anything from history? Carmen Reinhart and Kenneth Rogoff's book on the history of crises, "This time is different", which I mentioned at the beginning, reflects on precisely this question. The authors cite two important reasons why lessons have not been learned from history. They are ignorance and arrogance, that is, in better Finnish, ignorance and arrogance. Ignorance means that history is not known, and therefore one cannot imagine all the risks. People, markets and entire societies have a short memory. Past mistakes and the resulting crises remain dusty entries in the history books that are not read, or at least not known to economic influencers. It can be assumed that the steady and favourable money market developments of the early 2000s (the so-called "soft market"). Great Moderation) contributed to banks, borrowers and securities investors underestimating financial market risks before the fall 2008 crash. Arrogance, on the other hand, has to do with thinking that we are wiser and more developed than previous generations and are therefore able to avoid their mistakes, and to cope with situations in which our predecessors fell. There were signs of this, too, in the most recent financial crisis. It was speculated that the modern financial system, modern advanced risk management methods and efficient information intermediation serving investors would help the market manage risks that in the past would have caused great damage. However, experience showed that market risks were much higher than could have been estimated on the basis of a short history, and that the protection afforded by risk diversification was overestimated in the event of very wide-ranging shocks to the economy. Ignorance and arrogance had led to unsustainable accumulation of risks and indebtedness, which are still being dismantled. * Eino Leino's "Bank Lords" includes all the elements familiar from later crises. It involves taking risks, embezzling, carrying out hostile corporate hijackings and over-indebtedness. Leino addresses the issue from the point of view of the morality of those involved in these actions. Alongside the moral aspect, a structural perspective can be placed. What if, in the end, human activity, even with its imperfections, takes place only on the terms of the environment? Isn't the reason for crises then in the system in which people operate, and not in their personal weakness? If this is the case, it is not enough to demand a moral awakening, but the rules of the game must be changed. Lessons must be learned from crises. It is an unfortunate fact that banking legislation and supervision often lag behind market developments and it is only crises that get the necessary reforms under way. This has happened many times in history, and it has also happened now with the last financial crisis. The critical attitude of public opinion towards banking is strongest in those countries where, during the crisis experienced, a large amount of society's funds have been committed to bailing out the banks. Criticism is natural. It is a reaction to imprudent and inept risk-taking, and to the perceived fact that in recent decades banks have become too far removed from their service role in the service of saving, investment and economic growth and have moved into the world of short-term profit - the casino economy. At the same time, banking is an indispensable part of a well-functioning economic system. Banks are needed to pool savings funds into credits, they are needed to convert depositors' liquid investments into longer-term loans, and they are needed to assess the creditworthiness of various investment objects. The sector must therefore be strengthened and reorganised by various means, and confidence in the constructive role of banking in society must be restored. The latest financial crisis has triggered many projects to improve banking regulation, not least here in Europe. There is even talk of regulatory tsunamis in the banking sector, and it has also been claimed that the new regulation will hinder bank lending. In this context, I cannot go into more detail about the various reform projects that are under way in the regulation of the banking sector. They concern, among other things, the prudential requirements of banks, the strengthening of banking supervision and the powers to intervene in a timely manner in order to save society's resources and implement investor responsibility. It has been necessary to strengthen the regulation of banks and the financial markets. But the question of rules and morality is not an either-or question. Not everything can ever be regulated, and even the best rules will not help if they are not taken seriously and properly enforced. Ultimately, the sustainability and success of banking depends on the values, goals and culture of the people involved. I have been closely involved in the preparation of a proposal for new rules that would better distinguish between traditional banking and securities trading. Regulation in this area has already been tightened up in a number of countries. Two years ago, a working group set up by the European Commission, which I chaired, made a recommendation to regulate the structures of banks at European level. One of our arguments for separating securities trading from traditional banking was that the hopefully customer-oriented corporate culture that prevails on the basic banking side should be kept separate from the pursuit of short-term profits in securities trading. At the beginning of this year, the Commission presented its proposal for the restructuring of banks, based on the report of my working group. The progress of the reform will now depend on negotiations with the European Parliament and the Council. * Maintaining a healthy culture in the financial sector requires stronger institutions. It also requires an understanding relationship with the history of the industry, to avoid ignorance and arrogance. Here, fiction also has its own meaning. An old text, such as 'Bank lords', gives a perspective that is too often lacking in the financial world. However, even in this company, I do not want to flatten fiction as just a tool for profit considerations: "Bank lords" are also a pleasure to read. Liikanen (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagLiikanen)

Kaiken kaikkiaan 1910-luvun alun rahamarkkinatilanne oli suurin piirtein sellainen kuin miksi Eino Leino sen kirjassaan maalasi. Suomen kauppatase oli k<8a><8a>ntynyt vuoden 1907 kansainv<8a>lisen laskusuhdanteen j<8a>lkeen selv<8a>sti alij<8a><8a>m<8a>iseksi. Alij<8a><8a>m<8a> rahoitettiin runsaalla p<8a><8a>omantuonnilla, jonka seurauksista Leinokin puhuu. Vuoden 1912 vaiheilla p<8a><8a>omantuonti Suomeen pys<8a>htyi ja rahamarkkinat kiristyiv<8a>t selv<8a>sti. T<8a>h<8a>n kiristymiseen Leinokin viittaa. Kireytt<8a> kesti vuoden 1913 lopulle saakka. Suomessa ei kuitenkaan n<8a>in<8a> vuosina koettu yleist<8a>, ns. systeemist<8a> finanssikriisi<8a>, sellaista, joka olisi koetellut koko pankkij<8a>rjestelm<8a><8a>mme niin kuin 1930-luvulla tai 1990-luvun alussa. Leinon materiaalina <d3>Pankkiherroissa<d3> ei olekaan kokonaisvaltainen finanssikriisi, vaan er<8a><8a>t kavalluksiin ja n<8a>ytt<8a>v<8a>sti ep<8a>onnistuneisiin liiketoimiin liittyneet pankkiskandaalit. Suomen siihenastisen pankkihistorian suurin konkurssi oli koettu vuonna 1901, kun Suomen Maanviljelys-ja Teollisuuspankki Oy, oli joutunut suoritustilaan suurien luottotappioiden vuoksi. Pankin p<8a><8a>johtaja Otto Hjelt erotettiin virastaan ja h<8a>n pakeni Yhdysvaltoihin v<8a>ltt<8a><8a>kseen pahemmat seuraukset. Maanviljelys-ja Teollisuuspankin pes<8a><8a> selvitettiin aina vuoteen 1917 asti. Lopputuloksena sen konkurssista oli, ett<8a> pankin osakkaat menettiv<8a>t sijoituksensa kokonaan ja tallettajat menettiv<8a>t saamisistaan yli 30 %. Suomen historian ehk<8a> legendaarisin kavallus oli tapahtunut vuonna 1912. Tuolloin k<8a>vi ilmi, ett<8a> Suomen Yhdyspankin Tampereen konttorinjohtaja Nils Idman oli petoksin ja v<8a><8a>renn<9a>ksin kavaltanut noin 9 miljoonaa silloista markkaa. Idman sai teostaan 10 vuotta kuritushuonetta. Kansallisbiografia kertoo, ett<8a> Idmanin vyyhteen sekaantunut Pohjoismaiden Osakepankin Tampereen konttorin esimies Albert Snellman teki jutun paljastuttua itsemurhan. My<9a>s Suomen Pankin Tampereen konttori oli my<9a>nt<8a>nyt Idmanille suuria luottoja, jopa aivan viime hetkill<8a> ennen t<8a>m<8a>n paljastumista, ja Suomen Pankin konttorinjohtaja eli <d3>komisarius<d3> Adolf Lindeblad joutui eroamaan. <d3>Pankkiherrojen<d3> kirjoittamisen aikaan tuorein suomalainen pankkiskandaali oli Nykarleby Aktiebankin kaatuminen vuoden 1913 lopulla. Pankki oli pieni, mutta juttu her<8a>tti eritt<8a>in suurta huomiota. L<8a>hteiden mukaan Nykarleby Aktiebank oli harjoittanut <d3>kevytmielist<8a> luotonantoa<d3> ja sen kirjanpitoa oli v<8a><8a>rennetty. Marraskuussa 1913 pankin p<8a><8a>johtaja Georg L<9a>nnestr<9a>m teki itsemurhan, mink<8a> j<8a>lkeen toimeenpannussa tarkastuksessa k<8a>vi ilmi, ett<8a> pankki oli konkurssikyps<8a>. Pankin tappiot osoittautuivat niin suuriksi, ett<8a> tallettajat menettiv<8a>t konkurssissa sijoituksistaan l<8a>hes 36 %. Osakkaat menettiv<8a>t sijoituksensa kokonaan. N<8a>m<8a> tapaukset varmasti toimivat aineksina ja her<8a>tteen<8a> kun Eino Leino kirjoitti <d3>Pankkiherroja<d3>. Helpon rahan ja keinottelun kuvaamisen kannalta Leino oli ehk<8a> kuitenkin liikkeell<8a> hiukan liian varhain. Ensimm<8a>isen maailmansodan syttymisen j<8a>lkeen Suomessa nimitt<8a>in k<8a>ynnistyi varsinainen pankkiboomi, joka jatkui 1920-luvun alkuvuosiin asti. Sen k<8a>ytt<9a>voimana oli, ett<8a> sodan setelirahoituksen aiheuttama rahanrunsaus ja inflaatio ruokkivat spekulaatiota ja pankkisektorin ep<8a>tervett<8a> kasvua. Muutamassa vuodessa Suomeen perustettiin tuolloin yhteens<8a> 16 uutta liikepankkia, joista kuitenkin vain harva osoittautui olojen vakaannuttua i elinkelpoiseksi. Syntyneet ongelmat hoidettiin useimmissa tapauksissa fuusioimalla heikot pankit vahvempiin, joten suurilta konkursseilta v<8a>ltyttiin. * Rahoitusmarkkinoiden kriisit ja keinottelu ovat tietysti olleet monien muidenkin romaanien aiheena. Otan t<8a>ss<8a> esiin vain kaksi, joiden vertaaminen <d3>Pankkiherroihin<d3> tuntuu kiinnostavalta. Leinon <d3>Pankkiherroja<d3> on verrattu muun muassa Tom Wolfen tunnettuun bestselleriin <d3>The Bonfire of the Vanities<d3> (Turhuuksien rovio), jossa menestyv<8a> investointipankkiiri Sherman McCoy tuhoutuu 1980-luvun New Yorkissa. Kirjoissa on yhteist<8a> se, ett<8a> painopiste on kriittisess<8a> tapainkuvauksessa enemm<8a>n kuin varsinaisessa keinottelussa, joka kuitenkin muodostaa tapahtumien v<8a>ltt<8a>m<8a>tt<9a>m<8a>n taustan. Kirjojen ero on mielenkiintoinen. Siin<8a> miss<8a> Leinon kirjan polttopisteess<8a> on yksil<9a>n ja sit<8a> kautta koko liikemiesluokankin moraali, Wolfe kuvaa laajasti yhteiskunnallisia ristiriitoja, joita p<8a><8a>omamarkkinoiden vapautuminen ja varallisuuserojen kasvu 1980-luvun New Yorkissa aiheuttivat. Yhteist<8a> on tuhlailevan ja kevytmielisen el<8a>m<8a>ntavan kuvaaminen ja kritiikki, mutta Leinon psykologisen n<8a>k<9a>kulman sijaan Wolfen kirjassa n<8a>k<9a>kulma on sosiologinen. Leinon <d3>Pankkiherroissa<d3> ratkaiseva j<8a>nnite on p<8a><8a>henkil<9a>iden sis<8a>ll<8a>, mutta Wolfen <d3>Turhuuksien roviossa<d3> j<8a>nnite on yhteiskuntaluokkien, Park Avenuen ja Bronxin v<8a>linen, ja my<9a>s rotujen v<8a>linen. 1980-luvulla alkanut varallisuuserojen leventyminen, johon on samalla liittynyt arvopaperimarkkinoiden merkityksen kasvu, on viime aikoina ollut kansainv<8a>lisen keskustelun polttopisteess<8a>. N<8a>in varsinkin sen j<8a>lkeen kun ranskalainen Thomas Piketty julkaisi paljon huomiota her<8a>tt<8a>neen kirjansa <d3>P<8a><8a>oma 21. vuosisadalla<d3>. Piketty pelk<8a><8a>, ett<8a> l<8a>nsimaat ovat varallisuuden keskittymisen takia palaamassa sen tyyppisiksi yhteiskunniksi, jollaisia ne olivat ennen ensimm<8a>ist<8a> maailmansotaa <d0> aikaan jota <d3>Pankkiherroja<d3> kuvaa. Leinon kirja osoittaa t<8a>llaisen tulevaisuudenkuvan varjopuolet. Wolfe varoittaa siit<8a> erityisen tehokkaasti, vaikka kehitys oli 1980-luvulla vasta alkanut. Leinon <d3>Pankkiherroilla<d3> on vertailukohtia my<9a>s aikalaistensa joukossa. Yksi huomattava sellainen on amerikkalaisen Upton Sinclairin vuonna 1908 kirjoittama pieni avainromaani <d3>The Moneychangers<d3>, joka ilmestyi aikanaan my<9a>s suomeksi, nimell<8a> <d3>Rahanvaihtajat<d3>. Sen suomensi muuten Yrj<9a> Sirola, sanomalehti Ty<9a>miehen toimittaja ja my<9a>hemmin kommunistijohtajana kuuluisaksi tullut mies. H<8a>n oli oleskellut useita vuosia Amerikassa ja varmaankin siell<8a> tutustunut Sinclairin kirjaan. Sinclairin <d3>Rahanvaihtajat<d3> kuvaa Wall Streetin jo mainitsemaani suurta p<9a>rssiromahdusta vuonna 1907, ja sen taustoja. Teemoiltaan kirja muistuttaa l<8a>heisesti Leinon <d3>Pankkiherroja<d3>. Sinclair kuvaa yl<8a>luokan tuhlailevaa el<8a>m<8a><8a> ja liike-el<8a>m<8a>ss<8a> vallitsevaa petollisuutta. Molemmat kirjat p<8a><8a>tyv<8a>t joidenkin p<8a><8a>henkil<9a>iden kuolemaan. Mutta siin<8a> miss<8a> Leinon painotukset ovat moraaliset, Sinclairilla painotukset ovat selv<8a>sti poliittiset. Sinclair kiinnitt<8a><8a> <d3>Rahanvaihtajissa<d3> p<8a><8a>huomion kartelleihin ja trusteihin finanssikriisin syin<8a>, sek<8a> hallituksen ja lehdist<9a>n korruptoituneisuuteen liike-el<8a>m<8a>n paineiden ja houkutusten edess<8a>. Siin<8a> miss<8a> Leino kuvaa ihmisten tuhoutumista psykologisesta n<8a>k<9a>kulmasta, Sinclair kuvaa sit<8a> yhteiskunnallisesta ja rakenteellisesta n<8a>k<9a>kulmasta. Politiikka n<8a>ytt<8a>ytyy Sinclairilla yht<8a><8a>lt<8a> korruptoituneena taloudellisten intressien v<8a>likappaleena, mutta toisaalta mahdollisuutena muuttaa asioita. Niinp<8a> kirjan lopussa sen p<8a><8a>henkil<9a> Allan Montague, liikejuristi, ilmoittaa ryhtyv<8a>ns<8a> politiikkaan muuttaakseen maailmaa. Mit<8a><8a>n t<8a>llaista toivoa ei Leinon kirja <d0> eik<8a> Wolfen <d3>Turhuuksien roviokaan<d3> <d0> tarjoa. * Er<8a>s talouskeskustelun ajankohtaisia kysymyksi<8a> juuri nyt on, voiko politiikka <d0> siis lains<8a><8a>d<8a>nt<9a> ja julkinen valvonta <d0> vastedes est<8a><8a> finanssikriisien syntymisen. Pankkikriisit ovat olleet toistuva ilmi<9a> markkinataloudessa. Kriisien j<8a>lkeen on monesti tehty suuriakin muutoksia pankkitoiminnan s<8a><8a>ntelyss<8a>, talouspolitiikassa ja kansainv<8a>lisess<8a> rahaj<8a>rjestelm<8a>ss<8a>. Tarkoituksena on ollut v<8a>ltt<8a><8a> kriisien uusiutuminen. Silti kriisej<8a> syntyy. Her<8a><8a> kysymys, miksi. Eiv<8a>tk<9a> ihmiset todellakaan opi historiasta mit<8a><8a>n? Carmen Reinhartin ja Kenneth Rogoffin kriisien historiaa k<8a>sittelev<8a>ss<8a> kirjassa <d3>This time is different<d3>, jonka alussa mainitsin, pohditaan juuri t<8a>t<8a> kysymyst<8a>. Kirjoittajat mainitsevat kaksi t<8a>rke<8a><8a> syyt<8a>, miksi historiasta ei ole opittu. Ne ovat ignoranssi ja arroganssi, eli paremmalla suomenkielell<8a> tiet<8a>m<8a>tt<9a>myys ja ylimielisyys. Tiet<8a>m<8a>tt<9a>myys tarkoittaa sit<8a>, ett<8a> historiaa ei tunneta, eik<8a> siksi osata kuvitella kaikkia riskej<8a>. Ihmisill<8a>, markkinoilla ja kokonaisilla yhteiskunnilla on lyhyt muisti. Menneet virheet ja niist<8a> johtuneet kriisit j<8a><8a>v<8a>t p<9a>lyttyneiksi merkinn<9a>iksi historian kirjoissa, joita ei lueta, tai ainakaan talousel<8a>m<8a>n vaikuttajat eiv<8a>t niit<8a> tunne. Voidaan olettaa, ett<8a> 2000-luvun alun tasainen ja suotuisa rahamarkkinakehitys (ns. Great Moderation) vaikutti siihen, ett<8a> pankit, velanottajat ja arvopaperisijoittajat aliarvioivat finanssimarkkinoiden riskej<8a> ennen syksyn 2008 romahdusta. Ylimielisyys puolestaan liittyy siihen, ett<8a> ajatellaan, ett<8a> olemme viisaampia ja kehittyneempi<8a> kuin edelliset sukupolvet ja pystymme siksi v<8a>ltt<8a>m<8a><8a>n heid<8a>n virheens<8a>, ja selvi<8a>m<8a><8a>n tilanteista, joihin edelt<8a>j<8a>mme sortuivat. T<8a>st<8a>kin oli merkkej<8a> viimeisimm<8a>ss<8a> finanssikriisiss<8a>. Arveltiin, ett<8a> nykyaikainen rahoitusj<8a>rjestelm<8a>, nykyajan kehittyneet riskienhallintamenetelm<8a>t ja sijoittajia palveleva tehokas informaation v<8a>litys auttaisivat markkinoita hallitsemaan riskej<8a>, jotka aikaisemmin olisivat aiheuttaneet suurta vahinkoa. Kokemus osoitti kuitenkin, ett<8a> markkinoiden riskit olivat paljon suuremmat kuin lyhyen historian perusteella olisi voitu arvioida, ja ett<8a> riskien hajauttamisen tarjoama suoja oli yliarvioitu kun talouteen kohdistui hyvin laaja-alaisia h<8a>iri<9a>it<8a>. Tiet<8a>m<8a>tt<9a>myys ja ylimieli olivat johtaneet kest<8a>m<8a>tt<9a>m<8a><8a>n riskien kasautumiseen ja velkaantumiseen, joita edelleenkin puretaan. * Eino Leinon <d3>Pankkiherroissa<d3> ovat mukana kaikki my<9a>hemmist<8a>kin kriiseist<8a> tutut ainekset. Siin<8a> otetaan riskej<8a>, kavalletaan, suoritetaan vihamielisi<8a> yrityskaappauksia ja ylivelkaannutaan. Leino k<8a>sittelee asiaa n<8a>iss<8a> toimissa mukana olevien moraalin n<8a>k<9a>kulmasta. Moraalisen n<8a>k<9a>kulman rinnalle voidaan asettaa rakenteellinen n<8a>k<9a>kulma. Ent<8a> jos ihmisen toiminta ep<8a>t<8a>ydellisyyksineenkin loppujen tapahtuu lopuksi vain ymp<8a>rist<9a>n ehdoilla? Eik<9a> syy kriiseihin silloin ole systeemiss<8a>, jossa ihmiset toimivat, eik<8a> heid<8a>n henkil<9a>kohtaisessa heikkoudessaan? Jos n<8a>in on, ei moraalisen her<8a>tyksen vaatiminen riit<8a>, vaan toiminnan pelis<8a><8a>nt<9a>j<8a> on muutettava. Kriiseist<8a> t<8a>ytyy ottaa opiksi. On valitettava tosiasia, ett<8a> pankkilains<8a><8a>d<8a>nt<9a> ja <d0>valvonta usein laahaavat markkinoiden kehityksen j<8a>ljess<8a> ja vasta kriisit saavat tarvittavia uudistuksia k<8a>yntiin. N<8a>in on k<8a>ynyt monta kertaa historiassa, ja n<8a>in on k<8a>ynyt my<9a>s nyt viimeisen finanssikriisin yhteydess<8a>. Yleisen mielipiteen kriittinen suhtautuminen pankkitoimintaan on voimakkainta niiss<8a> maissa, joissa paljon yhteiskunnan varoja on koetun kriisin aikana sitoutunut pankkien pelastamiseen. Kritiikki on luonnollista. Se on reaktio varomattomaan ja taitamattomaan riskinottoon, ja siihen, ett<8a> pankkien on koettu viime vuosikymmenin<8a> et<8a><8a>ntyneen liiaksi palveluteht<8a>v<8a>st<8a><8a>n s<8a><8a>st<8a>misen, investointien ja talouskasvun palveluksessa ja siirtyneen lyhytn<8a>k<9a>isen voitontavoittelun <d0> kasinotalouden <d0> maailmaan. Samalla pankkitoiminta on v<8a>ltt<8a>m<8a>t<9a>n osa hyvin toimivaa talousj<8a>rjestelm<8a><8a>. Pankkeja tarvitaan kokoamaan s<8a><8a>st<9a>varoja luotoiksi, niit<8a> tarvitaan muuttamaan tallettajien likvidit sijoitukset pitempiaikaisiksi lainoiksi, ja niit<8a> tarvitaan arvioimaan eri investointikohteiden luottokelpoisuutta. Toimialaa on sen vuoksi vahvistettava ja tervehdytett<8a>v<8a> eri keinoin ja luottamus pankkitoiminnan rakentavaan yhteiskunnalliseen rooliin on palautettava. Viimeksi koettu finanssikriisi on k<8a>ynnist<8a>nyt monia hankkeita pankkis<8a><8a>ntelyn tehostamiseksi, ei v<8a>hiten meill<8a> Euroopassa. Pankkialalla puhutaan jopa s<8a><8a>ntelytsunamista, ja uuden s<8a><8a>ntelyn on v<8a>itetty my<9a>s haittaavan pankkien luotonantoa. T<8a>ss<8a> yhteydess<8a> en voi ryhty<8a> k<8a>ym<8a><8a>n tarkemmin l<8a>pi eri uudistushankkeita, joita pankkialan s<8a><8a>ntelyss<8a> on meneill<8a><8a>n. Ne koskevat muun muassa pankkien vakavaraisuusvaatimuksia, pankkivalvonnan vahvistamista sek<8a> niit<8a> valtuuksia, joilla ongelmiin ajautuneiden pankkien toimintaan voidaan puuttua ajoissa yhteiskunnan varojen s<8a><8a>st<8a>miseksi ja sijoittajavastuun toteuttamiseksi. Pankkien ja rahoitusmarkkinoiden s<8a><8a>ntelyn vahvistaminen on ollut v<8a>ltt<8a>m<8a>t<9a>nt<8a>. Mutta kysymys s<8a><8a>nn<9a>ist<8a> ja moraalista ei ole mik<8a><8a>n joko-tai -kysymys. Kaikkea ei koskaan voida s<8a><8a>nnell<8a>, ja parhaatkaan s<8a><8a>nn<9a>t eiv<8a>t auta, jos niit<8a> ei oteta vakavasti eik<8a> valvota kunnolla. Viime k<8a>dess<8a> pankkitoiminnan kest<8a>vyys ja menestys riippuu siin<8a> mukana olevien ihmisten arvoista, tavoitteista ja toimintakulttuurista. Olen ollut tiiviisti mukana valmistelemassa ehdotusta uusiksi s<8a><8a>nn<9a>iksi, jotka erottaisivat periteisen pankkitoiminnan ja arvopaperikaupan paremmin toisistaan. T<8a>t<8a> asiaa koskevaa s<8a><8a>ntely<8a> on jo kiristetty useissa maissa. Kaksi vuotta sitten Euroopan komission asettama ty<9a>ryhm<8a>, jota johdin, teki suosituksen pankkien rakenteiden s<8a><8a>ntelemiseksi Euroopan tasolla. Yksi perusteemme arvopaperikaupan erottamiselle perinteisest<8a> pankkitoiminnasta oli, ett<8a> t<8a>ytyisi pit<8a><8a> peruspankkitoiminnan puolella vallitseva, toivottavasti asiakasl<8a>ht<9a>inen yrityskulttuuri erill<8a><8a>n arvopaperikauppaan kuuluvasta lyhytaikaisten voittojen tavoittelusta. Komissio antoi t<8a>m<8a>n vuoden alussa pankkien rakenteiden uudistamista koskevan ehdotuksensa, joka perustuu ty<9a>ryhm<8a>ni raporttiin. Uudistuksen eteneminen riippuu nyt Euroopan Parlamentin ja Neuvoston kanssa k<8a>yt<8a>vist<8a> neuvotteluista. * Terveen toimintakulttuurin yll<8a>pit<8a>minen rahoitusalalla vaatii entist<8a> lujempia instituutioita. Se vaatii my<9a>s ymm<8a>rt<8a>v<8a><8a> suhdetta toimialan historiaan, tiet<8a>m<8a>tt<9a>myyden ja ylimielisyyden v<8a>ltt<8a>miseksi. T<8a>ss<8a> kaunokirjallisuudellakin on oma merkityksens<8a>. Vanha teksti, sellainen kuin <d3>Pankkiherrat<d3>, antaa perspektiivi<8a>, josta rahamaailmassa liian usein on puutetta. En kuitenkaan halua t<8a>ss<8a>k<8a><8a>n seurassa latistaa kaunokirjallisuutta vain v<8a>lineeksi hy<9a>tyn<8a>k<9a>kohdille: <d3>Pankkiherroja<d3> on my<9a>s nautinto lukea.
