Title: Learning from history. 120th anniversary celebration of the Economic Society
text: Chief Executive Erkki Liikanen: You can  and should  learn from history. Economic Society's 120th anniversary, Helsinki, 27.10.2014. . Speech . Monday27 October 2014,6:00 PM Erkki Liikanen Governor of the Bank of Finland Economic Society's 120th anniversary helsinki, 27 October 2014 YOU CAN  AND SHOULD  LEARN FROM HISTORY The Bank of Finland celebrated its 200th anniversary three years ago. The brand year was in many ways an enriching experience. The experience was further deepened by anttiKuustera's and Juha Tarkka's historical works on the Bank of Finland through the ages. The history work depicts how well integrated the financial market in the Baltic Sea region was in the late 1700s. The work tells how enlightened and reform-minded Russian central officials were at the beginning of the 1800s. It also depicts how important a driving force Finland's accession to the international gold standard in the late 1870s was for our country's economic development. And it depicts Finland's integration with the international monetary system after The Second World War and integration with the European Union in the 1990s. The Economic Society of Finland celebrates its 120th anniversary today. Its one hundred and twenty-year course contains several milestones in the history of Finland and Europe. Many times of transition are reflected in our lives to a surprising degree to this day. You can  and you should  learn from history. THE GLORIOUS EPOCH The period between the 1870s and The First World War has been commonly referred to as la belle epoque. The Economic Society was founded in the midst of this glorious epoch. During these decades, the world, Europe and Finland experienced a very big change. Internationalization and technological development were drivers of change in the economy. Distances shrank thanks to new transportation and means of communication, such as railroads and steamships, telephone and telegraph, and the wireless signal. World trade grew by leaps and bounds. World trade and mobility were promoted by the global integration of financial markets. The increased stability brought about by the international gold standard also contributed to this development. Most countries in the world joined the gold standard by the 1870s. The Grand Duchy of Finland took this step in 1878. Russia joined only a couple of decades later. Finland's accession to the gold standard was of crucial importance for the economic development of our country. Thus, Finland's monetary system was integrated with the Western world. Why did neo-Renaissance-style stone palaces grow on cards time up like mushrooms out of the earth in Helsinki in the early 1880s? Why did the same happen in many other European countries? The answer is the gold standard, which gave private domestic players access to the international credit market. The glorious era was marked by immense optimism. The world opened up opportunities for those who dared to take the chance. Scientific progress, the higher level of education and the increased interdependence instilled hope that the world could be controlled and conflicts regulated by negotiation. Since the Napoleonic Wars, there had been peace on the European continent, excluding the war between Prussia and France in 18701871. The educated classes had begun to think that the interdependence had become so great that it effectively ruled out war between the great powers. War had certainly been waged in the peripheral areas. The Grand Duchy of Finland also received its own baptism of fire during the Crimean War. An influential thinker and representative of the educated classes appeared in England in the early 1900s, Norman Angell, journalist and writer. He became known for his book The Great Illusion, which came out in 1910. In the book, he argued that everyone is a loser in a war between modern industrialized countries. The reason was the interdependence of countries as a result of trade agreements and credits. According to Angell, ideas, such as that war could increase national wealth, were outdated. The time was ripe for rational diplomacy, in which all governments understand that resolving disputes through negotiation is a better strategy than war. History tells us that Angell's forecast did not materialize. THE GREAT WAR I'm reading a quote: "On the first of August, just before seven o'clock in the evening, Germany declared war on Russia. On the evening of the second of August, the German troops penetrated the Principality of Luxembourg and Belgium after Brussels had been faced with ultimatums to let the German columns into the country according to Schlieffen's plan. On the third of August at 18.15, Germany declared war on France. Britain announced that it would come to Belgium's rescue, if the country's borders were violated. And by the fourth of August, it was clear that Germany had penetrated Belgium." 1 World War I had begun. The quote is taken from Francois Cochet's book La Grande Guerre. In the background was a complicated network of alliances and security guarantees that, after the escalation of the conflict between Austria and Serbia, operated in a way that no one had control over anymore. The glorious epoch had come to an end. The Economic Society turned 20 years old. When the war broke out at the turn of the month JulyAugust 1914, the reception was enthusiastic. The formed class tuned into the general euphoria. Sociologist Max Weber immediately wrote that the war "in all its horror was a great and wonderful thing worth experiencing". Author Thomas Mann labelled the war as something "cleansing and liberating, an incredibly hopeful event". Enthusiasm quickly began to wane. The war was not short, as intended, but it dragged on, the number of people killed increased and the economic problems were brought to a head. As a rule, war cannot be financed solely with tax revenue in the long run, but the state must rely on loans. Most often, the loan is entered into the country's own central bank. The repayment of the loan then hits the savers and holders of monetary assets, who see the real value of their assets decrease as a result of inflation. It doesn't hurt to have friends to borrow from. The United States initially stayed out of the war, but the American banks, most notably J.P. Morgan, granted generous loans to England and France. When, in April 1917, the United States joined the war, the reason was not only the Germans' submarine blockade, but also the need to secure the claims of its own banks. The Allies had to win the war. Otherwise, the U.S. banks would have started to falter. THE BITTER LEGACY OF THE GREAT WAR Finns' knowledge of the First World War is insignificant. Even the Thirty Years' War is better known to us. This is regrettable, because it is difficult to understand today's Europe without knowing the background and consequences of the war. Max Jakobson often visited Brussels in the early 1990s and he pointed out that the core of European integration is foreign to The Finns, as Finland did not participate in the First World War. About the First World War, it is said that it was a war that broke out by accident and that no one wanted. Nor would anyone have wished or been able to foresee the outcome of the war. The borders of Europe and the Middle East were redrawn. The empires of Austria-Hungary, Russia and Germany fell apart, as did the Ottoman Empire. Britain's hegemony began to creak at the seams at the same time as the importance of the United States increased. Russia was driven into the arms of the Bolsheviks. As a result of the war, many small nations became independent, among them Finland. A large part of the borders that arose after the war were created artificially. Almost all of them have at some point been subject to tensions, which have sometimes been serious. Tensions remain. For example, the borders drawn by Britain and France on the ruins of the Ottoman Empire in the Middle East have been the scene of crises and acts of violence in recent months. One of the great questions of the time is whether all states will survive. The border between Denmark and Germany is the only one of the borders that came into being after the First World War that has never been subject to any tensions. In the referendum held after the war, the inhabitants of northern Schleswig decided to join Denmark, while the inhabitants of Middle Schleswig wanted to remain part of Germany. The terms of the Treaty of Versailles aroused bitterness among the losers, especially in Germany. Particularly sharp criticism of the terms of the peace treaty was voiced by John Maynard Keynes. He predicted in 1919 that the deliberate impoverishment of Central Europe would "destroy the formation and advancement of our entire generation." Twenty years later, signs were seen that Keynes' prophecy would come true. The second losing state, the bankrupt Austria, was treated differently.2 At the League of Nations, which had been formed in conjunction with the Versailles Peace Treaty, a separate Economic and Financial Commission was established in 1920 tasked with getting Austria's economy back on its feet. The U.S. provided debt financing against government guarantees. The package included a hard clean-up. Among other things, fifty thousand civil servants lost their jobs and the pensions of the former empire's civil servants were reduced. In economic terms, the case of Austria proved to be a success. It had to serve as an example when the International Monetary Fund began to develop models of action to help troubled countries. The flip side of it all was that Austria's political development towards democracy suffered from the limited right to self-determination. THE CRAZY YEARS The 1920s were marked by modernism and the people's desire to forget about the war. Electricity, radio, cars, film and jazz music made inroads into everyday life. Posterity gave this era the name les annees folles, the crazy years. In America, the term roaring twenties, the merry or stormy twenties, was used. In Finland, the boom took off in 1924. That year, the Economic Society celebrated its 30th anniversary. By then, it was clear that Finland would return to the gold standard to a new gold parity that somewhat corresponded to the prevailing exchange rate level.3 Until then, it had been expected that the return to the gold standard would take place to the pre-war parity. That would have meant severe deflation, especially lower property prices. Under these conditions, no one was expected to start any construction projects. Eliel Saarinen, who had designed the Helsinki Railway Station and Finnish banknotes (1909 and 1922 types), moved to the United States for lack of work. When the expectations of a return to the gold standard of the old parity disappeared, all the dams burst and the whole of Front Toolo was filled with construction. By 1929, the economy was clearly overheating. Finland would probably sooner or later have suffered a self-inflicted recession. On October 29, 1929, almost exactly 85 years ago, stock prices in New York plummeted. This event set in motion a dynamic that led the world into the Great Depression. THE GREAT DEPRESSION The Great Depression was a traumatic experience. The causes of it have been widely debated over the decades. Economics changed, and different schools have their own interpretations of the causes of the Great Depression. The fact remains that the Great Depression testified that the market economy, the banking system and economic policy had gone wrong. Something had gone wrong in earnest. One of the foremost researchers on the Great Depression has been the professor of economics at Princeton University, Ben Bernanke, who in the early 2000s became first a member of the executive board and later head of the central banking system in the United States. Bernanke gave a speech in November 2002 under the title Making Sure "It" Doesn't Happen Here. The word "it" in the headline referred to deflation. Bernanke had analyzed the depression of the 1930s in depth and had become convinced that one of the most important tasks of economic policy is to do everything possible to prevent a repeat of the catastrophe of the 1930s. Macroeconomic policy is thus not only about cyclical policy, but also about risk management and crisis resolution. In his speech, Bernanke enumerated a number of measures that reduce the likelihood of a deflationary circle. According to Bernanke, if a country is hit by deflation after all, it should act proactively and aggressively. The measures also include, where necessary, massive purchases of securities on the market. Purchases can focus both on sovereign debt and on private debt securities  either directly or indirectly by granting banks credit against collateral in the form of eligible private debt securities. If necessary, it is possible to go further than that and, for example, implement substantial tax cuts or finance budget deficits with central bank debt. In January this year, the Bank of Finland's Bank Council met Bernanke in Washington a few days before the end of his term of office. We asked him: Now that it's been 6 . years since the outbreak of the financial crisis, can it be said that all the lessons of the Great Depression were taken advantage of? Did something happen that could not be predicted because of the historical experience? As far as the political conclusions are concerned, the answer was the same as in 2002. But one thing had come as a surprise to him: the complexity and vulnerability of the major international financial institutions. It has required and requires a lot of new work. THE RELAUNCH IN THE 40S The Second World War meant a long break in trade and credit relations. Without a well-functioning monetary system, mutual credit relations and multilateral trade, the world would not have been able to recover from the chaos created by the war. In the midst of the ongoing world war, the representatives of 44 allied countries gathered in July 1944 in Bretton Woods to negotiate the principles of the global monetary system. In the conference, the USSR was also represented. Of the Nordic countries, Iceland and Norway participated, and Denmark as an observer. At the same time as the delegations of the Allied countries arrived in Bretton Woods, Finland in Tali-Ihantala fought its fiercest battles of the entire World War. The United States had severed its diplomatic relations with Finland. The new international monetary system was designed on the basis of the proposals of the American and British governments. The leading figures in the negotiations were US Deputy Treasury Secretary Harry Dexter White and the famous British economist John Maynard Keynes. Finland's relations with the victorious powers after the war were regulated by the Armistice Agreement, which was signed on September 19, 1944. The agreement had consequences for Finland's creditworthiness, which was overshadowed by the doubt that Finland would be able to pay war reparations to the Soviet Union and Finland's domestic political situation in general. Under these uncertain conditions, the Economic Society turned 50 years old. Finland's path to membership of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank was by no means straight forward. Ratification of the peace treaty was delayed in 1947. In the same year, Finland's application for UN membership foundered on great power conflicts. Finland was finally admitted as a member of the IMF and the World Bank at the second meeting of the organizations in September 1947. The following year, the Cold War began. It is uncertain whether Finland would then have managed to get into the Bretton Woods organisations any longer. At the same time, reconstruction had begun on the European continent. The United States had in 1948 deployed the comprehensive Marshall Plan to restore the finances of European countries. Western European countries participated in the aid plan with the exception of Spain, the Nordic countries with the exception of Finland, and Greece and Turkey. Finland could not participate in the programme for foreign policy reasons. Marshall aid ceased in 1951. The Marshall Plan was supplemented in 1950 by the European Payments Union (EPU). The aim was to enable multilateral trade between the Western European countries. The payments union is considered to have been a success. Ronald McKinnon, among others, argues that the Union has had more significance for the recovery of Europe than Marshall aid.4 During the payment union, trade between the countries of Western Europe more than doubled. The Union was wound up in 1958, when the convertibility of the currencies was reintroduced. "NEVER AGAIN" The Second World War can be considered a continuation of the First World War. It was even more devastating than the first. After the war, former enemies stated: "Never again". The founding father of the EU, Robert Schuman, had to feel the first world war very personally. His home area in Elsass-Lorraine had been part of Germany before the First World War. During World War I, Schuman served as a printer in the German Army. In May 1950, Robert Schuman, then French Foreign Minister, dropped a bomb. At a weekly press conference of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs at the Quai d'Orsay, he proposed that France, Germany and other interested European states should leave their right of self-determination in coal and steel into the hands of a common, supranational organization. The proposal received a great deal of attention in several parts of Europe, but not in Finland. The Finnish Embassy in Paris reported on the matter for the first time in September, when negotiations were already very advanced. Robert Schuman and Jean Monnethade learned from the experience of the First World War. They realized that the interdependence resulting from trade and credit relations was not enough to prevent war. Common institutions were also needed, which at the same time meant a restriction on national sovereignty. In 1958, the European Coal and Steel Community was enlarged into the European Economic Community. The development of the single market took great strides forward in the 1960s, when the EC countries mutually abolished customs duties. At the same time, convertibility of currencies for commercial transactions was introduced. FINLAND'S OVERALL EU POLICY LINE In 1947, Finland had concluded a trade agreement with the Soviet Union, which was in force until 1992. The trade agreement contained a broad most-favoured-nation clause, which gave Moscow a tool for monitoring Finland's integration decisions. Finland's goal, however, was to develop trade with both East and West, although both parties to the Cold War placed restrictions on the countries within their own circle of interests to trade across the Iron Curtain. The biggest concern for Finland was that our worst competitors, such as Sweden, would gain an unreasonable competitive advantage. Then the Swedes also came to Finland's aid, because the Iron Curtain could have settled over the Gulf of Bothnia if Finland had been cut off from the western market. Since 1948 and until the end of the Cold War, Finland managed in one way or another to reach the same integration agreements as Sweden: GATT, EFTA, free trade agreements with the EEC and finally membership of the EEA. The world was changing. The shifts in power in the Eastern European countries, the reunification of Germany, the independence of the Baltic countries and, finally, the disintegration of the Soviet Union were reflected both on the map of Europe and in the political power relations of the continent. Finland's attitude towards Europe began to take shape in August 1991 after the coup d'etat in Moscow had failed. Some political parties had already activated themselves in favour of EC membership in the past. President Mauno Koivisto also publicly raised the issue at the end of September 1991. The rest is history. On the agenda of the Maastricht Summit in December 1991, the presidency had made a note of the opening of negotiations with Austria and Sweden. The proposal was not accepted, but Finland had understood the message. Now it was a matter of acting if Finland wanted to negotiate simultaneously with Austria and Sweden. Finland acted quickly and decisively. On 18 March 1992, the Parliament approved Finland's application for EC membership. On the same day, the application for membership signed by the President and the Prime Minister was handed over to Brussels. Membership negotiations began in February 1993 and were concluded within just over a year. In October 1994, a referendum on EU membership was held. The Economic Society celebrated its 100th anniversary. During the ongoing negotiations, the European Community was reconstituted into the European Union  the same Union to which we belong and to which Finland, together with Sweden and Austria, joined at the beginning of 1995. Finland's overall EU policy during the first 15 years of EU membership highlighted the impact at common tables. For the first time in its entire existence, Finland was involved in making decisions that had direct or indirect consequences for the world around us. Our long-time permanent EU representative Jan Store recently published a book that has aroused great interest. In his final report, he recalls how The Economist in 1999 defined Finland's actions in the EU: "Despite Finland's position on the edge of Europe, finns have, ever since the beginning of membership in 1995, mastered the EU's rules of the game in an almost unbelievable way. Many people look at Finland as a prime example of how a small Member State should act in the EU institutions; not preach like the Swedes, not make themselves awkward like the Danes, not be overambitious like the Austrians, but act modestly and purposefully by sticking to their principles without losing a sense of proportion." The economic crisis caused problems for Finland's European policy. Overall, the crisis gave rise to more dividing lines within the EU than in the past. Arbitration countries emerged between the euro area countries and those countries that had not adopted the euro as their currency. Dividing lines also emerged within the euro area between countries in need and countries in need. Economic crises always lead to difficult situations. When total output decreases, unemployment grows and public deficits are created, the government must make difficult decisions. In addition, we must also take a stand on the crisis policy of the euro area and our participation in it. For a long time, the discussion was dominated by the erroneous notion that the causes of Finland's primary economic problems lay outside our country, for example, in Greece or the Economic and Monetary Union (EMU). We concentrated on criticizing and teaching others. As always, pride took precedence over fall. The problems were not seen in their proper light. The sharp decline in the electronics sector and the adjustments in the forest industry affected Finland at the same time as the international financial crisis. In the shadows and independently of the financial crisis, a serious and long-standing structural problem has arisen in Finland. The solutions to the national crisis are to be found in Finland, the solutions to the financial crisis in Europe. At the European level, yesterday the ECB took an important step in building the banking union, when it published the comprehensive assessment of European banks. We have been an active participant in the process. In Finland, structural reforms are very topical. Pension reform is critical and must be implemented. But we also need structural reforms in the product and labour market. How should Finland then act in Europe and in other international contexts? If the facts change, you have to think again. The logical thing is to set a positive agenda, formulate and prioritize the issues and try to pursue them together with other countries. It may be easier to get on the sidelines and oppose all the changes, but then no solutions are created. There, too, we do best if we define our own goals and try to gain support for them in others. It will only succeed if we are also prepared to support others when they make legitimate claims. When the general attitude is constructive, it is easier to gain understanding from others when you yourself have exceptional interests to defend or are even difficult. Finland has voluntarily joined a large community with which we share the same values, and build common institutions. I would like to extend my best wishes to the Economic Society, which today celebrates its 120th anniversary. 1 So begins Francois Cochet's book La Grande Guerre. Fin d'un monde, debut d'un siecle, Ministre de la Defence, Paris 2014. Title: European financial markets and monetary policy as drivers of economic growth
text: President Erkki Liikanen: Europe's financial markets and monetary policy as drivers of economic growth. Helsinki, 26.1.2015. . Speech . Monday26 January 2015, 5:00PM President and CEO Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland Speech at OP-Pohjola Group Research Foundation's theme day "Euro area financial markets in the face of the new" Helsinki, 26.1.2015 EUROPEAN FINANCIAL MARKETS AND MONETARY POLICY AS DRIVERS OF ECONOMIC GROWTH Firstly, monetary policy Monetary policy has been conducted in a challenging environment in recent years. The financial crisis challenged the traditional monetary policy-making in a new way. As is well known, the primary objective of the European Central Bank is to maintain price stability. The target is defined in such a way that annual HICP inflation over the medium term should be below, but close to, 2%. The central bank's secondary objective is to support the EU's overall economic policy when the achievement of the objective of price stability is not jeopardised. How has the ECB succeeded in its core mission? In the long run, the objective of price stability has been well achieved. The average inflation rate has been close to, but below, 2% over the course of the euro. However, the very last few months have been a challenging period in terms of price stability. Inflation rates have remained below one per cent and will remain below target for the next couple of years, according to forecasts. We will return to this a little later. Since August 2007, the European Central Bank and other central banks have been operating under exceptional circumstances. With the bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers in September 2008, the financial turmoil escalated into a large-scale, global financial crisis. The lesson of the Great Depression was that the liquidity of banks must be secured against collateral in all circumstances. In October 2008, in line with the practice adopted in Finland in the 1990s, the ECB moved to a policy of full distribution to safeguard liquidity in the banking system. The second lesson was that monetary policy needs to be eased quickly. Interest rates were aggressively lowered since the same October. These measures were able to calm the financial markets. Nevertheless, the systemic crisis led to a deep recession. Interest rate cuts were resumed at the end of 2011. Now, in practice, the zero limit has been reached. The deposit rate of the Central Bank is negative. The mandate has not limited the ECB's ability to conduct an accommodative monetary policy. The financial crisis turned into a sovereign debt crisis in some euro area countries in 2010 and 2011. In the second half of 2011, doubts also spread about the ability of some European banks to raise financing on the market. For its part, the ECB responded to these problems through non-standard measures such as the Securities Purchase Programme (SMP) and exceptionally long refinancing operations (VLTROs). They eased for a while, but the crisis did not end there. In Europe, the sovereign debt crisis and the European confidence crisis came to a head in the summer of 2012. As the infection spread to Italy and Spain, the existence of the single currency was called into question. Resolving the crisis of confidence required exceptional and decisive measures. What was important was the aforementioned decision of the Eurozone Summit in 2012 to build a banking union in Europe. In the preparation and implementation of decisions, European decision-making has been able to work quickly and of high quality. Another important pillar was the determination of the European Central Bank. In July 2012, Mario Draghi delivered his famous speech in London, stressing that the ECB was prepared, within the framework of its mandate, to do whatever it takes to ensure the stability of the euro. The measures were decided by the Governing Council at its next meeting at the beginning of August 2012, clearly defining the country's own responsibilities and the division of labour within the international institutions. If a programme country that complies with these conditions is found to have acted in accordance with its commitments, the ECB may purchase their sovereign bonds on the secondary market. There was no limit on purchases in advance. The measures gradually restored confidence. The functioning of the financial markets returned. However, country-specific differences in financial intermediation remained: the ability of the banking system to function differed from one country to another. Where the banking system was operational and the economic outlook was positive, monetary policy was effectively transmitted. Where the banking system continued to have problems and the prospects for economic growth were also weak, credit interest rates remained clearly higher. In the wake of the financial and sovereign debt crisis, the Eurosystem has therefore faced a new challenge: prolonged low inflation. There is hardly any scope for monetary stimulus through conventional monetary policy, as nominal interest rates have been brought close to zero. The ECB therefore took important new decisions in June and September to make monetary policy more effective. Furthermore, as the Council had unanimously committed itself to continuing to take further action in the event of prolongation of the problems brought about by low inflation, it was decided to launch extensive preparations in November. At the same time, it was noted that the situation will be reassessed in early 2015. Last Wednesday and Thursday, the Council then made its assessment. Additional measures are needed. At its meeting, the Governing Council decided to extend the securities purchase programme to government bonds. At the same time, we announced that we would keep monetary policy interest rates down and expand purchases of securities by private and public issuers by EUR 60 billion per month until September 2016, and in any case until inflation is sustainably on a path consistent with the medium-term objective of price stability. Another important message was that the Governing Council's decision on the extended purchase programme is a monetary policy measure to safeguard price stability and is therefore in line with the Treaty and has a clear legal basis. The unity of monetary policy is confirmed by the adoption by the Governing Council of the decision on the purchase programme and its modalities. In the event of any credit losses arising from government bond purchases under the extended purchase programme, the losses shall be borne by the national central bank that purchased the securities. This covers 80% of the purchase programme. Other risks, i.e. purchases of securities by European multinational institutions and the ECB, are divided according to the capital key. According to the ECB Charter, risk-sharing is a matter for the Council to decide, and these decisions are not related to monetary policy coherence in the euro area or reduce the effectiveness of the purchase programme. On this basis, a consensus solution was reached within the Governing Council, which could take into account concerns about the channelling of risks from one country to another. The Governing Council's decision to extend asset purchases will lead to an increase in the ECB's balance sheet by at least a good EUR 1000 billion and thus also to an increase in the amount of central bank money in the economy. The extended purchase programme will lower interest rates, ease the financing conditions of the economy and increase confidence in the growth of the euro area economy, increase demand and increase inflation. The ECB's actions are historic in that, despite the multinational structure, the Eurosystem has at its disposal equivalent and equally effective monetary policy instruments with other central banks. Now to the financial markets and the banking union In the course of 2014, the ECB carried out a comprehensive assessment of banks' balance sheets before their supervision was transferred to the Supervisory Board set up within the ECB. The balance sheets of the banking system have been scanned and banks' resilience assessed through a stricter stress test. The measures have been taken to ensure the ability of banks to lend to the euro area economy in the future. According to global banking regulation, or the so-called banking regulation. In addition, the gradual entry into force of Basel III has already substantially strengthened the solvency and liquidity of banks. In Finland, the support generated by the accommodative monetary policy in the euro area has been strong. This has been significantly influenced by the stable domestic banking sector. The domestic banking sector has been able to provide finance to both firms and households at relatively low cost in European comparisons during the years of the global financial market crisis and the European sovereign debt crisis. This has been contributed to by the good creditworthiness of domestic banks, which has kept the cost of market funding for domestic banks low compared to many other European players. On the other hand, interest rate fixings on domestic loans, e.g. in mortgage lending, have intensified the passage of a light monetary policy. In Finland, the existence of a strong and stable banking sector is therefore of paramount importance for the smooth transmission of finance, because despite the gradual change, the banking sector remains the most significant source of corporate debt financing in Finland. For a long time, the development of the volumes of lending to non-financial corporations in Finland was at a good level in a European comparison. Recently, lending to non-financial corporations in Finland has also grown only slowly, although still faster than the euro area average. There are undoubtedly many different factors behind this. The weak outlook for the real economy affects the demand for and need for credit by non-financial corporations. From Finland's point of view, this gives cause for concern. In Finland, productive investments have been low in recent years and the capital stock has even contracted. Financial intermediation without major disruptions is a prerequisite for economic growth. How can the Banking Union improve the transmission of monetary policy and the functioning of financial markets, the efficiency and stability of financial intermediation? The aim of the banking union is to ensure equal supervision of major banks in all member states. Through the harmonisation and intensification of supervision, the banking sector will be more stable, more sustainable and better able to function and fulfil its role, even in economically weaker times. The correct pricing of risks will be improved and, as part of this, investor responsibility will be strengthened; in resolution, the bank's shareholders and creditors bear the losses, in which case this must also be taken into account in the pricing of the original risks. In banking supervision, the ECB has taken over supervisory tasks on 4.11.2014 and the governance structures of the SSM have been put in place. The single crisis resolution mechanism is about to get under way, legislation has been adopted and appointments to senior positions in the SRB have been made. The SRM will start operating from the beginning of 2015 and the full resolution powers will enter into force on 1.1.2016. Another important reform is macroprudential policy and its launch. Macroprudential policy complements the toolbox for managing, anticipating and preparing for systemic crises, but also complements the toolbox for the correct targeting of monetary policy. In the current context of the euro area, the importance of macroprudential policy is being fleshed out because, while an accommodative monetary policy is needed in the euro area, macroprudential policy can curb excesses in countries where overheating is feared and where tightening measures are needed to maintain stability. Macroprudential policies are primarily aimed at reducing the severity of financial crises and the likelihood of their occurrence. The tools used to promote macroprudentiality work through two goals. Firstly, the instruments strengthen the risk tolerance of key players in the financial system. On the other hand, the instruments prevent and mitigate the accumulation of systemic risks in the financial system, be they cyclical or structural systemic risks. The implementation of macroprudential policy will also start in Finland this year. In Finland, the Board of the Financial Supervisory Authority has the power to decide on the activation of macroprudential instruments, but the decision is based on cooperation between the Bank of Finland, the Ministry of Finance and the Financial Supervisory Authority. The past crisis years contained many important lessons. One of the lessons is related to the global nature of financial markets and financial intermediation and the complex network of interactions and interdependencies. A complex network of financial markets will only function smoothly when there is sufficient trust in the network's actors and when the risks in the system are priced correctly. Ensuring reliability and transparency requires that, in a complex operating environment, supervision must be brought into line with the level at which operations are located. Supranational banking supervision is responsible for this task. Another of the main lessons of the crisis was the strong link between the smooth transmission of finance and growth in the real economy: since the effective transmission of monetary policy requires a stable financial system, on the one hand, well-managed and viable banks are needed, and, on the other hand, capable authorities with the tools to safeguard and promote the stability of the financial system. Both the banking union and macroprudential policy and its instruments respond to these new challenges.

Toinen t<8a>rke<8a> viesti oli, ett<8a> EKP:n neuvoston p<8a><8a>t<9a>s laajennetusta osto-ohjelmasta on rahapoliittinen toimi hintavakauden turvaamiseksi ja siksi perustamissopimuksen mukainen ja oikeusperustaltaan selv<8a>. Sitten rahoitusmarkkinoista ja pankkiunionista Vuoden 2014 aikana EKP suoritti pankkien taseiden kattavan arvion, ennen kuin niiden valvonta siirrettiin EKP:n yhteyteen perustetulle Valvontaelimelle. Pankkij<8a>rjestelm<8a>n taseet on l<8a>pivalaistu ja pankkien h<8a>iri<9a>nsietokyky arvioitu aiempaa tiukemmalla stressitestill<8a>. Kotimainen pankkisektori on kyennyt v<8a>litt<8a>m<8a><8a>n rahoitusta niin yrityksille kuin kotitalouksillekin eurooppalaisessa vertailussa varsin edullisin kustannuksin globaalien rahoitusmarkkinoiden kriisin, ja eurooppalaisten valtioiden velkakriisin vuosina. Title: Opening speech of the Kimmo Pyykk Art Museum
text: Director General Erkki Liikanen: Opening speech of the Kimmo Pyykko Art Museum. Kangasala, 31.1.2015. . Speech . Friday 6 February2015,11:00 AM President Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland Kangasala, 31.1.2015 OPENING SPEECH OF THE KIMMO PYYKKo ART MUSEUM Since the above is an overview of Kimmo Pyyko's career as an artist, I want to focus on five stages or times in Kimmo Pyyko's path as an artist. The first two are set at a time I looked at from afar, the last three up close. First, the 1960s. A lot of exciting things happened then. Assi and I were still at school in Mikkeli. Fortunately, we were able to see glimpses of helsinki going on in the library's press room. Kimmo Pyykko had started to make figurative works with surreal, hybrid characters that talked about great things. "The Little Soldier" (1966) exorcised war and militaristic upbringing. "Cardinal" (1966) asked about the responsibility of religious organizations. The greatness of "Napoleon" (1968) shrunk amusingly: the big body of the work is the size of the emperor's ego, but the head so small that only one thought seems to fit there. In addition to the world's crises and big questions, Kimmo Pyyko's work has a plot that reflects on individual experience and loneliness. It often manifests itself in sculptures with female figures, such as "Condemned" (1968). "The Fugitive" (1967), a bomb-shaped sculpture with human running feet, combined the weapon of destruction and the distress of the fleeing person in a memorable way. The work is an icon of its decade and painfully as relevant as it was half a century ago. No wonder Pyykko received the Spurs of Criticism in 1968, at that time still quite a new award. Previously, it had been received mainly by representatives of music and the performing arts Then the 1970s. The FAQ was at the height of its power. I was about to elect him twice as president, first by emergency law in Parliament in 1974 and then as an elector in 1978. He was not only a strong president, but also the superior figure of the decade. THE FAQ was a great writer, with a name and a pseudonym. He was a well-known fitness enthusiast. At a rehabilitation facility in Peurunka, he was tested and leaked out that the over-70s are in the condition of a 40-year-old. That's not all: A little later, he went public as a talented sculptor. Maarit Tyrkko said in her book that she was right in her element as an artist. He publicly presented two works: "So it is if it seems like it" and "Bread Shovel". The footnote mentioned that Pyykko had been a technical assistant. I suspect that Kimmo was more like a trailing skier. How much did he make and how much did Kekkonen? I would like to see a small play or movie about it. Kimmo Pyyko's artistic collaboration with the president revealed one important feature of Kekkonen, a certain self-irony. However, as an artist, Kimmo Pyykko had to carry two burdens for a long time, jealousy of the friendship of the "ruler" and suspicion of selling his free "soul". Then there is the 1980s. Since Kimmo Pyykko had helped make Urho Kekkonen's famous bread shovel sculpture and it was used to finance Kekkonen's election campaign, it became a natural task for him in 1981. At that time, Kekkonen fell ill and resigned. A new presidential battle was launched. I was responsible for Mauno Koivisto's campaign. What better way to show that we are serious than for Pyykko to make a sculpture of "Manu" for this election. Thus was born a sculpture known for its eyebrows and strong facial features. It was made into large and small reliefs and badges, by selling them the campaign was financed. Pyykko as a sculptor was one of the bridges from Kekkonen's time in Koivisto' s time. Koivisto was not in his element as a sculptor, he was more of a carpenter. At the beginning of 1982, Mauno Koivisto also left the Bank of Finland and served as President of the Republic for two terms. Finally, to the 2000s. Two of Kimmo Pyyko's works have become very familiar to us during this time. One was a large wood carving, "The Witcher". The then Governor of the Central Bank of Luxembourg, Yves Mersch, wanted to buy an original, Finnish work for the bank's European collection. He ended up choosing Kimmo Pyyko's "Poppamies". He was fond of the forms and material of the work. The name caught my eye, Poppamies. This week, the ECB decided to engage in large-scale purchases of securities. Yves Mersch and I were making up our minds. He is currently a member of the Executive Board of the ECB. Someone said that the Central Bank is like a witch-huntsman, it creates money from scratch. However, this is not the case. Even the sculpture reminds us that we are not a "Pop man". We create money only by granting credit to banks against collateral or by buying securities. However, sometimes too much is expected of central banks. Another, even closer to us has been Kimmo Pyyko's bronze sculpture "The End of the Journey". It's a worn, leather-looking flight bag. which the passer-by has left on the floor on his return from the last voyage. The bag is slightly open and inside is a lonely shiny little bird. I saw this sculpture in the summer of 2004 in Salmela. At Assi's request, we travelled one Friday to a cottage in Mikkeli via Salmela. On the same day, I had returned from a 14-year business trip to Brussels and on Monday I was starting at the Bank of Finland. Brussels had been preceded by 19 years as a Member of Parliament, party secretary and minister for 19 years. Bronze work, The end of the journey crashed. I didn't get it out of my mind. Somehow it reflected the moods of that moment. Now the trips are done. I finally went to Kimmo in December and got this piece. I drove my own car and carrying the sculpture to the car was no small thing. The snow work was undone on the street in front of our home and I had to park the car far from the side of the street. Then, as I laboriously carried the heavy sculpture, a woman's high-pitched scream could be heard from the car behind me. "Outrageous parking". However, I took the sculpture inside before I came to fix the parking. But it wasn't good enough for the lady. He had taken a picture of the car and sold his revelation seven days  to the magazine with the headline: Outrageous parking! The whistleblower got a decent tip reward for it. A great art purchase, as its acquisition in that form, too, spread to the public consciousness. But there that bag rests peacefully at home. Sometimes I hear a bird singing from inside it. When I pack my bag for the trip again in the early morning, it feels as if the bird is looking for a long time and saying, "I wonder if it's time to stop those trips sometimes." The trips haven't quite ended, but the bag reminds us that the day will come too. I would like to congratulate Professor Kimmo Pyykko on a fine collection spanning decades. I would like to congratulate the municipality of Kangasala for the beautiful museum. With these words, I will open this exhibition.

Title: The importance of facts in economic policy
text: Director-General Erkki Liikanen: The importance of facts in economic policy. Lecture at the University of Turku 23.3.2015. . Speech . Monday23 March 2015,10:00 AM Erkki Liikanen Lecture at the University of Turku 23.3.2015 THE ROLE OF FACTS IN ECONOMIC POLICY Ladies and gentlemen, It is a great honour to give a lecture here at the University of Turku, which is a major centre of research and teaching. I have learned to appreciate the research contribution of the University of Turku in the areas of life in which I have worked or in which I have practiced. On the hobby side, I have had a lot of contact with Timo Soikkanen and Kimmo Rentola. During and after the years of politics, Jaakko Nousiainen was for me the undisputed authority in the study of politics. Many people have become familiar with economics. Paavo Okko also from the years I was ambassador and commissioner in Brussels. I would like to thank Professor Matti Wiberg for his kind invitation. My topic today is the importance of facts in economic policy. This is a topical issue because Finland and Europe are known to face major economic challenges. Facing them requires a correct analysis of what the starting points and possibilities are. In the debate on economic policy, we sometimes try to appeal to facts and sometimes they are selectively forgotten. The role of an expert is also a hot topic: are the assessments of the situation offered by economist experts genuinely objective, or are political objectives hidden in them? Less than four decades ago, in 1977, the then Governor of the Bank of Finland Mauno Koivisto, an alumnus of the University of Turku, spoke on almost the same topic in this same forum. He described the situation at the time like this: "If you look at how many different perceptions in modern society go by the name of knowledge, it is worth however, in an old fashioned way, also emphasizes the importance of wisdom." Koivisto continued: "Research-based information is usually quite incomplete and even unreliable, but nevertheless it is the best information available, and in most cases it is the most explicit information, in which case the known gaps and errors in the reasoning process can best be demonstrated." Hardly anyone can disagree that political decision-making should be based on facts. On the other hand, mere facts are not enough to justify action, values, goals and visions are also needed. In a democracy, the definition of the objectives of economic policy is the responsibility of the elected politicians, who therefore represent the values of the citizens. Making choices between conflicting objectives is precisely the task for which the political process has been built. The choices to be made should reflect citizens' preferences, but they must be based on facts, on knowledge of what is possible and on the most correct picture possible of the consequences of the various measures. Thus, the decision-maker has to rely on the information that the experts produce for him. In economic policy, therefore, the responsibility of economists and statisticians is great. It is important for democracy that they do not try to guide decision-makers according to their own opinions. In the interaction between politics and research, the role of economists has often become to remind decision-makers of economic realities that can be unpleasant. More than 150 years ago, the British historian and archconservative Thomas Carlyle established the term 'the dismal science' for economics. Apparently, Carlyle had in mind Thomas Malthusi's population theory, according to which the population would always strive to grow faster than the production of living needs, so the majority of humanity would be doomed to permanently balance on the borderline of the subsistence minimum. Even in the current economic debate, there are echoes of Carlyle's distrust of economists. They are sometimes suspected, as a profession, of being nothing more than drivers of misery and cuts. There has also been a desire to label economists as apostles of lack of alternatives. There have been doubts about the value of economics. It has sometimes been thought that economists' speeches conceal ideological and political objectives under the cloak of science, which are then pursued in the name of objective truth. This debate has intensified during the economic crisis of recent years, when many countries have had to take politically difficult decisions to resolve banking crises and manage government deficits. Of course, economic arguments are often invoked in political discourse. That is natural and relevant. It is not always easy to distinguish between, on the one hand, analysis that strives for objectivity and, on the other hand, rhetoric that selectively appeals to economics. Economists would do well to focus on the former in order to avoid the impression that all economic argumentation is tendentious manipulation. ON THE DOCTRINE OF ECONOMIC POLICY An important milestone in defining the relationship between economics and politics was the theory put forward by the Dutchman Jan Tinbergen. Tinbergen put forward his theory in 1952 in the book "On the Theory of Economic Policy". Tinbergen's pioneering work was later rewarded when, in 1969, he became the first Nobel Laureate in Economics (together with the Norwegian Ragnar Frisch). Jan Tinbergen's philosophy today no longer represents the last word in research. However, because of its clarity, it is still a good point of reference when the issue is discussed. I will go through some of its main points here. The economic policy process, according to Tinbergen, has five stages: 1. Definition of the status quo. 2. Forecast of how the economy would develop if economic policy were to continue unchanged. 3. Studying the impact of economic policy options. 4. Decision-making, i.e. making choices between alternative policies. 5. Implementation of policy decisions. Tinbergen saw economic policy from the perspective of national economic governance. He distinguished between economic policy instruments on the one hand and economic policy objectives on the other. Famous is the so-called. Tinbergen's principle that there should be as many instruments of economic policy as there should be objectives. According to Tinbergen, it is up to the political decision-maker to set the objectives of economic policy and to determine the framework within which different means can be used. He must reflect the political preferences of society and decide how to weight different goals, even conflicting ones. On the other hand, the task of the economist is the analysis of the means. Economic analysis cannot, on the basis of facts alone, lead to solutions to the problems of economic policy. But nevertheless, economic analysis has three important functions: The economic analysis must assess the compatibility of the economic policy objectives with each other and also the objectives . compatibility with available policy instruments. By locating possible contradictions, the analysis can delimit the options for decision-making and thus . contribute to economic policy-making. If the objectives are sufficiently well defined, the economic analysis can find those values of the instruments with which the objectives are . would be realized. Tinbergen's model highlights the difference between the roles of decision-maker and draftsman. It corresponds to the difference between values and facts. From today's perspective, these divisions may seem natural. But at the time of Tinbergen, they were radical. What was radical was precisely to put economics in a clearly instrumental role, that is, to distinguish between analysis and political decision-making. In this, he deviated from the pre-Keynes mainstream, which saw the task of economics mainly to explain and justify the solutions produced by the market. At the height of Tinbergen's influence, policy analysis and quantitative planning were the buzzwords of the day. To do this, economics had to be developed into objective and quantitative. The necessary knowledge base had to be formed. To this end, a system of national accounts was developed, such as gross domestic product and its components, and statistics began to be applied to model the functioning of the economy. Economists began to be seen as "economic engineers" who solved the optimization task defined by politicians. Also in Finland at the turn of the 1950s and 1960s, there was an active discussion about the essence and role of economics. This debate took place, in particular, in the form of the so-called "green card" formed by the young economists of the time. In the O group. It was also joined by Mauno Koivisto after he moved from Turku to Helsinki. Most of the members of the O Group worked at some point at the Institute of Economics of the Bank of Finland. One of the steepest figures in the O group was Olavi Niitamo, who represented a sharply positivist position. According to it, subjective and political elements could be eliminated from economics by moving to the strictest possible mathematical approach. He even wrote in the Journal of The National Economy in 1960 that "there is probably no fundamental difference between the models of explanation of economics and, for example, physics. Both are probabilistic models and the difference is only in the degree of accuracy of the explanation." Niitamo later became director general of statistics finland. Niitamo's disputing partner was another member of the O-Group, Jouko Paunio, who was of a more moderate opinion. He considered economics to be ultimately a humanistic science. Paunio wrote that an economist should strive for objectivity in his research work, but at the same time reminded that economics is not a natural science. According to Paunio, "It is the economist who is engaged in science, which is in close contact with economic policy, with the practical activities that are directed at economic life. Because of this, for everyone the economist, as if by himself, has a personal idea of the direction in which economic life should be steered by means of economic policy. On the other hand, economics is still at such a level of development today that it somehow effortlessly allows the personal appreciations of the researcher to influence the research work intended to be objective.' Over the decades, the Tinbergen model has received a lot of criticism. One of the themes has been the question of the possibility of objective research in the social sciences in general, which is what Paunio also referred to in that quote. This problem was highlighted, among other things, by the Swede Gunnar Myrdal, who in 1974 received the Nobel Prize in Economics. Myrdal represented a much more sceptical position than Paunio on the possibilities of objectivity. He considered that it was impossible for an economist to separate his own values and political opinions from his work. In Myrdal's view, this had to be acknowledged, and since an unbiased analysis was therefore an impossibility, economists just had to be open about their own starting points and perspectives. Myrdal represented extreme relativism. For him, economics was by definition political. The responsibility for whose analysis could be trusted and whose advice had to be listened to remained with the politician in Myrdal's model. WHAT DOES THIS DEBATE LOOK LIKE FROM A MODERN PERSPECTIVE? It is important for the functioning of democracy that an objective knowledge base is sought as a basis for decision-making. It is unlikely to ever be fully achieved, but the aim is to achieve it. The task of the study is to expand the common knowledge base on which competing opinion leaders can rely. You can approach this by taking the example of climate research. There is a widespread perception that global warming, caused by carbon dioxide and methane emissions, poses a serious threat to the future of humanity. In the end, this should not be a matter of opinion: it is the responsibility of the study to find out whether global warming and the human contribution to it are true or not. It would even be problematic to consider that the results of the various climate scientists only reflect their political opinions, and one could safely choose what one believes. Society must be able to rely on the scientific process and its purposes. Otherwise, we will be completely lost. It would also be dangerous to accept the idea that political decision-makers or economic interest groups should be allowed to guide the work of climate scientists. My example was from the side of natural science, where the requirement of objectivity is easier to implement than in the social sciences. However, even in economic research, the goal of objectivity is as necessary as in climate research. If I think of my own experience as a decision-maker, I would not want to rely on an expert who acts on a pre-established political agenda. The decision-maker feels particularly uncomfortable if he or she notices that the preparation has only tried to justify the position that the decision-maker already had. A glaring example of what abandoning the objective of objectivity can lead to is the misrepresentation of Greek government deficit statistics in the first decade of the 2000s. It lulled creditors and the European Union into a false sense of security about what was happening in Greece's public finances. The facts were revealed after the change of government in the autumn of 2009. Indeed, Greece's actual deficit was many times higher than had previously been announced. Greece's creditworthiness plummeted and it was no longer able to cover its deficit on the private loan market. It became dependent on credits from other euro area countries and implemented what was agreed as a condition for them a rigorous adjustment programme. The Greeks have had to pay a high price for the long-standing cover-up of the economic situation. As a result of the euro crisis, the importance of economic statistics in the economic policies of the euro area countries has become even more important. New, stronger procedures have been put in place to ensure that member states do not run into difficulties such as those in Greece. Economic statistics, such as GDP and public sector deficit and debt statistics, are no longer just background information used for economic policy to support decision-making, but increasingly binding norms have been built on them. The emphasis on the normative role of economic analysis places increasing demands on statistical production and the analyses derived from it to be as objective as possible and trusted by all parties involved. It can be said that we are increasingly dependent on a clear adherence to the distinction put forward by Tinbergen between objective work as economists and political decision-making. A more general issue in this regard is the relationship between the preparation of civil servants, on the one hand, and political preparation and decision-making, on the other. For a long time, political preparation was carried out in the party circle. Mauno Koivisto was minister of finance when party support stabilized. It provided an economic basis for the parties' programming. The preparation of civil servants, on the other hand, was separate from this in the ministries. Over the years, the situation has changed. The parties' resources have been reduced and have been deliberately reduced. Similarly, the number of political assistants to ministers within ministries has increased sharply. Several ministers also have political secretaries of state today. At worst, this may have led to three developments: First of all, the responsibility of civil servants has become blurred and with it the preparation of officials has deteriorated due to the preparation of civil servants. and the boundary of political preparation is not visible. Secondly, the development that has taken place has weakened the popular movement character and independence of the parties vis-a-vis the state. . Even at this level, the boundaries are blurred. Thirdly, those who have been in political assistant positions for a long time have sometimes had the refractive error that they do not see . position vis-a-vis elected decision-makers who enjoy the confidence of parliament. I have great respect for both elected political decision-makers and civil servants who carry out independent work with official responsibility. I have been in both positions. I have also enjoyed the guidance of distinguished officials. When I was a young minister, the State Secretary was Teemu Hiltunen, and the President of Postipankki was an experienced civil servant and minister HeikkiTuominen. The difference between the duties of a political decision-maker and an official became clear. In recent years, there has not always been the same clarity. The appearances of civil servants on the political side, which raise their own profile, have raised questions. Of course, an official can increase his momentary popularity by belittling politicians and their talents. It is not really clear what an official needs such popularity for. Of course, we must have freedom of opinion. But the official also has a duty, with his expertise and preparatory work, in every way to facilitate the making of difficult decisions. In addition to a couple of outside comments: One stage where the difference between political alignment and the preparation of civil servants should be visible in our circumstances is the compilation of the Government Programme. As a policy document, the government programme should be strategic and ultimately owned by the parties that put it together and the elected ministers. The working group chaired by Olli-Pekka Heinonen made a lot of proposals worth considering. Another question is how far the major economic issues will be resolved already in the government negotiations. If the Prime Minister and also the Minister of Finance are already known when drawing up the government's economic programme, this will provide opportunities, in the light of historical experience, to organise the work effectively. CENTRAL BANKS AND DEMOCRACY After the above, the representative of the Central Bank must, of course, look in the mirror. What is the relationship between democracy and economics in monetary policy? In what sense do central banks exercise political power? If they take political decisions, how does that fit in with democratic principles? The independence of central banks is a key element of a modern monetary and economic policy package. It is a key principle in all developed countries. In the euro area, for example, the autonomy of the ECB and the national central banks in relation to political decision-making has been taken to a very advanced stage. When deciding on monetary policy, the central banks of the Eurosystem are not allowed to take instructions from political bodies. The central banks of other countries, such as the United States, Britain or Sweden, also conduct monetary policy independently in relation to the governments of their countries. The independence of the central banks of the euro area has both political and economic reasons. Politically, the role and functions of the European Central Bank were defined between 1988 and 1992 in a process that culminated in the signing of the Maastricht Treaty. In practice, it was clear from the outset that agreement on the establishment of monetary union could only be reached on condition that the objective of the single monetary policy was defined as price stability and that the single central bank was independent in its task. This is understandable, bearing in mind that the formation of monetary union meant, for the acceding countries, a permanent renunciation of monetary sovereignty. From the point of view of the countries to join, this required maximum certainty as possible as to what form the single monetary policy would take. Any departure from the principles of central bank independence and price stability would have been unacceptable for those countries that had already achieved high monetary policy credibility before the formation of monetary union. Such countries included: Germany and Holland. On the other hand, countries seeking to join the monetary union that had historically enjoyed weaker monetary policy credibility also had to share in the benefits of a credible monetary policy, such as permanently moderate interest rates and low inflation expectations. Such countries included: Italy and Spain, and perhaps partly Also Finland. The end result was that the eurosystem's central banks became very independent, but this autonomy is delegated in a democratic order to carry out a predetermined task. The primary objective of monetary policy is price stability and, secondarily, without jeopardising price stability, central banks must support other economic policy objectives in the Union, such as balanced economic growth. In line with this, monetary policy is now very accommodative. Last year, the European Central Bank was entrusted with a new role as the highest banking supervisor in the euro area. It could not have been given this necessary task if there had not been a guarantee of the independence of the Central Bank and the impartiality of its decisions. One might ask how the independence of central banks views the picture of economic policy outlined by Tinbergen as a process in which experts map out the options and their implications, but political decision-makers decide on the policy pursued. This question brings us to the theoretical side of the independence of central banks. According to modern economics, the key weakness of Tinbergen's model of economic policy is that it does not take into account the importance of policy expectations. Expectations of how politics will be conducted in the future affect the mechanisms of economic activity today. This is particularly true of monetary policy, where the management of inflation expectations is key. Economic policy instruments cannot therefore be used on the assumption that the mechanisms of operation of the national economy are independent of the policies pursued. In this case, Tinbergen's idea of first clarifying the operating mechanisms of the economy and only then deciding on measures, in its original form, no longer applies. In its stark form, this criticism has been represented in particular by RobertLucas, who was awarded the Nobel Prize in Economics for his research in 1995. Lucas' ideas also included a particularly strong confidence that economic policy would not be able to systematically improve economic stability and that, for example, cyclical policies would not be beneficial. He takes an extreme position on this issue, and there are good reasons to disagree. But the more general idea, stemming from Lucas's work, that economic policy should be thought of through rules of conduct and ways of reacting rather than through individual measures, is widely accepted by economists. Lucas' criticism also influences how Tinbergen's idea of the relationship between political decision-making and the analysis that underpins it should be interpreted. When the role of expectations is central, as in monetary policy, policy choices need to be understood more broadly than individual guidance measures, strategic rather than tactical. After this change, tinbergen's model is again usable. For example, in monetary policy, it is up to the political decision-makers to decide on the objectives of monetary policy, after which the central bank is set to implement the chosen line. In this architecture, one of the tasks of economists is to produce information on the basis of which politicians can define the tasks of the Central Bank and make their delegation decisions correctly. Monetary policy is the realization of the task assigned in this case. Price stability is at the heart of the task. Thus, the power of the Central Bank is delegated and limited. The delegation of practical monetary policy to the Central Bank also serves as a political commitment to the chosen objectives. This is particularly important in monetary policy, where the credibility of the policy is a key condition not only for maintaining monetary stability, but also for the central bank's ability to smooth out economic fluctuations, without compromising the stability of the value of money. Although central banks in the euro area and elsewhere carry out a limited monetary policy function, their activities are not mechanical. It requires in-depth analysis, preparation and, ultimately, responsible consideration of how best to carry out the assigned task. The role of central banks in the debate on economic policy is based precisely on this. In connection with the preparation of monetary policy and the prudential supervision of financial markets, central banks, including the Bank of Finland, carry out a wide-ranging analysis of economic developments and future prospects. Particular care will be taken to identify threats to the balance of the economy and the stability of the financial sector. Through the analysis, the Bank of Finland also makes its contribution available to policymakers. Experience has shown that it is precisely because of the bank's independence that it may be of particular interest. The aim is that the objectivity of the central bank's contribution can be trusted in society at large. It has sometimes been asked why we do not provide more detailed advice on how to solve the economic problems of Finland (or the euro countries). The answer to this is obvious: given the position of the Central Bank, it must be possible to rely on the objectivity of the analysis it produces. If, in addition, we were to offer recommendations that clearly contained political value choices, this would blur the picture of the Bank's remit and the role of its analysis in economic policy. Thank you!
