Title: Speech at the opening of the "Our Common Debt" exhibition at the Bank of Finland's Monetary Museum
text: President and CEO Erkki Liikanen: Speech at the opening of the exhibition "Our Common Debt" at the Bank of Finland's Monetary Museum. Helsinki, 21.4.2015. . Speech . Tuesday 21 April 2015,11:00 AM Check against delivery Ladies and gentlemen, I welcome everyone to the opening of the monetary museum's new temporary exhibition. This time's exhibition the theme is "Our Common Debt". It deals with the history of government borrowing and, to a lesser extent, with the present. The exhibition has been built in cooperation with the State Treasury. Most of the material on display is from the State Treasury's collections. This is the first time that the State Treasury's historical collection of bonds has been made available to the public to this extent. I would like to take this opportunity to express my special thanks to Mika Arola and Suvi Asikainen, who have been responsible for the exhibition from the State Treasury. On the Bank of Finland's side, the coordinators have been Vappu Ikonen and Jaakko Koskentola. In addition, I would like to thank architect Teemu Taskinen for the graphics and the overall design of the exhibition. The exhibition has been made into also an online virtual exhibition. It was created by Outi Kotala. Tonight at 5 p.m. Dr. Mika Arola from the State Treasury will hold the Money Museum's Studia Monetaria series here a public presentation on government borrowing from the 1800s to the present day. Of course, you are all welcome. ** Finland's central government debt has traditionally been relatively small, which was an exception among European countries. After all, they became heavily indebted from the late 1970s onwards. I remember when, at the end of the 1980s, I discussed sovereign debt with an OECD official. I told him that our sovereign debt was "fifteen per cent of GDP". He looked at me and said, "do you mean fifty, five-o?" I replied, 'well, fifteen, one-five'. In the early 1970s, when economic growth, inflation and progressive taxation brought money to the Finnish treasury at a record pace, the debt was almost completely paid off. At that time, it was even possible to consider the question of whether the state needs to take out a loan at all. The Minister of Finance was Johannes Virolainen. Mauno Koivisto, the then Governor of the Bank of Finland, said that he had told the Estonians that there must always be enough presence on the international loan market to keep the name of the country in the memory. Central government debt remained low until the economic crisis of the early 1990s. During the ensuing recession, the debt started to rise, but in the early years of EU membership, a clear decline was achieved again. That is a good thing. Finland's situation would be much worse than it is today if we had had to face the crisis of 2008 with a high level of indebtedness. Since the onset of the financial crisis, government debt has been growing rapidly. This year it will cross the EUR 100 billion mark. At the same time, Finland is testing the common fiscal rules for the euro area, which we ourselves have been working on. The change from the situation just a few years ago has been rapid. ** The bond market is going through very exceptional times. Investors' yield requirements for loans from creditworthy countries have dropped to close to zero, and loans can even be obtained at a negative interest rate. Even long-term interest rates are at record lows. The low level of interest rates in the sovereign debt market is partly due to the central bank purchase programme, which was launched in the euro area at the beginning of March. The purchases are significant in scope. Central banks did not start buying bonds to facilitate the financing of government deficits, but for monetary policy reasons, in order to achieve the ECB's price stability objective. Accordingly, inflation should return to close to two per cent over the medium term. The effects of the purchases have been a step in the right direction. Last week, the ECB underlined again that purchases will continue at least until the end of September 2016 and, if necessary, beyond, until the Governing Council considers that inflation rates will return to their aim in a sustained manner. ** The current low interest rates may tempt too casually towards government indebtedness. However, the mathematics of borrowing show that staring at nominal interest rates is deceiving. In the long run, the extent to which a given level of debt burdens public finances does not depend on the nominal interest rate, but on the real interest rate and economic growth. Changes have taken place in Finland, which is why we need to be very cautious about taking on debt. Long-term growth expectations have recently declined due to, among other things, the shrinking working-age population. This contraction looks set to continue well into the future, while labour productivity growth has also slowed down. In conditions of low growth, reversing the debt/GDP ratio is a much more demanding task than it would be in a period of high growth. ** According to a forecast published by the Bank of Finland last December, halting the growth of Finland's public debt required adjustment measures of approximately EUR 5 billion in the next few years. At that time, the sustainability gap was estimated at 4% of GDP. The latest data suggest that the fiscal outlook is still somewhat weaker than these six months ago. Against this background, the recent official estimates of the Ministry of Finance on the outlook for general government finances and the need for adjustment can be considered justified on a scale. It is essential to continue the budgetary adjustment process. This is because the current problems are, for the most part, not cyclical, but longer-term. In the absence of strong economic growth, without further adjustment measures, our common debt would only continue to grow. It is important that the fiscal adjustment programme is decided at the beginning of the parliamentary term. A credible programme is sufficiently concrete and binding. The entry into force of the actions can be phased, but it is important that some of the actions enter into force as early as 2016. ** The exhibition, which is now being opened, shows how important international creditworthiness has been for Finland at different times. Securing access to foreign credit was the main objective already when Finland linked the markka to the northern European silver standard region in 1865, and again when Finland joined the gold standard in 1878. After independence, Finland's position in the international loan market was initially poor, but a determined policy improved creditworthiness. Risto Ryti, governor of the Bank of Finland, summed up the goal in 1925 by saying: "It is not enough to have a good monetary system, it is also required that our monetary system be such that it is trusted abroad." Experience with the functioning of the euro area shows how important confidence in the financial stability of a country in the euro area is, including for a country in the euro area. Those countries whose public finances have not been mistrusted have performed well as members of the euro area. On the other hand, the countries with which suspicion has arisen have, in turn, been forced to implement particularly tough fiscal policies. When used in moderation, government borrowing is a useful tool that provides flexibility and investment opportunities. After all, this is where the value of a country's creditworthiness lies. But if moderate use turns into addiction, it becomes a problem. Indebtedness then becomes a burden that eats away at the flexibility and freedom of choice in the state economy. I do not believe that the line between moderation and dependence should be tested. ** I welcome you to visit this interesting exhibition!

Title: Interview in Handelsblatt
text: Governor Erkki Liikanen: Interview in Handelsblatt, 27 April 2015. . Speech . Monday27 April2015, 12:00 PM Governor Erkki Liikanen Interview in Handelsblatt, by Michael Maisch and Jan Mallien Published on 27 April 2015 an edited transcript of the interview Handelsblatt: Mr. Liikanen, the biggestproblem for the euro zone right now is Greece. The Greekfinance minister recently said that there will be a deal and that the opinions are converging. Is he right? We all hope so. It very much depends on Greece. They need to deliver and then there will be a solution. The issues that need to be solved are domestic issues. They had a positive trend in the economy last year. The current uncertainty has caused problems. Your colleague Benot Coeure just said, a Grexitisnot an option. But isnot the situation so serious, that the ECB should prepare for a worst case scenario,just to be on the safe side? We are a rules based institution, and the emergency liquidity the national central bank is providing for the Greek banking system is a tool covered by those rules. I do not make any further comments. The other big topic on the agenda for the Eurozone is QE. The markets have reacted quite strongly on the program. Did this come as asurprise for you? The purchases are going well. We should not focus too much on short term effects. For me the asset purchase programme is like a marathon. There are ups and downs, but the target must be clear. Our aim is to achieve price stability. The important thing when running a marathon is: You have to be stable and you must not get excited. The IMFhas revised upwards its growth forecasts for some Eurozone countries. How much is that due to QE? There were some other positive events at the same time. The falling oil prices are of course helping the European economy. One side effect of the monetary policy is the lower exchange rate of the euro. But also on fiscal consolidation many European countries have made progress. Thereos less need for radical budget cuts. And there have been some structural reforms. Do you thinkthere would have been a possibilityto avoid QE? No. The programme was important because we had this very low inflation for a very long time. If low inflation turns into a negative spiral it is very difficult to turn. We acted at the right time, we were well prepared and the execution was well handled. But we must remember the marathon. The first kilometers are easy. Some economists are alreadydemanding a reduction ofthe bondpurchases. Does the ECB need an exit strategy? If we start to hesitate, that would be the worst solution of all. We have built up expectations and now have to deliver. We need to be firm to fulfill our commitment. For us price stability is the target and we havenot achieved that yet. Are you concerned that QE mightlead to dangerous bubbles in the capital markets? We certainly have to be careful. If interest rates remain very low for a long time, that can create risks. Therefore the discussions about what we central bankers call macroprudential policies are very important. We have to set regulatory and supervisory rules to prevent risks. We must be firm if needed. Is the ECBs mandate for macroprudentialpolicy strong enough? We should have an open mind to reinforce the set of tools and to ask for more, if needed. There is a need to learn as we go. One problem that concerns me is linked to the capital requirements for banks which are based on risk weighted assets. What exactlyis the problem? If a bubble starts to develop, it is often linked to housing prices. If you want to fight the bubble you would raise the capital requirements for bank lending. But the risk weighting for mortgages is very low, while the risk weighting for credits to SMEs is rather high. So banks might be tempted to limit their lending to SMEs instead of cutting mortgages. You are one ofthe most prolific experts on banking regulation. Arenot these happy times for you? Big banks like Deutsche Bank, Barclays or HSBC are allgetting smaller and less dangerous. We have been certainly doing a lot in Europe. We are implementing the stricter capital and liquidity rules under Basel III, there has been this massive comprehensive balance sheet assessment and the European Banking Union with its resolution rules. So does this mean that the problem of banks that are too big to failhas been finally solved? If it comes to banking regulation we are much further in our marathon, than for example with the asset purchase programme. I would say we have passed the 30 kilometer mark. But if we want to complete this journey we also have to deal with the structural problems in the banking markets. That means we have to avoid that bigger banks which still profit from an implicit state guarantee are taking excessive risks. You prepared areport for the European Commission on that topic. You and your team came to the conclusion that banks of a certain size should separate their riskier activities especially in proprietary trading from the rest of the business. Now itlooks like your proposals mightbe watereddown. I think nobody is contesting our analysis, the problem still exists. Our conclusion was, if these risky positions become very big, they should be funded by the market not through deposits or any form of funding enjoying an implicit government guarantee. We came up with two proposals: Either we would ask the banks for more capital for the trading book or we would suggest a mandatory separation. Butthe EU parliament and the Council are now discussing different options. Thatos true one option is that the supervisors would under certain conditions have the right to separate a bank. Where they will draw the line between these powers and a mandatory separation one will see. I will make my comment when the product is finished. The new EU Commissioner Jonathan Hill seems sometimes more concerned aboutthe possible negative impact of new regulation on growth than about the further stabilization of the financial system. Does that concern you? Two remarks on that. First: The previous commission was fighting against a very severe crisis. This crisis is the crisis of our generation and it has been bad for growth. We simply had to fix those problems. And secondly, the regulators should always justify themselves, they should always assess the impact of the new rules as well as possible. The ECBis now responsible for the supervision ofthe bigger banks in the Eurozone. Isnot there an inherent conflict of interestbetween this task and monetary policy? That is a very good question. Here in Finland banking supervision and monetary policy are separated, but they belong to the same family. The benefits are, they are sharing the same administration, the same IT services and people are rotating between the two institutions, but there is still a separation. If we could find a similar long term solution for the ECB and the banking supervision in the Eurozone it wouldnot be bad. Why wasnot the banking supervision set uplike this right from the start? The European Treaty allows the EU to delegate tasks only to existing institutions. But donot get me wrong. There might be some imperfections, but in my view the Banking Union is the biggest step in the European Integration since the introduction of the euro.

Title: High school graduation ceremony in Puumala
text: Director General Erkki Liikanen's speech at the graduation ceremony of upper secondary school in Puumala 30.5.2015 . Speech . Saturday 30 May 2015, 10:15 AM Director General Erkki Liikanen Speech at the closing ceremony of upper secondary school Puumala, 30.5.2015 Puumala has been providing upper secondary education for 41 years. Today, the last students will receive their caps in Puumala. I congratulate all the new students who are getting their caps today. Getting a high school in Puumala was an important step in 1974. A big step in our school system was also the transition to comprehensive school, which had started two years earlier in Lapland and, exceptionally, also in Puumala. Why is that? Let's find the answer to that from afar. After the war came the baby boomers. Until the summer of 1950, the annual birth rate was over 100000. Finland had fought a heavy war. However, the high birth rate and reconstruction spoke of optimism and faith in the future. The baby boomers, the last of which I am, were taught in the parallel school system. After four years of primary school, the pupils were divided  usually irrevocably  into primary and secondary schools. Those from a modest background usually stayed on the folk school road. Our parents usually did not have the opportunity to go to secondary school. That's why when our class matriculated from the Mikkeli Lyceum in 1969, we were all the first students in our family. My father had moved from a rural municipality as the youngest in a family with 11 children to work in the city of Mikkeli, and my mother's path had been an evacuee path from Karelia. Like most other families with children, our family received an arava loan to build in Mikkeli. Many people also moved from Puumala for work. Jaakko Lopponen moved from Partalansaari and his family to Mikkeli and also to Lahemaki. Jaakko came to Kymi as an engineer, and the boys started their schooling in Mikkeli and graduated from the Lyceum a few years earlier than I did. Paavo and Pauli Lopponen are good friends of mine and also the first students in their family. Money was tight in many families, including Liikanen, even though his father worked two jobs. One form of additional income was that our family had children attending secondary school in full-board families living in rural areas. At the same time, we had Pekka from Suomenniemi, who attended the Mikkeli Lyceum, and Saara from Puumala, who attended the Mikkeli coeducational school. This is how I got in touch with Puumala. Sarah's parents lived in Otansalo. I got there at the age of 13 for a whole ski holiday. During the day, I was involved in the log forest, mainly pruning branches. Twice a week we went to experience the winter nets and got some handsome pikes and mats. There was also one exceptional day in the week: kinkers were held in the reeds. The experience will not be forgotten. I got to know a lot about island life, its advantages and disadvantages. An interesting memory yet: The Summas sent fish by bus from time to time. I went to sell them to the neighbours and that's how my daughter's way to school was covered. The 1960s launched a major comprehensive school reform. Reino Oittinen, director general of the School Board, was minister of education in the governments of Rafael Paasio and Johannes Virolainen Mauno Koivisto when a major reform was announced in the port. It was a great demonstration of the Finnish people's desire for education and reform: everyone wanted to be offered a unified comprehensive school, regardless of their parents' financial status. In 1969, Puumala came to the attention of finnish schoolchildren. The Youth Information Centre organized a continuous camp at Rokansalo School throughout the summer, which was attended by hundreds of young people from all over Finland. All the main viziers of the Finnish Teenage League spoke there. One camp manager was Jorma Westlund, who became the political secretary of the Minister of Education 2.5 years later. The previous Foreign Minister, ErkkiTuomioja, was also so fascinated by the scenery that he even went to see the cottage plots. One of the participants was Riitta Ahmavaara, a young man from Helsinki, who works here in Puumala and Lintusalo as an entrepreneur. MattiViialainen from Lintusalo, on the other hand, still attended middle school in Puumala, but still had to go to upper secondary school in Mikkeli. In January 1972, I was elected to Parliament. Elementary school laws had been enacted, but practical implementation was ahead. The plan was to start in Lapland in 1972, to proceed towards the south so that Helsinki would be the last to move in 1978. However, the municipal politicians and the mayor of Puumala were vigilant. Why can't Puumala also be among the first to move as an experimental municipality? The background was the desire for education, but also the fact that state subsidies for primary school were higher. Mayor Raimo Kainuja's shop stewards Veli Huttunen, Taisto Kivisto, Alpo Valtonen and Taisto Silvan became very familiar at that time and later. The head of the provincial government's education department, Vaino Saari, was also very helpful. The Minister of Education was Ulf Sundqvist and his political secretary was the just-mentioned Jorma Westlund. Jukka Sarjala, whose roots in Kangasniemi, was also the Counsellor of Education at the Ministry of Education. He was also helpful. As a result, Puumala emerged from the crowd and started comprehensive school earlier than the rest of the region. August 8, 1972 is still remembered in Puumala. I was sitting on the stairs of my father-in-law's cottage in Anttola when a huge lightning sound could be seen in the sky in the direction of Puumala. The storms in Puumala knocked down large areas of forest. The storm was commemorated a couple of years ago. Together with the municipal representatives of Puumala, we were even able to meet Finance Minister Paul Paavela on the matter. As a result, an additional justification was added to the article on general state subsidies to municipalities: when granting subsidies, special attention had to be paid to municipalities that have suffered storm damage. The transition to comprehensive school and the storm damage had made Puumala familiar to the decision-makers of the kingdom. The following winter, in 1973, work began here to establish a high school. Many meetings were held around the issue, in which, in addition to the previous ones, the chairman of the school board, Eino Hakuli, and the secretary of the school administration, Tapio Holopainen, were present. In the autumn, the matter progressed to a conclusion in the municipal bodies, and immediately after that, the director general of the school board, Erkki Aho, and his family visited Puumala. The school board supported the project because of the long and difficult journeys to school. I had come to know them in Otansalo. Then we went to see the Minister of Education, Ulf Sundqvist, and the permission to establish the upper secondary school was obtained in May 1974. By the way, Minister Sundqvist left for the army after he had granted his permission. This is how Puumala wrote his own chapter on the history of general education; was the first to go to primary school in the region and also got his own upper secondary school. The excellent history of the upper secondary school tells many great stories about the 41-year journey. The teachers have worked with great commitment and many young people have received the entire basis of general education in Puumala. It has been a great and valuable investment and none of it goes to waste. Times are changing and baby boomers are getting smaller. A couple of years ago, the story of the Mikkeli Lyceum ended, today the last students from Puumala are graduating. There is wistfulness and joy in the mind at the same time. Sadness that this story is coming to an end. But on the other hand, it is a joy and pride that we have been able to be involved in building such a great story of education. Times have also changed in that our age group was always the first student in their family. The educational base has expanded and educational and life careers are expanding and moving in all directions. There are new opportunities and new uncertainties in life and future prospects. The new information society and the Internet offer countless opportunities. Retrieving information has become fast and its cost is low. Distance is no longer a cost in obtaining knowledge. As users of information technology, you are in a good position to make use of these electronic channels on offer. Electronic channels make networking easier. It is more important than ever in studies and working life. Through networks, you can find information, friends, partners and even jobs. It opens windows and creates opportunities that you might not otherwise find. Internationality is increasingly present in our lives. It can be seen as trips abroad, exchange students, foreigners in Finland and foreign series on television. The international environment is rewarding but challenging. Language skills give the keys. It is important to maintain an open mind, a desire for knowledge and a positive attitude towards life. The transformation of media and information connections is also changing communication. You can keep in touch with friends and acquaintances even from a long distance. It makes it easier to move to a foreign place. The support and presence of family and friends will help with the challenges ahead. Close people create security and help you think about the most important things. The Finnish school system is still one of the best in the world. You, the new students of Puumala Upper Secondary School, are well prepared to meet the challenges of the future in Finland and elsewhere. The rapid pace of change in the world is increasing the need for multi-skilled workers. We must have the courage, on the one hand, to create our own educational and career path and, on the other hand, to remain prepared for change. You have to seize the opportunity when you come across one. At the same time, the desire to constantly learn and the readiness to innovate help to cope. Kielitaito antaa avaimet. T<8a>rke<8a><8a> on s<8a>ilytt<8a><8a> avoin mieli, tiedonhalu ja positiivinen el<8a>m<8a>nasenne. Median ja tietoyhteyksien mullistuminen muuttavat my<9a>s yhteydenpitoa. Suomen kouluj<8a>rjestelm<8a> on edelleen yksi maailman parhaista. Teill<8a> tuoreilla Puumalan lukion ylioppilailla on hyv<8a>t valmiudet vastata tulevaisuuden haasteisiin Suomessa ja muualla. Tulee tarttua tilaisuuteen silloin kun sellainen tulee vastaan. Samalla halu oppia jatkuvasti ja valmius uudistua auttavat p<8a>rj<8a><8a>m<8a><8a>n. Title: Economic relations between Finland and Russia 18652015
text: Director General Erkki Liikanen: On economic relations between Finland and Russia 1865d02015. Mikkeli, 8.7.2015. . Speech . Wednesday8 July2015,5:00 PM Director General Erkki Liikanen Headquarters Summer Symposium Mikkeli 8.7.2015 Esityskalvot (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches/documents/150708_el_paamajasymposium.pdf) (PDF) . ON ECONOMIC RELATIONS BETWEEN FINLAND AND RUSSIA 1865d02015 (Figure 1) "Russia has been a good neighbour for us in general, many countries have much more difficult neighbours." (Mauno Koivisto, Russian Idea, p.298) This quote is from Mauno Koivisto from his 2001 book The Idea of Russia. His books also appeared in Russian. Countries tend to trade the most with their neighbours. It is influenced by the short geographical distance and low freight costs. In addition, we have gotten to know our neighbours well and got along with them in different circumstances. There is a long history together, although sometimes it may have included difficult periods as well. Difficult periods have usually also been reflected in financial interactions. Economic relations between Finland and Russia over the past 150 years follow these general developments. Trade has generally been brisk in both directions, companies and entrepreneurs have invested across the border. But sometimes political factors and even wars have also had a significant impact on Finland's economic relations with Russia and also with other countries. Over the past 150 years, for example, Russia's share of Finland's exports has fluctuated from zero to nearly 100 between percent. (Figure 2) Russia, Sweden, Germany and the United Kingdom have been the most important trading partners in the long history of foreign trade. The changes reflect both political and economic factors. The figure also puts our economic relations with Russia in context: The story of Finland over the past 150 years is also the story of the internationalization and integration of the Finnish economy into the world economy, east and west. In this story, the Bank of Finland has played a role. The largest spikes, exceptionally large and small trade shares, are associated with the two world wars of the last century: during the First World War, the war almost completely closed the Baltic Sea to Finnish merchant ships. Almost the only possible trading partner was Russia, of which Finland was an autonomous part. During the Second World War, trade with Russia was at a standstill. But in general, with the exception of the period between the world wars, Russian trade has been an important part of Finland's foreign trade, even in politically d0 or even geopolitically d0 difficult times. At the same time, however, it is worth remembering that mutual economic exchange depends not only on political conditions, but also on the economic resources and opportunities of those who trade. The neighbourhood promotes trade and tourism, but purchasing power is key. As you can see from the figure, from the very beginning of the 1900s until well into the 1970s, Finland's most important export country was great Britain, with the exception of exceptional times. This also indicates the position of the British economy at that time. According to the estimate of the well-known economic historian Angus Maddison, Great Britain, in terms of total production, was almost the size of the entire Russian Empire as late as the eve of the First World War in 1913. From a Finnish perspective, Great Britain was easier to reach by sea routes than most of the vast Russian land. In foreign trade, Finland was and is behind the seas. The overwhelming majority of our foreign trade is carried out by ship. The rise of great Britain alongside and past Russia as Finland's most important export market in the second half of the 1800s is also an important part of Finland's increasingly deep integration into the global economy. At the same time, it is also an indication of how the Finnish economy benefited from the relatively liberal attitude of the Russian Empire to the affairs of the Grand Duchy of Finland, including trade policy. There were many other examples, not least the fact that the Bank of Finland was founded 49 years before the current Central Bank of Russia and the Finnish markka was pegged to the silver standard 150 years ago. The First World War destroyed a lot, and with it Finland's foreign trade also had to look for partly new markets. Political factors affected trade between Finland and the Soviet Union/ Russia very unfavorably. Relations between the Soviet Union and the outside world were very poor for many years, and only absolutely necessary goods were wanted to be obtained from abroad. This was also, in part, an ideological choice. Self-sufficiency in almost everything was considered a virtue. In that situation, trading has no chance of success. The Second World War, on the other hand, completely changed the situation also with regard to Finland's foreign trade. Great Britain's position as the main export country remained, but Russia came alongside it. However, it is also worth remembering how difficult the situation in Finland was immediately after the Second World War: a large part of the production capacity had been destroyed or had to be handed over to the Soviet Union. We were short of almost everything, even food. In this situation, imports from Russia were very important. (Figure 3) In addition to food, Finland was also able to buy fuels that were needed in industry. Part of this Finnish import, of course, returned to the USSR in the form of war reparations. As the political and economic situation stabilized in the 1950s, Finland traded briskly to both east and west. Trade with Western Europe and the United States was conducted on a commercial basis. The framework conditions for trade with the Soviet Union were determined by politics, but trade seems to have, at least in broad terms, followed the principle of comparative advantage: the Soviet Union, especially from the 1960s onwards, produced a lot of energy products for export, and Finland was happy to buy them. As we can see from the figure, the transition to a completely market-based system after the collapse of the USSR has not changed this thing for anything. For a long time, the period after the Second World War was a fairly balanced period for Finland's foreign trade and economic relations between Finland and the Soviet Union. The country structure of Finland's exports was diverse, and for a long time the Ussr, Sweden, Germany and great Britain were almost equally important in imports. But the combined influence of geopolitics and economic factors changed the situation in the 1970s. Two oil crises and the explosive situation in the Middle East skyrocketed the price of crude oil. In bilateral trade between Finland and the USSR, this meant that the increased value of Soviet imports was matched by increased exports across the eastern border. In the early 1980s, the Soviet Union's share of Finnish exports rose to over 25 per cent. The Soviet Union and Russia can be thought of as a kind of cushion for the Finnish economy against the effects of rising oil prices: The negative effects of oil prices are partly balanced by increased exports to Russia. This mechanism worked in both the 1980s and 2000s. But with the rapid fall in oil prices, the same mechanism works in the other direction: Finnish exports to Russia fall as the purchasing power of Russians decreases. This was the case in the late 1980s and again now in recent years. At the beginning of the 1990s, political factors were also strongly visible in the economic relations between Finland and Russia: the disintegration of the Soviet Union caused a downturn in trade between our countries for several years as the eastern neighbour sought its direction. Of course, it is an interesting question how much the fall in oil prices hastened the collapse of the USSR, but, as you can see from the next figure, our exports had been contracting for several years before this. (Figure 4) Of course, the special nature of trade in the East also added to this difficult situation: the ability of companies to export their goods to Russia depended not only on price and quality, at least in part, but also on other factors. When the demand in the USSR disappeared, a significant part of the products exported there could not compete with other competitive international markets. Industry underwent major structural change. Trade with the East thus brought in income, but also slowed down productivity growth in many sectors of the economy and delayed industrial restructuring. Of course, there are also examples of companies that, with income from eastern trade, financed their internationalization in the global market. Over the past 20 years, economic relations between Finland and Russia have become accustomed to a time when economic factors determine the volume of trade and investment. The single most important factor is the price of oil. The price of by far the most important export product of Russia determines the export earnings of Russia, which, in turn, are used for imports. Indeed, Russia has become a very open national economy. It imports a lot of consumer and investment goods, Russian companies have for many years been the largest borrowers in the European market. (Figure 5) The following describes the development of the past 20 years: the link between Finnish exports and oil prices is astonishingly clear until the 2009 crisis. After the crisis, the re-export of cars and telephones, for example, almost completely disappeared from our exports. Although the price of oil still largely determines Finland's export opportunities to Russia, we have also been able to prove again the importance of political factors in economic relations. Although, for example, russia's ban on the import of some food products to the EU countries is not particularly large in terms of Finland's entire exports, the effects on the food industry and agriculture have been very negative. How much the contraction of Russian exports has affected the Finnish economy. Most of all, the fall in oil prices has significantly reduced Russia's ability to import goods and services. According to calculations made at the Bank of Finland, our GROSS DOMESTIC PRODUCT would be about one per cent higher if our exports to Russia had remained at the 2013 level. Where do we go from here? In a positive scenario, geopolitical tensions will gradually ease. The key to this is to enable Ukraine to implement the provisions of the Minsk ceasefire agreement. Trade between Finland and Russia is largely determined by the price of oil and, for example, the very significant investments of Finnish companies in Russia. However, it should be remembered that in the coming years the Russian economy will not grow nearly as fast as it did between 2000 and 2008. The working-age population is shrinking, even faster than in Finland, and investment is already falling for the third year. In other words, even at best, our exports to Russia will only grow slowly in the coming years. If things get worse in international relations, we will be in a situation where the development of economic prosperity on both sides of the border will also be lower. Economic interaction will continue and many contacts and contacts will remain, but their positive economic impact will be less pronounced. Russia (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagRussia)

Title: Speech at the opening ceremony of jukka Mkel's art exhibition
text: Director General Erkki Liikanen: Speech at the opening ceremony of Jukka Makela's art exhibition. Helsinki, 20.8.2015. . Speech . Thursday20 August 2015, 6:00 PM President and CEO Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland Speech at the opening ceremony of Jukka Makela's sensitivity and power art exhibition Kunsthalle Helsinki, 20.8.2015 TWO STORIES ABOUT THE ACQUISITION OF THE BOARD The baby boomers born after the war changed Finland a lot. They consider that they created an important part of the Finnish welfare society. Some younger people, on the other hand, have felt that they have taken away opportunities for those who follow. In the field of art, the baby boomers brought the golden generation, whose works we have had and will enjoy. There is no controversy on this issue. One of the most significant events of the summer is the exhibition of Leena Luostarinen's life's work, which is still open at the Salo Art Museum and leaves no one cold. Many artists of this generation are living in their full period of creation. Jukka Makela is one of the most notable of them. Today we are at Kunsthalle Helsinki to open her new exhibition. Jukka Makela has worked as an artist for as many as five decades. During that time, the world and Finland have changed. Jukka Makela's career as an artist also includes many stages. He made his breakthrough in the 1970s. In 1999, Kiasma exhibited his work from three decades in an exhibition that received a lot of attention. I had already gotten to know Jukka Makela long before this Kiasma exhibition as a result of an educational episode. My wife's brother, Ilmo Issakainen, had always repeated for years that Finnish decision-makers look like uncivilized fools when they give interviews in their offices. In the background there is either a cluttered bookshelf, a queue of pennants received as a gift, or an old painting that a person does not know. Why hasn't anyone acquired a modern painting on their wall that means something to them? Yes, it would be different from the crowd. In the autumn of 1994, this came back to me. Finland, Sweden and Austria joined the European Union as new Member States. The first Finnish Commissioner was presented with his office. It was an empty space of 70 square meters. Then it was said that there is a budget for the furnishings, with which the Commissioner can furnish his office as he wishes. Art must be purchased with your own funds. I called llmo. Now let's first get a whiteboard, and only then decorate the office. After the discussion, we decided to go to Jukka Makela's house in Lallukka. I knew him as an artist, but Ilmo knew him personally. During a visit to Lallukka, I bought a large painting by Jukan Makela. It was hung in the office so that the painting filled the back wall of the main part. After that, the interior architect was tasked with furnishing the rest of the office. Transporting the painting to the office was a story in its own right. It was so large that it could not fit in the elevators and not turn from the stairs. A crane was eventually ordered in front of the commission's main building, which lifted it in through a window. It's even more annoying that there were no mobile phone cameras to capture the event back then. Jukka's coal work in the early 1990s was then visible for five years in all the pictures taken from the office of the first Finnish Commissioner. Today it delights us at home every day. A few years later, I also got to open Jukka Makela's exhibition in Antwerp, Belgium. When talking about Jukka Makela's art, we discuss to what extent it is a description of nature and to what extent it is abstract. In the end, this question seems to depend on the eye of the beholder. When it rained in Brussels in March, the snows of the Finnish spring came to mind. It was then that the painting looked like a spring sturgeon with dried tree branches. Whereas in Brussels things were not really progressing, it looked like the EU's complex decision-making structure, which was not clear. But never tired of looking at it. The work of art appeared again and again in a new light. The second episode is related to the Bank of Finland. The Bank of Finland had a valuable art collection, which, however, was never opened for citizens to see. Less than ten years ago, I invited the late Professor Leena Peltola to discuss the topic. He had been an art expert at the Bank of Finland and knew the collection well at the time. Leena Peltola strongly encouraged the bank's art treasures and the historic bank building itself to be made available to citizens. Among other reflections, we had one new visual problem. The main building of the bank, built in the 1880s, was restored in 2006. It was fitted with modern technology aids. On the wall of one of the most important halls, a large video projector, as in the past, was rumbling in the middle. It certainly was not a joy to the eye in the historic bank building, which had been drawn by ludwig Bohnstedt, a German architect born in St. Petersburg who won the first international architectural competition held in Finland. Many had thought of a solution to hide the cannon, but they were either unusable or prohibitively expensive. Leena Peltola suggested a different way out: get a spectacular painting next to the cannon that absorbs all interest. After that, no one will notice the cannon. Interesting idea, we noted. We asked for a proposal for an artist. A couple of days later, Leena called and told her that she had ended up with Jukka Makela. "He has large-scale paintings that fit the space. Ask him to present them.  So then the artist came to the bank. He had taken pictures of his large paintings and they were projected alternately on the wall of the bank next to the cannon. Leena Peltola was right. The video projector disappeared from the eyes. Jukka Makela's painting is now completely dominated by the Bank of Finland's so-called "painting". The back wall of the gold standard room. Art has many dimensions. Today we are opening Jukka Makela's new exhibition. It is extensive and extraordinary. It has a lot of work that is on display for the first time. There are two coal works from the 1990s, which I talked about above, in the exhibition, but everything else is paintings of this millennium and very many of the very last days. The exhibition says a lot about Jukka Makela's creative power today. I want to thank Jukka Makela for the exhibition, I want to thank Pirkko Tuukkanen, whose entire contribution only Jukka knows, but we know it is invaluable. I would like to congratulate Kunsthalle Helsinki on choosing an artist! With these words, I will open Jukka Makela's exhibition Sensitivity and Power.
