Title: Opening words in the money museum's exhibition
text: Director General Erkki Liikanen's opening words at the monetary museum's exhibition. Helsinki, 29.9.2015. . Speech . Tuesday 29September 2015,10:00 AM OPENING WORDS IN THE EXHIBITION OF THE MONETARY MUSEUM "THE IMAGE OF THE NATION . STATISTICS FINLAND 150 YEARS" Director-General Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland Monetary Museum Check against delivery Dear friends! I welcome you to visit the latest changing exhibition at the Money Museum. The exhibition has been organized in cooperation between Statistics Finland and the Bank of Finland and is entitled "Image of a Nation". The reason for organizing the exhibition right now has been the fact that Statistics Finland is celebrating its 150th anniversary. For us, Statistics Finland is a pleasant partner in this as in many other contexts. Cooperation between the Bank of Finland and Statistics Finland has always been close. The reasons are obvious. Monetary policy cannot be conducted without a proper and fresh knowledge base. The bank is a major consumer of statistics. *** Central banks have been using and producing statistics for a long time. The use of statistics expanded, especially in the 1920s, when monetary conditions began to be stabilized after the upheavals caused by the First World War. Particular interest was focused on price indices and balance of payments. A statistics department was established at the Bank of Finland as early as 1919. The division of labour between Statistics Finland and the Bank of Finland has varied. Recently, too, there have been changes. For example, the compilation of banking statistics was transferred from Statistics Finland to the Bank of Finland after eu membership began; on the other hand, the compilation of the balance of payments statistics, which had been the responsibility of the Bank of Finland since the 1930s, was transferred to Statistics Finland less than two years ago. In the development of statistical methods, the Bank of Finland has traditions to be proud of. In 1931, when Finland detached the markka from the gold standard, monetary policy needed new benchmarks to navigate. There was a desire to maintain the stability of the value of money. To this end, the Bank of Finland began to calculate its own, even weekly, consumer price index, following the example of the Central Bank of Sweden. Some problems arose in calculating the index, so the bank hired a young statistician Leo Tornqvist to study how the consumer price index should actually be calculated. In 1936, Tornqvist published the result of his research in the bank's Monthly Bulletin: a logarithmic, variable-weight chain index, which today is known throughout the world as the Divisia-Tornqvist index formula. It is probably still the most accurate price index of its kind that has been invented. Central banks are at least as interested in price indices even today, when price stability has been set as the main objective of monetary policy, even if they do not produce the indices themselves in developed countries. We no longer see the need for weekly price indices, but otherwise the quality requirements of the indices are high. Moreover, the measurement of inflation is becoming increasingly difficult today as the development of information technology changes the quality of many products in a way that is difficult to quantify. *** Decision-making in society must be based on researched information. Statistics must strive for objectivity, and the different roles of the data producer and the political decision-maker must be kept clear. This has been highlighted in the EU, where the coordination of economic policies between member states and jointly agreed rules are ultimately based on statistics. They must therefore be absolutely reliable and objective, and the independence of the statistical authorities must be beyond any doubt. Five years ago, when europe's sovereign debt crisis erupted, there was an appalling observational lesson about how dangerous it is if confidence in economic statistics fails. That must not happen again. *** Finland is facing years of radical reform of the national economy and the public sector. Statistics play an invaluable role in this. After all, development cannot be achieved without measurement. Peter Drucker, one of the gurus of modern business management, once said: 'If you can't measure it, you can't improve it'. If something cannot be measured, it is difficult to lead, and what cannot be led is difficult to implement. There are many types of measurement, and not all metrics are numerical or statistical. But the responsibility of the developer of the meters is great: it is necessary to measure things that matter, even if it is difficult. Otherwise, it threatens to happen as it did to the man in the story, who searched for his lost key under the beam of light on the lamppost just because it was too dark elsewhere. One important area for development, the need for measuring which has been highlighted in recent years, is the productivity of public services. The growth of the national economy has long been a disappointment, and it is reflected in the tax base and, consequently, in the resources of public finances. At the same time, however, the demand for and need for public services is constantly increasing, partly because of the ageing of the population, but also for many other reasons. In order to solve the problem, increasing the productivity of public service production is a matter of destiny for Finland, and a policy aimed at this requires good indicators of productivity in the result. Traditionally, national accounts have measured public output on the basis of the inputs used. Under the current circumstances, this solution is becoming increasingly difficult to defend. Efforts to better measure public service provision and its benefits are more important today than ever. *** The exhibition now being opened at the Monetary Museum, entitled "The Image of the Nation", was built in cooperation between Statistics Finland and the Bank of Finland. On Statistics Finland's side, reija Helenius, Leila Kaunisharju, Mervi Ukkonen, Marketta Lukkari, Sirkka-Liisa Lonnrot, Jukka Hytonen and Matti Okko have been involved in the work; From the Bank of Finland Vappu Ikonen, Jaakko Koskentola and Juha Tarkka. The exhibition architect has been Teemu Taskinen, and the digital exhibition, which opens online, has been built by Outi Kotala. Mauri Antero Numminen kindly agreed that his singing Act on Statistics Finland could be included in the video presented at the exhibition. The "statistical Finns" from different decades featured in the exhibition were photographed by photographer Sanna Peurakoski, whose models were Johanna Eerola, Minttu Kuula and Jarno Talvitie. Their outfits were obtained from the costume shop of the National Theatre. I would like to express my sincerest thanks to all the designers and builders of the exhibition. I congratulate Statistics Finland on its 150 years of operation and predict that, in a changing world, the importance of the work it does will continue to grow. I also believe that the cooperation between our institutions will continue and deepen. Congratulations, and welcome to the exhibition! Liikanen (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagLiikanen)
text_original: P<8a><8a>johtaja Erkki Liikasen avaussanat rahamuseon n<8a>yttelyss<8a>. Helsinki, 29.9.2015. . Speech . Tuesday 29September 2015,10:00 AM AVAUSSANAT RAHAMUSEON N<80>YTTELYSS<80> "KANSAKUNNAN KUVA .TILASTOKESKUS 150 VUOTTA" P<8a><8a>johtaja Erkki Liikanen Suomen Pankin rahamuseo Check against delivery Hyv<8a>t yst<8a>v<8a>t! Toivotan teid<8a>t tervetulleeksi tutustumaan uusimpaan Rahamuseon vaihtuvaan n<8a>yttelyyn. N<8a>yttely on j<8a>rjestetty Tilastokeskuksen ja Suomen Pankin yhteisty<9a>n<8a> ja sen otsikkona on <d3>Kansakunnan kuva<d3>. Aiheen n<8a>yttelyn j<8a>rjest<8a>miselle juuri nyt on antanut se, ett<8a> Tilastokeskus t<8a>ytt<8a><8a> 150 vuotta. Meille Tilastokeskus on mieluinen partneri t<8a>ss<8a> niin kuin monessa muussakin yhteydess<8a>. Suomen Pankin ja Tilastokeskuksen yhteisty<9a> on aina ollut tiivist<8a>. Syyt ovat ilmeiset. Rahapolitiikkaa ei voida harjoittaa ilman kunnollista ja tuoretta tietopohjaa. Pankki on tilastojen suurkuluttaja. *** Keskuspankit ovat k<8a>ytt<8a>neet ja tuottaneet tilastoja jo kauan. Tilastojen k<8a>ytt<9a> laajeni varsinkin 1920-luvulla, kun rahaoloja alettiin vakauttaa ensimm<8a>isen maailmansodan aiheuttamien mullistusten j<8a>lkeen. Mielenkiinto kohdistui varsinkin hintaindekseihin ja maksutaseeseen. Suomen Pankkiinkin perustettiin tilasto-osasto jo vuonna 1919. Ty<9a>njako Tilastokeskuksen ja Suomen Pankin v<8a>lill<8a> on vaihdellut. Viime aikoinakin on tapahtunut muutoksia. Esimerkiksi pankkitilaston kokoaminen siirtyi EU-j<8a>senyyden alettua Tilastokeskukselta Suomen Pankille; toisaalta maksutasetilaston laadinta, joka oli ollut Suomen Pankin vastuulla aina 1930-luvulta asti, siirtyi vajaat kaksi vuotta sitten Tilastokeskukseen. Tilastomenetelmien kehitt<8a>misess<8a> Suomen Pankilla on perinteit<8a>, joista voi olla ylpe<8a>. Vuonna 1931, kun Suomi irrotti markan kultakannasta, rahapolitiikalle tarvittiin uusia kiintopisteit<8a>, joiden mukaan suunnistettaisiin. Rahan arvon vakaudesta haluttiin pit<8a><8a> kiinni. Suomen Pankki alkoi t<8a>t<8a> varten laskea omaa, jopa viikoittaista kuluttajahintaindeksi<8a>, Ruotsin keskuspankin esimerkki<8a> seuraten. Indeksin laskemisessa ilmeni joitakin ongelmia, joten pankki palkkasi nuoren tilastotieteilij<8a>n Leo T<9a>rnqvistin tutkimaan, miten kuluttajahintaindeksi oikeastaan pit<8a>isi laskea. Vuonna 1936 T<9a>rnqvist julkaisi pankin Monthly Bulletin-julkaisussa tutkimuksensa tuloksen: logaritmisen, muuttuvapainoisen ketjuindeksin, joka nyky<8a><8a>n tunnetaan koko maailmassa Divisia-T<9a>rnqvist -indeksikaavana. Se lienee edelleenkin lajissaan tarkin hintaindeksi mit<8a> on keksitty. Keskuspankit ovat ainakin yht<8a> kiinnostuneita hintaindekseist<8a> my<9a>s nyky<8a><8a>n, kun hintavakaus on asetettu rahapolitiikan p<8a><8a>tavoitteeksi, vaikka ne eiv<8a>t kehittyneiss<8a> maissa itse indeksej<8a> tuotakaan. Viikkotason hintaindekseille ei en<8a><8a> n<8a>hd<8a> tarvetta, mutta muuten indeksien laatuvaatimukset ovat korkeat. Inflaation mittaaminen on sit<8a> paitsi nyky<8a><8a>n yh<8a> vaikeutumassa kun tietotekniikan kehitys muuttaa monien tuotteiden laatua tavalla, jota on vaikeata kvantifioida. *** Yhteiskunnallisen p<8a><8a>t<9a>ksenteon pit<8a><8a> perustua tutkittuun tietoon. Tilastoinnin pit<8a><8a> pyrki<8a> objektiivisuuteen ja tiedon tuottajan ja poliittisen p<8a><8a>t<9a>ksentekij<8a>n erilaiset roolit on pidett<8a>v<8a> selvin<8a>. T<8a>m<8a> on korostunut EU:ssa, jossa j<8a>senmaiden keskin<8a>inen talouspolitiikan koordinaatio ja yhdess<8a> sovitut s<8a><8a>nn<9a>t perustuvat viime k<8a>dess<8a> tilastoihin. Siksi niiden on oltava ehdottoman luotettavia ja objektiivisia, ja tilastoviranomaisten riippumattomuuden on oltava kaikkien ep<8a>ilysten ulkopuolella. Viitisen vuotta sitten Euroopan valtionvelkakriisin puhjetessa saatiin kauhistuttavaa havainto-opetusta siit<8a>, kuinka vaarallista on, jos luottamus taloustilastoihin pett<8a><8a>. Sellainen ei saa toistua. *** Suomella on edess<8a><8a>n kansantalouden ja julkisen sektorin radikaalin uudistamisen vuodet. Tilastoilla on t<8a>ss<8a> korvaamaton osuutensa. Kehitt<8a>minen ei nimitt<8a>in onnistu ilman mittaamista. Nykyaikaisen liikkeenjohdon guruihin kuulunut Peter Drucker sanoi aikoinaan: <d2>If you can<d5>t measure it, you can<d5>t improve it<d3>. Jos jotakin ei voida mitata, sit<8a> on vaikeaa johtaa, ja se, mit<8a> ei voi johtaa, on vaikea toteuttaa. Mittaamista on monenlaista, eiv<8a>tk<8a> kaikki mittarit ole numeerisia tai tilastollisia. Mutta mittarien kehitt<8a>j<8a>n vastuu on suuri: on mitattava asioita, joilla on merkityst<8a>, vaikka se olisikin vaikeaa. Muuten uhkaa k<8a>yd<8a> niin kuin tarinan miehelle, joka etsi kadonnutta avaintaan lyhtypylv<8a><8a>n valokiilan alta vain siksi, ett<8a> muualla oli liian pime<8a><8a>. Yksi t<8a>rke<8a> kehitt<8a>miskohde, jonka mittaamisen tarve on viime vuosina korostunut, on julkisten palvelujen tuottavuus. Kansantalouden kasvu on jo pitk<8a><8a>n muodostunut pettymykseksi, ja se n<8a>kyy veropohjassa ja sit<8a> kautta julkisen talouden resursseissa. Samalla julkisten palvelujen kysynt<8a> ja tarve kuitenkin koko ajan kasvavat, osaksi v<8a>est<9a>n ik<8a><8a>ntymisen takia, mutta my<9a>s monen muun syyn vuoksi. Jotta ongelma voitaisiin ratkaista, julkisen palvelutuotannon tuottavuuden kohottaminen on Suomelle kohtalonkysymys, ja t<8a>h<8a>n t<8a>ht<8a><8a>v<8a> politiikka vaatii tulokseen hyvi<8a> tuottavuuden mittareita. Perinteisestih<8a>n kansantalouden tilinpidossa on julkista tuotantoa mitattu k<8a>ytettyjen panosten perustella. T<8a>m<8a> ratkaisu on nykyisiss<8a> oloissa k<8a>ym<8a>ss<8a> yh<8a> vaikeammaksi puolustaa. Ponnistukset julkisen palvelutuotannon ja siit<8a> saatavan hy<9a>dyn paremmaksi mittaamiseksi ovat nyky<8a><8a>n t<8a>rke<8a>mpi<8a> kuin koskaan. *** Rahamuseossa nyt avattava n<8a>yttely, jonka otsikkona on <d3>Kansakunnan kuva<d3>, on rakennettu Tilastokeskuksen ja Suomen Pankin yhteisty<9a>n<8a>. Tilastokeskuksen puolelta mukana ty<9a>ss<8a> ovat olleet Reija Helenius, Leila Kaunisharju, Mervi Ukkonen, Marketta Lukkari, Sirkka-Liisa L<9a>nnrot, Jukka Hyt<9a>nen ja Matti Okko; Suomen Pankista Vappu Ikonen, Jaakko Koskentola ja Juha Tarkka. N<8a>yttelyarkkitehtina on ollut Teemu Taskinen ja verkossa avattavan digitaalisen n<8a>yttelyn on rakentanut Outi Kotala. Mauri Antero Numminen suostui yst<8a>v<8a>llisesti siihen, ett<8a> h<8a>nen laulamansa Laki tilastokeskuksesta voitiin sis<8a>llytt<8a><8a> n<8a>yttelyss<8a> esitett<8a>v<8a><8a>n videoon. N<8a>yttelyss<8a> esiintyv<8a>t <d3>tilastosuomalaiset<d3> eri vuosikymmenilt<8a> on kuvannut valokuvaaja Sanna Peurakoski, jonka malleina olivat Johanna Eerola, Minttu Kuula ja Jarno Talvitie. Heid<8a>n asunsa saatiin Kansallisteatterin puvustamosta. Lausun parhaat kiitokset kaikille n<8a>yttelyn suunnittelijoille ja rakentajille. Onnittelen Tilastokeskusta sen 150-vuotisen toiminnan johdosta ja ennustan, ett<8a> muuttuvassa maailmassa sen tekem<8a>n ty<9a>n merkitys edelleen kasvaa. Uskon my<9a>s instituutioittemme v<8a>lisen yhteisty<9a>n edelleen jatkuvan ja syvenev<8a>n. Onneksi olkoon, ja tervetuloa n<8a>yttelyyn! Liikanen (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tag=Liikanen)

Title: Interview with Brsen-Zeitung
text: Governor Erkki Liikanen: Interview with Bsrsen-Zeitung, 6 October 2015 . Speech . Tuesday 6 October 2015,12:00PM Governor Erkki Liikanen Interview in Bsrsen-Zeitung, by Mark Schrsrs Published on 6 October 2015 an edited transcript of the interview Bsrsen-Zeitung: Mister Liikanen,the Euro area economy is growing, even above its potential rate, the credit cycle has turned into positive territory, unemployment is declining is there right now really aneedfor the European CentralBank (ECB) to think about loosening further the already unprecedentedly loose monetarypolicy? If I may I would like to start the discussion from another angle from inflation. Please. We have an inflation target of below but close to 2%, in the medium term. At the moment the inflation rate is very low and well below this target, and even our forecast for 2017 is a little below the target. If we take our mandate seriously we cannot ignore that and we have to be vigilant. This is even more the case because risks for growth and inflation are tilted to the downside. But youore right, there are also some positive developments. The PMIs are positive, especially for the countries in the Euro area periphery. Lending is also improving, even if this is not fully reflected in the real economy so far. So, whatdoes that mean for the question of additional monetary stimulus? First of all this means that we have decided on an asset purchase program in January this year and that we have said, that this will go on until September 2016 or beyond, if necessary. We have to stick to that and implement it fully. We also should not forget: Monetary policy always works with a lag. If I compare the situation with a marathon I would say that we are only at kilometer 15. Letos keep the tempo and letos stick to our plan. And if things change, we should not draw any hasty conclusions. So it is premature that market participants increasingly see an expansion of the asset purchase program (Quantitative easing,QE) as a done deal? We have said that we are going to buy until September 2016. And we have committed ourselves to buy longer if it becomes necessary. Our program is flexible enough to be adjusted regarding the size, the composition and the duration. This holds true. We do not need to say more at the moment. Butisnotthere again arisk that also due to the ECBos communication expectations mount enormously and thatthe ECB finally has to deliver in order to avoid anegative market reaction? It is very important for us to follow what markets think. And we communicate in a way that market participants understand what we do and why. But we decide on our policies ourselves and completely alone. Marketso mood changes daily our policy aims at the medium term. So you are not afraid of becoming a prisoner of the markets? No. Our mandate and our analysis drive us not the markets. And this is how it should be: We could not let markets dictate our policy. Economyis also alot aboutpsychology. Donot you think that it would strengthen the confidence in the Euro area economy if the ECB starts talking more about the positive developments and not always only about the risks? This is a very good point. We have to tell the good news, but we also have to talk about the problems. We have to get the balance right. If you talk about risks you refer to China and the oilprice, right? The situation in China and the Emerging Markets and the low oil price are the biggest downside risks at the moment. But it is too early to tell whether these developments are temporary or have lasting implications. For example the low oil price seems to be supply-side driven that would be less problematic compared to demand driven factors. Iom sure when we meet in Maltae e at the next monetary-policy meeting on October, 22the e we will already know much more. The renewed fallin oilprices have pushed the inflation rate again below zero in September, to 0,1%. But in the pastthe ECB has always arguedthatit has to olook througho such extreme fluctuations in the oilprice. Yes, we have always said that we need to look through the changes in relative prices. What is important for us are the second-round effects. We have argued this way when oil prices went up and that must also be the case when oil prices go down. And do you see such effects? It is still a little bit too early to say. But what we observe are some new developments: For example how quickly changes in the short-term inflation impacts the longer-term inflation expectations and how much impact the oil prices have on these expectations at the moment. We should not be too hasty with conclusions, but we have to analyze it. We need more time to do that work. The longer-term inflation expectations should notbe influenced by recent oil price developments. Do you thinkthat especially the market-based inflation expectations are still areliable indicator? Whenever inflation expectations go down more than we like to see we have to be careful and monitor it whatever the reasons are. The question is how we react. But one thing is clear: We have to be loyal to our mandate. This holds true if inflation is too high and also if inflation is too low. Do you see a risk of deflation in the Euro area at the moment? Deflation is definitely less of a risk at the moment than it was at the end of last year. But we need to be careful and consistent in our assessments. Some observers see the renewed drop in inflation as an indication thatQE is not working. Our program is a long-term project and we do not question it every single day because it is working: It had an impact on inflation expectations and it is supporting the economy. Would an expansion ofQE really have abig impact? The experience ofthe US central bank Fed seems to signal that there is a diminishing return with every new QE program? Some people even say the most efficient measure is the announcement itself. But seriously: We implement now what we have decided. We should not be impatient now. If you speculate too early about doing more it also weakens what you have already decided on. I hope it will be enough to buy until September 2016. If not we have said what we have said. But again: We should not be impatient. If the GoverningCouncil comes to the conclusion that more QE is needed would itbe more efficientto expand the program or to increase the monthly-run rate of60bill. Euro? When we decided on the program the most important thing to me was the Forward Guidance. To me the commitment for the accommodative monetary policy is the key. Some experts argue that under the current rules the ECB would notbe able to expand the program significantly because the ECB would soon run out of bonds for countries like Germany. We had this kind of discussion even more when we started the asset purchase program. Back then it was said we would run out of bonds within weeks. This has not happened. I am not worried about our capability to deliver what we promise. Can you imagine that the ECB stops buying accordingto the capital key, because atthe moment it buys large amounts ofGerman bunds or would such a decision call into question thatQE is monetary policy instrument? I would not change anything now. We have planned this program very carefully. In case there is a need to actis it also an option to cut interest rates further,for example the deposit rate of d0,2%, or does the ECB stick to its statement that the interest rates have reached their lower bound? We have said that and I have nothing to add to that. The more the ECBloosens its policythe more difficultthe exit is going to be. Should this play a bigger role in the considerations? When you have the risk of deflation you are in a new territory. We have had to innovate new instruments. But you can be assured: It is deeply in our mindset that we want to bring this policy to an end. If you look at the US experience you see how difficult the exit can be. But for us this is a luxury problem for the distant future. When our economy starts to improve on a broad base I will be happy to deal with the problem of the exit. When we get there we will be ready and able to exit. You are a member of the GoverningCouncil since 2004. Al lot of critics say that the ECB has moved awayfrom its approach of following a more cautious osteady-handpolicyo and that ithas started, like the Anglo-Saxon central banks, to intervene more pro-actively and aggressivelyin the markets. How do you see the development ofthe ECB? Yes, the ECB has changed. But the world has changed even more. These crises should not have happened because everybody thought that markets would always correct themselves. This belief has proven to be overly optimistic. This also means that from time to time central banks have to play a bigger role. You also have to admit that the so.called Anglo-Saxons are not always wrong. We should have enough self-confidence to follow what has proven its value for other central banks. But one thing has absolutely not changed: our commitment to our mandate, to price stability. We are deeply rooted in the European tradition of monetary policy which is very much linked to the Bundesbank. The Bundesbank was the best central bank in the world for decades. But alot ofpeople see especiallythis connection as being cut off completely. I donot agree. Price stability and independence have been very important for the Bundesbank and they are also important values for the ECB. In the Euro crisis the ECB has also become apolitical actor for example as a member ofthe Troika. Donotyou see the ECBos independence at risk? In the crisis many people wanted the ECB to be on board. But I would say that we should keep our distance to the political processes. This is also reflected in many decisions: For example we do not buy government bonds of a country under a rescue program as long as this program is under review. Butis there really a distance ifthe ECB -through the purchase ofgovernmentbonds -becomes the biggest creditor of the Euro area member states?The President of Bundesbank,Jens Weidmann, says it blurs the line between fiscal and monetary policy. Jens Weidmann is a highly respected member of the Governing Council and this is a very good point. But it is not the case that the governments drive us. There is no ofiscal dominanceo. We decide on our monetary policy absolutely independently. Some experts even argue that a centralbank solely focused on the stability of money is no longer up.to-date. First of all: Price stability is our primary mandate. But as long as price stability is not at risk the EU treaty foresees that the can support the economy more general. But more generally speaking: The best contribution that central banks can make to sustainable growth and employment in the long-term is to guarantee price stability. Atthe moment centralbanks worldwide are very much concerned aboutincreased uncertainty and volatility in financial markets. But is higher volatility not usualin asituation in which we stand on the cusp of changing times due to the upcoming lift-offbythe Fed andisnot it a problem if monetary policy always steps in as soon as there is stress? You are absolutely right, higher volatility is nothing abnormal when you have reached a turning point. And it is definitely not our task as a central bank to react to every single market fluctuation. But uncertainty and volatility can have negative impact on the real economy if they last for a long time. We have to monitor that very closely. Another topic: In the Greek crisis there was for the first time ever dapublic debate about a country leaving the Euro area. What are the implications for the monetary union andfor the ECB? I have been to Greece recently right after the election. My message was pretty clear: Greece has to deliver now! There is an agreement and it has to be implemented completely. The European institutions and the member states have gone to their outermost limits. To implement the agreement is the best that the decision-makers can do for their country and for Europe. But what has happened in Greece recently will stay in everybodyos memory. Some observers argue that the discussion about aGrexit has also putinto question the irreversibility of the Euro. I would say letos not put into question the irreversibility of the Euro. And I donot think that this has happened. We had some specific problems with a single country. And my impression is that other countries have learned their lessons: Donot get so far. It is much better to solve your problems earlier and on your own before all the others also sit at the table and interfere. What lessons should be drawn for the monetary union? The five EU Presidents have calledfor much more integration and centralization culminatingin the call for an EU finance ministry. Bundesbank PresidentWeidmann has criticized that the proposals lack the right balance between common liability and control. The most important steps we need to do now are the full implementation of the banking union and the capital markets union. Already at the time when the monetary union was created a lot of experts said that these parts were missing but this was neglected. But is has proven to be a fallacy to think that every country could deal best with its banks alone. We need common rules. With the capital markets union we will get via the financial markets a better risk sharing across countries. This is very important. Another issue is the question. How far can we get with the fiscal union? And what is your answer? A fiscal union is an intellectually interesting concept and Iom not against more integration in the area of fiscal policy. But this does not work without strong democratic legitimacy. But such big steps are not going to happen soon. Butis the monetary union viable without a fiscal union?A lot ofpeople doubt it. Besides the banking union and the capital markets union another precondition would be that the fiscal rules are respected. They are too complicated and they need to be simplified. But what really counts in the end is that the fiscal rules are respected. Finally we also need better discipline through the financial markets. When you callfor the fullimplementation ofthe banking union does this also mean that you are pleading for a common depositguarantee system in the Euro area? A common deposit guarantee scheme would serve the aims of the banking union. But it could only be implemented gradually. How do you assess the current situation ofthe European banks? In many respects they still seem to lagbehind their US counterparts. The Euro area economy is still weak, interest rates are low, non-performing loans in some countries are high this all puts pressure on the banks. On the other hand there are also positive developments. The ECBos banking supervision arm has concluded its comprehensive assessment, and measures to recapitalize banks have been implemented in most parts. What we need now is to harmonize the treatment of capital. There are still too many national solutions. Some banks might also need to reassess their business model. But this is not for the authorities to decide. Many European bankers complain about too much regulation also in comparison to the US. There are certainly some points we have to look at again closely. One example: Under Basel III risk weights for housing are very small, but risk weights for credits to small and medium size enterprises are very high. But historically crises mostly started in the housing market. We might have a problem there. But all in all Iom fine with the regulation. And what aboutthe otoo-big-too-failo-problem there has been the oLiikanen reporto of an expert group you have chaired? A lot has happened in dealing with these big banks regarding capital requirements, resolution, TLAC buffers. But there are still cases in which an implicit government guarantee for big banks lead to cheap funding for these institutions which is used for excessive risk taking especially when it comes to proprietary trading and market.making. We should not ignore or forget this problem. When it comes to the problem of too big to fail, we have gone a long way but not all the way. Butyou donot see a risk of overregulatingbanks? Of course we must be careful not to overregulate. But you also donot have to always buy every argument of lobbyists.

Title: Interview with CNBC
text: Governor Erkki Liikanen: Interview with the CNBC, 12 October 2015. . Speech . Monday12 October 2015, 4:30 PM Governor Erkki Liikanen An interview with the CNBC, Geoff Cutmore, conducted on Saturday 10 October in Lima Published on 12 October Transcript excerpts Governor Liikanen on banking sector: CNBC: Is there any room do you think to review the capital requirements that are likely to be imposed on the banks by the ECBos regulatory function and I ask this because the Commission is now saying that regulation shouldnot get in the way of the opportunity for growth. And we know that the bankers themselves are crying foul and are worried that they are going to be less competitive compared to the U.S. or other parts of the world. Is there perhaps a need to review the capital requirements that the ECB us going to impose. Governor Liikanen: We, of course, follow the international rules which have been set out by Basel committee where everybodyos in and itos very important that we respect those rules. But there are some details that we need to look through. One is of course complexity. Second is, I give you one example, about SMEs. When we went through the reform and we assessed the capital requirements on the basis of the risk-weighted assets which means that housing has very low-risks weights and SMEs very high-risk weights. But if you look at the experience of the crisis, housing has been the biggest source of risk weights problems. So perhaps there is something wrong there because you should be able to diversify risks: You have many SMEs you finance but housing you must be careful because bubbles are very heavy because they have deep impact on the whole population. I think we must be able to look at the details but letos not open the whole Pandora box. We are the generation that has gone through the worst financial crisis since the 1930s. We trusted too much on the self-regulation. There must be rebalancing. Owners must put capital into the banks. Banks must have the liquidity. But of course if there are evident complexities that donot serve the main purpose then of course you must need to look at it. CNBC: So I just want to understand that very clearly because I think it is a very important point. Are you saying that maybe a blanket approach on risk-weighted assets is not the right approach? Governor Liikanen: I said on this particular issue on the SMEs. So that we say that housing risk weights are very small, low. For SMEs very high. In that particular issue it doesnot work in the right way. It wasnot our purpose to make funding of the SMEs more complicated and perhaps make it easier to create a bubble in the housing market. It should be perhaps more balanced. I just want to show that if there is a problem as this has been identified, we must be able to look at it. Governor Liikanen on monetarypolicy: CNBC: I canot let you go without asking how the board currently sees conditions. We talked a bit about growth --less so about inflation. The market seems to be drawing its own conclusion that, at some point, there will be another move to deepen or to some extend the current QE program. Is the market wrong in jumping to these conclusions already? Governor Liikanen: When we took the important step in January, that we started this broad-scale asset purchases, we were very careful with our communication. And what is critical for me is the long-term commitment. We will continue the program as long as needed to get inflation back in a sustainable way so that it respects our target for price stability which is below but close to two in the medium term. So this long-term commitment is most important. Of course the first part of the sentence is we buy 60 billion per month until the end of September next year. If we compare that to a marathon, we have just passed 15K. But most important is the commitment even beyond if needed. Our commitment is linked to our strategic price stability target. CNBC: And just so I can understand how the council is considering the risks at the moment. Obviously oil and deflation and the consequences of that and have been understood and I think discussed clearly. But here at this meeting so much of the focus has been on the new threat of leverage in emerging markets. Can you help us understand how much that is coming into council considerations as you think about what might be triggered for further action? Governor Liikanen: The impact of the emerging economies is perhaps more important on the growth. Still it has been marginal, perhaps the revision has been only 0.1 percent but it has been bigger there. But the second point is when the growth in China has been more limited than before and the supply of oil is more abundant. Oil price has been going down. These of course have impact on the growth and the inflation outlook. But still today it is perhaps too early to say if this impact is transitory or temporary or if itos having a long-term impact. The change in energy prices is not a major concern. Concern comes if there is a secondary effect later. And we meet in Malta later and thatos the moment to see the issue -whether itos transitory or it is having a lasting impact. CNBC: And on that issue of transitory. Oil is back at 50 a barrel. Do you think that the decline will in fact turn out to be transitory and very low inflation expectations are excessively low at the moment? Governor Liikanen: There are two issues. One is the change in relative prices like the oil prices and second is impact on the inflation outlook, for instance if there is secondary impact on rate formation or its impact on rate expectations. I would say that the first is easier and with the second part one must be extremely careful, monitor closely, take into account every single aspect and then see whether we need to take decisions. But anyhow, I just want to make it very clear: If needed, if warranted, we are able to act within the present program and if needed able to continue beyond September. But it is not the time yet. We will assess that every meeting when we meet.

Title: Memoirs of Ben Bernanke The Courage to Act
text: Governor Erkki Liikanen on the memoirs of Ben Bernanke oThe Courage to Acto . Speech . Saturday 17October 2015,9:00 AM Governor Erkki Liikanen Submitted to Helsingin Sanomat (in Finnish) The author has been Governor of the Bank of Finland and a member of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank since 2004. BERNANKE STEERED THE USA THROUGH THE CRISIS In his memoirs,the unflappable central banker describes his experiences in his own inimitable style. In early 2002, Ben Bernankeos secretary at Princeton asked the professor: oGlenn Hubbard is on the line. Will you take the call?o Hubbard, President George W. Bushos leading economic adviser and at that time on leave of absence from Columbia University, had a question: oWould you be interested in coming to Washington to discuss with the President a post at the Federal Reserve?o The rest is history. Bernanke first became a member of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, moved on to serve in the White House as chairman of President George W. Bush's Council of Economic Advisers and finally became Chairman of the Federal Reserve from 2006 to 2014. Thus, the leading researcher of financial crises was head of the USAos central bank when the world stumbled into the great financial crisis of 2007d2009. Bernanke visited Finland just a week ago. He told us he had written his memoirs personally. Amongst the numerous works dealing with the financial crisis, Bernankeos position, expertise and clear, individual style of writing makes this book undoubtedly the pick of the crop. The path of this young Jewish man from a small town in the American South to the elite universities of the North describes one of the paths available in the America of those days. Bernanke grew up in South Carolina, which in the 1960s was still a segregationist state. The assassination of Martin Luther King in 1968 appalled the young Bernanke as did the fact that even generally nice people could react to the assassination with satisfaction. In the early 1970s, Bernanke left to study first at Harvard and then at MIT. At the latter, his professor was Stanley Fischer (today Vice Chairman of the Federal Reserve), who had served earlier as thesis supervisor for the Finnish economist and investor Pentti Kouri. Fischer encouraged Bernanke to read the Monetary History of the United States by Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz.. He was swept away and from then on concentrated on monetary and macroeconomic questions. One of Bernankeos recognised contributions to economic theory is the concept of the ofinancial acceleratoro, which he used to explain the depth of the Great Depression of the 1930s. According to Bernanke, in a depression the flow of credit dries up, leading to a further exacerbation of the situation. Banks become more careful as their losses grow. At the same time the solvency of borrowers is weakened. As the sources of credit run dry, this inhibits household purchases and corporate investment. A healthy financial system is, therefore, extremely important to the national economy. This observation provides the key to Bernankeos actions during the financial crisis. Bernankeos memoirs describe the phases of the financial crisis above all in the United States, but he also deals with the close cooperation between central banks globally and the crises in other regions. Bernanke was the primus motor when dollar funding was secured not only for banks within the USA, but also for those abroad, through the aegis of other countrieso central banks, and for the exceptional interest rate reduction coordinated between all the leading central banks in October 2008. He also deals with Europe and the ECB. Bernanke valued the input at a critical stage by the ECBos Jean-Claude Trichet. The two men shared the same negative opinion of the debt restructuring in respect of Greece in 2010, although they occasionally differed in their monetary policy decisions. Bernanke writes appreciatively of Trichetos successor Mario Draghi another product of MIT and his work in conquering Europeos economic problems. In the economic crisis of 2008, President George W. Bush trusted Bernankeos judgement from the outset. Bernanke, for his part, is grateful to Bush for shouldering the responsibility during the extremely critical weeks of 2008 irrespective of the political costs. But the measures required to save the financial system in the United States, and perhaps globally also aroused opposition. The strongest attacks came in the 2012 presidential primaries for the Republican Party. The Republicanso hostility towards the Fed and Bernanke personally clearly bothered him. oI did not leave the Republican Party. I felt that the party left me,o Bernanke states. Finland makes a brief appearance in connection with the rescue operation for Bear Stearns. The Fed wanted for the first time in 60 years to use the exceptional possibility of granting credit directly to a single bank. This required the support of all five members of the Board. The problem was that one of the five, Rick Mishkin was at the time visiting the Bank of Finland and at that precise moment was skiing in Lapland. He could not be reached by an encrypted phone line. However, a solution was found. Nevertheless, the next member of the Federal Reserve Board to visit the Bank of Finland, Randall Kroszner did not dare come until the situation had calmed down. Title: Speech at the 100th anniversary of reisjrvi Cooperative Bank, 22 November 2015
text: President and CEO Erkki Liikanen: Speech at reisjarvi Cooperative Bank's 100th anniversary celebration, 22.11.2015 . Speech . Sunday 22November 2015, 10:00 AM President and CEO Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland Speech at Reisjarvi Cooperative Bank's 100th anniversary celebration Reisjarvi, 22.11.2015 OSUUSPANKKITOIMINTA The cooperative fund business founded in Germany landed in Finland in the early 1900s. Cooperative funds usually operate locally, and members often knew each other. Only hardworking and reliable persons were eligible as new members. Loans were granted only for objects that increased production, and their use was closely monitored. The predecessor of Reisjarvi Cooperative Bank, keskikylan osuuskassa, was founded in April 1915. Today we can celebrate the bank's 100-year history. Reisjarvi received its second cooperative fund in January 1916. Otto Liikanen, among others, was elected to the board of the Kangaskyla cooperative fund, which was established at that time. According to the history that has just been published, the cooperative operated in the houses of cashier Antti Viljanmaki and chairman Otto Liikanen for its first two decades. Who was Otto Liikanen? He was born in the rural municipality of Mikkeli and left for America at the age of 20 in search of a better livelihood. There he met Amanda (Manda) Maria Kumpumaki from Reisjarvi. They married in 1907 and then decided to return to Finland and settle in Otto's home region of Mikkeli. Manda's father, Gabriel Kumpumaki, died in January 1908 shortly after the young couple returned, and Manda's mother, Gustavus, was widowed. At the funeral, the widow became so enamored with her Son-in-Law from Savo that she asked the young couple to stay in the house. The matter did not turn into a savonian project that is not ready to start, but the solution was made right away. In April 1908, Otto and Manda moved to Reisjarvi. After the rocky fields of Savo, Otto fell in love with the rockless lands of Ostrobothnia, which were much easier to clear. Two of Otto's sisters, Hilma and Elina, also moved to work in Reisjarvi. After that, Hilma married Heikki Pesola in the same year that Otto was founding Osuuskassa. Elina later married Kalle Puurula. The siblings had a total of 29 children. Otto Liikanen had to go through the hardest season during the shortage years of the 1930s. He was a co-owner and guarantor of a local sawmill that went bust. Otto and Manda's house went to a forced auction as collateral. They finally got it back. But the losses were palpable. The equity ratio of the cooperative funds was low, but the smallness of the loss buffer was compensated by the unlimited additional obligation of the members of the cooperative fund for the debts of the cooperative fund. In other words, if one of the members of the fund left his loan unmanaged, the others had to make up for the shortfall that had arisen. The resulting social pressure maintained a high debt-paying morale. Cooperative funds adhered to one of the most important principles of banking - the feeling of your customers. Reisjarvi Cooperative Bank has remained vibrant throughout history through the transition periods and, like other cooperative banks, has played a significant role in developing the locality and its business life, as well as supporting association activities. As a cooperative fund, its activities included not only lending, but also education, education and the promotion of thrift in the spirit of the cooperative idea. It also contributed to the habituation of those living in the countryside to the monetary economy. More broadly, it has played an important role in promoting association activities. Cooperative banks are cooperatives owned by their members. For cooperative banks, a key source of new capital is often the accumulation of retained earnings through profitable business operations. For this reason, small cooperative banks operating locally typically have large capital buffers and also good solvency. In addition, cooperative banks often have more deposits than loans on their balance sheets. Thus, banks do not have to finance their lending with securities-based liabilities, which in a crisis situation may prove to be a less stable source of financing than deposits. Cooperative banks often focus on the development of local business, which emphasizes the exploitation of local information and the so-called "green light". soft information. In terms of type, their business model can be defined as relationship banking. It plays a key role in lending small businesses. In her doctoral dissertation, Eeva Kerola, an economist at the Bank of Finland, has studied the success of cooperative and savings banks during the economic crisis in Europe. Compared to commercial banks, cooperative banks with a close-knit group structure in particular have recently performed well. During the crisis, their profitability has remained stable and has improved relative to commercial banks. In addition, their credit ratings have deteriorated less than commercial banks. During the crisis, banks operating under the public relations model offered more favourable conditions and continued to lend. Thanks to good information, they also survived with fewer credit losses. All in all, according to Kerola's doctoral dissertation, cooperative and savings banks had a mitigating effect on the effects of the crisis. CHANGES IN THE BANKING ENVIRONMENT For banks, the world looks very different today than it did 10 years ago. At that time, finland's economy had been growing continuously for a decade. Credit made its trade, and banks' mortgage portfolios grew rapidly, even though interest rates were clearly higher than at present. Banking regulation and supervision also differed from the current one. On the reform of the prudential regulation of banks, the so-called . On Basel II, agreement had been reached, but the regulation was still based on the previous Basel I. Supervision was national and there were considerable differences between countries in the content of supervision and in the content of banking regulation. In many ways, the current situation is different from 10 years ago. The volume of Finland's GDP has remained lower than in the peak years and is not expected to return to the record level of 2008 for a long time yet. We can talk about the lost decade of economic growth. The situation in the financial markets has also changed. Interest rates are historically low, and the shortest EURIBOR rates have sunk into negative territory. The average interest rate on the mortgage portfolio is lower than ever before (1.3%). Nevertheless, loan growth has remained subdued, partly as households have become more cautious. The development described above is based on both international and domestic factors. The global financial crisis that erupted in 2007 and the subsequent european sovereign debt crisis and the deep recession in the real economy changed the situation. The Finnish economy has been weighed down by both cyclical and structural factors. Our goods exports decreased. Exports of mobile phones contracted sharply after 2007. The spread of online magazines and e-readers reduced the demand for paper and the slowdown in global economic growth reduced the demand for investment goods. Every year, more people leave the working-age population than enter it. The difficulties of the Russian economy have also been passed on to Finnish exports. CHANGES IN BANKING REGULATION - BASEL The regulation and supervision of banks has also changed. The crisis highlighted serious shortcomings in the prudential regulation of banks. European banks had been required to have insufficient own funds in relation to the risks, and their own funds contained items that did not cover losses in a crisis situation. In addition, liquidity that used to work well between banks, which was previously taken for granted, dried up at times, causing problems in the banking system and, more broadly, in financial intermediation. There was a broad reaction to the situation. The Financial Stability Board (FSB), which coordinates the policies of the financial sector, stressed the importance of improving the risk-bearing capacity of financial institutions. Preparations were made for a new banking regulatory package, Basel III. Among other things, it required banks to set aside more and, in particular, better quality own capital for their risks. The Basel III recommendations have been transposed into legislation at EU and national level. The new definitions of solvency have been applied since the beginning of 2014. Much progress has been made, but the work continues. PANKKIUNIONI Since the summer of 2012, Europe has made rapid progress in building a banking union. For the time being, the banking union consists of single banking supervision and single resolution. Its third element, a common deposit insurance scheme, is the next challenge, which requires all national systems to be on the same level. The objective of SSM is effective, supranational and consistent supervision. Banks in the euro area are supervised by a single supervisory mechanism consisting of the European Central Bank and the national supervisory authorities of the euro area countries. The largest, with a balance sheet of over 30 billion. credit institutions in euros are under the direct supervision of the ECB, including the 4 largest credit institutions in Finland. The single resolution has also been promoted. A single resolution mechanism has been established in the euro area, consisting of the Single Resolution Board and the national resolution authorities, in Finland the Financial Stability Authority. Its task is to ensure the orderly resolution of problem banks in the banking union countries in such a way as to minimise the impact on the real economy and public finances. The mechanism will have full resolution powers from the beginning of 2016. The division of labour is similar to that of banking supervision: the SRB is responsible for the resolution of significant banks and cross-border banks supervised by the ECB, and the NRAs are responsible for the resolution of other banks. From the beginning of next year, investor responsibility will apply, in which bank creditors will participate in the recovery efforts of banks in difficulty. There is a major paradigm shift, as it will no longer be assumed that the state and taxpayers will ultimately bear the costs of rescuing problem banks. The aim of the COMMON DEPOSIT INSURANCE SCHEME is to increase the resilience of the financial system and to reduce the link between banks' and sovereign problems. This year, the European Commission will publish its proposal for a common deposit insurance scheme. The Commission is likely to propose, at least in the initial phase, an insurance scheme based on existing national deposit guarantee schemes, which would work like reinsurance. There are currently large differences in the funding rates of national deposit guarantee schemes, and a move to common funding would require closing these differences. Therefore, the construction of a common deposit insurance scheme is not without its problems. However, when it comes to decision-making, we must be able to look far enough into the future. The safety net created by the common deposit guarantee scheme would limit the risks to public finances, especially in countries where the banking sector is concentrated like Finland. THE CURRENT SITUATION IN THE FINNISH BANKING SECTOR The current environment in which banks operate is characterised by slow economic growth and low interest rates. The ECB's monetary policy has been strongly accommodative. In addition to the low key interest rates, the ECB implements a comprehensive securities purchase programme. Money market interest rates are low across the board, and short-term EURIBOR rates have sunk into negative territory. The fall in market interest rates has been passed on to the borrowing rates of non-financial corporations and households, as variable rate loans make up a large part of the loan portfolio. Indeed, the margin between loan and deposit rates has decreased. In addition to the low level of interest rates, the slow growth in loan and deposit volumes has weighed on banks' net interest income, which has reduced its share of banks' total income. No major change in this is expected, as financial markets expect interest rates to remain low also in the coming years. However, other income has partly compensated for the subdued development of net interest income. Banks have actively marketed higher-yielding investment and saving products than deposits, such as asset management, mutual funds and insurance savings. In particular, the popularity of investment funds has increased, which has increased banks' commission income. Profitability has also been supported by slow cost growth and low credit losses. Overall, the risk-bearing capacity of the Finnish banking sector has remained good. Banks have a sufficient amount of own funds, and the quality of own funds is high. MAKROVAKAUSPOLITIIKKA Financial supervisors have traditionally focused on the supervision of individual financial institutions. The international financial crisis, on the other hand, gave impetus to the new so-called financial crisis. the development of macroprudential policies. It pays wider attention to risks to the financial system which, if realised, could also cause serious disturbances to the real economy. The objective of macroprudential policy is to reduce the likelihood of such threats and to minimise the impact of actual threats. To achieve this objective, public authorities need a macroprudential toolbox. Finland's macroprudential authority is the Financial Supervisory Authority, whose Board of Directors decides on the variable capital add-on requirement, the so-called capital add-on. on the setting of the countercyclical buffer. The objective of the variable capital add-on is to mitigate changes in the credit cycle and thus contribute to the stable development of financial intermediation. In addition, at the beginning of next year, the so-called "green belts" will come into force. macroprudential instruments that allow public authorities to set a maximum loan-to-value ratio for mortgage lending, the so-called mortgage lending ratio. the loan ceiling, as well as the additional capital requirements imposed on four credit institutions considered to be of systemic importance for the Finnish financial system. It is important for the effectiveness of macroprudential policies that macroprudential instruments are available even before a potential crisis, so that public authorities can act swiftly if necessary. GENERAL ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT IN FINLAND Despite the improved outlook for the euro area, finland's economic growth has been subdued. As I said above, the Finnish economy has been hit by many different shocks at the same time, which have narrowed the bottom of industry and exports and dampened economic growth. The important thing is to recognize the facts. Many of these problems are long-term and will not go away as the economic cycle changes. That is why we need structural reforms. Pension reform is one of them. On the other hand, it is important that the government and parliament also proceed in the so-called "green light". with regard to the health and social services reform. We must be able to increase productivity everywhere, including in public services. Common funds must do more. Finland lost its cost competitiveness strongly between 2008 and 2009. First, the increase in nominal wages significantly exceeded the pace of competitor countries, and then, with the recession, productivity plummeted. It would be very desirable for the social partners to find solutions in their negotiations to improve cost competitiveness. Well-functioning public finances and services are one of the pillars of the welfare society. When our national product has contracted markedly, the national economy's ability to finance shared services has decreased. Finland's rate of indebtedness cannot continue clearly faster than the others. The problems of the Finnish economy are great, but we also have our strengths. We have a good education system and a functioning administration. We have women and men widely available on the labour market. We can trust the judiciary and we have no corruption. The country has a lot of entrepreneurial and innovation potential. On the basis of these strengths and a correct assessment of the situation, it is now necessary to build a foundation for growth and employment. This will require a concerted effort by all. I would like to offer my best congratulations to reisjarvi cooperative bank, which is celebrating its 100th anniversary.
