Title: Optimism, pessimism and realism in economic policy, 27 November 2015
text: President Erkki Liikanen: Optimism, pessimism and realism in economic policy, 27.11.2015 . Speech . Friday 27 November 2015,2:00 PM President and CEO Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland Speech at Mauno Koivisto lecture at the University of Turku Turku, 27.11.2015 Esityskalvot (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches/documents/el-27-11-2015.pdf) . OPTIMISM, PESSIMISM AND REALISM IN ECONOMIC POLICY Ladies and gentlemen, Thank you for the invitation to give this year's Mauno-Koivisto lecture. It is a great honour and a pleasant task. I have chosen the importance of optimism, pessimism and realism in economic policy as my subject. I chose the topic because of its topicality, but it also touches on Mauno Koivisto in that he famously gained the reputation of a persistent pessimist in the 1970s. Mauno Koivisto was the Governor of the Bank of Finland at a time when Finland had to radically revise its economic growth prospects. Koivisto became president of the Bank of Finland in 1968, at a time marked by great growth optimism from a modern perspective. The prospects for the prospects of a rapid rise in living standards were downright utopian. Economic policy was thought to be able to guarantee rapid and undisturbed economic growth long into the future. However, after a few years, the growth folded. The turning point is considered to be the first oil crisis of 1973. Then, for a long time, the world drifted into stagflation, a state characterised by lower growth and higher inflation than usual. It took time for it to be understood that the changes that had taken place were structural, and there was no going back to the old rate of growth. In 1974, shortly after the oil crisis, Helsingin Sanomat organized a forecasting competition in which economic influencers were asked to draw the GDP curve for the following years with their free hand. The curve drawn by Director General Koivisto was different from that of the other participants. He predicted a very long and deep recession ahead. Koivisto was one of the first to see that the world had changed and also conveyed this message to the domestic public. Based on his prediction, financial journalists named Koivisto the "economic pessimist of the year". Although the recession of the 1970s became even deeper and longer than Koivisto had predicted, koivisto's reputation as a pessimist remained. The citizens sensed that Koivisto was not trying to at least flatter, but told things as they were. It was even considered one of the main reasons for his popularity. In Finland, the problems came to a head when, after the mid-1970s, a current account crisis occurred. In order to resolve it, recourse was made to the international monetary fund's support credit and the associated austerity programme. Urho Kekkonen declared a national emergency, which was resolved by Martti Miettunen's emergency government. Balancing the economy was a painful process. I vividly remember when, as a young member of parliament at a meeting of a parliamentary group, I asked Koivisto, following well-known academic economists: "The current account must be balanced, but wouldn't a slower schedule be better for economic growth?" Koivisto didn't like my question at all. He was indignant that I belonged to young people who had read the books and who did not understand the realities of economic policy. I have lingered here in the history of Koivisto's term as President because it feels familiar when compared to the current economic situation and the debate on economic policy. Also in the mid-1970s, both in Finland and elsewhere in the industrialised countries, a situation arose in which the previous model of economic growth had reached an impasse and a new basis for growth had to be sought. Previous expectations and thought habits had to be reassessed. *** Even today, Finland is going through a period of transition. As with the turnaround of the 1970s, the current upheaval was preceded by an exceptionally favorable period that lasted more than ten years. During the period from the beginning of EU membership until the financial crisis of 2008, Finland's national economy was one of the most successful in Europe and the world. Now, however, Finland's economic growth has stagnated and turned into a contraction in production and income generation, which has been going on for a long time. The balance of the national economy has deteriorated. However, it took too many years for the situation to really wake up and realize its seriousness. Why did it take so long to recognize and acknowledge the economic crisis? There are several reasons for this. First of all, at the beginning of the negative turnaround, the basic balance of the Finnish national economy was historically good. We had a large current account surplus then, so we as a nation had clearly more income than we spent. A similar situation exists on the fiscal side. Finland's general government finances as a whole showed a surplus, and the general government debt that had grown during the recession of the 1990s had been paid off at a good pace. Even on the employment side, the starting point was relatively good. The unemployment rate had fallen to around 6 per cent. From this point of view, it was possible to weaken the balance of the economy for many years before the seriousness of the situation began to dawn on the Finns. Another reason for the slow perception of the nature of our problems was that the turnaround in the Finnish economy, which has now proved to be structural  the end of growth  coincided with the slump in world trade caused by the international financial crisis. In the year following the collapse of the Lehman Brothers bank, there was a drastic dive in international trade and production, affecting all countries, including Finland. The signals of the financial crisis and the beginning of our own structural crisis were mixed together. It took some time for it to become clear that Finland would not recover from that dip at the same rate as most of the other industrialised countries. The third reason was that Finland belonged to the euro area, which softened the effects of the negative turnaround on Finland. The European Central Bank lowered its key interest rates shortly after the crisis began. The expansionary effect of this was felt particularly strongly in Finland, as in Finland, banks' lending rates are generally linked to short-term market rates. Indeed, bank lending in Finland has continued to be higher than average in the rest of the euro area in recent years. The fourth reason is that the contraction of the working-age population has mitigated the impact of job losses on the unemployment rate. The fifth reason is that households' real disposable income and private consumption have continued to grow, albeit at a slowdown, despite the end of general economic growth. While the total output (GDP) of the national economy has contracted clearly from its peak in 2008, according to Statistics Finland's figures, households' disposable real income was nearly ten per cent higher last year than in 2008. This has mitigated the prospects for an economic turnaround in everyday life. The increase in household incomes has been supported by the general government deficit, which at the same time has meant a rapid increase in public debt. The sixth reason may be psychological. It is humane that the worst news should first be thwarted. There is a well-known Kubler-Ross theory about this in psychology  a theory known as a model: People tend to initially look for reasons to deny inconvenient facts. At the next stage, the damage is then angered. Koivisto has also often emphasized this. It is only when it is realised that the denial of the facts cannot continue any longer that people can move on. *** During the past year, too, there have often been speeches in which the seriousness of the state of the national economy has been questioned. The reports produced by officials have been deemed to be tendentiously pessimistic. It has even been claimed that the assessment of the situation was guided by an attempt to seek the numbers to justify actions motivated by a political agenda. In two respects, this denial has been particularly striking: firstly, the depth of Finland's fiscal imbalances and the need to adjust them have been called into question. Secondly, attempts have been made to circumvent the fact that Finland's cost competitiveness has been severely weakened and is a brake on industrial recovery and employment growth. As counterproposals, it is said that this changes when comparing with other countries and changing the period of comparison. One can often disagree on economic policy and its objectives. This is natural, because economic policy has to make choices that are ultimately based on values and reconciling the interests of different social groups. This is not to say that the facts can be freely selected according to it, which leads to a more comfortable picture of the tasks ahead. When Mauno Koivisto specifically wrote a doctoral dissertation on sociology at this university, I would like to quote Patrick Moynihan, professor of sociology at Harvard: "Everyone has the right to their own opinion, but not to their own facts." Moynihan later also served as a Democratic senator and U.S. ambassador to the UN. Let's open it up a bit. In a democracy, economic policy is based on political debate and the idea that values and facts can be separated. It is important for the functioning of democracy that an objective knowledge base is sought as a basis for decision-making. It is unlikely to be fully achieved, but the aim is to achieve it. Efforts must be made to respect the difference between values and facts. The task of the study is to broaden the common knowledge base on which competing opinion groups can rely and which they can accept as starting points. In the preparation of economic policy, this is an important task of the civil service. If there is no common factual basis, or if the possibility of objectivity is also disputed, then social debate and the democratic process as a whole will become really difficult, if not impossible. Under such circumstances, any solution seems to either side to be injustices based on incorrect information or even a lie. The approach can be taken by taking an example of the relationship between climate research and climate policy. It is becoming increasingly clear that global warming, caused by carbon dioxide and methane emissions, poses a serious threat to the future of humanity. In the end, this should not be a matter of opinion: it is the responsibility of the study to find out whether global warming and the human contribution to it are true or not. Climate scientists do not agree on everything, and that is not even to be expected. But this does not negate the principle that research should be expected to strive for objectivity. It would even be problematic if it were accepted as a starting point that, on the climate issue, for example, the results of scientists only reflect their political opinions. One could therefore safely choose what to believe and who to believe. If that happens, humanity will be incapable of doing anything about climate change. Rational politics is based on the fact that society can rely on the scientific process, its purposes and the possibility of objective knowledge. My example was from the side of natural science, where the requirement of objectivity is perhaps easier to implement than in the social sciences. However, even in economic research, the goal of objectivity is as necessary as in climate research. If I think of my experience as a decision-maker, I certainly would not want to rely on an expert who acts on a pre-established political agenda. The decision-maker will also feel uncomfortable if he or she finds that the preparation has only tried to justify a position that the decision-maker already had, or that he or she was thought to have. *** A glaring example of what abandoning the objective of objectivity can lead to is the misrepresentation of Greek government deficit statistics in the first decade of the 2000s. It lulled creditors and the European Union into a false sense of security about what was happening in Greece's public finances. The facts were revealed after the change of government in the autumn of 2009. Indeed, Greece's actual deficit was much higher than had previously been announced. Once this became clear, Greece's creditworthiness plummeted and it was no longer able to cover its deficit on the private loan market. It became dependent on credits from other euro area countries and implemented the austerity adjustment programme agreed as a condition for the loans. The Greeks have had to pay a high price for the long-standing cover-up of the economic situation. As a result of the euro crisis, the importance of economic statistics in the economic policies of the euro area countries has become even more important. New, stronger procedures have been put in place to ensure that member states do not run into difficulties such as those in Greece. Economic statistics, such as GDP and public sector deficit and debt statistics, are no longer just background information used for economic policy to support decision-making, but increasingly binding norms have been built on them. Such an emphasis on the role of economic statistics places increasing demands on statistical production and the analyses derived from it being as objective as possible and trusted by all parties involved. *** A classic of economic policy theory, the Dutchman Jan Tinbergen discussed the relationship between civil service preparation and politics as early as 1952 in his very influential book "On the Theory of Economic Policy". He stressed the importance of the distinction between objective and political dimensions. Tinbergen's pioneering work was later rewarded when, in 1969, he became the first Nobel Laureate in Economics (together with the Norwegian Ragnar Frisch). Although Jan Tinbergen's book dates back decades, its philosophy is nevertheless a good point of reference when discussing the issue due to its clarity. The economic policy process, according to Tinbergen, has five stages: 1. Definition of the status quo. 2. Forecast of how the economy would develop if economic policy were to continue unchanged. 3. Studying the impact of economic policy options. 4. Decision-making, i.e. making choices between alternative policies. 5. Implementation of policy decisions. Tinbergen distinguished between economic policy instruments on the one hand and economic policy objectives on the other. Famous is the so-called. Tinbergen's principle that there should be at least as many instruments at the disposal of economic policy as there are objectives. According to Tinbergen, the roles of politician and expert should be clearly separated. It is the task of the political decision-maker to set the objectives of economic policy and to determine the framework within which different means can be used. The decision-maker must reflect society's preferences and decide how to weight different goals, even conflicting ones. On the other hand, the task of the economist is to map out the status quo and analyze the available means. Economic analysis cannot, on the basis of facts alone, lead to solutions to the problems of economic policy. But economic analysis, however, in Tinbergen's view, has three important functions: The economic analysis must assess the compatibility of the economic policy objectives with each other and also the compatibility of the objectives with the available policy instruments. By locating potential contradictions, the analysis can limit the options for decision-making and thus contribute to economic policy-making. If the objectives are sufficiently well defined, the economic analysis can find the values of the instruments at which the objectives would most likely be achieved. In Tinbergen's theory, the difference between the roles of decision-maker and draftsman corresponds to the difference between values and facts. From today's perspective, these divisions may seem natural. But at the time of Tinbergen, they were radical. And it's good to try to hold on to them even today. *** A more general issue in this regard is the relationship between, on the one hand, the preparation of officials and, on the other hand, political preparation before the actual decision-making. For a long time in Finland, the political preparation of matters was carried out within the framework of political parties. Mauno Koivisto was minister of finance when party support stabilized. It provided an economic basis for the parties' programming. The preparation of civil servants was separate from this in the ministries. Over the years, the situation has changed. The parties' resources have been reduced and have been deliberately reduced. Similarly, the number of political assistants to ministers within ministries has increased, although it took some step backwards recently, how large, I cannot judge. As a result, the responsibility of civil servants has been blurred and, as a result, the quality of preparation has deteriorated, as the line between official preparation and political preparation is not visible. Secondly, the development that has taken place has weakened the popular movement nature of the parties and their independence vis-a-vis the state. Even at this level, the boundaries are blurred. That is not good for democracy. I have great respect for both elected political decision-makers and civil servants who carry out independent work with official responsibility. I have been in both positions. I have also enjoyed the guidance of distinguished officials. When I was a young minister, The State Secretary was Teemu Hiltunen and the President of Postipankki was an experienced civil servant and minister Heikki Tuominen. The difference between the duties of a political decision-maker and an official became clear at that school. In recent years, there has not always been the same clarity. It often seems to an outsider that political assistants go into the field of civil servants, and officials go into the field of politics. *** To return to the relationship between optimism and pessimism in the debate on economic policy: There has been an interesting contradiction in the debate: When the message about the state of the Finnish economy has been deliberately suspected of being pessimistic, in the context of the euro area crisis, there has been accusation of unwarranted optimism and denial of problems. In the midst of the financial crisis, there is a desire to make statements in support of confidence. Just think of the alternative. However, to accuse oneself of naive optimism is unreasonable when you consider how tough decisions have been taken in the end to lift the euro area out of the eye of the crisis. One good example is the establishment of single banking supervision, which led national authorities to abandon the previous of his power. The construction of a single resolution system and the implementation of investor responsibility is another example. False optimism and false pessimism both have their own dangers. That is why building a common, realistic factual basis as a basis for decision-making is more important in Finland now than it has perhaps been for decades. This places even higher demands on objectivity than usual for the machinery for preparing economic policy, for research institutes and also for the work of economists within organisations. Such a demand is not a pipe dream, but the lifeblood of effective social debate and political decision-making. Optimism is important in the sense of understanding that problems can be solved when they are tackled. Optimism in economic policy becomes counterproductive if it manifests itself in the form of a denial of problems and adaptation needs. *** There are also grounds for optimism in Finland. The basic strengths of Finland's national economy  its fundamentals  remain strong. This is also reflected in the fact that in those competitiveness comparisons where the emphasis is on economic fundamentals and not on the cost level, Finland ranks well. For example, in the latest report published by the World Economic Forum two months ago, Finland was the fourth best European country and ranked eighth in the global comparison. Despite the slight decline, the ranking was still good. The list of strengths is handsome. The WEF drew attention to the following, among others:  Our public institutions are functional and transparent  Finland's innovation capacity is top-notch  Our education system is excellent  Our banking system has evolved  Our technological capabilities are good  Finnish infrastructure is of a high standard Finland's starting point for success in international competition is therefore in good shape in many respects. But at the same time, it must be stressed that, despite these proven strengths, the actual performance of our economy is not good. Since 2008, it has shown itself to be significantly worse than the average for euro area countries. This year, we are already completing a nine-year period during which Finland's national economy has not grown at all. A similar stagnation in growth has not been experienced before in Finland's recorded economic history. It does not seem to be possible to convert the undeniable strengths of the Finnish national economy into sustainable economic growth. It is obvious that success will require major changes, at least in public finances and the labour market. Two sore questions stand out above all others. One of them is Finland's price competitiveness. The second is the general government deficit. Let's start with competitiveness. How bad or good is Finland's current price competitiveness now, and how good should it be? Competitiveness can be measured directly, by means of international cost and price comparisons or by looking at how competitiveness is reflected in practice. In his studies published last summer, Lauri Kajanoja has, to his credit, examined the issues related to benchmarking competitiveness and tried to find the most reliable and justifiable way to answer the question of what the state of Finland's price competitiveness is in relation to other countries and what it should be in order to support balanced economic growth. When assessing competitiveness, in addition to the wage level prevailing in the various countries, many other factors must be taken into account, such as differences in productivity between countries, the level of non-wage labour costs and, in addition, the price development of exported products, i.e. the terms of trade. The most common measure is relative unit labour costs, which describes the evolution of labour costs relative to competitor countries, adjusted for changes in productivity. The figure shows that relative unit labour costs have developed unfavourably for us. They are now at least ten per cent higher than they were before the financial crisis  and back then we had a thriving mobile phone sector that could pay high wages. Now a large part of that ability to pay wages has disappeared. Therefore, in order to assess the severity of the competitiveness problem, it is not sufficient to compare the change in the relative cost level in Finland with the situation in one of the more or less arbitrarily selected reference years or in the analogue country. The key is to analyse what level of price competitiveness would be compatible with the balance of the national economy. After all, the adequacy of price competitiveness is recognised by its consequences. Good competitiveness is one that leads to export success that allows for balanced growth of the national economy. The signs of the developments that have now taken place are bad. From the peak reached in 2007, the volume of industrial output has decreased by a quarter. It is true that part of this is due to a single market change, the collapse of the mobile phone sector. But if you look at an industry other than the electronics industry, its production has also fallen by almost a fifth. The decline in industry is due to a contraction in exports. In part, of course, one can blame the difficult conditions on the international market, but that does not explain everything. In fact, since 2007, Finnish exports have developed clearly weaker than in the analogue countries, which have also had to compete in the same difficult conditions. The underlying cause of the problems is therefore low competitiveness, which is of course not only due to past wage increases, but also to many other things, among them the defeat of our mobile phone sector in the technology competition in the sector and the constant increase in the need for labour in the care and health sectors. But in order to put the economy back on a growth path, Finland's competitiveness should be brought to a level where our export sector can also thrive in the current, increasingly difficult market conditions and from finland's current technological starting point. The Kajanoja study I mentioned came to the conclusion that the need to correct Finland's cost competitiveness - relative labour costs  is in the order of 10-15 per cent. Kajanoja estimates that such a competitiveness improvement would be needed in order for Finland to return to the growth path without the current account being thrown out of sustainable balance as a result of the recovery. The challenge is great, and it's no wonder there's a temptation to explain it away. However, this temptation should be resisted. Another sore point in the debate, along with competitiveness, is the public deficit. Until 2008, the income and expenditure of the municipalities and the state as a whole were fairly closely balanced for us, and thanks to the accumulation of social security funds, the entire general government finances showed a surplus. After the fall in GDP in 2009, the combined deficit of municipalities and central government rose to around EUR 10 billion and has remained in this magnitude since then. This has been going on for seven years now. At the same time as the weakening of central and local government finances, the previously large surplus of social security funds has also been reduced to a small amount. In fact, the deterioration in Finland's public finances in recent years has been exceptionally large even by European comparison. According to estimates by the European Commission From 2008 to 2014, Finland's general government structural deficit increased more than in the other EU countries and much more than in the other euro area countries. At the same time as crisis countries such as Greece, Ireland, Portugal and Spain have made significant adjustments, we have seen a significant increase in our structural deficits. The fact that this has been possible is, of course, due to the fact that our starting point was so much better than that of the countries mentioned, which have gone through the financial crisis. The fact that it has so far been possible for us to allow this increase in the general government deficit has supported domestic demand and thus partly explains why the weakening of the economic base has not yet been fully reflected in the everyday life of the average Finn. Of course, this is no consolation to the large number of citizens who, as a result of finland's loss of competitiveness and the upheavals in the world market, have been forced to give up their jobs or whose economy has otherwise deteriorated. But it shows that maintaining the current prosperity, let alone increasing it, requires putting the national economy on a more solid footing. In September, the Ministry of Finance published the so-called "Green Paper". in the context of the General Government Fiscal Plan, its latest estimates of the structural share of Finland's general government deficit and the extent to which it can be estimated to be due to weak economic cycles. According to that estimate, more than half of the deficit has become structural. The Bank of Finland will publish its own, independent assessment of the state of Finland's general government finances in connection with the Finnish economic forecast in less than two weeks' time, on Thursday 10 December. I cannot prejudge the numerical estimates that will be published at that time, but it is clear that the situation is so serious that the work of restoring public finances to a sustainable path must be pursued with determination. The assessment of both the competitiveness gap and the structural deficit in the public sector are the most crucial tasks in terms of the economic policy situation. They are not easy tasks but require serious, professional work. They are also difficult because the results can be difficult to accept. But still, the analysis should not be colored, neither optimism nor pessimism, but realism. It means acknowledging the facts. Economic policy must be able to rely on a reliable knowledge base produced by officials in statistics offices, ministries and the Central Bank, and critically evaluated by experts from various research institutes and organisations. This critical assessment of the factual basis is, of course, important. But it also involves the responsibility of keeping the debate on economic policy on track where it is possible to discuss solutions. This is especially the case now, when the Finnish economy is in the worst predicament for a long time. Instead of denying problems, we need to find solutions to them. A way out of problems must be built on the basis of realistic analysis. For that, on the other hand, we need a positive, even optimistic attitude instead of cynicism. The position of decision-makers is not easy. In this they need our support.

Title: Speech at the Sammat Independence Day celebration on 6 December 2015
text: President and CEO Erkki Liikanen's speech at sammat's independence day celebration 6.12.2015 . Speech . Sunday 6 December 2015, 12:00 PM President and CEO Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland Speech at Sammat's Independence Day celebration Sammatti, 6.12.2015 Dear festive audience! Ladies and gentlemen! Elias Lonnrot, the son of a tailor from Sammat, was five years old when two emperors, Napoleon of France and Alexander I of Russia, gathered for peace negotiations in the summer of 1807 in Tilsit. Tilsit is located in Kalingrad, which is now part of Russia. Napoleon had been successful in many battles and the resources of the Russian army began to decline. The negotiations were conducted in French, one of the heads spoke it without emphasis. He was Alexander I. In the negotiations, peace was made and an alliance between the parties was agreed. It was important for Napoleon to enclose England under an embargo. After various stages, it became Russia's task to involve Sweden in the alliance. Sweden responded negatively in January 1808. In late February, Russian troops crossed the border. The result was the Finnish War of 18081809, at the end of which Finland became part of Russia. After the end of the war, the Emperor convened the Diet of Porvoo, where, in a well-known speech, he elevated Finland to the ranks of nations. Finland became an autonomous part of Russia, the Grand Duchy. A pro-reform period followed, during which important national institutions were established, such as the Bank of Finland, which was founded in 1811. Elias Lonnrot came from humble circumstances, and therefore it was not easy to get to his studies despite the gifts. He eventually matriculated in his early twenties and was admitted to the Turku Academy in 1822. His fellow students included J.L. Runeberg and J.V. Snellman, two other future figures of the nation. Already at the age of 26, Lonnrot headed for his first poetry collection trip. The rest is history. The first version of the Kalevala appeared ten years later. Lonnrot became the second father of the Finnish literary language after Mikael Agricola, and the Kalevala became a source of exhaustive inspiration in the creation of the nation and its culture. The next major turning points date back to the 1860s. Emperor AlexanderII had risen to power in the late 1850s and he convened the estates in Helsinki for the first time in over 50 years in the autumn of 1863. The legislative work resumed. There were many, even major, changes. Local government gradually shifted from the church to the municipalities. Another important change was that the Bank of Finland was transferred to the estates, i.e. the legislators. This happened, but only later, due to J.V. Snellman's opposition. Banking delegates of the Finnish Parliament history dates back so far. J.V. Snellman had a great influence on the history of the Finnish markka. Before the Crimean War, roubles were used as money in Finland, and the country was firmly on the silver standard together with Russia. However, the outbreak of war in 1854 triggered a monetary crisis, as a result of which the exchangeability of the ruble for silver had to be abolished. It brought many difficulties. When the value of money was no longer tied to silver, it quickly began to decline. There was a shortage of change because the silver coin disappeared into the coffers of speculators. The worst thing for Finland was that exchange rates in relation to traditional trading partners in Sweden and northern Germany began to fluctuate. Trade and access to foreign credit became more difficult. The Finns wanted a solution to the question of money. The Emperor responded to the petitions by awarding Finland its own currency, the Mark, in 1860. However, it was defined in relation to the banknote ruble, its quarter. When the banknote ruble remained legal tender, this reform did not yet bring a solution to the main problem of how to return to the silver standard. When Snellman became chief of finance in 1863, he took it upon himself to tie the mark to the silver standard. Snellman traveled to St. Petersburg to negotiate on the matter and obtained the emperor's consent that the mark could be redefined, not the ruble in general, but specifically the silver ruble as a quarter. The Imperial Manifesto, which stipulated that domestic and Russian silver coins would henceforth become the only legal means of payment in Finland, was published 150 years ago, in November 1865. The introduction of its own currency, the markka, was not an instrument of isolation, but precisely an integration project. The decisive factor was that the mark was tied to the silver standard. Because of this, the statue of Snellman is in front of the Bank of Finland. However, times were not easy. The banknote ruble had weakened drastically, and the markka with it. Tying to the silver standard meant a jump-like strengthening of the markka. After that, an international financial crisis arose. In 1867, Finland was hit by a great extinction. Even after the import of foreign grain, the shortfall was as much as a third of normal demand. There was a great famine with hordes of beggars and epidemics. In alleviating it, Snellman was considered a failure and was forced to resign from the Senate. The reason was procrastination in importing grain, not the silver stock. Due to the silver standard, the chances of obtaining credit had increased. In 1865, exactly 150 years ago, two great men of our culture, Jean Sibelius and Akseli Gallen-Kallela, were born. They rose to the top of our culture at a very young age. The inspiration for their first major works was Lonnrot's Kalevala. In 1889, Akseli Gallen-Kallela painted his first major work in Paris, Aino-Triptych. This is part of the Collection of the Bank of Finland. Gallen-Kallela was a 24-year-old artist who had to convince his father-in-law of his ability to support his daughter Mary. He wanted to show it with a great painting work dominated by Aino and Vainamoinen. Aino became Gallen-Kallela's first major work. Its second version was completed in 1891 and can be seen at the Ateneum. It already has Mary's "imprint". Jean Sibelius, on the other hand, began composing Kullervo at the age of 25 in Vienna in 1891. When he returned to Finland in the autumn, he had the opportunity to listen in person to Larin Paraske. Kullervo premiered in the spring of 1892 was a great success. Even before Kullervo, Sibelius had begun composing the texts of Lonnrot's third fellow student, J.L. Runeberg, into songs. Sibelius married Aino Jarnefelt in the summer of 1892. The work of Sibelius, Gallen-Kallela and many other creative artists was inspired for a long time by the Kalevala and its birthplaces. But even that didn't mean isolation from the rest of the art. Sibelius spent long periods abroad and his music is ultimately universal. World War I broke out in 1914. It changed the world and Europe and left a long mark. The losses and internal problems suffered in the war drove Russia into a revolution in the spring of 1917. Finland sought to take advantage of the opportunity by seeking greater autonomy or independence. The Provisional Government took a negative view of it. The matter could only be decided when the Constituent Assembly met. The coming to power of the Bolsheviks in November changed the situation. Finland's political field was divided in how independence was to be pursued. Finally, the parliament met on 6.12.1917 and approved the declaration of independence issued by the bourgeois senate, that is, the government. Russia recognized the month of Finland, January 4. Sweden and France followed, and So did Germany. Sibelius's music was a symbol of a new, free Finland. Finlandia was the central number at the independence concert in Stockholm. His music  Finlandia and Jaeger March  was also played on 13 January 1918 at the Independence Festival held at the Finnish National Theatre. According to Erik Tawaststjerna's biography, Sibelius considered the organization of the independence celebration in those circumstances to be somewhat "malapropos", i.e. inappropriate. The Civil War broke out just two weeks later in late January. Finland was divided and the scars left over from it were deep. Sibelius's Ainola was located deep on the side of the Reds. Gallen-Kallela's Kalela, on the other hand, was on the other side of the border. Jean and Aino Sibelius feared, also for their lives. After his discussions, Robert Kajanus conveyed the information that the people's delegation wanted to safeguard Sibelius's integrity. Sibelius generally sought to keep his distance from politics, even though his circle of acquaintances, like himself, belonged to whites. Of course, there were slight differences of opinion even in the circle of acquaintances. Gallen-Kallela, on the other hand, joined Mannerheim's troops, first as a cartographer, but then at headquarters, where he designed the decorations. The Civil War ended in May 1918 with the victory of the whites. Let me quote Tawaststjerna again: "In June, the jaeger guard officers' embassy visited Sibelius in Aino and handed him a flower device. The roses delighted him, but the thorns at the same time reminded him that he had been dragged into politics: "I suffer from looks and prospects for the future. I'm afraid of the worst... The whole of Finland during the war i.e. in the sign of militarism. No understanding whatsoever of the symphonists' aspirations." Gallen-Kallela was also overwhelmed by similar feelings: "Tired of all the belligerence... I want to delve into myself again: Maybe I'll find a new path in it." After the end of the Civil War, the prison camps and the fate of those who lost became a sore point for years to come. In the Ekenas prison camp in the first winter, 1/3 died of starvation or epidemics. How was it possible that Finland could be restored by the outbreak of the Winter War in 1939? KyostiKalliopiti of the Agrarian League gave a famous speech back in May at the Church of Nivala: Reconciliation, not revenge. In July, J.V. Stahlberg was elected president. They played a major role in building reconciliation along with the social democrats elected to parliament. What about Mannerheim? He was, above all, a general of the whites in the 1920s. In 1930, he became chairman of the Defense Council. From the middle of the decade, he worked for the Nordic trend. In the rest of the Nordic countries, the Social Democrats were in government. Mannerheim began to present himself cautiously, but consistently in favor of reconciliation. During the war, he also made bold decisions himself, for which no one's prestige would have been enough. Instead of celebrating the victory in the War of Independence, a day of remembrance for the fallen began to be celebrated. It was followed by the January engagement between employers and employees. Let us return to Sibelius. His active compositional work continued after the Civil War. He received a new version of the 5th symphony in 1919, followed by the 6th and 7th symphonies and finally Tapiola in 1926. Sibelius was 60 years old at the time. Akseli Gallen-Kallela continued his work in the Kalevala district of Lonnrot. Koru-Kalevala was published in 1922. The overall illustration does not have time to be completed. Gallen-Kallela died in March 1931. Jean Sibelius composed The Mourning Call for the Funeral. It was Sibelius's last work. Sibelius lived to be 92 years old. I have wanted to deal with three great people who have meant a lot to Finnish identity today. We are celebrating the anniversary of Jean Sibelius and Akseli Gallen-Kallela, and we are doing it in Elias Lonnrot's home municipality, Sammat. Next, on finland's economy. The economic outlook has remained subdued. The problems in the economy have proven to be long-term. Since 2008, exports and business investment in export sectors have declined particularly much. Public finances are in a weak state. Relative to GDP, general government deficit has deepened by more than 3 per cent and general government debt by more than 60 per cent. Without new decisions, debt growth will continue at a rapid pace. More asylum seekers have arrived in Finland this year than in previous years. The impact of increased immigration on the long-term development of general government finances largely depends on the employment of persons remaining in Finland and their descendants. Immediately after immigration, the employment rate is lower than the average for the entire population, but over time, more and more people can be expected to find employment as language skills and other conditions improve. Research suggests that the integration measures of the authorities may have a significant impact on the employment of immigrants. In order to solve the long-standing problems of the economy, there has been a need to make progress in many areas. The first is to improve cost competitiveness. The second is structural reforms that improve the conditions for economic growth and the long-term sustainability of public finances. Thirdly, we need to halt the growth of public debt through adjustment measures. Cost competitiveness in Finland has deteriorated significantly, especially since 2007. Especially in export sectors, the profitability of production in Finland has deteriorated. The autumn 2013 wage settlement halted the decline in cost competitiveness, but did not yet lead to a substantial improvement in it, as the rate of increase in labour prices has also remained lower than usual on average in trading partner countries. Solutions are now needed that lead to a sufficiently large and sufficiently rapid improvement in cost competitiveness. Such solutions would improve the prospects for export and employment in export sectors. At the same time, they would sustainably improve the conditions for favourable employment development in the domestic market industries. In the field of structural reforms, the pension reform approved by Parliament this year is of great importance. Progress should also be made elsewhere. One is to complete the health and social services solution in such a way that the productivity of public services increases. Anti-competitive regulation can also be reduced in different sectors. The increase in public debt would be a lesser problem if strong economic growth were to be expected over a longer period of time. In Finland, on the other hand, the additional debt that is now being taken on will have to be managed in the future in a situation where a smaller part of the population is of working age and a larger part is retired, and where more people than at present need care and health services. In order to halt the increase in public debt, savings will have to be made. If no adjustment is made, today's young people will, in due course, have to both pay for the majority of the baby boomers' pensions and service the debts of the previous generation. In addition, they are forced to find a job in an economic situation, the problems of which, in a bad case, have still not been solved. The Finnish economy is going through a difficult phase. But even from these difficulties, a way out can be built through consistent and responsible action. I believe that the public understands the seriousness of the situation. They are prepared to play their part when the adjustment measures are made fairly for everyone and when we know that they are a condition for better growth and employment. Jaakko Valtanen, former Commander of the Finnish Defence Forces, gave an impressive interview to Helsingin Sanomat today. He says in an interview: "Cheer patriotism has no longer appealed to people since the wars". "The essential thing now is that we feel affection for the society we have chosen. That society can provide a decent person's life, livelihood and interpersonal relationships. That people have faith in the future." Happy Independence Day. Snellman matkusti Pietariin neuvottelemaan asiasta ja sai keisarin suostumuksen sille, ett<8a> markka voitiin m<8a><8a>ritell<8a> uudelleen, ei yleisesti ruplan, vaan nimenomaan hopearuplan nelj<8a>sosaksi. Keisarillinen manifesti, jossa m<8a><8a>r<8a>ttiin, ett<8a> kotimainen ja ven<8a>l<8a>inen hopearaha tulisivat t<8a>st<8a> l<8a>htien ainoiksi laillisiksi maksuv<8a>lineiksi Suomessa, julkaistiin 150 vuotta sitten, marraskuussa 1865. Oman rahayksik<9a>n, markan k<8a>ytt<9a><9a>notto ei ollut erist<8a>ytymisen v<8a>line, vaan nimenomaan integraatiohanke. Ratkaisevaa oli se, ett<8a> markka sidottiin hopeakantaan. T<8a>m<8a>n vuoksi Snellmanin patsas on Suomen Pankin edess<8a>. Ajat eiv<8a>t kuitenkaan olleet helpot. Setelirupla oli ehtinyt rajusti heikenty<8a> ja markka sen mukana. Sitominen hopeakantaan merkitsi markan hypp<8a>yksenomaista vahvistumista. Sen j<8a>lkeen syntyi viel<8a> kansainv<8a>linen finanssikriisi. Vuonna 1867 Suomea kohtasi suuri kato. Ulkomaisen viljan tuonnin j<8a>lkeenkin vajaus oli per<8a>ti kolmannes normaalista tarpeesta. Syntyi suuri n<8a>l<8a>nh<8a>t<8a> kerj<8a>l<8a>islaumoineen ja kulkutauteineen. Sen lievitt<8a>misess<8a> Snellmanin katsottiin ep<8a>onnistuneen ja h<8a>n joutui eroamaan senaatista. Syyn<8a> oli viivyttely viljantuonnissa, ei hopeakanta. Hopeakannan vuoksi mahdollisuudet saada luottoa olivat lis<8a><8a>ntyneet. Vuonna 1865, t<8a>sm<8a>lleen 150 vuotta sitten syntyi kaksi kulttuurimme suurmiest<8a>, Jean Sibelius ja Akseli Gallen-Kallela. He nousivat kulttuurimme k<8a>rkeen hyvin nuorella i<8a>ll<8a>. T<8a>m<8a> kuuluu Suomen Pankin kokoelmaan. Gallen-Kallela oli 24-vuotias taiteilija, jonka piti vakuuttaa appensa kyvyst<8a><8a>n el<8a>tt<8a><8a> t<8a>m<8a>n tyt<8a>r Mary. H<8a>n halusi osoittaa sen suurella maalausty<9a>ll<8a>, jota hallitsevat Aino ja V<8a>in<8a>m<9a>inen. Ainosta tuli Gallen-Kallelan ensimm<8a>inen suurty<9a>. Sen toinen versio valmistui vuonna 1891 ja on n<8a>ht<8a>viss<8a> Ateneumissa. Siin<8a> on jo Maryn <d3>j<8a>lki<d3>. Jean Sibelius taas aloitti Kullervon s<8a>vellysty<9a>n 25-vuotiaana Wieniss<8a> vuonna 1891. Palattuaan Suomeen syksyll<8a> h<8a>n sai tilaisuuden kuunnella henkil<9a>kohtaisesti Larin Paraskea. Kullervo kantaesitys kev<8a><8a>ll<8a> 1892 oli suuri menestys. Sibelius oli jo ennen Kullervoa alkanut s<8a>velt<8a><8a> L<9a>nnrotin kolmannen opiskelutoverin, J.L. Runebergin tekstej<8a> lauluiksi. Sibelius avioitui kes<8a>ll<8a> 1892 Aino J<8a>rnefeltin kanssa. Se muutti maailmaa ja Eurooppaa ja j<8a>tti pitk<8a>n j<8a>ljen. Sodassa k<8a>rsityt tappiot ja sis<8a>iset ongelmat ajoivat Ven<8a>j<8a>n kev<8a><8a>ll<8a> 1917 vallankumoukseen. Suomi pyrki k<8a>ytt<8a>m<8a><8a>n tilaisuutta hyv<8a>kseen laajempaa itsem<8a><8a>r<8a><8a>misoikeutta tai itsen<8a>isyytt<8a> hakemalla. V<8a>liaikainen hallitus suhtautui siihen kielteisesti. Asia voitiin p<8a><8a>tt<8a><8a> vasta, kun perustuslakia s<8a><8a>t<8a>v<8a> kansalliskokous kokoontuisi. Bolshevikkien tulo valtaan marraskuussa muutti tilanteen. H<8a>nen musiikkiaan <d0> Finlandia ja J<8a><8a>k<8a>rimarssi <d0> soitettiin my<9a>s 13. tammikuuta 1918 Kansallisteatterissa pidetyss<8a> itsen<8a>isyysjuhlassa. Pelk<8a><8a>n pahinta... Koko Suomi sodan ts. militarismin merkeiss<8a>. Ei mink<8a><8a>nlaista ymm<8a>rt<8a>myst<8a> sinfonikoiden pyrkimyksi<8a> kohtaan.<d3> Samantapaisten tunteiden vallassa oli my<9a>s Gallen-Kallela: <d3>V<8a>synyt kaikkeen sotaisuuteen<c9> Tahdon syventy<8a> taas itseeni: Ehk<8a> l<9a>yd<8a>n siit<8a> uuden polun.<d3> Sis<8a>llissodan p<8a><8a>tytty<8a> vankileirit ja h<8a>vinneiden kohtalo muodostuivat kipe<8a>ksi asiaksi vuosikausiksi eteenp<8a>in. Talouden pitk<8a><8a>n kest<8a>neiden ongelmien ratkaisemiseksi on tuonut useaan tarpeen edet<8a> monella saralla. Ensimm<8a>inen niist<8a> on kustannuskilpailukyvyn parantaminen. Toisen muodostavat sellaiset rakenteelliset uudistukset, jotka parantavat talouskasvun edellytyksi<8a> ja julkisen talouden pitk<8a>n aikav<8a>lin kest<8a>vyytt<8a>. Kolmanneksi tarvitaan julkisen velan kasvun pys<8a>ytt<8a>mist<8a> sopeutustoimien avulla. Kustannuskilpailukyky on Suomessa heikentynyt merkitt<8a>v<8a>sti etenkin vuoden 2007 j<8a>lkeen. Syksyn 2013 palkkaratkaisu pys<8a>ytti kustannuskilpailukyvyn heikkenemisen, mutta ei viel<8a> johtanut sen oleelliseen paranemiseen, sill<8a> ty<9a>n hinnan nousuvauhti on my<9a>s kauppakumppanimaissa keskim<8a><8a>rin pysynyt tavallista hitaampana. Nyt tarvitaan ratkaisuja, jotka johtavat kustannuskilpailukyvyn riitt<8a>v<8a>n suureen ja riitt<8a>v<8a>n nopeaan paranemiseen. Samalla ne parantaisivat kest<8a>v<8a>ll<8a> tavalla suotuisan ty<9a>llisyyskehityksen edellytyksi<8a> kotimarkkinatoimialoilla. Rakenneuudistusten saralla eduskunnan t<8a>n<8a> vuonna hyv<8a>ksym<8a>ll<8a> el<8a>keuudistuksella on suuri merkitys. Muuallakin tulisi edet<8a>. Yksi on sote-ratkaisun saattaminen maaliin siten, ett<8a> julkisten palvelujen tuottavuus nousee. Kilpailua rajoittavaa s<8a><8a>ntely<8a> voidaan v<8a>hent<8a><8a> my<9a>s eri toimialoilla. Julkisen velan kasvu olisi pienempi ongelma, jos odotettavissa olisi vahvaa talouskasvua pidemm<8a>n aikaa. Suomessa sen sijaan nyt otettavaa lis<8a>velkaa joudutaan tulevaisuudessa hoitamaan tilanteessa, jossa nykyist<8a> pienempi osa v<8a>est<9a>st<8a> on ty<9a>i<8a>ss<8a> ja suurempi osa el<8a>kkeell<8a> ja jossa nykyist<8a> useampi tarvitsee hoiva-ja terveyspalveluja. Jotta julkisen velan kasvu saadaan taittumaan, s<8a><8a>st<9a>j<8a> joudutaan tekem<8a><8a>n. Jos sopeuttamistoimia j<8a>tet<8a><8a>n tekem<8a>tt<8a>, nykyiset nuoret joutuvat aikanaan sek<8a> maksamaan valtaosan suurten ik<8a>luokkien el<8a>kkeist<8a> ett<8a> hoitamaan edellisen sukupolven velat. Lis<8a>ksi he joutuvat l<9a>yt<8a>m<8a><8a>n ty<9a>paikan taloustilanteessa, jonka ongelmia ei huonossa tapauksessa edelleenk<8a><8a>n ole ratkaistu. Suomen talous el<8a><8a> vaikeaa vaihetta. Mutta n<8a>ist<8a>kin vaikeuksista voidaan rakentaa tie ulos johdonmukaisella ja vastuullisella toiminnalla. Uskon, ett<8a> kansalaiset ymm<8a>rt<8a>v<8a>t tilanteen vakavuuden. He ovat valmiita kantamaan oman osuutensa, kun sopeutustoimet tehd<8a><8a>n kaikkia oikeudenmukaisesti koskien ja kun tiedet<8a><8a>n, ett<8a> ne ovat paremman kasvun ja ty<9a>llisyyden ehto. H<8a>n sanoo haastattelussaan: <d3>Hurraa-is<8a>nmaallisuus ei ole sotien j<8a>lkeen en<8a><8a> puhutellut ihmisi<8a><d3>. <d3>Olennaista on nyt se, ett<8a> tunnemme kiintymyst<8a> sit<8a> yhteiskuntaa kohtaan, jonka olemme valinneet. Title: Finnish economy, monetary policy and financial stability. Helsinki, 10 December 2015.
text: Determined action needed to strengthen the economy Releases (/en/media-and-publications/releases/) . Press releasenumber 27 . Thursday10 December 2015, 11:00 AM The problems in the Finnish economy have turned out to be long-term in nature. Recovery is gradually getting underway, but in 2016 Finland will be one of the most weakly growing economies in the euro area. Since 2008, there has been a particularly strong decline in exports and investment in the export industries. d4The outlook for the Finnish economy is burdened by industrial restructuring, weakened cost-competitiveness and a contracting working-age population. Turning this trend around is vital and will require determined action,d5 said Governor Erkki Liikanen today at the launch of the latest issue of the Bank of Finland journal Euro & talous. In Finland, the price of labour has risen faster than average among the countryd5s trading partners, while companiesd5 wage-paying capacity has developed more weakly, particularly since 2007. In the export industries, profitability has declined. d4In Finland, we need solutions that can substantially improve cost-competitiveness. This will bolster confidence and improve the outlook for economic growth as exports and investment gather strength,d5 Governor Liikanen pointed out. Finlandd5s public finances remain weak. The GDP ratio of the general government deficit is now over 3%, and general government debt over 60%. In the absence of new decisions, the debt will continue to grow rapidly. d4When an economy can look forward to a prolonged period of strong growth, growing public debt is less of a problem. This is, however, not the case at the moment. Taking on more debt simply passes the burden onto the young, who will also be forced at the same time to bear the costs of health and care services as well as pension costs to the extent that pensions are under-funded,d5 Liikanen continued. Improving the possibilities for growth and ensuring the sustainability of the public finances requires structural reforms. d4The pension reform will reduce the sustainability gap and is a significant achievement. Swift progress is also required with other reforms. It is vital that social and healthcare reform is carried through in such a way as to improve productivity in the public services,d5 Liikanen said. In Finland, the current low level of interest rates has bolstered the economy particularly well via the lower rates of loan interest for households and businesses. d4The better the measures to repair the economy succeed, the more monetary policy can support growth in Finland,d5 Liikanen underlined. Monetary policy measures have significantly eased financial conditions and supported the real economy in the euro area. Euro area inflation has, however, hovered around zero for over a year already, and the inflation outlook remains very weak. At its December 2015 meeting, the Governing Council of the ECB decided on a further easing of monetary policy. The deposit rate was lowered to -0.3%. In addition, the Eurosystemd5s expanded asset purchase programme was extended to run to March 2017, and, if necessary, purchases will also continue beyond that date. d4The Governing Councild5s decisions were taken in order to secure a sustained adjustment in the path of inflation consistent with its aim of achieving inflation rates below, but close to, 2%, and to secure the anchoring of medium.term inflation expectations in accordance with this target,d5 Governor Liikanen emphasised. The Eurosystem will also reinvest the principal payments on the securities in the purchase programme as they mature. Determined action needed to strengthen the economy . Title: Kalevi Sorsa and central bank. Helsinki, 15 December 2015.
text: President Erkki Liikanen: Kalevi Sorsa and the Central Bank. Helsinki, 15.12.2015. . Speech . Tuesday 15December 2015, 2:00 PM President and CEO Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland Moment for Kalevi Sorsa event Helsinki, 15.12.2015 KALEVI SORSA AND THE CENTRAL BANK Ladies and gentlemen, In the 1970s, relations between the governments and the Bank of Finland were sometimes tense. This was also the case when Kalevi Sorsa was prime minister. There were then many in the Social Democrats who saw the independence of the Central Bank vis-a-vis the government as a problem in terms of coordinating economic policy. There were also those who believed that the Central Bank should be transferred to the direct authority of the government and the Ministry of Finance. Peter Nyberg and Eero Vuohula also wrote a well-known article on the subject in the Review of the Labour Economic Research Institute. Tensions in the relationship between the government and the bank became most evident in the early days of the Sorsa II government. The situation came to a head with the devaluation in February 1978 and the subsequent resignation of the government. After this crisis, Sorsa gave a speech at the SDP Party Council that attracted a lot of attention, in which he said that there was such a contradiction between the independence of the Bank of Finland and the leadership of the government that "Finland is growing a snake of two-headed economic policy in its bosom". The statement was strong. What had happened? Before that speech, the Bank of Finland and its President, Mauno Koivisto, made the devaluation in a way that put in front of the government's fait accompli. Norway had devalued its crown on February 10, 1978. It was Friday. This took place between the electorate elections and the electorate meeting. The 1978 presidential electorate elections had been held on January 15 and 16. Urho Kekkonen's electoral alliance had gained 259 electors. It is part of the spirit of the times that the result was hardly wondered at. Raino Westerholm received 25, Veikko Vennamo10 and AhtiSalonen 6 electors. The electors had been convened on Wednesday, 15.2.1978. On Sunday 12 February, Director-General Mauno Koivisto announced on television that the devaluation of the Norwegian krone also affected the position of the Finnish markka. The next day, on Monday, the Bank of Finland closed the foreign exchange market completely, and in that situation we were waiting for decisions. For Prime Minister Kalevi Sorsa, Koivisto proposed a devaluation of the markka by 8 per cent. This would already be the third devaluation of the Finnish markka in 12 months, as two devaluations had already taken place in 1977. The economic situation in Finland was difficult. Economic growth was at a standstill and unemployment had risen to a record level of 7% so far. The Finnish markka was subject to continued mistrust in the foreign exchange markets. The short-term market rate applied in the interbank day credit market had risen to as much as 23%. In 1977, the Sorsa II government had begun a series of stimulus packages. Just a couple of months before the devaluation of Norway, the government had decided on a third stimulus package, including reductions in employers' social security contributions. The trade unions had participated in the stimulus package by agreeing to postpone the wage increases already agreed on the grounds that devaluation would be avoided. In this situation, drifting into devaluation was very embarrassing for the government. Kalevin viisi vuotta kest<8a>neest<8a> kaudesta pankinjohtajana muistetaan kuitenkin parhaiten h<8a>nen tulopoliittinen sopimusehdotuksensa syksylt<8a> 1991, jolla koetettiin alentaa ty<9a>voimakustannuksia ja v<8a>ltt<8a><8a> ajautuminen pakkodevalvaatioon. Kalevi ryhtyi t<8a>h<8a>n ep<8a>kiitolliseen teht<8a>v<8a><8a>n p<8a><8a>ministeri Esko Ahon, valtiovarainministeri Iiro Viinasenja Suomen Pankin p<8a><8a>johtaja Rolf Kullbergin pyynn<9a>st<8a> tilanteessa, jossa ty<9a>tt<9a>myys oli jyrk<8a>ss<8a> nousussa ja Suomen markkaan kohdistui ep<8a>luottamusta niin, ett<8a> valuuttavaranto oli hyv<8a><8a> vauhtia hupenemassa. Kuten useimmat muistavat, Kalevi Sorsa hoiti oman osuutensa ja h<8a>nen v<8a>litysehdotuksensa hyv<8a>ksyttiin keskusj<8a>rjest<9a>tasolla 21. p<8a>iv<8a>n<8a> lokakuuta. Sopimus olisi alentanut ty<9a>voimakustannuksia noin 7 prosentilla. Loppujen lopuksi aika ei riitt<8a>nyt liittotason neuvotteluihin, valuuttaspekulaatio kiihtyi ja markka laskettiin kellumaan marraskuun 12. p<8a>iv<8a>n<8a>. Seuraavana p<8a>iv<8a>n<8a> sille vahvistettiin uusi kurssi, joka merkitsi 14 prosentin devalvaatiota (muodollisesti; k<8a>yt<8a>nn<9a>ss<8a> markka heikkeni 10 prosenttia). Kaleville t<8a>m<8a> oli tietysti valtava pettymys ja h<8a>n oli valmis eroamaankin. Presidentti Koivisto sai h<8a>net kuitenkin puhutuksi pysym<8a><8a>n virassaan. T<8a>m<8a> kaikki tuntuu tietysti kovin tutulta kun seuraa t<8a>m<8a>n p<8a>iv<8a>n yhteiskuntasopimusneuvotteluja. Historia ei toista itse<8a><8a>n ja jokaisella vuosikymmenell<8a> on omat haasteensa. Mutta ehk<8a> on hyv<8a> muistaa, ett<8a> vaikeissa paikoissa on oltu ennenkin. Kalevi Sorsa oli niiss<8a> monta kertaa.

Title: Director General Erkki Liikanen writing in Ilta-Sanomat on 16 January 2016
text: Director General Erkki Liikanen: article in Ilta-Sanomat 16.1.2016 . Speech . Saturday 16 January 2016, 9:00AM President and CEO Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland Article in Ilta-Sanomat 16.1.2016 ( ) PRESIDENT AND CEO ERKKI LIIKANEN'S ARTICLE IN ILTA-SANOMAT 16.1.2016 In the euro area, economic growth has been strong, but Finland is still struggling. What is needed now is a shared vision and a company-specific agreement based on trust, writes Erkki Liikanen, President of the Bank of Finland. International news reports uncertainty in emerging economies. Nevertheless, the global economy has continued to grow. In advanced economies, including the euro area, growth has been even stronger than in the past. However, Finland is lagging behind, and the country's economy is still struggling. It would be of paramount importance for us to be able to participate in the growth. Finland's exports have contracted more than any other developed economy. At the same time, jobs and investment in exporting companies have fallen sharply. No one can deny these problems. It is widely understood that we need more investment to create jobs and restructure our economy. Despite this, the confusion and contradiction of the economic debate confuses many. However, is there a syndicate that would create a sustainable way out of problems? 1. On the one hand, it is said that there is a serious problem with Finland's competitiveness. On the other hand, it is said that Finland is one of the most competitive countries in Europe. How is such a contradiction possible? In the comparison of the World Economic Forum (WEF) in Davos, Finland still ranks in the top position. The Economic Forum measures many important prerequisites for growth: How widespread is corruption? Is the justice system reliable? Is the financial system working well? What is the level of primary education? What condition are the ports and railways in? Do women participate in the labour market? They are important prerequisites for economic growth and in Finland they are in good shape, but they are not enough. We must also be able to turn these strengths into high-quality goods and services at competitive prices, that is, to realise our potential. We have failed to do that in recent years. The functioning of the labour market has played a part in the problems, and in some of the issues concerning the labour market in the above-mentioned comparison, Finland ranks very far from the top. Are wages in Finland, then, clearly higher than in others? No, but wage costs have risen clearly more than others over the past 10 years. At the same time, as productivity growth has stagnated, the ability of the entire national economy to pay wages relative to other countries has weakened. We have therefore lost many more jobs in industry and exports than others. Wages in Finland rose particularly much compared to other countries immediately after the onset of the international financial crisis. The rise was the result of the federal agreements concluded just before the crisis in 2007 and 2008. When the crisis hit, wage growth quickly subsided in other countries. At the same time, productivity declined sharply in Finland. Has anything been done to remedy this? The moderate wage settlement in autumn 2013 halted the deterioration of the situation. That is all well and good, but unfortunately it is not enough. We should also make up for past losses. What is needed is a solution that limits wage increases to what the open sector can pay and measures that quickly bridge the gap with competitor countries. If cost competitiveness can be improved, Finnish exporters can make more profitable offers and win back markets. The production and jobs of exporting companies will increase, and the conditions for new investments will also improve. As the income of the national economy increases, the positive impact on domestic market companies and, more broadly, on employment will also spread. Some critics have said that the contraction in mobile phone production was not solely due to domestic costs. They are right. The industry underwent a drastic change in technology and business model, which Finland could not respond to. But the rise in domestic cost levels over the past decade has held back and is holding back the creation of new jobs and investment in other export sectors. When it comes to creating new businesses to replace lost production, you have to be broadly competitive. When companies prosper and their productivity and ability to pay wages increase, this is later reflected in wage developments. The sooner competitiveness improves, the faster employment will improve and the better we will be able to absorb the fluctuations of the global economy, which have not stopped. Correcting competitiveness is a necessary, but not sufficient, condition for Finland's success. In addition, we must make use of our proven potential. Finland has strong ict expertise and business activities that utilise it. Finland is therefore in a position to be at the forefront of digitalisation on a broad front, both when creating new business activities and when reforming the ways of working in industry and services. 2. On the one hand, efforts are required from the central organisations to achieve a social contract and, on the other, there is a desire to decentralise contractual activities to enterprises. Are these not contradictory objectives? Experience has shown that the balance of economic development can be strengthened by the fact that the wage-paying capacity of the open sector, i.e. export companies and firms competing with imports, also determines the framework for agreements in other sectors. This requires economic cooperation and coordination. That is what failed badly in 2007 and 2008. The aftermath of failure is long. In the future, it will be up to the social partners to decide how sectoral employers' and employees' organisations negotiate and coordinate working time and pay solutions suitable for their sector and the economy as a whole at the level of central organisations. It is also important that solutions are taken at company level to ensure, on the one hand, the profitability of the company and, on the other, the positive development of jobs. If the company's order backlog is strong, working hours can be arranged in such a way that productivity increases by agreement. When the economic cycle weakens again, it would be important at company level to seek solutions flexibly that avoid or at least minimise job losses. Workplace-specific agreements require mutual trust, while trust requires a broad flow of information in both directions. Productivity is not increased by grinding or dictation, but by jointly sought solutions that support the company's success, the conditions for growth and job retention. So we need both: a common vision and a company-specific agreement based on trust. Our situation is so difficult that it can only be overcome well by combining solutions that improve competitiveness in the short term and developing contractual practices that support the safeguarding of growth and employment within the framework of economic and monetary union. 3. In addition to export problems, the Finnish economy has been weighed down by the decline in the working-age population, which has continued since 2010. The economy is dominated by structural problems. Due to changes in the industrial and age structure, the causes of the contraction in real GDP and government deficits are not temporary, but long-term. Therefore, structural reforms are needed to boost economic growth and safeguard the balance of public finances. The agreement on pension reform was therefore a significant achievement. In addition to the pension reform, the health and social services reform related to the social and health care sector is a historically large-scale reform project. The reform provides an opportunity to improve productivity. Services are human work, which is based on the huge collection of information and the processing of databases. Digitalisation plays a key role in this. Finland was one of the world's leading countries in the digitalisation of the tax system. The electronic prescription was delayed for an unreasonably long time, but its benefits can be seen today. The health and social services reform is an opportunity to take a major step in promoting the productivity and digitalisation of public services. This requires strong leadership and a greater capacity for reform. 4. Major structural reforms would make it easier to achieve a balance in public finances. Can they help to postpone the reduction of the deficit to the next generation? Finland's level of public debt is not exceptionally high, but the pace of indebtedness in Finland is among the fastest. If we were to expect a long period of strong economic growth, we could theoretically think about postponing the adjustments. Unfortunately, Finland's growth will, at best, be slower than in the previous decades. This is due, on the one hand, to the contraction of the labour force and, on the other hand, to the weakening of productivity growth due to a decline in industry and investment compared to the pre-crisis period. If, in this situation, it is decided to pass on the adjustment to the next generations, what will it mean? In any case, today's young people will have to bear the brunt of the growing health and care services caused by ageing, as well as the financing of pensions where they are not funded. The funding ratio is about 25 per cent. In addition to this, the fiscal adjustment would be transferred to them, as the previous age groups did not want to do so while working. It is unreasonable to pass on the eating debt to the younger generations. The fiscal adjustment must take into account at least two factors. It is important that the adjustment measures do not undermine the conditions for longer-term economic growth and employment. It is also important that the adjustment measures treat the different population groups fairly. 5. The ECB's monetary policy stance is strongly accommodative. How could it support finland's economic recovery? The European Central Bank, the Eurosystem and the Bank of Finland, as part of it, have strongly supported price stability and economic recovery through their accommodative monetary policy. Not only short-term but also long-term interest rates have fallen. Low interest rates have increasingly been passed on to support borrowers. At the same time, the divergence in monetary policy easing vis-a-vis other central banks has also had a positive impact on euro area growth through exchange rates. As a result, the economic outlook for the euro area has broadly improved over the past year. It also supports Finland's export opportunities. The more Finland takes care of its own competitiveness, the greater the benefits it will derive from the single monetary policy and also from the recovery of the euro area.

Jos t<8a>ss<8a> tilanteessa sopeutus p<8a><8a>tet<8a><8a>n siirt<8a><8a> seuraaville sukupolville, mit<8a> se merkitsee?
