Title: Mannerheim and reconciliation. Finnish History Days, Lahti 5.2.2016.
text: Director-General Erkki Liikanen: Mannerheim and reconciliation. Finnish History Days, Lahti 5.2.2016. . Speech . Friday 5February 2016,2:00PM Mannerheim and reconciliation Director General Erkki Liikanen Finnish History Days, Sibelius House, Lahti 5.2.2016 at 5 p.m. The body of the presentation  the presentation given may differ On February 26, 1919, Regent Mannerheim visited the Mikkeli Lyceum. He had accepted the position two months earlier. Mannerheim spoke to all the Lyceum students: "Let the white snows we see around us today be, and the blue sky curving over them as a metaphor for the moods of the youth; snow, in which no traces of the passer-by are yet visible, and a high trace of the sky, which is not obscured by clouds. May the minds of our youth be as pure and their thoughts just as high. That is the future of our fatherland, the future that we who have lived through the events of the present, wish our beloved Finland bright and happy." Kari Selen states in his book Mannnerheim's Speeches that the event certainly pleased schoolchildren, because the regent promised after his speech that the following Monday would be a day off. Mannerheim was still speaking in the evening at the Seurahuone in Mikkeli with arrangements for dinners: "I've already enjoyed the hospitality of this city before. It was when the battle for the future of this country was still being fought." At the same time, he thanked him for the peace of mind he received in Mikkeli. So this happened in February 1919. From 1964 to 1966, almost half a century later, Mannerheim deeply divided the Mikkeli City Council. The city board and council discussed the location of mannerheim's statue on several occasions. The left-wing majority did not want it in the square, in the heart of the city. After many stages, it was finally decided to place it on the Square of Greater Savonia, which is a beautiful place, but half a kilometer from the center. At the time of the decision-making, I was in the first grade of upper secondary school at the same Mikkeli Lyceum where Mannerheim had spoken in 1919. The question of Mannerheim and post-civil war reconciliation has been a matter of concern ever since. In 2003, almost 40 years later, the issue was raised again in the city bodies. At that time, the council decided to move it to the Government Square in Mikkeli. My intention today is to seek answers to four questions: 1. How was national unification after the Civil War and before the Winter War possible at all? 2. What was Mannerheim's contribution to national unification? 3. Why were the wounds of the Civil War still open for so long again after the war? 4. Why, as one symbolic example, was the location of mannerheim's statue such a difficult question for so long in Mikkeli? HeikkiYlikangas wrote in 1993 that the Civil War is neutral compared to the concepts of war of independence, civil war or class war. That is why I am talking about the Civil War today. The overall picture of the Civil War began to take shape in historical research when Jaakko Paavolainen's works Political Violence in Finland appeared. The first part, The Red Terror, was published in 1966 and the second part, The White Terror, in 1967. The books gave the number of victims. I still remember when my high school history teacher Heikki Palmen told me that they were new studies of history for him. He had thought that at least as many, if not more, whites had died. Palmen was a man who read a lot. I borrowed Paavolainen's books from the city library and plunged into the stages of the national tragedy. Even later, Paavolainen published the studies Prison Camps in Finland and The National Tragedy. When Jaakko Paavolainen died a few years ago, Professor Timo Soikkanen wrote that Paavolainen's works were revolutionary both in the study of history about 1918 and in the deconstruction of the associated trauma. He put the numbers of casualties killed in and after the war approximately in place. Vaino Linna's Here Under the North Star had appeared earlier, between 1959 and 1962. It was not a study of history, but it was a great literary trilogy of the stages of the nation. The castle also had a significant influence on the discussion of the events of 1918. Immediately after the end of the Civil War, Kyosti Kalliopuhui, the central leader of the Peasants' Union, in the Nivala Church. The line of the rock was reconciliation, not revenge. "We must create a Finland in which there are neither red nor white, but only Finns who love their motherland, citizens of the Republic of Finland, who feel that they are members of society and who enjoy themselves here," said Kallio on May 5, 1918. In the 1917 elections, 92 social democrats or socialists had been elected to parliament. After the civil war, some of them were imprisoned, some had fled to Russia and some did not feel able to participate in parliamentary activities under those circumstances. Only two attended parliamentary sessions. The Parliament was dissolved and the last session of the Stub Parliament was held two days after Mannerheim's visit to Mikkeli. The new Parliament met in April 1919. There, the Social Democratic Party had 80 representatives, the Agrarian League 42, the Coalition Party 28, the Progress Party 26 and the Swedish People's Party 22. In July, Regent Mannerheim confirmed the new form of government, and a week later K.J. Stahlberg defeated Mannerheim in the presidential election conducted by parliament by a vote of 143 to 50. Mannerheim was supported by the National Coalition Party and the Swedish People's Party. Stahlberg was voted for by the Progress Party, the Agrarian League and the Social Democratic Party. The attitude towards Mannerheim was deeply divided. He had strong supporters and unyielding opponents. Political conditions were unstable. At first, governments sat for a hundred to two hundred days. Conflicts between the bourgeois parties were related to the aftermath of the civil war and the language issue. The controversy over whether Finland should be a republic or a kingdom had also deeply divided. Under Stahlberg's leadership, the republicans and those who emphasized the importance of reconciliation were neck and neck in the years after the Civil War. It was not easy for everyone to adapt to it. During Stahlberg's term, Mannerheim visited the Presidential Palace only once for dinner and even then left immediately after the meal had ended. Mannerheim took a very different position on many key issues than the president and the government. Mannerheim's speeches at the end of 1919 and in 1920 were sharp. He did not approve of the large-scale reds amnesty for prisoners, and no attempt to start peace negotiations with Soviet Russia. "Mannerheim seemed to be more on the right than the right," it was said. Many also felt that Mannerheim was ready to lead a military force from Finland in support of the troops of Russian white generals in order to overthrow the Soviet government in Russia. Mannerheim sharply criticized the government's amnesty policy in November 1920: "You will understand that when everything that has been bought with heavy victims within two short years is traded away as change between the state parties, that when one is prepared to open the borders of the country to thousands of those from whose bullets our best sons fell." The severely scarred wound was associated not only with the civil war itself, but especially with executions and prison camps. According to Paavolainen, the victims of the Red Terror rose to 1800 white. Whites, on the other hand, died as victims of terror a total of 8400 Reds, including 364 underage girls. The darkest chapter in the tragedy were the prison camps. As many as 13500 Finns died of disease and malnutrition in the prison camps. Military and civilian authorities blamed each other for what happened after the war. The Finnish Civil War lasted a hundred days and the total number of victims rose to 1% of the population. The Spanish Civil War lasted a thousand days and, according to new studies, the total number of victims rose to 1.5-2% of the population. Both civil wars were total conflicts and they can be compared to each other," says Jukka Kekkonen, Professor of Legal History. In Fellman's Park here in Lahti, a red prison monument was unveiled 60 years after the Civil War in May 1978. President of the Republic Urho Kekkonen also honoured the occasion with his presence. The unveiling ceremony of the monument was attended by 30,000 citizens. Among them were many who were in the same place as prisoners in the spring of 1918. We came here to Lahti from Mikkeli for a bus. I was a 27-year-old MEMBER of Parliament. We also had a long-time and respected member of the Mikkeli City Council and also of the City Board, Maire Haapasalo, who started her career as a journalist. He knew and knew Fellman's history better than others. Here in Lahti, the impression was left that his family had had some connection to the events in Hennala and Fellman, but the matter was not cleared up at the time. His spouse was long-time Member of Parliament and Minister of the 2nd Government of Ahti Karjalainen K.F. Haapasalo. What was Mannerheim's contribution to the treatment of red prisoners? Matti Klinge says that Mannerheim was absent from Finland since 1.6.1918. That summer, prison camp deaths were at their worst. According to Klinge, Mannerheim had tried to prevent "white terror" during the war and opposed the mass imprisonment of the Reds. In March 1918, he issued an order according to which those who surrendered in the conquest of Tampere must be treated as prisoners of war. In the final stages of the war, Mannerheim had banned summary executions. Each prisoner's case had to be heard in court. However, the executions continued in a confused situation. In his memoirs, Mannerheim wrote that he had proposed to the Senate that ordinary Red Guards, even those who had been imprisoned with a gun in hand, be released from the camps without further ado. Only serious crimes had to be brought to court. The Minister of Justice of the time, OnniTalas, vehemently denied Mannerheim's claim. According to him, Mannerheim did not propose the release of prisoners in the spring of 1918. According to Talas, his will would have been fulfilled. Two episodes were related to Mannerheim and the red prisoners after the capture of Tampere. Mannerheim had visited a military hospital with white and red wounded. He reportedly accidentally handed out badge ribbons to the Reds as well. It became clear at the end of the round. He got really angry. Mannerheim had commanded the Reds apart, even into the street. In the end, the order was watered down. The history of the Finnish Red Cross, written by Gunnar Rosen, also tells about another case. A couple of weeks after the previous event, a new order for the day was issued in Mannerheim's name. The effects of the food shortage had begun to be seen. The order of the day stipulated that the daily ration of bread and flour for the wounded was 250 grams for the whites and 75 grams for the reds. A.J. Palmen, the chief physician who had twice been imprisoned by the Red Guards, protested sharply and wrote that the order was indefensible from the point of view of medical care. He continued, "Since I cannot accept the above procedure, and under no circumstances do I, as a doctor, consider myself capable of taking part in the torture of defeated enemies, I may hereby declare that I will cease to function in the hospital entrusted to me if the procedure laid down in the order is followed." Many doctors, even because of their social backgrounds, were sympathizers of whites, but they adhered to medical ethics in their work and dealt with victims in the same way. Prison camps were a difficult subject. Jean Sibelius's diary, which was published in Finnish last year, tells one episode. Sibelius's own diary entry was made on July 20, 1918, i.e. just over two months after the end of the Civil War. To quote Sibelius: "I was out for a walk in the morning and by chance I met one of the workmen. I got angry and we parted in disagreement. He was emotional and full of pity for the innocently suffering Reds. We all know that in our prison camps they die like flies, but there is nothing we can do about it now. That's just the way things are now." The time was not at all easy for Sibelius. ErikTawastsjerna wrote about the second event a month earlier: The Jaeger Guard went to greet Sibelius in Ainola and handed him a flower device. "The roses delighted him but the thorns reminded him that he had been dragged into politics". Sibelius writes in his own diary: "I suffer from glances and future prospects. I'm afraid of the worst... The whole of Finland is a war i.e. a war. in the sign of militarism. No understanding whatsoever of the symphonists' aspirations." In his book Mannerheim, Veijo Merit sums up the discussion about the treatment of red prisoners: When there was constant controversy about who bore the responsibility, no one did. At the same time, hunger and disease killed a startling number of Finnish women and men in prison camps. The prime ministers who led the governments of the early years of independent Finland came from the Agrarian League, the Progress Party or the Conservative Party. In 1925, LauriKristian Relander of the Agrarian League was unexpectedly elected president of the second Republic. At the end of 1926, kallio's 2nd government was overthrown. The bourgeois parties could not agree on a new government. The formation of a government that would have included left and right is out of the question at the time. In the end, President Relander gave the task of forming a government to the leader of the largest parliamentary group, Vaino Tanner. As expected, Tanner received a negative response from other parties. Relander urged to continue and was even ready to accept a one-party government. Relander told Tanner that the trend so far was unhealthy, the nation was divided, and the events of 1918 still played some part in dealing with politics. It had to be taken away. This is how the Tanner government was formed. Professor Vaino Voionmaa became Minister for Foreign Affairs. For the first time, a woman, Miina Sillanpaa, joined the board. The government's proposal for an amnesty law was one of the most pressing issues. In the end, by a vote of 96 to 94, a motion was passed that pardoned the rest who had been convicted solely of participation in or in connection with the Civil War. Those who suffered the punishment were restored to civic trust. When President Relander fell ill in May 1927, he was in office. President Tanner received a parade of the Defense Establishment, which was also attended by units of the Guards Corps. The issue was the subject of heated debate. Tanner said he had done his duty and therefore the matter did not cause him any conscientious objections. After losing the presidential election in 1919, General Mannerheim was excluded from state duties. Kari Selen stated that Mannerheim was in a way an "outsider" in Finland. He had returned to Finland after 30 years in Russia. The only group to which he firmly belonged were the white generals. In 1918, Sophie Mannerheim, the general's sister, had started to assist, among other things, orphaned children of the Red Guards. He founded a nursing home for them, which was named Children's Castle. He got his brother involved in the idea of creating a nationwide child welfare organization, which happened in 1920. When the organization held its first meeting, General Mannerheim said in his inaugural speech that he was hesitant to take the initiative because he was unfamiliar with the field. Sophie Mannerheim, on the other hand, knew the history of child welfare work. It originated from the call-ups during the Boer War in Britain, which revealed in a horrific way a different picture of the health of the people than had been thought. Sophie Mannerheim was similarly awakened by the misery of remote areas. Mannerheim also started a long term later as chairman of the Finnish Red Cross. How did the general come to prevail in this position? The initiator was Richard Faltin, Finland's first military doctor. He had started his career in Krasnoye Selo in Ingria. When the Russo-Japanese War broke out in 1904, Faltin had travelled to Manchuria to become chief physician. There was one ambulance and three military hospitals from the Finns. In the great battle of Mukden, the losses amounted to 90,000 men. One day after the fighting, an exhausted, young cavalry lieutenant colonel with a high fever appeared in the Red Cross ambulance. He was Carl Gustaf Mannerheim. Faltin took care of Mannerheim's condition. When the same Faltin in 1922 asked him to be the chairman of the Red Cross, Mannerheim did not feel that he could refuse. Mannerheim also travelled abroad in Red Cross duties. Among other things, he participated in the meetings of the International Red Cross in Geneva. The union was operated by two committees, one focused on peacetime and the other on wartime. Mannerheim led both. He also created the field hospital system that was ready when the Winter War broke out. At that time, the Red Cross was not yet the current NGO. District and basic organizations were created only in the 1950s. In 1928, Mannerheim took two initiatives. First of all, he proposed the establishment of a Red Cross hospital and donated a considerable sum as a nest egg. The hospital was completed with donated funds in 1932. Mannerheim spoke at the inauguration and President Per-Erik Svinhufvud was also present. Mannerheim stated that the hospital "trains the most qualified forces for the tasks which, according to the lofty principles of the Geneva Convention, are the responsibilities of the Red Cross associations in the event of epidemics, war and persecution." The hospital is known as Toolo Hospital and is part of the Hospital District of Helsinki and Uusimaa. The initiative of the second concerned the holding of a series of radio presentations. Its purpose would be to "awaken from one's own, small hobbies, strife and strife, and to spread among them civil peace and a sense of community." Mannerheim continued as chairman of the Finnish Red Cross, even though he had to sit full-time in the General Staff from 1931 onwards. Of Mannerheim's surviving public speeches of the time, he gave several of them at events organised by the Finnish Red Cross. Mannerheim had moved to St. Petersburg at the age of 20 in 1887 and returned from there in 1917, when he was 50 years old. For three decades, his contacts with Finland had been limited to a small group of Finland-Swedes. Through the Finnish Red Cross and the Finnish League for Child Welfare, Mannerheim gained a more diverse picture of Finland and the Finns. It may have had a bearing on his perceptions and attitudes. The Red Cross came to the fore even after the war, when the General Staff of the Finnish Defence Forces had donated its assets to the Finnish Red Cross before the abolition. It included property acquired with state money. The Red Cross stuck to the letter of the will. When the negotiations between the Finnish Defence Forces and the Finnish Red Cross reached an impasse, Mannerheim was still looking for help in finding a compromise. In addition to his organizational duties, he represented the Finnish state at a few international events. In November 1932, he attended the commemoration of Gustav Adolf's 300th birthday in Lutzen. There Mannerheim gave Finland's greeting. On the way, he also stayed in Berlin, where The Finnish Envoy was Vaino Vuolijoki. After talking with the general, Vuolijoki wrote to Vaino Tanner that Mannerheim is much better than his reputation and recommended that the Social Democrats should not reproach him too much. The middle-group governments, which were aiming for the middle ground of politics, and also the minority government of the Social Democrats, suffered a setback in the atmosphere of the Great Depression in 1929. The focus of politics shifted to the right. At its core was the anti-communist movement. Svinhufvud returned first as prime minister in 1930 and then as president. According to Timo Soikkanen, Lapuan Liike tore apart the budding defragmentation. The tense mood is illustrated by the fact that, in the run-up to the 1933 elections, the right wing demanded a ban on the Social Democratic Party for treasonous activities. The Social Democrats, on the other hand, demanded that the IKL's relationship with the banned Lapua movement be clarified and that attention be paid to the relations between the IKL and the Coalition Party. Because of this, there was little time left for defragmentation, only the years 19331939 before the wars. Mannerheim, according to Eric Heinrichs, bid farewell to the role of white general only 15 years after the end of the Civil War. It happened at the 15th anniversary of the end of the war in 1933. At that time, Mannerheim stated that it was no longer necessary to ask where each had been in 1918. Yrjo Niiniluoto, in his book The Great Role, considered it a bold attempt to liquidate the past. In 1967, Kalle Lehmus, who headed the Information Department of the General Staff, published The Unknown Mannerheim, which brought many more nuances. According to him, in the 1930s Mannerheim sought contacts with the social democratic governments of the Nordic countries. One of the objectives was to de-escalate tensions in Finland. In January 1935, Mannerheim held a press conference in which he emphasized the necessity of a Nordic orientation. According to Linden, there were two reasons for this. First of all, Mannerheim believed that anchoring Finland in the direction of neutral Sweden and Norway would convince the Soviet Union that Finland has no intention of supporting the possible belligerent efforts of some superpower, mainly Germany, against the Soviet Union. Another reason for domestic politics; it would make it easier to achieve language peace and, at the same time, cooperation with countries dominated by the labour movement could de-escalate conflicts in Finland as well. In December 1935, parliament adopted a position paper on the Nordic trend. For the right wing, it meant, above all, defence policy, and for the Swedish People's Party and the Social Democrats, it also meant foreign, economic and cultural policy. In 1937, Kyosti Kallio was elected President of the Republic. Svinhufvud returned to Luumaki. Kallio paved the way for red mullet cooperation. The government of Prime Minister A.K. Cajander was the first in which the left and bourgeois parties were together. The government included the Agrarian League, the Social Democrats and part of the Progressive Party. The first red mullet government was a significant step towards the unification of the nation. The right-wing opposition spoke of "the return of the blood flows of 1918." Another factor that laid the foundation for the unification of the nation was strong economic development. It enabled the red mullet government to pursue a reform policy. Finland's national product grew at the top rate in Europe towards the end of the decade. Mannerheim had no connections with the largest party of that time, the Social Democrats. He tells about this in the 2nd part of his memoirs. He notes that the government's so-called "black market". The thrift committee was formed in 1931 by J.K. Paasikivi, Risto Ryti and Vaino Tanner. He went to see Paasikivi and Ryti in the defence budget issue, but not Tanner. Mannerheim writes about this afterwards in his memoirs. "I did not know Mr Tanner, the head of the Socialist Party. During the War of Independence, the cooperative movement he led, Elanto, with its warehouses, had formed the backbone of the rebels' maintenance, and since 1919 he had been a staunch opponent of defense appropriations. When I had reason to assume that Mr Tanner was not inclined to take account of my points of view, I refrained from visiting him." Mannerheim regrets this in his memoirs and says that if he had known Tanner then as he later came to know him, he would probably have tried, even though he could not have hoped for much success in his proselytizing. In late May 1937, Mannerheim organized a dinner at his home. Among the dinner guests were also two ministers, Vaino Tanner and Vaino Voionmaa. Mannerheim had stated that they were the first social democrats in his home. This was 19 years after the end of the Civil War. According to Tanner' s account, Mannerheim tried to get into a conversation with them for two, but because of the other guests, it did not work out. However, there was one thing Tanner had noted down. When he had asked Mannerheim about the danger of war, he had replied: "War is in some ways a bit like what was once in St. Petersburg with Yevropeiskaja Gastinitsa (a well-known place of restaurants and entertainment). We didn't usually decide to go there specifically, but we always had to go there in some way." On June 4, 1937, Mannerheim turned 70 years old. It was one kind of measure of national unity. The celebration was mainly a non-socialist holiday, but there were hardly any gravelly voices from the left either. Minister Hannes Ryoma was part of the government's congratulatory delegation, and The Speaker of parliament Vaino Hakkila read the parliament's petition at the citizens' party. The changed tone of Mannerheim's speeches was also noticed on the left. Vaino Tanner spoke in Naantali in July 1938 on behalf of the workers: "In its (labour) opinion, the bitterness towards the winner of the war, the white General Mannerheim, has evaporated. On the contrary, it has acknowledged his many manly statements in recent years." It is known that Mannerheim and Tanner's views on the possibility of war diverged. In August 1939, Germany and the USSR, the old enemies, concluded a non-aggression pact. It seemed like a bombshell to the opinions of the parties. The extreme right and the communists had justified their policies on the opposing side, but in this way the mother countries betrayed their supporters. Vaino Hakkila wrote polemically that the Berlin-Moscow agreement caused such a short circuit in the heads of the "supporters of dictatorial doctrines" that indeed all the lights went out. The result was a truly miserable confusion and the collapse of the ideology." The morale of the communists was also deeply influenced by the persecutions carried out by Stalin in Karelia, in which a considerable number of Finnish noble brothers were executed. The far right, on the other hand, collapsed its bottom when Germany invaded Czechoslovakia. It was considered to be directed against all small states and their rights. Lehmus said that Mannerheim had made two decisions with his own authority, by which he was expressly trying to promote reconciliation. First of all, he decided to end the celebration of victory in the War of Independence, which took place on May 16. The Winter War had shown the unity of the nation, and there was no longer any desire to celebrate in public the events that aroused bitter memories in a large part of the population. Instead, a day of remembrance for the fallen began on May 19. The importance of the decision is also emphasised by Niiniluoto. Secondly, he also laid a wreath on the graves of the Reds. It was also a recognition to those who fought for the Reds or otherwise acted that they, too, had acted for their convictions with the aim of an independent Finland. Thus, the stigma of treason was removed. Perhaps the biggest and most visible amicable settlement, however, was the January engagement of 23.1.1940. At that time, in the midst of the Winter War, employers issued a declaration in which they recognized trade unions as counterparties. The Parties agree that they will henceforth endeavour to reach an agreement through negotiations. The midwife of the January engagement was K.A. Fagerholm. Lehmus, among others, also claims that Mannerheim and Rudolf Walden, minister of defence and director of the United Paper Mills, were key background influencers. Just over two years later, Mannerheim turned 75. A small-scale birthday party was held in a train carriage in Immola. The birthday is also remembered for the fact that Hitler unexpectedly went to congratulate Mannerheim. That conversation was recorded and the tape has been used a lot because in it Hitler spoke in a "normal" voice. Before that, however, the President and the government had offered their congratulations and told Mannerheim about the title of Marshal of Finland. After that, it was the parliament's turn to congratulate. At that time, the Bureau announced that parliament had decided to give Mannerheim his own home in Helsinki. This is how the Kaivopuisto apartment became Mannerheim's property. Next in line for congratulations were representatives of the Central Organisation of Finnish Trade Unions SAK, the Metalworkers' Union and the Woodworkers' Union. Under the leadership of Eero A. Wuori, President of the Central Organisation of Finnish Trade Unions (SAK), they said the following: "The working people have attached particular value to your determined efforts, which have been aimed, in particular, at wiping out the traces left by the 1918 cases from among our people. The working people see that, by doing so, you have been the influential builder of the united front that has been a fundamental prerequisite for the success of the struggles of our people in recent years." Mannerheim attached special importance to the congratulations. He said: "Nothing pleases me more than to see here with me representatives of the Working People of Finland, who make up a huge part of the constructive power of our people. Your beautiful greeting gives me a very special joy and at the same time the satisfaction of seeing in it a testimony of the fulfillment of my dreams and aspirations from decades ago. The contribution of the Finnish working population to the fierce struggle of recent years, both at the front and in the factories and jobs in their home region, deserves great recognition." After the trade union movement, it was the turn of the Finnish Defence Forces, the Union of Brothers in Arms, the Knights of the Mannerheim Cross and the Uusimaa Dragoon Regiment. The greeting from the trade union movement was immediately after the state, which probably shows its great importance to Mannerheim. Mannerheim's memoirs contain three pictures of the events of the birthday. Together are the President and the Minister of Defence bringing the state's congratulations, in another the congratulations of the SAK embassy and in the third the mentioned meeting with Adolf Hitler in a train carriage. Why, then, in the 1960s, even in Mikkeli, did the placement of Mannerheim's statue open the wounds of a difficult civil war? This question plagued for years. One explanation may be given by Timo Soikkanen, to which I referred above. Research data on the civil war was just coming. The traumas were unraveled. A prerequisite for this was correct knowledge. The knowledge base came only later. But something even more had to do with the events in Mikkeli. My father, Eino Liikanen, was born in 1925, so he made it to the front during the Continuation War. I remember asking him twice who he had voted for. First in 1958 parliamentary elections. He said that he had voted for A.F. Oar, a silent general, who was a candidate in the constituency of Mikkeli. Title: Monetary policy and publicity. Transparency column on the Freedom of The Press 250 Years website, 22 February 2016.
text: President Erkki Liikanen: Monetary policy and publicity. Transparency column of the Freedom of the Press 250 Years website 22.2.2016. . Speech . Tuesday 23February 2016,9:00 AM Transparency column: Monetary policy and publicity Director General Erkki Liikanen Published 22.2.2016 On the 250th anniversary website ( ) The famous Freedom of the Press Act of 1766, the anniversary of which is being celebrated this year, included two pillars: on the one hand, the abolition of prior censorship of printed matter and, on the other hand, the implementation of the principle of public access to documents. Both were radical reforms. The principle of public access enshrined in the law was unique in the whole world. Today, it would be difficult to imagine a democratic state governed by the rule of law without freedom of the press and public access to government. Implementing transparency is all the more important and also the more difficult the bigger and the organization is. In the EU, for example, the continuous improvement of administrative and political transparency is particularly important for the sake of public confidence. At the same time, the fragmentation of the 'public space' within the Union, due to the many languages and traditions, makes it a challenge to implement transparency effectively. The Nordic countries, not least Finland, have played a key role in promoting openness. Since the 1990s, the relationship between central banks and the application of the principle of public access to official records has undergone a downright revolutionary change. This has happened not only in Europe, but also in other developed countries. For a long time, it was thought that in order for monetary policy to succeed, it was necessary to keep the arguments and plans for it secret. In this respect, monetary policy was perhaps compared to the defence planning of states or to the most sensitive negotiations in international diplomacy. Illustrative of the mindset was the motto "never explain, never apologize" by Montagu Norman, the legendary president of bank of England. Now those days have come a long way. Central banks are now more transparent about the basis and implementation of their policies than ever before. This is a global phenomenon in which euro area central banks such as the ECB and the Bank of Finland have been closely involved. The latest concrete example of increased transparency is that last year the European Central Bank began to publish comprehensive reports on the meetings at which the Governing Council takes its monetary policy decisions. In this way, the rationale behind monetary policy  and the counter-arguments on the table  come to the fore, giving those interested a more meek picture of the Governing Council's activities and thinking. The publication of the reports of the meetings follows on from many of the forms of transparency already introduced by the ECB. These include press conferences after monetary policy meetings on questions and the regular publication of the economic forecasts used by the Council and the so-called 'monetary policy outlook'. forward-looking communication, which the ECB has been conducting systematically since summer 2013. The transparency of central banks serves a dual purpose. One relates to their role as public authorities. As public authorities, they must be accountable to citizens and to those political bodies that have delegated monetary policy decision-making to independent central banks. The independence of central banks and the transparency of their decision-making are, in a way, different sides of the same coin, which must be balanced with each other. The increase in the transparency of central banks has gone hand in hand with the increase in their operational autonomy. This, too, is a global change that took place during the 1990s. The purpose of central bank independence is to ensure confidence in the value of money by protecting monetary policy from political and other pressures that could disrupt that confidence. However, independence is conditional on a clear mandate and accountability of the central bank in terms of how it has acted to safeguard its objective of price stability. Monetary transparency complements the more formal systems of accountability of central banks vis-a-vis political bodies, in the case of the ECB, the European Parliament and its committees, and in the case of the Bank of Finland, the Parliament, the Banking Board elected by it and the Parliamentary Finance Committee. In addition to the implementation of accountability, another purpose of the increase in central bank transparency has been to increase the effectiveness of monetary policy. The impact of monetary policy on financial markets, inflation and cyclical developments is only partly based on current monetary policy measures, and to a large extent on the expectations of the public - i.e. companies, households, labour market organisations and investors - on future policy. The majority of the effects of monetary policy are realised through expectations. Managing expectations is a key element of monetary policy. Transparency enhances the credibility of the Central Bank's communications and thus helps to keep monetary policy expectations and the Central Bank's plans in line with each other. Let's take an example. In the current economic climate, where inflation in the euro area, which has been below forecasts for a long time and below the target of around 2%, strongly requires an accommodative monetary policy stance, the European Central Bank has sought to convince the markets and the general public that a light monetary policy will continue in the future for as long as necessary to achieve price stability. When communication meets the expectations of monetary policy in line with these intentions, the effectiveness of the policy can be maximised. When considering the value of transparency, one cannot ignore the impact that transparency of activities and debate has on their quality. This aspect was central to Mr Chydenius's famous report on freedom of the press. In it, Chydenius explained how open criticism ensures that the strongest arguments in politics win and the weaker ones have to give way. Transparency also ensures that legitimate principles are invoked in decision-making: for example, members of the Council should not appeal to national interests, but should look at monetary policy from the point of view of the euro area as a whole. The increased transparency of the discussions in the Governing Council also contributes to ensuring that this principle is also respected and to demonstrating to the public that the Council's action in this regard, too, meets the requirements of good monetary policy-making. Title: ECB's monetary policy. Helsinki, 21.3.2016.
text: Governor Liikanen: The monetary policy measures and forward guidance together constitute a comprehensive response Releases (/en/media-and-publications/releases/) . Press releasenumber 4 . Monday21 March 2016,11:05AM The slowdown in the growth rates of global trade and the emerging economies, as well as the increase in financial market uncertainty early in the year have weakened the outlook for the euro area economy. Growth in global trade is dampened particularly by weaker growth in the emerging economies, including China. In the euro area, growth continues to rest on domestic demand. In 2015, the average annual inflation rate for the euro area was 0%, the lowest outcome since the start of Monetary Union. The slow pace of inflation has mainly reflected the low price of oil. In February 2016, inflation was -0.2%. The slowdown in inflation has been broadly based. In view of the weakened economic and inflation outlook, the Governing Council of the ECB decided in March 2016 on several measures in pursuit of its price stability objective. These measures included lowering all key interest rates, extending the asset purchase programme to cover debt securities issued by the corporate sector, and expanding the volume of monthly asset purchases. In addition, with the aim of further incentivising bank lending to the real economy, banks can obtain very long-term loans in targeted longer-term refinancing operations. d2The monetary policy measures and forward guidance together constitute a comprehensive response. The new measures will accelerate the return of inflation to levels below but close to 2%, and support the recovery of the euro area economy,d3 said Erkki Liikanen, Governor of the Bank of Finland, at todayd5s press conference. The package is aimed at further easing financing conditions in the euro area and stimulating new credit provision. d2Taking into account the current inflation outlook, our policy rates are expected to remain at present or lower levels for an extended period of time, and well past the horizon of the asset purchases. If the outlook or financing conditions deteriorate, the ECB still has capacity to boost inflation and growth,d3 Governor Liikanen emphasized. d2The new longer-term refinancing operations offered to banks will improve their capacity to lend to the real economy. In the euro area, monetary policy feeds through to the real economy mainly via the banks. It is crucial for economic recovery that the banking sector is in good shape,d3 Governor Liikanen stressed. The accommodative monetary policy is gradually increasing demand in euro area countries, which will also help Finland. The low interest rate level is reflected in low rates on corporate loans and housing loans. As these loans mainly bear a variable rate and the banking system is in good shape, the transmission of monetary policy is particularly effective in Finland. d2Turning the Finnish economy onto solid growth requires improved cost competitiveness and structural reforms. When this creates a need to expand production, accommodative monetary policy improves financial conditions and supports firmsd5 decisions to invest and create jobs,d3 said Governor Liikanen. Title: Speech by Director General Erkki Liikanen at Antti Suvanno's farewell reception on 11 April 2016
text: President and CEO Erkki Liikanen's speech at Antti Suvanto's farewell reception 11.4.2016 . Speech . Tuesday 12 April 2016,4:00 PM President and CEO Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland Speech at Antti Suvanto's farewell reception Helsinki, 11.4.2016 There are people and economists for many purposes. When times are difficult and the winds are blowing, they behave differently. Some are carried away by the wind like a bark ship. They drift. Others, on the other hand, have a keel. Then a competent sailor can also navigate the headwind and take the boat to its destination. When there is a keel, does not drift, but advances. Antti Suvanto is an economist with a keel. He doesn't drift with the winds of favor. Antti comes from Ostrobothnia. But it's not exactly a stereotype. One senior economist at the bank said that when Antti comes to the table, you can't tell from his face whether he's telling a joke or pulling a snub. When there is a strong keel, poker is also enough. Ostrobothnians and Savonians stand out from each other. The bottomers are always serious, the Savonians are just as often stunned. Antti's expression comes from Ostrobothnia. But he's hard to predict because he freaks out, but doesn't know how often. Behind the friendly essence, if necessary, you can find an Ostrobothnian character and edge. That's what we've seen again today Winter. Antti Suvanto has held many positions at the Bank of Finland. He has done analysis, compiled a story about individual phenomena on which others have been able to build. He has been a respected supervisor who has encouraged his subordinates and transferred his tacit knowledge and contacts widely. He also performed a lot himself, as a writer and speaker. He is an economist valued by all and enjoys widespread confidence. No gifts are allowed here. However, with the right of the host, I make an exception. Antti and Marja are music lovers. Among the great composers of the last century was Dmitry Shostakovich. Jean Sibelius even ranked him among the top three. Julian Barnes has published his critically acclaimed book Noise of Time this year. It relies on facts, but where there are gaps, Barnes creates the story. The message is: Even in the midst of the noise of time, you need to see the most essential. Statisticians and economists are familiar with the concept of Noise of Data, data noise. There, too, it is necessary to separate from the data what is important, relevant. Good judgment helps with that. That's what Antti has, he's focused on what's essential. I want to give this book to Antti, the composer, the conductor and, if necessary, also the solo player. At the same time, I would like to tell you that even if Antti ends his full-time employment, he will not lose anywhere. He has promised to be available. We have a few interesting ideas in this regard. Thank you Antti for the many years together.

Title: Opening words in the Money Museum's exhibition on the recession period of the 1930s. Helsinki, May 10, 2016.
text: Director General Erkki Liikanen: Opening words in the monetary museum's exhibition on the depression of the 1930s. Helsinki, 10.5.2016. . Speech . Tuesday 10 May 2016,11:00AM Check against delivery Dear friends, I welcome you to the opening of the new exhibition at the Money Museum. The subject of this exhibition is the Great Depression of the 1930s. The exhibition is open from today until next Christmas. The Great Depression of the 1930s is one of the phases in history that has most changed economic policy thinking. Its importance in this sense can be compared to the oil crisis of the 1970s and - time will tell - perhaps the global financial crisis of recent years. The lessons of the 1930s have influenced monetary policy in many ways. One lesson is that central banks take the prevention of a deflationary spiral very seriously. The second lesson is to safeguard the liquidity of the banking system during the crisis. Everyone who has studied economic history, and especially monetary policy, has gone through the Great Depression. One key figure in mediating the lessons of history in recent years was the previous governor of the Federal Reserve, Ben Bernanke. Prior to his career as a central bank, he had been a professor and had just studied monetary policy in the 1930s. The Bank of Finland's Board of Governors visited the United States in the spring of 2014, when we had the opportunity to meet Chairman Bernanke just before the end of his term of office. We asked him what he considered to be the most important lesson of monetary policy during the Depression of the 1930s. Bernanke's response was the importance of securing banks' liquidity and operational capacity. After all, in the 1930s, hundreds of banks in different countries collapsed due to payment difficulties. The loss of liquidity and the loss of credit turned an already difficult economic crisis into deep deflation and the collapse of the real economy in many countries, especially in the United States. Another lesson, according to Bernanke, was that monetary policy must move quickly. As a result, interest rates were reduced exceptionally rapidly since the autumn of 2008. Bernanke also said that what surprised him the most during the financial crisis of recent years was how quickly and strongly the crisis was transmitted from one country to another. In this respect, the world is completely different from what it was in the 1930s, as a result of the internationalisation of the financial markets and financial institutions, as well as electronic commerce. During the crisis that erupted in 2008, central banks have been much more determined and active than they were in the 1930s, and their international cooperation has worked better. But it has also been learned that monetary policy alone cannot fix all the problems raised by the financial crisis. It also requires a great deal of structural action in the other areas of economic policy. In Finland, the depression of the 1930s, then called the period of shortages, was clearly shorter than in continental European countries or the United States, but even here it caused unemployment, debt problems and bankruptcies, as well as criticism of the Bank of Finland's monetary policy. With the help of this interesting exhibition, you can get acquainted with these issues in a versatile way. Vappu Ikonen has borne the main responsibility for putting the exhibition together. Vappu has been helped in this work above all by the museum's chief curator Jaakko Koskentola and the chairman of the museum's management team Juha Tarkka. The exhibition architect has been Teemu Taskinen. Outi Kotala has been responsible for the production of the slide show in the exhibition space and the virtual exhibition, which will be opened online. Jorma Saarikko has been responsible for the presentation technique used. I would like to thank everyone involved in the construction of the exhibition and wish the exhibition a lot of interested audiences. Welcome to visit the exhibition!

Title: Bank of Finland Economic and Financial Comittee (EFC) dinner, 10 June 2016
text: Governor Erkki Liikanen: Bank of Finland Economic and Financial Comittee (EFC) dinner, 10 June 2016 . Speech . Friday 10 June 2016,10:00 AM Speech by Governor Erkki Liikanen, Bank of Finland Economic and Financial Committee (ECF) dinner Helsinki, 10 June 2016 Dear friends, As we all know, 9th of May in 1950 Robert Schuman made his great proposal, drafted by Jean Monnet, to create a coal and steel community. A year later six founding members signed the Treaty of Paris, which founded the basis for the new union. Many of those countries are here today. Finland was far away, in a divided Europe. When did we have the first contact with this process? It was by chance in the spring of 1953. Robert Schuman had left the French Government earlier in the same year due to a political crisis. At the same time the Foreign Trade Association in Finland wanted to have a famous guest speaker. An active press counsellor of the Finnish embassy in Paris met by chance former minister in a social occasion and passed him the invitation. There is no one who has an emptier calendar than a fresh former minister. So Schuman accepted the invitation right away. When the Foreign ministry in Helsinki heard about this, they wanted to cancel the invitation, but it was too late. When the visit finally took place, the Government decided not to devote any official attention to Robert Schuman. As expected, the visit created a strong negative reaction from the Soviet Union. A week later, Pravda wrote that the visit was undeniably connected with discussions against stepping up trade between Finland and the Soviet Union. President of the Republic, Juho Kusti Paasikivi, however, received Schuman and wrote in his memoirs: " I explained my own view and the position of Finland. He understood it well. Schuman is indeed an intelligent and charming man." This was 53 years ago. Europe was deeply divided into two hostile blocks. Finland followed European construction from a distance, if at all. The destiny of this country has always been linked to the relations between great powers. We have been "a land in between". Culturally, Finland shows many influences. We have got much through Stockholm, and from famous German university towns. Architecturally, the neo-classic centre of Helsinki resembles St. Petersburg. As a political entity, Finland had emerged as a result of the Peace Treaty of Tilsit, in 1807, negotiated by Napoleon and Tsar Alexander I (en francais). Napoleon encouraged the Russian emperor to conquer Finland from Sweden. Alexander I succeeded and established the autonomous Grand Duchy of Finland, where he ruled as constitutional monarch although he remained an autocrat in Russia. Important institutions of this country were developed during the autonomy, long before independence. Among them, the Bank of Finland was established in 1811. It is the fourth oldest central bank. Finland obtained its own monetary system in 1860. It was seen as a means of integrating the country's monetary system with the European monies. The currency, markka, was defined as being equal to the French franc in metallic content. In 1906, 110 years ago, Finland became the first country in Europe to grant universal suffrage to all women, still being a part of Russian empire. Finland became independent in 1917. Independence was followed by three months of tragic civil war. However, the democratic institutions survived and did not cease to function, even during the Second World War. Jean Monnet never came to Finland. But we had something in common with him: He was a cross country-skier as all the Finns are. He developed his great idea about Coal and Steel Union during a two-week cross-country randonnz on the Alps. When he skied the whole day, it cleared his mind and in the evening he put the ideas on paper. In two weeks the project was ready and he passed it to Robert Schuman. During the war, Jean Monnet often repeated that there could be no peace in Europe, if the nation states continued to be structured around the sort of sovereignty that leads to politics of national privilege and economic protectionism. Coincidentally, the same J.K. Paasikivi also wrote during the war that the limitation of raison doztat is the question upon which hinges the future of not only small states, but also the large states, and humanity as a whole. Ultimately, Monnet and Paasikivi were talking about the same thing. Finland joined the International Monetary Fund early. But the tensions between super powers went fast high and our margin of manoeuvre all but disappeared. In 1960 UK, Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Austria, Switzerland and Portugal created EFTA. Finland was able to join a year later, with a special association agreement. But in 1973 the UK moved on to the EEC, Denmark followed. Finland had to find an arrangement with the EEC. This led to a free-trade agreement with the EEC. In the end of the cold war the window to relations to the West opened and Finland used it early 1992. The president of the republic Mauno Koivisto said in his famous speech that we want a seat around the table where the decisions are taken. Finland wanted to become a full member of the European Union. What is most essential in the EU? It is that the guiding principle is law, not force. Legitimacy and the rule of law govern relations between member states. The task of the European institutions is to monitor legality and compliance of all activities with the EU treaties. Finally, taking into account the history of Finland, a small country, so often shaken by the storms of our continent, it is no surprise that Finnish European policies -from the very first day -have been community-oriented and supporting strong common institutions. We have all had our internal challenges later, but I still believe that this is the majority opinion. Two years ago President Mauno Koivisto, who had opened out path to the EU, had his 90th birthday. President Koivisto said on his birthday that he belonged to the generation who had to fight for independence during the war. Later his generation worked for European Integration. They were ready to pool the sovereignty with others, to have more influence. And he continued: oThis happened. The pessimists were wrong.o Another great Finn from the same generation, Max Jakobson, has more than anyone else explained the history of Finland to the international readers. The most famous of his books is called oThe diplomacy in the winter waro. His daughter told in the funeral of her father about their joint walk in 1997, when Finland had been a member of the EU for two years. oListen, just during recent times I have understood, that for the first time in her history Finland is genuinely independent,o Max Jakobson had said. Being a member of the European Union has given us a say in many areas. We are more than ever before in our history there where the decisions are taken. Ladies and Gentlemen, Dear friends, We are having this dinner in the house of the National Opera. Music, from classical to metal rock is a corner stone of our cultural life. But you will not hear rock today. Instead you will hear later tonight one of the famous songs of Jean Sibelius, A Dream of the Night. The singer is a great soprano Mari Palo. But she will start with a jewel among opera arias, a Song to the Moon in Rusalka, by a Check composer Antonin Dvorak. And she will finish with a well-known peace from My Fair Lady. The musical was composed by Frederic Lsewe, who was born in Berlin from Austrian parents. He moved to the US in his early 20oies. I want to wish you warmly welcome to dinner!

Title: Interview with La Repubblica, 22 June 2016.
text: Governor Erkki Liikanen: Interview with La Repubblica, 22 June 2016. . Interview . Wednesday22 June 2016,12:00 PM Governor Liikanenos interview in La Repubblica, by Ferdinando Giugliano Published on 22 June 2016 An edited transcript of the interview Britain maydecide to leave the EU. What would be the economic andfinancialimpact of this decision? I have learnt early never to reply to hypothetical questions. I can only say that we hope that the UK stays in the EU. It is in the interest of the EU and of the UK. Referenda are always for the voters to decide, from the outside you canot do or say much. What is the ECBdoingto prepare for apossible oLeaveo vote? Of course we must always be ready for everything, but for now all I can say is that I hope they stay inside. Moving on to monetarypolicy, the quantitative easing programme is setto end in March, unless you decide to extendit. Will you back an extension? We must look at monetary policy as a package of measures. Our aim is price stability, defined as inflation close but below 2% in the medium term. This target is symmetric. The challenge is that when inflation is very low, the instruments are not symmetric because you have the zero-lower bound. In this context we must look at three things: monetary policy instruments, including traditional ones such as interest rates and non-traditional ones such as negative deposit rates; second, forward guidance which postpones the expected tightening of monetary policy; and thirdly the large-scale asset purchases that pull the yield curve downwards. These three measures are all helping to achieve the target of price stability and support the economy. We have done so much, so far, and we are just starting to implement two important parts of the package: to buy corporate bonds and to conduct the second series of targeted longer-term refinancing operation. We just need to implement these with steady hand. I am convinced that we will deliver. Whatos your assessment of the European recovery? In general, the euro area economy has been recovering, and the recovery has been broad-based. Somehow, this is sometimes forgotten. Even in my country, Finland, people focus on issues such as Greece and donot see that this recovery has already continued for some time and that monetary policy is keeping its force. Of course, our concern is a prolonged, too low inflation. Therefore we need to implement our programmes with a Do you think we are at afloor for interest rates? We have carefully formulated our forward guidance, that rates will remain at the present or lower level for an extended period of time, and well past the horizon of our net asset purchases. There is no need to change our forward guidance: it has served us well and gives a framework for our measures. The corporate bondpurchases is a big step. There are criticisms that you are distortingthe corporate bond market by choosing one company over another. How do you respond to that? When we started to discuss the large-scale asset purchases, experts in the Bank of Finland proposed to have corporate bonds on the agenda. We have been investing in corporate bonds for decades and are now one of the six banks that are implementing the programme. Corporate bonds enable us to strengthen the pass-through of our monetary policy to the financing conditions of the corporates and to enlarge the universe of the purchases. There are also countries in the euro area where the sovereign bond market is very limited. We purchase corporate bonds that have an investment grade rating. There is always criticism, but all in all, I believe we have been very consistent with the implementation of the asset purchase programme. Moving on to banks, in Italythere has been widespread criticism ofthe bail-in mechanism which some,including the Bank of Italy, say increase financial instability. Are you concerned aboutthis issue? If we have learnt something from the crisis, it is that this asymmetry in the market, where profits are private and losses are to the taxpayers, does not work in the long-term. I am sure that this fundamental idea is still the right one. Of course, when you move from one stage to another, there can be difficulties and there can be criticism. Even in my country it is the same. It is very important that banks inform the citizens so that when they buy securities they know what risks are involved there. It is very important investors know there are implications. Critics say you are treating banks as cheese shops, assuming you can easily close one and go and buy cheese from adifferent one. But banks are different andthere can be systemic implications from applying bail-in to some investors. How do you respond? In the long-term the clarity of business environment and regulation is very important. For me the legislation has been an important step in the banking union. First, we have created a single supervisor for over 130 banks and we are introducing coherence in the supervisory practices. This is going pretty well. The second part has been the recovery and resolution framework. When you make such a substantial reform it is important to keep in mind the long-term goal: profits and losses would be shared by the same stakeholders. I am aware the transition can cause problems for smaller banks. For big banks, we have one supervisor, looking at them in a coherent manner. But we also have thousands of small banks, and we need to adopt the same culture, both for supervisors and the banks. But this takes time. Some economists, includingthe Governor ofthe Bank ofItaly Ignazio Visco, say we need a backstop atthe European and national levelto avoid a crisis from getting out ofhand. Do you think they are right? In the transition period, some assistance can be justified, but you should not replace the idea of bail-in with common funds. If we talk about a solution like insurance, which means risk-sharing, there is a case for creating a Sometimes the risk is that people just want to focus on the backstop and forget everything else. So you thinkbanks should be in the same position before you have a jointdeposit guarantee scheme? Ecofin said in the conclusions: oNegotiations at the political level will start as soon as sufficient progress has been made on the risk reductiono. This seems to be now the political framework. Before you take the final step, banks should be in the same position. I support the logic that in the end this kind of insurance-based, risk-sharing is justified and important. You must move in parallel in all these areas. In your 2012 report you recommended separatingthe trading activity of banks from retail activities. What was the logic behindthat? The logic is simple. Bank funding typically benefits from an implicit government guarantee, which is based on the deposit insurance. If this guarantee is also behind high-risk activities, such as proprietary trading or other large.scale market-making activities, this can lead to excessive risk-taking. A lot has happened in the markets since we published the report, as we have seen that many of the banks that had very large portfolios in this trading side have downsized them. Our proposal was not for this financial cycle, but for the long term: you can have commercial and trading activities in the same company, but they must be separated, so that market-making and proprietary trading are financed properly on the markets. The proposal is now sitting in the European Parliament, and we will see what happens. Do you have a sense of when they willdecide on it? Of course I talk to them, but there are many other important issues on their table at the moment. It is up to them to decide. You also recommended banks should have sufficientbail-inable debt and a clear hierarchy of instruments to be used in bank resolution. There is a discussion going on about the so-called TLACa buffer banks should have to spare taxpayers in case they are resolved. Some countries,including France andItaly, are sayingthatthe Single Resolution Board is asking too muchfrom the banks. Where do you stand? I understand one preoccupation of the banks. There has been a long process of reforms, changes, which have been pretty heavy, particularly for the smaller banks, who donot have the corporate services to run these all the times. We should be able to get to a new position, where we can say, thatos it for now, then we take a pause. This does not mean we are done forever, but take a pause. I think the time when this pause would be justified is coming close. I often talk to banks, including small-and medium-sized ones, so I appreciate their concerns. However, the banking lobbies often make one mistake: if they lobby against everything, this weakens their position. But I understand well that at some point they need to know that now we consolidate the reforms, take a pause, so that they can develop their business model, concentrate on that. From the reforms we have passed we can say that the banks are more stable, they are better-capitalised, but in the medium term they must be also profitable. Profits are important for the stability of the banking system, as banks must be able to finance capital losses, which can come from lending and risk-taking. This issue of long-term profitability is there and I donot contest it. It has improved. The comprehensive assessment of 130 banks was very important. It has not been contested. There were some very good aspects: for example, it was conducted at the European level, so there was no national regulatory capture. People had to treat banks equally and they did not have any bias. So it has been more credible and the recapitalization was very important. Often banks have used retained profits for recapitalization, this has made banks stronger, better-capitalised, more transparent. Of course, there are still a few pending issues, one is of course non-performing loans. If banks have a major problem with NPLs, their capacity to lend is more limited. This whole question of NPLs includes many questions: what kind of legal procedures you should have in case of bankruptcy, accounting rules, what kind of vehicles you create for handling NPLs. At the end of the day, of course, you need to have capital to finance them. These are the issues that remains on the table and it is important for the European banking system and national supervisors to deal with them. Italian banks have asubstantial problem with NPLs. Policy-makers in Rome complain thatEuropan supervisors are obsessing about NPLs, while caring less about other issues,including trading losses,for example on derivatives. Do you agree with this concern? If one does an analysis of how the lending is related to the level of NPLs there is a correlation: the more NPLs you have, the slower your lending grows. So for banks to deliver their task of lending, it is important they downsize their NPLs. But of course, my working group in the report was proposing changes to bankso trading activity. So we should not forget any risks. I know it is not a quick fix, but the bankso capacity to lend is dependent on not having a too high burden of NPLs. Everyone is entitled to his own opinion, but we should have the same facts. Are you concerned that the ECBos hyper-active monetary policy may be contributingto financial instability? ECB Governing Council has been consistent: if you study our communication since December 2014, we have always linked asset purchases and forward guidance together. It has been very coherent, from meeting to meeting. Forward guidance stays there and you reinforce it with particular measures. It is not hyper-active, but it is active, because the situation has been very difficult. And monetary policy is working. If you look at the European recovery, it is clear that monetary policy has played its role. The transmission channels are many, but in a marathon you should not stop half-way, you need to keep the tempo and patience, and deliver. Also, the Governing Council has shown its capacity to act and communicated in a coherent and consistent manner. In these difficult times there has been an institution that is strong in its commitment and consistent in its actions. We have delivered, but the ECB canot do everything. Thatos of course the big issue of structural reforms: we often talk about them in a too general manner, but they are needed to create dynamism in the economy, improve competitiveness, so that companies can have trust in the future and can decide to invest. It is important to create the willingness from companies to move on, since the financing problems are more limited than they were before. And companies should also do their part. Are you afraid that Brexit could derail the European recovery? There is one issue of which I am sure: for Finland, the EU has been the right choice. We have been able to join a Union where the relations between States are based on law, not on force. This has been the case for us since 1995. We will not give away this choice, since it is critical for our country. If you look at the challenges we have around, we would be much weaker if we were to act all alone, we would be in a much worse position. In the political area, I am convinced there is a very broad European attitude in favour of this choice of the EU, when we take into account our history. I have seen the speeches by David Cameron and Gordon Brown making these points, presenting the case in a way we can share. We have these populist tendencies which come and go, but would we really like to turn back?

Title: Book review  Robert J. Gordon:  The Rise and Fall of American Growth
text: Governor Erkki Liikanen: Book review Robert J. Gordon: The Rise and Fall of American Growth . Speech . Friday 5August2016,10:00AM Governor Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland Book review published in Finnish in Helsingin Sanomat, 1 July 2016 ROBERT J. GORDON: THE RISE AND FALL OF AMERICAN GROWTH, PRINCETON, USA, 2016 Has long-term economic growth come to a halt in the developed countries? This question has been at the centre of international debate among economists for the last year or so. The renowned economic historian and growth researcher Robert J. Gordon made his contribution to the debate at the beginning of the year with an over 700-page study of US growth from 1870 to the present day. Gordon divides the period into the unprecedented ospecial centuryo 1870d1970 and into the time of slowing growth that followed it. The former was characterised by major technological breakthroughs such as electricity and the internal combustion engine, with the impact of inventions on productivity growth being highest in the years 19201970. Subsequent innovations in information and communications technology were also revolutionary, but were restricted, in Gordonos view, to a narrower field of human activity, and therefore their impact has not been so extensive. Another difference is that the fruits of the innovations of the special century were widely distributed among citizens. The period after this is characterised by a strong increase in inequality. Gordonos book is also a social history. It describes vividly the great impact of technological development on the nature of work in agriculture and industry. Work became safer, and real earnings rose. Rooseveltos legislation also contributed to this. The technological breakthrough in homes was equally impressive; indoor plumbing and refrigerators were introduced and raised the quality of life. In Finland, this change came much later. Many Finns still remember that time. Once, as a young Member of Parliament, I accompanied a British diplomat on a speaking engagement to Kangasniemi in Eastern Finland. For him, the biggest surprise of the whole trip was the fact that, in 1973, the home where the speech was made had no running water inside. The whole region, moreover, had not yet been electrified. At the end of his book, Gordon analyses the headwinds facing US economic growth. The four most important of these are rising inequality, stagnating education, an ageing population and rising general government debt. Finland has all four challenges, but two more stark, two less serious. Finland is ageing more quickly than the USA and public indebtedness is still growing. Basic education puts us in a better position, however, and the trend with regard to inequality has not been as steep. Growth-retarding pressures, moreover, are arising from climate change. If adjustments are made in an orderly manner, the costs will be lower. The US elections will have an important impact on the implementation of the Paris Agreement. Another problem is the decline in industrial jobs, to which globalisation and technology have contributed; this has reduced average real incomes. The issue is reflected in political debate in the USA, and in Europe, too. Gordon recognises the revolutionary nature of information and communications technology. Why doesnot he believe that it will bring a new wave of productivity growth? He gives explanations, bigger and smaller. Why havenot smartphones and tablets increased productivity? Two examples of reasons: people visit entertainment websites during work time and also use time to send personal e-mail and shop online. He is also concerned that various online services greatly disturb the concentration of teenage boys in particular, adversely impacting learning outcomes. Gordon is a respected researcher. His view that the best innovations are behind us is challenged by many. One challenger is Professor Joel Mokyr, a colleague of Gordon at Northwestern University. Mokyr considers globalisation and speed to be a major change. If something is invented, it is immediately everywhere. He is convinced that scientific development is advancing rapidly and that change will only accelerate. Another well-known technology optimist, Professor Erik Brynjolfsson of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, will visit Finland in August. Gordonos economic history is impressive. I also share his concern about the headwinds to growth. But I donot believe that that peopleos capacity to innovate is on the decline. ICT and the internet are great facilitators.

Title: The slowdown in growth has had an impact on the monetary policy environment and interest rates. Helsinki, September 29, 2016.
text: Front page . Media and Publications . Releases . The ECB's monetary policy measures signal a strong commitment to price stability Releases (/en/media-and-publications/releases/) . Bulletin No. 18 . Thursday 29.9.2016, 11.00 The euro area economy is expected to grow at a moderate pace in the coming years. This view is supported by recent Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections, including the Bank of Finland's forecast for the international economy. Downside risks to the economic outlook relate mainly to factors external to the euro area. Inflation has remained around zero for about three years now, but is expected to pick up gradually, supported by monetary policy. Monetary policy has been significantly eased to maintain price stability. Key actions in this regard have included lower interest rates, large-scale purchases of securities and forward guidance. "There is a commitment to continue this action for as long as is necessary from the perspective of price stability. With a strong commitment to price stability, the effectiveness of monetary policy will increase and inflation expectations will remain anchored," said President Erkki Liikanen today at a press conference for Euro & Economy. "The Governing Council will monitor and analyse economic developments very closely on the basis of the most up-to-date information and forecasts and assess the impact of the monetary policy taken," said President Erkki Liikanen. It will take time for extensive monetary policy measures to pass through to the economy. Monetary policy has been able to contribute to the economic recovery in the euro area. However, it alone cannot bring about long-term economic growth. Structural reforms need to be accelerated in all euro area countries in order to accelerate potential output growth. The slowdown in the growth of the working-age population and productivity is dampening growth opportunities worldwide. When an ageing population approaching retirement age in developed countries saves, and asian countries also save a lot, there is a high demand for safe investments. This has contributed to a wide-ranging fall in real interest rates. "All economic policy factors need to try to prevent subdued growth and low inflation from becoming long-term," stressed Director-General Erkki Liikanen. Euro & economy publication website .
