Title: The Euro and the Battle of Ideas
text: Book Review: The Euro and the Battle of Ideas, Governor Erkki Liikanen . Speech . Friday 7 October 2016,4:00PM Finnish version of the review will be published on Saturday 8 October. Books have been written about the Economic and Monetary Union which include a lot of opinions but fall short on history and research. In this regard, the recently published The Euro and the Battle of Ideas (Princeton University Press 2016) stands apart. The book is authored by a group of three writers with diverse backgrounds: Markus Brunnermeier, a leading younger-generation economist of German origin, HaroldJames, an esteemed scholar of economic and German history, born in England, and Jean-Pierre Landau, who has acted as Deputy Governor of the Banque de France. The book describes extensively the differences between the German and French visions, perhaps more than necessary for some readers. Germans are depicted as favouring rules, the French discretion; Germans insisting on responsibility, and the French calling for solidarity; and the Germans suspecting solvency problems where the French think liquidity is the matter. The perceived differences are traced in the book to certain formative historical experiences of these nations. However, one is well-advised to recall the characterisation by Hans von Ploetz, former Secretary of State at Germanyos Foreign Office: The positions of Germany and France are often so far apart that when they are reconciled, the opinions of many others will have been taken into account in the process. According to the book othe Finns, Austrians, and sometimes Slovaks and Poles behave as if they are more Germanic than the Germans, and France is often seen as a champion of the Mediterranean Europe.o The walk on the beach in Deauville, France by Nicolas Sarkozy and Angela Merkel in October 2010 figures out already in the introduction of the book. It has been told that during this walk they made a compromise on government debt restructuring: Germany would show some flexibility on fiscal rules if France would, in return, accept oan adequate participation of private creditorso. The backdrop was the Greek sovereign debt crisis and the desire to end government liability for crises, which had gone on since the Lehman Brothers collapse of 2008. In his memoirs, the US Secretary of the Treasury Tim Geithner states that he objected to the debt restructuring at the time, as it could have been followed by a huge wave of contagion to other countries. Jean-Claude Trichet, President of the ECB, was afraid of the same. Markets did indeed react abruptly. Yields in peripheral countries soared violently. The crisis not only re-escalated but also spread to Spain and Italy. EU criticism is often dominated by complaints of encroaching Brussels supremacy. In a broad number of ways, this book demonstrates that in fact, during the financial crisis, power shifted out of Brussels to the capitals of the member states. It criticises the Commission president Josz ManuelBarroso for not giving a single major speech on the subject for he was worried that the Commission might be discredited it overstretched politically. However, another explanation may be that whenever taxpayerso money is at stake, the European Commission is hardly given a say beyond the (relatively small) EU budget. Moreover, the IMF was also wanted on board. Debt restructuring was back on the agenda as the markets temporarily calmed down in summer 2011, and Greek debt to private investors was cut the following year. Summer 2012 marked a new turning point in the crisis. First, in the June summit in Brussels, the heads of state decided on the creation of the banking union. It was a major step forward The establishment of the banking union and its three pillars single banking supervision; resolution mechanism involving stronger early intervention powers for the authorities and investor liability; and deposit guarantee are diligently described in the book. Later, in July 2012, the ECB President Mario Draghi stated the famous words in London: oWithin our mandate, the ECB is ready to do whatever it takes to preserve the euro. And believe me, it will be enough.o The ECB Governing Council acted accordingly in August and September. According to the book, the implicit support of Ms. Merkel and Finance Minister Wolfgang Schsuble was one of the reasons why the speech had such an impact. The Euro and the Battle of Ideas is an impressive accomplishment. It is an extensive analysis of the Economic and Monetary Union, the financial crisis and its political background and examines the subject in a critical but balanced manner. I really welcome that esteemed economists and historians have gone to such an effort. There are details that I recall differently. At any rate, the book is a stimulating read, and will deepen and broaden any readers perspectives.

Title: The emergence and success of companies; economic growth and employment. Investment Invest event, Helsinki, 1 December 2016.
text: President and CEO Erkki Liikanen: The emergence and success of companies; economic growth and employment. Investment Invest event, Helsinki, 1.12.2016. . Speech . Thursday1 December 2016, 4:00 PM President and CEO Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland Award ceremony at Investment Invest: Private Investor's Choice 2016  Finland's most reliable and attractive listed company Helsinki, 1.12.2016 THE EMERGENCE AND SUCCESS OF ENTERPRISES; ECONOMIC GROWTH AND EMPLOYMENT Introduction The emergence, success and destruction of enterprises are key drivers of economic growth, employment and productivity development. Production is created in enterprises, and the more productive the enterprises are, the more value added is generated. Jobs are created in new companies or in companies that are already in operation. Jobs are lost when companies cease to operate, or existing companies lay off workers. The development of jobs and productivity is positively affected, firstly, by the creation of more new enterprises, secondly, by fewer existing enterprises to close down, thirdly, by the employment of existing companies, and fourthly, by the reallocation of resources between companies? Can it be said which of these is the most important? Economics has its own branch of research that studies in particular the impact of business dynamics on the national economy. In this speech, I will therefore discuss the role of enterprises in the background of productivity and employment trends in the national economy. Growth and productivity Productivity developments are crucial for long-term growth and competitiveness. In the long term, economic growth is primarily due to the increase in labour productivity brought about by technological progress. In parallel with technological advances, recent research considers the reorientation of economic resources to more productive use as a key source of productivity growth. Differences in productivity between countries may be partly due to differences in resource allocation. The productivity of the national economy may lag behind competitor countries due to the fact that within industries labour and capital are not in the best use. Even within narrowly defined industries, productivity differences between firms are large and their productivity is very asymmetrically distributed. In general, there are only a few relatively high-productivity companies operating in the industry and the majority of the operators are relatively low-productivity companies. Indeed, particularly from the point of view of economic policy, it can be misleading to speak of an 'average enterprise'. The productivity of a national economy or industry does not depend solely on the productivity of the average enterprise, but on how the factors of production are distributed between different enterprises. Productivity and the efficient use of economic resources naturally improve as the share of high-productivity firms increases at the expense of low-productivity firms. In a well-functioning economy, the most productive companies are large and growing, and the companies with the lowest productivity are small and contracting (Haltiwanger (2011), CompNet (2015)). How do new and existing companies in the market affect productivity? The operating environment of companies is constantly changing and affects productivity and profitability. Changes in the operating environment create conditions for the emergence of new companies and force companies already on the market to adapt and adapt their activities. Those companies that are able to regenerate, survive the competition and grow, those that fail to adapt will contract or leave the market. Productivity growth and the reorientation of resources are generated through several channels: firstly, new companies enter the market, secondly, selection occurs, some companies survive, some exit the market, or thirdly, existing companies renew internally or resources are redirected between them (see, for example, Hyytinen and Maliranta 2013). The productivity effects of companies of different sizes and ages depend on differences in productivity on the one hand and on the size of the enterprises on the other. The productivity growth of new enterprises is often faster than that of the old ones. However, the productivity of new firms tends to be below average initially, so the impact of new firms on productivity growth in the economy as a whole may initially be negative. Over time, new enterprises grow at the expense of the old ones, and the resulting positive effect on productivity will only become apparent with a delay. Young companies that survive the competition grow faster than old ones. The exit of companies from the market has a positive impact on productivity when low-productivity firms are eliminated. According to a study by Hyytinen and Maliranta (2013), the most important source of productivity growth in the economy is the gradual renewal of relatively old companies. Even if the change in productivity is not as great as in young enterprises that are rapidly increasing their productivity, the impact can be large due to the relatively large size of these enterprises. This observation is also noteworthy from the point of view of economic policy. Jobs are created in companies In addition to productivity, enterprises play a key role in employment development. In Finland, the debate on job creation is often conducted on a general level. The creation of new businesses and the growth of existing ones are important for job creation. It is clear that, accordingly, the contraction and closure of companies mean the destruction of jobs. However, not all companies create new jobs. A large proportion of all new jobs are created by a very small number of companies. In Finland, gazelle companies that grow very fast, i.e. more than 20% a year, account for about 6% of companies, but it is in these companies that about half of all new jobs are created. At the same time, in a large number of enterprises, job creation remains very low and the number of companies making job losses is considerable, regardless of the economic situation. In the debate on economic policy, the role of SMEs as employers is often raised. Indeed, a large proportion of new jobs in the national economy are created by SMEs. At the same time, it should be remembered that a very large proportion of SMEs are companies with one or only a few employees that are not growing and that is not their aim. Studies show that a more important factor in job creation than the size of a company is the age of the company: new enterprises create jobs in particular. Among the new ones there are a relatively large number of so-called . gazelle companies that are growing and increasing the number of jobs at a rapid pace. However, in the case of young companies, the up-or-out dynamic is emphasized. Of these companies, only a small number survive beyond the valley of death in the first years. But at the same time, it should be remembered that even if a large number of start-ups do not ultimately succeed and close down in the first couple of years, those that continue often grow rapidly in the years immediately after their establishment. However, the rate of job growth in enterprises rarely continues over long periods of time. This slowdown in growth rates is common, at least for the fastest growing companies. The term 'gazelle' perhaps gives the wrong impression of fast-growing companies, as there is no permanent group of companies that grow year after year clearly faster than other companies. The point is that some companies grow much faster than others during their life cycle, either through their own operations or through acquisitions. Then let's look at the figures of recent years in Finland. In recent years, the number of start-ups has declined and the growth in the number of enterprises that have closed down has stalled. In 2015, the enterprise stock was on level with 2013. At the same time, the creation of new jobs has decreased. However, the share of start-ups in Finland among all enterprises is low in international comparison. In many countries, start-ups account for about 1525% of all companies, while in Finland it is less than 10%. Although job creation in young enterprises is significant, the destruction of jobs in them is also great. More permanent changes in the number of jobs are essential. Along with start-ups, large companies are also needed. While new and small enterprises can be important for job creation (employment growth), a large proportion of jobs (level of employment) are in large enterprises. Small and large enterprises do not live in isolation, but form a complex of interacting companies, in which large companies provide SMEs with a market and outsourcing agreements. (Nightingale & Coad 2013) However, employment is not the only objective of economic policy. Policies aimed at employment growth in companies alone can be very problematic in the long run if it is at the expense of productivity growth in companies (Aiginger, 2006, 2007). It should be remembered that it is productivity growth that is key to a country's long-term economic growth. Conclusions Enterprises play an important role in both productivity growth and employment growth. American professor John Haltiwanger (2011) states that a well-functioning economy is flexible enough to allow the reallocation of resources that improve productivity, while minimizing the costs of change. Friction exists in all economies. But the weakest productivity and growth performance occurs where product, capital and labour markets are the most rigid. The problem with politics is that it is difficult to identify fast-growing companies in advance, and rapid growth does not necessarily predict rapid growth in the future. The most important thing, therefore, is for decision-makers to remove obstacles to the growth and mobility of companies, both new and existing, and to create the best possible conditions for the creation of new businesses. The market then decides which of them will be most successful. Title: Monetary policy and economic outlook. Helsinki, 13 December 2016.
text: Monetary policy will continue to support price stability and growth Releases (/en/media-and-publications/releases/) . Press releasenumber 25 . Tuesday 13 December 2016,11:00 AM The global economic recovery has continued. The economic outlook nevertheless contains uncertainties from potential changes in the international political arena. d4Protectionist views have been raised at the same time as there is a great need for international cooperation to resolve climate, refugee and economic challenges,d5 said Bank of Finland Governor Erkki Liikanen today at the release of the latest issue of the Bank of Finland Bulletin. The economic expansion in the euro area is expected to proceed at a moderate but firming pace. The risks surrounding the euro area growth outlook remain tilted to the downside, and inflationary pressures continue to be subdued. The ECB Governing Council decided in December 2016 to continue the expanded asset purchase programme (EAPP) until the end of 2017, or beyond if necessary, until the pace of inflation is sustainably restored in line with the price stability objective. Purchases to the value of EUR 80 billion per month will continue until March 2017. Thereafter they will continue at a monthly pace of EUR 60 billion. d4The very substantial amount of monetary support is preserved in the euro area. Favourable financing conditions are important for price stability and economic recovery,d5 Governor Liikanen continued. ECB monetary policy has also supported growth in Finland. Economic growth in the euro area improves Finnish companiesd5 opportunities to increase exports to other euro area countries. In addition, financing costs have decreased in Finland owing to an efficient transmission of monetary policy, and interest rates on household and corporate loans are low. This has served to bolster consumption and investment. The Finnish economy is recovering. Growth has been largely dependent on householdsd5 consumption and housing investments but is forecast to gradually become more broadly based. Exports will gradually recover as growth continues in Finlandd5s export markets and Finlandd5s own cost-competitiveness improves. It is important to strengthen the underpinnings of growth by continuing structural reforms and securing a favourable operating environment for business. Labour productivity growth is often faster in young companies than in more established ones. On the other hand, the most important source of productivity growth across the economy as a whole is a gradual renewal in established companies. Meanwhile, a substantial proportion of new jobs are emerging among new and rapidly growing companies. Companies that will grow rapidly are hard to identify in advance, and rapid growth that has already occurred cannot necessarily anticipate a continuation of the same trend. It is the role of economic policy to create equal opportunities for different types of companies. d4When the economy is able to renew itself by improving productivity and generating jobs, this will boost economic growth and the outlook for the public finances. It will also reduce the risk of increased marginalisation and lack of opportunities,d5 Governor Liikanen underlined. Euro & talous publication website . Thursday12 January 2017,7:30PM Governor Erkki Liikanen The Embassy of Finland, Paris, 12 January 2018 FINLAND AND EUROPE The delivered text is authentic It has been almost 67 years since journalists met on the evening of May 9, at the Quai d'Orsay for the minister's weekly press conference. They expected the usual routine, but the minister in question, Robert Schuman, read them a two-page statement in a "deaf and hesitant" voice that hit them like a bomb. "It is no longer a question of vain words, but of a bold act, a constructive act. The France acted, and the consequences of its action can be immense. It acted essentially for peace. For peace to really have a chance, there must first be a Europe. "This is how Schuman began his speech, which culminated in the proposal to create a coal and steel community. It was in the coal and steel sector, the raw materials of the war, that Schuman first wanted to establish a Community. Schuman said it explicitly: "The solidarity of production that will thus be forged will show that any war between France and Germany becomes not only unthinkable but materially impossible. " The French initiative has received considerable attention in different parts of Europe. But the Finnish embassy in Paris did not report on this in Helsinki until September, when negotiations on the establishment of the Coal and Steel Community were already well advanced. The Treaty establishing the European Coal and Steel Community was finally signed in April 1951. The treaty largely followed Schuman's initial conception. And it was on the same basis that the European Economic Community, the EEC, was founded six years later. In Finland, Robert Schumann, the composer whose name is written with two n's, was much better known than the founding father of Europe. Robert Schuman was a leading politician in post-war France. Juho Kusti Paasikivi had a similar statu in Finland. Schuman became Prime Minister in 1947, when Paasikivi had already assumed the presidency of Finland. The Schuman government lasted only one year, after which Schuman served as foreign minister in eight successive governments. Paasikivi and Schuman each inspired their country's foreign policy in the late forties and early fifties, but Paasikivi played this role longer and, finally, as president in the years -46-56. The priorities of the French and Finnish governments were hardly comparable. Paasikivi was primarily concerned with building a relationship of trust with the Soviet Union, while ensuring that his country continued to abide by the rules of democracy and the market economy. As for Schuman, his main problem was Germany and, above all, how to eliminate forever the possibility of a new armed conflict between France and Germany. On the domestic political scene, both were anxious to limit the weight of the Communist Party. As you well know, at the origin of Robert Schuman's initiative was Jean Monnet, who at the time headed the Commissariat au Plan. I'll talk about Monnet later. Schuman and Paasikivi's careers and worldviews, however, have some things in common. Schuman was originally from Alsace-Lorraine, a region which, until the First World War, was part of Germany. He attended school in Metz and studied law in Munich and Berlin. Schuman, needless to say, knew Germany well; he even held an administrative job in the German army during the war. Paasikivi was an influential figure in Finland at the time when it constituted an autonomous Grand Duchy within the Russian Empire. He was a leading expert on Russian issues. At the beginning of his studies, he specialized in Russian language and literature and spent six months in Novgorod. Subsequently, he too chose the legal profession. During the 1910s, the relationship with Germany was the subject of heated controversy in Alsace-Lorraine. Political opinion was sharply divided. Some wanted the region to become a German state in their own right, while others aspired to a return to the French zone of influence. The former wanted an autonomous AlsaceLorraine, with its own constitution, its own government, and independent of the Bundesrat. It is interesting to note that during the debates, the example of Finnish autonomy was occasionally mentioned as a reference. As he is well known, Jean Monnet was originally from the Cognac region. It was Jean Monnet's father who created the Monnet brand in 1901. The cases of cognac were shipped by the Monnet company to Berlin, New York, St. Petersburg and London. The idea that these crates were expected all over the world stimulated the young man's imagination. In search of adventure, he left school at the age of 16 and set off to discover the vast world, first two years in London, after Canada and finally the United States. By the age of 20, he had already seen much of the world. Monnet returned to Cognac just before the First World War and started working in the family business. However, Monnet continually reflected on the great problems of war and peace. He was concerned about the poor organization of Allied supplies purchases. Monnet managed to get in touch with the French Prime Minister and present his ideas to him. This unknown 26-year-old, son of a cognac merchant, made a deep impression on the Prime Minister. He sent it to the Minister of War and Monnet soon found himself in London, tasked with organizing the combined supply of the Allies. With such a background, he became Deputy Secretary-General of the League of Nations. A few years later, however, bad news came to him from Cognac. The market had collapsed and Monnet's sister went to Geneva to ask her brother to return to take care of the family business. To the surprise of his colleagues, Monnet returned to Cognac at the age of 36 to run the family business. As soon as business had been put in order in Cognac's company, Monnet entered the world of banking. He started working for an American investment bank in Paris. He led the negotiations on the stabilization of the zloty in Warsaw. In 1929, he moved to the United States to work in San Francisco. Monnet summed up his period in San Francisco, which ended in 1932, as follows: "In San Francisco I made a lot of money, then lost a lot of money, the only thing I added to my capital was experience." At the same time, the family received good news. The company acquired a new customer, ALKO, the Finnish state-owned alcohol monopoly. Over the years, Monnet has become a well-known and respected brand in the Finnish market. During the same period, J.K. Paasikivi was the president of Kansallis-Osake Pankki Bank, a large Finnish bank until 1934. J.K. Paasikivi was a great expert on Russia. He was already the head of the delegation that in 1920 negotiated peace between Finland and Soviet Russia. He was also in a key position in negotiations with our neighbour before, during and after the Second World War and also served a period as ambassador to Moscow. Jean Monnet's contacts with Moscow were limited professionally, but important for his personal life. In 1929, Jean Monnet had fallen in love with an Italian woman during a dinner in Paris. This young woman was already married and she could not get a divorce. Eventually, after some complicated maneuvers, Monnet took his beloved Silvia to Moscow, where Catholic marriages were not recognized. They married there in 1934, with the help of the Russian authorities. In 1936, Monnet returned to Washington, D.C., where his family lived until the end of the war. He established an extensive network of contacts in this city. He was a friend of a renowned journalist, Walter Lippmann, and Monnet was an influential figure in circles close to President Roosevelt. When the war broke out, MP Robert Schuman was in charge of the evacuation of his constituency of Thionville. In 1940, he was appointed French Under-Secretary of State for Refugee Affairs. When the French government was transferred to Vichy, Schuman followed suit. But when all constitutional powers were conferred on Marshal Petain, Schuman left Vichy and returned to his constituency in August 1940. There he was soon arrested by the Germans. Two years later, he managed to escape and joined the resistance until the end of the war. Paasikivi served as ambassador to Moscow from April 1940 until the end of June 1941, although he returned to Finland in March. During the war, he maintained numerous contacts with Finnish political and economic leaders. For his part, during the war, Monnet was involved in various international operations, and enjoyed the confidence of President Roosevelt. I am simply referring to a historical episode in Monnet's life during the war. In July 1940, Monnet was in London. De Gaulle, too, had already settled in London. Monnet proposed to the British government that it take a sufficiently spectacular step to galvanize the French government. He proposed the creation of a close union between England and France, with a common currency, a customs union and equal citizenship rights for nationals of both states. Winston Churchill hesitated, but he nevertheless submitted the proposal to his government for discussion. To his surprise, the government welcomed the proposal enthusiastically and approved it on July 14, 1940. Charles de Gaulle did the same and he became, the next day, a historical figure through his speech to the BBC. De Gaulle did not like the federal accent of Monnet's text, but he understood that, for the sake of pragmatism, the great evils need the great remedies. The reaction in France was amazement. It simply seemed impossible to put the roof on the house before the walls were built. It was hoped, however, that the French Prime Minister would have a little more time. But history has decided otherwise. Questions of national sovereignty and reason of state During World War II, Monnet repeatedly emphasized the need for European integration. He was not an idealistic federalist; he was above all a man endowed with practical sense. Monnet had been disappointed by the League of Nations' inability to act. He was convinced that the interdependence of nations was a reality and that exacerbated nationalism was at the root of the majority of conflicts. He was equally convinced that Europe's political stability and economic prosperity required the creation of a free trade area. But it was not enough to eliminate customs duties, union was necessary in other areas as well, among which Monnet envisaged money, prices, industrial and agricultural production as well as communications. For Monnet, Europe would never know peace, if it continued to emphasize a type of national sovereignty leading to imbalances and protectionism. If the European states were to isolate themselves from each other again, it would once again be necessary to constitute disproportionate years. And, soon, it would be war again. Around the same time, in the summer of 1944, Paasikivi was reflecting on the fate of small countries. His study of history had made him pessimistic: "States act in the name of reason of state, that is, simply in their interest. This notion is frightening, it has the color of blood." He continued: "To date, no system has been devised that can put a brake on the reason of state and protect other countries from it." When Monnet spoke of nationalism and national sovereignty, Paasikivi wrote about reason of state. In the final analysis, they dealt with the same subject. For Paasikivi, it was first necessary to find a way to set limits to the reason of State; for Monnet, the first difficulty was to circumscribe national sovereignty. The starting point of Paasikivi's reflection was the fate of small countries, but it went far beyond that: "Reaching limits to reason of state and reconciling it with morality is a question that, of course, concerns above all the future of small countries, but which, in the final analysis, will also determine the future of large countries and humanity as a whole." History had not only made Paasikivi pessimistic, it had also made him cautious. For his part, when his many initiatives earned him accusations of excessive optimism, Monnet systematically replied: "I am not optimistic. I am determined. " As for Schuman, he summed up his thought in his unpublished memoirs: "The hard lessons of history have taught the man of the frontier that I am to be wary of hasty improvisations, projects that are too ambitious, but they have also taught me that when an objective, carefully considered judgment based on the reality of the facts and the best interests of men, leads us to new, even revolutionary initiatives, it is important ... to stick to it firmly and persevere. " Birth of a great idea The paths of the prudent minister, Robert Schuman, and the daring man of action, Jean Monnet, crossed during the post-war period. In February 1950, Monnet had travelled to the Alps for a two-week ski tour. Although he had a guide to show him the way, Monnet found himself alone in the evening: evolving in the world of concepts, he traced his own track, which was to lead him to the great innovative ideas that he then laid on paper. When it returned, the proposal was ready: the France should take the initiative to create a coal and steel union, which would make it possible to resolve the thorny conflict over the management of coal and steel and to normalize relations between France and Germany. On May 1, Schuman sent a message to Monnet: "I have read your proposal. I make it my business." The central idea of Schuman's initiative was that, in the fields of coal and steel, the Member States would agree to give up part of their national sovereignty, under the aegis of a community. The Christian Democrats gave him their full support. The conference of social democrats, an opposition party, opposed it. Only one of them, a little-known young MP, defended the plan with warmth. The Assembly went to Strasbourg, the High Authority and the Court of Justice to Luxembourg. At the same time, Schuman's position as French foreign minister was under threat. Pinay's government fell in December 1952 and Schuman left foreign affairs in January 1953. "Visitor full of intelligence and charm in Finland" A few weeks later, the Finnish Foreign Trade Association was looking for a speaker for the occasion. The committee of the Foreign Trade Association was delighted. But difficulties soon arose. According to Brotherus, the foreign minister went so far as to ask France's ambassador in Helsinki to cancel Schuman's planned visit to Finland. The neighbor was Jean Monnet. Louis Carre had simply invited his neighbor to meet the important host. Monnet and Kekkonen had a long conversation in English, although the newspaper does not say what about it. This is the only meeting between Jean Monnet and a Finnish head of state. At the instigation of the Benelux countries, negotiations had been initiated with a view to creating a European Economic Community (the EEC). The negotiations led to the conclusion of the Treaty of Rome in 1957. Under the terms of this Treaty, the Member States have relinquished part of their national sovereignty in certain well-defined areas, in particular in the fields of customs policy, trade policy, competition policy and agricultural policy. The guiding principle of the founding States of the EEC was the idea that together, European countries would be more powerful and stronger than alone. Gathered in a Community, the Member States would acquire an economic and political "added value" which they could not obtain individually. Finland was far from all this. The Soviet Union regarded the EEC as a Western alliance and not as a partner. Finland had little room for manoeuvre and every step was closely monitored. In Finland, European integration was little known  if it was. Finland joined EFTA as an associate member in 1961. When the UK decided to leave EFTA to join the EEC, it was Finland's first Brexit. We were obliged to negotiate a free trade agreement with the EEC. Which was not easy. After the Single European Act, Jacques Delors made a proposal on the European Economic Area. We have concluded the negotiations. We had obtained access, but we were not equal with the member states. Finland had no say in Community policy. The conclusion was clear. Mauno Koivisto, our President at the time, spoke to Parliament in 1992: We want to be around the table where decisions are taken. We want to have our say. We want to be a constructive member. I also want to go back to Paasikivi's memoirs. What is the essential characteristic of the European Union, if not that the fundamental principle that guides it is law - not force? Finland concluded accession negotiations on 1 March 1994, the same day that President Koivisto's term of office ended and Martti Ahtisaari made his solemn commitment to the Finnish Parliament. Legitimacy and the rule of law are the guiding principles governing relations between Member States. As guardian of the Treaty, the Commission's task is to ensure the legality of all activities and compliance with the founding treaties of the European Union. The European Court of Justice independently settles disputes concerning the legality of such actions. The principle of legality and common institutions represent an important protection for all Member States, regardless of their size or population. This is especially true for the small Member States. This is the most essential. Once we have taken a chair around a table in an institution that respects these principles, we do not leave it! But in Europe, we need to do better, of course! We need to focus on the essentials. To conclude: I would like to highlight two priorities where action at European level is necessary and also the most effective. First of all, the banking and capital markets union must be completed. We had a long crisis after 2008. Economic and Monetary Union must be strengthened through these important projects. We have made good progress, but we must complete them. Then we were confronted by a crisis of immigration and refugees of war and economy. We must ensure the control of our external borders and we must broaden the Consensus of the European Union on migration policy and apply the principles of responsibility and solidarity. And of course, all European actions must be complemented by national actions. Thank you for your attention.

Monday16 January 2017,5:00 PM CEO Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland Speech at Pentti Hakkarainen's opening reception Helsinki, 16 January 2017 Dear friends, Pentti, I am so happy that so many foreign and Finnish guests have come here today. Pentti is making history. In two weeks he will be the first member in the history of the Bank of Finland who has served all three 5-year mandates as a board member and after this all is not retiring. The retirement age is still far from him and will go even further. Pentti has been a great colleague. Out of his many qualities I just mention three. First, he is always available. Whatever is the issue or how difficult it could be, he never runs away. He gives his support even when you still hesitate to ask. If you need a stronger defense, he can play libero. If you need attack, he can make goals. His 24/7 availability has been a huge asset for the bank. And to have such a deputy governor is a rare privilege. In theory, this could sometimes be a problem for Hannele. Second, Pentti is curious, he wants to know more and he wants to learn. Curiosity is an important quality for a creative working environment. People must be ready to make questions. Often those which look simple, are the most difficult. Third, one issue dominates in his mind: how to improve efficiency and productivity. How to get more out of our resources? Could we do this all by spending less? And here Pentti does not give up. Never. Dear friends, Pena already has a rare career behind her. Han had been responsible for the financing of one oral company and had been responsible for two management position of a large bank before joining the Bank of Finland. He has been at the Bank of Finland for 15 years now. In this background, it has sometimes been the case that Pena was the most active member of the executive board and at the same time the official who knew the details best. There may have been times to keep up with others or endure. I would also like to thank Pentti for numerous moments of discussion during the past 12 years. The world has been in turmoil and there has been a need to stop, even for half an hour. Have sat down, had a cappuccino, maybe even smoked a small cigar, when it was legal. And discussed. I still miss those moments. Dear friends, When people leave an institution we invite friends and colleagues to a reception to say good-bye. But Pentti is not leaving. He is starting a new career as a European member in the Single Supervisory Mechanism of the ECB. Pentti had a unanimous support for this task in the ECB Governing Council. I am sure he will do a great job in Frankfurt. So we dont say good-bye, hyvssti, we say as the French do: au revoir, goodbye only until we meet again, au revoir, nskemiin, nskemisiin. Thank you, Kiitos Pena.

Title: On European integration, the Treaty of Rome and Finland's path in Europe. Speech at the 60th anniversary of the Treaty of Rome, Helsinki, 25 March 2017.
text: Director-General Erkki Liikanen: on European integration, the Treaty of Rome and Finland's path in Europe. Speech at the 60th anniversary of the Treaty of Rome, Helsinki, 25.3.2017. . Speech . Saturday 25 March2017, 3:00PM President Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland 60th anniversary of the Treaty of Rome Helsinki, 25.3.2017 ON EUROPEAN INTEGRATION, THE TREATY OF ROME AND FINLAND'S PATH IN EUROPE President Urho Kekkonen began his second term in March 1962 with a major election victory. Behind them were the note crisis and discussions in Novosibirsk with Prime Minister Hrutshev. John F. Kennedy was halfway through his short presidency. The domestic political situation in Finland was tense. 39-year-old Ahti Karjalainen had become prime minister for the first time. Shortly after the elections, President Urho Kekkonen made a state visit to France at the invitation of President Charles de Gaulle. Ahead of the trip, the international situation had escalated due to the Cuban Missile Crisis. The visit started at 24.10 and lasted almost two weeks. The arrival day dinner at the Elysee Palace was described by 33-year-old Counsellor Jussi Makinen in his book: "I also prepared a draft of Kekkonen's speech, which he gave to General de Gaulle at the dinner offered in his honour at the Elysee Palace on 24 October 1962. The speech, to which Kekkonen did not make a single change, reads in its entirety as follows: " Makinen then publishes the entire speech and continues: "My honour was not limited only to the fact that I had been able to draft the text of the speech, but since Kekkonen did not speak French, he also commissioned me to read the speech in French after he had given it to General de Gaulle in Finnish. The next day, when I heard the speech of the President of the Republic of Finland in my own voice on the French radio, I felt grateful that in this way I was able to serve my country." "As the second long discussion on the first day of the visit drew to a close, President Kekkonen raised the issue of enlarging the European Single Market and Finland's export interests to the common market. General de Gaulle replied that this economic question he preferred to address in the presence of his advisers and suggested that it be raised at a meeting the following day, to which he, for his part, would invite (Prime Minister) Pompidou and (Foreign Minister) Couve de Murville." And later Makinen continues: "It was a very significant speech," said Pompidou to me. "There were important ideas in it that I often come to think about. I hope that I will have the opportunity to discuss these matters with President Kekkonen. Because the ideas put forward by President Kekkonen in his speech are very important for France as they are for Finland. They are very essential for the development of the whole world." After all, there is nothing about the discussions related to the EEC itself in Jussi Makinen's book: "I talk to Kekkonen". I understand Kekkonen's position on the book very well. When Makinen asked the president to comment on the manuscript, Kekkonen replied: "The book is not about me, but about you". Juhani Suomi has gone through the debates related to Europe in his book The President. Finland notes that de Gaulle was open-minded in the discussions, which later helped Kekkonen to analyse the development of Europe. De Gaulle could not accept a bipolar world, the intermediate world between the United States and the USSR was important. In order to be able to control its interests, that middle world would have to unite. De Gaulle left no doubt under whose leadership this should happen. According to Finland, he had already stated in his message through the ambassador that "the real Europe is France". De Gaulle sought to realize the "intermediate world idea, with the help of a strong European EEC. According to him, the purpose of economic cooperation was to lay the foundations for political cooperation, a Union that would also extend into the area of defence. At the supranational level, he did not want to extend cooperation and sharply criticized those who wanted it. After the official part of the visit, the president spent a free weekend in Paris. Juhani Suomi has published Jussi Makinen's colourful description of the weekend in his book The President. Helsingin Sanomat, on the other hand, reported in a one-column little news story that Urho Kekkonen visited Louis Carre's house at the weekend and met Jean Monnet. They talked for a long time in English. According to the newspaper, "Mr Europe", despite being 74 years old, had seemed refreshed and brisk. Louis Carre was a successful Parisian art dealer. Alvar Aalto had drawn a house for him in a small village 40 kilometers from Paris. Another architectural option had been Le Corbusier. The presentation of the municipality mentions not only Louis Carre, but also another prominent figure who lived in the same village. He was Jean Monnet, the 'founding father' of the European Union, as the French put it. Monnet, the son of a cognac merchant from Cognac, made a remarkable career in international positions and banking, and after the war settled in this small village. Louis Carre and Jean Monnet were thus neighbors and friends. De Gaulle's sharp criticism was, above all, jean monnet. De Gaulle and Monnet knew each other for a long time. I will mention only one, but an episode from the time of the war: In July 1940, the French government faltered between the continuation of the war and the armistice. Monnet was in London at the time and he worked hard to encourage the French government to continue the war. De Gaulle had also already settled in London. Jean Monnet suggested that the British Government should make another dramatic move to encourage the French Government. The proposal was: To create a deep union between England and France. The Union would have a single currency, it would form a customs union and its citizens would have common citizenship rights. Quite a proposal, even in the light of today. Winston Churchill hesitated, but nevertheless submitted it to his government. To Churchill's surprise, the government welcomed it enthusiastically and adopted the proposal on 14 July 1940. So did Charles de Gaulle, who became a figure in history the next day with his speech to the BBC. De Gaulle did not like the federalist tone of Monnet's text, but as a pragmatist he understood the necessity of dramatic initiatives. De Gaulle had only met Monnet once before, on his last visit to London. However, it was hoped that the French Prime Minister, Paul Reynaud, would use it to take more time. But the reception was dismayed. Several ministers said Britain was trying to subjugate France as its domino state. Marshal Petain, who was still a minister at the time, said that to unite with Britain is the same as to ally with the body. Although there had been cooperation in the diplomatic sphere, a large part of the army, and especially the navy, was very suspicious of Britain. And no extra time was taken. Petain came to power and began armistice negotiations with Germany. France was lost. Eric Rousssel, who wrote a biography of Jean Monnet, estimates that this episode left a permanent rift in de Gaulle's relationship with Monnet. de Gaulle gave an interview about it published after his death, to which Monnet later reacted. It was a peculiar post-mortem, All in all, President Kekkonen's visit to Maison Carre lasted an hour. A short guest list for the event has been found in the archives. According to it, Louis Carre had also invited Maire Gullichsen. What were Urho Kekkonen and Jean Monnet talking about? Unfortunately, there is no memo on the discussion. In addition to European integration, there would have been many topics for small talk. For the novelist, it would be an open treasure trove. Markus Leikola has recently published an excellent historical novel, The Street of the New World. In the second part, he could build the content for the conversation as well. Karo Hamalainen wrote a book about Paavo Nurmi, in which he goes through Nurmi's imaginary conversations with Urho Kekkonen and Risto Rydi. Here are three examples of possible topics for discussion: First, both were cross-country skiers. In February 1950, Monnet and a guide went on a ski hike in the Alps. In the evenings, by the fireplace, he wrote down his thoughts. At the end of the two-week trip, he had a proposal for coal and steel cooperation ready. This is what Monnet says about the ski hike in his memoirs. Both knew that cross-country skiing brightened thoughts. Another topic could have been Moscow. Jean Monnet's wife, Silvia, was also present at Maison Carre. They had their own special relationship with the Soviet Union. Jean and Silvia Monnet were married in Moscow in 1934. At a dinner in Paris, Monnet was head over heels in love with an Italian, Catholic lady. The husband was there. It was impossible to get rid of the difference. The only way Monnet could think of was to get to Moscow, which did not recognize Catholic marriage. The Soviet authorities helped them to the port of marriage. What might the archives tell us about that? And thirdly, Alko OY had already brought Monnet cognac to the shelves in 1934. It was a well-known, better brand of cognac in Finland. In the same year, Monnet suffered heavy losses as a banker in San Francisco. Tamminiemi's butler said that Monnet cognac was a valued brand in the house. It is interesting that during a state visit, the President of Finland met a person whose views were strongly rejected by the President of the host country. Who arranged the meeting between Monnet and Kekkonen? A year ago, I asked Ossi Sunelli, who was part of the travelling party, and Matti Hakkanen, who was serving as an assistant in Paris at the time. According to both estimates, the invitee must be the art dealer Louis Carre. He had simply summoned his neighbour, Jean Monnet. Ambassador Gunnar Palmroth would not have done so. During their visit, Monnet and de Gaulle increasingly expressed contrasting views on the fundamental issues of European integration, deepening and enlargement. According to President de Gaulle, national sovereignty was inviolable, he did not accept strong European institutions and he was negative about qualified majority voting. A few years later, with his 'empty chair policy', he froze the eec's entire operation. Monnet, on the other hand, considered that the objectives of the EEC and effective decision-making could only be safeguarded by qualified majority rules and common, independent institutions. These were two important prerequisites for effective decision-making. They are the deepening of it. During the visit, the first EEC enlargement negotiations were underway with the UK, Ireland, Denmark and Norway at the time of Kekkonen's visit. The usual problems were on the table, above all agriculture. The Conservative government was in favour of membership, Labour had turned against in opposition. de Gaulle took advantage of this when, in January 1963, he vetoed the enlargement negotiations with Britain. An additional reason was in the background: "England has become a satellite of the USA. The Scandinavians are satellites of England," de Gaulle told his spokesman Alain Peyrefitte. Monnet, on the other hand, was pro-enlargement. He had been in England during the two wars and respected the tradition of democratic institutions and freedom of speech in the country. Monnet strongly condemned de Gaulle's decision: 'Instead of creating a European Union with Great Britain and basing it on a partnership between Europe and the USA, we have achieved a desunion and the dangers that this entails'. In his book The President, Juhani Suomi estimated that de Gaulle "could rightly see a guarantor that the development of the organization (i.e. the EEC) would not endanger Finland's interests". On the other hand, there is no mention of monnet's meeting and his views on the development of the EEC. One year after Kekkonen's visit, US President Eisenhower met de Gaulle in Paris. He asked about Monnet. De Gaulle replied, "He makes good cognac. Unfortunately, that's not enough for him". Jean Monnet never visited Finland. Instead, another founding father of the EU, Robert Schuman, who took the initiative to establish the Coal and Steel Community drafted by Monnet in 1950, later visited Finland. The Treaty establishing the European Coal and Steel Community was signed in the spring of 1951. Robert Schuman's visit to Finland took place in 1953. The invitation to visit had been backed by the Finnish Foreign Trade Association, but the trainman in Paris was Press Counsellor Heikki Brotherus. In his memoirs, he said that he had therefore received a letter from Permanent Secretary Tarjanne accusing him of high-handedness. In his book, Brotherus claimed that the Foreign Ministry had gone so far as to ask the French ambassador to Finland to cancel Schuman's visit. Where did we go in the spring of 1953? Stalin had died in March. The election of the new Soviet leadership was followed with great interest. Prime Minister Urho Kekkonen represented Finland at Stalin's funeral. After returning from the funeral, Kekkonen told President Paasikivi that his mind in Moscow had calmed down. The new leader Malenkov is a man of Stalin's spirit and will pursue the same policy. The new government was organized according to a precise plan and Malenkov and Beria agreed. Robert Schuman's visit took place three months after he left the French Government. At the weekly meeting, Ralf Torngren told President Paasikivi that the leadership of the Foreign Trade Union wants to make the visit a big deal, but the government does not. He stated, according to Paasikivi's diaries, that "the government does not hold dinner, nor any other attention." That is why Prime Minister Urho Kekkonen did not meet WithChuman. However, President J.K. Paasikivi was listening to Robert Schuman's speech on 9.4.1953 and also received him the next day. Paasikivi spent an hour talking with Schuman. Schuman assessed germany's future and believed that the Coal and Steel Community would contribute to eliminating antagonism between Germany and France. Paasikivi explained Finland's position. "Schuman is indeed a pleasant and intelligent man," Paasikivi summed up in the diaries of his meeting. Although the government did not organise the programme, The Minister of Social Affairs in Kekkonen's government, Vaino Leskinen, took him to a private dinner at the Workers' House in Helsinki, where a guest met trade unionists. There are no notes on this discussion either. It was part of the picture of the time that Pravda wrote about the visit a week later. According to Pravda, it could not be denied that Schuman's visit was linked to the debate against the revitalisation of trade between Finland and the Soviet Union, which has been undertaken by right-wing socialists. That's how Leskinen got his share, too. The article was written by Stefan Smirnov, who later served in the Finland unit of the international department of the NKP until the 1980s. Inkeri Hirvensalo and Pekka Sutela have just published a book on the history of eastern trade. It will be discussed tomorrow at the Money Museum. It provides a background to the Soviet view. In the memoirs of Paasikivi and Jean Monnet, there are interesting similarities between the war years. During his time as a senior official in the League of Nations, Jean Monnet was disappointed with the organisation's ability to function. He was convinced that interdependence between peoples is a fact and that uncontrolled nationalism is the root cause of wars. Monnet was convinced that both political security and economic prosperity in Europe depended on the creation of a common free trade area. But it is not enough simply to abolish customs duties: we need a Union in other areas, among which he listed money, prices, industrial and agricultural production and transport. Monnet stressed that there can be no peace in Europe if states are rebuilt on the basis of a national sovereignty that leads to a policy of prestige and economic protection. If the countries of Europe are to protect themselves against each other again, then the creation of large armies will be necessary again. And before long, war will ensue. In the summer of 1944, Paasikivi pondered the fate of a small state on his own behalf. He had become a pessimist while reading history. "The states acted in the interest of the Staatsrason state. It's awful, blutrotig blood red." And Paasikivi continued: "So far, no system has been found that would restrict the Staatsrason and protect other states against it." Where Monnet spoke of nationalism and national sovereignty, paasikivi wrote about the staatsrason. At its core, both were talking about the same thing. Paasikivi said the key question is how to limit the staazrason. Monnet, on the other hand, considered it a fundamental problem how to limit national sovereignty. Paasikivi's starting point was the fate of a small country, but he did not limit himself to it: "The limitation of the Staatsrason, its relationship with morality, is a question on the resolution of which the future of small countries in particular depends in the first instance, but also, in the end, the future of large and human beings as a whole". History had made Paasikivi a pessimist on the one hand and cautious on the other. When Monnet was accused of being overly optimistic in a number of initiatives, he always replied: 'I am not an optimist, I am determined'. The Schuman-Monnet initiative led to the creation of the European Coal and Steel Community. Its headquarters were based in Luxembourg and its parliament in Strassbourg. Jean Monnet became its first director. The next integration effort after the Coal and Steel Community was related to defence. However, the proposal for a defense community fell through at the French National Assembly in 1954. The new attempt was made to create nuclear cooperation on the one hand and the common market on the other. In particular, the Netherlands and its Foreign Minister, Willem Beyen, worked for the common market. He took the initiative to relaunch the customs union in April 1955. It was adopted by the Benelux countries as a joint initiative. The Foreign Ministers of the six Community met in Messina, Italy, in June 1955 and set up a Belgian minister, Paul-Henry Spaak, to chair a committee tasked with preparing for the establishment of the European Economic Community. A british representative was also invited. It sub-working group reworked the text both to become a common market and to create an energy community. Spaak's rapotti was announced in April 1956. The negotiations leading up to the creation of the EEC took place at the Chateau Val-Duchessee in Brussels. The Treaty of Rome was signed in March 1957 and the EEC became operational at the beginning of 1958. Where did Finland go at that time? At the beginning of the 1950s, Finland was politically and economically very isolated. Finland was one of the first to become a member of the IMF in 1948, but then the wall came up against it. Finland had submitted an application for MEMBERSHIP of the UN, but the Soviet Union vetoed the membership of Finland and Italy because the West did not accept Bulgaria, Romania and Hungary. Finland did not become a member of the UN until the end of 1955. When the Spaak report, which formed the basis of the Treaty of Rome, was nearing its end in the circle of six in 1956, it was an eventful time in Finnish domestic politics in Finland. In March, President Urho Kekkonen took office with the narrowest possible majority. Juhani Suomi writes One Voice about the President. The general strike began on the same day. And where did Finland's trade policy activity head then? Finland had been forced to opt out of the Marshall Plan at the insistence of the Soviet Union. In this way, we were also excluded from the OEEC, the European Economic Organisation, which was set up to coordinate it. In 1957, Finland launched a exploratory talks on possible OEEC membership. Finland was the only European market economy outside the OEEC. Included was Austria, which was occupied until 1955. The OEEC had signalled that Finland would be welcome. For the Soviet Union, however, this was too much, as membership would, in its opinion, have increased Finland's dependence on the West too much and weakened relations between Finland and the Soviet Union. Finland was actually informed of the negative position adopted by the Soviet Union in March 1958, after which the membership project was put on hold. It had to be completely buried when the K.-A. was formed in August 1958. The Fagerholm government was caught up in a foreign policy crisis known as the night frosts, which ended with the resignation of the government that same year. However, the collapse of the OEEC membership did not have time to cause major economic problems for economic relations with Western Europe. Finland had become a foreign member of the European Payments Union in 1957 with the so-called Helsinki Protocol, which allowed Finland to engage in multilateral trade. The solution to the problem of multilateral trade was the convertibility of currencies, which was carried out at a global level, led by the International Monetary Fund. The general convertibility of currencies advocated by the Imf was carried out in Europe from the beginning of 1959, when all currencies became freely convertible against each other, and now also against the US dollar. Finland was involved in this, and the mark became a "hard" currency freely convertible into other currencies for foreigners. At the same time, the majority of imports were exempted from the licence requirement in one fell swoop. Thus, setbacks in attempts to participate in European economic integration were compensated at the global level. Following britain's withdrawal from the negotiations that led to the creation of the EEC in November 1955, it made a proposal to expand the OEEC into a free trade area. However, charles de gaulle, who was elected president of France in 1958, took a negative position on this proposal. For a long time, the process of European integration was divided into two different paths. Britain reacted by putting together a free trade area, EFTA, around it. It was important for the Nordic countries because they were traditionally very dependent on trade with Britain. Although EFTA was built into a much looser organisation than the EEC, Finland still had difficulty in getting involved. When EFTA was the subject of intensive negotiations between the future member states during 1959, the United Kingdom did not want Finland to participate in the negotiations. The Soviet Union, for its part, demanded an assurance from President Kekkonen that Finland would not join EFTA. Even the YYA Agreement was invoked. According to Juhani Suomi, Kekkonen came to the conclusion early on that the solution should be some kind of external membership. The solution was associate membership, in which Finland would be placed on a commercially equal footing with the EFTA countries proper after the transition periods, but it would have a limited position in the organisation's decision-making. However, Kekkonen did not set out to implement this solution until the Soviet Union's acceptance of the idea had been received. The breakthrough in this was when Hru.t.ev visited Kekkonen's 60th birthday in the autumn of 1960. ( After the celebration at the Finnish National Theatre in Tamminiemi at 23.00. The event ended at 5.00 A.m. J.Suomi) In this way, EFTA became, through a special arrangement, an important operating environment for Finnish trade policy. Finland became a full member only in 1986, 26 years after its founding. Finland faced its first Brexit when Britain, Ireland, Denmark and Norway negotiated a membership agreement with the EEC in 1972. Finland had to negotiate its own free trade agreement with the EEC. It wasn't simple. Juhana Aunesluoma's book On the Road to Free Trade describes the stages in detail. I was able to follow the process as a young member of parliament and as a substitute member of the Committee on Foreign Affairs. One of the most difficult issues was the rules of origin. According to that provision, the manufacturing process giving rise to the treatment of a customs advantage had to be carried out in the same country. Jacques Delorsin became President of the Commission at the beginning of 1985. With the support of member states, he launched the single market programme. It deepened integration and at the same time made decision-making more efficient. The EFTA countries feared that they would be caught up in the new trade barriers. Austria even membership of the EEC. In January 1989, Mr Delors proposed the creation of a European Economic Area in the European Parliament. This offered the way for the EFTA countries to gain access to the internal market without membership. The underlying idea was that there was no desire to proceed with enlargement before deepening. The proposal for the European Economic Area suited Finland well. Membership remained a sensitive issue in terms of foreign policy. The EEA Agreement would bring the benefits of the internal market without the political costs of membership. Eea membership took place after complicated stages at the beginning of 1994. But at the same time, one thing became clear: we can have access to the internal market, but not a say in decision-making. In the autumn of 1991, major changes began. An attempted coup in the USSR failed in August and at the end of the year the Soviet Union broke up. During the autumn, Finland applied for a new anchor. One turning point in the decision-making process was the Maastricht Summit in December, where, alongside other major issues, a proposal to open accession negotiations with Austria and Sweden popped up. President Mauno Koivisto announced in his inaugural address to the Diet in February 1992 that Finland wants a place around the table where decisions are made. We wanted influence. We want to be a constructive member. Why we wanted influence: the essence of the EU is that it is there that relations between countries are determined by law and not by force. Legitimacy and the rule of law are always in the interests of a small state and, even a little further, in the interests of a large one. Finland's negotiations on EU membership ended on 1 March 1994. In the morning, Mauno Koivisto was still president, and during the day the duties were transferred to Martti Ahtisaari. When Mauno Koivisto turned 90 in autumn 2013, he said that he belonged to a generation that first fought for independence and then sought to promote integration. They were prepared to give up sovereignty when they were counterbalanced by more influence. And he continued, "This is what happened. The pessimists were wrong". Linda Jakobson again recounted one walk with her father at Max Jakobson's memorial service that year. It happened in 1997. Suddenly, Max Jakobson had stopped and said, "Listen, it's only in recent years that I've realized that, for the first time in its history, Finland is now truly independent." Both have been patriots, including front-line men. But at the same time, they have been committed to a common Europe and to internationalism. The Juncker Commission has just published a document outlining five alternative paths. This includes a lot of good questions and the exchange benefits welcome to inspire discussion. The heads of the big four countries have announced their support for a Europe of different speeds. The Prime Minister of Finland has come out in support of working together. Options can be combined: The first scenario, although it has a bad title in the official translation: 'carry on as before' forms a good basis. We rely on common institutions and a common treaty. On their basis, the law determines, not power. At the same time, the third scenario, those who want to can do more together, can complement it. That is what economic and monetary union and Schengen mean. Of course, there is a limit to how many different configurations can work effectively. Juncker also spoke about these problems in the European Parliament. The option to hold off. The fourth scenario, if properly thought out, can be part of the whole. Let us not add new tasks too lightly, but let us focus on the essentials, those areas where action at European level adds value. In this way, proposal 1 would be supplemented, where applicable, by scenarios 3 and 5. I would like to highlight two areas here. Of course, there are others. The banking union, or even more broadly the financial union, must be completed. The union's two pillars, the single banking supervision and the bank resolution framework, have been implemented, but the third, the single deposit insurance scheme, has largely not been implemented. The expert working group chaired by Antti Suvanto concluded that a common deposit insurance scheme based on an insurance-type arrangement is a coherent part of the banking union. It would also make it easier to deal with the problems of banks separately from the state. By the way, it would also be in Finland's interest. The second area relates to common external border controls. Uncontrolled migration some time ago showed that poorly functioning external border controls and free movement to the internal market are an impossible equation. Common and effective management of external borders is a necessary condition for a smoothly functioning internal market. There are also a number of extremely important issues on which the EU must defend its achievements. One is freedom of trade. Of course, we also need to find out and make adjustments to how inclusive growth can be created within its framework. Another big issue is the Paris Agreement on climate change. It was a breakthrough and its implementation must be safeguarded. There's a lot more, but I'll leave the list here. Title: The ECB's monetary policy continues to be exceptionally lighthearted. Helsinki 30 March 2017
text: Monetary policy continues to be highly accommodative Releases (/en/media-and-publications/releases/) . Press releasenumber 8 . Thursday30 March 2017,11:00AM The euro area economy has now benefited from four years of unbroken growth. The monetary policy of the ECB has been highly accommodative, lowering funding costs for households and non-financial corporations alike. In Eurosystem staff projections, growth is expected to remain both broadly based and positive. Nevertheless, the euro area is still recovering from the financial and debt crisis. Despite ongoing moderate growth, inflation has only started to increase in the past few months on account of rising oil prices. At the same time, the risks of deflation have been substantially receding ever since last summer. There is still unutilized capacity in the economy, and wage growth is moderate. With inflation expectations remaining low, there is little sign of higher inflation in the medium term. 'A very substantial degree of monetary accommodation is still needed in the euro area for underlying inflation pressures to build up and support inflation in the medium term,' said Governor Erkki Liikanen today at the press briefing for the publication of the latest issue of the journal Euro & talous. Policy rates are at a historical low. The deposit rate has been at -0.40% since March 2016. The key ECB interest rates are expected to remain at present or lower levels for an extended period of time, and well past the horizon of net asset purchases. In December 2016, the ECB Governing Council decided to continue the asset purchase programme (APP) until the end of March 2017. At the same time, the Governing Council decided that monthly purchases would again amount to db60 billion until the end of December 2017. 'Purchases will continue until we see a sustained adjustment in the path of inflation consistent with our inflation aim,' stressed Governor Liikanen. 'Should the economic outlook weaken or the financial market situation no longer contribute to increasing inflation, the duration or volume of purchases can be adjusted.' Like other euro area countries, Finland is benefiting from the accommodative stance of monetary policy. Stable economic growth in the euro area and globally means that Finnish exports will also pick up and the composition of growth is will broaden. Nevertheless, Finnish growth is set to remain below pre-crisis levels. Weakened cost-competitiveness was one element behind the contraction in Finnish exports since 2008. 'The Competitiveness Pact is forecast to bring about tangible improvements in cost-competitiveness. Going forward, it is key for unit labour cost growth to remain below those of trading partners in the coming years even after the expiration of the Competitiveness Pact,' said Governor Erkki Liikanen. For stronger economic growth in the euro area as in Finland, it is key for international trade to remain free and undisturbed. The benefits of globalisation have not been equally distributed: income inequality within advanced economies has increased, and many people have lost their job to structural change. 'We need to pay more attention to reducing the risk of increased marginalisation and lack of opportunities,' said Governor Liikanen. Education plays a key role here. Taxation, income transfers and public services are all relevant to employment. An efficient financial system and developing a competition-friendly regulatory environment will support potential growth and employment. Euro & talous publication website .
