Title: Jaakko Honko public lecture 4.4.2017
text: President Erkki Liikanen: Financial markets and their regulation after crises: reforms and future challenges. Helsinki, 4.4.2017. . Speech . Tuesday 4April2017, 5:00PM President and CEO Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland Financial markets and their regulation after crises: reforms and future challenges Jaakko Honko public lecture 4.4.2017, Aalto University School of Business Helsinki 4.4.2017 FINANCIAL MARKETS AND THEIR REGULATION AFTER CRISES: REFORMS AND 1 FUTURE CHALLENGES In the summer, it will be ten years since the first phase of the global financial crisis began in August 2007. The last free weekend in July before the crisis is very much on the mind. The Bank of Finland organised a seminar at SuomiAreena in Pori. Speakers included ECB President Jean-Claude Trichet, Aalto University Professor Matti Pohjola and Federal Reserve Bank Senior Economist CraigHakkioja MIT Professor BengtHolmstr9am. I looked through what was thought of the global economic outlook in early 2007. As recently as April 2007, the International Monetary Fund stated that "the favourable global economic outlook continues to provide a strong basis for the stability of the global financial system". However, the report included a scenario analysis of the contagious effects of subprime credit write-down that could threaten the stability of the global financial system. The Bank for International Settlements, the BIS, was also not in a state of crisis in July 2007. The bank has been recognised for regularly reminding of risks before the crisis. In its annual report for 2007, the BIS states that "our ability to assess the likelihood and interdependence of these risks is limited". The mention is in the context in which the BIS describes the risks threatening the global economy. The crisis has profoundly affected many things. Financial market regulation in advanced economies has been stepped up. Economics has engaged in a lot of introspection. It is now understood that serious disturbances in the financial markets and their consequences for the real economy must be better integrated into macro-models. The financial crisis has been a reminder of the magnitude of the losses in economic growth caused by severe disruptions in financial markets. A stable financial system is a prerequisite for sustainable economic growth. This should not be forgotten either, at a time when there is criticism of regulatory reforms in the air. One of the main causes of the financial crisis was d0 paradoxically d0 that a large-scale crisis among the world's most developed at the heart of the financial market was not considered possible. Before the crisis, there was a strong belief in self-regulation and self-correcting ability of the financial system. For example, there is the rapidly growing value-paperization of mortgages in the United States. The sale of packaged mortgages to other investors, including the European banking sector, was seen as a new and effective form of risk diversification. However, when the crisis erupted, global diversification turned into a contagion channel for risks. The global links between banks and other financial institutions had become so complex that mortgage risks in the US turned into a shock much larger than their size, threatening to freeze the market. Bengt Holmstr9am has analysed, also in his jaakko Honko lecture here in 2012, what are the prerequisites for liquidity in the debt market and why liquidity can also quickly disappear in a crisis situation. There was also a belief in self-regulation by financial institutions, as it was thought that bank owners and investors have strong incentives to control banks' risk-taking. Alan Greenspan later stated that he was disappointed in this regard. After the financial crisis, a reassessment of the financial system's capacity for market discipline and self-regulation had to be reassessed. The existence of systemic risks is now being taken seriously. It has become clear that individual actors and institutions do not have sufficient incentives to prepare for risks at the system-wide level. Careful and effective regulation and supervision are needed to help. Let us recall the main causes and lessons of the financial crisis. Through them, the value of regulatory reforms for national economies can be understood. 1. Causes and lessons of the global financial crisis: synthesis The causes of the financial crisis can be divided into three parts that are intertwined: 1) there were macroeconomic determinants, (2) the shortcomings of monetary and macroprudential policies in the pre-crisis years and (3) problems with the development of financial markets and their regulation and supervision. First explanation: Macroeconomic background factors A key macroeconomic determinant of the crisis was the current account imbalances, in particular between the United States and China, which was boosted by strong economic growth in China and many other Asian countries. Prosperity was accumulated in these countries, while the experience of the Asian financial crisis in the late 1990s created an incentive for them to buffer their economies against potential crises. The countries compiled substantial current account surpluses, which they invested specifically in the US market. At the same time, there was confidence in the ability of the US financial system to channel investments into profitable and safe targets. This abundant supply of outside capital pushed U.S. long-term interest rates down. In an environment of falling interest income, pressure arose to create new lucrative investments. These were offered, among others, by subprime credits, for which there was also a political order in the United States. Another macroeconomic background factor was that economic growth had long been stable. Cyclical fluctuations had levelled off. It was largely attributed to modern monetary policy. Since the stock market crash of 1987, we had also become accustomed to central banks being able to stabilise the markets with their liquidity supply if necessary. The flip side of these positive developments was that there was a growing sense of security and risk awareness Decreased. Second Explanation: Monetary and macroprudential policy shortcomings The second explanation for the financial crisis relates to the monetary policy pursued in the years before the crisis, but also to the absence of macroprudential policies. During the 2001 terrorist attack and other millennial shocks, U.S. monetary policy had been lightened. The lightness was sustained by concerns about deflationary developments. The housing market was seen to heat up, but when the series of rate hikes began, in retrospect, it did not work sufficiently. Should the bubble in the US housing market have been burst by more decisive monetary policy? The challenge was that monetary policy provided one instrument, but in this case there were two objectives: price stability and financial stability. Macroprudential policy instruments to safeguard the stability of the financial system were lacking. In principle, there were means of banking regulation, but the structure of regulation in the United States was fragmented, which made decision-making difficult. This has also been described in his memoirs by Greenspan's successor, Ben Bernanke. By the way, the Parliamentary Banking Council met Bernanke during his last working week in Washington. We were chaired by another Ben, Mr Zyskowicz. Bernanke is a well-known scholar of the Great Depression. We asked: What was surprising or new about this crisis? He replied: "We knew that interest rates needed to be cut quickly and the economy revived. But what was new was the complexity of international financial institutions. Third explanation: Financial market imbalances Indeed, the third explanation for the financial crisis relates to the liberalisation of the international financial system, which had been going on for a long time before the crisis, and to the problems of financial innovation and regulation. From the 1980s onwards, the liberalisation and deregulation of international financial markets accelerated. In part, this was a natural consequence of developments in information technology and financial risk management methods. This was also due to a paradigm shift that highlighted the importance of markets that function as freely as possible in promoting economic growth. In the late 1990s, the so-called "green belt" was abandoned in the United States. The Glass-Steagall Act, which had separated investment and deposit banking. In addition, wall street's large investment banks, which had traditionally operated as partnerships, turned one after another into limited liability companies. The role of these regulatory and structural changes in the genesis of the financial crisis remains to be studied, but they very likely increased risk-taking. One of the changes in banking in the pre-crisis decade was the proliferation of the 'originate and distribute' business model and the inclusion of increasingly risky assets. Banks started to package the credits on their balance sheets and sell them on to investors, often through special purpose vehicles. The activity is called securitization. This was justified by more effective risk diversification, as the risks inherent in credit were basically transferred to a large number of investors away from banks' balance sheets. But in doing so, the traditional link between the borrower and the lender was also broken. As a result, the criteria for lending were relaxed. There were other reasons behind this. Securitisation and the use of special purpose vehicles allowed for a lower solvency requirement under the then rules, even if the risks had remained virtually unchanged. By reducing the amount of equity required for solvency requirements, the percentage return on equity was increased. In other words, banks were able to (ostensibly) improve their profitability by increasing their leverage. When the crisis erupted, it turned out that the risk rating and pricing process for securitised items did not work flawlessly. The products were too complicated. Risks were underestimated, in particular for macro and systemic risks. Credit rating agencies' own financial incentives jeopardised their independence and were likely to contribute to the failure of ratings. Closely related to the create-and-diversify model was the fact that the structure of banks' own fundraising changed radically in the pre-crisis period. The relative share of deposits declined as banks financed the rapid growth of their asset masses, especially through short-term market financing. This exposed banks to liquidity risk, a modern version of bank flight, which materialized when problems with subprime credit were revealed. Perhaps the biggest failure of bank regulation was insufficient prudential requirements. Exploiting the gaps contained in them contributed to the rapid growth of banks' balance sheets. At the same time, the actual risk buffers were reduced. In addition, the regulation allowed the partial use of low-quality solvency capital, which did not provide a buffer against losses. This was a key mistake. Tim Geithner, the first finance minister in barackObama's administration, notes in his memoirs that the main cause of the crisis was the investment and commercial banking business model, which combined low equity and very short-term market financing. The authorities allow this to happen. There is a broad consensus on Geithner's conception. The problem was common in Europe and the United States. What factors basically led to excessive leverage and short-term market financing growth for banks? According to one explanation, it was about the typical euphoria that periodically takes over the financial markets. This was also fuelled at the time by the macroeconomic factors I was talking about. I also mentioned above that overheating was further accelerated by the belief in the ability and incentives of leading financial institutions to keep their risks under control. I witnessed a historical exchange of views on the subject. The imf's then chief economist, Professor Raghuram Rajan, questioned the belief in the self-management of financial markets at Jackson Hole in 2005. He analysed three problems: front-loaded performance bonuses encouraged greater risk-taking, there was too much reliance on risk diversification, and there was a belief that liquidity was endless. His summary was that this development has not made the international financial system safer, but more risky. Larry Summers, among others, harshly criticized him, stating that Rajan was a Luddite. Luddites destroyed spinning machines in the early days of the Industrial Revolution. Later history proved Rajan right. In addition to Rajani's views, the problem created by the incentives for excessive risk-taking by financial institutions that have grown too large and complex has been highlighted. Investors expected that in the crisis the most significant the banks are ultimately bailed out with public money. The key banks were too big to fail and therefore received financing too cheaply. They were able to increase their risks and leverage. A spiral follows in which their size increases even more. The owners benefit but the cost of hidden insurance provided by taxpayers rises because the profits are private, but the losses are the taxpayers'. The financial crisis had its roots in the United States, but the risks had also spread to Europe. The regulatory and supervisory shortcomings were largely similar. What was done to prevent the problems from reoccurring? The key preparatory work for the reforms has been carried out on the basis of consensus between central banks and supervisors. The secretariat of the various bodies is located in Basel, under the care of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS). A key role at international level has been played by the Financial Stability Board, which was headed until 2011 by Mario Draghi.Today, the President of the Bank of England is MarkCarney. It assesses vulnerabilities in the global financial system and proposes actions to address them. Another important player is the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, chaired by Stefan Ingves, governor of the Central Bank of Sweden. Its mission is to develop the regulation, supervision and practices of banks worldwide. In addition to these, there is the Group of Governors and Supervisors of central banks, which is the supervisory and coordinating body for the work. Its current chairman is Mario Draghi. The United States is centrally involved in all the work. The most prominent representative of the central bank has been fed governor or executive board member Don Tarullo. The regulatory standards prepared by the Basel Committee are not directly legally binding. However, they are usually monitored. In the EU and its Member States, the prudential and liquidity regulation of banks follows very closely the recommendations of the Basel Committee. A lot has happened in the United States since the turn of the year. First, Patrick McHenry (1/31/2017), chairman of the House Financial Services Committee, strongly criticized the Fed's actions in a letter to Chairman Janet Yellen. Then there was the Presidential Executive Order (2/3/2017), which said that the new administration should promote the interests of the United States in the negotiations on financial regulation. Janet Yellen responded in the letter that the Fed has the power and responsibility to negotiate with foreign counterparties about regulation and does so for the benefit of the United States. For his part, Don Tarullo announced his resignation. He is leaving his position this week. Let me now turn in more detail to how the post-crisis regulatory reforms have unravelled the problems and what measures are still in progress. I will try to give the full picture, but my focus is, of course, on Europe. 3. Major changes in financial regulation and supervision The regulation and supervision of financial institutions and markets failed before the global financial crisis. The authorities did not recognise the warning signs of the crisis or the channels for its spread. Neither the market nor the academic economists did any better. Regulation may even have contributed to the crisis. After the crisis, it was necessary to radically reform supervision and regulation. It is worth highlighting three sets of reforms. Firstly, the banks' ability to absorb losses has been significantly strengthened. Before the financial crisis, banks needed to have at least 2% of the best-quality equity or equity capital relative to their risk-weighted exposures as protection against losses. Now, in many countries, the largest banks are required to have the highest quality own funds five times more than before. Thanks to this, banks are more resilient to crises. Banks' ability to cope with liquidity crises has also been strengthened. The global financial crisis started as a liquidity crisis as banks lost confidence in each other. They did not dare to grant each other even short-term unsecured loans in the interbank loan market. It was Rajan who had warned of this. The new requirements will ensure that banks have sufficient cash and other highly liquid assets on their balance sheets. A smaller share of banks' borrowing may consist of short-term financing, which in crisis situations often stops quickly. Secondly, no bank should be 'too big to fail', so to speak. Systemically important banks have been subject to more supervisory and capital requirements than other banks. These banks are also required to issue debt instruments that, in the event of a crisis, can either be cancelled or converted into share capital in order to strengthen the bank's solvency. The authorities have also been given stronger powers to manage and resolve crises in order to restructure banks facing problems, primarily with regard to the bank's shareholders and the so-called 'crisis management'. at the expense of junior brothers. Thirdly, the global financial crisis at the latest showed that monetary policy geared towards price stability and institutional supervision of financial institutions controlling the solvency and risk-taking of financial institutions do not automatically guarantee the stability of the financial system as a whole. The authorities needed a stronger mandate to ensure the stability of the financial system as a whole and to take measures to safeguard that stability. In order to safeguard the stability of the financial system, public authorities need to be able to identify the systemic risks that generate and intensify financial crises more reliably and at an earlier stage. In Finland, concerns have been raised especially about the ever-increasing indebtedness of Finnish households and structural vulnerabilities related to the Finnish housing market and mortgage lending. Identifying risks is not enough to prevent financial crises. Public authorities therefore also need measures aimed at preventing systemic risks and imbalances in the financial system, thereby reducing the likelihood of financial crises. These new instruments are called macroprudential instruments. Examples of macroprudential instruments include the maximum loan-to-value ratio for mortgages, i.e. the so-called mortgage lending ratio. the loan ceiling, which entered into force in Finland at the beginning of July 2016. It limits the maximum size of new mortgages in relation to the collateral on the loan. The amount of the loan ceiling is decided by the Board of the Financial Supervisory Authority. It may lower the loan ceiling if the stability risks associated with mortgage lending are estimated to have become dangerously high. The Bank of Finland's well-known position is that the macroprudential toolbox targeting household indebtedness and mortgage lending should be strengthened in Finland from the current level. Banking union strengthens supervision and resolution in Europe The seeds of the global financial crisis were sown in the United States, but many European countries suffered the most from the financial crisis and the subsequent escalating euro area sovereign debt crisis. Finland was spared the banking crisis, but as a result of the collapse of exports, Finland's GDP contracted by 8% in 2009. The experience of the financial crisis revealed in stark terms that, on the one hand, european integrated banking and financial markets and, on the other hand, nationally fragmented banking supervision and resolution were an unsustainable combination. If large financial institutions have significant business activities in many countries, their supervision and resolution must also be on a broader basis. As a result of the establishment of the banking union, the supervision of banks in the acceding countries was transferred to the SSM attached to the European Central Bank. The largest banks were transferred to direct supervision by the ECB. The SSM ensures strict and consistent supervision of banks operating in many countries, while drawing on the local expertise of national financial supervisors. The Single Resolution Mechanism (SRM) aims to contribute to ensuring that the crisis management of failing multinational banks can in future be handled in a coordinated and organised manner. Even the largest multinational banks must not be too big to fail. Recently, the so-called "cash flow" enjoyed by large banks in their cost of raising funds. the implicit state guarantee has been significantly reduced. It tells us that the market has begun to take the government's goal as intended. The third, as yet unfinished, element of the banking union is the single centralised deposit insurance scheme in the banking union. I will come back to that at the end of my presentation. Risks change Since the crisis, the global financial system has become more stable and secure. However, the risks to stability are like viruses that are constantly mutating. Often they become irritated when they react to drugs developed for previous diseases. In hockey terms, the challenge of controlling the financial markets is to "skate to where the puck goes next, not where it is." In order to achieve their price stability and other objectives, central banks have in recent years kept their key interest rates exceptionally low and, in some countries, even negative. Expansionary monetary policy has been essential in a world that has slowly recovered from the crisis. As a detrimental side effect, low interest rates can increase incentives for risk-taking and fuel the rise in asset prices. Lending in some countries has started to grow at an ominous pace. Macroprudential instruments must then be used. The financial sector is also changing. Soon, two of Finland's four largest credit institutions will be able to operate in Finland as branches of a foreign bank. Banks are also expanding their business into new, even surprising areas. The boundaries between banking and other business activities are blurring. Banks are also challenged by new players who make use of new technologies. It is, of course, possible for the banks to respond to this in the same way. In Finland, for example, the banking sector has long been a forerunner in many operating models related to digitalisation. Digitalisation brings benefits, but perhaps also new risks that are still difficult to identify. On the other hand, international financial activities have also been simplified in a healthy way in recent years. A few examples: (i) Banks engage in fewer short-term securities trading than in the crazy years. (ii) Many major international financial giants have cut their sprawl and simplified their structures. (iii) The use of complex artificial financial instruments with no genuine added value has decreased. (iv) The markets for financial derivatives are more transparent. 4. Future prospects Have the regulatory reforms since the financial crisis gone too far for the financing needs and growth of the economy? A recent study has drawn attention to the fact that the recovery in bank stock valuations after the global financial crisis and the European sovereign bond crisis has been slow compared to other crises. The study suspects that the reason for this is overly strict regulation2. The regulatory reforms have been significant, but they have also been given time to adapt. On the other hand, the environment of low interest rates has posed challenges for some banks, depending on the interest rate fixing of their balance sheets and the structure of their own fundraising. The bottom line is that banks' profitability can no longer be based on the fact that their own financing is supported by public safety nets, which allows for high leverage and, consequently, a seeming improvement in profitability. Owners and investors must also be prepared to bear the risks: profits and also losses. The new resolution legislation provides the means to ensure that risks are genuinely passed on to bank owners and debt investors. This may result in bank owners and debt investors being able to demand higher risk premiums in the future. However, there is no going back to the era of inefficient regulation and to the risks ultimately borne by taxpayers. d3Varjopankkitoimintad3 An important question when assessing post-crisis regulation is whether the reformed regulation of banks will increasingly drive banking and its risks into the so-called "black market". to shadow banks. These are financial services companies that operate similarly to banking but are less regulated. Shadow banks played a significant role in the emergence of the financial crisis, as some of the real risks of banks were hidden off banks' balance sheets. Since the crisis, different views have been expressed on risk management in the shadow banking sector. So far, however, no significant regulation of shadow banks has been undertaken. Instead, banks' links to the shadow banking sector will be regulated more effectively than in the past. In the United States, post-financial crisis Dodd-Frank legislation allows the authority to bring a shadow bank that has become a systemic threat under supervision. In Europe, this possibility does not exist at the moment. In September, the Bank of Finland will organise an international conference on shadow banks at the House of the Estates, where the theme will be discussed further. (Welcome!) Completing the banking union In Europe, a key remaining task is the completion of the banking union. The two pillars of the banking union, the Single Banking Supervision and the Bank Resolution Framework, are well implemented, but the third, the Single Deposit Insurance Scheme, is incomplete. The common deposit guarantee scheme has been a controversial element, but I agree with the working group chaired by Antti Suvanto: if implemented correctly, insurance-type deposit insurance is a consistent part of the banking union. The main beneficiaries are small and concentrated banking systems, where banking risks are correlated between different actors. It should also be said that one of the problems of the European financial system is its high bank-centricity and, accordingly, the relatively small role of financial intermediation outside the banking system. This structural feature increases the fragility of the European financial system. For this reason, the completion of a parallel Capital Markets Union is important for the Banking Union. It can also be facilitated by the implementation of structural regulation of banks. There are already signs of a revival of venture capital investment in Europe. In Finland, we are rightly proud of the popularity of Slush and much related to it. It is important to work to ensure that there are no obstacles at the various stages of the expansion of promising new companies due to structural bottlenecks in financing. On the other hand, it is important to remember that venture capitalists also carry out a key pruning exercise in a market economy: it is often said that there is no shortage of funding, but at most of good ideas to be financed. This aspect should also be borne in mind when considering various measures. 5. Finally I have referred above to Professor Raghu Rajan's proven crisis prophet from 2005. He wrote a book in 2010 about the remaining hidden breaking points of developed economies and societies especially based on the experience of the United States. According to Rajan, a key breaking point has been caused by the global relocation of jobs to countries with lower production costs. This has led to a weakening of the relative position of the lower-skilled workforce and created uncertainty. Before the financial crisis, this was corrected, according to Rajan, by promoting the provision of low-cost mortgages to people who did not have the ability to pay. It was from this thinking that subprime credits were born and the consequences of its experiment we know today. But the underlying problem has not disappeared. Globalisation has lifted hundreds of millions of people out of the worst poverty in developing countries. That is a great achievement. But at the same time, declining sectors and regions have emerged in developed countries and people have lost their jobs and prospects for the future. It has also brought its political risks. Rajan's one policy recommendation in 2010 was to expand the provision of education. It is now collectively seen as the most important. Education also supports labour mobility and thus employment. Taxation, transfers and public services also play an important role in good employment. Pro-competitive regulatory development and a well-functioning, stable financial system also support the conditions for economic growth and its ability to adapt to change. 1I thank Esa Jokivuolle and Jukka Vauhkonen for their help. Title: Speech on the occasion of the ECB Supervisory Board meeting, concert at the Temppeliaukio Church. Helsinki, 11.5.2017.
text: Speech on the occasion of the ECB Supervisory Board meeting, concert at the Temppeliaukio Church. . Speech . Thursday11 May 2017,7:00PM Governor Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland On the occasion of the Supervisory Board meeting in Helsinki Concert at the Temppeliaukio Church 11 th May 2017 Ladies and Gentleman, Basel is a household name in this audience. The Basel Committeeos recommendations and their implementation have long been a key focus in your work. And even now we are discussing whether there will be a Basel 3.5 or Basel 4. In midsummer last year, BIS held its regular annual meeting in Basel. We Nordics donot especially like to spend midsummer in a city. The only right place is to be by a lake with family and friends around a campfire. But once more last year we had to fly to Basel. From Midsummeros Eve to the following Sunday. But then came the good news! We learned that a famous modern opera by Karlheinz Stockhausen was to be performed that very Sunday in Basel theatre. This opera, Donnerstag aus Licht, has cult status among many musicians and artists of the younger generation. Its premiere was in 1981 in Milanos La Scala. We got the tickets and entered. It was a six-hour performance with great singers, musicians and dancers. The story was the autobiography of the composer. There are three roles: the composer, his strict father and his fragile mother, Eva, who was taken into a mental hospital. It was a moving experience that we will not forget. This very opera performance was later nominated opera production of the year by the respected opera magazine Opernwelt (oOpera worldo). Evas challenging role was sung by Anu Komsi, who will sing for us today. Anu Komsi has made many performances to great acclaim around the world. She is also famous for her interpretations of contemporary Finnish composers such as Magnus Lindberg and Esa-Pekka Salonen. She presented Lindbergos oAccusedo with Toronto Philharmonic Orchestra in February and in the Independence Day concert in Helsinki in December. She has also recorded the premiere of Esa-Pekka Salonens oWing on Wingo with her sister, Piia Pauliina Komsi. This was composed by Salonen for the inauguration of Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles, designed by Frank Gerry. Next week they will sing oWing on Wingo in three concerts with the New York Philharmonic Orchestra in New York City. Three years ago, in the middle of a beautiful July in the lake area in Eastern Finland we heard that Anu Komsi was giving a concert together with Marzi Nyman in the huge wooden church in Puumala. We were surprised, because we knew Marzi Nyman as a leading jazz musician of his generation. He was even nominated Jazz Musician of the Year by Pori Jazz festival in 2003. By the way, Pori is famous not only for jazz but also for the topical discussions organized during its festivals. Just two examples: Jacques Delors spoke there in 1994 just before Finland joined the EU. Jean-Claude Trichet, for his part, participated in a panel in summer 2007. This turned out to be the last weekend before the turbulence took over the financial markets. We took first a boat and then a car and hurried to the church. We knew Anu Komsi can sing anything. But I was very curious to know how Marzi Nyman plays organ. And he did not disappoint. Marzy Nyman and Anu Komsi play for us here tonight. When we sat in the huge wooden church, I saw Sakari Oramo, chief conductor of the BBC Symphony Orchestra and also Principal Conductor of the Stockholm Royal Philharmonic Orchestra sitting there. I asked: oAre you also playing?o oNo, I am the driver,o was his reply. This was true. He drove back with his wife Anu Komsi all through the white night from Eastern Finland to Kokkola, their home town on the west coast. It was a long drive, at least six hours. In Kokkola, Anu Komsi and Sakari Oramo will be organizing an Opera Festival again this summer. Sakari Oramo began his career as a violinist and even recorded the great violin concerto of Jean Sibelius in his youth. He became concert master of the Radio Symphony Orchestra and also began to study conducting. The rest is history. He moved on and began to conduct in Finland and other Nordic countries. Then he was invited as a visitor to conduct the City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra. Soon after, he was appointed to follow Simon Rattle as the chief conductor. Sakari Oramo was then 30 years of age. He stayed there for 9 years as chief conductor. Last August, Sakari Oramo conducted the last night of the famous Proms at Royal Albert Hall in London. Those who heard the event will not forget either the music or the speech. He has done tens of recordings. Last year he received an award for best recording for his thrilling 1st and 3rd Symphonies by Nielsen with the Royal Stockholm Philharmonic Orchestra. He has been visiting conductor in leading philharmonic orchestras. In April he conducted the Wiener Philharmoniker in Vienna. Friends of music got great news just six weeks ago. Sakari Oramo was invited to become Professor of Orchestral Conducting at the Sibelius Academy of the University of the Arts in Helsinki, from January 2020 for five years. This means we can not only continue to enjoy his music, but we, our children and grand-children will also enjoy the music of his students for decades to come. But tonight, Sakari Oramo is not driving, he is not conducting and he is not teaching. He will play violin. Once more, I am happy to present to you, Anu Komsi, Marzi Nyman and Sakari Oramo! Title: Opening words of the BOFIT Russia briefing. Helsinki, May 24, 2017
text: Director-General Erkki Liikanen: Opening words of the BOFIT Russia factsheet. Helsinki, 24.5.2017 . Speech . Friday 26May 2017,9:35 AM President Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland Opening words BOFIT Russia briefing 2017 at the House of the Estates 24.5.2017 Welcome to the Bank of Finland's Research Institute for Transition Economies' traditional information session on Russia. As in previous years, researchers at the Bank of Finland discuss the current situation and future prospects of the Russian economy from different perspectives in their presentations. The Russian economy is returning to growth, although the development of different sectors of the economy is still very different. However, today is also a good day to look back a bit; very often in the history of countries, the same themes are repeated from year to year and decade to decade. Understanding history, not just economic history, is therefore important. Tomorrow, President Mauno Koivisto, who also served as governor of the Bank of Finland from 1968 to 1982, will be laid to rest in the grave. Mauno Koivisto's term as Director-General was also in many ways related to trade between Finland and our eastern neighbour, but also to Finland's progressive integration with the rest of Europe. At that time, the Bank of Finland handled payment transactions related to eastern trade to and from Finland, and it was possible to observe from the front row how the first oil crisis and the multiplication of oil prices in a short time increased trade between Finland and the Soviet Union. In the mid-1970s, the Soviet Union's share of Finland's exports rose to about 20 per cent, driven precisely by the price of oil: When the value of Finland's imports to the Soviet Union rose, exports to the East also had to increase, according to the logic of eastern trade at the time. And increased export earnings, of course, allowed the USSR to import even more goods from abroad. However, this increased exports to the East were far from enough to make up for the losses in other markets, and During Mauno Koivisto's presidency in 1975, Finland was forced to borrow from the International Monetary Fund in the form of a so-called "foreign exchange fund". as an oil credit. At the same time, Finland committed to a loan programme that, among other things, curbed the growth of domestic demand and promised to limit energy consumption. In other words, although Finland's exports to the East benefited from higher oil prices, the situation was the opposite for the level of the national economy as a whole. Finland was and is an energy-importing country. The link between the economy of our eastern neighbour and the price of energy is returned to in almost all the presentations in this factsheet. Energy is still By far Russia's largest export product, as HeliSimola describes in her presentation. In recent years, productive investment in Russia has declined. Here, however, again, the energy sector has gone in a different direction, there has been an increase in capacity. In his presentation, Vesa Korhonen sheds light on the development of Investments in Russia, and Laura Solango's presentation on reforms in the banking sector also talks about the financing opportunities for investments. Of course, Mauno Koivisto's interest in Russia was not limited to the economy. He acquired knowledge of the Russian language and became extensively acquainted with the history of our neighboring country. In his book "The Idea of Russia", published in 2001, Mauno Koivisto interestingly detailed the thinking and differences between two reformer ministers of the Tsarist period, Sergei Witte and Pyotr Stolypin. Both had a clear understanding that the Russian economy needed significant reforms in order to be able to guarantee its citizens a rising standard of living and to maintain the legitimacy of the political system. Both men were supporters of a strong central power, and both were able to push through even difficult changes, including: Witte the monetary reform of 1897, which stabilized the value of the ruble. Stable rubles were needed in order to obtain long-term loans from abroad. They, on the other hand, were needed for large investment projects, for example on the railways. Of course, these reformers have not been forgotten in Russia either, and there is no doubt about the need for reform either. In his presentation, Iikka Korhonen goes through the reform packages currently being prepared in Russia, and one of the groups carrying out these reform programmes has even taken its name from Stolypin. Time and the world around us are different, but perhaps in the group's proposals for development driven by a strong central power, parallels can be seen more than a hundred years ago. But, as we hear, other proposals for reforms have also been made. Once again, welcome to the Russia factsheet! Title: Monetary policy and the Finnish economy. Helsinki, 13 June 2017.
text: Monetary policy still accommodative in Finland, the economy has turned, further measures needed to make this turn sustainable Releases (/en/media-and-publications/releases/) . Press releasenumber 14 . Tuesday 13 June 2017, 11:00 AM At its meeting last week, the Governing Council of the ECB decided to continue its accommodative monetary policy stance. Monthly securities purchases to the value of EUR 60 billion will continue at least until the end of the current year. They will continue beyond this date if inflation is not observed to be sustainably approaching the price stability objective. The Governing Council does not expect to raise its key policy rates for a considerable time. The current monetary policy stance has clearly bolstered economic growth and supported improved employment throughout the euro area, including Finland. 'Economic performance is, however, not yet sufficiently strong to raise euro area inflation in line with the monetary policy objective. This is why the ECB will need to continue to pursue a very substantial degree of monetary accommodation to secure a sustained return of inflation rates towards levels that are below, but close to, 2%,' said Bank of Finland Governor Erkki Liikanen today at the press briefing for the release of the latest issue of the Bank's journal Euro & talous. 'In Finland, economic growth has strengthened following several weak years, and growth is forecast to continue. At the same time, economic activity has become more broad-based. Exports have started to increase, while the growth in domestic demand continues', observed Governor Liikanen. Although the outlook for the Finnish economy has brightened, the situation remains vulnerable. Export earnings are still below the level of 2008, the industrial base has narrowed and the number of industrial jobs has declined exceptionally steeply. A substantial reduction in the general government deficit is not forecast. The measures taken in recent years to strengthen the economy have been important. The Competitiveness Pact, the measures taken to balance the public finances and the pension reform decided in 2015 have made a positive contribution to improving the economic outlook. 'The economy has turned. In order to make this turn sustainable, further measures are needed. Cost.competitiveness needs to improve even after the expiration of the Competitiveness Pact. Additional measures will be needed to strengthen the public finances. Further structural reforms are vital in improving the conditions for economic growth,' Governor Liikanen underlined. Title: ECB monetary policy, European Economic and Monetary Union and the Finnish economy. Helsinki, 28 September 2017.
text: Accommodative monetary policy to continue until a sustained adjustment in the path of ination is reached Releases (/en/media-and-publications/releases/) . Press releasenumber 21 . Thursday28 September 2017,11:00AM The euro area is experiencing broadly based economic growth. Confidence in the economy has increased and investment levels are on the rise. The economic expansion is projected to be solid in the coming years, across a range of economic sectors and countries. Yet, this upturn in growth has not led to a satisfactory rise in the rate of inflation. At the beginning of 2017, rising energy costs and food prices were the primary contributors to inflationary pressure. Since then, however, their impact has lessened. 'The amount of underutilized capacity within the economy is expected to gradually be taken up, and the global economy's generally favourable outlook will support growth in the euro area. Together these factors support expectations that the inflation rate will slowly return to the policy objective, even if inflation has so far remained relatively subdued. A very substantial degree of monetary accommodation is still needed in the euro area for underlying inflationary pressures to gradually build up,' said Governor Erkki Liikanen today at the press briefing for the publication of the latest issue of the Bank of Finland's journal Euro & talous. Economic activity has received significant support from ECB monetary policy in recent years. Policy rates are at an historical low and are expected to remain at their current levels for a prolonged period of time, even past the duration of the expanded asset purchase programme (EAPP). Monetary policy will maintain accommodative financing conditions until the sustainability of the price stability objective is secured. The EAPP will be extended to the end of December 2017, at the very least, and beyond if required. 'The ECB Governing Council will this autumn decide on the calibration of its policy instruments beyond the end of the year, taking into account the expected path of inflation and the financial conditions needed for a sustained return of inflation rates towards levels that are below, but close to, 2%,' added Governor Liikanen. 'The ECB's policy target is symmetrical. It is of equal importance to act effectively on inflation levels that are above or below the price stability objective.' The euro area's accommodative monetary policy has also bolstered the recovery of the Finnish economy. Lending rates remain low, and the euro area has seen continued economic growth, which is important for Finland's export sector. Furthermore, Finnish exports are receiving support both from the outlook for the global economy and from the Competitiveness Pact, which came into force at the turn of the year. 'Finland's economic recovery is now more broadly based and robust than before, owing to the upturn in exports and corporate investment,' said Governor Liikanen. It is important that the measures designed to strengthen Finland's economy continue to be implemented. 'The decline in cost-competitiveness has been turned around and the situation improved. It is essential to sustain this progress and recover the losses of the past decade,' pointed out Governor Liikanen. Most urgent are measures to foster growth in employment and productivity as well as strengthen the public finances and improve their long-term outlook. Euro & talous publication website . Title: Mauno Koivisto as a financial man and decision-maker
text: President and CEO Erkki Liikanen: Mauno Koivisto as a financial man and decision-maker. Helsinki, 25.11.2017. . Speech . Saturday 25 November 2017, 1:30 PM President and CEO Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland Mauno Koivisto as financial man and decision-maker Mauno Koivisto's legacy carries seminar 25.11.2017, Helsinki MAUNO KOIVISTO AS AN ECONOMIST AND DECISION-MAKER In August 1967, two months before the appointment of the Governor of the Bank of Finland, the Prime Minister raised the issue in the party committee of the Social Democratic Party. A concise minutes of the debate have been drawn up: Rafael Paasio addressed the question of the governors of the Bank of Finland, saying that it will soon have to be addressed. "We don't have our own candidate, karjalainen, Rossiya Aura have been on display." Aura's candidacy is more related to the city of Helsinki's leadership question, and (Teuvo) Aura himself is not interested in SP. Karjalainen himself, on the other hand, says that he is indifferent to it. (Veikko) Kokkola (Chairman of the Board of Governors) announced this morning that he had spoken with (Klaus) Waris (Governor of the Bank of Finland), who again expressed his regret that Koivistoole did not want to. Within the Bank of Finland, rossi is considered to be the next candidate after Koivisto. In Waris' opinion, Karjalainen would have difficulties, as Rossi would leave immediately if Karjalainen, who has never managed a bank, was elected and could not do so. (Olavi) Lindblom returned to Koivisto, from where kekkonen said that now a large party does not want one man in order. Lindblom knew that Waris had talked to Karjalainen after hearing Koivisto's position and said that Karjalainen, as the strongest candidate, should start familiarizing himself with banking matters and go around the world's banking circles in order to establish relations. Karjalainen had stated that he himself would agree to it, but later said that the party would not allow it. Lindblom stressed that we should talk to Koivisto once again. Paasio recalled that the matter was seriously discussed when elanto's CEO was elected, when Koivisto had given Elanto priority. (Veikko) Helle pointed out that it was easier to get a Social Democrat as a co-operative shop manager than as a manager of the Bank of Finland. He was still in favour of discussions with Koivisto. (Erkki) Raatikainen threw out the name Prof. Jouko Paunio, who had been at the Bank of Finland Research Institute and is a Social Democrat. If Rossi is appointed director general, Paunio should be taken into account for the vacant director position, although Viita would also be an issue. (Pentti) The cloak told ross, under whom he had been for many years, that he is not a fighter, but ready for reconciliation. . .. The party committee decided that there would be further discussions with Koivisto and then we would return to the matter again". Two months later, a discussion on the successor to Klaus Waris took place in the Bank of Finland's Board of Governors. Mauno Koivisto had finally given up Elanno and given his consent. The negotiations resulted in two main candidates: Minister of Finance Mauno Koivisto and Minister for Foreign Affairs Ahti Karjalainen. Karjalainen had been on the bank's board of directors for a decade, but most of it was on leave as a minister. Tuure Junnila of the Conservative Party opposed both candidates as political and instead proposed Dr. Reino Rossi, who served on the board of directors, as director general. After that, a special voting order was made on the proposal of chairman Veikko Kokkola. First, a vote was cast between Karjalainen and Rossi, and the winner was set against Koivisto. Karjalainen dropped Ross. After that, in the final vote, Koivisto defeated Karjalainen by a vote of 5 to 3, with one member abstaining. Koivisto was voted for by the left-wing majority of the banking council; the centrist members voted for Karjalainen and Junnila abstained. President Kekkonen's pseudonym Liimatainen gave suomen Kuvalehti support for Koivisto's appointment because it would help the incomes policy solution, the "aftermath of devaluation". Mauno Koivisto also had a background in banking. He had completed his doctoral dissertation on sociology, and Professor Esko Aaltonen had asked Koivisto to be his assistant in Turku. He did not become an assistant. However, the name of the daughter comes from this job title. Joonas Laherma, ceo of the Helsinki Workers' Savings Bank, asked Koivisto to become the director of the Helsinki Workers' Savings Bank in 1957. Koivisto had already received an order book for the post of assistant, but after hesitation answered no to it and left for Helsinki. Timo Helel8a, who worked in the research department at the Bank of Finland, was both Tellervo and Mauno Koivisto's friend from Turku. Helel8a called Koivisto a so-called "witch hunt". The O-group, which included many young economists of the time, e.g. Erkki Laatto, JussiLinnamo, Olavi Niitamo, Jouko Paunioja Jaakko Lassila. O-Group members mostly work at the Bank of Finland and Statistics Finland. The group became an important community for Koivisto. In this way, Koivisto had been close to the economists of the Bank of Finland for a decade before his term as President. From now on, I will divide my presentation into four parts. 1. What were the major economic issues during Koivisto's time as President? 2. Koivisto moved twice from Panki to become prime minister. What was the contribution of the co-chairs Rafael Paasio and Kalevi Sorsa to this? 3. How did Finland's position in Europe change during Koivisto's presidency? 4. Koivisto and his archives settled at the Bank of Finland after his presidency. What did posterity get? 1. WHAT WERE THE MAJOR FINANCIAL ISSUES DURING KOIVISTO'S TERM AS PRESIDENT? 1. Liinamaa agreements, FAQ agreement, income policy 2. The dollar was decoupled from the gold standard in 1971. 3. The energy crisis of the 1970s, low growth and high inflation 4. Problems with external balance. Finland's IMF programme in 1975. 5. Interest rate policy returned to the arsenal of the Central Bank. Kekkonen stated above that he justified the choice of Koivisto with his opportunities to support a moderate income policy. Incomes policy thinking had been brought to Finland by the just-mentioned Timo Helel8a and Jouko Paunio at the Bank of Finland. In 1965, the Economic Council commissioned them to conduct a report. Helel8a and Paunio wrote that "an absolute prerequisite for a successful employment policy in Finland is that a consistent income policy be pursued alongside employment policy." The Liinamaa I Treaty was concluded in March 1968 and the Liinamaa II Treaty followed in the autumn of 1969. These were successful. Since the inflationary FAQ agreement of December 1970, the situation deteriorated. The 1970s saw the collapse of the international exchange rate system, which also drew the Finnish markka with it. The USA waged war in Vietnam and its government deficit also increased for domestic reasons. Gold flowed out of the US and uncertainty increased. In August 1971, President Nixon announced that the dollar would be decoupled from gold. International payment transactions stopped, and exchange rates began to fluctuate. It drove the Board of Directors of the Bank of Finland to make difficult choices. Will the dollar follow, or did you have to apply for a new benchmark for the value of the markka? At first, the markka followed the weakening dollar, which for a long time bothered Koivisto. In 1973, the bank's management decided to start monitoring an index of currencies important for foreign trade, a kind of basket of currencies. In 1977, a new monetary law was adopted. According to it, on the proposal of the Bank of Finland, the government decided on the limits at which the currency index could fluctuate. The Bank of Finland's task was to ensure that the variation remained within those limits. Mauno Koivisto was careful about the division of labour between the Government and the Bank of Finland. Mauno Koivisto was the Governor of the Bank of Finland in the 1970s, when the growth expectations of the economy had to be radically revised downwards both globally and in Finland. The very beginning of the 1970s was still a time of rapid growth and high employment. Then the growth folded. The turning point was the first oil crisis in the fall of 1973. The world was plunged into stagflation, a time of lower growth and higher inflation. It took time for the changes to be understood to be structural. There was no going back to the old growth rate. After the first oil crisis, in 1974, Helsingin Sanomat organized a forecasting competition in which economic influencers were asked to draw the GDP curve for the following years with their free hand. Koivisto's curve was different from that of the others. He predicted a long and deep recession ahead. Koivisto was one of the first to see that the world had changed. He had already talked about the impact of the contraction of oil reserves a year earlier. Why is that? One of the reasons was that Mauno Koivisto had been following the Club of Rome's discussion about the limits of growth even before the energy crisis. He knew Pentti Malaska, a professor from Turku who was a member of the Club of Rome. Koivisto became an honorary member of the Club of Rome. The recession of the 1970s became even deeper and longer than Koivisto had predicted, but Koivisto's reputation as a pessimist remained. The citizens sensed that Koivisto was not trying to at least flatter, but told things as they were. It was considered one of the main reasons for his popularity. As Minister of Finance, Koivisto struggled with central government indebtedness. President Koivisto's main problem was the current account deficit and the indebtedness of Finland's national economy. The problems escalated after the mid-1970s and Finland entered a current account crisis. In order to resolve the current account crisis, recourse was finally made to the IMF's support credit and the austerity programme attached to it. Kekkonen declared a national emergency, and Martti Miettunen's emergency government was formed to resolve it. Balancing the economy was a painful process. I remember well when, as a young member of parliament and a fresh master's degree, I asked Koivisto at a meeting of the parliamentary group, following well-known academic economists: "The current account must be balanced, but wouldn't a slower schedule be better for economic growth and employment?" Koivisto didn't like my question at all. He was indignant that I belonged to young people who had read the books and who did not understand the realities of economic policy. Later, I understood the background of the discussion better when I read Jouko Paunio's speech at the Science Days in 1977, in which he d1 an old friend d1 strongly criticized Koivisto's policy. As inflation accelerated in the 1970s, the use of interest rate policy became topical. But pushing through the interest rate hikes in the banking council was difficult. Under Klaus Waris, it didn't work out once. Mauno Koivisto tried often. The proposals were first withdrawn, and then halved, but changes in base rates reverted to the instruments of central bank policy. When Mauno Koivisto became president, the bank's board of directors included both Aarre Simonen, the true leader of TPSL, and Ahti Karjalainen, who was also the figurehead of the Center Party during his banking years. The demand for the independence and independence of the Central Bank's Executive Board was in a different light from what it is today. Mauno Koivisto did not stand alone in the basic tasks of the Central Bank either. A couple of examples of this. Koivisto was known to be well versed in the theorists of socialism and social democracy. In 1970, Berlin, directed by Kalle Holmberg, was performed at the Helsinki City Theatre in the throes of order. The play told about Berlin in 1919, when the Social Democratic Defense Minister Gustav Noske defeated the communists' coup attempt. The play caused a great stir and also enthusiasm on the radical left. It took Mauno Koivisto to heart and he wrote a two-part review of it in the Finnish Social Democrats in October 1970. "And what was the situation like in 1919 for the workers' movement and what kind of confrontation did there be? (Unfortunately, I've had all sorts of other things to do in recent years that have disrupted my theoretical pursuits, so I can't quickly come up with any more specific text now)". "I see the biggest difference in the attitude towards power: the Social Democrats aspire to political power, but are willing to share it. The Communists have declared that they are seeking power with the express intention that power will then not be shared with anyone." The persons mentioned in the review were: Hannu Taanila,Eetu Salin,V.I. Lenin,KarlKautsky,Eduard Bernstein,Rosa Luxemburg,DanielCohn d0Benditja Lev Trotsky". Another example: Koivisto often wrote and talked about left-wing cooperation even during his time as director general. The last article in his Book of Wrong Politics is titled Moving Forward. It is dated 1.5.1976. "We have been told to carry each other's burdens. It is a righteous and righteous thing. But in these present circumstances, it is easy for the one whose burden is borne to climb on top of the burden himself." My recollection of the speech was more colorful: "When we returned from a difficult task at the front, the guy got tired and asked if you would take my backpack? I took a backpack. Then we went forward again and he asked: Would you take my rifle? I can't cope anymore. I also took a rifle. We continued our journey again. Then he became exhausted again and asked: Can I get on your back? I'm all over the top. It was too much." I remember the speech well. It was Mauno Koivisto's May Day speech in Mikkeli Church Park in 1976. I was there as the opening speaker. Ingvar Carlsson has also visited Mikkeli, the godmother of Bor8cs. The coexistence of the Government and the Bank of Finland was not always easy. Critical was in the early spring of 1978. The situation came to a head with the devaluation in February and the subsequent resignation of the government. Sorsa later gave an eye-catching speech at the SDP's party council. He said there was such a contradiction between the independence of the Bank of Finland and the leadership of the government that "Finland is growing a snake of two-headed economic policy in its bosom." What had happened? The Bank of Finland and its president, Mauno Koivisto, devalued in a way that put the government in front of a fait accompli. Norway had devalued its crown on February 10, 1978. It was Friday. This took place between the 1978 electorate elections and the electorate meeting. The elections had been held in January and the electors had been convened on Wednesday 15.2.2010. Urho Kekkonen's electoral alliance had gained 259 electors. It is part of the spirit of the times that the result was hardly wondered at. On Sunday 12 February, Director-General Mauno Koivisto announced on television that the devaluation of the Norwegian krone also affected the position of the Finnish markka. After the announcement, retreat was impossible. For Prime Minister Kalevi Sorsa, Koivisto proposed a devaluation of the markka by 8 per cent. This would have been the third devaluation of the Finnish markka in 12 months. In 1977, the Sorsa II government had begun a series of stimulus packages. Before the devaluation of Norway, the government had decided on a third stimulus package. The government leadership sought to break free from the inflation-devaluation spiral. The trade unions had contributed to the package by agreeing to postpone the wage increases already agreed on on the grounds that devaluation would be avoided. The descent into devaluation was very embarrassing for the government. On the other hand, Koivisto saw devaluation as the only fast-acting way to end the mistrust of the markka's exchange rate that prevailed in the foreign exchange market. By decision of the Bank of Finland, the foreign exchange market remained closed throughout the presidential election week. The day after President Kekkonen was elected for the 5th time, the Bank of Finland made a formal proposal to the Government to devalue the markka by 8%. No prior agreement had been reached with the government on the size of the devaluation. The Board of Sorsan II had to either accept or reject the proposal. A majority of the government approved the bank's proposal by a vote of 8-4, but prime minister and finance minister Paul Paavela voted against. The situation was exceptional. Prime Minister Sorsa therefore tendered the resignation of the Government. A new government was soon appointed on the same basis. It was Sorsa IIb. At the 175th anniversary of the Bank of Finland, eight years after the episode, Prime Minister Kalevi Sorsa said that while government representatives had explained their economic policy plans to the Central Bank, "our central bank was wrapped up in its rustling mystique". "No, mystery seems to be the besetting sin of central banks everywhere," he continued, quoting Montagu Norman, the legendary governor of the Bank of England, whose motto was 'Never apologise, never explain': don't apologise, and don't explain. "That's how a political decision-maker would work, if only he could," Sorsa decided. What do tensions look like in the light of today? The role of the Central Bank has changed, we are part of the European System of Central Banks. Exchange rates are floating. The Central Bank has been given autonomy in the exercise of a clear mandate, the task of price stability. Strengthening the independence of central banks requires transparency and accountability. The effectiveness of monetary policy is also enhanced through successful communication. Mauno Koivisto held the post of Director General for 14 years and a month. Three times he was on leave of absence, and the task was left to deputies, Reino Rossi, Aarre Simosen, or Ahti Karjalainen. On net, Koivisto was president and CEO for 8 years and 10 months. 2. KOIVISTO TWICE TRANSFERRED FROM THE BANK TO THE POSITION OF PRIME MINISTER. WHAT WAS THE CONTRIBUTION OF THE CHAIRMEN, RAFAEL PAASIO AND KALEVI SORSA? Year1968. Mauno Koivisto only had 80 days as director-general when he became prime minister again. How was that possible? Rafael Paasio's majority government had started after the 1966 elections. The Social Democratic Party returned to government after an eight-year hiatus and the SKDL for the first time since the 1940s. The expectations were high and so was the disappointment. After the presidential elections of 1968, the opposition against Rafael Paasio wanted to oust him from the post of party chairman. The way forward was to separate the roles of prime minister and president. Surprisingly for many, Paasio chose the position of chairman. This was how a new prime minister had to be elected. Title: Book review  Jean Tirole, Economics for the Common Good, Princeton University Press 2017
text: Governor Erkki Liikanen: Book review Jean Tirole, Economics for the Common Good, Princeton University Press 2017 . Speech . Friday 5January2018,1:45 PM Governor Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland Book review published in Helsingin Sanomat on 4 January 2018 JEAN TIROLE: ECONOMICS FOR THE COMMON GOOD, PRINCETON UNIVERSITY PRESS 2017 Jean Tirole became Nobel laureate in 2014. Tirole has told that the prize changed his life in one respect. Until then, he had engaged in discussions with researchers and also with policymakers, but suddenly he found himself being stopped in the street by people who wanted to know what economic research is and how it can promote well.being. People were asking whether economics could resolve the great challenges of our times. This prompted Tirole to leave the academic ivory tower and write a book on how economic research can serve in resolving pressing problems and in gaining a better understanding of the world we live in. The result is an impressive book in which he presents a wide range of questions and provides answers from the perspective of economics in an easily readable form. Jean Tirole has exceptional qualifications for the task. On the one hand, he has published a remarkable amount of research literature, and on the other he is a modest person who also appreciates the work of others. The book contains over 500 pages, but each of its 17 chapters can be read independently. Jean Tirole emphasises that economics is a science of the means, not of the aims. Common objectives of society rely largely on values. Therefore, the mandate to define these objectives is created by democratic elections. Economics, in turn, can provide an input when the goal is to find tools for meeting the objectives at the lowest possible cost. Economic research can also be of significance when it contributes with the analysis of the multifaceted economic problems to laying a foundation for decision-making. What is the role of the market for economists? Tirole stresses that the market is an instrument, not an end in itself. He describes situations in which the market fails. This happens when buyers have insufficient information about products or when consumers only think about their immediate gratification or make decisions involving higher costs than their payment capacity. Market failures also occur if an economic actor has too significant market power. If the market functions properly it can improve efficiency, but there is no reason to assume that it will deliver equity. This is why both the state and the market are needed. They are complementary not substitutes for another. The state cannot ensure a decent life for its citizens without a market. The market, in turn, needs the state to guarantee that the judicial system operates smoothly and that market failures are addressed. Increasing competition with regulatory decisions has brought considerable advantages to consumers. An example: during my term in the European Commission, we drew on Jean Tiroleos research work and expertise when we proposed the unbundling of the local loop in 2000. Broadband prices declined rapidly and most households gained access to broadband. This was an important step in the development of the information society. The book also describes the most recent advances in economics, which relate to information theory and game theory. Tirole has also published several well-known articles with Bengt Holmstrsm who was awarded the Nobel Prize in 2016 for his research in information economics. Tirole writes a lot about incentives. Incentives affect the behaviour of firms and individuals. However, a financial incentive does not always lead to the intended results. As an example, Tirole refers to blood donation: when people started to get a financial reward from donating blood, the number of donors plummeted. Donors were not motivated by money but instead by the possibility to contribute to the common good. Jean Tiroleos Economics for the Common Good is one of the most important economics books of the year. It is valuable to policymakers, since it proves that economics has produced many tools that can be used in finding the best possible solutions. The book also sends an important message to economists, that they should bring their important contribution to the societal debate by sharing the results of their research. Economists may have their own personal views on values, but objectives based on values of society must be left to the democratic process.
