Title: Significance of the Civil War Memorial Year  speech at the opening of the Bank of Finland 1918 exhibition on 31 January 2018
text: President Erkki Liikanen: The significance of the Civil War Commemoration Year  speech at the opening ceremony of the Bank of Finland 1918 exhibition 31.1.2018 . Speech . Wednesday31 January 2018, 1:00 PM President Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland Significance of the Civil War Commemorative Year Opening of the Bank of Finland 1918 exhibition 31.1.2018 MEANING OF THE CIVIL WAR COMMEMORATION YEAR Dear invited guests, dear friends! The exhibition, which opens today at the Monetary Museum, deals with one of the most difficult topics in Finnish history, the Civil War of 1918. When we are at the Bank of Finland, we focus on how the war affected the monetary conditions in Finland and the Bank of Finland. Finland's development into an independent republic, Nordic democracy, welfare state and full member of the European Union has been a multi-stage process. The Civil War of spring 1918 is perhaps the most tragic phase of this narrative. It continues to divide opinions even after a hundred years. Nevertheless, it is important that the whole in its commemorative year is discussed and based on the extensive research that has been done on it. It is also important that the background and events of the spring of 1918 would now form as nuanced and objective a picture as possible as part of Finnish history based on research. The historic nature of the Civil War does not mean that there are no lessons to be learned from it. Our national tragedy bears stark proof of the consequences that suspicion, hatred and political immaturity can lead to. The background was the economic collapse and plight of 1917. In finland's current stable conditions, it can be forgotten how fragile and slowly strengthening democracy is. There are far too many examples of this in other parts of the world, including in recent years and decades. If the Year of Commemoration of the Civil War helps Finns to appreciate and cherish the social reconciliation and stability we have achieved over the decades that followed, then the commemorative year will not be wasted. The parliament's commemoration last Friday was very successful in this respect. *** Marjaliisa and Seppo Hentila summed up in their book German Finland 1918, published last year: The end result that Finland as a nation and state has achieved has by no means been self-evident. The fact that Finland became an independent republic built on the Western model required three things, according to them: Germany had to lose world warBol.the aeviks had to manage to stay in power in RussiaThe Whites had to win Finnish Civil War If even one of these had gone differently, Finland would have become a very different country," Hentilat points out. The list of hentiles was written from the point of view of the spring of 1918. Among the events that preceded it, one could add the Russian Revolution and the Brest-Litovsk peace talks that began in December, which marked a German victory (albeit temporary) on the Eastern Front of the World War. These, too, were key events for Finland's fate. Although modern research already knows how to place Finland's independence in the major political context of the time, I believe that the images of most Finns are still dominated by the "national narrative" of the Civil War, which is directly inherited from the years of the Civil War. When the events are put into an international context and the military strength of the various parties is taken into account, the conclusion is reached that the outcome of the Finnish Civil War was practically resolved already when Germany decided to intervene in Finland and when the Bolshevik Government of Russia had accepted the idea that the country should give Germany a free hand over Finland. The decision on german intervention arose at a meeting on February 13 in Bad Homburg. Immediately afterwards, General Ludendorff ordered and also received a request for help from Edvard Hjelt, the representative of the Finnish Senate in Berlin, which justified the expedition to be sent to Finland. The Senate of Vaasa did not hear about the matter until weeks later, in March 1918. Even before the outbreak of the Finnish Civil War, Lenin had come to the conclusion in January that peace had to be made with Germany. He initially struggled to get the rest of his party's leadership on its heels, but in February the Bol.vivik leadership already saw that its options were either peace or destruction. From Finland, Lenin said already on 17.2.: "We have done what we have been able to do." At this point, the Finnish Civil War had been going on for three weeks. In February, Germany also presented Russia with its final peace terms, which, as expected, included russia having to withdraw its army from Finland. Russia's agreement was a no-brainer. The Brest-Litovsk Peace Treaty was concluded on 3.3.1918. Germany was interested in peace because it hoped peace on the Eastern Front would help it to a quick victory in the West. For the Bolshevik government, it was a question of securing its own existence. However, it considered the concessions it had made to be temporary, as it considered the realisation of the revolution in Western Europe, too, to be only a matter of time. The agreement reached in February between the Bolshevik government of Russia and Imperial Germany was poorly suited to finland's prevailing picture of the nature of the civil war. The Senate of Vaasa wanted to emphasize that Finland is fighting the independence struggle with German support against Bolsist Russia. The People's Commissariat, on the other hand, relied on the Bol.A. government as practically its only supporter and then did not realize that Lenin's realpolitik calculations worked against it. The international background of the Finnish Civil War can be seen as one example of how weak small nations are in a world where the politics of force override the principles of international law. It reminds us how important it is for relations between countries to be based on law and common institutions. It stresses the importance of multilateral international structures such as the European Union, the OSCE and the UN, especially for small countries. *** The position of the Bank of Finland in the events of the spring of 1918 is not very well known. Few people think that the Bank of Finland operated for almost three months in the hands of the People's Delegation and was the main financier of its activities. The events of the spring of 1918 showed how, even under exceptional circumstances, economic life could not function without means of payment and, for example, the payment of wages could not proceed without regular money supply. On both sides of the front, means of payment and credit were needed for the needs of both the military and business life. In a way, the problems of the People's Delegation and the Senate were opposite: the Bank of Finland's banking board had the supporters of the People's Delegation have a majority and hold the Bank of Finland and the printing press. When other banks were closed, it was difficult to make the distribution of money and, for example, the weekly payment of wages work. In the north of the country, which is held by the Senate, private banks were operating, but there was not enough cash. The Senate of Vaasa had to develop various exceptional solutions to compensate for the fact that the Central Bank and its largest branches had remained in the hands of the opposing party. The consequences of the Civil War for the value of money are easy to guess. The swell of the banknote system, the faltering government and the shortage of goods due to the war collapsed the value of the Finnish markka. In fact, as early as 1917, rising inflation was one of the main reasons for the economic distress that exacerbated the social situation in Finland to the point of explosion. It was in 1917 that the Finnish economy collapsed deeper than at any time in its history, even taking the years of the last wars as a comparison. *** The exhibition at the Monetary Museum, which is now opening, features civil war-era means of payment from both sides of the front line, as well as documents depicting financial management in the exceptional circumstances of the time. An interesting object in the exhibition is, among other things, the five-penny designed by Akseli Halonen, which remained the only type of money for the people's delegation. Until then, the front of the five-penny had been the subject of a double eagle. In the new political situation, this did not fit, and Halonen replaced it with a fanfare horn and flag theme. After the Civil War, Halonen worked as an illustrator for Helsingin Sanomat, among others. Other rarely seen items on display are the banknotes of The Vaasan Osake-Bank, strictly speaking, the konttocurant cheques that the Senate of Vaasa issued to alleviate the lack of means of payment. These money substitutes were designed by Akseli Gallen-Kallela, who became the court designer of finland, which was otherwise independent during the Civil War. Among other things, he designed decorations, uniforms, and also made his own proposal for the Flag of Finland - which, however, did not materialize. Finally, I would like to thank the designers of the exhibition: Vappu Ikonen, who has borne the main responsibility, as well as Jaakko Koskentola and Juha Tarkan. The exhibition architect was Teemu Taskinen. Special thanks are also due to Antti Heinonen, formerly Chief Treasury Officer of the Bank of Finland and Banknote Director of the European Central Bank, who has helped put the exhibition together with his expertise. In Antti's book "Money of War and Peace", which appeared last year, there is an interesting description of the monetary economy of the Civil War period. Tonight at 5 p.m., Antti Heinonen will give a presentation on the history of banknotes from 1918 in the Studia monetaria series of the Monetary Museum. I recommend it to everyone. Welcome to visit the exhibition! Kansanvaltuuskunnan ja senaatin ongelmat olivat tavallaan vastakkaiset: Suomen Pankin pankkivaltuustossa oli kansanvaltuuskunnan tukijoilla enemmist<9a> ja hallussaan Suomen Pankki ja setelipaino. Kun muut pankit olivat kiinni, rahan jakelua ja esimerkiksi viikoittaista palkanmaksua oli vaikeata saada toimimaan. Senaatin hallussa olevassa maan pohjoisosassa taas yksityispankit toimivat, mutta k<8a>teist<8a> ei ollut riitt<8a>v<8a>sti. Vaasan senaatti joutui kehitt<8a>m<8a><8a>n erilaisia poikkeusratkaisuja korvatakseen sen, ett<8a> keskuspankki ja sen suurimmat haarakonttorit olivat j<8a><8a>neet vastapuolen k<8a>siin. Sis<8a>llissodan seuraukset rahan arvolle ovat helposti arvattavissa. Setelist<9a>n paisuminen, hallitusvallan horjuvuus ja sodasta johtuva tavarapula romahduttivat Suomen markan arvon. Itse asiassa jo vuonna 1917 kiihtynyt inflaatio oli yksi t<8a>rke<8a> syy siihen taloudelliseen ahdinkoon, joka k<8a>rjisti yhteiskunnallista tilannetta Suomessa r<8a>j<8a>hdyspisteeseen. Suomen talous romahti juuri vuonna 1917 syvemm<8a>lle kuin koskaan historiansa aikana, vaikka vertailuun otettaisiin viime sotien vuodet. *** Nyt avattavassa rahamuseon n<8a>yttelyss<8a> on esill<8a> sis<8a>llissodan ajan maksuv<8a>lineit<8a> rintamalinjan molemmilta puolilta sek<8a> dokumentteja, jotka kuvaavat finanssihallintoa ajan poikkeuksellisissa oloissa. Kiinnostava kohde n<8a>yttelyss<8a> on muun muassa Akseli Halosen suunnittelema viisipenninen, joka j<8a>i ainoaksi kansanvaltuuskunnan omaksi rahatyypiksi. Siihen asti viisipennisen etupuolella oli ollut aiheena kaksoiskotka. Uudessa poliittisessa tilanteessa t<8a>m<8a> ei sopinut, ja Halonen korvasi sen fanfaaritorvi-ja lippuaiheella. Halonen toimi sis<8a>llissodan j<8a>lkeen muun muassa Helsingin Sanomien kuvittajana. Muita esill<8a> olevia harvoin n<8a>htyj<8a> kohteita ovat Vaasan Osake-Pankin setelit, tarkkaan ottaen konttokuranttisekit, joita Vaasan senaatti laski liikkeeseen maksuv<8a>lineiden puutteen helpottamiseksi. N<8a>m<8a> rahan korvikkeet suunnitteli Akseli Gall<8e>n-Kallela, josta tuli sis<8a>llissodan aikana muutenkin itsen<8a>isen Suomen hovisuunnittelija. H<8a>n suunnitteli muun muassa kunniamerkkej<8a>, univormuja ja teki my<9a>s Suomen lipuksi oman ehdotuksensa -joka ei kuitenkaan toteutunut. Haluan lopuksi kiitt<8a><8a> n<8a>yttelyn suunnittelijoita: Vappu Ikosta, joka on kantanut p<8a><8a>vastuun, sek<8a> Jaakko Koskentolaa ja Juha Tarkkaa. N<8a>yttelyarkkitehtina toimi Teemu Taskinen. Erityisen kiitoksen ansaitsee my<9a>s Antti Heinonen, aiemmin Suomen Pankin ylikassanhoitaja ja Euroopan keskuspankin setelijohtaja, joka on asiantuntemuksellaan auttanut n<8a>yttelyn kokoamisessa. Antin viime vuonna ilmestyneess<8a> kirjassa "Sodan ja rauhan rahat" on mielenkiintoinen kuvaus sis<8a>llissodan ajan rahataloudesta. T<8a>n<8a> iltana kello 17 Antti Heinonen pit<8a><8a> t<8a><8a>ll<8a> rahamuseon Studia monetaria -sarjassa esitelm<8a>n vuoden 1918 setelihistoriasta. Suosittelen sit<8a> kaikille. Title: On the development of economic and monetary union.
text: Erkki Liikanen: Statement to the Parliament's Economic Committee on the development of economic and monetary union. Helsinki, 14.2.2018. . Speech . Wednesday14 February 2018,4:00 PM President Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland Statement to the Parliament's Economic Committee on the development of economic and monetary union 14.2.2018 Case: E 115/2017 vp Government report: European Commission proposals for the development of economic and monetary union (/link/d71bc62a78b145359ba5b1a144b419ed.aspx) ON THE DEVELOPMENT OF ECONOMIC AND MONETARY UNION Completing the banking union is a key issue for stability and therefore a priority for central banks. Significant progress has been made in the banking union area since 2012 with the creation of single banking supervision and the Single Resolution Mechanism. At the same time, financial stability in the euro area has improved. However, work to strengthen the financial system in the euro area and increase stability must continue. It is essential to consolidate confidence in the liquidity and solvency of euro area banks in such a way as to reduce or eliminate the likelihood of shocks to the stability of the banking systems of the euro area as a whole or its member states. Progress has been made in this regard. In further work, it is worth considering the stability of the banking system at the top of the list support the strengthening of deposit guarantee and resolution schemes. The objective of the deposit guarantee scheme is to stabilise customers' confidence in the continuous liquidity of bank deposits. In this way, deposit runs from one bank or country to another due to mistrust can be avoided. In addition, it is also possible to prevent potential problems in a single bank from spreading through the contagion effect into mistrust of the banking system as a whole. The confidence-building effect achieved with the deposit guarantee scheme requires sufficient resources and secured liquidity from the deposit insurance funds. The stronger and more credible a deposit guarantee scheme is, the more effective it is at reassuring depositors and the less likely it is that it will need to be used. The resolution system is already in place. It makes it possible to intervene in the activities of underperforming or over-risk banks even before their equity capital and, in the resolution procedure, eligible liabilities eligible for bail-in in accordance with the principle of investor responsibility have run out. This will minimise the risk that the costs of banking problems would be borne by taxpayers. Due to the confidence in the system, the Resolution Fund also needs to be supported by a final backstop. It would also protect the Deposit Guarantee Fund from losses. The sustainability of a possible new European deposit insurance scheme has been assessed in a study that will soon be published. According to this, now that the position of banks has been improved by strengthening their capital and ensuring that they have sufficient items on the balance sheet that are subject to investor responsibility, even in the event of a large-scale banking crisis, deposits could be secured by a common deposit guarantee fund financed by the banking sector. Interestingly, once the payments have been collected from the banks according to the 'polluter pays' principle according to their risks, there would also be no significant claims flows between countries. A common deposit insurance scheme ,which would be stronger in terms of resources than national schemes, would significantly increase the stability of the euro area banking system compared to the current situation where national funds are responsible for deposit insurance. The aim should be to achieve the same sustained level of confidence in liquid bank deposits across the euro area. In principle, a common deposit insurance scheme is of the greatest benefit to countries with a highly concentrated banking system that is large in relation to the size of the economy, i.e. there are few but large banks. The implementation of a single deposit insurance scheme can be facilitated by reducing the amount of non-performing loans (NPLs) recovered during the financial crisis or the subsequent euro area debt crisis. It is right that these inherited problems should be dealt with with national resources, in accordance with the guidelines laid down by the Commission. This should be made possible by means of transitional provisions. Therefore, they should not be eliminated now, but only after reducing the risks. It is also important to act for the future. Currently, Common Banking Supervision (SSM) is developing guidance for a new NPL provisioning policy to increase banks' credit loss provisions and resilience. In addition, a new accounting standard, IFRS 9, entered into force at the beginning of the year, according to which anticipated provisions for credit losses are recorded already when granting credits. It is also important that banks' exposure to risks in their home countries is reduced and capital to cover these risks is improved. The solution model advocated by experts at the Bank of Finland is based on the premise that, as part of the completion of the banking union, the bank will be required to have more capital if it wants to own a large amount of individual state debt. An additional capital requirement based on concentration risk would provide an incentive for banks to diversify their sovereign bond holdings and support market-based risk sharing in the euro area. The negative market impact of the requirement would probably be less pronounced than other regulatory options. A capital add-on based on concentration risk in the banking union would provide an incentive to reduce divergences in banks' home country risks. The requirement would ensure that the risks of concentration of banks' holdings of government bonds in relation to their own capital are reduced in accordance with an appropriate timeframe. It is important to strengthen banks' loss-absorbing capacity to ensure that, in the event of a resolution, investor responsibility is implemented as defined by EU law. The ultimate goal is that, in a resolution situation, investor responsibility is realised and that taxpayers' money in the form of state aid is not needed to deal with the problems of crisis banks. The minimum requirements for the bank's own funds and remeasable liabilities, which safeguard banks' resilience, should therefore be finalised (the so-called "revolving credits"). MREL requirements). It is important to reach agreement on the proposals made by the European Commission in November 2016 to amend the legislation on bank resolution. It is key to the convergence of banks' risk levels that uniform regulatory requirements are defined for all banks and that their uniform implementation by public authorities across the banking union is key. However, with regard to timetables, the market and stability effects of the measures should be taken into account. Title: Book review - Stephen Kotkin:  Stalin Vol. II. Waiting for Hitler 19281941, Allen Lane
text: Governor Erkki Liikanen: Book review -Stephen Kotkin: Stalin Vol. II. Waiting for Hitler 1928-1941, Penguin Press, 2018 . Speech . Monday19 March 2018,10:10AM Governor Erkki Liikanen Bank of Finland Book review publisehd in Helsingin Sanomat on 17 March 2018 BOOK REVIEW -STEPHEN KOTKIN: STALIN VOL. II. WAITING FOR HITLER 1928-1941, PENGUIN PRESS 2018 AN AMERICAN PERSPECTIVE PLACES THE FINNISH WINTER WAR IN THE GEOPOLITICAL FRAMEWORK OF THE SOVIET UNION. Last August Princeton university professor Stephen Kotkin gave a speech at an international conference in Aspen, Colorado. His analyses of Russia were distinctive and incisive. When I went to thank the professor he asked whether I knew Kimmo Rentola. Kotkin had familiarised himself with the Finnish professoros articles on the Winter War for his own research on Stalin. Kotkin had begun work on a trilogy on Stalin, and the first volume had already been published. It was a huge success among the critics. The second volume, Waiting for Hitler, discusses the events of the Soviet empire from 1928 onwards and was published last autumn. Henry Kissinger wrote in his famous book Diplomacy (1994): oStalin was indeed a monster; but in the conduct of international relations, he was the supreme realist patient, shrewd and implacable, the Richelieu of his period.o Kotkin challenges Kissingeros view. Stalin was all the things Kissinger stated, but he was never only that. Stalin was more of a gambler than most people have understood. Kotkin mentions four gambles taken by Stalin. The first was the forced collectivisation and dekulakisation. Stalinos justification for his action was that capital was needed for a rapid industrialisation of the country. Not much capital could be extracted, though. The greatest risk of collectivisation was famine, which actually materialised in many regions. The second gamble involved the cleansing of the party and army at the same time as the Soviet Union was already involved in wars in Spain and China and was soon to be in conflict with Germany. These purges also featured in director A. J. Annilaos latest film, which is based on Antti Tuurios novel Ikitie (oThe Eternal Roado). If the worst had come to pass, the purges could have threatened the very existence of the Soviet Union. The third gamble was the treaty with Hitler and the division of Europe by a oPact of Bloodo, even if the justifications for this were economic in nature. The pact between Hitler and Mussolini was also identically titled, before it was later renamed the oPact of Steelo, due to the negative reception in Italy. Kotkin considers that Stalinos fourth and final gamble was the Soviet invasion of Finland and the resulting Winter War. Stalin embarked on this gamble with Finland unprepared and without realising he was doing so. This was Stalinos first test in the arts of modern warfare. According to Kotkin, the results initially proved disastrous. The book dedicates as many as 60 pages to detailing the negotiations preceding the Winter War and the war itself. Kotkin not only draws on Soviet archives but has also studied Finnish biographies and research literature. Jakobson, Ksksnen, Mannerheim, Manninen, Rentola, Sarola-Kuusinen, Tanner, Tuominen and many others are named among the bookos references. The value of Kotkinos monumental work for a Finnish reader is that it places Finland in the geopolitical framework of the Soviet Union. It provides an impressive chronicle of Soviet history and simultaneously paints a detailed portrait of Stalinos person, characteristics and life. Kotkin raises a fundamental question for the reader: would it have been possible to avoid the Winter War by agreeing to Stalinos demands on the borderline adjustments and the Hanko military base? The late Finnish president Mauno Koivisto discussed the issue in his final book Itsensiseksi imperiumin kainalossa (oIndependence under the arm of an empireo) (2004). Koivisto wrote: oTo date, there is no evidence that the Soviet Unionos plans for Finland would have diverged from those for the Baltic States. Perhaps war in autumn 1939 was a necessary prelude to new negotiations, who knows.o Kotkinos book pays a great deal of attention to culture. A year ago, the Finnish National Opera performed Shostakovichos Lady Macbeth. Stalin went to see this in January 1937. A few days later an article appeared in Pravda entitled oA muddle instead of musico. It had been penned by Platon Kerzhentsev, the eager new chairman of the Committee for Artistic Affairs, and not by Stalin, as rumoured. The opera was not showcased again for several decades. Title: The Future Challenges of Central Banks
text: Governor Erkki Liikanen: THE FUTURE CHALLENGES OF CENTRAL BANKS. Banque de France, Paris, 29 June 2018. . Speech . Tuesday 3July 2018, 4:49PM Governor Erkki Liikanen Banque de France Paris, 29 June 2018 FUTURE GAMES OF CENTRAL BANKS First of all, I would like to thank Francois Villeroy, my colleague and friend, for his invitation. I have the utmost respect for the Bank of France, its traditions and its ongoing efforts to promote European ideals. The Bank of France is one of the strongest banks in the Eurosystem, both in terms of its operational capacity and the quality of its studies. After the years of the "Great Moderation", we experienced the international financial crisis that turned into a double recession in Europe. Eventually, the economic recovery is beginning to pave the way for some form of "normalization" of monetary policy. However, this "normalization" does not mean a return to the past financial context or to central banks considered normal a decade ago. Central banks need to think about their role in the economy and society. I see several good reasons to do so. One of them is that the practical needs for monetary policy in the post-crisis period have led to a . development of the scale and scope of central bank operations much greater than was considered normal before the crisis. By necessity, central banks have shown their pragmatic side by helping to restore financial stability and overcome the danger of deflation. The second reason for reflecting on the current role of central banks is related to the changes . societal observed in recent years. A trend towards increasing skepticism about established institutions has emerged in many countries, a kind of alienation from the institutional structures of democratic societies. As independent public institutions operating under the law, central banks must pay attention to these developments. Central banks need to find ways to encourage public support for their status and mandate. In Europe, a particular aspect of this societal change is emerging. The rise of nationalism has fuelled a certain scepticism about the European project in general and, occasionally, about the euro. It is obvious that the euro is today so vital for our economies and the political construction of our continent that its legitimacy must not be threatened. The institutional architecture supporting the common currency must be protected and strengthened. That is why central banks in Europe need to think carefully about how to meet this challenge. A third reason is technological and concerns in particular the wave of digitization or even the . Digitizing. This is not a new phenomenon, even in the banking sector. But there are reasons to think that the digitization process has now reached a point where it can have disruptive potential without previous. This can transform the nature of the banking sector beyond what we can predict. For Central banks, this can lead to existential questions about, among other things, the role of central money. and the integrity of the settlement system. I will focus here on the first two of these drivers of change. Monetary policy strategy First of all, when talking about monetary policy, we must distinguish between objectives and tools. The range of tools used by central banks has certainly expanded considerably compared to the practices of the 2000s. Currently, the ECB is in the process of gradually reducing and concluding its net bond acquisition programme at the end of the year. This conclusion reflects the Governing Council's view that the euro area economy is gradually returning to normal. However, the new monetary policy instruments are now and definitively part of the central banks' toolbox and can be reactivated if the situation so requires. Although monetary policy instruments have changed significantly over the past decade, the objectives of monetary policy have not been called into question. Price stability remains the primary objective of monetary policy. Our commitment to price stability has survived all tests: it has not prevented monetary policy from supporting economic activity and employment in a meaningful way. Despite this, it is occasionally necessary to interpret monetary policy strategy in new contexts. What does this mean today? Some economists have proposed an alternative monetary policy strategy, called "Price Level Targeting." I believe that price level targeting involves many practical difficulties related to communication but also to how it works if the target is not completely credible. Adopting it would also represent a radical change, making communication problems particularly difficult. The benefits of targeting could be achieved by committing to a goal of "below but close to 2 percent, on average over the entire business cycle. In my opinion, monetary policy should therefore aim for an inflation rate of "below but close to 2 percent" over the medium term. This means that, regardless of their direction, deviations from the average inflation rate should be seen as undesirable. Stabilitefinanciere Let us now turn to financial stability, which remained underdeveloped when EMU was created. Perhaps the neglect of financial stability was due to the reluctance to address politically difficult issues, or perhaps it was an illusory optimism overestimating the stability of financial and money markets in general. We have paid a heavy price for this negligence. I argue that the fact that the Eurozone has experienced a long period of low growth is linked to the financial fragility of its architecture. Some items in the invoice are not not yet fully settled, such as non-performing loans inherited from the crisis years, still on the balance sheets of some banks. Great institutional progress has been made in the area of financial stability, in particular since 2012, when the Banking Union project was launched with the unification of banking sector supervision and the creation of the Single Resolution Mechanism. These are great European achievements. However, it is necessary to continue working on three sites: First, the Single Resolution Fund needs a fiscal safety net to ensure its ability to . operate in all circumstances and ensure the orderly resolution of institutions in difficulty. Bottom of single resolution is privately financed, its cost being borne by the banks, but it needs this liquid safety net to eliminate any doubt about its effectiveness. Secondly, a European deposit insurance scheme must be created, based on proportional payments. the risks involved. This will ensure the resilience of deposit markets within our currency area by levelling trust in bank deposits, regardless of the country of origin of the bank receiving the deposit. Thirdly, the Capital Markets Union must be created. This is a priority often emphasized by Francis. Villeroy. I appreciate his European commitment and consistency on this issue. I support him and share his opinion. The development of European securities markets would help the system shift some of the risk associated with asymmetric economic fluctuations to private investors. Currently, and especially before the euro crisis, cross-border capital flows within Europe have been generated far too much by banks, as they borrow on international markets and lend on their domestic markets. This makes banks too vulnerable to country risk. Central bank communication and relationship with policy makers and the public The media environment and the political field have been radically transformed in recent years, not everywhere in the same way, but I believe that the implications for central banks are largely similar in many countries. These changes are the result of a mixture of several factors. One of them is the social media revolution, which has reduced the prestige and influence of journalism and traditional mass media. Explanations related to the real economy are to be found in globalization and the technological revolution that increase feelings of insecurity. There are two historians whose expertise on Russia I greatly appreciate, Helene Carrere d'Encausse and Stephen Kotkin. The latter recently wrote in the journal "Foreign Affairs" about the current model of globalization: "This reoriented economic activity increases domestic inequality of opportunity and the feeling of betrayal of politicians in rich countries. For some of the losers, the wound is compounded by what they feel is a cultural insult, as their societies lose their familiarity. Western elites have focused on reaping the benefits of globalization rather than minimizing its costs, and as a result, they have supercharged the process and aggravated its conflictual consequences.  Kotkin's analysis is a critique of how the recent economic transformation has been managed. Continuing this reasoning, the current crisis of legitimacy of democratic institutions would therefore be a consequence of the social blindness of political and economic decision-makers in Western societies. It is not necessary to fully share Kotkin's analysis, but he has raised important points and the new media and political environment requires a certain reorientation of public institutions, including including central banks. The most radical expression of Euroscepticism is visible outside the Eurozone. But for the Eurosystem central banks, the erosion of confidence in the common currency would be a very development. unfortunate can make their work more difficult. The necessary changes include improved communication and voluntary accountability to the public. In the new political environment of communications, we need to develop new forms of transparency and new channels of interaction with civil society. It would be arrogant to assume that central bank officials have all the wisdom and information necessary to run the financial markets. It is fatal to give the public the impression that this is what we think of ourselves. Confidence in central banks is important for the credibility and success of monetary policy. A high level of public confidence can also give central banks a natural and constructive role in their respective countries' economic policy discourses. A central bank, even an independent one, does not need to become a technocratic institution isolating itself in its "ivory tower" and studying economics from a deliberately narrow point of view. On the contrary: the contribution of an impartial central bank and source of economic expertise can foster economic debate and policy formulation, while maintaining a strong engagement with society at large. As Nobel laureate Jean Tirole wrote in his book "Economy of the Common Good," economics is the science of means, not ends. It is a statement that legitimizes the participation of economists in political discussions. Tirole sees a neutral expert role, where economists can participate without entering the political field. We must be humble and avoid the arrogance of the past. Economists cannot derive normative value judgments from their technical knowledge. The choice of political objectives and priorities must be left to political decision-makers. One of my priorities as Governor has been to strengthen the role of the central bank in national policy debates in Finland. We have regularly conducted and published independent analyses of the problems of the Finnish economy. We frequently had in-depth exchanges with policy makers and organisations of particular interest, such as labour market organisations. For example, we have followed and frequently commented on the development of the competitiveness of the Finnish economy, which deteriorated significantly just before the international financial crisis. Our participation in the economic policy discussions was well received and we contributed positively to the wage negotiations aimed at restoring the competitiveness of the Finnish economy. This trust is the fruit of the impartiality of our contributions. On another level, our economists of all ranks visit universities, schools, companies and trade unions directly. These visits of course serve the communication objectives but this is not the only advantage, or even necessarily the most important. We learn a lot from the questions asked by untrained people with good judgment. The interaction generated by these visits is also a learning experience for staff. This allows you to better understand the different needs and learn to better communicate with people who are neither colleagues nor financial experts. The experience was more positive than expected. To increase our visibility, we use social media. Economists at the Bank of Finland have, in recent years, been encouraged to participate in social media. By using social media, they can grow their professional networks and increase the number of followers. Social media is particularly useful for disseminating and promoting studies, blogs and comments published on the Bank of Finland website. The message should be as simple as possible, but not simpler (Einstein). Conclusion Ladies and gentlemen: The most important strategic issue concerns the ability to manage continuity and change: Central banks, like other organizations, must adapt and change in order to survive. In the present circumstances, I think the need for adaptation is particularly strong. We must remain vigilant with regard to the demands for change brought about by the financial, social and technological environment. At the same time, central banks are, like many other public institutions, guardians of continuity. The mandate that our political leaders have given us is very explicitly about continuity: central banks are the guardians of the value of the currency (in the name of price stability), financial stability, the security and safety of payment systems, etc. At the general level, the challenge is to find the right balance between change and adaptation, continuity and persistence. It is an arduous task that we must carry out, using our leadership and combining ingenuity and team spirit. Thank you for your attention! Erkki Liikanen

Un haut niveau de confiance publique peut aussi donner aux banques centrales un r<99>le naturel et constructif dans les discours de politique <8e>conomique de leur pays respectif. Une banque centrale, m<90>me ind<8e>pendante, n<d5>a pas besoin de devenir une institution technocratique s<d5>isolant dans sa <c7> tour d<d5>ivoire <c8> et <8e>tudiant lconomie d<d5>un point de vue d<8e>lib<8e>r<8e>ment <8e>troit. Au contraire : la contribution d<d5>une banque centrale impartiale et source d<d5>expertise <8e>conomique peut favoriser le d<8e>bat <8e>conomique et la formulation des politiques, tout en entretenant un engagement fort avec la soci<8e>t<8e> au sens large. Comme Jean Tirole, laur<8e>at du Prix Nobel, l<d5>a <8e>crit dans son livre <c7> <83>conomie du bien commun <c8>, lconomie est la science des moyens, pas des fins. C<d5>est une d<8e>claration qui l<8e>gitime la participation des <8e>conomistes aux discussions politiques. Tirole voit un r<99>le d<d5>expertise neutre, o<9d> les <8e>conomistes peuvent participer sans p<8e>n<8e>trer le champ politique. Nous devons <90>tre humbles et <8e>viter l<d5>arrogance du pass<8e>. Les <8e>conomistes ne peuvent pas tirer des jugements de valeur normative de leur savoir technique. Le choix des objectifs et priorit<8e>s politiques doit <90>tre laiss<8e> aux d<8e>cideurs politiques. Une de mes priorit<8e>s en tant que Gouverneur a <8e>t<8e> de renforcer le r<99>le de la banque centrale dans les d<8e>bats de politique nationale en Finlande. Nous avons r<8e>guli<8f>rement men<8e> et publi<8e> des analyses ind<8e>pendantes des probl<8f>mes de lconomie finlandaise. Nous avons eu fr<8e>quemment des <8e>changes approfondis avec les d<8e>cideurs et les organisations d'int<8e>r<90>t particulier, comme les organisations du march<8e> du travail. Par exemple, nous avons suivi et fr<8e>quemment comment<8e> le d<8e>veloppement de la comp<8e>titivit<8e> de lconomie finlandaise, qui s<d5>est d<8e>t<8e>rior<8e>e sensiblement juste avant la crise financi<8f>re internationale. Notre participation aux discussions de politique <8e>conomique a <8e>t<8e> bien re<8d>ue et nous avons positivement contribu<8e> aux n<8e>gociations salariales destin<8e>es <88> restaurer la comp<8e>titivit<8e> de lconomie finlandaise. Cette confiance est le fruit de l<d5>impartialit<8e> de nos contributions. Sur un autre niveau, nos <8e>conomistes de tout rang rendent directement visite aux universit<8e>s, <8e>coles, entreprises et syndicats. Ces visites servent bien s<9e>r les objectifs de communication mais ce n<d5>est pas le seul avantage, ni m<90>me n<8e>cessairement le plus important. On apprend beaucoup des questions pos<8e>es par des gens non form<8e>s dot<8e>s de bon jugement. L<d5>interaction g<8e>n<8e>r<8e>e par ces visites constitue aussi une exp<8e>rience d<d5>apprentissage pour le personnel. Cela permet de mieux comprendre les diff<8e>rents besoins et d<d5>apprendre <88> mieux communiquer avec des personnes qui ne sont ni des confr<8f>res ni des experts financiers. L<d5>exp<8e>rience a <8e>t<8e> plus positive que pr<8e>vue. Pour renforcer notre visibilit<8e>, nous utilisons les m<8e>dias sociaux. Les <8e>conomistes de la Banque de Finlande ont, depuis quelques ann<8e>es, <8e>t<8e> encourag<8e>s <88> participer aux m<8e>dias sociaux. En utilisant les m<8e>dias sociaux, ils peuvent d<8e>velopper leurs r<8e>seaux professionnels et augmenter le nombre d<d5>abonn<8e>s. Les m<8e>dias sociaux sont particuli<8f>rement utiles pour diffuser et promouvoir les <8e>tudes, blogs et commentaires publi<8e>s sur le site Internet de la Banque de Finlande. Le message doit <90>tre aussi simple que possible, mais pas plus simple (Einstein). Conclusion Mesdames et messieurs : La question strat<8e>gique la plus importante concerne l<d5>aptitude <88> g<8e>rer continuit<8e> et changement : Les banques centrales comme d<d5>autres organisations, doivent s<d5>adapter et changer pour survivre. Dans les circonstances pr<8e>sentes, je pense que le besoin d<d5>adaptation est particuli<8f>rement fort. Nous devons rester vigilants vis <88> vis des exigences de changement induites par l<d5>environnement financier, social et technologique. En m<90>me temps, les banques centrales sont, comme beaucoup d<d5>autres institutions publiques, gardiennes de la continuit<8e>. Le mandat que nos dirigeants politiques nous ont donn<8e> concerne de fa<8d>on tr<8f>s explicite la continuit<8e> : les banques centrales sont les gardiennes de la valeur de la devise (au nom de la stabilit<8e> des prix), de la stabilit<8e> financi<8f>re, de la s<8e>curit<8e> et de la s<9e>ret<8e> des syst<8f>mes de paiements, etc. Au niveau g<8e>n<8e>ral, le d<8e>fi est de trouver le bon <8e>quilibre entre changement et adaptation, continuit<8e> et persistance. C'est une t<89>che ardue que nous devons mener, en utilisant notre leadership et en combinant ing<8e>nuit<8e> et esprit dquipe. Je vous remercie de votre attention ! Erkki Liikanen

Title: Financial market shocks  an unexplained phenomenon for analysts
text: Deputy Governor Pentti Hakkarainen Hannes Snellman Financial Law Seminar 2008 Financial Market Turbulence  A Conundrum for Analysts? Financial market turmoil  an unexplained phenomenon for analysts The turbulence in the financial markets raises two questions. Is turbulence the cause of the weakening of economic growth? Or is it a symptom of even more serious economic shocks? The theme of the event is appropriate to this day, as the current financial market turmoil is quite a mystery. The term 'conundrum' was introduced into common use by The Governor of the Federal Reserve, Alan Greenspan. By that he meant that long-term interest rates remained low, despite the fact that the central bank had raised its short-term policy rates several times. The Fed began a gradual (at a measured pace) rate hike in June 2004. Interest rates were raised by a quarter of a percent at almost every central bank interest rate meeting until June 2006. Despite the withdrawals, interest rates on long-term bonds remained low. Greenspan was fascinated by this phenomenon, for which he used the term 'conundrum'. The globalisation of financial markets, the strong accumulation of savings and surpluses in growing economies and the so-called 'green belt' created the basis for this phenomenon. The China phenomenon, which led to products being priced at lower prices on the world market, even though their quality improved. The riddle of the financial markets There is now a new unexplained phenomenon in the financial markets, the 'conundrum'. The shocks hit the core of the financial market in the interbank deposit and loan markets. For several years now, a number of risks had been identified for the stability of the financial markets, including: 1 Low risk premiums in almost all products where investors and financial market participants can take risk and price it. 2 The excessive sufficiency of funding, which made it possible to finance almost all projects on exceptionally favourable terms. 3 A frenzied search for returns that increased the risk positions of institutional investors and MFIs operating in the financial markets. Despite the risks identified, the financial markets are functioning steadily and profitably. In August 2007, an unprecedented change took place. A liquidity crisis arose in which MFIs were unwilling to lend to each other on the same terms as before, without good collateral (see chart on page 4). The interbank market has been efficient. Pricing is based on bank-to-bank settlements and loans for different lengths of running time, from overnight arrangements to two-month-long arrangements. In August 2007, this market stopped like a wall. It surprised MFIs and analysts with its intensity and speed. Banks were ready to lend to each other on the same terms as before, only on either of the so-called "greenfields". repo trades or against a security deposit. Unsecured lending, which determines, among other things, euribor, instantly became more than half a percentage point higher. Causes of turbulence The causes of the liquidity crisis are manifold. In simple terms, they can be classified as the widespread use of financial innovation and the expansion of a new approach to financial activities. For several years, there was a strong risk appetite and low risk premiums in the market, the availability of financing was excellent. In times of low interest rates, increasingly high-risk positions were taken to seek returns by indebtedness and accepting increasingly poor creditworthiness. This became the optimal operating model for MFIs. The old operating model based on bank financing increasingly gave way to the new world of securitisation. In the "Old World", the bank issued a loan to the borrower and monitored throughout the loan period the ability of the borrower to take care of the repayment of the loan. In the New World, the chain of financial intermediation lengthened. Loans were sold through financial intermediaries. The bank whose books the loans came from valued them by packaging the loans and selling the package with its risks to investors. The new operating model fuelled the emergence of financial innovation and changed the traditional operations of financial institutions by separating different risk elements into, for example, special purpose vehicles and credit default derivatives. A large part of the lending and its risks were transferred outside the banking sector and, at the same time, outside supervision. The incentives of intermediaries selling loans and final investors did not coincide. It was essential for the new operations that the rewards and incentives were volume-based. Commissions were granted to loan sellers, loan packagers, creditworthiness assessors and various experts, loan package splitters and sub-sellers, and derivative builders. Due to the long chain, the end investor was left with a risk that was difficult to manage. The new approach increased the efficiency of the financial system. The benefits included improved access to finance, lower prices and risk management. In the new model, liquidity is linked to the market's ability to trade, i.e. to the fact that these different products can be traded efficiently. Securitisation increases the liquidity of the market and, on the other hand, is based on the fact that the market is liquid. Market liquidity is also important for valuation in normal times, when there are no difficulties with trading, i.e. the value of assets can be determined on the basis of the cash flow they generate. In tighter times, the importance of liquidity increases in valuation and can be a decisive component of it. When there are problems with the liquidity of a financial instrument, its value can be significantly negligible in relation to the cash flows it generates. In the new approach to financial markets, financial instruments are continuously valued. Thus, they have a direct impact on the net assets and own capital of investors and MFIs. A liquidity shock can also create a solvency shock for financial markets and operators. Tobias Adrian of the Federal Reserve and Hyun Song Shin from Princeto-n University, who have recently studied this, have concluded that a new channel for the transmission of financial crises has emerged, in which market liquidity problems affect all players immediately. The more the operating model is based on securitisation, the stronger and more immediate this effect will be. The crises of the previous operating model spread like a domino effect from one financial institution to another. In today's operating model, crises affect everyone and immediately. It is not just a question of risk or increased risk, but of uncertainty. The classic distinction between uncertainty and risk is that uncertainty concerns a situation for which there is no probability distribution for outcomes, while for risk it can be estimated. At the moment, the problems are based on uncertainty and the fact that not all parties have the same information. Creditworthiness assessments, which have translated uncertainty into risk, have been used to reduce this problem. Creditworthiness assessors are open about their methods, but there has been a widespread and deep misunderstanding of what the real purpose of the rating is. This is particularly evident in structured products, where creditworthiness assessments are identified with regular bond products. Creditworthiness assessors have made an assessment of the repayment of the credit and not of the market value of the product. Disturbances surprised The unexpectedness of the financial turmoil is illustrated by the fact that the main difficulties have been felt by first-class players. Northern Rock was a respected basic business mortgage bank in Britain and Societe Generale is known in France for its good risk management. Bear Stearns is at the forefront of Wall Street investment houses and has sold its services and own shares, among other things, suggesting that in the last 86 years they have not made a loss-list financial statement. Other reputable banks such as Citibank, Merrill Lynch, UBS, Hong Kong Shanghai Banking Corporation, Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, etc. have been subject to write-downs and various capital shortfalls. Crisis prevention How to solve the crisis, have been avoided and avoided in the future? Financial actors and researchers have put forward different solutions. Central banks have added liquidity to the market in a non-profitable way, acting as banks' banks. Last Friday saw a new form of central bank involvement, when the Fed financed Bear Stearns by the investment bank JPMorgan Chase in such a way that the financial intermediary bank did not incur a separate risk to the financial intermediary bank. The risk is borne by the Fed. The arrangement differs from previous liquidations, where there has been action against full collateral or in the case of so-called liquidation. repo-trades. Central banks have also been expected to support financial market stability through monetary policy. Different central banks have acted differently in this regard. The Fed has been cutting interest rates rapidly. It seems that it has put the functioning of the financial markets ahead of the containment of inflation. The ECB has kept the monetary policy stance unchanged. A few smaller central banks have even raised their interest rates, despite the fact that this may have a negative impact on the stability of financial markets. Secondly, there have been calls for more supervision and for supervisors to keep a tighter grip on financial activities. This has been justified, for example, by the fact that excesses such as subprime lending can be prevented. The third proposal is that the range of complex financial innovations should be reduced to standardised products that would be traded on regulated marketplaces, e.g. on regulated marketplaces. on the stock exchanges. The fourth requirement has been that the capital and requirements of monetary financial institutions must be tightened and that various off-balance-sheet items and special purpose vehicles must be taken into account. Liquidity buffers for monetary transactions have also been called for. All four of these proposals have been opposed, arguing that they would lead to backward developments. The involvement of central banks, both as a liquidity provider and as a supporter of financial stability for MFIs, is alienated, as it can lead to moral hazard. If the stability of the financial markets is strengthened by a loose monetary policy, it carries the risk of a vicious circle of inflation. There are doubts about the ability of public authorities to substantially enhance supervision in the current financial market operating model. The authorities are always behind in time in their supervision. The products are developed so quickly that they are not sufficiently known. It has been emphasised that, in addition to regulatory oversight, the market discipline and mutual disclosure obligations of market participants should be strengthened. There is opposition to the simplistic standardisation of financial products as it hinders innovation and the intensification of the financial markets. The problem with the proposals to tighten capital requirements has been that it would reduce the return on financial activities and increase the cost of financing. It is also estimated that these requirements would in any case be circumvented in different ways. Finally In conclusion, various means should be further explored. Possibly combining different actions and preserving the dynamics of the financial markets, progress should be made towards enabling the markets themselves to resolve the situation quickly, taking into account the different characteristics of globalised financial markets. It is neither realistic nor even desirable to return to past regulation. Frederic Mishkin, a member of the fed executive board last Friday, said that because of financial innovation, "bad things happen, because in the long run they bring benefits". text_original: Deputy Governor Pentti Hakkarainen Hannes Snellman Financial Law Seminar 2008 Financial Market Turbulence  A Conundrum for Analysts? Rahoitusmarkkinoiden hirit  selittmtn ilmi analyytikoille Rahoitusmarkkinoiden turbulenssi hertt kaksi kysymyst. Onko turbulenssi taloudellisen kas-vun heikentymisen syy? Vai onko se oire viel vakavammista talouden hiriist? Tilaisuuden teema sopii thn pivn, sill nykyinen rahoitusmarkkinoiden hiri on melkoinen mysteeri. Termin conundrum toi yleiseen kyttn Yhdysvaltain keskuspankin pjohtaja Alan Greenspan. Hn tarkoitti sill pitkien korkojen pysymist alhaisina siit huolimatta, ett keskus-pankki oli korottanut lyhytaikaisia ohjauskorkojaan useamman kerran. Fed aloitti asteittaisen (at a measured pace) korkojen noston keskuussa 2004. Korkoja nostettiin neljnnesprosentti melkein jokaisessa keskuspankin korkokokouksessa keskuuhun 2006 saakka. Nostoista huolimatta pitkaikaisten joukkovelkakirjojen korot pysyivt alhaalla. Greenspania ih-metytti tm ilmi, josta hn kytti termi conundrum. Ilmille loi pohjaa finanssimarkkinoiden globalisoituminen, sstmisen ja ylijmien voimakas kasautuminen kasvaviin talouksiin ja ns. Kiina-ilmi, jonka johdosta maailmanmarkkinoilla tuotteet hinnoiteltiin entist alhaisempiin hin-toihin, vaikka niiden laatu parani. Rahoitusmarkkinoiden arvoitus Rahoitusmarkkinoilla on nyt uusi selittmtn ilmi, conundrum. Hirit iskivt finanssimark-kinoiden ytimeen pankkien vlisille talletus- ja lainamarkkinoille. Jo usean vuoden ajan rahoi-tusmarkkinoiden vakaudelle oli identifioitu useita riskej, mm. 1 Alhaiset riskilist lhes kaikissa tuotteissa, joissa sijoittajat ja rahoitusmarkkinoilla toimivat voivat ottaa riski ja hinnoitella sit. 2 Ylenmrinen rahoituksen riittvyys, jonka ansiosta lhes kaikkiin hankkeisiin sai poikke-uksellisen edullisin ehdoin rahoitusta. 3 Kiivas tuotonhaku, joka kasvatti rahoitusmarkkinoilla toimivien institutionaalisten sijoittajien ja rahalaitosten riskipositioita. Tunnistetuista riskeist huolimatta rahoitusmarkkinat toimivat vakaasti ja tuloksellisesti. Elo-kuussa 2007 tapahtui ennennkemtn muutos. Syntyi likviditeettikriisi, jossa rahalaitokset eivt olleet halukkaita lainaamaan toisilleen entisin ehdoin, ilman hyv vakuutta (ks. kuvio sivulla 4). Pankkien vliset markkinat ovat olleet tehokkaat. Hinnoittelu perustuu pankkien keskinisiin tal-letuksiin ja lainoihin, joita tehdn eripituisille juoksuajoille, yli yn jrjestelyst aina kahden-toista kuukauden mittaisiin jrjestelyihin. Elokuussa 2007 tm markkina pyshtyi kuin seinn. Se ylltti rahalaitokset ja analyytikot voimakkuudellaan ja nopeudellaan. Pankit olivat valmiita lainaamaan toisilleen entisin ehdoin vain joko ns. repo-kaupoin tai turvaavaa vakuutta vastaan. Vakuudeton lainananto, jossa mritetn mm. euribor, kallistui hetkess yli puoli prosenttiyk-sikk. Turbulenssin syit Likviditeettikriisin syyt ovat moninaiset. Ne voidaan yksinkertaistaen luokitella finanssi-innovaatioiden laajaan kyttn ja rahoitustoiminnan uuden toimintamallin laajentumiseen. Useiden vuosien ajan markkinoilla oli voimakasta riskinottohalua ja alhaiset riskilist, rahoituk-sen saatavuus oli erinomainen. Matalien korkojen aikana tuottojen hakemiseksi otettiin yh suu-rempia riskipositioita velkaantumalla ja hyvksymll yh huonompaa luottokelpoisuutta. Tst tuli rahalaitoksille optimaalinen toimintamalli. Vanha pankkirahoitukseen perustuva toimintamal-li vistyi yh enemmn uuden maailman, arvopaperistamisen alta. Vanhassa maailmassa pankki antoi lainan lainanottajalle ja seurasi koko laina-ajan lainanotta-jan kyky huolehtia lainan takaisinmaksusta. Uudessa maailmassa rahoituksen vlittmisen ketju piteni. Lainoja myytiin rahoituksen vlittjien kautta. Pankki, jonka kirjoihin lainat tulivat, arvo-paperisti niit paketoimalla lainoja ja myymll paketin riskeineen sijoittajille. Uusi toimintamal-li ruokkii finanssi-innovaatioiden synty ja muutti perinteist rahoituslaitosten toimintaa erilais-ten riskielementtien erottamisella mm. erillisyhtiihin ja luottoriskijohdannaisiin. Suuri osa lai-nanannosta ja sen riskeist siirtyi pankkitoimialan ja samalla valvonnan ulkopuolelle. Lainoja myyvien vlittjien ja loppusijoittajien kannustimet eivt olleet yhtenevisi. Uudelle toiminnalle oli keskeist, ett palkkiot ja kannustimet olivat volyymiperusteisia. Palkkioita mynnettiin lainan myyjille, lainojen paketoijille, luottokelpoisuusarvioitsijoille ja erilaisille asi-antuntijoille, lainapaketin pilkkojille ja edelleenmyyjille sek johdannaisten rakentajille. Pitkn ketjun johdosta loppusijoittajalle ji vaikeasti hallinnoitava riski. Uusi toimintamalli lissi rahoitusjrjestelmn tehokkuutta. Hytyj olivat rahoituksen saatavuu-den parantuminen, hinnan alentuminen ja riskien hallinnointi. Uudessa mallissa likviditeetti on sidoksissa markkinoiden vaihdantakykyyn eli siihen, ett nill eri tuotteilla voidaan kyd kauppaa tehokkaasti. Arvopaperistaminen lis markkinoiden likviditeetti ja toisaalta perustuu siihen, ett markkinat ovat likvidit. Markkinoiden likvidiys on trke mys arvon mrityksen kannalta normaaliaikoina, jolloin vaihdantaan ei liity vaikeuksia eli varallisuuserien arvon voi mritt niiden tuottaman kassavirran perusteella. Tiukempina aikoina likvidiyden merkitys kasvaa arvon mrityksess ja voi olla sen ratkaiseva osa. Kun rahoitusinstrumentin likvidiyteen liittyy ongelmia, sen arvo voi olla huomattavan vhinen tuottamiinsa kassavirtoihin nhden. Uudessa rahoitusmarkkinoiden toimintamallissa rahoitusinstrumentit arvostetaan jatkuvasti. Nin niill on vlitn vaikutus sijoittajien ja rahalaitosten nettovarallisuuteen ja omiin pomiin. Lik-viditeettishokista voi synty rahoitusmarkkinoille ja toimijoille mys vakavaraisuusshokki. Tt viimeaikoina tutkineet Tobias Adrian Yhdysvaltain keskuspankista ja Hyun Song Shin Princeto-nin yliopistosta ovat todenneet, ett on muodostunut uusi rahoituskriisien tartuntakanava, jossa markkinalikviditeettiongelmat vaikuttavat kaikkiin toimijoihin vlittmsti. Mit enemmn toi-mintamalli perustuu arvopaperistamiseen, sit voimakkaampi ja vlittmmpi tm vaikutus on. Aiemman toimintamallin kriisit levisivt dominoefektin lailla rahoituslaitoksesta toiseen. Nyky-toimintamallissa kriisit vaikuttavat kaikkiin ja vlittmsti. Kyse ei ole pelkstn riskist tai kasvaneesta riskist vaan epvarmuudesta. Klassinen erottelu epvarmuuden ja riskin vlill on se, ett epvarmuus koskee tilannetta, jonka tulemille ei ole todennkisyysjakaumaa, kun taas riskille se voidaan arvioida. Tll hetkell ongelmat perustuvat epvarmuuteen ja siihen, ett kaikilla osapuolilla ei ole samaa tietoa. Tt ongelmaa on pyritty vhentmn luottokelpoisuusarvioinneilla, joissa epvarmuus on muunnettu riskiksi. Luottokelpoisuusarvioijat ovat avoimia menetelmistn, mutta on vallin-nut laaja ja syv vrinymmrrys siit, mik on luokituksen todellinen tarkoitus. Tm on nky-nyt erityisen selvsti strukturoiduissa tuotteissa, joissa luottokelpoisuusarvioinnit on samaistettu tavallisiin joukkovelkakirjatuotteisiin. Luottokelpoisuusarvioijat ovat tehneet arvion luoton ta-kaisinmaksusta eivtk tuotteen markkina-arvosta. Hirit yllttivt Rahoitusmarkkinoiden hiriiden ylltyksellisyytt kuvaa se, ett suurimmat vaikeudet ovat koh-distuneet ensiluokan toimijoihin. Northern Rock oli Britanniassa arvostettu perusliiketoimintaa harjoittava asuntoluototuspankki ja Socit Gnrale on Ranskassa tunnettu hyvst riskienhal-linnastaan. Bear Stearns on Wall Streetin investointitalojen krke ja myynyt palvelujaan ja omia osakkeitaan mm. viittaamalla siihen, ett viimeisen 86 vuoden aikana he eivt ole tehneet tappiol-lista tilinptst. Alaskirjaukset ja erilaisten pomavajeiden tyttmiset ovat kohdistuneet muu-tenkin hyvmaineisiin pankkeihin, kuten Citibank, Merrill Lynch, UBS, Hong Kong Shanghai Banking Corporation, Morgan Stanley, Bank of America jne. Kriisien ehkiseminen Miten kriisi ratkaistaan, olisi vltetty ja tulevaisuudessa vltetn? Rahoitusalan toimijat ja tutki-jat ovat esittneet erilaisia ratkaisuja. Keskuspankit ovat lisnneet markkinoille likviditeetti ta-vanomaisesti pankkien pankkina toimien. Viime perjantaina tuli uudenlainen keskuspankin osal-listuminen, kun Yhdysvaltain keskuspankki Fed rahoitti investointipankki JPMorgan Chasen v-lityksin Bear Stearnsia siten, ett rahoituksen vlittvlle investointipankille ei muodostu tst rahoituksesta erillist riski. Riskin kantaa Fed. Jrjestely poikkeaa aiemmista likviditeetin vah-vistamisista, joissa on toimittu tytt vakuutta vastaan tai ns. repo-kaupoin. Keskuspankeilta on odotettu mys rahapolitiikan keinoin tukea rahoitusmarkkinoiden vakaudelle. Eri keskuspankit ovat tss suhteessa toimineet eri tavoin. Fed on alentanut korkoa nopeasti. Nytt silt, ett se on asettanut rahoitusmarkkinoiden toimivuuden inflaation hillitsemisen edel-le. EKP on pitnyt rahapolitiikan virityksen entiselln. Muutamat pienemmt keskuspankit ovat jopa nostaneet korkojaan siit huolimatta, ett rahoitusmarkkinoiden vakaudelle tll voi olla kielteisi vaikutuksia. Toiseksi on vaadittu, ett valvontaa pit list ja ett valvojien tulisi pit tiukempi ote rahoitus-toiminnasta. Tt on perusteltu mm. sill, ett subprime-lainoituksen kaltaiset ylilynnit voitai-siin est. Kolmas ehdotus on, ett monimutkaisten finanssi-innovaatioiden kirjo pitisi supistaa standardoituihin tuotteisiin, joilla kauppaa kytisiin sdellyill markkinapaikoilla esim. prs-seiss. Neljs vaade on ollut se, ett rahalaitosten pomaa ja vaatimuksia pit kirist ja erilai-set taseen ulkopuoliset ert ja erillisyhtit on huomioitava. Mys likviditeettipuskureita rahalai-toksille on vaadittu. Kaikkia nit nelj esityst on vastustettu perustellen niiden johtavan takaperoiseen kehitykseen. Keskuspankkien osallistumista sek likviditeetin antajana ett rahalaitosten rahoitusmarkkinoiden vakauden tukijana vierastetaan, sill se voi johtaa moraalikatoon (moral hazard). Mikli rahoi-tusmarkkinoiden vakautta vahvistetaan lysll rahapolitiikalla, sen riskin nhdn inflaation noidankeh. Viranomaisten kyky tehostaa valvontaa olennaisesti nykyrahoitusmarkkinoiden toimintamallissa epilln. Viranomaiset ovat valvonnassaan aina ajallisesti jljess. Tuotteet ke-hittyvt niin nopeasti, ett niit ei tunneta riittvsti. Onkin korostettu, ett viranomaisvalvonnan ohella pitisi vahvistaa markkinoilla toimivien omaa markkinakuria ja keskinist tiedonantovel-vollisuutta. Finanssituotteiden yksioikoista standardoimista vastustetaan, koska se ehkisee innovointia ja ra-hoitusmarkkinoiden tehostumista. Pomavaatimusten kiristmisehdotuksissa on nhty ongelma-na se, ett kiristminen pienentisi rahoitustoiminnan tuottoa ja rahoituskustannukset kasvaisivat. On mys arvioitu, ett nit vaatimuksia joka tapauksessa kierrettisiin eri tavoin. Lopuksi Yhteenvetona voi todeta, ett eri keinoja tulee edelleen tutkia. Mahdollisesti eri toimia yhdistel-len ja rahoitusmarkkinoiden dynamiikka silytten tulisi edet siin, ett markkinat itse pystyisi-vt ratkaisemaan tilanteen nopeasti huomioiden globalisoituneiden rahoitusmarkkinoiden eri ominaisuudet. Ei ole realistista eik edes toivottavaa palata menneeseen stelyyn. Viime perjan-taina Fedin johtokunnan jsen Frederic Mishkin totesi, ett finanssi-innovaatioiden johdosta bad things happen, because in the long run they bring benefits. Kuvio: Rahamarkkina- ja ohjauskorot euroalueella

Title: The role of the Bank of Finland through the eyes of a new member of the Board of Directors
text: Board member Marja Nyk8anen: The role of the Bank of Finland through the eyes of a new member of the Board of Directors. Helsinki, 1.2.2017. . Speech . Wednesday1 February 2017,4:43 PM Member of the Board of Directors Marja Nyk8anen From the Bank of Finland speech at the Finland 100 years seminar of the Banking Department of the Bank of Finland. Helsinki 1.2.2017 Presentation slides (pdf) (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches/documents/2017-02-01-suomen-pankki-role. the new-executive-board-and-silmiin_marja_nykanen.pdf) THE BANK OF FINLAND'S ROLE IN THE EYES OF THE NEW EXECUTIVE BOARD MEMBER I would like to welcome you to the Finland 100 years seminar of the Banking Department of the Bank of Finland. My topic is defined as "the role of the SP through the eyes of a new board member" and I will now talk about it with about 7 hours of experience. In this introduction, I will address monetary policy and banking supervision during and after the financial crisis. Has the financial crisis been overcome? At least the crisis has changed shape along the way. It has five different stages to identify. In particular, I will briefly go through the first three phases of the crisis and, because of my own background, I will approach the subject from the point of view of monetary policy and also from the point of view of banking supervision. With the crisis, monetary policy and banking supervision became closely intertwined. The financial crisis accelerated the reform of European banking supervision. The financial crisis and subsequent events have had a significant impact on the Bank of Finland's activities in implementing the single monetary policy. The role of the Financial Supervisory Authority as a banking supervisor has perhaps undergone an even greater change as it has become part of the single banking supervision system in the euro area. From the subprime crisis to the financial crisis (2007-2008) and the global recession (2009-2010) The first symptoms of the subprime crisis in the US housing market (stage 1) in the euro area were already visible in the interbank market in the second half of 2007, but it was not until Lehman Brothers went into liquidation in September 2008 that triggered a trajectory that jeopardised the functioning of the global financial system as a whole. It dawned on market participants that large and influential financial institutions can also fail. It eroded mutual trust in the financial markets and the interbank money market came to a standstill. In the second phase of the crisis, the financial crisis was transmitted from the financial markets to the real economy. World trade collapsed at the end of 2008 and the national products of developed countries contracted drastically in 2009. As demand declined, inflation declined to negative levels in many countries. The Eurosystem reacted decisively at different stages of the crisis. In October 2008, the ECB launched a series of reductions in key interest rates. By mid-2009, the ECB had cut interest rates by 3.25 percentage points to 1%. The ECB also abandoned its quantitative control of liquidity and started to implement the so-called liquidity controls. the policy of full allocation in fixed-rate monetary policy operations. The liquidity risk was reduced because banks received the amount of financing they wanted from the central bank in exchange for collateral. As monetary policy interest rates approached zero, the ECB gradually adopted unconventional monetary policy instruments. For example, the effect of interest rate cuts was further postponed by implementing fixed-rate long-term (6-12 months) credit operations. The lending capacity of banks was strengthened through the covered bond purchase programme. In the first and second phases of the crisis, the ECB continued to act only through the banking system in an effort to enhance the transmission of credit to the economy. Sovereign debt and confidence crisis (2011 d0 2012) In the third phase of the crisis, risk premiums for banks and governments, especially in the euro area peripheral countries, started to grow and economic developments and credit risks in euro area countries diverged. Government risks disrupted the transmission of monetary policy: market interest rates rose even as the Governing Council lowered the key ECB interest rate. The Eurosystem responded again to the crisis with interest rate policy and liquidity management. In the autumn of 2011, interest rates began to be cut again and banks were offered extra-long central bank loans (VLTROs). In addition, emergency funds from the EU and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) supported the weakest euro countries: first Greece, Portugal and Ireland, followed by Italy and Spain. The pivotal moment of the financial crisis was a speech by ECB President Mario Draghi in London in July 2012. Draghi promised to do "everything necessary to secure the euro." The market impact of the speech was immediate and powerful. Pressures on sovereign bond markets in the periphery of the euro area eased and the climate of confidence began to improve. Normalisation of financial markets (2013-2014) The euro area summit took a decision on the creation of a banking union in 2012. Plans to reduce the link between banks and sovereigns in the long term became clearer. The Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM) was kicked off at a record pace and became operational in early November 2014, when some 120 of the largest banking groups in the euro area were transferred directly to the ECB. The start of ECB supervision was preceded by a comprehensive review of banks' balance sheets carried out in 2014. It assessed the quality of banks' credit portfolios and certain other balance sheet items. Banks were required to provide additional capital, if necessary, to cover the valuation deficits identified. During 2014, it was also decided to set up the Single Resolution Mechanism (SRM), the resolution authorities implementing it and the fund to manage the funds raised for resolution. The euro area resolution authority became operational at the beginning of 2015 and the national authorities organised themselves. Banks started to collect contributions to the Resolution Fund. The aim of the bank resolution regulation and the aforementioned authorities is that crisis banks would no longer be bailed out with taxpayers' money, but that the bank's owners and creditors would bear the banks' losses. Macroprudential supervision can also be considered the output of the financial crisis. It was created because it was seen as necessary to extend supervision not only to the monitoring of the situation of individual supervised entities, but also to a more general level of macroprudential and systemic risks. The aim was to identify, prevent and limit these risks. Despite the normalisation of financial markets, inflation and inflation expectations were dampened to a slower pace than the Eurosystem's price stability objective. In the summer of 2014 the Governing Council lowered one of its key interest rates, the overnight deposit rate, to negative levels. The Council also stepped up the easing of monetary policy through new non-standard means such as forward guidance, targeted longer-term refinancing operations (TLTROs) and a negative overnight deposit rate, as well as direct purchases of covered bonds and asset-backed securities (ABS). A period of low growth and inflation (2015 -) Despite the normalisation of financial markets, the monetary policy environment at the turn of 2014-2015 was challenging: the longer-term economic outlook was subdued and the geopolitical situation (the Crimean and Ukrainian crises) increased uncertainties. Markets expected inflation in the euro area to remain low. With a zero interest rate limit, the ECB was virtually no longer able to support economic growth and boost inflation through interest rate policy. At its January 2015 meeting, the Governing Council decided on a sovereign purchase programme and started in March 2015. The initial amount of the purchase programme was EUR 60 billion/month (3/2015 d0 3/2016). The Governing Council has announced that it will extend the purchase programme at least until the end of this year. By then, the Eurosystem has purchased more than db2200 billion in debt securities. Eur. In March 2016 the Governing Council added corporate loans to the purchase programme. Six national central banks, including the Bank of Finland, started to carry out these purchases. Torsti Silvonen from the European Central Bank will explain in more detail the ECB's purchases of securities in his presentation. The monetary policy implemented has been passed on to the real economy The PURCHASE PROGRAMME is transmitted to the economy through financial markets. First, the balance sheet of the Central Bank and the liquidity of the banking system will increase. At present, the excess liquidity of the euro area banking system is close to db1300 billion. Eur. The PURCHASE PROGRAMME has had a significant supporting effect on economic growth and inflation. Short-term interest rate expectations in the euro area are very low and retail bond rates have fallen broadly in the euro area. Households have increased their demand for credit. In turn, investment opportunities for companies have been improved by lower interest rates on both bank loans and corporate bonds. The position of exporters, in particular, has also been improved by the weakening of the euro. Increased economic activity has boosted euro area real GDP growth and, in part, inflation expectations. The rise in long-term 10-year interest rates in recent months reflects rising inflation expectations. The national economies of Finland and the euro area are closely linked, so the purchase programme has also had a significant positive impact on the Finnish economy. There are still 11 months left in the purchase programme, so at this stage it can at most be the subject of interim financial statements. Monetary policy has been transmitted to the real economy, but transmission has been slower than thought. As the objective of price stability has not been achieved and the key interest rates remain close to the zero interest rate limit, non-standard monetary policy instruments are still needed. Common banking supervision in the euro area has been a step in the right direction. It has been possible to weaken the link between banks and sovereigns, banks have strengthened their solvency and supervisory practices have been harmonised. Examples of the latter include the harmonisation of options and discretions allowed by prudential regulation, the harmonisation of internal models for measuring risks and the harmonisation of the definition and treatment of bad loans. There are differences in the condition of banks: there are countries where banking is profitable and banks are solvent. On the other hand, there are countries where overcapacity in the banking sector and/or the high volume of bad loans cause difficulties for banks. The digitalisation of banking, new players and operating concepts, and low interest rates are challenging the sustainability of banks' business models across the euro area. The financial crisis is over, but its shadow is long. There is still work to be done in both monetary policy and banking supervision. I wish you a fruitful seminar. board (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagjohtokunta) Board member (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagJohtokunnan Member) speech (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagpuhe)
