Title: Introductory remarks at the 2nd Annual Nordic Cyber in Finance Conference
text: Deputy Governor Marja Nyksnen: Introductory remarks at the 2nd Annual Nordic Cyber in Finance Conference, Helsinki, 29 November 2018 . Speech . Thursday29 November 2018,9:00 AM Marja Nyksnen Deputy Governor of the Bank of Finland Introductory remarks 2nd Annual Nordic Cyber in Finance Conference Helsinki, 29 November 2018 INTRODUCTORY REMARKS AT THE 2ND ANNUAL NORDIC CYBER IN FINANCE CONFERENCE HOSTED BY THE BANK OF FINLAND, HELSINKI, 29 NOVEMBER 2018 Ladies and Gentlemen, You are all warmly welcome to this conference, entitled "Nordic Cyber in Finance" and hosted by the Bank of Finland. As we know, in the world of digital technology, everything happens at lightning speed what was breaking news yesterday, may already feel old and familiar tomorrow. Therefore, I will only be half-joking when I say that we, the Nordic central banks, have a long tradition of co-hosting a Cyber Conference every year, as this is already the second event of its kind. The first one was organised in wonderful Copenhagen, one year ago, by our dear Danish colleagues from Danmarks Nationalbank. The event was so well organised that it will be difficult to improve on it, but one thing we have added is an event hashtag #cyberinfinance. After all, the Bank of Finland already has 90 experts active on Twitter. One of them, by the way, is a robot who tweets real-time economic forecasts. Let's see if @SPNowCast has tweeted anything this morning. Today we will continue the discussion started in Copenhagen, and focus on a handful of timely themes within the domain of cyber security. Among these, we will hear very substantive presentations on hybrid threats, as well as data breaches, which has been a topic much talked about throughout the year. Slide 3: Parallels between the financial crisis and cyber risks In my opening remarks, I wish to raise awareness of one additional important topic. That is the link between cyber risks andfinancial stability. To simplify the issue, whereas we are already striving to make sure that a single bankercannot bring down the entire financial system, in the future we also have to make sure that a single hackercannot bring it down either. Let me now elaborate on this notion. This year marks the tenth anniversary of the global financial crisis. The roots of the crisis were in the US mortgage market, but there were complex interdependencies, and global imbalances, which contributed to the problem. I will not delve deeper into the sequence of events, as they have been covered in many good books and articles. Instead, I wish to look at some of the key lessonsfrom the crisis, and to draw parallels between them and the cyber risks we are facing today. 1. The GreatCyber-Moderation? The years preceding the global financial crisis were commonly described as "The Great Moderation" by economists. The concept refers to the long period of low volatility in financial markets and relative calm in the wider economy. Business cycles were subdued and banks were profitable year in, year out. To many, it seemed as if financial institutions had permanently mastered risks, and the world had found a way to grow steadily without recessions. As we now know, that long period of relative calm was suddenly disrupted by the collapse of Lehman Brothers and the credit crunch and the recession that followed in the real economy. The Great Moderation had only been a mirage. We have witnessed many serious cyber incidents in the last few years, some with international significance. But none so far have directly disrupted critical market infrastructures, such as payment systems. Is this because we have comprehensively mastered the risks, or have we merely been lucky, so far? What we can learn from the financial crisis is that just because we have avoided a systemic cyber event so far does not mean that the risk of one occurring has decreased. We should not let ourselves lull into a false sense of confidence. 2. Interconnectedness When the financial crisis unfolded, it became clear that financial institutions were much more interconnected and dependent on each other than either market participants or regulators had previously understood. Financial risks became systemic, because banks had correlated exposures, and because a complex web of contractual obligations created contagion channels for the crisis to spread. The growth of digital technology in the financial sector has created another kind of complex web between financial institutions, namely one of computers and information systems. This will be further accentuated by the emergence of Open Banking. We should therefore apply the concepts of correlated exposures and contagion channels also from a cyber security point of view, and make sure cyber events have a limited impact, if and when they occur. 3. Bank resilience Resilience is a word that is used by both the financial community and the cybersecurity community. The financial crisis taught banks, and banking regulators, that it is essential to maintain sufficient capital buffers to create resilience against unforeseen financial shocks. The most important regulatory steps taken in Europe to make the banking sector financially more resilient are the creation of the banking union and the development of a new macroprudential framework. Cyber security experts, on the other hand, talk about cyber resilience, when they refer to an organisation's ability to withstand, contain, and recover from cyber attacks. The Financial Stability Board has recently published a Cyber Lexicon ( ) where this concept has been carefully explained. Going forward, both types of resilience are important for financial institutions. But cyber resilience cannot be built by adding capital buffers. Each type of resilience requires its own policy tools. 4. Preparedness and contingencies Capital buffers can protect a bank from financial shocks by improving its long-term solvency, but it is also important for the bank to hold sufficient liquidity to be able to meet its short-term financial obligations. The importance of, and distinction between, liquidity and solvency became a central topic during the global financial crisis. The analogy to financial liquidity in the cyber security context are contingency arrangements. Contingency planning and backup systemsenable financial institutions to continue operating while a cyber event is occurring and until a problem has been fixed. Independent control over critical infrastructures, such as payment and settlement systems, has to be maintained, to prevent a potential cyber event from causing a disruption in the wider economy. In Finland, a viable national back-up system for payments is needed and is currently work in progress one that can be deployed in emergency situations without the need of international assistance. Dear friends, As you can see, there are many parallels between financial stability and cyber security. I have already highlighted four of them: false confidence, interconnectedness, resilience, and contingency planning. Before I conclude, let me add two more. 5. Understandingthe risks of new innovations Before the global financial crisis, there was talk about innovation in the financial sector. But instead of FinTech, it referred to financial innovation. What was meant by that term at the time were new financial products, often securitised investment offerings, such as Mortgage Backed Securities or Credit Default Swaps. While these then new innovative products helped create more efficient markets, they also brought with them plenty of new risks. There was not enough time and not enough experience to understand the true risk profiles of some of these products. As a result, risks were more than often mispriced and under-regulated. Again, we can see a parallel in cyber security. Today, the emergence of FinTech is bringing to the market new offerings for both households and businesses. There is now a wide selection of payment apps, investment tools, and other types of digital financial services available. Many of these are based on technologies, such as artificial intelligence and open interfaces, of which we do not have much experience yet. It is important that we analyse carefully how these products work, so that we have a good understanding of the risks involved. This also requires regulators to move out of their traditional comfort zone, and become more knowledgeable about technology. 6. Divergent risk preferences Finally, I would like to remind ourselves of the concept of moralhazard, which became important during the global financial crisis. A central dilemma in the financial sector has always been the trade-off between risk and reward. Financial businesses, such as banking, trading, or insurance, are essentially about calculated risk-taking. However, in many cases the risk appetiteof individual financial institutions is too high from the point of view of the rest of society. There is thus a negative externality with regard to risk-taking, which can lead to what economists call moral hazard. Does this old dilemma of divergent risk preferences repeat itself in the case of cyber risks? At least in theory, that may be the case. Let me be clear, there is currently no reason to think that our banks and other financial institutions were not, and indeed are not, well protected against cyber risks. But the financial crisis showed us that systemic risks are risks which an individual institution is not taking into account unless motivated to do so by regulators. As an example, an individual bank does not necessarily know whether it is a single-point-of-failure in the wider financial system. In such a case, it is the regulator who needs to see the bigger picture; it is the regulator who needs to identify concentrations of risks, and then use policy measures to introduce precautions. The types of precautions are different in the case of financial risks and cyber risks, but the basic principle is the same. Ladies and Gentlemen, Dear Friends, We have had many financial crises in history, but none of them have been caused by a cyber event, at least not so far. But the concept of systemic risk has become broader, and cyber security is becoming an integral part of the financial stability framework. Based on the experience from the global financial crisis, combined with an increasingly complex industry landscape driven by digitalisation, regulation in the financial sector is more necessary than ever. But it doesnot have to mean over-regulation. One has to find the rightbalance between creating a safe and sound business environment, while also allowing innovation to take place. It also means finding the appropriate tools and responsesto the risks at hand. Since the threats to financial stability are becoming increasingly technological, and also more global, this calls for more cooperation between authorities, both within a country but also between countries. A global response is needed, by putting to best use the international institutions that have been established in recent years for maintaining financial stability. I hope these thoughts will motivate a lively and productive discussion in all the sessions today. Let me wish you all a pleasant stay in Helsinki. Thank you. cyberInFinance (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagcyberInFinance) cyber (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagcyber) CyberSecurity (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagCyberSecurity) CyberResilience (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagCyberResilience) CyberThreats (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagCyberThreats) Marja Nyksnen (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagMarja Nyksnen) digitalisation (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagdigitalisation)

Title: How can banks help COVID-19 resilience and recovery
text: Deputy Governor Marja Nyksnen: How can banks help COVID-19 resilience and recovery . Speech . Thursday22 April 2021, 4:00 PM Deputy Governor Marja Nyksnen Keynote Speech at Sustainable Investment Forum Europe 2021 22 April 2021 HOW CAN BANKS HELP COVID-19 RESILIENCE AND RECOVERY? Ladies and gentlemen! It is an honour to be invited to give this keynote speech on such an important topic in such an interesting forum. Last spring, giving a virtual keynote speech in an online conference was something new and exciting. Today, over a year later, it is not like that anymore. Hopefully, it wonot be too long before we get back to a bit more of a normal situation again. Today, in this virtual contribution, I will be talking first about the reaction of the authorities to the economic shock from the COVID-19 pandemic. Then I will talk about how banks have been a part of the solution. Finally, I will conclude by looking at the future and talk about how increasing the role of the capital markets can help to increase the resilience of the EU economy. Central Banks,Supervisors and public authorities support bank lending In the early spring of 2020, the effects of COVID-19 started to become clearer, and, for a brief moment, it seemed as if the economy would go into freefall. However, the public authorities responded swiftly and decisively in order to minimize the social and economic costs of the pandemic and the lockdowns. Central banks were among the first responders, with the ECB pandemic emergency purchase programme, PEPP, now standing at 1,850 billion euro. In addition, the ECB has been offering a significant amount of financing to banks through targeted longer-term refinancing operations. Fiscal authorities around the world made emergency payments and gave support for companies and households. The EU even reached an agreement where the EU itself would secure 750 billion euro from the markets and distribute it among the Member States. In addition to direct financing, countries in Europe made changes to insolvency laws to prevent companies going bankrupt. In several countries a moratorium was put in place to help households and companies with debt repayments. Furthermore, public guarantees were extended to bank loans to ensure that companies could attain credit. Supervisors used the flexibility built into the legislative framework and relaxed the available capital buffers, further enabling banks to keep lending. And these are just some of the examples of how the public sector has supported the economy amid COVID-19. Banks have been part ofthe solution The banks have seized the opportunity given by supervisors, central banks and the public authorities to maintain their lending to the real economy. By enabling access to funding, banks have allowed companies in the real economy to keep people on their payroll despite the uncertainty. At the same time, public support to households, companies especially SMEs and the moratoria have kept delinquencies at a record low in many countries. This has meant that bank balance sheets have not seen an increase in NPLs as one would have assumed given the economic shock. But history has shown that there is a lag between an economic shock and the associated insolvencies. In this crisis, given the moratoria and other public support measures, it is to be expected that this lag might be longer than in previous crises. Thus, it is premature to extrapolate the future losses in this crisis from the credit losses so far. And, therefore, it is imperative that banks maintain prudent capital positions to maintain their resilience and to ensure that this crisis will not become a banking crisis. Because of this, it is a bit disappointing to see that few banks are not heeding the supervisorso recommendation to restrict dividends for the time being. This behaviour is unfortunate for two reasons. Firstly, it dilutes the bankso capital buffers, thus making them more susceptible to any future deterioration in economic conditions. This will increase the risks to financial stability. Secondly, such behaviour may even seem like profiteering from the crisis. A better than expected situation in any bank now is not due to the excellent business skills or risk management at the bank, but is more of a windfall from the multi-trillion euro of public support. In future,the capital markets willplay arole in sustainable finance by complementing bank lending Once again, this crisis has shown the extent of Europeos dependency on banks to provide funding for the real economy. Now, donot get me wrong, we need banks and their role will still be critical in the future. But it is time to turbocharge the development of the Capital Markets Union, the CMU. The CMU would provide complementary funding sources for companies, especially in turbulent times when banks are not able to lend as much as needed. Furthermore, the capital markets could allow riskier companies to attain funding, as bank loans are not suited for all. The CMU would also allow banks to attain funding, securitize their loans and sell them to investors. This could have the potential to distribute risks more evenly across countries, thus absorbing future shocks. Furthermore, active capital markets require banks to act as intermediaries, thus it could provide stable or even a countercyclical source of revenue for banks. It is also critical that we build back better after COVID-19, focusing on environmental sustainability and helping the EU and Member States to transition to climate neutrality by 2050. The capital markets would enable different types of green instruments to be developed to help towards this goal. And, as the current crisis has shown, there are ample opportunities for Member States and the EU to issue social bonds that can help to build more inclusive and equitable societies. Efficient and liquid capital markets could provide a solid foundation for extending this. To conclude The public authoritieso role in helping society cope with the economic impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic has been significant. Most EU banks have understood the gravity of the situation and have continued to provide funding to households and companies while at the same time preserving prudent capital positions. Going forward, we need to increase the role of the capital markets to enhance the resilience of our economies. For this we need the CMU, which could help the EU to become socially, environmentally and economically more sustainable. I think it is a goal worth pursuing. covid-19 (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagcovid-19) Marja Nyksnen (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagMarja Nyksnen) sustainable nance (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagsustainable nance) banking union (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagbanking union)

text: Bank Manager Matti Louekoski's speech at CM-Urakointi Oy's annual meeting . Speech . Thursday14 February 2002,12:00 AM The EU is enlarging and looking for a way out - how will our economy change? A good knowledge of history is a solid basis for planning for the future. Even when planning the future of the EU, it is good to remember that the successes achieved and the perceived misfortunes have shaped attitudes and capabilities in the further development of the system. Based on the ???nstic experience of the Finns, it can be said that our existence since 1995 has not revolutionized our el?m??, but has had a significant impact on it in many ways. In fact, the effects began as early as when our country's eu membership began. The changes have by no means taken place without painful consequences, but the benefits of time have begun to weigh heavily on the scales. For my part, I would venture to pit??? Finland's Chensest experience as quite a success for the EU. In economic policy, and in monetary policy in particular, the EU's neutrality marked a clear change of policy. In entering the Union, Finland was forced to abandon its previous policy of inflation and devaluation, which had essentially been based on the large-scale and deep-seated deliberations of the financial markets. The EU is committed to a freely functioning market. In the division of economic policies, macroeconomic price stability is the responsibility of central banks. In all EU countries, it is the primary and by far the most important aspect of monetary policy. Finland was one of the first countries to join the euro area, whose monetary policy is discussed in the Governing Council of the ECB. The loss of monetary self-efficacy has been considered by some to be a great loss. The ??nostic experience of monetary policy together has at least been one of the worst fears. Although monetary policy in the euro area is not geared to the needs of the Finnish economy, it has always been satisfactory for the Finnish economy. In the economic turmoil of the time, we have enjoyed the benefits of a large currency area in terms of its stability. One can only imagine the pressures on our monetary policy in recent times if the monetary conditions in Europe, and with it in Finland, had been the same as at the beginning of the last decade. Enlarging the EU The European Union began as a coal-and-tersycommunity of six countries and expanded in several stages into an economic union of twelve countries and the present Union of fifteen. After a few years, we will be the next leap forward as the expansion moves to Eastern Central Europe. ?m? expansion differs in many ways from previous ones. Enlargement will open up a previously inexperienced gap in living standards for the EU's guerrillas. Another significant difference is that there are more new Member States joining than ever before. Up to 10 new Member States could enter the Union in the first instance, and as soon as the beginning of 2004. The common market after the next enlargement will cover countries where the difference in wage levels is five times, or even more. This state of affairs is a matter of concern to EU citizens and p?t?ji?. Even so, the biggest fears are related to the ty? market and future movements of ty? power. Many people who are simply employed, or under-calibrated citizens of the new Member States, move in large numbers on the free labour market to the old Member States. Many, on the other hand, believe that most of the n?isth fears turn out to be more unfounded. The enlargement of the Union is not expected to lead to an uncontrolled flow of migrants. Based on previous integration experience, the issue may even be against the p?in. Accession to the Union is likely to stimulate economic development and open up entirely new economic opportunities in the acceding countries. In this situation, citizens choose whether to participate in the rapid growth process - and the success it brings - in their own country. In addition to the selection situation described above, the new Member States are old cultural states whose citizens are proud of their roots as much as the citizens of the old Member States. From Finland's point of view, it will be interesting to see whether, in the future, we will have to make greater efforts than before to attract skilled new labour to the country. It is quite different from the fear of being buried under the vy?ry of the cheapening power of expansion. There is no point in pointing out that the northern, peripheral location is probably not a great temptation. Many experts have drawn attention to the fact that the largest group of migrants from the new Member States may be well-trained experts. They are able to adapt relatively easily to the new environs. They are also best able to hy?ty about the high standard of living in the old Member States. Such a leak would be very heavy for the losing countries. The EU's support system is designed to balance much smaller income inequality in the union's old member states, and they will not function in their current form in an enlarged Union. That is why there is a need for relocation periods and possibly more extensive renovations of the support systems. The most widely debated system is the common agricultural policy in its present form, which, even in the meantime, could hardly be easily adapted to an enlarged Union. The problem is also that it is precisely the agricultural support systems that are among the most attractive attractions in favour of membership in favour of the countries that have applied for it. Whatever happens to the EU's support systems, it is clear that the distribution of subsidies alone does not guarantee sustainable economic growth. However, it is a prerequisite for bridging the gap in living standards or substantially reducing them at present. Even in the present Member States of the Union, there are examples of effective aid approvals (Ireland) and regions (Greece and Italy) where even substantial aid has not helped to close the gap in living standards with the rest of the EU. It is very important that the economic policies of the applicant countries themselves determine how quickly they can feel that they are reaching the standard of living of the present Member States. The EU's support systems can help with the process, but the point is that they cannot rely on the safety net. The governance of the applicant countries, both public and private, is also crucial to the success of this process. For example, the law is readily available for formal approval, but its application is quite a challenge for the applicant countries. A bad administrative culture, especially corruption, must be eradicated from the path of stable social development. As the EU has expanded over the years, it has become increasingly difficult to make decisions based on a long consensus. Significantly, it will become even more difficult as a result of the next enlargement. Just over a year ago, in Nice, the heads of state negotiated a new treaty which, in technical terms, makes it possible to admit new Member States. However, the agreement does not solve, not even to a great extent, the problems associated with eu decision-making. Solutions to improve the efficiency of work are one of the challenges that are not at all a challenge. Cooperation expands and deepens If one megatrend in the development of the EU is enlargement, the other is the constant deepening of cooperation. The deepening of cooperation has always been driven by individual major projects. In the economic sphere, there have been two such countries: the common market for goods and the single currency. In addition, the common agricultural policy can be well considered, at least initially, to be a deeper economic project. A couple of years ago, at their meeting in Lisbon, the EU's ministers also piled on a project of great proportions: making the EU the most competitive and dynamic information society in the world. It is indeed a challenging objective, and in order to achieve it, for example in relation to the United States, we need to take force to enable the average American to buy half as much as the average European with his salary. Significant gap in living standards. Compared to the United States, the root cause of Europe's slow economic growth and low standard of living is the structural robustness of the economies. Above all, ?m? ?kyy is the unfortunately high level of employment and, in general, the low level of participation in the labour market. The challenge now is to break down the rigidities without, at the same time, dismantling the qualities of the welfare state worthy of a shilling. The Czech project in Europe is still in its early stages. Financial market integration Financial markets in Europe, particularly in recent years, have undergone significant integration. The best example is the unsecured short-money market for banks, which currently operates smoothly across the euro area. The market for government bonds and other bonds also has many features of the common market. Despite the advent of the euro, the market continues to operate at national level and form a rather fragmented whole. A fundamental obstacle to financial transactions in the countries of the euro area has been removed, namely the certainty of exchange rate developments. This has opened up, for the first time, a real opportunity has opened up for the Member States to create europe-wide and efficiently functioning financial markets. The creation of a common financial market was the subject of a decision at the European Council in 1998. The aim is for the market to function by 2005. The pursuit of the goal and its implementation will have a significant impact on our efforts in Finland. It is difficult to concretise the impact of the common financial market. However, it can be concluded that the common financial markets are likely to be dominated by large and medium-sized enterprises. Large companies - for example, the ten largest in Finland - have traditionally been able to effectively access the financial markets worldwide. Our small and medium-sized enterprises, on the other hand, can hardly hope to receive similar services outside the well-functioning common financial markets. As the integration of financial markets progresses, the question of where the current framework for the prudential supervision and crisis management of financial markets in the EU is sufficient under conditions where the boundaries of national markets may have disappeared altogether. The very recent examples of major disasters in the financial markets challenge the supervisory authorities not only to develop their own competence, but also to rapidly expand and deepen international cooperation.

Title: Speech at the Internationalising Economy seminar
text: Bank Manager Matti Louekoski's speech at the Kansainvslistyvs economy seminar . Speech . Saturday 4 January 2003, 12:00 AM Tiivistelms The internationalisation of the finnish economy can be viewed from many angles. In the business economy, internationalisation is considered to be a natural thing. The small size of the domestic market already forces companies to plan their operations internationally if they intend to aim for a medium size even in Europe. Especially in the areas of technology that have been very successful in recent years, internationalisation is the point of the whole operation. In more traditional industries, internationality has been a natural thing. In the forest industry, for example, the international expansion of marketing and production has been in favour of counter-cyclically. It has also been necessary to locate production in different parts of the world in order to be able to take advantage of the different trends in the market. At the same time, it has been possible to compensate for differences and fluctuations in raw material prices and other production costs. In terms of the conditions of economic development as a whole, the opening up of the European market has been of paramount importance. In particular, the integration of EMU has meant a fundamental change in the way in which it operates - stabilisation. At the same time as administrative and operational boundaries have been lowered, the established conditions of the larger common sphere of activity have become a source of economic turmoil. The competitiveness of Finland and Finnish companies has developed very positively in the new circumstances. So has the financial markets. Inflation, for example, has been better controlled in the long term and interest rates are substantially lower than they were in the past. Even in the new activity, the benefits will not be free of charge. On the other hand, their adoption requires a strong investment in development, austerity, long-term management and cost discipline. At the same time, the balance of public finances has been shunted. So the new action is challenging, but it's also fair in the way that self-inflicted mistakes become o-penalizingo vslitchmssti. If, for example, costs are unleashed, then the next loss of competitiveness will cause a wave of stubbornness. Devaluation or other previously used constables cannot be called upon to help. The only way to avoid places of danger is to be patient and to be tall. This is subject to the requirements of all parties involved in the management of the house.

Title: Summary of speech, Current information on insurance and financial supervision and legislation
text: Summary of bank manager Matti Louekoski's speech, News on supervision in the insurance and banking sector and legislation . Speech . Tuesday 1 June 2004,12:00 AM The global operating model of the financial markets has changed drastically over the past 20-30 years. The liberalisation of financial markets, internationalisation, the establishment of European monetary union, technological development and the increase in shareholder value have significantly increased competition in the financial markets and across national borders. Firms in the financial sector have reacted to the change in activity and the intensification of competition in various ways, including by spreading to new industries and by forming larger financial firms through mergers and acquisitions. European banks and insurance companies have responded to the change in their activities, in particular by forming larger national units. Not all the structural arrangements have been successful. In Ersisss cases, difficulties have arisen in overcoming the risks that have arisen. Cross-border mergers and acquisitions have so far been relatively rare. However, the EU's wide-ranging policies and planned projects to promote financial integration will lower the barriers to entry in the past. It is probably only a matter of time before cross-border mergers and acquisitions of financial firms begin to become more common in Europe. The Nordic countries have been at the forefront of integration in chechnya and in many other respects. That is why the dangers, risks and threats of integration are the first to emerge. In part, this development is the result of traditional Nordic cooperation, the spirit of which is like a natural merger of business. The action is familiar. One of the key risks associated with the integration of European financial markets is that a common European integration can, in the worst case, make it more difficult for national authorities to ensure the stability of national financial markets and to ensure the prevention and management of crises in national financial markets. The conflict between the common European law and the national level supervision and crisis management can be great, for example, in the supervision of foreign branches of banking groups. According to the eu banking lawsdsnnsn home country principle, the supervisory responsibility for a bank's foreign branches lies with the supervisors of the country in which the bank is registered. The home country principle of banking supervision can be problematic, especially in crisis situations, in countries with significant-sized foreign branches of banks. Therefore, the functioning of the cooperation of supervisors and the exchange of information is of paramount importance. Greater harmonisation of control methods in the european enclave would facilitate cooperation between supervisors and the exchange of information. The narrow observance of the 'domestic principle' alone is not enough to control. For the Bank of Finland, the contribution to the overall stability of the financial markets is that Finnish supervisors have it is sufficient to control the financial companies operating in Finland, regardless of the country in which the companies are registered. Supervisors are particularly empowered to manage crisis and emergency conditions.

Title: Speech at the CFO-Summit seminar
text: Bank Manager Matti Louekoski's speech at the CFO-Summit seminar . Speech . Wednesday9November 2005, 12:00 AM The development of the Finnish economy (points of the speech) The growth of the Finnish economy has been relatively good. But from a favorable nsychvss economic developments however, there are structural risks There have been no major changes in finland's economy during the past year, despite the fact that the contract dispute in the paper industry caused a loss of production. They reduce the growth rates for the year by an estimated nearly one per cent. Similarly, economic growth is expected to accelerate next year. According to the Bank of Finland's recent macroeconomic forecast, growth in the average year is expected to reach just over 2%. This is a good achievement at the euro area level. Industrial output growth has been weaker in recent months than previously estimated. In August, output in the electronics industry contracted further, and in September, too, its output grew rather slowly. The production of the forest industry has been caught up in the early summer, so growth has been faster. Finland's economic growth is currently based on strong domestic demand. Private consumption has continued to grow briskly and is also projected to continue to grow moderately over the past few years. Good income and employment trends will increase the purchasing power of households, and household optimism is expected to be shining in the past few years. However, consumption growth may be threatened by the heating of the housing market and high household borrowing. A significant increase in interest rates would be sensitive to a slowdown in the growth of consumer demand. This could be accompanied by a reversal of the long-standing rise in house prices, which would intensify the reactions to consumption. Finland's exports are supported by the continued favourable development of the global economy and world trade. In China, output and aggregate demand have continued to grow strongly, and the recovery in euro area output growth and domestic demand is also clear. Finnish exports and imports have developed in much the same way, but the value of imports has grown much faster than the value of exports. The problem has also been the growing share of imported input in both Finnish industrial production and exports. Indeed, the current account surplus is projected to decline substantially over the past few years. Finland's export structure, despite its diversification, is a constant risk in the global economy, where Finland's position in individual market areas and industries may change unexpectedly. Between 2001 and 2003, Finnish exports grew modestly, despite the fact that world trade increased rapidly. Since then, exports to Russia in particular have increased. Deliveries to Vensjs increased by about 30% per year (from early 2004 to early 2005). However, the growth in Vensjsn exports is partly due to the transit of durable goods, not to products actually produced in Finland. Exports of ship deliveries and electronics industry products are expected to increase over the past few years, but the capacity of the forest industry, for example, may have to be dismantled in Finland even more than estimated. There is already an example of this. The problem in recent years has been the weak development of export prices to Finland in the export sectors, especially in the electronics industry. Recently, the terms of trade have been weakened by the increase in world market prices, which has led to a sharp increase in Finnish import prices. Finland's terms of trade have been deteriorating continuously for several years now. In the electronics industry, productivity growth has lowered the prices of mobile phones, for example. The price development of paper products has become weak in recent years; export prices declined throughout 2004. In the United States, the demand for newsprint has been falling for a long time. It is possible that the use of information technology has finally begun to reduce the demand for paper. The weak development of export prices has become a structural problem for Finland. Exports have increasingly focused on product groups where competition is particularly fierce. In the absence of pricing power for exporters, the development of exports is increasingly dependent on relative costs. There is a particular risk that export prices will develop less favourably than expected, but productivity growth will not compensate for the former situation, so that the profitability of exporters will be undermined. A deterioration in the terms of trade may also have an impact on domestic consumption. Even if exports increase, domestic income generation weakens and may lead to a reduction in household consumption opportunities. So far, the effects of the decline in the terms of trade in households have been mitigated by the fact that the prices of many durable goods have fallen as a result of intensified international competition. If the fall in prices is prolonged, the result will be a slowdown in the growth of household consumer demand. In any case, the trendy decline in the terms of trade indicates that households' indebtedness is not growing at the rate that the general economic picture would suggest. Thus, it is possible that the recent rapid increase in indebtedness has not been fully based on realistic income expectations. Economic developments in Finland in recent years have been supported by the stability of monetary conditions achieved during emu, which are reflected in low interest rates and low inflation. In Finland, inflation has remained even lower than in the rest of the euro area for a long time. This has been partly due to increased competition in the hysdyke market as well as in many services. Changes in car and alcohol taxation have played a significant role in the background of low inflation in recent years. An important aspect of price developments is the volatility of raw material prices, which is rapidly increasing in domestic energy price developments. This is a good example of the price spikes in fuel prices caused by the hurricanes in the Gulf of Mexico. Increased competition, on the other hand, may lead to lower prices in services, for example. Moderate and long-term wage agreements have been conducive to prolonged inflation developments in recent years. The rise in earnings level has slowed down slightly in Finland over the past three years. However, the rate of increase in labour costs has exceeded the average level of the euro area. Under the current TUPO agreement, contractual wages will only be reviewed if inflation exceeded 2.6% in 2005. As inflation has remained around 1% recently, the inflationary condition cannot be triggered. The resulting wage pressures are therefore not expected next year. On the other hand, there is a risk that the reduced availability of skilled labour will lead to an increase in wage drift in many sectors and, consequently, to an increase in inflationary pressures. The lack of productive investment is starting to pose a threat to economic growth and productivity development in Finland. Our good competitiveness in accordance with the competitiveness measurements is at odds with the fact that we have lost export markets and foreign investment to Finland has remained constant. The level of investment is already present in the structure of Finland's foreign trade. At the same time as the import rate is rising in a trend-like manner, there is little sign of diversification of exports. Without a clear increase in the investment rate, the current share of exports in GDP will begin before a long-term decline. Finland's investment rate has developed weaker in recent years than in many competitor countries. For example, in the year, the amount of productive investment does not increase from the previous year. In recent years, the focus of investment has been on construction, the growth of which, in turn, is expected to level off in a couple of years. The share of machinery and equipment in investments in Finland is small compared to international standards. It has even contracted in recent years. In part, it can be explained that Finnish companies have moved production abroad. By contrast, research and development activities have remained better in Finland. Sufficient productive investment is a prerequisite for renewing outdated capacity and keeping production technology up-to-date. They are also a prerequisite for diversifying the productive fabric and increasing productivity, as well as for maintaining international competitiveness. In many sectors, there is still a need for new obsolete capacities. As a result, growth in productive investment is projected to recover in 2006d 2007, although expansion investments are relatively low. However, the investment rate of the economy as a whole is projected to rise only slightly. If the investment rate, and in particular investment in machinery and equipment, were to improve clearly over the current period, it would support both the continuation of favourable productivity developments and the growth potential of the economy over a longer period of time. Employment has improved during the year, but the upward trend towards the end of the year would be slightly flatter than forecast. Although the decline in the employment rate has continued, the employment rate is still at the same level as a year ago. In addition to tyshchen, the problem in Finland is beginning to be the availability of suitable workpower. This is due to factors arising from the situation and market mismatches. At worst, the capacity constraint may even weaken Finland's export opportunities and, in addition, its propensity to import. The simultaneous existence of Tyshchimpism and a shortage of labour indicates an increase in structural employment. The education and skills of advanced long-term workers often do not meet the requirements of new jobs. In addition, tystchmst and open positions are often located in different parts of Finland, and it is not always easy to move to a job due to the segregation of the housing market, for example. House prices differ greatly from each other in different parts of Finland, which raises the thresholds for moving. According to a study carried out by the Bank of Finland, the efficiency of the labour market has deteriorated since 2000. In particular, companies in the construction sector and many service sectors will find it more difficult to find the right workforce, regardless of the economic situation. For a slightly longer period of time, the Finnish tys market is starting to have a strong influence on the development of the new age group and the transfer of the large classes to the economy. They represent significant challenges not only to the adequacy of the labour force, but also to the balance of public finances. In relation to the msssss of the Elskelsisten mssrs, the mssrss of the working people will grow strongly already in the last decade. It has many implications: lowering tax revenues, increasing expenditure on pensions and increasing the demand for public services (especially care services). In part, it puts an increase in the national economy at the expense of consumption. In the 2010s and 2020s, when the large classes that emerged after the war, the financial burden on the 2010s and 2020s increased the economic strain on the iksn. The entire dependency ratio will stabilise from the 2020s d 2030s to a more epstull than it is today. The implementation of the reform has been estimated to extend the average working time by 2d3 years. If you were to do so, you would probably be able to avoid the burden of the situation. According to a study carried out by the Bank of Finland, the need to increase employment premiums would be reduced by an estimated 3% to one. The need to increase taxation would also be more important. Similarly, it would be a smaller loss of employment for a long period of time. In many other industrialised countries, however, Finland is quite well prepared for the problems arising from the situation: the system has been funded and recently reformed to meet future challenges. However, the problem of age and exclusion is serious in Finland, as it is even earlier than many other countries and comes to the fore more sharply. An effective way of alleviating the burden on public finances is to use technology more effectively, particularly in the provision of public services. It makes it possible to satisfy the demand for additional services, even though a larger proportion of service providers are employed in the local government sector in the past few years. In Finland, it would be a problem that although we are good at producing new technical products, we are other countries in the new technology system. There are exceptions, such as the Finnish banking sector, where we are new technology countries. It would be desirable for the same increase in the level of productivity in the field of public services. All in all, the municipal side should focus more on the efficient provision of services than on moving municipal borders. I don't know if the optimal size of municipalities is lsydettsvisss, but with the current more efficient, the service system that transcends municipal boundaries is easy to develop. Whether there is the political will to do so is another matter. In the light of the outcome, it can be said that the Finnish economy is therefore very favourable for the years. However, it is very much beyond the years and foreshadow future problems. The main factors guiding our development are globalisation, technological development and demographic developments. Finland's problem is, among other things, that our exports are concentrated largely in sectors where international competition is intensifying and prices are falling. Finland must be able to attract high-level investments to the country more effectively than at present, which will diversify the structure of our exports and increase productivity. The functioning of the housing market and the labour market must be improved, as its inoperability is widely reflected in the economy: for example, in household risks and income trends. A great deal of experience and know-how was lost in the tys market during the past few years, as the large classes of age move to the university. It is now high time to ensure that the labour market has sufficient capable resources to ensure that the "generational change" goes smoothly. Our goal must be to ensure that in finland in the future there will be enough work and work. We also want to compete to ensure that Finland remains a high-tech and other high-skilled society. It takes people, ideas and investments.

Changes in Finland over the past 20 years have been big The liberalisation of the financial markets took place with the well-known repercussions, then came the banking crisis and the subsequent recovery, and finally the major structural changes followed. The major change has been accompanied by rapid technological development and its hustle and bustle in banks and the financial sector. Customer interaction has changed profoundly thanks to the Internet and other new service channels. The financial sector is being transformed everywhere by a few agents of change, of which technological progress and the transformation of information technology are the most important. It changes the nature of the activity in a permanent way. New business opportunities are opening up and things can be done more efficiently than before. The pace of technological progress is not slowing down, but accelerating. So the change is accelerating. From the point of view of an individual company or bank, rapid technological development means a constant challenge to adapt business strategies and to ensure that customers keep up with the change. 2. An essential part of the reform is that the banking sector has genuine incentives to develop its own risk management. The new solvency requirements can have a major impact on, for example, banking competition and, through it, on the need to improve operational efficiency. A major reform was also a major reform for companies listed in the so-called IFRS. From 2007 onwards, ti-lin?sten IFRSs also apply to all bond issuers. A major, fundamental change is the emergence of an EU-wide financial market and the introduction of the euro. Financial market integration is rapid in Europe and around the world. Integration, even in the case of the financial markets, means a long process for which it is unthinkable to have a p??tepistet. A similar interlinkage is exemplified by the mortgage market; the loan is now accompanied by more insurance policies than before. 5. In Finland, the size of the financial sector relative to the national economy is quite small All international comparisons are reported. There are many reasons for this, including the traditionally small financial wealth of Finns. Similarly, the banking crisis, for example, cut off significant parts of balance sheets and assets. Finland ik??ntyy In Finland, the ageing of the structure will take place at a very rapid pace in the coming years. It is difficult to predict how the ageing of the bank will affect banking, but reliability and ease of use of services are likely to be emphasised as a guideline for banking operations. Households are on a larger scale, for example, investment funds. Seven challenges for the future 1. Customers have changed and will continue to do so Customers are likely to become more demanding, for example, in terms of quality of service and internet usage. The challenge, especially for local banks, is that part of the customer base does not live in the bank's area of operation. How can you connect with and have customer relationships with these customers in a tough competitive situation? 2. Technological development continues and accelerates Technology and its transformation affect all activities in the financial markets. Individual operators must be able to correctly apply new technologies in their own operations. Technological change makes it possible to improve productivity and efficiency. Title: Economic policy opportunities in Euro-Finland, at a seminar of the Taxpayers' Federation
text: President Matti Vanhala's speech: Opportunities for economic policy in Euro-Finland, seminar of the Central Union of Taxpayers . Speech . Tuesday 11 January 2000, 12:00 AM Seminar of the Central Union of Taxpayers 11.1.2000 Chairman of the Board Matti Vanhala: 1. Although it will only be possible to assess the usefulness of the EU's economic and monetary union in the future, on the basis of long-term experience, it must nevertheless be considered - and therefore as for the time being - that the potential for securing favourable economic development in Finland has also increased. Monetary union gives a country with even a small currency a moderate guarantee of stable monetary conditions, i.e. a stable monetary situation. a stable price level and, in a broad sense, a stable monetary system. Through this, monetary union will remove the traditional hssspesske of our national economic development. Economic policy can thus focus on furthering the actual objectives set for economic development, but instead on concentrating efforts on combating financial market problems from domestic and foreign countries. In chemistry, the existence of monetary union brings economic policy peace. 2. However, the existence of monetary union brought with it a significant change in the game of economic policy. Even in monetary union, economic development is driven above all by the decisions of economic powers other than the government and the central bank. Companies, municipalities, etc. in a market economy, decisions are made on their own initiative in Chechnya. But in monetary union, neither the government nor the central bank has any chance of correcting or compensating for possible mistakes in other parts of the economy. There is no national exchange rate elasticity, for example. competitivenessThe adverse employment effects of income solutions are irreparable by public action. Not through tax policy or other economic policy. The employees of the various sectors will have to face the consequences of their own, both good and bad, with greater probability. In the context of monetary union, responsibility for economic development is partly on a healthier footing than in the past. Of course, this does not guarantee that the overall economic points, e.g. employment objectives, gain sufficient weight in the making of the national economy. 3. There are so far 11 Member States in the EU's Economic and Monetary Union. In the context of a single monetary policy and eleven different economic situations, it is essential that the fiscal policy of each country and the economic and structural policies of the government in general are the principles of national economic policy. It is not possible to eliminate cyclical fluctuations by means of economic policy. But if we had relied on national monetary policy in the past to curb cyclical pressures, we would have to resort to national fiscal policy in the future. This is a new set-up which will give rise to intense reflection on the possibilities and conditions of fiscal policy in the member countries of the Monetary Union. In a monetary union of simultaneous economic development, the use of national fiscal policies must be carefully guarded. In Finland, in connection with current income negotiations, this means that income solutions may not limit or tie up the leeway of fiscal policy. 4. Monetary union will not determine a nation's economic future. The ECONOMIC AND MONETARY UNION of the EU is a czech republic for Finland, because it will hopefully help to permanently eliminate the traditional hsiristekijs of the Finnish economy, the sharp fluctuations in the monetary economy. However, this is not enough. to solve Finland's employment problems; . bring public finances that are based on excessively high tax rates and excessive expenditure volumes to the brink. to the bottom; safeguard the sustainability of public finances in the event of a change in the structure; . in particular, not to secure the long-term success of the Finnish economy, which are linked above all to the . to increase the flexibility of the economy in all its aspects and to increase the mental pssoma. The questions referred to above are inextricably linked. Securing the financial basis of the welfare state in the event of a change in the structure requires a significant increase in the employment rate - which, in turn, requires a significant reduction in the tax burden. In any case, when it comes to ensuring the balance of the state's finances over the economic cycle, we also have to face the major issues of prioritisation of public expenditure finances. These are the real structural challenges and fateful issues of the Finnish economy. Monetary union in the EU does not provide solutions to them, but it does not restrict them from being tackled. In a global competitive economy, each country must also survive on its own and through national action in the conditions of monetary union.
