Title: How does (economic) policy affect the national economy and investment?
text: Board Member Olli Rehn: How does (economic) policy affect the national economy and investment? Helsinki, 21.9.2017. . Speech . Thursday21 September 2017,10:00 AM Olli Rehn, Member of the Board of Directors Bank of Finland How does (economic) policy affect the national economy and investment? Securities magazine Rahapsivs 2017 Helsinki, 21.9.2017 (pdf) (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches/documents/2017-09-21-olli-rehn-securities-mint.pdf) HOW DOES (ECONOMIC) POLICY AFFECT THE NATIONAL ECONOMY AND INVESTMENT? Good listeners, The theme of my speech is omite's (economic) policy affecting the national economy and investment? o. Although the answer seems obvious to many, it is worth considering the questions in more detail. First a general comment and then an example from the Bank of Finland's field of activity. In general, political, economic, technological and cultural changes are taking place at different times of d stable development and, on the other hand, economic continuity manifest themselves at very different rates in different regions. The long periods of continuity of politics and ideology are often interrupted by rapid and skkinsnish periods, such as the four-decade-long period of cold war in 1989-91 or the terrorist attacks of september 2001. Economic and technological development, on the other hand, is progressing in the deepest streams and more continuously. In the long run, it follows the period of technological innovation described by economist Joseph Schumpeter and the periods of their consolidation. The aim is to influence their adoption by means of policy measures to strengthen structural competitiveness d knowledge, research and innovation d activities. In the shorter term, economic developments are characterised by fluctuations in demand and supply, which John Maynard Keynes was looking for. Monetary and economic policies aim to smooth out cyclical fluctuations and support sustainable growth, financial and price stability, as well as high levels of employment and well-being. I will look at the question of the angle of my own area of responsibility. On the Board of directors of the Bank of Finland, I am responsible for the implementation of monetary policy, such as purchase programmes. Their decision-making is centralised to the Governing Council of the ECB, but the implementation is decentralised to the national central banks. Traditionally, the central bank, also the European Central Bank, conducts monetary policy through the key interest rate. If inflation falls too low, it will seek to revive the economy and return the reduced inflation to its target level by lowering the central bank's credit and deposit rates. This is reflected in the level of interest rates on short-term loans on the market. As a result of the continuity of low interest rates, the central bank is also able to reduce interest rates on longer-term loans. It is precisely the reduction in longer market and banking interest rates that is essential, since it has the strongest impact on the recovery of investment and consumer demand. However, in exceptionally difficult circumstances, such as in recent years following the onset of the financial crisis, the effectiveness of traditional interest rate policy is not sufficient. Although central bank interest rates and their also short-term market rates were pushed to zero, the economy did not recover sufficiently and inflation fell well below the ECB's price stability target, which is olshell but below 2% inflationo. At its worst, there was a threat of a deflationary spiral. When a deflationary spiral threatens or inflation persists at exceptionally low levels, traditional interest rate policy can be thwarted by large-scale purchases of securities, which have been resorted to by several central banks in recent years. The ECB has taken three types of action: firstly, it lowered central bank interest rates to zero, and the deposit rate has been negative since 2014. Secondly, it has been implementing a large-scale purchase programme since 2015. Thirdly, banks have been offered a great deal of longer-term financing. These measures, in particular the large-scale purchase programmes, are primarily aimed at bringing longterm interest rates down one and increasing the money supply beyond what could have been achieved in the traditional contexts of monetary policy. How, then, do the direct purchases of securities by the Central Bank through the financial markets enter the real economy? In the oSyssys phase, the money supply first needs to be used in the liquidity of banks. Large purchases of securities by the central bank increase the amount of deposits held by commercial banks in the central bank. When it is expensive to lie down with deposits at the central bank, purchase programmes can be used to directly stimulate bank lending, which has emerged from the shock of the financial crisis. Indeed, lending has been clearly recovering in recent years. In the implementation phase, this is reflected in the real economy by increasing investment and increasing demand or by strengthening consumer demand. The real economy has recovered. For example, the exchange rate of the euro reacts strongly to purchase programmes. The euro started to weaken already in 2014, as market expectations of the purchase programme intensified. This contributed to the rebalancing of the euro area economy. The recent appreciation of the euro against the dollar, on the other hand, reflects an improvement in the growth rate in the euro area, but also an increase in the security of the United States. At the moment, the exchange rate of the euro is quite close to its long-term average. Under the ECB's purchase programmes, central banks purchase both government bonds and private sector bonds, secured loans from designated banks and investment-grade corporate bonds. Why, then, is the weight of purchases in government bonds? There are several reasons for this. Firstly, as a public authority, the central bank, in all its activities, pays attention to the risks arising from these, and in particular to the credit risks arising from central bank operations. The credit risk associated with government bonds is generally clearly lower than that of private sector bonds. Secondly, experience has shown that the effectiveness of purchasing programmes is based on their long-term size. The total procurement under the Eurojsestelm purchase programme amounts to approximately 2000 billion. the euro scale, and the current euro system buys a variety of bonds for an average of 60 billion. euros per month, which means purchases of about one billion euros a month in Finland as well. Large-scale purchases are only possible on the sovereign bond market, which is many times larger than the private debt securities market. Thirdly, research and experience with the purchase programmes show that the effectiveness of purchases is greater than the longer the central bank buys on the market. Loans issued by governments are typically clear longer than loans from banks or companies, which is also in favour of their use in order to guarantee the effectiveness of the purchase programmes. Then they will have heard whether it is right for central banks to influence the prices of securities through their actions, as is the case with the purchase programmes. Is such an action appropriate for the Central Bank, or would it even be a question of manipulating the market? The answer is that the impact of the euro system purchase programmes of recent years on long-term interest rates and, therefore, on the real economy and general inflation developments, has been an absolutely central part of the mechanism for the transmission of monetary policy. The ECB's monetary policy has been effective in influencing the easing of deflationary pressures and has been in the right direction. Without the market effects achieved, the effectiveness of monetary policy would have been deficient, as shown in the following slide. The legal side of the answer is that the ECB has the right and the duty, in accordance with its mandate under the EU Treaty, to use the directives given to it as it sees fit to achieve its objectives, primarily price stability. The purchase of securities is one of the assets that were explicitly given to the ECB in the Treaties when the Bank was set up. The applicability of securities purchases to the monetary policy toolbox has been challenged before the Court of Justice of the EU in mid-2015 following a question put to it by the German Constitutional Court. The decision taken at that time supported the ECB's position that the question of whether the measures are necessary and proportionate to achieve the monetary policy objectives. The ECB's purchases of securities have been necessary to safeguard the convergence of monetary policy, and the positive results achieved show that action has been necessary and necessary to restore price stability in the euro area. They have also supported sustainable growth and employment. All in all, the intensification of economic activity and the improvement in employment in the euro area is also a key factor for the economy and society as a whole, including investors. This weighs more on the scales than on the sidelines of light monetary policy, as the sharp rise in asset values is hardly regretted by equity investors. We are still a long way from the kind of overheating that preceded the financial crisis, as shown in the attached figure. As a result of monetary policy, both non-financial corporations and households have started to grow moderately. However, it would be disastrous for the economic development of the euro area if the over-indebtedness of some households and businesses made it unduly difficult, for example, for young households or prevented them from starting new businesses. Among other things, in the context of macroprudential policy, both in Europe and in Finland, we also strive to ensure that over-indebtedness does not recur. The impact of securities purchases on public finances has also been discussed. In the same way as the stimulus policy in general, the central bank's purchases of securities also reduce interest rates in general and thus reduce the debt servicing costs of the state as well as other debtors. However, the fact that part of the central government debt under the purchase programmes is also transferred to the central bank does not alter the commitments relating to the payment of government debt d the state amortizes and amortizes its debt to the central bank in the same way as it does to private creditors. Summa summarum: After all, central bank bond purchases are a very similar central bank policy to central bank interest rate cuts. The differences are in the lhinns instruments. However, d despite all the exceptional measures, d inflation is one below target, in particular the so-called inflation rate. core inflation. One might well ask, of course, where the exceptional shift in the monetary policy toolbox has been experienced basically due to. The problem of the zero interest rate limit and the resulting reliance on large-scale purchase programmes in monetary policy is new and exceptional compared to history. Why is normal interest rate policy not now sufficient to achieve the objectives of monetary policy? It is essential to note that the effects of interest rate policy do not depend only on the level of interest rates, but on their level in relation to the neutral, i.e. the so-called "interest rate". natural interest rates. A natural interest rate is an interest rate that prevails when price developments are stable and production potential is equal. The natural interest rate is not constant over time, but changes depending on, among other things, the prevailing inflation expectations, how the situation develops, and the potential for returns in the real economy. Several studies have attempted to assess the natural level of interest rates in recent years, and the results suggest that natural interest rates would have fallen markedly since the end of the financial crisis. According to them, the natural real interest rate would have sunk to around zero and, in some studies, even fallen into negative territory. This is due, among other things, to the slowdown in growth and productivity growth. Various studies have been reported, for example, by Lauri Vilmi in the Bank of Finland's Euro & Talous publication a year ago. The low natural level of interest rates is, of course, a challenging manifestation from a monetary policy point of view, which most obviously explains why central bank interest rates printed at around zero (and negative for the deposit rate) alone have not been sufficient to achieve price stability in line with the ECB's objective. It is difficult to predict the future development of the natural interest rate. Whether it can be expected to return to the level to which it was used before the financial crisis depends, inter alia, on the development and productivity growth rate. These developments will also have an impact on the future conduct of monetary policy by central banks and on the choice of monetary policy instruments. As a result, the circle will close, meaning that monetary policy will eventually be linked to the real economy. As previously announced, the Governing Council has decided to continue its purchases of securities by 60 billion until the end of 2017. the monthly pace of the euro. During the autumn, the Governing Council of the ECB will decide on the level and timing of the purchase programme (ocalibrationo) for the period after the turn of the year. The adjustment of the size and timing of the pace of the purchase programmes is therefore necessary, but the accommodative monetary policy stance will continue until the price stability objective is fully achieved. It should be in the long term itself, not only in the short term, but also in the medium term, without the lightness of monetary policy. The ECB's purchase programmes therefore have different levels of interest rate policy than traditional interest rate policy, but the objectives of the policy are exactly the same as to stimulate the d economy and bring inflation back to the target path. The work will continue until the target has been reached, with markets and investors in place. Olli Rehn:How does (economic) politics affect the national economy and investment? Helsinki, 21.9.2017. Arvopaperilehden Rahapiv 2017 Helsinki, 21.9.2017 (pdf) (/globalassets/fi/media-ja-julkaisut/puheet/documents/2017-09-21-olli-rehn-arvopaperi-rahapaiva.pdf) MITEN (TALOUS)POLITIIKKA VAIKUTTAA KANSANTALOUTEEN JA SIJOITTAMISEEN? Hyv kuulijat, Puheenvuoroni teemaksi on merkitty miten (talous)politiikka vaikuttaa kansantalouteen ja sijoittamiseen?. Vaikka vastaus tuntuu monesta itsestnselvyydelt, kysymyst on paikallaan pohtia tarkemmin. Ensin yleinen kommentti ja sitten esimerkki Suomen Pankin toimialalta. Yleisesti ottaen poliittiset, taloudelliset, teknologiset ja kulttuuriset muutokset etenevt eri aikajnteill  vakaa kehitys ja toisaalta epjatkuvuudet ilmenevt hyvin eri tahtiin eri elmnalueilla. Politiikan ja ideologian pitkt jatkuvuuden kaudet katkeavat usein nopeisiin ja kkinisiin knnekohtiin, kuten neljn vuosikymmenen mittaisen kylmn sodan kauden pttyess vuosina 1989-91 tai sen jlkeisen rauhanomaisen vaiheen pttyess terrori.iskuihin syyskuussa 2001. Taloudellinen ja teknologinen kehitys puolestaan etenee syvin virtoina ja jatkuvammin. Pitkll aikavlill se noudattaa taloustieteilij Joseph Schumpeterin kuvaamia teknologisten innovaatioiden lpimurtoa ja niiden vakiintumisen kausia. Niiden hydyntmiseen pyritn vaikuttamaan rakenteellista kilpailukyky  osaamista, tutkimusta, innovaatiotoimintaa  vahvistavilla politiikkatoimilla. Lyhyemmll aikavlill talouden kehityst leimaavat kysynnn ja tarjonnan vaihtelut, joihin John Maynard Keynes etsi lkkeit. Raha-ja talouspolitiikalla pyritn tasaamaan suhdannevaihteluita ja tukemaan kestv kasvua, rahoitus-ja hintavakautta sek korkeaa tyllisyytt ja hyvinvointia. Tarkastelen tt kysymyst oman vastuualueeni nkkulmasta. Vastaan Suomen Pankin johtokunnassa rahapolitiikan toimeenpanosta, kuten osto-ohjelmista. Niiden ptksenteko on keskitetty EKP:n neuvostolle, mutta toimeenpano on posin hajautettu kansallisille keskuspankeille. Perinteisesti keskuspankki, mys Euroopan keskuspankki, harjoittaa rahapolitiikkaa lhinn ohjauskoron kautta. Jos inflaatio painuu liian alas, se pyrkii elvyttmn taloutta ja palauttamaan alentuneen inflaation tavoitetasolle laskemalla keskuspankin luotto-ja talletuskorkoja. Tm heijastuu vlittmsti markkinoiden lyhyiden lainojen korkotasoon. Viestittmll alhaisen korkotason jatkuvuudesta keskuspankki pystyy mys alentamaan pidempien lainojen korkoja. Nimenomaan pidempien markkina-ja pankkikorkojen lasku on olennaista, koska sill on voimakkain vaikutus investointien ja kulutuskysynnn elvyttmisess. Poikkeuksellisen vaikeissa olosuhteissa, kuten viime vuosina finanssikriisin kynnistymisen jlkeen, perinteisen korkopolitiikan teho ei kuitenkaan riit. Vaikka keskuspankkikorot ja niiden myt lyhyet markkinakorot painettiin nollaan, talous ei elpynyt riittvsti ja inflaatio ji selvsti alle EKP:n hintavakaustavoitteen, joka on mritelty lhell mutta alle 2% inflaatio. Pahimmillaan uhkana oli deflaatiokierre. Deflaatiokierteen uhatessa tai inflaation pysyess sitkesti poikkeuksellisen alhaisella tasolla perinteist korkopolitiikkaa voidaan tydent laajamittaisilla arvopapereiden ostoilla, joihin useat keskuspankit ovat viime vuosina turvautuneet. EKP on toteuttanut kolmenlaisia toimia: Ensinnkin se laski keskuspankkikorot nollatasolle, ja talletuskorko on ollut negatiivinen vuodesta 2014. Toiseksi se on toteuttanut laajamittaista osto-ohjelmaa vuodesta 2015. Kolmanneksi pankeille on tarjottu runsaasti pitempikestoista rahoitusta. Niill toimilla, etenkin mittavilla osto-ohjelmilla, pyritn ensisijaisesti laskemaan pitki korkoja yh alemmas ja lismn rahan tarjontaa yli sen, mit rahapolitiikan perinteisill vlineill olisi voitu saada aikaan. Miten sitten keskuspankin suorat arvopaperiostot vlittyvt rahoitusmarkkinoiden kautta reaalitalouteen? Sysysvaiheessa rahan tarjonta nkyy ensin pankkien likviditeetiss. Keskuspankin isot arvopaperiostot kasvattavat liikepankkien keskuspankissa pitmien talletusten mr. Kun talletusten makuuttaminen keskuspankissa on kallista, niin osto-ohjelmien avulla voidaan epsuorasti elvytt pankkien lainanantoa, joka on krsinyt finanssikriisin aiheuttamasta shokista. Lainananto onkin ollut viime vuodet selvsti elpymn pin. Vlittymisvaiheessa tm heijastuu reaalitalouteen kasvattamalla investointeja ja yllpitmll tai vahvistamalla kulutuskysynt. Nin reaalitalous on elpynyt. Esimerkiksi euron kurssi reagoi voimakkaasti osto-ohjelmiin. Euro alkoi heikenty jo vuonna 2014, kun odotukset osto-ohjelmasta voimistuivat markkinoilla. Tm osaltaan edesauttoi euroalueen talouden tasapainottumista. Euron dollarikurssin viimeaikainen vahvistuminen puolestaan heijastaa kohentuneita kasvunkymi euroalueella, mutta toisaalta mys lisntynytt epvarmuutta Yhdysvalloissa. Tll hetkell euron kurssi on melko lhell pitkn aikavlin keskiarvoaan. EKP:n osto-ohjelmissa keskuspankit ostavat sek valtioiden velkakirjoja ett yksityisen sektorin velkakirjoja, nimittin pankkien vakuudellisia lainoja sek investointiluokan yrityslainoja. Miksi sitten mrllisesti ostojen ppaino on valtionlainoissa? Thn on useita syit. Ensinnkin, julkisena viranomaisena keskuspankin tytyy kaikissa toimissaan kiinnitt huomiota niist aiheutuviin riskeihin, ja aivan erityisesti keskuspankkioperaatioista aiheutuviin luottoriskeihin. Valtiolainoihin liittyv luottoriski on yleens selvsti pienempi kuin yksityisen sektorin velkakirjoissa. Toiseksi, kokemus on osoittanut, ett osto-ohjelmien teho perustuu pitklti niiden suureen kokoon. Eurojrjestelmn osto-ohjelman thnastiset hankinnat ovat noin 2000 mrd. euron mittaluokkaa, ja tt nyky eurojrjestelm ostaa erilaisia velkakirjoja keskimrin 60 mrd. euron edest kuukaudessa, mik tarkoittaa Suomessakin noin miljardin euron ostoja kuukausittain. Nin laajamittaisten ostojen toteuttaminen on kytnnss mahdollista vain valtionlainamarkkinoilla, joiden mittaluokka on moninkertainen yksityisiin velkapaperimarkkinoihin verrattuna. Kolmanneksi, tutkimus ja osto-ohjelmista saadut kokemukset osoittavat, ett ostojen teho on sit suurempi, mit pidempi lainoja keskuspankki ostaa markkinoilta. Valtioiden liikkeeseen laskemat lainat ovat tyypillisesti selvsti pidempi kuin pankkien tai yritysten lainat, mik mys puoltaa niiden kytt osto-ohjelmien tehon takaamiseksi. Silloin tllin on kuultu epilyj siit, onko oikein, ett keskuspankit toimillaan vaikuttavat arvopaperien hintoihin niin kuin osto-ohjelmissa tapahtuu. Onko tllainen toiminta keskuspankille sopivaa vai olisiko kysymys markkinoita jopa vristvst manipulaatiosta? Vastaus lhtee siit, ett viime vuosien eurojrjestelmn osto-ohjelmien vaikutukset pitkiin korkoihin ja siit edelleen reaalitalouteen ja yleiseen inflaatiokehitykseen ovat olleet aivan keskeinen osa rahapolitiikan vlittymismekanismia. EKP:n rahapolitiikka on vaikuttanut tehokkaasti deflaatiopaineiden vistymiseen ja on ollut vaikutuksiltaan tarkoitetun suuntaista. Ilman saavutettuja markkinavaikutuksia rahapolitiikan teho olisi jnyt puutteelliseksi, kuten seuraava kalvo kertoo. Vastauksen juridinen puoli on, ett EKP:lla on EU:n perussopimuksessa mritellyn mandaattinsa mukaan oikeus ja velvollisuuskin kytt sille annettuja vlineit parhaaksi katsomallaan tavalla sille mrttyjen tavoitteiden, ensisijaisesti hintavakauden, saavuttamiseksi. Arvopaperiostot kuuluvat niiden vlineiden joukkoon, jotka EKP:lle perussopimuksissa eksplisiittisesti annettiin kun pankki perustettiin. Arvopaperiostojen soveltuvuutta rahapolitiikan keinovalikoimaan on ksitelty EU:n tuomioistuimessa keskuussa 2015 Saksan perustuslakituomioistuimen sille esittmn kysymyksen johdosta. Tuolloin tehty pts tuki EKP:n kantaa, jonka mukaan tmnkin vlineen kytss kyse on viime kdess siit, ovatko toimet tarpeellisia ja oikein mitoitettuja rahapolitiikan tavoitteiden saavuttamiseksi. EKP:n arvopaperiostot ovat olleet tarpeellisia rahapolitiikan vlittymisen turvaamiseksi ja niill saavutetut mynteiset tulokset osoittavat, ett toimet ovat olleet tarpeellisia ja hydyksi hintavakauden palauttamisessa euroalueelle. Ne ovat mys tukeneet kestv kasvua ja tyllisyytt. Kaiken kaikkiaan euroalueen taloudellisen aktiviteetin voimistuminen ja tyllisyyden koheneminen on koko kansantalouden ja yhteiskunnan, mys sijoittajien, kannalta mynteist. Tm painaa enemmn vaa'assa kuin kevyeen rahapolitiikkaan liittyvt sivuilmit, kuten varallisuusarvojen voimakas nousu -mist osakesijoittajat sinns tuskin ovat pahoillaan. Olemme viel kaukana sellaisesta ylikuumenemisesta, joka edelsi finanssikriisi, kuten oheisesta kuvasta nkyy. Elvyttvn rahapolitiikan avulla sek yritysten ett kotitalouksien lainakannat ovat alkaneet maltillisesti kasvaa. Euroalueen talouskehityksen kannalta olisi kuitenkin turmiollista, jos joidenkin kotitalouksien ja yrityksien ylivelkaantuneisuus vaikeuttaisi kohtuuttomasti esimerkiksi nuorten kotitalouksien asemaa tai estisi uusien yritysten perustamisen. Muun muassa makrovakauspolitiikan vlinein pyrimme niin Euroopassa kuin Suomessakin mys huolehtimaan siit, ettei ylivelkaantuminen en pse toistumaan. Keskusteltu on mys arvopaperiostojen vaikutuksista valtiontalouksiin. Samaan tapaan kuin elvyttv korkopolitiikka muutenkin, mys keskuspankin arvopaperiostot laskevat yleist korkotasoa ja siten alentavat valtion niin kuin muidenkin velallisten velanhoitokuluja. Se, ett osto-ohjelmien myt osa valtion velasta ptyy keskuspankin omistukseen, ei kuitenkaan milln tavalla muuta valtion velanmaksuun liittyvi sitoumuksia  valtio lyhent ja kuolettaa velkaansa keskuspankille yht lailla kuin yksityisillekin velkojille. Summa summarum: Keskuspankin velkakirjaostot ovat loppujen lopuksi hyvin samankaltaista keskuspankkipolitiikkaa kuin keskuspankkikorkojen laskut. Erot ovat lhinn instrumenteissa. Silti  kaikista poikkeustoimistakin huolimatta  inflaatio on yh tavoitetta hitaampaa, etenkin ns. pohjainflaatio. Voidaan tietysti hyvin kysy, mist koettu poikkeuksellinen siirtym rahapolitiikan keinovalikoimassa pohjimmiltaan johtuu. Korkojen nollarajan ongelma ja niist johtunut turvautuminen laajamittaisiin osto-ohjelmiin rahapolitiikassa on uusi ja historiaan verrattuna poikkeuksellinen asia. Miksi tavanomainen korkopolitiikka ei nyt ole riittnyt rahapolitiikan tavoitteiden saavuttamiseksi? Olennaista on huomata, ett korkopolitiikan vaikutukset eivt riipu vain korkojen tasosta sinns, vaan niiden tasosta suhteessasiihen, mik on kulloinkin vallitseva neutraali eli ns. luonnollinen korkotaso. Luonnollinen korko on korko, joka vallitsee hintakehityksen ollessa vakaata ja tuotantomahdollisuuksien ollessa tydess kytss. Luonnollinen korko ei ole ajassa vakio, vaan muuttuu mm. sen mukaan, mitk ovat vallitsevat inflaatio-odotukset, miten sstmiskyttytyminen kehittyy, ja millaisia tuottomahdollisuuksia on saatavissa reaalitalouden puolelta. Luonnollista korkotasoa on viime vuosina yritetty arvioida useissa tutkimuksissa, ja tulokset viittaavat siihen, ett luonnollinen korkotaso olisi alentunut selvsti finanssikriisin jlkeen. Luonnollinen reaalikorko olisi niiden mukaan painunut nollan tuntumaan ja joissakin tutkimuksissa painunut jopa negatiiviseksi. Tm johtuu mm. tyikisen vestn kasvun sek tyn tuottavuuden kasvun hidastumisesta. Eri tutkimuksista on tehnyt selkoa mm. Lauri Vilmi Suomen Pankin Euro & Talous -julkaisussa vuosi sitten. Matala luonnollinen korkotaso on tietysti rahapolitiikan kannalta haasteellinen ilmi, joka mit ilmeisimmin selitt sen, miksi nollan tuntumaan (ja talletuskoron osalta negatiiviseksi) painetut keskuspankkikorot eivt viel yksinn ole riittneet hintavakauden toteuttamiseen EKP:n tavoitteen mukaisella tavalla. Luonnollisen koron tulevaa kehityst on vaikea ennakoida. Voidaanko sen odottaa palaavan lhemms tasoa, johon ennen finanssikriisi totuttiin, riippuu mm. vestkehityksest ja tuottavuuden kasvuvauhdista. Tm kehitys vaikuttaa jatkossa mys keskuspankkien rahapolitiikan tuleviin toimintamuotoihin ja rahapolitiikan vlineiden valintaan. Nin ollen ympyr sulkeutuu eli rahapolitiikka kytkeytyy lopulta reaalitalouteen. EKP:n neuvosto on pttnyt jatkaa arvopaperiostoja aiemmin kerrotun mukaisesti v. 2017 loppuun asti 60 mrd. euron kuukausitahtia. Tmn syksyn mittaan EKP:n neuvosto ptt osto-ohjelman tasosta ja aikataulusta (=kalibroinnista) vuodenvaihteen jlkeiselle ajalle. Osto-ohjelmien virityksen tarkentaminen mittaluokan ja aikataulun suhteen on siis edess, mutta kasvua tukevaa rahapolitiikkaa jatketaan, kunnes hintavakaustavoite tyttyy kestvll tavalla. Sen tulee pit itsen yll ei vain lyhyell vaan mys keskipitkll aikavlill ilman rahapolitiikan kevytt mitoitusta. EKP:n osto-ohjelmissa on siis kytss eri vlineet kuin perinteisess korkopolitiikassa, mutta politiikan tarkoituspert ovat aivan samat  talouden elvyttminen ja inflaation palauttaminen tavoiteuralle. Ty jatkuu kunnes tavoite on saavutettu, markkinoita ja sijoittajia yllttmtt. Olli Rehn:Miten (talous)politiikka vaikuttaa kansantalouteen ja sijoittamiseen? Helsinki, 21.9.2017. Title: Forests and economy in Savo and Finland  history of sawmills
text: Board member Olli Rehn: Metsst and the economy in Savo and Finland d the history of sawmills. Otava, 22.9.2017. . Speech . Friday 22 September 2017,11:30 AM Olli Rehn, Member of the Board of Directors, open doors of The Bank of Finland Versowood Otava, 22.9.2017 METST AND THE ECONOMY IN SAVO AND FINLAND d THE HISTORY OF SAWMILLS Thank you for the invitation to the Otava sawmill d i.e. versowood's Otava unit open house. I feel like I'm at home, because it's only a short rowing distance from our msk beach and we're on my route by land. The sawmill industry has a long tradition in Finland and Savo. In many ways, the history of the sector is linked to the long-term arc of the development of the Finnish national economy and the rise in the standard of living of the Finns. The development and implementation of new technologies have been key to the growth. Increased productivity has made it possible to improve living conditions and well-being. From the outset, the sawmill industry has been a precursor to the development of new production methods and hysdyntsmisesss d i.e. innovation, as they say today. The first water sawmills were built already in the 1500s in connection with the crown estates. At that time, Finland was still a relatively ksyhs and syrjsinen country, but the first steps of industrialization were taken at an early age. However, sawing with the old water saws was slow and the hsvik was large. In the late 1600s, the first new type of fine-grain sawmills developed by the Dutch was built in Inkoo and Pernissn. New sawmills made it possible to multiply production capacity. The first sawmills for the export of sawn timber were established as early as the 1700s. In the late 1800s, the Finnish sawmill industry became a large-scale industry, as sawmills became more common and the market was taken over by the use of hchyry power. In 1860, the timber industry accounted for about 30% of goods exports and forest-based exports for just over half of exports. The industrial hysdynching of the Mikkeli pitsjssss forests began in the 1770s with the addition of a hydroelectric sawmill established in Korpikoski. Kicked off in the mid-1800s. Political pushches opened up space for the development of the sawmill industry: freedom to conduct a business from the 1860s the construction of the Lsht and Savo railway, which was completed in 1889. Under self-indulgence, a powerful and diverse wood processing industry had emerged in Finland. The share of the timber industry in exports had risen by half and more than 75 % of exports were based on forests. After the Second World War, finland's economy grew rapidly. The standard of living measured by gross domestic product doubled twice in twenty years. Finland caught up with other countries and became one of the wealthiest countries. At the same time, the industry diversified. However, the importance of metssala to finland's national economy remained considerable and its share of exports remained high. In 1955, up to 95% of goods exports originated from Finnish forests. It is not for nothing that metsss has been called green gold. In recent decades, Finnish industry and its exports have diversified dramatically. There have been upper and lower. On the whole, however, the prosperity of nations will continue to increase the use of processed wood products in the world. However, the relative importance and prices of processed wood, pulp, sawn timber and paper are changing. The 2000s and the difficulties of the forest industry The decline in demand for paper hit the Finnish forest industry in the 2000s. It was important for the economy as a whole, and especially in the provinces, where the sector was of great importance. In the years since the turn of the millennium, the share of the forest industry in Finland's GDP has declined and that of the lumberjacks has shrunk by about 35,000 people, which corresponds to about 1.5% of all employment. The change has been particularly noticeable in traditional forest industrial locations. South-Eastern Finland has been the biggest contributor to the cuts in production in the sector. In absolute terms, the kouvola (3700) and Helsinki regions (4000) have the highest number of jobs in the sector. In relative terms, the largest number of jobs in the forest industry has been found in Imatra, Kouvola and Jsmssls, where the number of jobs lost has been almost 10 per cent of all jobs. However, there are differences in the regions in how the decline of the forest industry has been reflected in the overall size of the region. In the sub-regions of Kotka-Hamina, Kajaani and Jakobstad, tysss has grown despite the disappearance of jobs in the forest industry. However, the bottom of the forest industry is clear and investment has re-emerged. The forest industry is recreating its skins, as it has done so many times before throughout history. Sawmill industry The sawmill industry is an export sector for the Finnish economy. Approximately three quarters of the sawn timber produced in Finland is exported. The importance of the sector is underlined by its high degree of domesticity. The sawmills use domestic raw materials and domestic labour. That is why of all our industries, it is in the sawmill industry that the share of domestic value added to exports is the highest. About three quarters of export earnings to Finland. Over the past 40 years, the productivity of the wood industry has increased more than fivefold. In other words, one tysntekijs currently produces more sawn timber than 5 tysntekijs in 1975. The rate of productivity growth has been twice as high as in the rest of the economy. The situation of the international and Finnish economies The revitalisation of the forest industry is, of course, also part of the better vibe of the finnish economy as a whole. The strengthening of growth reflects the improvement in the global economy, in particular in the euro area. Light monetary policy has played a part in the improvement of the economic situation. The light monetary policy has improved opportunities for business investment by lowering the price of borrowing money and also by creating a favourable framework for banks' own financing in the euro area as a whole. The gradual strengthening of the economic situation has fuelled the positive sentiment and further contributed to the strengthening of the economic cycle. The higher-than-expected growth of exports and the acceleration of investment growth have improved the forecasts. (SP 2.1%). Finland's exports are now strong both to the euro area and outside the euro area. Growth in the euro area, China and japan has picked up. On the other hand, Brexit is now predicted to dampen uk growth. In the United States, the acceleration of growth is overshadowed by the new administration's difficulties in bringing about reforms. In spite of this, the global economy is, on the whole, in a better position than it was a year ago. Domestic economic policies support the conditions for growth. After all, an evss has been created to improve the competitiveness of exports. Wages have also risen more slowly in the first half of the year than in competitor countries. In the short term, the biggest economic development-related uncertainties in the second half of the year are related to the strength of growth in construction and investment in general and to market solutions. Economic policy in support of growth In the longer term, the conditions for the sustainable growth of the Finnish economy are created by strengthening the productive potential of the economy, i.e. by strengthening productivity, labour supply and investment. The strong growth in productive investment is now also in terms of the growth of production potential and prosperity in the economy as a whole. The Versowood sawmill is, of course, a good example of such an investment. It is supported by the labour market solutions of recent years and the Competitiveness Pact. At the same time, there are concerns about the risk of indebtedness in the national economy. At the moment, Finland is experiencing high levels of indebtedness, as well as households and public finances. This has been partly the norm in relation to the cyclical downturn, as households and public finances seek to offset the impact of the economic cycle on consumption. However, indebtedness must not become a structural manifestation. The growth and indebtedness of the national economy must be in line with the expected increase in income. The problem with the rush of economic upturns is often that they are too quick to share the projected good and even the reforms already planned. Past challenges and those that are a little further in the future are forgotten. The Finnish economy is also affected by EU-level balances. From the point of view of the metss and other bioeconomy, it is important that the calculation methods for carbon sinks were changed in a direction that is more favourable to Finland and in the direction of the wastewater. Hyvst ystsvst, Versowood's Otava sawmill is a great example of Finnish know-how and a long-term company that bears fruit through the ups and downs of the economy. The Finnish economy is growing and prospering precisely because of the influence of such companies and entrepreneurs. Successes! Title: Opening remarks in the session "The European Spring?"
text: Board member Olli Rehn: Opening remarks in the session "The European Spring?", Washington, 13 October 2017. . Speech . Friday 13October 2017, 5:30PM Olli Rehn Member of the Board of Bank of Finland At the the Reinventing Bretton Woods Committee seminar oThe Quest for Normality in an uncertain World?o, Washington, 13 October 2017 (Presentation ppt) (/globalassets/fi/media-ja-julkaisut/puheet/documents/2017-10-13-olli-rehn-european. spring.pdf) OPENING REMARKS IN THE SESSION oTHE EUROPEAN SPRING?o Ladies and Gentlemen, The title of this panel is quite evocative. It recalls visions of regeneration and new growth. The title also reminds us of the historic events of 1968, the oPrague springo and the oParis springo. They proved to be short-lived. If there is now a European spring, let us hope its impact is more lasting. True, there are reasons for optimism. The euro crisis is behind us and economic fundamentals in Europe are strong and improving. For the euro area as a whole, the recovery is now in its fifth year and broad-based in terms of both countries and sectors involved. Most importantly, the employment situation, which is the Achilleso heel of European societies, is gradually improving. The euro area unemployment rate is at the lowest level since the end of 2008. The number of employed is growing for the fourth consecutive year. A suspicious feature of the recovery is that the inflation rate has been very low compared to the ECB definition of price stability (of below but close to two per cent). In particular, ocoreo inflation, which excludes the most volatile components of food and energy prices, has been hovering around one per cent for several years. The Eurozone recovery is a result of the positive feedback loop between the growing world economy, the largely completed fiscal and balance-of-payments adjustment, and much improved credit conditions. The expansionary monetary policy of the ECB has been indispensable, and will be needed as long as price stability again is self.sustaining. As a sign of stronger fundamentals, the current accounts of the ex-deficit countries have also swung to balance or surplus. The Eurozone current account balance shows a sizable surplus, giving scope for increased investment in the coming years. As a result of the better of economic fundamentals, the political risks to Europeos progress seem now larger than the economic ones. While the situation in Catalonia remains tense and feeds uncertainty though with a limited market impact so far the overall political situation in the Eurozone reflects more constructive undercurrents. The recovery itself is creating political room for manoeuvre; and at the same time, the European sense of belonging together has strengthened on the face of world events. We should now use the improving economic circumstances and the political window of opportunity for pursuing a serious reform of the euro area, in order to make it a genuine stability union. The first and foremost priority is to complete the banking union. We have already successfully unified banking supervision under the ECB and created the single resolution mechanism, including bail-in rules and early intervention and resolution instruments for failing banks. What we still need to do to complete the banking union is two things. First, to create a credible fiscal backstop for the bank resolution fund. Second, to build a common European Deposit Insurance Scheme. To be politically feasible, these remaining elements will require convincing measures of risk reduction, and possibly some co-insurance features in their construction, at least in the first phase. Going further, we have the Commissionos policy paper, the initiative of the French President and the non-paper of the German Ministry of Finance on the table. None of these alone cannot carry the day. In reforming the architecture of the Eurozone we would do well to combine the best elements of German and French thinking, which is elegantly described by Markus Brunnermeier, Harold James and Jean-Pierre Landau in their milestone oThe Euro and the Battle of Ideaso. The next reform of the Eurozone architecture should aim at producing a plausible, viable synthesis between, on the one hand, the core principles of oGermano economic philosophy, which calls for properly tuned incentives and rules, and those of oFrencho economic philosophy, which emphasizes insurance and stabilization I would call this a European synthesis. (And I use the quotation marks deliberately, as these national adjectives are only proxies for two economic philosophies, not owned just by the two countries.) I found the joint contribution of 15 French and German leading economists, published in September, most relevant in this regard, with its call for a constructive rethinking of the inherited national positions on the question of the future development of the EMU. That means building a solid stability union that emphasizes each member stateos own responsibility and joint structures to preserve financial stability. The first principle of a stability union is that each member state should primarily be responsible for its own economic policy, and the rules and incentives should be designed accordingly. The second principle is that there needs to be sufficient capacity to joint Eurozone action to preserve financial stability in case of market turbulence. Moreover, it is essential that steps towards further sharing of risk are equally matched by steps to reduce risk. This goes both for public finances and the banking union. Let me conclude by correcting one flaw that is often seen in the media. The dichotomy of ofederation or deatho as options for the Eurozone is raised frequently, for propaganda reasons. It is a fake news and has no factual basis. The euro area will not become a federation or transfer union, but it will not break up just because of not becoming one. Instead, we need both a sense of direction and a sense of realism. The essential guiding principle in reforming the Eurozone economic governance is that we must work to ensure financial stability through co-insurance and risk sharing, while any step towards increased solidarity and merger of economic risk should be combined with increased responsibility and economic sustainability. In the meantime, we Europeans need to continue reforming our real economies and the European social model. Not nostalgically clinging to the status quo, since that would only lead to a permanent economic decline and social stagnation. Not dismantling the European model, because we believe in the combination of a stability culture, entrepreneurial drive and social justice. But instead, by genuinely reforming and modernizing Europeos social market economy, for the sake of sustainable growth and job creation. Title: Financial stability as a priority for the reform of the euro area
text: Olli Rehn, Member of the Executive Board: Financial stability as a priority for the reform of the euro area. Public hearing of the Finance Committee and the Grand Committee. Helsinki, 19.10.2017. . Speech . Thursday19 October 2017, 12:30 PM Olli Rehn, Member of the Executive Board, Bank of Finland Joint public hearing of the Finance Committee and the Grand Committee on economic and monetary union (EMU) in depth Helsinki, 19.10.2017 FINANCIAL STABILITY THE FOCUS OF THE REFORM OF THE EURO AREA Thank you for the invitation to the joint public hearing of the Finance and Grand Committee. This is a very timely occasion, as the next stage in the reform of the EU's economic and monetary union is the process of reforming the EU's economic and monetary union. With a proactive approach, Finland can influence the direction of the solution, especially as many of the key players ? the Commission and the other Member States ? do not have a common understanding of the direction of emu development. On the other hand, the basis for the reform is that the basic elements of the euro area economy are now in better shape than they have been for a long time. The recovery started in 2013 and growth is now more broad-based than before. Even in crisis countries, budgetary and current account balances have been brought under control and employment in the euro area has improved significantly. Recovery does not mean going back to the pre-crisis situation. In 2010 ? 12, difficult steps were taken to overcome the crisis and stabilise the economy. The stability mechanism created at that time and the reforms carried out strengthened the euro area's ability to resist and move on a sustained growth path, which paved the way for the ECB's purchase programmes in August and September 2012. Stable growth and employment require that one of the fragile points of economic and monetary union, as revealed by the crisis, be rectified. As Finland is a member of the euro area, it is of course also in our interest that the Economic and Monetary Union should function steadily and support sustainable growth and employment. That is why the Finnish debate on economic and monetary union should move from the setting up of crisis management to the planning phase of a stable system. The most important lesson of the crisis is the importance of the stability of the financial system for the growth and stint of the national economy. Part of this is a banking union that strengthens the stability of financial systems and builds better financing conditions for companies of all sizes ? and thus sustainable growth and jobs for citizens. Significant progress has been made on the banking union through the creation of a single banking supervision and resolution mechanism. In resolution, the responsibility of investors has been increased. At the same time, financial stability in the euro area has improved. Like all other central banks, the Bank of Finland considers that there are reasons to continue to strengthen the basis for the euro area's financing system. What would we particularly like to focus on? 1. First, the common deposit guarantee scheme must be sufficient to maintain a high level of trust, even in bad times. The mere existence of national deposit guarantee schemes is not sufficient to maintain the confidence of depositors in the event of serious crises. The construction of a common deposit insurance scheme could well be carried out on the basis of the principle of insurance, which could be the case with the new proposal adopted by the Commission last week. Progress in the field of a common deposit insurance scheme is very important, especially for small countries such as Finland, where the banking system is concentrated and where large banks operate in the size of the country. 2.However, the completion of the banking union requires that problems inherited from the period prior to the banking union, such as the large volume of unmanaged credit, have been resolved to ensure that risks are mitigated at the same time as common structures are strengthened. There is also the question of how the sovereign debt held by the banks is accounted for in the bank. Many banks in the euro area have a large number of debt securities from their home countries on their balance sheets, which feeds into the harmful link between public finances and national banking systems. There are reasons why we are looking for a solution so that the bank takes into account the risks of government bonds over a long period of time. However, care should be taken to ensure that the negative market effects of the transition phase are mitigated. 3.There are also reasons to strengthen the Single Resolution Fund. It would need to be backed up by a contingency system, which was agreed between the Member States four years ago (2013), but which has not yet been implemented. The contingency system would act as the last piece of work to be activated if the resources of the ? European Resolution Fund, which is in place only after the implementation of investor responsibility, proved to be sufficient to deal with the p??komisations. The European Commission rightly stated last week that this kind of contingency planning should be put in place as soon as possible. In the Commission's view, the European Stability Mechanism (ESM) could act as a system for which it would need a dedicated lending mandate. It could also be a key part of the mandate of the European Monetary Fund, if it were to be set up. Resolution and deposit guarantee schemes that support financial stability play a key role in the functioning of the monetary union. Their credibility already proves that they need to be used. 4. With regard to the development of EMU, Finland should take the initiative and be active. Now is the right time for this, when the various countries and the Commission have made proposals. Why not pursue a European synthesis of the various parties involved? One interesting suggestion, for example, is the petition published in September by 15 German and French economists to promote constructive cooperation and hopefully to resonate. This combines the construction of a stability union in accordance with German economic thinking with the emphasis of French thinking on investment and growth. The coordination of economic policies is an example of an area where such synthesis is needed. In this area, there is a strategy based on the same level of solidarity and stability mechanisms, on the one hand, and market discipline, on the other. The confrontation is exaggerated. That is why market discipline is needed: under normal circumstances, the economies of the euro area countries should be kept healthy enough to play the role of market discipline and debt arrangements, and to act as a deterrent that they do not often have to resort to. The committee asked for cooperation to proceed, either by governments or by strengthening the role of the Commission. From Finland's point of view, it is worthwhile to be concerned about the future of the common process, since it is the most effective method in terms of the legitimacy and efficiency of the work of the p????ensen , i.e. it creates the conditions for the emergence of a ????? and all the Member States, including the smaller ones, are involved in influencing the process 5. An acceptable alternative is to strengthen economic and monetary union in which the Member States' own responsibility for economic growth and employment, as well as the joint coordination of economic policies, are balanced with its insurance cover, which is what common structures provide for risk management. Now that the reform of the euro area is under way, Finland can actively influence the outcome of a stability union such as this one. The Bank of Finland and its experts are also involved in the preparation of Finland's position papers on the development of monetary union. speech (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagpuhe) Olli Rehn (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagOlli Rehn) Emu (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagEMU) euro area (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tageuroalue) renewal (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?taguudistaminen) rahoitusvakaus (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagrahoitusvakaus)

Thursday19 October 2017, 12:30 PM Johtokunnan jsen Olli Rehn Suomen Pankki Valtiovarainvaliokunnan ja suuren valiokunnan yhteinen julkinen kuuleminen Talous-ja rahaliiton (EMU) syventmisest Helsinki, 19.10.2017 RAHOITUSVAKAUS EUROALUEEN UUDISTAMISEN PAINOPISTEEN Kiitn kutsusta thn valtiovarain-ja suuren valiokunnan yhteiseen julkiseen kuulemiseen. Tilaisuus on kovin ajankohtainen, sill EU:n talous-ja rahaliiton uudistamisen seuraava vaihe on kynnistymss. Suomi voi aloitteellisella otteella vaikuttaa ratkaisun suuntaan, etenkin kun monilla keskeisill toimijoilla  komissiolla ja muilla jsenvaltioilla  ei ole EMU:n kehittmisen suunnasta viel yhteist nkemyst. Uudistustylle luo pohjaa toisaalta se, ett euroalueen talouden perustekijt ovat nyt paremmassa kunnossa kuin aikoihin. Elpyminen kynnistyi kevll 2013 ja kasvu on nyt entist laaja-alaisempaa. Kun Suomi on euroalueen jsen, on luonnollisesti mys meidn etumme mukaista, ett talous-ja rahaliitto toimii vakaasti ja tukee kestv kasvua ja tyllisyytt. Siksi suomalaisen talous-ja rahaliittoa koskevan keskustelun olisi siirryttv kriisinhallinnan asetelmista vakaan jrjestelmn suunnittelun vaiheeseen. Kriisin trkein opetus on se, miten suuri merkitys rahoitusjrjestelmn vakaudella on kansantalouden kestvlle kasvulle ja tyllisyydelle. Trke osa tss tyss on pankkiunioni, jolla vahvistetaan rahoitusjrjestelmn vakautta ja rakennetaan parempia rahoitusolosuhteita kaikenkokoisille yrityksille  ja siten kestv kasvua ja tyt kansalaisille. Samalla euroalueen rahoitusvakaus on parantunut. Yht kaikki muiden keskuspankkien tavoin Suomen Pankki katsoo, ett tyt euroalueen rahoitusjrjestelmn perustan vahvistamiseksi on syyt jatkaa. Mihin jatkotyss tulisi mielestmme erityisesti keskitty? 1. Ensinnkin yhteisen talletussuojajrjestelmn tulee olla riittvn vahva yllpitmn luottamusta huonoinakin aikoina. Pelkt kansalliset talletussuojajrjestelmt eivt ole riittvi tallettajien luottamuksen yllpitmiseksi vakavien kriisien kohdatessa. Yhteisen talletussuojan rakentaminen voitaisiin hyvin kynnist jlleenvakuutuksen periaatteella, miss lhtkohtana voisi pit komission viime viikolla antamaa uutta esityst. Riskien vhentmiseen liittyy mys kysymys pankkien hallussa olevan valtionvelan ksittelyst pankkisntelyss. Monilla euroalueen pankeilla on taseessaan paljon niiden kotivaltioiden velkapapereita, mik ruokkii haitallista kohtalonyhteytt valtiontalouksien ja kansallisten pankkijrjestelmien vlill. Tm olisi kuitenkin tehtv huolella niin, ett siirtymvaiheen kielteiset markkinavaikutukset kyetn ehkisemn. 3.Mys yhteist kriisinratkaisurahastoa on syyt vahvistaa. Sek sntj ett markkinakuria tarvitaan: sntjen olisi pystyttv normaalioloissa pitmn euroalueen maiden taloudenpito niin terveell kannalla, ett markkinakurin ja velkajrjestelyjen rooliksi jisi toimia sinns hydyllisen pelotteena, johon ei tarvitsisi usein turvautua. Title: Appearance before the Parliamentary Committee of Inquiry into the Spanish crisis and the financial sector assistance programme
text: Olli Rehn: Appearance before the Parliamentary Committee of Inquiry into the Spanish crisis and the Spanish financial sector assistance programme . Speech . Thursday2 November 2017, 3:00PM Olli Rehn Member of the Board of Bank of Finland Appearance of Olli Rehn before the Parliamentary Committee of Inquiry into the Spanish crisis and the Spanish financial sector assistance programme Madrid, 2 November 2017 (Presentation pdf (/globalassets/fi/media-ja-julkaisut/puheet/documents/2017-11-02-olli-rehn-madrid.pdf)) Check against delivery APPEARANCE OF OLLI REHN BEFORE THE PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE OF INQUIRY INTO THE SPANISH CRISIS AND THE SPANISH FINANCIAL SECTOR ASSISTANCE PROGRAMME Distinguished Speaker Ana Mara Pastor Julin, Honourable Members of Congreso de los Diputados I. INTRODUCTION Let me first thank you for the invitation to appear before this Parliamentary Committee of Inquiry into the Financial Crisis in Spain and the Financial Sector Program. I have been asked to give testimony on the different dimensions of the financial crisis in Spain and the financial sector reform program, as a former Vice-President of the European Commission responsible for economic and monetary affairs. In my presentation, I will set the Spanish crisis into its context of the Eurozone crisis and focus on three main issues: first, on the causes of the financial and economic crisis in Spain (on this, I can be relatively brief, since the causes are rather well-known by now, and I can broadly agree with Deputy Director-General Servaas Deroose of DG ECFIN who appeared here earlier today);second, on the remedies and decisions related to the financial sector program and its policy outcomes by looking at the progress in economic recovery;and third, on the lessons that can and should be learnt from the Spanish crisis as well as the wider Eurozone crisis for reforming the Economic and Monetary Union. Before dwelling into substance, I need to make two reservations: first, my term responsible for economic and monetary affairs covered the years 2010-14, so I will focus on that period; second, I am speaking in my personal capacity, not on behalf of the Bank of Finland. II. THE CONTEXT: THE EUROZONE CRISIS For a start, it is useful to look at the overall evolution of the Eurozone economy in the last decade, seen below from the simple but telling perspective of real GDP in the Eurozone in 2008-2017. The Eurozone debt crisis evolved in various stages and was an adjacent to the financial crisis, which started in 2007.8 in the United States and became a global one in 2008-9. In Europe, the global financial crisis turned into a debt crisis which is often perceived as a public debt crisis, but actually was at its root a balance of payment crisis, or a crisis of macroeconomic imbalances, caused by the increase in both private and public debt, in the Spanish case mostly private debt, especially related to the boom in the construction sector and the real estate market. Essentially, the crisis was a classic story of boom and bust, the accumulation of large economic and financial imbalances, unwinding of those imbalances and dealing with the consequences of these unwindings. The strength of the housing boom was intensified by several factors: mortgage interest rates fell a lot, making mortgages extremely cheap. Banks used securitization intensively. As the crises hit, the property developers were left with thousands of unsold and even unfinished properties and a piles of debt. The most intense period of the Eurozone crisis was between 2010 and 2013. The chronology of the crisis can be divided into five stages: 1. As a prologue, the global financial crisis in 2007-9, which hit the Eurozone hard and reduced its GDP by the dramatic 4.5 percent. However, by effective global policy coordination, very substantial monetary and fiscal stimulus packages were agreed, which helped the world economy to recover in the course of 2009-10. Yet, the unemployment rate in the Eurozone jumped in two years of the financial crisis by 2.5 percentage points, i.e. from 7.5% in mid-2007 to 10.0% in end-20091. This led to large structural unemployment and thus to deep social and human scars in Europe. 2. The outbreak of the Greek crisis and the pressing, improvised debt crisis management in 2009-10, with Greece at its epicenter. The Greek program was decided in May 2010. Soon after, Ireland (in November 2010) and Portugal (in April 2011) had to request a conditional financial assistance program, too. The EU was caught off-guard by the debt crisis, without any viable financial stability tools at its disposal, and with the weight of the global financial crisis still on its shoulders. However, at this stage it was still mostly a matter of small states, and thanks to the new tools that were created (particularly the reform of economic governance through the so-called six-pack legislation, as well as the European Financial Stability Mechanism and European Financial Stability Facility, or the EFSM and EFSF), the small states' bushfires were successfully prevented from turning to continent-wide forest fires. 3. The Italian and Spanish crises of 2011-12, which constituted a creeping, protracted confidence crisis and even more dangerous stage than the first one. Both countries faced immense market pressure and very high bond yields, which led to credit rating downgrades and threatened the sustainable service of their public debt. Even France was touched by these headwinds. The credit downgrades and the simultaneous deleveraging and increase of non.performing loans in the banking sector had negative ramifications to the lending capacity of these countries' banks. This in turn led to a decline in private lending to enterprises, especially SMEs, and became a form of a liquidity trap. 4. The stabilization was reached after strenuous efforts in 2012-13, with the combination of the re-instated credibility of fiscal policy by the member states, the creation of the permanent European Stability Mechanism and the ECB's bold action to contain the contagion in the financial markets. During these years, the rebalancing of the Eurozone economy gathered pace, especially in the countries that had had large current account deficits. But its economic performance was dualistic: the financial markets and public finances stabilized first, while sustained growth and job creation only recovered with delay, from spring 2013 on. 5. The stage of recovery and growth was reached in 2013 and has since been going on. Yet, the recovery was for many years fragile and haunted by deflationary dangers, geopolitical tensions and governance weaknesses. In 2016-17 the Eurozone growth however accelerated, and its per capita growth was stronger than that of the United States. In 2018, the Eurozone will be growing for the fifth year in row. Inflation is still under control or rather, below the price stability target which should be reached in a sustainable manner and this reduces pressures for rapid reactions in monetary policy that could slow down the growth rate. III. FINANCIAL SECTOR PROGRAMME In July 2012, the Eurogroup decided on a conditional financial assistance program for Spain which implied granting a maximum of 100 billion euros of loans for bank recapitalization to Spain. A program seeking to reform the banking sector was approved in July. The program included a first-aid reserve of 30 billion euros. Something had been learned in crisis management by 2012. For once, the Eurogroup and the Commission worked closely in tandem and decided to overshoot rather than undershoot, which was crucial for the credibility of the Spanish rescue operation and for the financial stability of the Eurozone. This was decisive to show that we were finally if not ahead but at least not behind the curve. The markets took our commitment to effectively recapitalize the Spanish banking sector very seriously, as the maximum figure 100 billion euros was assumed to be clearly above the expected needs. In the end, Spain used only around 41 billion of the financial sector assistance programme of 100 billion. I can say we worked very well with the respective Spanish Governments. Moreover, the competent preparation by the Spanish authorities, not least by the central bank,Banco de Espaa, was crucial for the success of the Spanish program. This was substantially aided by the high-quality work of the Commission mission team, led by Deputy Director-General Servaas Deroose. IV. IMPRESSIVE RECOVERY IN SPAIN We should try to learn lessons of the crises but also the lessons of the recoveries. The recovery in Spain has been impressive. Once the GDP started to grow, the rate of growth has been strong (slide 4) The competitiveness has improved in terms of unit labour costs (slide 5) The deleveraging of the Spanish corporate sector has been painful (slide 6) Corporate borrowing does not decline anymore (slide 7) The loan quality has improved in terms of the share of non-performing exposures (slide 8) The amount and share of housing-related doubtful is steeply declining (slide 9) V. LESSONS Against this backdrop, it is more than warranted to properly analyse the lessons learnt from the Eurozone debt crisis. Generals, as the saying goes, are always preparing for the previous war. Maybe so, but, the euro area debt crisis has provided a wealth of lessons of general application. Based on the crisis experience, I see the following three lessons as key issues for rebuilding the EMU: 1. Financial stability was grossly neglected before the crisis, and this should now be corrected by completing the banking union. Based on my experience in the fire brigade during the debt crisis, stability of the financial system is crucially important for the macro-economy, i.e. for sustainable growth and employment. The nadir or rather, the worst rock-bottom of the crisis followed the worst phase of market turbulence, which raged untamed until the European Stability Mechanism was put in place and the ECB had launched its unconventional monetary policy measures as the lender of last resort. As Daniel Gros has noted, financial stability proved to be the "neglected stepchild" of the Maastricht Treaty. As a result, we Europeans paid a bitter price in the form of a double-dip recession in 2008d2012 and suffered years of high unemployment. Against this backdrop, the near-term focus should be kept on finalisation of the banking union. Our goal should be a strong banking union based on the bail-in principle, which means that the private sector, the owners and the investors, should bear losses for bank failures before taxpayers. What we still need to do is two things. First, to create a credible fiscal backstop for the bank resolution fund. Second, to build a common European Deposit Insurance Scheme. To be politically feasible, these remaining elements will require convincing measures of risk reduction, and possibly some co-insurance features, at least in the first phase. Legacy bank problems at the national level should not be shifted on to the euro-area level. Member states should work out the legacy problems on their own. This is what recent solutions to winding up troubled banks have sought to achieve. 2. For the sake of financial stability, and also to prevent future crises, the EMU needs a lender of last resort and an effective financial stability mechanism, which it now has, but can be further developed. That's why we must recognize the critical importance of the function of the lender of last resort both for solvent sovereigns and for solvent financial institutions in the case of market panic. In practice, this means that any jurisdiction, including the Eurozone, must possess a financial stabilization mechanism, or a big bazooka (in the popular language and financial journalism), so that a central bank, a separate stability fund, or both, have the tools to come to the rescue in a crisis and subdue even a major market panic. It is needed proactively and permanently to pre-empt them. One of the lessons of the crisis is that prevention is always better than correction. The ESM can be further developed by e.g. reinforcing its capacity to take decisions and extending its toolbox with a more effective and workable precautionary credit instrument. 3. In building the stability union, the main responsibility for economic policies should rest with the member states, while this responsibility should be balanced with the insurance provided by common structures, especially as regards ensuring financial stability. Going forward further and maybe deeper as well we have the Commission's policy paper, the initiative of the French President and the non-paper of the German Ministry of Finance on the table. None of these alone can carry the day. Therefore, the next reform of the Eurozone architecture should aim at producing a plausible, viable synthesis between, on the one hand, the core principles of "German" economic philosophy, which calls for properly tuned incentives and rules, and those of "French" economic philosophy, which emphasizes insurance and stabilization I would call this a European synthesis or Spanish and Finnish, why not! Here I use the quotation marks deliberately, as these national adjectives are only labels for two economic philosophies, not owned just by the two countries. I found the joint contribution of 15 French and German leading economists, published in September, most relevant in this regard, with its call for a constructive rethinking and re-consideration of the inherited national positions on the question of the future development of the EMU. That means building a solid stability union which emphasizes each member state's own responsibility and joint structures to preserve financial stability. The second principle is that there needs to be sufficient capacity for joint Eurozone action to preserve financial stability in case of market turbulence. Moreover, it is essential that steps towards further sharing of risk are equally matched by steps to reduce risk. This goes both for public finances and the banking union. VI. CONCLUSIONS The euro area will not become a federation or transfer union, but neither will it break up just because of not becoming one. In any case, its architecture must be further reinforced, and there is a third way by combining risk reduction and risk sharing. The dichotomy of 'federation or death' has been put forward too often, and frequently for propaganda reasons. It is fake news, and has no factual basis. The euro area will not survive by simply becoming a federation or transfer union, but neither will it break up just because of not becoming one. Life is seldom black-and-white. Instead, there is a third way we need both a sense of direction and a sense of realism. The essential guiding principle in reforming the Eurozone economic governance is that we must work to ensure financial stability through co-insurance and risk sharing, while any step towards increased solidarity and merger of economic risk should be combined with increased responsibility and economic sustainability. The most promising and, to my mind, preferable option for the Eurozone reform is to strengthen such a stability union in which the Member States' own responsibility for sustainable economic growth and employment, on one hand, and the common economic policy co-ordination with its insurance coverage of joint structures providing risk management, on the other hand, are in balance. I wish we can work together with the "Congreso de los Diputados" for such a genuinely European outcome. Thank you for your attention. 1Eurostat, Euro area unemployment at 9.1%. Such anniversaries always get us to have a gun for a while and reflect on the achievements of past generations. Especially in the year of the 100th anniversary of our self-sufficiency, a little remembrance of history is in order, even one that is older than Finland's self-worth. That older history includes, among other things, the dynamism of s?shshbanks. In economic terms, Finland's history has been a success story. In the late 1800s, our country was one of the most kchymost corners of Europe. The newly created Lammi S???bank was located in a country whose industrialization had just begun. Since then, we have caught up with economic development, where we have remained despite the setbacks of the last decade. It is difficult to unequivocally measure the rise in living standards. In peacetime, real GDP per person is still a measure of the satisfactory standard of living of the VHhinch?nk, and according to that metric, our standard of living has risen tenfold in a few generations. We can feel a small sense of national pride with a clear conscience. There were no Lammi S??shbanks, but it is about as old as Finland as a developing nation and a dynamic economy. When your bank was founded, The Seven Brothers of the Stone was a new, almost printed book. Jean Sibelius was a schoolboy who, only a few years ago, would write the first s?vellyksens on the notes.
