Title: Finnish economy in euro time
text: Member of the Board Pentti Hakkarainen: Finnish economy in euro time . Speech . Monday19 April 2004, 12:00 AM Seminar 19.4.2004 at THE NOBEL INSTITUT, Oslo Ladies and Gentlemen, first of all I would like to thank for this opportunity to give a presentation on the Finnish economy in euro time. In my presentation to you today I would like to put before you the challenges Finland is faced with in its membership in the EMU the Economic and Monetary Union. There are three angles to evaluate the Finnish economy in 'euro time'. First it can be viewed from the point of entry, i.e. the economic circumstances at that time and the debates regarding our entry. Then secondly we can look at the current economic situation. Thirdly we must assess the economic outlook, and there I will take you through some key points of the bank's forecast for the coming 2 years. Last of all I will conclude by highlighting some potential challenges we have in our economy. Perhaps a word of caution is needed. We have been a member of the monetary union only 5 years, which may be far too short a time to come to final conclusions on the subject. I will nevertheless try to provide you with an early assessment of Finland's economic performance. Above all, one issue that I would like to highlight is the fact that Finland does not stand in isolation. When assessing the position we are in and the challenges that lie ahead, we must recall that we are irrevocably linked to the euro and more than ever must see ourselves in a global perspective. Thus, developments of the global economy not only European but also United States' and Asian economies should be taken into account when assessing Finland's economic development. Entering into the monetary union Without doubt, the Finnish decision to join the monetary union was not motivated by economic considerations alone. Political motives played an important role as well. One of the key expectations was that being part of the 'inner circle' of the European Union would bring with it the chance to maximise Finland's influence in Europe. Yet, without doubt, economic considerations were crucial and constantly referred to in heated debates on whether or not to join. Finnish monetary policy had traditionally suffered from a lack of credibility, where devaluation was repeatedly used as a means of restoring competitiveness and this was directly reflected in interest rates. Critics blamed this for many of the structural problems the country suffered from, such as large investment rates relative to growth and the chronic weakness of the current account. It was anticipated that monetary policy credibility would strengthen, and that interest rates would be lower and more stable if the country were to join the monetary union. This should in turn enhance investment and economic growth. However, there were also some concerns expressed regarding losing our independent monetary policy and the possibility for devaluating our currency in case of unforeseen economic adverse shocks. Generally speaking when there are shocks affecting different countries differently, i.e. so called asymmetric shocks, each country can use its monetary policy or exchange rate movements to adjust accordingly. It should be pointed out that most of the studies made before the EMU showed that the economic structure of Finland deviated clearly from the rest of the EU. Therefore the expected difficulty of adjusting to asymmetric economic shocks without national money was considered the main objection to Finland's membership. Experiences and outcomes of Finland joining the EMU Looking at Finland's official membership of the EMU at the beginning of 1999, when the union became a reality in the sense of permanently fixed exchange rates and a single monetary policy, we can see in retrospect that Finnish monetary policy converged almost completely with that of Germany already much earlier. Inflation fell been below 2% and the floating exchange rate was fairly stable already from 1994 onwards. Let me remind you of the fact that when Finland joined the euro, the country had just recovered from very severe economic and financial crises. This means that, the effects of our membership are intrinsically mixed with the effects of the crises, such as the significant depreciation of the currency, a sudden increase in government debt, and mergers and acquisitions as well as privatisations in both banking and industry sectors. The Finnish experience in the early 1990s stood out from similar experiences of its neighbouring Nordic countries; not least because of the coinciding sudden collapse of Soviet export markets which strongly intensified the crises. Over only a few years, our GDP decreased by an unprecedented 10% and unemployment rate increased from below 4% close to a staggering 18%. While another factor and one that makes it difficult to isolate the positive effects of the EMU is the remarkable impact of the so called 'new economy' in Finland. From late 1990s onwards our economic performance has been dominated by the exceptional growth of the high-tech electronics industry led by the success of Nokia. The information and communication technology sector as a whole contributed to a so strong a boom that the effects of the new monetary regime are hard to distinguish from technology-related changes in the economy. Current economic situation and outlook for the future Let me now turn to the current economic situation. To a large extent, the expectations we had of the effects EMU membership have, in fact, materialised. Credibility in monetary policy has been achieved as the promise of lower interest rates has become a reality. Although this is, indisputably, partly an international phenomenon, interest rates in Finland have been somewhat lower and more stable than in Sweden and the UK, who both remain outside the monetary union. In the environment of the common monetary policy, Finnish economic development has clearly exceeded the average of the other Eurosystem members (slide: Total output). This is partly due to a powerful but favourable asymmetric shock in the form of an IT boom that was much stronger in Finland than in the euro area on average. The slide shows also that the euro area is far from being homogenous yet and Germany's economy in particular has been lagging, which has had a downward effect on the area's overall GDP levels. Without doubt, one essential development has been the increasing level of openness in the economy. This has taken place at several levels as the share of exports in the country's GDP has increased. But the change has been substantial in the financial markets with a very rapid growth in portfolio investments and direct investments. The improvement of the current account is all the more significant, since Finland had not had large current account surpluses for several decades. Moreover, these surpluses have been recorded at a time when economic growth is robust previously periods of robust economic growth were typically associated with large external deficits. The increase in foreign direct investment has happened together with a sharp improvement in the profitability of export industries and a decline in their domestic fixed investment. The period has also seen the expansion of Finnish multinational companies on an unprecedented scale. Much of direct Finnish investment abroad has been in the form of takeovers, especially in the forest industries, however there have also been plenty of industrial greenfield projects in foreign markets. Fundamentally, Finland is in shape. The country's economy is doing well; in fact it is showing higher-than-average results against its fellow euro area members. This is set against the backdrop of a world economic situation which has taken a cyclical change for the better during the course of 2003 with growth being driven by the United States and several countries in Asia. Although recent developments have been favourable, there are still uncertainties about growth continuing over the longer term due to major imbalances in these big economies. All things considered, Finland has emerged well from the extended international recession. Its balance sheets have remained relatively strong and the prospects for growth in domestic demand in the immediate years ahead appear bright. The Bank of Finland forecasts slightly less than 3% annual GDP growth for the coming 2 years. We foresee that this growth will be sustained by quite strong household consumption, the gradual stimulus to the export sector from the improving world economy and a gradual recovery in investment. We should note that growth will however remain clearly slower than in the late 1990s. The information technology boom brought with it a remarkable growth in industrial production from the electronics industry (slide: Industrial output in Finland). However, as far as exports are concerned, the electronics industry is still supported by almost equal shares in the export market with the more traditional Finnish strong industrial pillars of the paper and forestry sector as well as the metals industry. Although it is felt that Finland's exports over the next few years are likely to be rather lacklustre, compared with the brisk pace of the international economy, a 7% growth forecast for export markets is likely to permit healthy growth of as much as 5 to 6% in Finland's export of goods and services. We foresee that the inflation outlook is probably going to remain subdued. The inflationary pressures on goods and services have eased although housing prices have accelerated, largely as a result of the low interest rates. It is likely that the strengthening economy and continuing low interest rates will keep these housing prices on a gentle upward curve, at least for some time, and we see that there is a clear risk of overheating in the housing market. The outlook for public finances is stable even though there has been a decrease in general government revenue relative to GDP, partly due to tax cuts, and central government will move slightly into deficit later this year. Overshadowing all of the positive development is unemployment. The upward turn in the world economy has not yet been reflected in exports and industrial output in the manner expected. In fact, industrial employment has been in decline for almost two years already, and the overall employment rate for 2006 is forecast as being a dismal 68%. The unemployment rate, meanwhile, is falling far too slowly, which can, in turn, have an adverse affect on consumer sentiment. This brings us to an essential indicator of economic growth confidence, both industrial and consumer confidence (slides: Consumer confidence and Industrial confidence indicator). In fact, confidence indicators have been good in forecasting growth, since there has been a tight correlation between the confidence expressed and the actual economic development that follows behind. In Finland, confidence indicators are clearly at higher levels than in the euro area. Apart from the impact of the increased value of the euro, Finnish industry has been hampered by its production structure, which is not oriented towards the growth sectors of world trade. This means that, contrary to expectations, Finland has been slow to benefit from the return to growth elsewhere in the world. There is a clear need for Finnish industry to become more responsive to the global competition. Downside risks and upside surprises To recall a point I made earlier Finland is not an economy in isolation of the global economy and the sluggish pace of recovery in fixed investment is a key issue facing our industry. A rise in US long-term interest rates and the continued depreciation of the dollar would have a negative effect on the entire world economy. Another, very different sort of risk to the international economy concerns the low level of interest rates, the present abundance of global liquidity and the opening up of the Chinese economy, where there is an increased danger of over-investment and, by extension, overheating. This could lead to a serious crisis first in China, and repercussions could also be felt in many traditional sectors in the industrialised nations. Despite this, the tentativeness of the forecast for the world economy also leaves space for positive surprises. If we look for a moment towards the United States we can see that major improvements in productivity and cost savings have enabled companies recently to strengthen their balance sheets considerably. There could, therefore, be a surprise on the way in the shape of a strong recovery in investment. Challenges ahead After these positive conclusions regarding Finland's EMU membership, let me say a few words of caution and explain some of the challenges the Finnish economy will face in the future. One of the major aspects of the future economic development relates to the fact that, according to demographic forecasts, the Finnish population will be ageing faster in the next couple of decades than that of most other European countries. It has been assessed that there will be a substantial extra burden on public finances in terms of pensions and other expenditures related to an ageing population. Despite the growth of the economy, employment in the industrial sector has diminished in recent years. We cannot avoid the fact that overall investment activity in Finland has remained low in fact the flow of direct investment would appear to be more outward than inward and there has been little increase in the country's productive capacity. The entry of the ten new member countries into the European Union in two weeks' time will surely intensify the competition for the placement of new factories and jobs. Moreover, the enlargement will undoubtedly intensify tax competition within the European Union a particular challenge to countries like Finland with high personal and marginal income tax rates. The response to these global challenges is to increase the dynamism and efficiency of the Finnish economy, have competitive tax rates, place even greater emphasis on research and development, maintain high level of education, and improve the efficiency of its public services. It is obvious that we cannot succeed in the global competition with conventional means like low-costs, natural resources, abundance of work force, etc. Finland would have to face most of these challenges, regardless of whether it was a member of the euro area or not. However, we believe that EMU membership provides us with a more stable monetary environment and a larger "home market". These characteristics seem to create confidence among business leaders, and even with the man in the street, in their expectations relating to future economic situation. Final conclusions Ladies and Gentlemen, having now taken you through our economical experiences in euro time, the key messages that I would like you to take away with you today are -that the decision to join the single currency has, for the time being, proven to be a sound solution for Finland, -that we are clearly able to benefit from being members of the euro area, and -that the Finnish economic outlook is rather bright, yet subject to international economic development. All in all, Finnish EMU membership seems, at this early stage, to have fulfilled most of its promises and enable Finland to have avoided most of its risks. The structural effects on the economy appear to have been favourable, as predicted. Clearly however, more time has to pass and the performance of the economy over more than one economic cycle has to be observed before any definite conclusions on these issues can be attempted.

Monday31 October 2005, 12:00 AM The economy is also volatile but crooked: lack of investment The rapid growth of the world economy gives the Finnish economy good points. The prolonged period of monetary easing, which has been triggered by, among other things, low loans, high and still rising asset prices, such as house prices in America and several European countries, could lead to corrections that would also give the Finnish economy a boost to global economic growth. Consumer demand is growing Growth continues to be driven by strong domestic demand. Private consumption will increase over the last few years, as well as good income trends and low interest rates will prolong the purchasing power of households. Households' confidence in the favourable development of the economy is essential. In addition, interest rates are in t?rke?, since, due to the rapid indebtedness of households, an unexpected rise in interest rates would be susceptible to a fall in consumer demand. The increase in consumption is also accompanied by risks of weaker than forecast development. The reversal of the long-standing rise in house prices is another risk which, if realised, would weaken consumer demand. Investments v?h?isi? The development of productive investments has been weak in recent years. The investment rate is less than 20% of GDP. Investment is a lifeline for a sustained rise in living standards. The current pace is eroding the basis for economic growth. In many sectors, there is a need to renew outdated capacity. It is therefore reasonable to expect that investment growth will accelerate. There is something strange about the fact that private investment is not growing much, even though financing is available on exceptionally favourable terms. Vienniss? hintaongelmia Exports also include water, and this supports the favourable development of the world economy and world trade. At the same time, when the import rate is rising in a trend-like fashion, there is no sign of diversification of exports. Without a clear increase in the investment rate, the current share of exports in GDP will begin before a long-term decline. Another problem is the weak development of export prices. Exports have increasingly focused on product groups where competition is particularly fierce. In the face of global competition, it is not possible to transfer our own home-made costs to the price. There is a risk that export prices will fall at an accelerated rate and that productivity will not increase sufficiently. The profitability of Czech export companies is deteriorating. Indeed, the terms of trade have declined continuously since 2002 and are projected to decline over the forecast horizon. On the other hand, studies show that a very important factor explaining the level of productivity is the structure of society, including political decision-making. Entrepreneurs and enterprises have the right, a legitimate interest, to demand from the municipalities of the economic area, as well as a responsible approach to developing the operating conditions for the economy. Title: Bank Director's speech at the Helsinki Region Chamber of Commerce's Traffic Days 2006
text: Speech by Bank Director Pentti Hakkarainen at the Helsinki Region Chamber of Commerce Traffic 2006 . Speech . Tuesday 14 March 2006, 12:00 AM Current challenges for the economy(summary) The global economy has grown at an exceptionally rapid pace in recent years and will continue to grow. As for the development of the world economy, there are some strange manifestations: the high price of sljy, growth is concentrated in different ways in different parts of the world, especially the abundance of money in the world, and the peculiar set-up of indebted and financing countries. The rapid growth of the world economy gives the Finnish economy good points. Our country may be in a state of flux. Good operating conditions must be ensured for businesses, businesses and the business community. It is not just a matter of attracting new players, but also of strengthening existing ones. The global economy is gaining momentum The global economy continues to grow at a rapid pace. The economic upturn that intensified in the second half of 2003 is predicted to be the end of the year d although the fastest phase is already behind us. The growth has been in the same way as in the various economic areas (Figure 1). In the United States, growth continued briskly last year, still based above all on strong private consumption. The effects of the cyclones on the nshytchvsvst and then. In Asia, China shows no signs of slowing down and japan's economy has finally improved. Last year, its growth reached lshes 3%. The pace of growth in the euro area has been subdued as expected, but since the second half of last year, signs of a strengthening of growth have increased. In addition to exports, investment demand is now also supporting production growth. The pain point remains household consumer demand, which has remained subdued. However, there are large country-specific differences in the structure of growth in the euro area. In addition to China, the other BRIC countries, Russia, Brazil and India, will contribute to the growth of the world economy. Economic growth in Vensjs, largely due to the high price of sljy, continues at an annual rate of about 6%. Brazil, too, has emerged from its economic plight. Its economic growth is likely to continue at a rate of 3-4%. India and the economy are often unnecessarily d overshadowed by China. However, its economy is growing rapidly, at around 7% a year, and the country is expected to become one of the most significant economies in the future. Extraordinary developments in the world economy, pre-skemschismis The global economy has exceptional characteristics; The price of sljy has reached an unforeseeable high level, growth is different around the world and investment is low in developed countries, liquidity, money, is very high, some countries are getting into debt and many new countries are becoming wealthier. In addition, the ilmist are supranational. ... the price of ljy rose as a result of a wide variety of factors generally regarded as one-off reasons; e.g. the uncertainties caused by the war in Iraq (Figure 2). Since then, the high price of sljy has been boosted above all by strong demand, while free production capacity has become scarce. Of course, the supply has played its own role, but it has played a more important role. Now, however, on the basis of futures prices and various forecasts, sljy and sljysts refined products such as motor fuels will remain expensive in the lshi years. ... The consumption of ljy has already increased for a long time more than the processing capacity of sljy. The effects of high prices on economic activity have so far been reduced to strong economic growth, and the increase in the price of sljy has hardly led to an acceleration in the rate of price or wage growth in other products. Asia is experiencing the fastest global economic growth, based on investment and exports. They have fuelled the growth of industrial production. In the United States, on the other hand, growth has been driven above all by activity in the household sector, which has been driven by strong private consumption and the heating up of the housing market. In the euro area, growth, in turn, was based on exports until the end of last year. As a result, the structure of growth has diverged quite significantly in recent years across the world economy. This, on the other hand, has been reflected in differences in current account developments. Traditionally, the growth structure has been more or less the same in different parts of the world, but now the whole economy is doing well, but for different reasons. Is the mismatch of the economic slowdown different from the nshty in our economic history? The level of investment is particularly prevalent in many advanced economies. The situation is different in the fast-growing Asian countries, especially in China. If investments are made, but they do not generate significant growth figures in the statistics, then investments are generally cheap. At the moment, growth potential is being created in Asia. The high level of willingness to invest in developed countries, high interest rates in Asia, the current monetary policy and the monetary policy pursued by central banks have created a situation in which real interest rates have fallen very low globally (Figure 3). There is a lot of money available and at an exceptionally low cost. The financial nature of the investment targets has contributed to the fact that the assets have been diverted to housing, capital shares and other assets. It is easy to create bubbles in the prices and values of this situation. Partly due to monetary policy with low interest rates, partly rising house prices and other reasons, households have become rapidly indebted d especially in the USA, but also in many European countries. On a global scale, it is also quite abundant that just a few years ago, ksyhins or otherwise considered to be countries in economic distress are financing the current account deficit of the world's richest country, the USA (Figure 4). The investments of China, India, Russia, Korea and many other growing economies in dollar-dollar bonds amount to approximately 2.7 trillion, or 2700 thousand million, the amount that could be used to make up for the US current account deficit for about 4 years. This situation means that these countries are financing the americans' celebration of consumption. Global economic corrections The imbalances that arise in the economy will be smoothed out in due course and excesses will be corrected. There are therefore reasons to investigate and anticipate what may be the corrections and their effects. Longterm interest rates have been low due to high liquidity. The situation will change if inflation expectations increase, if the level of investment rises or if Asian countries do not invest at the same rate as before in dollar bonds. If only something comes to fruition, it is obvious that interest rates will rise. At worst, this would lead to a slowdown in investment growth, lower house and fixed prices and lower share prices in the United States. The banking sector could also play its part in the addition of bad debts and non-performing loans. This would be further reflected in the tightening of credit conditions for businesses and consumers. Financing the us deficit problem has not been a problem for the country itself. In the last quarter of last year, or 3 months, preliminary data show that USD 250 billion flowed into the country. However, when there are limits to indebtedness, the problem unravels either uncontrollably or in a controlled manner. These are issues that have a key impact on the world economy. The uncontrolled correction is accompanied by a sharp depreciation of the dollar as foreign investors revise their dollar investments. At the same time, interest rates on dollar bonds are rising. As a result, housing values can kssntys invoice. Over-indebted households face financial difficulties. Consumer demand has a direct negative impact. As a result, the US economy would probably fall into recession or even recession, and it would easily lead to a global economic downturn. A controlled solution is desirable. It requires cooperation between several countries. In the USA, a reduction in the size of the general government budget would be desirable. Asian countries must continue to liberalise their economies, strengthen private consumption and allow their currencies to float more freely. In Europe, there are reasons why productivity growth is being promoted, particularly in the services sector, as a result of lower prices for services and an increase in the purchasing power of households and a strengthening of consumer demand. Finland's economy is growing Economic growth in Finland continues to be favourable (Figure 5). Due to the contract dispute in the paper industry, GDP growth slowed down to just over 2% last year but is expected to accelerate again in 2007 to just over 3% and continue at around 3% in 2007. Inflation is also accelerating. The reason for this is largely the sharp rise in energy prices that has already taken place, which is gradually taking the form of an increase in costs. However, in the lshi years, inflation remains under control and is below 2%. It is below the inflation rate of many of our competitors and strengthens the price competitiveness of our economy. A slowdown in global economic growth would also give a boost to the Finnish economy. The challenges lie in the high level of consumer demand, the rise in investment levels and the growth of exports. In Finland, consumer demand is growing The growth has been based on longterm strong domestic demand, especially household consumption and construction (Figure 6). Private consumption is likely to grow quite well even over the past few years, as well as a moderate real income trend, a recent improvement in employment and low interest rates, and a prolonged increase in the purchasing power of households. It is essential that household confidence in the favourable development of the economy continues to be maintained. Investments in our country vshsisis The development of productive investments has been weak in recent years. Worryingly, investment in machinery and equipment is below 6% of GDP, which is clearly lower than in the euro area, not to mention the United States (Figure 7). Investment is the lifeblood for a sustained rise in living standards. The current pace is eroding the basis for economic growth. In many sectors, there is a need to renew outdated capacity. It is therefore reasonable to expect that investment growth will accelerate. In terms of investments in machinery and equipment, however, there is no substantial change in the nskyvisss. In fact, according to an investment survey by the Federation of Finnish Industries, the growth in the value of fixed investment in industry will fall from last year's rate of 7% to about 1% in 2000. Price problems for Finnish exports Our exports are in the favourable development of world trade. However, there are problems with the structure of Finland's foreign trade. The first is the one-sidedness of exports. At the same time, when the import rate is rising in a trend-like fashion, there is no sign of diversification of exports. Another problem is the weak evolution of export prices (Figure 8). Exports have increasingly focused on product groups where competition is particularly fierce. There is a risk that export prices will fall at an accelerated rate and that productivity will not increase sufficiently. The weakening of the average ratio of export and import prices, the terms of trade, means that the revenue accrual in Finland is clearly developing at a slower pace than gdp growth could lead to the desired increase in household indebtedness and the fiscal base of public finances. The export is also the responsibility of the Vensjsn trade. Our geographical position provides opportunities for further expansion, e.g. for the export of consumer goods to Russia. Vensjs has recently become one of Finland's largest trading partners. However, the excellent export figures are partly due to exports. It applies above all to mobile phones and other electronics (Figure 9). Exports refer to the import of goods from abroad, first across finland's customs border, storage and, more recently, their export to Vensjs. In the statistics, these goods are recorded as imports and exports to Finland without being produced or, more specifically, processed in Finland. Thus, exports are different from traditional transit exports, i.e. transit trade, which are not included in Finland's international trade statistics. Common to both trade flows is that their effects on domestic income generation and employment are comparable. Finland must ensure competitiveness The favourable economic development is characterised by significant risks arising from the structure of our national economy. We cannot be lulled into a sense of good faith and believe that growth would continue without measures to improve the competitiveness of our national economy and strengthen the growth potential of the future. The improvement in the investment rate, and in particular in investment in machinery and equipment over the last few years, is needed in order to continue the current favourable productivity development and strengthen the growth potential of the economy over a longer period of time. We must also continue to invest in research and development. In particular, R&D investments in our traditional industries d in international comparison from the large countries of Finland's R&D expenditures are largely due to only one industry, the electronics industry. The right attitude plays a significant role. According to studies, a very important factor explaining the level of productivity is the structure of society, including political decision-making. We have shown speed in this area, for example, by providing energy supplies in the future. text: Bank Manager Pentti Hakkarainen's speech at the 60th anniversary seminar of OP Fixed Centres . Speech . Wednesday9August 2006,12:00 AM How long and fast will the housing market integrate? The cross-border movement of people, goods and services has an impact on the market. The European Union will create the most uniform conditions of action and competition throughout its territory. Financial markets in the euro area are long-term integrated. Such development increases competition, productivity and well-being. It will have a greater impact on the housing market and financing in Finland as well. A special feature of Finnish mortgage lending is the high proportion of variable rate loans, the risk of which is particularly noted by the extension of maturities. Housing market The housing market is becoming more integrated, but there are still national characteristics. Integration has intensified, especially since the 1990s. Sssntelys has been dismantled. The single currency and interest rates and the coordination of economic policies will harmonise the operating conditions in the euro area market. The integration process will be reinforced by the services directive, which has been ratified in return and which removes obstacles to crossborder housing construction, housing transactions and fixed housing. There will continue to be national factors due to the different economies of the countries, the state of play, the climate and the housing finance system. In the future, the requirements for the size, quality and price of dwellings will be integrated, as homebuyers will have better information and opportunities to compare housing in different countries. Construction companies are internationally established and as they operate more and more across borders, it is natural to expect more uniform standards than before. Foreign fixed investors have come to Finland and Finnish fixed investors are also investing abroad. Changes in different markets are closely monitored. Changes in the value of fixed assets in New York, for example, can have a direct impact on the fixed values of investors in European metropolises, including finland's largest cities. Asuntorahoitus The development of the housing market is linked to the integration of the housing finance system. In addition, one element of the objective of Europe's Economic and Monetary Union, an integrated financial market, is the harmonisation of housing finance. Although the financing conditions have started to vary from one euro area country to another, national differences persist, in particular as regards the forms of housing finance, interest rates and the criteria for borrowing rates. For example In Denmark, housing finance involves special fixed credit institutions and bonds issued by them. On the other hand, in many countries, among others. In Finland and Germany, a bank loan is a form of financing. Around half of all mortgages in the EU-15 are at fixed interest rates, while in Finland more than 90% is taken out as a variable rate loan, more commonly linked to euribor. In Finland, there has already been fierce competition in the price of mortgages and longer repayment periods for a long time. Price competition has contributed to the use of variable rate loans. Short-term market interest rates are low and have been tempted to tie the interest rate of the loan to them. This means that interest rate risk has been transferred from banks to households. But do households have the knowledge and control over interest rate risk? Banks are already providing basic advice to borrowers on risk. In addition, it is common to carry out solvency tests and warn against over-indebtedness. In view of the long maturities and the high proportion of variable rate loans, banks must ensure that those with housing loans are aware of the risks and means of hedging themselves. In addition, they shall develop interest rate risk hedging instruments that are suitable for individuals. Companies already have, for example, interest rate swaps and interest rate options that can be further developed into suitable mortgage products. Summary The direction of development of the housing market and d financing is clear; integration. Some of the effects are already nshty. This trend is slowed down by differences in national systems and consumer habits, which do not change momentarily. So there will be more repercussions. In the fixed market, international dependence has increased. Changes elsewhere have a direct impact on fixed markets and prices, as well as on investor participation and, in other respects, through the development of the global economy. Competition continues in Finnish housing finance. So far, banks have been able to make up for the narrowing mortgage margins with additional volumes. As a result of the ever-increasing supply of foreign banking services, financial institutions will continue to compete on price with a variety of products and services. In Finland, housing financing is predominantly variable-rate and borrowers have an interest rate risk related to the financing. Those with housing loans should therefore be provided with adequate means of hedging against interest rate risks. Title: Bank Manager's speech "A globalising economy and its impact on regional banking"
text: Bank Director Pentti Hakkarainen's speech "Globalising economy and its impact on regional banking" at the 100th anniversary celebration of Kiuruvesi Cooperative Bank . Speech . Sunday 19 November 2006,12:00AM Bank Manager Pentti Hakkarainen Kiuruvesi Cooperative Bank's 100th anniversary celebration Kiuruvesi 19.11.2006 Cooperative banking was mobilized by force, the state and the people's movement working together, more than a hundred years ago. Although the funds provided in the form of loans came from the State, the characteristic feature from the outset has been locality and customer involvement. This activity has been going on for a hundred years, and so has Kiuruvesi. The time has been full of many things, with wars and economic recessions. And cooperative banking has endured all the changes, and even strengthened. Has it been possible to operate on the edge of Yl?-Savo in Kiuruvesi, on its own terms and conditions? Will the profitability of cooperative banks in a globalised economy continue and will the local bank continue to meet all the demands that are already expected to be brought about by future developments? How are the effects of a rapidly changing world being felt? There is always confidence in the future. But are there now more challenges or challenges that are more difficult to cope with than in the last hundred years? It is worth looking first at the operating environment that prevailed in the early days of the cooperative fund and the conditions that have been endured over time. Then it is good to look at the challenges of the future and how the much-vaunted globalising economy will affect regional banking. Kiuruvesi Cooperative Bank's history book "Strong roots, leafy wood" is an excellent description of what has happened in the bank's operations and activities. In this context, I will highlight the key development features from a slightly different angle and also a global perspective as an addition to the description in the history book. Globalisation is often talked about and has become a rather detached phrase. It may be that the general public already thinks that events in the rest of the world have not affected you. I will tell you in a moment that they worked and will continue to do so. Action in Yl?-Savo a hundred years ago A hundred years ago, our country was among the most kchy countries in Europe. The economic situation was particularly difficult in It?-Suomi, where for centuries it had been lived on slash-and-burn farming. In the second half of the 1800s, however, the time of slash-and-burn farming began to be over. V?est?n subsistence was based solely on agriculture and forestry, the yield of which had been so low that it was impossible to afford anything more than that. As a good indication of the modesty of the conditions, it is not until 1904 that it was not until 1904 that the church was brought to the meeting place of the municipality. The pressure for reform was pressing and the transition to animal husbandry turned out to be a major change in agriculture. However, ?m? required investment in livestock shelters, el?im and milk-processing equipment. The existing financial institutions did not provide the loans needed to carry out the reforms, but the solution was to use the local cooperative funds. They made it possible to finance the necessary investments and to overcome the vicious circle of poverty. It doesn't seem like it's like a hundred years ago, it was a completely separate el?m?? that wasn't too influenced from the outside. The economy, too, and the activities of the cooperative fund were free from anything further afield, not to mention the authorship of the world economy. We did as we wanted. However, the truth is different. It seems that the beginning of the 1900s was a time of global trade. Agriculture and its products operate on the terms of the world market. Agricultural products were the main goods of foreign trade, and trade was duty-free. Dairy products, meat and eggs were exported. Grain was imported duty-free from abroad, especially from Russia and Germany. The effects of world trade were felt v?lichch?sti. Pressure from the world market also led to the cessation of grain cultivation. They switched to animal husbandry and cultivated the feed grain they needed. The outbreak of world war I interrupted the globalisation that had taken place in the spirit of free trade, and the whole of Finnish society was plunged into a deep crisis. The first stage was the breakdown of trade relations, which resulted in the collapse of grain imports and Finland's entry into a food crisis. The next stage was the foreclosure of the Ven?j? market, when the entire export industry had to look for new markets. Around the same time, the external framework of world trade also changed, as the ideology of free trade was revolutionised and one country after another switched to a protectionist trade policy. Taught by the food crisis, the objective of Finland's agricultural policy was to ensure national self-sufficiency, which meant the resurgence of grain farming and the growth of arable land by clearing the land. ?ss? succeeded, which is why in concrete terms n?kyi my?s Kiuruvesiell?. However, agricultural production, especially in livestock products, exceeded domestic demand and there was a relatively painful adjustment process, as the export markets for butter and milk were not open. In Particular, the Ven?j? market was subject to permanent foreclosure in It?-Suomi. The most difficult situation was in the early 1930s, when the global depression was at its deepest. However, the situation stabilised in the second half of the decade and the years were the "golden years" of Finnish rural society. The speech about the country spirit was not just a matter of words. The belief in a peasant small-scale symbiosis of agriculture and forest economy was firm. There were other major changes in the development of our society. The region's strong momentum and economic growth were driven by settlement activity in the 40s and 50s. Sith was followed by a knuckle; a major change in Finnish society, in which agriculture contracted drastically and forests collapsed. This was a major blow, especially for small agricultural and forestry farms, where typically low agricultural incomes were increased by participating in forests. In fact, there were quite a lot of small-scale land and forest holdings in the region as a whole, and the development of the whole region was quite a blow. The region was used, and especially in the 70s, to the rest of the world, from the countryside to the city and all the way to Sweden. The 80s and 90s coincide with the casino era and the boom in overinvestment. What followed was the recession in the past, in which the country was blown away and the banks were hit hard by bad debts. That time did not allow for kiuruvett?k?k?n syrj?n, and many activities from dairies to various services have had to be stopped under more efficient operating methods. The effects were not the worst overall. The principles of prudence, customer knowledge and good solvency in banking proved to be correct. The deep recession of the first half of the 1990s interrupted a long period of continuous growth. Edess? was a rigorous process of adaptation that all of us in Chels?? have experienced firsthand. During the years of the wars adaptation had taken place in the protectionist anti-globalisation spirit. Now Finland's position had fundamentally changed since joining the EU. Free trade and a free market economy had emerged as the motto. In rural areas, however, faith in the future faltered and there was a general sense of global development. The recession was a good example of how the events of the global economy rocked the whole of Finland. The economic plight was not just homemade, even though excesses were made and mistakes were made in one's own housekeeping. As a result, the Finnish banking sector became dangerously fragile. One banking group collapsed l?hes completely. The industry had to be heavily restructured even during the move. The number of people in the banking sector halved in the first half of the 90s. In banking, the emphasis was on risk management and ensuring solvency. The cooperative bank group reformed the group structure and formed an interconnection. Some of the banks are excluded, forming their own Local Cooperative Bank Group. Overall, the banking industry became more efficient and efficient, so that Finnish banks are currently among the most progressive and efficient in the world. The experience of the last ten years also shows how the Finnish rural community has once succeeded in adapting. These fears have not materialised. Although the number of people working in agriculture has rapidly declined, production has either remained stable or increased. In agriculture, too, there is a significant increase in productivity. Despite its location in Syrj?isest?, Kiuruvesi has succeeded in its own "area of expertise", which has made it possible to make a successful transition from the s??tele economy to the harsh world of the free market. The change that has taken place over the past hundred years can be well illustrated by numbers and by looking at ??rip?it?. In the early 1900s, the V?ki number was about 10,000 and had grown to about 16,000 by the 60s, it now began to decline back towards 10,000 inhabitants. During this time, the economic structure of Kiuruvesi also changed. Whereas in the 1940s more than 90% of the inhabitants made their living from agriculture and forestry, it is 24%. Agriculture is still of great importance. This is why we should welcome the desire of agricultural enterprises to develop and renew themselves. The size of the premises has increased and the premises have been modernized by investing in new technology. This success shows that Kiuruvesi is the largest producer of milk and beef in Finland. In a hundred years, the share of v?est? needed to provide services has risen from 2% to 52% ? i.e. in various services in the municipality, commerce and transport, the v?ki has increased 25-fold compared to a hundred years ago. And t?n??n Kiuruvesi el??? l?hes 20 times more of the industry than a hundred years ago, the industry accounted for 1% of the total industry and now about 19%. Toimintaymp?rist? l?hitulevaisuudessa The future is reflected in europe's progress in integration, strong internationalisation and the pre-modern pace of the global economy. The usual topics in our discussions are EU directives and their effects, our children's and grandchildren's studies or jobs abroad, the rapid growth of the American economy or even China. Indeed, a great change has occurred in our worldview. Accession to the European Union and economic and monetary union (EMU) brought about changes in agricultural activity, in all areas of industry and even in political decision-making. One or more of the issues that affect us will be resolved in Brussels. Not that being out of the EU would have changed a lot. As a small economy, Finland is dependent on the environment and the world economy. Good examples are Denmark or even Sweden. Both of them follow the same principles of monetary policy as we do, even though they are outside the euro area. Economic and monetary union has a direct impact on banking. N?in also to the celebrating Kiuruvesi Cooperative Bank. In addition to the fact that we now have a single currency for the whole of the euro area, the interest rate and the monetary conditions are the same across Europe. In addition, financial markets are becoming increasingly integrated in Europe. The banking sector will have more supranational, foreign supply than before. There are already products that are easy to market and manage; debit or credit cards and consumer loans. More complex and good customer knowledge requires products, such as various long-term products and mortgages, will come with time. In their production, economies of scale are high and distribution margins are small due to increasing competition. Banks are facing new, complex solvency requirements and risk management requirements. Accounting and its accounts are also becoming more international. Foreigners have entered the Finnish banking market through corporate arrangements, either through mergers or acquisitions. The last example is the sale of Sampo Bank to Den Danske Bank last week. The same payment area, SEPA, will create its own spice. It will make it easier to handle all types of payments within the euro area across national borders. It increases competition in financial services. Consumers are becoming more and more comfortable, and the provision of services and competitiveness will be put to the test again. In addition to the international development, new domestic banks are entering the market. Tapiola Bank has only just started and S-Bank is coming as early as next year. New to the banking competition is v?ri?. For customers, the changes are hy?dyllisi?. Every need is filled with service and products. There are new products for the regular banking services all the time ? mortgages, interest rate caps, options, various insurance products and the list could go on for however long. Competition long prices and other conditions well. Does a regionally operating bank, which is small throughout the market, have the opportunity to meet these challenges? Stankym?t for a longer future Banks have v?lineet to serve their customers regardless of time and place. The history book of Kiuruvesi Cooperative Bank contains a good, illustrative account of how Paula Pennanen, a native of ??lch and who has lived in different parts of the world, uses the banking services of Kiuruvesi Cooperative Bank under the branches of a banana tree in Kenya. An interesting detail is that even his salary bank is a bank that celebrates its celebrations! Customers are increasingly using banking services, even if they are not in Kenya. They make life easier in many ways. The location of the bank's branch is not as decisive as it used to be. For many households, the bank has become a kind of housekeeper. From bank statements n?hd?n income and expenses. At the same time, accounts of past times are generated and plans and plans for the use of funds can be made. The asset situation can be viewed on-line at any time. A locally operating bank has inherent strengths in the competition. In banking, there will always be things where local customer knowledge and v?litchn customer encounters are invaluable. N?in is involved in a number of services for human and corporate clients, in particular for the financing of SMEs. Services and products can be found to best suit each of the service selections. In the case of personal customers, the activities of banks have changed to the demanding provision of customer advice in the form of payments. It is not easy to deal with n?iss? matters with internet services alone. Kiuruvesi Cooperative Bank has excellent opportunities to p?rj?ch. Customers receive services in a modern way. In all banking, sound prudence is essential. Most of the funds of others, i.e. the depositors' own funds, are not the bank's own funds, and therefore no excessive risk can be taken in the operation. The key to success will continue to be customer knowledge and service. Another aspect of a cooperative bank is that it is its own company, in which the management has its own responsibility. In particular, the Bank's governing body, executive board and board of directors also play a specific role. They are responsible for ensuring that the bank's management knows its business and that the lines of operation are correct. There are reasons to emphasize and appreciate the responsibility and responsibility, as its effects will only last for years, sometimes decades. Finally, but not v?hemm?n t?rkehn?, one of the basic prerequisites for success, or as the strategy analysts would say in tv comments, is the dependence of the local bank on its own territory and its people. The bank works well for a long period of time, and only as well or badly as it operates. The vitality and vitality of the region is a prerequisite for everything. All the well-being of the region is finally based on successful and strong livelihoods. The basic needs and comfort of the residents must be taken care of. It is not just a question of caring for the sick or the elderly, of schools or of access to municipal services, but also of matters such as cultural services. It is a major challenge to ensure the vitality of the region as the v?est? becomes more and more active. The situation is the same in the whole of Yl?-Savo. The responsibility for creating a good framework for action lies primarily with the social institutions, but this alone will not help to wait for public administration measures. Development must also involve companies, entrepreneurs and individuals. The local bank has an important role to play in strengthening activity in the region. It is also in the bank's own interest. However, this does not mean financial participation, but encouragement of new projects and the strengthening of a reform-oriented and mysthetic climate. The Bank can play its part in ensuring the development of the region.
