Friday 5February 2016,12:00PM Commentary at the Ministry of Finance's mini-seminar on promoting financial stability Pentti Hakkarainen, Vice Chairman of the Board of Directors, Helsinki, 5.2.2016. Presentation body d the presentation held may differ METS IS NHTV PER POUND This expert report examines the significant structural vulnerabilities in the Finnish banking system, which could lead to particularly high economic consequences of banking crises and other serious financial crises in Finland. In particular, vulnerabilities include: Strong concentration of the Finnish banking sector, . the important role of banks in financing the private sector. the strong dependence of banks on international financial markets and the Nordic banking system. . The financial crises we have experienced have shown that, in order to safeguard the stability of individual financial institutions, the stability and supervision of private financial institutions are not always sufficient to safeguard the stability of the entire financial system. Even if individual financial institutions act correctly and in accordance with their own priorities, their activities as a whole may at times give rise to dangerous developments in the financial system d such as excessive lending or excessive risk concentrations. In order to identify such risks and combat them, there is a need to forest for the trees. The so-called. macroprudential analysis and policies in order to identify and address risks to the stability of the entire financial system in a timely manner. BANKS' POWNREQUIREMENTS EIVT EST ACCESS TO FINANCE FOR COMPANIES As part of this theme, the potential impact of banks' requirements on companies' access to finance is also relevant to this theme. Occasionally, accusations are heard of tightening claims and other forms of tightening of the terms of financing of companies. There are reasons to take this seriously, especially in the current economic climate. The costs of the claims have been investigated by the Bank of Finland. According to the studies, the impact of the tightening of prudential requirements on the price of loans was not true of the essential mssr. In Finland, the solvency of the banks was already so strong that banks have not had to start acquiring their own Pssoma due to the new, tightened solvency requirements. Indeed, the price of bank loans in Finland has been driven in particular by the competition of banks for loan customers, not so much as solvency or other banking conditions. The report to be published contains an in-depth analysis of the impact of national requirements on the cost of financing and, consequently, on economic growth. In addition, the costs have been estimated, especially in Finland. The empirical and theoretical results presented in the report reinforce the assessment that the adverse effects of increases in the requirements on the financing of companies have probable to have been small. Banks' solvency problems weaken their ability to also provide credit to households and businesses in crisis situations. During the financial crisis and in the years since then, it has been conclusively observed that banks' lending capacity has been best preserved in those countries where banks' solvency and liquidity were strongest before the start of the crisis. In countries where weak banks ran into problems, the damage to the overall economy multiplied. Finland and the other Nordic countries are examples of countries where the strength of the banking sector softened the effects of the crisis. In many of the countries most severely affected by the crisis, the weakness of the banking sector contributed to exacerbating the crisis. According to the experience of the bank sector as a whole, the solvency of the entire banking sector must be ensured in order to enable banks to face bad times. MACROPRUDENTIAL POLICY STARTED IN FINLAND IN 2015 A new strand of economic policy d macroprudential policy d was launched in Finland at the beginning of 2015. For more than a year now, a macroprudential decision has been made in Finland on the basis of the new Credit Institutions Act in order to achieve financial stability. The Board of the Financial Supervisory Authority prepares quarterly decisions on macroprudential measures in Finland. The European Central Bank has the possibility to set stricter requirements than national standards for macroprudential measures, including those at EU level. It is gratifying that the Finnish authorities now have the means that would have been needed thirty years ago to curb the credit expansion that existed at the time. After the liberalisation of the financial markets, bank lending accelerated to uncontrollable dimensions in Finland at the end of the 1980s. At the time, the Bank of Finland and the Finance Minister did not have prepared any legislative instruments to d macroprudential measures d to slow down credit growth. At the end of 1988, when no other means could be found, the Finance Minister, under the leadership of Erkki Liikanen, the then Minister of Finance, the current Head of The Bank of Finland, planned to set a ceiling of 10% on the growth of credit, above which a special tax would be levied. In the end, the plan was not implemented, but instead the Bank of Finland decided to increase the banks' cash reserve requirement by means of a special interest-free additional deposit obligation, which had been conditioned on the growth of credit.1 As a result of this measure, credit growth was eventually halted d but not too comprehensively. Contrary to guidance, one banking group continued its brisk lending, eventually failing to overcome its problems. The most serious consequence of the excessive trend in indebtedness was the collapse of the entire Finnish economy, with disastrous and long-term consequences. If macroprudential measures had been in place at the end of the 1980s, the authorities would have been able to act in good time to curb overheating in lending and finance systems and to strengthen banking systems. The economic and human costs of the recession would probably have been higher than the actual costs. A new macroprudential policy has begun in Finland in a context of weak economic conditions. On the other hand, the operating model of low interest rates creates incentives for rising indebtedness and rising asset prices. Problems may also arise as to how funding is channelled to different borrower sectors. From the point of view of economic growth, it is to be hoped that funding will be sufficiently channelled into productive investment by companies. From a stability point of view, these concerns relate in particular to the increased indebtedness of households. It is the case that banks maintain their strong solvency. GOOD FOR THE INTERNATIONAL LEVEL In Finland, when you think about what is needed to achieve financial stability, it is necessary to look at the big picture. First of all, it should be borne in mind that the risks to the stability of the financial system in today's dynamic and integrated world economy are very diverse and changeable, which is why different levels are needed to support stability. The Finnish financial system is part of the Nordic banking system and the international financing system. In order to ensure fair conditions of competition and to limit the ssntelyarbitras, it is necessary to ensure that macroprudential standards are at international level. At the same time, it is necessary to assess how the various instruments work together and how contradictory or unnecessary measures work together. The risks of the financial system spread rapidly across borders. When macroprudential positions are as similar as possible in different countries, the responsible authorities are in a better position to counter threats to stability across borders. It is natural that the greatest attention in macroprudential policy has been focused on the banking sector, which remains the most important part of the financial system in Finland as well. However, particularly in the EU, efforts are being made to develop macroprudential measures that are not directly targeted at the banking sector. In particular, the European Commission's initiative to build a domestic market union has increased the pressure on the Community. JRJESTRYRISK BUFFER KYTETTVISS IN MOST OTHER EU. ASHORE The additional requirement to be imposed on all banks, if necessary, is the systemic risk buffer requirement, which is a structural macroprudential requirement. As stated in the report to be published, the Finnish financial system has a number of structural vulnerabilities that require Finnish banks to have strong solvency to cover risks. The system of using the risk buffer has been made possible in most EU countries. It has been found, for example, in Sweden, Denmark, Norway and Estonia. Our banking sector is strongly linked to foreign banking systems. It is important that macroprudential balances in Finland, and especially in the other Nordic countries, are comparable. sssn also drew attention to its country report on Finland published by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in autumn 2015. The IMF considers that it would be justified to strengthen Finland's macroprudential framework with a systemic risk buffer, which would bring Finland's financial assets more into line with the home countries of foreign banks operating in the system. It is clear that the so-called 'bank credits' which are significant from the point of view of the financing system. O-SII buffers are similar in some respects to the system risk buffer. However, where appropriate, the system risk buffer requirement may be imposed on the banking sector as a whole and its maximum size is higher than the O-SII buffer requirements. The provision of a risk buffer does not imply that the requirement is imposed automatically on banks. The conditions for setting the requirement and the impact are assessed. This takes into account the state of the economy and the financial system in a diverse and thorough manner. The buffer is used separately on the basis of an estimate of the buffer. FINALLY It is also necessary for the fire brigade to start procuring fire-fighting equipment when the house is already on fire. Vslneet must be purchased before then. Vslines must be suitable for extinguishing both attic and forest fires. In the same way, the macroprudential authority shall ensure in good time a sufficient amount of macroprudential funding, which it may, at its discretion, use in order to counter various stability threats to the financial system. The system risk buffer would be part of the system. From the national nsks angle and to the vssntelyarbitras, the Finnish authorities have the same high-quality macroprudential standards as the authorities of other countries. Presentation body d the presentation held may differ ECONOMIC CURRENT AFFAIRS REVIEW AND DEVELOPMENT OFTENT Ty... KEEPV IN FINLAND Thank you for the invitation to your seminar to speak on economics. My theme is to look at the ways in which the myhnexual development of our economy and our economy is ensured, especially from the Finnish nskskulma and the Czech Republic. The interest of representatives of the plastics industry in the economy has long roots. I even have the fact that the world's first plastics industrialist, Leo Baekeland, the inventor of bakelite, was very interested in economics. A few words about Baekeland: hsn was a Belgian-born chemist who emigrated to the United States as a young man and became rich after the invention of a new type of photographic paper, the patent for which hsn sold to Kodak. After that, as a financially independent man, Hsn devoted his hobby to materials research, resulting in the world's first plastic, bakelite. Hsn then founded a company called Bakelite Corporation, which began to manufacture the revolutionary substance. Leo Baekeland was one of the celebrities of his time and a highly sought-after speaker. In 1907, just the same year that hsn announced the invention of bakelite, Baekeland gave a speech to the American Chemists' Association, in which hsn urged chemists to take an interest in economics as well. Hsn said, among other things, nsin: oEEconomics, unlike most other sciences, can be mastered without any kind of study. All bias, petty greed, self-love and justice are rejected. o The economists do not quite agree with Baekeland's opinion! Yes, or so, but there seems to be some bias and greed in the current economic debate. I am now experiencing -those vices vsltsen .ksyds lspi the current quite challenging problems of the economy and the main problems of Finnish economic policy. CHINA AND EMERGING ECONOMIES Let me start with the state of the international economy. (slide 2) Since the turn of the year, international financial markets have focused on China, but also on the sharp fall in the prices of sljy and other raw materials, as well as on the state of the US economy. In particular, the march rates have largely declined partly in line with the development of the Chinese exchange rate. In advanced economies, the main share price indices are now at the levels of late autumn 2014. (slide 3) China's economy continued to grow last year, with GDP growth slowing slightly to 6.9%. China's economic certainty is longterm linked to the fact that the structure of growth is changing. In particular, investment growth has slowed down considerably in China. sms is partly related to the weakness of fixed investment, but there are also a wide range of infrastructure projects at the moment than in 2010 d 2012. The slowdown in industrial output growth is partly due to the relatively weak development of exports. By contrast, private consumption continues to grow strongly in China. In addition, it is expected to account for more than half of gdp growth of around six per cent in the year. The change in China's growth model will, among other things, meet all the demand directly related to construction. At the same time, the demand for services is growing sharply. sms nskyy also in china and eu vslisesss trade and tourism. (slide 4) All in all, it can be said that there has been a shift in international economic growth. Since the onset of the financial crisis, developments in the long-term emerging economies were significantly better than in the developed economies. Recently, however, economic growth has slowed down in the emerging economies, while in the developed economies it has accelerated. (slide 5) Developments have been particularly weak in Russia and Brazil d partly due to lower prices of raw materials on the world market. The price of a barrel of raw sturgeon has fallen from around 45 last fall to around 30. ... The reason for the fall in the price of ljy has largely been the increase in the production of sljy in the OPEC countries. In the financial markets, the security associated with the growth rate of the Chinese economy is also part of the reason for the fall in the price of sljy. The prices of many other raw materials have also fallen. Chelshn has also contributed to the slowdown in China's economic growth and the changing structure of China's growth. (slide 6) One of the economies in the greatest difficulty is now Vensjs. According to preliminary figures, the country's GDP contracted by 3.7% in 2015. Private consumption and real income fell by around 10%, while investment contracted by around 8%. Investments have declined in Vensjslls in the middle of 2012. The development of investment reflects the long-term problems of the Russian economy. Weak economic shocks and the price of financing can be expected to weigh on investment further in 2016 . In the Russian economy, the year can become as weak as the previous one. In September 2015, the Bank of Finland predicted a 2% contraction in Russian GDP in 2016. At that time, however, the price of raw material was clearly higher than it is today. If the price of sljy remains at its current level, Vensjs's export earnings will fall further than before, which will also be reflected in private consumption and investment. (slide 8) THE US-EURO AREA ECONOMY One of the most strongly grown developed economies in recent years is the United States. Economic growth has continued around 2%, although growth moderated slightly over the past year. Recent indicator data on the US economy are partly contradictory, with strong developments in consumption and employment, while weak industrial performance. The Federal Reserve raised its key interest rate in December, which was held in December before it was raised to zero for 7 years. Following some conflicting data on the state of the US economy in recent weeks, there has been a lively debate about the timing of the central bank's next expected rate hike. (slide 9) The euro area economy continued to grow over the past year. At the same time, the employment rate has continued to decline from its high level. (slide 10) Despite economic growth, inflation in the euro area has remained low. Annual HICP inflation stood at 0.4% in January 2016. Inflation has been weighed down in recent months in particular by the fall in the price of sljy. The rise in the prices of other hysdykes has also remained subdued. (Slide 11) The ECB's monetary policy has been eased as before. In the mid-2014 elections, new monetary policy measures have been introduced. The new securities purchase programmes are part of this action. The second consists of additional measures to support lending. In addition, the interest rate on banks' central bank deposits has been reduced below zero. In the long run, as a result of past action by the Central Bank and the Central Bank, financing conditions for non-financial corporations and households have eased. While monetary policy has not eased in the same way in other countries, the external value of the euro has weakened. The lightening of monetary policy will contribute to the recovery of credit demand, consumption, investment and exports in the euro area. The aim is to achieve an inflation rate of less than 2% in the medium term. A light monetary policy also supports the Finnish economy. (Slide 12) DIFFICULT STATE OF THE FINNISH ECONOMY Finland's economic development has continued to be very subdued compared to other countries. GDP remained broadly unchanged last year, and the latest indicator data do not indicate a strengthening of the situation. The trend has remained around 9 per cent in recent summer. (slides 13 and 14) The development of the Finnish economy has been weak since the end of 2008. GDP per capita is now about 9% lower than in 2007. This indicates the formation of income. Production has been reduced, as well as a reduction in productivity and employment. When the generation of income per capita is more stable than before, the increase in expenditure will have to be financed by more debt than before. The subdued development of the international economy in recent years explains only part of the weakness of the Finnish economy. The weak performance is also due to industrial restructuring, the decline in cost competitiveness, the evolution of the structure of the d whereas growth in the labour market has also been reduced d and, more recently, the weakening of the Vensjs economy. (Slide 15) The economic dependency ratio has weakened, i.e. the share of those working in the labour market has decreased. The mssss of the tysllis has grown, while the mssss of the elskelss and the tystchmis has grown. This is partly due to the fact that larger classes of people have been in the economy and, on the other hand, to the fact that the employment situation has deteriorated. (Slide 16) Economic headwinds have been triggered in particular by a contraction in exports and investment in export sectors. However, consumption has continued to grow. Exports amounted to 12% between 2008 and 2014. Today, exports are roughly one-fifth lower than at their peak in the second quarter of 2008. In one developed economy, exports have not declined by much. (Slide 17) As the generation of income in the economy has contracted and expenditure is financed more by debt than before, public debt and household debt have increased. Finland's general government deficit is now around 3% and its public debt is above 60% of GDP. Without new pockets, debt growth will continue at a rapid pace above 68% in 2017. In the euro area, on the other hand, the average sub-base has fallen to around 2% of GDP. (Slide 18) As the population grows, a larger share of public expenditure will be needed to pay the pensions. In 2007, the share of elfs in primary government expenditure was 29%, and in 2017 it is projected to be as high as 32%. In addition, the worsening of employment has led to an increase in expenditure on employment. From the sschen angle, the increase in expenditure on pensions and employment has taken up space for other public expenditure. The key questions in Finland's economic policy will be whether this development will continue, and what is the alternative? MEASURES TO REMEDY THE ECONOMIC SITUATION Now that the state of the international economy and the Finnish economy has been examined, the listeners will have a good idea of what they are doing. The current problem of the economy will not be solved by talking alone, but by means of difficult and responsible measures. (Slide 19) The Bank of Finland has highlighted the corrective measures that can be taken to solve the problems of the Finnish economy. They include three areas. The first is structural reforms that improve the productive potential of the economy and the sustainability of public finances. Reforms have been carried out in Finland. One of these is the elske reform, which can be used as a step towards solving the problems of the economy. Furthermore, reforms are needed. Secondly, an increase in public debt is necessary. The current problems of the Finnish economy are not of such a nature that they can be solved by means of a fiscal stimulus. The third element of the measures is the restoration of cost competitiveness. The public perception of recent economic policy has become muddled, and progress in all three areas of economic policy mentioned above is still incomplete. However, all these advances have been made. It is now up to the government to function, and solutions will emerge. If there are no solutions, there is a risk that the Finnish tys will be too expensive to fly the oulos flago and at the same time the burden of indebtedness will be passed on to the next generation. In order to finance this development, we are not going to run away from difficult actions.

Tyttmyysaste trendi on viime kevst lhtien pysytellyt 9. prosentin tuntumassa. (kalvot 13 ja 14) Suomen talouden kehitys on ollut heikkoa jo vuoden 2008 lopulta lhtien. Henke kohti laskettu BKT on nyt noin 9 % pienempi kuin vuonna 2007. Tm kertoo tulonmuodostuksen vhenemisest. Tuotantoa on pienentnyt sek tyn tuottavuuden ett tyllisten mrn pieneneminen. Kun henke kohti laskettu tulonmuodostus on aiempaa vhisempi, joudutaan menojen kasvu rahoittamaan aiempaa enemmn velalla. Kansainvlisen talouden vaimea kehitys viime vuosina selitt Suomen talouden heikkoudesta vain osan. Tmn taustalla on yhtlt se, ett aiempaa suurempia ikluokkia on jnyt elkkeelle, ja toisaalta se, ett tyllisyystilanne on huonontunut. Keskeisi kysymyksi Suomen talouspolitiikassa tulevat olemaan, tuleeko tm kehitys jatkumaan, ja mik sen vaihtoehto on. Ensimmisen muodostavat sellaiset rakenneuudistukset, jotka parantavat talouden tuotantomahdollisuuksia ja julkisen talouden kestvyytt. Uudistuksia on Suomessa tehty. Kaikilla niist etenemist on kuitenkin tapahtunut. Trke on nyt, ett hallituksen toimintakyky silyy hyvn, ja ratkaisuja syntyy. Mikli ratkaisuja ei synny, vaarana on, ett suomalainen ty liian kalliina ulosliputetaan ja samalla velkaantumisen taakka siirretn tulevalle sukupolvelle. Title: Prerequisites for economic growth
text: Vice Chairman of the Board Pentti Hakkarainen: Prerequisites for economic growth. Oulu, 16.5.2016. . Speech . Monday16 May 2016,4:00 PM Pentti Hakkarainen Vice Chairman of the Board Martti Ahtisaari Institute's Economic Forum "Prerequisites for Economic Growth" Oulu, 16.5.2016 Esityskalvot (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches/documents/160516_ph_puhe_oulun_yliopisto.pdf) . (pdf) FINLAND'S ECONOMIC SITUATION DIFFICULT, BUT THERE ARE OPPORTUNITIES FOR ECONOMIC GROWTH Good listeners. The theme of my presentation is the prerequisites for economic growth in Finland. There has been public debate and characterized the situation as a hopeless, lost case. The situation in Finland is still exceptionally difficult. It is based on a number of authors. Exports are subdued and investment vshsiset. The Finnish economy has been buoyed by international development, and the sign of growth is only a year. One of the reasons for the difficulties in the economy is the drastic restructuring of industry, which has also hit Oulu hard. But in the same way as in Oulu for centuries, you should not hope for too much help from outside, but you yourself should take action. Tar and salmon gave rise to their own strong economy. As demand withered away, there was a shift to basic industry. As it faced its own challenges, Oulu was developed into an advanced technology centre with a brisk approach. The importance of the investments made in the university has been absolutely central. When difficulties were experienced in electronics in recent years, the role of the region has been developed for projects in the Arctic region and Oulu has been developed into a city in northern Scandinavia, especially in economic terms. Similarly, the difficulties of the whole of Finland can be overcome. In order to deal with the difficult economic situation, measures have been identified and now is the time for implementation. What are the measures and conditions for generating economic growth? [slide 2] Firstly, let's take a moment to look at the situation. Since the financial crisis, finland's GDP growth has been modest and the pre-crisis level has not been reached. Last year, modest growth of 0.5% was recorded after three years of recession. However, recent forecasts suggest that growth is improving slightly, from zero to one per cent, which is good news. However, the beginning of 2016 has not brought clarity to the plight of industry and exports. In the forecasts, growth is therefore strongly based on growth in domestic demand, i.e. consumption and investment, especially in construction and some individual large productive investments. [slide 3] After the good news, the worse news is that the growth of the longer term is weak. It is clear that the lost level of total production will not be able to catch up in the lshi years, so that we will return to the previous trend of GDP growth. But, for example, the Bank of Finland estimates that the growth rate over a longer period of time will also be slower than what we have been used to in the past - the annual growth rate of GDP is around 1%. [slide 4] A one per cent increase is something that Finland has not been used to before. New things to share will be scarce if: at all. Growth in the 2010s is in danger of becoming weaker than that of The Czech Republic. The slow growth puts us in a whole new situation, and the challenges it poses are a little more difficult. Why, then, has growth slowed down? And why isn't the previous growth rate? [slide 5] In the 10-year period since 2004, the average growth rate has been 1.3%. With a period from 2014 to a year Growth in 2020 is projected to slow down to an average of 0.8%. The slowdown in growth is due to the the change in the structure of production, i.e. the restructuring of industry and its contraction. Growth in the coming years will be based on productivity growth. In particular, the expected acceleration of average growth in the 2020s from 0.8% to 1.1% is due to the recovery in the rate of productivity growth, due to historical developments, however, productivity growth requires both productive investment and R&D investments d both have shown weak performance in recent years. On the other hand, it is a brake on growth because of the contraction in the labour market and thus the economic economy. is tyspanos vshenee. In addition to the favourable demographics of recent years, the rise of the long recession of recent years d the rise of structural labour d sss remains the ballast of the economy. [slide 6] In 2010, we have already seen a decline in 2010, slightly earlier than in the rest of Europe. In the future, the average annual contraction will be 0.2% per annum. The decline will continue into the 2020s. Thus, the measures taken to increase the participation rate of the force are very much in the same way. [slide 7] Global growth is also slowing down, and we are not expecting a particularly China-like pull-up from abroad. Global growth concerns concern, among other things: -Normalisation of monetary policy in the United States, -price developments in the euro area, -price developments in the UK, prices of sljy and other raw materials, and -slowdown in economic growth in China and changes in its structure. [slide 8] Finland's high cost level and problems in the export industry have also been reflected in investments that have historically fallen to a very low level. In particular, productive investment has declined. So much so that they are hardly enough to keep the economy as a whole growing population. In addition, the willingness to invest may have led to a lower willingness to invest, as both the growth of the domestic market in Finland is meagre. However, the combined consumption of households and the public sector has developed in a negative way with exports and investment. Household consumption has been supported by low interest rates, while public consumption has been supported by fiscal stimulus. [slide 9] The change in the structure of growth d from export-driven to consumption-driven growth - has affected both household and public sector indebtedness, as well as in the current account. While households' income generation and the development of tax revenue have been weak, but the consumption of households and the public sector has been reasonably strong, the domestic sector as a whole has become heavily indebted. The poor performance of exports in relation to consumption is again reflected in the meltdown in the current account. It is worthwhile for a small open economy to get into debt in the event of a temporary recession, as it will smooth out the domestic economic cycle, but there are also dangers. Indebtedness will become structural if it continues, even if long-term growth remains weak. In Finland, the possibility exists. And the growing burden of debt will be on narrower shoulders in the future, as the economic dependency ratio weakens as a result of ageing and poor employment trends. [slide 10 or 11] The structures of the welfare state are not now at the bottom of the table. When growth is projected to be sluggish over a longer period of time, the current expenditure-based approach will not bridge the gap between revenue and expenditure. It will lead to an increase in public sector indebtedness. [slide 12] Another problem is that debt stimulus leads to higher prices and supports imports, not helping the export industry, on the other hand: Solving the problem of the competitiveness of the economy would require slower price and cost developments than those of its competitors over a number of years. [slide 13] The contraction of the private sector and productive activity is also causing the destruction of more enterprises in Finland than new ones have been destroyed, and the net change in the stock has even fallen into negative territory. Chams speaks of the plight of industry. The emergence of new enterprises is tsrkehs from two autumns. Firstly, the emergence of new enterprises is strongly correlated with both productivity and employment. Secondly, productivity growth is positively correlated with the development of employment. The acceleration of productivity growth will therefore not destroy jobs, at least in the middle of the world. The emergence of new enterprises thus contributes to the growth of the economy and through productivity and employment. [slides 14-17] In order to strengthen future growth, measures other than low monetary policy interest rates and ample liquidity are needed. They can support the economy on a cyclical basis, but not on a permanent basis. Growth based on indebtedness (household or public finances) is not sustainable. I said at the outset that action must be taken. Simply waiting for an international cyclical upturn to lift Finland out of recession is not responsible. It is not right to accept the slow economic growth as a model for the future. The younger generations would have to pay an exorbitant share of the debt burden, while their incomes are predicted to decline and their chances of employment would remain poor. Reforms have been made to improve economic structures and competitiveness, although there are often short-term costs. The structure of the economy will be improved by strengthening the operating conditions in the industrial and other sectors of industry, where we have special expertise. Training is not available for the hunnch, as it ensures long-term competitiveness. In the public sector, there are reasons to seek efficiency through competition. In addition, there are reasons to be at the forefront when new technology can be used. To conclude, I will summarize what I have said by looking at economic growth over several decades. The period under review could also be the last couple of hundred years, because in fact our prosperity is based on the development of that period. In the 1800s, humans lived in many areas of Finland together with cattle, and at that time there were repeated nslsnhsdists. It is precisely thanks to economic growth that Finnish society has entered the current welfare model, which takes care of the weak, the sick and the elderly. The means have been foreign trade, an improving level of education and an open-minded use of technology to increase productivity. Some people have the question of why economic growth is necessary. And in our situation, where, as a result of the development of the situation, the development of the population is predicted to be the same, can growth be achieved? And there is also the question of why we should not be satisfied with the current level and without future economic growth. Is economic growth always even desirable and good? Economic growth is not just an end in itself, but its goal is to create prosperity that can take care of both itself and others. Our welfare society requires that the current generation takes care of the previous generation, which has already been displaced. The correct distribution of the fruits of economic growth is ensured by the democratically elected members of our society. Economic growth is not a matter of clarity in itself, but requires renewal, especially in order to increase productivity. Increasing productivity does not mean grinding or increasing the pace of work, or the abundance of natural resources, but it is much more diverse. It is a question of operating methods, organisational structures and technology. Examples include how nurses' cooperation improves flexibility through additional and new ways of working, or how the effectiveness of treatment increases with more empathy for the patient, or how the teacher can encourage his or her students to hymn their mental potential more than before. This is not only desirable, it is a condition for the growth of prosperity.

(pdf) SUOMEN TALOUSTILANNE VAIKEA, MUTTA TALOUSKASVULLE ON MAHDOLLISUUKSIA Hyvt kuulijat. Esitykseni teemana tnn on talouskasvun edellytykset Suomessa. Julkisuudessa on asiasta debatoitu ja luonnehdittu tilannetta toivottomaksi, menetetyksi tapaukseksi. Suomen tilanne onkin edelleen poikkeuksellisen vaikea. Sen taustalla on useita tekijit. Vienti on vaimeaa ja investoinnit vhiset. Suomen talous on jnyt kansainvlisen kehityksen vauhdista ja merkkej kasvun kynnistymisest on vain vhn. Yksi syy talouden vaikeuksiin on teollisuuden raju rakennemuutos, joka on nkynyt mys tll Oulussa voimakkaasti. Mutta samalla tavalla kuin tll Oulussa jo vuosisatojen ajan, apua ulkopuolelta ei kannata toivoa liikaa vaan on itse ryhdyttv toimiin. Tll tervasta ja lohesta kumpusi oma vahva talous. Niden kysynnn kuihduttua, siirryttiin perusteollisuuteen. Sen kohdatessa omia haasteitaan, reippailla otteilla Oulusta kehitettiin edistyksellinen teknologiakeskus. Yliopistoon tehtyjen panostusten merkitys tss on ollut aivan keskeinen. Kun elektroniikan puolella koettiin viime vuosien aikana vaikeuksia, on seudun roolia kehitetty arktisen alueen hankkeisiin ja Oulua brndtty pohjoisen Skandinavian pkaupungiksi, erityisesti taloudellisessa mieless. Samoin koko Suomen vaikeudet ovat voitettavissa. Vaikean talouden tilan kntmiseksi on toimet identifioitu ja nyt on toteutuksen aika. Mit ovat toimet ja edellytykset, joilla saadaan talouskasvua aikaan? [kalvo 2] Ensin tmn hetken tilanteesta. Suomen bruttokansantuotteen kasvu on jnyt finanssikriisin jlkeen vaatimattomaksi eik kriisi edeltnytt tasoa ole saavutettu. Viime vuonna pinnistettiin vaatimattomaan 0,5 prosentin kasvuun kolmen taantumavuoden jlkeen. [kalvo 7] Mys globaalisti kasvu on hidastumassa, eik ole odotettavissa erityist Kiina-ilmin kaltaista vetoapua ulkomailta. Maailmantalouden kasvuhuolet koskevat mm. -Yhdysvaltain rahapolitiikan normalisoitumista, -euroalueen hintakehityst, -Britannian EU-kansannestyst, -ljyn ja muiden raaka-aineiden hintakehityst sek -Kiinan talouskasvun hidastumista ja sen rakenteen muuttumista. [kalvo 8] Suomen korkea kustannustaso ja vientiteollisuuden ongelmat ovat heijastuneet mys investointeihin, jotka ovat laskeneet historiaansa nhden hyvin alhaiselle tasolle. Erityisesti tuotannolliset investoinnit ovat supistuneet. Jopa niin paljon ett ne tuskin riittvt pitmn koko talouden pomakannan kasvussa. Mys vestn ikntyminen on voinut alentaa investointihalukkuutta, kun sek tyvoiman ett kotimarkkinoiden kasvunkymt Suomessa ovat laihat. Kotitalouksien ja julkisen sektorin yhteenlaskettu kulutus on kuitenkin kehittynyt pinvastaisesti viennin ja investointien kanssa. Kotitalouksien kulutusta on tukenut matala korkotaso, julkisessa kulutuksessa nkyy finanssipolitiikan elvytys. [kalvo 9] Kasvun rakenteen muuttuminen  vientivetoisesta kulutusvetoiseen kasvuun -on nkynyt sek kotitalouksien ett julkisen sektorin velkaantumisessa, ett vaihtotaseessa. Viennin heikko menestys suhteessa kulutukseen nkyy taas vaihtotaseen ylijmn sulamisena. Pienen avotalouden kannattaa velkaantua tilapisen taantuman sattuessa, koska se tasoittaa kotimaista suhdannetta, mutta tss piilee mys vaaransa. Velkaantumisesta tulee rakenteellista jos se jatkuu, vaikka pitkn aikavlin kasvunkymt pysyvt heikkoina. Suomessa tm mahdollisuus on olemassa. Ja kasvava velkataakka on tulevaisuudessa entist kapeammilla harteilla, kun taloudellinen huoltosuhde heikkenee ikntymisen ja heikon tyllisyyskehityksen vuoksi. [kalvo 10 tai 11] Hyvinvointivaltion rakenteet eivt ole nyt kestvll pohjalla. Kun kasvun arvioidaan jvn hitaaksi pidemmll aikavlill, nykyisill menoperusteilla tulojen ja menojen vlist kuilua ei saada kurottua umpeen. Se johtaa julkisen sektorin velkaantumisen kasvuun. [kalvo 12] Toinen ongelma on ett velkaelvytys johtaa hintojen nousuun ja tukee tuontia, eik auta vientiteollisuutta, pinvastoin: Talouden kilpailukykyongelman ratkaisu vaatisi kilpailijamaita hitaampaa hinta-ja kustannuskehityst useiden vuosien ajan. [kalvo 13] Yksityisen sektorin ja tuotannollisen toiminnan supistuminen nkyy mys siin ett Suomessa tuhoutuu tll hetkell enemmn yrityksi kuin syntyy uusia  yrityskannan nettomuutos on painunut jopa negatiiviseksi. Tm kertoo teollisuuden ahdingosta. Uusien yritysten syntyminen on trke kahdesta syyst. Ensiksi, uusien yritysten syntyminen korreloi voimakkaasti sek tuottavuuden ett tyllisyyden kanssa. Toiseksi tuottavuuskasvu korreloi positiivisesti tyllisyyskehityksen kanssa. Tuottavuuskasvun nopeutuminen ei siis ainakaan keskimrin tuhoa typaikkoja. Uusien yritysten syntyminen siis edesauttaa talouden kasvua sek tuottavuuden ett tyllisyyden kautta. [kalvot 14-17] Tulevan kasvun vahvistamiseksi on tehtv muitakin toimia kuin rahapolitiikan matalat korot ja runsas likviditeetti. Nm voivat tukea taloutta suhdanneluontoisesti, ei kuitenkaan pysyvsti. Myskn velkaantumiseen .kotitalouksien tai julkisen talouden -perustuva kasvu ei ole kestv. Jo alussa totesin, ett on ryhdyttv toimiin. Pelkstn sen odottaminen, ett kansainvlinen suhdannenousu nostaisi Suomen taantumasta, ei ole vastuullista. Myskn hitaan talouskasvun hyvksyminen tulevaisuuden mallina ei ole oikein. Nuoret sukupolvet joutuisivat maksamaan kohtuuttoman osan velkataakasta samalla kuin heidn tulojensa ennustetaan heikkenevn ja tyllisyysmahdollisuuksien pysyvn huonoina. Onkin tehtv talouden rakenteita ja kilpailukyky parantavia uudistuksia, vaikka nill usein onkin kustannuksia lyhyell aikavlill. Talouden rakenteita parannetaan vahvistamalla toimintaedellytyksi niill teollisuuden ja muiden elinkeinojen aloilla, joissa meill on erityisosaamista. Koulutusta ei saa jtt hunningolle, sill se varmistaa pitkn aikavlin kilpailukyky. Julkisessa sektorissa on syyt hakea tehostamista kilpailun avulla. Lisksi meidn on syyt olla reippaassa etunojassa kun uuden teknologian kytt voidaan hydynt. Loppuun tiivistn sanomaani tarkastelemalla talouskasvua usean vuosikymmenen ajalta. Tarkastelujakso voisi olla mys viimeiset parisataa vuotta, sill itse asiassa tuohon ajanjakson kehitykseen perustuu tmn pivn vaurautemme. Viel 1800-luvulla ihmisi asui Suomessakin monilla alueilla savupirteiss yhdess karjan kanssa ja tuolloin krsittiin toistuvista nlnhdist. Niist lhtkohdista suomalainen yhteiskunta on juuri taloudellisen kasvun ansiosta tullut nykyiseen hyvinvointimalliin, jossa huolehditaan heikoista, sairaista ja vanhuksista. Keinoina ovat olleet juuri ulkomaankauppa, paraneva koulutustaso ja tuottavuutta lisvn tekniikan ennakkoluuloton kyttnotto. Joillakin teill ehk on mieless kysymys, miksi talouskasvu on tarpeen. Ja miten tilanteessamme, jossa vestn ikntymiskehityksen johdosta tyllisten mrn ennakoidaan vhenevn, voidaan kasvua saada aikaan? Ja ehk viel sekin kysymys, ett miksi ei voitaisi tyyty nykyiseen tasoon ja el ilman tulevaisuuden talouskasvupyrkimyksi. Onko talouskasvu aina edes toivottavaa ja hyv? Talouskasvu ei ole tavoite vain sellaisenaan vaan sen pmrn on luoda hyvinvointia, jolla voidaan huolehtia sek itsest ett muista. Hyvinvointiyhteiskuntamme edellytt, ett nykyinen tysskyv sukupolvi huolehtii osaltaan edellisest, jo tyvoimasta pois siirtyneest sukupolvesta. Talouskasvun hedelmien oikein jakautumisesta huolehtii yhteiskuntamme demokraattisesti valitut pttjt. Talouskasvu ei ole itsestn selvyys vaan se edellytt uudistumista, erityisesti tuottavuutta lismll. Tuottavuuden lisminen ei tarkoita hiostamista tai tiiviimp tytahtia taikka luonnonvarojen hydyntmist aiempaa runsaammin, vaan se on paljon monimuotoisempaa. Kysymys on toimintatavoista, organisaatiorakenteista ja teknologian hydyntmisest. Kytnnn esimerkkein kvisivt vaikka se, miten sairaanhoitajien yhteisty paranee joustavuutta lisvill ja uusilla toimintatavoilla, tai lkrin hoidon teho kasvaa lisntyneell empatialla potilaan ksittelyss, taikka miten opettaja saa kannustettua oppilaitaan hydyntmn henkist potentiaaliaan entist enemmn. Tllainen ei ole vain toivottavaa, vaan se on hyvinvoinnin kestvn kasvun ehto.

Title: Financial stability
text: Nordic links and household debt create risks for financial system Releases (/en/media-and-publications/releases/) . Press releasenumber 10 . Thursday19 May 2016,11:00AM The Finnish financial system has remained stable despite the weakness of the economy. Risks related to lending, debt accumulation and asset price developments are not directly threatening. d4The stability of the financial system is not facing imminent threats. Even so, stability needs to be fostered. Interconnectedness and concentration make the financial sector vulnerable. The weak cyclical situation also needs to be monitored,d5 pointed out Bank of Finland Deputy Governor Pentti Hakkarainen today at the press briefing for the publication of the new issue of the journal Euro & talous. The already high level of household debt relative to disposable income has continued to rise. The pace of indebtedness has, however, slowed, and relative housing prices have declined close to their long-term averages. Financial system participants have strengthened their capital positions, thereby improving their ability to lend and absorb losses. However, the low level of interest rates and the weak economic situation, should it prove prolonged, will put a strain on the profitability of banks and insurance companies. In Finland, a few large market participants hold significant market shares in banking and in non-life and earnings.related pension insurance sectors. The financial markets in Finland are, in fact, more concentrated than elsewhere in the euro area. d4It is necessary to ensure that there is a sufficient degree of competition in banking, insurance and pension insurance. The competitive situation will be changing with the entry into the banking sector, in particular, of new market participants making use of the opportunities offered by digitalisation,d5 said Deputy Governor Hakkarainen. The size of the banking sector relative to the economy is considerable. Dependence on market-based funding exposes banks to disruptions on international financial markets. Banks in Finland are also closely interlinked with other Nordic countries, where financial and housing market problems would rapidly spill over to Finland. d4Close monitoring, including of the other Nordic countries, is required to preserve the stability of the financial markets,d5 stated Deputy Governor Hakkarainen. Macroprudential policy, on which the Board of the Financial Supervisory Authority decides, serves to strengthen the stability of the Finnish financial system. The tools applicable in this new sphere of economic policy include countercyclical capital buffer requirements and the loan-to-value cap. However, in international comparison, there are still shortcomings in the macroprudential instruments available in Finland. d4The financial markets are seamlessly integrated. It is important for the Finnish macroprudential toolkit to be comparable with those of other Nordic countries and the Baltic States,d5 emphasised Deputy Governor Hakkarainen. Macroprudential measures must be timed with due consideration to the weak cyclical environment.

It is important that the tests are viewed in the correct light, not as a guarantee of a trouble-free future or as a cross-bank affair. The banks' stress test can be compared with the car inspection. Banks need to operate businesses and they are regularly tested. The same thing sr it with cars. Through a car inspection, it can be guaranteed that the car meets minimum requirements for use. But a flawlessly completed inspection cannot guarantee that a crash cannot occur or that no problems with the car will arise in the future. Like a inspected car, a stress-tested bank can meet new times and suffer problems. A highly qualified bank may find itself at risk because of its own oetgsrder by taking all the large and excessive risks. Its management can cut the bank badly, leading to disaster. No test can provide an absolute guarantee of a risk-free future. However, there are differences in the approach to the car inspection. Stress tests must ensure that banks' problems can spread to the rest of the economy and society. What is being tested? The countervailing power of banks is demonstrated by various adverse risk scenarios, which are not likely but sufficiently feasible. Now the negative scenarios include three oer e.g. strong market gains, weaker economic performance sn what was predicted by the European Commission, credit problems and price falls on the banks. Very common sr to manifest flaws in the tests without having goett through all the work that has actually been done. Some experts have suggested that the greatest economic development in the tests has not been satisfactory, and that the tests should otherwise have been stricter. Some commentators have flagged that only 51 bankso have been checked and that many banks have been excluded. In addition, it is pointed out that history shows that we have seen how the tests can give grsnt light to banks that after At mster serissa problems. Some banks have for their part hsvda that they sr bsttre sn others and hsnvisited to the test results. The most important thing is that the sndoe is not how dire prospects are for the economic situation or how strict the conditions are for the future. The setting of the circumstantial ssent, but snnu more important sr a reasonably detailed elucidation of the Bank's functions showing how different factors affect its activities. The banking stress tests have evolved a lot over the last ten years. In 2016, the European stress tests have drawn on the experience of the previous stress tests. The tests now out provide very detailed information; up to 17,000 data points and tens of pages with many information tables for each bank. All banks are treated in the same, harmonised way. It sr much, much more sn only the banks' capital nivoe that was published. Once the stress tests are reasonably detailed and when they have been published, all external actors d soevsl authorities such as banks, investors and inssttare, as well as all other actors d can submit their own actions and analyses. This sr what hsnde also Hssoe in that hsr case. Immediately when the test results were issued, financial analysts in investment banks and banking firms gave their own estimates. They could use their own forecasts or circumstantial circumstances for the economic environment in the future. The banking supervisor EBA published on its website a programme which encourages all interested parties to feed in their own assumptions regarding economic developments and look at the impact of various factors on banks' performance. The published stress tests may have left many people unaware of the fact that banking supervisors are conducting the tests continuously. The ECB carried out the same test on all the banks under its supervision. National supervisors monitor all banks and use different future scenarios. Where are only results for the 51 largest international banks now published? Why have the results of tests on smaller banks not been made public? In fact, smoe banks that have traditional banking activities and mainly domestic investment and lending activities can be analysed more closely and based on their own financial reporting. It can also be noted that the current performance and performance reporting requires fairly comprehensive descriptions of the risks sven from smoe banks. Large banks, which have complex operations and operations in many countries, the management of risks can be accurate and inconclusive from only official and financial reporting. The banks operate as a complex and their operating environment is fast and fast, and they have risks compared to the traditional banking risks. They have typically expanded into investment activities with many complicating products that can trigger exposures that cannot be highlighted in numerous reports to provide a satisfactory picture of potential problems. It sr svoert sven for experts to analyse risk positions vsl and to estimate risks rstt. Doe and doefore people who are concerned about sad events where banks have fallen into serious difficulties and caused serious problems not only for the bank, but also for the parties and the rest of the economy. This is precisely where there is a need for public stress tests, carried out by banking supervisors, which provide information on risks and potential outcomes in the event of uninvolved circumstances. The banks' stress test d and the publication of the results d have become an increasingly important part of the monitoring work. One of my colleagues in the Federal Reserve, i.e. the US Federal Reserve, pointed out that the stress test sr the most important and strongest government activity to help banks keep up with the times. Through stress tests, authorities can guide banks to build up risk buffers. The very knowledge of stress tests has a major impact, not only on the banks but also on the confidence of the public. Title: How strong is the foundation for economic growth in Finland?
text: Executive Board Vice-President Pentti Hakkarainen: How strong is the foundation for economic growth in Finland? Mariehamn, 15.8.2016. . Speech . HOW STRONG IS THE FOUNDATION F... IS THE FINANCIAL SITUATION IN FINLAND? After a loeng period of dsmpad tillvsxt, a turnaround has now taken place and the economic outlook for Finland is showing a weak upturn. Title: Where does well-being come from? Finns' journey from the cascades towards the digital world
text: Vice Chairman of the Board Pentti Hakkarainen: Misch well-being is born? Finns' journey from kaskimaki towards the digital world. Iisalmi, 17.9.2016. . Speech . Saturday 17September 2016,2:45 PM Keynote speech by Pentti Hakkarainen, Vice Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Bank of Finland At the regional meeting of the Yls-Savo Youth Chamber of Commerce in Iisalmi 17.9.2016 Presentation body d the presentation held may differ Pictures (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches/documents/160917-mista-wellness-syntyy_yla-savon. . Youth Chamber of Commerce images.pdf)(PDF) Good ladies and gentlemen! The Finnish economy is in a difficult situation. Although economic growth has picked up, it has not strengthened as usual, and the Ychchyms have remained subdued and stable. In my speech, I will discuss the economic nskymis and those factors that mssrsssvsvs. Although Finland is heavily dependent on international economic development, the keys to favourable development are ultimately long in our own countries. If Finns are entrepreneurs and invest in the future, the prerequisites for the development of our well-being can be good. Let me start with the global economy. [Figure 2] Over the past few years, the responsibility for the global economy has changed. So, in the years when the international financial crisis weighed heavily on the developed economies, growth in the emerging economies was much stronger. Overall, their financial systems were not in crisis and their domestic demand held its own. The situation changed when China's economic growth began to slow down and the prices of sljy and other raw materials began to fall a few years ago. Many emerging economies depend on export earnings from raw materials. Development weakened in countries that had previously grown rapidly, such as Brazil, South Africa and Russia. The effects of the contraction of the Russian economy have also been strongly felt in Finland. At the same time, developed economies had survived the worst effects of the international financial crisis. Of course, the consequences of the crisis will continue to be felt, as the debt burdens of households and governments, for example, are higher than before. Nevertheless, in the United States, the recovery process is now long, and the euro area economy has also been growing for a few years. Economic developments in various countries have been supported by strong monetary stimulus. What about the future? According to forecasts, the development of emerging economies is now improving. In China, the gradual slowdown in growth continues, but e.g. It has already been possible to reach some kind of grounding. In the advanced economies, growth is expected to continue. However, it is still not expected to be very strong, and new eps backuptekijs have emerged. [Figure 3] Many of them are linked to recent trends in international politics. In Europe and the United States, national interests and international cooperation have increasingly emerged. Armed conflicts continue in Lshi-idssss. There have been a number of terrorist attacks in Europe. One of the key factors for Europe's economic development is the UK's EU solution. *** The development of the Finnish economy has been known to be weak for several years. The level of GDP is still significantly lower than in 2008, just before the onset of the international financial crisis. In a short period of time, the economy has suffered a number of powerful blows. In addition to the general subdued nature of the international economy, the Finnish economy has been weighed down by problems in the electronics and lumberjack industries, rising domestic cost levels, the contraction of growth in the labour market and, more recently, the weakness of the Vensjs economy. The headwinds have been particularly strong on exports. [Figure 4] Since 2008, Finnish exports have contracted more than those of other developed economies. In fact, there has not been a single large and long-term contraction in exports for decades in another developed economy. The development of business investment has also been exceptionally weak in Finland. Household demand has remained much stronger. Before the international financial crisis, Finland did not experience the same strong growth in household debt or rising house prices as many other developed economies. So there has not been the same need to reduce household debt or house prices as in many other countries. The operational capacity of the financial system in Finland has remained good. Last year, the downturn in the Finnish economy was prolonged, and the economy grew slightly. Household consumer demand has continued to increase, while construction has continued to grow. The employment situation has improved somewhat. However, exports and business investment have remained subdued. All in all, Finland's economic development has been strongly ambivalent since 2008. While exports, manufacturing and business investment have contracted, private consumption and service production have increased. The decline in export earnings has meant that consumption growth has been strongly debt-driven. The expenditure of both households and the public sectors has been higher than their income. The latest forecasts estimate that economic growth in Finland will continue, although not very fast. However, it is certain how long even such growth can continue in Finland if exports and business investment do not recover. Strongly debt-driven growth is not at the bottom of the table. In Finland, measures are now needed to improve the conditions for improving the sustainability of exports, investment and employment. This is key to restoring cost competitiveness and structural reforms that improve the growth potential of the economy. *** [Figure 5] The current economic uncertainties are partly related to the question of whether the trend in the long term of economic growth is slowing down. After the difficulties of recent years, is there some kind of new normality in international economic development that is weaker than in the past? One of the factors behind the prerequisites for economic growth is the development of vsests. In advanced economies, the vsests is getting older. The number of people aged 15d64, who are counted as Tysikss, has already declined in Finland, and the same will soon happen in many other EU countries. In the United States, too, the growth of the number of employees is slowing down significantly. However, the development of economic prosperity over a long period of time is not primarily related to development, but to productivity. The increase in productivity means that the same contribution can be used to produce more and better goods and services. In recent years, the slowdown in productivity growth has repeatedly been negative in the developed economies. The future of productivity development is now the subject of lively debate among economists. Many people risk that productivity growth in the coming decades will not be as rapid as in the past. The same risk also applies to Finland. I will come back to these questions at the end of my speech. *** If we want to understand the development of the Finnish economy since the 1800s, productivity growth plays a key role. [Figure 6] Production per capita in Finland grew rapidly compared to most other countries for most of the 1900s, when productivity growth was rapid. How well has Finland become one of the most developed economies in the world? The fact that Finland had a "persssshiihtsjsn advantage" does not alone explain the rise. Most of the countries in the world were backward compared to the wealthiest economies in the late 1800s, and almost all of them are still Sith. Finland is one of the very few that managed to be caught during the 1900s. In addition to Finland, there are hardly any similar success stories other than Norway and Japan. The key factors behind Finland's success include international connections, an increase in the level of competence and, in many respects, strong institutions. [Figure 7] Industrialisation linked to international trade is often a key factor in the success of the Finnish economy. The economy of a small country can prosper among the larger ones by specializing in certain export industries where economies of scale can be achieved. This can be successful, for example, in sectors where raw materials are abundantly extracted from the home country. This kind of success was foretold in Finland already in the 1600s and 1700s, when Finland was the world's largest producer of tar. During the actual industrial mass production, the success of the forest industry has been partly the same. However, such an increase in industrial production based on economies of scale does not alone explain Finland's success. The world's wealthiest economies had a significant head start over Finland in terms of productivity, except in industry and in many service sectors. Over the decades, smsk's lead has narrowed or disappeared. International links are linked to Finland's industrialisation and rapid productivity growth in many ways. Trade links have made it possible to increase exports and import raw materials and semi-finished products needed by industry. In addition, the cross-border mobility of people and people has contributed to the introduction of new technologies and the development of skills. Over the decades, finland received countless amounts of foreign direct investment d especially from the most developed economies. Their country also received the necessary financing for investments from abroad. This type of investment was often accompanied by the adoption of frontier production methods. In many cases, these advances required the development of the personnel's skills. Nsin was born out of demand for higher education than before. When it was received, the pool of experts grew and its readiness to take on more and more new technologies. Good development fed itself. Vshitelle also grew the Finns' own ability to invest, finance investments and develop production methods. Enterprise and risk-taking. Many of the companies now operating in Finland have a background in tssss, in a development that began in the second half of the 1800s. One example is Stora Enso. Its Finnish operations are rooted in Wilh, founded in Fredrikstad, Norway, in 1860. Gutzeit & Co in a hsyry sawmill. Hans Gutzeit, who inherited the sawmill, began to apply for a new place for it in Finland, where logs were more readily available than in Norway. In 1872, hsn built a sawmill in what was then Kymi, in the area of the present-day city of Kotka. It became the largest and most modern in Finland, and its powerhouse was a hchyry machine with a power of one hundred horsepower. The sawmill was run by professional men from Norway who moved to Kym with Hans Gutzeit. The sawmill began to be called the Norwegian sawmill, by which name it was known for decades. A multi-stage development began, which has led to stora Enso being one of the world's largest forest industry associations. Another example is Outokumpu Oyj. In 1910, its lshchi point was a copper ore mill made in the city of Outkumpu in Kuusjsrven pitsjssss. The technology, i.e. the electrolytic method used to separate copper, was initially obtained from Norway. The operation of the mine was not without its problems, and in the late 1910s the company was leased for three years to the Norwegian company Hybinette. In the 1920s, the owner of the mine became the State of Finland. Copper was produced with the energy of the Imatrankoski power plant. In 1944, the military situation on the Isthmus front became difficult. For the war economy, the transfer of the srkesn copper smelter from Imatra to Harjavalta now became vsltsmsch. The increase in the supply of Sshks and the increase in the price after the war boosted the energy of the sssching method, i.e. the development of flame smelting. It is said to have been one of the most significant inventions of the 1900s in the field of copper metallurgy. The flame smelting method was productized d first for its own Harjavalta smelter in 1949 and then sold more widely to the world, the first of which was to Furukawa in 1956. The procedure turned out to be a vote of confidence; more than half of the world's current copper production is produced using the flame smelting method developed by Outokumpu. On the basis of flame smelting technology, Outotec, a leading expert in metal technology, developed into a separate resin company. The current Outokumpu Oyj produces stainless steel and is the largest company in its field in Europe, if not in the world. The third example is Neste Corporation. It was preceded in 1948 as a state entity in a field that was long-standing for Finns at the time. The purpose of the company was to secure finland's sljyn maintenance. Neste gained a significant competitive advantage over its competitors with its technologically advanced process of refining sulphur fuel from highly sulphur-containing venslsisests raw. As a result of its own research, Neste has developed a technology for the production of renewable diesel from vegetables and fats from the food industry. In February 2014, Talouselsms magazine selected the invention as the most revolutionary Finnish business innovation. Today, Neste is a large company that produces a wide variety of processed products from raw materials and other materials. ssls from Savo to similar in global competition to psrjssvis companies such as Olvi, Ponsse, Normet, Genelec, etc. are based on world-class expertise in their own industry and technology. As economists have tried to find out why some countries have been more economically successful than others over a long period of time, and where lively economic activity generates growth, no simple explanations have been provided. For example, abundant natural resources can explain the development of society and, in the worst case scenario, can even be a factor in the development of society and a factor that slows down economic growth. Of the various easily measurable quantities, there has been no desire to explain the factors. Careful examinations have focused on highlighting the institutions of society and the economy. This is well described in the book Why Nations Fail by two professors Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson. Finland's successes can also be explained not only by the existence of international links, but also by other institutional factors. [Figure 8] The most important institutional strengths of Finland from an economic point of view are considered to be a reliable judiciary, efficient public administration, corruption, good quality of basic education, infrastructure and the broad participation of women in the labour market. Although there is always room for improvement, Finland compares with many other countries in terms of nshden mystified institutions. At least some of them have probably been among Finland's strengths for a long time, so they can be the backbone of Finland's long-term success. The institutional strengths mentioned above create opportunities for favourable economic development. For example, when the functioning of the judiciary has been reliable, foreign companies have dared to make direct investments in Finland. In the same way, Finnish entrepreneurs have dared to take financial risks in their operations, as they have been able to rely on the psssevsnss themselves to enjoy the fruits when the project is successful. In all the other countries, the situation has not been as good as it has been. The stability of public finances and monetary conditions also provides opportunities for economic growth. When public finances are at the bottom of the table, companies do not have to worry about increasing taxation in the future. When monetary conditions are stable, companies do not have to worry about the movement of prices or financial charges in the future. The most important events for the stability of monetary conditions in Finland were the emergence of the Finnish markka in the 1860s, the decoupling of its value from the development of the Vensjsn ruble, and the tying of the value of the markka to silver and later to gold. The transition to the international gold standard also made it easier to obtain financing for Finland, which was located far from the financial centres of Europe. *** Let us return to the current challenges of today's economy and the Finnish economy. As I said earlier, the key to growth is now the restoration of cost competitiveness and structural reforms to support growth potential. This refers to research data and experiences from Finland and other countries. [Figure 9] Can a longer historical perspective teach us anything about overcoming the current difficulties of the Finnish economy? At the very least, it refers to the role of international contacts. In addition, it refers more generally to the importance of institutions. Catching up with the institutional strengths of the Finnish economy is essential in the current situation. We will continue to need a reliable and efficient public administration and judiciary, good basic education and infrastructure, corruption and the broad participation of women in the labour market. *** The international debate on the future development of productivity growth concerns long-term technological progress and its consequences. Historical analyses have highlighted the importance of major technological advances in the long term for productivity development. In the 1800s, the development of chyry power and railways was revolutionary. In the early 1900s, the harnessing of sshksn and the internal combustion engine had wide-ranging effects. In recent decades, information technology has played a similar role. It is a long-term question of how much we can expect from information technology in the years to come. Have the greatest effects on productivity and well-being already been felt, or is shsnastic development only a foretaste of what is to come? Is the impact of digitalisation on par with previous technological revolutions? Answers to these questions will only come from the test of time. [Figure 10] In any case, it is clear that digitalisation will continue to change societies in the future. Computers and robots have destroyed many jobs and created a lot of new ones, and this trend will continue. There are also estimates that technological progress could lead to a permanence increase in the number of people. However, history and economics do not wholeheartedly support this kind of nskemysts. Previous ones too technological revolutions have destroyed jobs, but human beings have still shilled their value. However, there are reasons to take the concern about growing inequality in the context of technological developments. In recent decades, digitalisation, in combination with globalisation, has particularly affected middle-income jobs in developed economies. In economic policy, it is necessary to take into account trends. The people who lose their jobs must be able to use their skills. The exclusion of the labour market and the lack of transparency is an obstacle. It is at the heart of society in okoo in terms of the conditions for economic growth. [Figure 11] Economic policy, on the other hand, should not be used to push technological advances and globalisation to the national border. The conditions must be in place for innovation to be taken into use, and we have the potential to be at the forefront of technology. The journey of Finns from the kaskimas towards the digital world can continue successfully. Lshteits Acemoglu, Daron d Robinson, James: Why Nations Fail. 2012. Kokkinen, Arto: How did Finland rise?
