Title: Honorary Doctor's Speech "How does the current crisis influence economic and financial research?" Turku School of Economics Doctoral Conferment
text: Johtokunnan jssen Seppo Honkapohja: Kunniatohtorin puhe "How does the current crisis inuence economic and nancial research?" Turun kauppakorkeakoulun tohtoripromootio 14.5.2010 . Speech . Friday 14May2010,12:00 AM Seppo Honkapohja Kunniatohtorin puhe Turun kauppakorkeakoulun tohtoripromootio 14.5.2010 HOW DOES THE CURRENT CRISIS INFLUENCE ECONOMIC AND FINANCIAL RESEARCH? Honorable Rector Mr. Virtanen, Director of the School Mrs. Lshteenmski, Conferrer Mr. Paasio, Professors, Young Doctors, Colleague Honorands, Ladies and Gentlemen The current economic and financial crisis has now lasted over two and half years. It is the biggest peace-time economic crisis since the Great Depression of the 1930s. The Second Great Contraction, as it is often called, has had huge ramifications to economic and business life. The crisis has also sparked as indeed it should a lively debate about misguided orientations in economic and financial research. Today I want to offer a short overview of new research directions that economics and finance seem to be taking. There was no single cause for the Second Great Contraction. A number of developments in the financial system contributed to a huge credit boom that turned into a global crisis. The boom was fuelled by financial innovations, which initially looked good but turned out to be disastrous. There were also macroeconomic causes. Global imbalances between countries, in particular between China and the United States, had a major impact by providing funds to the boom. Monetary policy in the early years of the past decade has also been blamed, though there are disagreements about its significance. Looking at the financial system, one set of problems arose from distorted incentives in financial intermediation. Attempts to improve distribution of risks motivated wide-spread issuance and sale of asset backed securities. These included bundles of mortgages, consumer credit and business loans, as well as further layers of structured assets. One problem in the process of securitization was that it weakened lenderso incentives to properly assess borrower quality. A second distortion turned out to be the fact that, for a number of reasons, risks were not sufficiently spread outside the banking system. A third distortion has been the form of remuneration. Many contracts essentially offered unbounded upside rewards but capped downside losses and thus encouraged excessive risk taking. Information problems were another cause for the financial crisis. The new complex securities that were created in the hectic boom were one source of information problems. Assessing risk exposure and the value of even simple bundled securities is not straight-forward. These assessment difficulties were multiplied in more sophisticated securities that included embedded options, multi-layer structures, and hierarchies. Another set of information problems arose from the appearance of significant counterparty risk during the crisis and its impact on the behavior of highly-leveraged financial intermediaries. Financial-system causes for the crisis have taught important lessons for economic and financial research. The problems just outlined are amenable to economic analysis. However, the appropriate theories are quite different from the efficient markets hypothesis which postulates that financial markets function well and are free from bubbles and excessive volatility. There were also macroeconomic causes for the Second Great Contraction. Of these, the phenomenon of global imbalances is more a failure of economic policy and politics than of economic science. However, some major lessons for macroeconomic research have also become apparent. Study of economic history should have a much more prominent place in macroeconomics curricula. It has become painfully clear that financial booms and busts occur with significant regularity. They are not just a orare evento. Deeper understanding of earlier financial crises yields insights to the analysis of the current crisis. Right now, it is particularly instructive to study the history of past sovereign debt crises. Recent economic history also teaches another, very different lesson. Academics and policy makers should not be fooled by periods of macroeconomic tranquility. The two decades before the current crisis called the Great Moderation were, overall, a period of relative calm in the international economy. Great Moderation influenced risk perceptions of actors in financial markets, including regulators and central bankers. In addition, it influenced the views of the economics profession about the role of money and credit in the macro economy. The canonical macroeconomic models relegated money and credit to a side show. The key frictions in the economy were thought to be in the real sector. The current crisis has made it clear that credit, and banking must have a central place in macroeconomics. Moreover, financial factors are not just small frictions that can somewhat amplify business cycles in the economy. The financial system can occasionally be a source of major shocks and disruptions. Understanding their consequences will require a new generation of macroeconomic models. To conclude, it may be recalled that, after the work of John Maynard Keynes, the Great Depression of the 1930s led to a revolution in macroeconomics. In contrast, the Second Great Contraction has so far not brought about a scientific revolution. We are seeing a lively reassessment and reorientation of prevailing economic and financial theories. It is encouraging that the economics profession is taking initial steps in new research directions underscored by the crisis.

Title: Lessons from the financial crisis on monetary policy, financial stability and regulation. Money, Macro and Finance Research Group, 42nd Annual Conference
text: Member of the Board Seppo Honkapohja: Lessons from the nancial crisis on monetary policy, nancial stability and regulation. Money, Macro and Finance Research Group, 42nd Annual Conference, Limassol 3.9.2010 . Speech . Friday 3September 2010, 12:00 AM Member of the Board Seppo Honkapohja: Money, Macro and Finance Research Group, 42nd Annual Conference, Limassol 3.9.2010 Slides (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and.. interviews/documents/100903_mmf_conference_limassol.pdf)(pdf) Let me first say that I am very happy to participate in the panel in front of this group of economic researchers. I want to thank the organizer for inviting me to the panel. It is a common view that there are a great many causes for the current economic and financial crisis. These range from (i) very favorable macro-financial conditions before the crisis, (ii) significant financial imbalances that remained concealed for a long time, and (iii) mistakes by the financial markets, institutions and supervisors. See slide 1 for a more detailed list. [Slide 1] There are a large number of good discussions of these causes and no doubt, the analysis of them will become more refined over time. I will not discuss them further, except to note that the multitude of causes is a big challenge for research and the area provides many good research topics. The impact of financial instability on the real economy has been the key element in the current crisis. This observation has several important consequences. (i) Money and credit must be central in macroeconomics and policy. (ii) The financial system is occasionally the key source of disruptions to the real economy. (iii) Achieving financial stability (FS) is of major importance for the real economy. In addition, I want to note that concerns about public debts are the third stage in the current financial crisis. This is an unsurprising development as many financial crises in history have had three stages: banking and/or currency crisis, recession in the real economy, and public debt crisis. My remarks in the panel focus on two topics. First, I address some aspects of the changing views about macroeconomic/price stability (PS) and financial stability (FS). Second, I want consider the sovereign debt crisis by looking at what we know about these crises in the past. Let me start with the relationship between PS and FS. Slide 2 present a simplified interpretation of the traditional view of this relationship. [Slide 2] A key idea is that achieving FS contributes to achievement of PS, but link is relatively weak. Monetary policy affects the real economy and its transmission works to a large extent via interest rates that in turn affect the situation of financial institutions. In terms of FS the relation is nevertheless weak, provided monetary policy focuses on PS and is successful in achieving macroeconomic stability. Apart from the cost of finance, the links from the financial system to the real economy are weak. Regulatory policy naturally influences the stability of the financial system. This view suggests a clear assignment between monetary policy and FS policy. Monetary policy should be assigned to achieve macroeconomic/price stability, whereas regulatory policy is the key tool to address FS. The objectives and instruments are different, though there is some natural interaction. Communication is crucial for the two sets of policies and it is important to distinguish between FS and PS policy communication. This traditional view about the connections between PS and FS has been altered by the events in the financial crisis. Financial instability during the crisis had major consequences for the real economy. Indeed, it resulted in a very rapid decline in real activity in 2008 and early 2009. Slide 3 sketches how the traditional view about the connections between PS and FS has been changed by what happened during the crisis. [Slide 3] There are several phenomena that are important topics for further research for both theoretical and, in particular, empirical work. One issue is the risk-taking channel of monetary policy, according to which low interest rates lead to more risk-taking and leverage by banks. The mechanisms behind financial frictions and constraints that quickly and in an apparently nonlinear fashion emerged in the crisis are another important topic for further work. In this area new research has already been initiated and the area will most likely become an even more important in the future. Another lesson from the events in past three years is that both monetary and fiscal policies are needed in the clean.up of major failures of finance and the resulting recessions. Policy-makers have cooperated extensively during the current crisis. This effort has been successful in preventing a melt-down of the international financial system that would also have led to a much worse outcome in the real economy than what happened in 2008-2009. More generally, in my opinion there are several lessons for monetary policy from the crisis. I will not go into details here but here is a list of issues that are under discussion and would benefit from an academic input as well. (i) A very rapid overall credit growth should always be a warning signal. Such growth is likely to be associated with strong asset price increases. (ii) In terms of objectives monetary policy should remain focused on the maintenance of price stability over the medium term. Moreover, monetary policy should not be burdened with other objectives. (iii) Institutional independence of the central bank is essential. The experiences from the current crisis have not altered this underpinning of modern central banking. Regulatory measures are the other main set of policies. There are two parts to regulatory policies. First, during a financial crisis there will typically be a need to initiate crisis management. A lot has been said and written about this topic. Let me just point out that regulatory management during a financial crisis must take care of the potentially necessary recapitalization of banks, and it may also have carry out restructuring of financial systems. Finally, its objective should the eventual creation of sustainable business conditions for banks and other institutions. Another aspect of regulatory change is the new regulatory and supervisory initiatives inspired by a financial crisis. At the moment we are seeing this kind of response to the current crisis. The plans under discussion include reformed high.quality capital and liquidity standards for banks, and the regulations are likely to have wide coverage of financial institutions. An important innovation coming from the current crisis is the concept of macro-prudential regulation that focuses on systemically important financial institutions. This is a very new area with many open issues and there are surely good and important research issues in this area. Let me now move to the second part of my remarks that are directed the sovereign debt crisis. We know from basic economics that successful resolution of a fiscal crisis has two crucial parts. Turning primary public balance, i.e. balance between expenditure and revenues excluding interest payments, gradually positive is one key step. The other basic step is resumption of economic growth, so that the growth rate of real GDP is preferably higher than the average level of real interest on public debt that a country is paying. The current fiscal situation is challenging in many countries. This is shown, for example, by the computations by the IMF done in early part of 2010 in Slide 4. [Slide 4] Major corrections in the fiscal balances need to be carried out. There is a large literature estimating the effects of different types of fiscal consolidations. The basic messages from this literature are the following. A fiscal consolidation usually has short run costs in terms of reduced growth and a temporary worsening the public debt-to-GDP ratio. One message is that a consolidation should be relative large and persistent, i.e. last for several years. Initial conditions also matter best chances for success are when the fiscal deficit is large and the public debt position is unsustainable in the long run. There are also differences in effects between expenditure cuts and tax increases. I will not go into the details. In principle, one should adopt measures that have small fiscal multipliers as this minimizes the negative short-run effects. In the long run, the effects of a fiscal consolidation are often positive as growth speeds up. To achieve this, a consolidation should primarily focus on expenditure cuts rather tax increases. The reason is that tax increases are often distortionary and tend to reduce economic growth. However, in reducing government expenditures one should avoid cuts in productive public spending, as such cuts can have negative effects on growth. Initial conditions of the economy also matter. Best success seems to be in a odifficulto initial situation, i.e. when the government sector is relatively large and the initial public debt-to-GDP ratio is relatively high. There are even situations with non-Keynesian short-run effects, in which the fiscal multipliers are negative and thus expenditure cuts are expansionary even in the short run. These possible Non-Keynesian effects operate through expectations about improvements in the future fiscal situation and also faster economic growth. The basic idea is that Non-Keynesian effects can arise when a country is in an unsustainable situation (expectations of a omesso in the future) and the consolidation succeeds in changing these expectations. Let me next look at some examples of public debt dynamics after a financial crisis. [Slides 5-9]. A key feature of a fiscal consolidation is that the actual process of debt reduction takes many years. The crises of Finland and Sweden, which erupted in 1991, involved major increases in public debt and it then took over ten years to reduce the debt-to-GDP ratios by 20-30 percent. Mexico 1994 is another example with smaller build-up of debt but it took five years to reduce the debt ratio to the pre-crisis level. Sometimes, there is only stabilization of the public debt to GDP ratio as a result of the crisis. Korea in the 1990s and Spain in the 1970s are two examples. Current discussions about public debt problems in many Western market economies illustrate a fundamental difficulty in public debt crises. Realistic time horizons for fiscal action by a government and market perceptions of the speed of public decision making are very different. Carrying out a fiscal consolidation is inherently a very slow process as indicated by the examples just discussed. Even drawing up plans for the fiscal actions takes non-trivial amount of time. These uncertainties trouble the markets, lead to rumors and occasional herds that move the market sentiments. To minimize these uncertainties it is important to try to anchor expectations about future fiscal developments. Clear multi-year fiscal programs to improve credibility and significant size of the consolidation can help here. Likewise, front-loading may well be a good thing. Focusing on items with small fiscal multipliers should also provide some relief. Credibility of the consolidation will depend on its execution. The plans should not be overly ambitious, so that they can be carried through the political decision-making process. Goals should be set somewhat conservatively in order to minimize the probability of disappointments in the early years. Development of better fiscal institutions is vital for improving credibility and, in the longer run, reputation. The experiences of Finland and Sweden during the 1990os crises provide examples of the role of improvement of fiscal institutions. Both countries made reforms that gave better centralized control for policy-making about fiscal decisions, in particular the budget process. One useful innovation was the adoption of multi-year expenditure ceilings and other practices that helped to achieve the fiscal consolidations. Improvement of fiscal institutions is currently a major objective in the EU and euro-system fiscal institutions. Enforcement of the Stability and Growth Pact has clearly been inadequate before the current crisis. Major steps are now being taken to strengthen the European fiscal institutions. These include the European Financial Stability Mechanism (ESFM) and European Financial Stability Facility (EFSF), stronger surveillance of budgetary policies and the Van Rompoy task force on economic governance in the EU. In UK, the new government has established an Office for Budgetary Responsibility that will monitor the fiscal situation in the UK in the coming years.

Title: How will economics change after the financial crisis? VATT's 20th anniversary seminar
text: Board member Seppo Honkapohja: How will economics change after the nanny crisis? VATT's 20th anniversary seminar 1.10.2010 . Speech . Friday 1 October 2010, 12:00 AM Seppo Honkapohja VATT's 20th anniversary seminar 1.10.2010 Speech liittyv?t Membranes (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and. . interviews/documents/101001_sh__vatt.ppt) (PPT) Puheeseen liittyv?t Membranes (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and. . interviews/documents/101001_sh__vatt.pdf) (PDF) HOW WILL ECONOMICS CHANGE AFTER THE FINANCIAL CRISIS? Dear General, ladies and gentlemen, Introduction The current economic and financial crisis has now lasted more than three years. The crisis has been the most difficult in peacetime since the Great Depression of the 1930s. The current crisis, often referred to in English as eethe Second Great Contractionee, has had a major impact on various countries and the global economy. The loss of output has been significant in the economic areas of the world economy and for some years before most market economies have reached the pre-crisis standard of living in terms of GDP. In Finland, for example, the level is not expected to be reached until 2012. Economists ? with some exceptions ? could not have foreseen a future crisis, which has given rise to strong criticism of economics and a lively debate on erroneous trends in economic and financial science research. Some economists, such as Paul Krugman of the New York Times in September 2009, have called for a fundamental reorientation of economics. Others have defended economics, pointing out that there are a lot of examples of so-called economics in recent research. eerelevantsee of research areas. It is not surprising that there is a wide range of opinions in the debate, and there is no consensus. There is no attempt to create a systematic overview of the debate at the moment. L?hdenk's movement from the other direction, i.e. I will briefly look at the causes of the economic crisis and, on the basis of them, comment on the problem areas of economics and what changes, according to my observations, have begun to take place in economics. Towards the end of my presentation, I will move on to a more general level and briefly reflect on the methodological points of macroeconomics and the pressures for their change. Causes of the economic crisis [Figure 1: Causes of economic crises] At the moment, researchers and researchers and the committee's leadership on the developments that led to the economic crisis is that there is not just one specific reason for the crisis. The crisis arose from the combined influence of many authors. Macroeconomic and financial conditions before the crisis were exceptionally favourable. Growth was brisk, inflation remained low, liquidity was well available, financial market volatility was low and risk premia were low. Conditions fuelled not only rapid economic growth, but above all the strong credit cycle, during which many imbalances did not receive sufficient attention. Housing and fixed prices rose to high levels in many countries, fuelled by strong credit and indebtedness growth. The banking system relied more broadly on the securitisation of credit, which was imagined to be the risk of financial providers. Macroeconomic factors also played a role. Credit growth, particularly in the United States, was based on significant global imbalances in the country, with investment surpluses flowing from developing countries to rich countries, especially the United States. Of the ep?balistic, the czech situation is the situation of China and the United States. During the crisis, the balance narrowed somewhat, but it has not improved. Monetary policy and low interest rates at the beginning of the last decade have been so criticised. Low interest rates encouraged higher returns in the search, leading to underpricing of risks and excessive risk-taking. [Figure 2: Causes of economic crises, continuation] The problems encountered in the functioning of the financial markets, financial institutions and the social economy constitute the third strand of the causes of the economic crisis. One element was the increase in the incentives for financing. Efforts to improve risk-sharing are widely motivated by the issuance and sale of asset-backed securities, including bundled mortgages, consumer loans and corporate loans, as well as other structured products. The securitisation of credits undermined lenders' incentives to assess the borrower's solvency. The problem turned out to be that, for a number of reasons, the risks did not spread sufficiently beyond the banking system. When the market entered a crisis, a significant part of the bad loans were the responsibility of the banking system, which led to large losses and, in many cases, to the withdrawal of banks from public funds. The fee structures applied to the siphons of financial institutions are also included in the incentives. Many contracts did not limit returns, but there were limits on losses, which encouraged excessive risk-taking. Various information problems also contributed to the financial crisis. One of the key assets was the new complex securities created during the credit boom. Even assessing the risks and value of simple packaged securities is not straightforward. The assessment problems were further complicated by the introduction of very complex securities, which included options and other instruments of different types and levels. Information problems were also caused by significant counterparty risks arising during the crisis and their impact on the use of high-leveraged counterparties. Weaknesses were also revealed on the financial and ? control side. Going into the details, it can be noted that before the financial crisis, in the years leading up to the financial crisis, the change in the financial system was exceptionally rapid and that the system did not keep up with the development of the financial system. The crisis has shown that self-isolation and market demands are not sufficient to guarantee the stability of the financial system. ?m? is one of the teachings of the events of recent years. [Figure 3: Basic Education] The escalation of the crisis into a global downturn in the real economy in the second half of 2008 is evident from which lessons are learned. The financial system is sometimes central to the real economy and its impact on the wider spectrum. In the autumn, safeguarding the stability of the financial system will be part of economic policy in the future. Similarly, money, credit and banking must play a central role in macroeconomics, even if some of the cyclical fluctuations in market economies are ee normal and the financial system at that time is not the stability of the economy. The crisis has also been a lesson in macroeconomic policy. The monetary policy stimulus measures of the central banks, on the one hand, and the fiscal stimulus measures of the governments of the various countries, on the other, were able to be implemented in cooperation, which prevented the crisis from turning into a genuine global recession. However, the great recession experienced in eetoinen has been the most dangerous macroeconomic situation since the Second World War. There are reasons to point out that the crisis is not yet over and new h?iri?ich may well be encountered. The typical third phase of the financial crises, the sovereign debt crisis, did not really take until the beginning of the year and will take many years to deal with it. The final exit from the crisis is still a long way off, although most national economies have caught up with economic growth. Title: Opening words, changing exhibition of the Money Museum
text: Board member Seppo Honkapohja: Opening words, monetary museum's changing nsytilu, 20.1.2011 . Speech . Thursday20 January 2011,3:00 PM Seppo Honkapohja Opening words in the changing nsyttelysss oThree currencies,two centuries, one Bank of Finlando Bank of Finland Monetary Museum 20.1.2011 On behalf of the Bank of Finland, I have the pleasure of opening nsyttely oThree currencies, two centuries, one bank of Finlando in the Monetary Museum of the Bank of Finland. This is one of the events of the Bank of Finland's centenary year 2011. In December 1811, the Waihetus, Loan and Depositioni Contori was founded, which was renamed the Bank of Finland in 1840. Only the Swedish Riksbanken, the Bank of England and the Banque de France are older. Over the past 200 years, Finland has had three currencies d Vensjsn ruble, Finnish markka and euro. For citizens, a change in a currency or a monetary unit is always a czech event. The change in something that is often discussed affects all citizens and forces them to rethink the prices and wealth values of hysdys. Tssss nsyttelysss tells about the monetary changes carried out during the 200-year history of the Bank of Finland. Changes in the currency or monetary unit are anchored in the events of different periods of time, as well as in the living conditions of citizens and their changes. The first change in monetary conditions came about when Finland became a Grand Duchy under Vensjs. Waihetus., Loan and Depositioni -Contori issued ruble and kopeekkamsrsisis banknotes to eliminate the shortage of cash. However, the thalers of swedish rule remained in use until the early 1840s. At the beginning of 1841, Vensjs initiated a monetary reform in which paper or bank rubles of varying values were replaced by silver rubles. The old banknotes were collected and exchanged for new banknotes from the Bank of Finland, which can be redeemed with silver. At the same time, the Swedish peafowl camps were picked up. The transition from ruble to mark was made in 1860. The reason for this was the collapse of the ruble in the 1850s as a result of the Crimean War. Because of the war, Vensjs gave up the silver standard. When the exchange of banknotes for silver escalated, the exchange of the ruble was first restricted and the company was also abolished. In December 1859, the Senate of Finland proposed that the banknotes should not be in denomination ksypis, but that their value should be valued in the St. Petersburg bay. Chekhsn refused and in February 1860 the Bank of Finland proposed issuing its own monetary unit, the markka. On 4.4.1860, Alexander II made a declaration of the amended monetary unit to the Grand Duchy of Finland. After the issue of the markka, monetary conditions remained difficult, as Russian banknotes still had to be redeemed in Finland at their face value. The Senate began to investigate the restoration of the silver standard, and after various stages, the Finnish markka was attached to the silver standard on 8.11.1865. However, the world market price of silver fell at the turn of the 1860s d70s, which led to many countries switching to the gold standard. A new monetary law on Finland's transition to the gold standard entered into force at the beginning of 1878. In the reform, the Finnish markka formally acquired the same value as the French franc, i.e. 0.2903 grams of gold. However, Finland was not in a currency union with France. Vensjs took over the gold standard in 1897. Markka's existence was threatened at the turn of the 1900s, during the years of oppression. Vensjs sought to harmonise the monetary system in the Grand Duchy's own monetary unit. By decree, the gold ruble was made into money in Finland. However, the first world war and the collapse of the gold standard were brought together by the Finnish and Russian monetary systems. Finland gave up the gold standard in 1915. In the early days of Finland's self-decline, monetary conditions were mixed. In Finland, the gold standard came into force again in 1925, although the markka was clearly lower than before the World War. However, the second international gold standard was vulnerable and began to collapse in 1931. Finland gave up the gold standard in October 1931 and joined the so-called Gold Standard. to the pound club in 1933. The wars that broke out in the autumn of 1939 led to a large-scale squalification of the foreign exchange and financial markets. The state financed the war effort with banknote financing, which led to high inflation. 1946 In Finland, a banknote cut was carried out due to high inflation. The operation also financed the state, since the other side of the banknote was a forced loan to the state. In 1948, Finland joined the International Monetary Fund. The mark became a convertible currency ten years later, although travel currency, for example, was used after the sssdel. In 1963, the reform of ksytchraha took place, when two zeros were dropped from the mark and the pennies were taken again. The most recent monetary reform was the introduction of the euro in 1999. The euro was initially the currency of account and the euro notes and coins were introduced at the beginning of 2002. As far as the planning and compilation of the project is concerned, I can tell you that the idea for the work was born at a meeting of the museum's management group. It was curated by the museum's chief curator Jaakko Koskentola and the nsyttelytyhmhmhmsn were juha Tarkka, advisor to the board of directors, and Vappu Ikonen, a document service officer. The graphic layout of Nsyttely was created by architect Teemu Taskinen. The photographic material is from the collections of the Bank of Finland, the State Art Museum, the Finnish Heritage Agency's photo archive and the Helsinki City Museum. My sincerest thanks to those responsible for the implementation of the campaign. I am pleased to announce the opening of oThree currencies, two centuries, one bank of Finland.

Title: Speech on the occasion of the book launch of "Anticipating the Wealth of Nations"
text: Member of the Board Seppo Honkapohja: Speech on the occasion of the book launch of "Anticipating the Wealth of Nations", London, 5 December 2011 . Speech . Monday5 December 2011, 1:00 PM Speech on the occasion of the book launch of "Anticipating the Wealth of Nations: The Selected Works of Anders Chydenius (1729-1803)" by Maren Jonasson and Pertti Hyttinen Seppo Honkapohja, Bank of Finland. Finnish Embassy, London, 5 December 2011 It is a great honour and pleasure for me to discuss this book from the economics point of view. I should point out right away that I am a macroeconomist by background and not a specialist in economic history or history of economic thought. As an undergraduate I became aware of Chydeniuso important work through a summary article and I even tried to read his most important work but got discouraged by its old-fashioned translation. The publication in English of this collection of the works of Anders Chydenius is a landmark in Finnish economic and more generally social history of thought. Moreover, the translation uses modern English, which is important to enhance the readership of the book. I will not discuss Anders Chydeniuso life and career as an influential politician and intellectual in Sweden (and Finland as part of Sweden) in the 18th century. At the outset it must be said the breadth and depth of Chydeniuso writings is amazing. His writings convey that he was a passionate supporter of free trade, freedom of business and occupation, the rights of the rural labourers, as well as freedom of information and religion. The new collection on display contains Chydeniuso most important economic writing, his writing about freedom of information and social rights and also his auto-biography. My remarks will focus on Chydeniuso economic ideas and writing as nowadays he is perhaps most known for his thoughts about economic liberalism. It must be acknowledged at the start that many arguments by Chydenius are similar to those of Adam Smith. Chydeniuso most important writing, titled oThe National Gaino, was published in 1765, i.e., eleven years before the publication of Adam Smithso Wealth Nations. The latter is of course considered to be the decisive precursor to modern economics. I will shortly make some comparisons of economic ideas of Chydenius and Smith. Before discussing Chydeniuso economic writings in detail, I want to start with some remarks about the background and roots of his economic writings. Generally, scholarly economic writings in the 18th century Sweden can be said to correspond broadly to the major ideas and themes in economic doctrines in other countries in Europe. Sweden was well connected to the rest of Europe even. At the time the dominant school of economic thought was mercantilism, a doctrine that emphasized government control of foreign trade as the most important way for ensuring prosperity and security of the state. Mercantilist policies included high tariffs on manufactured goods, monopolized markets with staple ports, export subsidies, restricting imports, maximal use of domestic resources, and banning exports of gold and silver. Mercantilist doctrines were initially formed well before the 18th century. In Sweden the views of the economics scholars who were active in the first half of that century are nowadays considered to belong to the realm of relatively standard mercantilist thinking. In particular, the importance of attaining a favorable balance of trade was emphasized as it provided the basis for heavy regulation of the economy. However, something called oreform.mercantilismo emerged from the earlier oold mercantilisto thought. Reform-mercantilism is said to have formed a bridge with the more modern liberal economic thinking. A number of important Swedish writers are considered to belong to this reform group. Historians of Swedish economic thought usually place also Anders Chydenius in this group of reform-mercantilists who favored liberal economic attitudes and were critical of the usual mercantilist economic policies. If one looks at the writings of Chydenius, it is notable that he rather sparsely refers to other economic writers. Even Swedish writers are not mentioned that often in his work even though it is known that he interacted widely with the Swedish politicians and intelligentsia. As a starting point, it should be noted that Chydenius placed much less emphasis on the role of manufacturing than was done by mercantilists and correspondingly more on the role of agriculture. For this reason Chydenius is also placed in a school of writers called proto-Physiocrats. Initially, Physiocrats emphasized the role of agriculture on the basis of a onatural ordero which should govern living together of people. They were critical of the regulations that supported manufactures and they favored unlimited trade d they had grain trade in mind. It can be argued that Chydenius made an additional contribution to the views of the proto-Physiocracts, because Chydenius was insistent on free market and free trade quite broadly. He was against economic regulation as a matter of principle, not just to give more scope for agriculture. The school of Physiocrats also had a role in some ideas and doctrines presented in the Wealth of Nations. In particular, the concept of intertwined circular flows describing the organism of an economy was first formally presented Quesnaios Tableau Economiques in 1758. Adam Smithos concept of the invisible hand or, in modern terms, general equilibrium of markets relies on the idea of circular flows. In contrast, the idea of circular flows cannot be found in Chydeniuso writings. Let me now come back to the economic writings of Anders Chydenius. I already mentioned that his most important work is oThe National Gaino, published in 1765. The piece starts with the idea that the surplus of value of exported commodities over value of imported ones is called othe profit of the nationo. This sounds like a mercantilist notion, but Chydenius does not move on to the idea that an export surplus in the form of money is particularly good for the country. Instead, he says that the owealth of peopleo consists of the value of products brought about with the help of othe number of people and their diligenceo (p.145). Chydenius also entertains the coarse form of the idea of ocomparative advantageo, so that Sweden should use cheap labor and ample raw materials. This would make workers to focus on production that delivers highest incomes, maximum employment and increase exports. I must point out that comparative advantage is nowadays one of the corner-stones of modern economic theories of international trade. In the National Gain one can also find great deal of emphasis on freedom of enterprise and markets. Let me quote: oIf the door to profit is opened by free enterprise, every man will be fully employed within a few years; if that does not happen, however, the nation will inevitably, regardless of all other measures, become as drowsy as it was beforeeo (p.156). These ideas are very similar to doctrines that Adam Smith endorsed in his Wealth of Nations. One way to see the relation is to think of Adam Smithos concept of the division of labor as the fundamental element in improving the productivity of labor. Freedom to move from one occupation or industry is required if the gains from division of labor need to be attained. Constraints on mobility would diminish these gains. The collection contains four most important writings of Anders Chydenius. I have already commented on the National Gain. The other three writings deal with: (i) emigration of people from Sweden and measures address the problem, (ii) the staple system that limits exports of goods as a weakness of the country, and (iii) a natural system of finance as a remedy to the problem of inflation and weakness of the copper markka coinage. Each of the three writings contains surprisingly modern ideas. For example, writing (i) mentions the pursuit of happiness and benefits as a reason for emigration. In other words, people think rationally about mobility. Writing (ii) is strong pamphlets against regulation, especially those on exports. Writing (iii) is critical of the usual reasoning about the source of inflation suggesting instead that the large issue of bank notes as the problem. The essay also argues that the planned remedy, restrictions on the supply of money would lead to problems of deflation. I will not comment on these other essays in detail. I want to add that each of the four writings is accompanied by a commentary by Professor Lars Magnusson from Uppsala University. Magnusson is a very prominent scholar in economic history and history of economic thought. Magnussonos comments place each piece of writing in its surrounding political environment. This enhances the use of the book. Looking at the overall profile of Chydeniuso economic writings, it must be noted that Chydenius was primarily a politician and a remarkable intellectual. The four writings take the form of essays or pamphlets and they were published in a very short period 1765-1766. These observations deliver one contrast between Chydenius and Adam Smith. Smith was largely an academic scholar who studied in Glasgow and Oxford and became a Professor at Glasgow University in 1751. Wealth of Nations took ten years to write. It must be emphasized that the economic thinking of Anders Chydenius and Adam Smith are independent from one another despite the eleven year difference in the publication dates of The National Gain and the Wealth of Nations. Anglo-Saxon books about the history of economic thought do not mention Chydenius, because his writings appeared in Swedish and until now they have not been properly published in English. There have been a couple of earlier translations but their quality is not that high and the places of publication are obscure to the bigger world. The current collection of Chydeniuso most important writings finally rectifies the omission. I have made some brief comparisons of the writings of Chydenius to those of Adam Smith. I will not say more about this, but I want to make a comment about the title of the book. The word oanticipatingo in the title has some different meanings in English. As the writings of Chydenius ja Smith were made independently of each other, the neutral interpretation of the word oanticipateo as meaning odo something earlier thano (Oxford English Dictionary) is the correct one. There is no causal connection, but this does not reduce the significance of Chydenius. He was an influential intellectual who had many original ideas worthy of study by historians of economic and social thought. All significant scholars have intellectual predecessors and contemporaries. The real issue is whether a scholar has made contributions that improve and add to the existing intellectual and political knowledge and arguments. My remarks will focus on Chydenius economic ideas and writing as nowadays he is perhaps most known for his thoughts about economic liberalism. It must be acknowledged at the start that many arguments by Chydenius are similar to those of Adam Smith. Chydenius most important writing, titled The National Gain, was published in 1765, i.e., eleven years before the publication of Adam Smiths Wealth Nations. The latter is of course considered to be the decisive precursor to modern economics. I will shortly make some comparisons of economic ideas of Chydenius and Smith. Before discussing Chydenius economic writings in detail, I want to start with some remarks about the background and roots of his economic writings. Generally, scholarly economic writings in the 18th century Sweden can be said to correspond broadly to the major ideas and themes in economic doctrines in other countries in Europe. Sweden was well connected to the rest of Europe even. At the time the dominant school of economic thought was mercantilism, a doctrine that emphasized government control of foreign trade as the most important way for ensuring prosperity and security of the state. Mercantilist policies included high tariffs on manufactured goods, monopolized markets with staple ports, export subsidies, restricting imports, maximal use of domestic resources, and banning exports of gold and silver. Mercantilist doctrines were initially formed well before the 18th century. In Sweden the views of the economics scholars who were active in the first half of that century are nowadays considered to belong to the realm of relatively standard mercantilist thinking. In particular, the importance of attaining a favorable balance of trade was emphasized as it provided the basis for heavy regulation of the economy. However, something called reform.mercantilism emerged from the earlier old mercantilist thought. Reform-mercantilism is said to have formed a bridge with the more modern liberal economic thinking. A number of important Swedish writers are considered to belong to this reform group. Historians of Swedish economic thought usually place also Anders Chydenius in this group of reform-mercantilists who favored liberal economic attitudes and were critical of the usual mercantilist economic policies. If one looks at the writings of Chydenius, it is notable that he rather sparsely refers to other economic writers. Even Swedish writers are not mentioned that often in his work even though it is known that he interacted widely with the Swedish politicians and intelligentsia. As a starting point, it should be noted that Chydenius placed much less emphasis on the role of manufacturing than was done by mercantilists and correspondingly more on the role of agriculture. For this reason Chydenius is also placed in a school of writers called proto-Physiocrats. Initially, Physiocrats emphasized the role of agriculture on the basis of a natural order which should govern living together of people. They were critical of the regulations that supported manufactures and they favored unlimited trade  they had grain trade in mind. It can be argued that Chydenius made an additional contribution to the views of the proto-Physiocracts, because Chydenius was insistent on free market and free trade quite broadly. He was against economic regulation as a matter of principle, not just to give more scope for agriculture. The school of Physiocrats also had a role in some ideas and doctrines presented in the Wealth of Nations. In particular, the concept of intertwined circular flows describing the organism of an economy was first formally presented Quesnais Tableau Economiques in 1758. Adam Smiths concept of the invisible hand or, in modern terms, general equilibrium of markets relies on the idea of circular flows. In contrast, the idea of circular flows cannot be found in Chydenius writings. Let me now come back to the economic writings of Anders Chydenius. I already mentioned that his most important work is The National Gain, published in 1765. The piece starts with the idea that the surplus of value of exported commodities over value of imported ones is called the profit of the nation. This sounds like a mercantilist notion, but Chydenius does not move on to the idea that an export surplus in the form of money is particularly good for the country. Instead, he says that the wealth of people consists of the value of products brought about with the help of the number of people and their diligence (p.145). Chydenius also entertains the coarse form of the idea of comparative advantage, so that Sweden should use cheap labor and ample raw materials. This would make workers to focus on production that delivers highest incomes, maximum employment and increase exports. I must point out that comparative advantage is nowadays one of the corner-stones of modern economic theories of international trade. In the National Gain one can also find great deal of emphasis on freedom of enterprise and markets. Let me quote: If the door to profit is opened by free enterprise, every man will be fully employed within a few years; if that does not happen, however, the nation will inevitably, regardless of all other measures, become as drowsy as it was before (p.156). These ideas are very similar to doctrines that Adam Smith endorsed in his Wealth of Nations. One way to see the relation is to think of Adam Smiths concept of the division of labor as the fundamental element in improving the productivity of labor. Freedom to move from one occupation or industry is required if the gains from division of labor need to be attained. Constraints on mobility would diminish these gains. The collection contains four most important writings of Anders Chydenius. I have already commented on the National Gain. The other three writings deal with: (i) emigration of people from Sweden and measures address the problem, (ii) the staple system that limits exports of goods as a weakness of the country, and (iii) a natural system of finance as a remedy to the problem of inflation and weakness of the copper markka coinage. Each of the three writings contains surprisingly modern ideas. For example, writing (i) mentions the pursuit of happiness and benefits as a reason for emigration. In other words, people think rationally about mobility. Writing (ii) is strong pamphlets against regulation, especially those on exports. Writing (iii) is critical of the usual reasoning about the source of inflation suggesting instead that the large issue of bank notes as the problem. The essay also argues that the planned remedy, restrictions on the supply of money would lead to problems of deflation. I will not comment on these other essays in detail. I want to add that each of the four writings is accompanied by a commentary by Professor Lars Magnusson from Uppsala University. Magnusson is a very prominent scholar in economic history and history of economic thought. Magnussons comments place each piece of writing in its surrounding political environment. This enhances the use of the book. Looking at the overall profile of Chydenius economic writings, it must be noted that Chydenius was primarily a politician and a remarkable intellectual. The four writings take the form of essays or pamphlets and they were published in a very short period 1765-1766. These observations deliver one contrast between Chydenius and Adam Smith. Smith was largely an academic scholar who studied in Glasgow and Oxford and became a Professor at Glasgow University in 1751. Wealth of Nations took ten years to write. It must be emphasized that the economic thinking of Anders Chydenius and Adam Smith are independent from one another despite the eleven year difference in the publication dates of The National Gain and the Wealth of Nations. Anglo-Saxon books about the history of economic thought do not mention Chydenius, because his writings appeared in Swedish and until now they have not been properly published in English. There have been a couple of earlier translations but their quality is not that high and the places of publication are obscure to the bigger world. The current collection of Chydenius most important writings finally rectifies the omission. I have made some brief comparisons of the writings of Chydenius to those of Adam Smith. I will not say more about this, but I want to make a comment about the title of the book. The word anticipating in the title has some different meanings in English. As the writings of Chydenius ja Smith were made independently of each other, the neutral interpretation of the word anticipate as meaning do something earlier than (Oxford English Dictionary) is the correct one. There is no causal connection, but this does not reduce the significance of Chydenius. He was an influential intellectual who had many original ideas worthy of study by historians of economic and social thought. All significant scholars have intellectual predecessors and contemporaries. The real issue is whether a scholar has made contributions that improve and add to the existing intellectual and political knowledge and arguments. Title: Opening of the Last Marks exhibition
text: Board member Seppo Honkapohja: The last marks .nsyttely opening . Speech . Friday 27 January 2012, 1:00 PM LAST MARKS -NYTTELE OPENING 27.1.2012 BANK OF FINLAND MONEY MUSEUM TYPES OF FINNISH MARKKAMRISET BANKNOTES IN 1945d2002 It is my pleasure to welcome you all to the opening ceremony of the Bank of Finland's Monetary Museum, which changes every year. The theme of the year is the last marks. It presents the Finnish markkamsrsisis banknotes from the 1945 model to the issue of euro banknotes in 2002. At the end of February 2012, the Bank of Finland will stop redeeming mark banknotes issued after 1945, the 10th anniversary of the euro exchange. The text is based on a book of the same name written by Antti Heinonen and published by the Bank of Finland, which has been presented publicly by sske. It consists of two parts. Proposals for sketch competitions on the subjects of the banknotes in 1947 and 1982 were presented on the walls and walls. Multimedia presents the types of banknotes that were used in Finland after the Second World War. BANKNOTE REFORM IN THE 1940S At the beginning of the 1940s, the Bank of Finland and its banknote printing house began to design a new banknote model. Twenty years had passed since the last banknote reform (which had been abolished in 1922). In addition to the development of the graphic industry, the danger of the development of the graphic industry had also been increased. Another justification for the reform was the lack of banknote paper and its raw materials, which advocated a reduction in the size of banknotes. In 1939, a banknote of 5000 marks had been issued. Due to the high inflation during the war, it was planned to take a persti 10000 mark banknote in the form of a loan. In addition to the denomination of the banknotes, the Board of Trustees had also made preliminary consideration of the design of the design of the banknotes. However, the plans were rethought due to banknote cutting. According to the Government's press release, in 1946 the largest banknotes of 500, 1000 and 5000 marks were cut in half. The banknotes lost half of their value to the payment engine, with the other, or right, forming a forced loan to the state. At the same time, all the denominations, including FIM 100 and lower value banknotes, were exchanged for new ones in the early months of 1946. 1947 DESIGN CONTEST The next renewal of banknotes took place in 1946. The design was the subject of a competition open to Finnish artists, which prompted the design of the sketch for five different banknotes. The competition received 18 entries. The jury unanimously awarded the first prize (FIM 150,000, in today's money approximately EUR 8,000) to the pseudonym oSampoo (sculptorsjs Tapio Wirkkala), the second prize (FIM 100,000, in today's money approximately EUR 5,300) to the pseudonym oTys mies honoro (Tapio Wirkkala) and the third prize (FIM 75,000, in today's money approximately EUR 4,000) to the pseudonym oSuomen Leijonao (architect Matti Visanti). On the basis of the results of the competition, the Board of Trustees commissioned Tapio Wirkkala, together with the professionals of the printing industry, to start drawing up two models of banknotes. One of the banknotes would be embodied (front of the banknote) and the other exclusively other patterns and ornaments (back side). The Board of Governors decided, on the basis of printing and banking technology, that the new banknotes, regardless of their denomination, would all be the same size. The Bank's Board of Governors also decided on the design of the banknotes. A portrait of J.V. Snellman, the second largest president of the Republic, K. J. Stoehlberg, and the third largest incumbent president, J.K. Paasikivi, were chosen for the largest banknote. (In the design competition, Tapio Wirkkala had, however, sketched portraits of cultural figures on the banknotes.) The banknotes were put into circulation in late 1955, with the exception of the 1000 markka banknote, which was put into circulation in 1956. BANKNOTE REFORM IN THE 1980S AND 1990S Lshestyttsesss in the 1980s we were in a situation where the appearance of the setelistsn was based on a series issued in 1955, which had been diligently changed from the 1963 monetary reform. Two zeros were dropped from the denomination of the Chells banknotes. The series also included a 500-mark banknote designed by a group of artists of the printing house. The series of banknotes represented the philosophy of decades ago in terms of subject matter and graphic design. The reason for the renewal was the rapid development of copying techniques and the addition of the mechanical display and authentication of banknotes. In 1981, the Bank's Board of Directors set up a thematic committee, which, after selecting the topics, continued as a design committee. In many European countries, there was a desire for banknotes to indicate the country's cultural heritage, and popular subjects were national cultural artists, scientists and other scholars. The committee proposed the subject of the banknotes and the threefold division of Finnish history: the time of Swedish rule, the period of autonomy and the time of self-independence. The design competition for the draft banknotes was closed because it would take a very long time to get the result of the public competition. A group of artists from the banknote printing company Torsten Ekstrsm, Paavo Huovinen, Eeva Oivo, Pentti Rahikainen and Pirkko Vahtero were invited to the sketch competition, as well as the subject matter committee jssen, graphic designer Erik Bruun. Of the anonymous proposals, the design committee considered Torsten Ekstrsm's draft series to be the best, the stylistic artistic performance of Pentti Rahikainen's proposal and Eeva Oivo's proposal as a very illustrative implementation of era thinking. The final series of banknotes was created in cooperation. Torsten Ekstrsm generally designed the fronts of the banknotes and the back of Erik Bruu. The studio of the banknote printing house under the leadership of Pentti Rahikainen was responsible for other artistic details related to the safety of banknotes. Eeva Oivo painted pssosa from portraits, and Paavo Huovinen fashioned all the basic images of watermarks and painted a portrait of Sibelius. Kai Wuorio was responsible for his expertise in printing technology. In the series of banknotes, the high value banknotes represented the oldest period and the progress towards modern times, and the values were decreasing. The subject of the originally planned 5000-mark banknote was the period of Swedish rule and the period of the emergence of vernacular culture. Mikael Agricola's portrait on the front page and Turku Cathedral on the back symbolize the era. Sketches were made, but it was never put into circulation. 1000 marks was worth the largest banknote when the new series was introduced. Its subject was swedish rule a period, especially a period of trade liberalisation and economic activity. On the front page, the themes are symbolized by the image of Anders Chydenius and the sailing ship of the 1700s. The King's Gate of Suomenlinna was designed on the back side. The 500 and 100 mark notes were decorated with designs from the period of autonomy. On the front of the 500-mark banknote was Elias Lsnnrot, and on the back side there was a Finnish landscape, Punkaharju, which was strongly represented in art. The 100-mark banknote depicted the strong rise of Finnish culture, with Jean Sibelius's youth picture on the front and a landscape of Sibelius's music on the back. The 50- and 10-mark notes, on the other hand, were the subject matter of self-reliance. It is symbolized by Alvar Aalto and Finlandia Hall, on the one hand, and Paavo Nurmi and the Olympic Stadium on the other. The 10-mark note was replaced by a coin in 1993 and at the same time a 20-mark note representing the war period was put into circulation. The person selected the writer Vsins Linna and the back page focused on the buildings of the Tammerkoski highland and finlayson weaving mill, which depicts the industrialising country. The banknote was designed by graphic designer Erik Bruun. The portrait of the writer Linna was based on a photograph taken by the Picture Sisters. It is pleasing to note that the opening ceremony will be attended by banknote designers and heidsn lsheisissn, among others, Maaria Wirkkala, Petra Wirkkala, Erik Bruun and Torsten Ekstrsm. My sincerest thanks to those responsible for the implementation of the campaign. Architect Teemu Taskinen has supported the Money Museum in the design. I am pleased to announce the opening of the oLast Marks o. Bank of Finland (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagBank of Finland)

Friday 27 January 2012, 1:00 PM VIIMEISET MARKAT -NYTTELYN AVAUS 27.1.2012 SUOMEN PANKIN RAHAMUSEO SUOMEN MARKKAMRISET SETELITYYPIT VUOSINA 19452002 Minulla on ilo toivottaa teidt kaikki tervetulleeksi mys Suomen Pankin rahamuseon vuosittain vaihtuvan nyttelyn avajaisiin. Tn vuonna nyttelyn teema on viimeiset markat. Nyttely esittelee Suomen markkamrisi seteleit vuoden 1945 mallista vuonna 2002 toteutettuun euroseteleiden liikkeeseenlaskuun asti. Suomen Pankki lopettaa niden vuoden 1945 jlkeen liikkeeseen laskettujen markkaseteleiden lunastamisen helmikuun 2012 lopussa, jolloin eurorahanvaihdon pttymisest on kulunut 10 vuotta. Nyttelyn teksti perustuu Antti Heinosen kirjoittamaan ja Suomen Pankin julkaisemaan samannimiseen kirjaan, joka on sken esitelty julkisesti. Nyttely koostuu kahdesta osasta. Pytvitriineiss ja seinill esitelln seteleiden aiheista vuosina 1947 ja 1982 jrjestettyjen luonnoskilpailujen ehdotuksia. Multimediassa esitelln Suomessa toisen maailmansodan jlkeen kytss olleet markkamriset setelit tyypeittin. SETELIEN UUDISTAMINEN 1940-LUVULLA Suomen Pankissa ja sen setelipainossa ryhdyttiin 1940-luvun alussa suunnittelemaan uutta setelimallia. Edellisest seteliuudistuksesta oli kulunut lhes kaksikymment vuotta (siit oli ptetty vuonna 1922). Graafisen teollisuuden kehityksen myt mys vrentmisen vaara oli lisntynyt. Toinen trke peruste uudistukselle oli puute setelipaperista ja sen raaka-aineista, mik puolsi seteleiden koon pienentmist. Vuonna 1939 oli laskettu liikkeeseen 5000 markan seteli. Sota-ajan nopean inflaation vuoksi suunniteltiin perti 10000 markan setelin ottamista kyttn. Seteleiden nimellisarvon lisksi johtokunta oli alustavasti pohtinut mys seteleiden ulkoasun suunnittelun jrjestmist. Suunnitelmat menivt kuitenkin uusiksi setelinleikkauksen vuoksi. Valtioneuvoston ptksen mukaan uudenvuodenyn 1946 suurimmat eli 500, 1000 ja 5000 markan setelit leikattiin kahtia. Setelit menettivt puolet arvostaan maksuvlineen, jolloin toinen eli oikea puoli muodosti pakkolainan valtiolle. Samalla kaikki seteliarvot, mys 100 markkaa ja sit arvoltaan pienemmt setelit, vaihdettiin uusiin vuoden 1946 alkukuukausina. VUODEN 1947 SUUNNITTELUKILPAILU Seuraava setelien uusiminen kynnistyi vuonna 1946. Suunnittelusta ptettiin jrjest suomalaisille taiteilijoille avoin kilpailu, joka ksitti luonnoksen suunnittelun viitt eri seteli varten. Kilpailuun tuli mraikaan menness 18 ehdotusta. Palkintolautakunta ptti yksimielisesti antaa ensimmisen palkinnon (150 000 markkaa, nykyrahassa noin 8 000 euroa) nimimerkille Sampo (kuvanveistj Tapio Wirkkala), toisen palkinnon (100 000 markkaa, nykyrahassa noin 5 300 euroa) nimimerkille Ty miehen kunnia (Tapio Wirkkala) ja kolmannen palkinnon (75 000 markkaa, nykyrahassa noin 4 000 euroa) nimimerkille Suomen Leijona (arkkitehti Matti Visanti). Kilpailun tuloksen pohjalta johtokunta antoi Tapio Wirkkalan tehtvksi yhdess setelipainon ammattilaisten kanssa ryhty laatimaan kahta setelimallia. Toisessa seteleist olisi henkilkuva (setelin etusivu) ja toisessa yksinomaan muita kuvioita ja koristeita (takasivu). Pankkivaltuusto ptti paino-ja pankkiteknisist syist, ett uudet setelit olisivat nimellisarvostaan riippumatta kaikki samankokoisia. Pankkivaltuusto ptti mys seteleihin tulevista kuva-aiheista. Arvoltaan suurimpaan seteliin valittiin J. V. Snellmanin, toiseksi suurimpaan tasavallan ensimmisen presidentin K. J. Sthlbergin ja kolmanneksi suurimpaan istuvan presidentin J. K. Paasikiven muotokuva. (Suunnittelukilpailussa Tapio Wirkkala oli tosin luonnostellut seteleihin kulttuurihenkiliden muotokuvia.) Setelit laskettiin liikkeeseen loppuvuodesta 1955 lukuun ottamatta 1000 markan seteli, joka laskettiin liikkeeseen vuoden 1956 puolella. SETELIEN UUDISTAMINEN 1980-JA 1990-LUVULLA Lhestyttess 1980-lukua oltiin tilanteessa, jossa kytss olevan setelistn ulkoasu perustui vuonna 1955 liikkeeseen laskettuun sarjaan, johon oli tehty ahkerasti muutoksia vuoden 1963 rahanuudistuksesta lhtien. Tllin seteleiden nimellisarvosta pudotettiin pois kaksi nollaa. Sarjaan oli listty mys setelipainon taiteilijaryhmn suunnittelema 500 markan seteli. Kytss oleva setelisarja edusti aihepiiriltn ja graafiselta ilmeeltn vuosikymmenten takaista ajattelua. Uudistamiselle oli perusteena sek kopiointitekniikan nopea kehitys ett mys seteleiden koneellisen ksittelyn ja aitoustarkistuksen lisntyminen. Vuonna 1981 pankin johtokunta perusti aihepiiritoimikunnan, joka aiheiden valinnan jlkeen jatkoi designtoimikuntana. Monissa Euroopan maissa haluttiin seteleiden osoittavan maan kulttuuriperint ja suosittuja aiheita olivat kansalliset kulttuurihenkilt -taiteilijat, tiedemiehet ja muut oppineet. Toimikunta ehdotti seteleiden aiheeksi ja Suomen historian kolmijakoa: Ruotsin vallan aika, autonomian aika ja itsenisyyden aika. Seteliluonnoksien suunnittelukilpailu ptettiin pit suljettuna, koska julkisen kilpailun tuloksen tystminen veisi hyvin pitkn ajan. Luonnoskilpailuun kutsuttiin setelipainon taiteilijaryhmn jsenet Torsten Ekstrm, Paavo Huovinen, Eeva Oivo, Pentti Rahikainen ja Pirkko Vahtero sek aihepiiritoimikunnan jsen, graafikko Erik Bruun. Anonyymein jtetyist ehdotuksista designtoimikunta piti parhaana Torsten Ekstrmin sarjaluonnosta, tyylikkn taiteellisena suorituksena Pentti Rahikaisen ehdotusta sek aikakausiajattelua hyvin havainnollistavana toteutuksena Eeva Oivon ehdotusta. Lopullinen setelisarja syntyi yhteistyn. Torsten Ekstrm suunnitteli yleens seteleiden etusivut ja Erik Bruun takasivut. Setelipainon ateljee Pentti Rahikaisen johdolla vastasi muista seteleiden turvallisuuteen liittyvist taiteellisista yksityiskohdista. Eeva Oivo maalasi posan muotokuvista, ja Paavo Huovinen muovasi kaikki vesileimojen peruskuvat sek maalasi Sibeliuksen muotokuvan. Kai Wuorio vastasi painoteknisest asiantuntemuksesta. Setelisarjassa arvoltaan suuret setelit edustivat vanhinta aikaa ja nykyaikaa kohti edettess arvot pienenevt. Alun perin suunnitellun 5000 markan setelin aiheena olivat Ruotsin vallan aika ja kansankielisen kulttuurin syntymisen kausi. Mikael Agricolan muotokuva etusivulla ja Turun tuomiokirkko takasivulla symboloivat aikakautta. Setelist tehtiin luonnoksia mutta sit ei koskaan laskettu liikkeeseen. 1000 markkaa oli arvoltaan suurimmaksi seteliksi, kun uusi sarja otettiin kyttn. Sen aiheena oli Ruotsin vallan aika, erityisesti kaupan vapautumisen ja taloudellisen vilkastumisen aika. Nit teemoja symboloivat etusivulla Anders Chydeniuksen kuva ja 1700-luvun purjelaiva. Takasivulle suunniteltiin Suomenlinnan Kuninkaanportti. 500 ja 100 markan seteleiss kuva-aiheet olivat autonomian ajalta. 500 markan setelin etusivulla oli Elias Lnnrot ja takasivulla taiteessa voimakkaasti esill ollut suomalaismaisema, Punkaharju. 100 markan seteli aihe kuvasti suomalaisen kulttuurin voimakasta nousua, etusivulla oli Jean Sibeliuksen nuoruudenkuva ja takasivulla Sibeliuksen musiikkia ilmentv maisema salojrvelt. 50 ja 10 markan seteleiss aihepiirin oli puolestaan itsenisyyden aika. Sit symboloivat yhtlt Alvar Aalto ja Finlandia-talo sek toisaalta Paavo Nurmi ja olympiastadion. 10 markan seteli korvattiin kolikolla vuonna 1993 ja samaan aikaan laskettiin liikkeeseen sotien vlist aikaa kuvaava 20 markan seteli. Henkilvalinta ptyi kirjailija Vin Linnaan ja takasivun aiheeksi tuli teollistuvaa maata kuvaavaa teemaa kuvaavat Tammerkosken yljuoksun ja Finlaysonin kutomon rakennukset. Setelin suunnitteli graafikko Erik Bruun. Kirjailija Linnan muotokuva perustui Kuvasiskojen ottamaan valokuvaan. On miellyttv todeta, ett avajaisissa on mukana setelien suunnitteluun osallistuneita ja heidn lheisin mm. Maaria Wirkkala, Petra Wirkkala, Erik Bruun ja Torsten Ekstrm. Parhaimmat kiitokseni nyttelyn toteutuksesta vastanneille. Arkkitehti Teemu Taskinen on ollut suunnittelussa Rahamuseon tukena. Minulla on ilo julistaa Viimeiset markat  -nyttely avatuksi. text: Seppo Honkapohja, Member of the Executive Board: "Vsestsn iksntyminen: an economic resource and cost factor", Helsinki 4.9.2012 . Speech . Tuesday 4September 2012, 4:00 PM Seppo Honkapohja, johtokunnan jsen,Suomen Pankki Vanhus-ja lhimmispalvelun liiton seminaari 4.9.2012,tiivistelm Sodan jlkeinen syntyvyys kasvoi Suomessa enemmn kuin muualla ja laski nopeammin. Title: Awards for the Talousguru competition
text: Board member Seppo Honkapohja: Talousguru.competition award ceremony 1.3.2013 . Speech . Friday 1 March 2013, 12:00 PM Seppo Honkapohja, Member of the Board of Directors Bank of Finland Speech at the award ceremony of the Talousguru competition 1.3.2013 Congratulations to all the finalists. The financial guru competition was now held 16 times. The competition is organised by the Association of Teachers of History and Social Studies (HYOL), the Bank of Finland and the Federation of Finnish Financial Services. The Association of Financial Journalists and the Association of Finnish Upper Secondary School Students support the competition. In the year, about 900 students from 120 upper secondary schools around Finland took part in the Economic Guru competition. The top ten qualified for the finals in Helsinki. As in previous years, all ten finalists in the finals of the year are exceptionally talented financial experts. The competition is demanding and success requires an active economic hobby - the knowledge of the economics course given in upper secondary school alone is not enough for success. The contestants must also be proficient in oral argumentation, as the competition will include a presentation section. The latter skill is necessary in many jobs of an economist. In this year, it has been decided that financial literacy is not limited to individual upper secondary schools in the city region, but that the economy is of interest to the environment of Finland. There have been competitors from The Psskaupunki region, Oulu, snekoski, Mariehamn, Turku and Tampere. Looking at the group of finalists, one might find that young people's financial literacy is at a high level. However, it should be remembered that this is the smallest special group. Unfortunately, the economy is not of the same interest to all peers. We at the Central Bank are concerned about the state of general financial literacy. It is important that everyone can judge the opportunities associated with their own finances and to assess the risks involved in the different solutions. Special attention is paid to the financial literacy of young people. Society as a whole is overwhelmed by the fact that young people learn how to do a well-thought-out economic process. Good financial information helps to make a well-considered economic aspect of the situation. Poor financial literacy, on the other hand, can cause costs to the national economy due to social problems, for example. Young people are forced to deal with economic issues at a very early stage and should be offered a way to get a clear picture of the economy. The Bank of Finland cooperates with history and social studies teachers and supports teaching financials in schools in different ways. Sprjestss e.g. visits by schoolchildren to the Central Bank, training sessions for economics teachers and the production of learning materials. A new Eurocampus website is launched. The site contains a variety of economic-related games, activities and videos, as well as young people's own blog posts about the economy and money management. The winners of the Economic Guru competition have received cash prizes and newspaper prizes. What is most appreciated, however, is the opportunity offered to the final competitors to apply for a direct university study place in economics at a few universities through their success in the competition. In recent years, the University of Helsinki, the Svenska Handelshsgskolan and Jyvsskyls University School of Economics have been involved. Aalto University has joined in the year, and it wants to offer the top three finishers in the competition a direct chance to study. Those who have followed the competition can certainly agree with the fact that universities have been far-flung in offering direct study places to young people. Each of the finalists is certainly in an excellent position to succeed in their studies in economics. Economics is currently needed in a wide variety of tasks and institutions. Through their studies in economics, many have become economists within the walls of the country. Good luck to the competitors! Bank of Finland (/en/other-pages/tag-search/?tagBank of Finland)
