Title: EMU 2.0: the euro world after the reforms
text: Seppo Honkapohja, Member of the Executive Board: EMU 2.0: the euro world after the reforms. Helsinki, 23.1.2014. . Speech . Thursday23 January 2014, 12:00 PM Seppo Honkapohja Board of Directors and The Economics Association 23.1.2014 Esityskalvot (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches/documents/taltietyhd_22012013_sh.pdf) (PDF) . EMU 2.0: THE EUROZONE AFTER REFORMS 1. INTRODUCTION: EMU 1.0 Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), which began in January 1999, is the outcome of a long-standing process of general and economic policy cooperation. Its earliest roots go back to 1950, when the European Payments Union was abolished. However, in the late 1960s, it is a natural idea to identify european exchange rate system problems and potential stability. They sparked a debate on monetary integration and led to the emergence of a so-called 'green card'. To the Werner report. The report was published in 1970 and was set up as the treaty of monetary union in 1980. This meant the irrevocable convertibility of currencies, the freedom of movement and fixed exchange rates, either through national monetary symbols or through the European Community currency unit. The report proposed, on the one hand, the relatively smooth establishment of a system of European central banks and, on the other hand, quite strongly a central body of other economic policies under the auspices of the European Parliament. This body would have power over national budgetary policy (mssrs, financing) and structural and regional policy.1 With the collapse of the Bretton Woods system, european monetary and exchange-rate cooperation intensified in the so-called 'green belt'. the European Monetary System (EMS) and, as part of it, the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) were established in the late 1970s on the basis of an initiative agreed between Germany and France. The EMS was a very German- and Bundesbank-driven monetary and exchange rate system because the other currencies were anchored in the D-mark. In the early years of the EMS, inflation fell to ten per cent between 1980 and 1986. When the social movements were sssnnsstel, the EMS countries had the opportunity for a degree of autonomy in economic policy. In addition, it was possible to change exchange rates. In the early days of the EMS, the reorganisation (realignment) took place several times, but gradually the situation stabilised. On the other hand, the pressures to liberalise the 1980s created new guarantees for the European monetary system. In the late 1980s, developments brought forward proposals for deeper monetary integration and led to the development of Delors. to set up a committee in 1988. The Committee proposed a rapid transition towards the single currency and the creation of a European Central Bank. The Treaty of Maastrict set out a plan for the transition to economic and monetary union. The EMS crisis of 1992 did not derail the monetary union project to the detriment of many. The easing of the ERM's exchange rate pipelines and the disciplined action of the central banks calmed the markets, allowing the EMU project to continue.2 The chronological summary of the background and origins of EMU ignores the wide range of political orientations and negotiations in which cooperation between Germany and France, in particular, has played a key role. Political processes show that the emergence of economic and monetary union was not merely a development of the system of economic policy or monetary policy, but was a general European policy policy in the great mssr. Emu 1.0, the first version of economic and monetary union established under the Maastrict Treaty, was essentially monetary union, since it brought about a single monetary policy and a centralised monetary policy decision-making for the euro area. However, the role of the national central banks is significant, for example, in the design and implementation of monetary policy and in other areas of central bank policy. In other economic policies, responsibility lies with the Member States. They were responsible for their public finances on their own, although the Stability and Growth Pact imposed restrictions on budgetary and public debt. In particular, it should be noted that banking supervision remained a national responsibility, even though the need for joint supervision had been raised as part of a common European financial market. In the context of the adoption of the banking directive and the establishment of monetary union, there was quite a lot of discussion among experts as to whether the single banking market and monetary union also require a centralised approach to banking supervision. However, there is no need to get to the bottom of the matter. Banking supervision entrusts the responsibility of banks in the okotimaao (the licensing system) and thus the last Member States. During the financial and economic crisis that began in 2007, EMU 1.0 has changed significantly and continues to do so. My presentation looks at the changes. First of all, there are reasons to recall the main features of the economic development of EMU 1.0 and the problems that led to the crisis. 2. THE ROAD TO THE CRISIS The emergence of economic and monetary union meant a significant fall in interest rates for most of the Member States, including Finland. The fall in interest rates was partly reversed even before the start of economic and monetary union and continued for a year or two after its start. As a result of these developments, the spreads in the interest rates on government debt in the euro area Member States vis-a-vis Germany narrowed to a very low level. The size of the interest rate differentials was independent of the state of public finances in the individual countries. [FIGURE 1] Partly as a result of the fall in interest rates, economic growth accelerated in many Member States, as shown in Figure 1. The graph shows the evolution of gdp levels in Spain, Ireland, Italy, Greece and Portugal (GIIPS countries), i.e. the countries that have since been in crisis, between 1998 and 2013.3 The graph also shows the time series of GDP developments in Germany and France. The GIIPS countries' paths to the crisis were by no means the same. In Spain and Ireland, the acceleration of growth was accompanied by a strong fixed boom and higher constant prices. Greece's problem was massive overheating, which was based on a significant increase in private consumption. In fact, in Italy and Portugal, there was hardly any acceleration in economic growth. The crisis in these countries was caused by more general weak development, a lack of economic reforms and debt problems. A common feature of the GIIPS countries was the increase in each country's external indebtedness, which contributed to the deepening of current account problems already in the early years of EMU. The current account deficits were a clear signal of the imbalance in economic growth, but this was not given sufficient attention. In the GIIPS countries, the export-to-GDP ratio remained substantially unchanged after the euro era. The ratio did not start to grow until after the recession of 2008-2009. EMU 2.0 At the heart of the economic crisis, economic and monetary union has been and continues to be developed in many areas. Although some of the measures are currently in the middle of implementation, we can already talk about EMU version 2.0. We have therefore moved on to the new version of EMU. The operational mechanisms of crisis management and the division of the various institutions are one of the most advanced aspects of the crisis. a shaped section of changes in the way EMU works. Priority in crisis management is, of course, given to the crisis countries' own adjustment efforts to correct the imbalances. These operations are time-consuming and often require bridge financing from external public institutions, as the financing provided by the market may have been blocked. Bridge funding provides opportunities for systematic adaptation, without which the crisis could become chaotic. Since overheating, over-indebtedness and possibly price bubbles have arisen before the onset of the financial crisis, the crisis phase has led to an adjustment downward spiral. Bridge funding cannot eliminate the need for adaptation. The crisis in the euro area has also taught us that the EU must have the means to provide financial assistance. The European Stability Fund (ESM) now exists as a permanent provider of crisis financing. In addition to the ESM, the involvement of the International Monetary Fund has proved to be humble. The IMF has long experience and procedures for dealing with financial crises. The European Central Bank, for its part, is responsible for the long term concerned with the liquidity needs of the financial services and the transmission of monetary policy to the Member States. [FIGURE 5] The reformed Economic and Monetary Union relies on better market discipline on the one hand and better market discipline on the other, both for the Member States and the financial systems. The diagram in Figure 5 illustrates the whole. First of all, there are reasons to comment on the role of the market in the reformed Economic and Monetary Union. Hopefully, the way the market operates has changed as a result of the crisis. Before the crisis, the discipline imposed by the financial markets on the public finances of the Member States was seriously deficient. Interest rate differentials before the crisis years did not at all reflect the state of public finances in the various countries. For example, Greece, which was heavily indebted and unbalanced, received financing at a slightly higher interest rate than, for example, Germany or Finland. Indeed, the development of the market before the crisis years was a bubble in the same way as the subprime crisis in the United States. The sharp rise in public debt interest rates during the crisis was, in turn, part of the general re-pricing of risks that occurred when the markets woke up to the financial crisis. The reforming EMU needs better market discipline and market players will hopefully monitor the public finances of the various countries more closely than before. Emu's new economic policy framework aims to provide better information. [FIGURE 6] Figure 6 illustrates the reformed approaches to the Member States. The economic policy framework and coordination have been substantially reformed. The aim is to steer the economic policies and economic development of the Member States in a more diverse way than in the past. The Stability and Growth Pact has been reformed in many ways and new economic policy packages and pacts have been developed. The political crisis caused CDS prices to rise in early 2013. Prices began to fall again when a solution to the crisis was found. It is important to see that the crisis in Portugal did not cause a significant contagion impact on other GIIPS countries. The Banking Union, which is currently under construction, is the second package of major reforms. The banking union is necessary because the EU's financial markets are long-term integrated and the largest banks operate in many Member States. At the heart of the crisis, it was recognised that there was a need to try to weaken the tight linkage between the public finances and banks of the countries. Many banks in crisis countries own significant amounts of government bonds and, on the other hand, the state is responsible for the restructuring or winding-down of a bank in difficulty, which may require significant funds. [FIGURE 7] The right half of Figure 7 illustrates the new market discipline in the financial system. The graph shows the evolution of credit risk prices of large European banks since the beginning of 2011. In the depths of the crisis, CDS prices rose sharply, while in the autumn of 2012, the development of cds has been mixed. There has been a positive trend in prices since the autumn of 2012, although there has been quite a large variation. The left half of Figure 7 illustrates the features of the banking union. The banking union has three components: a single financial supervision, a single crisis management mechanism and a deposit insurance system. The common charter is very much part of the banking union, as it will bring more uniform requirements to the EU countries. It should be stressed that the banking union does not contain the bank support described in a separate box, which has helped to rescue banks from systemic banking crises. A well-functioning banking union is likely to result in the use of bank support. The Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM) is already in the high phase and is due to become operational in November of this year. Prior to the establishment of joint supervision, a so-called "joint surveillance" is carried out. a comprehensive assessment of the balance sheets of the large banks entering direct supervision of the ECB in a comprehensive manner and a consistent assessment. The assessment will ensure that the ECB will start its role as supervisory authority "from a clean sheet". This assessment will be carried out on 130 banking groups. In terms of balance sheet, the groups cover about 85% of the euro area banking sector. The assessment consists of three parts: risk assessment, asset quality assessment and stress tests. In the long run, a political consensus has also been reached jointly on the Resolution Mechanism (SRM), which is being revived or a bank in a situation is being wound up in an orderly manner.8 A key principle of the SRM is bail-in, whereby the responsibility for financing the winding-down of a crisis bank is placed primarily on owners and investors. Investor responsibility will enter into force from 2016 onwards. The joint resolution fund has also largely been agreed upon. It is proposed that the fund be built gradually over the next ten years. The third part of the banking union, the development of deposit insurance, is currently at the stage of a directive. According to the directive, deposit guarantees in different countries will be harmonised, but the system will be nationalised. 4. ECONOMIC AND MONETARY UNION NTENT The economic situation in the euro area is currently better than a year ago. The current account and government deficits are disappearing, or at least have decreased significantly. According to forecasts, public indebtedness is stabilising in many GIIPS countries and is gradually starting to decline. Economic growth in the GIIPS countries has increased or is increasing. The decisions taken in crisis countries and at EU level, as well as the ECB's OMT monetary policy programme, have all had an impact on the situation. The consequences of the crisis in the GIIPS countries are notoriously very serious. Reducing widespread employment is a slow process and a significant reduction in high levels of indebtedness will take at least ten years, depending on future economic development and the targets to be set for debt levels. Repair processes are subject to various risks. If risks materialise widely in many countries, the situation in the euro area could become more difficult again. To sum up, it must therefore be said that the situation remains fragile and risky. We are only at the beginning of the recovery. The economic crisis, which is already in its sixth year, is not over. Economic and monetary union has been and will continue to be in the throes of change. Coordination of economic policies and its monitoring has significantly improved. The plans for the banking union are long in coming and the first parts of it are in the process of being implemented. Economic and monetary union is undergoing a major reform of all the measures and measures. It should be stressed, however, that the essence of EMU remains unchanged. The reforming economic and monetary union remains the federation of self-states and not the federation. These changes will help to correct the major weaknesses identified through the crisis. New policies and institutions will strengthen the euro area economy and the economic policy framework. Of course, the effectiveness of these reforms will only become effective in the future, when the euro system faces new shocks and challenges. EMU 2.0: EUROMAAILMA UUDISTUSTEN JLKEEN 1. JOHDANTO: EMU 1.0 Tammikuussa 1999 aloittanut talous-ja rahaliitto EMU on pitkn yleis-ja talouspoliittisen yhteistyn lopputulos. Sen varhaisimmat juuret ulottuvat vuoteen 1950, jolloin Euroopan maksu-unioni kynnistyi. Ehk luontevana lhtpisteen voidaan kuitenkin pit 1960-luvun lopulla krjistyneit eurooppalaisia valuuttakurssijrjestelmn ongelmia ja potentiaalista epvakautta. Ne kirvoittivat keskustelua monetaarisesta integraatiosta ja johtivat nk. Wernerin raporttiin. Raportti julkaistiin vuonna 1970 ja siin asetettiin pmrksi kynnist rahaliitto vuonna 1980. Tm tarkoitti tydellist ja peruuttamatonta valuuttojen vaihdettavuutta, pomaliikkeiden vapautta sek tysin kiinteit valuuttakursseja joko silyttmll kansalliset rahasymbolit tai Euroopan Yhteisn rahayksikn kautta. Raportissa ehdotettiin yhtlt suhteellisen vljsti Euroopan Keskuspankkien jrjestelmn perustamista ja toisaalta varsin voimakkaasti muun talouspolitiikan keskittmist Euroopan parlamentin alaiselle keskuselimelle. Tll elimell olisi ptsvaltaa kansallisen budjettipolitiikan (mr, rahoitus) sek rakenne-ja aluepolitiikan suhteen.1 Bretton Woods -jrjestelmn romahdettua Euroopan raha-ja valuuttapoliittinen yhteisty tiivistyi nk. valuuttakrmeen myt ja 1970-luvun lopulla syntyivt Euroopan rahajrjestelm (EMS) ja sen osana valuuttakurssimekanismi (ERM) pitklti Saksan ja Ranskan sopiman aloitteen pohjalta. EMS oli hyvin Saksa-ja Bundesbank-vetoinen raha-ja valuuttapoliittinen jrjestelm, koska muut valuutat oli ankkuroitu D-markkaan. EMS:n alkuvuosina inflaatio hidastui kymmenest kahteen prosenttiin vuosina 1980 -1986. Kun pomaliikkeet olivat snnsteltyj, oli EMS:n jsenmailla mahdollisuus jonkinasteiseen talouspolitiikan autonomiaan. Lisksi valuuttakursseja oli mahdollista muuttaa. EMS:n alkutaipaleella nit uudelleenjrjestelyj (realignment) tapahtui useasti, mutta asteittain tilanne vakautui. Toisaalta 1980-luvun kuluessa syntyneet paineet pomaliikkeiden vapauttamiseen loivat uusia epvarmuuksia Euroopan rahajrjestelm kohtaan. Nm kehityskulut nostivat 1980-luvun lopulla esiin ehdotuksia syvemmst rahaintegraatiosta ja johtivat Delorsin johtaman komitean asettamiseen vuonna 1988. Komitea ehdotti nopeaa siirtymist kohti yhteist rahaa ja Euroopan keskuspankin perustamista. Maastrictin sopimuksessa vahvistettiin suunnitelma siirtymisest talous-ja rahaliittoon. 1992 kynnistynyt EMS:n kriisi ei monien ylltykseksi saanut rahaliittohanketta pois raiteiltaan. ERM:n valuuttakurssiputkien leventminen ja keskuspankkien kurinalainen toiminta rauhoittivat markkinat, jolloin EMU-projekti saattoi jatkua.2 Tm kronologinen tiivistelm EMU:n taustasta ja syntyvaiheista sivuuttaa moninaiset poliittiset linjaukset ja neuvottelut, joissa erityisesti Saksan ja Ranskan yhteisymmrrys on ollut keskeinen osa. Nm poliittiset prosessit kertovat, ett talous-ja rahaliiton synty ei ollut pelkstn talouspolitiikan tai rahapolitiikan jrjestelmn kehittmist, vaan se oli suuressa mrin yleist Eurooppa-politiikkaa. Maastrictin sopimuksen nojalla kynnistyneen talous-ja rahaliiton ensimminen versio EMU 1.0 oli ennen kaikkea rahaliitto, sill se aikaansai yhden rahapolitiikan ja keskitetyn rahapoliittisen ptksenteon euroalueelle. Kansallisten keskuspankkien rooli silyi kuitenkin merkittvn esimerkiksi rahapolitiikan suunnittelussa ja toteutuksessa sek erill muilla keskuspankkipolitiikan lohkoilla. Muussa talouspolitiikassa vastuu silyi jsenvaltioilla. Ne vastasivat julkisesta taloudestaan itsenisesti, joskin vakaus-ja kasvusopimus asetti budjettialijm ja julkista velkaa koskevia rajoituksia. Erityisesti on todettava, ett pankkivalvonta silyi kansallisella vastuulla, vaikka yhteisen valvonnan tarpeesta oli esitetty nkemyksi osana yhteisi eurooppalaisia rahoitusmarkkinoita. Pankkidirektiivin stmisen ja rahaliiton muodostamisen yhteydess kytiin melko paljon keskustelua asiantuntijoiden kesken siit, vaativatko yhteinen pankkimarkkina ja rahaliitto mys pankkivalvonnan keskittmist. Asiassa ei kuitenkaan psty eteenpin. Pankkivalvonta ji pankkien kotimaan (toimiluvan myntjn) ja siten viime kdess jsenmaiden vastuulle. Vuonna 2007 alkaneen finanssi-ja talouskriisin myt EMU 1.0 on merkittvsti muuttunut ja muuttuu edelleen. Esitykseni tarkastelee nit muutoksia . Aluksi on syyt palauttaa mieliin EMU 1.0 ajan talouskehityksen keskeiset piirteet ja kriisiin johtaneet ongelmat. 2. TIE KRIISIIN Talous-ja rahaliiton synty merkitsi useimmille jsenmaille, Suomi mukaan lukien, huomattavaa korkotason laskua. Korkotason lasku kynnistyi osittain jo ennen talous-ja rahaliiton alkamishetke ja jatkui vuoden pari sen kynnistytty. Tmn kehityksen seurauksena euroalueen jsenmaiden julkisen velan korkoerot suhteessa Saksan supistuivat hyvin pieniksi. Korkoerojen suuruus oli kytnnss riippumaton yksittisten maiden julkisen talouden tilasta. [KUVIO 1] Osaltaan korkojen laskun seurauksena monien jsenmaiden talouskasvu kiihtyi, kuten Kuviosta 1 on nhtviss. Kuviossa on esitetty Espanjan, Irlannin, Italian, Kreikan ja Portugalin (GIIPS-maiden) eli sittemmin kriisiin ajautuneiden maiden BKT:n tason kehitys vuodesta 1998 vuoteen 2013.3 Kuviossa ovat mys Saksan ja Ranskan BKT:n kehityst kuvaavat aikasarjat. GIIPS-maiden tiet kriisiin eivt suinkaan olleet samanlaisia. Espanjassa ja Irlannissa kasvun kiihtymisen myt kynnistyi voimakas kiinteistbuumi ja kiinteisthintojen nousu. Kreikan ongelmana oli valtava ylikuumeneminen, joka perustui merkittvss mrin yksityisen kulutuksen kasvuun. Itse asiassa Italiassa ja Portugalissa talouskasvu ei kiihtynyt juuri lainkaan. Niden maiden kriisin taustalla olivat yleisempi heikko kehitys, talousuudistusten puute ja velkaongelmat. Yhteinen piirre GIIPS-maille oli kunkin maan ulkoisen velkaantumisen kasvu, joka nkyy vaihtotaseongelmien syvenemisen jo EMU:n alkuvuosien aikana. Vaihtotaseen vajeet olivat selke viesti talouskasvun tasapainottomuudesta, mihin ei kuitenkaan kiinnitetty riittvsti huomiota. Kuvio 2 havainnollistaa tt kehityst.4 [KUVIO 2] Kuvion 2 vaaka-akselilla on vaihtotaseen alijm ja pystyakselilla julkisen talouden alijm vuosina 2002 -2012. Maan nimeen liittyv nuoli osoittaa ajanjakson lhtvuoden 2002 datapistett. Kyrien suunta lhtpisteist on aluksi posin vaakasuoraan vasemmalle eli havaintojakson alkuvuosina vaihtotaseet heikkenivt, kun taas julkisen talouden tila ei kovin paljoa muuttunut. Ajanjakson myhempin vuosina kyrien suunta kntyy osoittamaan melko suoraan alaspin, mik tarkoittaa julkisen velkaantumisen krjistymist. Tm kyrien suunnan muutos tapahtui globaalin finanssikriisin kynnistytty. Samaan aikaan GIIPS-maiden julkisen velan korot alkoivat nousta voimakkaasti, kun julkisen talouden velkakriisi niss maissa toden teolla krjistyi. Jakson 2002 -2012 viimeisin vuosina kyrien suunta on kntynyt oikealle eli vaihtotaseiden vajeet alkoivat pienenty. Mys julkiset vajeet ovat pienentyneet. Italia muodostaa jonkinasteisen poikkeuksen thn dynamiikkaan: sen kyr on osoittanut useasti eri suuntiin. Todettakoon, ett vastaavaa dynamiikkaa ei ole nhtviss ns. korkean luottoluokituksen euromaissa (Alankomaat, Belgia, Itvalta, Ranska, Saksa, Suomi), kuten Kuviosta 3 on nhtviss. [KUVIO 3] Eri maiden talouskehityksen heterogeenisuus ja euroajan alkuvuosien ongelmat nkyvt mys eroina GIIPS-maiden ja koko euroalueen erkaantuneessa vientikehityksess. GIIPS-maissa vienti/BKT suhde pysyi oleellisesti muuttumattomana euroajan kynnistymisen jlkeen. Tm suhdeluku alkoi kasvaa vasta vuosien 2008 -2009 taantuman jlkeen. Korkean luottoluokituksen euromaissa vienti/BKT suhdeluku kasvoi asteittain vuosien 2008 .2009 syvn taantumaan saakka, mink seurauksena viennin osuus supistui. Tmn jlkeen tilanne on jlleen kohentunut. Kaiken kaikkiaan euroalueen vienti suhteessa BKT:een on kasvanut euroaikana hyvin, kuten Kuvio 4 osoittaa. Thn menness viennin BKT-osuus on noussut 12 prosentista noin 20 prosenttiin euroajan kuluessa. Tmn kehitys on ollut nopeampaa kuin esimerkiksi Yhdysvalloissa tai Japanissa, kuten Kuviosta 4 voidaan havaita. [KUVIO 4] Talouskehityksen eroja voisi havainnollistaa mys kustannuskilpailukyvyn (yksikktykustannusten) kehityksen erojen kautta. GIIPS-maissa yksikktykustannukset nousivat voimakkaasti vuoteen 2008 tai 2009 saakka. Kilpailukyvyn heikentyminen on yksi osoitus talouksien ylikuumenemisesta. Viime vuosina kilpailukyky on selvsti parantunut sen jlkeen kun sopeutuminen alaspin kynnistyi. Italia on poikkeus tss kehityskulussa.5 Tll hetkell GIIPS-maiden vaihtotaseongelmat ja julkisen talouden alijmt ovat merkittvsti pienentyneet ja osin poistuneet. Niden maiden ennustetaan tn vuonna psevn kiinni positiiviseen talouskasvuun. Tm on nhtviss Kuviossa 1 esitetyist EU:n komission ennusteista vuosille 2014 ja 2015. Talouskriisi ei kuitenkaan ole ohi, sill kriisimaissa velkatasot ja tyttmyysasteet ovat korkealla. Ylikuumenemisen ja korkean velkaantumisen edellyttm alaspin sopeutuminen on ollut tuskallista ja siit kumpuavat poliittiset paineet vellovat voimakkaina.6 [Kuvio 1 uudelleen] 3. EMU 2.0 Talouskriisin myt Talous-ja rahaliittoa on kehitetty ja kehitetn edelleen monella saralla. Vaikka osa nist toimenpiteist on tll hetkell keskell toteutusta, voidaan mielestni jo puhua EMU:sta versio 2.0. Olemme siis siirtymss EMU:n uuteen versioon. On syyt huomauttaa, ett uusien toimintamallien implementointi ja toimivuus on posin viel testaamatta. Siksi versio on 2.0 eik 2.x, x>0. Vlittmn kriisinhoidon toimintamekanismit ja eri instituutioiden tynjako ovat yksi kriisin edetess myt muotoutunut osa-alue EMU:n toimintatapojen muutoksia. Etusijalla kriisinhoidossa ovat luonnollisesti kriisimaiden omat sopeutustoimet tasapainottomuusilmiiden korjaamiseksi. Nm toimet vievt aikaa ja vaativat usein ulkopuolisten julkisten instituutioiden siltarahoitusta, koska markkinoiden tarjoama rahoitus on saattanut tyrehty. Siltarahoitus antaa mahdollisuuksia suunnitelmalliseen sopeutumiseen, jota ilman kriisi voisi muuttua kaoottiseksi. Koska ennen finanssikriisin puhkeamista on syntynyt ylikuumenemista, ylivelkaantumista ja mahdollisesti hintakuplia, kriisivaiheessa on vistmtt edess sopeutuminen alaspin. Siltarahoitus ei voi poistaa tt sopeutumistarvetta. Euroalueen kriisin myt on opittu, ett EU:lla on oltava vlineet tarjota rahoitustukea. Euroopan Vakausvline EVM on nyt olemassa pysyvn kriisirahoituksen tarjoajana. EVM:n lisksi mys Kansainvlisen valuuttarahaston mukanaolo on osoittautunut hydylliseksi. IMF:ll on pitk kokemus ja menettelytavat finanssikriisien hoitoon. Euroopan keskuspankin tehtv on puolestaan pit huolta rahoitusjrjestelmn likviditeettitarpeista ja rahapolitiikan vlittymisest jsenmaihin. [KUVIO 5] Uudistettu Talous-ja rahaliitto nojaa yhtlt parempaan markkinakuriin ja toisaalta parempiin sntihin, jotka kohdistuvat sek jsenvaltioihin ett rahoitusjrjestelmn. Kuviossa 5 oleva kaavio havainnollistaa tt kokonaisuutta. Aluksi on syyt kommentoida markkinoiden roolia uudistuneessa Talous-ja rahaliitossa. Markkinoiden toimintatapa on toivottavasti muuttunut kriisin seurauksena. Ennen kriisi rahoitusmarkkinoiden asettama kuri jsenmaiden julkisille talouksille oli vakavasti puutteellinen. Korkoerot ennen kriisivuosia eivt lainkaan heijastaneet eri maiden julkisen talouden tilaa. Esimerkiksi pahasti velkaantunut ja tasapainottomasti kasvanut Kreikka sai rahoitusta vain hieman korkeammalla korolla kuin esimerkiksi Saksa tai Suomi. Markkinoiden kehitys ennen kriisivuosia olikin kupla vhn samaan tapaan kuin subprime-kriisi Yhdysvalloissa. Kriisin aikana tapahtunut raju julkisen velan korkojen nousu oli puolestaan osa yleist riskien uudelleen hinnoittelua, joka tapahtui markkinoiden havahtuessa rahoituskriisiin. Uudistuva EMU tarvitsee parempaa markkinakuria ja markkinoiden toimijat toivottavasti seuraavat eri maiden julkisia talouksia aiempaa tarkemmin. EMU:n uusi talouspoliittinen kehikko pyrkii tarjoamaan thn aikaisempaa parempaa informaatiota. [KUVIO 6] Kuvio 6 havainnollistaa uudistuneita toimintatapoja jsenvaltioiden osalta. Talouspolitiikan sntj ja yhteensovittamista on huomattavasti uudistettu. Tavoitteena on ohjata jsenvaltioiden talouspolitiikkaa ja talouskehityst aikaisempaa monipuolisemmin. Vakaus-ja kasvusopimusta on uudistettu monilla tavoilla ja uusia talouspoliittisia paketteja ja sopimuksia on kehitetty. Oheinen Kuvio 6 kuvaa talouspolitiikan uuden snnstn, jossa on kolme keskeist osaa: Kuuden kohdan paketti (Six-Pack), Kahden kohdan paketti (Two-Pack) Euromaille sek Talousunionia vahvistava sopimus (nk. Fiscal Compact).7 En mene tss yksityiskohtiin. Haluan kuitenkin huomauttaa, ett uudessa kehikossa koko kansantalous ja erityisesti sen vaihtotaseen tila otetaan kriittiseen tarkasteluun. Tm tehdn nk. makrotalouden eptasapainoa koskevan menettelyn avulla. On mys hyv todeta, ett voimassa olevia sntj on tiukennettu knteisen nestysmenettelyn avulla. Markkinoiden kuri julkiselle taloudelle nkyy Kuvion 6 oikeanpuoleisessa osiossa. Siit nhdn kuinka GIIPS.maiden luottoriskihinnat ovat laskeneet voimakkaasti kesst 2012 lhtien. Portugali vuonna 2013 on poikkeus thn havaintoon. Poliittinen kriisi knsi CDS-hinnat nousuun alkuvuodesta 2013. Nm hinnat alkoivat uudelleen laskea, kun kriisiin lytyi ratkaisu. On trke havaita, ett Portugalin kriisi ei aiheuttanut merkittv tartuntavaikutusta muihin GIIPS maihin. Parhaillaan rakenteilla oleva Pankkiunioni on toinen suurten uudistusten kokonaisuus. Pankkiunioni on tarpeellinen, koska EU:n rahoitusmarkkinat ovat pitklle integroituneet ja isoimmat pankit toimivat monissa jsenmaissa. Kriisin myt havaittiin, ett on tarpeen pyrki heikentmn maiden julkisten talouksien ja pankkien tiukkoja kytkentj. Monet kriisimaiden pankit omistavat merkittvsti valtion obligaatioita ja toisaalta valtion vastuulla on vaikeuksiin ajautuvan pankin saneeraus tai alasajo, mik saattaa vaatia merkittvi varoja. [KUVIO 7] Kuvion 7 oikea puolisko havainnollistaa uutta markkinakuria rahoitusjrjestelmlle. Kuviossa esitetn eriden isojen eurooppalaisten pankkien luottoriskihintojen kehitys vuoden 2011 alusta lhtien. Kriisin syventyess CDS.hinnat nousivat voimakkaasti, kun taas syksyst 2012 lhtien kehitys on ollut mynteist. Niss hinnoissa on ollut mynteinen trendi syksyst 2012 lhtien, joskin niiss on esiintynyt melko suurta vaihtelua. Kuvion 7 vasen puolisko kuvaa pankkiunionin ppiirteet. Pankkiunionissa on kolme posaa: yhteinen rahoitusvalvonta, yhteinen kriisinhallintamekanismi ja talletusvakuutusjrjestelm. Yhteinen sntkirja on hyvin trke osa pankkiunionia, sill sen avulla saadaan EU maihin aiempaa yhtenisemmt sntelyvaatimukset. On korostettava, ett pankkiunioni ei sisll kuviossa erillisell laatikolla kuvattua pankkitukea, jonka avulla on pelastettu pankkeja systeemisiss pankkikriiseiss. Toimiva pankkiunioni luultavasti vhent pankkituen kytt. Yhteinen valvontamekanismi (SSM) on jo ylsajovaiheessa ja sen on mr aloittaa toimintansa tmn vuoden marraskuussa. Ennen yhteisen valvonnan kynnistymist suoritetaan ns. kattava arvio, jossa EKP:n suorassa valvontaan siirtyvien suurten pankkien taseet arvioidaan kattavasti ja yhtenisi kriteerej kytten. Arvion avulla varmistetaan, ett EKP aloittaa tehtvns valvontaviranomaisena "puhtaalta pydlt". Tm arviointi kohdistetaan 130 pankkiryhmn. Taseella mitaten ryhmt kattavat noin 85 % euroalueen pankkisektorista. Arvioinnissa on kolme osaa: riskiarviointi, saamisten laadun arviointi ja stressitestit. Pitklle menev poliittinen yksimielisyys on saavutettu mys yhteisest kriisinratkaisumekanismista (SRM), jota kytetn elvytettess tai ajettaessa hallitusti alas ongelmiin joutunut pankki.8 Keskeinen periaate SRM:ssa on sijoittajavastuu (bail-in), jolloin kriisipankin alasajon rahoitusvastuu kohdistetaan ensisijaisesti omistajille ja sijoittajille. Sijoittajavastuu tulee voimaan vuodesta 2016 alkaen. Mys yhteisest kriisinratkaisurahastosta on suurelta osin psty sopuun. Rahasto on esitetty rakennettavaksi asteittain seuraavan kymmenen vuoden aikana. Pankkiunionin kolmas osa, talletussuojan kehittminen on tll hetkell direktiiviasteella. Direktiivin mukaan eri maiden talletussuojat tullaan harmonisoimaan, mutta jrjestelmt jvt kansallisiksi. 4. TALOUS-JA RAHALIITON NKYMT Euroalueen taloudellinen tilanne nytt tll hetkell paremmalta kuin vuosi sitten. Vaihtotaseen ja julkisen talouden alijmt ovat poistumassa tai ainakin ne ovat pienentyneet merkittvsti. Ennusteiden mukaan julkisen velkaantuminen on vakautumassa monissa GIIPS-maissa ja se alkaa asteittain knty laskevalle uralle. GIIPS.maiden talouskasvu on kynnistynyt tai se on kynnistymss. Tehdyt ratkaisut kriisimaissa ja EU-tasolla sek EKP:n rahapoliittinen OMT-ohjelma ovat kaikki mytvaikuttaneet thn tilanteeseen. Kriisin seuraukset GIIPS-maissa ovat tunnetusti hyvin vakavat. Laajalle levinneen tyttmyyden alentaminen on hidas prosessi ja korkeiden velkaantumisasteiden merkittv alentaminen tulee viemn ainakin kymmenen vuotta riippuen tulevasta talouskehityksest ja velkatasoille asetettavista tavoitteista. Nm korjausprosessit ovat alttiita erilaisille riskeille. Mikli nm riskit toteutuvat laajalti monissa maissa, euroalueen tilanne voi vaikeutua uudelleen. Nkymien yhteenvetona on siis todettava, ett tilanne on edelleen hauras ja riskialtis. Olemme vasta elpymisen alussa. Jo kuudetta vuotta jatkuva talouskriisi ei ole ohitse. Talous-ja rahaliitto on ollut ja tulee olemaan muutoksien kourissa. Talouspolitiikan yhteensovittaminen ja sen seuranta ovat merkittvsti kohentuneet. Suunnitelmat pankkiunionista ovat pitkll ja sen ensimmiset osat ovat toteutusvaiheessa. Talous-ja rahaliitto on uudistumassa merkittvsti kaikkien niden ptsten ja toimenpiteiden myt. On kuitenkin korostettava, ett EMU:n perusolemus on ennallaan. Uudistuva talous-ja rahaliitto on edelleen itsenisten valtioiden liitto eik mikn federaatio. Niden muutosten avulla korjataan kriisin kautta havaittuja isoja heikkouksia. Uudet toimintamallit ja instituutiot tulevat epilemtt vahvistamaan euroalueen taloutta ja talouspoliittista ohjausjrjestelm. Luonnollisesti niden uudistusten toimivuus tullaan nkemn vasta tulevaisuudessa, kun eurojrjestelm kohtaa uusia sokkeja ja haasteita. text: Board member Seppo Honkapohja: North Karelia Economic Forum -North Carelia Economic Forum. Outokumpu, 21.3.2014. . Speech . Friday 21 March 2014, 3:00 PM Seppo Honkapohja North Karelia Economic Forum, opening words Outokumpu 21.3.2014 Slides (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and. . interviews/documents/140321_pkfoorumi_avaus_sh.pdf) (PDF) NORTH KARELIA ECONOMIC FORUM -NORTH CARELIA ECONOMIC FORUM Hyvst talousfoorumin osanottajat, ladies and gentlemen It is my pleasure, on behalf of the Jsrjestsjis, to welcome you to the North Karelian Economic Forum, which is the provincial union issnnsi. The programme has been implemented jointly with the North Karelian delegation. The theme of the forum is the challenges of economic growth in Europe and Finland and also the perception of the direction of the future development of North Karelia. The focus of the discussions will be on the weak economic performance of Europe and Finland since 2008. Figure 1 illustrates the situation. This forum focuses on the growth challenges in Europe, Finland and the region of North Karelia. Let me start with Figure 1. CHART 1 Figure 1 shows a good starting point for our discussions. Growth performance of the United States, Euro area and Finland has been very slow and all three entities have fallen far behind the past trends. In the recovery from the crisis, performance of the euro area has been noticeably worse than that of the United States, while Finnish performance is somewhat worse than that of the euro area average. CHART 2 Let me focus on Finland a little bit more. Figure 2 shows the time paths of industrial production levels in major sectors: forest industry (in yellow), metal excluding electricity and electronics (in red), electricity and electronics (in green) and chemicals (in blue). Major shocks have hit our two biggest sectors. There is a gradual decline in the forest sector while in the electronics we see a huge drop in 2009 and further gradual decline after that. These shocks are not the only difficulties faced by the Finnish economy. The problem with population aging and declining labor force at present and in the future is a known problem. The latest shock comes from the crisis in Ukraine. The Russian economy is going to be adversely affected. We already know that the Russian rouble and stock markets have significantly depreciated. This is bound to have an adverse impact on Finnish exports to Russia. These exports are over 9 percent of total Finnish exports. Clearly, these shocks mean that the Finnish economy faces a difficult period ahead. This period is likely to be lengthy and policies have to try to mitigate the impacts of these shocks. In particular, strengthening our industrial base into new areas and directions is a very timely goal for Finland. (I use the term "industry" in a broad sense and include the service sectors.) I will not try to pre-empt our speakers today. Let conclude by pointing out that Northern Karelia region is known for its innovative activities in the forest sector, one of the problem sectors mentioned above. In this region there are new companies that are extending the use of wood in very novel directions. Let me just mention two new wood products. The first example is pyrolysis oil that is obtained from wood biomass waste and is a new substitute for fuel oil. The second example is dissolving pulp that is a potential substitute for cotton in textile industry. As many participants know, there are several other North Karelian firms that produce new and products in the forest and other industries. After these remarks we move to the program of the Forum.

Title: Speech at the Banking Association's event
text: Bank Manager Sinikka Salo's speech at the Banking Association's event . Speech . Tuesday 21 November 2000,12:00AM Member of the Executive Board Sinikka Salo Finnish Banking Association event at Kalastajatorpa 21.11.2000 I would like to thank the banking associations at the outset for giving me the opportunity to speak to a representative group of Finnish information officers and bank management. This opportunity is especially pleasing to me when it comes soon, just three weeks after I have returned to Finland and started working at the Board of Directors of the Bank of Finland. I liked the event to be very meaningful anyway. Because of the fact that there are good dialogues between information and banking institutions, which is why faster changes are taking place in the banking world. Banks are such a central part of society that they are naturally always under the magnifying glass of the media, as, of course, is the case. Changes in banking apply to everyone. The analyses provided by the information relays are absolutely central to what is happening in the banking sector, and why. It is the duty of bankers and journalists to ensure that customers and citizens get as good an overview as possible - not just of what is happening, but also of the deeper processes that are changing the banking industry. If this is to be done, it will not only be the banks, but the economy and society as a whole. The lack of confidence during the banking crisis in the context of public opinion and the banking sector provided many lessons in the relationship between public opinion and the banking sector. *** I have promised to talk about the current challenges facing banking from the point of view of the Central Bank. It has to be said that my own personal approach to the matter is quite pan-European, and although I have been following the financial market developments in Finland as well, it may be that my emphasis on this is reflected in the concerns and ideas that are heard in pan-European forums - and some of them in Finland may seem more like current events in Finland . On the other hand, the current debate on the financial sector is not national, but is becoming international (which is also a challenge for the media). The banking sector is notoriously undergoing a drastic change, not only in Finland, but also in other parts of Europe and the whole world. Banks are rethinking their products, markets and distribution channels. At the same time, the corporate structure of the sector is changing through various industry arrangements, as mergers and group formations are examples of the sector. Internationalization is one of the clearest trends. The second is the industry drift: the vision that the whole banking sector as a separate industry is hsmsrtymssss, while the boundary between securities and investment services and insurance in relation to traditional banking is becoming increasingly hazy. It is more common to talk about the financial services sector in general rather than the banking sector. As in a market economy in general, the driving force behind change is competition and innovation, which force companies to rethink their operating concepts and improve their efficiency. The current changes in the banking sector are due, on the one hand, to the impact of new technologies on business opportunities, competition and product development, and, on the other hand, to the effects of monetary union, which are one of the European financial markets. There is a customer (i.e. the depositor, the investor, the person who uses the payment service, the person in need of financing) .as long as healthy competition remains the driving force behind the change and security is not compromised. According to the tasks entrusted to it, the central bank's angle to the upheaval is the result of the upheaval. In principle, it is customary to distinguish between three functions of central bank activity: monetary policy, payment systems and the supervision of the stability of financial markets. *** In the area of payment systems, the Central Bank naturally plays a central role as a hub for payment transactions at national level and now also in the context of the euro area. This is the result of central bank payments. In the euro area, the objectives of central banks are defined as stability, efficiency and security of payment systems. One aspect of efficiency is the convergence of the euro area's financial markets, which is an essential part of the achievement of monetary union. In the recent development of European payment systems, it is possible to record from the central bank's corner both considerable achievements and major challenges. A major recent achievement in the development of the payment system has been the construction of a common wholesale payment system for the euro area, i.e. a system of payments by large banks. The construction of the European central banks has played a key role. TARGET .maksujsestelmsllslls, which is served by various private systems. However, only part of the payment transactions are international payments (about 40% of the value). It can be said that, in the case of large payments by banks, the euro area now has a single payment system and, through it, a very similar money market for banks. Large payments travel in real time and quite cheaply from one bank to another, if not right from Hanko to Petsamo, then at least from Helsinki to Lisbon. Now to the challenges. Customer payments have so far been placed under the responsibility of the private sector - banks - as is natural in a market economy - to meet the requirements of monetary union . There is still a lot to be done in this sector. Unfortunately, it has to be said that, despite EMU and all the technical developments, there is still no uniform system of payments in Europe. There seems to be a lot of interest, at least in the rest of Europe, in the change that the Finnish banking network has undergone. In principle, the next threat to the sector would be the acceleration of competition, but market integration (due to EMU and banking) is now expected to be more intense. At the same time, however, the increasing complexity and internationalisation of the banking sector make the implementation of banking supervision in the new circumstances even more challenging than before. In particular, the effectiveness of national authorities in international markets has been discussed. Will the outcome be trusted if the bank is supervised and managed by a foreign authority? How do you deal with it if the domestic deposit insurance system has to compensate for large losses of foreign depositors? Recommendations developed in other similar for a, on the other hand, have a decisive impact on, for example, EU directives and the laws of different countries. One of the reasons for my optimism is the change in the tax treatment of deposits that took place last summer. At the same time, the incipient decline in government debt is creating more space in the financial markets for private, long-term debt securities. Hopefully, nsms opportunities will be able to be used as a good idea for the Finnish housing finance system. In this context, it is also welcomed by the Special Mortgage Credit Bank Facility, which entered into force at the beginning of this year. If new types of institutions are successful, then we will need to increase the level of interest rates and securitisation of loans in housing finance. The housing sector (households and landlords) would not be as exposed to interest rate risks in the future as it is today. This requires the ability to provide information and coherence in policy. Sits central banks are pursuing. *** Talking about the challenges of banking does not describe the rosy moods in which the Finnish financial sector has been living for the past couple of years. Rather, one could speak of some kind of rush of opportunity caused by the history of the banking crisis, the painful but successful restructuring of the sector, the historically high level of profitability, the growth of the securities market in the past and the staggering niggles that have been opened up by the new internet and mobile technologies. In addition to this, mention should be made of the increase in Finnish wealth and the increase in the opportunities for households to acquire funds, which has a beneficial effect on some of the activities of banks. In many cases in the banking sector, waves of optimism such as those in the past have turned into disappointments in a short period of time. Even now, the future of banking depends not only on the industry's own strategic wisdom, but also on general cyclical developments, with all their certainty. From the central bank's point of view, it is appropriate to stress the importance of prudence when, in the future, the possibilities of hysdynnets. It's not empty talk now. Nevertheless, I want to be an optimist and believe that Finnish banking is now, historically speaking, exceptionally good at meeting the challenges it faces. Hystyjins are the customers who can have access to the international payment, investment and financing opportunities made possible by the new, large European financial markets and new technologies. If the challenges are met correctly in the eastern years, I believe that in the future the public image of banking will improve.

Toisaalta varsinkin suurten yritysten riippuvaisuus pankkiluotoista on vhenemss sit mukaa kun markkinat kehittyvt ja yritykset rahoittavat toimintaansa yh enemmn suoraan tukkumarkkinoilta. Yksi rahapolitiikan harjoittamisen kannalta potentiaalinen ongelmakohta euroalueen pankkirakenteissa on niiden epsymmetrisyys eli yh suuret maittaiset erot. Eri maiden luottomarkkinat poikkeavat melko paljon toisistaan siin suhteessa mik on pankkien merkitys kotitalouksien ja yritysten luotonantajina ja mink tyyppisi rahoitustuotteita pankit asiakkailleen tarjoavat. Tss suhteessa ei EMUsta huolimatta ole tapahtunut nopeaa yhdenmukaistumista eri jsenmaissa. Pitkn plle tietty rahoitusrakenteiden yhdenmukaistumista voidaan odottaa, mutta erot kansallisessa lainsdnnss esim. pomaverotuksen alalla sek erot asuntomarkkinoilla ja eri maiden yritysrakenteessa aiheuttavat sen, ett kansalliset erikoispiirteet eivt varmasti kokonaan poistu ainakaan nyt nkpiiriss olevana aikana. Mik merkitys tll luottorakenteiden epsymmetrisyydell on? Se tarkoittaa kytnnss muun muassa sit, ett sellaiset maat, joissa vaihtuvakorkoisilla pankkilainoilla on suhteellisen suuri merkitys yritysten rahoituksessa ja asuntorahoituksessa, altistuvat markkinakorkojen vaihtelulle jossain mrin enemmn kuin muut. Suomi on tllainen maa. Meill nykyn melkein 90 % kotitalouksien lainoista on sidottu euribor-korkoihin tai pankkikohtaisiin viitekorkoihin, mik merkitsee markkinakorkojen muutosten suhteellisen nopeaa vlittymist vanhojenkin lainojen kustannuksiin -Suomessa nopeammin kuin joissakin muissa maissa. Rahapolitiikkaa on kuitenkin hoidettava piten silmll koko euroalueen tilannetta, eik korkopolitiikan mitoituksessa voida (eik pidkn) ottaa huomioon yksittisten maiden erityisongelmia. Siksi voisi olla eduksi, jos Suomenkin luottomarkkinoiden rakenne mys korkosidonnaisuuksien osalta lhenisi euroalueen yleislinjaa. Arvioisin olevan syyt uskoa, ett meill Suomessa on viime aikoina avattu tie sellaisiin rakennemuutoksiin, jotka vhentvt asuntorahoituksen riippuvuutta talletusmuotoisesta sstmisest ja lyhytaikaisista markkinakoroista. Yksi syy thn optimistiseen ksitykseeni on viime kesn tapahtunut talletusten verokohtelun muutos. Tm on tehnyt eri sstmismuodot kotitalouksien kannalta aiempaa tasavertaisemmiksi, ja aiempi lyhytaikaisia pankkitalletuksia yksipuolisesti suosinut tilanne on poistunut. Alkuvaiheessa verotuksen muutos on nyttnyt suosineen sijoitusrahastoja, joihin on virrannut varoja, vaikka osakemarkkinabuumi on muuten osoittanutkin jhtymisen merkkej. Sstmisen verokohtelun nyt siis muututtua aiempaa neutraalimmaksi kotitalouksien obligaatiosstmisen kasvulle (joko suoraan tai luultavammin rahastojen kautta) on luotu paremmat edellytykset. Samalla valtion velan alkanut supistuminen luo yh enemmn tilaa rahoitusmarkkinoilla yksityisille, pitkaikaisille velkapapereille. Niill kertyt varat sopivat kansainvlisen kokemuksen mukaan hyvin asuntorahoitukseen kytettviksi. Toivottavasti nm mahdollisuudet kyetn kyttmn hydyksi Suomen asuntorahoitusjrjestelm kehitettess. Tss yhteydess tytyy mys toivottaa tervetulleeksi erityisten kiinnitysluottopankkien toiminnan mahdollistava lainsdnt, joka tuli voimaan kuluvan vuoden alusta. Jos nm uudenlaiset laitokset menestyvt, ehk meill pstisiin asuntorahoituksessa laajempaan kiintekorkoisuuteen ja lainojen arvopaperistamiseen. Nin asuntosektori (kotitaloudet ja vuokranantajat) eivt olisi tulevaisuudessa niin alttiita korkoriskeille kuin nykyn. Keskuspankin vastuulla on toimia niin, ett rahapolitiikan strategia ja sen reagointitapa laajasti ymmrretn ja nin pankit ja niiden asiakkaat osaavat mitoittaa velkaantumisensa ja lainojensa korkoehdot realistisesti. Tm vaatii lpinkyvyytt tiedotuksessa ja johdonmukaisuutta politiikassa. Sit keskuspankeissa tavoitellaan. *** Pankkitoiminnan haasteista puhuminen ei ehk tysin kuvaa niit ruusuisia tunnelmia, joissa suomalainen rahoitusala on viimeiset pari vuotta elnyt. Voisi ehk pikemminkin puhua jonkinlaisesta mahdollisuuksien huumasta, jonka ovat aiheuttaneet pankkikriisin jminen historiaan, alan kipe mutta onnistunut saneeraus, historiallisella huipputasolla pyriv kannattavuus, arvopaperimarkkinoiden ennennkemtn kasvu ja ne huikaisevat nkymt joita uusi internet-ja mobiiliteknologia ovat avanneet. Tmn lisksi on mainittava viel suomalaisten varallisuuden kasvu ja kotitalouksien sstmismahdollisuuksien lisntyminen, mik vaikuttaa suotuisasti pankkien joihinkin toimintoihin. Monesti aikaisemmin pankkialalla tmntapaiset optimismin aallot ovat lyhyess ajassa vaihtuneet pettymyksiksi. Nytkin pankkitoiminnan tulevaisuus on sidoksissa paitsi alan omaan strategiseen viisauteen, mys yleiseen suhdannekehitykseen kaikkine epvarmuuksineen. Keskuspankkinkkulmasta kuuluu asiaan korostaa jrkevn varovaisuuden merkityst kun tulevaisuudessa hmttvi mahdollisuuksia hydynnetn. Eik se ole tyhj puhetta nytkn. Silti haluan olla optimisti ja uskon, ett suomalaisella pankkitoiminnalla on nyt historiallisesti katsoen poikkeuksellisen hyvt lhtkohdat vastata kohtaamiinsa haasteisiin. Hytyjin ovat asiakkaat, joiden ulottuville voidaan saada entist tehokkaammin ja ktevmmin ne kansainvlisen maksamisen, sstmisen, sijoittamisen ja rahoituksen mahdollisuudet, joita uudet, laajat eurooppalaiset rahoitusmarkkinat ja uusi teknologia tekevt mahdollisiksi. Title: Speech at the Economic and Financial Forum in the Local Government Sector
text: Bank Manager Sinikka Salo's speech at the Municipal Economic and Financial Forum . Speech . Wednesday7 February2001,12:00AM EMU yes euro 1. Central bank information work in EMU Under the conditions of monetary union, communication between monetary policy and the real economy is now as much the same as in the past. It is possibly even more demanding than before, as the monetary policy institutions in EMU are structured in a new way and the finnish national system is a little more complex. This has increased the need for information. On the other hand, monetary policy is better than that. After all, the aim is stability and minimisation of excess costs. Money should be a point of reference in the economy and not a point of reference. That is why monetary policy in EMU is also more successful, and Finland's membership of the monetary union is more humble, what the drama and the monetary sector offer us Finns. As a result of EMU, monetary policy in Finland has started to be fairly stable and predictable - at least compared to the storms that took place a dozen years ago, and often before. Despite the increase in predictability, monetary policy will continue to have to react to changes in the economy, and these reactions will also have an impact on Finland. It is therefore fair to say that understanding the logic of monetary policy and its aspirations is one of the most important prerequisites for good economic management. Not only for those who have to operate in the money and cash markets, as many do, but more generally also for all those who make forward-looking pricing and purchasing markets. I would go so long as to say that one of the most important things a national central bank can do in the context of monetary union for the economic success of its own country is to ensure that the general public, both professionals and laypeople, understand monetary policy as well as possible and that it rarely makes errors of judgement as far as possible as possible about where the policy is going. After all, the world is always turbulent and economic signals cannot be mechanically interpreted. That is why it is important that the way of thinking of the makers of monetary policy - the way in which the signals of the economy are thought - becomes as common as possible. At the service of the European Central Bank in Frankfurt, it was clear that the information strategy for the monetary union as a whole would include national central banks (in fact, I would like to use the English term 'communications strategy' in a little more detail and to talk about a communication strategy rather than an information strategy) - so, it is clear how long the ECB will have to rely on the NATIONAL CENTRAL BANKS in its communication strategy. In Frankfurt, it is not possible to write bulletins, but it is not possible to participate in the debate on the economic and political circles of the various countries so that the specific situation and current problems of each country receive the attention they deserve. 'Euroland', or euro area, is not a single country, but a multipolar economic area, albeit with a single financial market, but different economic structures and different economic policy concerns in different regions, not to mention differences in languages and cultures. -I wonder if it needs to be pointed out that the European economic policy debate is also becoming more broadly based today. Today, in all the euro countries, the interest of citizens is focused above all on economic issues at national level. Communication with the domestic general is therefore not an ancillary function of the Central Bank, but part of its core task, and therefore participation in the economic policy debate is maintained by the Bank of Finland. It is, of course, the responsibility of domestic fiscal and labour market policy to ensure that Finland's economy balances in monetary union is the responsibility of domestic fiscal and labour market policy, but the Bank of Finland's role is to contribute to supporting this policy, i.e. to ensure that responsibility for balance is taken in Finland. We strive to ensure that monetary policy in Finland is also trusted and that all the information that the bank has to provide to support other economic policies is also available to the various parties. 2. The ECB's monetary policy strategy It is well known that the ECB's monetary policy objective is to pursue price stability throughout the euro area. 'The euro area as a whole' implies that the policy is not tailored to the needs of any individual country or group of countries. In the same breath, it is worth noting that, from Finland's point of view, it is also worthwhile to be: even if we Finns were to decide on the monetary policy of the euro area alone, it would still not be worthwhile for us to take only finland's cyclical situation as a point of monetary policy for the whole of monetary union, not even if our own situation was somewhere different from the others, as it was a year or two ago. It is in the interest of each Member State and of Finland that the euro area economy as a whole remains in balance. In the context of the single currency, we are all in the same boat, equally dependent on the stability of the price level of the euro area, that is, the value of the euro, and, above all, on the confidence it enjoys. That is why the monetary policy interests of the various member states of the ECB are converging in the long term, and this is the starting point for monetary policy-making. The Governing Council has criticised price stability as meaning that the rate of increase in consumer prices should remain below two per cent over the medium term. In recent months, inflation rates in the euro area have crossed the border and have risen by three per cent. A forecast published by the ECB in December estimated that the two per cent critical limit could be exceeded in another year. That calculation, however, was conditional on exchange rates, interest rates and the price of sljy in late autumn. The conditions for inflation to fall below two per cent already in the year have clearly improved due to favourable exchange rate developments and a fall in the price of sljy. -The easing of inflationary pressures is driven by a clear change in the global economy in recent months, even weeks. In the United States, in particular, economic forecasts have been revised downwards, and the concern about overheating of demand in the past has turned into speculation as to how great the probability of a recession could be. Despite the change in the nitty-gritty in the USA, the conditions for balanced growth in the euro area are, however, still very good, partly thanks in part to the protection afforded by monetary union. The ECB has published a so-called "green card". a two-pillar strategy describing how monetary policy is set in such a way that the objective of price stability can be achieved. The first pillar is monetary. A reference value has been set for the growth rate of money, which is used when monetary developments are monitored. According to the reference value, an annual growth rate of 4.5% in money can be expected to be consistent with price stability. The amount of money in cash is counted as a very wide range of bank deposits and securities issued by banks. For a long time, monetary growth has been above the reference value, but has recently slowed down, partly partly as a result of the tightening of monetary policy in the past. In December, the annual growth rate of money was 4.9%. The second pillar of the monetary policy strategy is a 'broad assessment of inflationary pressures', which refers to a forward-looking analysis of the real economy. The important role of this is played by the macroeconomic forecasts, or rather the estimates, which are drawn up on the basis of the Council's work. A six-monthly publication of the monetary policy criteria for the financial markets and the general public has now begun to be made clearer. In market comments and in the press, monetary policy in the euro area is often commented on in relation to exchange rate developments - in particular, the dollar value of the euro is of interest. It is natural enough, because exchange rates fluctuate psivitsin, but the meanings of the exchange rate are also exaggerated. The ECB has not set a target level for the exchange rate, and the monetary policy objectives have been determined solely in terms of price stability. Thus, the stability of the purchasing power of the euro is the stability of the euro in the internal part of the euro area, not the stability of exchange rates, nor the evolution of exchange rates dictates monetary policy. Of course, the exchange rate plays a role in inflation, as the depreciation of the euro in the foreign exchange markets may lead to higher import prices and inflationary pressures in the euro area. The exchange rate is linked to the monetary policy strategy solely and exclusively through this, as part of a comprehensive assessment of inflationary pressures in the 'second pillar' I mentioned. The two-pillar strategy of monetary policy is not of a mechanical nature. It is based on the idea that both the growth of money and the general inflation rate must be carefully interpreted and weighed in order to distinguish the transient hsirist from long-term changes and to correctly weight the signal values of the various indicators. In addition to the technology of economists, it takes a lot of wisdom, a lot of wisdom, a sense of what is really happening in the economies of the euro area. That is why monetary policy-making and the latest interpretation of the situation take place in the Governing Council, which, through the presidents of the various national central banks, has a broad understanding of economic developments in the euro area as a whole. In the deliberations of the Council, the contribution of the national central banks is significant 3. The role of the Bank of Finland in the euro system I would like to correct one commonly used refrain: neither Finland nor the other Members of the European Monetary Union can be said to have given up their monetary policy - they have simply combined it. Finland does not have a "foreign" monetary policy, but we have our own, common monetary policy throughout the euro area. The structure of the European System of Central Banks , or more precisely the 'euro system', is structured in such a way that a Member State is not only an object of monetary policy, but also a subject of monetary policy. This is the case that the euro system is a coalition of national central banks in which they, through the European Central Bank, jointly decide on monetary policy that has been raised as a common concern. The Bank of Finland's common role in the euro system is to participate in the preparation of the euro system. When Mr Vanhala participates in meetings of the Governing Council of the ECB, where monetary policy is discussed, he is a member of the Council, as well as any other member of the Council , such as Ernst Weltekell of the German Bundesbank or Jean-Claude Trichet of France. Only the ECB's own finances, such as its distribution of profits, are proportional to the size of each Member State. Of course, the 'one jssen, one ssni' principle is based on the point I mentioned by sske, the fundamental convergence of the monetary interests of the various countries. If it weren't for the nsin, the whole system would naturally be impossible, and it wouldn't have been built in the first place. In the preparation of the proposal, the involvement of the national central banks is quite extensive. There are 13 committees supporting the ECB's policy preparation, including the Monetary Policy Committee, which prepares the macroeconomic projections published by the ECB. Under the auspices of the committees, in turn, there are various permanent and national task forces. A total of forty experts from the Bank of Finland will take part in the committee and group meeting in Frankfurt. A larger number of people are also serving in the field of analysis and statistics. The bank's second role is to represent the euro system in Finland. This is partly operational: the Bank of Finland must be involved in the operational implementation of monetary policy, which is decentralised to the various national central banks. The payment transactions of commercial banks, the deposit of their reserves, money market operations that control interest rates, the issue of banknotes and coins, the investment of foreign exchange reserves - almost all central bank transactions are carried out by the national central banks. However, as I have already pointed out, the representation of the euro system in Finland also implies an obligation to communicate and market, on the one hand, to collect points and, on the other hand, to assess the demands placed on the Finnish economy and economic policy by means of a monetary policy aimed at European price stability. By virtue of its position, the Bank of Finland is obliged to analyse the issues and the unique possibility of analysing the economic development of Finland from the perspective of European monetary policy and the effects of European monetary policy on the perspective of the Finnish economy. 4. EMU for Finland There is already so much experience of monetary union that the picture of its effects and the adaptation needs it entails begins in Chechnya. Monetary union has had some impact on Finland's macroeconomic development. Interest rates and exchange rates have been fixed on the basis of the single monetary policy, and monetary policy balances must have been somewhat different from what would have been done under the conditions of a floating mark. However, it would not be worth exaggerating. Strong links bind the economies of all European countries to each other - both the members of monetary union and the 'outs'. However, the biggest effects have -as expected - been political and psychological. We have all been able to see how Finland's weight in European economic policy has grown, and we have, in a way, moved to the 'guerrilla ring'. This has, of course, had not only political but also economic consequences. Phosss come with psychology and confidence in the picture. When, in the past, a well-known Spanish banker was asked why he was in favour of his country joining the monetary union, he replied that the Spaniards had argued that they had not considered their money to be an 'exotic currency'. I am sure that our mark has, like peseta, from time to time been deprived of its exoticism. Exoticism, or bad notoriety, was paid for in the past as a considerable amount of stability, as trust in the markka ranged from unduly good to unduly bad. The result was not only fluctuations in interest rates, but also unnecessary difficulties for the foreign operations of small and medium-sized enterprises. The local government sector also has experience. 5. The role of municipalities in EMU Finland When considering joining the monetary union, there was quite a lot of discussion in Finland about what monetary union would mean for Finland's regional economy and public finances. Both issues are central to municipalities, as they account for two thirds of public finances and when it is the municipalities that face the problems of regional development first. As is well known, Finland is undergoing considerable regional structural change, including the concentration of economic growth and new jobs in a few growth centres. Ilmissn also includes the concentration of economic growth in a few technically and scientifically demanding industries, such as the electronics industry. It is possible that finland's member monetary union has played some part in the success of Hi-Tech d Finland. The permanently locked exchange rate relative to continental Europe has certainly contributed to the availability of pssoma and encouraged Finnish companies to choose competitive pricing. However, I do not believe that monetary union is far from being the driving force behind structural change. The general trend towards globalisation is almost certainly a much stronger driver of change than monetary union. From the point of view of regional development, it is actually the case that Finland's membership of the monetary union has softened the adaptation to structural change of regions dependent on the forest sector and agriculture. If the Finnish markka had floated, it is very possible that, under the conditions of rapid economic growth and the current trade balance, the mark would have been under considerable pressure to strengthen. The real incomes of the forestry and agricultural sectors would have been lower than they have now enjoyed under the conditions of monetary union. At the same time, at the level of the overall economy, we have had to worry about the threat of overheating. In this sense, emu membership has been more of an income base for agriculture and forestry than a sith. This has been counterbalanced by the strong globalisation of new jobs in knowledge-intensive fields in university towns. On the fiscal side, the most well-known part of monetary union is the standards limiting public debt, which are currently included in the EU's Stability and Growth Pact. The purpose of these standards is to ensure that the common currency is not destabilised in the country by a fiscal policy. The Stability and Growth Pact is criticised for excessively restricting the room for manoeuvre in public finances. After all, the agreement requires that each country's public finances should be in medium-term balance and, on a cyclical basis, a maximum of 3% of the deficit (with the exception of situations of an exceptionally deep recession, in which the deficit could be higher). This kind of criticism is most often misguided. The agreement hardly excludes any economic strategies. In fact, the public finances of European countries are so worrying that the obligations of the Stability and Growth Pact can rightly be too lax. In Finland, too, the public sector is well oversized, especially due to the accumulation of social security funds. There are good reasons for this, especially in the context of the recent boom, where there has been room to correct balance sheets that have been hit by the recession. The Stability and Growth Pact does not require us to be over-the-top, so it does not, in the current circumstances, constitute a 'straitjacket' for Finland's economic policy in any way. The requirement for scarcity in the general expenditure economy is due entirely to the economic fundamentals and the risks associated with the tax base and EMU. I do not want to see the seriousness of the issues relating to the finances of the municipalities. The situation of municipalities as part of the dynamics of the public sector is exceptionally difficult because of the fact that regional development is so important and because the challenges of ageing will put a strain on the budgetary allocations of municipal health and care services in the future. In addition to the well-known issues, there is also the question of preparing for future cyclical fluctuations. The future development of the tax base will not always be as favourable as it has been in many municipalities in recent years. There are reasons for the municipalities' finances to be more cautious about indebtedness and even cyclical tendencies, the deficits intended to be temporary, than in central government finances. There are reasons to consider whether the current financial situation of the municipalities is stable, how it will certainly withstand the more difficult times that are to come in due course. I will not comment further on the report prepared by the liquidator Pekkarinen. The issues of municipal income distribution, which are the subject of the report's actual proposals, are clearly beyond the competence of the Central Bank. However, the report also draws due attention to macroeconomic issues, namely the special features of the Finnish tax system, which apparently make the income base of municipalities more variable than it would be. It is precisely this that makes it difficult for local government finances to adapt to cyclical changes. Pekkarinen rightly points out that the dependence of municipalities on the joint tax is, in fact, rare from an international point of view and difficult when the revenue from the joint tax is very strongly cyclical. What will happen to local government finances when there is sometimes a transition from a boom to a recession and corporate profits fall? Will there then be a gaping hole in the municipal budget? Traditionally, the aim has been to keep municipal budgets broadly in balance, regardless of cyclical fluctuations. This is justified. If, as a result of the economic cycle, the cyclical economy generates a sub-economy, it is better that they are generated in the state budget than in a very fragmented municipal field. Tax forms that vary widely in terms of yield are therefore best suited as state revenues. Pekkarinen sets as the objective of the report to increase the stability of municipal tax revenues, but does not propose any changes to the extent to which the proceeds of the joint taxation belong. Apparently, hsn has not come up with an alternative that would have seemed politically realistic. From the point of view of local government finances, it would be much better if the joint tax were a state tax. So it is in other countries. The share of municipalities in other taxes, such as the tax on wage income, could be correspondingly higher. Pekkarinen hopes that a discussion will be held on the possibility that the stability of the municipalities' tax base would be resolved either by the state equalising the accounts paid to municipalities in the four-year period or by establishing a joint cyclical adjustment fund for municipalities. He does not make a concrete proposal because he considers that the time is not ripe for change. Personally, I consider the proposals to be very difficult to implement and whether they can ever mature to be feasible. The functioning of cyclical funds and cyclical adjustment procedures is determined by the fact that the cyclical fluctuations do not follow the rhythm of the economic cycle, and generally not before the date, if at all, the level of tax accrual is "normal" and because we are above or below the long-term average. How, then, do you know how to manage the cyclical adjustment? In september, I think that the problem dependence of municipalities on the joint tax is difficult to solve with funds or equalisation procedures. I would like to call for an open-minded examination of the different forms of taxation between municipalities and the state. ***** 6. The importance of the eurocite system There is already experience of the economic policy and financial market implications of monetary union - as well as of the challenges that required adaptation. At the micro level, the effects of monetary union, on the contrary, will not really be felt until January and February 2002. Czech euro banknotes and coins will be used. According to the EU recommendation, the vast majority of payments in euros would take place in as little as two weeks from the beginning of 2002, provided that the conversion of ATMs to euros takes place at the expected pace and if trade gives the general change in Greece in euros from the beginning of the year. In monetary terms, the exchange of money does not mean big, it is like just the last seal of change. As a logistical operation, of course, it is very demanding. Some 130 million banknotes are withdrawn and almost a total of many new banknotes are put into circulation. On the coin side, the number of pieces is roughly tenfold. It is also a demanding operation for the general public, companies, trade and even municipalities, all of which will have to convert their invoicing, bookkeeping and other information systems into line with the new monetary unit. The costs of the changeover to the euro (NOTE: transition period from 1.1.1999 to 31.12.2001, and the exchange period from 1.1.2002 to 28.2.2002) will be considerable and there will probably be difficulties. It should be remembered, however, that hysdies are also large, although they often only accumulate over a long period of time, in the years to come and in decades. The use of euro banknotes and coins requires extensive communication from the Bank of Finland. The Bank of Finland participates in the euro 2002 information campaign, which is a joint effort of the central banks of the euro area and the ECB, and is also implementing a Finnish campaign. The aim of the central banks is to familiarise citizens, in particular, with the external and authenticity of euro coins and the timetable for issuing them. The target group is not only a large general group, but especially those professional groups that are able to find out about the new money or are able to effectively disseminate information about the new currency. The most czech groups are the banks, the trade and the tourism sector, as well as the police and the education administration. Through this, we hope to reach schoolchildren, among others. The Bank of Finland has already signed more than 40 cooperation or partnership agreements. with entities. The Bank of Finland assists the partners in communicating the euro and, in return, the partners take care of informing their own personnel and customers. The nskyv part of the Bank of Finland's mass media campaign will take place at the end of 2001. At that time, the nshdssn e.g. an extensive tv advertising campaign. The use of the euro in Finland is also reflected in the joint euro information campaign of the Minister of Finance and the European Union. The various campaigns are coordinated in the midst of the prevention of incidents and information blackouts. The local government sector has extensively analysed the measures required for the changeover to the euro and has also estimated the associated costs. In most municipalities, the challenges are likely to be more related to accounting, tariffs and invoicing, i.e. account money, because the money is used in the municipalities, except for sports and sports services.
