Saturday 5 May 2001, 12:00 AM Globalisation issues and challenges Introduction The Finnish matriculation examination is characterised by a strong tradition of social dimensioning, which has manifested itself more strongly, more subduedly. It is obvious that the students of the Faculty of Political Science have an emphasis on the social angle, as they study topics that touch on power and politics in different areas of society. Each generation has its own "stuff". I myself studied in the late 1960s and at the turn of the 1970s - a time of real turmoil, when people wanted to change the world radically and quickly. At the time of the Czech Republic, I liked the characterization of the 1800's Finnish matriculation examination, which I picked up from the book by Matti Klinge and Laura Kolbe. "Finnish student", i.e. "students always want to be and think they are the leaders of the people and the owners of the future". Of course, Nsin is not, at least not tsysin, but more often than not, the legitimacy of tsms's faith is called into question. Yet it is believed, and so I suppose the ideas and enthusiasm to promote social debate and development come from young people. When I thought about the subject of my speech, I tried to consider what would now be the "own stuff" in which the students of the Faculty of Political Science would like to "own the future". In my mind, one obvious topic is globalisation. I therefore chose globalisation and the challenges it poses to the international community as the subject of my speech. Globalization, the new economy -critique of globalization In recent years, the debate on economic policy has been going on for a long time around two megatrends: the 'new economy' and the 'globalisation'. In fact, the disputed arguments are so closely related that neither can be properly understood separately. Interestingly, however, they are generally viewed in a very different way. The new economy has generally been seen as a positive revolution that promises a rapid increase in prosperity in the world without much inflation or a polluting "chimney industry", and which can free people up for truly global, vslichmsn interaction and information gathering on the recipient's terms. On the other hand, globalisation, on the other hand, appears most of the time as a threat in public debate. The criticisms are directed at, among other things: the social and environmental consequences of globalisation. It is based on the fear that development trends known as globalisation will simultaneously lead to the escalation of poverty problems in developing countries, the destruction of jobs in industrialised countries and the accelerated destruction of the environment. Significant criticism also focuses on the impact of globalisation on the relationship between economic and political power in the world. Pelschis, that the power of the market has been stripped of control by the kssist and governments. It is thought that when the market has become so large that the national government cannot control it, they will in turn begin to control the governments. This leads to the erosion of national sovereignty. It is believed that the fates of the whole world will also be passed on to human market forces. A situation arises, if the spacecraft on Earth did not have a captain to steer: "nobody is in charge". At the same time, the power of the market with which globalisation is identified is not as anonymous and value-free as market optimists suggest. It is thought that power is concentrated more in the hands of large multinationals, which today, in terms of power relations in their favour, are supposedly capable of dictating the coherence of economic policy and the direction of economic development worldwide. Another concentration of power that has been criticised by law is the international economic organisations, in particular the Imf, the World Trade Organisation and the World Bank, which contribute to globalisation and act in accordance with the objectives of the International Monetary Fund, the World Trade Organisation and the World Bank. Globalisation is not just an economic, economy-driven manifest But globalization is not a separate manifestation with distinct "own" effects: it is in a wider context. Media researcher Marshall McLuhan coined the term "world village" back in the 60s, and it wasn't a good idea to describe the obvious ones that have given rise to the current globalisation debate. McLuhan nski that the world is changing, above all because of the growing importance of mass media. However, there could be no idea of the more revolutionary possibilities offered by technology. In the current debate, globalisation is often the subject of economic-driven development. After all, the debate is very much about the political, social and environmental consequences, since the market and business in general are more easily crossed over national borders. However, the economic nsks angle is very superficial and easily leads to simple management decisions about how to deal with the globalization image. The merit of McLuhan's world village award is precisely that it gives priority to the factors that influence globalisation: technological change and the next cultural change. From the point of view of the world's worldview, the driving force behind globalisation is the general expansion of the circle of people, which technology has made possible. Elsms is basically globalized in two autumns. First of all, thanks to new technologies, telecommunications have become enormously more efficient in a few years, and therefore cultural influences and market knowledge are spreading in one more abundant stream and reaching a single larger proportion of the world's people. It's easier to get things from around the world that we're interested in, whether commercial, entertainment, or cultural. It is precisely the same technological advances that are leading to the talk of a 'new economy' that are globalising the whole of people's circles. And since technological progress is in a way irreversible - once invented, it is not easy to get the invention of the "one-way" globalisation process. Along with technology, another reason for globalization is the political changes that have occurred in recent years. Since the fall of communism and many right-wing dictatorships, governments today do not restrict people's contacts with the people internationally in many countries as before. This would be more difficult in the modern technological environment. The political changes which have led to the expansion of democracy and civil liberties in the world do not appear to have been technologically independent. It is very clear that technological advances have not led to a society controlled by the 'big brother' as George Orwell once did, but rather to the extent that centralised control of use and information has become more difficult than before. The opening up of the circle of people's contacts and the similarity of their countries also played a part in the collapse of communism in the social system. The globalisation of the economy in one way or another is a consequence of the emergence of the world village and the associated spread of the democratic and free model of society. That is precisely why the idea that the globalisation of the economy is somehow indistinguishable from the general cultural change that exists cannot be true. The market is formed by how modern people elsvst: consume, work, ssssvsvst and move, whatever entertainment or culture they follow, and so on. The transformation of people into inhabitants of the world village, and why, hopefully, at the same time its citizens, will globalise their economic relations, as well as with the rest of the world. The functioning of the market then reflects their needs and skills, but also their morals. Evaluation of criticism It is actually a little strange against this background that the criticism of culture and values directed at the ssian Elsmsntavas is directed precisely against 'globalisation'. One cynical explanation, hopefully epstosi, could be that the criticism is essentially hypocritical: it is only the resistance to change that has arisen in rich societies to the new situation caused by the inclusion of developing countries in the world economy as more serious competitors. In other words, there is a loss of jobs in sectors where production in developing countries is increasing and, in general, greater structural changes. If it were, criticism of globalisation would only be a new, more hypocritical form of the demand to protect the industries of the industrialised countries from competition, the restructuring of the world economy and the need to condemn developing countries to poverty and dependence on the financial aid of the rich countries in the future, instead of being able to stand on their own two feet. Another easy explanation, which is contemptuous of the criticisms that has been made, could be that it would be based on a lack of awareness of the situation in developing countries: if it had not been noticed that globalisation, and only it, offers the developing countries a real chance for a better economic future, or if it had not been noticed that in developing countries globalisation threatens the economic and political elites of those countries, and that they have only been able to do so as far as they have been able to artificially shunning protectionism and isolationist policies. The first option available to globalisation is not a natural idyll, but a gunshot, a lack of choice. However, I do not want to believe that criticism is explained only by selfishness or ignorance. There is also a genuine value base behind the debate and the criticism of globalisation. The critique appeals to ideals such as opposition to poverty, cherishing the environment and democracy, with which there can be no difference of opinion. In that sense, it is a positive indication of how strong a force public opinion based on moral principles can be. Unfortunately, however, criticism is generally based on a very superficial assessment of the causes and consequences of globalisation. In particular, the forms of criticism show that it is also apparently based on a misrepresentation of tsys, which are the motives behind international economic policy organisations such as the IMF and the WTO in their attempts to develop the economic and political structures required by a globalising economy. Of course, illegality and other mild-mannered criticisms cannot be accepted. Criticism of globalisation is of great importance if and when it leads to higher ethical requirements, what is bought, what is produced and how it is produced. Pitss notices that the controlling influence of global public opinion on the activities of multinationals is precisely the political manifestation characteristic of the "world village". Criticism is also of great importance in persuading international organisations to act more transparently and to show how their objectives and strategy relate to generally accepted values. However, it is completely misguided if it wants to limit the opening up and globalisation of the world. Globalisation is not only irreversible, but also, in essence, a huge positive force. It is precisely the people and the community who are most affected by globalisation and the opportunities it offers that are the greatest problems. The challenges of globalisation for international cooperation Globalisation policy therefore does not seem to me to be able to ask the question of whether globalisation is good or bad, but rather to ask what common challenges it poses to international society and how to respond to such challenges. In relation to ssss, I am inclined to think about things from the point of view of realpolitik. It should be remembered that the alternative to development based on government agreements, which is being built by the international d IMF, WB, WEO, is not harmony led by some ideal, enlightened autocrat, but the economic and political fragmentation of the world into competing trading blocs. What would follow would be a slowdown in economic development and the transformation of trade into an instrument of power politics by the strong players in the world economy. It is therefore the case that the work of the Czech Republic (IMF, WB, WTO) is moving forward, and this is only possible if all the significant countries feel it makes sense for them to participate in the work and implement the agreements reached. Of course, the sms point sets its own limits on how the psschisxs can be done. At a time, various international organisations, especially the International Monetary Fund, are making efforts to implement so-called 'green belts'. in order to create a new international financial architecture in order to safeguard the more stable functioning of international financial markets and thus increase the security of the position of countries dependent on the domestic market (i.e. those in need of credit or investment). The question is a programme of enormous proportions, demanding over a long period of time, consisting of many different areas. This will address a number of key problems: the development of economic policy and access to economic information; the establishment of international quality standards for the supervision and infrastructure of financial markets; and seek to increase the responsibility and coordination of investors in the event of problems. The Fund plays a key role in coordinating and supervising the development of reforms and the implementation of these reforms. However, better functioning of the financial markets alone is not enough to bring about the transfer of productive resources from richer countries to more mature countries. What is also needed is to safeguard and extend the freedom of trade flows. In order to better enable the countries to participate in the nitty-gritty of the rapid integration of the world economy, the richest countries should boldly open up their markets to the products of these countries. This would cause adjustment difficulties for a small proportion of the richest countries, but both the developing countries and the majority of the industrialised countries would be in a state of stupor, while the former would be in the form of higher earnings, while the former would be in terms of low prices and new consumer goods. Furthermore, the prosperity of developing countries creates new markets for the products in which the rich industrialised countries specialise - for example, ksnnyks! A key issue for developing countries would also be the export production of subsidies from the industrialised countries. Nsms subsidies keep the world market prices of many products artificially low and are, on the whole, undeniably damaging, the only ones that in the industrialized countries rely on subsidies in the industries. Given the background, it is strange that the WTO's action is opposed by precisely those groups of people who feel that they are on the side of the developing countries. Finally Good political science students, celebrating jug-sledgehammers. Of course, when I was thinking about the speech at first, I had a topic related to monetary policy and EMU, which I am naturally more familiar with. However, globalisation is such an attractive subject that I deliberately wanted to identify a little with my youth and studies and boldly set out to "own the future". I cannot really say whether my speech would have been as you have heard without my experience of the operation of the financial markets, or of the activities or activities of international organisations, or of my observations of politics. In any case, I want you to have your thoughts as a target for the jug-pouring. At the same time I want to myshs reveal to you, why in the past I switched to political science and economics d after all, I am originally a mathematician and a statistician. The reason was precisely my interest in society, in the analysis of power and power. Of course, I did not think of becoming the "leader of the people", in accordance with klinge and Kolbe's observation of the Finnish student world that I quoted at the beginning - I am not, but I had some hopes of becoming the "owner of the future" and making a small contribution to the way the world goes. I am happy to acknowledge that the Faculty of Political Science was an excellent choice for me.

Yksi kyyninen selitys, toivottavasti eptosi, voisi olla, ett kritiikki onkin pohjimmiltaan tekopyh: taustalla olisi vain rikkaissa yhteiskunnissa syntynyt muutosvastarinta sit uutta tilannetta kohtaan, jonka kehitysmaiden mukaantulo maailmantalouteen yh varteenotettavampina kilpailijoina aiheuttaa. Jos nin olisi, globalisaatiokritiikki olisi vain uusi, entist tekopyhempi muoto vaatimuksesta suojata teollisuusmaiden elinkeinoelm kilpailulta, pysytt maailmantalouden rakennemuutos ja nin tuomita kehitysmaat tulevaisuudessakin kyhyyteen ja riippuvuuteen rikkaiden maiden taloudellisesta avusta sen sijaan ett ne pystyisivt seisomaan omilla jaloillaan. Toinen helppo, esitetty kritiikki ylenkatsova selitys voisi olla, ett se perustuisi tietmttmyyteen kehitysmaiden tilanteesta: ikn kuin ei olisi huomattu, ett juuri globalisaatio ja vain se tarjoaa kehitysmaiden vestlle todellisen mahdollisuuden taloudellisesti parempaan tulevaisuuteen, tai ikn kuin ei olisi huomattu, ett kehitysmaissa globalisaatio uhkaa lhinn noiden maiden taloudellisia ja poliittisia eliittej, ja niitkin vain siin mrin kun ne thn saakka ovat voineet keinotekoisesti hyty protektionismista ja eristytymispolitiikasta. Globalisaation ensiksi tarjolla olevana vaihtoehtona ei ole luonnonmukainen idylli, vaan pyshtyminen, kyhyys ja vaihtoehdottomuus. En kuitenkaan tahdo uskoa, ett kritiikki on selitettviss vain itsekkyydell tai tietmttmyydell. Kyll keskustelun ja globalisaatiokritiikin taustalla on mys aitoa arvopohjaa. Kritiikkihn vetoaa sellaisiin ihanteisiin kuin kyhyyden vastustaminen, ympristn vaaliminen ja demokratia, joista ei voi olla eri mielt. Siin mieless se on positiivinen osoitus siit, kuinka vahva voima moraalisiin periaatteisiin nojaava kansalaismielipide voi olla. Valitettavasti kritiikki nytt kuitenkin yleens perustuvan hyvin pinnalliseen nkemykseen globalisaation syist ja seurauksista. Erityisesti kritiikin saamat muodot osoittavat, ett se perustuu mys ilmeisesti tysin virheelliseen kuvaan siit, mitk ovat kansainvlisten talouspoliittisten jrjestjen kuten IMF:n ja WTO:n vaikuttimet, kun ne yrittvt kehitt globalisoituvan talouden vaatimia taloudellisia ja poliittisia rakenteita. Kritiikkiin liittyvi laittomuuksia ja muita lieveilmiit ei tietenkn voi hyvksy. Globalisaatiokritiikill on mielestni mynteinen merkitys jos ja kun se johtaa yh korkeampiin eettisiin vaatimuksiin siin, mit ostetaan, mit tuotetaan ja miten tuotetaan. Pit huomata, ett maailmanlaajuisen kansalaismielipiteen valvova vaikutus monikansallisten yritysten toimintaan on juuri "maailmankyllle" ominainen poliittinen ilmi. Kritiikill on mys mynteinen merkitys, kun se saa kansainvliset jrjestt toimimaan avoimemmin ja osoittamaan, miten niiden tavoitteet ja strategia liittyvt yleisesti hyvksyttyihin arvoihin. Se osuu kuitenkin mielestni kokonaan harhaan, jos se tahtoo rajoittaa maailman avautumista ja globalisoitumista. Globalisaatio on paitsi peruuttamatonta, mys perimmltn valtava positiivinen voima. Ongelmat ovat suurimpia juuri niill ihmisill ja yhteisill, jotka eivt pse osallisiksi globalisaatiosta ja sen tarjoamista mahdollisuuksista. Globalisaation haasteet kansainvliselle yhteislle Globalisaatiopolitiikka ei siksi minusta voi lhte kysymyksest, onko globalisaatio hyv vai pahaa, vaan on kysyttv, mit yhteisi haasteita se kansainvliselle yhteislle aiheuttaa ja miten nihin haasteisiin on vastattava. Tss suhteessa olen taipuvainen ajattelemaan asioita reaalipolitiikan kannalta. On muistettava, ett sen hallitusten vlisille sopimuksille perustuvan kehityksen vaihtoehtona, jota kansainvliset jrjestt  IMF, WB, WEO .rakentavat, ei suinkaan ole jonkun ideaalisen, valistuneen itsevaltiaan johtama harmonia, vaan maailman taloudellinen ja poliittinen pirstoutuminen keskenn kilpaileviin kauppablokkeihin. Tst seuraisi taloudellisen kehityksen hidastuminen ja kaupan muuttuminen viel ilmeisemmin maailmantalouden vahvojen osapuolten harjoittaman valtapolitiikan instrumentiksi. Trkeint on siksi, ett niden jrjestjen (IMF, WB, WTO) ty etenee, ja se on mahdollista vain, jos kaikki merkittvt valtiot kokevat kannaltaan mielekkksi osallistua thn tyhn ja toteuttaa aikaansaadut sopimukset. Tm nkkohta asettaa tietysti omat rajansa sille, miten ptksi voidaan tehd. Tll hetkell eri kansainvlisiss jrjestiss, varsinkin Kansainvlisess Valuuttarahastossa ponnistellaan ns. uuden kansainvlisen rahoitusarkkitehtuurin luomiseksi, jotta voitaisiin turvata kansainvlisten rahoitusmarkkinoiden entist vakaampi toiminta, ja siten list pomamarkkinoista riippuvaisten (eli luottoa tai sijoituksia tarvitsevien) maiden aseman turvallisuutta. Kysymyksess on mittasuhteiltaan valtava, pitkn ajan vaativa ohjelma, joka koostuu monista eri osa-alueista. Siin puututaan moniin keskeisimpiin ongelmavyyhteihin: talouspolitiikan lpinkyvyytt ja taloustiedon saatavuutta kehitetn; luodaan kansainvlisi laatustandardeja rahoitusmarkkinoiden valvonnalle ja perusrakenteelle; ja pyritn lismn sijoittajien vastuuta ja koordinaatiomahdollisuuksia ongelmatilanteiden varalta. Valuuttarahastolla on keskeinen rooli niden uudistusten kehittelyss ja mys kytnnn toteuttamisen koordinoinnissa ja valvonnassa. Rahoitusmarkkinoiden parempi toiminta ei kuitenkaan yksin riit aikaansaamaan tuotantoresurssien siirtymist rikkaista maista kyhempiin maihin. Lisksi tarvitaan mys kauppavirtojen vapauden turvaamista ja laajentamista. Jotta kyhimmt maat voisivat paremmin pst osallisiksi niist hydyist, joita maailmantalouden nopea yhdentyminen tuo, rikkaimpien maiden pitisi avata rohkeasti markkinoitaan niden maiden tuotteille. Tst aiheutuisi sopeutumisvaikeuksia pienelle osalle rikkaimpien maiden vest, mutta sek kehitysmaat ett teollisuusmaiden vestn valtaosa hytyisivt, edelliset parempien ansioiden, jlkimmiset taas edullisten hintojen ja uusien kulutustavaroiden muodossa. Lisksi kehitysmaiden vaurastuminen luo uusia markkinoita niille tuotteille, joihin rikkaat teollisuusmaat ovat erikoistuneet -esimerkiksi knnykille! Kehitysmaiden kannalta keskeinen asia olisi mys subventioiden vhentminen teollisuusmaiden vientituotannossa. Nm subventiot pitvt monien tuotteiden maailmanmarkkinahintoja keinotekoisen matalina ja ovat kokonaisuutena ottaen kiistatta vahingollisia, ainoina hytyjin ne, jotka teollisuusmaissa tyskentelevt tukipalkkioiden varassa pyrivill toimialoilla. Nit taustoja ajatellen on outoa, ett WTO:n toimintaa vastaan hykkvt juuri ne ihmisryhmt, jotka kokevat olevansa kehitysmaiden asialla. Lopuksi Hyvt valtiotieteen ylioppilaat, juhlivat kannunvalajat. Alun perin puhetta miettiessni minulla oli tietenkin mielessni lhemmin rahapolitiikkaan ja EMUun liittyv aihe, jonka luonnollisesti tunnen paremmin omakseni. Globalisaatio on kuitenkin niin houkutteleva aihe, ett halusin tahallani hieman samaistua nuoruus-ja opiskeluaikoihini ja ryhty rohkeasti "omimaan tulevaisuutta". En oikein osaa sanoa olisiko puheeni ollut kuulemanne kaltainen ilman sit kokemusta, joka minulla on rahoitusmarkkinoiden toiminnasta, tai kansainvlisten jrjestjen toiminnasta tai toiminnasta eriss kansalaisliikkeiss, tai ylipns havainnoistani politiikasta. Joka tapauksessa haluan jtt nm ajatukset teille kannunvalannan kohteeksi. Samalla haluan mys paljastaa teille, miksi aikanaan vaihdoin valtiotieteelliseen ja siell kansantaloustieteeseen  olenhan alun perin matemaatikko ja tilastotieteilij. Syyn oli nimenomaan kiinnostukseni yhteiskunnasta, vallan ja vallankytn analyysist. En luonnollisestikaan ajatellut tulevani "kansan johtajaksi" alussa siteeraamani Klingen ja Kolben suomalaista ylioppilasmaailmaa koskevan havainnon mukaisesti -enk sit olekaan, mutta kyll minulla hieman oli toiveita tulla "tulevaisuuden omistajaksi" ja vaikuttaa pienelt osaltani maailmanmenoon. Title: Speech at the Days of Social and Health Security
text: Speech by Bank Director Sinikka Salo on social and health security . Speech . Friday 17 August 2001,12:00AM Suomi2015 (lyhennelm?) There is often a conflict between economic efficiency and social security. However, it would be in the interests of social debate if, instead of focusing on the confrontation between the most important aspects of the situation, we concentrated on a debate on how effective production and social security can best support each other. In fact, the challenges facing Finnish society over the past 10-20 years specifically required economic policy and social security as a single whole. It is well known that the economy functions most effectively when social security and services are in order, while poorly functioning social and health services certainly hinder the development of the entire national economy. However, social security is also an intrinsic value, and that is why it is not "repayable by itself". The development of the national economy is therefore one of the key factors in considering the future of the social sector. I would say that economic development is one of the three fundamental forces that will determine the framework for action in the social sector in the current period. The second force is the development of v?est?, and the third is the internationalisation of Finland, both at the European level and globally. Finland's v?est? is growing rapidly. So R?j?ht??k? in Finland is an el?ke bomb? I do not think so. The decisive factors are the changes in the employment sector, the development of employment and the growth of the economy, as well as the return on the funds. The situation, as it is, could be summed up by saying that the el?ke bomb is enough to tick, but its magnitude is somewhere between m??r's ep?varma and it can also be dismantled by the joint efforts of economic and social policy. It is sometimes suggested that for the large classes, it would solve Finland's problem of employment, as jobs would be freed up for younger people. Unfortunately, it is not a simple matter. If and when a growing bill of income has to be paid for by taxing the work, the fact that the large classes will be taxed will almost mean an increase in taxation. If weakly k?y, the ?m? can destroy those places of work that from the great age classes were "liberating". The solution to this question cannot be dealt with lightly by simply increasing social security contributions. The employment effects and, through that, other negative social effects would be too bad. In part, it is possible to solve the problem of the cost of living expenses by increasing the participation of those who are involved in the work. Indeed, the government has set itself the goal of raising the average level of the population by 2-3 years. Another objective is to increase the employment rate, at least to 70%, which would increase the number of "payers" in society and the level of expenditure incurred by employment and stature. Estimates of the el?ke bomb, like other calculations on the financing of social security, are related to estimates of the future carrying capacity of the economy Economic growth is for the future of the welfare society a significant point, but social policy cannot be lulled into economic growth alone. Growth has not, until then, eliminated social problems in Finland, and the mere increase in the production of goods will not do so in the future either. Although economic growth basically brings so-called additional distribution to the national economy, it does not, however, provide an automatic solution to the question of the financing of the welfare state. The problem is the so-called 'Baumol disease', which is due to the fact that technological progress has not traditionally increased the productivity of public services as is the case in industry. If economic growth is unilaterally based on improvements in industrial productivity, the tax base and tax revenues will increase sufficiently, but at the same rate the cost of production of public services will also rise, since long-term wages will follow the growth of productivity in the private sector. As a result, despite economic growth, the production of public services will be stagnating unless taxation is constantly increased. The political symptoms of Baumol's disease are the growing dissatisfaction with the fact that the m??r? and quality of public services, without a constant increase in taxation, do not keep pace with the general development of living standards, and the pressure to solve the ?m? dilemma at administrative costs, either to increase the pace of public service provision or to constantly increase the pace of public sector salaries, and then to pay for the public sector all the time after the private sector pays. N?m??ks can do the trick momentarily, but it is clear that neither means offers a workable solution for the long term, at least not one that is compatible with the provision of high-quality services. Are there any symptoms of Baumol's disease in Finland? And if so, can the disease be cured? The option of ever-tightening taxation to finance health and other social services seems to us to be at least exhausted. In any case, the expected upward pressure on el?ke payments is unlikely to make room for an increase in other taxes. The improvement of employment, which is absolutely thrke? and economic reasons for the development of social cohesion, requires, rather, an overall tax burden, not a tightening of the tax burden. On the other hand, in Finland, the production costs of at least the health care sector and possibly other welfare services have fallen sharply in recent years. Finland's development in relation to the situation is exceptional, both historically and internationally. It appears that we have been stopping the progression of Baumol's disease for several years and shows that this disease is not a law of nature, but at least sometimes a disease. Certainly some of the increase in productivity has been achieved by means that have now been exhausted, but hopefully there will also be the impact of product development and technology, i.e. a development that can continue for a long time. Baumol's disease can be called milder if the growth of the national economy can be put on a broader footing than just dependent on an increase in industrial productivity. Economic growth based on improved employment will bring resources to the economy and also to the public sector without the baumol disease being eradicated. It stresses the importance of increasing the employment rate. Another way is to reform the production of public services so as to reduce the gap between the productivity development of public services and private goods production. In the case of Miss??n, I am not offering as a solution the solution to the increase in the pace of employment, but I am referring to the innovation-based increase in productivity, the constant hushing of new technologies and product development in the production of welfare services. One way of encouraging service providers is to encourage a wider use of private outsourced services and also to encourage competition from municipal service organisations. Within the framework of the EU's economic policy coordination, Finland has also been urged to address the issue of ???. The ?h?nastic nature of the EU's social policy coordination has been an effective solution, for example, because the mobility of the eu's social policy has been a so-called 'green light'. "social tourism" in eu countries has not been a real problem.. However, the situation may change in the future, for example as a result of enlargement, and pressure may well arise to improve the coordination of social policies. However, experience shows that the EU, especially on the social side, is very slow in moving, and any changes are likely to be far behind. Global integration is likely to be a stronger social factor than the EU's action, including social policy for the future. I cannot go into more detail on the matter now, but I would say that the threat of global tax competition is long overstated. People want social security and are prepared to pay for it if it is effectively managed. However, competition will certainly become a problem in cases where the social security system is very inefficient, i.e. unable to produce a result commensurate with its costs in terms of the welfare of the employees and the quality of the location of the enterprises. For example, large-scale long-termism, with its associated problems of fragility, will certainly make it more difficult for social security systems to be able to operate in a globalised world. In this sense, globalisation affects the social security sector in the same way as it does in the private sector: it rewards efficient and innovative organisations, but it can cause a crisis in poorly managed organisations. According to my opinion, the successes of Finnish society over the decades can be measured for a very long time, as how its social sector copes with the challenges ahead. But the success of the social sector depends on how the economic basis of the welfare state can be safeguarded and further strengthened. However, economic growth and reliance on the pull of "economic engines" such as the export industry are not enough, but rather a challenge for innovation and continuous guerrilla renewal for welfare service organisations. As an economist, I have stressed the importance of being an economist. But a high level of employment is actually much more fundamental to the objective of denying economic people, which is to achieve this. From the ty?market to the sidelines, there is an additional risk that people will get upset anyway. This, in turn, increases the likelihood of social and health problems. In addition to social policy measures, there is a need to promote tax and labour market policies, which are crucial to securing the future of the 'Finnish model' of social security. If we succeed in keeping people healthy and able to last longer, improve the profitability and stint of work, and open up the welfare services sector to new innovations and the introduction of new technologies, the Finnish welfare society, as a renewed and reformed company, will also be able to prosper in the coming decades. Title: Speech at the Employees' Euro Night
text: Bank Manager Sinikka Salo's speech at the Euro evening for wage earners . Speech . Wednesday17 October 2001,12:00AM The euro and the Finnish economy I would like to thank you for giving me the opportunity to discuss with you the euro and the importance of monetary union for the Finnish economy. There is an extraordinary amount of interest in this matter right now, which is, of course, due to the changeover of banknotes at the turn of the year, the so-called euro conversion. The euro will also become part of every citizen's daily life, from the pay slip to the cashier of the milk shop, and the change is very much in the mood. As an economist, however, I believe that the impact of the change that exists is smaller than what happened in Finland a few years ago, when Finland actually joined the European Economic and Monetary Union. After all, we have been in the middle of monetary union for almost three years, and Finland's monetary policy was harmonized to meet the requirements of monetary union for some time before. So when I think about the effects of monetary union on the Finnish economy, I think first and foremost of how monetary policy has changed, how the Finnish financial markets have integrated with the rest of Europe and how companies are currently operating in a market of 300 million people. The issue of common euro banknotes is, of course, a significant matter, both in terms of symbolic value and as a technical operation, but it is after all only the tip of the mountain in all respects, which is what monetary union means for the economy. Finland has thus been a member of the European Economic and Monetary Union for almost three years. This is such a long time that the picture of the effects of EMU - its hysdyism and the adaptation needs it entails - begins in Finland as well. One obvious and important influence on joining the monetary union was, of course, the elimination of exchange rate fluctuations vis-a-vis the other euro countries. Since 1999, the monetary units of the Finnish markka and the other euro countries have not really been exchange rates, but fixed conversion rates, which will also be used at the turn of next year when the euro definitively replaces the national monetary units. The stabilisation of exchange rates and the single monetary unit will link the Finnish economy more closely to the euro area market as a whole and to the foreign competition faced by companies. At the same time, they benefit the consumer and improve the internationalisation of enterprises, especially small enterprises. As about a third of Finland's exports go to the euro area, the effects of the elimination of foreign exchange rates are not quite as great as in many continental European countries, whose exports are still more clearly directed towards the euro area. Another effect of monetary union has been the convergence of interest rates. Interest rates applied in Finland are currently charged on the euro area-wide money market with a uniform level of interest rates. The Interest Rate is controlled by the European Central Bank through its monetary policy, which it implements in conjunction with the national central banks, such as the Bank of Finland. The convergence of money market interest rates has not led to a uniform convergence of bank borrowing rates or deposit rates in the euro area, but interest rates have rather widened and I believe that the development of the banking market will increase competition and harmonise bank interest rates in the current context. Interest rates have been lower in recent years than they have been for a long time, and in fact it is far into the history of the gold standard until the years before we meet the same low interest rates that we have enjoyed in recent years. The difference with recent decades is particularly clear: in the past, Finland struggled with the persistent problem of inflation and, therefore, with higher interest rates than other European countries. The problems of monetary union have now eased. The integration of exchange rates and interest rates has very rapidly changed the structure and functioning of the financial markets. Investment and securities markets, in particular, have become national to pan-European. This has already been of great importance to large borrowers and investors. For example, Finnish tyselske funds have diversified their portfolio investments on a very large scale to the European market. The banking world is now increasingly prepared for the fact that the competition for private investors and borrowers will also become more international. The use of the Internet and the expected reduction in the cost of credit transfers in the euro area will have an impact on the direction of the euro area. When finland was considering joining the monetary union, there was a lot of discussion about what monetary union means for national economic policy. The question was, is it an invaluable instrument of economic policy when one's own interest rate policy cannot react to Finland's particular cyclical problems? And how great are the risks when the opportunity to compensate for the loss of competitiveness caused by excessive wage increases, for example, by devaluing and removing it? And can the end of national monetary policy be compensated for by other means? These questions can hardly be answered with certainty, even in the member states. However, it is clear that the need for a national cyclical policy depends at least on whether finland's cyclical phase differs from the rest of Europe: if the economic cycles of the Finnish economy vary at the same rate as in the other euro countries, then the single monetary policy can be expected to be better suited to Finland's needs. If you look at recent developments, you will see that cyclical fluctuations have in fact been significantly synchronised with the rest of the euro area, although they have been relatively steeper than in the middle of monetary union. As for the risks of competitiveness and the need for devaluation, it must be remembered that the possibility of devaluation was always a double sword. While exchange rate flexibility made it possible to restore lost competitiveness by a simple means of economic policy, the mere existence of such a means of avoiding inflationary expectations and the temptation to raise difficult economic policy problems by resorting to inflation-accelerating solutions. Leaving exchange rate policy out of the toolbox of Finnish economic policy for good is therefore not only a challenge, but also an opportunity. If our economy's previous sensitivity to inflation was due to the weak credibility of monetary policy, now the problem should not exist. The existence of monetary union has put an end to devaluation speculation and creates the confidence needed to ensure that economic policy solutions are compatible with stable monetary stability. Wage and price developments in recent years are relatively encouraging. Fortunately, although finland's national economy has grown rapidly, inflation has risen well above the general level of the euro area. It is to be hoped that this will be a sign of the stabilising effect of monetary union on inflation expectations and wage formation. However, as expected, the greatest effects of monetary union have been political and psychological. We have all been able to see how Finland's weight in European economic policy has grown, and we have, in a way, moved to the 'guerrilla ring'. This has, of course, had not only political but also economic consequences. Phosss come with psychology and confidence in the picture. When, in the past, a well-known Spanish banker was asked why he was in favour of his country joining the monetary union, he replied that the Spaniards had argued that they had not considered their money to be an 'exotic currency'. I am sure that our mark has, like peseta, from time to time been deprived of its exoticism. Exoticism, or bad notoriety, was paid for in the past as a considerable amount of stability, as trust in the markka ranged from unduly good to unduly bad. The result was not only fluctuations in interest rates, but also unnecessary difficulties for the foreign operations of small and medium-sized enterprises. What about the future? How does it affect the functioning of the euro-parliament? As reported, the finnish economy has changed more and faster in a few months than in the long run. This is due to a very favourable development over several years. The achievements of the Finnish national economy between 1994 and 2000 are truly remarkable. The total output of the national economy grew for seven years at an annual rate of about five per cent, i.e. almost one and a half times during that period. Compared to the rest of the euro area, the Finnish economy grew at roughly twice the rate. At the same time, some 300,000 new jobs were created and central government finances were balanced. Last year, central government finances were oversized for the first time in a decade. On the business side, a significant development feature was the significant improvement in the solvency of enterprises, which was common in Finland in the 1980s, not to mention the economic crisis of the early 90s. The period of rapid growth is now over, and economic growth in Finland has stopped in recent springs and summers, and has even become negative. This is mainly due to the contraction in output in the INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY sector, which started in the United States last year and has since spread to other parts of the world and other industries. The certainty of future development has grown all over the world. A very rapid recovery of the economic cycle was expected in the United States, but this has so far been disappointing. In recent weeks, economic security has been further fuelled by the terrorist attacks in the United States and their military consequences in Central Asia. World political events clearly had a negative impact on consumer and investor confidence. It seems that the common factor in this has postponed the recovery of the international economy further into the future. Forecasting agencies in Finland have been rapidly lowering their estimates of economic growth in Finland and next year. The Bank of Finland updated its own cyclical forecast at the beginning of September, just before the terrorist attacks took place in America. At that time, we predicted growth of 1 1/2% for the year, and we estimated that next year economic growth would recover to around 2 1/2%. The figures are quite modest compared to what we have become accustomed to in recent years. The change in the forecasts for Finland was due in particular to the poor export performance in the early part of the year, which is now reflected in production, income and employment, but also in the consumption and investment opportunities of companies and households. In September, we also predicted that the employment rate would rise next year. It is precisely the case that it rises somewhat above ten per cent. The change in forecasts in the direction of the Czech Republic has given rise to a number of questions. Finns have a very traumatic experience in their memory of the recession of the early 1990s. Now that economic growth has stalled, many are wondering whether the economic situation is similar to the situation of a decade ago. Is it possible that we will end up in a crisis similar to the one we had then? The current situation is sufficiently reminiscent of the situation in 1991, in that it is a period of rapid growth that has come to an end. Now, as then, changes in the international economy have halted the growth of Finnish exports. As then, the international environment is now a special factor that is particularly acute in finland. Ten years ago, the special factor was the collapse of the Soviet Union and the end of trade with it, which affected us more than other countries. One of the most important factors is that the recession began in the telecommunications and information technology sectors, which are of particular importance in Finland - after all, the growth of the Finnish economy at the end of the 1990s accounted for a fairly large part of the growth of the electronics industry. shsn similarities then almost pssttyvstkin. However, despite the totality I have mentioned, the current economic situation is radically different from that of ten years ago. At that time, Finland's national economy had reached an impasse due to foreign and domestic indebtedness. Consumption and investment depended on borrowing, and when the limits were reached in relation to the balance, the government was steep. Now the situation is quite different. Take foreign indebtedness, for example: whereas before the last recession, in 1990, Finland's current account deficit was 30 billion marks, we have now had an annual surplus of about FIM 60 billion. This huge figure means that the national economy as a whole has not now exceeded its means, but that Finnish companies and households have had much more income than expenditure in recent years. sms gives the national economy a solid buffer against worse times. In terms of domestic indebtedness, the situation is also much better now than it was in the early 1990s. At that time, the debt of companies and households to banks rose to an all-time high, relative to their income. The ratio of corporate and household debt to income is now about a third lower, so they are clearly vulnerable than they were then. And if you look at the situation of the banks, their solvency is now significantly better than it was in the early 1990s. However, the significant difference between the current situation and that of ten years ago is how the money market now works, and the change that has taken place is largely related to Finland's EMU membership. Ten years ago, the contraction of exports, the difficulty of borrowing abroad and the weakening of banks' solvency led to exchange rate speculation against the Finnish markka and a sharp rise in interest rates. The rise in interest rates hit the then heavily indebted national economy particularly hard. The result was financial difficulties, bankruptcies and bad debts. The reaction of the financial markets to the reversal of the economic cycle has been almost counterproductive. Inflationary pressures have eased and interest rates may have been lowered. The fall in interest rates has been particularly strong in the United States, but even in Europe the ECB has been able to lower its key interest rates. Most recently, exactly one month ago, interest rates were reduced by half a percentage. From the point of view of our own economic situation, this has been very appropriate. The three corona reductions carried out in this year have clearly had an impact on, among other things: Euribor rates and banks' own prime rates, to which Finnish loans are linked. Thus, the euro area and, with it, the Finnish financial markets have clearly eased in the economic cycle, which contributes to supporting economic activity. Ten years ago, the financial markets, in a similar phase of the economic cycle, were on the other hand tightening more sharply until 1993, more than two years after the start of the crisis. This comparison illustrates the extent to which Finland is in a state of certainty as a member of the monetary union. The fact that we are part of a European currency area means that Finland's exceptionally high dependence on the telecommunications sector, which is now experiencing setbacks, has not been passed on through exchange rate fluctuations or interest rate reactions as a stability for the rest of the economy. EMU has therefore been a stabilising factor in the current situation. The ECB's assertiveness and the confidence it enjoys in monetary policy have kept inflation expectations in the euro area under control and allowed for a gradual relaxation of monetary policy. I do not want to see the significance of the economic changes that have taken place, but monetary union will make it easy for economic policy or any other kind of economy. In municipal finances, for example, adjusting to tax revenues can be very difficult. It is clear that monetary union cannot solve economic problems that have non-monetary roots. But on the other hand, in the stable environment created by monetary union, the basic elements of the economy - such as productivity, competitiveness, solvency of enterprises and innovativeness - are the most effective. As the basics of finland's economy are in better shape today than they have been for decades, the prerequisites for a revival of economic growth are good for us, despite the setbacks of recent months. In this context, it is appropriate to say a few words about how monetary policy in the euro area is currently conducted. Both monetary policy tasks and its institutions, i.e. those which conduct monetary policy for european citizens, were laid down in the Maastricht Treaty, which was signed in 1992. The principles chosen for the system were the central bank system, formed of the national central banks and jointly of the European Central Bank, in which the decision-making is centralised, but in which banking transactions, including the implementation of monetary policy, take place at the national central banks of the Country. The national central banks of the euro area and the European Central Bank, which are jointly responsible for monetary policy in the region, are referred to as the Euro-System. The National Central Banks (NCBs) own the European Central Bank and play a decisive role in its decision-making. The highest body of the ECB is the Governing Council, which comprises the presidents of all the central banks participating in monetary union. From Finland, the Council thus includes Matti Vanhala, Director of the Bank of Finland. In addition to the presidents of the national central banks, the governing council is also composed of six members of the Executive Board of the ECB. The Executive Board of the ECB is the operational steering body, which is permanently based in Frankfurt and prepares the meetings of the Governing Council and is responsible for the implementation of these decisions. The Executive Board of the ECB is supported by a total of thirteen committees composed of representatives from both all the NATIONAL CENTRAL BANKS and the ECB. The committees each specialise in their own area of central banking. So we have the Monetary Policy Committee, the Market Operations Committee, the Payments System Committee and so on. The importance of the committee institution is that cooperation with the Eurojs system is not limited to formal decision-making and its implementation according to common guidelines. Thanks to the committees, the implementation of monetary policy and the preparation of various development projects are now carried out in close cooperation across the entire system. A large number of different working groups and task forces are also operating under the auspices of the committees. Civil servants in central banks - such as the Bank of Finland - are of a very international nature today, due to committee work, among other things. In order to safeguard the political independence of monetary policy, the Maastricht Treaty stipulated that both the national central banks and the ECB must be financially independent and, in the performance of their decisions, themselves. The persons elected to the executive boards of the central banks shall be inseparable during their term of office and may not, for monetary matters, receive the office from outside the Public Sphere, even from national governments or parliaments. In the decision-making of the Governing Council of the ECB, all members of the Council have one ssni. Thus, when Mr Vanhala attends meetings of the Governing Council of the ECB, where monetary policy is discussed, he has as much power as everyone else in the Council - for example, Ernst Weltekell of the German Bundesbank or Jean-Claude Trichet of France. Only the ECB's own finances, such as its distribution of profits, are proportional to the size of each Member State. The 'one member state, one ssni' principle is based on the fundamental convergence of the monetary policy interests of the Member States. If it weren't for the nsin, the whole system would naturally be impossible, and it wouldn't have been built in the first place. It is worth emphasising this point. The ECB's monetary policy objective is to pursue price stability throughout the euro area. 'The euro area as a whole' implies that the policy is not tailored to the needs of any individual country or group of countries. This was not a contradiction for a single Member State: even if we Finns were to decide on the monetary policy of the euro area alone, we would not be able to take only finland's cyclical situation as a point of monetary policy for the whole of monetary policy in the monetary union, even if our own situation were different from the others. It is in the interest of each Member State and of Finland that the euro area economy as a whole remains in balance. In the context of the single currency, we are all in the same boat, equally dependent on the stability of the price level of the euro area, that is, the value of the euro, and, above all, on the confidence it enjoys. As a result, the monetary policy interests of the countries that have joined the euro area are converging in the long term, and this is the starting point for decision-making in the Governing Council. How has the emergence of monetary union affected the operations of the Bank of Finland in Finland? The main changes have taken place in the bank's institutional position, not in its operations. The central bank, which managed its own money and acted under the guidance of the Parliamentary Banking Council, has become a part of the Monetary Union itself, active in the preparation of European monetary policy and representing Finland in the Eurojs system. The bank's second role is to represent the Eurojs system in Finland. This is partly operational: the Bank of Finland must be involved in the operational implementation of monetary policy, which is decentralised to the various national central banks. The payment transactions of commercial banks, the deposit of their reserves, money market operations that control interest rates, the issue of banknotes and coins, the investment of national foreign exchange reserves - almost all central bank transactions are carried out by the national central banks and in Finland the work is carried out by the Bank of Finland. But the representation of the Eurojs system in Finland also implies an obligation to communicate and market, together with the collection of points from the Finnish economic debate and, on the other hand, from the presentation of the demands made by European monetary policy on the Finnish economy and economic policy. By virtue of its position, the Bank of Finland is obliged to analyse the issues and the unique possibility of analysing the economic development of Finland from the perspective of European monetary policy and the effects of European monetary policy on the perspective of the Finnish economy. That's what we do. What is monetary policy aiming for? How will it react to future news and changes in the economy? In order to answer these questions, the Governing Council has defined a strategy for its monetary policy consisting of three elements: an operational assessment of price stability and two so-called pillars. The ECB Charter, which sets the bank's task of maintaining price stability in the euro area, does not specify what price stability means. The Governing Council of the ECB has therefore been forced to deal with it itself. It has been assumed that, in the context of price stability, the rate of increase in consumer prices should remain below two per cent over the medium term. Consumer prices are measured by means of the so-called Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices, which is calculated in the same way in all EU Member States. -In recent months, inflation rates in the euro area have exceeded the two per cent mark and have risen as high as three per cent. However, according to forecasts, inflation is now slowing down, so that the mssritels of price stability, which therefore speaks of "medium time", is unlikely to be broken. In addition to the definition of the objective, the strategy includes two pillars which describe how monetary policy is pursuing its objective. The first pillar is monetary. A reference value has been set for the growth rate of money, which is used when monetary developments are monitored. According to the reference value, annual monetary growth of around 4.5% can be expected to be consistent with price stability. As a measure of the amount of money, the M3 figure is used in particular, which includes, in addition to money, bank deposits and securities issued by banks to a very large extent. -The interpretation of the growth of money has recently been clearly hampered by investment movements in the euro area and other countries, as well as by the fact that, during falling share prices, the popularity of bank deposits in Europe has increased dramatically. The second pillar of the monetary policy strategy is a 'comprehensive assessment of future price developments and associated risks', which refers to the forward-looking analysis of the real economy. This draws attention, for example, to the relationship between demand and supply in the euro area hysdyke and labour markets, as well as to inflationary pressures from commodity prices such as the price of sljy. In the context of analyses under the second pillar, the important role is played by macroeconomic forecasts, or rather by the estimates that are drawn up on the basis of the Council's work. Estimates have now begun to be published on a semi-annual basis, which is hoped to clarify the rationale for monetary policy in terms of the money market and the wider general context. The two-pillar strategy of monetary policy is not of a mechanical nature. It is based on the idea that both the growth of money and the general inflation rate must be carefully interpreted and weighed in order to distinguish the transient hsirist from long-term changes, and so that the signal values of the various indicators can be correctly weighted. In addition to the technology of economists, it takes a lot of wisdom, a lot of wisdom, a sense of what is really happening in the economies of the euro area. That is why monetary policy-making and the latest interpretation of the situation take place in the Governing Council, which, through the presidents of the various national central banks, has a broad understanding of economic developments in the euro area as a whole. In the deliberations of the Council, the contribution of the national central banks is significant. In the economic press, monetary policy in the euro area is often commented on in relation to exchange rate developments ,in particular, the dollar value of the euro is of interest. It is natural enough to have exchange rates fluctuating, but the significance of the exchange rate is also exaggerated. The ECB has not set a target level for the exchange rate, and the monetary policy objectives have been determined solely in terms of price stability. Thus, the stability of the purchasing power of the euro is the stability of the euro in the internal part of the euro area, not the stability of exchange rates, nor the evolution of exchange rates dictates monetary policy. Of course, the exchange rate plays a role in inflation, as the depreciation of the euro in the foreign exchange markets may lead to higher import prices and inflationary pressures in the euro area. The exchange rate is linked to the monetary policy strategy only through this, i.e. as part of a broad assessment of inflationary pressures in the 'second pillar' I mentioned. From the very beginning of monetary union, the exchange rate of the euro attracted a great deal of attention because the value of the euro against the dollar fell almost continuously from the beginning of 1999 to the autumn of 2000. Since then, the euro has fluctuated somewhat, but it has not been deteriorating in trend. At the same time, the debate on the exchange rate has been diluted. The shape of the ECB's monetary policy and the functioning of its strategy can be followed by anyone interested. Once a month, following a meeting of the Governing Council of the ECB, a press release on monetary policy is issued and a press conference is held in which Wim Duisenberg, the President of the ECB, answers questions from the press. A press release and a summary of the discussion at the press conference will be posted on the Bank of Finland's internet site for general use immediately in the press conference and in the Finnish language. When you read the press release, you will immediately see that it is organised by means of strategic pillars: first, comments are made on the growth of money and bank credit under the pillar, and then you move on to the second pillar, such as cost pressures and the demand situation. The same structure is also given to the monetary policy reviews which the ECB publishes in its monthly bulletin.
