Tm vertailu osoittaa havainnollisesti, miten tllaisissa epvarmoissa oloissa Suomelle on hyty rahaliiton jsenyydest. Se, ett olemme osa eurooppalaista valuutta-aluetta merkitsee, ett Suomen poikkeuksellinen suuri riippuvuus nyt takaiskuja kokeneesta tietoliikennesektorista ei ole vlittynyt valuuttakurssivaihteluiden tai korkoreaktioiden kautta epvakautena muuhun talouteen. EMU on siis ollut nykyisess tilanteessa vakauttava tekij. EKP :n itsenisyys ja sen rahapolitiikan nauttima luottamus ovat pitneet inflaatio-odotukset euroalueella hallinnassa ja tehneet mahdolliseksi rahapolitiikan asteittaisen keventmisen. En tll halua vhtell tapahtuneiden taloudellisten muutosten merkityst enk vitt, ett rahaliitto tekisi talouspolitiikan tai muunkaan elmn helpoksi. Esimerkiksi kunnallistaloudessa sopeutuminen vheneviin verotuloihin voi olla hyvinkin vaikeaa. On selv, ett rahaliitto sinns ei voi ratkaista sellaisia taloudellisia ongelmia, joiden juuret ovat muualla kuin rahataloudessa. Mutta toisaalta rahaliiton luomassa vakaassa ympristss talouden perustekijt -sellaiset kuin tuottavuus, kilpailukyky, yritysten vakavaraisuus ja innovatiivisuus -psevt parhaiten vaikuttamaan. Kun Suomessa nm talouden perusasiat ovat nykyisin paremmassa kunnossa kuin vuosikymmeniin, edellytykset taloudellisen kasvun elpymiselle ovat viime kuukausien takaiskuista huolimatta meill hyvt. Ehk on paikallaan sanoa tss yhteydess muutama sana siit, miten rahapolitiikkaa euroalueella nykyisin hoidetaan. Sek rahapolitiikan tehtvist ett sen instituutioista, eli niist laitoksista, jotka rahapolitiikkaa Euroopan kansalaisia varten hoitavat, ptettiin Maastrichtin sopimuksessa, joka allekirjoitettiin vuonna 1992. Jrjestelmn pperiaatteiksi valittiin kansallisista keskuspankeista ja yhteisest Euroopan keskuspankista muodostettu keskuspankkijrjestelm, jossa ptksenteko on keskitetty, mutta kytnnn pankkitoimet, mukaan lukien rahapolitiikan toimeenpano, tapahtuvat posin kansallisissa keskuspankeissa. Euroalueen kansallisia keskuspankkeja ja Euroopan Keskuspankkia, jotka yhdess vastaavat alueen rahapolitiikasta kutsutaan Eurojrjestelmksi. Kansalliset keskuspankit omistavat Euroopan keskuspankin ja ovat ratkaisevasti mukana sen ptksenteossa. EKP:n korkein pttv elin on neuvosto, johon kuuluvat kaikkien rahaliitossa mukana olevien keskuspankkien pjohtajat. Suomesta neuvostoon kuuluu siis Suomen Pankin pjohtaja Matti Vanhala. Kansallisten keskuspankkien pjohtajien lisksi neuvostossa istuvat mys EKP:n johtokunnan jsenet, joita on kuusi. EKP:n johtokunta on vakituisesti Frankfurtissa tyskentelev operatiivinen johtoelin, joka valmistelee neuvoston kokoukset ja vastaa niiss tehtyjen ptsten toteuttamisesta. EKP:n johtokunnan tukena on kaikkiaan kolmetoista komiteaa, joissa on edustajat sek kaikista kansallisista keskuspankeista ett EKP:st. Nm komiteat ovat erikoistuneet kukin omaan keskuspankkitoiminnan osa.alueeseensa. Niinp meill on rahapolitiikan komitea, markkinaoperaatioiden komitea, maksujrjestelmkomitea ja niin edelleen. Komitealaitoksen merkitys on siin, ett yhteisty Eurojrjestelmss ei rajoitu muodolliseen ptksentekoon ja sen toimeenpanoon yhteisten suuntaviivojen mukaan. Komiteoiden ansiosta rahapolitiikan toteutus ja erilaisten kehityshankkeiden valmistelu tapahtuu nykyisin koko jrjestelmn laajuisena, tiiviin yhteistyn. Komiteoiden alaisuudessa toimii viel suuri joukko erilaisia tyryhmi ja task forceja. Virkamiesty keskuspankeissa -kuten Suomen Pankissa -on mm. komiteatyn vuoksi nykyn erittin kansainvlist luonteeltaan. Rahapolitiikan poliittisen riippumattomuuden turvaamiseksi Maastrichtin sopimuksessa sdettiin, ett sek kansallisten keskuspankkien ett EKP:n on oltava taloudellisesti riippumattomia ja ptksenteossaan itsenisi. Keskuspankkien johtokuntiin valittavat henkilt ovat virkakausiensa kestess kytnnss erottamattomia ja he eivt saa ottaa rahapoliittisissa asioissa vastaan mryksi miltn ulkopuolisilta tahoilta, edes kansallisilta hallituksilta tai parlamenteilta. EKP:n neuvoston ptksenteossa kaikilla jsenill on yksi ni. Kun pjohtaja Vanhala osallistuu EKP:n neuvoston kokouksiin, joissa rahapolitiikasta ptetn, hnell on siis siell yht paljon nivaltaa kuin kaikilla muillakin neuvoston jsenill -vaikkapa Saksan Bundesbankin Ernst Weltekell tai Ranskan Jean-Claude Trichet'll. Vain EKP:n omasta taloudesta kuten sen voitonjaosta ptettess nimrt ovat suhteessa kunkin jsenmaan kokoon. Tllainen yksi jsen, yksi ni -periaate perustuu jsenmaiden rahapoliittisten etujen perimmiseen yhtenevisyyteen. Ellei nin olisi, koko jrjestelm olisi luonnollisesti mahdoton eik sit olisi alun perin nin rakennettukaan. Tt seikkaa kannattaa korostaa. EKP: n rahapolitiikan tavoitteeksi on asetettu hintavakauden tavoittelu koko euroalueella. "Koko euroalueella" merkitsee, ett politiikkaa ei rtlid minkn yksittisen maan tai maaryhmn tarpeisiin. Tss ei oli yksittisen jsenmaan kannalta mitn ristiriitaa: vaikka me suomalaiset psisimme yksin pttmn euroalueen rahapolitiikasta, ei meidn siltikn kannattaisi ottaa vain Suomen suhdannetilannetta koko rahaliiton rahapolitiikan lhtkohdaksi, ei sittenkn, vaikka oma tilanteemme olisi muista poikkeavakin. Jokaisen jsenmaan ja nin mys Suomen etu on, ett euroalueen talous kokonaisuutena pysyy tasapainossa. Yhteisen rahan oloissa olemme kaikki samassa veneess, samalla lailla riippuvaisia euroalueen hintatason eli euron arvon vakaudesta, ja etenkin sen nauttimasta luottamuksesta. Nin ollen euroalueeseen liittyneiden maiden rahapoliittiset edut ovat pitklti yhteneviset, ja tm on lhtkohtana ptksenteolle EKP:n neuvostossa. Miten rahaliiton syntyminen on vaikuttanut Suomessa Suomen Pankin toimintaan? Suurimmat muutokset ovat tapahtuneet pankin institutionaalisessa asemassa, eivt niinkn sen kytnnn toiminnassa. Omaa rahaa hallinnoineesta, Eduskunnan pankkivaltuuston ohjauksessa toimineesta keskuspankista rahaliiton myt tullut Eurojrjestelmn itseninen osa, joka toimii aktiivisesti vaikuttavana osapuolena Euroopan rahapolitiikan valmistelussa ja edustaa Suomea Eurojrjestelmss. Pankin toinen, yht trke rooli on edustaa Eurojrjestelm Suomessa. Tm on osittain operatiivista tyt: Suomen Pankin tulee osallistua rahapolitiikan operatiiviseen toteutukseen, joka eurojrjestelmss on hajautettu eri kansallisiin keskuspankkeihin. Liikepankkien vlinen maksuliikenne, niiden varantojen tallettaminen, korkoja ohjaavat rahamarkkinaoperaatiot, setelien ja kolikoiden liikkeeseen lasku, kansallisen valuuttavarannon sijoittaminen -melkein kaikki kytnnn keskuspankkitoimet toteutetaan kansallisten keskuspankkien toimesta ja Suomessa tmn tyn tekee Suomen Pankki. Mutta eurojrjestelmn edustaminen Suomessa merkitsee mys yhteydenpito-ja markkinointivelvoitetta, yhtlt nkkohtien kermist suomalaisesta talouskeskustelusta ja toisaalta arvioiden esittmist siit, millaisia vaatimuksia eurooppalainen rahapolitiikka Suomen taloudelle ja talouspolitiikalle asettaa. Suomen Pankilla on asemansa vuoksi velvollisuus analysoida nit kysymyksi ja mys ainoalaatuinen mahdollisuus nhd sek Suomen talouskehitys eurooppalaisen rahapolitiikan perspektiivist ett Euroopan rahapolitiikan vaikutukset Suomen kansantalouden perspektiivist. Tmn me nemme tehtvksemme. Ent mit rahapolitiikka tavoittelee? Miten se tulee reagoimaan tuleviin uutisiin ja talouden muutoksiin? Vastatakseen nihin kysymyksiin EKP:n neuvosto on mritellyt rahapolitiikalleen strategian, joka koostuu seuraavista kolmesta elementist: hintavakauden operationaalisesta mritelmst ja kahdesta niin sanotusta pilarista. EKP:n peruskirja, joka asettaa pankin tehtvksi hintavakauden yllpitmisen euroalueella, ei tarkemmin mrittele, mit hintojen vakaus tarkoittaa. EKP:n neuvosto on siksi joutunut itse mrittelemn tmn ksitteen. Mritelmksi on otettu, ett hintavakauden vallitessa kuluttajahintojen nousuvauhdin olisi pysyttv keskipitkll aikavlill alle kahden prosentin. Kuluttajahintoja mitataan niin sanotun yhdenmukaistetun kuluttajahintaindeksin avulla, joka lasketaan samalla tavalla kaikissa EU:n jsenmaissa. -Viime kuukausina inflaatiovauhti euroalueella on ylittnyt kahden prosentin rajan ja kynyt jopa kolmessa prosentissa. Ennusteiden mukaan inflaatio on nyt kuitenkin hidastumaan pin, joten hintavakauden mritelm, jossa siis puhutaan "keskipitkst aikavlist" tuskin tullaan rikkomaan. Strategiaan kuuluu tavoitteen mrittelyn lisksi kaksi pilaria, jotka kuvaavat, miten rahapolitiikka kytnnss pyrkii tavoitettaan toteuttamaan. Ensimminen pilari on rahataloudellinen. Rahan mrn kasvuvauhdille on asetettu viitearvo, jota kytetn, kun rahatalouden kehityst seurataan. Viitearvon mukaan rahan mrn noin 4,5 prosentin vuotuisen kasvun voidaan odottaa olevan sopusoinnussa hintavakauden kanssa. Rahan mrn mittarina kytetn erityist M3-lukua, johon lasketaan kteisen rahan lisksi hyvin laajasti pankkitalletuksia ja pankkien liikkeeseen laskemia arvopapereitakin. -Rahan mrn kasvun tulkintaa ovat viime aikoina selvsti vaikeuttaneet sijoitusten liikkeet euroalueen ja muiden maiden vlill sek se seikka, ett laskevien osakekurssien aikana pankkitalletusten suosio Euroopassa on kovasti kasvanut. Rahapolitiikan strategian toinen pilari on "tulevan hintakehityksen ja siihen liittyvien riskien laaja arviointi", mill viitataan reaalitaloudelliseen, eteenpin katsovaan analyysiin. Tss kiinnitetn huomiota esimerkiksi kysynnn ja tarjonnan vliseen suhteeseen euroalueen hydyke-ja tymarkkinoilla sek raaka-ainehinnoista kuten ljyn hinnasta tuleviin inflaatiopaineisiin. Toiseen pilariin kuuluvussa analyyseissa merkittv rooli on kokonaistaloudellisilla ennusteilla, tai paremminkin arvioilla, joita eurojrjestelmss laaditaan snnllisesti neuvoston tyn perustaksi. Nit arvioita on ryhdytty nyt snnllisesti -puolivuosittain -mys julkistamaan, mink toivotaan selventvn rahapolitiikan perusteita rahamarkkinoiden ja laajan yleisn kannalta. Rahapolitiikan kahden pilarin strategia ei ole luonteeltaan mekaaninen ptssnt. Se perustuu ajatukseen, ett sek rahan mrn kasvu ett yleiset inflaationkymt on huolellisesti tulkittava ja punnittava, jotta ohimenevt hirit voidaan erottaa pitkvaikutteisista muutoksista, ja jotta eri indikaattorien signaaliarvoja voidaan oikein painottaa. Tm vaatii ekonomistien tekniikan lisksi paljon viisautta, nkemyst ja tuntumaa siit, mit euroalueen talouksissa on todella tapahtumassa. Siksi rahapoliittinen ptksenteko ja tilanteen viime kden tulkinta tapahtuu EKP:n neuvostossa, jolla on eri kansallisten keskuspankkien pjohtajien kautta laaja tuntuma talouskehitykseen koko euroalueella. Tss neuvoston suorittamassa harkinnassa kansallisten keskuspankkien panos on merkittv. Talousalan lehdistss euroalueen rahapolitiikkaa kommentoidaan usein suhteessa valuuttakurssikehitykseen .varsinkin euron dollariarvo on kiinnostuksen kohteena. Tm on kyll luonnollista, koska valuuttakurssit heilahtelevat pivittin, mutta vlist valuuttakurssin merkityst mys liioitellaan. EKP:hn ei ole asettanut valuuttakurssille mitn tavoitetasoa, ja rahapolitiikan tavoitteet on mritelty yksinomaan hintavakauden kannalta. Thtimess on siis euron ostovoiman vakaus euroalueen sisll eik valuuttakurssien vakaus sinns, eik valuuttakurssikehitys mitenkn sanele rahapolitiikkaa. Valuuttakurssilla on tietenkin merkityst inflaation kannalta sit kautta, ett euron heikkeneminen valuuttamarkkinoilla voi aiheuttaa tuontihintojen nousua ja nin inflaatiopaineita euroalueella. Valuuttakurssi kytkeytyy rahapolitiikan strategiaan vain tt kautta, siis osana sken mainitsemaani "toiseen pilariin" sisltyv inflaatiopaineiden laajaa arviointia. Euron kurssi kiinnitti heti rahaliiton alkuaikoina runsaasti huomiota siksi, ett euron arvo suhteessa dollariin laski melkein yhtjaksoisesti vuoden 1999 alusta vuoden 2000 syksyyn. Sen jlkeen euron dollarikurssi on tosin vaihdellut jonkin verran, muttei en ole ollut trendimisesti heikkenev. Valuuttakurssista kyty keskustelu on samalla laimentunut. EKP:n rahapolitiikan muotoutumista ja sen strategian toimintaa kytnnss voi seurata kuka tahansa kiinnostunut henkil. Kerran kuussa EKP:n neuvoston kokouksen jlkeen annetaan lehdisttiedote rahapolitiikasta ja jrjestetn tiedostustilaisuus, jossa EKP:n pjohtaja Wim Duisenberg vastaa lehdistn kysymyksiin. Sek tiedote ett yhteenveto lehdisttilaisuudessa kydyst keskustelusta viedn Suomen Pankin internet-sivulle yleisn kyttn heti lehdisttilaisuuden ptytty -ja Suomen kielell. Tiedotetta lukiessa huomaa heti, ett se on organisoitu strategiapilarien avulla: ensiksi kommentoidaan ykkspilariin kuuluvia rahan mrn kasvua ja pankkiluottoja, ja sitten siirrytn toisen pilarin asioihin, kuten kustannuspaineisiin ja kysynttilanteeseen. Saman rakenteen lyt mys niist rahapoliittisista katsauksista, jotka EKP snnllisesti julkaisee kuukausikatsauksessaan.

Title: Speech at the National Housing Research Seminar
text: Bank Manager Sinikka Salo's speech at the national housing research seminar . Speech . Tuesday 20 November 2001,12:00AM On the functioning of the housing market in modern Finland At the outset, I would like to thank the Finnish Real Estate Association and the Real Estate Association of Southwest Finland for this opportunity to come and talk about the housing market, which, as you know, has been close to my heart  after all, I have also done my doctoral dissertation on the housing market. And although I haven't done any research on the housing market for years now, I've made some effort to follow it. Especially when I return to my home country  after almost six years in Central Europe and thus gaining personal experience of living in Germany , I would like to say that the single most important thing I would like to see corrected in Finland is still the housing market. I had been given the title "The Perspective of Finance on Housing". Since I do not believe that housing finance in the traditional sense is a problem area for housing policy in the current circumstances, I have taken the liberty in this speech to look at other issues relating to the housing market that I believe to be more important. Of course, I also deal with housing finance and financial matters. And even though we are in a research seminar, I have taken on a somewhat "provocative" role for myself? Our lowest housing level in the EU In this role, I will first present a few facts for background: Finland is still overcrowded  the average size of our apartments is the smallest of the EU countries. The most densely populated countries in Europe (Germany, the Netherlands; population density more than ten times that of Finland) are more sparsely and of higher quality. For example, in the Netherlands (the highest population density in the EU), 71% (!) of dwellings are single-family houses and the average size of dwellings is 98 m2. Germany and Denmark also have a high living space. In addition, rental apartments also make up a large part of the housing stock. In Finland, the average size of apartments is 76 m2, single-family houses make up 40.5% of apartments and rental apartments 30%. Housing is one of the most important factors in a household's well-being. The fact that we live too cramped and expensive and have a housing shortage, especially in growth centres and in the Helsinki metropolitan area, will keep the housing market in a "constant crisis". It is intolerable that it is not possible to acquire even a reasonable family home with a normal wage income, and that rental housing is not available either. In addition, the housing stock is of poor quality  small apartments in standardised prefabricated blocks of flats. Housing overcrowding in finland is the order of the day  especially in the Helsinki metropolitan area and in growth centres. According to studies, the majority want to live in detached houses, but the majority of new production is production in blocks of flats and too small. Household preferences are not realized. It is costly for society to build 'wrong' housing that is not wanted except 'for as long as it has to'. Ahead is the demolition, the unification of small apartments. The question also arises as to the importance of the lack of rental housing for labour mobility, an increase in which would be desirable. Also  and this is related to households' need for indebtedness  the financial planning of young first-time homebuyers over the life cycle would be made easier if, before "establishing" and acquiring their own home, one could live reasonably in a rented dwelling and save before buying one's own home. In this context, it should be noted that the average level of household indebtedness in Finland is not high (approx. 60% relative to disposable income), but of course the scope for indebtedness, especially among young people, is limited. All in all, we can say that our housing situation is very poor by European standards (by all conventional indicators). Despite the lower level of housing, the income share spent on housing is even higher than the EU average  so we get less real value for money in housing. What is the reason for this? What is the reason for this poor state of affairs? In the search for ways to solve housing problems, various factors in the economy must be considered very broadly. Housing policy is not just some kind of subsidy policy or a policy of arava, but housing policy is all those measures that affect the functioning of the housing market. And it is worth pointing out that the housing market can, in a way, distinguish between many different markets: the real estate market, where the prices of old homes are formed, and the new construction market, where the prices of new homes are formed. In the short term, the supply of housing (the existing housing stock) is rigid, so the price level of apartments is mainly determined by demand. In the longer term, the supply through new production and its price level affect the price development of the entire housing stock. Supply, on the other hand, depends to an important extent on the functioning of the land market and the functioning of the building inputs market, as well as on the available labour force, i.e. the functioning of the labour market. Since a home is usually not bought without loan financing and since the apartment is also an investment object, the functioning of the housing market is closely linked to the financial market. When economic units simply buy the services of residential properties owned by others, we are talking about the rental market. For this presentation, I looked at what I thought about the functioning of the housing market about ten years ago when I was still actively engaged in research on the housing market and looked at what has been done since then. (At that time, for example, I wrote an article together with Heikki A. Loikkanen in the Journal of the National Economy entitled "Promoting the functioning of the housing market".) At that time, we proposed that the quality and cost of our housing level would be the same. by promoting the functioning of the market, it will be brought to a Nordic level by the year 2000. This has not been achieved. But has anything changed since those times? Revitalising land markets is key Ten years ago, we attached great importance to reviving the land market, and I still think that this is the most important issue in terms of housing for Finns. It is quite obvious that we do not have enough plots available in growth centres. Plot prices are unreasonably high in regional centres. The land market is not working properly. In order to promote the functioning of the land market, it is necessary to increase the supply of building land and make it more flexible. Even if you can't make land, you can make land! Measures are needed concerning both town and country planning procedures and tax matters, etc. incentives which, by their steering effect, contribute to the provision of the necessary building land. Long-term planning must aim for perseverance. (Apparently, during and after the depression years, municipalities reduced their investment in zoning and zoning staff.) In fact, municipalities, for example, have quite effective means at their disposal to promote these goals: they have a monopoly on town and country planning, which should be used to create housing areas that are rational and comfortable in terms of urban structure. Cities' and municipalities' own land use and land acquisition must be made more efficient. Privately owned land should also be zoned if this is desirable for the appropriate development of the urban structure. Construction in urban areas should progress on zoning grounds with the aim of creating a pleasant community. Municipal boundaries or land tenure relationships should not be a hindrance. Zoning should not, for example, be allowed to: create intermediate areas, which, however, are later to be made available for residential use. Outside urban centres, the basic option should be considered to be more single-family house construction instead of blocks of flats. Municipalities have the right to redeem land. It should be used more sensitively. Town and country planning procedures should be speeded up and appeal periods reduced. The taxation of the increase in value resulting from zoning and the more significant introduction of a property tax would contribute both to the supply of land to the market and to the more efficient use of the existing housing and other building stock. (It should be noted that a property tax as a "stable tax revenue" would be more appropriate for municipalities compared to a corporation tax, the return of which varies and is therefore more uncertain. Indeed, Finland is one of the few western European countries where corporation tax is paid to municipalities and where property taxation does not play a significant role as a means of financing local government. ) Promoting the so-called free rental market, i.e. private investors What has been the development of the rental market? The inoperability of the rental market was quite obvious 10 years ago  for example, the dismantling of rent regulation had only just begun. Since then, rent control for privately owned rental apartments has been completely dismantled. Similarly, there has been a shift to a more neutral taxation of rental income with other investment income. However, the private rent supply for both private and institutional investors is still too small  it should be made to grow. This is influenced by many factors (e.g. plot policy  e.g. pension funds may not be able to invest in properties on rented plots), but it is clear that even the slightest risk of restoring rent control  something that has sometimes been glimpsing in speeches lately  will deter investors. Financing perspective on housing  funding is not a key problem From the problem of private rental housing, I can move on to commenting on the financial perspective of housing, which was my original title. I will explain a little later why financing in the traditional sense, that is, when it comes to lending for housing, is no longer a problem. The financial aspect of housing, on the other hand, could be linked to the question of how financial markets could help to manage regional house price fluctuations, promote the functioning of the market for private rental housing and thus facilitate regional mobility. For example, in addition to existing real estate companies, companies that would own properties around the country could be listed on the stock exchange. The advantage for these companies would be that the returns on their shares would depend less on regional price differences. Thus, living in rented accommodation and investing in the shares of these companies could reduce the risk of capital losses compared to owner-occupied housing. The background is that, for example, the turnover of production technologies increases the need for regional labour mobility, which, however, is reduced by owner-occupied housing: it is difficult for a person living in owner-occupied housing to move from a declining area to a growing centre due to the probable capital loss caused by the apartment. If, on the other hand, you lived in rented accommodation (to a high standard, as in countries where rented housing is quite common, e.g. in a rented apartment). In Germany and Switzerland  in the last mentioned country, 60% of apartments are private rentals!)) and, in addition, invest in the shares of such a company, be able to live well, but at the same time also secure the diversification of his investment. If you live in an owner-occupied apartment, the investment portfolio is one-sided. In other words, the financial markets could, in the current circumstances, produce investment services that would allow households to better manage their wealth and, at the same time, to choose their form and place of living more freely in different situations of life. This would certainly contribute to the supply of free private sector-funded rental housing. On the other hand, traditional housing financing  mortgage lending  has not been a key problem in Finnish housing policy for a long time. We no longer have a 'capital shortage'. Finnish financial system and housing financing the stigmatised rationing and administrative steering, which led to the majority of financial intermediation taking place through channels where the price mechanism did not work much, was already achieved in the 1980s. Who remembers anymore that under credit rationing conditions, the average "hard money" mortgage was still 7-9 years in the early 1980s, and in order to get a loan, you had to save 20-40% of the purchase value of the apartment in advance. Under credit rationing conditions, access to finance limited the demand for housing, which was then unwound in the context of the liberalisation of the financial markets with the removal of the constraint on the availability of mortgage credit. The bursting of pent-up demand caused the housing market to overheat, price rise and a large bubble, which subsequently burst with notorious consequences. Mortgages are now available at market prices, and as interest rates in the euro area are low  thanks to the credible monetary policy of the European Central Bank (ECB)  mortgages are also available at rates that have never been so low. Competition has also reduced the premium relative to the reference rate. It is true that mortgages are still short-term, but that is not because longer loans are not available. For some reason  historically  consumers and homebuyers do not yet seem to have realised the benefits of long loan periods. In Finland, the credit system in terms of interest rate fixing differs somewhat from the prevailing system in the EU. After all, 90% of household loans are tied to EURIBOR rates or bank-specific reference rates. Housing financing is deposit-based and depends on short-term market interest rates, and bond-financed mortgages have not achieved a significant position for us. There is no legal or tax barrier to the growth of household bond savings (either directly or probably through funds). (The tax treatment of deposits does not currently differ from that of other investment objects, and the legislation enabling mortgage banks to operate has also been corrected.) The incipient decline in government debt is also creating more and more space in the financial markets for private, long-term debt securities. According to international experience, the funds raised with these would be suitable for very long-term and fixed-rate housing financing, i.e. for securitisation of housing finance. In this way, the housing sector (households and landlords) would not be as exposed to interest rate risks in the future as it is today. It has to be said, however, that the ECB's monetary policy has already proved credible  i.e. that price stability in the euro area has been maintained at relatively low interest rates and with low interest rate movements. This means that the interest rate on variable rate mortgages has also remained low and fluctuated quite a bit, which perhaps partly explains the low demand for fixed-rate mortgages. In addition to the fact that the range of mortgages in terms of interest rate fixing and maturity has increased, we can now be calmer than before when it comes to interest rate developments. As a member of EMU, we belong to a large monetary area with a long-term and credible monetary policy. (It should be noted that, from the point of view of the transmission of monetary policy, a shift in housing finance to a more securities-based approach might be desirable. This would bring our housing finance system closer to the average euro area housing financing and the transmission of monetary policy. Countries  such as Finland  where floating rate bank loans play a relatively large role in corporate and housing financing are exposed to fluctuations in market interest rates to some extent more than others.) All in all, however, I would like to say that traditional credit financing is not one of the main problems of housing and housing policy in Finland. Financial institutions are able to pass on the type of loans that households want  also for a much longer period than at present. As I said, there are no formal, regulatory or legal barriers to the emergence of a fixed-rate, long-term loan market. For example, there are currently two real estate credit banks operating in Finland  Sampo Bank and OP Bank Group each have their own  as well as the 140-year-old Finnish Mortgage Association. Savings Bank Aktia has also announced that it will establish its own mortgage bank. which will be operational in 2002. Other banks can also set up their own if the need arises. Targeting public support to households requires more flexible supply The amount of public support for housing distributed annually is significant  in 1999 it amounted to 17 billion. Marks. The support is mainly either direct or indirect income and tax support. The share of financial assistance is about 15%. In general, there should be wisdom in the use of aid  so that grants and subsidies do not overly distort the functioning of the market. Above all, aid should not flow capitalised into increases in house prices. After all, in unregulated conditions, the subsidy is mainly for the benefit of the most inflexible factor  and the more inflexible the factor is. It can be said that in the past decades, the subsidy policy, above all tax deduction rights, contributed to our rigid plot policy, the shortage of rental housing, and the supply more generally, to the fact that the price level of apartments in Finland remained high, i.e. households received a reduction in housing costs as lower taxation, but had to pay a higher price for their apartment. It can therefore be said that the success of a demand-driven support system  the right to tax deductions, income subsidies  depends essentially on supply flexibility. When the supply is flexible, then the probability that the subsidy will benefit the household for which it was originally intended increases, i.e. the subsidy lowers housing costs and does not capitalize on housing prices. For this reason, too, flexibility in supply should be promoted. As far as supply-oriented support schemes, i.e. subsidies for the construction or renting of housing, are concerned, finland has been subjected to a number of unfair 'deadlocks' in the housing market. For example, in Helsinki, the so-called. There are features of HITAS housing that essentially hinder the appropriate use of the existing housing stock: The resale prices of HITAS apartments located on subsidised rental plots in municipalities are indexed to their construction costs. As a result, the price ratios of dwellings of different ages, locations and qualities do not correspond to their use value ratios. On the other hand, their price ratios to the rest of the dwelling stock vary both from one object to another and from one time to another. This results in arbitrary redistribution of wealth and lock-in phenomena that limit migration and thus cause massive welfare losses. The procedure for allocating housing is also questionable. The functioning of the housing market and the rational allocation of support require that housing support is not tied to the characteristics of real estate, but to the characteristics of households. Therefore, efforts should be made to get rid of HITAS and similar arrangements. Finally  towards continental European living Housing is one of the largest items of household expenditure and the largest single acquisition cost  the predictability and stability of the housing market is therefore important. We have not had a lack of funding for a long time now, and Finland's membership of EMU has brought stability to our financial markets in terms of interest rates. The financial markets offer a wide range of mortgage lending opportunities. Our low level of housing, high prices and rents and housing problems in general are home-based, the result of many long-standing regulatory measures that have been partially dismantled but not fully overcome. The land market, in particular, works poorly for us, which is, of course, strange considering that we live in the most sparsely populated country in Europe. On the other hand, from an optimistic point of view, this should be a challenge. The real price and rent level of apartments is ultimately determined by the supply side of the apartments. If the construction industry and its input markets (including the land and construction materials market) become more efficient so that new dwellings can be placed on the market at lower prices than before, the real price and rent level of the entire housing stock, including old dwellings, will decrease. When how we live in the future will depend centrally on the supply of housing, and the main supply factor is the availability of plot land, we should have a good chance of overcoming this problem. In fact, we should not settle for anything less than to develop Finland into a model country for housing. I would even go so far as to say that housing is one of our most important "competitiveness factors". If we do not improve it, we will have difficulty keeping our well-educated own citizens in the country, and we will not be able to attract other talents here either. (service) jobs in growth centres are also not created when there is a shortage of housing. These jobs are such that, far from being created elsewhere in the country (in my opinion, the housing shortage in growth centres cannot manage regional policy for the benefit of regions with net migration losses), they are not created at all. Despite the fact that we now live poorly by eu standards, it is quite realistic to think that we will raise our housing level higher than others. The level of housing should be the great attraction for Finland. In my opinion, Finland could be a real dream country if our level of housing were what it should be, taking into account our income level and the fact that there is plenty of space and wood (building material) in our country.

Title: Speech at the Future 2020! event
text: Bank Manager Sinikka Salo's speech future 2020! d at the event . Speech . Friday 8March 2002, 12:00 AM Technological development and the future of the public sector My good listener. First of all, I would like to thank you for the great opportunity offered to me at the Future 2020 seminar to discuss the Finland of the future with you. Reaching into the future seems to be particularly well suited to Oulu, a city that has become one of the symbols of the Finnish technology miracle in recent years. My intention is to consider the importance of technological development for the future of the public sector. The combination of "new technology" and "public sector" may seem peculiar to someone. After all, the image of the public sector is not very high-tech. At the level of perceptions, new technology has been combined with lHinns IT companies, the telecommunications industry, industrial automation, and so on. Perhaps the first thing that comes to mind in the service sector is the banks, where transactions have completely changed over the past two decades as a result of automation and electronics. The public sector, on the other hand, is associated with much softer images of the past, of schools and health services. Another image of the public sector has to do with bureaucratic administrative agencies. Someone may be able to say that the new technology is particularly relevant and stigmatising precisely for these activities. In my mind, however, it is precisely the case that matters. I would therefore like to take the opportunity afforded to me to assure you that technology innovation will be absolutely crucial to the future of the public sector over the next few decades. The significance of this is so great that it does not affect the 'micro-level', i.e. the organisation of chelons in hospitals or schools, or some of the citizens' interactions with the authorities: the effects are much more far-reaching. It seems clear to me that the question of the new technologies in public service provision in Finland will very soon be at the centre of the entire debate on economic policy and the whole of social policy. How this issue is resolved depends not only on the future size and character of the public sector, but also on the future of the nordic welfare model as a whole. The subject matter is for me as a citizen, as a woman, as a representative of the Central Bank. As a citizen, like other Finns, I am interested above all in the fact that the availability and quality of welfare services will also be sufficient in terms of the availability and quality of welfare services in the future. I am also interested in what kind of taxation is needed to finance these services. Basically, I am a so-called "happy taxpayer" enough to think that I do not hate taxes, but consider them essential and part of the modern welfare society. In the same breath, however, I would like to say that, of course, taxation must also be high and encouraging, and it should not be tightened so much that it seriously hinders the functioning of the labour market or slows down economic growth too much. As a woman, I am interested in the future of the public sector because public service provision is so female-dominated and, on the other hand, because it increases the freedom of women to choose their role in society. The education and health sectors, in particular, are notoriously female-dominated and have lower pay levels than many male-dominated sectors. At the same time, it has long been part of the Nordic model of gender equality that the responsibility for caring for children and the elderly does not fall on female children, child sid or elderly daughters or ministchss, but that women are social services that enable women to play an active role in the care of women, even if the family has small children or elderly people in need of care. -The support provided by the public sector for the participation of women is not only a question of equality, but also a question of economic efficiency. Society cannot afford to use women's work or to take it for only half-heartedness. The question of the future of the public sector and the impact of technological developments on it is also a matter for the Central Bank. You ask why: after all, interest rates and other monetary policy are the responsibility of the central banks, while public finances are, of course, primarily the responsibility of the government and the municipalities. In all countries, the close interest of central banks in the management of public finances is due to the interdependence of monetary and other economic policies, since sound public finances are a key condition for the success of monetary policy. If public finances run into financial difficulties, the financial system and the functioning of the monetary system as a whole are jeopardised. -The example of such a situation came a few months ago in Argentina, where the failure of public finances also caused a financial crisis, even though the country's monetary system was supposed to be built with the help of dollar connections, in principle, very securely. Finland's national economy is now on a fairly stable footing, probably more stable than ever, thanks to emu neutrality and well-managed central government finances. However, looking to the future, public finances in particular face serious challenges, and the debate also touches on the bank of Finland's operating field, monetary balance and Finland's successes as part of the European economic policy system. That's one of the reasons why I consider the topic to be so tsrkesnsn. The purpose of this seminar is to see the future of the seminar for about 20 years. Although it is dangerous to imagine that the future will continue to develop the trend of humanity as it is, it is still a good idea to begin to look at how the world has changed over the last 20 years. Let us start looking at the development of the economy as a whole and move on to budgetary issues only after that. *** Since 1980, Finland's national economy has grown at an average annual rate of around three per cent. This means that the total volume of goods and services produced has almost doubled in just over 20 years. At the same time, there has been almost no change in the labour economy: in 1980, the number of employees and enterprises totalled about 2.3 million, which is why in 1980 it was worthwhile. In fact, the number of hours worked has decreased slightly, as the number of holiday and part-time employment relationships has increased. Thus, when the economic activity of the national economy has not increased, at least not in addition, it can be said that the growth of the economy as a whole has been achieved through an increase in productivity. The improvement in labour productivity has been based in part on investments that have increased the production of machinery, equipment and other production facilities, but to a large extent also on technical progress, which has made the use of inputs more efficient, so that at the same time inputs can produce much more goods and services today than they did two decades ago. In recent years, economists have been studying productivity growth to explain how much it has done, and the prevailing trend today is probably that more than half of the productivity gains have been due to the use of new technologies. There will probably never be any certainty about the percentages in this case, but it is clear that technological progress has played a crucial role in the engine of economic growth. Formerly the public sector? According to statistics, the growth of public service production over the last two decades has been much faster than the average for the economy as a whole. Since 1980, the number of people working in public has increased by about 40%; there are now more than 560,000. Almost a quarter of the labour force provides public services. Longer on the horizon, the change has been more radical. When Pekka Kuusi once wrote his famous book "Social Policy of the 60s", only 8% of the labour force was employed in the production of public services. It is clear that, as the use of labour input has grown, the number of public services provided has also increased greatly. According to Statistics Finland's calculations, the share of public services (measured in terms of value added) in the value of the output of the entire national economy is now about 18%. Two decades ago, the share was just over 14% There are no comprehensive and reliable estimates of the development of labour productivity in public activities as a whole. This is due to the fact that it is very difficult to measure the amount of production when the products do not have a market price. What is certain, however, is that the growth of public service production in recent decades has been based on the increase in the power of the economy, on the other hand, rather than in any other economy in which productivity growth has been a key factor. The characterisation of fiscal growth is not a reproach. It is simply a question of the fact that the increase in average productivity in the economy as a whole is based on the industry of pssos, where technological progress and new investments have increased productivity very rapidly. On the one hand, the productivity development of public services, but also of the private services sector, has been much slower than that of industry. For example, in the private health sector, productivity has only decreased over the past 9 years, according to Statistics Finland's calculations. How to proceed? Can Chyhsnastic trends continue? The growth in demand for welfare services and other services provided by the public sector, or at least in the need for them, does not indicate any signs of slowing down, and there is reason to assume that it will continue to grow at the same rate as demand for market hysdys. In fact, I consider the growth in the need for services to be certain and the corresponding growth in service production to be certain. If and when there is a nsin, the question can be asked as to how the services will be produced and paid for in the future. Can development continue along the same lines as in recent decades? A closer look at the last question reveals that the financing of public services cannot be based on general economic growth alone in the long term. Although economic growth does, of course, add to the national economy, so to speak, an increase in the size of the common cake does not bring an automatic solution to the question of the financing of the welfare state. One often wonders why the financing of social services is becoming so difficult, or even more difficult, politically and economically, even though Finland is richer than ever before. After all, the name implies that, for example, 20 years ago, the real income of the Finnish economy was almost half as low as it is today. You would think, then, that we as a society today could afford much more than we did then, and that if economic growth continued, in twenty years' time we would be able to afford much more than we do now. Shouldn't it become easier and easier for society to provide security and welfare services? Unfortunately, it is not a simple matter. Rather, economic growth in line with trends observed up to shs, based on productivity growth in goods production and private services (such as transport, telecommunications and finance), does little to facilitate the financing of public services. The reason for this is the so-called Baumol disease, an unfortunate but universal economic manifestation caused by the fact that there has generally been no increase in productivity in public service provision, or at least not as much as in the private sector, and especially in industry. In Baumol's disease, the difference in productivity between the private and public sectors means that public services are becoming relatively more and more expensive in terms of economic growth. The tax base and public sector tax revenues will also increase in line with economic growth, but at the same rate will the cost of producing public services rise if and when wages for the long term follow the growth of productivity in the private sector. As a result, the company will not be able to increase the production of public services except by increasing taxation. If the share of public services in production is to be constant in real terms, this is only possible if taxation is constantly increased at the same rate as the productivity of the private sector. As economic growth progresses, a national economy with Baumol disease has three bad and one good option. The bad options are as follows: 1. tax rates are constantly rising, at the same rate as the production of public services is growing; or 2. the production of public services is not increased, although the economy is otherwise growing; or 3. real wages in the public sector are not raised at the rate of the real wage level in the rest of the economy, but are given year after year. after the wages paid in the market sector. Nsms are all siechschmis options. The constant, trend-like tightening of taxation would lead to one of the worsening incentive problems in the labour market and to a weakening of the labour market, which contributes to the tax base. If we fall into this scenario, the sustainability of public sector funding will be questionable for the long term. A reduction in the growth of the output of public services, on the other hand, would lead to a deterioration in the level of service provided by welfare services and to growing dissatisfaction with the ability of the public sector to respond to its tasks. Apparently, the share of the private market sector in the traditional management of public authority would increase, which would erode the Nordic model of equality thinking, with the wealthiest buying expensive private services for themselves and relying on the decaying public supply of the wealthier. The third bad option, the deliberate reduction of real public sector wages, on the other hand, is likely to be a viable option from the point of view of labour market policy and would not only certainly lead to a reduction in the quality of services. Why was that a good option? The only option that will ensure the long-term development of the Finnish welfare society, as we are used to it, would be to substantially accelerate productivity growth in public services, as much as possible to increase productivity in the private sector. The size of public services could grow with the rest of the economy and the tax rates needed to finance them could remain stable. The crucial role of productivity developments in the financing of public services is illustrated by the following simple calculation example. If productivity in the private sector were to increase by 3.7% per year over the next 19 years, productivity would double by 2020. Chems is an optimistic, but not entirely impossible scenario. Let us now think that productivity in public services would not increase at all at the same time. However, if the amount of public services provided were to increase in proportion to the growth of the rest of the economy, the tax rate at which the services are financed would also have to be doubled. On the other hand, as I have already mentioned, if productivity in public services were to rise at the same rate as in the private sector, a standard tax rate would already be sufficient to maintain a stable share of public services in total output. The principled and formulaic examinations are very topical, as it is already the case that the Finnish public sector will be under considerable cross-pressure in the coming decades. The demand for services is growing rapidly due to, among other things, the emergence of services and the medicalisation of society. Not only does the general level of income rise, but the demand for public services also increases, as the demands of people in general, and especially in health and care services, rise. The main trend, however, is ysestsn iksning. While there are now about four jobs for about every person over the age of 65, in the 2020s, according to forecasts, there will already be a situation where there will be two jobs for every elderly person. In a recent study (Parkkinen 2002), the VATT Institute for Economic Research has investigated the effects of age on care expenditure. According to it, by 2020, society's expenditure on care services per Finn would increase by almost 30%. But VATT's calculations are based on the current real prices of care services, so we do not take into account the impact of Baumol's disease, which will continue to raise the real prices of services and make the future much gloomier - unless the productivity of public services increases. The financing of public services is hampered not only by the increase in the need for public services and their tendency to become more expensive year on year, but also by the fact that the increase in expenditure on energy, which has been the subject of much debate in recent years, competes, in a way, for the same resources as the production of public services. Studies by the Finnish Centre for Economic Safety and Security, for example, have estimated that the tysntekijsils and the tyselske fees collected from employers will rise sharply in the 2020 years, even before 2020 to more than a quarter of the wage income. If the tax rate, including contributions, is not wanted or can not be clearly increased, it is clear that the intensification of service provision will play a key role in resolving the conflict that exists. At the same time as the demand for services is growing, the increase in the level of wages in the public sector is also under pressure. The public sector must be able to compete with the private sector for competent power, unless the productivity and quality of public action is to be compromised. In addition, it must be taken into account that the public sector is dominated by women, and when an attempt is made to increase the level of pay for women, it is likely to mean an increase in the relative level of pay in the public sector, not a decrease in it. Huttunen himself is judged to be conservative. It is certainly to be hoped that the completion of the project will speed up the debate on the future of public service provision and bring it to a more concrete level. *** In my speech, I have tried to explain how central to increasing the productivity of public service provision must be in the survival strategy of the welfare state. It is clear that only the intensive use of new technologies in the public sector - on the same scale as that undertaken in the private sector - can cure our national economy from Baumol disease and save the Nordic model for a long period of time. I have understood that the development of welfare technology in Oulu, for example, has been included as one of the focus areas of product development in research. The development of technology is vsltsmschnch. In addition, however, it is also necessary to create in society the conditions, attitudes and incentives that ensure that innovations that increase productivity are really widely adopted. This may require structural changes in the way the production of welfare services and other public services is organised. The development of the private sector is, of course, driven by competition between producers in terms of quality and price. In its broad economic policy guidelines, the EU has jointly agreed to take measures from Finland to increase competitiveness in the production of public services. Of course, the implementation of this requires a very clear organisational separation between the service provider and the provider, and the readiness of the organisations ordering the services to put the various public service providers out to tender on a national and, why not, international scale. Promoting competition may be one way, but there is certainly a need for others. In any case, I would like to believe that the challenge that exists will be tackled in time and that the next two decades will, therefore, become an era that will revolutionise our current approach to public service provision and the importance of technology. Knowing that it is you, the good listeners, that you have to make a significant contribution to the Finnish welfare society's response to its next challenge.

Huttunen itse pit arviotaan konservatiivisena. On todennkist ja mys toivottavaa, ett projektin valmistuminen vauhdittaa julkisen palvelutuotannon tulevaisuutta koskevaa keskustelua ja tuo sen thnastista konkreettisemmalle tasolle. *** Olen puheenvuorossani koettanut selvitt, miten keskeisess avainasemassa julkisen palvelutuotannon tuottavuuden kasvattamisen on oltava hyvinvointivaltion selviytymisstrategiassa. Miten tst tehtvst voidaan suoriutua? On selv, ett ainoastaan uuden teknologian voimaperinen kyttnotto julkisella sektorilla -samassa mitassa kuin sit yksityisellkin sektorilla on ryhdytty hydyntmn -voi parantaa kansantaloutemme Baumolin taudista ja pelastaa pohjoismaisen mallin mys pitkll aikavlill. Olen ymmrtnyt, ett juuri tll Oulussa on esimerkiksi hyvinvointiteknologian kehittminen otettu kaukonkisesti yhdeksi tutkimuksen tuotekehittelyn painopisteeksi. Teknologian kehittminen on vlttmtnt. Tm saattaa vaatia rakennemuutoksia siin, kuinka hyvinvointipalvelujen ja muiden julkisten palveluiden tuotanto on jrjestetty. Kilpailun edistminen saattaa olla yksi keino, mutta muitakin varmasti tarvitaan. Joka tapauksessa haluan uskoa, ett thn ksill olevaan haasteeseen onnistutaan ajoissa tarttumaan ja ett seuraavat kaksi vuosikymment nin ollen tulevat muodostumaan aikakaudeksi, joka mullistaa nykyiset ksityksemme julkisesta palvelutuotannosta ja teknologian merkityksest siin. Tiedn, ett juuri teill, hyvt kuulijat, on tarjottavananne merkittv panos, kun suomalainen hyvinvointiyhteiskunta vastaa thn seuraavaan haasteeseensa.

Title: Speech at a seminar of the Finnish Department of the European Cultural Foundation "Whose culture is being talked about? - the cultural content of the Northern Dimension of Europe'
text: Bank Manager Sinikka Salo's speech at the Seminar of the European Culturestishn Finland Department "Whose culture is being talked about? -The cultural insufficiency of Europe's Northern Dimension' . Speech . Thursday30 May 2002, 12:00 AM The euro, European identity and national identity The euro d our single currency The adoption of the single currency by the twelve countries that have joined monetary union is the most tangible and tangible demonstration of the progress of European integration, even if it does not really matter more than some of the previous steps in the process of integration. In fact, there is good reason to suggest that the EU's internal market, created in 1992, has played a greater role in economic development than monetary union. However, money is such a sensitive part of people's everyday life that the symbolic significance of common euro banknotes is of a completely different order from the fact that goods and services circulate in the EU's internal market without barriers from one country to another. The monetary economy is not isolated from general economic, political and social development. That is why, right now, with the advent of the euro banknotes, it is interesting to consider the question of what the adoption of the single currency actually reflects the stage of development achieved by European integration, and why the formation of monetary union could play a role in further integration. The development of European integration is often cited d especially in Finland - explained very one-sidedly as a product of economic forces. It is thought that the internationalisation of production, trade and finance would be the driving force behind EU integration, and that political and institutional changes would be as if subordinate to the basic principles of the economy. However, this clearly underestimates the ideological and political aspect of the EU's development. It is certainly true that political and economic integration will help Europe to be more successful in the modern world economy. However, even a cursory examination of history shows that the internationalisation of the economy does not automatically and everywhere lead to political integration, not even economic policy. Moreover, European integration is a long-standing expression of political will for a stronger, more united and more peaceful Europe. Like the other dimensions of EU integration, monetary union is a long-standing product of political will. The formation of monetary union at least proves that the will to integrate and the confidence they have placed in their European integration partners have been quite strong in recent years. As a result of the establishment of monetary union, the acceding countries are now even more interdependent, so that the problems of economic policy in any member state would affect, through a single monetary market, the value of the euro, interest rates and the economic situation throughout the monetary union. In view of their dependence, monetary union requires a high level of confidence in the Member States that the finances of all the other Member States will be sound. Similarly, it has required the readiness to commit to common the standards by which confidence is ensured. So: common interests, common obligations. In spite of the dependence of the Member States, monetary union is not, of course, primarily a product of new risks, but has already proved to be an important stabiliser of economic development in the euro area. Hystyjins has been particularly the countries whose monetary policy before monetary union lacked credibility. Even in Finland, we have not been able to enjoy such a balanced money market for decades as in recent years. If there have been problems with economic development, it would be difficult to believe that they were due to the financial conditions. The monetary system established on the basis of the Maastricht Treaty, which includes the self-determination of the central bank, the designation of price stability as an objective of monetary policy, and the implementation of budgetary policies in the Member States, has proved its worth. More broadly, the functioning of monetary union has shown that the European Union is capable of creating strong institutions capable of pursuing credible and long-term policies. However, monetary union has not turned the EMU countries, let alone the EU as a whole, into a truly federal state. When monetary union was set up, some of its opponents argued that the adoption of the single currency would mean abandoning one of the essential elements of a sovereign state for the country that would join it, and that it would jeopardise its self-sufficiency and political freedom. This is unlikely to be the case. When considering the link between money and the state's self-sufficiency, there are reasons to note that the idea of a national monetary policy is in reality younger than the idea of a nation-state and its political sovereignty. It is worthwhile to do so for a moment. In the second half of the 1800s, when the idea of nation states and the world unity they formed matured, the monetary systems of the various countries were generally based on the gold standard, and the gold standard monetary system did not allow for a nationally differentiated monetary policy. Although the names of the monetary units used in the gold standard countries differed from each other, they were manifestations of only one measure of value, gold. For example, in the countries of the Latin Monetary Union, which included Belgium, Switzerland, Italy and Spain in addition to France, all countries' monetary units  francs, lira and pesetas  had been valued as equivalent to the French franc, but were still not seen as a threat to the national freedom of those countries. When the Finnish markka switched to the gold standard in 1878, the value of the Finnish markka was also valued at the level of the French franc. As such, long-term integrated, European monetary conditions have been shining since the 1870s for about 40 years, and would probably have stayed longer if the first world war had not collapsed the gold standard in the monetary system. However, it was the same decades that were the golden age of European nationalism. Why, then, is economic and monetary union, EMU? The fact that economic and monetary union does not, in the present way, traditionally imply a federal state d which, incidentally, is not at all unambiguous: for germans, for example, it means a decentralization of long-term work, while for the British it means concentration - it is above all the case that the economic policy cooperation of its member countries is based on sssnch, i.e. based on standards mutually agreed between governments and coordination on the basis of them. It is characteristic of the United States and federal states such as the United States that a large part of the executive power is concentrated in the hands of the federal government or the like. According to the Erssritelm, the EU's political system could be described as "a set of complex networks which, in some cases, are connected to each other, in other cases are partly disconnected from each other." Without going into the broad question, it can be said, taught by the history of the EU, that the EU is looking for its own future form in its own pockets and is not copying the existing model. Even in the future, d at least the EU will focus more on the development of the system of enlargment than on the establishment of centralised administration. Why is monetary union important for further integration? One of the effects of the single currency is psychological. As I have already mentioned, the euro has made EU integration an unprecedented part of people's daily lives. It is thus helping to build a stronger awareness among us, with the use of EUR 300 million, of the fact that we are part of a European society whose successes and destinies are interlinked. As a symbol, it must be very effective in the chechen sense. At the same time, it is clear that the euro can only be properly implemented, provided that monetary policy is well managed and that the value of the single currency remains stable and credible. An escalation in monetary policy would certainly give the whole of European integration a bad echo. The second importance is economic: the single currency and the integration of markets in the euro area. Of course, the impact is particularly strongly felt in the financial markets, which are already in many respects d e.g. So-called. for the short money market - merged into a single, continent-wide entity. The internal market requires closer integration of the banking and securities markets. Integration will continue and will be one of the main drivers of change which will also stimulate economic activity and policy integration. By way of example, one can cite the need for harmonisation of commercial and company law and the need to develop cooperation between national financial supervisors and, before the long term, to set up competent financial supervisory bodies at Union level. In addition to civic awareness and economic integration, the single currency also plays a role in the enlargement of the EU. The monetary credibility and stability created by EMU are, by name, one of the reasons why the countries of Central and Eastern Europe are invariably particularly interested in joining the EU and, in due course, in monetary union. Many countries have bad experiences similar to those of Finland or, for example, Italy and Spain, and how difficult it is to build credible monetary policy structures on their own, without an institutional basis similar to that of the Maastricht system. They also need a large, integrated euro area market to finance the growth and renewal of their own economy. EMU and its criteria for membership are already having a favourable effect on the monetary policy of the applicant countries. The success of monetary union presupposes that the economies of the applicant countries achieve a balance in line with the criteria even before they join monetary union. The criteria concern, among other things, inflation, interest rates and the balance of public finances. These criteria provide the economic policies of the applicant countries with the clear external benchmarks needed for a credible economic policy. Monetary union is therefore the result and demonstration of political will, and it also contributes to the further process of integration. It should be noted, however, that monetary union is only part of europe's overall integration process and is not the only force. With this comment, I would like to stress that the single currency should not be given too much political value. Given the great symbolic value of monetary union, it is only natural that there should be a temptation to introduce new members into monetary union even before their economies have matured and adapted to the demands of EMU. This applies above all to the stability of budgetary policy and banking systems. It is essential for the future economic development and political unity of the EU that the stability of the single currency should not be jeopardised by taking the risk of compromising the convergence criteria of monetary union on political grounds. This would not only jeopardise the monetary stability of the euro area, but would also slow down the consolidation of the economic policies of the new Member States in line with European stability policies. In the chechen minds, the existence of monetary union is more of a seal that shows and consolidates the level of integration already achieved, rather than a means of achieving a lack of integration. European identity and national identity, European civil society European integration as a political programme requires, in order to be successful, the development of a European civil society in which European political awareness and public opinion are born and influenced. Without the development of such a European civil society, the European political institutions will not be able to function properly and achieve the legitimacy they deserve. European civil society, on the other hand, cannot be born unless a European identity develops among the citizens of the Union. Of course, a European identity cannot be created if Europeans give up their national identity and become Europeans instead. Europe is not a new nation state. European identity is created through the realisation that Europeans are better able to realise their national identity together than in isolation. The history of Europe and Europeanism is notoriously bleak. Its horrors have been due partly to sick nationalism, which has been driven by the division of people into omeihino and otoisiino on the basis of nationality or ethnic origin, and partly by political movements that have imagined that they could solve social problems by denying the fundamental principles of the rule of law, an open society and democracy. The ideological background to European integration lies precisely in the historical experience and its lessons. On this basis, the EU's development is driven by the pursuit of peace, political freedom and economic prosperity. The European Union is, above all, a commonwealth of values, and the political power of Europe and economic success depend on the basis of values in the last few years. The EU's values are the values of an inclusive, open and democratic society in which human rights and the market economy play a central role. European countries have also always attached particular importance to social cohesion and solidarity. The values on which the EU is based are best summarised in the criteria that were criticised at the Ksspenhamina Summit in Mid-1993, when it was considered what conditions the former socialist countries of Central and Eastern Europe could join as Members of the Union. According to these criteria, eu membership requires, first of all, stable administrative institutions guaranteeing respect for the principles of democracy, the rule of law, respect for human rights and the protection of minorities. It also requires a functioning market economy and the ability to withstand competitive pressures and market forces within the Union. Thirdly, the new Member States wishing to join the Union will be required to be able to assume the responsibilities of membership, including the objectives of economic and monetary union. The idea of a European identity has recently been challenged, in a way, on two sides. Both civil society and major politics have highlighted the global angle and the corresponding global responsibilities for issues such as the environment, the economies of developing countries and global security problems. This development requires a European identity as part of the global political arena. The key question is how to make Europe a reality in the world. On the other hand, stronger nationalist, or at least anti-internationalist, political currents have emerged in the estuary of Europe, which are negative about EU integration in general, and at least towards the enlargement of the Union itself or the development of the EU's global role. The point is that a European identity cannot be defined through negations, i.e. it should be said that there is a non-European and, as such, something to be rejected. The power of Europeanism is not to reject the oei-Europeano. It is not through the msssrity that Europeans are required to reject their traditional national identities and identities. European identity is only positively defined - through the universal values and principles on which European integration is based. Similarly, it can be said that national identity and European identity do not compete with each other. This is because the European political and social context and the European institutions create the best conditions for the realisation of the national culture and characteristics of each country. Thriving societies and cultures have never been the ones that seek to isolate themselves, but rather those societies that are best able to interact creatively with the common society and the economy. In the early days of Finnish culture and national herssm, it was extremely clear, for example, in the basics of Snellman's nationality. And the most eloquently written about it is Aleksis Kivi, whose Seven Brothers is in fact the story of how true freedom finally comes about - not through separation, but on the other hand, on the basis of coexistence and citizenship, responsible participation in the world from many parts of the world to ksssin. When the Finnish national idea has its roots in nsisss ideas, it certainly gives us excellent points of understanding the relationship between national identity and Europeanism in a positive way. Finally Ladies and gentlemen, despite the diversity of European cultures, there is the ultimate, somewhat mythical, kssite of European unity, which we Finns also share. It's easy to recognize: I myself recognized the similarities in culture, institutions and customs at a young age when I was first on a school exchange in the Black Forest and as a senior oau pair in Paris. The commonality I experienced was only strengthened during the 5th year I lived in Germany. In Central European thinking, integration has traditionally meant, above all, peace and security. Integration is a political project d the dream of the wise and the ambition of the vskevs. The common quest for efficiency and effectiveness, a collective ambition, has led European nations to accept restrictions and sanctions. The joint project has introduced a new structure into the ancient European context. This has not (been) the same for us Finns d nor for many others who had joined the EU more d who had diverted our interest after the war and who were primarily involved in the project (and to whom the project was marketed) primarily as an economic d common market. This helps to explain why, so often in Finland, we take the form of the rest of Europe: we even talk about "Finland and Europe" while we talk about "Finland and the rest of Europe". Of course, we Finns also share European values and integration in a broad European mindset. And although integration is cumbersome, it is progressing d oL'Europe difficileo is the apt name for the work on the history of integration that I am currently reading. Firstly at the European Monetary Institute (EMI) to assess the number of countries needed to establish monetary union, and then after the establishment of monetary union, to set up the European Central Bank (ECB) showed me, even on a personal basis, the strong will and the passion for integration to d the desire for workable solutions and compromises. At that time, it finally dawned on me how we can be involved in a historically unique project. A project in which countries voluntarily and peacefully surrender their sovereignty for the common good. European integration as a political programme requires the development of European civil society to be successful. It is not the euro, but the conscious action of eu citizens d i.e. also the Finns - for our better continent- will carry europeanism! The siss market and the single currency are, in fact, only means. It is essential (in the words of Jacques Delors) for Europeans to work together and to build together a Europe whose richness lies in its diversity, its strength in solidarity and its influence in its strength and generosity. o
