Symbolina se on tss mieless varmaankin hyvin tehokas. Samalla on selv, ett tmnkin tehtvns euro voi tytt kunnolla vain, sill edellytyksell, ett rahapolitiikkaa hoidetaan hyvin ja yhteisen rahan arvo pysyy vakaana ja uskottavana. Eponnistuminen rahapolitiikassa antaisi koko eurooppalaiselle integraatiolle varmasti huonon kaiun. Toinen merkitys on taloudellinen: yhteinen raha lis markkinoiden yhdentymist euroalueella. Erityisen voimakkaasti tm vaikutus tuntuu tietysti finanssimarkkinoilla, jotka jo nyt ovat monilta osiltaan  esim. ns. lyhyen rahan markkinoiden osalta -sulautuneet yhdeksi, koko mantereen laajuiseksi kokonaisuudeksi. Sismarkkinoiden tysimrinen hydyntminen edellytt pankki-ja arvopaperimarkkinoiden yhdentymisen tiivistymist. Yhdentyminen tulee jatkumaan, ja se on yksi keskeisi muutosvoimia jotka vauhdittavat mys taloudellista toimeliaisuutta ja talouspoliittista integraatiota. Tst esimerkkein voi mainita kauppa-ja yhtioikeuden sdsten harmonisointitarpeen ja mys lisntyvn tarpeen kehitt kansallisten rahoitusvalvojien yhteistyt ja ennen pitk perustaa unionin tasoisia, toimivaltaisia rahoitusvalvontaelimi. Kansalaistietoisuuden ja talouden yhdentymisen lisksi yhteisell rahalla on merkityst mys EU:n laajentumisen kannalta. EMUn luoma rahapoliittinen uskottavuus ja vakaus ovat nimittin yksi niist syist, joiden vuoksi Keski.ja It-Euroopan maat ovat poikkeuksetta erittin kiinnostuneita liittymn EU:hun ja sen kautta aikanaan mys rahaliittoon. Monilla nist maista on samantapaisia huonoja kokemuksia kuin Suomella tai vaikkapa Italialla ja Espanjalla siit, kuinka vaikeata on rakentaa uskottavia rahapolitiikan rakenteita yksin, ilman Maastrichtin jrjestelmn kaltaista institutionaalista perustaa. Ne kaipaavat mys psy euroalueen laajoille, yhdentyville pomamarkkinoille rahoittaakseen oman taloutensa kasvua ja uudistumista. EMU ja sen jsenyyskriteerit vaikuttavat hakijamaiden rahapolitiikkaan edullisesti jo nyt. Rahaliiton jsenyys edellytt, ett hakijamaiden talous saavuttaa kriteerien mukaisen kestvn tasapainon jo ennen liittymist rahaliittoon. Kriteerit koskevat mm. inflaatiota, korkoja ja julkisen talouden tasapainoa. Nm kriteerit antavat hakijamaiden talouspolitiikalle selket ulkoiset kiintopisteet, joita uskottava talouspolitiikka tarvitsee. Rahaliitto on siis poliittisen tahdon tulos ja osoitus, ja mys osaltaan mytvaikuttamassa integraatiokehityksen jatkumiseen. On kuitenkin huomattava, ett rahaliitto on kuitenkin vain osa Euroopan yleist integraatiokehityst, eik se riit ainoaksi kyttvoimaksi. Tll huomautuksellani haluan korostaa sit, ett yhteiselle rahalle ei saisi asettaa liikaa poliittista vlinearvoa. Rahaliiton suuren symboliarvon vuoksi on luonnollista, ett on olemassa kiusaus ottaa rahaliittoon uusia jseni jo ennen kuin niiden taloudet ovat kypsyneet ja sopeutuneet EMU.jsenyyden asettamiin vaatimuksiin. Tm koskee ennen muuta budjettipolitiikan kestvyytt ja pankkijrjestelmn vakautta. EU:n tulevan taloudellisen kehityksen ja poliittisen yhtenisyyden kannalta on olennaista, ett yhteisen rahan vakautta ei saa vaarantaa ottamalla sellaista riski, ett rahaliiton konvergenssikriteereist tingittisiin poliittisin perustein. Tllainen ei ainoastaan vaarantaisi euroalueen rahataloudellista vakautta, vaan mys hidastaisi uusien jsenmaiden talouspolitiikan vakiintumista eurooppalaisen vakauspolitiikan mukaiseksi. Tsskin mieless rahaliiton jsenyys on pikemminkin sinetti, joka osoittaa ja vakiinnuttaa jo saavutetun integraation tason, kuin keino puuttuvan integraation toteuttamiseksi. Eurooppalaisuus ja kansallinen identiteetti, eurooppalainen kansalaisyhteiskunta Euroopan integraatio poliittisena ohjelmana vaatii menestykseen, ett tytyy kehitty eurooppalainen kansalaisyhteiskunta, jossa syntyy ja vaikuttaa eurooppalainen poliittinen tietoisuus ja kansalaismielipide. Ilman tllaisen eurooppalaisen kansalaisyhteiskunnan kehittymist eurooppalaiset poliittiset instituutiot eivt voi kunnolla toimia ja saavuttaa niille kuuluvaa legitiimisyytt. Eurooppalainen kansalaisyhteiskunta ei puolestaan voi synty, ellei unionin kansalaisten keskuudessa kehity eurooppalaista identiteetti. Eurooppalainen identiteetti ei luonnollisestikaan voi synty siten, ett eurooppalaiset luopuisivat kansallisesta identiteetistn ja ryhtyisivt sen sijaan eurooppalaisiksi. Eurooppa ei ole uusi kansallisvaltio. Eurooppalainen identiteetti syntyy sit kautta, ett oivalletaan, ett eurooppalaiset pystyvt toteuttamaan kansallista ominaislaatuaan paremmin yhdess kuin eristytyen. Euroopan ja eurooppalaisuuden lhihistoria on tunnetusti synkk. Sen kauhut ovat osaksi johtuneet sairaasta nationalismista, jonka kyttvoimana on ollut ihmisten jakaminen meihin ja toisiin kansallisuuden tai etnisen taustan perusteella, ja osaksi poliittisista riliikkeist, jotka ovat kuvitelleet voivansa ratkoa yhteiskunnallisia ongelmia kieltmll oikeusvaltion, avoimen yhteiskunnan ja demokratian keskeiset periaatteet. Euroopan integraation aatteellinen tausta on juuri tss historiallisessa kokemuksessa ja sen opetuksissa. Tlt pohjalta EU:n kehityksen kyttvoimana on pyrkimys kestvn rauhaan, poliittiseen vapauteen ja taloudelliseen vaurauteen. Euroopan unioni onkin ennen muuta arvoyhteis, ja sek Euroopan poliittinen voima ett taloudellinen menestys lepvt viime kdess tmn arvoperustan varassa. EU:n arvot ovat lnsimaisen, avoimen ja demokraattisen yhteiskunnan arvot, joissa ihmisoikeudet ja markkinatalous ovat keskeisess asemassa. Eurooppalaisissa maissa on mys aina annettu erityist arvoa yhteiskunnan koheesiolle ja solidaarisuudelle. EU:n perustana olevat arvot on ehk parhaiten tiivistetty kriteereiss, jotka mriteltiin Kpenhaminan huippukokouksessa keskuussa 1993, kun pohdittiin, mill edellytyksill It-ja Keski-Euroopan entiset sosialistiset maat voisivat liitty unionin jseniksi. Niden kriteerien mukaan EU:n jsenyyteen vaaditaan ensinnkin vakaat hallinnolliset instituutiot, jotka takaavat demokratian ja oikeusvaltion periaatteiden noudattamisen sek ihmisoikeuksien kunnioittamisen ja vhemmistjen suojelun. Jsenyyteen vaaditaan mys toimiva markkinatalous sek kyky kest unionissa esiintyvi kilpailupaineita ja markkinavoimia. Kolmanneksi unioniin pyrkivilt uusilta jsenilt vaaditaan kyky omaksua jsenyyteen liittyvt velvollisuudet, talous-ja rahaliiton tavoitteet thn mukaan lukien. Eurooppalaisen identiteetin ajatus on viime aikoina haastettu tavallaan kahdelta puolen. Yhtlt sek kansalaisyhteiskunnassa ett suurpolitiikassa on korostunut globaali nkkulma ja sen mukaiset globaalit vastuut esimerkiksi ympristkysymyksist, kehitysmaiden taloudesta ja maailmanlaajuisista turvallisuusongelmista. Tm kehitys vaatii mrittelemn eurooppalaisen identiteetin osana maailmanlaajuista poliittista kentt. Keskeinen kysymys on tllin, miten eurooppalaisuutta toteutetaan maailmannyttmll. Toisaalta Euroopan sisll on noussut yh vahvempia nationalistisia tai ainakin kansainvlistymisen vastaisia poliittisia virtauksia, jotka suhtautuvat negatiivisesti EU-integraatioon yleens, ja ainakin unionin itlaajenemiseen tai EU:n globaalin roolin kehittmiseen. Olennaista on, ett eurooppalainen identiteetti ei voi mryty negaatioiden kautta, eli niin, ett sanottaisiin, mik on ei-eurooppalaista ja sellaisena torjuttavaa. Eurooppalaisuuden kyttvoimana ei ole ei-eurooppalaisen torjuminen. Se ei myskn mrity sit kautta, ett eurooppalaisia vaadittaisiin hylkmn perinteiset kansalliset olemuksensa ja identiteettins. Eurooppalainen identiteetti on mriteltviss vain positiivisesti -niiden universaalien arvojen ja periaatteiden kautta, joille eurooppalainen integraatio perustuu. Vastaavalla tavalla voidaan todeta, ett kansallinen identiteetti ja eurooppalainen identiteetti eivt kilpaile keskenn. Tm johtuu siit, ett eurooppalainen poliittinen ja yhteiskunnallinen nyttm ja eurooppalaiset instituutiot juuri luovat parhaat edellytykset kunkin maan kansallisen kulttuurin ja kansallisten ominaispiirteiden toteuttamiseen. Kukoistavat yhteiskunnat ja kulttuurit eivt ole milloinkaan olleet niit, jotka pyrkivt eristytymn, vaan pinvastoin: juuri ne yhteiskunnat, jotka ovat parhaiten kyenneet luovaan vuorovaikutukseen kansainvlisess yhteisss ja taloudessa, ovat mys olleet sisllltn rikkaimpia. Suomalaisen kulttuurin ja kansallisen hermisen alkuaikoina tm nhtiin tavattoman selvsti, se kuuluu esimerkiksi Snellmanin kansallisuusksityksen perusteisiin. Ja kaunopuheisimmin asiasta on kirjoittanut Aleksis Kivi, jonka Seitsemn veljest on itse asiassa kertomus juuri siit, kuinka todellinen vapaus lopultakin syntyy -ei erillisyydest, vaan pinvastoin yhteisllisyydest ja kansalaisuudesta, vastuullisesta osallisuudesta maailmaan monista lhtkohdista ksin. Kun suomalaisen kansallisaatteen juuret ovat niss aatteissa, antaa se varmasti juuri meille erinomaiset lhtkohdat ymmrt kansallisen identiteetin ja eurooppalaisuuden suhde positiivisella tavalla. Lopuksi Arvoisat kuulijat, huolimatta eurooppalaisesta kulttuurien kirjosta on olemassa perimminen, hieman myyttinen eurooppalaisen yhtenisyyden ksite, jonka mys me suomalaiset jaamme. Se on mielestni helposti tunnistettavissa: itse tunnistin samankaltaisuudet kulttuurissa, instituutioissa ja tavoissa hmrsti jo nuorena tyttn kun olin ensin koululaisvaihdossa Schwarzwaldissa ja vhn vanhempana au pairina Pariisissa. Kokemani yhteisyys vain vahvistui niin 5. vuotena, jotka asuin Saksassa. Keski-eurooppalaisessa ajattelussa integraatio on perinteisesti merkinnyt ennen kaikkea rauhaa ja turvaa. Integraatio on poliittinen hanke  viisaiden unelma ja vkevien kunnianhimo. Yhteinen pyrkimys tehokkuuteen ja tuloksellisuuteen, kollektiivinen kunnianhimo, on saanut eurooppalaiset kansakunnat hyvksymn mryksi, sntj, rajoituksia ja pakotteita. Yhteishanke on tuonut ikivanhaan Eurooppa-ksitteeseen uutena aineksena toimintaan thtvn rakenteen. Tm ei ehk ole (ollut) yht selv meille suomalaisille  eik monille muillekaan myhemmin EU:iin mukaan tulleille  jotka olimme sodan jlkeen suunnanneet kiinnostuksemme muualle ja jotka nkivt hankkeen (ja joille hanke markkinoitiin) ennen kaikkea taloudellisena  yhteismarkkinoina. Tm ehk osaltaan selitt sen ett niin usein Suomessa otamme etisyytt muuhun Eurooppaan: me jopa puhumme "Suomesta ja Euroopasta" kun meidn pitisi puhua "Suomesta ja muusta Euroopasta". Tokihan mys me suomalaiset jaamme eurooppalaiset arvot ja mys integraation laajassa eurooppalaisessa mieless. Ja vaikka integraatio on vlill vaivalloista, se etenee  L'Europe difficile on osuva nimi integraation historiasta kertovalle teokselle, jota parhaillaan luen. Tyskentely ensin Euroopan rahapoliittisessa instituutissa (EMI) rahaliiton perustamiseksi tarvittavaa maiden lhentymist arvioiden ja sittemmin rahaliiton perustamisen jlkeen Euroopan keskuspankkia (EKP) pystyttmss osoitti minulle henkilkohtaisestikin kytnnn toiminnassa integraatiota ajavan vahvan tahdon ja vkevn intohimon  halun lyt toimivia ratkaisuja ja kompromisseja. Tuolloin minulle viimeistn valkeni, miten historiallisesti ainutlaatuisessa hankkeessa voimme olla mukana. Hankkeessa, jossa maat vapaaehtoisesti ja rauhanomaisesti luovuttavat suvereenisuuttaan yhteisen hyvn vuoksi. Euroopan integraatio poliittisena ohjelmana vaatii menestykseen eurooppalaisen kansalaisyhteiskunnan kehittymist. Ei euro sinns, vaan EU:n kansalaisten  siis mys meidn suomalaisten -mrtietoinen toiminta paremman maanosamme puolesta kantaa eurooppalaisuutta! Sismarkkinat ja yhteinen raha ovat itse asiassa vain keinoja. Olennaista on (Jacques Delorsin sanoin) eurooppalaisten tahto el yhdess ja rakentaa yhteist Eurooppaa, jonka rikkaus piilee sen monimuotoisuudessa, vahvuus sen solidaarisuudessa ja vaikutusvalta sen voimakkuudessa ja jalomielisyydess.

Title: Remarks in the 30th Economics Conference 'Competition of regions and integration in EMU'
text: Pankinjohtaja Sinikka Salon puhe: Remarks in the 30th Economics Conference 'Competition of regions and integration in EMU' . Speech . Friday 14June 2002,12:00 AM Regional policies anddifferences in economic structures In a globalising world, resources need to be continuously reallocated according to changes in demand for products, changing competitive positions and production methods. As technology has developed and economies have opened themselves up to trade, reallocation has taken place in much larger regional entities than earlier. There has also emerged a tendency for people and firms to cluster together with those that share their particular know-how and skills. Europeos economic geography is changing because of these trends and pressures known popularly as 'globalisation'. These regional developments do not originate from European integration, but are likely to have been strengthened through the increased competition it has brought about. At the same time integration through increased trade, financial market integration and more similar macro economic policy frameworks should have a synchronising impact on the economic performance of countries participating in the EU and in particular on the EMU. In general, assessments regarding performance of the monetary union during its first three and half years are positive. Alexander Italiener also concluded his illuminating presentation on differences in macroeconomic performance in the EMU by expressing 'moderate optimism'. Based on the Finnish experience, one can agree with the sentiment. Finland, as a small open economy with specialised industrial structure -paper and electronics (Nokia) -was generally regarded as most prone to asymmetric shocks. However, since the early years of the 1990s when the policies aiming at joining the EU and the EMU were adopted, the economic cycle has been more synchronised with the average cycle in the euro area, albeit with higher amplitude. Even during the last half of the 1990s, when GDP growth in Finland clearly exceeded the average growth in the EU, inflation remained rather close to that of the euro area average. Moreover, the recent rapid slowdown of demand in the IT-sector, which hit the Finnish economy more heavily than other euro area countries, did not significantly change the situation. The ECB monetary policy reaction to a decrease in interest rates was largely taken as being well-suited to the Finnish IT sector and the economy as a whole, while a credible common monetary policy prevented the difficulties of the IT.sector from spilling over into other sectors in the economy. In the following, I am going to focus on differences in regional structures, questions of specialisation, and regional policies. I do not even try to answer the difficult question of how much divergence in structures is sustainable, posed in the title of this panel session -I refer to the 'common understanding' that polarisation is bad and should be avoided. According to recent studies, clustering and specialisation need not lead to polarisation, because as it is argued 'most regions should be able to specialise in something'. However, risk of polarisation cannot be ruled out, if policies try to freeze existing patterns of economic structures although they are no longer competitive. Therefore, issues of regional and cohesion policy have become increasingly important on the policy agenda in the EU, in the wake of enlargement. *** The accession countries are much poorer than the existing EU countries. The planned enlargement of the EU into a union of 25 member states will therefore necessarily entail a dramatic increase in economic and social inequality in the Union, both between Member States and between regions. Even though this increase in inequality is, in a sense, only a notional consequence of the change in boundaries, the political consequences for the EU are by no means notional. Increased differences will be duly reflected in political agenda. The allocation of the EU structural and cohesion funds is where the conflict of interest will be seen at its clearest, but similar tensions have arisen or are likely to arise in other fields, such as agricultural policy, freedom of movement, incomes policies etc. There is, I expect, a broad consensus about what could be called the two-pillar approach for cohesion policy in the EU. The first pillar is the recognition by less prosperous nations and regions that they bear the primary responsibility in tackling their own poverty, which is crucial, for it is not only good economic policy, but is key to good governance. The second pillar is that the EU must provide support for its least developed regions. The distinction between these two pillars is of course clear only in theory. In practice national and community policies are highly interrelated, especially as far as regional policy in its strictest meaning is concerned. But nevertheless, it is conceptually and politically important to clearly bear this separation of responsibilities in mind. With regard to national policies, in a welfare state well-developed public services and high level, highly progressive taxation tend to reduce inequality in society in general and consequently reduce regional inequality. In Finland, for example, the poorest of the country's 20 regions contribute, in the form of taxes to the central government budget, less than 70 % of what they receive from the budget in the form of expenditure, whereas some other regions pay some 50 % more than they receive. The effect of this redistribution of income on regional income differences is substantial. I doubt whether many accession countries at their present level of development could benefit much from an immediate adoption of a full-scale welfare-state and it is likely that they have to tolerate much greater regional differences than most of the present member countries. But there may be something to be learnt from the underlying ideology of the (efficient) welfare state and some of its features could perhaps be adopted in the new member states without too heavy a budgetary burden. In particular, in view of the high level of unemployment and rapid ageing of the population, one of the main challenges for the accession countries is to increase labour force participation and employment. This requires supportive infrastructure and services to be provided by a welfare state, notably such as facilities for childcare and care of the elderly that particularly support the participation of women in the work force. Wage moderation and increased wage differentiation according to productivity and skills are both essential ingredients in any policies targeted at higher growth and higher employment. Wage flexibility will remain important even after the elimination of fundamental labour market imbalances, especially for countries which aim joining the euro area in the relatively near future. In the monetary union each country has to live up to the goal of price stability. Countries joining the monetary union must have institutions, economic structures and policy discipline suited for specifically that. Meanwhile it should be stressed that for less prosperous accession countries, the main policy priority is to adopt an over-all policy framework that is strongly oriented towards high and sustainable economic growth. This will entail encouraging new activities and combinations of activities, but regional policy objectives should be subordinated to aggregate economic policy objectives. *** At the European Union level, one of the key issues in the policy debate is the establishment of a financial framework for the enlargement process. It is vital that some of the issues are solved for the period 2004-2006, but the main problems seem to lie with the next financial perspective 2007-2013. It seems that the continuation of present community policies after enlargement would imply substantial budget pressures. There is a risk that the current limit of 1.27% of GDP for the Communityos own resources would be exceeded and by the end of the period this could be an excess that is more than merely marginal. Instead of increasing the European citizens' tax-burden, efficiency of the Communityos policies should be more in focus. The main targets for improvements are the Common Agricultural Policy and Cohesion Policies, by the simple fact that they together take up some 80 % of total Community expenditure. It is generally accepted that the Community Cohesion Policy should continue to target the least developed regions. After accession into the EU, the least developed areas will be in the new member countries and thus structural and cohesion funds will be redirected to these countries. This will imply substantial transfers from the EU budget to the new member countries. Great attention is needed to ensure that the recipients have the capacity to absorb them. Under the current rules for the period 2000-06, transfers from the Structural and Cohesion Funds are limited up to a maximum of 4 % of national GDP a year in all Member States. In view of the limited administrative and absorption capacity of most of the new EU-countries, the Commission proposal in the recent information note Common Financial Framework 2004-2006 for the Accession Negotiations, confirming the same ceiling for overall structural financial support for 2004-2006, is a step in the right direction. This ceiling would seem appropriate even after 2006. Strict application of limits without exceptions would help prevent misunderstandings and the culture of rent-seeking in the new member states. In this regard one might question whether it is helpful to refer possibilities of additional financing in exceptional cases, such as 'projects of a particular Community interest in relevant circumstances', as suggested by the Commission in its First progress report on economic and social cohesion. To avoid the risk that cohesion policies freeze existing patterns of economic activity and thereby increase the likelihood of the polarisation they seek to prevent, refocusing of cohesion policies would be needed to contribute to the objective of increasing regional growth prospects and competitiveness. Instead of resisting inevitable changes, the authorities should perhaps even aim at speeding up the adjustment of the economy to the new economic.political environment. The experiences of some countries suggest that rapid adaptation to changing circumstances in the form of even large migration flows is feasible and in the end may even be optimal. One approach to regional policy, that has sometimes been successful, is to favour viable growth centres. As an example, much of the northern part of Finland has become or is in the process of becoming very sparsely populated. At the same time, the main centre of the area, Oulu, has successfully transformed itself, over only a couple of decades, from a stagnant smokestack-industry town into a dynamic business metropolis specialising in mobile and other information technology as well as biotechnology. This transformation has, without doubt, been helped by active regional policies that focused on the relatively rich local centre and not on the whole area. A decisive move was probably the establishment of the University of Oulu, which started its operation in 1959. In particular, the faculties of technology and medicine have played a central role as promoters of local growth and have close connections with the local high-tech companies. *** In my contribution to the debate I have highlighted some aspects of regional policies in preventing polarisation in economic structures and performance. It is important to avoid policies that would freeze existing structures of economic activity if they were not viable. Let me finish my contribution by referring to recent discussions on institutional reforms: We need more transparency and efficiency, also in the administration of the communityos regional policies, which is very complex. At the same time, very little is known of the effects of different programmes. It is important to recall the need for transparent and efficient programme evaluation, detection of fraud or non-conformity with financial rules, and harmonised application of sanctions in the different Member States in the case of shortcomings. More effective use of regional policies also requires greater synergy with other Community policies in the areas of research, innovation and education.

Title: International Household & Family Research Conference
text: Pankinjohtaja Sinikka Salon puhe: International Household & Family Research Conference . Speech . Friday 19July 2002, 12:00 AM Consumers and families as market actors I am very honoured to have been invited to give this speech at your conference dinner. The role of consumers and families as members of global consumption society and as market partners, which is the focus of your conference is indeed a very well chosen topic. I do not have competence to make any in depth comments on the very interesting and topical items on your agenda. But I would like to start by highlighting the role of consumers and consumer interest groups as market actors in a global context, thus relating your conference also to the "hot" issue of globalisation. Our daily life has become more global. Technological development has greatly favoured information transmission and mass media, and thus new cultural tendencies and market information are spreading rapidly and reaching more and more people. It is easy for example through internet -to find issues and things we are interested in from all around the world irrespective the nature of our interests be it cultural, commercial, entertaining etc. The process has proceeded so far that it seems justified to say that we are now living in a "global village". (This term was introduced as early as in the 1960s by the "media guru" Marshal McLuhan, while presenting his vision of the impact of developments in mass media on daily life of people.) One aspect of this development is that the scope of consumer choice has expanded and the share of goods, and increasingly also services, marketed globally in the average consumption basket has increased greatly. Comparison of prices and purchases of goods over country borders has enhanced market competition. Consumers have benefited from lower prices, but perhaps even more important also from the point of view of a consumer -have been the dynamic effects that follow from opening of global markets for innovative and well-operated firms. I have no doubt that these changes in consumption patterns follow from rational decisions by well-informed market actors rather than say, the marketing efforts of large multinational companies and that the globalisation process has made a significant contribution to the welfare of most of us. We can now see clearly the benefits from the globalisation in developed world, but of course the greatest potential for improvement is in the developing world. The emerging market economies have already taken significant steps in gaining access to the global market. Being in the position of a latecomer, they have been able to adopt directly modern technology in consumption, without having to travel through all generations of technology. For example, consumers in developing countries are directly adopting radio-based mobile phone technology, skipping heavy and capital intensive fixed-line telecommunication systems altogether. The pace of the diffusion process can be astonishing. To mention just one example, the number of mobile phone users in China increased in June this year by 4,8 million, that is about the size of the population of Finland. Another, often overlooked aspect of globalisation is that markets reflect not only the needs and preferences but also the knowledge and the moral of global villagers. In the end, it is the consumers who decide in what kind also ecologically and socially -of village we live. There are now many examples which show that the opinions of global consumers, with regard to what products are produced and how, cannot be neglected. In order to maintain their image and brands, multinational companies cannot isolate their production in developing countries from the ethical values of their consumers in the developed world. Globalisation is a deep process with far-reaching consequences for practically the whole population of the world. It is associated with many challenges, and its benefits are not shared equally by all. But overall, I am rather confident that technological change and globalisation taken as a whole will bring with themselves a tremendous increase in the living standards of the now poorest people. While saying this, I admit that it is a risky business to make forecasts. Therefore, being a central banker and thus highly risk averse, it would be wiser for me to refrain from speculating any further about future developments in this field. Therefore, I am now going to turn to issues relating more closely to central banking. *** In Europe, economic integration has proceeded further than in other parts of the world. To some extent, European integration is a reflection of the broader process known as globalisation, and its underlying forces are much the same. But there are also significant differences. The most prominent one is that while globalisation has mainly -but of course not only -been a market-led process, the European integration has to a large extent been created by a deliberate political will. An important difference is also that Europe has created community institutions under the umbrella of the European Union. Some of these institutions have significant union-wide powers, whereas the global governance is almost entirely based on voluntarily intergovernmental co-operation. When the European integration process was initiated, more than 50 years ago, memories of World War II were still vivid. The main purpose was to create an environment of economic prosperity and stability that would prevent any future wars between Europeans. The main tool chosen to achieve this goal was deep trade integration and the gradual convergence of economic policies. Indeed, from the very start the Treaty explicitly envisaged the creation of a common market based on the four freedoms of movements: goods, services, workers and capital, which were finally laid down in the Single Market Programme of 1985. After the adoption of this Programme it became increasingly clear that the potential of the internal market could not be fully exploited while the relatively high transaction costs linked to currency conversion and the uncertainties associated with exchange rate fluctuations persisted. The existence of separate currencies and different exchange rates indeed appears to be a barrier to trade and in particular to the retail trade, as has been witnessed by recent empirical economic research. The reasons for this are likely to be of micro-economical rather than of macro-economic origin, such as transaction costs and different information problems including the difficulty of price comparisons. From this point of view, the single currency should be seen as a necessary complement, the crowning achievement of the Single Market, as well as, as facilitating further economic integration. Currently, the euro area comprises a single market of twelve EU countries with free movement of capital, labour, goods and services and with a single currency for more than 300 million Europeans. In this respect the euro area is comparable with the two major economies in the world, the US and Japan. *** Monetary policy in the euro area countries is on the responsibility of the European Central Bank. According to the EU Treaty, the main goal of the monetary policy of the ECB is the maintenance of price stability in the euro area. The clear priority given to the price stability objective is based on the fact that monetary policy will make the best overall contribution to improving economic prospects and raising living standards by maintaining price stability in a credible and lasting way. The ECB does not have either the means or the responsibility for ensuring a high level of employment and real growth, beyond the positive impact of price stability. The European Central Bank has defined price stability as increase in consumer prices in the euro area, as measured by the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP), less than 2 % annually. Many people think that a positive inflation target is better than stability in price level because inflation is less dangerous than deflation. But a much more convincing argument for the ECB definition of price stability is that it allows for some inaccuracy in the measurement of the price level. Most central statistical offices are not able to properly account for improvements in the quality of consumer goods and therefore published consumer price indices -including the HICP -give a downward biased estimate of the true inflation. Furthermore, the ECB definition indicates a medium term objective, not to be adhered mechanistically from month to month or even necessarily annually. From the point of view of the consumer, price stability is useful because it reduces noise from price comparisons. Empirical evidence has shown convincingly that low inflation is closely related to stable inflation. The consumer is therefore less uncertain about real interest rates and other inter-temporal relative prices in an environment of stabile prices than in inflationary conditions. Empirical evidence also shows that the variability of relative prices correlates positively with the rate of inflation. Therefore the consumer is also less uncertain about contemporaneous relative prices in an environment of stabile prices than in inflationary conditions. *** Before joining the EMU (Economic and Monetary Union), the problem of asymmetric business cycles was discussed in Finland and elsewhere. Some sceptics believe that because in a monetary union there is no national monetary policy available to counteract asymmetric shocks to the economy, monetary union cannot last very long. For example, Professor Milton Friedman said recently in the context of his 90th birthday that he expects that the EMU will have a much shorter life than he has had. He said that it is good if the monetary union in Europe will last for 15 years. Here I must say that I cannot agree with him. To some extent, I can rely on empirical evidence. The Finnish business cycle was, in the past, usually very different from the "core" European countries. Therefore, the worry was that common monetary policy, geared to "average" European needs, would be sometimes too lax and sometimes too tight for Finland. The former situation would cause inflation to get out of control; in the latter case, policy would curtail aggregate demand too much and could cause an unnecessary recession. I do not want to sound imprudent, but I think that the experience, which we have so far, suggests that these fears were probably exaggerated. Economic fluctuations in Finland have become significantly more synchronised with the rest of the euro area, although the amplitude of the fluctuations in our economy are still steeper. The past inflationary character of our economy was mostly due to weak credibility of our monetary policy. Now this problem does not exist any more. Being a member in the EMU with a credible monetary policy has finally ended devaluation speculations and brought about the credible price stability that is needed for solutions to build sustainable welfare. It is thus not surprising that wage and price developments in Finland during the past years have been very encouraging. *** Ladies and Gentlemen, Let me once again congratulate you for the very interesting topic of your Conference. It goes without saying that choices of consumers and families are decisive to economic developments. Consumer has always been a King, and will remain so, even increasingly in a globalised world. Without denying the role of policy makers I as a central banker -would like to highlight the important contribution that the stability oriented monetary policy can make by providing a stability "anchor" for consumers' decisions on consumption and investment -it is thus very much up to consumers to decide whether consumption and production are ecologically and socially sustainable and how the welfare in the world is achieved. In the end, markets reflect our needs and skills, but also our moral. I wish you all the success in your conference and hope that you also have some time to enjoy your stay in Helsinki.

Tuesday 3September 2002, 12:00 AM Financial market trends and the future of Europe Ladies and gentlemen, my intention is to discuss with you the future direction of European development, particularly with regard to the angle of the financial markets. The subject is very much the subject, not only for me and the other representatives of the central banks, but for the european economy as a whole and also for EU policy and for all Europeans. Many of the profound processes shaping the future of Europe are, by name, very closely linked to the functioning and development of financial markets. The connection is two-way. As European political structures change, the financial markets reflect changes, and I believe that in ten years' time the European financial markets will be in many respects different from today's. On the other hand, developments in financial markets will also have an impact on how Europe can reform and develop in the coming years. In particular, financial market policy plays a key role in the EU's efforts to build a more economically coherent and dynamic Europe. *** One of the main upheavals on our continent is the forthcoming enlargement of the EU. It is, of course, part of the economic and political changes in Europe that began twenty years ago since the collapse of Communism. The EU's enlargement project shows that changes are continuing, not only in the applicant countries, but throughout Europe, and therefore also apply to all current EU countries. Just think of the very topical debate on the reform of the EU's political structures: it has become more intense precisely because the EU's member state is growing in the last few years. The expansion of the financial markets is linked in particular to the fact that the role of the financial markets is the huge influx of investment efforts that the future new Member States will need to reach the old EU countries in terms of the level of development and efficiency of their economies. At the more technical level, successful implementation of enlargement requires, in particular, the intensification of the banking and financial sectors in the applicant countries and the development of their financial supervision. sms is Chelkeys, so that in a few years' time the frenzy of EU enlargement is not followed by a hangover of financial crises. Another process of change that is taking place at the same time is the guerrilla integration of the EU, which is constantly progressing and its promotion is, as we know, a key objective of common policy. This process is now, with the completion of the enrolment market and monetary union, moving towards greater integration of European financial markets. Integration concerns, inter alia, securities markets, payment systems and markets for various banking and financial services. It also has an impact on politics: the role of the financial markets in the economy is so central that, as they merge with the rest of the economic policy cooperation of the EU countries, there will be a single more demand. Financial supervision is at the forefront of the Czechskin point, but many other areas of economic policy, such as taxation, are also at the forefront of the debate. It can be said that, right now, the integration of the financial markets is one of the key drivers of European political integration. In relation to Chelse, it coexists with the new challenges of security and environmental policy. This is the third key process which, even in the future, will have a profound impact on European economic and social policy and also on the functioning of the financial markets. However, the effects of economic integration on the financial markets are not clear in themselves, but depend to a large extent on how economic policy solves the problems of economic policy and labour policy. It is probable that the d will be substantially increased in Europe over the next decade. It is therefore predicted that this will make the European securities markets, and in particular the stock markets, much larger in volume than they have been up to now. The growing importance of elske funds and dssstiside as investors continues to influence the distribution of economic power in the business sector, including the governance and operation of large companies. The four-year-old key process I would like to mention is technological development. Although the worst ohypeo environment for new information technologies has been eroded in the last couple of years, it is clear that its effects on the economy and society are only just beginning. It is obvious that new technologies and the development of the information society are having an impact on European financial markets by changing the way financial markets operate: I am referring, for example, to trade in financial services on information networks or to the development of payment in financial services. Thus, technology affects the marketing, production and distribution of financial services. However, the fact that the functioning of the financial markets has a decisive influence on the dynamism of the European economy, i.e. europe's ability to develop and adopt technological innovations. It is precisely in the autumn that the convergence of the financial markets and, through it, the improvement of efficiency is at the heart of the eu's overall strategy. As well as expectations about the future significance of the Shkssi trade, as well as confidence in the ability of financial markets to sift through the best and most viable technology projects, there have been serious setbacks in the last two years or so. The prestige of Internet and mobile technology has plummeted and many projects for which funding was previously available have proved to be disappointing. At the same time, more emphasis has been placed on the ability of the financial markets to cope with the assessment of far-reaching projects and the supervision of management. Epsilyksis and criticism have been voiced, particularly in the United States, but there is no reason to blindly trust that conditions in Europe are better in terms of market efficiency than on the other side of the Atlantic. However, in this context, it must be said straight away that the role of the financial markets in directing finance cannot be easily compensated for. For example, the excesses associated with the financing of the technology boom show shortcomings in the efficiency and ssntelysss of the functioning of companies and financial markets, but it does not suggest that the functioning of the financial markets is relevant to the success of the economy: lsksy is precisely anti-banking. In the light of recent experience, legislation, central banks and other public authorities need to invest more in financial market policy and the architecture of financial market infrastructures than had been the case in the last decade. *** The importance of the development of financial markets as central to the future of Europe as a whole is well reflected in the EU's economic development strategies. The Lisbon European Council in 2000 criticised the development of a strategy for the EU for the next decade of the 2000s. At the time, the strategy was summed up in the demand that, over the course of a decade, Europe should become the most competitive and dynamic knowledge-based economy in the world, capable of sustaining economic growth, creating new and better jobs and increasing social cohesion. The Lisbon Strategy was designed to enable the EU to meet the challenges of global competition and the development of information technology. However, the strategy does not only focus on the economy and technology, but also wanted to emphasise the social dimension of the structural change sought. In the strategy, the economy is not an end in itself, but while pursuing a dynamic economy based on knowledge and technology, the desired structural change is to be integrated into a European model of society with an emphasis on social cohesion. At the heart of the strategy, as well as economic dynamism and social cohesion, is the improvement of employment and the integration of cohesion. In formulating the strategy, Europe's strengths were the excellent macroeconomic stability achieved through the institutions of economic and monetary union and the excellent level of education. On the other hand, the persistently high level of employment and underdevelopment of the services sector, particularly in the field of information technology, are problems. Another problem is the scarcity of high-quality it experts in Europe. The strategy pays particular attention to the financial markets. This is due to the fact that, in a market economy, it is the long-term functioning of the financial markets that determines the achievement of the strategy's objectives, the designation of the size and orientation of new investment and, consequently, the long-term growth of productivity. The strategy states that efficient and efficient financial markets will support growth by improving the allocation of ssoms and lowering the cost of transactions. It therefore plays a key role in the development of new ideas and in the development of new ideas and in the promotion of enterprise in Europe. In particular, the development of the risk finance market is a prerequisite for innovative SMEs, and thus also for the emergence of new jobs. That is why the strategy places the emphasis on the implementation of a truly integrated siphon market in the financial services sector. There is a great deal to be gained from those companies, which are in principle large enough to attract the interest of foreign investors, but still so small that the marketing of shares abroad has been too expensive until the scale of their activities. An EU group of experts chaired by Pehr Gyllenhammar has estimated that by simply improving the functioning of financial markets, economic growth in the EU countries could be accelerated by half a per cent per annum, and by some extent more than that. There is certainly a great deal of room for interpretation and uncertainties in relation to such estimates, but the impact on growth of this kind would, of course, be of great importance for europe's rigour, competitiveness and also for the budgetary finances of European countries. On the other hand, the stability of the financial markets, if badly ksy, could cause not only economic damage, but also setbacks and eps stability in the political development of Europe. Financial and banking crises tend to destroy not only the economic pssoma and jobs, but also the political and social pssoma, and therefore the stable functioning of the market is a broad social issue. What, then, are the most important development needs of the market? The main problem facing European financial markets today is considered to be the fragmentation that continues to afflict them. Despite the adoption of the single currency and the united states, the financial markets in the EU operate in a common way in many respects with national differentiation. The most advanced convergence has been in the short-term money market for banks, which are already integrated. The situation on the securities markets is worse, due, inter alia, to national differences in legislation and the fragmentation of securities settlement and settlement systems. International securities trading is much more cumbersome and expensive than national securities trading within the EU. In particular, the integration of the stock market is still less well than that of the bond market. This has most recently been the focus of alexandre Lamfalussy's group reports, on the basis of which reforms are being pushed forward. The situation on the financial services market is still more favourable than on the stock market, and national borders have a major impact on trade in financial services, even within the euro area. The European payment system is also very fragmented. Although a different standardisation process has been carried out for a long time, paying from one EU country to another is much more difficult, slower and more expensive than paying in one country, especially for households and small businesses. It is well known that the Commission has intervened with its regulation on the pricing of payment services, which as early as next year (from 1.7.2003) restricts the right of banks to charge higher fees for cross-border credit transfers than for domestic payments. Regulation alone is not enough to fix the problem, and that is why it is a reason why fragmentation in the payment system is detrimental to the real common market, not only in financial services, but also in many other products. The payment system is the infrastructure for the functioning of all markets. Another problem with the financial markets in the euro area, along with their fragmentation, is the lack of efficiency. The cost structure of banks and securities securities is quite heavy in many European countries, for example compared to the United States or, for example, the Nordic countries, and there is a fairly widespread consensus that there is potential for significant costs in the production of financial services. In part, inefficiency is the result of market fragmentation, which has restricted competition and made an expensive cost structure possible. The question of costs is also a question of stability, because only a profitable and cost-effective banking sector can generate sufficient income financing and ensure that its solvency is sufficient for a long period of time. The third problem facing European financial markets is that, as markets develop and integrate, financial supervision threatens to develop and develop afterwards. After all, European financial supervision is based on the so-called 'financial supervision'. the principle of the home country, so that a greater proportion of the international activities of the financial industry are controlled by an authority in a country other than the one in which the service is sold. In more cases, deposit insurance may also be the responsibility of a country other than the one in which the risks that led to the problems were taken or where the eligible depositors reside. At the same time, the decline of banking-securities and insurance activities poses new challenges for supervisory organisations. The multiplicity of authorities places great demands on their flow of information and operational cooperation. These requirements will increase as the integration of financial markets in Europe progresses in line with the objectives. *** The implementation of the Lisbon strategy in financial market policy was to be based on a programme adopted by the EU the previous year, which specifically aimed at making financial markets in the EU more coherent and efficient. The programme is the FSAP d Financial Services Action Plan d which was adopted in 1999 and runs until 2005. In total, FSAP initially included 42 different proposals for measures to create a single, efficient and stable financial market in Europe. The proposals sought to contribute to four strategic objectives: The wholesale financial market was converging in the EU; The development of an open and secure financial services market; ensuring the continued stability of EU financial markets; The removal of tax obstacles in line with the financial markets The first of the strategic objectives of the action plan is a truly convergent European wholesale financial market. This is developing projects to focus on the securities and derivatives markets where fragmentation problems are most serious. According to the FSAP, the availability of investment securities across the EU is uniform, so that one prospectus is sufficient for the sale of securities throughout the EU. The information on the financial statements of companies is the same as the so-called financial information. on the basis of the IAS standard. The international operation of the Eu ropean Funds must be facilitated. The functioning of securities settlement systems needs to be improved and their costs reduced. In the financial services market, the FSAP wants to make it easier to trade financial services such as mortgages and insurance in eu countries. In this region, the proposals for the development of the FSAP concern, above all, the implementation of consumer protection in cross-border trade in financial services. Another common priority is the creation of an integrated payment system in the EU. On the financial stability side, the FSAP and the supervisory authorities in the EU are essentially cooperating. The programme also includes the development of regulations on the reorganisation of credit institutions and insurance companies. On the taxation side, the FSAP aims to achieve a partial level of taxation of interest income, which should also be applied in all Member States. For example, the aim is to ensure that differences in the tax treatment of deposits do not lead to comparable competition in the banking market. *** Since the adoption of the FSAP and the Lisbon Strategy, a great deal has happened. Within the EU, the A significant number of FSAP initiatives have already progressed to the level of directives or regulations, although much of the work has already been done to promote the integration of financial markets and a significant number of initiatives within the framework of the FSAP. This has to be done largely by the economy. It should be remembered, by name, that the financial world does not consist of developmental, top-level strategies, not directives, but business operations. That is why the FSAP and other such programmes only prove their worth in the European economic test. For example, the European banking sector has reacted to the EU regulation on the pricing of international payments traffic, to which I mentioned earlier, by setting up a joint venture called the European Payments Council, which has set itself the objective of achieving the vision of a single European payments area. Among other things, Khrjests is advocating the establishment of a pan-European payment clearing house during the Lshi years. This would be a milestone in the real integration of the European payment systems, which would require a substantial reduction in the cost of production of international payment services. While integration and development programmes have been developed and worked on, the environment has changed rapidly. Most of the news has been bad for the financial markets. Globally, growth expectations for the IT and telecommunications sectors have declined. The slowdown in economic growth has weakened the budgetary balance of states everywhere. The terrorist attacks that took place a year ago on 11 September have brought security issues and global security cooperation to the forefront. Most recently, attention has focused on the question of what kind of information the financial markets rely on. The accounting scandals that started in Enrono and WorldComo have shaken confidence in the management of companies and in the market information they distribute, especially in the United States, but it seems clear that the lessons of these events cannot be ignored in Europe either. If the EU's financial market policy were based solely on the olaissez faireo d-style dismantling of the market, the events of the last two years would certainly have caused great difficulties in trying to achieve uniformity and to make European financial markets more efficient. However, the FSAP and other market infrastructure reforms are still progressing, mostly in line with the original objectives and guidelines. The EU's programme for the integration and enhancement of financial markets has so far proved to be a good idea. This is due to the fact that the programmes have focused on building a coherent legal and other infrastructure on which the market could operate efficiently (openly and competitively) and at the same time convergently. The key, then, is that the opening up of competition should be part of the process of making the market more stable, more stable and safer. Similar developments in the SSS are also carried out at the global level within the IMF, the BIS and the Financial Stability Forum, but the problems awaiting their solution are, of course, greater than those of the EU's guerrillas, where the countries' points of contact with each other and their political interdependence with each other is greater than in global cooperation. The single monetary policy in the EMU area has also contributed to the development of european financial markets. The construction of a single financial market is intended to transform the economy of the eu as a whole, including, of course, the current applicant countries. The intended impact will not only extend to credit institutions and processors and the rest of the financial sector, but to industry, trade, services and public finances. As a result of this change, all sectors will be radically Europeanised, as markets and corporate finance and ownership structures in Europe will merge more and more together. The building will also be transformed by the institutions, i.e. the governments and authorities of the EU countries, as well as the Commission, the ECB and other joint institutions. The importance of a common policy and competences at Community level will be emphasised. The suspense and supervision of the financial markets require such a high degree of political and authority cooperation that, for its part, there is also a strong deepening of political integration within the EU. All in all, the development of financial markets is at the heart of the EU's economic policy cooperation over the years. At the same time, this is an excellent example of the hysdys that European integration can achieve. Epsilin, that without a common EU policy in the region, the economy of our continent would hardly be able to find a common, open and secure financial market in the future. The EU's single policy on the financial markets will also strengthen the negotiating position of Europeans in global for a, where European stocks can gain the weight they deserve on the basis of the economic weight of our continent.
