Viime aikojen kokemusten perusteella lainstjien, keskuspankkien ja muiden viranomaisten on panostettava rahoitusmarkkinapolitiikkaan ja rahoitusmarkkinoiden perusrakenteiden arkkitehtuuriin enemmn kuin viime vuosikymmenell oli tehty. *** Rahoitusmarkkinoiden kehittmisen koko Euroopan tulevaisuuden kannalta keskeiseksi nhty merkitys tulee hyvin esiin EU:n talouden kehittmisstrategioissa. Lissabonissa kevll 2000 kokoontunut Eurooppa-neuvosto mritteli EU:lle kehittmisstrategian 2000-luvun ensi vuosikymmeneksi. Strategian sislt tiivistettiin tuolloin vaatimukseen, ett tmn vuosikymmenen aikana Euroopasta tulisi maailman kilpailukykyisin ja dynaamisin tietopohjainen talous, joka kykenee yllpitmn kestv talouskasvua, luomaan uusia ja parempia typaikkoja ja lismn sosiaalista yhteenkuuluvuutta. Lissabonin strategia laadittiin, jotta EU voisi vastata globaalin kilpailun ja tietotekniikan kehityksen haasteisiin. Strategiassa ei kuitenkaan ole keskeist vain talous ja teknologia, vaan siin haluttiin niden ohella nimenomaan korostaa tavoitellun rakennemuutoksen sosiaalista dimensiota. Strategiassa talous ei ole itsetarkoitus, vaan samalla kun tavoitellaan dynaamista, tiedon ja teknologian hydyntmiseen perustuvaa taloutta, tavoiteltu rakennemuutos tahdotaan yhdist eurooppalaiseen, sosiaalista yhteenkuuluvuutta painottavaan yhteiskuntamalliin. Strategiassa keskeiseksi sek talouden dynamiikan ett sosiaalisen yhteenkuuluvuuden kannalta nhdn tyllisyyden parantaminen ja syrjytymisen ehkiseminen. Strategiaa muotoiltaessa Euroopan vahvuuksina mainittiin talous-ja rahaliiton instituutioiden avulla saavutettu erinomainen makrotaloudellinen vakaus ja vestn hyv koulutustaso. Toisaalta ongelmina nhtiin sitkesti korkeana pysyttelev tyttmyys ja palvelusektorin alikehittyneisyys, erityisesti tietotekniikan hydyntmisen osalta. Ongelmaksi nhtiin mys korkeatasoisten tietotekniikan osaajien niukkuus Euroopassa. Strategiassa kiinnitetn erityist huomiota rahoitusmarkkinoihin. Tm johtuu siit, ett markkinataloudessa juuri rahoitusmarkkinoiden toiminta pitklti ratkaisee strategian tavoitteiden toteutumisen, nimittin uusien investointien mrn ja suuntautumisen ja siten mys tuottavuuden pitkn aikavlin kasvun. Strategiassa todetaan, ett tehokkaat ja lpinkyvt rahoitusmarkkinat tukevat kasvua parantamalla pomien kohdentumista ja alentamalla pomakustannuksia. Niill on siksi keskeinen rooli uusien ideoiden kehittelyss ja kyttnotossa sek yrittjyyden edistmisess Euroopassa. Erityisesti riskirahoituksen markkinoiden kehittminen on trket innovatiivisille PK -yrityksille, ja siten mys uusien typaikkojen synnylle. Siksi strategiassa korostetaan todella yhtenisten sismarkkinoiden toteuttamisen trkeytt mys rahoituspalvelusektorilla. Erityisen paljon voitettavaa on niill yhtiill, jotka ovat periaatteessa kyllin suuria herttkseen ulkomaisten sijoittajien kiinnostusta, mutta kuitenkin sen verran pieni, ett osakkeiden markkinointi ulkomaille on thn asti ollut niiden toiminnan laajuuteen nhden liian kallista. Pehr Gyllenhammarin johdolla toiminut EU:n asiantuntijaryhm on arvioinut, ett pelkstn rahoitusmarkkinoiden toimintaa tehostamalla voitaisiin EU-maiden taloudellista kasvua kiihdytt puolella prosentilla vuodessa, ehk jonkin verran ylikin. Tllaisiin arvioihin liittyvt tulkinnanvaraisuudet ja epvarmuudet ovat varmasti suuria, mutta tt luokkaa olevalla kasvuvaikutuksella olisi tietenkin erittin suuri mynteinen merkitys Euroopan tyllisyyden, kilpailukyvyn ja mys Euroopan valtioiden budjettitalouden kannalta. Toisaalta rahoitusmarkkinoiden hirit ja epvakaus, jos huonosti ky, voisivat aiheuttaa paitsi taloudellista vahinkoa, mys takaiskuja ja epvakautta Euroopan poliittisessa kehityksess. Rahoitus-ja pankkikriiseiss tapaa tuhoutua paitsi taloudellista pomaa ja typaikkoja, mys poliittista ja sosiaalista pomaa, ja siksi markkinoiden vakaa toiminta on laaja yhteiskunnallinen kysymys. Mitk sitten ovat markkinoiden trkeimmt kehittmistarpeet? Euroopan rahoitusmarkkinoiden ehk suurimpana ongelmana nykyn on pidettv niit edelleenkin vaivaavaa pirstoutuneisuutta. Huolimatta yhteisen rahan kyttnotosta ja yhdest, yhtenisest rahapolitiikasta rahoitusmarkkinat toimivat EU-alueella yh monessa suhteessa kansallisesti eriytynein. Pisimmlle yhtenistyminen on edennyt pankkien vlisill lyhyen rahan markkinoilla, jotka ovatkin kytnnss jo tysin integroituneet. Arvopaperimarkkinoilla tilanne on huonompi, mik johtuu muun muassa lainsdnnn kansallisista eroista sek arvopaperikaupan selvitys-ja toimitusjrjestelmien hajanaisuudesta. Kansainvlinen arvopaperikauppa on EU-alueen sisllkin nin ollen paljon hankalampaa ja kalliimpaa kuin kansallinen. Erityisesti osakemarkkinat ovat integroituneet viel heikommin kuin joukkovelkakirjamarkkinat. Thn on viimeksi kiinnitetty huomiota Alexandre Lamfalussyn tyryhmn raporteissa, jolta pohjalta uudistuksia pyritn viemn eteenpin. Rahoituspalvelujen vhittismarkkinoilla tilanne on viel eptyydyttvmpi kuin osakemarkkinoilla ja kansalliset rajat vaikuttavat kytnnss erittin paljon rahoituspalvelujen vhittiskauppaan jopa euroalueen sisll. Mys Euroopan maksujrjestelm on erittin pirstaleinen. Vaikka erilaista standardointityt on tehty jo pitkn, kytnnss maksaminen EU-maasta toiseen on paljon hankalampaa, hitaampaa ja kalliimpaa kuin maksaminen yhden maan sisll, varsinkin kotitalouksien ja pienyritysten maksuissa. Thn asiaan Komissio on tunnetusti skettin puuttunut maksupalvelujen hinnoittelua koskevalla regulaatiollaan, joka jo ensi vuonna (1.7.2003 alkaen) rajoittaa pankkien oikeutta peri rajat ylittvist tilisiirroista korkeampia palkkioita kuin kotimaisista maksuista. Regulaatio ei yksin riit ongelmaa korjaamaan, ja siksi on syyt pelt, ett maksujrjestelmn pirstoutuneisuus haittaa psemist todellisiin yhtenismarkkinoihin ei vain rahoituspalvelujen, vaan monien muidenkin tuotteiden markkinoilla. Maksujrjestelmthn ovat kaikkien markkinoiden toiminnan kannalta vlttmtn infrastruktuuri. Toinen euroalueen rahoitusmarkkinoiden ongelma, niiden pirstoutuneisuuden ohella siis, on puutteellinen tehokkuus. Sek pankkien ett arvopaperiprssien kustannusrakenne on monissa Euroopan maissa varsin raskas, esimerkiksi Yhdysvaltoihin tai vaikkapa Pohjoismaihin verrattuna, ja melko laajasti ollaan yht mielt siit, ett rahoituspalvelujen tuotannossa on mahdollisuuksia huomattaviin kustannussstihin. Osittain tm tehottomuus on seurausta markkinoiden pirstoutuneisuudesta, joka on rajoittanut kilpailua ja tehnyt kalliin kustannusrakenteen mahdolliseksi. Kustannuskysymys on mys vakauskysymys, koska vain kannattava ja kustannustehokas pankkisektori voi generoida riittvsti tulorahoitusta ja nin huolehtia vakavaraisuutensa riittvyydest pitkll aikavlill. Kolmas Euroopan rahoitusmarkkinoiden ongelma on, ett kun markkinat kehittyvt ja yhdentyvt, rahoitusvalvonta uhkaa jd tss kehityksess jlkeen. Euroopan rahoitusvalvontahan perustuu ns. kotivaltioperiaatteeseen, joten rahoitustoimialan kansainvlistyess yh suurempaa osaa toiminnasta valvoo jonkin muun maan viranomainen kuin sen, jossa palvelu myydn. Mys talletusvakuutus saattaa yh useammassa tapauksessa olla jonkin muun maan vastuulla kuin sen, jossa ongelmiin johtaneet riskit on otettu tai jossa korvauksiin oikeutetut tallettajat asuvat. Samalla pankki-arvopaperi-ja vakuutustoiminnan lhentyminen aiheuttaa uusia haasteita valvontaorganisaatioille. Viranomaisten monilukuisuus asettaa suuria vaatimuksia niiden vliselle tiedonkululle ja operatiiviselle yhteistylle. Nm vaatimukset kasvavat sit mukaa kun rahoitusmarkkinoiden yhdentyminen Euroopassa tavoitteiden mukaisesti etenee. *** Lissabonin strategian toteuttaminen kytnnn rahoitusmarkkinapolitiikassa ptettiin perustaa EU:n jo edellisen vuonna hyvksymn ohjelmaan, joka tht nimenomaan rahoitusmarkkinoiden yhtenistmiseen ja tehostamiseen EU-alueella. Tm ohjelma on niin sanottu rahoituspalvelujen toimenpidesuunnitelma eli FSAP  Financial Services Action Plan  joka hyvksyttiin kevll 1999 ja ulottuu vuoteen 2005. Kaiken kaikkiaan FSAPiin sisltyi alun perin 42 eri ehdotusta toimenpiteiksi, joilla Eurooppaan voitaisiin luoda yhteniset, tehokkaat ja vakaat rahoitusmarkkinat. Ehdotuksilla pyrittiin edistmn nelj strategista tavoitetta: Rahoituksen tukkumarkkinoiden tysi yhtenistminen EU-alueella; Rahoituspalvelujen avointen ja turvallisten vhittismarkkinoiden kehittminen; EU:n rahoitusmarkkinoiden jatkuvan vakauden varmistaminen; Veroesteiden poistamisen rahoitusmarkkinoiden yhtenistmisen tielt Ensimminen toimenpidesuunnitelman strategisista tavoitteista on todella yhteniset eurooppalaiset rahoituksen tukkumarkkinat. Tss kehittmishankkeet keskittyvt lhinn arvopaperi-ja johdannaismarkkinoihin, joissa pirstoutuneisuuden ongelmat ovat vakavimmat. FSAP:in mukaan sijoituspoman saatavuus EU:n laajuisesti on yhtenistettv siten, ett yksi tarjousesite riitt arvopaperien myyntiin koko EU:n alueella. Yritysten tilinptsinformaatio on yhtenistettv ns. IAS -standardin pohjalle. Elkerahastojen kansainvlist toimintaa EU:n sisll on helpotettava. Arvopaperikaupan selvitysjrjestelmien toimivuutta on parannettava ja niiden kustannuksia alennettava. Rahoituspalvelujen vhittismarkkinoilla FSAP haluaa helpottaa rahoituspalvelujen kuten esimerkiksi asuntolainojen ja vakuutusten kauppaa EU-maiden vlill. Tll alueella FSAP:n kehittmisehdotukset koskevat ennen muuta kuluttajasuojan toteuttamista rajat ylittvss rahoituspalvelujen kaupassa. Toinen vhintn yht trke prioriteetti on integroidun vhittismaksujrjestelmn luominen EU-alueelle. Rahoitusmarkkinoiden vakauden kehittmisen puolella FSAP tht valvontaviranomaisten vlisen yhteistyn olennaiseen tiivistmiseen EU:ssa. Ohjelmaan kuuluu mys luottolaitosten ja vakuutusyhtiiden tervehdyttmistoimia koskevien sdsten kehittminen. Verotuksen puolella FSAP pyrkii korkotulojen verotuksen osittaiseen yhtenistmiseen mrmll koroille minimiverotaso, jota kaikissa jsenmaissa olisi vhintnkin sovellettava. Tll pyritn esimerkiksi siihen, ett erot talletusten verokohtelussa eivt vristisi pankkikilpailua yhtenistyvill markkinoilla. *** Sen jlkeen kun FSAP ja Lissabonin strategia hyvksyttiin, on tapahtunut paljon. EU:n piiriss on tehty mrtietoista tyt rahoitusmarkkinoiden integraation edistmiseksi ja huomattava osa FSAP:n sisltyvist aloitteista on jo edennyt direktiivi-tai regulaatioasteelle, joskin paljon tyt on viel tekemtt. Tmn tyn on tapahduttava suurelta osalta talouselmn toimesta. On nimittin muistettava, ett rahoitusmaailma ei koostu kehittmisptksist, yltason strategioista eik direktiiveist, vaan kytnnn liiketoiminnasta. Siksi FSAP ja muut tllaiset ohjelmat osoittavat arvonsa vasta eurooppalaisen talouselmn kytnnn testiss. Esimerkiksi eurooppalainen pankkisektori on reagoinut tuossa edell mainitsemaani kansainvlisen vhittismaksuliikenteen hinnoittelua koskevaan EU-regulaatioon perustamalla European Payments Council.nimisen yhteistyjrjestn, joka on asettanut tavoitteekseen toteuttaa vision yhtenisest eurooppalaisesta maksualueesta. Jrjest ajaa mm. yleiseurooppalaisen maksujen selvityskeskuksen perustamista lhivuosien aikana. Tm olisi trke virstanpylvs Euroopan vhittismaksujrjestelmien todellisessa yhdentymisess, joka edellytt kansainvlisten vhittismaksupalvelujen tuotantokustannusten tuntuvaa alentumista. Samalla kun integraatio-ja kehittmisohjelmia on kehitetty ja tystetty kytntn, ympriv maailma on muuttunut nopeasti. Enimmkseen uutiset ovat olleet rahoitusmarkkinoiden kannalta huonoja. Tietotekniikka-ja telekommunikaatiosektorin kasvuodotukset ovat maailmanlaajuisesti laskeneet. Talouskasvun taittuminen on heikentnyt valtioiden budjettitasapainoa kaikkialla. Vuosi sitten syyskuun 11 pivn tapahtuneet terrori-iskut ovat nostaneet turvallisuuskysymykset ja globaalin turvallisuusyhteistyn etualalle. Viimeksi huomio on suuntautunut kysymykseen, millaisen informaation varassa rahoitusmarkkinat toimivat. Enronista ja WorldComista alkaneet kirjanpitoskandaalit ovat horjuttaneet luottamusta yritysten hallintoon ja niiden jakamaan markkinainformaatioon varsinkin Yhdysvalloissa, mutta tuntuu selvlt, etteivt niden tapahtumien opetukset voi jd huomiotta Euroopassakaan. Jos EU:n rahoitusmarkkinapolitiikka perustuisi pelkkn laissez faire tyyliseen sntelyn purkamiseen, viimeisten kahden vuoden tapahtumat olisivat todennkisesti aiheuttaneet suuria vaikeuksia pyrkimyksille yhtenist ja tehostaa Euroopan rahoitusmarkkinoita. Nin ei kuitenkaan ole kynyt, vaan FSAP ja muukin markkinoiden perusrakenteiden uudistamisty etenee edelleen, ja enimmkseen alkuperisten tavoitteiden ja suuntaviivojen mukaisesti. EU:n rahoitusmarkkinoiden integraatio-ja tehostamisohjelma on siis toistaiseksi osoittautunut ehk yllttvnkin myrskynkestvksi. Tm johtuu siit, ett ohjelmat ovat keskittyneet rakentamaan yhtenist juridista ja muuta perusrakennetta, jonka varassa markkinat voisivat toimia tehokkaasti (avoimesti ja kilpailullisesti) ja samalla yhtenisesti. Avaimena on siis, ett kilpailun avaaminen kytketn osaksi prosessia, jossa markkinoita kehitetn vakaammiksi, lpinkyvmmiksi ja turvallisemmiksi. Vastaavaa sntelyn kehitystythn tehdn nykyn mys laajasti globaalilla tasolla IMF:n, BIS:n ja Financial Stability Forumin piiriss, mutta siell ratkaisuaan odottavat ongelmat ovat tietysti viel suuremmat kuin EU:n sisisess tyss, jossa maiden lhtkohdat ovat sittenkin lhempn toisiaan ja maiden poliittinen riippuvuus toisistaan on suurempi kuin globaalissa yhteistyss. Mys yhteinen rahapolitiikka EMU-alueella on osaltaan tukenut Euroopan sisist rahoitusmarkkinoiden kehittmistyt. Yhtenisten rahoitusmarkkinoiden rakentamisen on tarkoitus muuttaa koko EU:n talouselm, tietysti nykyiset hakijamaat mukaan lukien. Tavoiteltu vaikutus ei ulotu vain luottolaitoksiin ja prsseihin ja muualle rahoitusalalle, vaan teollisuuteen, kauppaan, palveluihin ja julkiseen talouteen. Kaikki nm sektorit tulevat kynniss olevan muutoksen seurauksena radikaalisti eurooppalaistumaan, kun markkinat ja yritysten rahoitus-ja omistusrakenteet sulautuvat Euroopassa yh enemmn yhteen. Rakennusty tulee mys muuttamaan tekijitn, eli EU-maiden hallituksia ja viranomaisia sek mys komissiota, EKP:ta ja muita yhteisn toimielimi. Yhteisen politiikan ja yhteistason toimivaltuuksien merkitys tulee korostumaan. Rahoitusmarkkinoiden sntelyn ja valvonta vaativat niin laajaa poliittista ja viranomaisyhteistyt, ett tm ty omalta osaltaan voimakkaasti syvent mys poliittista integraatiota EU:n piiriss. Kaiken kaikkiaan, rahoitusmarkkinoiden kehittmisty on keskeisell sijalla EU:n talouspoliittisessa yhteistyss lhivuosina. Samalla tm tykentt on erinomainen esimerkki niist hydyist, joita eurooppalaisella integraatiolla voidaan saavuttaa. Epilen, ett ilman EU:n yhteist politiikkaa tll alueella maanosamme talouselm tuskin psisi hytymn yhtenisist, avoimista ja turvallisista rahoitusmarkkinoista nkpiiriss olevassa tulevaisuudessa. EU:n yhteninen rahoitusmarkkinapolitiikka vahvistaa mys eurooppalaisten neuvotteluasemia globaaleilla foorumeilla, joissa eurooppalaiset nkkannat voivat nin saada sen painon, mik niille kuuluu maanosamme taloudellisen painoarvon perusteella.

Title: Speech at the "Head up towards tomorrow" seminar
text: Speech by Bank Manager Sinikka Salo at the seminar "Pss pystysss towards tomorrow" . Speech . Wednesday2 October 2002, 12:00 AM EMU and Finland's economic policy Dear participants in the seminar, ladies and gentlemen! Finland has been a member of the European Economic and Monetary Union for almost four years. It's so long that the picture is so long that the picture The effects of EMU - its hysdyism and the adaptation needs it causes - will also begin in Finland. I would like to use my speech to explain the ECB's monetary policy framework and how the single currency and integrated European financial markets are important for the European internal market and for Finland. I would also like to talk about the challenges of economic policy, the most important of which is the adjustment pressures on public finances, including Finland. EMU and EU financial integration One obvious and important influence on joining the monetary union was, of course, the elimination of exchange rate fluctuations vis-a-vis the other euro countries. From 1999 onwards, the monetary units of the Finnish markka and the other euro countries did not actually have exchange rates, but fixed conversion rates, which were also used at the turn of last year when the euro finally replaced the national monetary units. The single currency unit links the Finnish economy more closely to the euro area market as a whole. At the same time, being part of the monetary union will benefit the consumer and improve the chances of internationalisation, especially for small enterprises. Another effect of monetary union has been the convergence of interest rates. Interest rates applied in Finland are currently charged on the euro area-wide money market with a uniform level of interest rates. The interest rate is controlled by the European Central Bank, which conducts monetary policy jointly with national central banks such as the Bank of Finland. Interest rates have been lower in recent years than they have been for a long time, and in fact it is far into the history of the gold standard until the years before we meet the same low interest rates that we have enjoyed in recent years. The difference with recent decades is particularly clear: in the past, Finland struggled with the persistent problem of inflation and, therefore, with higher interest rates than other European countries. The problems of monetary union have now eased. The integration of exchange rates and interest rates has contributed to the integration of financial markets and changed the structure and functioning of financial markets. In particular, investment and securities markets have changed or are changing from national to pan-European. This has already been of great importance to large borrowers and investors. For example, Finnish tyselske funds have diversified their portfolio investments on a very large scale to the European market. The banking world is now increasingly prepared for the fact that the competition for private investors and borrowers will also become more international. Internet usage and the expected fall in the cost of credit transfers in the euro area will have an impact on the direction of the euro area. Many of the deep processes shaping Europe's future are closely linked to the functioning and development of financial markets. The connection is two-way. As European political structures change, the financial markets reflect changes, and I believe that in ten years' time the European financial markets will be in many respects different from today's. On the other hand, developments in financial markets will also have an impact on how Europe can reform and develop in the coming years. In particular, financial market policy plays a key role in the EU's efforts to build a more economically coherent and dynamic Europe. It is only under the conditions of a single financial market that a large enclave of more than 300 million inhabitants of the EU will be able to operate a encyclopedia d where goods, services and greece can move freely and which now have a (pssos) single currency. The EU expert group chaired by Pehr Gyllenhammar estimated that by simply improving the functioning of the financial markets, economic growth in the EU countries could be accelerated by half a per cent per annum, and by some extent more. There is certainly a great deal of room for interpretation and uncertainties in relation to such estimates, but the impact on growth of this kind would, of course, be of great importance for europe's rigour, competitiveness and also for the budgetary finances of European countries. However, the integration of financial markets into pan-Europeans is still half-hearted, as the financial markets are fragmented in many respects. An example of this situation is the banking market and payment transactions, where national borders have a significant impact on trade in financial services, even within the euro area. The region is of particular interest to small and medium-sized enterprises d and also to ordinary Finns: more payments than before, for example. For our children studying in continental Europe, our holiday apartments for rent in Spain, etc. In the financial services market, the EU wants to facilitate cross-border trade in, for example, mortgages and insurance, and the proposals for development are mainly concerned with the implementation of consumer protection. Another priority for the CZECH EU is the creation of an integrated payment system within the EU. Although a different standardisation process has been carried out for a long time, paying from one EU country to another is much more difficult, slower and more expensive than paying in one country, especially for households and small businesses. The EU has intervened in this matter by means of the Regulation on the pricing of payment services, which as early as next year (from 1.7.2003) will restrict the right of banks to charge higher fees for cross-border credit transfers than for domestic payments. However, a regulation as such is not sufficient to remedy the problem, but requires economic action. As a positive development, it can be seen that the European banking sector, for example, has reacted to the above. regulation in the desired way by setting up a cooperation called the European Payments Council, which has set itself the objective of achieving the vision of a single European payments area. Among other things, Khrjests is advocating the establishment of a pan-European payment clearing house during the Lshi years. This would be a milestone in the effective integration of the EU's payment systems, which would require a substantial reduction in the cost of producing cross-border payment services. All in all, the development and convergence of financial markets is at the heart of the EU's economic policy cooperation over the years. At the same time, this is an excellent example of the hysdys that European integration can achieve. Without a common EU policy in the region, our continent's economy is unlikely to be able to find a common, open and secure financial market in the future. The EU's common policy on financial market issues will also strengthen the negotiating position of Europeans in global for a. The European nsskans can gain the weight they deserve on the basis of the economic weight of our continent. The ECB's monetary policy The ECB's monetary policy objective is to pursue price stability throughout the euro area. 'The euro area as a whole' implies that the policy is not tailored to the needs of any individual country or group of countries. ssss is not a single From the point of view of the member state, there is a contradiction: even if we Finns were to make the monetary policy of the euro area on our own, we could not just take finland's cyclical situation as a point of monetary policy for the whole of monetary union, not even if our own situation is different from the others. It is in the interest of each Member State and of Finland that the euro area economy as a whole remains in balance. The Governing Council has set out a strategy for its monetary policy which sets out as closely as possible how financial information about the euro area is used to assess risks to price stability and to make interest rate adjustments. By means of a strategy that is as transparent as possible, we aim to ensure that the general d professionals and laypeople alike understand monetary policy as well as possible and as rarely make errors of judgement as to where the policy is going. I will not go into more detail about the details of the strategy, I am referring in part to, for example, the ECB's monthly bulletin, which is also published in Finnish and can be ordered (free of charge) from the Bank of Finland in addition to the fact that it is also published on the Internet. What I would like to say, however, is that although the ECB Charter, which sets the bank's mandate for maintaining price stability in the euro area, does not specify what price stability means, the Governing Council has ruled it out. It has been assumed that, in the context of price stability, the rate of increase in consumer prices should remain below two per cent over the medium term. This excludes from price stability high inflation as deflation. It should also be noted that, although with a rather detailed description of the strategy the ECB strives for transparency, the strategy is not a mechanical strategy. It is based on the idea that both the growth of money (the so-called first pillar) and the general inflation indicators based on the real economy (the so-called second pillar) must be carefully interpreted and weighed in order to distinguish the transient hsirst from long-term changes and to correctly weight the signal values of the various indicators. In addition to the technology of economists, it takes a lot of wisdom, a lot of wisdom, a sense of what is really happening in the economies of the euro area. Monetary policy decision-making and the latest interpretation of the situation take place in the Governing Council, which, through the presidents of the various national central banks, has a broad understanding of economic developments in the euro area as a whole. In the deliberations of the Council, the contribution of the national central banks is significant. In the economic press, monetary policy in the euro area is often commented on in relation to exchange rate developments ,in particular, the dollar value of the euro is of interest. It is natural enough that exchange rates fluctuate, but their meanings are often exaggerated. Title: Opening speech at the Baltic seminar organised by the Bank of Finland's Research Institute for Transition Economies (BOFIT)
text: Opening speech by Bank Director Sinikka Salo at the Baltics seminar of the Bank of Finland's Institute for The Study of Transition Economies (BOFIT) . Speech . Monday18 November 2002, 12:00 AM Baltic statesThe challenges of becoming a Member State of the EU Ladies and gentlemen, Over the past ten years, the process of European integration has intensified. The successful adoption of the single currency by the twelve countries that have joined the monetary union is the most important and concrete demonstration of the progress of European integration up to and including, of course, the creation of an EU internal market d which, for the most part, was introduced in 1992 - was already an essential step for the economy. The changes have been major, taking us in the right direction. The historic process of European integration, which began in 1950, is not now a stop. The EU is enlarging and cooperation between the Member States is deepening at the same time. Next month's European Council in Ksspenhamina will decide on the accession of ten new Member States to the European Community. It also includes our neighbours Estonia, Lithuania and Latvia. Enlargement presents challenges both for the EU as an institution and for the new Member States. The eu's challenges lie above all in its sizzle-making. It must reform its institution for the production of the PFsch so that it operates efficiently and democratically, even in conditions where 25 of the current 15 countries are involved in the making of the PFsch. Discussions on these issues are known to be heated. Another challenge for the EU's action is that, after enlargement, the EU will become more heterogeneous than it is today, not only for several years, but also for decades. The standard of living in the new Member States is clearly much lower than in the present countries. During the Lshi years, the challenge is related to the institutions of the Member States and the implementation of the legislation. From the point of view of the functioning of the EU, it is necessary to ensure that, in relation to the relationship, there is also a high common level in all the new Member States. *** For ten years now, the policy of Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and the other new Member States has been consciously designed and calibrated to meet the requirements of european organisations. The demands for membership were to be met, and political changes should not lead to any slippage. It is true that, in most of the applicant countries, changes in governments have not brought much change in economic policy, legislation or institution-building. The policy has been longstanding, consistent and comprehensive. The nation has had a goal that has been pursued with a common effort. As bitter as relations between new parties and new politicians may have sometimes been, the basics have not been disputed. A consistent policy has been good for economic activity. In Estonia, for example, private practice was so extensive and rapid that the private office could be abolished as unnecessary last year. Economic activity, including international trade and payment transactions, was liberalised more quickly and more closely than in any other country. The use of one's own money made it possible to control inflation, which had galloped wildly. The fixed exchange rate system is anchored in the stability of economic policy, while balanced budgetary policies supported it. The use of one's own money was a success story for all three Baltic states. The exchange rate of the Estonian krone has been tied to the euro for over ten years, first to the German mark, then to the euro. The history of Latvian Latin and Lithuanian Litas is a little shorter, but with total success. The test of the stability of the new currencies was the 1998 Russian crisis. The stability of the currencies was a good indication of the confidence of market participants in the exchange rate policy of the countries and, more generally, in the economic policy line. *** Accession to the EU does not mean joining the euro area, even though all ten new Member States have expressed a desire to adopt the euro as quickly as possible. Initially, the new Member States are the so-called "green countries". derogation lands. In the context of monetary union, the member states have to agree with the conditions laid down in the Maastricht Treaty for joining the monetary union It seems natural that the countries should adopt them at different rates. For some of the new Member States, achieving the criteria in the shi years seems possible for sys, but many may have difficulties with all the criteria. In addition to the inflation criterion, there are challenges in meeting the criterion of permanent stability, particularly in the public sector, as the structural changes in the economy in many countries have not yet been completed. In addition, the eu's membership of the EU itself entails additional costs. The impact of this has been estimated at around 5% of GDP compared to 2004. In addition, the European monetary and financial system, the so-called European Monetary and Financial System, is a member of the European Monetary System. The ERMII presents challenges, in particular with regard to the timing of the closure of the central rate and, more importantly, the timing of the changeover to the euro. According to the Maastricht criteria, a Member State must participate in exchange rate arrangements for a period of two years without devaluation or significant currency devaluation. Successful adherence to the course requires a long-term and consistent policy on the part of the applicant countries. As far as the ERM is concerned, it has to be said that the Member States are expected to participate in the system. On the other hand, there is no compulsion to participate, and therefore it is not necessary to take place immediately after eu membership. The applicant countries must carefully consider when they are in a position to fix their exchange rates and commit themselves to the austerity of the ERM II d conditions. On the other hand, it should be borne in mind that ERM II d d and the market in terms of the choice of equilibrium rate provides a framework that promotes both real and nominal convergence and guides both the market in the choice of equilibrium rate. ERM II can serve as a framework to provide both stability and flexibility (wide ranges), which is why many applicant countries are at the stage of their current (both real and nominal) adjustment process. The supranationality and broad territorial coverage of ERM II after enlargement will d make it weaker than many other -one-centred exchange rate systems in a globalising world. *** Good listeners, Throughout its history, European integration has progressed d at a slower pace d in recent years, by such leaps and bounds that it was impossible to imagine 10-15 years earlier. The euro is a good example of the power of integration. Of the Countries of the Sea, the euro is currently used only in Finland and Germany. In Sweden, however, preparations are currently being made for the adoption of the euro, and in Denmark, too, public opinion on the euro is rather mixed. By April or May 2004, our Baltic neighbours will also be members of the EU. Their aim is to adopt the euro as soon as possible. It is therefore credible and even probable that in the course of time the euro will become the single currency of all the countries of the Sea. At the Bank of Finland, we are proud of the help we have been able to provide to research in the Baltic states, which has been carried out at BOFIT for more than ten years. Naturally, however, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have created their own success stories themselves. We look forward to continuing our cooperation with these countries within the new framework that will soon become a reality, that of the European Union. I am pleased to open the seminar, which I believe will be interesting and humble.

text: Bank Manager Sinikka Salo's keynote speech at moodi r.y.'s 35th anniversary celebration . Speech . Saturday 8 February2003,12:00AM Dear students, dear professors, dear friends! I find it very pleasing to visit student events and to meet students, but at the same time it always makes me and probably many other people who have reached the stage of the university always feel a little wistful. A huge amount of cherished memories from my student years come to mind. I am particularly reminded of the youthful enthusiasm and joy of learning that we experienced at the time. Now it's only really understood why the meaning of the spirit of the student years is the whole myshemmssss elsmssss. d Hopefully, even the current generation of students will be able to resist the temptations of cynicism and a positive attitude towards the world, learning and the importance of new knowledge. After all, studying should not only be about acquiring knowledge and skills, but also about becoming part of a particular professional community, joining its values and its incorporation into one's own function in society. In this matter, the activities of students are, of course, of great importance and work. I find it particularly a pleasure and also an honour to be part of mood's anniversary celebration, as I myself have studied statistics (in fact, statistics was my mainstay in my master's degree in political science). I had great personalities as teachers, including professors Seppo Mustonen and Leo Tsnqvist d both pioneers in statistics. I have a great love for statistics and statistics. Although my own career ultimately turned me into an economist and not a statistician, throughout my professional career I have been dealing with statistics and their analyses, indices and indicators, as well as as a researcher and now in the process of making decisions and forming opinions and positions. "Belief is never the vssrti of knowledge", and I can say that my appreciation of the field of statistics, and the emphasis on the systematic analysis of information, which is emphasized by studies in statistics, has always been high and has only increased in recent years. I am, of course, a major weekly consumer of economic statistics and analyses, but I have also had to play my part in developing the statistics, namely harmonising them within the euro area. In addition, I have also found myself in the position of producer, because the Bank of Finland is one of the most czech statistical producers in Finland, and the production of financial statistics in the bank is my area of responsibility. Without forgetting the methodological importance of statistics, in my speech I will focus specifically on the accuracy of statistical production and the quality of statistics. *** Statisticians have often been considered number pysrittsjins, whose job is to psstys on the pers shelfes of libraries. Although I understand the enormous social importance of the things described by the statistics, the role of the statistician is too often very passive and dry. I don't know if there ever was a perss in such an image, but the information that in modern times couldn't be further from reality. Many contemporary discourses have underlined the social importance and responsibility of the statistician profession. I simply mean that in the information society today, the production and use of statistics has increased. The change that has taken place has been significant and is mainly due to internationalisation. The internationalisation of economic policy and environmental policy, among other things, has changed the role of statistics in politics. In the past, statistics were used to be used to provide information, and it was thought that the conciseness and management of information is an aid to the making of information, but nevertheless clearly subordinate to politics. Today, the situation has changed, and statistics have become more and more often the norms of information. sms has raised the field of statistics in a new way to the centre of social psychology, not subordinated to politics, but alongside politics. European integration is a good example of this. The reason is that a united Europe relies on harmonised indicators. As stated, the European Union does not have a centralised administrative apparatus, neither in economic policy, nor in social policy, nor in environmental policy, nor in other key areas. However, Europe is pursuing an ambitious and more intensive coordination of economic policies. However, a common policy is not based on a common administration, but is based on common standards, which are then imposed by the administration at national level. In economic policy, for example, we have a Stability and Growth Pact, the purpose of which is to ensure that the Member States of monetary union do not improve at each other's expense or otherwise improve the economic situation of other Member States. The agreement covers the amount of public debt and public deficits in the member states of the euro area. In any case, there are numerous coordination processes in economic policy which coordinate the policies of the Member States through peer pressure and commonly agreed standards. All economic policy standards are based on statistics: national accounts, employment statistics, financial statistics, and so on. If statistical standards have become increasingly important in the context of European integration, then the corresponding figure is also evident at global level. Take, for example, environmental policy. The Kyoto Agreement, the pssch trade, the whole international cooperation that will test the planet for future generations, is based on the use of statistical indicators as policy norms. Another example of the growing importance of statistics in global politics is the need to stabilise the development of international financial markets, the so-called new international financial architecture. In recent years, the Czech Republic has been built in cooperation with international organisations. A key element of the new financial architecture is the development of standards for the insularity, quality and speed of completion of economic statistics in different countries. We have thus entered a world in which international political cooperation is increasingly active through statistical methods and their standardisation. At the same time, politics at national level is increasingly forced to mirror itself against the norms that have been criticised at European or global level. The indicators are the statistics produced by the national authorities. *** While the role of statistics has emerged as a point of reference and a yardstick for politics, the role of statistical authorities has also come into a new light. The recent public exchange of views between Minister Lipponen and Heli Jeskanen, director of the Central Statistics Office, about the criteria for compiling statistics and the possible halving of Finland's employment rate, had certainly been reflected in the lengthy newspapers and, to my knowledge, reflected real differences of opinion on how Finland's statistical production would be handled. Rather, it underlined the high quality standards that international statistical cooperation imposes on the economic statistics of the various countries. At the same time, it also brilliantly highlighted how Czech statistics are in today's society, and how czech matters are the independence and undeniable professionalism of the statistical authorities. After that example, everyone understands how damaging it would be if it were to be a matter of how much it would be for the statisticians to take political expediency points into account. For those of us central bankers, an example of the independence and objectivity of statistical production concerns the European Stability and Growth Pact, which I mentioned earlier. Recently, some European countries have struggled to accommodate the deficits of public finances within the limits set out in the Treaty. The credibility of the coordination of economic policy in Europe as a whole depends on whether the national statistical authorities can be trusted to do so in a cold and objective manner, at the same rate of professional integrity. If I were to refer to epsillchis, the whole european structure of economic policy would be plunged into a crisis of confidence. The statistical authorities are more strongly associated with the group of public authorities, whose absolute independence and integrity are essential for their activities. After all, the Court of Justice has a long history as an institution whose raison d'etre depends on their independence and independence. At the time of the establishment of the European Monetary Union, it was clear that the central banks were also included in the same group. Allow me to say a few words about the central banks as well. When european monetary union was being planned, the key issue was the reliability and credibility of monetary policy. Many European countries had complained of confidence in the value of their currencies, which had been the result of high inflation, high interest rates and currency speculation. The single European currency had to be set up on such a basis as to put an end once and for all to this kind of confidence in the European Union. The solution was to make the European Central Bank a self-governing and independent institution, but with a clear, statutory objective: to achieve price stability in the euro area. Economic cycles vary, but experience shows that the institutional structure of monetary union is successful. Europe as a whole has not enjoyed lower interest rates and lower inflation for decades than it does today. Monetary policy confidence has radically improved. Currency crises, which at the beginning of the last decade caused great devastation in many European countries, including Finland, have made history. *** Dear statisticians, In my speech, I have highlighted the growing social importance of the statistical sector. A statistician has hardly ever been a mere act of smashing numbers into someone else's raw material. Today, and most recently today, statistics are an objective set of economic, social and environmental indicators that can only be used by a dedicated and professionally ethical community. Professional ethics are born out of professional pride and nsyryness d pride in one's own work and nurturing in relation to learning and renewal. So be proud to be a statistician. Thank you for the event and wish your association the success of the long and fine traditions of the Finnish statistical profession!

Title: Speech in Malta
text: Pankinjohtaja Sinikka Salon puhe Maltalla . Speech . Friday 28 March 2003, 12:00 AM The Relevance of Fiscal Soundness for MonetaryStability Remarks in the SUERF (The European Money and Finance Forum) Seminar "Securing Financial Stability: Problems and Prospects for new EU Members", jointly organized with the Central Bank of Malta on 28 March, 2003 First of all let me thank the organisers for this opportunity to talk in front of this distinguished audience. I have attended SUEF meeting more or less regularly since early 1980s and it is a great pleasure to be here again. Large changes are about to happen in the economic scene in Europe over this period and this is very much reflected both by the place and the participants of this seminar. I very much welcome these changes. I understand that I am supposed to tackle the issue of fiscal soundness and monetary stability from the point of view of a practitioner rather than providing any academic insight in the issue. This is no doubt my approach. However, when preparing this presentation I browsed some recent academic literature on the subject and I could not resist the temptation to provide some very "subjective" reflections of how to apply them in practice. Anyhow my approach in the paper that I am going to summarise to you is very "practical" relating to the assessment of fiscal stability in the accession countries. *** Relations between fiscal and monetary policies have been and are likely to remain the subject of many discussions in both academics and policy-making circles. Of these discussions, the best known is perhaps the so-called opolicy mixo debate. This is concerned mainly with the design of fiscal and monetary policy responses to different macroeconomic disturbances, or more recently, design of different policy rules to be applied to different probability distributions of disturbances. The relation between fiscal soundness and monetary stability is a closely related but nevertheless distinct issue. It is concerned with disturbances that are of fundamental or extreme nature and it always has a bearing on the possibility of fundamental policy failures. Of the different aspects of fiscal soundness and monetary stability, this presentation will focus on the sustainability of public finances and the risk of high inflation. High inflation is -at least in its extreme form of hyperinflation .largely a modern phenomenon, related to the need to print paper money to finance large fiscal deficits. These deficits are often but not always caused by exceptional events such as wars, revolutions, collapses of empires, and establishment of new states. It would be interesting and in the present economic situation, some would say more timely -to discuss also the other side of the coin, namely the relationship between fiscal stability and deflation, but I must leave this issue out of this presentation. For me, it is a side issue and the main theme is complicated enough even without it. My presentation is structured the following way. I first discuss two rather different academic approaches that consider the relationship between fiscal soundness and monetary stability. No in-depth survey of the literature will be attempted here; my purpose rather is just to give some glimpses of research that has been done on this subject. (References to some recent literature are provided on my main paper.) Thereafter I summarise in general terms some of the main steps usually adopted in practical assessments of the sustainability of public sector indebtedness. Finally, in line with the general theme of this seminar, I discuss some of the fiscal challenges the accession countries may encounter in the coming years. Although the level of government indebtedness in most accession countries is now rather low and in any case lower than in most of the present member states, fiscal deficit are high and, in view of the forthcoming pressures, may rise further. The medium-term picture foreseen by the countries themselves in their Pre-Accession Economic Programmes is very favourable, but I see a risk of increasing deficits and of a continuous increase in the level of governmentso indebtedness. Such fiscal policies would place a heavy burden on national monetary policies in the new member states. Furthermore, fiscal pressures in the new member states may intensify political pressures to weaken the rules of fiscal surveillance in the EU. There is thus a risk that the enlargement will both directly and indirectly increase the burden fiscal policies places on monetary policies. *** In the "theoretical part" of my paper I summarise two strands of academic discussion relating to relation between fiscal policy and inflation, notably the so-called inflation tax literature and the fiscal theory of the price level. The latter literature distinguishes between monetary dominant (or Ricardian) and fiscally-dominant (or non-Ricardian) equilibria or regimes. In the monetary dominant regime fiscal primary surplus adjusts, given any sequence of prices, to guarantee fiscal solvency, whereas in the fiscally dominant regime the government's inter-temporal budget constraint is satisfied only for some price paths and the price level is assumed to settle itself to a path satisfying the government budget constraint. Interestingly, it has been suggested in a paper published by the EU Commission Services that the EMU is a monetary dominant regime, provided that the Stability and Growth Pact is respected. Inflation-tax literature In the so-called inflation-tax literature, connection between fiscal policy and inflation is studied in a simple demand-for-and-supply-of-money framework. Inflation is treated as a tax on money balances and fiscal policy is connected with inflation through seigniorage revenues obtained from increasing money supply. The cost of increased money supply is borne by holders of money balances as the purchasing power of money decreases. A substantial body of empirical evidence confirms that inflation is highly correlated with money growth, the long.run correlation between these two variables being close to one-to-one. In high inflation countries, the connection between money growth and inflation is broadly contemporaneous. In low-inflation countries, the effects of money growth are distributed rather evenly across the current and previous periods, and the short run correlation between contemporaneous and even lagged money growth and inflation appears to be in general rather low. As to the relationship between public finances and money supply, a plausible and often advanced hypothesis is that money supply and seigniorage income should increase as a function of the fiscal needs, as reflected by the size of the budget deficit. However, empirical evidence of this link is weak. In their recent empirical analysis Fisher et. al. found a negative relationship between budget balance and seigniorage in their cross-sectional data, but the coefficient was small. A ten-percentage-point increase in deficit leads on average to a 1,5 percent increase in segniorage revenue. Furthermore, even this weak relation seems to derive mainly from some exceptional observations with very high levels of seigniorage (over 6 per cent of GDP). These exceptional observations included, by the way, one accession country, namely Malta. For the lower-inflation countries the coefficient is even lower and insignificant. The basic message of the inflation tax literature for the analysis of fiscal soundness and monetary stability is that in some circumstances, monetary financing may be the only source of finance available for the government and that monetary financing is bound to affect the functioning of the monetary system. These are still valid messages. There is also some research on inflation tax as an element in an optimal or efficient system of taxation. I am not convinced of the usefulness of this type of analysis and, to save time, I will not deal with this issue in my presentation I have discussed it briefly in my main paper. To summarise: There seems to be a widespread conviction that high inflation is almost always caused by fiscal pressures. Against that background, the lack of a firm ex post correlation between deficit and seigniorage may be surprising. However, among other harmful things, high inflation disrupts the budgeting of expenditures and wrecks tax collection systems. Thus, government receipts and disbursements are likely to vary erratically, which may explain the lack of a correlation between fiscal deficits and inflation. Fiscal Theory of the Price Level Another, recent strand of academic discussion, called the fiscal theory of the price level, deals explicitly with fiscal and monetary policy and their interactions. The theory focuses on the governmentos inter-temporal budget constraint and the sustainability of the fiscal position. There are many ways to state the governmentos inter-temporal budget constraint. One useful way to write it is in terms of the change of the (net) debt ratio, or (1) db/dt -s (i g -p) b e. Here b is the governmentos net debt and s primary surplus, both as per cent of GDP. db/dt denotes the change in the debt ratio whereas i is the (average) interest rate on debt, g the growth rate of real GDP and p the rate of inflation. The stock-flow adjustment term e captures, as per cent of GDP, all other effects on the change in the debt ratio such as reevaluations of debt items etc. The fiscal theory of the price level assumes that agents optimise their behaviour over time in anticipation of future economic developments, including the expectation of future policy actions. There is also a shift of emphasis towards the analysis of budgetary and monetary policy rules, rather than single decisions, and their time-consistency. The inter-temporal and optimising character of analysis makes models complicated and difficult to analyse, even given their strong simplifying assumptions. Nevertheless, the theory has made many interesting contributions to the analysis of fiscal soundness and monetary stability, including the analysis of the institutional framework needed to govern the interactions between monetary and fiscal policy I mentioned earlier as an example a justification for the Stability and Growth Pact. I will not try to provide even a selective survey of the results of the analysis here; rather, my intention is to draw some more or less subjective lessons from the literature. Compared to the inflation tax literature, the fiscal theory of the price level extends both the time perspective and the spectrum of liabilities and assets considered in the analysis. Instead of a single instantaneous rate of inflation, the whole time path of the price level is relevant, and instead of the stock of money, the whole portfolio of government liabilities and assets is considered at least in principle. Results from the theory illustrate the fact that irrespective of the starting position, the burden of irresponsible fiscal policies, if followed persistently over time, becomes excessive in the end even for strongly stability oriented monetary policies. The risk of vicious debt dynamics is rather explicit in equation (1). If primary budget deficit is large (as reflected in a large negative value of s), debt tends to increase. When debt becomes large enough, it starts to grow at an accelerating rate, as nominal interest rate normally exceeds nominal output growth. At this stage, there is not much to be done to increase the real rate of growth (g) and there are also limits to feasible primary surpluses (s). For very high debt ratios, unsustainable debt dynamics can only be reversed if the rate of interest on debt (i) is low enough and the rate of inflation (p) is high enough, i.e. through monetary financing. In rational expectation models, this is of course clearly perceived by the public well before its actual occurrence. Furthermore, models considered in the literature clearly illustrate the fact that monetary and fiscal policies need to be consistent in order to be able to produce balanced and harmonious policy outcomes. In fact, there is no guarantee in these models that a uniquely determined, well-behaving equilibrium time path for the price level exists, even for policy rules which in themselves seem to be quite sensible but not mutually consistent. For example, inflationary and deflationary spirals, stochastically fluctuating explosive inflation or sunspot equilibria may emerge even if monetary authorities let money stock grow at a constant rate or follow a Taylor rule. Even though this literature has provided many useful insights, I have some doubts about the extent to which its results are relevant from an empirical or political point of view. By their very nature, analytical models are highly simplified and therefore unrealistic representations of complex reality. At least for the moment, the contributions from this literature have been more conceptual in nature, and the models involved appear to have left little marks on the way debt sustainability or interactions between fiscal and monetary policies are analysed in practice. *** Having had a look at the recent strand of theories about the relation between fiscal soundness and monetary stability let me now turn to assessment of government debt sustainability. Debt sustainability and some reflections on ofiscal dominanceo The concept of fiscal dominance is related to the concept of government debt sustainability. In practical work on debt sustainability by institutions like the IMF, the governmentos intertemporal budget equation like (1) above is also the cornerstone of the analysis, but rules of thumb and back-of-the-envelope computations replace the solution of forward-looking rational expectations differential equations. In all likelihood, one is forced to rely on judgement. This is in part related to the fact that the authorities seldom have any well-defined opolicy ruleso assumed in the theory or, if they have, follow them with the consistency assumed in academic models. While the role of the monetary policy in the sustainability analysis is crucial, in practical work it is usually specified only indirectly through macroeconomic assumptions about inflation, interest rates, exchange rates etc. The imprecise character of policy rules makes debt sustainability a rather vague concept. In practical terms, a governmentos liability position can be regarded as sustainable if, given the cost of financing the government faces in the debt market, the government indebtedness does not grow continuously without major correction in the balance of income and expenditure. The exclusion of major corrections in income or expenditure captures the notion that there are social and political limits to adjustment that determine the willingness to pay. The first step in a sustainability assessment is to determine the starting position. In theoretical models, this step is trivial but in actual assessments it may be difficult. The compilation and dissemination of basic data such as level of public sector indebtedness, primary balances, interest bills, the real interest rates, etc are complicated by difficulties such as outright lack of data and imprecisely defined off-budget and contingent liabilities. A major step in the exercise is to project key macroeconomic variables, such as interest rates, rates of economic growth, and exchange rate changes, together with the flows of revenues and expenditures over sufficiently long period. To the extent that these variables are influenced by government policies, this part of the assessment is intrinsically uncertain. An almost overwhelmingly difficult decision is to determine the point at which the government can no longer be expected to be able to continue servicing its debt without unrealistic corrections in income or expenditure. No single threshold such as a given level of indebtedness can reliably define this point. For some developing countries, a government debt level of 40 per cent of DGP may be unsustainable whereas some other countries have successfully managed a public sector debt in excess of 100 per cent of GDP. Ultimately, assessments of sustainability can be only probabilistic. An increase in public sector debt is likely to increase the perceived risk of unsustainable public finances and thereby the perceived risk of a future loosening of the monetary policy and ultimately of monetary financing. The size of the perceived risk depends on many things such as the level of government debt, the soundness of the fiscal policy framework as well as the status of and the credibility of the monetary policy strategy adopted by the central bank. An increase in indebtedness gives rise to less concern if it is associated with strong and credible overall policy framework and with strong commitments by the fiscal authorities to restore the debt level to a low level within a realistic timetable. The composition of debt as well as related ostock-flowo corrections in the level of indebtedness symbolised by e in equation (1) are also relevant. For example, debt denominated in domestic currency may bring with itself a temptation to inflate in order to reduce the real value of the debt. As the risk is recognised by the public, inflationary pressures in the economy may emerge as domestic debt increases even if the government has no intention to take recourse to monetary financing. Comprehensive medium-to-long-term fiscal programmes can be a key element in both in assessing and in shaping policies to avoid the risk of fiscal unsustainability. For that purpose, the stability and convergence programmes drafted by the EU member states now include a section analysing the sustainability of public finances from a longer run point of view. This work is based on and complemented by in-depth analyses by the Economic Policy Committee on the effects of ageing and the governmentos contingent liabilities. While official fiscal programmes may be useful, their usefulness depends entirely on the assumptions used in programmeos projections. The experience from the convergence and stability programmes suggests that official programmes tend to suffer from optimistic assumptions. Moreover, usually only marginal deviations from the baseline forecast are considered in them and thus they do not provide proper stress tests for analysing the consequences of substantial risks to fiscal soundness. *** Fiscal challenges in the accession counties In view of the main theme of this seminar, I will now venture to reflect on fiscal challenges in the accession countries, keeping an eye on the soundness of public finances. This is a complex and sensitive topic. My intention here is not to try to present an exhaustive discussion of it dthat would clearly be beyond my competence but rather only to restate some of the points I have made earlier on fiscal soundness and monetary stability in somewhat more concrete terms, using accession countries as illustrative material. As to the starting point, the public sector indebtedness in the 10 accession countries is not alarming, given the relatively high level of economic development achieved by these countries. In 2001, the ratio of government debt to GDP ratio was higher than 60% of GDP only in Malta. On the other hand, the balance of income and expenditure is less favourable and many accession countries have large budgetary deficits. In 2001, five accession countries, including the three largest countries (Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary) ran deficits above 3% of GDP. I have no data for 2002, but the deficit estimates presented in the last yearos Pre-Accession Economic Programmes range from near zero in Estonia to between 5% and 7% of GDP in the Czech Republic, Hungary, Malta and Poland. Given the low or moderate level of indebtedness, high deficits indicate, in general, large primary deficits. In view of the large primary deficits there may be a risk that at least some of the accession countries are in the early phase of a perhaps rapid debt accumulation process. In fact, the debt ratio has already started in some countries to increase very rapidly. The risk of prolonged debt accumulation stems, among other things, from following fiscal challenges now facing the accession countries: Accession countries are undergoing tremendous structural and institutional changes, including the need to upgrade public infrastructure and to fulfil the commitments entailed in the European Agreement. These will have in future significant budgetary implications. While accession countries will benefit in net terms from the EU accession, the impact on budgets is thought to be negative. Investment in public infrastructure, complying with EU environmental standards and the implementation of also rest of the EU acquis implied by the accession will be only partly compensated by net transfers and positive budgetary effects of tax harmonisation. In particular, absorbing structural and cohesion funds requires domestic fiscal co-financing. The financial sector in most accession countries is still at an early stage of development and therefore governments must rely heavily on foreign savings to finance public deficits. This exposes them to balance of payments difficulties. Lack of progress in reining in excessive deficits could undercut market sentiment and economic activity in countries with large external deficits. Sharp stock-flow corrections may increase public debt. These corrections may include the impact of exchange rate changes on foreign currency-denominated public debt and the public assumption of private debt (for instance as a result of privatisation deals, bailouts, calls of public guarantees etc.). The share of foreign currency denominated debt out of total public debt is significant in many accession countries already now and may increase in the future. In some cases, government guarantees may also be a matter of concern. The ageing of the population will affect profoundly economic developments in all EU countries, including the future members. It remains to be seen whether its effects are comparable to events like wars or end of empires, which in the past have been the major driving force behind fiscal and monetary instability. Anyway, while many accession countries have implemented comprehensive reforms of their pension systems, I expect that the ageing of the population poses considerable challenges for most if not all of them, especially in view of the consequences of the expected increase in labour mobility after the accession. A scenario of growing or perhaps even accelerating public sector indebtedness seems to be in contrast with the scenarios presented in the accession countrieso Pre-Accession Economic Programmes. Last year, the programmes forecast progressive fiscal consolidation at general government level, with budgetary positions in 2005 ranging from balanced budgets (Bulgaria, Estonia) to a deficit of 3.1 % and 5.5 % in Malta and Czech Republic, respectively. According to the programmes, the debt ratio would have risen significantly only in the Czech Republic and, to a lesser extent, Latvia and Poland. While the scenarios in Pre-Accession Programmes certainly were not infeasible at least at the time of their drafting, they fail to be fully convincing. To some extent this is due to a lack of a throughout long-term sustainability analysis in the programmes, but a more important reason is the assumptions used in the programmes. The Pre-Accession Programmes assume high and even accelerating growth rates so that in all programmes the 2005 growth rate is the highest one projected. While the accession countries generally managed to post growth rates of 2-5 per cent in 2002, this was only because robust domestic demand helped to offset the impact of slowing exports. Large current account deficits underscore the risks related to these trends. In order to permanently achieve growth rates assumed for the later years, accession countries should achieve a significant acceleration in the pace of the catching-up process. Only by taking early action to dispel even the slightest doubts about fiscal developments which may over time lead to an erosion of debt sustainability one can be assured that macroeconomic environment is favourable for the achievement of this key priority. Although the situations may differ, there is perhaps a general need to strengthen mediumterm budgetary frameworks in the accession countries. There are several elements common to all strong medium-term fiscal frameworks. First of all, programmes should be based on realistic or preferably even cautious macroeconomic assumptions. Second, a careful review of government spending priorities and tax cut commitments is needed to secure a momentum of fiscal consolidation and the credibility of medium-term budget targets. In this respect, I note that most Pre-Accession Programmes fail to provide policy commitments to credibly underpin a medium-term path of fiscal consolidation. Nevertheless many of them envisage significant reductions of primary expenditures, in contrasts with the rigidity of primary expenditures recorded in the past. Finally, there is evidence showing that the institutional design of the budget process has affected fiscal outcomes in accession countries. Budget institutions that appear to be supportive for achieving fiscal discipline are those that strengthen the role of the minister of finance in the budget process and limit the autonomy of spending ministers and individual legislators without responsibility for the budget. Conclusions Fiscal soundness is essential for monetary stability. There is much evidence, some of which has been provided rather recently by the accession countries, that it is impossible to maintain price stability without sound public finances. Compared to those examples, the situation in Europe is now comforting. Many EU countries have achieved price stability, and also the accession countries have progressed considerably towards this goal. The fact that risk of high or even moderate inflation is now more or less latent implies that public finances must be on a relatively sound footing. Nevertheless, adopting a longer time perspective, there is no reason to believe that public finances have become for good irrelevant for monetary stability. I have argued in this presentation that there is no clear line of demarcation separating sound public finances from unsound public finances. Rather, there is a risk of unsound public finances, which more or less continuously depends on a great number of variables such as the level and composition of liabilities, credibility of the fiscal and monetary policy, of the commitments adopted by the government etc. At very low risk levels the probability of a budgetary collapse is virtually zero and the burden the risk places on monetary policy is insignificant. In such a situation a weakening in the governmentos budgetary position may have insignificant effects on monetary policy. At very high level of risk, the burden be-comes overwhelming, and a weakening in the governmentos budgetary position may again be insignificant, because the collapse is doomed to be inevitable anyway. I would think that the situation relevant for both member and accession countries is somewhere between these two extremes. This means that much depends on the policy adopted by the authorities. An increase in deficit increases the risk of unsound public finances and thereby complicates the task of maintaining monetary stability. In the accession countries, debt ratios are relatively low. With their higher expected growth rates, accession countries may feel that they are facing favourable debt dynamics, at least in comparison with the present member countries, and that their fiscal policies do not pose any concern for monetary stability. I do not think that this conclusion is warranted. On the contrary, fiscal pressures seem to be emerging at an alarming rate. Successful real convergence is likely to require substantial public expenditure to finance public investment and the expenditure needed to fulfil the obligations of the EU membership. Public expenditure needs also to be stepped up in order to maximise the benefits from the EU membership through structural and cohesion funds. These challenges, some of which have already contributed to a widening of the fiscal deficits in the accession countries, may lead to a further weakening of the budgetary discipline. A relaxation of budgetary discipline in the new member states would impose a heavy burden on their national monetary policies and could complicate the goal of attaining substantially higher levels of real and nominal convergence. Instead of a weakening of the budgetary discipline, the new member states would benefit from adopting strong and realistic stability-oriented medium-to long-term fiscal frameworks, including where needed changes in budgetary institutions. Once the accession countries join the EU, the Treaty provisions and all secondary legislation on economic and budgetary policy, in particular the Stability and Growth Pact, will apply to them. This, I believe, is one of the great benefits from the accession. Given the expected state of public finances in the new member states, some of the new member states may have difficulties in complying with the requirements of the pact. In view of the size of the economies, such difficulties would not necessarily directly threaten the monetary stability in the euro area, even in the case these economies would be part of the area. Rather, the main risk to monetary stability is an indirect one, namely that political pressures to loosen the pact may intensify after the accession. In a monetary union, fiscal rules like the Stability and Growth Pact are an essential element of overall policy framework. Therefore, even though one could allow more room for country specific factors in the interpretation of the Stability and Growth Pact in the future, the temptation to weaken it is dangerous and should be firmly resisted.

Wednesday2 April 2003,12:00 AM Economic development and monetary policy Good listeners, First of all, I would like to thank you for the invitation of the Members of The European Union to come and speak at your event. I thought of the time allotted to me by thinking, above all, about the longer period of growth in the EU and the euro area, when structural challenges have to be addressed - and when I am the representative of the Central Bank, in particular, the European integration of the financial markets. But in the past, very briefly, the short-term economic shocks, to which it is difficult to say what new ? guarantees are exceptionally high. *** In the bank's recently published forecast, the economic recovery is still expected to be postponed, as well as globally, that at home ? for reasons, above all related to the international situation, the security of the economic situation is still in place: in addition to the bloated current account deficit and the indebtedness of the household sector, the emergence of ?ss? the third factor of imbalance in the public sector is when the public sector deficit grows to more than 4% of GDP in that year. The impact of this factor on the dollar exchange rate is certain ? a weakening of the dollar and an orderly appreciation of the euro would be desirable ? rapid corrections instead of eiv?t.
