Title: Social policy and sustainable economy
text: Bank Manager Sinikka Salo's speech: Social policy and the sustainable economy . Speech . Thursday12 February2004,12:00 AM Speech at the Forum for the Development of Social and Health Policy by the Swedish Leadership, 12.2.2004 Ladies and gentlemen, I would like to express my sincerest thanks for the invitation to the Forum for the Development of Social and Health Policy by the Ministry of Health and Social Policy. It is a great honour for me to be able to speak to you, because I have a great deal of respect for the benefit of disadvantaged people in the organisations you represent. There is often a desire for a conflict between economic efficiency and the social sector. In my speech, I will try to clarify why there is no such confrontation, i.e. why social policy and the economy are intertwined. Our well-being services are facing great challenges for decades. The pressures come from two different directions of my nshdss. The globalisation of national economies is likely to continue at the current rate. As China, India and other wealthy countries of Asia join the international labour market, companies operating in Finland, our wage earners and our political employees will have to stretch their talents to ensure that employment and living standards remain at a high level. Another direction that, in Finland, as in other industrialized countries, will put pressure on the welfare state in the Lshi years is the development of vsests. In addition to the development of this trend, public expenditure on pensions and health care is aiming to increase substantially. Indeed, the future success of our economic policy will be measured for a very long time, as we succeed in singing the basic principles of our nordic welfare model, which enjoys broad support, in new, more challenging circumstances. The question of securing welfare services is often a matter of mere political will, i.e. a purely political issue of income distribution. This is a simplification that goes too long. In addition to the political will, there are many other things to be taken into account, not the functioning of the economy. That is why the debate on the future of social and health policy is not a good thing for social work professionals alone. Especially when outlining the longer-term development of the sector, a broader angle that takes into account the economy as a whole is downright vsltsmssn. The important framework for social and health care in Finland is given by our membership of the European Union, despite the fact that responsibility for policy clearly lies with the Member States in the policy area, not with the Community. When all, or almost all, eu member states are struggling with similar problems, the exchange of information and experience between countries has been an important means of outlining common problems and policy responses. The EU's Lisbon strategy The Lisbon European Council of 2000 therefore criticised the development of a strategy for the EU for the next decade of the 2000s. The essence of the strategy was summed up at the time by the demand that the strategy be held during the decade. Europe would become the most competitive and dynamic knowledge-based economy in the world, capable of sustaining economic growth, creating new and better jobs and increasing social cohesion. The Lisbon Strategy was designed to enable the EU to meet the challenges of global competition and the development of information technology. However, the strategy does not only focus on the economy and technology, but also wanted to emphasise the social dimension of the structural change sought. The strategy aims for a dynamic, knowledge- and technology-based economy, combined with a European social model with a social cohesion-oriented approach. In the strategy, the strategy is to improve the level of employment and to improve the level of integration. The strategy is built on three basic pillars. First of all, therefore, there is a desire to hold on to the 'social cohesion', i.e. solidarity- which is firmly part of the European tradition in the future. Success in this area depends on a strong and well-functioning economy. The second pillar of the strategy is therefore a sound macroeconomic policy. In other words, the single monetary policy, which is the responsibility of the ECB, and the national budgetary policy, which is the responsibility of the Member States, must provide the most stable framework possible for the private sector to operate. The third pillar, on the other hand, is the reform of production structures and the labour market in order to modernise the economy and revive the capacity for growth. The aim of the structural reforms is to increase the level of employment and, through new production methods, to increase productivity. It should be noted that the third pillar also includes the integration of financial markets, i.e. the achievement of well-functioning EU-wide financial markets. This is due to the fact that, in a market economy, it is the long-term functioning of the financial markets that determines the achievement of the strategy's objectives, the designation of the size and orientation of new investment and, consequently, the long-term growth of productivity. Economic problems of European countries The Lisbon strategy is based on the economic problems of european countries, in particular the slowdown in economic growth and the difficulties in public finances, and on the other hand, the awareness that economic problems have constantly put their stamp on public finances and have made it difficult to achieve social cohesion. In Belgium, Italy, Ireland and Greece, government debt increased uncontrollably in the 1970s and 1980s. Of the Countries, only Ireland has managed to escape its debt trap since then, thanks to economic policy guidelines and favourable external factors. The other countries, on the other hand, continue to be in the debt swamp. Italy remains the most net indebted of the world's major industrialised countries, although Japan is well ahead of it. In the 1990s, heavily indebted European countries were saved from bankruptcy, probably simply because they succeeded in becoming the father of EMU. In the euro area, the expectations of low interest rates in these countries have been realised, probably even above all expectations. Despite the low level of interest rates, part of europe's heavily indebted countries' public expenditure still goes to interest on debts. If debt servicing expenditure is taken away from public expenditure, public finances are clearly overspending, generally around 5 or 6% of GDP. In reality, including debt service expenditure, public finances in the countries are clearly understated. In some indebted countries, too, there is already a three per cent threshold. A huge amount of tax revenue, i.e. 5 or 6% of GDP, will therefore have to be used for interest on government debts instead of welfare services. This may explain political preferences or historical traditions better in low-level welfare countries. Sustainability of Finland's public finances In Finland, the government debt-to-GDP ratio is about 44 per cent, or more than in most other EU countries. The financial situation of the public sector as a whole is improved by the fact that the central government, and in particular the employment funds, have substantial financial claims to offset their debts. Thanks to the partial funding of the pensions, the financial assets of the public sector are already higher than the public debt and are constantly growing faster. The state and the municipalities take out enough additional loans, but the ssssch of the institutions exceeds the borrowing of the state and municipalities. Compared to other EU countries, Finland's general government finances can be considered to be excellent. On the other hand, like most other countries, Finland has prepared for these challenges by funding a significant part of its future expenditure, its public indebtedness and the reform of the social security system and taxation in a way that encourages work. Is the public sshsschm in Finland actually excessive? Would it be better to use tax revenue for different areas of social and health care than for the accrual of financial receivables? I believe that it would not be difficult for anyone to come up with a large number of items in need of additional funding. Although finland's fiscal situation is now sound and clearly better than in most other EU countries, it requires careful assessment. The challenges are related to the future nibbles. The power of the government is increasing and public expenditure is increasing. The change in the structure of the Vsestss in Finland will be the fastest in the EU countries by 2020. Last October, the Finance Minister drew up new estimates of the longterm duration of the budgetary financing base. According to the calculation published in Finland's stability programme, the current policy will maintain its general government finances in excess until 2025, i.e. until 2025, public financial assets would be accumulated. However, after that, public finances become sub-national and financial assets start in the tenth or fifteenth year. Since then, public sector indebtedness is starting to grow at an accelerating rate. In other words, according to the finance minister's calculation, public finances will not be on a longer basis if the current policy is continued. The challenges posed to the public sector by this phenomenon were also highlighted by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in its latest country review of Finland. According to the IMF, the budget line of the Government Programme is too lsyss. In view of the challenges of this situation, Finland's public finances should aim to exceed the current target of around two per cent, rather than the current target of around two per cent. By this, public finances would remain stable even after 2025. I do not wish to comment on the question of exactly what the fiscal stance in Finland should be. However, in order for our welfare services to be in reasonable shape in the future d when the challenges are greater than they are today - and not just for a while, it is of paramount importance that the state and local government debt should swell. This means a constantly strict and prudent budgetary policy. Municipalities, and especially the state, may well accumulate debt for a year or two. However, borrowing is prudent and borrowing is only taken out on a temporary basis. If the level of indebtedness exceeds a certain point, it is difficult to contain it; rather, it tends to grow at its own pace. Since then, welfare services are very difficult to satisfy at the level. The looming problems in two decades' time may seem far-fetched and, of course, the long-term calculations and scenarios contain a great deal of certainty. However, even if they are indicative, the calculations illustrate the fact that public finances are managed over a very long period of time. 20 years from the Czech angle is not a long time. History provides a good example of how the welfare state can be destroyed by an failed policy. On the negative side, the best example is Argentina, where the exceptionally high standard of living since the war, and with them welfare services, was destroyed by poor policies over two generations. Now the country's debt problems are absolutely overwhelming. It is quite wise to be lulled into the idea that we can take the constant improvement and increase in welfare services, or even the maintenance of existing services as something that has been given. In Finland, with the exception of the IMF, hardly anyone has called for fiscal tightening in the debate on economic policy. On the other hand, the pressure on the budget line in the government programme is growing. There are calls for further tax cuts and for an increase in expenditure. Despite the government's strict spending limits, the politically-wise easiest way to meet these demands would be by a compromise that reduced taxation and increased spending. I think that would be a very bad choice. The wise thing to do would be to pursue a prudent fiscal policy. Interest rates on debt, Stability and Growth Pact In addition to the amount of debt, central and local government debt expenditure is significantly affected by d in particular for long-term indebted countries d interest rates. In terms of interest rates, the euro area countries are now in the same boat for a long time. In addition to the single monetary policy and the integration of financial markets, interest rates in the euro area have fallen significantly. If long-term interest rates in the euro area rise because other countries take out additional loans, the production of welfare services will not only increase in the countries that take on debt, but also in Finland. On the one hand, because finland's government debt servicing costs are increasing, but also because public borrowing and rising interest rates are causing the willingness of the private sector to borrow and invest and thereby slow down economic growth. Welfare services in Finland should therefore ensure the stability of public finances in euro area countries other than Finland. To serve this purpose, a Stability and Growth Pact was concluded. It protects us against mistakes on the part of other countries. Good listeners! The countries of the European Union are committed to stability in their economic policies. There are difficult alternatives to this line. People need to be confident that the framework for economic activity will continue to be stable - public finances will remain stable and prices will remain stable. Within the framework of the eu's economic policy division, this means primarily that the ECB is concerned about price stability in the euro area and that the Member States, in turn, keep excessive borrowing. The growth of the economy and the growth potential of the economy The various expenditure pressures that come from the whispering, in particular the increase in income and health expenditure, have been the subject of much public debate. What has become clear to me is the risk of economic growth, the slowdown and, or possibly even the end of, economic growth that is comparable to them. The effects of this trend on gdp growth are already clear. On average, total output in the EU countries is growing at a rate of one per cent than in the United States alone, as a result of the slower or no growth rate in the autumn alone. Nskspiirisss is already a contraction of the force in the future. It is worrying if the economy also becomes more stable and productivity growth slows down. However, a trendy decline in output is not a scenario. On the other hand, we must consider all possible means of achieving this. As a key element of the European Lisbon strategy, I mentioned the creation of well-functioning European financial markets. There is no possibility of examining them d I would point out, however, that the integration of national financial markets into truly functioning pan-European financial markets could, according to various estimates, increase the d the potential for growth is very significant. The financing of welfare services cannot be attributed to tax increases; also, public investment in education cannot be reduced However, when considering future solutions, we are faced with the possibility of a slowdown in growth. In addition, the financing of welfare services is also threatened by the erosion of the tax base due to the globalisation of the economy and tax competition. It would therefore be a frivolous idea to base the financing of welfare services on tax increases. In most European countries, the current increase in the level of taxation in relation to total output of several percentage points, i.e. an average of around 5 % of gdp, is required. It is, of course, only a question of a pressure calculation, but it would be clear to everyone that the problem of financing welfare services cannot be solved in this way in a sustainable way. Welfare expenditure cannot also be financed by cutting public investment. On the other hand, public expenditure should be directed as far as possible in order to promote economic growth, i.e. investment in education and other long-term public investment should in the future be increased rather than increased. Welfare system can be used to increase the productivity of services In order to secure the funding of welfare systems, it is necessary to reform the systems themselves. In my view, an essential feature of a well-functioning welfare society is that the up-to-dateness of public services is constantly assessed. In the old formulas, jsmshchchhim would shun tightly. In several contexts, I have stressed the need to improve the efficiency of the provision of welfare services. The whole core problem with the financing of welfare services seems to be that productivity in the public sector is rising more slowly than in the private sector. Wages in both sectors, on the other hand, are rising more or less, or at least at the same rate. In addition to the correct content and sizing of public services, it is necessary to ensure the most efficient allocation of resources and the availability of the necessary resources in the future. There are large and quite permanent differences in efficiency in public service production, which cannot be explained by the circumstances. For example, it has been estimated that the productivity of social and health services and education services could increase by between 10% and 20% if all services were produced as efficiently as the most efficient of the moment. Greater productivity growth in Chechnya can be achieved by reforming structures, operating methods and the use of information technology. This is in line with the Lisbon strategy, with the combination of the information society and the welfare society, in which we in Finland should be in the best position to operate in the previous sectors. The intensification of public services is unfortunately often the case. Nshdssn, the question is the constant tightening of the pace of work and the deterioration of the interests of the tysntekijs. In the name of the Costsssch, the public sector, and in particular the municipal employers, have adopted a large-scale project, even in sectors where the work is very stable for a longer period of time. Such tricks are not a step intensification, nor can proper results be achieved for a longer period of time. Nskyvisss is also starting to be a situation where there is a shortage of power. At the end of the day, other methods will have to be used in order to provide a skilled workforce to manage public services. Instead of exploiting the labour force, the efficiency of the work should be improved by stopping the work of unnecessary chels, concentrating on the essentials and carrying out the tasks as efficiently as possible. The fact that the public sector has resorted to methods such as the pstkstys suggests to me that the main challenges facing the public sector are related to the ability of the public sector to organise public sector work and, more broadly, production in an efficient and long-term manner, i.e. to omanagemento broadly understood. A lot has been done in Finland in recent years to reform the welfare state. The productivity of the health sector, and possibly of other welfare state functions, has clearly improved over the last ten years. But the tys continues. As I said, the most important challenge for the success of Finnish society in the decades is to reform the production of public sector services so that the gap between the productivity development of public services and private goods production continues to widen. Part of the shsnastic productivity increase in the public sector may have been achieved by means that have now been exhausted. I hope - and I believe - that there will also be an impact on product development and technology, i.e. the kind of development that exists in Finland as an application of cutting-edge technology and that can continue in the future. In addition to the new technologies in the public sector, great opportunities have opened up for work and productivity gains. In addition to the fact that information technology is used in the care services themselves, it is of course also useful in the organisation of services, where the greatest amount of information is likely to be available. The production of social and health care services can be made more efficient, for example, by reforming municipal and service structures, regional cooperation and networking. Scale and specialization benefits as well as joint service can be hysdynchss. In the context of the reform of production methods, technical tools have often only played a catalyst role, so that in terms of productivity growth, changes have occurred in ways of thinking and working methods. With regard to increasing productivity growth in the production of services, I would like to stress that this is not a question of reducing the quality of services d as is often suggested in public. It is a question of ensuring that high-quality services are provided efficiently d professionally and reliably. People are also willing to pay taxes. *** Ladies and gentlemen! The social and health care sector in Finland and other European countries will face major challenges even in the past few years. The challenges are very similar in all European countries. We are unlikely to be able to correctly assess all future developments for a moment. What is certain, however, is that the reforms for high-quality welfare services are vsltsmstsmis. In order to safeguard welfare services, it is necessary to work on a broad front. European countries have already responded in different ways to the challenges ahead. From the point of view of the welfare services, the opening of the welfare services was a general economic strategy adopted for the EU in Lisbon in 1990, in which social cohesion and a strong economy were thought of as two sides of the same coin: The maintenance of welfare services requires a strong economy, but a strong economy also requires the services of the welfare state, which yllspitsvsv and additionalssvsvst to be involved in the same thing in Europe. It is well known that the economy works better when social services are in order. Of course, social security is also an intrinsic value and therefore it is a value even when it does not pay back itself. The economy must function for the last few people. In my opinion, this is also at the heart of the Lisbon Strategy. The objectives of the strategy are still very topical, even though its implementation has been partly faltering. Strong public finances and sound monetary policy are vital pillars in preparing for future changes. The functioning of the internal market has been promoted, for example, by the implementation of integrated European financial markets. The key to saving the welfare state is to renew the outdated structures of the economy. This means creating entirely new jobs in the industrial and service sectors, based on high-level technology. On the other hand, a great deal can be achieved by new production methods and increased productivity at existing sites. Given its size alone, the social and health care sector plays a key role in increasing the productivity of the public sector. As part of efforts to improve the efficiency of public service, the role of the private sector in the provision of public services will certainly be strengthened in the future. In connection with the flexible operation of the public sector, the sydentsvien jsrjestsjen and the so-called "public sector" work. the role of the third sector in the provision of public services is also likely to be played by the third sector. However, I do not have the prerequisites to go into the work in more detail. However, I would like to say that it is not, of course, the responsibility of the Member States to fill in potential gaps in public welfare services. Rather, it is up to the people who have set themselves to pursue their own self-imposed goals. I wish you every success in your work and in your challenging tasks.

Jotta hyvinvointipalvelumme voidaan pit kohtuullisessa kunnossa mys tulevaisuudessa  jolloin haasteet siis ovat suuremmat kuin nykyisin -eik vain tll hetkell, on mielestni kuitenkin aivan ensiarvoisen trke est valtion ja kuntien velkaa paisumasta. Tm tarkoittaa jatkuvasti tiukkaa ja harkitsevaa budjettipolitiikkaa. Kunnat ja etenkin valtio voivat hyvin kartuttaa velkaa vuoden tai kaksi. Vain suuntaa-antavinakin laskelmat kuitenkin havainnollistavat sit tosiasiaa, ett julkista taloutta pit hoitaa hyvin pitkjnteisesti. Tst nkkulmasta 20 vuotta ei ole pitk aika. Kielteisess mieless parhaan esimerkin tarjoaa Argentiina, jossa sodan jlkeinen poikkeuksellisen korkea elintaso ja niiden mukana hyvinvointipalvelut onnistuttiin tuhoamaan huonolla politiikalla kahden sukupolven aikana. On sangen epviisasta tuudittautua siihen ajatukseen, ett voisimme ottaa hyvinvointipalvelujen jatkuvan parantumisen ja lisntymisen tai edes nykyisten palvelujen silymisen ennallaan itsestn annettuna. Suomessa kytvss talouspoliittisessa keskustelussa ei -IMF: lukuun ottamatta -juuri kukaan ole vaatinut finanssipolitiikan kiristmist. Pinvastoin, paineet hallitusohjelmassa mritellyn budjettilinjan hllentmiseksi nyttvt olevan kasvamassa. Vaatimuksia esitetn sek verotuksen uusista kevennyksist ett menojen kasvattamisesta. Tm olisi minusta sangen huono valinta. Viisasta olisi harjoittaa varovaista finanssipolitiikkaa. Velan korkotaso, vakaus-ja kasvusopimus Velan mrn ohella valtion ja kuntien velkamenoihin vaikuttaa merkittvsti  etenkin pitklle velkaantuneiden maiden osalta  korkotaso. Korkojen suhteen euroalueen maat ovat nyt pitklti samassa veneess. Yhteisen rahapolitiikan ja rahoitusmarkkinoiden integroitumisen myt euroalueen korot ovat lhentyneet toisiaan merkittvsti. Jos pitkt korot euroalueella nousevat koska muut valtiot ottavat lis lainaa, hyvinvointipalvelusten tuotanto krsii paitsi velkaa ottavissa maissa mys Suomessa. Nin yhtlt siksi, ett Suomen valtion velanhoitokulut kasvavat, toisaalta siksi, ett julkinen velanotto ja korkojen kohoaminen syrjyttvt yksityisen sektorin halukkuutta ottaa lainaa ja investoida ja tt kautta hidastavat talouskasvua. Hyvinvointipalveluiden silyttmiseksi Suomessa tulisikin siksi turvata julkisen talouden vakaus mys muissa euromaissa kuin Suomessa. Tt tarkoitusta palvelemaan solmittiin vakaus-ja kasvusopimus. Se turvaa meit muiden maiden virheilt. Hyvt kuulijat! Euroopan Unionin valtiot ovat sitoutuneet talouspolitiikassaan vakauteen thtvn linjaukseen. Tlle linjalle on vaikea nhd varteenotettavia vaihtoehtoja. Ihmisten on voitava luottaa siihen, ett jatkossakin taloudellisen toiminnan puitteet silyvt vakaina -julkinen talous silytt tasapainonsa ja hinnat pysyvt vakaina. EU:n talouspolitiikan tyjaon puitteissa tm tarkoittaa ensisijaisesti sit, ett EKP pit huolta euroalueen hintavakaudesta ja jsenvaltiot puolestaan pidttytyvt liiallisesta velanotosta. Vestn ikntyminen ja talouden kasvupotentiaali Vestn ikntymisen myt tulevat erilaiset menopaineet, erityisesti elkkeiden ja terveydenhoitomenojen kasvu, ovat olleet julkisessa keskustelussa runsaan huomion kohteena. Selvsti vhemmlle huomiolle on jnyt vhintn niiden veroinen ikntymisest aiheutuva riski, nimittin talouskasvun hiipuminen ja tai mahdollisesti jopa loppuminen. Ikntymisen vaikutukset kokonaistuotannon kasvuun nkyvt jo nyt selkesti. EU-maiden kokonaistuotanto kasvaa keskimrin prosenttiyksikn hitaammin kuin Yhdysvalloissa pelkstn siit syyst, ett tyntekijiden mr kasvaa hitaammin tai ei lainkaan. Nkpiiriss on jo lhitulevaisuudessa tyvoiman supistuminen. Huolestuttavaa on, jos tyvoiman ikntymisen myt talous mys jykistyy ja tuottavuuden kasvu hidastuu. Trendinomainen tuotannon supistuminen ei kuitenkaan ole vlttmtn skenaario. Meidn tulee pinvastoin mietti kaikkia mahdollisia keinoja sen vlttmiseksi. Ern Lissabonin strategiaan keskeisen kuuluvana keinona mainitsin edell eurooppalaisten toimivien rahoitusmarkkinoiden luomisen. Niiden tarkastelemiseen ei ole tss yhteydess mahdollisuutta  toteaisin kumminkin, ett kansallisten rahoitusmarkkinoiden integroiminen todella toimiviksi Euroopan laajuisiksi rahoitusmarkkinoiksi voisi eriden arvioiden mukaan list EU:n  ja mys Suomen  kasvumahdollisuuksia varsin merkittvsti. Hyvinvointipalvelujen rahoittamista ei voida laskea verotuksen kiristmisen varaan; myskn julkisia investointeja koulutukseen ei voida karsia Tulevia ratkaisuja mietittess joudumme kuitenkin pitmn mieless kasvun hiipumisen mahdollisuuden. Lisksi hyvinvointipalvelujen rahoittamista uhkaa mys veropohjan murentuminen talouden globalisoitumisen ja lisntyvn verokilpailun myt. Olisikin mielestni kevytmielist laskea hyvinvointipalvelujen rahoitus verotuksen kiristmisen varaan. Useimmissa Euroopan maissa elke-ja terveydenhuoltoetuisuuksien silyttminen nykyiselln edellyttisi useiden prosenttiyksikkjen, ehk keskimrin noin 5 prosenttiyksikn, korotusta verotuksen tasossa suhteessa kokonaistuotantoon. Kysymys on tietenkin vain painelaskelmasta, mutta kaikkien pitisi ymmrt, ettei hyvinvointipalvelujen rahoitusongelmaa voida ratkaista tll tavalla kestvsti. Hyvinvointimenoja ei voida myskn rahoittaa karsimalla julkisia investointeja. Pinvastoin julkiset menot tulisi suunnata mahdollisimman pitklle talouskasvua edistvsti, toisin sanoen investointeja koulutukseen ja muihinkin pitkvaikutteisiin julkisiin investointikohteisiin tulisi tulevaisuudessa pikemmin list kuin vhent. Hyvinvointijrjestelm turvattavissa lismllpalvelujen tuottavuutta Hyvinvointijrjestelmien rahoituksen turvaaminen edellytt mielestni itse jrjestelmien uudistamista. Hyvin toimivan hyvinvointiyhteiskunnan luonteeseen tulee minusta kuulua olennaisena piirteen se, ett julkisten palvelujen ajanmukaisuutta arvioidaan jatkuvasti. Vanhoihin kaavoihin jmhtmist pitisi karttaa tiukasti. Useissa yhteyksiss olen painottanut tarvetta tehostaa hyvinvointipalvelujen tuottamista. Hyvinvointipalvelujen rahoittamisen koko ydinongelma tuntuu olevan se, ett tyn tuottavuus nousee julkisella sektorilla hitaammin kuin yksityisell sektorilla. Palkat sit vastoin nousevat molemmilla sektoreilla jokseenkin tai ainakin lhes samaa vauhtia. Julkisten palvelujen oikean sislln ja mitoituksen ohella on vlttmtnt varmistaa voimavarojen mahdollisimman tehokas kohdentaminen ja kytt sek tarvittavan tyvoiman saanti tulevaisuudessa. Julkisten palvelutuotantoyksikiden vlill on suuria ja varsin pysyvi tehokkuuseroja, joita ei voida selitt olosuhdetekijill. On esimerkiksi arvioitu, ett sosiaali-ja terveyspalvelujen ja opetuspalvelujen tuottavuus voisi kasvaa 10 -20 prosenttia, jos kaikki palvelut tuotettaisiin yht tehokkaasti kuin tmn hetken tehokkaimmat. Ttkin suurempaan tuottavuuden kasvuun voidaan pst rakenteita, toimintatapoja ja tietotekniikan kytt uudistamalla. Tm on Lissabonin strategian mukaista tietoyhteiskunnan ja hyvinvointiyhteiskunnan yhdistmist, jossa meill Suomessa pitisi olla mit parhaat edellytykset toimia edellkvijn. Julkisten palvelujen tehostaminen ymmrretn valitettavan usein vrin. Nhdn, ett kysymyksess on tytahdin jatkuva kiristminen ja tyntekijiden etujen huononnukset. Kustannussstjen nimiss julkinen sektori ja erityisesti kunnalliset tynantajat ovat ottaneet kyttn laajamittaisen ptktyn, sellaisillakin aloilla joilla tynkymt ovat pitemmn plle erittin vakaat. Tllaiset temput eivt ole tyn tehostamista, eik niill voida pitemmn plle saada aikaan kunnollisia tuloksia. Nkyviss alkaa mys olla jo tilanne, jossa tyvoimasta on pulaa. Viimeistn silloin joudutaan turvautumaan toisiin menetelmiin, jotta saataisiin ammattitaitoista tyvoimaa hoitamaan julkiset palvelut. Tyvoiman riiston asemesta tyn tehokkuutta tulisi parantaa lopettamalla tarpeettomiksi tulleiden tiden tekeminen, keskittymll olennaisiin asioihin ja suorittamalla tehtvt mahdollisimman tehokkaasti. Se, ett julkisessa sektorissa on turvauduttu ptktyn tapaisiin menetelmiin, viittaa minusta siihen, ett julkisen sektorin suurimmat haasteet liittyvt viime kdess kykyyn organisoida julkisen sektorin tyntekoa ja laajemmin tuotantoa tehokkaasti ja pitkjnteisesti, siis johtajuuteen laajasti ymmrretyss mieless. Hyvinvointiyhteiskunnan uudistamiseksi on Suomessa viime vuosina tehty paljon. Terveydenhuoltosektorin ja mahdollisesti eriden muidenkin hyvinvointivaltion toimintojen tuottavuus on selvsti parantunut viimeisten kymmenen vuoden aikana. Mutta ty jatkuu. Kuten totesin, Suomen yhteiskunnan menestyksen kannalta ehk keskeisin lhivuosikymmenten haaste on julkisen sektorin palvelujen tuotannon uudistaminen siten, ett ero julkisten palvelujen ja yksityisen tavaratuotannon tuottavuuskehityksess edelleen pienenee. Osa julkisen sektorin thnastisesta tuottavuuden noususta voi olla saavutettu sellaisin keinoin, jotka on nyt loppuun kytetty. Toivon -ja uskon -kuitenkin, ett mukana on mys tuotekehittelyn ja teknologian vaikutusta, eli sellaista kehityst, jota Suomessa huipputeknologian soveltajana on ja joka voi jatkua tulevaisuudessakin. Uuden teknologian myt mys julkisessa sektorissa ovat avautuneet suuret mahdollisuudet tyn jrkeistmiseksi ja tuottavuuden lismiseksi. Sen lisksi ett tietoteknologiaa kytetn hyvksi itse hoitopalveluissa, sit luonnollisesti on kytettv hyvksi mys palvelujen organisoinnissa, joissa todennkisesti on saatavissa eniten sstj. Sosiaali-ja terveysalan palvelujen tuotantoa voidaan tehostaa mm. kunta-ja palvelurakenteita uudistamalla, seutuyhteistyll ja verkottumisella. Mittakaava-ja erikoistumisetuja sek yhteispalvelua voidaan hydynt. Tuotantotapoja uudistettaessa tekniset vlineet ovat usein olleet vain katalysaattorin asemassa siten ett tuottavuuden kasvun kannalta trket muutokset ovat tapahtuneet ajattelutavoissa ja tyskentelymenetelmiss. Kun puhutaan tuottavuuden kasvun nostamisesta palvelujen tuotannossa, haluan korostaa, ett kyseess ei ole palvelujen laadun heikentminen  niin kuin julkisuudessa usein nkee esitettvn. Kyse on siit, ett laadukkaat palvelut tuotetaan tehokkaasti  ammattitaitoisesti ja luotettevasti. Nist ihmiset ovat mys valmiita maksamaan veroja. *** Arvoisat kuulijat! Suomen ja muiden Euroopan maiden sosiaali-ja terveysala tulee olemaan suurten haasteiden edess lhivuosinakin. Haasteet ovat hyvin samanlaisia kaikissa Euroopan maissa. Emme varmaankaan osaa tll hetkell arvioida oikein kaikkia tulevia kehityslinjoja. Varma asia kuitenkin lienee se, ett laadukkaiden hyvinvointipalvelusten silyttmiseksi uudistukset ovat vlttmttmi. Hyvinvointipalvelusten turvaamiseksi joudutaan tekemn tyt laajalla rintamalla. Euroopan maat ovat jo reagoineet eri tavoin edess oleviin haasteisiin. Hyvinvointipalvelujen nkkulmasta mielestni trke avaus oli EU:lle Lissabonissa vuonna 1990 hyvksytty yleinen talousstrategia, jossa sosiaalinen koheesio ja vahva talous ajateltiin saman asian kahdeksi eri puoleksi: Hyvinvointipalvelujen yllpito vaatii vahvaa taloutta, mutta mys vahva talous edellytt hyvinvointivaltion palveluja, jotka yllpitvt ja lisvt tyvoimaan osallistumista ikntyvss Euroopassa. Tiedetn, ett talous toimii paremmin kun sosiaalipalvelut ovat kunnossa. Luonnollisesti sosiaaliturva on mys itseisarvo ja siksi se on jrjestettv silloinkin kun se ei maksa itse itsen takaisin. Talouden tulee toimia viime kdess ihmisi varten. Mielestni tm on mys Lissabonin strategian ydinkohta. Strategia on tavoitteiltaan edelleen hyvin ajankohtainen, vaikka sen toimeenpano on osin kangerrellut. Vahva julkinen talous ja vakaa rahapolitiikka ovat ensiarvoisen trkeit tukipilareita edess oleviin muutoksiin varauduttaessa. Sismarkkinoiden toimintaa on edistettv mm. toteuttamalla eurooppalaiset integroituneet rahoitusmarkkinat. Avainasemassa hyvinvointivaltion pelastamiseksi on talouden vanhentuneiden rakenteiden uusiminen. Yhtlt tm tarkoittaa kokonaan uusien, korkean tason teknologiaan nojaavien teollisuus-ja palvelualan typaikkojen luomista. Toisaalta paljon voidaan saavuttaa hydyntmll uusia tuotantotapoja ja lismll tyn tuottavuutta olemassa olevilla typaikoilla. Pelkstn jo kokonsa perusteella sosiaali-ja terveysala on avainasemassa, kun julkisen sektorin tuottavuutta kohotetaan. Osana julkisen palvelun tehostamispyrkimyksi yksityisen sektorin osuutta julkisten palvelujen tuottamisessa tullaan tulevaisuudessa todennkisesti vahvistamaan. Thn liittyen julkisen sektorin toimintaa joustavasti tydentvien jrjestjen ja ns. kolmannen sektorin merkitys julkisten palvelujen tuottamisessa on todennkisesti mys lisntymss. Thn trken tehtvkenttn minulla ei kuitenkaan ole edellytyksi paneutua tarkemmin. Se kuitenkin toteaisin, ett jrjestjen vastuulla ei luonnollisestikaan ole julkisten hyvinvointipalvelujen mahdollisten aukkokohtien paikkaaminen. Pikemminkin jrjestjen tulee tavoitella omia, itsenisesti asetettuja tavoitteitaan. Toivotan teille onnea ja menestyst trkeiss ja haasteellisissa tehtvissnne.

Title: Equality and fairness in management
text: Bank Manager Sinikka Salo's speech: Equality and fairness in management . Speech . Wednesday17 March2004,12:00AM Speech by Bank Manager Sinikka Salo Equality and justice tyselsmssss d power and responsibility at the d seminar 17.3.2004 Ladies and gentlemen, In my presentation, I will examine the subject given to me, the importance of equality and justice, from the nsks corner of the management of the Bank of Finland. The Bank of Finland is an interesting topic of discussion for many because of its own special nature, after all, it is an institution whose activities are based on its ability to create money, and it is, in a way, secretive. However, the Bank of Finland can also be viewed from the more general angle of management, as an organisation of more than 600 employees, which, although it has its own characteristics, but at the same time represents as an illustrative "case" the problems arising in the management of the financial industry and the public sector. The Bank of Finland highlights in an interesting way many of the management challenges typical of modern times. They are due to the Bank's unique position as the Central Bank of Finland, but there is no particular mystique to management in the Central Bank. As elsewhere, stakeholders and individuals demand a great deal from our management today, and issues of fairness and equality arise alongside performance-oriented management and the prerequisites for a well-functioning organisation. From a management point of view, the Bank of Finland's operations highlight three key features: the first is the bank's character as an expert organisation that invests in research. The second is the internationality of the entire organisation. The third challenge for management is the constant and extraordinarily rapid change in financial markets and monetary policy, which forces effective environmental analysis, continuous reform of operating models and skills, and the reorientation of people. Let's start with the change. Like many other financial sector organisations, the Bank of Finland has been very deep on changes over the past fifteen years. The background, of course, is Finland's entry into monetary union and, in parallel with the Ministry, the enormous structural change that has taken place in the Finnish financial markets and banking sector. As a result of this change, the central bank implementing national monetary policy has become part of the euro system, which prepares and implements the common monetary policy of the euro area. The role and powers of the Financial Supervisory Authority have been strengthened and attached to the Bank. The central bank has become increasingly important as a payment centre and the national payment system it manages has been integrated into the trans-European target payment network. In addition to monetary union, the bank's responsibilities as a statistical authority have clearly expanded, while many of the functions associated with its old role as an authority, such as the payment of clerical movements and trade payments, have been removed. The financial service has been completely reformed, and the old branch network has largely been replaced by cooperation with private service providers, and so on. The list of changes in the Bank of Finland's lspiksymi could go on for a long time, and the process of change is not over, because European integration and wider globalization are constantly revolutionizing the central bank's operating field in Finland as well. A great deal of resources are devoted to anticipating changes and analysing their impact. In the new context, the central bank's activities are characterised by an international character that encompasses the entire organisation, all its units and functions. The international nature of the Bank of Finland is not only a question of operational action to implement a common and coherent European monetary policy, but also of international cooperation in the reform of operations and the preparation of monetary policy. Cooperation is therefore a long-standing d and most of the question of expert friendliness, planning and influencing in forums where the Finnish people's word weighs just as much as they can make their expertise and interaction skills possible. The system of the European Central Bank takes place in tenth committees and working groups, which prepare the european central banks' common monetary policy and their activities for the development of financial markets and payment systems. Of course, all of the Bank's operational activities are international due to long-term coordination. In the context of the environment, which is characterised by constant change on the one hand and the profound internationalism on the other, the Bank's strategy has been to invest in expertise. As part of an international network and in a rapidly changing operating environment, a bank can only succeed if its staff is able to compete with internationally competitive expertise and influence. It is therefore necessary to develop expertise at international level and to focus it on issues that are central to the future of the Bank of Finland and the Finnish financial markets. Above all, it is necessary to motivate and mobilise the Bank's expert base for self-help and creative work. The Bank of Finland is currently an expert organisation, with approximately 650 employees with 56% university degrees and about 50 postgraduate degrees. The bank is being developed in a conscious way, specifically in the direction of an expert organisation. R&D expenditure accounts for five per cent of all expenditure and education input is about 4 per cent of the wages and salaries sum. The organisation is, by public sector standards, and the central bank is quite flat, the level of office is vshsn, so the co-operation of experts with the management is relatively vslichnchnt. Managing experts requires a lot from supervisors and senior management. It clearly requires delegation, trust, and self-reliance, because creative work and external influence can only be led by general objectives and not by detailed guidelines. A major challenge for the management is therefore to build a vision that describes the objectives of the activities, which is sufficiently illustrative, so that it coordinates the work of creative people into a coherent and psmssrs-conscious whole, but at the same time sufficient general and forward-looking, so that it does not prevent an open-minded work in order to introduce new operating models and ways of working. Forming and communicating the vision and the strategy that guides its implementation to all levels of the organization is a key management tool in the Bank of Finland, as in other development-oriented organizations. We already have a long tradition of strategy at the Bank, which became established as part of the annual operational planning already during sirkka Hsmslsisen's presidency. But even if explaining the objectives to the personnel is a matter of leading an expert organisation, it is not a dispute. In addition, it is possible to engage and motivate experts and, of course, other people to strive to achieve the vision. ssss management faces the demand for justice and its constituent equality. An organization that breaks the expectations of the tysntekijsidens, what it is like to be guided by fair management and equal treatment, loses a lot of loyalty and motivation. Particularly sensitive in relation to the ssss are expert organisations, for which the personal motivation of experts is definitely the most czech and decisive factor for success. The requirement of fair management must be incorporated into formal management systems and management systems. However, this is only the formal side of the matter, and the requirements of fairness and equality are tested in the field of human management, which is more art than formalistics. Even the best official documents will not suffice if you get tangled up. The policies guiding the Bank of Finland's operations emphasise the need to adapt operating methods to pluralistic working relationships. As I have already said, cost awareness and economic and efficient action, as well as networking and transparency d all of which is reflected in the guidelines - are also fair activities. The Board of Directors of the Bank of Finland also strives to be transparent and to communicate its strategy in a transparent manner. Nsin lays the foundations for equality and justice. Thn haasteeseen ei minkn organisaation johtoporras pysty yksin vastaamaan. Organisaation menestys ratkaistaan jokaisen yksiln henkilkohtaisen luovuuden ja innostuksen kautta, joita johdon tytyy oppia edistmn. Yhteisen vision merkitys tss tunnetaan. Title: The future of the euro
text: Bank Manager Sinikka Salo's speech: The future of the euro . Speech . Monday22 March2004,12:00AM The presentation is based on my article published on Channel 9/03 Presentation at the Direction for Finland seminar 22.3.2004 Ladies and gentlemen! I have been asked to speak at an event on the future of the euro. An interesting and broad theme can be found in different ways. In this context, I am looking at the future of the euro from the international angle. As a major currency, the euro will have to compete for its position on the international financial markets with the US dollar and other leading currencies, and one might ask how it will compete with the euro. I believe that the success of the euro on the international financial markets is a good omen for its success as domestic money. It is even possible to go any longer and say that the future of a currency as a currency depends on the last minute how successful it is in the international competition with other currencies. Adoption of the euro the biggest change since the bretton-woods djs system collapse The introduction of the euro at the beginning of 1999 was the biggest change in the international monetary system since the breakaway of the Bretton Woods system, created after the Second World War, and the gradual floating exchange rates of the currency were floated following the easing of the us dollar in August 1971. However, many observers, particularly in the United States, but also in France and other European countries, have, in the case of the euro, possibly marked the point of entry in the euro. The U.S. dollar was renamed its leading currency after the bretton woods system collapsed. If the euro, over time, challenges the hegemony of the dollar, its adoption should be compared in historical significance with the change in currency conditions caused by the first World War, in which the dollar rose alongside the pound and passed as the world's leading currency. Stages of the currency in connection with the phases of the state that issued it The phases of a currency are generally closely linked to those of the state that issued it. The status of official money in the payment system is mostly secured by law, and thanks to this, even bad money can continue to occupy its position in its home country through exchange and value. On the other hand, a legal monopoly cannot guarantee success on the international foreign exchange market. In conditions of free currency and currency movements, the true quality of any currency, but especially of freely convertible money in a large currency area, is constantly assessed in the face of competition against other currencies on the international foreign exchange market. Competition is not only, or even primarily, about exchange rates, but about the willingness of the various players in the national economies to use different currencies for the different purposes of money, i.e. as a measure of value, exchange and value. The outcome of the euro political conference The euro was the result of political ps fights and many of its characteristics were reproduced as a result of the political psss ksdesss in the process of making essentially political decisions. It may therefore seem to be an exception to the fact that the fate of the currencies is determined by the last central competition. In essence, however, the history of the birth of the euro supports rather than refutes the thesis on the importance of competition between currencies. Although in the process of emergence, the pressures of competition were influenced by politics rather than by the market mechanism, the impact of currency competition on the outcome can be clearly seen. One of the factors that contributed to the emergence of the czech euro was that the currencies of most EU countries proved to be weak in conditions where not only goods but also countries moved across borders. The fragility of European currencies became clear during the crisis of German integration in 1991-92, when waves of speculation severely destabilised the European exchange rate system and were in fact destroyed altogether. The euro inherited its characteristics from the German mark Although all the currencies of the countries that have joined the monetary union have merged with the euro, the euro cannot be considered the heir to all its predecessor currencies in the same way. On the other hand, the euro inherited its characteristics only from the strongest predecessor, the German mark. The main institutional features of economic and monetary union, and in particular the ideas of monetary stability as the primary consideration of monetary policy and the independence of monetary policy from other policies, were incorporated into the Treaty as such in the legislation of the Federal Republic of Germany. The ecb's monetary policy implementation also has much the same features as the policy previously pursued by the Bundesbank. From the Czech angle, the euro did not emerge from the historical void, as is often thought. Rather, it is the latest link in the chain of natural development of European currencies. In order to avoid the situation, I should say two things that are very much related to the context of the German mark and the euro. First, although Germany emerged as Europe's leading economic power after the war, the triumph of the German mark was not based, at least not primarily, on the country's economic or political success. Rather, the characteristics of the German mark are inherited from the law to the euro in the implementation of monetary policy because they are generally good currency characteristics. Germany had a self-absorbed and strong central bank, whose well-known and recognised objective of monetary policy was monetary stability. The Maastricht Treaty ensured the conditions for the exchange of money for the euro. Secondly, the euro is by no means the sole heir to the German mark. Commenting on the outcome of sweden's EMU referendum, Lars Heikensten, president of sweden's central bank, said that there was no substantial difference between the monetary policy of the euro area and the monetary policy of Sweden. Like the ECB, the primary task of the Riksbank is to preserve the stability of the value of money, and it can only succeed if it has sufficient self-efficacy and other conditions for the successful performance of its tasks. This requires a strong institutional position and an orthodox monetary policy, and in relation to this, over the last two decades, conditions in Sweden have become markedly similar to those of the German Bundesbank, although there is, of course, no reason to talk about copying it. Similar changes have also taken place in the monetary policy of other countries. That is why, in Heikensten's opinion, the ECB's addition to the Riksbank, as well as many other central banks outside the euro area, are doing well as pupils of the Bundesbank. For the euro, the adoption of the ECB's role and the principles of its monetary policy in the other leading industrialised countries will mean the stabilisation of international monetary conditions. This makes it easier for the ECB to conduct monetary policy from outside the euro area. On the other hand, international competition between currencies has intensified as more countries are able to conduct monetary policy. Conditions are constantly changing. Too strict adherence to the tradition of the Deutschmark and the slavish rambling of the policy of the Bundesbank at the time will not guarantee great success for the Central Bank, and the ECB has not collapsed in its monetary policy. Mundell's criteria for currency success There is not much research data on economics - let alone a solidly grounded theory - on what made the international success of currencies. The future of the euro cannot be predicted by scientific models. However, the economic literature has provided some estimates, based on past experience, which support the international successes of the currency. Robert Mundell, a Nobel Prize-winning economist, has cited the following five authors: 1. The large size and prosperity of the currency area. 2. Sufficient and efficient financial markets. 3. Consistent and predictable monetary policy. 4. Sissic and external political stability. 5. Currency convertibility in all circumstances. -Criterions size In terms of the Vsk century, the euro area is one of the largest economies in the world. More than 300 million people live in the euro area. people, when, for example, the population of the United States is less than 280 million. and Japan's only 127 million. people. Gross domestic product in the euro area is just over 16% of the world's GDP, about 6% less than that of the United States (22%), but more than double that of Japan (7%). If and when all THE EU countries, including 10 new countries are admitted to the EU on the first May Day, join the euro area over time, the figure will increase by about half. In this way, therefore, the euro area could become a much larger currency area than the United States. However, the increase in total output in the euro area would probably be higher than that of the inhabitants. The total production per capita of the new Member States is clearly lower than the average in the current EU countries, and will continue to be so in the long term. The increase in production at the level of production will be influenced by the growth rate of production. In the countries of Europe, and especially in the euro area, production growth over the last ten to fifteen years has clearly been slower than in the United States. Indeed, the main economic policy challenge facing Europe is to stimulate economic growth. The underlying economic problems are largely structural, and there are hardly any quick-acting pop-ups to fix them. A substantial acceleration of economic growth is the aim of the Lisbon Strategy, which is a joint adoption by the EU countries. sms is built on three basic pillars. Firstly, social cohesion, which is firmly part of the European tradition. co-determination, solidarity . want to stick to it in the future. The second pillar of the strategy is sound macroeconomic policies, which are required for success under the first pillar. In other words, the single monetary policy, which is the responsibility of the European Central Bank, and the national fiscal policy, which is the responsibility of the Member States, must provide the most stable framework possible for the private sector to operate. The third pillar is the reform of production structures and markets in order to modernise the economy and revive the capacity for growth. The aim is to increase the level of employment and, by means of new production methods, to increase productivity. The third pillar also includes the integration of financial markets, i.e. the creation of well-functioning EU-wide financial markets. This is because, in a market economy, it is the long-term functioning of the financial markets that determines the achievement of the strategy's objectives: the importance and orientation of new investment and, consequently, the long-term growth of productivity. If EU countries succeed in implementing the reforms under the Lisbon Strategy, their economic growth could accelerate significantly. Eu enlargement may also boost economic growth in the EU and the euro area in the future. Due to the low level of productivity, the new Member States will be able to increase their production faster than the current Member States and possibly also the United States. Increasing competition and expanding markets also offer the old Member States the opportunity to accelerate their own economic growth, not by speeding up the implementation of reforms by the old Member States. To sum up, I would consider that, on the basis of the size of the currency area, the euro has all the prerequisites for success internationally, in the best case scenario even in the long term to compete on an equal footing with the dollar. However, in order to realise this potential, structural weaknesses in European economies, which are driven by faster output growth, need to be addressed. It is worthwhile to undertake reforms swiftly, because then, in addition to the fact that economic problems are becoming more acute in the current situation. -Criterion of successful monetary policy The european central bank's overall climate of monetary stability is a reality not only for euro area citizens, but also for non-euro area users of the euro. It is clear that the ECB's stability orientation is likely to support the international role of the euro. The success of the ECB's monetary policy is based on the Treaty, which explicitly makes price stability the sole priority of the European Central Bank and provides the ECB with sufficient financial resources to achieve this objective. While the ECB can and should support the achievement of the EU's other objectives, this action must not jeopardise the achievement of the primary balance. The ECB has been responsible for monetary policy in the euro area for more than five years. It is a short time to assess the success of the policy. It can be said, however, that until then monetary policy has been more successful than probably anyone expected or even hoped for before the ECB became operational. The ECB's assertiveness and the confidence it enjoys in monetary policy have kept inflation expectations in the euro area under control and enabled monetary policy to gradually relax. Indeed, throughout the existence of monetary union, inflation expectations in the euro area have remained under control at low nominal interest rates, which can be seen as a sign of confidence in the ECB's monetary policy. In fact, there is a history of the gold standard up to the years before we meet the same low interest rates that we have enjoyed in Europe in recent years. In weighing up the future of the euro, Mundell considered that the five success factors, namely the size of the currency area and the central bank's monetary policy, clearly speak in favour of the success of the euro. I am prepared to agree with this assessment. As far as the functioning of the financial markets and political stability are concerned, the picture cannot, on the contrary, be absolutely unambiguously mystic. -Criterion- the functioning of financial markets As far as the functioning of the financial markets is concerned, the euro has also made significant progress in Europe. The strengthening of the credibility of the price stability and, for its own part, the creation of an integrated system of large payments, the creation of a target system for large payments, provided an important boost to the integration of the EU's financial markets. Indeed, some of the euro area's financial markets have already been integrated; in particular, the unsecured short-money market for banks now operates smoothly across the euro area. The market for government bonds and other bonds is also relatively long-term integrated. Progress has also been made in other market segments. For example, the liquidity of financial instruments has increased and the range has increased. Despite significant progress, the financial markets in the euro area as a whole remain rather fragmented. The integration of European financial markets is being held back by a large number of different frictions. Integration includes, inter alia, the various types of legislation (such as the procedures relating to bankruptcy and taxation legislation) and the differences between supervisory systems and administrative authorisation procedures. Financial market infrastructures, such as securities clearing houses, are expensive, fragmented and operate differently in different countries. Because of all the factors involved, it is much easier to buy or sell financial services in the euro area than it is to buy or sell financial services from one country to another, and even something as simple as paying becomes more difficult as soon as one of the parties is from another euro country. In terms of the commonality and depth of the financial markets and thus the liquidity of the currency, the euro area is likely to remain in the remainder of the United States for a long time. As a result, the average competitive position of the two currencies may be more stable or tilted in a different direction than the comparison of total output alone or the currencies shown. Despite this, however, I am very optimistic about the future integration of the financial markets. The benefits of a truly Pan-European financial market are simply too great for us to be able to accept them. The development is likely to proceed gradually, with the initial aim of linking nationally active markets into a network of markets. Experience with the short-term money market without the use of the euro suggests that, on the whole, a reasonably well-functioning market can be built, even if the market institutions themselves remain national. As the integration of European financial markets progresses, it will also support the international role of the euro. However, the majority of the well-functioning pan-European financial markets are repaired by the citizens of the European countries themselves. -Criterion of political stability The main obstacles to the future of the euro concern the ability of the euro area to cope with various economic and political crises. Nsits epsilys is known for its lack of a strong political center. At present, economic and monetary union is not a traditional federal state. Each Member State remains responsible for its own economic policies. In economic and monetary union, however, national room for manoeuvre in economic policy is limited by the coordination of economic policies at community level in the Member States. Economic policy coordination on a social basis is a special feature of Europe. It is sometimes thought that the strengthening of cooperation in the EU's economic policy means a narrowing of the economic policy autonomy of nation states such as Finland. In a way, the idea of sticking to the point of view that all parties are forced to make compromises that sometimes seem awkward. Similarly, it is probably a fact that the large countries have a greater say, at least on an individual basis, in eu political decision-making and, more generally, in international cooperation, than the smaller countries. However, the idea of a loss of self-efficacy is also one-sided in relation to the fact that it does not take into account the increase in influence that we gain by participating in the eu's decision-making. However, it is in the interest of all Europeans, including Finns, that the common ssnns on which the EU is founded are sufficient and that the joint institutions also have sufficient powers. The recent increase in budget deficits has prompted a legitimate debate on the fact that there should be no free-riders in the monetary union. If the Member States of monetary union want to continue to enjoy the stability of monetary union, they must also play their part in supporting and eroding stability. The budget deficits are part of the safeguards on the basis of which the decisions on joining the monetary union were made. In addition to budgetary discipline, a common policy may be needed in situations where serious crises threaten the stability of financial markets. As the integration of the financial markets continues to take place, the need for cooperation will increase. Banks and insurance companies together form larger international entities and their liabilities and risks are spread over the euro area and also globally. In the autumn, the EU countries are very much in close contact with the financial markets and in the supervision of the financial markets and in crisis management. In relation to the situation, the concentration of power in more cases at the community level seems to be somewhat of a development over time. Good listeners! In my presentation, I have assessed the future of the euro from the angle of the competition between currencies. Tsmsn nskskulma was brought to the economic debate by the famous German economist and philosopher Friedrich Hayek. In the 1970s, he was convinced that private money would quickly produce money issued by the national central banks if their exclusive right to issue legal money were abolished. Hayek's work was influenced by the epsilemshtsts much earlier experience of global high inflation, the root cause of which was the financing of public expenditure by the United States and other industrialized countries with banknote financing. It can be said that, since the 1970s, world monetary conditions did not develop much in the direction predicted by Hayek. The exclusive right of central banks to issue legal payments is one of the reasons why private currency has not taken over the market from central bank money. However, that cannot be the only reason. The name 'private currency' has not been used on the international money market, to which the exclusive rights of the national central banks do not extend. Although private money has not become a significant competitor to central bank money, Hayek's idea of the great importance of money competition has proved to be of great importance. However, instead of at the national level, the competition between currencies is at international level. The consequences of currency competition have been dramatic over time. It is no exaggeration to say that the monetary conditions in Europe and throughout the world have changed fundamentally, precisely in line with The Autumn and The Hayek's prediction, so that weak currencies have collapsed and good currencies have prospered. The emergence of the euro from the nsks corner. Bad currencies were replaced by a new and better one, the euro. In terms of its characteristics, it can be a genuine heir to the best-performing European currency in international competition, the German mark. The European Central Bank and other institutions responsible for the infrastructure of the euro area's financial markets have succeeded in transferring the strong half of the German mark to the euro area level as a whole. However, there are many challenges for the future of the euro. As I mentioned, they have a lot to do with the future success of economic policy coordination and the development of a common capacity for financial supervision and crisis management. These issues are also contributing to the confidence enjoyed by the euro in the international market. The future development of the international role of the euro will depend to a large extent on the future success of Europe's economic and monetary policy. Success depends on sticking to the good elements of politics that are already in use, and we are trying to strengthen those elements that need to be strengthened. Of course, it is not worth pursuing a policy to promote the international use of the euro. The aim is the economic success and security of the citizens of the euro area. However, the international use of the euro is a significant symptom value. The euro will continue to operate internationally, at a time when monetary and economic conditions in the euro area are developing favourably.
