Title: Policy uses of and future developments in Balance of Payments Statistics - Some European Perspectives
text: Member of the Board Sinikka Salo: Policy uses of and future developments in Balance of Payments Statistics -Some European Perspectives . Speech . Thursday22 April 2004, 12:00 AM Frankfurt 22.4.2004 Introduction I think we all agree that good macro-economic statistics are essential for the smooth functioning of the Economic and Monetary Union, working under a single monetary policy and decentralised but co-ordinated fiscal policies. At the same time it is clear that the institutional settings of the EMU impose immense challenges for the collection, compilation and dissemination of statistical data. As for the conduct of monetary policy, a comprehensive set of timely, reliable, sufficiently-detailed and frequent aggregate-level statistics are crucial. Timely, reliable and frequent statistics are invaluable especially for a central bank like the ECB, operating in an environment where economic structures and the monetary policy transmission mechanism are not fully known and likely to undergo continuous change. As for the conduct of economic policies, national data may lose some of its significance in a monetary union, but nevertheless it tends to remain important, not only for national economic policies but also for their co-ordination. Since the launch of the EMU, Europe has improved tremendously in terms of the coverage and quality of aggregate time series at the euro area and EU level. This is true in particular for the balance of payments statistics, which are now compiled and disseminated monthly for both the euro area and the whole EU. These improvements have been largely a product of the close cooperation between the European statistical system, i.e. Eurostat together with the national statistical institutes, and the European System of Central Banks, these two systems sharing the responsibility for the balance of payments statistics in Europe. In spite of the substantial progress achieved since the launch of the EMU, there is still room for improvement. Aggregate level statistics have not yet achieved standards comparable to those of the other large currency areas, notably the United States. From the monetary policy perspective, action is needed in particular to improve the timeliness and quality of the euro area statistics. In the field of balance of payments statistics, the most urgent needs probably pertain to improvements in the quality of first monthly preliminary figures. The institutional structure of the EMU naturally tends to make not only statistical requirements but also the data collection and processing procedures unwieldy. Compilation of the aggregates requires harmonised data with sufficient coverage, and therefore collection and compilation procedures necessarily are more complicated than in the case of a single country. I do not know of any systematic comparative study on the efficiency of the production of statistics in major currency areas. However, even a casual comparison of Member States' national statistical systems gives some support to the notion that their efficiency varies quite considerably across Member States. This suggests that our statistical system, taken as a whole, cannot be fully efficient. To avoid misunderstandings, it is perhaps worth repeating that a comparison of aggregate level outputs and inputs between the euro area and other currency areas may be grossly unfair to the euro area, as data requirements and the conditions of the statistical system elsewhere may be very different from those in Europe. There is a strong public good element to aggregate statistics, and their production has always been and probably will always be financed mainly from public sources. In view of the formidable budgetary challenges that most if not all Member States are facing today and even more in coming years, it would be wishful thinking from the part of European statistical authorities, irrespective of their institutional background, to expect significant increases in the total amount of budgetary resources for the production of statistics in general or balance of payments statistics in particular. If we want to improve the timeliness and quality of balance of payments series, there seem to be no other options than to rebalance priorities within the statistical system. In my contribution, I would like to stress two aspects of this rebalancing of statistical priorities. In the first place, it is necessary to focus demand for aggregate data only on what is really needed for policy use, also taking into account the cost of production of aggregate time series. The potential need for statistics is unlimited and cannot be satisfied with limited resources. Setting priorities for the demand for statistics used for monetary policy purposes is mainly the responsibility of the ECB but as far as cost assessment is concerned, also national authorities responsible for the collection and compilation of data are involved. In the second place, it is absolutely vital to ensure, preferably in a co-ordinated manner, that statistics are collected and compiled as efficiently as possible, given the basic institutional constraints of the EMU. Setting priorities for the use of resources in the supply of statistics is mainly the responsibility of the national authorities, which are responsible for the collection and compilation of national data. However, the achievement of an efficiency frontier in the production of statistics may be impossible without substantial and constructive input from Eurostat and the ECB, which define the general conceptual framework as well as co-ordinate the collection and compilation of balance of payments data. In this contribution, my basic theme is that statistics, by their very nature, tend to be more or less incomplete and that the integration of markets due to globalisation and the single European markets has made them even more incomplete. My Danish college, Jens Thomsen, once put the very point very nicely -in the context of identifying balance of payment crises ex ante -by saying that when mistakes are analysed in retrospect, the relevant statistics which could have prevented a wrong decision being made always seem to be the ones which were missing at the time the decision was contemplated. Because statistics are anyway incomplete, there is no need for actuarial precision in the design of the statistical system. I shall argue that we need a more focussed approach. In particular, in the case of the balance of payments statistics the adoption of more up-to-date collection systems with greater reliance on corporate survey is needed. Challenges of globalisation for Balance of Payments statistics While it is often claimed that balance of payments statistics are now less important than they used to be say even twenty or thirty years ago I fully agree with Josz Vials' conclusion that, in spite of all the conceptual and operational challenges globalisation has put before the balance of payments statistics, balance of payments statistics continue to be very important, especially at the euro area level, for the monetary policy purposes. I would like to supplement his presentation, however, by arguing that statistical problems related to the globalisation process extend even further and deeper than he envisaged. I would like to start by drawing your attention to one well-known consequence globalisation has brought with it, namely the rise of very large global corporate units. A less well known but nevertheless evident fact is that these global companies are perfectly capable of growing and operating or at least maintaining their head office in a very small country. This development reflects the declining significance of national frontiers. It has taken place in Finland and probably also in some other smaller Member States, with the consequence that national statistical authorities are faced with the problem of recording the transactions of very large companies. These transactions may be extremely large, complex and numerous if compared with the transactions of onormalo enterprises operating entirely or mainly at national level. Let me illustrate some of the challenges large companies pose for statistics by using the Finnish ITC company Nokia as a concrete example. Nokia grew very rapidly in the 1990os. Measured by its stock value, at the height of the IT boom in 2000, it was among the 10 largest enterprises in the world. Its market value was then nearly double the value of the Finnish GDP, reflecting of course high expectations of future growth of sales and profit opportunities. Nokia's profits amount to several per cent of the Finnish GDP. After dividends and taxes, its undistributed profits are some 2% of our GDP. In national accounts, Nokia's undistributed profit is included in Finlandos national income, savings and current account surplus. This explains, in part, Finland's exceptionally high trade account surplus. However, some 90% of the company is owned by foreign investors. If undistributed profit to portfolio investment were allocated in national accounts and balance of payments in the same way as profit to direct investment, Finlandos national income, savings and current account surplus would have been annually some 2% lower than in published statistics. From an economic point of view, the current statistical figures can be regarded as misleading. In international investment position (IIP) statistics, shares are valued at market prices. In 2000 Nokiaos high market valuation was reflected in Finland's IIP statistics with the consequence that, measured by its net international investment position, Finland was at the time one of the most indebted countries in the world. Of course, in spite of these statistics, neither the government nor any other body had any rational reason to worry about our international net position, as Nokia was mostly owned by foreigners, and almost all of its sales and presumably also companyos profits were made outside Finland. Finlandos high indebtedness in 2000 was nothing more than a statistical artefact. This observation was confirmed by subsequent developments. Finlandos net position diminished to about one tenth of its peak value as Nokiaos share price declined to some one forth from its peak value or even lower. Nevertheless, Finnish IIP figures have already confused those economists who do not know statistical recording practices and the structure of the Finnish economyand are likely to continue doing so in the future, too. The problems large global companies cause to national accounts and balance of payment statistics are fundamental. While in institutional sector accounts households, public sector, non-financial corporations and financial institutions it is relatively easy to classify activities by nation for the household and public sectors, this has become increasingly difficult and in some cases outright impossible for the nonfinancial corporations and financial institutions sectors. For the corporate sector, foreign trade statistics can already now be characterised as being merely indicative. Statistics have been contaminated not only by the cross-border mergers and acquisitions but alsoand more importantly by the so-called invisible transactions; foreign trade of services and capital income and the financial flows of large multinationals whose share of total value of transactions is often substantial. As I already mentioned, the size distribution of relevant populations in economic and financial statistics, including the balance of payments, have become extremely skewed, as a consequence of the globalisation process. At the same time, many of the transactions made by these extremely large enterprises can be extremely complex. The existing balance of payments statistics already witness the quality implications of these phenomena; the most apparent case being the first monthly preliminary figures for the current year retained profits that are highly unreliable. In fact, proper data is available only a year or more after the first estimates. Preliminary figures are often subject to delayed major revisions. At the disaggregated level, these problems may hamper their use for monetary policy purposes. While the problems of extremely large corporations in relation to the size of the country and complex foreign trade transactions may be exceptionally acute in Finland, there cannot be any doubt that they are highly prevalent also in other Member States, at least in the smaller ones. Furthermore, these problems are likely to increase and become more intensive with the advancement of global integration. As many of the problems in the balance of payments statistics are universal, solutions to them should preferably be sought, in the first place, at international level. Some of the old typologies and classifications may have become outdated. It is a challenge for the international community to drop outdated dimensions from international standards. The IMF has already started preparations on the 6th Balance of Payments Manual. It is expected to be ready around 2008. Topics already under discussion include the increased consistency and integrity of national accounts and balance of payments statistics, the increased role of foreign asset positions, and the relation of statistical standards to international accounting standards. Attention has also been paid to balance of payments problems in monetary unions. In this context, I would particularly like to mention the need to harmonise further national concepts in national accounts and balance of payments statistics. This need is demonstrated by the large oasymmetries" seen in the balance of payments statistics for the major currency areas and the whole world. Another example I would like to mention are institutional sector figures in national accounts, where different treatment of depreciation allowances by different authorities make economically interesting comparisons very difficult. While revisions in international standards are important, the process whereby they are established is likely to be very slow. It may be too much to expect substantial progress already in the next balance of payments manual. In any case, some restructuring of statistics must be carried out in advance of the revision of the international manuals. Without prompt response at the European or Member State level, problems may emerge, as statistical concepts no longer are in line with relevant economic or business concepts. Unfortunately, these cases have not been rare in recent years in practice. Emerging single European markets: challenges for Balance of Payments Statistics While market integration has in the global context been largely a market driven process, in the European context it is an explicit policy goal of the highest priority. In many markets, integration at the European level has already proceeded significantly towards truly single markets. However, many European mar-kets, including those for financial and other services, are still highly segmented along national borders. Considerable policy effort, both in the context of the Lisbon strategy and elsewhere, has been devoted to removing the remaining legal and other factors which act as frictional elements in the creation of integrated European-wide markets. The establishment of fully integrated European-wide markets creates challenges for statisticians. Moreover, in some cases statistical issues may also be included in those frictional elements, giving rise to a consideration of different priorities. I would like to mention a couple of examples of difficulties related to balance of payments that affect re-cent policy issues in the EU more directly. The Regulation (2560/2001) on cross-border EU payments effectively made the cost of cross-border payments within the EU equivalent to the cost of domestic payments. At the same time, it relieved banks from all reporting requirements on cross-border euro payments below a threshold of EUR 12,500. In the framework of the regulation, the Commission will report no later than July 2004 on the advisability of increasing this threshold to EUR 50,000 as from January 2006. This rise in the threshold has been resisted on the grounds that it could pose a risk to the quality and detail in balance of payments. This clearly offers an illustration of a conflict between technical statistical requirements and the achievement of the broader economic and financial policy goals of the Community. Rather than resisting the rise of the threshold, Member States should be asked to accelerate their plans to modernise their data collection systems for balance of payments statistics. This is all the more relevant because the bias in errors and omissions in the euro area balance of payments continues to raise concerns. Much of the oasymmetrieso in European aggregate balance of payments statistics are due to the deficiencies of national data collection and compilation systems in Member States. In many countries work has already started on the improvement of existing data collection systems. In particular, Member States are introducing corporate surveys and building more accurate registers. Furthermore, they have committed themselves to compiling more reliable portfolio investment statistics, to building more accurate registers, to recording mergers and acquisitions, reinvested earnings and income more thoroughly, the latter being a major reason for existing asymmetries. These examples are only a sample of the existing quality projects. This work is very important both in principle and in practice. However, my personal feeling is that it would be more useful to focus directly on external transactions in order to reduce asymmetries in major currency areas' balance of payments. This is because it is practically impossible to remove all asymmetries from different national statistics, at least at reasonable cost. Another example with a significant European dimension I would like to take up here concerns the statute on the European Company, which is due to enter into force in October this year. This statute will remove some of the legal and regulatory impediments which thus far have prevented EU firms from fully exploiting the benefits of cross-border corporate restructuring. The European Company form would facilitate not only the merger of complicated group structures into a single legal entity but also the transfer of the company's head quarter from one Member State to another. Financial groups with pan-European or regional cross-border activities are also likely to be interested in the new company form. The new company form has important implications for financial stability, prudential supervision and crisis management. The statute may have significant implications also for money and banking statistics, specifically for balance sheet statistics relating to monetary financial institutions (MFI) but also to other financial intermediaries. In principle, a change in legal status will have no direct statistical impact, since for statistical purposes foreign branches and subsidiaries are treated identically, regardless of legal status. However, in practice there may be several indirect effects. There is also a risk that economic transactions pertaining to national areas would no longer correspond to existing statistical reporting and that the reorganisation of business activities could significantly affect the information content and usefulness of national statistics. An MFI operating as a European Company would be able to restructure its business activities on an ongoing basis and in a smoother fashion than is the case today. This could for example involve possibly recurrent reorganisations of branch activities across the European Company that might entail considerable implications on the statistical reporting of the various national branches. As an example of such a reorganisation, the administration of all derivatives business might be concentrated in one national branch. While the branches in the other countries may still continue to conduct derivative transactions with their customers, this activity made on behalf of the designated branch would no longer show up in the national statistics. That is, while the economic transactions still pertain to the various national areas, they may no longer correspond to the statistical reporting. In addition to derivatives, it is possible to envisage other examples of reorganisation, such as the concentration of the loan portfolio or securities holdings in the groupos head office. It may even be envisaged that a cross-border banking group may choose to record its deposit accounts in specific locations, for example in order to exploit differences in deposit guarantee systems. Such re-bookings could imply a substantial reduction in key items of the national monetary statis-tics of the countries hosting the groupos branches. These have become current issues in Sweden, Finland, Denmark and Norway, with the Nordic banking group Nordea Bank announcing its intention of becoming a European Company and already taking steps to implement this legal restructuring. As a European Company the Nordea Group would be a single legal entity under Swedish law, and its present subsidiaries outside Sweden would become its foreign branches. Its legal restructuring and the consequent adoption of a branch structure would therefore be a major challenge for statistical authorities in Sweden, Finland, Denmark and Norway as well as in the Baltic countries. Even though the implications for national monetary statistics may in some cases be substantial, the effect on euro area aggregates would be limited to situations where activities are transferred from or to euro area MFIs to or from non-euro area MFIs. However, this is precisely what is anticipated in the Nordea case, where the bank is active both inside and outside the euro area. The handling of Finnish clients directly from the head office would mean that under normal procedures different deposit, credit and other items would be recorded only in the balance of payments, not in Finnish or euro area monetary or credit aggregates. Nobody can say how predominant this kind of customer relationship would be, but at most, some 30-40% of the amounts currently recorded in Finnish MFI statistics could be transferred to Swedish statistics. Such reclassifications would show up clearly even in euro area monetary aggregates. As a further implication of the move to a single corporate structure, it is to be expected that cross-border banking groups will start to compile a single set of business accounts and be subject to the rulebook of a single supervisor. This is likely to generate a reorganisation of internal information management systems, as the ohome countryo reporting system becomes predominant. I would like to add a few remarks on this discussion. The imposition of extraordinary information requirements for a European company is expensive, and could run against the basic aims of the European Company statute. Therefore, reporting requirements to be imposed on European Companies need careful consideration. If the same data collection procedures are adopted as before, Nordea would not report at all to the Finnish authorities on its direct transactions from Finland to Sweden for the balance of payments statistics. In this case, the Finnish authorities would need to collect data for the balance of payments statistics from Finnish bank customers, as is standard practice with Finnish residents dealing with non-resident banks. However, in practice, this would be difficult if not impossible, at least for households. On the other hand, it is not inconceivable that Nordea could provide supplementary information voluntarily. This practice would not be in line with current practices in balance of payments and monetary statistics, and would be possible only as an unofficial supplementary system. Unofficial national figures could perhaps be published, but one can foresee that confusion and problems could arise, for example with respect to the confidentiality of the figures. Furthermore, while in the case of Nordea there is every reason to expect good cooperation between it and statistical authorities, the risk of non-cooperative companies in future cases cannot be excluded a priori. Nevertheless, in the future the use of complementary statistics is likely to emerge as an established procedure if the branch office structure becomes popular for banks operating across national borders. In any case, if the branch office structures and direct links between customers and head offices become prevalent, reliable national accounts and balance of payments statistics apparently require good cooperation between national authorities and possibly also multinational reporting systems. In order to prevent information requirements from becoming excessive, such systems should not try to cover all aspects and should avoid trying to include every detail. As long as there are no such complementary data, complementary data for banking statistics could in principle be collected by utilising balance of payments data. Under standard statistical procedures, this procedure would be very difficult, because the correspondence between balance of payments and monetary and financial statistics is still rather weak. Furthermore, balance of payments statistics do not include information on currency denominations, to say nothing of information on interest rates etc. Concluding remarks When European statisticians have encountered difficulties in the classification and compilation of balance of payments data for the euro area, their prevailing almost instinctive reaction seems to have been to increase the collection of more detailed information. This strategy of increasing details and developing almost real time registers has, however, obscured the difference between fast indicators and structural statistics. The costs of compilation are exploding and in spite of all the computations, fragmented data does not lend itself easily to fast and effective quality control methods. The outcome is that the data will be overly fragmented and difficult to handle. This development may lead to a vicious circle of growing IT and personnel costs, combined with explosive growth in the amount of information. Another approach could be to differentiate between the compilation of fast aggregate information and the compilation of structural statistics. As I have mentioned before, the respondent populations in financial statistics including the balance of payments are highly skewed. However, it is possible to identify reasonably nicely behaved subpopulations in view to the distributional properties. These subpopulations cover a relatively high proportion of the total value of the main aggregates facilitating low-cost collection and make possible the compilation of timely, nonbiased preliminaries of aggregates. These aggregates can be very useful, provided that their indicative nature is properly understood. On the other hand, the whole respondent population should be sufficiently covered for the more structural national statistics, which need not be as frequent and as timely as indicator statistics. In the EMU, as probably elsewhere, the backbone of the collection and compilation of statistical data is provided by basic national statistical information systems. These systems provide plenty of useful information, also for monetary policy purposes. However they tend to be expensive, rigid and are not easily adapted to rapid changes in the economic environment brought about by policy decisions and globalisation. By their very nature, statistics are incomplete. Furthermore, one consequence of global and Euro-pean integration seems to be that national statistics will become increasingly uncertain. This conclusion certainly concerns also balance of payments and international investment position statistics. This does not necessarily imply that the significance of balance of payments statistics has diminished. The implication is rather that the responsibility of the user of statistics has increased: he or she should be able to interpret time series properly and cautiously. If we want to maximise the support balance of payments statistics give to monetary policy uses, we should aim at developing good rather than perfect statistics. This implies that we should be selective when deciding what statistical items to produce; that the limited aggregate data set should be timely and reliable; and that data for it should be collected and processed as cost-effectively as possible, given the institutional constraints of the EMU. In order to improve timeliness, quality and cost effectiveness of balance of payments statistics, we should consider, in particular, a careful review of the sampling practices implemented at European and national levels. What we need for policy purposes is a focused approach. In the first place, in order to maximise the support statistics give to the ECB's monetary policy we should be extremely selective in deciding what statistics should be produced for policy purposes. Secondly, this focused set of statistics should be produced as efficiently as possible, while respecting existing institutional constraints in the production of statistics.

Title: Speech, "Globalisation and Finnish Housing"
text: Bank Manager Sinikka Salo's speech, Globalisation and Finnish housing . Speech . Tuesday 18 May2004,12:00AM Keynote speech at the Finnish Housing Fair's Casa humana d event in Helsinki, 18.5.2004 The development of housing policy over the last hundred years or so has meant that housing is in one broader social context. This development has taken many stages. In the early days of housing policy, more than a hundred years ago, its objectives were public health. The quality and space requirements of the apartments were standardised and the use of damp, dark and epshygienic premises was sought as apartments. Myshmma was joined by broader social policy objectives, as housing policy became more active in combating homelessness and the rsikes equalisation of housing conditions. The emphasis on social housing was part of the development phase. The post-war settlement policy, in turn, linked housing d and agricultural policy. Especially in the 1960s, housing policy began to be strongly influenced by the objectives of general economic policy, such as promoting economic growth and structural change in the economy. The aim was also to achieve this by means of housing construction. An example of this was the large-scale regional development projects, and it can be said that town planning and economic policy met each other at the final stage. Now we have a time when housing has to be thought of from a new and wider nsks angle. The new angle must be international. Once upon a time, housing policy must respond to the major challenges facing the whole of Finnish society, of which, as the major force of social change of the decade, to the globalisation of the economy. The question then arises as to the challenges posed by globalisation to housing policy, town and country planning and construction. Globalisation means many things, and its importance is not limited to the economy. It is powered by the spread of new technologies and the market economy system throughout the world. As a result, there is a staggering expansion of the scope for action and of the nssalas in all areas of human activity. At the same time, economic competition is intensifying and taking on new forms. Recently, there has been a lot of discussion about the so-called China, which refers to the relocation of production jobs from the old industrialised countries to the new, lower-cost countries. Of course, this is not just a question of price competition, but of the fact that many countries that were previously economically isolated and backward have now reached such a level of technical know-how that they are able to produce products that are already very demanding for the markets of rich countries. This is a major challenge and has caused great concern in the old industrialised countries. How do we respond to it? In this context, I would like to say that, overall, economic globalisation is seen as much more of an opportunity than a threat. It means leveling off opportunities in the world. It will lead to more jobs and an improvement in livelihoods in many countries in the past, while at the same time creating a demand for new products, goods and services in which the old industrialised countries now have to invest. Indeed, the problems of globalisation are due precisely to the difficulties of adaptation caused by structural change. The old rich countries will have to specialise in doing things that cannot be duplicated in countries with lower cost levels. This change will have major economic and social consequences. In the old industrialised countries, the fiercest competition in the countries, countries and regions is the highest in terms of high-skilled work, where the level of prestige and wages is highest. It is therefore a question, for example, of the location of activities such as research and development, marketing, management and finance. It is characteristic of these activities that they focus on each other's mobility. In the old industrialised countries, metropolises are growing and prospering where universities and the offices of large companies, research institutes and financial markets interact with each other. The growth sectors of physical production are growing in business and intangible production, which are concentrated in the largest growth centres. One can speak of London as a counterweight to the China-manifest. After all, London is an example of a European metropolis that has experienced strong growth and has been based on activities that have become more engrossed in globalisation than they have been. For Finland, the structural change taking place in the czech countries is a particularly major challenge. During the technology boom of the last decade, we have been too lulled into believing that major investments in technical education and product development will secure Finland's economic success. However, the technological lead is rapidly eroded by competition, and the maturation of technical products from revolutionary novelties to cheap bulk goods is taking place at a rapid pace under the influence of globalisation. At the same time, the transformation of the largest Finnish companies into multinationals or the merger into international groups has made Finland a clear location for the central management of the companies. If you have offices in Finland, the growth opportunities for Finnish design, marketing, law and finance will wither away. However, it is precisely the activities that high-income countries will have to consciously develop in the future. It is precisely the link between globalisation and the challenges of Finnish urban planning and housing policy that is clear. In Finland, care must be taken to ensure that our urban structure and housing market support Finland's success in the international competition between metropolisesses. We have traditionally paid a great deal of attention to income policy and tax policy as a means of safeguarding the competitiveness of companies. Much has also been invested in direct and direct support for research and development. However, I think it is clear that in Finland it would also be worthwhile to ensure that Finland, and in particular the Helsinki metropolitan area, offers an attractive and competitive location for the high-value activities I have already mentioned and an attractive place to live for the experts whose jobs are made up. All in all, the London report I referred to earlier, i.e. the competition between metropolises, was considered to be more threatening for Finland than the China report. The decline of Helsinki into a periphery would be a real threat to the development of the whole of Finland. At the moment, the situation is not good. One problem is that in Finland, and especially in the Helsinki region, the apartments are small by international comparison. The average size of apartments is slowly increasing, but we are not catching up with our competitors, because the average size of new homes in Finland is also clear from what is being built in other countries comparable to ours. Another problem that weakens the competitiveness of Finnish housing is that the quality of the housing stock does not correspond very well to the wishes of the residents. Finns mostly live in blocks of flats. Only about 40% of Finns live in detached houses, while, for example, 59% live in densely populated Denmark and 71% in the Netherlands. Even in Sweden, living in detached houses is more common than in our country. Only 35% of new dwellings are single-family houses, compared with 51% in Sweden, 60% in Denmark and 74% in the Netherlands. Despite the fact that, according to studies, the majority of Finns would like to live in detached houses and even though we would in principle have more room for construction than in most other countries. It all means that finland's housing stock should be improved quickly, especially in the Helsinki metropolitan area. Above all, the size of the apartments available must be increased and the quality of the apartments should better meet the wishes of the residents - this means, among other things, a rapid increase in the proportion of high-quality detached houses. The third factor that negatively affects the competitiveness of the Finnish housing market is the thinness and weak functioning of the rental housing market, especially the lack of supply of high-quality rental housing. The private rental housing market should also be made to function better than it is at present. This is relevant not only for the stay of foreign, temporary workers in the country, but also for the domestic mobility of the labour force. Not only does a well-functioning rental housing market help to mitigate the risks to households posed by fluctuations in housing prices. With a view to the development of a well-functioning rental housing market, it is necessary, inter alia, to try to revive the interest of institutional investors, such as insurance companies, in the production of rental housing. After all, in recent years, the assets of the hugely inflated tyselske funds have been invested in more foreign securities, and domestic investments in, for example, rental housing, have lost their importance. The two fundamental issues of housing policy have traditionally been the land issue and the financial question. It could also add design, i.e. architecture. Are nsms tekijst ok? Do they constitute unnecessary obstacles to the improvement of the quality of housing in Finland and especially in the Helsinki metropolitan area? Does Finland have any strengths that could be hysdynchss? Let's start with the positive things. These already include today's funding, which for decades was chronic scarcity in Finland. The stabilisation of Finland's monetary conditions on the occasion of joining the European monetary union changed the situation quite differently, and today's normal, commercial market provides access to finance at such a low cost that the state housing finance system has had to consider the need and legitimacy of its existence. Low and stable interest rates mean that the lack of financing or costs are not a key limiting factor in the development of Finnish housing. Another potential strength could be design, but I believe that in relation to the ssss, the Finns should return to their own traditions before the strength of the smsn becomes more widely used. For us, Finnish architecture is one of the building blocks of our national identity. Its international reputation is based above all on Alvar Aalto's tyshsn. Aalto sought to reform the functionalist way of building by bringing humanism and naturalness to it. Hsn did not believe in rationalistic or mechanical solutions, but wanted to give way to the unpredictability and diversity of elsms. At a time that was generally dominated by a blunt romanticism of efficiency and vulgssri social functionalism, Aalto sought inspiration in antiquity and the Italian Renaissance cities. The unique gift of Finnish architecture to the world is the humane okolmas tieo, which is set in the vsl of narrow efficiency thinking and epsinhuman monumentalism. At least it should be. Despite the fine traditions of Finnish architecture, Finnish housing construction has for decades invested more in efficiency than quality. It can, of course, be said that social reasons have forced it to do so. In the midst of the housing shortage, there was a tendency to believe that cheap construction with minimum standards represented the highest social morality: ornamentation was a crime, and beauty and quality were also things to bargain for. The number of apartments to be produced has been solved and the cost of the apartments was sought through serial production. Aalto nski early on that such a way of developing housing would be a stage of development. In 1939, in defending his Villa Maire d project, Hsn wrote as follows: o... the architectural case, in which individual instincts, personal instincts and cultural instincts form the basis of the task, (has) a peculiar far-reaching social significance if it is placed in the time perspective of the long term. It then, of course, refers to the new individualism which, as the production machinery evolves and the forms of organisation improve, makes it possible to take more flexible individuality into account in addition to the semi-developed machinery of primitive mass production. o The time that Ehks Aalto longed for has finally arrived. If and when globalisation takes hold of the competition between metropolitan areas in terms of the quality of housing and housing, it can be said that we cannot afford to use the opportunities offered by diverse and resident needs, humane construction. Building technology is not a hindrance. I hope not the puritanism of urban architects or municipal politicians either. From the point of view of society, high-quality construction is not even a cost factor, but a vsltsmstchity. What is needed for this is more permissive zoning and urban planning, which would give solvent demand room to influence the quality and orientation of construction. In Finland, housing has traditionally been tried with measures to support the development of demand. In the future, attention will be focused on the general demand for supportive measures to make the supply of housing more flexible: the demand for housing must be allowed to influence the orientation and quality of construction activities more than is currently the case. Making supply more flexible will also help to moderate the price level of housing. Now, for example, low interest rates are becoming capitalised by housing prices in growth centres due to the inflexibility of supply. In order to make supply more flexible, a special and decisive role is played by municipal zoning and plot policies. Through their land policy, municipalities could also increase competition and supply in the privately non-subsidised rental housing market. In a globalised world, the disadvantages of bureaucracy and restrictive sclerosis are felt in all areas of housing, including housing, and require the development of new ways of working in housing policy and town and country planning. Pidsn selvns, that the 10-year challenges of land policy in the local area require a substantial acceleration of the pace of town and country planning and a much more liberal land policy. In the City region, the news is that 18 new plots of detached houses will be zoned in the year. This can be seen as a scandal in the development of the Helsinki metropolitan area! Indeed, special efforts by the state are needed to create more space for high-quality housing construction. However, the question is a fundamental issue affecting the economic vitality and future of the whole country. Good listeners! The age of globalisation requires housing policy and related urban planning, town and architecture to be competitive and able to make the inhabitants as subjects and not as objects of politics. In order to develop the competitiveness of the housing sector, it is necessary to look for the natural strengths of Finland's growth centres and, in particular, the Helsinki metropolitan area, in housing. Nsms strengths are related to the space in Finland, the lsytheness of nature and, I hope, the ability of designers to draw from the human traditions of Finnish architecture. Competitiveness is not a pocket calculator, but rather, in the case of customers d ssss, the realization and acceptance of the d needs of the inhabitants. This means, for example, that quality in housing must not just mean building technology in the first place, but that people's diverse, even diverse needs determine the trends in housing. We would make Finland a model country for living!

Tuesday 18 May2004,12:00AM Juhlapuhe Suomen Asuntomessujen Casa humana tilaisuudessa Helsingiss, 18.5.2004 Asuntopolitiikan kehitys viimeisen noin sadan vuoden aikana on merkinnyt asumisen nkemist yh laajemmassa yhteiskunnallisessa yhteydessn. Tm kehitys on kynyt lpi monia vaiheita. Asuntopolitiikan alkuaikoina, runsaat sata vuotta sitten, sen tavoitteet olivat lhinn kansanterveydelliset. Asuntojen laatu-ja tilavaatimuksia normitettiin ja kosteiden, pimeiden ja ephygieenisten tilojen kytt asuntoina pyrittiin estmn. Myhemmin mukaan tulivat laajemmat sosiaalipoliittiset tavoitteet, kun asuntopolitiikalla ryhdyttiin aktiivisemmin torjumaan asunnottomuutta ja vhentmn asunto-olojen rike eptasa-arvoisuutta. Sosiaalisen asuntotuotannon korostaminen kuului thn kehitysvaiheeseen. Sodan jlkeinen asutuspolitiikka vuorostaan kytki asunto  ja maatalouspolitiikan toisiinsa. Varsinkin 1960 luvulla asuntopolitiikkaan alkoivat vaikuttaa vahvasti yleisen talouspolitiikan tavoitteet, kuten taloudellisen kasvun ja talouden rakennemuutoksen edistminen. Nit haluttiin tavoitella mys asuntorakentamisen keinoin. Esimerkkej tst pyrkimyksest olivat suurisuuntaiset aluerakentamishankkeet, ja voidaan sanoa, ett asemakaavoitus ja talouspolitiikka kohtasivat viimeistn tss vaiheessa toisensa. Nyt elmme jlleen kerran aikaa, jolloin asumista on ajateltava uudesta ja aiempaa laajemmasta nkkulmasta. Tmn uuden nkkulman on oltava kansainvlinen. Jlleen kerran asuntopolitiikan on reagoitava koko suomalaista yhteiskuntaa kohtaaviin suuriin haasteisiin, joista tmn vuosikymmenen merkittvimpn yhteiskunnallisena muutosvoimana talouden globalisaatioon. Onkin kysyttv, millaisia haasteita globalisaatio aiheuttaa asuntopolitiikalle, yhdyskuntasuunnittelulle ja rakentamiselle. Globalisaatio tarkoittaa monta asiaa, eik sen merkitys rajoitu vain talouteen. Sen kyttvoimana on uuden teknologian ja markkinatalousjrjestelmn leviminen kaikkialle maailmaan. Sen seurauksena on toimintamahdollisuuksien ja nkalojen huikea laajeneminen kaikilla inhimillisen toiminnan alueilla. Samalla taloudellinen kilpailu kiristyy ja saa uusia muotoja. Viime aikoina on keskusteltu paljon niin sanotusta Kiina.ilmist, jolla tarkoitetaan tuotannollisten typaikkojen siirtymist vanhoista teollisuusmaista uusiin, halvemman kustannustason maihin. Tss ei ole kysymys tietenkn vain hintakilpailusta, vaan siit, ett monet aikaisemmin taloudellisesti eristytyneet ja takapajuiset maat ovat nyt saavuttaneet sellaisen teknisen osaamisen tason, ett ne pystyvt tuottamaan jo hyvin vaativiakin tuotteita rikkaiden maiden markkinoille. Tm on merkittv haaste ja on herttnyt suurta huolta vanhoissa teollisuusmaissa. Miten siihen on reagoitava? Haluan tss yhteydess todeta, ett pidn talouden globalisaatiota kaiken kaikkiaan paljon enemmn mahdollisuutena kuin uhkana. Se merkitsee mahdollisuuksien tasoittumista maailmassa. Se johtaa typaikkojen lisntymiseen ja toimeentulon paranemiseen monissa aiemmin kyhiss maissa ja luo samalla kysynt uusille tuotteille, tavaroille ja palveluille, joihin vanhojen teollisuusmaiden on nyt panostettava. Globalisaation ongelmat johtuvatkin juuri tmn rakennemuutoksen aiheuttamista sopeutumisvaikeuksista. Vanhojen rikkaiden maiden on erikoistuttava tekemn asioita, joiden monistaminen halvemman kustannustason maissa ei ole mahdollista. Tm muutos johtaa suuriin taloudellisiin ja yhteiskunnallisiin seurauksiin. Vanhoissa teollisuusmaissa kovin kilpailu kydn siit, miss maassa ja mill alueilla tehdn korkeata osaamista vaativa ty, jossa arvonlisyksen mr ja palkkataso on korkein. Kysymys on siis esimerkiksi sellaisten toimintojen kuin tutkimus-ja kehitystoiminnan, markkinoinnin, liikkeenjohdon ja rahoituksen sijoittumisesta. Nille toiminnoille on ominaista, ett ne keskittyvt toistensa lheisyyteen. Vanhoissa teollisuusmaissa kasvavat ja menestyvt sellaiset metropolit, joissa yliopistot ja suuryritysten pkonttorit, tutkimuslaitokset ja rahoitusmarkkinat toimivat vuorovaikutuksessa toistensa kanssa. Fyysisen tuotannon vistyess kasvualat lytyvt nist liike-elm ja aineetonta tuotantoa palvelevista toiminnoista, jotka keskittyvt suurimpiin kasvukeskuksiin. Voidaan ehk puhua Lontoo-ilmist Kiina-ilmin vastapainona. Lontoohan on esimerkki eurooppalaisesta metropolista, jonka kasvu on ollut voimakasta ja perustunut toimintoihin, jotka ovat enemmn hytyneet globalisaatiosta kuin siit krsineet. Suomelle tm lnsimaissa kynniss oleva rakennemuutos on erityisen suuri haaste. Olemme viime vuosikymmenen teknologiaboomin aikana ehk liiaksikin tuudittautuneet siihen uskoon, ett suuret panostukset tekniseen koulutukseen ja tuotekehitykseen turvaavat Suomen taloudellisen menestyksen. Teknologinen etumatka on kuitenkin nopeasti kuluva kilpailutekij, ja teknisten tuotteiden kypsyminen vallankumouksellisista uutuuksista halvaksi bulkkitavaraksi tapahtuu globalisaation vaikutuksesta yh nopeammin. Jos pkonttorit lhtevt Suomesta, suomalaisen suunnittelun, markkinoinnin, juridiikan ja rahoituksen kasvumahdollisuudet kuihtuvat. Kuitenkin juuri nm toiminnot ovat niit, joita korkean tulotason maissa on tulevaisuudessa pyrittv mrtietoisesti kehittmn. Suomessa on huolehdittava siit, ett kaupunkirakenteemme ja asuntomarkkinamme tukevat Suomen menestymist tss kansainvlisess metropolien vlisess kilpailussa. Meill on perinteisesti kiinnitetty paljon huomiota tulopolitiikkaan ja veropolitiikkaan yritysten kilpailukyvyn turvaajina. Asuntojen keskikoko on meill kieltmtt hiljalleen kasvamassa, mutta emme ole saavuttamassa kilpailijamaitamme, koska mys uusien asuntojen keskikoko j Suomessa selvsti jlkeen siit, mit muissa meihin lhinn verrattavissa maissa rakennetaan. Tm siit huolimatta, ett tutkimusten mukaan valtaosa suomalaisista haluaisi asua pientaloissa ja vaikka meill periaatteessa pitisi olla rakentamiselle enemmn tilaa kuin useimmissa muissa maissa. Tm kaikki tarkoittaa sit, ett Suomen asuntokantaa olisi nopeasti parannettava, varsinkin Helsingin metropolialueella. Ennen kaikkea tarjolla olevien asuntojen kokoa on kasvatettava ja asuntojen laadun tulisi vastata paremmin asukkaiden toiveita -tm merkitsee mm. korkeatasoisten pientalojen osuuden nopeaa kasvattamista. Kolmas suomalaisten asuntomarkkinoiden kilpailukykyyn negatiivisesti vaikuttava tekij on vuokra.asuntomarkkinoiden ohuus ja heikko toiminta, varsinkin korkeatasoisten vuokra-asuntojen tarjonnan vhisyys. Yksityiset vuokra-asuntomarkkinat olisi mys saatava toimimaan nykyist paremmin. Tll on merkityst paitsi ulkomaisen, ehk tilapisen tyvoiman maassa oleskelun kannalta, mys tyvoiman kotimaisen liikkuvuuden kannalta. Sit paitsi hyvin toimivat vuokra-asuntomarkkinat auttavat vhentmn asuntohintojen vaihtelusta kotitalouksille aiheutuvia riskej. Toimivien vuokra-asuntomarkkinoiden kehittymisen kannalta olisi muun muassa koetettava elvytt institutionaalisten sijoittajien kuten vakuutusyhtiiden mielenkiinto vuokra-asuntotuotantoon. Viime vuosinahan huikeasti paisuneiden tyelkerahastojen varoja on sijoitettu yh enemmn ulkomaisiin arvopapereihin ja kotimaiset sijoitukset esimerkiksi vuokra-asuntoihin ovat menettneet merkitystn. Asuntopolitiikan kaksi peruskysymyst ovat perinteisesti olleet maakysymys ja rahoituskysymys. Thn voisi viel list suunnittelun eli arkkitehtuurin. Ovatko nm tekijt kunnossa? Muodostavatko ne turhia esteit asumisen laadun paranemiselle Suomessa ja erityisesti Helsingin metropolialueella? Onko Suomella vahvuuksia, joita voitaisiin hydynt? Aloitetaan positiivista asioista. Niihin kuuluu jo nykyn rahoitus, joka vuosikymmenien ajan oli Suomessa krooninen niukkuustekij. Suomen rahaolojen vakaantuminen Euroopan rahaliittoon liittymisen yhteydess muutti tilanteen aivan toisenlaiseksi, ja nykyn normaaleilta, kaupallisilta markkinoilta saa rahoitusta niin edullisesti, ett valtiollinen asuntorahoitusjrjestelm on joutunut pohtimaan olemassaolonsa tarvetta ja oikeutusta. Matala ja vakaa korkotaso merkitsee sit, ett rahoituksen puute tai kustannukset eivt ole keskeinen suomalaisen asumisen kehittmist rajoittava tekij. Toinen potentiaalinen vahvuus voisi ehk olla suunnittelu, mutta uskon, ett tss suhteessa suomalaisten pitisi palata oman traditionsa juurille, ennen kuin tmn vahvuus saadaan laajemmin kyttn. Suomalainen arkkitehtuuri on meille yksi trkeimmist kansallisen identiteetin rakennuspuista. Sen kansainvlinen maine perustuu ennen muuta Alvar Aallon tyhn. Aalto pyrki uudistamaan funktionalistista rakennustapaa tuomalla siihen humanismia ja luonnonmukaisuutta. Hn ei uskonut rationalistisiin tai mekaanisiin ratkaisuihin, vaan halusi antaa tilaa elmn arvaamattomuudelle ja monimuotoisuudelle. Aikana, jota yleens muuten hallitsi tyly tehokkuusromantiikka ja vulgri sosiaalifunktionalismi, Aalto etsi innoitusta antiikista ja Italian renessanssikaupungeista. Suomalaisen arkkitehtuurin ainoalaatuinen lahja maailmalle on humaani kolmas tie, joka sijoittuu ahtaan tehokkuusajattelun ja epinhimillisen monumentalismin vliin. Nin ainakin sen pitisi olla. Suomalaisen arkkitehtuurin hienoista perinteist huolimatta suomalaisessa asuntorakentamisessa on panostettu vuosikymmenien ajan enemmn mrlliseen tehokkuuteen kuin laatuun. Voidaan tietysti sanoa, ett sosiaaliset syyt ovat siihen pakottaneet. Asuntopulan vallitessa levisi ksitys, ett halpa rakentaminen minimistandardeilla edusti korkeinta yhteiskuntamoraalia: ornamentti oli rikos, ja kauneus ja laatukin olivat asioita, joista sopi tinki. Tuotettavien asuntojen lukumr on ratkaissut ja kustannussstj etsittiin sarjatuotannolla. Aalto nki jo varhain, ett tllainen lhestymistapa asuntorakentamiseen olisi jv tilapiseksi kehitysvaiheeksi. Hn kirjoitti vuonna 1939, puolustaessaan Villa Mairea projektiaan seuraavasti: ... arkkitehtonisella tapauksella, jossa yksilllinen elm, henkilkohtaiset vaistot ja kulttuuriksitteet muodostavat pohjan tehtvlle, (on) omalaatuinen kauaskantoinen sosiaalinenkin merkityksens, jos se asetetaan pitkn eteenpin thtvn aikaperspektiiviin. Se viittaa silloin tiet siihen uuteen individualismiin, joka tuotantokoneiston yh kehittyess ja jrjestelymuotojen parantuessa tekee mahdolliseksi joustavamman yksiln huomioimisen mys siin, miss tnn primitiivisen joukkotuotannon viel puolikehittynyt koneisto antaa leimansa asunnoille. Ehk Aallon kaipaama aika on vihdoin koittanut. Jos ja kun globalisaatio kynnist metropolialueiden vlisen kilpailun asumisen ja asuinympristn laadulla, voi sanoa, ettei meill ole varaa jtt kyttmtt niit mahdollisuuksia, joita monimuotoinen ja asukkaiden tarpeista lhtev, humaani rakentaminen tarjoaa. Rakennustekniikka ei ole esteen. Toivottavasti ei kaupunkiarkkitehtien tai kunnallispoliitikkojen puritaanisuuskaan. Korkealaatuinen rakentaminen ei yhteiskunnan kannalta ole edes kustannustekij, vaan vlttmttmyys. Se, mit sit varten tarvitaan, on sallivampi kaavoitus ja kaupunkisuunnittelu, joka antaisi maksukykyiselle kysynnlle tilaa vaikuttaa rakentamisen laatuun ja suuntautumiseen. Suomessa asumista on perinteisesti koetettu kehitt kysynt tukevin toimin. Tulevaisuudessa huomio on knnettv kysynt yleisesti tukevista toimista asuntojen tarjonnan joustavoittamiseen: asuntojen kysynnn on saatava vaikuttaa nykyist enemmn rakennustoiminnan suuntautumiseen ja laatuun. Tarjonnan joustavoittaminen edesauttaa mys asuntojen hintatason kohtuullistamista. Nythn esimerkiksi alhainen korkotaso on tarjonnan joustamattomuuden vuoksi kapitalisoitumassa kasvukeskusten asuntojen hintoihin. Tarjonnan joustavoittamisessa erityinen ja ratkaiseva asema on kuntien kaavoitus-ja tonttipolitiikalla. Tonttipolitiikkansa keinoin kunnat voisivat mys list kilpailua ja tarjontaa yksityisill vapaarahoitteisilla vuokra-asuntomarkkinoilla. Globalisoituvassa maailmassa byrokratian ja rajoittavan snnstelyn haitat krjistyvt kaikilla elmnaloilla, mys asumisessa, ja tm vaatii uudenlaisten lhestymistapojen kehittmist asuntopolitiikkaan ja kaavoitukseen. Pidn selvn, ett pkaupunkiseudun tonttipolitiikan selviminen lhimmn 10 vuoden haasteista vaatii kaavoitustahdin olennaista nopeuttamista ja paljon liberaalimpaa maankyttpolitiikkaa. Pkaupunkiseudulla uutiseksi nytt riittvn se, ett tn vuonna kaavoitetaan 18 uutta pientalotonttia. Tt voidaan pit Helsingin metropolialueen kehittmisen nkkulmasta skandaalina! Ehk tarvitaan tosiaan valtiovallan erityistoimia, jotta korkeatasoiselle asuntorakentamiselle saadaan tll enemmn tilaa. Kysymyksess on kuitenkin koko maan taloudelliseen elinvoimaan ja tulevaisuuteen olennaisesti vaikuttava asia. Hyvt kuulijat! Globalisaation aika vaatii asuntopolitiikalta ja siihen liittyen kaupunkisuunnittelulta, kaavoitukselta ja arkkitehtuurilta kilpailukyky ja kyky nhd asukkaat subjekteina eik politiikan kohteina. Asuntosektorin kilpailukyvyn kehittminen edellytt Suomen kasvukeskusten ja nimenomaan Helsingin metropolialueen luontaisten vahvuuksien etsimist mys asumisessa. Nm vahvuudet liittyvt Suomessa kytettviss olevaan tilaan, luonnon lheisyyteen ja toivoakseni suunnittelijoiden kykyyn ammentaa suomalaisen arkkitehtuurin humaaneista perinteist. Kilpailukyky ei ole taskulaskinksite, vaan se merkitsee asiakkaiden  tss tapauksessa asukkaiden  tarpeiden oivaltamista ja hyvksymist. Se merkitsee esimerkiksi sit, ett laadun ksite asumisessa ei saa tarkoittaa vain eik edes ensi sijassa rakennustekniikkaa, vaan sit, ett ihmisten monimuotoiset, jopa kirjavat tarpeet ratkaisevat asumisen kehityssuunnat. Meidn tulisi tehd Suomesta asumisen mallimaa!

Title: Speech, EU financial markets and payment traffic outlook
text: Speech by Sinikka Salo, Bank Director, EU financial markets and payments . Speech . Wednesday19 May2004,12:00AM Presentation at OpusCapita Plc's anniversary seminar in Tampere 19.5.2004 Europe's financial markets have also undergone significant changes. I believe that this will continue to develop and that european financial services will become national pan-European. It is clear that such a profound change in the European financial markets will have a significant impact on economic conditions in the Member States and, in some respects, on the world. Some of the euro area's financial markets are already fairly integrated. The best example is the unsecured short-money market for banks, which currently operates smoothly throughout the euro area. Significant progress has also been made in other areas, such as the sovereign bond market, but collectively, despite the monetary situation, the euro area financial markets in general remain heavily segmented along national borders. The transformation into a truly pan-European market is therefore, at most, half a lot. The integration of financial markets, as well as markets in general, is high on the EU's economic policy priorities. This is clear, for example, with the joint adoption by the Member States of the Lisbon Strategy, which includes a very concrete financial services action plan. According to the action plan, EU countries will, among other things, work towards the creation of an integrated securities market by 2005. A significant part of the legislation of the action plan and other measures have already been implemented. However, the full implementation of the action plan still requires a significant effort. Hardly anyone is able to accurately assess all the consequences of financial integration. However, according to a number of seemingly reliable estimates, integration can have considerable advantages. A common example of the link between financial markets and economic efficiency and growth is the United States. It is fairly widely believed that the large, deep and well-functioning us financial markets are, but of course not the only factor behind the country's high productivity and rapid economic growth. If that is the case, then the integration of the financial markets and the associated intensification would have a similarly positive impact on europe's employment, competitiveness and, through that, on the on-budget finances of european countries. Despite the political will at the level of the strategy, the creation of a common financial market is progressing slowly. Although the introduction of the single currency removed one of the main obstacles to the common market in the euro area, the emergence of a common market is still limited by a number of important frictional factors. This is partly based on the acceptance of existing conditions and the defence of local interests. Especially for the defense of financial centers ksydssn harsh wrestling. On the other hand, there are also genuine legal and technical problems with integration. This is intrinsically due to the fact that the national systems and laws have gradually been formed from each country's own pockets. Although market integration is now evident, in the past it has not been foreseen at all, at least not on the current scale. Despite the friction, I am optimistic about the integration process of the EU's financial markets. The benefits of a pan-European financial market are simply too great for us to be able to accept them. Epsselvsss is just that, on a schedule, we will eventually reach an integrated pan-European financial market in each sector. The convergence of the development and development of the financial markets will continue to be at the heart of the European Union's economic policy cooperation in the years, even after the financial services action plan is hopefully finalised in 2005. In the securities markets, following the implementation of the action plan, considerable additional efforts will be needed, in particular to integrate securities clearing and settlement systems. Outside the securities markets d for example in banking and insurance d the emergence of pan-European integrated financial markets will probably have to wait until an integrated securities market emerges. The combination of nationally segmented financial markets into one well-functioning and safe European financial market provides an excellent example of economic policy cooperation within the FRAMEWORK of the EU, which is of great importance for our future well-being. It is obvious that the cooperation between the Commission, the Member States d not the Member States of the EU d and the seamless legislation of the European Parliament is of paramount importance. However, these are self-motivated actions by the various participants in the financial markets to develop the European market. The role of central banks in the development of financial markets is a complex and complex issue. The European Central Bank's most important task is, of course, to establish a common monetary policy. The implementation of the single monetary policy, on the other hand, is primarily the responsibility of the national central banks of the euro area. The European System of Central Banks is not a general framework for financial markets laid down in the EC Treaty, but according to the Treaty it also contributes to the proper conduct of policies of the competent authorities with regard to the prudential supervision and financial organisation of credit institutions. However, the European Central Bank and the national central banks have d like central banks in general - also sought to influence the development of efficient markets and, to the satisfaction of this, have given their support to the emergence of a common financial market. In order to ensure the stability and reliable functioning of the financial system, the European Central Bank and the national central banks monitor and analyse the state of the euro area financial system and developments in its financial system. General supervision of the financial markets covers, in particular, the prudential and efficient supervision of the banking sector and of payment and settlement systems. *** The promotion of the proper functioning of the payment systems is laid down in the Treaty establishing the European Central Bank. Central banks carry out this task in different ways. Somewhere in the world, I will group it arbitrarily into three groups, i.e. the provision of payment services, the monitoring of the functioning and reliability of payment systems, and the development of payment systems. Central banks provide payment services primarily to commercial banks and, to varying extent, to others, such as the state, local banks and securities banks. The payment services provided by central banks constitute a small but very specific segment of the financial markets. In Finland, the Bank of Finland has traditionally offered payment methods primarily to banks and central banks and to central bank payments. For this purpose, since 1991, the SP has been using real time gross settlement (RTGS). Most of Finland's payments are settled in the banks' own, internationally advanced payment systems (POPS, PMJ). Nsisss SP is not a party, nor has it actively participated in their development, with the exception of the risk management sector. However, the margins of the systems are carried out by RTGS.jsestelmsss. In a number of central and eastern European countries, central banks play a much more important role, even in terms of payment as service providers. In order to become a reality, the single monetary policy requires that liquidity effects, and with them short-term money market interest rates, level off across the euro area. In order to implement the single monetary policy, there must therefore be a Europe-wide or euro area-wide payment system to help bridge liquidity and interest rate differentials between participating countries. At an early stage in the development of the european central banks' payment systems, the central banks agreed that everyone should have a functioning RTGS system before the single currency is adopted and that euro area-wide payments systems should be linked together with the national RTGS systems. There was a desire to adopt national systems in order to speed up the creation of a common system. It may also have contributed to the fact that the national systems were relatively new and did not want to be abandoned immediately after the end of the system. The European System of Central Banks (TARGET), which became operational in 1999, linked the RTGS system of the national central banks into a single entity, so that cross-border payments are made in real time using central bank money. Payments shall be irrevocable and final upon payment. TARGET has made an EU-wide system of central bank money in an excellent way. It has made it possible to implement monetary policy in a decentralised manner through the national central banks. At the same time, it has also contributed to the fact that the unsecured short-money market for banks is the most integrated segment of the financial markets in Europe, which I mentioned earlier. Over time, however, significant pressure has accumulated on the development of the system. The current TARGET is not in a position to meet all the requirements imposed on it by the current TARGET in the best possible way. The costs of the system are also heavy. However, the need to reform the entire system has become particularly topical as a result of the enlargement of the EU. The integration of the national RTGS systems of the new Member States into TARGET will require some and substantial changes in all of them. For some time now, it has been planned to build a new, technically more centralised payment system within the Framework of the European Central Bank. The plans for setting up the system are already long in coming. It is unlikely that target2 has been chosen as the name of the new system. As some of the new Member States may join the euro area as early as 2007, the new system should be ready by then in order for it to be available to the new euro area countries from the time of accession. TARGET2's structure is substantially different from the current TARGET. TARGET2 will become a centralised system operated by all central banks. However, the relationship between the NCBs and their own customers remains unchanged, i.e. the banks' accounts will continue to be in the accounts and balance sheets of the national central banks, and the banks will be linked to their own central bank in all matters relating to the account, just as they are at the moment. Only technology concentrates. The Central Banks of Italy, France and Germany have offered to build a common technical system for TARGET2. Target2's services have been designed to take account of banks' wishes. The accession of TARGET2 banks is also standardised throughout the EU. Banks will also seek to provide better liquidity management services than before. Pricing will also be harmonized, and the price of domestic and country-to-country payments will be the same. At the moment, the prices of payments made only from one country to another have been harmonised and the prices of domestic payments differ. It is hoped that the centralised solution will reduce prices. The price of cross-border payments will therefore fall, but the prices of domestic payments will not decrease in all euro area countries. Target2's cost and price level is raised by, among other things, better preparedness for various crisis and exceptional situations. The transition to the TARGET2 system will, in due course, in its own very narrow area, be a clear step towards pan-European, integrated financial markets. In relation to this, it reflects well the general trends in the financial markets. At the same time, it can be a long step towards a more concentrated financial market. Let me now turn to the question of the role of central banks as supervisors of payment systems. As supervisors, central banks do not, of course, act in the same way as market participants as they do in the payment of payments, but rather as a neutral player on the outside and upper side of the market, but at the same time well-informed. Traditionally, central banks have supervised the payment systems of banks, and this is still by far the most important supervisory function in terms of payment systems. National central banks also have different traditions in the oversight of payment systems. The Bank of Finland has traditionally intervened only when necessary, i.e. quite rarely. However, in the mid-1990s, it began to make a concrete assessment of the stability of finnish banks' payment systems. In part, the intensification of controls on payment systems was linked to preparations for the third stage of economic and monetary union. As a result, some changes were agreed with the banks to improve the risk management of the systems. In some other European countries, the Central Bank has traditionally supervised bank payment systems and even payment systems by assessing how they meet the requirements imposed by central banks. With regard to the euro area, the Governing Council adopted the principles of oversight of payment systems in 1999. Nsms was released the following year. According to them: The Council shall establish a common oversight policy for the oversight of the national systems. central bank of the general supervisor responsible for coordinating multinational systems, the Governing Council of the ECB. A great deal of attention has also been paid to the operation of payment systems in international cooperation. In particular, among the leading industrialized countries, that is, the so-called. The G10 central banks have drawn up basic principles for the so-called "common principles" in the BIS's Payments Committee (CPSS). SIPS for payment systems. The Governing Council has decided to apply the principles as such in the oversight of SIPS in the euro area and some of the principles in the oversight of other payment systems. In addition to technological developments, central banks have recently been paying attention to non-bank payment systems, in particular Sshksic money. In May 2003, the ECB published the security criteria for sshksic money and their suitability is to be examined by assessing how the monetary system is to be used. General supervision also includes preparing for crisis and exceptional situations. This is done at national level in conjunction with other authorities (Financial Supervisory Authority, Ministry of Finance). The importance of this has increased considerably in recent years. The development of payment systems, new systems and new parties pose new challenges for oversight. From national oversight to integrated oversight, the aim is to achieve uniform oversight in the euro area and to equal treatment of the parties involved. As is the case with the supervision of financial markets in general, progress is being made towards harmonised procedures in the supervision of payment systems. Harmonised oversight will require common procedures and will be developed in the future to assess the various aspects of payment. In the future, kriteerej may also be developed for different payment methods, for example. card payments. I shall conclude by reviewing recent developments and developments in european private payment systems. The ECB and the national central banks are actively involved in the development of the systems. However, it is clear that, in the development of private payment systems, their role is clearly smaller than in providing their own payment services or in monitoring the reliability of payment systems. As I said earlier, it was largely thanks to the European System of Central Banks' own TARGET system that the euro area money market, or more precisely the unsecured short-term money market for banks, was integrated in 1999. The integration of wholesale markets and wholesale payments was facilitated not only by TARGET, but also by the transition to the euro1 system, which had previously been used to pay ECU-sssisis in Europe at the beginning of 1999. On the German side, integration has not progressed as quickly as possible. The European Banking Association (EBA), which is responsible for EURO1, set up a so-called 'banking association' for smaller payments. STEP1 system. It began to operate in late 2000 and, however, the number of participants in STEP1 was relatively small, and the system did not meet the requirements for a euro area-wide system of payments, The Commission and the ESCB each initially sought to promote euromssism in the euro area on the basis of voluntary cooperation between banks. However, no significant progress could be observed. When the eurocheque was introduced at the beginning of 2002, the Commission began to prepare at a rapid pace a regulation on the development of cross-border payment of the euro. In 2002, a decree on The Constitution came into force, requiring the simultaneous pricing of domestic and cross-border payments to customers. Initially, the regulation only applied to card payments and ATM withdrawals, but since 2003 it has also extended to bank transfers of less than EUR 12,500. The regulation significantly accelerated the efforts of EU banks to improve cross-border payments. The largest banks and EU banking associations - which belong to the Finnish group Nordea and the Finnish Banking Association - founded the EPC (European paymets council) in mid-2002. It started to draw up plans for the creation of a single euro payment area (SEPA) in the euro area. The first objective was to create a crossborder system for crossborder transfers, which was therefore to be available in 2003. This goal was achieved ahead of schedule and STEP2 became operational in early 2003. The EU regulation on the pricing of payment services can be seen as a small but significant step forward in the integration of European financial markets. The regulation will have little effect on the payment transactions of large international companies, but it will make it easier and cheaper for small and medium-sized enterprises d and all ordinary Finns to make their payments abroad. However, the importance of the regulation is that it has given a significant boost to the cooperation between European banks. It is clear that epc will play a decisive role in the future payment system of Europe. EPC's current plans run until 2010. The aim is to achieve a step-by-step approach, in addition to bank transfers, other forms of payment within the euro area. The programme includes cards, direct debit, cheques and possible new forms of payment (e-money and telephone payments) in addition to credit transfers. In December 2003, the Commission published a communication entitled 'A new legislative framework for payment systems', which goes beyond EPC's plans. The aim is to create a modern uniform EU legal framework for payment services, which would allow free competition on uniform terms, safe payment, increase the efficiency of payment systems and ensure the legal position of all parties in the payment chain. For the time being, it is clear how the Commission will proceed on the basis of the communication. Also, the schedule is open. The harmonisation of the payment law is a thorny and challenging issue, given the large differences between national laws. The slow pace of integration also has other reasons, such as: National payment systems differ considerably from one another. In Finland, for example, the payment system is long-term electronicised and automated, while in Central and Eastern Europe, the systems are technologically considerably improved.
