Keskuspankkien nkkulmasta mielenkiintoinen kysymys epilemtt on se, millaiseksi keskuspankkien tai yleisemmin viranomaisten rooli Euroopan maksujrjestelmien kokonaisuudessa jatkossa muodostuu? Toteutuvan kehityksen myt paljastuu, miss mrin mahdollisten ongelmien ratkaisemiseksi riitt jonkinasteinen "epvirallinen taivuttelu", jossa keskuspankeilla saattaa olla keskeinen rooli, ja miss mrin tarvitaan lakiperusteista sntely, jonka luomisessa taas komissio, EU:n neuvosto ja Euroopan parlamentti olisivat avainasemassa. Hyvt kuulijat! Olen edell esittnyt muutamia esimerkkej meneilln olevista hankkeista Euroopan laajuisten rahoitusmarkkinoiden kehittmiseksi etenkin maksuliikenteen alueella. Jo tllainen pintapuolinenkin tarkastelu osoittaa, ett paljon on tekeill mutta paljon on viel tekemtt ennen kuin pstn Euroopan laajuisiin syviin rahoitusmarkkinoihin. Viime kdess kysymys on kansallisten menettelyjen ja snnsten yhteensovittamisesta, joka on hidasta. Eri maiden osapuolten olisi kuitenkin katsottava kansallisten lyhytaikaisten intressien yli, sill kiistatta yhtenisist hyvin toimivista Euroopan laajuisista rahoitusmarkkinoista tuleva hyty Euroopan elinkeinoelmlle ja kansalaisille on merkittv.

Title: The euro, financial markets and businesses
text: Bank Manager Sinikka Salo's speech: The euro, financial markets and companies . Speech . Saturday 11September 2004,12:00AM Speech at the 65th anniversary of vaasan yrittsjst ry 11.9.2004 Bank Manager Sinikka Salo Bank of Finland Dear guests, Vaasa has a long tradition of nurturing entrepreneurship. It is a great honour and pleasure for me to congratulate you. My own roots are also in Ostrobothnian enterprise. next year it will be 100 years since my grandfather founded a shop in Kortesjsrven Purmojsrve. The general feeling is that the number of companies is higher in Ostrobothnia than in the rest of Finland. The rights of Vaasa and other cities may have had a significant impact on the tune of enterprise in Ostrobothnia. In addition, it is probably the case that the Ostrobothnian character is the "madness" of the Ostrobothnians. well suited for business. You have to take a risk from your business. Ostrobothnia has a particularly large number of small and medium-sized enterprises. It has sometimes been suggested that the Ostrobothnian character is only suitable for managers of small and medium-sized enterprises. However, the success of the Ostrobothnians in the management of large companies has also proved their place in the management of large companies. Of course, good companies and business leaders are born much more than just in Ostrobothnia. Somewhere in the autumn, it seems to be born more in Ostrobothnia than elsewhere. The hard core of enterprise d the personality required for successful entrepreneurship d has, I believe, remained more or less the same throughout the ages. Year after year, people of a somewhat similar nature seek employment. On the contrary, the way in which companies operate, i.e. the framework for enterprise, has changed enormously in recent decades. The development of international integration of the economy has been particularly strongly influenced by the way in which enterprises operate. This has progressed both globally and regionally. Once the market has opened up, fewer companies will be able to hope to succeed with customs barriers or import restrictions. Similarly, the small size of the market is less likely to be an attempt to expand the company's activities. As a result of the global opening up of markets, the challenges and opportunities for entrepreneurs have both increased. In this context, there are reasons to point out that globalisation is, of course, much broader than the increase and expansion of foreign trade in goods and services, as well as the changes in jobs brought about by china, which is currently described in people's minds. The interaction of people across national and continental borders has increased in relations other than trade in goods and services. In the 1960s, like the famous media researcher Marshall McLuhan, it is quite justifiable to talk about the ssch corner in the world,of which we are all inhabitants. It can be said that, thanks to technological development and the opening up of connections, Vaasa has turned from a remote coastal city into a part of a large world village. Progress in regional integration has been fastest in Europe, where the European Union is the dynamo of the integration process. The European Union is often seen as an attempt by its Member States to meet the challenges of globalisation, but at the same time it is also a major driver of the integration process itself. Through the EU, European countries have the opportunity to rise alongside the United States as a political force influencing the global economy. On the other hand, it has a significant impact on the vitality and operating conditions of states and private citizens. In Finland, as in other EU countries, eu membership has had and will certainly affect the operating conditions of companies in many ways in the future. The consequence of this has been the transition to a single currency, the euro, and a single monetary policy by the ECB. Almost six years have passed since the changeover to the euro and, in concrete terms, the euro has already been in our pockets for three years. This is such a long time that some picture of the impact of the single currency and monetary policy is already beginning to take shape, although reliable impact assessments can only be made after a much longer period of time. The introduction of the single currency was a major change, the effects of which will be felt widely and for a long time in different areas of society. It is my intention to focus on two key areas, namely monetary policy and the financial markets. *** The influence of Nikhov and slitch on the accession to the monetary union was the impact of exchange rate fluctuations in the central euro area countries. The transition from national currencies and money markets to the euro and euro area money markets was a major change in all participating countries. However, the change was particularly marked in those countries whose tradition of monetary stability had been heverish before the introduction of the euro and where the money and foreign exchange markets were thus previously vulnerable to fluctuations in national and global market forces. The elimination of exchange rate risks and exchange rate exchange charges has benefited the consumer and helped internationalisation, especially small companies, which find it more difficult to operate in several currencies and to hedge exchange rate risks than large companies. Furthermore, as a major currency, the euro is not as easy a target for speculative currency hymns as many of its predecessor currencies, and it also provides good protection for euro area residents from speculative pressures on the foreign exchange markets. The fluctuations in the exchange rate of the euro against the US dollar and other currencies are, of course, a fact of life in the context of monetary union. Although the introduction of the euro has led to exchange rate risks for Finnish companies, the impact has naturally been greater for those central European countries where foreign trade, and especially exports, have been directed towards the guerrillas of the euro area. Approximately one third of Finland's exports go to the euro area, so due to the structure of our external trade, fluctuations in the exchange rates of the euro affect the Finnish economy more than the average euro area. From a Finnish point of view, the current situation naturally encourages the development of guerrilla trade in the euro area as it has turned into domestic market activity in every respect. The large domestic market, on the other hand, is a good basis for efforts in the fastest growing emerging markets, for example in Asia. Another effect of monetary union (in addition to the end of epartith exchange rate fluctuations in the euro area) was the convergence of interest rate developments in the euro area countries. The development of the shortest interest rates is determined by the key interest rates of the European Central Bank. Interest rates are, of course, the same throughout the euro area. The central bank is not in a position to control precisely the development of other interest rates, but all monetary policy developments have a significant impact on them through expectations. In various quarters, not in the United States, there was a great deal of sympathy for the monetary policy of the European Central Bank before monetary union began. The most significant experience of the first years of monetary union is that nsms epsluulos have been more or less completely destroyed. In its first five or six years, the European Central Bank's monetary policy, on the other hand, can be considered to have been more successful than hardly anyone could have anticipated or even hoped for. Despite the difficult conditions at the outset, I am referring in particular to the strong international boom and the rise in the price of sljy and other import hysdys. The European Central Bank has managed to achieve price stability in the euro area and has not even had to resort to a heavy-handed monetary policy. In other words, the European Central Bank's monetary policy has been credible. This is clear on interest rates in the euro area, which have been lower in all maturities in recent years than they have been for a long time. In fact, there is a history of the mentsvs until the years of the gold standard before there are similarly low interest rates as in recent years. Interest rates are low partly because inflation is low, but it is also very low in real terms, i.e. taking inflation into account. This provides good points for business. There are several reasons for the low interest rate. I would like to highlight two points. The firmly secured position of the Central Bank itself, the clear objective of monetary policy and the careful preparation of monetary policy were the key factors that enabled the European Central Bank to acquire monetary credibility as the new central bank in the near future. Economists have talked a lot about the advantages and disadvantages of both large and small currency areas. Experience in Europe and elsewhere suggests that the climate of stability created by a large monetary area and a stable monetary policy provides a vast majority of citizens and businesses with better positions than monetary policy, which can easily become tempted by market pressures in a small economy. The economic development of a large currency area is more stable than that of the subregions, because when assessing the average development of the subregions, the divergent development of the subregions somewhere in the region cancels each other out. In the same autumn, the monetary policy of a large currency area is generally more stable than that of a small currency area. Only stable variable interest rates have their advantages. I believe that stable monetary conditions in a large currency area are an advantage, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises. In general, the development of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) rarely coincides with the development of the national economy, and changes in interest rates determined by monetary policy are not particularly suitable for them, even when they are correctly dimensioned from the angle of the economy as a whole. While fluctuations in interest rates may make it more difficult to assess the present value of future expenses and cause other difficulties for entrepreneurs, activist interest rate policy is generally more of a subsidy for the development of small businesses than a subsidy. The special wishes of large companies may, on the contrary, be taken into account only too well by the authorities responsible for monetary and economic policy decisions in the country. One example of the excessive consideration of the specific interests of large companies in monetary and economic policy is provided by the inflationary and devaluation spiral of the Finnish economy d an integral part of which was the large-scale suffrage of the financial markets. after the war, and especially in the 1970s and 1980s. On the financial markets, the introduction of the euro has clearly accelerated the emergence of genuine pan-European financial markets. Changes in the financial markets generally take place, and changes in the single currency cannot be as drastic as the adoption of the single currency and the transition to a single monetary policy. However, I believe that, over time, changes in the financial markets are significant and will have a major impact on the economic development of European countries. Changes in the financial markets have a wide range of effects in many directions, but I would particularly like to stress the importance of a large and well-functioning financial market as a factor that has a positive impact on economic development. The fact that the introduction of the euro has calmed down monetary conditions in Europe has had a positive impact on the development of the financial markets. A much more important point, however, is that, for the first time in a long time, we have been given the opportunity to create a Europe-wide, truly integrated financial market and thus also to contribute to the functioning of the sizzle market d that Europe would genuinely operate as if it were the home market. The strengthening of the credibility of the stable price level and, for their part, the evolution of the payment systems d lshinns real-time transmission system for large payments operated by central banks TARGET . have given a new impetus to the process of integration of the EU's financial markets. Part of the euro area's financial markets are already integrated; for example, the unsecured short-money market for banks now operates smoothly and uniformly throughout the euro area. The markets for government bonds and other bonds are already functioning in many respects in a similar way throughout the euro area. Progress has also been made in other market segments. For example, the liquidity of financial instruments has increased and the range has increased. Despite what has been achieved, the financial markets in the euro area are still heavily segmented in many respects and the integration of the financial markets into pan-Europeans can still be considered to be at most half-hearted. The integration process is characterised by different national differences in legislation (such as bankruptcy and taxation legislation), supervisory systems and administrative procedures in the member states. Financial market infrastructures, such as securities clearing houses, also operate in slightly different ways in different countries. Due to all the factors involved, various financial transactions . for example, only making payments d are more difficult from one country to another than from one country to another. An example of this situation is the banking market and cross-border payment transactions to which I have already referred. National borders continue to have a major impact on trade in financial services, even in the euro area. This region is of particular interest to small and medium-sized enterprises, for which a natural market growth area is the single currency market, i.e. the euro area. Of course, this is also the case for ordinary Finns: more payments than before, for example. For our children studying in continental Europe, our holiday apartments for rent in Spain, etc. Similarly, for entrepreneurs looking for small foreign customers, it is important to ensure that future payments related to invoicing run as cheaply and quickly as possible. Indeed, the creation of an integrated payment system for the euro area and the EU as a whole is a priority for the CZECH EU. Although different standardisation work has been going on for a long time, paying from one EU country to another has been much more difficult, slower and more expensive than paying within one country, especially for households and small businesses. The EU intervened in this matter by means of the Regulation on the pricing of payment services, which, since 1.7.2003, has restricted the right of banks to charge higher fees for cross-border credit transfers than for domestic payments. However, the regulation as such does not in itself suffice to remedy the problem, but requires action by the parties to the financial markets, in particular the banks. A positive development can therefore be seen in the fact that the European banking sector has reacted to the above. regulation through the creation of a cooperation body called the European Payments Council, which has set itself the objective of achieving the vision of a single European payments area. Among other things, Khrjests is advocating the establishment of a pan-European payment clearing house during the Lshi years. This would be a milestone in the effective integration of the EU's payment systems, which would require a substantial reduction in the cost of production of payment services from one country to another. On the other hand, competition authorities and central banks must take the view that european cooperation between banks does not become a price cartel and that market power in the pricing of payment services is not ensured. Despite the various frictional factors holding back market integration, I am optimistic about the integration process of the EU's financial markets. The benefits of a pan-European financial market are simply too great for us to be able to accept them. Steps in the right direction are constantly being taken both by the legislation and by the financial sector itself, as the example I mentioned above of the development of an integrated payment system shows. The lowering of the barriers between the euro area countries and their trade and financial transactions in the single currency also poses a challenge and an opportunity. Economic success requires an understanding of the specific nature and prerequisites of each company and region, and its nskemists also from the nsks corner of the international customer. Increasing competition in an expanding market creates problems for those companies that are unable to offer quality that stands out from the rest. On the other hand, the opening up of markets will bring great opportunities for those companies that are able to take the initiative in their own and in the face of the high potential demand in continental Europe. The disadvantages caused by the 'exoticism' of one's own currency and own financial conditions in international operations have now disappeared, and the points of competition in this respect have evened out, not only for large companies, but also for small and medium-sized enterprises. right down to the grassroots. A well-functioning, truly Pan-European financial market will play a key role in the EU's efforts to build an economically coherent and more dynamic Europe, thanks to the so-called 'green belt' adopted in Lisbon in 2000. In line with the Lisbon Strategy. The combination of the development and development of the financial markets is therefore at the heart of the EU's economic policy cooperation over the past few years. This provides an excellent example of what can be achieved through European economic policy cooperation. Without policy cohesiveness, the economy of our continent is unlikely to be able to find a common, open and secure financial market in the future. Good listeners! In my presentation, I have examined the conditions for the success of enterprises and the economy as a whole from the central bank's corner, i.e. a stable monetary policy and large, well-functioning financial markets. The single monetary policy and the climate of stability built by the European Central Bank have created a favourable framework for the economic development of the euro area as a whole and also of Finland. Together with the euro, they have also accelerated the emergence of a well-functioning pan-European financial market. The monetary policy of the European Central Bank has already proved its worth. In other words, the foundation stone is already standing somewhat firmly in place. On the other hand, there is still a great deal of work to be done before we can talk about a truly Pan-European financial market. It will therefore take a great deal of effort to get the foundation stone in place. However, it is worth making an effort to ensure that a well-functioning financial market has an essential impact on economic development. Of course, stable monetary conditions and well-functioning financial markets alone are not enough to solve economic problems that have their roots in non-monetary economics. In recent times, the success of an individual national economy depends on the strength, courage and courage of private citizens. It is positive that in Finnish society the central importance of enterprise is now more important than perhaps in recent decades. The company is appreciated. The monetary economy or the means of economic policy more generally can only create the conditions for the real foundations of the success of competitiveness d so that innovation, enterprise and diligence make a difference. Of course, companies and entrepreneurs themselves play a key role. I wish you, ladies and gentlemen, vaasanyritsjst, still an innovative enterprise that requires at least a modicum of the famous "Ostrobothnian madness".

Title: Speech, "The country that paid its debts"
text: Pankinjohtaja Sinikka Salon puhe; The country that paid its debts . Speech . Wednesday17 November 2004, 12:00 AM At the reception of the exhibition in the Fullbright Center, 17 November 2004 Opening remarks by Ms. Salo, Member of the Board, Bank of Finland Your Excellency, Ambassador Mack, Mrs Mslss, Ladies and Gentlemen, I am honoured and pleased to have been invited to open this exhibition. Its theme "The country that paid its debts" refers to an interesting episode in relations between the United States and Finland. The exhibition also reveals how deep and good these relations are. Not only does the exhibition provide a fine example of the importance of sound reputation and fame, but also how to establish such a "brand". It may well be that this "brand" of being a country that pays its debts is one of the most successful promotion campaigns ever, for Finland. Let me provide you with some background on the exhibition and its theme. I'll start by quoting of the Times Sunday newspaper on 31st of May 1936, a large article entitled Why Finland pays its debt? which illustrates how, at that time, we Finns were known internationally. "The Finn is a rather dour, unsmiling fellow, who makes a fine friend but who takes life with great seriousness. He has a sturdy pride and self-respect. He wants to rely on himself. He asks no favours, and accepts no advice. He has an obstinacy and dogged determination that drives him on against tremendous odds. This doggedness has made him till the poor, rocky Finnish soil and to grow corn under conditions, which an English farmer would call impossible. It has enabled him to survive triumphantly six centuries of war and famine. And it is driving him to pay Finland's debt". *** Finlandos reputation as a reliable debtor was established in 1933, when Finland paid the food loan it had obtained from the United States in 1919, in full and on time. Finland was the United Stateso only debtor country that continued to pay its war-related debt until the end. To understand what this all was about, we need to go back to the times after World War I. International economic relations were fairly complicated as almost every European country was in debt to the US for loans used to finance the war and reconstruction. Germany, on the other hand, according to the Versailles Peace Treaty, owed reparation debts to the allied countries. The situation was later worsened by the emergence of international deflation which increased the real value of the obligations. Several international conferences were held in the 1920s, in order to resolve these international debt relations, and several plans were agreed, and institutions established, for example, the Bank for International Settlements (BIS). However, the debt situation was not progressing well. In 1931, US President Herbert Hoover granted its European debtor countries a year-long moratorium in an effort to facilitate international economic relations. The intention of the Hoover Moratorium was to postpone repayment of the debt by one year. The Moratorium did not mean the pardoning of debts, only their postponement. Payments to the US were to recommence in December 1932. Nevertheless, every other country with the sole exception of Finland took the moratorium to mean a pardon and left their debt unpaid from 1933 onwards. Thereby, Finland became the United Stateso only debtor country that continued to pay its debt until the end and this is why Finland got its reputation as a reliable debtor. Why did Finland pay its debt? This too has its own background. Finland's decision to pay the debt was not a mistake, but a conscious plan to improve Finland's bad reputation! In the 1920s, Finland had, indeed, the reputation of a bad debt payer. That was the result of a law issued in 1921 providing for the loan taken from France at the beginning of the 1920s to be paid back in Finnish markka. Since the markka was suffering from a strong inflation at the time, France ended up losing a significant amount of money at least in terms of gold. This pleased neither France nor the international financial markets. Officers in our Foreign Ministry were aware of the problems regarding reputation, and tried to find a way to mend it. Their hopes were fully satisfied when the US press paid a great deal of attention to Finlandos being one of only a few nations to continue its repayments. Indeed, as I mentioned earlier, paying back the debt was maybe the best promotion campaign ever for Finland and furthermore it was not expensive. One should mention that the size of the debt as a percentage of Finland's GDP was small, and its share of the US total receivables from Europe was actually negligible. So, the huge attention paid to the matter in the United States' media was, may I say, perhaps a bit out of proportion. But there was a principle at stake. The reason for the US media's strong reaction was naturally the Great Depression and the rage felt by American taxpayers against countries not paying their due. *** Between 1933 and 1936, almost 3,000 stories were published in American newspapers on Finland and the debt. Finland was portrayed as a small northern country that gives the shirt off its back, while its richer neighbours leave their debts unpaid. A quote from Christian Science Monitor of July 28 1933 goes: "The Finns are so pink-cheeked; they are gay, vital, and their hearts are so full of the joy of living. They know the true happiness to be derived from simple pleasures. A walk or a boat ride means more than a silly cinema in a too ornate movie palace". In December 1934, Finlandos continued payment of debt received plenty of attention in the press and, for example, a radio broadcast speech by President Roosevelt paid recognition to Finland on the debt matter. As an example of how well the Finnish authorities understood the PR value of repayments I quote the Governor of the Bank of Finland, Mr Risto Ryti. He visited the US in December 1934 and gave a widely quoted interview to the AP, in which he said that Finland could do nothing less: "It is only natural that we should. We signed the contract. We promised to pay. It is the only honest thing to do." Another quote in the Indianapolis Times 7th of December 1935 shows, how American citizens were taught some Finnish, too: "Hauskaa Joulua! On December 15th Finland will pay her semi-annual war-debt instalment of about a quarter of million dollars ---It's sure nice to think one nation will drop a remembrance in the lean old sock this year. In our best Finnish we wish her a Merry Christmas! Hauskaa Joulua!" From 1935 onwards, newspapers almost seemed to be waiting for June and December to gloat over otherso default and Finlandos exemplary payment of debt. Small articles described our geographical location, the countryos brave fight for independence and tendency to drink a lot of coffee. Instead of the small news and caricatures used so far to describe Finland, 1935 saw a turnaround, with more extensive and somewhat more truthful articles being written on the country like the article I quoted at the beginning. Even today, many American school children recall Finland as othe country that pays its debtso, since the fact is pointed out in at least a few text books. *** Finland continued to meet regular instalments until the 1940s, when a few yearso moratorium was called because of World War II. At that time, Finnish and US authorities also discussed whether it would be possible to invest the money repaid by Finland into something that would benefit Finland. This aim was met through the ASLA grant fund and Fulbright Centre established at the beginning of the 1950s. The last payment on the debt was made in accordance with a renewed, faster schedule in 1976. Plans for a scholarship fund were raised in public discussion already quite early on; a quote in the Tiffin Tribune on 26th of December 1935 says: "A recent Washington dispatch remarks, that some State Department officials have been wondering if part of these Finnish payment might not be set aside for a scholarship fund, for the education of Finnish students in American universities; and the idea has a good deal to recommend it. It would strengthen the bond of friendship and understanding between the two nations and it would be a tangible way of showing how this country appreciates the presence of one good debtor among a flock of deadbeats." *** Let me conclude my remarks by saying that the exhibition you are about to see shows some funny, some perhaps moving examples of the reflections in the US media. It is certain that the media and taxpayers were not only happy to receive the Finnish payments but also furious at the irresponsibility of the other countries. So, I hope you do not take the exhibition and the cartoons too seriously. But there is a lesson to be learned here nevertheless. And moreover, I am happy to confirm that according to the latest studies, Finland is still the least corrupted country in the world. I hope, that despite our reputed seriousness, developed as the result of centuries of wars and famine, we have learned to smile a little bit more by now! With this short introduction I wish all the success to the exhibition, which in a rather peculiar but nice way illustrates good relations between our nations!

Title: Monetary policy and financial markets in the EU
text: Bank Manager Sinikka Salo: Monetary policy and financial markets in the EU . Speech . Thursday18 November 2004,12:00 AM Sinikka Salo Bank Manager Bank of Finland Speech at Nordea's customer meeting Jyvsskylssss 18.11.2004 Ladies and gentlemen! The European Central Bank has been responsible for the monetary policy of the euro area countries since the beginning of 1999. The six-year period that has elapsed is too short to allow a reliable assessment of the success or success of the single monetary policy. However, I think that some cautious leadership can already be done now. There is no doubt that, in its first years, the European Central Bank's monetary policy has been more successful than hardly anyone could have expected or even hoped for. Despite the challenging conditions, I am referring in particular to the strong fluctuations in the prices of international economic cycles and other commodity prices - the European Central Bank has managed to keep prices stable in the euro area, without actually having to resort to a heavy-handed monetary policy. In other words, the single monetary policy has been credible from the outset. The credibility of monetary policy is most evident in euro area interest rates, which in recent years have been, on average, lower than they have been for a long time in all maturities. With the maturity of the European Central Bank's actual refinancing operations, which is now a week, the interest rate is in fact reduced by monetary policy. The interest rate is the same for the euro area as a whole, and as such it does not reflect the credibility or lack of monetary policy. The central bank influences the development of other interest rates through expectations, and it is not able to control them in the same way as policy rates. This provides an opportunity to assess the credibility of monetary policy. Interest rates in the euro area are currently low, partly because inflation is not particularly high, although it exceeds the European Central Bank's two per cent threshold for medium-term loans. However, interest rates, including longterm interest rates, are also low in real terms, i.e. taking inflation into account. This reflects the credibility of the European Central Bank's monetary policy in that borrowers and lenders believe that inflation and interest rates will remain under control in the future. We are now a very long way from the threats which some observers, especially outside observers, predicted would become a reality in a few years' time after the birth of monetary union. I can cite a number of reasons why the European Central Bank was able to acquire its monetary credibility as the new central bank with unprecedented speed. The law has made a significant contribution to the creation of monetary credibility. In law, the European Central Bank was well assured of its self-status, as well as that of the rest of the central bank. The power over monetary policy decisions was given entirely to the highest decision-making body of the European Central Bank, the Council, and the members of the Council were carefully protected from outside pressures. In addition, monetary policy was clearly given the primary objective of price stability. In addition to the framework established by the legislation, the careful preparation of the strategy and implementation of monetary policy also had its merit. Of course, part of the success has also been the fact that the members of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank have been able to use their self-sufficiency and discretion wisely. The European Central Bank's monetary policy strategy did not include a target level for the exchange rate of the euro. The value of the euro on international foreign exchange markets is given by the European Central Bank purely under the guidance of market forces, with the possible exception of some exceptional individual foreign exchange interventions. The rates of the other major currencies are also generally higher or higher in the same way. In conditions of floating exchange rates, even large exchange rate fluctuations are possible, ehksps vsistsmschmiskin. In the short period of its existence, the euro has also fluctuated considerably against other currencies. Its value fell since the beginning of 1999 to a low of around 85 cents in 2000. Since then, it has gradually strengthened to its current level of the dollar and 30 cents. In four years, therefore, the euro has appreciated against the US dollar by more than 50%. The pace of change, especially in recent times, can be seen as fast or, to use the adjective of Jean-Claude Trichet, president of the European Central Bank, even brutal. However, it should be noted that this has been a weakening of the dollar rather than a strengthening of the euro. Other currencies have also appreciated against the US dollar. Thus, the so-called "euro". the effective exchange rate has appreciated by more than 50 % per annum. But overall, the effective exchange rate of the euro has appreciated considerably over the years, by more than 30%. When, before monetary union was born, Finland discussed the possible pros and cons of monetary union, a great deal of attention was paid to the different structure of our economy from that of other European countries, especially those of Central and Eastern Europe, and in particular to the different structure of our foreign trade. As a small open economy, foreign trade is relatively more stable for Finland than for large countries. In addition to its exports, a large proportion, around two thirds, goes outside the euro area. In the other euro area countries, the ratio is clearly lower than the average, only around fifty per cent. In the context of finland's accession to monetary union, the single monetary and exchange rate policy was therefore considered to involve a high risk of exchange rate or price competitiveness. In particular, in the case that has since occurred, that in addition to the United Kingdom, Sweden would also be excluded from monetary union. Exchange rate risk and the possibility of restoring national competitiveness, if necessary through devaluation, were a weighty argument for many and even a decisive argument against joining monetary union in the minds of some. Due to the so-called asymmetry of the economy, the possibility of devaluing the currency was therefore considered, for reasons of competitiveness, to be an irreplaceable stockpile of our national economic policy and of our national economic policy. Personally, I don't share the sts, but I can consider it in the light of our previous history of monetary policy somewhere in the world. In this context, there are reasons to mention that, in the context of the debates on joining the monetary union, it was true that, in the debates, the relatively moderate fluctuations in exchange rates were likely to be in the opinion of all or almost all of the participants in the debate. If anyone had raised the issue of a 50% or even 30% revaluation of the single currency, this would have been seen as an epsrealistic possibility for Chys or, at most, as some kind of theoretical and worst-case scenario for the competitiveness of our industry. What is interesting about the realisation of the 'horror scenario' is that everyone seems to be very calm about it. That is, of course, absolutely right. Despite its strong appreciation, the external value of the euro is now only more or less at the 1999 level, as is Finland's price competitiveness. I would remind you that Finland joined the euro area at an exchange rate which was generally considered to be undervalued rather than overvalued. Despite the appreciation of the euro, the profitability of industry is at a good level, largely thanks to its own efforts in the past. Thus, at least from the nsks angle of Finnish companies, the appreciation of the euro is best understood as a return from the previous exceptionally low level to the normal level, not a deviation from the normal level to an exceptionally high level. There has been a lot of discussion among economists about the disadvantages and the problem of the large and small currency areas. Experience in Europe and elsewhere suggests that a large currency area and the climate of stability created by a stable monetary policy provides the vast majority of citizens and businesses with better prospects than the self-imposed monetary policy of a small individual economy, which can easily take shape under the pressure of speculation on the foreign exchange markets. As a large and strong currency, the euro offers the inhabitants of the euro area good protection against the pressures of the foreign exchange markets. Firstly, it is not as easy a target for speculative currencies from market forces as many of its predecessor currencies. But the second reason for the security of the euro is that monetary and exchange rate policy is protected not only from currency speculation, but also from the pressures of political pssching and interests. One might ask what would have happened if Finland continued to have its own currency and if the markka had strengthened to the US dollar by 50% in four years and the markka's currency index by 30%. It is never possible to get a real answer to this question. However, in the light of past experience, it is not inconceivable that we should have had a lively debate on the correction of the exchange rate of the markka in the past, and that economists and various political groups would be involved in the debate in addition to economists. It would not be impossible for attention in the debate to have been focused precisely on recent developments in the exchange rate since 2000 for purely expediency reasons. In an open economy, such a climate of debate easily leads to currency devaluations and high interest rates, and often expectations of self-feeding. Title: The euro, financial markets and entrepreneurship
text: Bank Manager Sinikka Salo: The euro, financial markets and entrepreneurship . Speech . Wednesday15 December 2004, 12:00 AM Sinikka Salo Speech at syl and ek seminar oEntrepreneurship and national competitivenesso Helsinki 15.12.2004 Ladies and gentlemen! Since the beginning of 1999, the European Central Bank has been jointly responsible for monetary policy towards price stability in the euro area as a whole. In this proposal, I will try to assess how the euro and the single monetary policy relate to entrepreneurship. The euro is part of the EU's single market programme The euro and European entrepreneurship are very closely interlinked. The dramatic political phases involved in the construction of monetary union and the intricacies of exchange rate policy in the run-up to monetary union have certainly become somewhat of an obstacle to the fact that the single currency is, after all, precisely part of the EU's single market programme. The rationale for its creation is based on the desire to build a large domestic market in Europe that would provide the best possible conditions for the entrepreneur. It is remembered how the EU Commission deliberately pushed the monetary union project forward under the symbol 'one market one money'. The importance of the single market programme, which began as early as 1992, for business is obvious. It has also been ensured, first of all, that all companies operating in the EU and EEA countries have a free passport for the entire European market: they only need a single licence, a 'single passport', as the saying goes. No one can discriminate against them. This will try to create as large, open and coherent a domestic market for European companies as possible, while this will make it more profitable to innovate and commercialise than it would be in a narrow and discriminatory market. The idea of a large common market is at the heart of the eu as a whole and, at the same time, the Union's greatest achievement in terms of business. The single market programme has many facets, such as trade policy, the setting of technical standards, the monitoring of competition policy at EU level, and so on. From my point of view, the lsheis side is, of course, the single currency, which has been created in order to make a real common market a reality. A single currency means much more than just 300 million people using the same banknotes. This means, among other things, that previously significant exchange rate risks in the euro area have disappeared; it also means that companies should continue to have a pan-European financial market guaranteeing the widest range of services at the most competitive prices; and its pitsisi means, moreover, that it would not matter for billing and the management of payment transactions whether transactions are carried out in the countries of the various countries of the euro area or within one country. The relevance of these objectives to the conditions for business activity is obvious, but they have not yet been realised. It is the case that central banks, other public authorities and private banks are consciously working to create a truly convergent monetary vyshck in the euro area. Deep and well-functioning financial markets are important for entrepreneurs, for example by improving the ability of innovative companies to finance their growth. The introduction of the euro has also improved the conditions for enterprise in Europe by creating a financially stable operating environment for enterprises. Stability and predictability are central to business planning, and a financially sound operating environment also includes stable and low interest rates. The euro's potential to create a truly Pan-European financial market has also improved. The ECB's monetary policy a success The six years that have passed since the introduction of the euro is too short a period for us to be able to make a reliable assessment of the success of monetary union and the single monetary policy. Unquestionably, however, it can be said that, in its first years, the European Central Bank's monetary policy has been more successful than hardly anyone could have anticipated or even hoped for. Despite the challenging conditions, d I refer in particular to the strong fluctuations in the prices of international economic cycles and other raw materials d the European Central Bank has managed to keep prices stable in the euro area. Interestingly, in fact, it has been possible to secure this without even having to resort to a heavy-handed monetary policy. The monetary policy of the European Central Bank is, of course, the subject of constant criticism from various quarters. We are, however, a long way from the horrors to which some, particularly outside observers d probably seriously d in the interests of d the fronts, predicted that monetary union would lead in a few years' time. The concerns were, in a way, umsrretchvisvish; the experience of numerous countries and central banks shows that monetary policy is not easy to conduct. Conducting monetary policy is particularly difficult for a new central bank that is just starting out. It was particularly challenging for the European Central Bank, which had to start operating in new and many respects, even in the pre-Russian conditions. Despite all this, the European Central Bank managed to quickly gain the confidence of the public and the markets in its monetary policy or, as economists say, to ensure the credibility of its monetary policy. The credibility of the single monetary policy will be clearly and tangible in the euro area's financial markets in the current low market interest rates and low inflation. Entrepreneurs and businesses cannot be created by means of monetary policy or other forms of central bank activity. However, through its actions, the Central Bank can support business activity and, for its part, create a favourable framework for doing business. It is now generally accepted that the Central Bank best promotes the conditions for enterprise by pursuing a long-term and consistent monetary policy and by establishing and maintaining stable monetary conditions. With regard to price stability in the euro area, the European Central Bank's monetary policy and, more generally, its efforts to build a climate of stability provide a model example of such policy. In addition, the central banks have to work to promote the smooth flow of payments, which is actually one aspect of monetary policy, broadly understood. *** In a large currency area, good points for enterprise Next, I will consider being part of the euro area d a large currency area d a little more carefully. There has been a lot of discussion among economists about the disadvantages and the problem of the large and small currency areas. The question can also be asked about the angle of enterprise. The experience of currency regions of different sizes is very varied, but on the whole they point in the direction that a large currency area can offer a longer period of time better points for enterprise than a small currency area. Firstly, the currency of a large currency area is not as easy a target for speculative currencies from market forces as many currencies in small currency areas. The second reason for the lack of speculative pressures in the case of the euro area is that the European Central Bank's monetary policy-making is better protected from pressures from political decision-making and interests than the central banks of most small currency areas. When Finland discussed its pros and cons before monetary union, a great deal of attention was paid to the structure of our economy, and in particular our foreign trade, which is different from that of other European countries. As a small, open economy, foreign trade is relatively stale for Finland than for large countries. Apart from Sith, the majority of our exports, around two thirds, go outside the euro area. In the other euro area countries, the ratio is only about half of the average. When discussing finland's accession to the monetary union, the single monetary and exchange rate policy was therefore considered to involve significant exchange rate risk. The exchange rate risk was assessed to be high, in particular in the case of d the subsequent implementation of the d case that our foreign trade, including Sweden and the United Kingdom, outside the monetary union. Due to the so-called asymmetry of the economy, the possibility of restoring national competitiveness, if necessary by devaluation, was a weighty or even decisive argument against joining monetary union, which was included in the monetary policy itself. Personally, I don't share the sts, but I can consider it in the light of our previous history of monetary policy somewhere in the world. Of course, this opportunity was lost when Finland joined the monetary union. In this context, there are reasons to mention that, in the context of the discussions on joining the monetary union, all, or almost all, of the participants in the debates were likely to see fairly moderate fluctuations in exchange rates. If anyone had raised the issue of a 50% or even 30% revaluation of the single currency, this would have been seen as an epsrealistic possibility for Chys or, at most, as some kind of theoretical and worst-case scenario for the competitiveness of our industry. During its short existence, the euro has previously fluctuated considerably against other currencies. Its value fell since the beginning of 1999 to a low of around 85 cents in 2000. Since then, it has gradually strengthened to the level of the dollar and 30 cents, and now even beyond. In four years, the euro has appreciated against the US dollar by more than 50%. Especially the recent pace of change can be fast. However, it should be noted that this has been a weakening of the dollar rather than a strengthening of the euro. Other currencies have also appreciated against the US dollar. But also the external value of the euro, that is, the so-called euro. the effective exchange rate has appreciated substantially in four years, by more than 30%. What is interesting about the realisation of the 'horror scenario' is that everyone seems to be very calm about it. That is, of course, absolutely right. Despite its strong appreciation, the external value of the euro is now only more or less at the 1999 level, as is Finland's price competitiveness. I would remind you that Finland joined the euro area at an exchange rate which was generally considered to be undervalued rather than overvalued. Despite the appreciation of the euro, the profitability of industry is at a good level, largely thanks to its own efforts in the past. Thus, at least from the nsks angle of Finnish companies, the appreciation of the euro is best understood as a return from the previous exceptionally low level to the normal level, and not as a deviation from the normal level to an exceptionally high level. One might ask what would have happened if Finland had continued to have its own currency and if the markka had strengthened to the US dollar by 50% and the markka's currency index by 30% in four years. It is never possible to get a real answer to this question. However, in the light of past experience, it is not inconceivable that we should have had a lively debate on the correction of the exchange rate of the markka in the past, and that economists and various political groups would be involved in the debate in addition to economists. It would not be impossible for attention in the debate to have been focused precisely on recent developments in the exchange rate since 2000 for purely expediency reasons. In an open economy, such a climate of debate easily leads to currency devaluations and high interest rates, and often expectations of self-feeding. In such a situation, it is difficult for the central bank to maintain a climate of stability for a very long time. The danger of continuing our long-term devaluation-inflation cycle would have been obvious; the currency would once have been allowed to be devalued in a situation where it should have been revalued. The scenario is, of course, sys hypothetical, and you can never get a clue. However, it is fair to suggest that our previous exchange rate debate and policy included a substantial dose of short-term devaluation. This policy sought to support growth and investment and was probably believed in many quarters to support enterprise as well. Tsms was a favorite vssrinkssity. The role of enterprise was used to support traditional industries in difficulty, the forest industry, and firms in difficulty, in particular large export companies. However, by shackling the functioning of the financial markets and directing scarce financial resources primarily to existing large-scale industry, the emergence and development of small and innovative enterprises were made more difficult d apparently unintentionally. Joining the euro area has significantly clarified the division of responsibilities in economic policy and, more generally, economic responsibilities. Economic policy responsibility for national price stability and competitiveness d i.e. price stability vis-a-vis the rest of the euro area and competitiveness in global markets clearly lies with fiscal and labour market policy, and not with the individual players in various entities, not with the companies. Errors in economic policy or business cannot be corrected by means of exchange rate policy in the same way as on many occasions in the past. In my opinion, most of the psschens in Finland are quite well understood. Both the public sector and companies knew how to use the incomes of the previous boom and the weak euro wisely, and inflation remained well under control. There will continue to be reasons for caution. There is now a boom in the world economy, but there is no guarantee that it will continue to be as strong as it is today. Exchange rate developments are still more difficult to predict than real GDP developments, but past experience suggests that large fluctuations in exchange rates are still possible and even probable in the future. Businesses should therefore also be prepared, among other possibilities, for the possibility that the euro will strengthen considerably in the current context. Finnish entrepreneurs have not been able to enter the euro area market. Although, in a way, our companies' domestic markets expanded in the euro area, the expansion of their home markets has not been particularly successful so far. However, exports from Finland to other countries in the euro area increased since the emergence of the euro area and peaked at around EUR 17 billion in 2001. Since then, however, annual exports to the euro area have declined and are now estimated at around EUR 14.5 billion. At the same time, exports to other countries have increased from EUR 22.5 billion to some EUR 23.5 billion. These numbers do not rule out the possibility that the euro has been adopted and exported to euro countries, possibly substantially. The effects have only masked the opposite effects of the international cyclical cycle. I believe, however, that our entrepreneurs would be able to make better use of the opportunities offered by the enlarged domestic market of the euro. Our small and medium-sized enterprises, in particular, would like to see their efforts to conquer the vast and prosperous markets of Central Europe. In spite of this, the market is unlikely to grow at the same rate as some other markets, which are geographically and culturally more distant. *** Europe-wide, truly integrated financial markets play a key role in promoting enterprise Let me now turn to the question of the importance of the use of the euro for the European financial markets. The introduction of the euro and the phytosanitary risks of the guerrillas in its region considerably calmed down the monetary conditions in Europe. This has already had its own positive impact on the integration of European financial markets. But for the time being, we are only at the beginning, and probably not even in the first place, how strong the impetus given by the single currency has been to create a truly unified financial market throughout Europe. Following the introduction of the euro, a certain part of the euro area's financial markets were integrated very rapidly; for example, the unsecured short-money market for banks now operates smoothly and uniformly throughout the euro area. Progress has also been made in other market segments. However, despite the progress made, euro area financial markets remain segmented in many respects. In the context of the integration process, there are differences between the laws (such as the Bankruptcy and Taxation Act) and the differences between the supervisory systems and administrative authorisation procedures. Financial market infrastructures, such as securities clearing houses, also operate in different ways in different countries, and it is not easy to combine them into a single whole. Some of the obstacles to the common market are of such a nature that they are fundamentally based on the passive or active defence of existing conditions. Despite the various frictions holding back market integration, I am optimistic about the integration process of the EU's financial markets. The benefits of a truly unified pan-European financial market are simply too great for us to be able to accept them. It could be said that the revitalisation of enterprise and economic dynamism is a crucial factor for Europe's rigour, competitiveness and the future development of the on-budget economy of the Member States. In turn, a well-functioning, truly Pan-European financial market plays a key role in reviving economic dynamission. The combination of the development and development of the financial markets is therefore at the heart of the EU's economic policy cooperation over the past few years. There is hardly any need to draw up a new major legislative programme. What is essential is the financial services action plan and the proper implementation of the supervisory framework. This provides an excellent example of what can be achieved through European economic policy cooperation. Without a conscious policy-sharing system, the economy of our continent is unlikely to be able to enjoy the benefits of the common, open and secure financial markets in the future. It is esimerkkins pssomasijoittajien merkitys The US financial markets are a good example of the benefits that a well-developed financial market offers to companies and businesses. Enterprise-based innovations, i.e. the commercial exploitation of inventories, have had a significant impact on the strong competitiveness of the country's economy and on its continued rapid growth. The rise of enterprise in the United States has only been largely possible thanks to active and skilled venture capitalists. Indeed, economists, business leaders and political psschens are now largely united in the view that viable investment activities are among the key factors in the country's innovation. In the same way, it is widely believed that the weakness of local investment activity is the cause of the weakness of Europe's economic dynamics. The per capita supply of at-risk alcohol in Europe has been roughly only about a fifth of that of the United States. The EU and the Member States have therefore recently paid attention to securing access to risk for small and medium-sized enterprises. Measures to increase the supply of risk hotspots in Europe are therefore welcome. However, it is worth noting that the financial markets form, in a way, a single whole and that the heyday of foreign investment activity in the United States is largely based on the functioning of other segments of the financial markets. I will mention just one example. The chances of exiting investments profitably have a significant impact on the willingness of local investors to make investments and to raise new investments. The development of private investment activities will therefore also depend on how well the financing system generates exit opportunities. The exit takes place, for example, by listing on the resin. In a small financial market, the exit possibilities are limited. This is well illustrated by a report by the Institute for Economic Development, according to which, despite the strong development in the 1990s, domestic financial markets do not meet the exit needs of local investors. According to the study, the reasons for this are, among other things, the strong cyclical nature of IPO opportunities, the volatility of the stock market and other characteristics of the domestic market. It is clear that the integration of Europe's financial and financial markets would provide significant opportunities to improve the exit possibilities of local investors and thus develop the entire portfolio investment activity. Good listeners! The Lisbon European Council in 2000 criticised the development of a strategy for the EU for the next decade of the 2000s. The main objective of the strategy is that, over the course of a decade, Europe should become the most competitive and dynamic knowledge-based economy in the world, capable of sustaining economic growth, creating new and better jobs and increasing social cohesion. The Lisbon objective is a challenging one, and it is not clear that we will succeed in achieving it. In my presentation, I have examined two cornerstones that are essential for achieving this objective, namely a sound monetary policy and a broad, well-functioning financial market. The single monetary policy and the climate of stability built by the European Central Bank have created a favourable framework for the economic development of the euro area as a whole and also of Finland. Together with the euro, they have also accelerated the emergence of well-functioning pan-European financial markets. The foundation stone of a sound monetary policy is already standing somewhat firmly in place. On the other hand, there is still a great deal of work to be done before we can talk about a truly Pan-European financial market. It will therefore take a great deal of effort to get the foundation stone in place. However, it is worth making an effort to ensure that a well-functioning financial market has an essential impact on economic development. Last but not least, I would like to stress that stable monetary conditions and well-functioning financial markets are not, of course, sufficient to solve the problems of the European economy, which have their roots outside the monetary and financial markets. The financial economy can only create the conditions for the real underpinnings of competitiveness to be d such as good level of education, innovation and diligence d to influence. Viimeisen muttei suinkaan vhisimpn asiana haluan korostaa sit, ett vakaat rahaolot ja hyvin toimivat rahoitusmarkkinat eivt tietenkn yksin riit ratkaisemaan Euroopan talouden niit ongelmia, joiden juuret ovat muualla kuin rahataloudessa ja rahoitusmarkkinoilla. Rahoitustalous voi vain luoda edellytykset sille, ett kilpailukyvyn menestyksen todelliset perustekijt  kuten hyv koulutustaso, innovatiivisuus ja ahkeruus  psevt vaikuttamaan. Menestyst voidaan ja tuleekin edist talouspolitiikan keinoin. Viime kdess menestys kuitenkin riippuu ratkaisevasti yrityksiss tehtvst tyst, siell vaikuttavasta nkemyksest ja rohkeudesta.

Wednesday1 June 2005, 12:00 AM Inflation control d European experience and implications for Russia European experience in winning inflation A remarkable feature in the economic development of the EU countries has been the con-vergence of inflation rates from a high and divergent level in the early 1980s to a consis-tently low and stable level achieved by mid-1990s and maintained thereafter. This im-provement of monetary stability must be regarded as a major achievement, especially as it has been accompanied by the virtual disappearing of chronic balance-of-payments problems which destabilized most European countries for decades. The convergence of European inflation rates was in part related to a worldwide process. In-flationary policies pursued in many European countries in the 1970s turned out to be unsuc-cessful and detrimental, especially in the context of increasing capital mobility. While Ger-many had led a relatively strict anti-inflationary monetary policy for long, a pivotal point in the reform of monetary policy was the adoption of a strict anti-inflationary monetary policy line by the Federal Reserve in the United States in the early 1980s. At the same time, the benefits of independence of central banks - la German Bundesbank d with price stability as the primary goal of monetary policy started to be increasingly recognized both in aca-demic and policy circles. Inflation of this size is harmful for any country, and it does not disappear by itself. Russia obviously has had to commit itself to combat inflation. Many countries have through their own policies and by establishing credible institutions succeeded in achieving low infla-tion. Clarifying the objectives of an independent and accountable central bank is part of the solution. Setting an explicit definition and goal for price stability is a good start.

Pienen maana hydymme eurooppalaisesta yhteistyst paljon, todennkisesti jopa enemmn kuin unionin suuret jsenmaat, jotka toisaalta uskoakseni tarvitsevat EU:ta kyll enemmn kuin usein myntvtkn. Meneilln olevat globalisaatioprosessit monessa suhteessa viel lisvt eurooppalaisen yhteistyn arvoa mys yritysmaailman kannalta. Mainitsen tss muutamia mielestni keskeisimpi esimerkkej tst. Ilmeisin esimerkki siit, miten EU auttaa suomalaisia globaalilla tasolla on EU:n kauppapoliittinen voima. Kun suomalainen elinkeinoelm tht aidosti maailmanlaajuisille markkinoille, on elintrke, ett suomalaisia tuotteita ei syrjit, vaan ne psevt niin sanotusti samalle lhtviivalle kilpailevien maiden tuotteiden kanssa. EU:n yhteinen kauppapolitiikka tyskentelee pitkseen markkinat avoimena mys suomalaiselle elinkeinoelmlle koko sill voimalla, mik EU:lla suurena kauppamahtina maailmassa on. Jonkinlainen paradoksi on, ett mit enemmn Suomen vienti suuntautuu EU:n ulkopuolelle, sit keskeisemmksi EU:n yhteinen kauppapolitiikka ja siten EU:n komission toiminta kannaltamme muodostuu. Toinen ja suomalaiselle elinkeinoelmlle yht trke eurooppalaisen yhteistyn muoto on sismarkkinat, jotka perustettiin vuonna 1992. Tllinhn tuli voimaan se yleisperiaate, ett tuotetta, joka on markkinoilla yhdess maassa, ei saa syrji muissakaan jsenmaissa. Varsinkin PK-yritysten kasvumahdollisuuksien kannalta on aivan valtava saavutus, kun nin luotiin nyt yli 450 miljoonan asukkaan yhteninen kotimarkkina-alue, jolla kaikkinainen syrjint on mrtietoisesti koetettu lopettaa ja on luotu "tasainen pelikentt". Kolmas eurooppalaisen integraation muoto, joka tukee suomalaisten toimintaa globaalilla tasolla, on yhteinen valuutta, euro. Ennen rahaliiton perustamista monet Euroopan maat, mys Suomi, krsivt kroonisesta rahataloudellisesta epvakaudesta. Maastrichtin sopimuksella luotu rahapoliittinen jrjestelm, joka koostuu yhteisest rahasta ja sit hallinnoivasta itsenisest ja uskottavasta keskuspankkijrjestelmst, on onnistunut rakentamaan koko euroalueelle historiallisesti poikkeuksellisen rahataloudellisen vakauden. Suomessa tm nkyy muun muassa ennennkemttmn matalana ja vakaana korkotasona ja lainapoman saatavuuden helpottumisena. Tm on globaalistikin katsoen merkittv kilpailutekij. Merkillepantavaa muuten on, ett juuri nill alueilla, joissa EU-integraatiosta saatu hyty on ollut suurin, keskeinen politiikan muotoilun rooli on unionitason toimielimill: komissio vastaa yhteisest kauppapolitiikasta ja sismarkkinoista, ja EKP yhdess kansallisten keskuspankkien kanssa yhteisest rahapolitiikasta. EU:n integraation suurin voima onkin ilmeisesti juuri sen ylikansallisissa instituutioissa, ja niihin perustuvat sen suurimmat menestykset. Kuten EU:n perustajiin kuulunut Jean Monnet sanoi: Ilman ihmisi mikn ei ole mahdollista, ilman instituutioita, mikn ei ole pysyv." Mutta instituutioita ei ole ilman sit poliittista tahtoa, joka perustaa ne ja antaa niille niiden tarvitseman legitiimisyyden. Henkilkohtaisesti uskon, ett nimenomaan EU:n yhteisten instituutioiden vahvistaminen on tehokkain tie Euroopan taloudelliseen ja muuhunkin edistykseen. *** Mutta palataan euroon, sill jos integraatioprosessissa yleisemmll tasolla tulisikin jonkinlainen vlisoitto, euro ja EKP:n yhteinen rahapolitiikka silyy luotettavana ja ty mm. rahoitusmarkkinoiden integroimiseksi jatkuu. Nm kysymykset ovat erityisen trkeit mys naisten kannalta. Yhteinen rahamme euro ja eurooppalaisen yrittjyyden toimintaymprist kytkeytyvt erittin tiiviisti yhteen. Yhteinen raha on osa EU:n yhteismarkkinaohjelmaa, jonka pyrkimyksen on rakentaa Eurooppaan laajat kotimarkkinat, jotka antaisivat yrittmiselle parhaat mahdolliset edellytykset. Avoimilla ja laajoilla yhteismarkkinoilla innovaatioiden tekeminen ja tuotteistaminen on kannattavampaa kuin mit se olisi suppeilla ja syrjivill kansallisilla markkinoilla. Ajatus laajoista yhteismarkkinoista on koko EU:n ydin ja samalla  kuten edell totesin  unionin suurin saavutus yritystoiminnan kannalta. Keskeinen merkitys tss on yhteisell rahalla, jonka kyttnoton seurauksena aikaisemmin merkittvt valuuttakurssiriskit poistuivat ja valuutanvaihtokulut jivt pois euroalueen sisisiss taloustoimissa. Nin luotiin pohja todellisten yhteismarkkinoiden toiminnalle. Muistakaamme, ett EU:n komissio ajoi rahaliittohanketta mrtietoisesti eteenpin tunnuksen "yhdet markkinat  yksi raha" alla. Mutta tyt on edelleen tehtv -yhteismarkkinat eivt viel toimi tydellisin. Viel emme saa hydynnetty kaikkia niit potentiaalisia hytyj, joita EU:n laajuiset, hyvin toimivat kotimarkkinat tarjoavat etenkin pienille ja keskisuurille yrityksille, joita naisten yritykset tyypillisesti ovat. Kuten edell totesin, euron kyttnotto rauhoitti tuntuvasti Euroopan rahaoloja. Tll vakaudella on jo ollut oma mynteinen vaikutuksensa Euroopan rahoitusmarkkinoiden yhdentymiseen. Yhteisen valuutan myt olemme lhempn tavoitetta, ett yritysten ja sijoittajien kytss olisivat Euroopan laajuiset rahoitusmarkkinat, jotka takaisivat kansalaisille ja yrityksille laajimmat palvelut kilpailukykyisimpiin hintoihin, ja joilla laskuttamisen ja maksuliikenteen hoidon kannalta ei pitisi olla merkityst, asioidaanko euroalueen eri maiden vlill vai yhden maan sisll. Niden tavoitteiden merkitys mm. suomalaisen yritystoiminnan edellytysten kannalta on ilmeinen, mutta nm tavoitteet eivt ole viel tysin toteutuneet. Euron kyttnoton jlkeen tietty osa euroalueen rahoitusmarkkinoista integroitui erittin nopeasti lhes tysin; esimerkiksi pankkien vliset vakuudettomat lyhyen rahan markkinat toimivat nykyisin kitkatta ja yhtenisesti koko euroalueella. Edistyst on tapahtunut muillakin markkinalohkoilla. Saavutetuista edistysaskeleista huolimatta euroalueen rahoitusmarkkinat ovat kuitenkin edelleen monessa suhteessa lohkoutuneet. Yhdentymiskehityksen tiell ovat erilaiset lainsdntn liittyvt erot sek valvontajrjestelmien ja hallinnollisten lupamenettelyjen erot. Rahoitusmarkkinoiden perusrakenteet kuten arvopapereiden selvityskeskukset toimivat mys eri maissa eri tavoin, eik niit ole helppo yhdist yhdeksi kokonaisuudeksi. Osa yhteisten markkinoiden esteist on luonteeltaan sellaisia, ett ne pohjimmiltaan perustuvat olemassa olevien olojen lyhytnkiseen puolustamiseen. Markkinoiden yhdentymist jarruttavista eri kitkatekijist huolimatta olen optimistinen EU:n rahoitusmarkkinoiden yhdentymiskehityksen suhteen. Edut aidosti yhtenisist Euroopan laajuisista rahoitusmarkkinoista yksinkertaisesti ovat liian suuret, jotta voisimme jtt ne hydyntmtt. Rahoitusmarkkinoiden kehittmisty ja stelyn yhtenistminen onkin EU:n talouspoliittisessa yhteistyss keskeisell sijalla lhivuosina. Oleellista on pttymss olevaan rahoituspalvelujen toimintasuunnitelmaan (Financial Services Action Plan  FSAP) sisltyvn rahoitusmarkkinalainsdnnn ja valvontakehikon kunnollinen toimeenpano. Jatkossa tavoitteena on mys toteuttaa vuoteen 2010 menness tysin yhteninen eurooppalainen maksualue (Single European payments area, SEPA) nykyisen pirstoutuneen maksujrjestelmrakenteen sijaan. Sill, ett maksusuoritukset kulkevat vaivattomasti ja kohtuuhintaisesti yli rajojen, on suuri merkitys esimerkiksi matkailun kannalta. Matkailun alueella toimivat yritykset ovat pieni, mutta monilla niist on markkinointikontakteja laajalti Manner-Euroopassa. Esimerkiksi Lapin matkailumarkkinat ovat jo integroituneet osaksi laajempia, Euroopan sismarkkinoita, euroalueen markkinoita. Asiakkaan kannalta maiden vliset raja-aidat madaltuvat, kun maksuliike rajan yli helpottuu. Hinnan noteeraaminen kotoisessa eurovaluutassa koko laajalla alueella, jossa asuu yli 300 miljoonaa ihmist, on tehostanut toimintaa olennaisesti ja kynnys tulla Suomeen on madaltunut. Rahoitusmarkkinoiden integraatioon liittyv tykentt tarjoaa erinomaisen esimerkin niist hydyist, joita mrtietoisella eurooppalaisella yhteistyll voidaan saavuttaa. On trke, ett nm kysymykset silyvt poliittisella agendalla. Euroopan laajuisten, hyvin toimivien rahoitusmarkkinoiden muodostumisen puolesta kannattaa ponnistella, sill  kuten edell olen pyrkinyt selostamaan  hyvin toimivilla rahoitusmarkkinoilla on yrittjyyteen ja Euroopan koko talouskehitykseen oleellinen, mynteinen vaikutus. Tllaisilla markkinoilla mys vaurastuvilla naisilla on enemmn mahdollisuuksia. Esimerkiksi Suomessa naisten osuus veronalaisesta varallisuudesta on kasvanut ja oli vuonna 2003 jo yli 40 %, pomatuloista naisten osuus on noin kolmannes, eli naisilla on mys lisntyvsti vaikutusvaltaa sijoitustensa kautta. Naisille puhuessani en malta olla pohdiskelematta, mikseivt naiset kyttisi tt omistajan valtaansa mys naiskasvoisemman talouselmn edistmiseksi. Naisethan voisivat esimerkiksi sijoittaa vain sellaisten yritysten osakkeisiin, joiden johtoelimiss on mys naisia. Tllaisen painostuskeinonhan raha tarjoaa. Luin skettin ern ruotsalaisen sijoitusrahaston johtajan  mieshenkiln  lausunnon rahastonsa sijoituspolitiikasta: he eivt sijoita yhtiihin, joiden hallituksissa ei ole yhtn naista. Vaikka naapurimaamme tunnetusti lienee meit tasa-arvo.mynteisempi, en usko tllaista tapahtuvan vain tasa-arvon vuoksi, vaan koska naiset ovat Ruotsissakin merkittv ja valistunut sijoittajaryhm. Tiedn, ett meillkin valistuneet talouselmn johtajat pyrkivt jo tmnkin vuoksi toimimaan naiskasvoisemman talouselmn puolesta. Arvoisat naiset! Olen tss puheenvuorossani pyrkinyt tuomaan esille esimerkkej niist talouspoliittisista kysymyksist, joiden olen arvioinut erityisesti innostavan naisia osallistumaan talouspoliittiseen keskusteluun ja ptksentekoon ja nkemn ne parantuneet mahdollisuudet, joita naisille on tarjolla. Kuten sanoin, ikntyvss Euroopassa  Suomi mukaan lukien  naisten panosta ei ole varaa jtt kyttmtt. Tmn tulisi rohkaista naisia aktivoitumaan viel enemmn. Naisten hyv koulutus ja tysipainoinen osallistuminen tyelmn, mist olemme tll Suomessa saaneet pohjoismainen hyvinvointivaltiomallimme tukemana nauttia, on edellytys mys tyelmn tasa-arvoisemmalle kulttuurille ja tukee siten mys tasa-arvoisempaa ja monipuolisempaa johtamis-ja keskustelukulttuuria kaikilla elmn aloilla. Koulutus ja laaja osallistuminen tyelmn on mielestni vlttmtn ehto sille ett naiset saavat enemmn poliittista ja taloudellista valtaa: Mys pttjin ja johtavassa asemassa olevien naisten asema liittyy kaikkien naisten asemaan yhteiskunnassa. Mutta hyv koulutus ja korkea tysskyntiaste ei ole riittv ehto, vaikka aiemmin niin ajateltiin. Monet selvitykset viittaavat jopa siihen, ett naiset korkeammasta koulutuksestaan huolimatta kokevat typaikkansa ja uramahdollisuutensa aikaisempaa eptasa-arvoisemmaksi. Tm ilmenee mys professori Sinikka Vanhalan tutkimuksissa, joissa hn raportoi naisten pettymyksist uransa ja vaikutusmahdollisuuksiensa suhteen. Hn toteaa: Vielkn ei selvsti nhd miten vahvasti tyelmss pelataan miesten pelisnnill. Mit ylemms mennn, sit tiukemmin eletn miesten luomassa kulttuurissa". Tmn kulttuurin murtamiseksi  mys talouspolitiikassa  tarvitaan vahvoja ja persoonallisia naisia, jotka panevat paljon peliin kulttuurin muuttamiseksi moniarvoisemmaksi. Toivotan teille rohkeutta ja intomielt. Siin miten Suomi rakentaa strategiansa globaalistuvassa ja integroituvassa maailmassa ei ole varaa jtt naisten ideoita kuulematta ja luovuutta hydyntmtt.
