ECONOMY NdbKYMdbT ? MILLdb FINLAND PdbRJdbdb? Good listeners! The world economy has developed quite favourably in recent years. Last year, total world production increased by about five per cent, and according to forecasts, growth will not slow down significantly in the year. Although growth is rapid, partly for cyclical reasons, it is not just a question of the most momentary upturn. The growth trend in world GDP has been picking up since the 1970s and is currently estimated to be around four per cent per annum. The long-term rapid growth of the global economy is largely due to two factors. In recent years, a great deal of new production technology has been introduced in both developed and developing countries. It has made production methods more efficient and created entirely new products. At the same time, the introduction of new technologies has essentially diminished the importance of geographical and cultural ethiss with the central states and peoples. The shrinking of ethisities is particularly evident in the production and transmission of information or information, and telecommunications form the dynamic core of the new technology. Influences and knowledge spread more quickly everywhere and reach a greater proportion of the world's people. Another major reason for the rapid growth of the world economy is the change in the direction of economic policy in a number of countries that had previously closed down. The countries have abandoned their growth strategies and opened up more and more to international trade and central co-employment. The opening-up will not only apply to international trade in industrial products. There has also been an increase in the mobility of other hy?dys, as well as in terms of technology, technology and workplaces worldwide. Indeed, world trade has grown faster than GDP, at an annual rate of between 5% and 10% in recent years. The development of production technology and the change in economic policy are not independent of each other. The reduction of barriers to the flow of information as a result of new technologies has made a significant contribution to the opening up and democratisation of economies and societies, both in Central and Eastern Europe and elsewhere. Technological advances have therefore not led to a society controlled by the 'big brother' as George Orwell once did, but rather to the contrary: centralised control of use and information has become more difficult than before. In addition to technological progress and the opening up of economies, the geographical location of enterprises has become more important and will continue to do so, and with the liberalisation of world trade, the home market hype given to companies by large sizes of land will decrease. For a small and well-located Finland, the changes seem to open up new opportunities. Finland is therefore in a position to compete in the international competition. One of the reasons for my optimism is that we have been doing well in the past, and that the favourable development of total production and prosperity in the last hundred or one hundred and fifty years is clear. The prerequisite, however, is that we continue to succeed in exchanging international trades in a competitive manner and specialising in it, where we are better than others. An integral part of the increase in production is the change in the structure of production. In the context of industrialization, the power of labour shifted from agriculture to industry. Finland and other long-term developed countries are now undergoing a new structural change, in which production is moving from manufacturing to manufacturing industrial products to high-productivity services. Low-productivity industrial sites and, increasingly, services are moving to countries with low cost levels, which are only just beginning their own industrialization. China-ilmi? affects all industries and there is no protection from high-tech sectors. As I have already said, knowledge and influences are spreading more quickly and more widely, and one of the peculiarities of the new technology is that it is relatively easy to transfer it to countries that are also developing. *** Regional integration is an essential part of the globalisation process. Although the European Union may well have been rooted in the post-war effort to ensure that peace is maintained in Europe, the EU has evolved more clearly over time as a response to the challenges of globalisation for European countries. Throughout its history, EU integration has ? despite occasional difficulties ? deepened and expanded, and this development continues. It is fair to say that, in a globalised and unstable global economy, the euro area and other EU countries are now economically stronger than they were before economic and monetary union. Economic and monetary union has proved to be an important stabiliser of economic development. In particular, the countries in the euro area whose monetary policy before monetary union was weak in terms of credibility have been particularly hy?tyjin?. Even in Finland, we have not been able to enjoy such a balanced financial market for decades as in recent years. N?in has been in spite of the extensive external h?iri?ist. The consequences of the War in Iraq or the sharp rise in the price of ?ljy on the European financial markets could have been quite turbulent under the conditions of separate currencies. Now the situation on the money markets has remained well under control all the time. This does not mean that there will be no reforms in Europe. In 2000, EU leaders agreed on a strategy for economic reforms, the so-called economic reform strategy. On the Lisbon Strategy. This strategy was reformed and the year before last, inter alia, so that ownership of the reforms ? i.e. the responsibility for planning and implementing them more clearly falls on the Member States. According to the Lisbon strategy, Europe should become the most competitive and dynamic knowledge-based economy in the world over the course of a decade, capable of sustaining economic growth, creating new and better jobs and increasing social cohesion. While the strategy aims at a dynamic economy based on knowledge and technology, structural change is being pursued in a single European model of society with an emphasis on social cohesion. Improving employment and improving the level of cohesion in economic dynamism and social cohesion and improving cohesion are central to economic dynamism. In a secure economic and political environment, it is necessary to strengthen those factors that promote trust and vision. In fact, there is no other way than to implement commonly agreed strategies and programmes in a conscious manner. Europe's difficulties have not been due to the fact that there is not really a long-term effort to accelerate economic growth. The objectives have been set out quite clearly in various quarters, most comprehensively in the Lisbon Strategy and, in particular, in the new national reform programmes, which were drawn up for the first time last year. The difficulty has been the ability to implement reforms to achieve the objectives. One of the main objectives of the reform of the Lisbon strategy was to improve the implementation of reforms. In recent years, at least some degrees of progress has begun to be made, which has also been the case with the recent acceleration of economic growth in the EU and the euro area. The Lisbon strategy has paid particular attention to the integration of financial markets. Structural changes in financial markets are generally rather slow. However, the last ten years have seen major changes in European financial markets. The introduction of the euro at the beginning of 1999 brought together the euro area's money markets and gave a significant impetus to the integration process of other segments of the financial markets. For the first time ever, the euro has also opened up the possibility of creating a deep and continental financial market. The integration of financial markets will promote competition in the financial markets and technical development, as well as broadening and deepening the financing process. Through this, it will enhance the efficiency of the production and strengthen the growth potential of real GDP. On the other hand, efficient and high-performance financial markets also support growth by improving the allocation of p??oms and lowering the cost of p??oma. Well-functioning financial markets enhance structural change by channelling economic resources from low-productivity sectors and firms to high-productivity sectors and firms. They also provide funding to accelerate the growth of the company's productivity and investment. It is often an investment in machinery and equipment, but more and more productivity is boosted by innovation and other intangible investments. The creation of deep and well-functioning financial markets in the euro area is a key effort to provide European companies with the widest, most open and coherent domestic markets possible. It is clear that, without a single financial market, the common market for services and goods cannot function optimally and companies can not refine their innovations and productise them in the best possible way. In other words, the whole idea of the guerrilla market will be halfway through, unless there is liquidity in Europe, deep financial markets. One area of the financial markets that needs to be developed in Europe is venture capital markets, where private and institutional investors finance non-cash companies on their own terms. The development of the venture capital markets is particularly important for innovative SMEs, and thus also for the emergence of new jobs. Starting a new technology business or implementing a major innovation project invariably requires external funding. The development of the pan-European risk finance market is particularly important in the case of companies, which are in principle large enough to attract the interest of foreign investors, but are so small that the marketing of shares abroad has, until then, been too expensive for the scale of their activities. The US financial markets are a good example of the benefits that a well-developed venture capital market offers to companies and entrepreneurs. Enterprise-based innovations, i.e. the commercial exploitation of inventories, have had a significant impact on the strong competitiveness of the country's economy and on its continued rapid growth. Economists, business leaders and political p??chens are now widely agreed that viable investment is one of the key factors in the country's innovation. In the same way, it is widely believed that the weakness of local investment activity is one of the causes of the weakness of Europe's economic dynamics. The per capita supply of at-risk alcohol in Europe has been roughly only about a fifth of that of the United States. The EU and the Member States have therefore recently paid attention to securing access to risk for small and medium-sized enterprises. The development of European financial markets also requires a new infrastructure, such as cross-border payment and settlement systems. I would cite the example of the Single European Payment Area (SEPA) project. SEPA's aim is to create a single payment area in Europe, where cross-border payment of euro-????ide payments in the EU is as easy, secure and fast as the payment of national contributions is at present. The project started in 2004 and is m??r? to get a p??chksis? in 2010. The first SEPA payment instruments are due to be introduced as early as next year. Building new markets and systems covering the whole of the euro area or even the whole of the EU requires considerable costs and is not easy anyway. In many cases, national and institutional conflicts of interest, for which there are no easy solutions available to all parties, are satisfactory to all parties. This is particularly the case in cases where economies of scale are considerable and the 'natural' solution would be to limit the number of operators to one. Because of conflicts of interest, the achievable longer-term hy?ddies are put in the background, but over time they are of a completely different order of magnitude than the costs. *** Good listeners! I have talked for quite a long time about the development of European financial markets. Despite the different pain points, the promotion of financial market integration is high on the agendas of the various European institutions. It is also one of the objectives of the Bank of Finland and the euro system as a whole, i.e. the European Central Bank and the national central banks of the euro area. A great deal of work has been done and is constantly being done across the board to break down the barriers to the integration of European financial markets. This is often completely hidden from the public eye. In spite of the Yhzchym?tchmyydest?, it is ?rke??. According to a number of seemingly realistic estimates, gdp in the euro area could be increased by as much as several per cent a year by up to several percentage points ? i.e. up to tenths of a per cent a year - if the barriers to financial integration could be completely removed. I believe that these estimates give a reasonably good picture of the economic importance of well-functioning and deep financial markets in Europe. *** Finland's survival strategy challenges? What about Finland's own efforts? It is quite obvious to us Finns that we have become very nervous about globalisation, and the EU and EMU also give us a solid foundation from which to build in the future. The Finnish social model can be described as a model that combines global IT know-how with an equal, networked (efficient) welfare state that acts as a factor that strengthens competitiveness. Until then, it has been very successful ? by many measures. But can it be in a globalised world? In my estimation, it can, but Finland naturally faces many challenges, of which I would like to highlight two of the most important ones: Firstly, the challenge is to integrate the information society and the welfare state into an efficient infrastructure. Although there is broad consensus on the objective of developing the information society, not enough has been done. The widespread application of information technology in society is still in its infancy or semi-final. After all, the aim is a knowledge-based form of production in all areas of society and the economy ? not just in the IT sector. A particular challenge is to resolve the conflict between outdated administrative structures and the information society. Although the combined expertise in information technology and well-being at the sites should be good, and although the use of information technology for welfare purposes in education, health care and social services is very advanced, their implementation is slow due to cumbersome organisations. Dynamism, awareness and commitment are needed. This is very challenging for the public sector, especially for the municipalities: the successes of Finnish society over the decades can be measured for quite a long time how the public sector copes with the challenges, i.e. how much the principles of the Nordic welfare state model, which enjoys great support, reasonable taxation that encourages work, and the good competitiveness of the economy can be measured. An efficient infrastructure linking the information society and the welfare state will contribute to the use of all resources, bring equality and security, and will also increase the competitiveness of enterprises and quality in general. Another challenge I would like to highlight is education and learning multicultural dialogue. The most important aspect of Finland's future membership is education. Finland has performed well in various educational comparisons. For example, a lot of attention has been paid to the results of the extensive international PISA survey, according to which Finnish comprehensive school pupils have excelled in reading and other competences. However, education alone is not enough, but a strong cultural, humanistic element must be included. From the North and Europe, finns have to survive in very different cultures. It is not only necessary to know how to trade, but also to be able to engage in genuine dialogue between cultures. We need to develop our cultural capacities ? learn how to live and work in a multicultural environment ? learn how to receive migrants. This is a major change of attitude. *** The importance of women-women entrepreneurship for the national economy? At the event, I was also asked to reflect on the importance of female entrepreneurship to the national economy. What is the role of women in the economic development of Finland and the EU as a whole? The question is easy to answer: absolutely crucial. The economic growth that is needed to increase and increase our well-being is generated by the contribution to the ? work??r?? and productivity ? how well and efficiently we produce goods or services. In a greying Europe, the growth of stubble is fading. It is estimated that the total production of the EU countries is growing at an average rate of up to one per cent slower than in the United States in the autumn alone, that in the old continent there will be no increase in the number of people working in the old continent, while in the United States it will not increase in the form of migrants, among other things. In terms of productivity, too, we have not succeeded in the opportunities offered by information technology, for example. Although Finland has so far had the best performance in the EU and in Europe as a whole, we cannot afford to be complacent. I spoke earlier about the Lisbon Strategy and its ambitions. It is clear that the economic growth needed to achieve prosperity cannot be achieved in Europe unless more women are recruited and employed. The key message is that Europe and the European form of life, prosperity and solidarity ? and the competitiveness and sufficient economic growth needed to maintain it depend on women. If, after ? more than 2000 years, it is finally necessary to heed the observation of the early European philosopher Plato that a state is not good if half of its talent is used. The target for the participation rate under the Lisbon strategy is 70% by 2010, while for women the target is 60%. N?it? goals can be considered modest from the Finnish n?k? angle, but there is also a lot of work to be done in them. In the EU and the euro area, the employment rate as a whole was just under 64% in 2005, while the employment rate for women was between 55% and 56%. N???k's figures show the potential in women when considering ways to increase the participation rate of women. In order to get women to work and stay in the workplace, there is a need for infrastructure ? including places for care and old people's homes ? which supports the reconciliation of work and the family. However, it has not been possible to provide sufficient services with private funds alone, and a public subventiota. This is the order for an effective Nordic welfare state model, i.e. a model characterised by publicly funded services supporting the reconciliation of merit and family life. It is no coincidence that the participation rate of women is at a high level in the Nordic countries, and at its lowest in countries where, for example, places for treatment have not been publicly funded. The recent increase in the participation rate of women in the countries has come at the expense of the fall in the birth rate. In Italy and Spain, for example, the birth rate has plummeted. The Nordic countries are the best in the world. We women haven't had to make a choice between a career and a family ? has been able to get both! The above-mentioned objective of increasing participation in the EU labour market would mean the creation of around 21 million new jobs in the EU by 2010. It is clear that the t?ysim???ninen of women's talent is also an attempt to be revived in Europe. Women entrepreneurs make up only about 27% of the average number of entrepreneurs in the EU. In Finland, the ratio is slightly higher, around one third. There is a need for new businesses and jobs, especially in the service sector, where women have high skills and in traditional and business sectors. Among other things, the need for more efficient public services, which I examined above, which involves, among other things, outsourcing services to services ordered from private providers and, in general, the demand for care services, offer good opportunities to become entrepreneurs. Many examples also show that women entrepreneurs have been able to build successful industries that have not been customary as long-term promising industries in modern Europe. *** Good listeners! Good businesswomen! The single monetary policy and the climate of stability built up by the European Central Bank have created a favourable framework for enterprise in the euro area as a whole. They have also accelerated the emergence of a pan-European, well-functioning financial market with the euro, but there is still a great deal of work to be done in the region before we can talk about a truly Pan-European financial market. However, it is worth the effort to achieve this objective, since, as I have tried to explain above, a well-functioning financial market has a fundamental mycultural impact on enterprise and on economic development as a whole. However, I would like to stress that the monetary economy or the means of economic policy in general can only create the conditions for the real foundations of successful business activity ? so that innovation, enterprise and diligence can be influenced. Of course, companies and entrepreneurs themselves play a key role. Increasing competition in an expanding market creates problems for those companies that are unable to offer quality that stands out from the rest. On the other hand, the opening up of markets offers great opportunities for those entrepreneurs who are able to take the initiative to take the initiative in terms of high potential demand from the euro area and the eu's internal market as a whole. Ladies and gentlemen, celebrated businesswomen! Quality, interaction skills and cultural understanding, innovation and courage to take risks are needed. The future for brave women is therefore good!

Talous-ja rahaliitto on osoittautunut merkittvksi taloudellisen kehityksen vakauttajaksi. Hytyjin ovat olleet varsinkin ne euroalueen maat, joiden rahapolitiikka ennen rahaliittoa krsi heikosta uskottavuudesta. Suomessakaan ei ole vuosikymmeniin saatu nauttia niin tasapainoisista rahoitusmarkkinoista kuin viime vuosina. Nin on kynyt mittavista ulkoisista hiriist huolimatta. Irakin sodan tai ljyn hinnan jyrkn nousun kaltaisten hiriiden seuraukset eurooppalaisilla rahamarkkinoilla olisivat saattaneet olla erillisten valuuttojen oloissa varsin turbulentteja. Nyt tilanne rahamarkkinoilla on pysynyt koko ajan hyvin hallinnassa. Tm ei suinkaan merkitse, etteik Euroopassa pitisi tehd uudistuksia. EU-maiden johtajat sopivat vuonna 2000 talousuudistusten strategiasta, ns. Lissabonin strategiasta. Tt strategiaa uudistettiin ja tervitettiin toissa vuonna mm. siten, ett uudistusten omistajuus  siis vastuu niiden suunnittelusta ja toteuttamisesta  lankeaa entist selvemmin jsenmaille. Lissabonin strategian mukaan Euroopasta tulisi tulla tmn vuosikymmenen aikana maailman kilpailukykyisin ja dynaamisin tietopohjainen talous, joka kykenee yllpitmn kestv talouskasvua, luomaan uusia ja parempia typaikkoja ja lismn sosiaalista yhteenkuuluvuutta. Samalla kun strategialla tavoitellaan dynaamista, tiedon ja teknologian hydyntmiseen perustuvaa taloutta, rakennemuutos tahdotaan yhdist eurooppalaiseen, sosiaalista yhteenkuuluvuutta painottavaan yhteiskuntamalliin. Sek talouden dynamiikan ett sosiaalisen yhteenkuuluvuuden kannalta keskeiseksi nhdn tyllisyyden parantaminen ja syrjytymisen ehkiseminen. Epvarmoissa taloudellisissa ja poliittisissa oloissa on trke vahvistaa niit tekijit, jotka edistvt luottamusta ja visiota. Tss oikeastaan ei ole muuta keinoa kuin toteuttaa yhteisesti sovittuja strategioita ja ohjelmia mrtietoisesti eteenpin. Euroopan vaikeudet eivt ole johtuneet siit, ettei tiedet mit talouskasvun nopeuttamiseksi oikeastaan pitisi tehd. Tavoitteet on esitetty varsin selkesti eri tahoilla, kattavimmin juuri Lissabonin strategiassa ja etenkin uusissa, viime vuonna ensimmist kertaa laadituissa kansallisissa uudistusohjelmissa. Vaikeutena on ollut kyvyttmyys toteuttaa tavoitteiden saavuttamiseksi vlttmttmi uudistuksia. Lissabonin strategian uudistuksen yksi keskeisist tavoitteista oli kohentaa uudistusten toteuttamista. Ehk viime vuosina tss on vhitellen alettu saavuttaa ainakin jonkin asteista edistyst, mik on saattanut nky mys EU:n ja euroalueen talouskasvun viimeaikaisena nopeutumisena. Lissabonin strategiassa on kiinnitetty erityist huomiota rahoitusmarkkinoiden integraatioon. Rahoitusmarkkinoiden rakenteelliset muutokset tapahtuvat yleens varsin hitaasti. Viimeisen kymmenen vuoden aikana Euroopan rahoitusmarkkinoilla on kuitenkin koettu suuria muutoksia. Euron kyttnotto vuoden 1999 alussa yhtenisti euroalueen rahamarkkinat ja antoi merkittvn sysyksen mys rahoitusmarkkinoiden muiden lohkojen integraatiokehitykselle. Euron myt Euroopalle on  ehk ensimmisen kerran  avautunut mahdollisuus luoda syvt ja lhes koko mantereen kattavat rahoitusmarkkinat. Rahoitusmarkkinoiden yhdentyminen edist rahoitusmarkkinoiden kilpailua ja teknist kehityst sek laajentaa ja syvent rahoituksen vlityst. Tt kautta se tehostaa pomien kytt ja vahvistaa kokonaistuotannon kasvupotentiaalia. Toisaalta tehokkaat ja lpinkyvt rahoitusmarkkinat tukevat kasvua mys parantamalla pomien kohdentumista ja alentamalla pomakustannuksia. Hyvin toimivat rahoitusmarkkinat tehostavat rakennemuutosta kanavoimalla talouden voimavaroja alhaisen tuottavuuden toimialoilta ja yrityksilt korkean tuottavuuden toimialoille ja yrityksille. Ne mys vlittvt rahoitusta yrityksen tuottavuuden kasvun nopeuttamiseen thtviin investointeihin. Nm ovat usein investointeja koneisiin ja laitteisiin, mutta enenevsti tuottavuutta kohotetaan innovaatioilla ja muilla aineettomilla investoinneilla. Syvien ja hyvin toimivien rahoitusmarkkinoiden luominen euroalueelle on keskeist pyrittess tarjoamaan eurooppalaisille yrityksille mahdollisimman laajat, avoimet ja yhteniset kotimarkkinat. On selv, ett ilman yhtenisi, rajattomia rahoitusmarkkinoita yhteiset markkinat palveluksille ja tavaroille eivt voi toimia optimaalisesti eivtk yritykset pse hydyntmn innovaatioitaan ja tuotteistamaan niit parhaalla mahdollisella tavalla. Toisin sanoen koko sismarkkinoiden idea j puolitiehen, ellei Eurooppaan saada likvidej, syvi rahoitusmarkkinoita. Yksi Euroopassa kehittmist kaipaava rahoitusmarkkinalohko on riskirahoitusmarkkinat, joilla yksityiset ja institutionaaliset pomasijoittajat rahoittavat oman poman ehdoin muita kuin prssiyrityksi. Riskirahoitusmarkkinoiden kehittminen on trket erityisesti innovatiivisille PK -yrityksille, ja siten mys uusien typaikkojen synnylle. Uuden teknologiayrityksen aloittaminen tai merkittvn innovaatiohankeen toteuttaminen vaatii lhes poikkeuksetta ulkoista rahoitusta. Erityisen paljon voitettavaa Euroopan laajuisten riskirahoitusmarkkinoiden kehittmisest on niill yhtiill, jotka ovat periaatteessa kyllin suuria herttkseen ulkomaisten sijoittajien kiinnostusta, mutta kuitenkin sen verran pieni, ett osakkeiden markkinointi ulkomaille on thn asti ollut niiden toiminnan laajuuteen nhden liian kallista. Yhdysvaltain rahoitusmarkkinat tarjoavat hyvn esimerkin eduista, joita hyvin kehittyneet riskirahoitusmarkkinat tarjoavat yrityksille ja yrittjyydelle. Yrittjyyteen perustuvilla yhtiill ja niden toteuttamilla innovaatioilla eli keksintjen kaupallisella hydyntmisell on ollut huomattava vaikutus maan talouden vahvaan kilpailukykyyn ja jatkuvasti nopeaan kasvuun. Ekonomistit, yritysjohtajat ja poliittiset ptksentekijt ovat nykyisin laajalti yht mielt siit, ett elinvoimainen pomasijoitustoiminta on maan innovatiivisuuden trkeimpi avaintekijit. Samalla tavoin uskotaan laajalti, ett pomasijoitustoiminnan heikkous on Euroopan talousdynamiikan heikkouden yksi trke syy. Riskipoman tarjonta asukasta kohden on ollut Euroopassa karkeasti ottaen vain noin viidennes Yhdysvaltain tasosta. EU ja jsenvaltiot ovatkin pyrkineet viime aikoina kiinnittmn huomiota pienten ja keskisuurten yritysten riskipoman saatavuuden turvaamiseen. Euroopan rahoitusmarkkinoiden kehittminen edellytt mys uutta perusrakennetta, kuten rajojen ylitse toimivia maksu-ja selvitysjrjestelmi. Mainitsisin tss yhteydess esimerkkin SEPA-eli Single European Payment Area .hankkeen. SEPAn tavoitteena on luoda Eurooppaan yhteninen maksualue, jossa euromristen maksujen maksaminen EU:ssa yli rajojen on yht helppoa, varmaa ja nopeaa kuin kansallisten maksujen maksaminen nykyisin. Hanke aloitettiin vuonna 2004 ja se on mr saada ptkseens vuonna 2010. Ensimmiset SEPA .maksuinstrumentit on tarkoitus ottaa kyttn jo ensi vuonna. Uusien, koko euroalueen tai jopa koko EU:n kattavien markkinoiden ja jrjestelmien rakentaminen vaatii tuntuvia kustannuksia eik ole muutenkaan helppoa. Monissa tapauksissa trmtn kansallisiin ja institutionaalisiin eturistiriitoihin, joihin ei vlttmtt ole tarjolla helppoja, kaikille osapuolille tyydyttvi ratkaisuvaihtoehtoja. Nin on asianlaita erityisesti niiss tapauksissa, joissa suurtuotannon skaalaedut ovat huomattavat ja "luonnollinen" ratkaisu olisi toimijoiden lukumrn rajoittuminen yhteen. Eturistiriitojen takia taustalle saattavat jd saavutettavissa olevat pidemmn ajan hydyt, jotka kuitenkin ajan oloon ovat aivan eri kertaluokkaa kuin kustannukset. *** Hyvt kuulijat! Olen puhunut varsin pitkn Euroopan rahoitusmarkkinoiden kehittmisest. Erilaisista kipupisteist huolimatta rahoitusmarkkinoiden integraation edistminen on korkealla Euroopan eri instituutioiden asialistoilla. Se kuuluu mys Suomen Pankin ja koko eurojrjestelmn  siis Euroopan keskuspankin ja euroalueen kansallisten keskuspankkien  tavoitteisiin. Eri puolilla on tehty ja tehdn jatkuvasti runsaasti tyt Euroopan rahoitusmarkkinoiden integroimisen tiell viel olevien esteiden purkamiseksi. Tm ty j usein kokonaan piiloon julkisuudelta. Nkymttmyydestn huolimatta se on trke. Useiden realistisilta vaikuttavien arvioiden mukaan euroalueen bruttokansantuotetta voitaisiin kasvattaa kymmeness vuodessa jopa useilla prosenttiyksikill  siis jopa prosentin kymmenyksill vuodessa -jos rahoitusmarkkinoiden yhdentymisen tiell viel olevat esteet saataisiin kokonaan purettua. Uskon, ett nm arviot antavat kohtuullisen hyvn kuvan hyvin toimivien ja syvien rahoitusmarkkinoiden taloudellisesta merkityksest Euroopassa. *** Suomen selviytymisstrategia -haasteita? Ent sitten Suomen omat ponnistelut? Meille suomalaisille on aivan ilmeist, ett olemme hytyneet suuresti globalisaatiosta ja mys EU ja EMU antavat meille vankan pohjan, jolta ponnistaa tulevaisuudessa. Suomen yhteiskuntamalli voidaan kuvata mallina, jossa maailmanlaajuinen IT-osaaminen yhdistyy tasa-arvoiseen, verkottuneeseen (tehokkaaseen) hyvinvointivaltioon, joka toimii kilpailukyky vahvistavana tekijn. Thn asti se on onnistunut erinomaisesti  monilla mittareilla mitaten. Mutta voiko se kest globalisoituvassa maailmassa? Arvioni mukaan voi, mutta Suomella on luonnollisesti monia haasteita, joista otan esille kaksi mielestni keskeisint: Ensinnkin haasteena tietoyhteiskunnan ja hyvinvointiyhteiskunnan yhdistminen tehokkaaksi infrastruktuuriksi. Vaikka tietoyhteiskunnan kehittmistavoitteesta vallitsee laaja yhteisymmrrys, sit ei ole viel pantu tytntn tarpeeksi. Tietoteknologian soveltaminen laajalti yhteiskunnassa on viel alkutaipaleella tai puolitiess. Tavoitteenahan on tietoon pohjautuva tuotantomuoto kaikilla yhteiskunnan ja talouden alueilla  ei pelkstn IT.sektorissa. Erityinen haaste on hallinnon vanhentuneiden rakenteiden ja tietoyhteiskunnan vlisen ristiriidan ratkaiseminen. Vaikka lhtkohtien informaatioteknologian ja hyvinvoinnin asiantuntemuksen yhdistmiseksi pitisi olla hyvt, ja vaikka informaatioteknologian kyttmisen pmrt hyvinvointitarkoituksiin koulutuksessa, terveydenhoidossa ja sosiaalisissa palveluissa ovat hyvinkin edistyneit, niiden toteuttaminen on hidasta raskaiden organisaatioiden takia. Dynaamisuutta, mrtietoisuutta ja sitoutumista tarvitaan. Tm on erittin haasteellista julkiselle sektorille, erityisesti kunnille: Suomalaisen yhteiskunnan menestyst lhivuosikymmenin voidaankin varsin pitklle mitata sill, miten julkinen sektori selvi nist haasteista, eli kuinka silytt suurta kannatusta nauttivan pohjoismainen hyvinvointivaltiomallin periaatteet, kohtuullinen tyntekoon kannustava verotus ja talouden hyv kilpailukyky vestn ikntyess. Tehokas tietoyhteiskunnan ja hyvinvointiyhteiskunnan yhdistv infrastruktuuri edist kaikkien resurssien kyttnottoa, tuo tasavertaisuutta ja turvallisuutta ja lis sek yritysten kilpailukyky ett elmn laatua yleens. Toisena haasteena otan esille koulutuksen ja monikulttuurisen dialogin oppimisen. Ehk kaikkein keskeisint Suomen tulevan prjmisen kannalta on koulutus. Suomi on menestynyt hyvin erilaisissa koulutusvertailuissa. Paljon huomiota on esimerkiksi kiinnitetty laajan kansainvlisen PISA-tutkimuksen tuloksiin, joiden mukaan Suomen peruskoululaiset ovat menestyneet erinomaisesti lukemisessa ja muussakin osaamisessa. Pelkk vlineellinen koulutus ei mielestni kuitenkaan riit, vaan mukaan on saatava voimakas sivistyksellinen, humanistinen elementti. Pohjolasta ja Euroopasta ksin suomalaisten on kyettv selviytymn hyvin erilaisissa kulttuureissa. On paitsi osattava kyd kauppaa mys kyettv aitoon kulttuurien vliseen dialogiin. Meidn on kehitettv kulttuurisia valmiuksiamme  opittava elmn ja toimimaan monikulttuurisessa ympristss  opittava mys vastaanottamaan siirtolaisia. Tm on suuri asennemuutos. *** Ent naiset -naisyrittjyyden merkitys kansantaloudelle? Tmn tilaisuuden jrjestjt pyysivt minua mys pohtimaan naisyrittjyyden merkityst kansantaloudelle. Mik on ylipns naisten rooli Suomen ja koko EU:n talouskehityksen kannalta? Tmn kysymykseen on helppo vastata: aivan ratkaiseva. Taloudellinen kasvu, joka on vlttmtn hyvinvoinnin yllpitmiseksi ja kasvattamiseksi syntyy typanoksesta  tyn mrst ja tuottavuudesta  siit kuinka hyvin ja tehokkaasti tuotamme tavaroita tai palveluksia. Harmaantuvassa Euroopassa typanoksen kasvu on hiipumassa. Arvioidaan, ett EU-maiden kokonaistuotanto kasvaa keskimrin jopa prosenttiyksikn hitaammin kuin Yhdysvalloissa pelkstn siit syyst, ett tyntekijiden mr ei vanhalla mantereella kasva kun taas Yhdysvalloissa tyntekijit tulee lis mm. siirtolaisina. Tuottavuudessakaan emme ole onnistuneet tysin hydyntmn mm. tietoteknologian tarjoamia mahdollisuuksia. Vaikka Suomessa olemme toistaiseksi prjnneet ehk parhaiten EU:ssa ja koko Euroopassa, meillkn ei ole varaa jd itsetyytyvisyyteen. Edell puhuin Lissabonin strategiasta ja sen kunnianhimoisista tavoitteista. On selv, ett ikntyvss Euroopassa ei voida saavuttaa taloudellista kasvua, joka tarvitaan hyvinvoinnin yllpitmiseksi, ellei naisia saada enemmn tyelmn ja yrittjiksi. Keskeinen sanoma onkin, ett Eurooppa ja eurooppalainen elmnmuoto, hyvinvointi ja solidaarisuus  ja sen silyttmiseksi tarvittava kilpailukyky ja riittv taloudellinen kasvu ovat aivan keskeisesti naisten varassa. Ikntyvss Euroopassa, jos miss on vihdoinkin  yli 2000 vuoden jlkeen otettava vaarin varhaisen eurooppalaisen, filosofi Platonin havainnosta, ett mikn valtio ei ole hyv, jos puolet sen lahjakkuudesta jtetn kyttmtt. Lissabonin strategian mukainen tyhnosallistumisasteen tavoite on 70 % vuoteen 2010 menness, naisten osalta tavoite on 60 %. Nit tavoitteita voi pit suomalaisesta nkkulmasta vaatimattomina, mutta niisskin on kovasti tekemist. Sek EU:ssa ett euroalueella koko tyllisyysaste oli vuonna 2005 hieman alle 64 %, naisten tyllisyysaste 55 -56 %. Nistkin luvuista nhdn selvsti naisissa oleva potentiaali, kun pohditaan keinoja tyhn osallistumisasteen nostamiseksi. Jotta naiset saataisiin lisntyvsti tyelmn ja pysymn siell, tarvitaan infrastruktuuri  mm. pivhoitopaikkoja ja vanhainkoteja  joka tukee tysskynnin ja perheen yhteensovittamista. Nit palveluja ei kuitenkaan missn ole riittvss mrin pystytty tuottamaan pelkstn yksityisin varoin, vaan tarvitaan julkista subventiota. Tss on tilaus tehokkaalle pohjoismaiselle hyvinvointivaltiomallille, eli mallille, jolle leimallista on, ett julkisesti rahoitetuilla palveluilla tuetaan ansiotyn ja perheen yhteensovittamista. Ei ole sattuma, ett naisten tyhn osallistumisaste on korkealla tasolla juuri Pohjoismaissa, ja alimmillaan maissa, joissa ei esimerkiksi pivhoitopaikkoja ole julkisin varoin jrjestetty. Niss maissa tapahtunut naisten viimeaikainen tyhn osallistumisasteen nousu on tapahtunut syntyvyyden laskun kustannuksella. Esimerkiksi Italiassa ja Espanjassa syntyvyys on romahtanut. Pohjoismaat selvivt tsskin parhaimmin. Meill naisten ei ole tarvinnut tehd valintaa uran ja perheen vlill  on voinut saada molemmat! Edell mainittu tavoite nostaa osallistumisaste EU:n tymarkkinoilla merkitsisi noin 21 miljoonan uuden typaikan luomista EU:ssa vuoteen 2010 menness. On selv, ett naisten lahjakkuuden tysimrinen kyttnotto mys yrittjyydess, jota ylipns tulisi elvytt Euroopassa, on vlttmtnt. Naisyrittji on keskimrin vain noin 27 prosenttia yrittjien mrst EU:ssa. Suomessa suhdeluku on hieman korkeampi, noin kolmannes. Tarvitaan uusia yrityksi ja typaikkoja etenkin palvelusektorilla, jossa naisilla on korkeaa osaamista sek perinteisill aloilla ett liike-elm palvelevilla aloilla. Mm. edell tarkastelemani tarve julkisten palvelujen tehostamiseen, johon liittyy mm. palvelujen ulkoistamista yksityisilt tuottajilta tilattaviin palveluihin sek yleens ikntyvn vestn lisntyv hoivapalvelujen kysynt tarjoavat hyvi mahdollisuuksia ryhty yrittjiksi. Monet esimerkit osoittavat mys, ett naisyrittjt ovat pystyneet rakentamaan menestyvi brndej sellaisillakin toimialoilla, joita ei ole ollut tapana pit lupaavina nykypivn Euroopassa. *** Hyvt kuulijat! Hyvt yrittjnaiset! Yhteinen rahapolitiikka ja Euroopan keskuspankin rakentama vakauden ilmapiiri ovat luoneet suotuiset puitteet koko euroalueen yrittjtoiminnalle. Ne ovat mys vauhdittaneet euron kyttnoton kanssa Euroopan laajuisten, hyvin toimivien rahoitusmarkkinoiden muodostumista, mutta tll alueella on viel tehtv kovasti tyt ennen kuin voidaan puhua aidosti Euroopan laajuisista rahoitusmarkkinoista. Tmn tavoitteen eteen kannattaa kuitenkin ponnistella, sill  kuten edell olen pyrkinyt selostamaan  hyvin toimivilla rahoitusmarkkinoilla on yrittjyyteen ja koko talouskehitykseen oleellinen mynteinen vaikutus. Haluan kuitenkin korostaa, ett rahatalous tai talouspolitiikan keinot yleisemminkin voivat vain luoda edellytyksi menestyksellisen yritystoiminnan todellisille perustekijille  niin ett innovatiivisuus, yrittjyys ja ahkeruus psevt vaikuttamaan. Niss perustekijiss yritykset ja yrittjt itse ovat tietenkin aivan keskeisess asemassa. Kiristyv kilpailu laajenevilla markkinoilla tuottaa ongelmia niille yrityksille, jotka eivt pysty tarjoamaan muista erottuvaa laatua. Toisaalta markkinoiden avautuminen tuo suuria mahdollisuuksia niille yrittjille, jotka pystyvt ottamaan aloitteen omiin ksiins ja lytvt euroalueelta ja koko EU:n sismarkkinoilta siell olevan suuren potentiaalisen kysynnn. Arvoisat juhlivat yrittjnaiset! Laatua, vuorovaikutustaitoja ja kulttuurien ymmrryst, innovatiivisuutta ja uskallusta riskinottoon tarvitaan. Tulevaisuus rohkeiden naisten kannalta nytt siis hyvlt!

Title: Finland's competitiveness and good jobs
text: Bank Manager Sinikka Salo's speech "Finland's competitiveness and good places" in Helsinki . Speech . Wednesday28 February 2007,12:00AM Summary of bank manager Sinikka Salo's speech at the Greens' 20th anniversary seminar in Helsinki 28.2.2007 FINLAND'S COMPETITIVENESS AND GOOD WORK... PLACES In my speech, I will discuss what kind of work finland will do in the future, and what kind of skills will give Finns the best opportunities to operate in the world of the future, which will be characterised by globalisation on the one hand and the structural changes caused by environmental and natural resource problems on the other. ohyviso jobs are needed d ohilt informationo jobs In the old industrialised countries, to which Finland also belongs, the fiercest competition in the countries, countries and regions is the one that requires high skills, the one with the highest level of value and ability to pay wages. In the context of activities, competitiveness is precisely one that is based on excellence in the area of so-called tacit knowledge. After all, tacit knowledge refers to competences that are difficult to write down on paper or otherwise formalise, difficult to transfer from one organisation to another d competence based on experience, cultural background and values. Its relative value increases as other things in the world become more mobile and easier to copy. Tacit knowledge is unique. Therefore, an organisation, a company or an entire society whose competitiveness is based on broad cultural know-how, superior interaction skills and networks, shared values that support innovation and cooperation is competitive in a deeper and more sustainable way than one that can provide a mere high level of technical performance. The question of destiny for Finland and the other European economies is how we succeed in the production of intangible services, cultivating our cultural and hysdynthe information technology in its efficient commercialisation. How does Finland find it attractive to ohyvis jobs for creative companies? The emergence of high-value jobs - "good jobs" depends very closely on how attractive Finland is perceived as a location for companies that create jobs. Much has been said about the costs of industrial production and their importance for the location of enterprises in the country. However, when it comes to the importance of taxation, it should be borne in mind that the location of companies and the attraction of talent to the country are influenced by many other factors. In my opinion, the importance of these factors has become too much for attention. High-value activities are characterised by the fact that they flourish in the light of each other. A cluster of excellence, metropolises, will be formed. It is obvious that in the old industrialised countries, metropolises are growing and prospering, where universities and the offices of large companies, research institutes and financial markets interact with each other. The growth of physical production is reduced by business activities and activities serving intangible production, which are concentrated in the most dynamic growth centres. And global know-how in the metropolises also requires other, more traditional services. Finland's success in a changing world so that we can offer more good jobs and continue to be at the forefront of economic restructuring requires us to meet at least four challenges. Challenge 1. Helsinkis has been developed as an international metropolis In Finland, the Helsinki metropolitan area in particular must provide a competitive location for high-value activities. The requirement for competitiveness applies to all factors affecting the location of corporate offices, but in the future, the attractiveness of the Helsinki region for experts in the field of work and housing will become one of the most important. At the moment, the critical issue is the supply of housing. In Finland, and especially in the Helsinki region, housing is small by international comparison and the housing market is weaker than in other comparable countries. Challenge 2. The humanities and cultural skills of the Finns have been developed. Technological know-how and investments in it are, of course, a prerequisite for success in the future. In addition to insinssri sciences, the emphasis in higher education must also be on humanities and cultural competence, very broadly understood. We need the ability to succeed in interacting in an open, multicultural world. Finns must also learn to open up their own society to a more mobile force. Challenge 3. The EU is a key part of Finland's globalisation strategy Especially for Finland and other small Member States, the EU is a key stepping stone to global interaction. It would be much more difficult for finns to influence global trade policy if we were not the member of the EU. On the other hand, it is thanks to the EU that Finnish growth companies will of course have access to a large domestic market where they cannot be discriminated against. This will increase the profitability of innovation and product development and contribute to the positive structural change in the Finnish economy. The same factors play a role in other Member States, and a common competition policy and a common market are crucial to solving Europe's economic problems. The integration of the financial markets is also of central importance, and we are only halfway there at most. The EU must now invest heavily, for example, in the development of European innovation funding. This is particularly important for the development of new high-value service companies and the development of information technology applications. Challenge 4: Linking the welfare society and the information society The question is how much support for our model of the welfare state, reasonable and supportive taxation and good economic competitiveness. The continuous improvement of the productivity of welfare services and administration is absolutely key, and information technology is the most important tool. A better integration of the information society and the welfare society will contribute to the use of all resources, will create security and, in addition, the competitiveness of enterprises and quality in general. The quest for 'better jobs' is also compatible with social and global responsibility. A thriving and modern high-value sector is increasing the tax base and helping to create a welfare society and other more traditional services. It does not compete with developing countries for their growth sectors in the same way as a traditional industrial-oriented strategy. The promotion of high-value service provision is consistent with the fact that the economic growth of the rich countries in the industrial world of the future will be directed mainly towards an increase in the production and consumption of intangible hysdys. The strategy thus supports a sustained development to which Finland is also well placed to adapt.

Tarvitsemme kyky menesty vuorovaikutuksessa avoimessa, monikulttuurisessa maailmassa. Suomalaisten on mys opittava avaamaan omaa yhteiskuntaansa kansainvlisesti yh liikkuvammalle tyvoimalle. Haaste 3. EU on nhtv keskeisen osana Suomen globalisaatiostrategiaa Erityisesti Suomelle ja muille pienille jsenmaille EU on keskeinen astinlauta globaaliin vuorovaikutukseen. Toisaalta juuri EU:n ansiosta suomalaisille kasvuyrityksille on ilman muuta tarjolla laajat kotimarkkinat, joilla niit ei voida syrji. Tm lis innovaatiotoiminnan ja tuotekehittelyn kannattavuutta ja nin osaltaan vauhdittaa Suomen talouden positiivista rakennemuutosta. Mys rahoitusmarkkinoiden yhdentymisen merkitys on tss keskeinen ja siin ollaan vasta korkeintaan puolitiess. EU:ssa on nyt panostettava voimakkaasti mm. eurooppalaisen innovaatiorahoituksen kehittmiseen. Tm on erityisen trke uusien korkean arvonlisn palveluyritysten kehittmisen ja tietotekniikan sovellusten kehittmisen kannalta. Haaste 4: Hyvinvointiyhteiskunnan ja tietoyhteiskunnan yhdistminen Kysymys on siit, kuinka yhdist suurta kannatusta nauttiva hyvinvointivaltiomallimme, kohtuullinen ja tyntekoon kannustava verotus ja talouden hyv kilpailukyky vestn ikntyess. Hyvinvointipalvelujen ja hallinnon tuottavuuden jatkuva parantaminen on tss aivan avainasemassa, ja tietotekniikka keinoista keskeisimpi. Parempi tietoyhteiskunnan ja hyvinvointiyhteiskunnan yhdistminen edist kaikkien voimavarojen kyttnottoa, luo turvallisuutta ja lis sek yritysten kilpailukyky ett elmn laatua yleens. Korkean lisarvon palvelutuotannon edistminen on sopusoinnussa sen kanssa ett rikkaiden maiden taloudellinen kasvu tulevaisuuden jlkiteollisessa maailmassa suuntautuu enimmkseen aineettomien hydykkeiden tuotannon ja kulutuksen lisntymiseen. Title: Speech "The euro, women and economic policy"
text: Bank Manager Sinikka Salo's keynote speech "The euro, women and economic policy" in Lapua . Speech . Wednesday7 March2007,12:00 AM CELEBRATORY SPEECH AT THE INTERNATIONAL WOMEN'S PdbIVdbN EVE EVENING IN LAPUA KR. OPISTO 7.3.2007 Ladies and gentlemen! Thank you very much for the opportunity to speak to you on the eve of the women's event! My title is 'The euro, women and economic policy', which is of particular interest to women right now and for women in particular! I justify the fact that women play a key role in the biggest role in meeting the future challenges of Finland and Europe! And the election is one of the opportunities to highlight ??nens?! I have summarised my remarks as follows: Let me first talk about the EU and its challenges and the importance of the euro for Finland and the EU's guerrilla market. The Lisbon Strategy, about which I am also talking, will not be realised without the contribution of women. The central message of my speech is that Europe and the European form of life, prosperity and solidarity ? and the competitiveness and sufficient economic growth of the economic life needed to achieve this are absolutely central to women. If, after ? more than 2000 years, it is finally necessary to heed the observation of the early European philosopher Plato that "a state is not good if half of its talent is not good". Secondly, I will look more closely at the role of women in the economy of an ageing Finland and Europe, ? and in increasing employment and productivity in entrepreneurial activities and in creating new intangible jobs in the service sector. Finally, on the economic policy guidelines, in particular the financing of the welfare state. *** The euro and the EU's internal market This year marks the 50th anniversary of the Signing of the Treaty of Rome by the European Integration Project. We Finns, who were only able to join the project 45 years later, after the end of the cold war, do not always remember that the EU's integration into Europe in order to guarantee peace and prosperity has been moving forward more slowly, ? ? Shilling faster. Over the last fifteen years or so, progress has been spectacular ? the EU's internal market in 1992, the single currency and monetary policy in 1999, enlargement in 2004 and, at the beginning of the year, with the accession of Bulgaria and Romania to the Treaty. At present, the EU comprises 27 states with 490 million people living on their territory. The euro area also expanded at the turn of the year when Slovenia adopted the euro. The euro area, whose monetary policy is the responsibility of the ECB and the Euro-System ? the ECB and the national central banks of the euro area ? now comprises 13 countries. In its more than 12 years of membership, Finland has lost its place in the EU and in the EU itself, but at the same time by working constructively to promote the EU's common goals. I would like to remind you that the EU is a key instrument for Finland, both economically and politically, when we participate in global integration. It can be said that in many respects the EU is like a stepping stone by which Finland rises to the global stage. Politically and psychologically, too, we have become stunned: In a way, we have moved on to the outer ring of Europe. As a small country, we enjoy a great deal of European cooperation, probably even more so than the large Member States of the Union, which, on the other hand, I believe need the EU more than they often do. In many respects, the ongoing globalisation processes add value to European cooperation. I will mention a few of the most important examples in my mind. The most obvious example of how the EU helps Finns on a global level is the EU's trade policy force. When a Finnish industry enters a truly global market, it is a matter of not discriminating against Finnish products, but on the same line as products from competing countries, so to speak. The EU's common commercial policy pushes the market open to Finnish industry with all the power that the EU has as a major trading power in the world. There is a kind of paradox that more Finnish exports are directed outside the EU, and that the EU's common commercial policy, and thus the work of the EU Commission, becomes more central to us. Another form of European cooperation for the Finnish industry is the EU's internal market, which was established in 1992. The general principle that a product on the market in one country must not be discriminated against in the other Member States came into force. It is a huge achievement, especially in terms of the growth potential of SMEs, to create a single domestic market with a population of more than 490 million, where all forms of discrimination have been deliberately tried to be stopped and a 'level playing field' has been created. This is of great importance for the global success of companies, as studies show that a sufficient large domestic market is a key success factor when growing companies seek to gain their own strength in the wider international market. It is true that the objective of the common guerrilla market is to be achieved, e.g. in the areas of trade in services, the European patent system and the payment system, but even the achievements of the czech republic are nothing short of human, when you consider all those political obstacles, the opening up of competition always has. The third form of European integration that supports the activities of Finns at a global level is the common currency, the euro. Prior to the establishment of monetary union, many European countries, including Finland, were aware of chronic financial stability. Exchange rate security and, owing to persistent inflation expectations, high interest rates weakened the economic and international successes of these countries. The monetary system created by the Maastricht Treaty, consisting of a single monetary system and a self-governing system and a credible central bank system, has succeeded in building a historically exceptional monetary stability for the euro area as a whole. In Finland, this is the case, among other things, in the form of low and stable interest rates and easier access to loans. Even on a global scale, this is a significant competitive factor. It is also noteworthy that it is precisely in the regions where eu integration has generated the greatest hy?a that the central role of policy-making is played by the Institutions at Union level: the Commission is jointly responsible for trade policy and the guerrilla market, and the ECB, jointly with the national central banks, for monetary policy. The greatest strength of EU integration apparently lies precisely in its supranational institutions, and it is on them that its greatest successes are based. As Jean Monnet said: "There is no way to have people, without institutions, why there is no lasting spirit." But there are no institutions without the political will to establish them and give them the legitimacy they need. Personally, I believe that it is precisely the strengthening of the EU's common institutions that is the most effective way to achieve economic and other progress in Europe. *** But let's go back to the euro, if there is some sort of phase of integration going on in the integration process at a more general level, the euro and the ECB's single monetary policy will remain reliable, and work on the integration of the financial markets, among other things, will continue. These issues are particularly important for women. Our single currency, the euro, and the functioning of European entrepreneurship are closely linked. The single currency is part of the EU's single market programme, which aims to build a large domestic market in Europe that would provide the best possible conditions for enterprise. In an open and extensive common market, it is more profitable to innovate and productise than it would be in a limited and discriminatory national market. The idea of a large common market is at the heart of the whole of the EU and at the same time ? as I said before ? the Union's greatest achievement in terms of business. A key element is played by the single currency, which, as a result of the non-use of the currency implications, eliminated previously significant exchange rate risks and the cost of exchanging currencies was eliminated in transactions in the euro area. N?in laid the foundations for the functioning of a genuine common market. After all, the EU Commission deliberately pushed ahead with the monetary union project under the symbol 'one market in one currency'. But there is still a common market that does not work the most closely. In the meantime, we will not be able to accept all the potential benefits that a well-functioning EU-wide domestic market offers, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises, which are typically women's enterprises. As I said before, the introduction of the euro considerably calmed down the monetary conditions in Europe. This stability has already had its own positive impact on the integration of European financial markets. In addition to the single currency, we are the goal of ensuring that businesses and investors, including consumers, should have a Pan-European financial market that would guarantee citizens and businesses the widest range of services at the most competitive prices, and which should not matter for invoicing and payment management whether transactions are conducted between the various countries in the euro area or the enclave of one country. The importance of these objectives, e.g. in terms of the conditions for enterprise, is obvious, but the objectives have not yet been achieved. Following the introduction of the euro, a certain part of the euro area's financial markets were integrated very rapidly; for example, the unsecured short-money market for banks now operates smoothly and uniformly throughout the euro area. Progress has also been made in other market segments. However, despite the progress made, euro area financial markets remain segmented in many respects. In the context of the integration process, there are different differences in legislation and differences in supervisory systems and administrative authorisation procedures. Financial market infrastructures, such as securities clearing houses, also operate in different ways in different countries, and it is not easy to combine them into a single whole. Some of the obstacles to the common market are of such a nature that they are fundamentally based on a brief defence of existing conditions. Despite the various frictions holding back market integration, I am optimistic about the process of integration of the EU's financial markets. The benefits of a truly unified pan-European financial market are simply too great for us to be able to accept them. The development of financial markets and the convergence of financial markets are therefore at the heart of the EU's economic policy cooperation. The Euroj?estelm? ? and the Bank of Finland as part of it ? are involved in the development of the system, in particular as regards the integration of payment systems. A key, topical project is the objective of creating a Single Euro payments area (SEPA) by 2010 instead of the current fragmented payment system structure. The fact that payments cross borders in an easy and affordable way is of great importance, especially for SMEs, but also for households. For example, companies operating in the tourism sector are small, but many of them have marketing contacts widely in continental Europe. Quoting the price in the homely euro currency over the entire wide area has significantly improved the efficiency of operations and the threshold for entering Finland has been lowered. For example, lapland's tourism market has already been integrated into the wider European internal market and the euro area market. From the customer's point of view, the borders between countries will be further lowered as cross-border payment transactions become easier. Of course, the easing of payment transactions will also make it easier for a household in Lapua to pay rent for their holiday home on the Costa del Sol in Spain or for a son or daughter studying in Germany. The work on the integration of financial markets is extensive and provides an excellent example of the benefits that can be achieved by a conscious European cooperation. It is a matter of fact that the issues are on the political agenda. It is worth making an effort to establish a europe-wide, well-functioning financial market, since, as I have tried to explain above, ? well-functioning financial markets have an essential, positive impact on enterprise and on the economic development of Europe as a whole. The integration of financial markets is also at the heart of the Lisbon Strategy, which ? as is well known ? was agreed in 2000, when the European Council ? the Heads of Government of the EU countries - criticised the development of a strategy for the EU for the next decade of the 2000s. At the time, the strategy was summed up in the demand that, over the course of a decade, Europe should become the most competitive and dynamic knowledge-based economy in the world, capable of sustaining economic growth, creating new and better jobs and increasing social cohesion. The Lisbon Strategy was designed to enable the EU to meet the challenges of global competition and the development of information technology. Its implementation is the responsibility of each Member State. The Lisbon Strategy, women and a greying Europe At the heart of the Lisbon strategy, both in terms of economic dynamism and social cohesion, is the improvement of employment and the integration of cohesion. The 2005 revision of the Lisbon Strategy sought to give new impetus to Europe's competitiveness and growth and confirmed that increasing the employment rate and creating new jobs also required the development of social security systems, the promotion of adaptability and the adaptability of enterprises and the flexibility of the labour market, as well as investment in human resources. The economic growth that is needed to increase and increase our well-being is generated by the contribution of the ? work??r?? and productivity ? how well and efficiently we produce goods or services. In a greying Europe, the growth of stubble is fading. It is estimated that total production in the EU countries is growing at an average rate of up to one per cent slower than in the United States in the autumn alone, that there will be no increase in the number of employees on the old continent, while in the United States it will not increase in the form of migrants, among other things. In terms of productivity, too, we have not succeeded in the opportunities offered by information technology, for example. On the other hand, expenditure on alcohol is increasing. We need both women's contribution and productivity. Although Finland has so far had the best performance in the EU and in Europe as a whole, we cannot afford to be complacent. Our problems are pan-European. The target for participation rates in the EU under the Lisbon strategy is 70% by 2010, compared with 60% for women. The Finnish Government Programme aims to increase the participation rate to 75 per cent. There is a lot of work to be done on these targets, as the employment rate in the EU is currently less than 66%. There is room for improvement in the EU, especially in terms of women's participation in the labour market. The employment rate for women in the EU is just over 57%, but in Finland it is around 66%. N???k's figures show the potential in women when considering ways to increase the participation rate of women. In order to get women to work and stay in the workplace, there is a need for infrastructure ? including places for care ? which supports the reconciliation of work and the family. However, it is not enough to be able to provide services with private funds alone, but a public subsidy is needed. This is the order for an effective Nordic welfare state model, i.e. a model characterised by publicly funded services supporting the reconciliation of merit and family, and thus the employment of women and a high level of education in order to increase employment and productivity. It is no coincidence that the participation rate of women is at a high level in the Nordic countries, and at its lowest in countries where, for example, places for treatment have not been publicly funded. The recent increase in the participation rate of women in the countries has come at the expense of the fall in the birth rate. In Italy and Spain, for example, the birth rate has plummeted. The Nordic countries are the best in the world. We women haven't had to make a choice for merit and the family's v?lill? ? has been able to get both! The Lisbon strategy also pays attention to enterprise and the importance of enterprise. The above-mentioned target of increasing the participation rate in the EU labour market to 70% would mean the creation of around 21 million new jobs in the EU by 2010. It is clear that the t?ysim???ninen of women's talent is also an attempt to be revived in Europe. Women entrepreneurs make up only about 27% of the average number of entrepreneurs in the EU. In Finland, the ratio is slightly higher, about a third, but we also ? even in Ostrobothnia ? additional companies and women entrepreneurs are needed. What kind of companies? What will be done in Finland in the future, and what kind of know-how will give Finns the best opportunities to operate in the world of the future, which will be characterised by globalisation on the one hand and structural changes caused by environmental and natural resource problems on the other. In the future, the toughest competition will be in the country and region, the one with the highest level of competence and ability to pay wages. In the context of activities, competitiveness is precisely one that is based on excellence in the area of so-called tacit knowledge. After all, tacit knowledge refers to competences that are difficult to write down on paper or otherwise formalise, difficult to transfer from one organisation to another ? competence based on experience, cultural background and values. Its relative value increases as other things in the world become more mobile and accessible. Tacit knowledge is unique. It is based on extensive cultural competence, superior interaction skills and networks, shared values that support innovation and cooperation. After all, it is women who have traditionally been strong in the regions. There is a need for new businesses and jobs, particularly in the service sector ? intangible information technology in the production of services, in the business sector and in the more traditional services. In a globalizing and integrating world and in Finland, women's multi-skills and cultural skills are czech. Among other things, the need to improve the efficiency of public services, including the outsourcing of services to services ordered from private providers and, in general, the need to increase the demand for care services and also good opportunities to become entrepreneurs. A key challenge for economic policy is the financing of welfare services The challenges of economic policy? Although the Finnish economy is on a more stable footing than in most other EU countries, the financing of the welfare state poses a challenge to our economic policy as our economy ages. Economic growth is needed, but economic growth alone cannot be relied on in order to finance the welfare state. A viable, if not the only, way of securing funding for our welfare system is to increase the efficiency of the welfare state. It is particularly important not only for taxpayers who use services, but also for the wage development of the personnel (of which women are women). Although Finland, as an information society, enjoys a broad degree of cooperation, this objective has not yet been achieved to a sufficient extent. The widespread application of information technology in society is still in its infancy or semi-final. After all, the aim is a knowledge-based form of production in all areas of society and the economy ? not just in the IT sector. Increasing productivity is particularly challenging, especially for the local government sector, which has a high degree of responsibility for service production. The successes of Finnish society over the decades can therefore be measured for a very long time, by how the public sector copes with the challenges, i.e. how much the principles of the Nordic welfare state model, which enjoys a great deal of support, reasonable taxation that encourages work, and the good competitiveness of the economy. The continuous improvement of the productivity of welfare services and administration is absolutely key, and information technology is the most important tool. In order to defend the welfare state, the productivity of the public sector will be enhanced by the fact that women in the public sector should be pushed more and more out of the backs of women in the public sector. That is certainly not possible. It may even be the case that it has gone too far. Instead, we need to consider how to integrate the Nordic welfare state into the information society so that efficiency increases and organisations become more streamlined. In other words, do the right things in the right place at the right time. Sitra's studies, for example, show that there is certainly a genuine rationalisation in the provision of public services, which is acceptable to both service providers and the use of services. In order to use the welfare state and services, women should move away from hedgehog defence. Women do not get to squat when they hear the words efficiency and productivity, because they are also their advantages. My advice to the defenders of the welfare state is that increasing the productivity of the public sector does not mean that the results are not the result of the work of carers, teachers or other service providers in the public sector, but that the results come from the reorganisation of activities and administration. When the system works efficiently, it also makes sense to the system. In an efficient system that provides high-quality services, we can afford and want to pay the taxes of the company that is able to do so. If the welfare state deteriorates and services are not available or of poor quality, the desire to pay stops. That is why it is also in the interests of women to make the public sector more efficient and rationalised. Ladies and gentlemen! The first unicameral parliament elected 100 years ago included many interesting and courageous women. The first champions have contributed to the fact that all posts are now open to a Finnish woman ? at least in principle ? all posts. Indeed, women have been involved in building Finnish well-being, and significant contribution has contributed to Finland's emergence as one of the richest countries in the world. So it's a pleasure to be a Finnish woman! It is obvious that we Finns have become very anxious about globalisation ? without participating in the international division of labour, a country like Finland, which has natural resources and a peripheral country, could not have developed into what it is today, one of the most prosperous societies in the world. History shows this, and the "second wave" of globalisation that is now going on has also been extremely advantageous for Finland economically. So, until then, we have been doing well and, although past success does not automatically guarantee a good result in the future, I am optimistic: the geographical location of companies, as a result of technological progress and the opening up of economies, will continue to play a role in the geographical situation of companies, and if the liberalisation of world trade continues, the disadvantages of the small size of the domestic market will also be felt by the small size of the domestic market. But the challenges we need to take on, if we do not change ourselves, do not play a constructive role in a changing global economy. Many of the products from which Finns have made their living are transferred to be manufactured in prosperous developing countries. At the same time, the rise in the price of raw materials and energy is also changing the conditions of production. We cannot stand still. Finns from the North and Europe have to survive in very different cultures. The ability to engage in genuine dialogue between cultures is required. Finns need to know how to live and work in a more open, multicultural eeworld village ? and also learn to receive the immigrants we so badly need in our society. ?m? is a big change of attitude for us Finns! But I believe that it is women, in particular, who can bring about a change in attitude. Women are needed more as influencers in the ? economy and throughout society. It is fitting to make my speech by quoting Hedvig Gebhard, Economic Counsellor ? member of parliament from the first parliament: "Every well-informed woman is a female candidate."
