Title: Impact of global financial markets on Finnish business
text: Bank Director Sinikka Salo: The impact of global financial markets on Finnish industry, Pori, 18.12.2008 . Speech . Thursday18 December 2008,12:00AM VTT Sinikka Salo Board of Directors and Bank of Finland Presentation at porin Seudun Kehitystsmiskeskus OY POSEK's event in Pori 18.12.2008 Speech liittyvst Patterns (PDF) (/globalassets/en/media-and-publications/speeches-and. interviews/documents/18122008_posek_kalvot_sinikkasalo.pdf) IMPACT OF GLOBAL FINANCIAL MARKETS ON FINNISH INDUSTRY Risks and their periodic realisation are an integral part of the functioning of financial markets. Reasonable hsiristilas are even thought to be hysdyllis: they are healthy risk awareness. This is one of the ways in which the market mechanism corrects itself. The financial market crisis that we are experiencing and that is currently experiencing cannot, of course, be a normal, healthy fluctuation. Its duration and depth are still subject to guesswork. But epsilemsts smskin hsiristila in time calms down. However, it is to be expected d and desirable . That in the aftermath of the crisis, the situation is quite different from that of the past, particularly as regards the management and supervision of the financial markets. In view of the crisis in the global financial system, economic reports and forecasting are accompanied by an exceptionally high level of certainty. In the following, I will try to look first at the causes and background to the current global financial market crisis, in order to better understand the mechanisms for integrating the crisis into the global economy as a whole and also into the Finnish economy. I have summarised my presentation as follows. First, I will look at the problems in the financial markets and their background, as well as the actions of the authorities at the global, EU and Finnish levels. I will then briefly examine the impact of the financial crisis on the world economy and the Finnish economy, highlighting how the current recession differs from the recession of the 1990s. Finally, d miksli time jss . I also consider the possible repercussions of the crisis on the future d sssing and supervision of financial markets . point of view. FINANCIAL MARKETS... N BACKGROUNDS In recent years and decades, the debt ratios of households and non-financial corporations have generally increased in the global economy and also in Finland. This development is a myshnteistic and reflects the evolution of the financing process. In financial markets, maturities and interest margins have decreased, while the development of risk diversification and technology have enabled banks to operate profitably in a context of reduced margins. At the same time, the strong growth in financing has been accompanied by problems, above all the underpricing of risks. As the credit portfolio grew, credit risks increased. At the same time, risk pricing has been shaky. In the middle of last year 2007, at the threshold of financial markets, the risks in international financial markets were so low that the situation was widely regarded as central: pricing in financial markets could not reflect the genuine cost of risks. Years of financial conditions played a part in underestimating the risks. There were good reasons for the favourable financing conditions: among other things, the shift of production to low-cost countries pushed down world trade prices, and in conditions of low inflation, central banks considered interest rates to be low. As the general level of interest rates declined in the financial markets, ample funding sought to seek investment targets from one of the riskier investments in order to achieve the usual level of returns. As a result, the quality of investments and debt material deteriorated. The most obvious example is provided by the partly reckless mortgage lending in the United States, and it is the instigator of the crisis. A key role in the problems of the US housing market was played by the securitisation of mortgages, i.e. the assembly, packaging and sale of individual mortgages as forward securities. In many cases, a multi-tiered chain was formed between the bank and the final investor, in which the securities resulting from the packaging of mortgages, and also car and other consumer loans, were repackaged two or three times into more exotic derivative securities. Risk diversification through secondary market trading and derivatives is a sinsnss mysnteists, but there are many problems associated with its uncontrolled use: 1. Incentives to monitor creditworthiness deteriorate. When a bank also credits someone else knows that the credit risk is borne by someone else, the risk assessment is not drawn up with the same care as if the risks were paid out of one's own purse. 2. The risk of risk and its use in different situations is reduced. When a security is transferred from the originator to the appraiser and the credit to the latter market investors, even in a multi-tiered transfer, the investor is in a weak position to form an informed assessment of the risk characteristics of the security resulting from the last package. Credit risk assessment relies heavily on a limited number of credit rating agencies. There was too much confidence in the risk ratings; The risk of complex securities by the rating agencies also proved to be weak. The ratings were based on the historically probative nature of households in different financial positions falling into a state of solvency under normal economic conditions. It was not possible to assess the credit risks associated with the perceived stagnation of the housing market and the fall in house prices. Even fine math doesn't help if genuine initial risk assessments are flimsy. 3. There has also been much criticism of the bonus system of MFIs. A typical feature of many investments is that the returns are front-loaded, but the risks are strongly back-loaded. If an investment person is rewarded in such a way that the premiums focus on the initial returns but not on the potential losses over the period, then the risk to the financial institutions and the economy as a whole will be substantial. It is precisely nsin nsytss in recent years that I have been ksyne. Many international banks facing problems bonus systems are superior to what is reasonable in terms of their benefits. 4. Securitisation was used not only to manage risks, but apparently also to circumvent the prudential requirements imposed on banks by the authorities. The solvency ratios imposed on banks set limits on the amount of risky loans that banks can hold on their balance sheets. The solvency ratio may have been transferred to off-balance sheet investment companies somewhere in the balance sheet. Although the investment companies have been formally independent of the banks, the banks have had to guarantee their activities. Thus, the exclusion of securities has not protected banks against risk. Summa summarum: Strong growth in financing, securitisation into complex products, and underpricing of risks led to a market where investors could not locate the risk and realistically assess its magnitude. ON THE IMPACT OF THE CRISIS After the start of the market, the risk premiums rose sharply. Banks paid huge margins for their borrowing. It was worth noting that the crisis has not exactly turned out to be in Quekh: the risk has risen for everyone. The risk in the interbank market, which before the crisis was a few hundredths of a percent, has been more than one percent, even more. See figure below (1). There are hardly any safe havens, the perceived risky players, in the financial markets. This situation reflects the certainty about the distribution of risks, which, even after the 1st year and despite many measures taken by the authorities, has not been resolved. The liquidity shock deepened and turned into a more serious crisis threatening the stability of several banks. As a result of losses and reductions in the value of their own capital, several large global banks faced solvency problems and sought to acquire new pssoma from the market and, for example, from the market. sovereign wealth funds. As the crisis has dragged on and liquidity problems have continued, mergers and bank takeovers by the authorities have resulted. In particular, the collapse of a large US investment bank, Lehman Brothers, on 15.9.2008 triggered a large-scale panic. Lehman's bankruptcy raised the risk premiums, which had already been somewhat reduced, to a new, higher level than before. The banks wanted to secure their own liquidity position and not lend to each other. There is still a high level of confidence in the market. The international hsiris has also been widely reflected in the Finnish financial markets and in the interest rates of many Finnish debtors through risk supplements to euribor rates, which are used as reference rates, although there have been hardly any problems with banks. The world's central banks have taken a number of steps to safeguard the functioning of the financial markets and, for example, in Paris, where the Eurogroup of 15 eurogroups met on 12.10.2008, the ECB announced that it would continue and intensify its efforts to safeguard liquidity, and also by agreeing with the Fed on the provision of dollar liquidity in Europe, by expanding the list of approved collateral materials. etc. All measures are aimed at eliminating certainty and making the financial system work, and to prevent the financial market crisis from being brought into line with the activities of firms and households in the so-called 'black market'. as a credit crunch. A credit crunch means that when banks' own losses and write-downs are reduced, banks are subject to a solvency requirement to reduce their receivables, i.e. their outstanding amounts. Chelsich's national economy may fall into recession or recession as lending to viable businesses, for example, deteriorates. The figure below (2) illustrates the obvious seriousness.. Governments have also agreed on a number of stabilisation measures to safeguard the deposit and market-based financing of banks, including by increasing the deposit guarantee scheme on a temporary basis, by providing state guarantees for bonds issued by banks up to five years, and by promising to secure a sufficient number of viable banks through state investments. The support measures for the banking sector have been quite massive. In the United States, crisis banks have had to be rescued and major support measures have been committed to prevent the credit crunch. In Europe, similar measures have been somewhat smaller in size, but nevertheless significant. In total, banks have written off more than 700 billion in their balance sheets. dollar after the crisis began. The same amount of new pssoma has been acquired. The guarantees given by the States are still many times greater. THE IMPACT OF THE FINANCIAL MARKET CRISIS ON THE GLOBAL ECONOMY Despite the support measures and strong stimulus measures, it is clear that global economic growth will slow down as a result of the crisis in the financial markets. It should be noted that the prolonged slowdown in global economic growth has been an expected (and also desired) development for reasons such as: The large us current account deficit has been considered a long period of time. It has been thought that it can only be used if the Americans take steps to reduce their consumption and increase their consumption. This would be reflected in a decrease in imports, and thus in a slowdown in exports from other countries to the United States and growth in countries d and thus worldwide as a whole. In many economies, there were clear signs of overheating, rising property prices and, in particular, house prices. The prices of raw materials were also high. Overall, inflation was higher. In the early autumn, at the international meeting, we discussed precisely the need for growth to moderate and to anchor inflation expectations worldwide. However, global economic growth has slowed down really dramatically in the last few months. The global economy has been growing very rapidly for a long time and a slowdown was to be expected without the financial market crisis, but of course the global financial market crisis is behind the rapid deterioration: The increase in financing costs d the increase in risk premiums and the tightening of loan conditions d are reflected in a slowing way in investment and consumption. The fall in asset prices is reflected in the impact on consumption. In the United States in particular, it is of great importance: the value of collateral on loans is falling. Tightening of access to credit d features of the credit d have a dampening effect on investment and consumption. The shortage of d the characteristics of the credit o credit o affects the new investment estsvssti. In addition to the general certainty, it increases the desire for and consumption. In essence, therefore, it is a lack of confidence in the financial markets d money does not move in the market. According to the latest forecasts for the global economy (eg. IMF, OECD, Eurojsestelm) major developed economies have entered a recession and forecasts have been revised briskly downwards. The forecasts for GDP growth next year for the euro area, the United States and Japan are a minus sign, and growth is not expected to pick up until 2010. Growth is also slowing down in developing countries d China, Russia, although growth rates in the countries are still positive. China's economic growth is expected to slow down to around 7-8% next year. China's GDP growth has been around 10% for a long time, and clearly in the upper half, so even though next year's figures are high, they will naturally be significantly lower than china has been used to in recent years. In order to compensate for the slowdown in exports in China, demand is being directed towards domestic infrastructure investment by using huge financial resources for large stimulus packages. The reduced prices of raw materials and energy are also supporting the stimulus measures. China's economy is about the same size as the German economy, so it already plays a very large role in supporting global economic growth, but of course it alone is not the engine of global growth. Economic growth in Russia is projected to slow down sharply. from about 8% last year to about 6% in Thns in the year. The GDP growth forecast for next year is 3.5%. Vensjs is still heavily dependent on price developments and, in addition, the financial markets in Vensjs are d unlike china's financial system d also exposed to the global financial crisis. To sum up the latest global economic forecasts published, global economic growth will fall below 4% in the year and will be just over 2% next year. The prolonged period of high growth in the global economy would now be clearly slower than before. How far? The most realistic scenario is to return to normal after a recession in a couple of years. The reason for this is that, as a result of the rather extensive measures taken by the authorities, the confidence of the banks will be restored and the credit mechanism will start to work again. I personally believe that this will happen. Despite the fact that this is an unprecedented global financial system, there is also a capacity to remedy the situation. Examples include the cooperation of the world's key central banks in providing liquidity to banking systems, as well as monetary policy d it should be mentioned that the interest rate cut in September by a consortium of key central banks was the first in history. Large-scale stimulus measures have also been taken in a coordinated manner, and protectionist measures to add trade barriers to trade have been put aside: the so-called 'trade war'. G20 members d also include representatives of emerging economies. it was precisely the World Trade Association (WTO) that called for the conclusion of the Doha Round. In the world, there should be more political will than usual to intervene in the functioning of financial markets and by strengthening the roles of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the Financial Stability Forum (FSF), which operates within the G7. Needless to say, it is clear that the EU should now be at the forums together to influence these issues. Naturally, one can think of worse scenarios for the global economy: oThe lost decadeo would mean that the the stimulus and coordination efforts would fail, and the global economy would enter a long period of japan's zero growth in the 1990s. Asset prices would continue to fall to longterm and low interest rates and deflation. oLarge Lamao, on the other hand, describes a scenario in which the credit mechanism does not work and fragments into a national one. A typical feature of the scenario is also uncoordinated economic policies and protectionism. The experience of the 1930s would therefore come true. As I said, I consider the two most extreme scenarios to be very specific. We live in a global world where economies depend on each other in science. *** THE FINNISH ECONOMY AND THE FINNISH FINANCIAL SECTOR It is, of course, clear that the Finnish economy cannot be isolated from the world's financial system during the crisis effects, even if there have been no significant outright losses from risky investments. I have already referred to the risk premiums for EURIBOR rates, which mean that Finnish borrowers whose loans are quite commonly linked to these reference rates are forced to pay a higher risk on their loans than onormal. On Tuesday last week, Suoman Pankki published its stability report. According to our assessment, the Finnish financial system remains stable. Finnish banking has so far been affected by the financial crisis as banks elsewhere. In this context, it is worth pointing out that the fundraising of deposit banks has been relatively largely based on deposits d and we remembered the lessons of our previous banking crisis on risk-taking. The direct effects of the international crisis are limited, but the effects are not. Among other things, the counterparty risk has increased. Similarly, as the economic situation deteriorates, the importance of credit risk will be emphasised in the future at the same time as banking income decreases. However, credit losses have still been relatively low. Overall, the solvency and liquidity of the banking sector have remained favourable, but profitability has declined. However, the banking sector faces major challenges in that banks should be able to fill the gap caused by the drying up of other financial instruments, especially in the financing needs of companies. When companies are unable to obtain direct access to finance on the market due to the inoperability of the corporate credit market, there is a higher demand for banks than is normal, for example. in the financing of the country. As a result, it is particularly important for banks to seek to use the opportunities available to strengthen their lending capacity. Sound prudence is part of banking, but if the banking sector as a whole digs into its potholes, the result will be difficulties in the corporate sector, which will not help the banks in the future, but on the other hand. REAL ECONOMY NKYMT The weakening of the global economy naturally also affects Finland. According to the bank's forecast revision published on 9.12.2008, growth in Finland is expected to fall into recession. I am not going to go into a detailed presentation of the forecast in more detail d it has been presented in our Euro&e-economy magazine and on our website, but a few words about it are still in order. Finland's growth has already slowed down quite significantly and next year's forecast for growth is negative (growth rate -.). Apart from the weakness in investment activity, this is due to the slowdown in growth in the Finnish export market, which is particularly strongly reflected in our exports, as the share of capital goods in our exports is high d and global economic growth is weakening, especially in terms of investment. We did not expect the economy to recover slowly until 2010. As business exports and investment face the global economic downturn most clearly, households and consumers play a key role in growth. In the Bank of Finland's forecast, the sssss rate will turn positive after a few years and the level of employment will decline. However, real household income is growing quite favourably due to wage settlements and falling inflation. Thus, those households who can be confident that their employment situation will remain good in their own economy have no reason to change their consumption or investment behaviour. It is in Tsrkess's mind not to stir up an over-the-top pessimism that, at worst, would begin to feed itself. We at the Bank of Finland do not predict a recession like the one in the early 1990s. Our forecast picture is quite different and is based on many of the strengths of our economy that Finland has built up since that recession: economic structures are more competitive, growth has not relied on foreign indebtedness in recent years, balance problems have been avoided during the economic upturn, public finances are firmly overflowing and we have room for stimulus, the banks are in a strong position. To illustrate the situation, I would like to see one film (3 ) concerning the current situation and its comparison with the two previous downturns. I do not want the situation to be serious, but our forecast is quite different from that of the Great Depression of the early 1990s d lshempsns onormaaliao cyclical downturn, although of course more serious. TRKE STABILIZING FACTOR EURO I would also like to remind you of the difference between the current situation and the situation in the early 1990s, i.e. to say a few words about the euro and the monetary policy of the European Central Bank. The introduction of the euro and central exchange rate risks 10 years ago brought considerable calm to European monetary conditions. A large euro area with a stable and credible monetary policy is a stabilising factor for the global economy and also facilitates cooperation between the main central banks. One can only imagine what the current turbulence in the financial markets d or in previous hsirs situations such as the situation caused by the terrorist attacks of 11 September 2001, or when the iraq wars broke out d would have happened in Europe if we had had more than one currency. There would probably have been quite a bit of wobble in the foreign exchange market, with adverse consequences for d myss for us in Finland. Now, on the other hand, the main central banks of the world d above all the European Central Bank and the entire Eurojs system, as well as the US Federal Reserve d have been able to act in a coordinated manner, agreeing, among other things, to safeguard the liquidity of the banking system and thus alleviate the crisis in the financial markets. In addition, the ECB has been able to do so. measures to support monetary conditions without jeopardising the basic situation. Monetary policy has been able to be measured from the angle of price stability, and as the global economy has weakened and, as a result, price expectations have rapidly come down, interest rates have been cut rapidly. It should also be noted that the euro area's membership also protects the euro area Member States from the balance of payments crisis to which Iceland, for example, has been hit. It is not the case that the euro has also grown in popularity in Denmark and Sweden, for example. I predict that the euro area will expand faster than was thought some time ago. WITH OPITTAVAA RAHOITUSMARKKINAKRIISIST? The financial crisis naturally raises a wide range of questions, and the search for answers is only just beginning. To conclude my presentation, I would like to take up a few thoughts: 1. One obvious question concerns the future of securitisation. Although the problems associated with securitisation are the core of the securitisation process, securitisation is not categorically condemned or attempted to stop. Properly managed, securitisation is an effective asset: it allows risks to be diversified from the relatively thinly-funded banking sector to financial funds, investment funds and other more strongly funded entities. By securitisation, e.g. the systemic risk in the housing market can be spread over more and stronger shoulders, and thus improve the financing system. Of course, this does not mean that it does not need to be done. In the future, securitisation will be able to be carried out in a way that incentives for responsible behaviour do not lead to the kind of excesses experienced in the United States. Products should be standardized in umsrrettsvssn form, the underlying debt securities should be well applied to the mssriteledjs kriteerejs. In Europe, securitisation in most countries is still in its infancy, so that systems can be built to be better on a country-by-country basis. 2. The broader question is how to deal with innovation in the financial markets. The emergence and wild growth of securitisation in the United States is one example in a series of innovations in the financial markets that, time and time again, bring the financial markets into unexplored waters. Myss in the future will new products whose activities were not initially carried out by the Company. This kind of innovation cannot be attempted by means of shunting. Instead, it is necessary to ensure that the risks arising from innovation do not threaten the infrastructure of the financial markets and, in particular, to safeguard the stability of deposit banks. In relation to chechnya, financial market authorities in many countries are the subject of serious debate. Many deposit banks, including in Europe, had acquired large positions on the US subprime securities market without the supervisory authorities having any knowledge of this. And even if the authorities had all the necessary information, you can ask whether the supervisor would still have understood the risks associated with these investments before they began to materialise in the middle of last year. 3. The discussion will also concern possible needs for new sshining. It will be necessary to consider ways in which deposit banks d the back of the financial markets d are able to protect themselves from the storms of the financial markets. Could it be possible to build better security barriers around deposit banks and to steer the investment activities of deposit banks in a way that would guarantee the ability of supervisors to ensure the solvency of banks? In the history of the financial markets, there have been stages in which deposit banking and investment banking have been separated by law. In this model, deposit banks are safe havens on the financial markets, where ordinary depositors can safely hold their funds, while investment banks can be used to seek better returns for those who have the will and the ability to bear the risk. Radical reforms are unlikely to be carried out once. It has to be said, however, that large investment banks in the United States have already taken place, either as a result of mergers, collapses or conversions. 4.It is still necessary to consider the structures for the management and supervision of the financial markets, particularly in the United States, where the crisis began, but also in Europe. Financial market supervision in Europe has not become more international at the same rate as banking, but the supervisory and crisis management structures have remained national for a long time. Cooperation with the national authorities has certainly been developed, but it is still clear that the fact that the fact that a heavily international euro area bank is in difficulties (Fortis) poses a wide range of difficult-to-resolve liability issues. Hsiris has once pointed out how tsrkess is, that the shunting and supervision of financial markets evolves with the process of integration of European financial markets. The EU needs a supranational European supervisor. Political leadership is needed to move these issues forward.
